units.la: ARCHIMEDES (Lector) sphæræ & cylindri rationem (in cujus inventione vehementius elaborasset) sepulchro suo incídi voluit. Et quidē si me de vigiliis studiisq; meis interroges, sepulcri mei columnam élogicę artis institutione desiderē. De causa voti respondebunt primó ad artis acburationē libri de inventione argumētorum & eorū dispositione ad iudicandum non solùm ab Aristotele organici, rhetorici, physici, sed à Cicerōe & Quintiliano tam multi oratorii: in quib. universis in duorum libellorū pugnum ratione uiaq; contrahendis omni studio diligentiaq; contendimus, ne qua particulæ cujusquam vel umbra illic cōfusa esset, cujus veritas nō hīc expressa tenearetur. Atq; hæc prima problematis archimedei conscientia erit. Respondebunt deinde ad logicæ usum, elegantiam, dignitatem, partibus omnibus explicandum, excitatæ logicis meditationibus cū populares poetarū, oratorū, historicorum eorū laudes, tum liberales & ingenuæ artes novi.corporis nova fpecie fui ftudiofis adolefcentiores, præclarifq; doti bus ornatiores & locupletiores factæ: acne qua agreftium procorum protervia timeretur, fuarum queq; fcholarum tanquam liberali cuftodia feptæ & comitatæ:Hæc fecūda problematis archimedei confcientia erit. Teftes igitur ifti logicā & ueritatē & utilitatē tot dierū noctiumq; uigiliis exquifitam teftati de voti noftri cauffa refpondebunt, teque (Lector) utfpero,commonefacient infanam nefcio quā in plerifq; omnibus Europæ academiis altercādi de fuis prę ceptis fophifticam, logicæ & ueritatis & utilitatis longè difsimilē effe, teq; ad ueriora & utiliora præftantifsimç facultatis ftudia præmiaq; inflammabūt. Ecquid uerò interea turbæ tam graves objectæ,theatra fcenicis probris extructa, tribunalia judicum pœnis minacia, dānatio tandem fœdis ignorantiæ calum niæq; notis infamis,è toto philofophiç regno manibus & lingua uelut amputatis inaudita profcriptio, an exiguā voti noftri cauffam perhibebunt? Quid cōfecuta
units.tr: Archimedes, reader, wished the rule of the sphere and cylinder (in whose discovery he had laboured more vehemently) to be carved on his tomb. And indeed, if you ask me about my vigils and studies, I would wish the institution of the art of logic to be inscribed on the column of my tomb. As to the cause of my vow, they will answer, first, the books on the invention of arguments and their arrangement for judgment, not only by Aristotle in the Organon, in the Rhetoric and in the Physics, but also by Cicero and Quintilian and so many other orators. In all of these we have striven with every care and diligence to compress them, in method and in substance, into the compass of two little books, so that no shadow of any particle would be confused there, whose truth was not held expressed here. This will be the first consciousness of the Archimedean problem. They will then answer for the use, elegance and dignity of logic, to be explained in all its parts: roused by logical meditations, the popular praises of poets, orators and historians, and the liberal and ingenuous arts, have been made new, as it were, in a new form of body for studious young people, and have become more adorned and more richly endowed with distinguished gifts; and lest the wantonness of rustic suitors be feared, each of their schools has been enclosed and attended, as by a liberal guardianship. This will be the second consciousness of the Archimedean problem. These witnesses, then, having testified that logic, sought out with the vigils of so many days and nights, is both true and useful, will answer for the cause of our vow; and, as I hope, Reader, they will remind you that the insane, I know not what, sophistical wrangling about its precepts in most of the academies of Europe is very unlike logic, truth and utility, and will inflame you to the truer and more useful studies of this most excellent faculty and its rewards. But what, meanwhile, of the so grave tumults raised against it, the theatres built with scenic reproaches, the tribunals of judges threatening penalties, the condemnation at last, infamous with the foul marks of ignorance and calumny, and the unheard-of proscription from the whole realm of philosophy, as if its hands and tongue had been cut off: will they report that the cause of our vow was a slight one? units.tr: EPISTLE.

units.la: secuta per Henricum regem à judicii tâ demētis invidia liberatio, & in solidam sanctioris judicii laudem regia professio?Quid postea cúm logicus hic ardor in religionis caussam invasisset, longé grauissima offensio ? vitæ falutifq; propterea tribus jam bellis civilibus jactatio nullámne voti nostri caussam indicabunt ? imó veró etiam admonebunt, ut Deo optimo & maximo gratias habeamus ,quód studiorum noftrorū cur sum his fluctibus exerceri, neq; tamen obrui voluerit: obtesterq; ut logicū lumē in bonis & veri percipiendi studiofis ingeniis accendat,cūq; ad ingenuas artes exornandum,tū ad cœlestia sacræ doctrinæ mysteria illustrandum magis ac magis augeat: perficiatque,ut isto in nominis sui gloriam epigramate logici epitaphii tabula concludatur.
units.tr: What followed when King Henry freed the subject from the envy of so great a judgement, and the royal profession brought him solid praise for sounder judgement? What followed afterwards, when this logical zeal had attacked the cause of religion, a far more serious offence? Will not the shaking of our life and safety, endured now through three civil wars, likewise point to the cause of our wish? Indeed, they will even admonish us to give thanks to God, most good and most great, that he willed our studies to be exercised amid these waves, yet not overwhelmed. I beseech him to kindle the light of logic in good minds, eager to perceive the true, and to increase it more and more both for adorning the liberal arts and for illuminating the heavenly mysteries of sacred doctrine; and may he bring it about that, for the glory of his name, the tablet of this logical epitaph be closed with this epigram.

units.tr: When Gaul was celebrating the troubled festival of Venus, and at the banquet served deadly poisons, Hymen and Love lit the marriage torches, while garlands and lyres were everywhere in the halls, pretending to be friendly.

units.la: Bellonæ junctus crudeles actus in iras Mars, manibus versans tela inimica suis.

units.la: Non lacrymas precium ve, preces, cum sanguine vitam Poscimus. hîs dictis, ensis & arma micant. In subitos subito convivia versa tumultus: Foedavit mensas appositasque cruor. Mutua contorquent conviva tela maniplis Incertis, multo sanguine terra madet. Senserunt armis Musae sua tecta moveri, Quaeq; sacros Hortos turbet, Erinnys adest. Hortos: in quorum medio diffusa per omnes En partes ramis fertilis arbor erat. Arbor erat: quam nulla modis melioribus unquam Mensura implebat: quae Nemus una fuit. Hanc simul invadit, nec non & missile sacro In trunco telum librat iniqua manus. Pallas opem poscit, pacem testata fidemq;: Pacem contemnunt, auxiliumq; fidem. His minime tuti sed defensoribus Hortus, Radix & Frondes, Ramus & Arbor erant. Dos, grave Pieridum munus, quod in arbore floret, Ramus erat, juvenum tam manifesta salus. In justos igitur solventes pectora luctus, Dicimus in tumulum talia verba tuum: In CINERES magnum convertit Gallia RAMVM Qui sparsi extremos Orbis ad usque sinus. Sed collecta Scholis servantur femina tantae Arboris, hic Ramus pullulat usq; Scholis. O dulces fructus, quos tu Germania servas, Calcitrat & multis turba scelesta modis. Vivant Scripta Scholis, belli quae flamma reliquit: Quae magni nobis cura doloris erunt.
units.tr: "We ask not for tears nor for a ransom, but for life with blood and prayers." At these words the sword and arms flash. Suddenly the banquet was turned into sudden tumult: blood defiled the tables and the dishes set upon them. The guests hurl weapons at one another in confused bands, and the earth is soaked with much blood. The Muses felt their dwellings shaken by arms, and Erinys, who troubles the sacred gardens, is present. The gardens: in the midst of them stood a fruitful tree, spreading its branches through every part. It was a tree such as no measure ever filled with better gifts; it alone was the grove. At once a hostile hand attacks it, and an unjust hand aims a missile at its sacred trunk. Pallas calls for help, attesting peace and good faith; they scorn peace, and help and faith. The garden, least of all safe for these, had its defenders: root and leaves, branch and tree. The dowry, the weighty gift of the Pierides, which flowers on the tree, was the branch, the plain salvation of the young. Therefore, with hearts loosed in lament for the just, we speak these words at your tomb: Gaul has turned the great BRANCH into ASHES, which was scattered to the farthest bays of the world. But the ashes of so great a tree are gathered and kept in the schools; here the branch sprouts up forever in the schools. O sweet fruits, which you, Germany, preserve, the wicked crowd kicks against in many ways. Let the writings live for the schools, which the flame of war has left behind; they will be for us a cause of great grief.

units.la: Fundamentum P. Rami in restituenda & reformada Dialectica, duplex erit, primum in artis praeceptis, secundu in artis exemplis & usu: in quo utroq; Aristotelem praecipue authore secutus est.Enim uero Dialecticam Aristoteles in libris & antiquorum, & aetatis suae philosophorum varie dispersam disipatamq;, magna cura colle git, librosq; de argumetis & argumetorum dispositione & judicio,id est de Logica,centu & quinquaginta minimum composuit,ut P.Ramus docuit primo Scholarum dialecticarum libro: e quib. libris adhuc supsunt tres & quadraginta. septe decim sunt in organo, quibus Porphyrius adjici solet: ut sint numero octodecim. Rhetorici sunt quatuor,Physicae octo primi, Philosophiae quatuordecim: in quibus,pauculis exceptis, omnia sunt de argumentis,deq; argumentorum judicio, id est, (ut dixi) de Logica. Ergo hic ager fertilissimus quidem est, & ab Aristotele (si ad veteres,unde conduxit,respiciatur)multis spinis ac fentibus expurgatus: Sed tn adhuc obfitus multis reliquis,& arandi,& colendi difficultatibus:quas fine dubio ipfe fuftuliffet Ariftoteles,fi diutius vixiffet,arareq; rurfus & iterare ac tertiare,modifq; omnib.excolere potuiffet.Sed poftreditu ab Alexandro, tredecim dutaxat anni,quotidianis duarum praelectionum curis, & tam multorum voluminum commentationibus occupati,non multum otii ad relegendu & retractandum habuere. Veruntamen hic etia Ariftoteles, tanqua bonus paterfamilias liberis,ita difcipulis falcem,fecurim, aratru, cylindrum, caeteraq; excolendi agri inftrumenta luculeta admodum reliquit,& unice comendavit. Ea autem funt axiomata illa & principia de materia formaq; artis,ut praecepta omnia fint primo kata wav̈os, de omni,id eft neceffario omninoq; vera:fecundo kaf' auto,per fe,id eft homogenea & cognata:tertio kathoλuπρωτα,universaliter prima,id eft ppria: ita ut generalia generaliter & femel doceantur: nude fpecialia per fingulas fpecies cocludatur. haec de materia artis praecepta funt, quae fi quis arbitretur aliorfum ab Ariftotele referri, ja miffo Ariftotelis nomine exiftimet a P. Ramo fieri artiu omniu communia , ut tantum cofideretur quam vere quaq; comode.De forma aute artis, res eft breuior:ut generalia precedant,fpecialia fequantur: naturaq; primum primo loco fit, fecundu fecundo,tertiu tertio,& ita deinceps: ut ab unitate per media genera ad individua multitudinem defcendatur: ut Plato loquitur, vel ysvinwtatov,generalifsimu primo loco:vw' allaλα subalterna intermedio: ἀδιαιρέτα, specialissima infimo loco sint, ut Peripatetici loquuntur. quae omnia secundo Dialecticae libro plenius exponêtur. haec(inquâ)ab Aristotele instrumêta coponendae artis Logicae singularia tradita sunt: non solùm seges ampla & copiosa relicta est. Primum igitur hoc studium P.Rami considerandû vobis erit in hac Logicae agricultura, ut Aristoteli obsecûdarit, ut tam multis libris involutam Logicâ ex Aristotelis legib. & principiis explicarit: Plurima sunt in Logicis Aristotelis libris Logica καθ' αὐτὸ, καθ' αὑτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτα, id est, absolutissima perfectissimaq; documenta: ea omnia, tanquam pretiosissimae Logici patrimonii opes, à P.Ramo retinentur & exornatur: salsa nô multa sunt, aliena sunt complura, sed multo plurima impropria, cû generalia specialiter & frequenter iterátur, eaq; plaga est omniû longe longeq; gravissima: methodusq; propterea cofusior, & in Organo, ut vulgò dispositû est ab interpretibus, hilterologiam mirabilem complexa, usuique (quod caput mali est) vehementer ac valde repugnantem, sicuti postea declaratis paribus explicabo. Ergo nô solûm cômodum, sed etiam jucundû nobis erit recordari, quomodo P. Ramus vera à falsis, homogenea ab alienis, propria ab impropriis sejunxerit, ut etiam quae deessent, undiq; coquisierit & addiderit: ut tam dissipatam tot tantarumq; rerum confusionem luce methodi atq; ordinis illustrarit: ad eamque rem breviter comparare singulis locis summatimq; subducere institui, quaecunq; á P.Ramo
units.tr: The foundation of P. Ramus in restoring and reforming Dialectic will be twofold: first in the precepts of the art, and second in the examples and practice of the art. In both he followed Aristotle above all as his author. Aristotle, with great care, gathered together Dialectic, which had been scattered and dispersed in various ways among the ancients and the philosophers of his own age, and he composed books on arguments, on the arrangement and judgment of arguments, that is, on Logic, at least one hundred and fifty, as P. Ramus taught in the first book of his Dialectical Lectures. Of these books, forty-three still survive. Seventeen are in the Organon, to which Porphyry is usually added, making eighteen. Four are rhetorical, eight are physical, and fourteen are philosophical. In these, with a few exceptions, everything concerns arguments and the judgment of arguments, that is, as I have said, Logic. So this field is indeed very fertile, and, if one looks back to the ancients from whom Aristotle took it over, it was cleared by him of many thorns and brambles. Yet it is still overgrown with many remaining difficulties of ploughing and cultivating, which Aristotle himself would undoubtedly have removed had he lived longer, and which he could have ploughed again, harrowed again, and tilled and improved in every way. But after his return from Alexander, he had only thirteen years, occupied with the daily cares of two lectures and with the composition of so many volumes, and so he had little leisure to re-read and revise. Nevertheless, here too Aristotle, like a good father of a family who leaves his children a fine supply of tools, left his disciples a sickle, an axe, a plough, a roller, and the other implements for cultivating the field, and he especially commended them. These are the axioms and principles concerning the matter and form of the art. The precepts concerning the matter are these: first, universal [κατὰ παντός], that is, true of everything and necessarily true; second, per se [καθ' αὑτό], that is, homogeneous and akin; third, universally first [καθόλου πρῶτα], that is, proper. So general things are to be taught generally and once only, and special things are to be concluded in each particular species. These are the precepts concerning the matter of the art. If anyone thinks they were referred by Aristotle to some other purpose, and supposes that P. Ramus, leaving aside Aristotle's name, made them common to all arts, let him consider only how true and how fitting they are. As for the form of the art, the matter is briefer: the general things should precede and the special things follow; what is first in nature should come first, the second second, the third third, and so on, so that one descends from unity through the intermediate genera to individuals and their multitude. As Plato speaks, the most general [γενικώτατον] should stand in the first place, the subordinate [ὑφ' ἄλλα] in the middle, and the indivisible [ἀδιαίρετα], the most special, in the last place, as the Peripatetics put it. All of these will be set out more fully in the second book of Dialectic. These, I say, are the singular instruments for constructing the art of Logic which were handed down by Aristotle, and a wide and abundant field was left not only for sowing. Therefore this first study of P. Ramus must be considered by you in this agriculture of Logic: how he followed Aristotle, and how he explained Logic, entangled in so many books, from Aristotle's laws and principles. Very many things in Aristotle's logical books are universal [κατὰ παντός], per se [καθ' αὑτό], and universally first [καθόλου πρῶτα], that is, most absolute and most perfect teachings. All of these, as the precious riches of Logic's inheritance, have been retained and adorned by P. Ramus. Not many things are unsound, many are foreign, but far more are improper, since general things are repeated specially and frequently, and this is by far the most serious fault of all. For this reason the method is more confused, and in the Organon, as it is commonly arranged by its interpreters, it contains a wonderful tangle of repetitions, and it is strongly and greatly opposed to practice, which is the chief defect, as I will explain with examples later. Therefore it will be not only convenient but also pleasant for us to recall how P. Ramus separated the true from the false, the homogeneous from the foreign, and the proper from the improper, and how he sought out and added whatever was lacking on every side, so that he might illuminate by the light of method and order such a scattered confusion of so many and so great matters. For this purpose I have resolved to set out briefly and in summary, place by place, all that has been dispersed by P. Ramus in the books of various schools, and also what has been disputed but not written down by him; indeed, whatever I heard and learned from him through constant and brotherly association.

units.la: variis variarum scholarum libris dispersa sunt, disputata etiam, neq; tamé ab eo descripta: imó verò quæcunq; pro assidua & fraterna consuetudine ex eo audivi ac didici. Atq; id P. Ramo primum restituendæ & reformandę Dialecticæ fundamentum propositum erit: secundum autem erit in exemplis & artis, & artificiosæ commentationis, id est, in usu artis & fructu demonstrando. Exempla verò poetarum & oratorum á P. Ramo multorum annorum professione & labore observata & animadversa equidem plurimi facio, quia demonstrat artis & veritatem & utilitatē. Hippocrates, Leo, Theudius, Hermotimus, Euclides, mathematicorum elementorum authores perhibentur: non quia elementa ipsa invenisse, sed quia facilius demonstrasse existimantur. At qui demonstratio logicorum theorematum vera & germana fit per exepla præstantium logicorum. Tota logica legitimè descripta definitionib. & partitionib. coponitur: quę quia principia sunt, aliam quàm insigniū exemplorū demonstratio nè non recipiūt: Et sic ἐμπειρία, ἱστορία, διὰ δνσις, ἐπαγωγὴ, experiētia, observatio, sensus, inductio (ut Aristot. 14. cap 1. Post & in Philosophia 1. cap. 1. li. bri profitetur) omnium artiū theorematā peperērūt. Quamobré nobilibus exēplis, variis præsertim ac disparibus, variasq; præstantium ingeniorū dotes in unā doctrinę gloriā veluti cōspirantiū demōstrationibus tantū tribuo, quantū accuratisimæ demonstrationi logicæ artis tribui possit. Exempla verò poetica & oratoria P. Ramus ad illustrandū & demonstrandū logicæ artis usum, quàm illustrissima Aristotele authore selegit. Sic enim nominatim jubet Aristot. octavo Topico, exemplis (qd' postea pleniús dicam) Homericis utendũ esse: Demostheneis pariter utendũ dixisset, si Demosthenis scripta tũ peinde celebrata fuissent. Et Aristotelei præcepti ratio magna prorsus est: Primúm puero à grámaticis & rhetoricis artib. ad logicá venienti poetę & oratores jam noti erűt artsu cósequentiũ scriptores adhuc ignoti. Deinde exépla hæc poetica & oratoria, usum artis Dialecticę talem demóstrant, qualis nẽpe apud principes ciuitatũ & populorũ doctores fuit: sic usus hic é politica illa Socraticę & Aristoteleę logicę dignitate ac præstátia deprometur: pretereaq; fructum grámaticæ puritatis & ornatus rhetorici dupliced gratis afferét: ut licet in iis Dialecticũ tátûm artificiũ discipulus meditetur, interea tamé fructus artificii & grámatici, & rhetorici, spóte & si ne labore cósequatur: ut qui cósuefcet politicorũ eiusmodi & popularium logicorũ more dissere re, cósuefcat interea, etiá nó cogitás, tamè eorũ more & loqui & dicere. His igitur Aristoteleis de caussis, P. Ramus exéplis illustribus & luculentis usus est: & illi secundi fundamenti prima pars fuit in exéplis magnorũ logicorũ, in quib. logicus artis suæ veritatem agnosceret, posteaque in perpetuis poematũ & orationũ operib. easdem logicas laudes sibi retexeret. hęc analysis est Aristoteli. Secunda pars est in uberiore quodá artis usu: neq; ampliús in cognoscendis alienis exéplis, sed in imitandis & similibus con-
units.tr: This will be the first foundation proposed for restoring and reforming Dialectic by P. Ramus; the second will be in the examples of the art and of skilful commentary, that is, in demonstrating the use and fruit of the art. Indeed, I greatly value the examples of poets and orators, which P. Ramus observed and noted through the labour of many years of teaching, because they demonstrate both the truth and the usefulness of the art. Hippocrates, Leo, Theudius, Hermotimus and Euclid are said to be the authors of the mathematical elements, not because they discovered the elements themselves, but because they are thought to have demonstrated them more easily. But the demonstration of logical theorems becomes true and genuine through examples of outstanding logicians. The whole of Logic, properly described, is constructed by definitions and divisions, and since these are principles, they do not admit any demonstration other than by examples of distinguished works. And so experience, history, inquiry, induction, experientia, observatio, sensus, inductio (as Aristotle professes, in the fourteenth chapter of his book and at the beginning of the Physics, chapter one), have produced the theorems of all the arts. For this reason, I attribute to the demonstrations of noble examples, especially varied and diverse ones, and to the varied gifts of outstanding minds, as if they were agreeing together for the glory of one doctrine, as much as can be attributed to the most accurate logical demonstration of the art of Logic. Moreover, P. Ramus chose poetic and oratorical examples to illustrate and demonstrate the use of the logical art, most illustrious, with Aristotle as his author. For Aristotle expressly commands, in the eighth book of the Topics, that Homeric examples (of which I will speak more fully afterwards) should be used; he would have said that Demosthenic examples should be used likewise, if Demosthenes' writings had been as celebrated then. And the reason for Aristotle's precept is entirely great: when a boy comes to Logic from the arts of grammar and rhetoric, the poets and orators will already be known to him, while the writers of the consequences of arguments will still be unknown. Next, these poetic and oratorical examples demonstrate the use of the art of Dialectic in the form in which it was found among the leading men of states and the teachers of peoples. Thus this use is drawn from that political dignity and excellence of the Socratic and Aristotelian Logic. Moreover, it will bring the fruit of grammatical purity and rhetorical ornament at no cost: so that, while the student meditates only on the dialectical skill in these examples, nevertheless the fruit of both the grammatical and the rhetorical skill is obtained spontaneously and without labour. For whoever becomes accustomed to argue in the manner of such political and popular logical examples, will at the same time become accustomed, even without thinking of it, to speak and to say things in their manner. For these Aristotelian reasons, P. Ramus used illustrious and brilliant examples. This was the first part of his second foundation, in examples of great logicians, in which the logician might recognise the truth of his art, and afterwards, in the lasting works of poems and orations, might find again the same logical praises for himself. This is the analysis of Aristotle. The second part lies in a more abundant use of the art, not in the mere recognition of foreign examples, but in imitating them, and in making similar ones and commenting on them, again with Aristotle as teacher and author.

units.la: fingendis & cōmentandis:idque rursus Aristotele magistro & authore. Aristoteles .n. in thesi (ait Tullius in Oratore) adolescentes non ad philosophorū morem,tenuiter disserēdi, sed ad copiam rhetorum,in utramq; partem, ut ornatiūs & uberiūs dici posset,exercuit. Itaq; P.Ramus perpetuò monuit, ut Aristotelea logicarū declamationū exercitatio teneretur,utq; Gramma-tica grammaticis, sic Dialeƈtica dialeƈticis magnorum authorum laudibus æmulandis, cō similibus etiā cōfingendis exerceretur, eademque quamplurimæ quamque accuratissimę imitationis & commentationis diligentia,perinde ut grámaticos,ita dialeƈticos fore. Hæc genesis est operis logici.Itaq; secundum P. Rami fundamentum in conformáda logica, est in usu artis, exemplis retexendis & confingendis.jam conferantur hæc cū logicis & libris & scholis:Exépla artis & artificiosæ exercitationis in logicis & libris & scholis longé dissimilia reperientur. In totis enim quadraginta quatuor libris illis,& præcipuē in Organo,longé secus factū est. Nam exempla illa Homerica nulla sunt admodum, sed confiƈta & feré duntaxat abecedaria:ut, Omne b esta: Omne c est b : Ergo omne c esta. q non modò logicum humanitatis usum nullum prorsus ostendunt,sed mētem auditoris excruciant,si mutas illas notas ad certi generis significationem velit referre. Et tamen hæc abecedaria figmenta, tanquam mathematica defenduntur etiam in Organo, & gloriosæ artis specie etiā laudátur.Enimverò (ajebat hīc P. Ramus) mathematici res objectas oculis & demonstratas appellant literis, tanquam vocabulis: ut, Esto linea a -- b: Esto (c), quadratu |a|. At totis Analyticis longè secus est: nec enim uel oculis, vel auribus argumentum vel argumentatio 5 proposita Homeri & Demosthenis, appellatur á logico literis, ut lineæ & circuli á geometra, sed literis ipsis, id est, mutis & nihil significatib. notis veluti phantasmata quædam offunduntur, quæ mentem auditoris, ut dixi, mirandum 10 in modum torqueát. Quare hęc exemplorū figméta nō sunt mathematica, & si maximè essent, ut sunt in Oragno quædam de trianguli tribus angulis, de diametro asymetro: attamen posteriores essent artis, nequedum Logicæ discipulo 15 perceptæ: ideoque vitiosa, quia ignota. Fingendi autem in artis explicatione licentia jam olim in scholis agitata est: & Cornificius antiquus rhetor (cujus Quintilianus meminit) quarto ad Herenium libro, in nostram hanc exemplorum 20 per varios & diversos authores inductionem invectus est, argumentis quatuor: primo, quia exempla (ait) adhibentur gratia demonstrandi, non confirmandi neque testificandi. Atqui (inquam) nihil demonstrarent, nisi confirma 25 rent & testificarentur, nec omnino argumenta essent, nisi arguerent. Deinde exempla hæc observata (ait) plerunque sunt eorum, qui artem nescierunt. Quid tum inquam? usum scierut artis parentem & magistrum. Tertio, quód exem 30 plorum per varios authores dispersorum inductione deterretur auditor artis. Ecquid (inquá)
units.tr: For Aristotle, in his theses (as Tully says in the Orator), trained young men not in the philosophers' manner of slender disputation, but in the abundance of the rhetoricians, on either side, so that it could be spoken more ornately and more richly. And so P. Ramus constantly advised that the exercise of Aristotelian logical declamations should be kept up, and that, just as Grammar is practised by grammarians, so Dialectic should be practised by dialecticians in emulating the praises of great authors, and also in devising similar ones; and that by the most careful diligence of very many and most accurate imitations and commentaries, dialecticians would be made just as grammarians are made. This is the origin of the logical work. Therefore, the second foundation of P. Ramus in shaping Logic lies in the practice of the art, in reconstructing and devising examples. Now let these things be compared with the logical books and the schools. Examples of the art and of skilful exercise will be found in the logical books and the schools very different from these. For in all those forty-four books, and especially in the Organon, things have gone quite otherwise. Those Homeric examples are almost nonexistent; they are invented and almost mere alphabets, such as: "Every b is a; every c is b; therefore every c is a." These not only show no use of the logical art in human affairs at all, but they torment the listener's mind if he wishes to refer those mute symbols to some kind of meaning. And yet these alphabetic fictions are defended even in the Organon as if they were mathematical, and are praised under the appearance of a glorious art. Indeed (P. Ramus used to say here), mathematicians call the things set before the eyes and demonstrated by letters, as by words: for example, "Let there be a line a--b; let there be the square (c) of a." But in the Analytics it is quite otherwise: for neither an argument nor an argumentation proposed by Homer or Demosthenes, which the logician does not name by letters, as the geometer names lines and circles, but by the letters themselves, that is, by mute symbols signifying nothing, are set before the eyes or ears, and these, as I said, wonderfully torment the listener's mind like certain phantoms. Therefore these fictions of examples are not mathematical; and even if they were most mathematical, as in the Organon are certain things about the three angles of a triangle, or about the incommensurable diagonal, nevertheless they would be later than the art, and not yet perceived by the student of Logic, and therefore faulty, because unknown. The licence of inventing examples in the explanation of the art has been debated in the schools for a long time already. Cornificius, an ancient rhetorician (whom Quintilian mentions), in the fourth book to Herennius, attacked this very induction of examples from various and diverse authors, with four arguments. First, because examples (he says) are used for the sake of demonstrating, not confirming or testifying. But (I reply) they would demonstrate nothing unless they confirmed and testified, and they would not be arguments at all unless they proved. Second, these observed examples (he says) are mostly those of men who did not know the art. What then, I reply? They knew the practice, which is the parent and teacher of the art. Third, the student of the art is deterred by the induction of examples scattered among various authors. What (I ask) ...

units.la: a potiùs, quàm vel apis in conficiendo melle florum per varias arbores collectione, vel Zeuxis in Helenę pictura é tot virginibus excipiêda venustate? Et tamen nô auditor & discipuli, sed artem cóstituentis doctoris terror hic essèt. Postremò, quód qui alienis quálibet egregiorũ authorũ exéplis illustrat artę à se cópositam, similis est mercatori purpuram publicanti, cujus copiá domi nó habeat: sed é vicinis officinis præcario petat. Enim uero mercator hic noster, doctrinæ tam præcepta á præstátibus & varijs authoribus obseruatione usus & animadversione, quám præceptorum exempla mutuatur. Quare tota Cornificii disputatio pro fictis exèplis adversus animadversa in magnis authoribus exépla, est illa quidé verbis & specie subtilis & ingeniosa, sed reipsa inanis & irridęda. Sed multò magis irridęda est pervulgata in logicorũ scholis opinio, Veritate in exemplis nó requiri. Ecquid igitur? quomodo Aristotelis principiis, historiæ & experientiæ, nó modò fícta, sed etiam falsa convenient? quomodo legi καταπαντὸς congruét? hæc erat P. Rami disputatio aduersus sicta & falsa exépla, é quib. fundi logici prima calamitas extitit. quód exèplis nó solū fictis, sed aliquádo falsis, certè ignotis ac prępostcris, præcepta quęlibet in logicá inducta sint, quæ exèplis, & tanquam vadimoniis Homericis induci nun quam potuissent: quæ Aristotelis ἱστορία καὶ ἰμάτια ἡ nunquam permisissent. Et tamen ista calamitas, foecúditate Aristotelearum declamationũ, si continuatæ essent, facilè compésata, quinetiá plané planè vindicata jampridé essem: Docuissetenim usus, quæ quibus theorematis exempla convenirent. At logicæ nescio quot ante seculorum scholæ,longé perniciosiorem artificiosæ exercitationis calamitatem sibi pepererunt,dum edictis & pœnis publicis poetas & oratores,quod in P.Rami judicio, etiá ab obtrectatoribus (ne qua gratiæ suspicio subesset) publicé testato & publicato legitur,exterminant:dum pro Aristo telea uberioris & ornatioris declamationis logica,incredibilé de præceptis duntaxat altercádo sophisticá exercent.Enimverò Socrates execrari solebat eum,qui primus utilitatem ab honestate sejunxisset: Ecquid facturum cesemus, si logicorum magistrorum opera, á dialecticę virtutis honestate sejunctam utilitatem illam Aristoteleam cerneret?Equidem commemini,quám frequenter quamq; graviter nostros homines hac de re P.Ramus admonuerit:ut de præstantissimæ artis dignitate paulò attentius cogitarent, neq; ex Aristotelea & Peripatetica schola Eubulideam & sophisticam diutius efficerent. Usum, usum (inquam) persæpe dicere solitus est solum correctorem tanti abusus & emendatorem futurum:sapientia antiquorum philosophorum,oratorum,poetarum,censuit de mundi partibus tres inhabitabiles esse, mediá æstu, duas extremas glacie & frigore: at nautarum & mercatorum vulgus,libros & literas ignorátium, totam illam sapientiam oculis corporis & navigationum suarum periculis, id est experientia refutauit. Quandiu disceptabitur de Logica,argu menta cupidis altercādi hominibus ad errores suos defendendum nunquam deerunt: at experientia, exercitatio, usus, captionibus eludi non pot, quin protinus error appareat. Sed hac de re scholę P. Rami variorum generum, item Proœmium reformandæ Parisiensis Academiæ loquitur, & loquetur amplius, solam de præceptis artis altercationem, meram inertiam esse. Ergo hoc fundamentū de arte, deq; artis usu, duplex P. Ramo ad constituendam & conformandam Logicam propositum deinceps erit.
units.tr: Or rather, than the bee's gathering of flowers from many trees to make honey, or Zeuxis's choosing of loveliness from so many virgins for his painting of Helen? And yet the listener and the students, not the teacher who sets up the art, would be terrified by this. Last, the man who illustrates with other people's examples, however fine, an art he has put together himself is like a merchant who sells purple cloth he does not have at home, and so begs it from neighbouring workshops. But our merchant here borrows the examples of the precepts from the same teaching: from the observation and attention he has given to excellent and various authors, as much as from the precepts. So the whole of Cornificius's argument for invented examples against examples observed in great authors is subtle and clever in its words and appearance, but in reality empty and worthy of ridicule. Yet much more worthy of ridicule is the opinion, widely held in the schools of the logicians, that truth is not required in examples. What then? How will fictional and even false examples agree with the principles of Aristotle, history and experience? How will the reading [καταπαντὸς] fit? This was P. Ramus's argument against fictitious and false examples, from which the first disaster of the logicians arose: that not only fictional but sometimes false, certainly unknown and absurd examples have been brought into logic to illustrate whatever precepts, examples which could never have been brought in, like Homeric pledges, and which Aristotle's [ἱστορία καὶ ἰμάτια ἡ] would never have allowed. And yet this disaster would easily have been made good by the fruitfulness of Aristotelian declamations, had they been continued, and indeed I would long since have been fully avenged on it: for experience would have taught which examples fitted which theorems. But the schools of logic, for I know not how many centuries, have brought upon themselves a much more pernicious disaster of artificial exercise, while by edicts and public penalties they banish poets and orators (as is read in P. Ramus's judgement, publicly attested and published, even by his detractors, lest any suspicion of favour should attach to it), and in place of the fuller and more ornate declamation of Aristotle they practise an incredible sophistry, quarrelling about precepts alone. For indeed Socrates used to curse the man who first separated usefulness from honour. What, then, shall we suppose he would do if he saw that by the work of the masters of logic that Aristotelian usefulness had been cut off from the honour of the dialectical virtue? I remember how often and how earnestly P. Ramus warned our people about this matter: that they should think a little more carefully about the dignity of this most excellent art, and should no longer, out of the Aristotelian and Peripatetic school, make it a Eubulidean and sophistical art for longer. Practice, practice, I say, he was wont to say very often, would alone be the corrector and reformer of so great an abuse. The wisdom of the ancient philosophers, orators and poets held that of the parts of the world three are uninhabitable, the middle one by heat and the two extremes by ice and cold; but the crowd of sailors and merchants, ignorant of books and letters, refuted all that wisdom by the evidence of their eyes and the dangers of their voyages, that is, by experience. As long as logic is disputed about, arguments will never be lacking for men eager to quarrel, to defend their errors; but experience, exercise and practice cannot be eluded by captious tricks, and the error at once appears. But on this matter the schools of P. Ramus, in various kinds of writings, and likewise the Preface to the reform of the Paris Academy, speak, and will speak further, declaring that mere quarrelling about the precepts of the art is pure inertia. Therefore this twofold foundation, concerning the art and the use of the art, is the one which P. Ramus has laid down for constituting and shaping logic from now on.

units.la: DIALECTICA.] Principio igitur Dialectica definitur Ars bene differendi. hæc definitio, ut loco & ordine, sic gravitate & pödere prima est, & diligenter accurateq; cóstituta integrum totius artis statum constituit: perversé aut atq; imperité confusa, totam artem pervertit: ea igitur attentisimé nobis consideranda. Generalis est res ipsa definita: generalia definitæ rei vocabula, ideoq; generaliter ad legē καθόλς πρῶτον definienda. Enim verò quanto studio in hanc confirmationem P. Ramus incubuerit, testis est secundus liber Scholarum dialecticarū. Sed gradatim agamus. Dialectica primùm est ars, id est comprehensio præceptorum in rebus æternis propriorum & ordine dispositorum, ad utilem vitæ finem spectantium, ut amplius intelligetur secundo libro. Quamvis enim natura pleriq; faciant, quod præceptis instituitur: ars tamen (ait Cicero 4. de Finibus, & 1. de Oratore) est dux certior, quàm natura: habet enim quædam quasi ad cōmonendū, quó quidq; referas: & quó intuens, ab eo quod tibi ppofueris, minús aberres.
units.tr: DIALECTICA.] First, then, dialectic is defined as the art of differing well. This definition, both in place and in order and in weight and importance, comes first; and if it is carefully and accurately framed it establishes the whole state of the art, but if it is confusedly and ignorantly stated it perverts the whole art. It must therefore be considered by us with the greatest attention. The thing defined is general, and the general words of the defined thing must therefore be defined generally, according to the rule [καθόλου πρῶτον]. Indeed, the zeal with which P. Ramus applied himself to this confirmation is witnessed by the second book of his Dialectical Scholars. But let us proceed step by step. Dialectic is first an art, that is, a comprehension of precepts, proper to eternal things and arranged in order, bearing on the useful end of life, as will be understood more fully in the second book. For although nature brings about many things that are instituted by precepts, art (as Cicero says in the fourth book of On Ends and the first of On the Orator) is a surer guide than nature: for it has certain points, as it were, to remind us to what each thing should be referred, and by keeping our eye on it we go less astray from what we have set before us.

units.la: DISSERENDI. Id est disputandi, disceptandi, ratiocinandi, ratione deniq; utendi: sic enim generaliter ars est definienda, ut tam laté pateat definitio hęc, quám laté patet usus humanę rationis. Nam si requiras, unde ars dialectica sumi debeat, utrúm é secta & opinione philosophi hujus, an illius, utrúm é schola praecipua aliqua, quales primo libro Scholarū dialecticarū quatuor insignes à P. Ramo expositæ sunt: respondeo ex eodem fonte hauriédam esse, unde philosophi omnes, quicunq; rectè ulla unquam in schola ratiocinati sunt, haurire debuerunt, é naturali nempe rationis usu: qui in biblitheca Aristotelis multiplex, & é uariis authoribus col lectus est: sed apparet idem usus etiá multó magis in exemplis magnorum & excellentiū poetarum, oratorum, philosophorum, jurecósultorum, omnis deniq; generis hominū. In uno non omnis generis exempla fortasse reperiëtur: observatione igitur & animadversione, adeoq; inductione, tota res exploranda & probanda est: Naturalis enim Dialectica, vis est rationis, mentibus nostris insita, per quam disputamus & ratiocinamur, per quam movemur, & excitamur ad inquisitionem & investigationē rerum: per quam, ut per solē mundus, sic animus partibus omnibus ad ratrocinandū illuminatur: per quá multis seculis antequam ulla de differendo litera effet, innumerabiles homines prudenter & acutè disputarunt, disseruerūt, ratiocinati sunt.
units.tr: DISSERENDI. That is, of disputing, disceptating, reasoning, and finally of using reason; for art must be defined in this general way, so that this definition extends as widely as the use of human reason extends. For if you ask whence the art of dialectic ought to be drawn, whether from the sect and opinion of this philosopher or that one, or from some principal school, of which four notable ones were set out by P. Ramus in the first book of his Dialectical Scholars, I reply that it must be drawn from the same source from which all philosophers who have ever reasoned rightly in any school were bound to draw: namely from the natural use of reason, which is manifold in the library of Aristotle and gathered from various authors. But it is plain that this same use appears much more in the examples of great and excellent poets, orators, philosophers, jurists, and finally of men of every kind. In one author perhaps examples of every kind will not be found; the whole matter must therefore be explored and proved by observation and attention, and so by induction. For natural dialectic is the power of reason, implanted in our minds, through which we dispute and reason, through which we are moved and stirred to inquiry and investigation of things; through which the mind, as the world by the sun, is illuminated in all its parts for reasoning; through which, for many centuries before there was any writing about disputing, countless men disputed, discoursed and reasoned prudently and sharply.

units.la: Sic ab Aristotele dicitur & in Ethicis, Virtutes
units.tr: So Aristotle says in the Ethics that virtues are natural

units.la: homini naturales esse: & in Topicis, Nativa ingenii indolem in differendo plurimum posse: & in Elechis deniq;, Idiotas uti Dialectica, & sine arte facere, quod artis praeceptis continetur. In describendis igitur Dialecticis praeceptis, propositá P.Ramo fuit naturalis bene differetium consuetudo, ut accommodatam naturae faceret artem, vel potius artem faceret naturae uelut effigiem quadam & imaginem. Hic enim doctor, artis logicae, pictor quidam esse debet naturalis logicae, neq; quicquid in praeceptis pingere, qd non ante in illa naturalis usus idea atq; veritate perspexerit. Quamobrem Dialectica ista vis generalis & rerum omnium communis generaliter & communiter definitur á P.Ramo.
units.tr: to man; and in the Topics that the native disposition of the mind has great power in disputing; and finally in the Sophistical Refutations that unlearned people use dialectic and do without art what is contained in the precepts of art. In describing the precepts of dialectic, therefore, P. Ramus proposed the natural custom of those who reason well, so that he might make the art suited to nature, or rather make the art as it were a likeness and image of nature. For the teacher of the logical art ought to be a kind of painter of natural logic, and should paint nothing in the precepts that he has not first perceived in that natural idea and truth of use. Hence dialectic, this general power common to all things, is defined generally and in common by P. Ramus.

units.la: Logica.] Dialecticae autem & Logicae vocabula pro eodem generaliter accipienda, ut διαλέγεσθαι και λογίζεσθαι differere & ratiocinari accipitur: utrunq; enim est idem quod ratione uti. Sic Plato in Alcibiade primo ait, διαλέγεσθαι, περὶ τῶ λόγῳ χρῆσθαι differere & ratione uti, idem esse. Dialecticam vero Plato primus appellavit hanc artem, ait Laertius in ejus vita: & generaliter eo nomine coplectitur totam rationis vim & facultate in Sophista, Phaedro, septimo de Republica. Sic Dialectici nomen generaliter usurpat in Cratylo, Phaedro, in eode septimo de Repub. Xenoph. 4. comment. ait, διαλέγεσθαι dici ἐν τῷ συνιόντας κοινῇ βουλεύεσθαι διαλέγοντας κατὰ γένη τὰ πράγματα: ex eo quod convenientes ad deliberandum in commune res per capita discerneret. Aristoteles autem etiam διαλέγεσθαι generaliter accipit primo Elenchorum, pro quovis usu rationis: sic in Philosophia, Dialecticae nomen pro tota rationis arte: & in Rhetoricis, τὰ διαλεκτικά, communi isto sensu & generali sumit. Logicam vero primus Aristoteles (si Vallae credimus) appellavit. & quidem verbum hoc tam generale est Aristoteli, quàm Dialecticae. Sic in Philosophia, λογικὰς ἀντιθέσεις argutias dicit: in Topicis, προτάσεως λογικῶν: in Physicis, ἀπορίαν λογικῶν, & hac eadem generali significatione, Tullius & Quintilianus Dialecticam & Logicam dixerunt. Quare Graeci pariter & Latini vocabula Dialecticae & Logicae generaliter acceperunt, λογιστικός, magis ad numerum refertur, unde λογιστικὸς & συλλογισμὸς pro computatione & calculo, sicut etiam λόγος, unde utrumque verbum factum est. & quidem Dialectica, Logica, διαλεκτικά, λογιστικά, praecipue ex syllogismi & argumentationis parte nominata sunt: quomodo fere & latina vocabula: Differendi enim nomen ab agricolis & olitoribus traductum esse Varro docet. Ut enim (ait) olitor disserit in areas sui cujusque generis res: sic in oratione qui facit, differere dicitur. Disputare, ut ait idem Varro est quasi purum facere, & per metaphoram, ratione uti, considerare, meditari, quòd virtus rationis humanae vera à falsis, utilia ab inutilibus, bona à malis discernit. Disceptare item sumitur ex veteri consuetudine Dialecticorum, quaestionem in varias partes distrahentium, cum alius partem unam, alius contrariâ gymnasticè exercitationis gratia in scholis arriperet. Quare latina vocabula, differere, disputare, disceptare, et fi originem tropi cõsideres, propriè ad judican‑ di partem, ut græca referuntur. Attamen doctri‑ næ constituendæ gratiâ, generaliter modò intel‑ ligátur, ad totam & generalem artis facultatem & inventionis & judicii significandū. Atq; Dia‑ lecticæ seu Logicæ nomen, Latini tentarunt la‑ tinè reddere: sed tamen græcis uti etiam malue‑ runt. Cicero in Lucullo: Dialecticam inventam esse dicitis, veri & falsi quasi disceptatricē. Quin‑ tilianus libri secundi capite vigesimo, Etiā (ait) disputatrix virtus erit. & capite secundo libri 12. Itaq; hæc pars Dialecticæ, sive illam disputatri‑ cem dicere malimus. Cic. lib. 3. de Finib. Quam‑ quam ea verba, quibus ex instituto veterū uti‑ mur, pro latinis, ut ipsa Philosophia, Dialectica, Rhetorica, Grammatica, Geometria, Musica, la‑ tinè dici poterant: tamē quia usu percepta sunt, nostra ducamus. Et Academico primo, Enitar ut latinè loquar: nisi in hujusmodi verbis, ut Phi‑ losophiam, aut Rhetoricam, aut Physicam, aut Dialecticam appellē, quibus ut aliis multis, jam utimur pro latinis, hæc ille. Quare ut quod insti‑ tui, concludam, cùm definita ratio sit generalis, cùm vocabula definitæ rationis generalia sint, definitio generalis facta est à P. Ramo, quæ totā & universam disseredi rationem complectere‑ tur: Sic enim decet ex Aristotelis lege καθόλυ πρῶτον, generalia generaliter explicari. Verumenim vero interpretes Aristotelis occurrent, Alexan‑ der, Porphyrius, Ammonius, eorumq; sectato‑ res & æmuli, qui nequaquam logicas illas Ari‑ stotelis leges ad Aristotelis Organum interpre‑ tandum & constituendum sibi proposuerunt. protinus enim confecta res esset, neq; jam P.Ramí diligentiam desideraret, sed falsæ opinionis ac persuasionis errore tantum attulerunt: ut nó verecundiús ac timidiús de divinis oraculis, quám de quibuscunq; scriptis Aristotelis cogitarent: omniaq; in Aristoteleo agro reperta, in eodem veritatis & utilitatis loco constituerent. Interpretes igitur hi, tali logica instructi, huic generali definitioni reclamabunt, neq; rationis usum illum generalem esse dicét: nominatimq; ex Aristotele primi Topici capite quinto proserent, hanc generalem logicam inveniri non posse: & si inventa sit, omnino tamen obscuram & molestam fore. hæc enim verba sunt in eo Organi loco. quin triplicem differendi doctrinam, apodicticam, topicam, sophisticam, pro illa una generali ab Aristotele factam esse dicent. Quæ omnia dici & agi in Organo P. Ramus confitetur: Sed Aristotelis legibus demonstrat esse contraria. Etenim ars illa communis, quæ negatur inveniri posse, non solùm inventa est, sed in Organo ipso tradita: imó laudata & celebrata. Adessent enim (ut optabat hic P.Ramus) Alexáder & Porphyrius, Organumq; ipsum corám proferret, & oculis pené corporis tam crassum errorem agnoscerent. Nam Categoremata, Categoriæ, ἐφόδια, Analytica priora tota, communia sunt & generalia: neq; ullius earū trium artium propria: & in his cōmunis doctrina est inveniendi medii & argumenti: ut nominatim primo Analytico, & reipsa in Categorematis & Categoriis comprehenditur. judicii autem doctrinam in enuntiato ἐρμηνεία: in syllogismo priora Analytica instituût. Itaq; P. Ramus his interpretib. ante oculos subjiceret, primis & præcipuis Organi libris communem & generalem doctrinam contineri, ideoq; assertionem illam Topici primi (quòd ars differendi communis inveniri non possit) esse falsam, legiq́ue Aristotelis καθ' αὑτὸ contrariam. In posterioribus autem Analyticis, ἀποδείξεις (quæ tanta duorum magnorum librorum pompa promittitur) tanquam conclufio propriæ affectionis de subjecto per caussam propriam, in liberalium artium doctrina nulla prorsus est: imò in rerū natura esse omnino non potest, ut in ipsis posterioribus Analyticis P. Ramus evidentissimè docuit. Et tamen totis illis Analyticis sicut in Topicis, nullum omnino est documentum logicū, nisi generale. Illic de causis, factis, subjectis, adjunctis, quæ eadem cum cæteris argumentis, in totis octo libris Topicis trecenties decies septies repetuntur: Tàtam enim in Topicis logicorū locorum tautologiam P. Ramus collegit: quin (quod etiam propositam) in iisdem Topicis, primo, tertio, septimo, Aristoteles commendat & celebrat quàm maximè uniuersales locos, quia sint (ait) ad plurima utilissimi. Et tamen tautologia ista tam hebes crassaq;, non est universæ logicæ, sed inventionis nis tantum: nec enim vel ἐρμηνεία, vel Analysis in Topicis iteratur toties. Quare & hic rursus à P. Ramo concluditur adversus istos interpretes, non
units.tr: Logic. The words Dialectic and Logic should be taken in general to mean the same thing, just as διαλέγεσθαι and λογίζεσθαι mean to discourse and to reason, since both amount to using reason. So Plato, in the first Alcibiades, says that διαλέγεσθαι, to discourse, and περὶ τῷ λόγῳ χρῆσθαι, to use reason, are the same thing. Plato was the first to call this art Dialectic, says Laertius in his Life, and under that name he generally embraces the whole power and faculty of reason, in the Sophist, the Phaedrus, and the seventh book of the Republic. Likewise he uses the name Dialectician in the general sense in the Cratylus, the Phaedrus, and the same seventh book of the Republic. Xenophon, in the fourth book of the Memorabilia, says that διαλέγεσθαι is used of people who meet together to deliberate in common and who sort things by kinds, because those who gather to take counsel together distinguish matters one by one. Aristotle too takes διαλέγεσθαι in general, in the first book of the Elenchi, for any use of reason. Thus, in the Philosophy, he uses the name Dialectic for the whole art of reason, and in the Rhetoric he takes τὰ διαλεκτικά in this common and general sense. Aristotle, if we believe Valla, was the first to call it Logic, and indeed this word is as general for Aristotle as Dialectic is. So in the Philosophy he calls subtle arguments λογικὰς ἀντιθέσεις; in the Topics he speaks of προτάσεως λογικῶν; in the Physics, ἀπορίαν λογικῶν; and in this same general meaning Cicero and Quintilian used the words Dialectic and Logic. Hence Greeks and Latins alike have taken the words Dialectic and Logic in general. Λογιστικός refers more to number, whence λογιστικὸς and συλλογισμὸς mean computation and calculation, and likewise λόγος, from which both words are derived. Dialectic and Logic, διαλεκτικά, λογιστικά, were named chiefly from the part concerning syllogism and argument, and the Latin words are much the same. For Varro teaches that the name of differing (differendi) was taken over from farmers and gardeners. As (he says) the gardener differs by arranging his plots, each according to its kind, so whoever does this in speech is said to differ. To dispute (disputare), as Varro says again, is roughly to make clear, and by metaphor, to use reason, to consider and reflect, because the power of human reason distinguishes true from false, useful from useless, good from bad. Likewise to dispute (disceptare) is taken from the old custom of the Dialecticians, who pulled a question into various parts, when one man seized one side and another the opposite, as an exercise in the schools for the sake of practice. So the Latin words to differ, to dispute, and to debate, if you consider the origin of the figure, refer properly to the part of judging, as the Greek words do. Yet for the purpose of setting up a doctrine they are understood only in general, to signify the whole general faculty of the art, both of invention and of judgement. And the Latins have tried to render the name of Dialectic or Logic into Latin, but they have preferred to use the Greek words too. Cicero, in the Lucullus: "You say that Dialectic was invented as a kind of judge of the true and the false." Quintilian, in the twentieth chapter of the second book: "Even virtue will be disputatious (disputatrix)." And in the second chapter of the twelfth book: "So this part of Dialectic, or we would prefer to call it the disputatious part." Cicero, in the third book of the De Finibus: "Although those words which we use by the practice of the ancients, such as Philosophy, Dialectic, Rhetoric, Grammar, Geometry, and Music, could be said in Latin, nevertheless, because they are established by usage, let us keep ours." And in the first Academica: "I will try to speak Latin; but except in words of this kind, such as when I call it Philosophy, or Rhetoric, or Physics, or Dialectic, which, like many others, we already use as Latin." So, to conclude what I set out to do: since the definition of reason is general, and the words for a defined reason are general, a general definition has been given by P. Ramus, which embraces the whole and universal reasoning of disputing. For thus, according to Aristotle's rule, καθόλυ πρῶτον, general things should be explained generally. But the interpreters of Aristotle will come forward: Alexander, Porphyry, Ammonius, and their followers and rivals, who did not at all propose to themselves, in interpreting and setting up the Organon of Aristotle, those logical rules of Aristotle. For the matter would have been finished at once, and would no longer need the diligence of P. Ramus; but they brought in nothing but the error of a false opinion and persuasion, so that they thought no less timidly and reverently about the writings of Aristotle than about divine oracles, and they set everything found in the field of Aristotle in the same place of truth and usefulness. These interpreters, equipped with such a logic, will cry out against this general definition, and will say that such a general use of reason cannot exist. Naming Aristotle, they will cite the fifth chapter of the first book of the Topics: that this general logic cannot be found, and that if it were found, it would nonetheless be wholly obscure and troublesome. For these are the words in that place of the Organon. Indeed they will say that Aristotle made a threefold doctrine of disputing, apodeictic, topical and sophistical, in place of that one general one. P. Ramus confesses that all these things are said and done in the Organon, but he shows by the laws of Aristotle that they are contrary to them. For that common art, which is said to be impossible to find, has not only been found, but is handed down in the Organon itself, and indeed praised and celebrated. For if Alexander and Porphyry were present (as P. Ramus wished), and the Organon itself were brought forward before them, they would recognise, almost with bodily eyes, so gross an error. For the Categoremata, the Categories, the ἐφόδια, and the whole of the Prior Analytics are common and general, and belong to none of those three arts in particular. In these there is a common doctrine of finding the middle term and the argument, as is expressly stated in the first Analytic, and is actually contained in the Categoremata and the Categories. The doctrine of judgement is in the ἐρμηνεία on the proposition, and the Prior Analytics set out the syllogism. So P. Ramus set before the eyes of these interpreters that the first and principal books of the Organon contain a common and general doctrine, and therefore that the assertion in the first Topics (that a common art of disputing cannot be found) is false and contrary to the law of Aristotle καθ' αὑτὸ. In the Posterior Analytics, however, the ἀποδείξεις (which is promised with such a great display of two large books), as the conclusion of a proper affection concerning a subject through its proper cause, there is absolutely none in the doctrine of the liberal arts; indeed it cannot exist at all in the nature of things, as P. Ramus has most clearly taught in the Posterior Analytics themselves. And yet in all those Analytics, as in the Topics, there is absolutely no logical teaching except a general one. There, causes, effects, subjects, adjuncts, which are the same as the other arguments, are repeated three hundred and seventy times in the eight books of the Topics. For P. Ramus gathered so great a tautology of the logical places in the Topics. Moreover (which also he proposes), in the same Topics, in the first, third, and seventh books, Aristotle commends and celebrates most highly the universal places, because they are, he says, most useful for very many things. And yet this tautology, so dull and gross, belongs not to the whole of logic but only to invention; for neither the ἐρμηνεία nor the Analysis is repeated so often in the Topics. Hence here again P. Ramus concludes against these interpreters that

units.la: nō duas logicas in Posterioribus & Topicis instituī, sed unam & eandem logicæ parte sæpius iterari & laudari: tautologiamq; tam molestā & odiosam, falsa duplicis doctrinæ specie prætextam, corrigendam esse ad legem Aristotelis, doctrinamq; generalem generaliter ac semel explicandam. Sed occurritur rursus ab his interpretibus; aliam logicam esse necessariorum, aliam probabilium seu contingentium: ideoq; apodicticam de necessariis, & topicam de probabilibus esse distinguendam. At hic P. Ramus hominum quorundam pertinaciam & stuporem admirabatur, manumq; quinq; digitis expansis ostentans, ajebat, non clarius palmam illam corporis oculis demonstrari, quám veritas hæc logicæ generalis ostenderetur. Etenim quamvis Dialectica præceptis cōstet omnino necessariis (secus enim ars non esset neq; καθ' αὐτὸ esset) attamen una communis sufficit & necessariis & contingentibus rebus edisserendis, ut patet in iis ipsis libris Apodicticis & Topicis, in quibus per eandem doctrinam causarum, effectorum, generis, speciei, & reliquorum sæpiùs iterată & cōfusam, necessaria & probabilia instituì vel ab his interpretibus affirmatur. Quare Dialectica unica generalis specialibus hisce necessitatis & probabilitatis differentiis abundé, vel interpretum cōfesione, sufficit. Atq; in isto necessitatis & probabilitatis elencho, ualdé simpliciter Alexander, Porphyrius, Ammonius, & interpretes reliqui seducti sunt, ad duas logicas speciales una generali constituendum: Sophistica autem
units.tr: two logics are not set up in the Posterior Analytics and the Topics; rather one and the same part of logic is repeated and praised too often, and this tautology, so tiresome and annoying, covered with the false appearance of a double doctrine, must be corrected according to the law of Aristotle, and the general doctrine must be explained generally and once only. But these interpreters object again: there is one logic of necessary things and another of probable or contingent things, and therefore the apodeictic, concerning the necessary, and the topical, concerning the probable, must be distinguished. But here P. Ramus wondered at the obstinacy and stupidity of certain men, and, holding up his hand with its five fingers spread, said that the truth of this general logic was shown no more clearly to the bodily eyes than that palm was. For although Dialectic consists entirely of necessary precepts (otherwise it would not be an art, nor would it be καθ' αὐτὸ), nevertheless one common art suffices for setting out both necessary and contingent things, as is plain in those very Apodeictic and Topical books, in which, by the same doctrine of causes, effects, genus, species and the rest, repeated often and confusedly, necessary and probable matters are set out, as these interpreters themselves affirm. Therefore one general Dialectic, without these special differences of necessity and probability, suffices abundantly, even by the confession of the interpreters. And in this refutation of necessity and probability, Alexander, Porphyry, Ammonius and the other interpreters were quite simply led astray, into setting up two special logics alongside one general one. But the Sophistical

units.la: b vitio-
units.tr: vice-

units.la: vitiorum (quæ tertia differendi ars ab interpretibus efficitur) per Aristotelis legem λαθ' ὣτὶ, locum in arte virtutum dialecticarū non potest habere: Vitia enim differendi virtutibus disseré di sunt heterogenea. Et tamé hæc tertia sophismatum logica valdé duas illas superiores, Apo-dicticam & Topicá refellit. Est enim illa tota generalis & communis: nec alia facta est apodicticæ, alia topicæ sophistica: quamvis sint é falsis alia impossibilia, alia contingentia, ut é veris, alia necessaria, alia tantum probabilia. Itaq; ut sophistica duorum generum impossibilium & contingentium, sic Dialectica duorum generum necessariorum & probabiliū, eadem & communis interpretibus videri debuit. Quamobrem Aristotelei Organi professores & lectores, qui usquam gentiū essent, P. Ramus ad sanctas illas & sacras Aristotelis leges revocabat, & familiariter admonebat, ut aliquando diligētius de tam turpi fædoq; sophismate cogitarent, neque se discipulofq; suos diutiús falli decipiq; paterentur: sed Aristotelis Organum perspiceret tam confusé triplicarū, ad perspicuam generis unitatem & simplicitatem esse revocandum, unamq; Dialecticam generalem, pro triplici, docendam ac de finiendam esse. De vocabulis autem Dialecticæ & Logicæ, res est expeditior: utrumq; enim interdum specialiter accipitur, non pro arte ulla speciali, sed pro artis opere probabili. sic Aristoteli dicitur Dialectica & interrogatio & propositio, sic Logica & quæstio & argumētatio & de monstratio, ut secundo libro Scholarum Dialecticarum {*}ticarum declaratur à P.Ramo: quomodo vide licet erant loquuti authores quidam, quorum libros Aristoteles collegerat. Nec sermo hic alienus sit, si attente considerétur. Quamvis enim di sputádi doctrina tota & una & necessaria sit, disputatio tamen multiplex esse potest, alia necessaria, alia probabilis : neque de verbis laborandum fuerit, intellecta re. Probabilis disputatio appelletur Dialectica & Logica: sed tamen ut antea in definitione, ita nunc in nomine rei, P.Ramus ad Aristotelem é sua lege judicem recurrit, & rogat quomodo contractionis hujus spina sit evellenda. Vocabula Dialecticæ & Logicæ modo generalia, modo non generalia sunt: Generalia, dicet Aristoteles, generalibus verbis, & generaliter explicanda: hæc enim lex est illa καθόλου πρῶτον. Quare P. Ramus vocabulis Dialecticæ & Logicæ, in ipsa Doctrina & arte declaranda, tantùm generaliter utitur. Ex hac igitur generali definitione, duo præterea P. Ramus deducit, primò artis finem esse generale, bené differre, non autè κατὰ μέρος, ut interpretes somnia runt: cùm ipsa (ut jam dixi) commentum sit in natura rerum impossibile: Sic Aristoteles 2. cap.
units.tr: the vices of arguing (which the third art of arguing, that of the sophists, is made of, according to the interpreters) cannot have a place in the art of the virtues of dialectic by Aristotle's law λαθ' ὣτὶ, since the vices of arguing are heterogeneous to the virtues of disputing. And yet this third, sophistical logic greatly refutes those two higher ones, the apodictic and the topical. For it is wholly general and common: there is not one sophistic of apodictic and another of topic, although some falsehoods are impossible and others contingent, and some truths are necessary and others only probable. Therefore, just as sophistic is one art of the two kinds of impossible and contingent, so dialectic of the two kinds of necessary and probable ought to have been seen by the interpreters as one and the same common art. For this reason P. Ramus called back the professors and readers of Aristotle's Organon, wherever they were in the world, to those holy and sacred laws of Aristotle, and admonished them as a friend that at last they should think more carefully about so shameful and foul a sophism, and not allow themselves and their pupils to be deceived and misled any longer; but that they should see that the Organon of Aristotle, confusedly divided into three, must be brought back to the clear unity and simplicity of a genus, and that one general dialectic must be taught and defined in place of three. As for the words Dialectic and Logic, the matter is more easily settled: each of them is sometimes taken in a special sense, not for any special art but for a probable work of the art. Thus Aristotle calls dialectic both questioning and proposition, and logic both inquiry and argumentation and demonstration, as P. Ramus explains in the second book of the Dialectical Scholars, in the way that certain authors, whose books Aristotle had collected, were accustomed to speak. Nor is this language foreign, if it is considered attentively. For although the doctrine of disputing is whole and one and necessary, disputation can nevertheless be manifold, some necessary, some probable; and there is no need to labour over words once the thing is understood. A probable disputation may be called dialectic and logic; but still, as before in the definition, so now in the name of the thing, P. Ramus has recourse to Aristotle as judge by his own law, and asks how the thorn of this confusion is to be pulled out. The words dialectic and logic are sometimes general and sometimes not: general things, Aristotle says, must be expressed in general words and explained generally, for that is the law καθόλου πρῶτον. Hence P. Ramus, in setting out the doctrine and art itself, uses the words dialectic and logic only in the general sense. From this general definition, P. Ramus further deduces two things: first, that the end of the art is to dispute well in general, and not κατὰ μέρος, as the interpreters have dreamed, since such a thing (as I have already said) is an invention impossible in the nature of things. So Aristotle, in the second chapter of the Topics, teaches the political discipline, as if you were to say that it has its end finally, when that is achieved which is contained within the powers of the art. Grammar is the art of speaking well, rhetoric of speaking well; therefore (you will say) the end of grammar is to speak well, and likewise the end of rhetoric is to speak well: so dialectic is the art of speaking well…

units.la: 1. Topici, docet disciplinam πολιτικὴν, tanquam diceres, finaliter habere, quàdo præstatur, quod artis viribus continetur. Grammatica, est ars bené loquendi: Rhetorica, bené dicendi: Ergo (dices) finis Grammaticæ, & bené loqui: finis item Rhetoricæ, bené dicere: Sic Dialectica est ars bené differendi: Ergo Dialecticæ finis est bené differere. Deinde ex eadem generali definitione,
units.tr: 1. Topics, he teaches that the discipline is πολιτική [politikē], as if you were to say that it has its end when that is accomplished which is contained within the powers of the art. Grammar is the art of speaking well; rhetoric, the art of speaking well: therefore (you will say) the end of grammar is to speak well, and likewise the end of rhetoric is to speak well. So dialectic is the art of disputing well; therefore the end of dialectic is to dispute well. Next, from the same general definition,

units.la: Ioan. 1.
units.tr: John 1.

units.la: ne,P.Ramus concludit,subjectum artis esse generale de omni ente & non ente, ut Ariftoteles nominatim profitetur:non autem de sola quæstione:cúm logicæ artis vis appareat in cogitandis argumentis,in enunciatis per fe manefeftis, in methodo. Non autem in solis enunciatis dubiis, syllogismo aliquo concludendis. unde sophisticam quæstionum in Logica doctrinâ esse convincitur, neq; magis ad Logicam, quàm ad Grammaticam attinere,quæ quæstionis genera sint:cúm fit ars utraq; tota communis omnium & dubiarum & non dubiarum rerum. Grammaticus de omni re bené loquitur:sic,ac multò magis, Dialecticus seu Logicus de omni re bene disserit. Sed de fine, deque subjecto Logicæ artis,P.Ramus secundo libro Dialecticarum scholarum copiofisimè disservit,quo in libro perspicietur, uti totum agrum logicum sine terminis ac finibus infinitè dispersum,& in tot illis voluminibus disipatũ, definitione in primis necessaria terminarit ac definierit:ut Aristoteli gratissimum opus ac optatisimum fecerit.In totis enim libris illis quatuor & quadraginta, definitio illa perspicuè proposita nusquam est:quæ tamen ex Aristotelis legibus debuit & esse (quia esset omnino necessarioq; vera, & homogenea, & propria)& primo loco esse, quia generalissima & naturâ esset prima. Ergo lætaretur Aristo teles, cúm logicum agrum fossa valloq; definitionis legitimæ ita conclusum & definitum cerneret.
units.tr: Ramus concludes that the subject of the art is general, concerning every being and non-being, as Aristotle expressly professes. It is not concerned with the question alone, since the power of the logical art appears in thinking out arguments, in propositions that are self-evident, and in method. Nor is it concerned only with doubtful propositions that are to be concluded by some syllogism. Hence it is shown that the sophistry of questions belongs in the doctrine of Logic no more than it belongs to Grammar to say what kinds of question there are, since each art is wholly common to all things, both doubtful and not doubtful. The grammarian speaks well about every thing; and so, much more, the dialectician or logician reasons well about every thing. But Ramus discusses at great length, in the second book of the Dialectical Scholae, the end and subject of the logical art. In that book it will be seen how he defined and bounded, first of all by a necessary definition, the whole logical field, which lay infinitely dispersed without terms or limits and scattered through so many volumes. He thus made it a most welcome and desired work for Aristotle. For in all those forty-four books, that clear definition is proposed nowhere, although by Aristotle's laws it ought to have been there, since it would be wholly necessary and true, homogeneous and proper, and in first place, because it is most general and by nature first. Therefore Aristotle would have rejoiced to see the logical field so enclosed and defined by the ditch and rampart of a legitimate definition.

units.la: Cap. II. De partibus Dialectica & inventionis.
units.tr: Chapter II. On the parts of Dialectic and of invention.

units.la: Dialecticæ partes duæ sunt: Inuētio & judicium.
units.tr: The parts of Dialectic are two: invention and judgement.

units.la: Invētio, pars Dialecticȩ de inveniendis argumentis. Argumētum, est quod ad aliquid arguēdum affectum est: quales sunt singulæ rationes solæ & per se consideratæ. Argumentum, est artificiale aut inartificiale. Artificiale, quod ex sese arguit. est autem primum vel á primo ortum. Primum, quod est suæ originis: estq; simplex aut comparatum. Simplex, quod simpliciter & absolutè consideratur. Simplex, est consentaneum aut dissentaneum. Cōsentaneum est, quod consentit cum re quam arguit: estq; cōsentaneū absolutè, aut modo quodā: Absolutè: ut caussa & effectum.
units.tr: Invention is the part of Dialectic concerned with finding arguments. An argument is that which is put forward to prove something, such as each single reason considered by itself. An argument is either artificial or inartificial. An artificial argument proves from itself; it is either primary or derived from the primary. The primary is that which is from its own origin, and it is either simple or compared. The simple is that which is considered simply and absolutely. The simple is either consonant or dissonant. The consonant is that which agrees with the thing it proves, and it is consonant either absolutely or in some mode. Absolutely, as cause and effect.

units.la: Magna P. Rami diligentia nobis apparuit in generali artis definitione confirmanda, contrarioq; specialium Logicarū sophismate refellendo: unde etiam confirmatio generalis partitionis, & refutatio cōtrarii sophismatis deducetur. Primùm igitur Dialecticæ artis partitio in Inuentionem & judicium, cum legibus Aristotelis congruit. Est enim κατὰ πάντος, καθ' αὑτὸ, καθόλης πρῶτον. congruit cum naturalis rationis usu: Argumenta enim quęrimus, deinde certa via & ratione disponimus ad judicandum: tertium munus rationis in differendo præterea nullum est. Itaq; concludere jam licet, duas hujus doctrinę partes esse, Inventionem & Iudicium: quod etiam dispositio dicitur: quia res certo genere difpositæ judicantur, ut fecundo libro patebit. Atque harum partium usus, licet in differendo conjunctus fit, præcepta tamen de inveniendo argumento, deq; disponendo & judicando, perenunciatum syllogismum & methodum feparan da sunt: ut in Grammatica arte, seorsum de vocabulis & eorum Syntaxi præcipitur: quamvis earum rerum usus in eadem oratione confusus ac permistus fit. hæc prima partitionis demonftratio, est é fundamentis illis Ariftoteleis de arte, deq; artis usu: altera demonstratio est é testimoniis Ariftotelis, Ciceronis, Quintiliani. Quicquid ab Ariftotele logicum præcipitur in toto Organo, precipitur de argumentis & argumentorum judicio. Sed hic agitur non de quacunq; comprehensione artis, sed de partitione corporis integri in sua prima membra: quæ ipsa duo, Inventio nempe & Iudiciŭ, tribus ab Ariftotele locis obscurius dividuntur: Primo in Prioribus Analyticis, totius hypothesis Logicę tres fiunt partes, inventio, compositio, resolutio: Deinde octavi Topici capite primo, locus est alter, sed obscurior, quod necesse fit primo locum invenire, fecudo interrogare & disponere, tum dicere ad alterum. At tertia pars redundat in utraque partitione: refo lutio enim illa, communis est & inventionis & iudicii meditatio: neq; novam artem continet. Et hæc ad alterum dictio, grammaticæ est, si pu ritas sermonis spectetur: vel rhetoricæ, si ornatus orationis. Tertius est Aristotelis locus primo cap.3. Rhetorici, ubi rhetoricæ quatuor siut partes, πίστις, τάξις, λέξις, ὑπόκρισις, probatio, dispositio, elocutio, actio. sed ibidem etiam veré dicitur, probationem & dispositionem, solas ad probandum & docendum necessarias esse: reliquas propter auditoris perversitatem invétas. hic Arist. locus etiam demõstrat in arte probandi & dicēdi, id est, in Dialeƈtica & Logica, duas illas inveniendi & disponendi partes solas esse necessarias & primarias. Ergo revera ac veritate Aristoteles, quávis in Organo distinƈté nó se quitur, attamen probat partitionem Dialeƈticæ in inventionem ac judicium. Ciceronis autē & Quintiliani sententia prefsior & accuratior hic est: Diligens disserēdi ratio, duas habet partes, unam inveniendi, alteram judicandi, ait initio Topicorum Tullius. Quintilianus item circa finem libri quinti, Dialeƈtici (ait) sibi & inveniendi & judicandi partes vendicant. Ergo testimonia hæc Aristotelis, Ciceronis, Quintiliani, partitionem Dialeƈticæ artis in inventionem & judicium confirmant. Sed tamen hi omnes rhetoricę arti has easdem partes inventionis & dispositionis etiam subjiciunt: in quo sunt ad λαβ̀ αὐτὸ revocandi: & logica illa justitiæ lege admonendi, præcepta artis unius propria, alterius artis aliena & impropria esse: doƈtrinam verò de ar-
units.tr: Ramus's great diligence became evident to us in confirming the general definition of the art and in refuting the contrary sophism of the special logicians, and from this the general confirmation of the partition, and the refutation of the contrary sophism, will also be drawn. First, then, the division of the art of Dialectic into invention and judgement agrees with the laws of Aristotle: it is said of all, per se, and first in universal [κατὰ παντὸς, καθ' αὑτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον]. It agrees with the practice of natural reason: we seek arguments, and then we arrange them by a certain method and reason for judging; there is no third task of reason in disputing beyond these. So we may now conclude that there are two parts of this doctrine, invention and judgement, which is also called disposition, because things arranged in a certain kind are judged, as will be clear in the second book. And although the use of these parts is joined together in disputing, the precepts on finding arguments, and on disposing and judging, must be separated from the discussion of the syllogism and of method, just as in the art of grammar precepts are given separately on words and their syntax, although the use of these things is mixed and confused in a single speech. This first demonstration of the partition rests on those Aristotelian foundations concerning the art and its use; the second demonstration rests on the testimonies of Aristotle, Cicero and Quintilian. Whatever logic Aristotle teaches in the whole Organon, he teaches about arguments and the judgement of arguments.
