But here we are concerned not with any comprehension of the art, but with the division of the whole body into its first members. These two, invention and judgement, are divided by Aristotle in three places, though less clearly. First, in the Prior Analytics, the whole hypothesis of logic becomes three parts: invention, composition, resolution. Then in the first chapter of the eighth book of the Topics there is another place, though more obscure: it is necessary first to find the place, second to question and arrange, and then to speak to the other. But the third part overflows into both divisions: that resolution is common to the meditation of both invention and judgement, and contains no new art. And that "speaking to the other" belongs to grammar, if the purity of speech is considered, or to rhetoric, if the ornament of the oration. The third place of Aristotle is in the first book of the Rhetoric, chapter 3, where the four parts of rhetoric are: proof [πίστις], arrangement [τάξις], diction [λέξις], delivery [ὑπόκρισις], that is, proof, disposition, elocution, action. But in the same place it is also rightly said that proof and disposition alone are necessary for proving and teaching, and the rest were devised because of the perversity of the hearer. This passage of Aristotle also shows that in the art of proving and speaking, that is in Dialectic and Logic, those two parts of finding and arranging alone are necessary and primary. Therefore, in truth and in fact, Aristotle, although in the Organon he does not follow the distinction clearly, nevertheless approves the partition of Dialectic into invention and judgement. The opinion of Cicero and Quintilian here is more exact and precise: "The careful method of reasoning has two parts, one of finding, the other of judging," says Tully at the beginning of the Topics. Quintilian likewise, near the end of the fifth book: "Dialecticians claim for themselves the parts both of finding and of judging." Therefore these testimonies of Aristotle, Cicero and Quintilian confirm the partition of the art of Dialectic into invention and judgement. But all of these also assign these same parts, of invention and disposition, to the art of rhetoric. In this they must be called back to the rule "take the thing itself" [λαβὲ αὐτό], and reminded by the law of justice that the precepts of one art are proper to it, and those of another art alien and improper.

units.la: gumentis & inveniendis & judicandis, logicæ artis esse propriam, omnes iidem authores confitentur: fateantur igitur, necesse est, in rhetoricis alienam & impropriam esse, planeq; sophisticam: & quidem tam alienam, tamq; sophisticam, quam de tropis & figuris elocutionis, deq; voce & gestu, actiōis doctrina sophistica & aliena esset in logicis. hanc P. Ramus ἀνόδειξιν ex Aristotelis lege sanciebat, afferebatq́ue præterea primos Aristotelis interpretes, partitionis hujus bipartitæ astipulatores & approbatores suisse: atq; in primis Adrastum illum, Simplicii testimonio Peripateticorum nobilissimum, qui ideo Categorias Topicis præpositas, τὰ πρὸ τοπικῶν nominabat: tum ad judicii partes, ἐρμηνείαν, ἀνάλυσιν utranq; cōponebat: elechos reservabat ad utriusq; partis vitia. his igitur & legū argumentis, & hominū testimoniis, P. Ramus partitione Dialecticæ in inventione & judicium approbat. Sed Alexander, & ab eo cæteri interpretes, Aristotelis logicam é scriptis potiùs quomodocunq; libris, quàm é principiis. Aristotelis & legib. interpretati, illā partitionem legitimā repudiarunt: & idem argumetum contra partitione generale, quod adversus definitione generale opposuerunt, quód differēdi ratio tripartita fit, apodictica, dialectica, sophistica. At enim (differebat hic P. Ramus, adversus eundem morbum idem remedium repetens) hæc tripartita distributio, est omnibus Aristoteleorum principiorū legibus cōtraria. Enimverò si puerū interrogē, Utrum Deus sanctas, sit oratio latina? iratus, opinor,respondebit, omnibus latinitatis legib. efse contrariā: quia ista duo nomina, neq; numero, neq; genere, neq; casu conveniat. At (inquá) partitio ista organica, consimilibus sophismatū sordibus sordidata est:Primo tripartita hæc distributio,nō est κατὰ ϖαντὸς: Nam falsum dicit affirmando totā Organi logici doctrinam in tribus illis differentiis & partib. contineri,cúm primi sex libri in Organo logico (κατηγορήματα Porphyrii, Aristotelis κατηγορίαι, tum libri duo de Interpretatione, deniq; duo de analysi priore, id est pars Dialecticæ prestatior & excellētior, de argumēto,enuntiato & syllogismo) in illa partitione nō cōtineātur: cúm etiā ἀπόδειξις illa, quæ tantopere jactatur,nulla ufquā fit,neq; per naturam esse posit. Itaq; qui primus partitus est logicā in tres illas partes, sophisticé & vitiosé est partitus, & in arte posuit, quod per legem κατὰ ϖαντὸς in arte esse non potuit:hoc primū sophisma partitionis hujus est contra primā legē. Secundó partitio hæc non est καθ' αὑτό in arte logica,quia sophistica vitiorum doctrina,nō est homogenea virtutum doctrinę: sed explicatis virtutibus,vitia inde contraria percipiuntur: imó (ait Aristoteles in Analyticis) vitiosa est definitio veri, nisi inde falsi cognitio fit manifesta. Quare cúm partitio hæc membrum corporis faciat,quod corporis nihil est,sophisma superiore gravius ostendit. Tertió,partitio hęc peccat contra legem καθόλου πρῶτον, quia generalia inveniēdi præcepta,per speciales quæstiones,apodictica, dialecticam,sophisticam,specialiter & sæpiús repetit. quæ tautalogia per legem illam valdé damnata est. Quare tertiu partitionis hujus sophisma gravissimum est omnium. Deniq; logici organi partitio prima, primo post definitione prima loco ex methodi lege cóstitui debuit. Atqui tripartita hęc partitio tádem in Analyticis proditur, ac ne proditur quidem: nec enim tota Logica usquam ab Aristotele nominatim ita divisa est, sed propositio dividitur in apodictica, dialecticam, sophisticam: & syllogismus é ratione propositionis, in apodicticum, dialecticum, sophisticum. Quare partitio logicæ trifariam facta in apodicticam, dialecticam, sophisticam, facta est contra omnes Aristoteleorum principiorum leges: nec oratio illa, Deus sanctas, magis est barbara, quàm hæc tripartita logicæ distributio sophistica. hæc igitur P. Ramus de partitione logicæ artis ita differebat, docebatq; usum artis partibus ita cófusæ ac perturbatę obscurissimum ac difficillimum esse factum. idque in primis ex altero illo usus fundamento, quod sibi propofuerat, animadvertendum & considerandū admonebat: quia ferè nulla logicæ artis utilitas in authoribus vel explicandis, vel imitandis per hác partitionem percipi posset. Disputatio superior de artis definitione, morsus doloris acres patronis erroris hujus attulit: hæc autem, mortis est instar, cùm Organi tanquam corporis membra, discerpi divellique partitione inventionis & judicii sentiant: Nam si (ut necesse est) inventionis judiciique partes singulæ, ac species separatim in suum quæque ordinem legibus Ariftotelis redigantur, falsa protinus & aliena, sed in primis iterata sæpiús apparebunt: & vix, ac ne vix quidem pro singulis libris singuli versus relinquentur. Itaque tanta rerum commutatio, tamque insolita μεταμόρφωσις, imperitis legum Aristotelearum & ignaris, acerba & gravis fuit: & inde judiciorû ac theatrorum turbę. Sed tamé nobilissimę artis & utilitas & dignitas tandem aliquando animos hominum capiet, amorefq; sui tá mirabiles excitabit, quám diras cótu melias adhuc perpessa est. Quapropter si Aristoteles logicum agrum tam tortuose antea & confragose pręruptum, nunc tandem viis tam planis & apertis distributum ex suis legibus & mâ datis aspiceret, magnam certè animo lætitiam caperet, tot postea seculis extitisse, á quo fieret, quod ipse tantopere factum desideravit. Sed de hac agricultura P. Rami, Dialecticę schole secûdo libro pleniús loquuntur.
units.tr: But that the doctrine of arguments, both of finding and of judging, is proper to the art of logic, all these same authors confess. Let them therefore admit, of necessity, that in rhetoric it is alien and improper, and plainly sophistical; and indeed as alien and as sophistical as the teaching on tropes and figures of speech, and on voice and gesture, that is delivery, would be sophistical and alien in logic. P. Ramus claimed this by a demonstration [ἀνόδειξιν] from the law of Aristotle, and he further asserted that the first interpreters of Aristotle were supporters and approvers of this twofold partition, and above all that famous Adrastus, most noble by the testimony of Simplicius among the Peripatetics, who for this reason called the Categories, placed before the Topics, the things before the Topics [τὰ πρὸ τοπικῶν]. Then he assigned to the two parts of judgement hermeneia and analysis [ἐρμηνεία, ἀνάλυσις], and reserved the elenchus [ἔλεγχος] for the faults of each part. Therefore, by these arguments from the laws and by these testimonies of men, P. Ramus approves the partition of Dialectic into invention and judgement. But Alexander, and after him the other interpreters, interpreted Aristotle's logic from the writings, however they came to hand, rather than from the principles of Aristotle and his laws; and so they rejected that legitimate partition, and raised against the general partition the same objection they had raised against the general definition, namely that the method of reasoning is threefold: apodeictic, dialectic, sophistic. But, Ramus argued, repeating the same remedy against the same disease, this threefold distribution is contrary to all the laws of the Aristotelian principles. Indeed, if I ask a boy whether "God holy" is a Latin sentence, he will, I think, angrily answer that it is contrary to all the laws of Latin, because those two words agree neither in number, nor in gender, nor in case. But, he went on, that organic partition is stained by similar sordid sophisms. First, this threefold distribution is not according to all [κατὰ παντὸς], for it falsely asserts that the whole doctrine of the logical Organon is contained in those three differences and parts, whereas the first six books of the logical Organon (Porphyry's predicables [κατηγορήματα] and Aristotle's Categories [κατηγορίαι], then the two books On Interpretation, and finally the two books of the Prior Analytics, that is, the more excellent and eminent part of Dialectic, concerning argument, the proposition and the syllogism) are not contained in that partition; and moreover that demonstration [ἀπόδειξις] which is so much boasted of nowhere exists, nor can it exist by nature. Therefore whoever first divided logic into those three parts did so sophistically and faultily, and placed in the art what by the law according to all [κατὰ παντὸς] could not be in the art: this is the first sophism of this partition, against the first law. Second, this partition is not per se [καθ' αὑτό] in the art of logic, because the doctrine of faults is not homogeneous with the doctrine of virtues; rather, once the virtues are explained, the contrary faults are perceived from them. Indeed (Aristotle says in the Analytics) a definition of truth is faulty unless the knowledge of falsehood becomes clear from it. Wherefore, since this partition makes a member of the body that is nothing of the body, it displays a sophism graver than the previous one. Third, this partition sins against the law first in universal [καθόλου πρῶτον], because it repeatedly restates the general precepts of finding by way of special questions, apodeictic, dialectic, sophistic. This tautology is strongly condemned by that law. Therefore the third sophism of this partition is the gravest of all. Finally, the first partition of the logical Organon should, by the law of method, have been set up in the first place, right after the first definition. Yet this threefold partition is at last set forth in the Analytics, or rather it is not set forth at all: nowhere does Aristotle name the whole of logic so divided. Rather, the proposition is divided into apodeictic, dialectic and sophistic, and the syllogism, according to the nature of the proposition, into apodeictic, dialectic and sophistic. Therefore the division of logic into apodeictic, dialectic and sophistic, made threefold, is contrary to all the laws of the Aristotelian principles; and that sentence, "God holy", is no more barbarous than this sophistical threefold distribution of logic. This, then, is what P. Ramus argued about the partition of the logical art, and he taught that the use of the art has become most obscure and difficult by such a confused and disordered division of its parts. He admonished that this should be noticed and considered especially from that other foundation of use which he had set for himself, because hardly any usefulness of the logical art, either in explaining or in imitating authors, could be perceived through this partition. The earlier discussion on the definition of the art brought sharp bites of pain to the defenders of this error; but this one is like death, since they feel the parts of the Organon being torn apart and pulled asunder, as if they were limbs of a body, by the partition into invention and judgement. For if (as must be) the individual parts and species of invention and judgement are separately brought into their own order by the laws of Aristotle, what is false and foreign, but above all what is repeated many times, will at once appear, and hardly, if at all, will a single verse remain for each single book. So such a change of things, and so unaccustomed a metamorphosis, was bitter and grievous to the unskilled and to those ignorant of the Aristotelian laws, and from it came disturbances of the courts and of the schools. But still the usefulness and dignity of this most noble art will at last capture men's minds and arouse in them a love of itself as wonderful as the dire opposition it has so far endured. Wherefore, if Aristotle were to look upon the logical field, so tortuously and roughly broken before, now at last laid out by clear and open paths according to his own laws and precepts, he would certainly feel great joy in his mind that, after so many centuries, someone had arisen by whom what he himself had so earnestly desired was done. But P. Ramus's cultivation of this field is discussed more fully in the second book of the Dialectic school.

units.la: Inventio] Adhuc duo prima artis lumina, definitio & partitio, defuerût Organo logico, sicuti sequentia quædá, quæ præcipuè adnotabimus. definitur autē à P. Ramo Inventio, é rebus quas interpretatur. Ei autem videbatur ἀνάλυσις vocabulum, ut alia deinceps pleraq; á Mathematicis ad logicam venisse, apud quos ἀνάλυσις proprie dicitur in numeris & magnitudinibus, ut datis duobus aut tribus numeris invenire tertiû vel quartû proportionalé : sic in lineis duabus vel tribus datis, sic invenire quadrati vel cubi latus. In logica aût non item est: é topicis enim nó potius invenís argumeta, quám ex etymologia vo-
units.tr: Inventio] Up to this point the two first lights of the art, definition and partition, were missing from the logical Organon, as were certain other things that we shall note especially. Ramus defines invention as the thing that its name interprets. He thought the word ἀνάλυσις [analysis] had come into logic from the mathematicians, among whom analysis is properly used of numbers and magnitudes, as when, given two or three numbers, one finds a third or fourth proportional, or, given two or three lines, one finds the side of a square or a cube. In logic, however, it is not like this. From the topics you do not so much find arguments, as from etymology you find words. Rather, you have the kinds of arguments set out, and with their help you may recognise examples in good authors, or draw them from your own store, as if from your pantry, things acquired by practice.

units.la: cum invenis voces, sed genera habes argumen torū descripta, quibus adjutus exēpla in bonis authoribus recognoscas, vel parta usu, tibi tanquam é tuo penu depromas. Argumentum] Definitur item argumentum, definitione generali, quod affectum fit ad aliquid arguendum, id est, explicandum. quomodo dicit poeta,
units.tr: cum invenis voces, sed genera habes argumentorum descripta, quibus adjutus exempla in bonis authoribus recognoscas, vel parta usu, tibi tanquam e tuo penu depromas. Argumentum] Argument is also defined by a general definition as that which is made to argue something, that is, to explain it, as the poet says: "Fear betrays degenerate spirits."

units.la: Degeneres animos timor arguit.—— id est ostédit, declarat. Argumentum autē id est in Logica, quod vocabulum in grammatica: sola videlicet ratio: nā vocabula, sunt symbola categorematū, ut Aristoteles cap. 1. lib. 1. de Interpretatione verisimé docet. utque é nominibus & verbis fit oratio, sic ex argumentis per nomina & verba significatis, efficitur enuntiatio. Argumentū igitur, sola est illa & separata ratio, sive per se sententia nullā cōstituit, sive constituit alī quā: Plerūq; enim argumentū uno verbo cōpre henditur, aliquando tota est enuntiatio, ut in cō paratis ἀναλυτικῶς tractatis videbimus. Neque veró argumetum tantummodo in syllogismo intelligendum, ut á Rhetoribus & Logicis vulgó intelligitur, cùm enunciatio dubia concluditur per aliquid tertium: sed omnis sententiæ partes argumēta sunt: ut cùm dico, Homo est animal. hîc duo argumēta sunt, species homo, & genus animal. Multis verò nominibus ab Aristotele res eadem nuncupatur, ac ne quis temerè erret, hæc auditori explicanda sunt. Grēcé igitur dicitur primò καλυπτόμενα, id est argumentum, quia κατηγορῶν, proprié est accusare, arguere: Dici autē potest latina saltem forma, catēgorema: unde κα- τηγογνωσία, doctrina categorematum apud Aristotelem. hoc autem verbum scholasticis quibusdam Logicis, uel potius ignaris usus logici, confusio nem attulit, cûm nihil arbitrarentur κατηγορεῖσθαι, nisi vocem simplicé de re aliqua affirmatá: cúm tamen, ut P.Ramus 3. Dialect. scholarũ docuit, Aristoteles id omne categorema faciat, quod aliquid arguit: sive una sit vox, sive multiplex, sive affirmata, sive negata. Argumēti præceptū di citur ab Aristotel. in Top.τόπος, id est locus, per metaphoram, quód certis præceptis, tanquā locis, commonstret unde argumēta petenda sint: quod Cicero & Quintilianus oftédunt. Cicero in Topicis: Inveniēdi veró arte, quę Topice dicitur, totā reliquerunt, & pars Dialecticæ de argu mentis τοπικὰ dicta, ut Quintilian. 14. cap.s. libri ait, de Dialecticis, qui sibi & inveniendi & judicandi vendicēt partes: quarum alteram τοπικῶν, alteram ἀρτυτικὸν vocát. Sed hac loci metaphora, artis cujusq; præcepta, loci posint appellari: & sic orat. 3. Tullius præcepta de ornatu, locos appellat, ideoque tropi nihil proprié significantis ambiguitatem P. Ramus evitavit. Secundó dicitur ἀρχὴ, principium, quod fit in Dialectica primum, unde postea enūtiationes existant. At hoc nimis commune P.Ramo visum est, & quamvis argumēta, principia sint in logicis, attamē quia verbum hoc erat magis usitatum in enuntiatis per se manifestis, ideo prætermisit. Tertió dicitur στοιχεῖον, id est elementum, quód sit simplicissimum & minimum: ut literæ, dicuntur elementa in Grammaticis: ignis, aer, aqua, terra, elementa in Physicis: ideoq; hoc verbũ ut in logicis iñ proprium,præteritum est. Quartó dicitur μέσον, id est medium, quód velut intermedium disponatur cum partibus questionis in syllogismo ad concludendũ quod volumus. quæ metaphora est à mathematicis,ut 2 ad 4,sic 4 ad 8:hic 4 est medium. sed metaphora hæc in enuntiato solo (ubi tamen est usus Dialecticî judicii primus) non convenit,quia duo tantùm sunt argumenta,neque ullum est medium. Itaque metaphora obscura hic est,& confusionem etiam Græcis interpretibus attulit, quæretibus in posteriore Analysi, quomodo definitio fit medium, quando sola cũ solo definito adhibetur. Tropi igitur improprii tanta obscuritas consultò fugienda fuit. Quintó dicitur ὅρος, terminus, quód propositione terminet: nam cũm dico, Homo est animal, homo & animal sunt termini enuntiationis, & argumenta duo species & genus: quomodo terminus dicitur á mathematicis,ut 1 & 2, sunt termini rationis duplę: quod in omni argumenti cõsideratione item verum est. Sed tamẽ mathematicum hoc verbũ minús in usu veré & politicæ logicæ tritum est,& ideo prætermissum. Sextó dicitur λόγος,id est ratio, quód fit cogitatio mentis. Sed hoc verbũ nimis generale videri possit, & totâ artem completi potius,quàm artis partem Septimó dicitur πίστις,id est probatio seu fides, quia facit ut rei credamus & assentiamur, quod in usu magis quàm superiora omnia versa tũ est,sed ad syllogismum feré respicit,& probationem enuntiationis dubiæ: Latiné argumentum tū proprie ab artis hujus doctoribus est appella tū, quia arguit: ideoq; ad docendum arte inventionis magis aptum P. Ramo & idoneum visum est. Est autem in omnibus argumentis mutua quedam duorum inter se affectio, ut caussarum cū effectis, subjectorū cum adjunctis, & in reliquis similiter, sicut é definitionibus singulorum percipietur: neq; unquam adhibetur argumentū ni si ad arguendū suum affectū: ut causse tantū arguūt effecta, & ab effectis solæ causse arguūtur, & sic in cęteris similiter.
units.tr: Degeneres animos timor arguit. That is, it shows and declares. In logic, however, argumentum means what the word means in grammar, namely only the reason; for words are the symbols of categorematic terms, as Aristotle very truly teaches in chapter 1 of book 1 of On Interpretation. And just as speech is made from nouns and verbs, so a statement is made from arguments signified through nouns and verbs. The argument, then, is that single and separate reason which, by itself, constitutes no sentence, or constitutes some sentence. For an argument is often comprehended in one word, and sometimes it is a whole statement, as we shall see in the treatises we are going to compare analytically. Nor is argumentum to be understood only in the syllogism, as it is commonly understood by rhetoricians and logicians, when a doubtful statement is concluded through some third thing. Rather, all the parts of a sentence are arguments. When I say, "Man is an animal," here there are two arguments: the species man and the genus animal. Aristotle gives this same thing many names, and so that no one may easily go wrong, these must be explained to the listener. In Greek it is first called κατηγορούμενα [kategoroumena], that is, argument, because κατηγορεῖν properly means to accuse, to argue. It can also be called, at least in Latin form, categorema, whence κατηγορηματικὴ θεωρία [kategorematike theoria], the doctrine of categorematic terms, in Aristotle. This word, however, has caused confusion among certain scholastic logicians, or rather among those ignorant of the use of logic, since they thought that nothing is κατηγορεῖσθαι [kategoreisthai] except a simple word affirmed of some thing. Yet, as Ramus taught in the third book of the Dialectic of the schools, Aristotle makes every categorema whatever that argues something, whether it be one word or many, affirmed or denied. The precept of the argument is called τόπος [topos] by Aristotle in the Topics, that is, place, by metaphor, because by fixed precepts, as by places, it shows whence arguments are to be drawn. Cicero and Quintilian point this out. Cicero, in the Topics: "They left the whole art of invention, which is called Topics, and the part of Dialectic concerning arguments called τοπικά [topika]," as Quintilian says in the fourteenth chapter of book 5, of the Dialecticians, who claim for themselves both the parts of invention and of judgment: one of which they call τοπικόν [topikon], the other ἀρτυτικόν [artytikon]. But by this metaphor of place, the precepts of any art may be called places, and so Tully in the third book of the Orator calls the precepts about ornament places. Therefore Ramus avoided the ambiguity of a trope that signifies nothing properly. Secondly, it is called ἀρχή [arche], principle, which is first in Dialectic, from which afterwards statements arise. But this seemed too common to Ramus, and although arguments are principles in the logical arts, he passed it over because this word was more usual for propositions that are evident in themselves. Thirdly, it is called στοιχεῖον [stoicheion], that is, element, because it is the simplest and smallest thing, as letters are called elements in grammar, and fire, air, water and earth are elements in physics. Therefore this word, as a proper term of logic, has been set aside. Fourthly, it is called μέσον [meson], that is, middle, because it is arranged as an intermediate with the parts of the question in the syllogism, to conclude what we want. This metaphor is from the mathematicians: as 2 is to 4, so 4 is to 8, and here 4 is the middle. But this metaphor does not fit a single statement (where, however, the first use of Dialectic judgment is found), because there are only two arguments, and there is no middle. And so this metaphor is obscure here, and it has also caused confusion for the Greek interpreters, who, when they asked in the Posterior Analytics how a definition becomes a middle when it is used only with the thing defined alone. Therefore such great obscurity of an improper trope was deliberately to be avoided. Fifthly, it is called ὅρος [horos], term, because it bounds a proposition. For when I say, "Man is an animal," man and animal are the terms of the statement, and the two arguments are species and genus. Thus term is used of mathematics, as 1 and 2 are the terms of a double ratio, and this is equally true in every consideration of an argument. But this mathematical word is less commonly used in the true and civil logic, and so it was passed over. Sixthly, it is called λόγος [logos], that is, reason, because it becomes a thought of the mind. But this word might seem too general, and would rather comprise the whole art than a part of it. Seventhly, it is called πίστις [pistis], that is, proof or belief, because it makes us believe a thing and assent to it. This is more usual in practice than all the preceding terms, but it refers mostly to the syllogism and to the proof of a doubtful statement. In Latin, the teachers of this art have properly called it argumentum, because it argues. Therefore this word seemed to Ramus more fitting and suitable for teaching the art of invention. In all arguments there is a certain mutual affection of two things with each other, as of causes with effects, of subjects with adjuncts, and similarly in the rest, as will be perceived from the definitions of the individual kinds. Nor is an argument ever employed except to argue its own affection: thus causes only argue effects, and effects only argue causes, and so similarly in the others.

units.la: Argumentū igitur] Sic igitur argumentū definitio est, deinceps dividitur dupliciter, ut sit artificiale vel inartificiale, q̄ partitione Aristoteles ostēdit ca. 2. primi Rhetoricorū, quæ falso quidē ad Theodecte, sed tū ad Theodecte inscribūtur: τ̄ ϸ ωίσιωμ, α̇ μὲν ἄτεχνοι ἀσίμ, α̇ ϸ ἔντεχνοι. ἔντεχνα ἁ ὅσα διὰ τῆ μεθόδε τὴ ἁ' ἡμῶν καλαισήμαδλύσαι Διωκτὸν. Probationes aliæ sunt inartificiales, aliæ artificiales: Artificiales, quæ per artem & nos ipsos comparari possunt. hic Aristoteles artificiale definit, quod per artem & per nos ipsos comparari potest: neq; tamen satis explicat Aristotelis definitionem veritatē illam artificialis argumēti, cūm artificiale argumentum possit etiam nobis afferri. quin ipsum inartificiale potest per arte & nos ipsos plerifq; in rebus coparari, ut postea é præcepto intelligetur. Sed é foresi Rhetorica id natum est, ubi orator sæpe accipit á litigatore inartificiales probationes. P. Ramus hic logicam legitimam & generale instituit: Itaq; non fori tantum, sed omnis & loci, & tēporis, & personæ, rei rationem habere debuit,& artificiale definire,quod per se argueret, & tanquâ plus artis ex sese haberet. Eadem partitio est etiam Arist. 8. cap.ad Alexandrum: ἀσι δὲ δύο τρόποι τῶν πίστεων, γὰρ γνουταί γὰρ ὰς μὲν αὐτῶν λόγων καὶ τῶν πραξέων καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὰς δ' ἀτεχνοι τοῖς λεγομένοις ἢ τοῖς πραττομένοις. Sunt autem duo modi probationum: sunt enim aliæ ex ipsis negotiis & actioibus & hominibus, aliæ autem adjunctæ sunt iis quę dicuntur & aguntur.hic verba sunt diversa,res eadé hanc Aristotelis partitioné Cicero & Quintilianus secuti sunt. Cicero in oratoriis dialogis, in partitionib.in topicis.Quintilianus lib. 5. cap. 1. hoc etiam addit:Ac prima quidé illa partitio ab Aristotele tradita, consensum feré omniú meruit, alias esse probationes, quas extra dicendi rationem acciperet orator,alias quas ex causa trahere ipse,& quodámodo gigneret: ideoq; illas ἀτέχνως,id est inartificiales,has ἔντεχνως,id est artificiales vocaverút. Hęc Quintil.ubi illud (feré) aliquid excipit:attamen nisi quód privatione facta est,partitio satis elegás & apta videatur:Sed tamen Aristoteles,& Aristotelé secuti,logicá in vétionis doctrinâ civilib. controversiis nó satis logicé subjecerút.Itaq; P.Ram.judicia illa summa Aristotelis,ut logica logicé proponeret, sequi debuit. Artificiale igitur definitur accuratiús,quod per se & sua natura fidé facit: ná cauf fis, factis , subjectis & reliquis artificialib. per se credimus:inartificialib. autè, id est testimoniis, nō credimus,nisi ratione causę,facti subjecti,& aliorū artificialiū. Artificiale]Deinceps neunitas
units.tr: Argumentum igitur] This, then, is the definition of argument. Next it is divided in two ways, into artificial and inartificial. Aristotle shows this partition in the second chapter of the first book of the Rhetoric, which is falsely, though not without reason, ascribed to Theodectes. Of proofs, some are inartificial, some artificial; artificial are those which can be prepared by method and by ourselves [ὅσα διὰ τῆς μεθόδου ἡμῖν κατασκευασθῆναι δυνατόν]. Here Aristotle defines the artificial as that which can be prepared by method and by ourselves. Yet he does not sufficiently explain the truth of that definition of an artificial argument, since an artificial argument can also be brought to us from elsewhere. Indeed, the inartificial itself can often be prepared by art and by ourselves in many matters, as will be understood later from the precept. But this partition arose from the forum of rhetoric, where the orator often receives inartificial proofs from the litigant. Ramus here establishes a general and legitimate logic, and therefore he had to take account not only of the forum but of every place, time and person, and to define the artificial as that which argues by itself and, as it were, has more art in itself. The same partition is also in Aristotle in the eighth chapter of the letter to Alexander: "There are two modes of proofs: for some arise from the things themselves and the actions and the men, others are attached to the things said and done" [ἔστι δὲ δύο τρόποι τῶν πίστεων, αἱ μὲν γὰρ ἐκ τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ τῶν πράξεων καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, αἱ δὲ ἄτεχνοι τοῖς λεγομένοις ἢ τοῖς πραττομένοις]. Here the words are different, but Cicero and Quintilian followed the same partition of Aristotle. Cicero in the Orator dialogues, in the Partitions, and in the Topics; Quintilian in book 5, chapter 1. He also adds this: "That first partition handed down by Aristotle has won almost universal agreement, that there are some proofs which the orator takes from outside the art of speaking, and others which he draws from the cause itself and, as it were, generates himself; therefore he called the former ἀτέχνως [atechnos], that is, inartificial, and the latter ἐντέχνως [entechnos], that is, artificial." So Quintilian; he excepts something with the word "almost", yet, except that it is made by privation, the partition seems fairly elegant and apt. But Aristotle, and those who followed Aristotle, did not sufficiently subject the doctrine of invention in civil disputes to logic. Therefore Ramus ought to follow those summary judgments of Aristotle, so that logic might set forth logically. The artificial, then, is defined more accurately as that which by itself and by its own nature makes belief. For we believe causes, deeds, subjects and the other artificial things by themselves; but we do not believe inartificial things, that is testimonies, except by reason of the cause, the deed, the subject and the other artificial things. Artificiale] Next, ...

units.la: Platonis in extremâ multitudinè, vel γενικώτατῶν Aristotelis, in ultima individua repeté præceps iret, partitiones à P. Ramo intermediæ factæ sunt, ut methodus gradatim & pedetentim descenderet: Igitur argumentum artificiale dividitur in primum & á primo ortu: quomodo Grámatici partiuntur vocabula in primitiva & derivativa. Est enim caussarum, effectorũ,subjectorum,adjunctorum,dissentaneorum, comparatorum Dialectica consideratio prima, tum ex his tanquam primis fontibus, nominis, divisionis, definitionis consideratio & doctrina derivatur, ut postea planiús intelligetur. Primum. ] Primũ est, quòd sit suæ originis, id est cujus consideratio prima est, nec ex sequentibus dependet: nã doctrina quidem caussarum (verbi gratia) potest intelligi sine doctrina definitionis: doctrina verò definitionis, dependet ex doctrina caussarum vel aliorum primorum argumentorum. Dividitur argumentum primum in simplex & cóparatum: Simplex verò, quod absolutæ conside rationis est, quòd neque par, neque impar, neq; simile, neque dissimile consideretur. Simplex deinde dividitur in consentaneum & dissentaneum: Dissentaneum autem in oppositis jam erat ab Aristotele significatum: consentaneum é regione facile fuit admimadvertere, quod cũ re conveniret: ut ex affirmato consentaneo, consentaneũ affirmaretur,é negato negaretur. Primi consentanei differentię sunt é 7.cap.1.Posteriorum: ubi Aristoteles facit homogenea ἁπλῶς ἢ πῶς absolutè aut quodammodo.
units.tr: Because Plato's extreme multiplicity, or Aristotle's most general kinds [γενικωτάτων], would otherwise rush headlong down to the ultimate individuals, Ramus introduced intermediate divisions, so that the method might descend gradually and step by step. Therefore the artificial argument is divided into the primary and that which arises from the primary, just as grammarians divide words into primitive and derivative. For the dialectical consideration of causes, effects, subjects, adjuncts, contraries and comparatives comes first, and from these as first sources the consideration and doctrine of name, division and definition is derived, as will be understood more clearly later. (First.) The first point is that it belongs to its own origin, that is, its consideration comes first and does not depend on what follows. For the doctrine of causes, for example, can be understood without the doctrine of definition, but the doctrine of definition depends on the doctrine of causes or the other first arguments. The primary argument is divided into simple and compared. The simple is that which is considered absolutely, that is, without regard to whether it is equal or unequal, like or unlike. The simple is then divided into consentaneous and dissentaneous. Aristotle had already indicated the dissentaneous in the case of opposites; the consentaneous, which agrees with the thing, was easy to notice by the converse: so that from an affirmed consentaneous the consentaneous is affirmed, and from a denied one it is denied. The differences of the primary consentaneous are found in Posterior Analytics 7, chapter 1, where Aristotle distinguishes the homogeneous as absolutely or in some way [ἁπλῶς ἢ πῶς].

units.la: Cap. III. De efficiente procreante & conservante.
units.tr: Chapter III. On the efficient cause, which produces and preserves.

units.la: CAussa, est cujus vi res est. Itaq; primus hic locus invētionis, fons est omnis scientię, sciriq; demū credit, cujus caussa teneat, ut merito dicat á Poeta, Felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas.
units.tr: A cause is that by whose power a thing is. Therefore this first place of invention is the source of all knowledge, and a person believes he truly knows only when he grasps the cause, so that the Poet rightly says: Happy is he who has been able to know the causes of things.

units.la: Caussa est efficiēs & materia, aut forma & finis. Efficiens, est caussa á qua res est: cujus etsi vera genera nulla sint, ubertas tamen permagna modis quibusdam distinguitur. primó quód procreet aut tueatur. Ovid 1. de Remed.
units.tr: The cause is efficient and material, or formal and final. The efficient cause is that from which a thing is. Although there are no true genera of it, its abundance is nonetheless very great and is distinguished in certain modes, first, because it produces or protects. Ovid, Remedia Amoris, book 1.

units.la: Ergo ubi visus eris nostra medicabilis arte, Fac monitis fugias otia prima meis. Hac ut ames: faciūt, hac quae fecere, tuentur Haec sunt jucundi caussa cibusq; mali.
units.tr: Therefore, when you have been made well by my medicinal art, take care to avoid idleness at the outset by following my advice. Those who make love, and those who have made it, keep it going; these are the cause of pleasant and of bad love.

units.la: Sic pater & mater procreant, nutrix tuetur. 4. Aeneid. (author,
units.tr: So the father and mother beget, and the nurse nourishes. Aeneid 4. (author,

units.la: Nō tibi diva parens generis, nec Dardanus Perfide, sed duris genuit te cautibus horrens Caucasus, Hyrcanaq; admorunt ubera tigres.
units.tr: No goddess was your parent, nor Dardanus, perfidious one, but the bristling Caucasus with its hard crags begot you, and Hyrcanian tigers gave you their teats.

units.la: Sic Romulus conditor Romanæ urbis, reges deinde reliqui, Cōsules, Imperatores, tutores, conservatores fuere.
units.tr: So Romulus was the founder of the city of Rome, and the later kings, consuls, commanders, guardians and preservers came after him.

units.la: Caussa est] Caussa definitur generaliter, cujus vi res est: αἰτία ἡγοῦ αἴτιον Graecè dicitur: & aliquādo generaliter quodvis argumentū, caussæ nomine significatur, proprie vero & specialiter hæc probatio. Significatur autem causa frequenter nominibus ἀρχὴς, στοιχεῖα, φύσεως, ἰδέας: principii, elementi, naturæ, essentiæ: sed duobus postremis etiam res tota suis causis constituta significatur, ut docetur quinto Philosophiæ: sed ἀρχῆς ἡ αἰτία eadem & una significatio est, quia se invicem consequuntur, ut est 2. cap. 4. Philosophiæ: Causa vero, primus Dialecticæ inventionis locus est, unde omnis scientiæ humanæ solida constansque cognitio demonstratioque deprompitur: tum enim vere proprieque scire judicatur, cum rei causam, propter quam res est, propria scimus: Sic Aristoteles τὸ ἐπίστασθαι καὶ ἡ ἐπιστήμη nomen definit in Posterioribus 2. cap. lib. 1. & infinite caeteris deinde libris repetivit: tametsi scientia cujuscunque rei sit, æternæ an caducæ, nihil ad logicam causarum topicam communem rerum omnium & generalem interest: tum enim vera scientia tenetur, cum ejus causæ tenetur: ideoque quacunque in arte vel genere verseris, præcipuum inventionis finem adeptus sis, cum causas perveideris: tamen quia præstantior æternarum rerum scientia sit, quam caducarum, scientiæ quoque nomen illic habetur præcipuum. Ergo meminerisab Aristotele scientiam definiri ex causis æternis ac propriis, propter quas res sit: eamque sententia dici ab eo ἀπόδειξις, quamobrem & propter quid: secus ê caeteris causis, vel quibusvis aliis argumentis, scientiam quandam secundariam gigni, eamque dici ὅτι, quia. Una vero causarum categoria, ut princeps est in argumentis, sic per universam Ariftotelis bibliotheca tautologias profufisimas habuit: ut hic Ariftoteleæ agriculturæ studio singulari sit opus: est enim caussarum velut oceanus in omnes partes effusus,in analytica,topica, physica, philosophica, nec ulla omnino in parte Logicæ graviùs in legem καθόλε πρῶτον pecca-tum est: Doctrina generalis tractatur totis fere Posterioribus Analyticis, sed præcipuè 11.12. 13.17. capitibus: eadem tractatur in totis Topicis, eademq; totis duobus primis libris Physicæ, eadem primis primorum de animaliũ ortu & partibus librorum capitibus, eadem totis duobus primæ Philosophiæ libris,ut fermé sex libri in unius caussæ argumento toties iterato sint cosumpti. Tot librorum materies P. Ramo in hoc caussarum capite redigeda,& ad leges Aristotelis dirigenda & conformáda proponitur: itaq; deinceps apparebit,quomodo falce & securi,cęterisque georgicis illis Aristotelis organis usussit. Felix]Locus est 2. Geergicũ, de causis physicis: hic autem ad Logicam laudem caussarum generaliter intelligitur.quale est illud Persii,
units.tr: A cause is: a cause is defined generally as that by whose power a thing is. In Greek it is called aitia, and sometimes any argument at all is named a cause generally, but properly and specifically this proof. The cause is frequently signified by the words principle [ἀρχή], element [στοιχεῖα], nature [φύσεως] and form [ἰδέα]: principle, element, nature and essence. But with the last two the whole thing constituted by its causes is also signified, as is taught in the fifth book of the Philosophy. But the cause and the principle [ἀρχῆς ἡ αἰτία] are the same and one meaning, because they follow one another, as in Philosophy 2, chapter 4. The cause, however, is the first place of dialectical invention, from which the solid and constant knowledge and demonstration of all human science is drawn; for then one is judged to know truly and properly when we know the cause of the thing, on account of which the thing is. Thus Aristotle defines the term to know and knowledge [τὸ ἐπίστασθαι καὶ ἡ ἐπιστήμη] in Posterior Analytics 2, chapter 1, book 1, and afterwards repeated it endlessly in the other books. Yet whatever the science of any thing is, whether of eternal or perishable things, it makes no difference to the general and common topic of causes of all things in logic: for true science is held when its causes are held, and therefore in whatever art or genus you labour, you have attained the chief end of invention once you have perceived the causes. Nevertheless, because the science of eternal things is more excellent than that of perishable things, the name of science is held there in its chief sense. Therefore remember that Aristotle defines science from eternal and proper causes, on account of which a thing is, and in his opinion this is called demonstration [ἀπόδειξις], by which and on account of which; but from other causes, or from any other arguments, a secondary sort of knowledge arises, and this is called that [ὅτι], because. The category of causes, being the chief of arguments, has produced such very great tautologies throughout the whole library of Aristotle that here is needed a singular diligence in Aristotle's agriculture: for the sea of causes is poured out in all directions, in the Analytics, the Topics, the Physics, the Philosophy, and nowhere in any part of logic has a more serious offence been committed against the law of the universal and first [καθόλου πρῶτον]. The general doctrine is treated almost throughout the whole of the Posterior Analytics, especially in chapters 11, 12, 13 and 17; the same is treated throughout the Topics, the same in the first two books of the Physics, the same in the first chapters of the books on the generation and parts of animals, and the same in the two books of First Philosophy, so that nearly six books have been consumed in the argument about one cause, repeated so often. The matter of so many books is proposed to be reduced by P. Ramus in this chapter on causes, and directed and conformed to the laws of Aristotle; so hereafter it will appear how he used the sickle and axe and those other agricultural instruments of Aristotle. Happy: this is a place in Virgil's Georgics 2 concerning physical causes, but here it is understood generally for the praise of causes in logic, like that line of Persius:

units.la: Discite nunc miseri, & caussas cognoscite rerum.
units.tr: Learn now, you wretches, and know the causes of things.

units.la: Caussa est efficies]Partitio caussarum in Aristotelis philosophia varia est, nunc in genera quatuor,efficiētem,materiam,formam,finem:nunc in modos varios, singularem,universalem,simplicem,compositam,actu,potētia, priorem, posteriorem,propinquiorem,remotiorem, per se, per accidés, ut videbis 2. Physico & in Philosophia 2.cap.5.lib. Sed harum minutiorum partitionũ nulla valde Aristoteli placuit:quatuor genera, efficientem, materiam, formam, finem præcipué probavit, & eadem P. Ramus est amplexa tus, naturaq; priora prępofuit, postposuit posteriora. Nam fi efficiens fit, & materia, non protinus erit forma & finis: sed cōtrá, fi forma fit & fi 5 nis, cęteras caussas necesse est antecessisse: ac cū dicitur primó cogitari fině, sané dicitur primó rem cogitari, fine quippe definitam : neq; argumentum, id est finem esse natura priorem cæteris caussis. Definitio Aristorelis de naturá prio- 10 re, alia in Categoriis. Aristoteles in Phil. 3. cap. 1. & 2. cap. 3. l. recte ait de causis, efficienté fini oppositam esse, quia effieiés fit prima, finis ultima. Ergo hæc de ordine caussarum, quas P. Ramus bifariam nominibus quatuor in genera duo par 15 titur: quomodo Aristoteles interdū genus unū exprimit p species duas, ut in Categoriis ἕξις καὶ διάθεσις, δύναμις καὶ ἀδυναμία: habitus & dispositio, potentia & impotentia: Hoc autem commune feré est efficienti & materiæ, quód tempore an- 20 tecedant effectum:neq; tamē id est perpetuum: ignis enim semper urit, neq; ideo hic efficiēs antecedit effectum. Quicquid fit, hę duæ caussę omnino commune nescio quid habet. Cicero in Topicis, caussarum genera duo facit, unū quod 25 vi sua efficit, ut ignis accendit: alterum sine quo effici non potest, ut locus, tempus, materia, ferramenta. Eandem partitionem sequitur in Partitionibus: & conficientes alias fecit absolutas, alias adjuvantes: addit etiam conficientes, quæ 30 propter principium aut propter exitum agant: in quibus finem complectitur. Ita uno efficientis nomine caussas omnes coplectitur, sicut uno effecti nomine, quicqd é caussis existit. Sed genera melius distinguentur in efficiente, materia, forma, fine. Primo quód] De hac caussa, Platonis locus in Philebo his verbis est: Soc. Sed vide, an tibi necessarium esse videatur, omnia quę fiunt per aliquá causam fieri. Pro. Mihi quidem, quomodo n. absq; ea fieret? Sic in Hippia majore: So. Atqui (ait) caussa ô Hippia, & id cujus caussa, ipsa caussa est, nonne aliud est? nec utiq; caussæ caussa fuerit: Sic vero considera, nonne caussam, id quod aliquid efficeret, esse cœstitit? Hippi. Constitit. So. Ab efficiente vero nō aliud fit, quám quod efficitur, non autę efficiens. hæc ille. Caussa efficiens ab Aristotele definitur tertio capite primi Philosophiæ, ἀρχὴ κινήσεως, principium motus: & 3. cap. secundi Physici, ἀρχὴ κινήσεως καὶ στάσεως ἢ ἡρεμίσεως, principium motus & status seu quietis: appellaturq; αἴτιον, τὸ ποιοῦν τι ποιόν καὶ γινωτικόν. Atque hujus caussæ topicum Aristoteles in primis sibi cótra veteres assumpsit, á quibus impoliti͏ùs & horridiùs expositum, & quidem magis à veritate ipsa coactis, quám ductis ulla arte: Itaq; ait in Philosophia 4. ca. primi libri: Obscurę tamē, nec quicquá aperté: sed ut in pugnis inexercitati pugiles faciùt: Etenim illi huc & illuc impulsi, egregias plagas frequeter imponùt, sed neq; hi arte, neq; illi omnino videtur sentire, quę dicát. Sic igitur Aristoteles de eficiéte, veterů philosophorum in logicis inscientiá coarguit, laudemq; doctrinæ hujus sibi attribuit, ut intelligamus ex isto laudis amore, quáti
units.tr: The cause is efficient: the division of causes in Aristotle's philosophy is various, now into four genera, efficient, material, formal and final; now into various modes, particular and universal, simple and compound, actual and potential, prior and posterior, nearer and more remote, per se and per accidens, as you will see in Physics 2 and in Philosophy 2, chapter 5. But none of these minor divisions pleased Aristotle greatly: he especially approved the four genera, efficient, material, formal and final, and P. Ramus has embraced the same, placing the prior by nature before and the posterior after. For if there is an efficient and a material cause, it does not at once follow that there is a formal and a final cause; but conversely, if there is a formal and a final cause, the others must necessarily have preceded: and when it is said that the end is thought of first, it is certainly said that the thing is first thought of, since it is defined by its end; nor is the argument, that is the end, prior in nature to the other causes. Aristotle's definition of what is prior by nature is given elsewhere, in the Categories. Aristotle in Physics 3, chapter 1, and Physics 2, chapter 3, rightly says that the efficient is opposed to the final among causes, because the efficient is first and the final last. Therefore these things are about the order of causes, which P. Ramus divides in two into four genera by names, as Aristotle sometimes expresses one genus by two species, as in the Categories: having and disposition, potency and impotency [ἕξις καὶ διάθεσις, δύναμις καὶ ἀδυναμία]: habit and disposition, potency and impotency. This, however, is nearly common to the efficient and the material cause, that they precede the effect in time; yet this is not perpetual, for fire always burns, and yet the efficient does not for that reason precede the effect. Whatever it is, these two causes have something entirely in common. Cicero in the Topics makes two genera of causes: one which produces by its own power, as fire kindles; the other without which it cannot be produced, as place, time, matter and tools. He follows the same division in the Partitions, and he made some causes absolute and others assisting; he also adds causes which act on account of the beginning or on account of the end, in which he includes the final cause. So by the one name of efficient he embraces all causes, just as by the one name of effect he embraces whatever arises from causes. But the genera are better distinguished as efficient, material, formal and final. Firstly, because: Plato's passage about this cause in the Philebus is in these words: Socrates: But see whether it seems necessary to you that everything which comes into being comes into being through some cause. Protarchus: To me indeed, for how could it come into being without one? So also in the greater Hippias: Socrates: But surely, Hippias, is the cause, and that of which it is the cause, itself a cause—is it not something else? Nor in any case would there be a cause of a cause. But consider it thus: did we not say that the cause is that which brings something about? Hippias: We did. Socrates: And from the efficient cause nothing comes but that which is effected, and not the efficient itself. So far Plato. Aristotle defines the efficient cause in the third chapter of the first book of the Philosophy as the principle of motion [ἀρχὴ κινήσεως], and in the third chapter of the second book of the Physics as the principle of motion and of rest or quiet [ἀρχὴ κινήσεως καὶ στάσεως ἢ ἡρεμίσεως]; and it is called cause [αἴτιον], that which makes something to be of a certain quality and which generates. And Aristotle especially took up for himself the topic of this cause, against the ancients, by whom it had been expounded more crudely and roughly, and indeed more by force of the truth itself than by any art in drawing it out. So he says in the fourth chapter of the first book of the Philosophy: obscurely, nor anything clearly, but as untrained boxers do in their fights: for they, struck this way and that, commonly land fine blows, but neither these nor those seem to know by art what they are saying. Thus Aristotle, concerning the efficient cause, convicts the ancient philosophers of ignorance in logic, and claims for himself the praise of this doctrine, so that from this love of praise we may understand how far Aristotle has made the topic of this kind.

units.la: Aristoteles Topicū generis hujus fecerit. Et certé efficiētis ubertatem variis nominibus in Philosophia proposuit, quæ P. Ramus nō ideo sub duxit, quod hic ulla vera genera efficiedi statueret, sed quód usum doctrinæ speraret hinc illuftriorem futurū. Efficienté vero, fi tépore præcedat, censet Ariftoteles ἀσυλλόγιστον vt est 12. cap 2. Post. Potest tamē aliquo syllogismi genere non tantū ex efficiēte, sed ex argumēto quolibet cōcludi. Efficientis aut partitio est prima illa quædā, quód efficiēs alia procreet, alia tueatur & cō servet: ⁊ Ariftoteles obscuriūs attigit in Philosophia I. cap. 5. libri. Principiū aliud quidē unde fit primū, cūm tñ non infit, & inde primūm motus solet inchoari, aut mutatio: ut liberi á patre & matre, & pugna á convitio: Aliud verò, cujus cōsilio movētur ea quæ movētur, & mutātur eā quę mutātur, ut sunt civitatū magistratus & po tētię & regna & tyrānides. Hic Aristoteles no tat caussas primó ꝓcreátes, ut patres sunt & matres: deinde cōservātes, ut magistratus & principes. sunt cōservatores imperiorū, regnorū, civi tatū: sed addit illas caussas exteriores, & has cōsilio agere: quę duę efficiēdi differentię diversæ sunt & dissimilis generis, nec bene oppositę: exteriores aūt caussę, sunt efficiēs & finis: interiores aūt & constituentes rem, materia & forma: Item aliæ agunt consilio & deliberatione, aliæ minimē. Sed hæc utraq; partitio non valde Logica est, neq; enim entis & non entis, ut omnia Logica esse debent, ideoq; de loco Aristotelis illo, quod erat communius, λογικώτερον, P. Ramus c
units.tr: Aristotle has made a topic of this kind. He certainly set out the richness of the efficient cause under various names in philosophy, and P. Ramus did not place these under a single heading because he thought there were any true kinds of efficient cause. He hoped rather that the use of the teaching would be clearer from this. Aristotle thinks that the efficient cause, if it precedes in time, is [ἀσυλλόγιστον], as in Posterior Analytics 2.12. Yet something can be concluded by some kind of syllogism not only from the efficient cause but from any middle term. The division of the efficient cause is the first one: that one efficient cause produces, while another preserves and maintains what has been produced. Aristotle touched on this rather obscurely in Physics 1.5. One principle is that from which a thing first comes, though it does not remain in it, and from which the first motion or change usually begins: as children come from father and mother, and a fight from an insult. The other is that by whose counsel the things that are moved are moved, and the things that are changed are changed: such as the magistrates, powers, kingdoms and tyrannies of states. Here Aristotle marks the causes that first produce, as fathers and mothers are, and then those that preserve, as magistrates and rulers are, who preserve empires, kingdoms and states. But he adds that these are external causes and that these act by counsel. These two differences of efficient cause are different and of unlike kind, and they are not well opposed. The external causes are the efficient and the final; the internal, which constitute the thing, are matter and form. Again, some act by counsel and deliberation, others not at all. But neither of these divisions is very logical, for they do not concern being and non-being, as all logical divisions ought to. Therefore, instead of that passage of Aristotle which was more common, [λογικώτερον], P. Ramus took

units.la: affumpfit. Cófervare veró,est efficere,sed adjuvando addendoq; toti particulam aliquam, ut in Officiis Cicero docet,gloriam in Repub,cóparari amore,gratia,fauore civium & opinione virtutis,eandemq; rebus iisdem conservari: ut hinc appareat, procreare & coferuare, non esse vera genera efficiendi:sed hoc ipsum,confervare,esse quoq; quoddam procreare:sed in aliqua totius particula. Tribus exéplis declaratur prima differétia efficientis : Primum est Ovidii de Remedio amoris,quod primum est,preoccupa re,ne amor adveniat:Secundũ est,admissi amoris caussas efficiétes expellere,quæ in otio præcipué sunt & procreantes & confervantes:Itaq; poeta demonstrationem problematis táquam geometricam hic adhibet: Tolle caussas (ait) su ituleris effectum.itaq; etiam mox subdit,
units.tr: up another. To preserve, however, is to produce, but by helping and adding some particle to the whole thing, as Cicero teaches in the De Officiis: glory in the commonwealth is acquired by the love, favour and goodwill of citizens and by the opinion of virtue, and it is preserved by the same things. From this it appears that to produce and to preserve are not true kinds of efficient cause; rather, this very thing, to preserve, is also a kind of producing, but of a part of the whole. The first difference of the efficient cause is illustrated by three examples. The first is from Ovid's Remedy of Love: that one must forestall love so that it does not arrive. The second is that one must expel the efficient causes of a love already admitted, which above all in idleness both produce and preserve it. So the poet applies here a demonstration of the problem as if it were geometrical. "Take away the causes," he says, "and you will have removed the effect." And so he soon adds:

units.la: Otia fi tollas,periére Cupidinis arcus,
units.tr: "If you take away idleness, Cupid's bows perish,"

units.la: Contemptæq; jacent & fine luce faces.
units.tr: "and his torches lie despised and without light."

units.la: Non tibi] Cúm Dido Aeneam neq; religione conjugalis fidei, neq; precibus ullis movere ac retinere posset, iis probris eum insectatur : primum removendo caussas procreates, tanquam falsas, quód neq; Venus fit ejus mater,neq; Anchifes pater: deinde tanquam veras fubjiciédo, quód Caucafus fit ei pater, durae cautes pro matre,nutrix tigris hyrcana. Romulus] Romulus primus Romam cödidit, deinde sex reges, tum varii Consules auxere, denique Im- peratores aliquot fæcula retinuere.
units.tr: "Not to you": when Dido could move and hold back Aeneas neither by the duty of marriage faith nor by any prayers, she assails him with these reproaches. First she removes the producing causes as false: that Venus is not his mother, nor Anchises his father. Then she sets down the true ones: that Caucasus is his father, hard crags his mother, and a Hyrcanian tigress his nurse. "Romulus": Romulus first founded Rome; then six kings increased it, then various consuls, and at last some generals kept it for several centuries.

units.la: Cap. IIII. De efficiente sola & cum aliis.
units.tr: Chapter 4. On the efficient cause alone and with others.

units.la: SEcundò, caussa efficiês sola efficit, aut cum aliis: earumq; omnium sæpé alia principalis, alia adjuvans & minií stra. 9. Aeneid. Nisus avocat ab Euryalo in se factæ cædis & culpam & pœnam, quia solus author fuerit.
units.tr: Second, the efficient cause either produces alone or together with others; and of all these, one is often principal and the others helpers and servants. Aeneid 9. Nisus takes upon himself, away from Euryalus, both the guilt and the punishment of the slaughter that was done, because he alone was its author.

units.la: Me me adsum, qui feci: in me convertice ferrū, O Rutili: mea fraus omnis, nihil iste nec aus, Nec potuit.
units.tr: "Me, me, here I am, the one who did it! Turn the steel against me, O Rutulians! All the fault is mine; he neither dared nor could do anything."

units.la: Solitaria caussa cum plerisq; & principalibus, & sociis, pro Marcello varié adhibetur: Nam bellicas (ait orator) laudes solēt quidam extenuare verbis, easq; detrahere ducibus, communicare cū multis, ne propriæ sint imperatorū. Et certé in armis, militū virtus, locorū opportunitas, sociorum auxilia, classes, commeatus multum juvant: maximam veró partem, quasi suo jure, fortuna sibi vendicat, & quicquid est prosperé gestum, id pené omne ducit suū. At veró hujus gloriæ, Cæsar, quam es paulò antē adeptus, socium habes neminem, totum hoc quantumcunq; est (quod certè maximum est) totum, inquam, est tum: um: nihil tibi ex ista laude centurio, nihil praefectus, nihil cohors, nihil turma decerpit: quinetiam illa ipsa rerum humanarum domina fortuna, in istius se focietatem glorię non offert: tibi cedit, tuam esse totam ac propriā fatetur. Instrumenta etiā in caussis adjuvantibus connumeratur. quo argumento impius Epicureus disputat mundum nunquam effe factum, 1. de Nat. Quibus enim (ait) oculis animi intueri potuit vester Plato fabricam illam tanti operis, qua cōstrui á Deo atque ædificari mundum facit? quæ molitio? quæ ferramenta? qui vectes? quæ machinæ? qui ministri tanti operis fuerunt?
units.tr: The solitary cause, with its principal and associated causes, is used in various ways in the case for Marcellus. For some people, as the orator says, are accustomed to belittle military praise, to take it away from the commanders, and to share it among many, so that it does not belong to the generals themselves. And indeed in war the courage of the soldiers, the advantage of the ground, the help of allies, fleets and supplies contribute greatly, and for the most part fortune, as if by right, claims the credit for herself, and she counts almost everything that has been successfully done as her own. But, Caesar, of this glory which you have lately won, you have no partner. All of it, however great it is (and it is certainly very great), is wholly yours. No centurion, no prefect, no cohort, no troop takes any part of this praise from you. Indeed fortune herself, the mistress of human affairs, does not offer to share in the glory of that man; she yields to you and admits that it is wholly your own. Instruments are also counted among the auxiliary causes. The impious Epicurean uses this argument to argue that the world was never made (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, book 1). For with what eyes of the mind (he says) could your Plato have seen that fabric of so great a work, by which he makes the world built and constructed by God? What machinery? What tools? What levers? What engines? What ministers were there for so great a work?

units.la: Secundo caussa] Partitio altera efficiētis, in sola & coficiente: quarū una plerūq; fit principalis, reliquæ sint adjuvantes, ut est in Platone & Aristotele. In primis (ait hospes in Politico) duas artes in omnibus quę fiunt, consideremus. Soc.
units.tr: Second cause: the other division of the efficient cause, into the sole and the concurrent cause. Of these, one is usually made principal and the rest are auxiliary, as is found in Plato and Aristotle. First (says the Stranger in the Statesman), let us consider the two arts which are present in all things that come into being. Socrates:

units.la: Quas? Hos. τλω ἡ γινόμως συναιτιον, τλω δ' αυτω αιτιαν: unam quidem generationis cōcaussam, alteram vero caussam. Soc. Quomodo? Hosp. Quęcunq; rem ipsam non efficiunt, sed efficientibus adjumenta suppeditāt: quibusq; absentibus nunquā earum unica opus institutum perficeretur, has suvaitiv, id est adjuvantes: opus autem ipsum perficientes, αιτίας, caussas appellamus. Soc. Consentaneum id quidem.hęc Plato. Caussa igitur hujusmodi, Gręcis est οωάντιον. quo verbo, quinto capite quinti Philosophię Aristoteles etiam utitur. Et capite secundo libri secundi Physicorum, facit artium alias ἀρχιτεκτονικὰς, id est principes & imperantes, alias ᾳοιητικὰς, id est effectrices & ministras: ut gubernator, princeps est causa navigationis: nautæ & remiges, ministri. Sic in Fato Tullius appellat causas principales & adjuvantes. Illa autem causa principalis, plerumq; pro absoluta usurpatur: ut cùm dicimus ab Alexandro Magno victos esse Persas, à Scipione Carthaginienses, à Cæsare Gallos: Hæc autem partitio secunda, tribus exemplis illustratur.
units.tr: Which? Stranger: one is the co-cause of generation [τὴν μὲν γενέσεως συναίτιον], the other the cause itself [τὴν δ' αὐτῷ αἰτίαν]. Socrates: How so? Stranger: Those things which do not themselves produce the thing, but supply help to the producers, and without which the work would never be completed by the one alone, these we call auxiliary [συναίτια], that is, contributing causes; but those which bring the work itself to completion we call causes [αἰτίας]. Socrates: That is certainly fitting. So Plato. Therefore a cause of this kind is called by the Greeks [συναίτιον], a word which Aristotle also uses in the fifth chapter of the fifth book of his Metaphysics. And in the second chapter of the second book of the Physics he makes some arts architectonic [ἀρχιτεκτονικάς], that is, principal and commanding, and others productive [ποιητικάς], that is, effective and serving: as the steersman is the principal cause of navigation, while the sailors and rowers are its ministers. Thus in the Fate, Tully calls causes principal and auxiliary. But the principal cause is usually taken for the complete cause, as when we say that the Persians were conquered by Alexander the Great, the Carthaginians by Scipio, the Gauls by Caesar. This second division is illustrated by three examples.

units.la: Meme] Primum exemplum est causæ solius efficientis. Me me, interficite, intelligitur: ut fit vox incredibili dolore propter amicum affecti: Cùm autem Nisus & Euryalus multis Rutulis cæsis & spoliatis, à Volscente hoste in sylva peremetur, Nisus elapsus, ut Euryalum captum & deprehensum animadvertit, rediit ad hostem, & se solum authorem factæ cædis confirmavit, ut pro amico moreretur. Bellicas] Exemplum secundum est de utroq; genere efficientis: Cotinet autem disimilitudinem rerum bellicarum & clementię Cęsaris: cujus utraq; pars ex causis efficientibus illustratur: In priore, quæ prota sis appellatur, sex sunt adjuvantes causæ, miles, locus, socius, clasis, commeatus, fortuna, quæ Cæsari victoriam comparant: in posteriore, unica est causa absoluta, quòd Cæsar solus author sit suæ clementię: eaq; amplificatur ex remotione aliarũ caussarũ adjuvantiũ, numero quinq;, centurionis, prefecti, cohortis, turmæ, fortunæ.
units.tr: Me me: the first example is of the sole efficient cause. "Me, me," meaning "kill me," is understood, as is the cry of one who is struck with incredible grief on account of a friend. When Nisus and Euryalus, after many Rutulians had been slain and stripped, were killed in the wood by the enemy Volscens, Nisus, having escaped, saw that Euryalus had been captured and seized, and returned to the enemy, and declared himself the sole author of the slaughter, so that he might die for his friend. Bellicas: the second example concerns both kinds of efficient cause. It sets out the difference between the military achievements and the clemency of Caesar, each part of which is illustrated through efficient causes. In the first, which is called the protasis, there are six auxiliary causes, soldier, place, ally, fleet, supplies and fortune, which secure victory for Caesar. In the second there is a single complete cause, namely that Caesar alone is the author of his clemency; and this is amplified by the removal of the other auxiliary causes, five in number: the centurion, the prefect, the cohort, the troop, and fortune.

units.la: Quibus enim ] Tertium exemplũ est de instrumentis, caussis nempe adjuvantibus. Velleius Epicureius irridet deum Platonis, á quo negat mundum esse constructum & ędificatum: Argumetum Velleii, est ex remotione caussarũ adjuvantium, ad elevandam divinam mundi fabricam: Deus non adhibuit ferramenta, vectes, machinas, ministros: non potuit igitur hunc mundum ædificare. Quę conclulio falsa & impia est, quia Deus non eguit his: solo enim nutu & verbo mundum condidit.
units.tr: Quibus enim: the third example concerns instruments, that is, auxiliary causes. The Epicurean Velleius mocks the god of Plato, by whom he denies that the world was constructed and built. Velleius's argument, drawn from the removal of auxiliary causes, is meant to diminish the divine construction of the world: God did not use tools, levers, machines or ministers; therefore he could not have built this world. This conclusion is false and impious, because God had no need of these things; for he created the world by his nod and word alone.

units.la: Cap. V. De efficiente per se & per accidens.
units.tr: Chapter V. On the efficient cause per se and per accidens.

units.la: TErtió, caussa efficiēs per se efficit, aut per accidens. Per se, quæ sua facultate efficit, ut quę natura vel cōsilio faciunt. Ventorum naturalis efficientia est primo Aeneid.
units.tr: Thirdly, an efficient cause either produces its effect per se or per accidens. It works per se when it produces by its own power, as things done by nature or by counsel do. The natural efficacy of the winds is described at the start of the Aeneid:

units.la: Incubuêre mari, totumque á sedibus imis, una Eurus, Notus ruũt, creberq; procellæ Africus, & vastos tollunt ad littora fluctus.
units.tr: They have fallen upon the sea, and the whole of it from its lowest depths: Eurus and Notus rush together, and the stormy Africus, and they raise vast waves toward the shores.

units.la: Consilii exemplum est Ciceronis de se confessio: Suscepto bello, Cæsar, gesto etiam magna ex parte, nulla vi coactus, judicio meo ac voluntate ad ea arma profectus sum, quę erat sumpta contra te. Per accidens efficit causla, quae externa facultate efficit, ut in his quae fiunt necessitate vel fortuna: necessitate, cum efficiens vi cogitur ad effectum: qualis est Pompejanorō excusatio: At mihi quidem(ait)si proprium & verum nomē nostri mali quæratur,fatalis quędam calamitas incidisse videtur, & improvida hominum mentes occupavi- se,ut nemo mirari debeat, humana cōsi lia,divina necessitate esse superata.Fortuna,est caussa per accidens,quãdo prę ter efficientis scopum, aliquid accidit. Si casu fortuito, ait Tullius 3. de Natur. Deor.Phæreo lasoni profuit hostis,qui gladio vomicam ejus aperuit, quam sanare medici non poterant.In hoc gene re caussarum,imprudentia connumerari solet. Ovid. 2. Trist.
units.tr: An example of counsel is Cicero's confession about himself: "When the war had been undertaken, Caesar, and carried on for the most part, I went over to those arms which had been taken up against you, not compelled by any force, but by my own judgment and will." An efficient cause works per accidens when it produces its effect through an external power, as in things that happen by necessity or by fortune. By necessity, when the efficient is forced by violence to the effect; such is the excuse of the Pompeians: "But to me, at least," he says, "if the proper and true name of our evil is sought, some fatal calamity seems to have fallen upon us and seized the improvident minds of men, so that no one should wonder that human counsels were overcome by divine necessity." Fortune is a cause per accidens whenever something happens beyond the aim of the agent. "If by chance," says Tully in the third book of On the Nature of the Gods, "an enemy benefited Jason of Pherae, who opened with a sword the abscess in his body, which doctors could not heal." In this kind of cause, imprudence is usually counted. Ovid, Tristia book 2:

units.la: Cur aliquid vidi? cur noxia lumina feci?
units.tr: Why did I see something? Why did I make my eyes harmful?

units.la: Cur imprudenti cognita culpa mihi est?
units.tr: Why has my fault become known to me, through my imprudence?

units.la: Inscius Actæon vidit sine veste Dianam:
units.tr: Actaeon, not knowing, saw Diana without her clothes:

units.la: Præda suis canibus nec minús ille fuit.
units.tr: He was no less prey to his own hounds.

units.la: Scilicet in superis etiam fortuna luenda est:
units.tr: Surely even among the gods fortune must be paid for:

units.la: Nec veniam,laso numine, casus habet.
units.tr: And chance, when a god is offended, has no pardon.

units.la: Hinc sumitur deprecatio: qualis est Ligario:Ignosce,pater,erravit, lapsus est, non putavit: fi unquam posthac. Et paulò post: Erravi, temerè feci, pœnitet ad clementiam tuam confugio, delicti veniam peto, ut ignoscas, oro. Fortunæ autem nomen, ignoratio caussarum cō finxit: cùm enim aliquid præter confiliû spemq; cōtigerit, fortuna vulgò dicitur, nec inscité Iuvenalis,
units.tr: From this is taken the plea for pardon, as in Ligarius: "Forgive me, father; he erred, he slipped, he did not think; if ever again..." And a little later: "I erred, I acted rashly, I repent; I flee to your clemency, I ask pardon for the offence, I beg you to forgive." The name of fortune was coined by ignorance of causes: for when something happens beyond plan and hope, it is commonly called fortune, and not unskilfully Juvenal says:

units.la: Nullum numen abest, si sit prudentia: sed te Nos facimus fortuna, deam, cœloq; locamus.
units.tr: There is no divinity absent, if there is prudence: but we make you, Fortune, a goddess, and place you in heaven.

units.la: Tertiò causa] Partitio ista tertia minùs multò Logica est, quàm superiores, & altero membro adiunctum aperte significat: ut potiùs adjunctum, quàm efficiens, dicenda videatur: tamen appellatur efficiens, & à philosophis ita proponitur: & quædam vis efficiendi permissa est: Itaq; ad usum P. Ramus retinuit, dum accuratius aliqd occurreret. Aristoteles aut ii. cap.
units.tr: Third cause] This third division is far less logical than the earlier ones, and by its second member it clearly signifies something added, so that it ought rather to be called "adjunct" than "efficient." Nevertheless it is called efficient, and the philosophers so propose it, and a certain power of efficiency is granted to it. Therefore P. Ramus retained it for practical use, while something more exact was not at hand. Aristotle, in the second book of the Posterior Analytics, chapter 2,

units.la: 2. Posteriorum, vocat illud per se, αὐτό: aliquado, ut 7. cap. 1. Phys. κατὰ τὴν ὁσίαν, & 5. c. 2. Physici, efficietis p se facit φύσιν καὶ ὀρμὴν ἢ προαίρεσιν, naturam & appetitum vel consilium. Idem in Ethicis ad N comachum 3. lib. Caussæ enim videntur esse natura & necessitas & fortuna & mens: in efficiente verò per se P. Ramus comprehendit τὸν νοῦν ἢ τὴν φύσιν: at ἀνάγκην καὶ τύχην comprehendit in efficiente per accidens. Incubuere] Aeolus oratione & precibus Iunonis adductus, ventos ex antro emittit in mare ad vexandas naves Trojanorum. hæc igitur est subitæ tempestatis descriptio ex ventis, caufsis efficiētibus: ubi ad incredibilē quandā tēpestatē explicādū, finxit poeta, qd̄ natura nō ferebat, vētos contrarios simul flare, ut Seneca ait in nālib. questionibus. qd̄ figmentū ex Homeri lib.5. Odysseæ imitatus est Virg. Suscepto] Ad augēdā Cēsarianę clemētiæ laudē, & ad causæ utilitatē, cōfitetur orator sefe cōsultó ac liberé arma cōtra Cæsarē suscepisse. Per accidēs] Verbū συμβεβηκὸς, accidēs, Aristoteli in Philosoph.ʒ. cap.5.lib. & 2.c. 6.lib. & 7.c.11.lib.significat quid dam αὐτόματον, ἀόριστον, ἄπιφον, ἄταλτον, Fortuitum, incertum, infinitum, inordinatū. Itaq; & id proprié ad locum adjunctorum pertinet, quatenus illam significat accidentiam: sed tamen efficientia hīc etiam quædam exprimitur. Necessitate] II.ca.2.Poster. appellatur ἀνάγκη βίαιος, necessitas violenta: ea veró, ut est in Philo.5.cap.5. παρὰ τὰ δρμὴν καὶ προαίρεσιν. contra voluntatem & consilių impedit & prohibet: Sic enim hīc accipitur non pro eo quod perpetuū sit atq; æternum, sed pro violentia: ut necessitas & violentia jam sit hīc idem. Violentū siquidem, necessariū dicitur: & ideo molestū, quemadmodū & Evenus inquit:
units.tr: calls that which is through itself "per se" (αὐτό). Sometimes, as in Physics 7, chapter 1, he speaks of "according to substance" (κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν), and in Physics 5, chapter 2, he says that the efficient cause itself makes things "by nature and impulse or choice" (φύσιν καὶ ὁρμὴν ἢ προαίρεσιν), that is, nature and appetite or deliberate purpose. The same is found in the Ethics to Nicomachus, book 3, where the causes are said to be nature, necessity, fortune and mind. In the efficient per se, P. Ramus includes mind (τὸν νοῦν) or nature (τὴν φύσιν), but necessity and fortune (ἀνάγκην καὶ τύχην) he includes in the efficient per accidens. They fell upon] Aeolus, moved by the speech and prayers of Juno, releases the winds from their cave into the sea to harass the ships of the Trojans. This, then, is the description of a sudden storm arising from winds as efficient causes; and where the poet is explaining an incredible tempest, he feigned what nature did not allow, namely contrary winds blowing at once, as Seneca says in the Natural Questions. Virgil imitated this fiction from the fifth book of Homer's Odyssey. Having undertaken] To increase the praise of Caesar's clemency, and for the advantage of his cause, the orator confesses that he himself deliberately and freely took up arms against Caesar. Per accidens] The word συμβεβηκός, "accident," in Aristotle, Philosophy 3, chapter 5, and book 2, chapter 6, and book 7, chapter 11, signifies something automatic, indefinite, unforeseen, uncertain, infinite, disordered: that is, fortuitous, uncertain, unlimited, unordered. Therefore it pertains properly to the place of adjuncts, insofar as it signifies that accidental quality; yet an efficient element is also expressed here. By necessity] In the second book of the Posterior Analytics, chapter 2, it is called violent necessity (ἀνάγκη βίαιος). That necessity, as it is in Physics 5, chapter 5, is contrary to impulse and choice (παρὰ τὴν ὁρμὴν καὶ προαίρεσιν): it hinders and prevents the will and counsel. For it is taken here not in the sense of what is perpetual and eternal, but of violence, so that necessity and violence are now the same here. For what is violent is called necessary, and therefore painful, as Evenus also says:

units.la: Πᾶν γὰρ ἀναγκαῖον πρᾶγμ', ἀνιαρὸν ἔφυ.
units.tr: For every necessary thing is by nature painful. [Πᾶν γὰρ ἀναγκαῖον πρᾶγμ', ἀνιαρὸν ἔφυ.]

units.la: Omne namque necessarium, res violenta est.
units.tr: For every necessary thing is by nature painful; a thing of necessity is a violent thing.

units.la: Et violentia, necessitas est quædam quēadmodum & Sophocles ait:
units.tr: And violence is a kind of necessity, as Sophocles says:

units.la: ᾿Αλλ᾽ ἢ βία μὲ ταῦτ᾽ ἀναγκάζει ποιεῖν.
units.tr: ᾿Αλλ᾽ ἢ βία μὲ ταῦτ᾽ ἀναγκάζει ποιεῖν.

units.la: Sed violentia me necessario hæc cogit facere.
units.tr: "But violence compels me by necessity to do these things."

units.la: Ac videtur necessitas ἀμετάπειστον τι ἄναυ ὀρθῶς, indissuasibile quiddam esse, & rectè: id enim contrarium est τῇ κατὰ τὸν προαίρεσιν νινήσει καὶ κατὰ τὸν λόγον. λογισμὸν, consilij & rationis affectioni. Hæc illic Ariftoteles.
units.tr: And necessity seems to be something [ἀμετάπειστόν τι], not to be persuaded otherwise, and rightly so; for this is contrary to the decision made by choice and by reason, to the affection of deliberation and of reason. So Aristotle there.

units.la: Pompejanorum] Excusat orator Pompejanos ad bellum civile cótra Cæsarem, veluti necessitate fatali impulsos, hæc græcis ἀμαρτίνη dicitur, cùm res aliter fieri non potest,atq; á Deo constitutum est intra fatalem cótinuationem ordinis sempiterni. Fortuna] Aristoteles 5. & 6. cap.2. Physici, τύχῃ καὶ αὐτόματον, fortunam & casum in efficientibus comprehendit. tametsi & ibidem, & in Philosophia 7.cap. 11. τύχῃ statuit in iis, quę consilio aguntur: αὐτόματον, in omnibus: Ideoq; in pueris, bestiis, lapidibus, non dici ἀτυχίαν καὶ ἀτυχίαν, bonam aut malam fortunam, nisi ὁμοιότητα, secundū similitudinem: ut Protarchus dicebat λίθος ἀτυχᾶς, lapides fortunatos esse, unde fiebant altaria, quia colerentur: αὐτόματον, veluti τὸ αὐτὸ μάταιον, ipsum frustra dicitur. At Aristo teles & fortuná & casum pro eodem promiscué sæpé aliás accipit, quomodo & P. Ramus accepit.
