Atheniensis apud Platonem disputat, res homínum in casu positas esse: & τύχῃ sic generaliter accipit lib. quarto de Legibus: At verò licet hoc quoque rectè affirmare in his ipsis. Clin.
units.tr: Of the Pompeians] The orator excuses the Pompeians for taking up civil war against Caesar, as if they were driven by fated necessity; by the Greeks this is called [ἀμαρτίνη], when a thing cannot be done otherwise, and it has been established by God within the fated continuation of an everlasting order. Fortune] Aristotle, in Physics 2, chapters 5 and 6, includes [τύχῃ καὶ αὐτόματον], fortune and chance, among efficient causes, although in the same place, and in the Philosophy 7, chapter 11, he holds [τύχῃ] to be in those things that are done by deliberation, and [αὐτόματον] in all things. Therefore in children, beasts and stones we do not speak of [εὐτυχίαν καὶ ἀτυχίαν], good or bad fortune, except [ὁμοιότητα], by similitude; as Protarchus used to say [λίθος εὐτυχᾶς], that stones are fortunate, whence altars were made, because they were worshipped. [αὐτόματον], as [τὸ αὐτὸ ματαίως], is said of the thing itself in vain. But Aristotle often takes fortune and chance indiscriminately for the same thing, as P. Ramus also took them. The Athenian in Plato disputes that human affairs are placed in chance, and he takes [τύχῃ] generally in this way in book 4 of the Laws. But indeed one may rightly affirm this also in these very things. Clinias.

units.la: Quid nam? Athen. Quod Deus quidem omnia, secundum autem Deum, τύχῃ ἢ καιρός, fortuna & occasio res hominū gubernent. Phæreo] Phalereo vulnus salutaris curatio fuit, qui ut Plin. libro 7. author est, jam deploratus á medicis vomicæ morbo, cúm mortem in acie quęreret, vulnerato pectore, medicinam invenit ex hoste. hostis igitur, curationis fortuita caussa fuit: non enim fanare inimicum volebat, sed necare: Cicero lib. 3. de Nat. Deor. non Phalereū, ut Plinius, sed Phæreum Iafonem nominat. Tale est de piscatoribus Milesiis exemplū, qui cūm piscīū capiendorum caussa, retia in mare demisissent, aureum tripodem ceperunt. piscatio ipsa fuit caussa capti tripodis, sed fortuita, quia talis eventus, neq; propositus, neq; provisus fuerat. Ovidius] Excusat Ovidius culpá suam, ob causam, quód aliquid fortuito viderit, quo Augustus Cæsar iratus est illi: cōmemoratq; simile casum Actæonis, qui cūm in monte Gargaphiæ, feras persequēs, nudā in fōte Dianā aspexisset, subitò ab ea in cervū cōversus, & à suis canib. dilaniat9 est.
units.tr: Clinias: What then? Athenian: That God indeed governs all things, but after God, [τύχῃ ἢ καιρός], fortune or opportunity, govern human affairs. Phaereo] The healing of the wound was salutary for Phalereus, who, as Pliny records in book 7, had already been given up by the doctors with the disease of an abscess, and while seeking death in battle, with his chest wounded, found a remedy from the enemy. So the enemy was the chance cause of the cure, for he did not wish to heal his enemy but to kill him. Cicero, in De Natura Deorum book 3, names not Phalereus as Pliny does, but Jason of Pherae. Similar is the example of the Milesian fishermen, who, having let down their nets into the sea to catch fish, caught a golden tripod. The fishing itself was the cause of catching the tripod, but a chance one, since such an outcome was neither intended nor foreseen. Ovid] Ovid excuses his fault, on account of the fact that by chance he had seen something, for which Augustus Caesar was angry with him; and he recalls a similar chance of Actaeon, who, while pursuing wild beasts on Mount Gargaphia, saw Diana naked at a spring, and was suddenly turned by her into a stag, and was torn to pieces by his own hounds.

units.la: Hinc sumitur] Cicero fingit per prosopopœiā, filium aliquem imprudentia lapsum, & idcirco veniam facti fui á patre deprecantem, tanquam non sponte, sed fortuito aliquo casu deliquerit.
units.tr: Hinc sumitur: Cicero, by prosopopoeia, feigns a son who has slipped through imprudence, and who therefore begs his father's pardon for his deed, as though he had done wrong not willingly but by some chance accident.

units.la: Fortuna] Fortuna, est ibidem Aristoteli quiddam παραλογου: ἀόριστον, ἀβέβαιον, ἀνθρωπίνῳ λογισμῷ ἀδηλλον, improvidum, incertum, dubium, humano judicio ambiguum: ejusq; afficientiam ignoratio caussarum confinxit. Fortuna enim, nullius per se caussa est, sed eventus, quem fortuitum dicimus, caussa quædam certa est, licet humanæ mēti ignota: ὡς δαίμων τι ἴσα καὶ δαιμονιώτερον, ut divinū quiddam & beatum, ut est 4. cap. 2. Physici. Non inscite juvenalis] Si intelligimus rerū caussas, videmus omnia divino consilio & prudentia regi & gubernari: sed quia eas frequēter ignoram9, ideo fortunæ locum tribuimus, deamque voca mus. Sic Academici interdum Deum appellát,
units.tr: Fortuna: in the same place, Aristotle says fortune is something paralogon [παραλογον], unexpected: indefinite, unstable, unknown to human reasoning, unforeseen, uncertain, doubtful, ambiguous to human judgment. Ignorance of causes has given it its effect. For fortune is not the cause of anything per se; but the event, which we call fortuitous, has some definite cause, though it is unknown to the human mind, hōs daimōn ti isa kai daimoniōteron [ὡς δαίμων τι ἴσα καὶ δαιμονιώτερον], like something divine and blessed, as in Physics book 4, chapter 2. Non inscite Juvenalis: if we understand the causes of things, we see that all things are ruled and governed by divine counsel and wisdom. But because we often do not know those causes, we give a place to fortune and call her a goddess. So too the Academics sometimes call God by that name.

units.la: d FortuFortunam, quód multa efficiat improvisa & inopinata nobis, propter obscuritatem ignorationēq; caussarū, ut ait Cicero primo Academico.
units.tr: Fortune, because she brings about many things for us that are unforeseen and unexpected, on account of the obscurity and our ignorance of causes, as Cicero says in the first book of the Academics.

units.la: Cap. VI. De Materia.
units.tr: Ch. VI. On Matter.

units.la: MAteria, est caussa ex qua res est. hoc argumento fićto apud Ovidium secundo Metamorphoseōs, Solis domus auro, pyropo, ebore, argēto cōponitur: Regia Solis erat sublimibus alta columnis, Clara, micāte auro flāmasq; imitāte pyropo. Cujus ebur nitidū fastigia summa tegebat: Argenti bisores radiabant limine valvæ.
units.tr: Matter is the cause from which a thing is. Ovid gives an illustration of this in the second book of the Metamorphoses, where the house of the Sun is built of gold, pyrope, ivory and silver: The Sun's royal palace stood high on towering columns, bright with glittering gold and imitating flames with its pyrope. Its gleaming ivory covered the topmost gables, and the silver double doors shone at the threshold.

units.la: Cęs.1.Bell.civil.Imperat militibus Cę sar ut naves faciāt, cujus generis eum superioribus annis usus Britanniæ docuerat: carinæ primùm ac statumina ex levi materia fiebant, reliquum corpus navium viminibus cōtextum, coriis integebatur.
units.tr: Caesar, Civil War 1: Caesar orders the soldiers to build ships of the kind that his experience in Britain in previous years had taught him. The keels and ribs were first made of light timber, the rest of the hull was woven of wicker, and it was covered with hides.

units.la: Materia] Materia sic definitur ab Aristotele 3. cap.2. Physic. ἔξ ἡ γίγνεται τὶ ἐνυπάρχοντος, ex quo fit aliquid, cúm insit: appellatur propré ab Aristotele ὕλη, materia: aliquando ἀνάγκη, necessitas, quód ea necessario concludatur, non absoluta quidē necessitate, sed ὑποθέσεως. quia si res sit, materiam esse necesse est: appellatur etiam interdum ὑποκείμενον, subjectū, sed minús proprié.
units.tr: Matter. Aristotle defines matter thus in the third chapter of the second book of the Physics: that out of which something comes to be, while it remains within it [ἐξ ἧς γίγνεταί τι ἐνυπάρχοντος]. Aristotle properly calls it hylē [ὕλη], matter; sometimes he calls it anankē [ἀνάγκη], necessity, because it is necessarily involved in the conclusion, though not with absolute necessity but a necessity of hypothesis: if the thing exists, the matter must necessarily exist. It is also sometimes called hypokeimenon [ὑποκείμενον], subject, but this is less proper.

units.la: Ut autem tota Dialectica est entis & non entis, sic locus materiæ Dialecticæ intelligendus est, non solum de materia physica & sensili: Nam artium mente conceptarum materiam, præcepta dicimus, at in animo corporeum & sensile nihil est, quomodo Aristoteles ait in Philosophia quinto & sexto capitibus libri primi, á primis philosophis ὕλην σωματικὴν materiam corporeā, á Pythagora & Platone ἀσώματον, incorpoream constituit: & rursus ibidem decimo septimi, iterum sexto octavi, duplicem esse ὕλην, τὴν μὲν αἰσθητὴν τὴν δὲ νοητὴν, materiam aliam quidem sensilem, aliam intelligibilem. Et omnino ait secundo quarti & tertio undecimi Philosophiæ, ἀρχὰς, sicut oppositā & comparata, esse τῶν ὄντων πρώτας διαφορὰς, ἐλλ' ἢ καὶ καθ' αὑτὸ πάθη, entis primas differentias & species & assectiones per se: idemque de omnibus Dialecticæ locis omnino dicendum, ut est octavo capite primi Elenchorum, ὅτι γὰρ κοινοί πρὸς ἅπαντα τίχνῶν ἡ διαλεκτική: hi nanque communes sunt ad omnem artem & facultatem. Ergo materiæ consideratio physicis artibus multo communior & generalior est: quod paulo diligentius admonendum P. Ramus censuit, ne quis hujus loci sensum ad res corporeas solum & manibus tractabiles attinere existimaret: Atq; hic ad laudem, præsentis de materia topici, judicium Aristotelis animadvertendum est, qui majore studio possessionem hujus doctrinæ affectavit quàm avarus quisquà pecuniam ullam concupivit. Antea in doctrina efficientis causæ, veteres philosophos inexercitatis pugilibus & apalæstris comparavit: in conftituenda autem materię doctrina appellat ἀγρὸς λογικὸς. id est agreftiores, & puerorum in cunis balbutientium persimiles. Materies vero efficientem sequi debet : ab hac enim sæpe efficitur,aut certe dolatur ac præparatur,ut est 2. capite 2.Physici.ὕλη καὶ ποιότης ἀλλὰ τίχνη τῶν ὑλῶν, ἀλλὰ μὴ ἀπλῶς, ἀλλ᾽ ἀὐφὺς,quoniā etiam faciunt artes materiam,aliæ quidem omnino, aliæ vero aptiorē, ut fecunda hæc caussa,fit velut effectus quidam primæ.Atq; hanc speciem caussæ Ariftoteles 12. ca.2.Pofter.multò justiùs ἀναλογίσεν facit,quàm efficientem : Attamen per materiam de effecto potest aliquid syllogismo concludi. Regia Solis] Exemplum fictum est, non verum. ideoq; τὴν μὴ ὕλην, materiam claram ac pellucidam auri, argenti,eboris, pyropi usurpat, ad fontem omnis claritatis & lucis arguendum.Forma etiam quædam hic attingitur é columnis,foribus,tecto; Cæsar]Cæsar ad Ilerdam in Hispania premebatur ab Afranianis,cúm intra flumina Sicorim & Cingam castrametatus esset,nec pontem haberet: has igitur perfectas naves carris iunctis devehit noctu millia passuū á castris viginti duo, militesq; his navibus flumen transportat,& difficultate sese expedit.
units.tr: Just as the whole of dialectic concerns being and non-being, so the place of dialectical matter must be understood not only as physical and sensible matter. For we speak of the matter of arts conceived in the mind as precepts, yet there is nothing bodily or sensible in the mind. As Aristotle says in the fifth and sixth chapters of the first book of the Physics, the first philosophers posited bodily matter [ὕλην σωματικήν], while Pythagoras and Plato posited incorporeal matter [ἀσώματον]. And again in the seventeenth chapter of the same book, and in the sixth chapter of the eighth book, he says that matter is twofold, one sensible [αἰσθητήν] and the other intelligible [νοητήν]. In general, in the second chapter of the fourth book and the third chapter of the eleventh book of the Philosophy, he says that the principles, as opposites and correlatives, are the first differences of being [τῶν ὄντων πρώτας διαφοράς], and the attributes in themselves [καθ' αὑτὸ πάθη], that is, the primary differences and species and affections of being. The same must be said of all the places of dialectic, as in the eighth chapter of the first book of the Elenchi: for dialectic is common to every art and faculty [κοινή πρὸς ἅπαντα τέχνη ἡ διαλεκτική]. Therefore the consideration of matter is much more common and general to the physical arts. P. Ramus thought this should be pointed out with some care, lest anyone suppose that the sense of this place pertains only to bodily things that can be handled. And here, to the credit of the present topic of matter, the judgment of Aristotle must be noted, who pursued possession of this doctrine with greater zeal than any miser ever coveted money. Earlier, in the doctrine of the efficient cause, he compared the ancient philosophers to untrained boxers and wrestlers; but in establishing the doctrine of matter he calls them a "logical countryside" [ἀγρὸς λογικός], that is, too rustic, and very like babbling children in their cradles. Matter, however, should follow the efficient cause, for it is often shaped by it, or at least hewn and prepared, as in the second chapter of the second book of the Physics: matter and quality [ὕλη καὶ ποιότης], for arts make matter, some altogether, others more fitting, since this secondary cause is like a kind of effect of the first. Aristotle, in the second chapter of the twelfth book of the Posterior Analytics, treats this kind of cause as analogous [ἀναλογισμός] far more justly than the efficient cause. Nevertheless, something can be concluded by syllogism about the effect through the matter. The royal palace of the Sun: the example is fictional, not true. Therefore Ovid uses the clear and transparent matter [τὴν μὴ ὕλην] of gold, silver, ivory and pyrope to show the source of all brightness and light. A certain form is also touched on here, in the columns, doors and roof. Caesar: Caesar was being pressed at Ilerda in Spain by the Afranians, and having encamped between the rivers Sicoris and Cinga, and lacking a bridge, he carried the ships, already built, on yoked wagons by night twenty-two miles from the camp, and transported his soldiers across the river with these ships, and so extricated himself from the difficulty.

units.la: Materia etiam latinè speciem materiæ significat,ligna nēpe,quibus ædificantur naves,ędes: quomodo & ὕλη significat græcé sylvam. Navis igitur é lignis,viminibus,coriis, id est materia sua, arguitur & explicatur.
units.tr: In Latin, materia also signifies the kind of material, namely the wood from which ships and houses are built; and in the same way hylē [ὕλη] in Greek means a wood. So a ship is shown and explained by its matter: of timber, wicker and hides.

units.la: Cap. VII. De Forma.
units.tr: Ch. VII. On Form.

units.la: CAussæ primũ genus ejusmodi est in efficiente & materia: fecundum sequitur in forma & fine Forma, est eaufa, per quam res est id quod est: ideoque hinc á cæteris rebus distinguitur: & forma simul cum re ipsa ingeneratur: Anima rationalis, est forma hominis: quia per eã homo est homo, & distinguitur á cęteris omnibus naturis: Geometricarum figurarũ in triangulis, quadrangulis sua forma est: Phyficarũ, cæli, terrę arborum, pifciũ sua forma est, unde præcipua rerũ ut natura est, sic erit explicatio, fi possit inveniri, ut in artificiosis rebus facilius occurret. Cæf. 7. Muri autē oēs „ Gallici hac feré forma sunt. trabes direćtæ perpetuę in longitudinē, paribus in „ tervallis diftātes inter fe binos pedes in „ solo collocātur: hæ revinciuntur intror „ sus, & multo aggere vestiuntur: ea autē quæ diximus intervalla, grandib. in fron „ te faxis effarciuntur. his collocatis & co „ agmētatis, alius insuper ordo adjicitur, „ ut idem illud intervallum fervetur, neq; „ inter fe cōtingāt trabes, sed paribus intermiffe spatiis, singulę singulis faxis in- „ d
units.tr: The first kind of cause is of this sort, in the efficient cause and the matter; the second follows, in the form and the end. Form is the cause through which a thing is what it is, and so it distinguishes the thing from other things; form comes into being together with the thing itself. The rational soul is the form of man, because through it man is man and is distinguished from all other natures. The form of geometrical figures lies in triangles and quadrangles; the forms of physical things, of the heavens, the earth, trees and fishes, are their forms. Hence the chief explanation of a thing's nature will be this, if it can be found, as it more readily occurs in artificial things. Caesar, book 7. The walls of the Gauls are almost all of this kind: straight beams, continuous in length, are laid on the ground at equal intervals, two feet apart. These are bound together on the inside and covered with a great deal of earth, and the intervals we mentioned are packed with large stones along the front. When these are laid in place and joined together, another row is added above, so that the same interval is kept and the beams do not touch one another, but, separated by equal spaces, each is tightly joined to the others with a stone set between.

units.la: terjectis arcte cotinearantur.sic deinceps omne opus contexitur, dum justa muri altitudo expleat. hoc cum in specie varietatem; opus deforme non est, alternis trabib.ac saxis, quae rectis lineis suos ordines servat:tum ad utilitate & defensionem urbium, summa habet opportunitatem, quod & ab incedio lapis, & ab ariete materia defendit: quae perpetuis trabibus pedes quadragenos plerunque introrsus revincta, neque perrumpi, neque distrahi potest. Sic forma Virgiliani potius explicatur Aeneidos primo: Est in secessu longo locus: insula portum Efficit obiectu laterum: quibus omnis ab alto Frangitur, ing; sinus scindit sese unda reductos. Hinc atq; hinc vasta rupes, geminiq; minatur In calum scopuli: quorum sub vertice late Aequora tuta silent: tum sylvis scena coruscis Desuper, horrentiq; atra nemo imminet umbra. Fronte sub adversa scopulis pendentibus antri: Intus aquae dulces, vivoq; sedilia saxo, Nympharum domos. Hic fessas non vincula naves Ulla tenent: unco non alligat ancora morsu:
units.tr: In this way the whole work is woven together until the wall reaches its proper height. Although this gives some variety in appearance, the work is not ugly, since the alternating beams and stones keep their rows in straight lines. It is also very well suited to the use and defence of cities, for the stone protects against fire and the timber against the battering ram; the beams, bound inward for forty feet or so, can be neither broken through nor pulled apart. The form is thus better explained by the passage of Virgil in the first book of the Aeneid: "There is a place in a long recess: an island makes a harbour with the barrier of its sides, against which every wave from the deep breaks and is divided into receding bays. On either side a vast cliff and twin crags threaten the sky; beneath their peaks the wide waters lie safe and silent. Above, a stage of shimmering woods, and a dark shade hangs over with bristling gloom. Beneath the facing front, under overhanging crags, is a cave: within are sweet waters and seats of living rock, the homes of the nymphs. Here no cables hold the weary ships, and no anchor binds them with its hooked bite."

units.la: Forma] Duae reliquae species causarum, commune genus unum habet, sed quod revera fit, nondum distinguere P. Ramus potuit. Forma definitur generaliter, non quidem physica illa tantum,
units.tr: Form] The two remaining species of causes share one common genus, but P. Ramus has not yet been able to distinguish what is actually done. Form is defined generally, not only that physical form which belongs to bodily and material things.

units.la: quæ corporearū rerum & materiatarū fit: Nam forma logica, ut materia, rerum omnium cōmunis est, qua nempe res est id quod est:unde etiā fit,ut á cæteris rebus differat. Formæ præcipua utilitas est unica, rē formare; unde distinctio á cæteris rebus sequitur:hęc utilitas duplex proponitur 14. cap.1. Topici: ἀ ... ad cognoscendū quid est unum quodque, & ad rationem ejusdem & diversi: Priore ratiõe describitur quod quid erat esse,ut 11. cap.1. Poster. ratio essentiæ, ut 1.cap.1.de ortu Animalium : essentia rei,ut 7.cap.1. Philos. ratio specifica & essentialis, ut 4. cap. 4. libri philosophiæ: specifica,completiva, constitutiva, ut apud Porphyrium: Appellatur vero etiā forma & ratio persæpe: interdū etiā species & exemplar,ut 2.ca. 5.Philos.Rationis secundę utilitas describitur á Porphyrio, qa species generis alias ab aliis dividit & distinguit:& appellatur tum proprié differentia. Et sic hoc nomen similitudini opponitur primi Topici cap.11.& 14. & é quatuor instrumentis cōmunibus ,duo fiunt illic ab Aristotele, similitudo & differētia. Ingeneratur ] Forma sola de caussis, est,simul congenita:ut scribit Aristoteles 11.cap.2.Posteriorum.In quo sanè id est animadvertēdum, quód materia modo quodá efficitur ab efficiente:at forma penitus efficitur,estque revera èssestus efficientis: & cùm architectus domū ædificat, facit domus materiam dolando poliendoque parte aliqua: sed formam penitus efficit. veruntamē forma facta longē plus adfert ad esse n tiam rei, quám materia: Est enim ipsamet essentia, aut certé præcipua pars essentiæ. Quemadmodū veró cognitio formarum, sciențiā persectam & absolutam effecit, ita homini perdifficilis est: qua de causa Timæus apud Platonem ait perpaucos homines veræ intelligentię esse participes. Communi quidem ratione & definitione intelligimus esse rerū formas: at quid singularis & unaquæque forma fit, ut leonis, equi, arboris, ab hominibus ignoratur, & si cognoscitur ut corporis humani, ut navis, vix multis rebus collectis exprimitur. Quapropter veteres philosophi hic valde fuerūt occupati, non in logica generalis argumenti definitione, sed in effigie. Pythagoras & Pythagorei dixerunt τὰ ὄντα, entia, μιμήσεις καὶ ὁμοιώματα, imitationes & similitudines esse numerorum: ἡ ἀριθμὸν, ἄνευ τῆς ἰσίας τῶν πάντων, & numerum, esse essentiam omnium. Plato paulò secùs docuit, res quidem non esse imitationes numerorum, sed idearum μεθέξεις, communicationes: ut communicatione, multa sint symbola ideis homonyma, ut author est Aristoteles primo libro Philosophiæ. Atqui in doctrina formę, vindicię Aristoteli aduersus antiquos philosophos nō defuere: Pythagorei, ait in Philosophia 5. & 6. c. li. 1. λίαν ἁπλῶς ἐπραγματεύσαντο, valde simpliciter & imperite id egerunt: Platonem vero per sua παραδείγματα τῇ ἰδέας, exemplaria & imagines idearum, ait ὑγρολογεῖν, ἡ ποιητικὰς μιμήσεις.
units.tr: For logical form, like matter, is common to all things: it is that by which a thing is what it is; hence also it differs from other things. The chief use of form is single: to give form to a thing. From this use the distinction from other things follows. This use is set out in two ways in the fourteenth chapter of the first book of the Topics: to know what each thing is, and to know the account of the same and the different. By the first account what-it-was-to-be is described, as in the eleventh chapter of the first book of the Posterior Analytics, the account of essence; as in the first chapter of the book On the Generation of Animals, the essence of a thing; as in the seventh chapter of the first book of the Philosophy, the specific and essential account; as in the fourth chapter of the fourth book of the Philosophy, the specific, completive, constitutive account, as Porphyry has it. Form and account are also often called by the name of species and exemplar, as in the second chapter of the fifth book of the Philosophy. The second use of the account is described by Porphyry: since species divide and distinguish one from another within a genus; and this is properly called difference. And so this name is opposed to similarity, as in the eleventh and fourteenth chapters of the first book of the Topics, where Aristotle makes two of the four common instruments: similarity and difference. Is generated: form alone of the causes is generated together with the thing, as Aristotle writes in the eleventh chapter of the second book of the Posterior Analytics. Here it must be noted that matter is in a sense produced by the efficient cause, but form is wholly produced, and is truly the effect of the efficient cause. When an architect builds a house, he makes the matter of the house by hewing and polishing some part of it, but he produces the form wholly. Yet the form contributes far more to the being of a thing than the matter does, for it is the very essence, or at least the principal part of the essence. But just as knowledge of forms makes science perfect and complete, so it is most difficult for man; for this reason Timaeus in Plato says that very few men share in true understanding. We understand by common reasoning and definition that things have forms; but what the particular and individual form of each thing is, as of a lion, a horse or a tree, is unknown to men, and if it is known, as of the human body or of a ship, it is hardly expressed even when many things have been gathered together. For this reason the ancient philosophers were greatly occupied here, not with the definition of the general logical argument but with the image. Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans said that beings [τὰ ὄντα] are imitations and likenesses of numbers, and that number [ἀριθμόν] is the essence of all things without which nothing is. Plato taught somewhat differently: that things are not imitations of numbers but participations [μεθέξεις] in the Ideas, communications, so that by this communication many things are symbols homonymous with the Ideas, as Aristotle reports in the first book of the Philosophy. Yet in the doctrine of form, Aristotle did not lack defenders against the ancient philosophers. The Pythagoreans, he says in the fifth and sixth chapters of the first book of the Philosophy, treated the matter very simply [λίαν ἁπλῶς] and without skill; and Plato, through his paradigms and the Ideas, which are exemplars and images of the Ideas, he says, talks nonsense [ὑγρολογεῖν] or speaks poetic imitations.

units.la: ταῖς μὲν λίγεν nugari, & poeticas metaphoras loqui, Deniq; formam,ait, σαφῶς ... ἀπεδλίδοκιν, perspicuè nullus exposuit: amavit nempe philosophus hic noster laudis hujus etiá patrimoniū.
units.tr: Some call it mere babbling and speak in poetic metaphors. Finally, he says, form was clearly [σαφῶς] ... explained by no one: indeed this philosopher of ours loved to claim this praise as his inheritance too.

units.la: Muri ] Ut superiora,efficientis & materię exempla,sic sequentia,formæ & finis: quávis unicum argumentum, multis tamen verbis arguunt & interpretantur.In Cęsaris exemplo, est etiá materia in trabibus,aggere,faxis:est etiam finis,ad propugnationem urbium:sed forma ipsa é materiæ perpetua dispositione atq; ordine,graphicé informatur, nec feré in exéplo ullo materiá solam deprehendes. Virgiliani ] Forma portus á Virgilio talis affingitur, qualis omnino possit optari, non qualis revera fit: Servius talem portū ait fuisse Carthaginis nouæ in Hispania, nec usquam esse in Africa. Pari veró elegátia portus pingitur é sinu,infula, rupibus, scopulis,nemore,aqua dulci, sedilibus : & finis etiá attingitur, quód hic & naves,& nautæ recreentur.
units.tr: Muri: As the earlier examples illustrate efficient cause and matter, so these illustrate form and end. Although each is a single argument, they set it out and explain it in many words. In Caesar's example there is matter in the beams, the earthwork and the stones; there is also the end, the defence of the cities. But the form itself is vividly portrayed by the constant arrangement and order of the matter, and in almost no example will you find matter alone. Virgiliani: Virgil ascribes to the harbour a form such as might be wished for, not one that actually exists. Servius says that such a harbour existed at New Carthage in Spain and nowhere in Africa. With equal elegance, however, the harbour is painted with a bay, an island, cliffs, reefs, a grove, fresh water and seats. The end is also touched on, since here both ships and sailors are refreshed.

units.la: Cap. VIII. De Fine.
units.tr: Chapter VIII. On the End.

units.la: FInis, est caussa cujus gratiâ res est, Physicis rebus finis homo propofitus est,homini Deus. Omniū artiū est aliquod fummumbonum & finis extremus,ut Grămaticę,bene loqui:Rhetoricę,bene dicere: Logicę,bene differere. Iuno 1. Aeneidos, connubii finem aflumit,cúm Aeolo Dejopejam pollicetur, solatii scilicet prolisque gratia.
units.tr: The end is the cause for the sake of which a thing exists. In physical things the end proposed is man; for man, God. Every art has some highest good and ultimate end: grammar, to speak well; rhetoric, to speak well (in the sense of eloquence); logic, to dispute well. In Aeneid 1, Juno takes up the end of marriage when she promises Deiopea to Aeolus, namely for the sake of comfort and offspring.

units.la: Sunt mihi bis septe prastăti corpore nymphæ: Quarũ, quæ forma pulcherrima, Dejopejam Connubio jungam stabili propriâq; dicabo: Omnes, ut tecum, meritis pro talibus, annos Exigat, & pulchra faciat te prole parentem.
units.tr: I have fourteen nymphs of outstanding beauty; of these I will join the most beautiful, Deiopea, to you in a lasting marriage and dedicate her as your own. May she, in return for such merit, spend all her years with you and make you a parent through a fair offspring.

units.la: In defensione Ligarii, Cicero Tuberonem accusatorē urget: cúm armorū contra Cæsarem susceptorū finem premit. Et certé (ait) contra ipsum Cæsarē est congressus armatus. Quid enim Tubero tuus ille districtus in acie Pharsalica gladi? agebat? cujus latus ille mucro petebat? quis sensus erat armorū tuorū? quæ tua mens? oculi? manus? ardor animi? quid cupiebas? quid optabas?
units.tr: In his defence of Ligarius, Cicero presses the accuser Tubero with the end of the arms taken up against Caesar. "And surely," he says, "he fought armed against Caesar himself. For what was your Tubero doing, drawing his sword in the battle line at Pharsalus? At whose side was that blade aimed? What was the purpose of your arms? What was your mind, your eyes, your hands, the ardour of your spirit? What were you desiring? What were you wishing for?"

units.la: Finis]Finis definitur ab Aristotele II.cap. 2. Posteriorum, τὸ τινὸς ἕνεκα, quod alicujus gratia: sed 3.cap.2.Physici, τὸ τέλος, τοῦτο δὲ ἔστι τὸ ἕνεκα, finis, est id cujus gratia. quomodo & Plato ante eum locutus erat: appellat etiā Aristoteteles αἴτιον τέλει, caussam finalem. Axioma illud 2. cap.1.Post. videtur loci hujus esse, διὸ ὑπάρχει ἕκαστον, ἐνῖνο μᾶλλον ὑπάρχει, propter quod est unūquodq; tale, illud magis. hæc definitio est generalis, & nomen generale: tamē Aristoteles videtur duas species finis efficere, dum modó materiæ finē appellat forma: modó totius rei compositæ finē id dicit, cujus gratia facta fit. Aristoteli igitur finis, est forma ipsa, cujus gratia materia dolatur, reque ipsa tandem absolvitur ac finitur: atq; ut ab efficiente effectum, a materia materiatum, a forma formatum, sic a fine finitum quidlibet intelligitur sed tamen quomodo finis sit duplex, Aristoteles ait 2. & cap. 2. Physici. Atqui nos utimur, tā quam nostri gratia sint omnia: sumus enim quo dāmodo & nos finis: dupliciter enim cujus gratiā. Hic duplex finis ab Aristotele proponitur, neq; tamē definitur aut nominatur. Nominatur autem 4. cap. 2. de Anima: ꝯ, dupliciter autem cujus gratia, & cujus, & cui. Simplicius aut in 2. cap. 2. Physici ait, τὸ τέλος, τὸ ἕνεκα, τὸ δὲ ᾧ, finis alius est cujus gratia, alius aut cui: ut forma domus, est finis, cujus gratia architectus materiā comparavit: at usus dom⁹, est custodia rerū, & tutela domini adversus quaslibet externas injurias. Atqui finis ille formalis, aut forma illa finalis, licet tam sit rerū omniū cōmunis, quàm est ipsa forma, a qua nunquā reipsa separatur: attamē quia distinctū caussæ genus nullum adfert, non est admodū propositus neq; tractatus pro logica caussa. Alter autē finis, qui est in usu & energia formæ, Philoponi sententia est absolutissimus, in usu quippe hominum. Enimverò feré quoties quamobrem, aut cujus gratia quidpiā factum, aut fiat, interrogatur, finis hic secundus intelligitur, nec habetur illius distinctionis ratio, cujus & cui, sed omnino cujus gratia, finem istū intelligimus: laudesque summę per Aristotelē fini tributæ, de hoc fi ne intelliguntur: & quidem nomine cujus gratia: sic enim Aristoteles 1. cap. 1. de Partibus animalium, cŭm de præstantia caussarum philosophatur : φάνιται δὲ πρώτη, ὧν λέγομεν ἐνεκα τινός. λόγος γὰρ ἐτὶ, videtur autem prima, quâ dicimus gratia cujus: hæc enim ratio est. & 2. cap. 5. Philosophiæ, τὸ γὰρ ἕνεκά ἐστι βέλτιστον, καὶ τέλος τῶν ἄλλων ὑπάν, quod cujus gratia est optimum, & finis est aliarum caussarum. his igitur locis Aristoteles si nem ait esse & primam caussarū, & optimā caussarum, & caussam deniq; caussarum. Itaq; si quis finem extenuare visus est, aut dicere, non esse commune artium rerumq; omnium, ut Aristippus, & quidam sophistę (ut est in Philosophia 2. cap. 3. lib.) qui in mathematicis dicebant per finem & summi boni rationem, nihil demonstrari. Aristoteles illis acriter resistit : Qui hoc dicūt (ait in Philosophia 3. cap. lib. 13.) mentiūtur: Demonstrat enim mathematicæ per finem & summi boni rationē : Non enim quia non nominat, dummodo opera resque demonstrant, ideo de bono nihil dicunt: Pulchri autem præstantissimæ species sunt τάξις, καὶ συμμετρία, καὶ τὸ ὡρισμένον, ordo, & symmetria & definitum, quæ maximè demonstrantur á mathematicis scientiis. Quare videmus quáto studio Aristoteles caussam hác finale extulerit. Itaq; tam præclaré exornatum patrimonium caussæ hujus, ut antea cęterarum caussarum, sibi ab atiquis philosophis vindicavit 6. cap. 1. Philosophiæ. Id veró cujus gratia actiones & mutationes & motus fiunt, quodammodo dicunt caussam: sic autem non dicunt, neque quomodo res ipsa postulat. Veruntamē hic secundus finis tam magnificē cōmendatus, tam studiosé vel ambitiosè potiús á philosopho vindicatus, P. Ramum valde anxium & suspensum tenuit, ut pene logicum ei nihil hic videretur: Nam quomodo logicum & omnis entis & non entis commune dicetur, quod sit speciale, & unius certę speciei, id est Dei & hominis proprium? Aristoteles .n.ii.cap.2.Posteriorū ait esse ἐν τῇ Διανοίᾳ, in ratiocinatione: q in Physicis ipsam appellat προαίρεσιν, deliberationem: quin 9.ca.2, Physici affirmat talem finem esse principium, τῆς πράξεως, ἀλλὰ τὸ λογισμὸς, nó actionis, sed ratiocinationis: ut finis, causa sit rei hactenus, dum ratiocinationis persuasio quædam efficienté movet. Aristoteles deniq; opponit ei αὐτόματον, fortuitū & temerariū: ut finis, circūstantia quæda videatur esse causæ efficiétis per se, nēpe aut cō silio & natura, aut per accidēs. Quod si fit, certè talis finis, logicū genus causæ nō videatur cōmune omnis entis & non entis, cúm sit speciale & proprium unius cujusdam entis, nempe utentis deliberatione & ratiocinatioe. Deinde si ἐνίφ γαα illa formæ, si factæ rei usus spectetur, talis finis, causa rei factę nequaquā videatur, cúm post rem factam accidat, sitque tempore posterior & efficiete, & materia, & forma. Hæc sunt quæ contra secundum finem pugnare P. Ramo videbantur: neque talis nodi solutio adhuc ulla satis idonea occurrit, sic ut antea de causa per accidens: hoc enim in categoria causarum indissolubile alterum videatur. Et utrunq; ex eadem circunstantia per se & per accidens. Verum enim uerò falsus P.Ramo videbatur vterq; locus ille qui fini & προδιρεσιν & λογισμὸν tribuit: præsertim cum Aristoteles ipse 8. cap. 2. Phyfic. differat naturā certo fine agere & tamen nō deliberare. Hæc enim prolixa est illius capitis disputatio: Neque porro absoluta perfectaque authori dominoq; suo res est, qua nondum potiatur. Et finem efficienti propositum esse, id est caussam cum alia caussa cōcurrere, nihil alienum videatur. Quare cùm caussa definiatur, cujus vi aliqd est, & vi finis, præcipué res fit ideo finé inter genera causarum P. Ramus retinuit, & suo cultu exornavit.
units.tr: Finis: Aristotle defines the end in the second book of the Posterior Analytics, ch. 2, as [τὸ τινὸς ἕνεκα] "that for the sake of which something is"; but in the Physics, book 3, ch. 2, as [τὸ τέλος], and [τοῦτο δὲ ἔστι τὸ ἕνεκα], "the end is that for the sake of which". Plato had spoken in the same way before him. Aristotle also calls the end [αἴτιον τέλει], the final cause. That axiom in the first book of the Posterior Analytics, ch. 2, [διὸ ὑπάρχει ἕκαστον, ἐκεῖνο μᾶλλον ὑπάρχει], "on account of which each thing is such, that thing is more so", seems to belong to this place. This definition is general, and the name is general too. Yet Aristotle seems to make two kinds of end: sometimes he calls the form the end of the matter, and sometimes he calls the end of the whole composite thing that for whose sake it is made. So for Aristotle the end is the form itself, for whose sake the matter is shaped and finally completed and brought to its limit; and just as the effect is understood from the efficient cause, the made thing from the matter, the formed thing from the form, so whatever is finished is understood from the end. How the end is twofold, Aristotle says in the second book of the Physics, ch. 2. And we use things as if all things were for our sake, since we too are in a sense an end; for the "for whose sake" is twofold. Aristotle sets out this twofold end but neither defines nor names it. He does name it in the second book On the Soul, ch. 2: and, the "for whose sake" is twofold, namely "for whose sake" and "for whom". Simplicius, in the second book of the Physics, ch. 2, says: [τὸ τέλος, τὸ ἕνεκα, τὸ δὲ ᾧ], the end is one thing, the for-the-sake-of-which, and another, the for-whom: for example, the form of a house is the end for whose sake the builder obtains the material, but the use of the house is the keeping of goods and the protection of the owner against any external injuries. Now that formal end, or final form, though it is as common to all things as the form itself, from which it is never really separated, nevertheless, since it brings no distinct kind of cause, is not greatly proposed or treated as a cause for logic. The other end, which lies in the use and activity of the form, is in Philoponus's opinion the most complete, since it is found in human use. Indeed, almost whenever we ask why or for whose sake something has been done or is done, we understand this second end, and no account is taken of the distinction between "for whose sake" and "for whom"; we understand the end simply as "for whose sake". The highest praises Aristotle gives to the end are understood of this end, and indeed under the name "for whose sake". So Aristotle, in the first book On the Parts of Animals, ch. 1, when philosophising about the excellence of causes, says: [φάνιται δὲ πρώτη, ὧν λέγομεν ἐνεκα τινός. λόγος γὰρ ἐτὶ], "the first seems to be that which we call 'for whose sake'; for this is the reasoning". And in the second book of the Physics, ch. 5: [τὸ γὰρ ἕνεκά ἐστι βέλτιστον, καὶ τέλος τῶν ἄλλων ὑπάν], "that for whose sake is the best, and is the end of the other causes". By these passages Aristotle says that the end is both the first cause, the best cause, and finally the cause of causes. Therefore if anyone has seemed to belittle the end, or to say that it is not common to the arts and to all things, as Aristippus and certain sophists did (as is said in the second book of the Physics, ch. 3), who claimed that in mathematics nothing is demonstrated through the end or the account of the supreme good, Aristotle resists them sharply. Those who say this (he says in the third book of the Physics, ch. 3, lib. 13) are lying: for mathematics demonstrates through the end and the account of the supreme good. For it is not because it does not name the good that it says nothing of the good, so long as its works and objects demonstrate it. The most excellent kinds of beauty are [τάξις, καὶ συμμετρία, καὶ τὸ ὡρισμένον], order, symmetry and the definite, which are chiefly demonstrated by the mathematical sciences. So we see with how much zeal Aristotle set forth this final cause. Thus he claimed for himself, from some earlier philosophers, the inheritance of this cause, now so splendidly adorned, just as he had done for the other causes, in the sixth chapter of the first book of the Physics. Those earlier philosophers spoke of the thing for whose sake actions, changes and motions occur as in some way a cause; but they did not speak of it as the thing itself requires. Yet this second end, so magnificently commended and so eagerly, or rather ambitiously, claimed by the philosopher, kept P. Ramus very anxious and in suspense, so that it almost seemed to him no logical matter at all here. For how can that be called common to all being and non-being which is special and proper to one definite kind, namely to God and to man? Aristotle, in the second chapter of the Posterior Analytics, says it lies [ἐν τῇ Διανοίᾳ], in reasoning; in the Physics he calls it [προαίρεσιν], deliberation; indeed, in the second chapter of the ninth book of the Physics he affirms that such an end is the principle [τῆς πράξεως, ἀλλὰ τὸ λογισμὸς], not of action but of reasoning. So far the end is a cause of the thing, in that the persuasion of reasoning moves the efficient cause. Finally, Aristotle opposes to it [αὐτόματον], chance and accident, so that the end seems to be a circumstance of the efficient cause, either per se, by design and nature, or per accidens. If this is so, such an end does not seem to be a logical kind of cause common to all being and non-being, since it is special and proper to one kind of being, namely to one who uses deliberation and reasoning. Next, if one looks at that form-related [ἐνίφ γαα] and at the use of the thing made, such an end does not seem to be the cause of the thing made at all, since it comes after the thing is made, and is later in time than the efficient cause, the matter and the form. These are the points which seemed to P. Ramus to tell against the second end; nor has any solution of this knot yet been found adequate enough, just as with the cause per accidens: for in the category of causes this seems to be another indissoluble knot, and both arise from the same circumstance, per se and per accidens. But indeed that passage which attributes to the end both [προαίρεσιν] and [λογισμόν] seemed to P. Ramus false, especially since Aristotle himself, in the eighth chapter of the second book of the Physics, distinguishes between acting by nature for a certain end and not deliberating. For that chapter of his is a long discussion. Nor is a thing yet owned and possessed by its master if it is not yet complete and perfect. And it seems nothing strange that the end should be set before the efficient cause, that is, that one cause should concur with another. Therefore, since a cause is defined as that by whose power something is, and especially by the power of the end, P. Ramus retained the end among the kinds of cause and adorned it with his own care.

units.la: Illud est Aristotelis antea jā citatum é 2. cap. 2. Physici, quód homo, fit finis omnium. Platonis illud est in multis locis, sed 7. de Republic. præcipué.
units.tr: That is Aristotle's saying, already cited earlier from Physics 2, chapter 2, that man becomes the end of all things. It is Plato's too, in many places, but especially in Republic book 7.

units.la: Id antea docuit Aristoteles, cûm dixit, finem esse optimam caussam: & 3. cap. 8. Politici ait, τὸ ἀνθρώπινον, id est optimam actionem, esse summum finem omnium virtutū, non solùm in actione, sed in animi contemplatione positarum: finis siquidem, est actio, & hujus gratia, facultas adhibetur.
units.tr: Aristotle taught this earlier when he said that the end is the best cause. In Politics 3, chapter 8, he says that the human good [τὸ ἀνθρώπινον], that is, the best action, is the highest end of all the virtues, and lies not only in action but also in the contemplation of the mind. For the end is action, and a faculty is employed for its sake.

units.la: Fictio poetica est non entis, ut superioraferè exempla: juno autem, aer est, & Aeolię insula læ septem prope Italiam vetofisimę: νύμφη lympha dicitur, mutato v in λ. hinc igitur regina aeris, & Aeolus rex ventorum, & Nympha ei promittitur, quia venti aquis aut excitantur aut fedantur. In hoc autem exemplo, forma quædam connubij est, ex stabilitate & proprietate dicatę uxoris. Hoc exemplum variis laudibus ornatum est & troporū & figurarū: ideoq; citatum varié, variis locis, varia de causa, modo propter tropos illos audaces, tribuētes animā rei inanimatę: modo propter anaphoram, quid, quid: modo propter epistrophen, agebat, petebat, cupiebas, optabas: modo propter polyptoton, quid, cujus, quæ: tum propter apostrophen & interrogationem λόγισμš: denique propter finis argumentum.
units.tr: This is a poetic fiction of something that does not exist, like most of the earlier examples. Juno is air, and the Aeolian islands, seven of them near Italy, are very ancient. A nymph is called νύμφη, lympha, with v changed to λ. Hence the queen of air, Aeolus the king of the winds, and a nymph is promised to him, because winds are either stirred up or calmed by waters. In this example there is a certain form of marriage, drawn from the constancy and devotion of the wife. The example is adorned with many tropes and figures, and so it is cited in various ways, in various places, and for various reasons: sometimes for those bold tropes that give a soul to inanimate things; sometimes for anaphora, quid, quid; sometimes for epistrophe, agebat, petebat, cupiebas, optabas; sometimes for polyptoton, quid, cuius, quae; then for apostrophe and the rhetorical question [λόγισμός]; and finally for the argument from the end.

units.la: Cap. IX. De Effectu.
units.tr: Chapter 9. On the Effect.

units.la: EFfectum, est quod é caussis existit. Sive igitur gignatur, sive corrumpatur sive modo quolibet moveatur quid libet, hic motus & res motu facta, essectum dicitur. huius loci sunt laudes & vituperationes: quarum pleni sunt libri sacri & profani. Aeneid. 6. facta variorum populorum comparatur ad nominis Romani laudem.
units.tr: An effect is that which comes into being from causes. So whether something is generated, or corrupted, or in any way set in motion, this motion and the thing made by motion is called an effect. To this place belong praises and censures, with which the sacred and the profane books are full. In the Aeneid, book 6, the deeds of various peoples are compared with the glory of the Roman name.

units.la: Excudent alÿ spirantia mollius æra: (tus: Credo equidē ducent vivos de marmore vul Orabunt caussas meliūs: cæliqueme atus Describent radio, & surgentia sydera dicēt: Tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memēto Hæ tibi erūt artes, Paciq, imponere moram, Parcere subiectis, & debellare superbos.
units.tr: Others will fashion bronze that breathes more softly, I believe, and will draw living faces from marble; they will plead causes better, and describe with the rod the motions of the sky and the rising stars. But you, Roman, remember to rule the peoples under your empire: these will be your arts, to impose the custom of peace, to spare the defeated and to subdue the proud.

units.la: Huc dicta scriptaq; referēda sunt. Pericles & Hortensius, bene dicēdi laude celebrantur: eodēq; argumento Demosthenes & Cicero etiam bené scribědi. Ad hunc etiam locum referuntur cŏsilia & deliberationes, etiāsi omnino ad exitum perductæ nō fuerint. Parmenio & Philotas morte mulctati sunt, qa cōjurationis in Alexandrū essent suspecti, ut Curtius & Arrianus meminerūt. De Lētulo & Cethego,aliisq; Catilinæ popularibus, Romani Senatus judicio sup pliciū sumptum est. Sunt etiā effecta vir tutum & vitiorū. Horatius hoc modo ebrietatis effecta describit:
units.tr: Things said and written belong here. Pericles and Hortensius are celebrated for the praise of good speaking, and by the same argument Demosthenes and Cicero for good writing too. Counsels and deliberations also belong to this place, even if they were never carried through to their outcome. Parmenio and Philotas were punished with death because they were suspected of a conspiracy against Alexander, as Curtius and Arrian record. Lentulus and Cethegus, and the other followers of Catiline, were put to death by the judgment of the Roman Senate. There are also effects of virtues and vices. Horace describes the effects of drunkenness in this way:

units.la: Quid nō ebrietas designat? operta recludit. Spes jubet esse ratas, in prælia trudit inerme. Sollicitis animis onus eximit, ac docet artes: Fœcundi calices quem non fecere disertum? Contracta quem nō in paupertate solutum?
units.tr: What does drunkenness not bring about? It unlocks what is hidden. It bids hopes be fulfilled, it thrusts the unarmed man into battle. It takes the burden from anxious minds and teaches arts. Which man has not been made eloquent by the generous cups? Whom has it not freed from his poverty?

units.la: Effectum ] Categoria caussarū locuples & copiosa fuit in Topicis quatuor generum, efficientis & materiæ, formæ & finis. Categoria effectorum sequitur, genere quidem logico, individua, attamen usu longé copiosissima. hoc argumentum in Philosophia Aristotelis dicitur proprié αἴτιατὸν, & Latiné usus pateretur, item proprié diceretur causatum: dicitur etiam πρᾶξις, ἔργον, ἐνέργεια, ποίησις, γένεσις, κίνησις, actio, opus, actus, essectio, generatio, motus: latinis effectū effectus, eventum eventus: Sed effectus vel effectum, si nomen spectes, proprié ad efficientem causam referrrefertur. & sané Latinis, ut Ciceroni in Topic. & Partitionibus, unicum est caussarum genus in efficientibus, ut antea diͤctum est, ut effectus efficientibus, táquam caussis omnibus inde respondeat: quanquam & finis incitat ad agendū, & forma materiaq; conftituút. Itaque effectum de caussis omnibus existit. ac quamvis nomen, generis unius originem referat, tamen quia omnium communem usum obtinuit, retineatur, & effectum, tanquam αἰτιατὸν, caussatum intelligatur. Verumenimvero ut caussarum locus infinita tautologia in omnem pené philosophiam effusus est, sic effectorum locus latisimé est difperfus: atque ut in illa Categoria, labor P. Rami perspectus est incolligendis totfrugibus, & expurgandis, & loco Ariftoteleis legibus imperato, recondendis: sic erit effectorū categoria. Primum é decem categoriis, una Ariftotelis est in actione & passione: in Posterioribus conjunctè tractantur: Effectorum locus cum cauffis, in Topicis parcissimé citatur: bis nempe: femel tertio, & iterū sexto. At locus hic, sex pené totos extremos Physicæ auscultationis libros, nomine motus, occupavit. Quamobrem Ariftoteleam P. Rami agricultura attendamus: ut tautologias tā multiplices repreferit, qua falce tā multas spinas amputarit. Eninvero generalis est effectorum locus, ut in toto Organo proponitur: Itaq; ad Ariftotelis legem καθόλᾳ πρῶτον, femel & generaliter est proponendus. Sed de phy ficis motibus, res P. Ramo fuit multo difficilior, quia rem physicam, non logicam complecti vie deandeátur:capita summatim hic attingam.Primùm definitio motus, quæ tamé accuratissima videtur,in physicis totam rem turbavit.Definitur 2. cap.3.Physici,ντιλίχεα τὰ ἀιωάμεα ἐντῷ ἢ τοιῶτοp,ιτὲ 5 τὰ ἀιωατὰ,ἢ ἀιωατόν. ιτὲ τὰ ζωντὰ, ἢ κινητὸν, motus est actus, potentia entis quatenus tale: possibilis, quatenus possibile: mobilis, quatenus mobile. qualis nempe motus fit in procreatione arboris initio ab imperfecte radicis germine, ad truncū 10 & ramos progressio. At ἐντελέχεια, fi perfectio fit (ut est in Ariftotelis Philosophia) idem quod ἐνέργεια, ἀρχὴ πλέωσις, non potest huic itioni ab imperfecto ad perfectum convenire: Sin autem ἐντελέχεια fit idem quod progressio ab imperfecto 15 ad perfectū, ut Ariftoteli ibidem dicitur ἐνέργεια ἀπλῶς, actus imperfectus, nihil aliud erit ἐντελέχεια quám κίνησις:totaq; hæc definitio non aliud significabit,quám motus,est mot9 mobilis quatenus mobile: nec omnino quicquam definiet. 20 Ergo labor Ariftotelis in colligendis & cumulandis Physicorum veterum commentis & placitis defatigati magn9 hic apparet: principia logica,leges, judicia illa summa non apparēt. Itaque P. Ramus defatigato succurrit, idque facit, 25 quod Ariftoteles optavit fecisse: Definitionem istam nihil definientem é medio tollit: motumque,idem quod effectum, facit:Idque de thefauris Ariftoteleæ bibliothecæ, P.Ramus item desumpsit. Caussa efficiens & movens,idem est,ut 30 antea ex Ariftotele patuit: sic enim principium motus est 3.ca. 2.Physici,& 2.cap.5.Philosophiæ: ergo motus, est effectus caussæ efficientis. Item agere & pati, & idem Ariftoteli 3. cap. 3. Physici, fæpeq; aliás quod movere & moveri: Ergo, ait P.Ramus, Ariftotelis sententia, actio & motus, idem est. Atqui hæc etiă affectus seu motus doctrina, logica est, non physica: Ariftoteles enim quæstionem hanc, Utrúm movere & moveri, sit idem quod agere & pati, ἀπορίαν λογικὴν, quæstionem logicam nominat 3. cap. 3. Physici, disputatque, actionem & passionem, motũ esse unicum, ratione tantúm differentem: ut motus idem, est in magistro διδασκαλία, doctrina, in auditore μάθησις disciplina: eadēq; via est Thebis Athenas, & Athenis Thebas, deniq; dubitat, utrúm eodē nomine, actio passioq; possit appellari: neq; putat, propter ὁμωνυμίαν: idq; rectè: Effectus enim, est adjunctum patiētis. Sed eadē res duobus in Logica ipsa locis lōgé testatiōr est: primo, ubi agere & pati, id est movere & moveri, de categoriis decē, una efficitur: secūdo, ad finem Categoriarum, caput præcipuū de motu, deque motus generibus, in Dialectica proponitur, & differentiē ipsorū inter se contrariæ explicātur. Quare tot testimoniis videmus doctrinā motus esse logicā. Sed tamē argumentũ in eadē Ariftotelis bibliotheca etiam contrarium est 1.cap.3. Physici, quód φύσις, id est natura, sit principiū motus, ideoq; sit Physici de motu præcipere. Atqui (ait P.Ramus) φύσις q proponitur philosophiē, corporū naturalium, non erat definienda principiū motus: hæc enim definitio, est logica definitio caussæ efficiētis, ut definitur 2.Physico, & in Philosophia 2, ca. 5. lib. Quamobrē videmus, ut Ariftoteleis argumētis & instrumentis logicus hic locus á P. Ramo expurgetur, ut motus neq; recté definitus, neq; justè physicis attributus: Sed saxũ hïc multò durius est, de generibus motuũ, quæ nullum doctrinæ micam habere P. Ramus asserit: utq; efficiētem, materiam, formā, finem, sic effectum specie individuum facit. Ergo quæstio hęc diligeter est attendenda. Aristoteles primo capite tertii Physici ait, quot species sunt en tis, tot esse species motus: entis autem species quatuor esse, substantiam, quātitatem, qualitatem, locum: quare motus item quatuor esse species, in substantia, formā & privatione: in quantitate, perfectum imperfectum: in qualitate, alibum nigrũ: in loco, suprá infrá. alibi motus istos appellat perspicuis nominibus γένεσιν, φθορὰν, αὔξησιν, μείωσιν, ἀλλοίωσιν, τὸ κατὰ τόπον μεταβολὴν: ortū, interitum, accretionem, imminutionem, alterationem, secundum locum mutationem. Quid igitur P. Ramus ad hūc Aristotelis syllogismum? sanè utrique parti resistit, & ait, verum non esse, adjūcti genera ex subjecto requirere: nec hominum genera é solis & terris ab homine habitatis probè & logicè dividi in Britannos, Hispanos, Gallos, Germanos, Italos, & infinita ejusmodi genera: sic neque genera motus commodé recenseri é generibus entum, non á quibus fiant, sed quibus accidant. Atque ita pars ista syllogismi, ut captiosa refellitur: neq; vero reliqua minús est aliena: Quatuor species entis hīc Melissus, aut Zeno nescio quis dixerat substantiā, quantitatem, qualitatem, locum. At, inquit P. RaP. Ramus, categoriæ, vel (ut Aristoteles loquitur) species entis, sunt in logicis decem: item 2. cap. 1. Physici, entis genera tria fiunt, substantia, quantitas, qualitas: locus autem nō adhibetur: item 1. cap. 5. Phys. primum genus motuū horū rejicitur, & tria tantùm genera retinentur, quantitatis, qualitatis, loci: deniq; in prima Philosophia, primæ entis species & differētię longè dissimiliter appellantur, caussæ, comparata, totaq; logicæ inventionis genera. Quapropter altera pars syllogismi, philosophorū in Aristotelis bibliothecam collectorū magnam inconstantiam & contradictione arguit: unde entium quadripartitam divisionem levissimam esse constat. Quare syllogismi hujus & propositio & assumptio multis modis captiosæ sunt, & veris in bibliotheca Aristotelis authoritatibus abundè cōfutatæ. Quapropter ubicunq; caussæ concurret ad aliquid efficiendum, effectio illa erit motus, sive substantia, sive quantitas, sive qualitas, sive quid libet aliud gignatur, sive etiā quod non sit, é fictis caussis comminiscamur, motus erit: generationi aut corruptio ejus ex quo res nova fit, annexa est: ut in substantia, cùm generatur seges, semē corrūpitur: Sic accretio, est generatio majoris quantitatis, & corruptio quædam pristini generis: sic alteratio, est caloris, frigoris, aut qualitatis cujuslibet novæ generatio, & corruptio pristinæ: progressio, est generatio quædā novi loci, mutatio corruptioq; pristini. Sed hoc Schole P. Ramí physicæ uberiūs & plenius explicabūt. Itaq; ut efficientis, materiæ, formæ, finis cōsideratio e generalis est per omne & ens & non ens communiter dispersa, sic effectorum seu motuum & doctrina & usus de factis, dictis, consiliis, omnibusq; corporis vel animi vel vtriusq; eventis, est intelligenda: Sic motus grammaticus, erit declinare nomina, conjugare verba, utraq; conectere, pronutiare & scribere, & similiter in caeteris artib9: deniq; movere & efficere, idem est: Itaque motus & effectus, idem: sed nomine effectus, non solum actio ipsa, sed opus etiam actione perfectu hic intelligitur. Huc dicta] Effectorum, ut dixi, species nullae sunt verae, attame modi quidam subjectis exemplis sunt diversi, ut dicta, scripta, & cofilia. Pericles] In cujus labris veteres comici, etiam cum ei maledicere(quod tum Athenis fieri licebat) dixerunt lepore m habitasse, ut est Oratorio primo, vel wáw suadendi deam sesitavisse, ut est in Bruto. Ideoq; ab Aristophane poeta dictus est fulgurare, tonare, permisere Graeciam. At nihil posteritati mansurisque mox literis reliquit, ait Quintilianus lib.12. cap.10. Hortefius ante Cicerone rex eloquentiae habitus est: & postea Ciceroni, quoad vixit, fecundus: at ejus scripta longe intra famam fuerunt, ait Quintilianus lib.11. cap. 3. Demosthenis autem & Ciceronis laus est utraq; bene dicendi tum voce, tum scripto. Parmenio & Philotas] Philotas filius ante lapidibus est obrutus: deinde Parmenio pater trucidat. Quintus Curtius de rebus gestis Alexandri scripsit latine libros decem, & in sexto habet hanc historiam. Arrianus scripsit octo graece, qui latine etiam conversi sunt, in quorum tertio, hanc historiam complexus est. Lentuli autem & Cethegi historia est in Sallustio, & Catilinariis orationibus Ciceronis. Horatius] Locus Horatii est primo libro epistolarum, in epistola ad Torquatum, causseq; illae ebrietatis antecedunt, potare, & spargere flores Incipiam, pariatq; vel inconsultus haberi.
units.tr: Effect] The category of causes was rich and copious in the Topics, in the four kinds: efficient and material, formal and final. The category of effects follows. As a logical genus it is indivisible, yet in use it is by far the most copious. In Aristotle's philosophy this subject is properly called αἴτιατὸν [caused thing], and in Latin it could properly be called the caused (causatum), if usage allowed. It is also called πρᾶξις, ἔργον, ἐνέργεια, ποίησις, γένεσις, κίνησις [action, work, activity, production, generation, motion], which in Latin are action, work, act, effection, generation, motion. In Latin they are "effect" (effectus) and "event" (eventum, "eventus"). But if you look at the name, "effect" (effectus or effectum) properly refers to an efficient cause. Indeed, for the Latins, as Cicero says in the Topics and in the Partitions, there is only one kind of cause, the efficient, as was said earlier, and the effect answers to the efficient cause as to all causes. Yet the end moves one to act, and form and matter constitute things. So the effect arises from all causes. Although the name points to the origin of a single genus, it has nonetheless gained common use among everyone, so it should be kept, and the effect is understood as the caused thing, αἰτιατόν. But truly, just as the topic of causes has spread out into almost all philosophy in endless repetition, so the topic of effects has been scattered very widely. And just as P. Ramus, in the category of causes, took pains to gather the fruits, to clean them, and to store them in a place ordered by Aristotle's laws, so will be the category of effects. Of the ten categories, the one on action and passion is treated together with the Posterior Analytics. The topic of effects is cited with causes only very sparingly in the Topics, namely twice: once in the third book and again in the sixth. But this topic occupied almost the whole of the last books of the Physics, under the name of motion. Therefore let us attend to P. Ramus's Aristotelian husbandry, which, with its hook, cut away as many thorns as it removed repetitions. For the topic of effects is indeed general, as it is proposed in the whole Organon; so, according to Aristotle's rule καθόλου πρῶτον [the general first], it must be proposed once and generally. But on physical motions, P. Ramus's task was much more difficult, since it seemed to embrace a physical rather than a logical matter. I shall touch on the main points here briefly. First, the definition of motion, which seems most precise, has thrown the whole matter into confusion in physics. It is defined in the Physics, book 3, chapter 1: motion is the act of a potential being as such: possible as possible, mobile as mobile. This is the sort of motion that occurs in the growth of a tree, the progress from the germ of an imperfect root to trunk and branches. But if ἐντελέχεια [actuality/completion] means perfection (as it does in Aristotle's philosophy), the same as ἐνέργεια [activity], then it cannot fit a progress from imperfect to perfect. But if ἐντελέχεια means the same as progress from imperfect to perfect, which in the same place Aristotle calls ἐνέργεια ἁπλῶς [activity simply], an imperfect act, then ἐντελέχεια will be nothing other than κίνησις [motion]; and this whole definition will signify nothing but motion, which is the mobile as mobile, and will define nothing at all. So Aristotle's labour in gathering and piling up the fancies and opinions of the ancient physicists is clearly seen to be wearisome; the logical principles, the laws, and those summary judgements do not appear. Therefore P. Ramus comes to the aid of the weary reader, and does what Aristotle wished to have done: he removes that defining-nothing definition from the middle, and makes motion the same as effect. And P. Ramus took this too from the treasures of Aristotle's library. That the efficient cause and the moving cause are the same, as was shown above from Aristotle, is clear: for the principle of motion is in the Physics, book 3, chapter 2, and in the Philosophy, book 2, chapter 5. Therefore motion is the effect of the efficient cause. Likewise, to act and to be acted upon, which in Aristotle (Physics 3, chapter 3, and often elsewhere) is the same as to move and to be moved. Therefore, says P. Ramus, according to Aristotle's opinion, action and motion are the same. And yet this doctrine of affection or motion is logical, not physical. For Aristotle, in Physics 3, chapter 3, calls this question, whether to move and to be moved are the same as to act and to be acted upon, a ἀπορίαν λογικήν [logical question], and he argues that action and passion are a single motion, differing only in reason, just as motion is in the teacher διδασκαλία [teaching], in the learner μάθησις [learning]; and the road from Thebes to Athens is the same as from Athens to Thebes. Finally he doubts whether action and passion can be called by the same name, and he does not think it is because of ὁμωνυμία [ambiguity], and he is right: for effect is an attribute of the one acted upon. But the same thing is far more clearly attested in two places in Logic itself: first, where to act and to be acted upon, that is, to move and to be moved, are made into one of the ten categories; second, at the end of the Categories, the chief chapter on motion and the kinds of motion is set out in the Dialectic, and their mutual contraries are explained. Hence we see from so many testimonies that the doctrine of motion is logical. But there is an argument to the contrary in the same library of Aristotle, Physics 1, chapter 3: that φύσις [nature], that is, nature, is the principle of motion, and therefore it belongs to physics to teach about motion. Yet (says P. Ramus) φύσις, which is proposed to philosophy as the nature of natural bodies, was not to be defined as the principle of motion. For this definition is the logical definition of the efficient cause, as it is defined in the Physics, book 2, and in the Philosophy, book 2, chapter 5. Hence we see that, by Aristotle's own arguments and instruments, this logical topic is purged by P. Ramus, so that motion is neither rightly defined nor justly attributed to physics. But the rock here is much harder: concerning the kinds of motion, which P. Ramus asserts have no crumb of doctrine in them, and which, just as he makes the efficient, matter, form and end, so he makes the effect a specific individual. Therefore this question must be carefully considered. Aristotle, in the first chapter of the third book of the Physics, says that as many kinds of motion as there are kinds of being. And there are four kinds of being: substance, quantity, quality, place. Hence there are likewise four kinds of motion: in substance, form and privation; in quantity, perfect and imperfect; in quality, white and black; in place, above and below. Elsewhere he names these motions by plain words: generation, corruption, increase, decrease, alteration, and change according to place: birth, death, growth, diminution, alteration, and motion with respect to place. What then does P. Ramus say to this syllogism of Aristotle? He certainly resists both parts, and says that it is not true that subordinate genera must be drawn from the subject, nor that the kinds of men are properly and logically divided, from the sun and the lands inhabited by men, into British, Spanish, French, German, Italian, and countless such kinds; so neither can the kinds of motion be conveniently listed from the kinds of being, not by what they arise from, but by what they happen to. And so that part of the syllogism is refuted as captious. Nor is the rest any less foreign. Melissus, or some Zeno, had said here that the four kinds of being are substance, quantity, quality, place. But, says P. Ramus, the categories, or (as Aristotle puts it) the kinds of being, are ten in the logical works. Likewise, in the Physics, book 2, chapter 1, there are three kinds of being: substance, quantity, quality; place is not used. Likewise, in the Physics, book 1, chapter 5, the first kind of these motions is rejected, and only three kinds are kept: of quantity, of quality, of place. Finally, in First Philosophy, the species and differences of being are named in quite different ways: causes, comparatives, and all the kinds of logical invention. Therefore the second part of the syllogism reveals the great inconsistency and contradiction of the philosophers collected in Aristotle's library, whence it is clear that the fourfold division of beings is very shallow. Hence both the proposition and the assumption of this syllogism are captious in many ways, and are thoroughly refuted by true authorities in Aristotle's library. Therefore, wherever causes come together to bring something about, that bringing about will be a motion, whether a substance, a quantity, a quality, or anything else is generated; and whether what is generated is something that did not previously exist, imagined from fictitious causes, it will be motion. Generation, or the corruption of that from which a new thing comes, is joined to it. Thus in substance, when corn is generated, the seed is corrupted. So growth is the generation of a greater quantity and a certain corruption of its former kind. So alteration is the generation of heat, cold, or any new quality, and the corruption of the former one. Progress is the generation of a certain new place and the change and corruption of the former. But the Schools of P. Ramus's physics will explain this more fully and completely. And so, just as the consideration of the efficient, matter, form and end is general, spread through all being and non-being alike, so the doctrine and use of effects, or motions, is to be understood concerning deeds, words, counsels, and all the events of body or mind or both. Thus grammatical motion will be to decline nouns, conjugate verbs, join both, pronounce and write; and likewise in the other arts. Finally, to move and to effect are the same. Therefore motion and effect are the same; but by the name of effect is understood here not only the action itself, but also the work brought to completion by the action. Of this place are] The praise of Caesar and of Marcellus in Cicero's speech for Manilius, the censure of Piso and Clodius in the orations against Piso and for his own house, are taken from here in large part. Aeneid, book six] The deeds of various peoples are compared here, to the praise of the Roman name: the Corinthians worked bronze, the Parians marble, the Babylonians and Egyptians the stars, more perfectly; the Romans, political discipline. Sayings] Of effects, as I said, there are no true kinds, yet certain modes differ with the subjects they are given, such as sayings, writings, and counsels. Pericles] On whose lips, the old comic poets said, even when people reviled him (which was then permitted at Athens), there dwelt grace, as is stated in the first book of the Orator, or that the goddess of persuasion sat there, as in the Brutus. Therefore the poet Aristophanes said that he lightened, thundered, and threw Greece into confusion. But, Quintilian says in book 12, chapter 10, he left nothing to posterity or to writings that would last. Hortensius, before Cicero, was held to be the king of eloquence, and afterwards, while he lived, second only to Cicero; but his writings fell well short of his fame, Quintilian says in book 11, chapter 3. The praise of Demosthenes and Cicero, however, is that both spoke well, both in voice and in writing. Parmenio and Philotas] Philotas, the son, was first stoned to death, and then his father Parmenio was butchered. Quintus Curtius wrote ten books in Latin on the deeds of Alexander, and in the sixth he has this story. Arrian wrote eight books in Greek, which were also translated into Latin, and in the third of these he gives this story. The story of Lentulus and Cethegus is in Sallust and in Cicero's Catilinarian orations. Horace] The passage of Horace is in the first book of Epistles, in the letter to Torquatus, and those causes of drunkenness come before it: "I shall begin to drink and to scatter flowers, and may I be thought thoughtless."

units.la: Hic vero septem ebrietatis effecta numerantur, quod arcana detegat, quod stulte confidentes & temere audaces faciat, quod ex animis scrupulum omnem evellat & eximat, quod sapientiae fatuam opinionem adferat, quod garrulos & loquaces efficiat, quod in summa paupertate dissolutos & prodigos reddat. Atq; haec de causarum & effectorum argumento: quod e causis ad effecta, dicitur Aristoteli διότι propter quid: contra ex effectis ad causas, dicitur ὅτι, quia: & illa quam haec probatio & explicatio longe praestantior est & excellentior: itaq; circulus mutuae affectionis hic magnus est, sed semicirculus ille clarior multo atq; illustrior.
units.tr: Here seven effects of drunkenness are listed: it reveals secrets; it makes men foolishly confident and rashly bold; it strips away and removes every scruple from the mind; it brings a foolish reputation for wisdom; it makes men garrulous and talkative; and in great poverty it makes them dissolute and prodigal. These points concern the argument from causes and effects. Aristotle calls reasoning from cause to effect διότι [dioti], "the reason why"; reasoning from effect to cause is ὅτι [hoti], "that". The latter kind of proof and explanation is far more excellent and outstanding. So the circle of mutual relation here is large, but that half-circle is much clearer and brighter.

units.la: ARgumentum modo quodam cõsentaneũ succedit:ut subjectũ & adjunctum. Subjectum est, cui aliquid adjungitur. Anima, est subjectum scientiæ,ignorantiæ,virtutis, vitii: Corpus,sanitatis, morbi,roboris,infirmitatis,pulchritudinis,deformitatis.Homo,subjectum est divitiarum,paupertatis,honoris,infamiæ,vestitus,comitatus.Locus, est spatium rei locatæ:Sic philosophi divinis entib9, licet parte & magnitudine carentibus, attribuūt locũ: sic Geometræ, locum lociq; differentias in rebus Geometricis:sic Physici etiam multó diligentiús,in rebus physicis considerant, in mundo,in elementis simplicibus, in rebus cõpositis. Sic Virgilius in Georgicis suum quemq; propositis rebus locum deligendũ admonet,ut segetibus, arboribus,vitibus,pascuis:
units.tr: The argument follows in a certain fitting order: the subject and the adjunct. The subject is that to which something is joined. The soul is the subject of knowledge, ignorance, virtue and vice. The body is the subject of health, sickness, strength, weakness, beauty and deformity. Man is the subject of riches, poverty, honour, infamy, clothing and companionship. Place is the space occupied by a thing placed. Thus the philosophers assign a place to divine beings, although they lack parts and magnitude; thus the geometers consider place and the differences of place in geometrical matters; and thus the natural philosophers consider it much more carefully in physical matters, in the world, in the simple elements, and in compound things. So Virgil in the Georgics advises that each thing proposed should have its own place chosen for it, as for crops, trees, vines and pastures:
