units.la: Et quid quæq; ferat regio,et qd quæq; recusét.
units.tr: what each region bears, and what each refuses.

units.la: Hic segetes,illic veniunt felicius uvæ:
units.tr: Here the crops, there the grapes come more happily;

units.la: Arborei fœtus alibi,atq; injussa virescunt
units.tr: elsewhere trees bear their fruit, and unbidden grasses grow green

units.la: Gramina.—
units.tr: (the grass).

units.la: Sensilia sensuum, & res virtutibus ac vitiis propositæ, subjecta virtutum & vitiorum hoc modo nominatur. Color, est subjectum visus: sonus, subjectum audi tus. quia hi sensus in his sensilibus occupantur & exercētur. Virtutes & vitia declaranturin Ethicis hoc argumēto:temperantia & intemperātia, voluptate:magnanimitas & ignavia, periculo: liberalitas & avaritia, divitiis. Sic res numerabilis, Arithmeticæ:mēsurabilis, Geometriæ subjicitur. Ejusmodi subjecto Cicero secunda Agraria disputat, inter Campanos nullam contentionem esse, quia nullus sit honor: Non glorię cupiditate (ait) efferebantur, propterea quód ubi honos publicē non est, ibi gloriæ cupiditas esse non potest: non contentione, necambitione discordes: nihil enim superat, de quo certaret: nihil quod contrā peterent, nihil ubi disiderent. Eodē argumento á Propertio dictum est,
units.tr: Sensible things, and things set over against virtues and vices, are named in this way as the subjects of the virtues and vices. Colour is the subject of sight; sound is the subject of hearing, since these senses are occupied and exercised in these sensible things. Virtues and vices are explained in the Ethics by this argument: temperance and intemperance by pleasure; magnanimity and cowardice by danger; liberality and avarice by riches. Thus the countable thing is subject to arithmetic, and the measurable to geometry. Cicero, in the second Agrarian Speech, argues on this kind of subject that there is no contention among the Campanians, because there is no honour among them. They were not carried away by a desire for glory, he says, because where there is no public honour there can be no desire for glory; nor were they at odds through rivalry or ambition, for there was nothing for them to contend over, nothing they might seek against one another, nothing for which they might quarrel. On the same argument Propertius has said:

units.la: Navita de ventis, de tauris narrat arator, Enumerat miles vulnera, pastor oves.
units.tr: "The sailor tells of winds, the ploughman of bulls; the soldier counts his wounds, the shepherd his sheep."

units.la: Argumentum modo] Duæ superiores categoriæ caussæ & effecti, latissimos fines & tautologias
units.tr: The argument just given: the two higher categories, cause and effect, have boundless scope and endless tautologies throughout the whole of Aristotle's works.

units.la: immensas in tota Aristotelis bibliotheca habuere, duae quae sequuntur, subjecti & adjuncti, per magnum item campū consimilis obscuritatis efficiunt: Categoremata Porphyrii hanc partitionem obscurius indicant: accidentis enim nomine, adjuncta apertius comprehenduntur: sped ciei autem nomine, subjectum obscuratur, cūm a Porphyrio specie proprium dicitur accidere, sed improprie cūm species tantūm referatur ad genus. In capite de accidente, συμβεβηκός, subjectum proprie accidenti opponitur: In Categoriis, partitio eadem subjecti & adjuncti paulo secūs comprehenditur, tanquam substantia una subjecta fit omnibus accidentibus novem reliquarum Categoriarum, nomen ipsum, συμβεβηκός interdum sic usurpatur: In Analyticis posterioribus συμβεβηκός & συμβεβηκὸς, subjectum & accidens, distinctius proponuntur: in Topicis de accidente problema praecipue factū est, & duo libri, secundus & tertius, eo accommodati: In Physicis cap. 14. libri 4. de loco & tempore fuerūt: quibus tautologiis tam multis intelligimus Philosophorum Logicorum, unde opera illa collecta sunt, ingenia feminibus partitioïs hujus gratia vidata parturiville magis quām peperisse. Quapropter Aristotelea τὰ λαθόντα πρῶτον falce vehementer hic opus est, ut res generalis semel & generaliter doceatur, caetera toties iterata amputentur. Ergo diligentiam P. Rami in observandis Aristotelis legibus & principiis hic agnoscamus, de subjecto jam separatim agamus. Subjecti locus, praeter tautologias illas ante memoratas, iteratur in Topicis novies: Id non est catholicum : Aristoteles in Philosophia II. cap.7.lib. docet essentiam suis accidentibus esse priorem, λόγῳ, γνώσει, χρόνῳ φύσει: ratione, notione, tempore, natura: quod generaliter de omni subjecto (si tamen omnino verum sit) queat intelligi. at subjectum proprio adjuncto quamvis & λόγῳ & γνώσει & φύσει sit prius & antiquius, attamen tempore prius non est. Locus] Haec definitio veteres philosophos atq; in primis Aristotelem, novem totis capitibus primis quarti Physici vehementer exercuit: Plato definierat χώραν ἡ διάστημα, regionem & spatium, quo res comprehenderentur: ut locus, non sit tantum ambitus locatae rei, sed totum interius spatium: cujus differentiae sunt non solum in ambitu dextum, sinistrum, ante, post: sed etiam sursum, deorsum, & loci medium deniq; intelligatur: quae dicuntur Aristoteli I. ca. 4.Physici.loci partes & species.8.cap.8.Physici, ἐναντιώσεις καὶ διαφορὰ, contradictiones & differentiae, quae non tantum constant θέσει πρὸς ἡμᾶς, situ quo ad nos, sed etiam τῇ φύσει ἡ δυνάμει natura & vi sua: quo ad nos enim situs mutatur, saepeque dextrum est nobis, quod erat sinistrum: Itaque quamvis locus, sit res plane logica, & spatii tantum designatione constet, stabilis tamen est, & fixas habet differentias & immutabiles, & quanvis ἀντιμετάστασις, transmutatio rerum locatarum vera sit, loci tamen στάσις ἀμετακίνητον, status immutabilis ab Aristotele defenditur. attamen non solum constans illa fixaq; loci designatio teneatur, sed affirmetur etiam generalis & omnium rerum communis,id est logica loci cõsideratio, quæ sit etiam rerum incorporearum. Sic enim Aristote les ait,ubi,esse categoriá, & genus entis: & antea Locū speciem entis: sicio. cap.8.Physici, primi motoris,quem facit ἀμφῇ, ἀμιγτῇ, sine parte, sine magnitudine, locum esse in suprema mūdi superficie: sic idem ȝ.cap.1. de Cœlo, ait cõsensu gentium, supremum locum mundi attributum Deo. Et certè si locus logicus, & sola spatii defignatione constans, divinis entibus attribuatur, ut naturæ illę sint infinitę: sic locus infinitus intelligetur: quomodo philosophus ille dixit, Deum, sphærá esse, cujus centrū esset ubiq;, peripheria nusquam: neq; mirabilius fuerit Deo locum, quám caussam, quám factū, quám quodlibet aliud logicū tribuere: nec logica tota esset entis & nó entis, nisi quoq; Dei esset. Ergo istá loci Dialecticam P. Ramus é novem capitum illorū sepibus extraxit, & é legibus Aristotelis, á Physica ad Logicam retulit. Sic geometrę] Aristoteles 6.ca.1.de Generatione, mathematicorū se discipulū profitetur in Philosophia de tactu & loco. Etenim mathematicis cõsimiliter de tactu & loco statuedū, sive sit utrumq; ipsorū separatum, sive secús.Itaq; Aristoteles mathematicos magistros secutus 1. cap. 6. Physici, tangere definit, quorum extrema sunt simul:simul aút,quę sunt in eodem loco.Tangant igitur,ait P.Ramus, periphęra & recta, sese:aut peripherę duę, & cōcludatur, Ergo extrema punćta erunt in eodem loco:sunt item lineæ in loco, sunt superficies in loco,nõ corpora solúm:quin Geometria de planis tribus, triangulo, quadrato, fexangulo, folidis duobus pyramide & cubo, completibus locum, citatur ab Ariftotele 8. cap. 3. lib. de Cælo, & de figuris complentibus locum P. Ramus accuratius in geometria. Deniq; Ariftoteles in Categoriis ait proprium effe magnitudinis, partes habere alicubi fitas: & Proclus ad 35. ppofitionem 1. elementorum, cúm theoremata Geometriæ topica & localia edifferit, locum, ait effe parallelogrammi fpatium inter duas parallelas có prehenfum. Quare geometricis rebus fuus etiá locus eft, tale nempe fpatiũ: imó á folis geometricis rebus locus occupatur: lux, color, ac multó minus naturæ divinæ, locum nullum occupant, licet in loco dicantur effe: At magnitudines non folúm funt in loco, fed occupant locũ: neq; duo corpora fimul effe poffunt: at lux duplex, triplex, centuplex, deniq; in eodé loco poteft effe, neq; tamen locum occupare, quin alia lux in eodem loco, vel millies major effe posfit. Quare magnitudo eft in loco, & locus eft fpatiũ rei locatæ: & fpatium quidé, fola defignatione cõftans. talis eft tota cæli & aftrorum pofitio & locatio, immutabili defignatione cõftans in parallelis, meridianis, & cæteris circulis.
units.tr: The two categories that follow, subject and adjunct, likewise produce a similar obscurity over a wide field. Porphyry's Categories indicate this division less clearly: under the name of accident, adjuncts are comprehended more plainly, but under the name of species the subject is obscured, since Porphyry says that a property belongs to a species, though improperly, as a species is referred only to its genus. In the chapter on the accident [συμβεβηκός], the subject is properly opposed to the accident. In the Categories the same division of subject and adjunct is treated somewhat differently, as if one substance were the subject of all the accidents of the nine remaining categories; the word itself [συμβεβηκός] is sometimes used in this way. In the Posterior Analytics, συμβεβηκός and συμβεβηκὸς, the accident and the subject, are set out more distinctly. In the Topics the problem of the accident is treated especially, and two books, the second and third, are devoted to it. In Physics book 4, chapter 14, it is treated in connection with place and time. From so many tautologies we understand that the minds of the logicians and philosophers, from whose works those collections were made, laboured over the seeds of this division and were in travail rather than bringing forth a birth. Therefore we need here the scythe of Aristotle, [τὰ λαθόντα πρῶτον], so that the general matter is taught once and in general, and the rest, repeated so often, is cut away. Let us therefore acknowledge P. Ramus's diligence in observing the laws and principles of Aristotle here, and now treat the subject separately. The topic of the subject, apart from the tautologies mentioned above, is repeated nine times in the Topics. This is not sound. Aristotle, in Philosophy II, chapter 7, teaches that the essence is prior to its accidents in logic, in knowledge, in time and in nature [λόγῳ, γνώσει, χρόνῳ, φύσει]: by reason, by notion, by time, by nature. This may be understood generally of every subject, if it is altogether true. But the subject is prior and more ancient than its proper adjunct both in reason, in knowledge and in nature, yet it is not prior in time. Locus (place): this definition greatly exercised the ancient philosophers, and Aristotle above all, in the first nine chapters of Physics book 4. Plato defined place [χώρα ἢ διάστημα] as the region or space in which things are contained, so that place is not merely the surrounding of the placed thing but the whole interior space. Its differences are not only right, left, front and back in the surrounding, but also up, down, and the middle of the place. These are what Aristotle calls the parts and species of place (Physics 1, ch. 4). In Physics 8, ch. 8, he speaks of opposites and differences [ἐναντιώσεις καὶ διαφοραί], which consist not only in position relative to us [θέσει πρὸς ἡμᾶς], but also in nature and power [τῇ φύσει ἢ δυνάμει]. For relative to us the position changes, and often what was left is right for us. Thus, although place is a thing purely logical, consisting only in the designation of space, it is nevertheless stable, and has fixed and unchangeable differences; and although the exchange [ἀντιμετάστασις] of placed things is real, the standing still of place [στάσις ἀμετακίνητον], an immovable state, is defended by Aristotle. Not only is that constant and fixed designation of place to be held, but the general consideration of place common to all things, that is, the logical consideration, is affirmed, and this extends also to incorporeal things. For Aristotle says that the place where is a category, and a genus of being, and earlier he calls place a species of being (Physics 8, ch. 8). And of the first mover, which he makes [ἀμφῇ, ἀμιγτῇ], without part and without magnitude, he says it is in the highest surface of the world. So in De Caelo 1, ch. 1, he says by the consent of the nations that the highest place of the world is attributed to God. And certainly, if logical place, consisting only in the designation of space, is attributed to divine beings, so that those natures are infinite, then place will be understood as infinite, just as that philosopher said that God is a sphere whose centre is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. Nor would it be more marvellous to attribute place to God than cause, or deed, or any other logical thing; nor would the whole of logic be of being and non-being, unless it were also of God. Therefore P. Ramus drew this logic of place out of the hedges of those nine chapters, and from Aristotle's laws transferred it from Physics to Logic. Sic geometrae (so do the geometers): Aristotle, in De Generatione 6, ch. 1, professes himself a disciple of the mathematicians in philosophy concerning contact and place. For contact and place must be determined for mathematical things in the same way, whether each is separate or otherwise. So Aristotle, following the mathematical masters, in Physics 1, ch. 6, defines touching as things whose extremities are together, and together [simul] are things in the same place. Therefore, says P. Ramus, a circumference and a straight line touch each other, or two circumferences; and it follows that the extreme points are in the same place. Lines are also in place, surfaces are in place, not bodies only. Moreover, Geometry, concerning the three plane figures, the triangle, square and hexagon, and the two solids, pyramid and cube, which fill place, is cited by Aristotle in De Caelo 3, ch. 3, and P. Ramus treats of the figures that fill place more exactly in Geometry. Finally, Aristotle says in the Categories that it is proper to magnitude to have parts situated somewhere; and Proclus, on the 35th proposition of Euclid's first book, when he discusses the topical and local theorems of geometry, says that place is the space of a parallelogram contained between two parallels. Hence geometrical things too have their own place, namely such a space; indeed place is occupied by geometrical things alone. Light, colour, and much less the divine nature, occupy no place, although they are said to be in a place. But magnitudes not only are in place but occupy it, and two bodies cannot be together. Yet light may be double, triple, a hundredfold, and may be in the same place without occupying it, since another light in the same place may be a thousand times greater. Therefore magnitude is in place, and place is the space of the placed thing; and this space is constant by designation alone. Such is the whole position and location of the heavens and stars, constant by an unchanging designation in the parallels, meridians and other circles.

units.la: Phyfici] Locus in Phyficis rebus minimé dubius eft, & hac de re eft 2. cap. 2. de Cælo, & fæpé aliás. Atq; hæc P. Rami confirmatio eft, quod locus fit fpatium rei locatæ. Contraria in Ariftotelis Phylofophia doctrina etiam eft, quód locus fit terminus corporis comprehédentis, primus immobilis: quod fi de folo corporũ phyficorũ loco diceretur, non effet tamen Ariftotelis haé ipsa de re, Philosophiæ consentaneum, qui mundani loci deorsum, collocat in centro mundi: & totum hoc spatium ab imo undiq; sursum, mundi locum facit. Quare definitio illa ita refellitur in physicis: neq; tria argumenta Aristotelis contra Platonem (quód locus non fit spatium) multó valentiora sunt: primò, quia locus fit tantum corporis: secundo, quia loca essent infinita: tertio, quia locus esset mutabilis. Primum Plato negaret, & placitum Aristotelis esse diceret: secundum concederet, eo modo quo magnitudinem vel divisione, vel additione infinitam concederet: tertium pro se arriperet, & diceret, spatiü designatione sola constans, immutabile esse: locum autem Aristotelis é superficie mutabilem esse, quoties corpus superficiei moveretur. Quamobrem Platonis locus teneatur, spatium nepe locatæ rei: qui sive fit oppletus corporeis rebus, sive non, ut vacuum in physicis rebus habeatur, nihil ad Logicá, quę est entis & nö entis: Campos Elysios, hortos Hesperidum & pleraq; alia loca poetæ fingüt: logicum hoc subjectum, & logicus locus est. Sed de doctrina illa Physica Aristotelis accuratiús suis locis Scholæ physicę P. Rami declarabunt. Georgicis] Georgica, sunt præcepta de agricultura, à γῆ, terra, & ἔργον, op9. In primo autem Georgico, Virgilius differētias locorum propositis rebus congruorū describit. Sensilia] Doctrina est Aristotelis in Philosophia 5. cap. 4. lib. ... subjecta quæ faciūt sensum: Aristoteles enim, sensus moveri censuit rebus extrinsecús incidentibus, & species colorum ad oculos, sonorum ad aures pervenire:ideoq; dicit sensus, & tanquam dicere, fensationes hinc fieri: hæc φαινόμενα vulgus in scholis appellat objecta:quomodo & Tullius loqui videtur:ut in Fato, Visum objectû imprimet illud quidem & quasi signabit in animo speciem suam. sed Ariftotelis verbum, ut dixi, est ὑποκείμενον, subjectum:res intelligatur.hoc autè argumento maxima pars philosophiæ & phyficæ & ethicæ explicatur. Artium omniû subjecta ejusmodi sunt, in quibus artes jam descriptæ, materia formaq; constantes occupātur: Sic Grammaticæ, Rhetoricæ, Logicę. Arithmeticæ, Geometriæ, subjectum, est res ex plicabilis per eas artes:quę ipsa est fermé diver fa á materia & præceptis artium ipsarum.Subjectum artium, etiam materia artium, aliquando subjectum dicitur,sed ambigué. Itaq; præstabit materiam artiû, & id quod suis præceptis interpretantur,appellare tantûm materiam:& id,circa quod exercêtur, appellare tantûm fubjectû. Cāpani in Italia,regni Neopolitani partem faciunt,de quorû moribus Liuius multa scripsit: ut alterum Consulem esse Cāpanû voluerint, ut sese Annibali adversus Romanos adjunxerint,tandêq; severitate magna mulctati, honorib. publicis omnibus spoliati, jus á magistratu Romano peterent. Locus est apud Propertium lib. 2. elegia prima, fubjectis variarum personarum,quod navita de ventis,arator de tauris,miles de vulneribus,pastor
units.tr: Physici] Place is least disputed in natural things, and Aristotle treats this matter in Book 2, chapter 2 of On the Heavens, and often elsewhere. This is P. Ramus's confirmation that place is the space of the thing placed. Aristotle's philosophy also holds the contrary doctrine, that place is the first immobile boundary of the containing body. Even if this were said only of the place of physical bodies, it would not be consistent with Aristotle's own philosophy on this point, since he places the lower regions of the cosmos at the centre of the world and makes the whole space from the bottom upward the place of the cosmos. So that definition is refuted in physics. Nor are Aristotle's three arguments against Plato (that place is not space) much stronger: first, that place belongs only to bodies; second, that places would be infinite; third, that place would be mutable. Plato would deny the first and say it is Aristotle's opinion; he would grant the second, in the way he would grant that magnitude is infinite by division or addition; and the third he would seize for himself, saying that space, which is constant by designation alone, is immutable, whereas Aristotle's place is mutable from the surface, whenever the surface of a body moves. Therefore Plato's view should be held, namely that place is the space of the placed thing, whether or not that space is filled with corporeal things, as the void is supposed to be in physics. This has nothing to do with logic, which deals with being and non-being. The poets invent the Elysian Fields, the gardens of the Hesperides and many other places; this logical subject is a logical place. But Ramus's physics school will explain Aristotle's physical doctrine more accurately in its own place. Georgicis] The Georgics are precepts on agriculture, from ge, earth, and ergon, work. In the first book of the Georgics, Virgil describes the differences of places suited to particular crops. Sensilia] This is Aristotle's doctrine in Physics book 5, chapter 4: the subjects that produce sensation. For Aristotle held that the senses are moved by external things striking them, and that the species of colours reach the eyes and of sounds the ears; hence he speaks of sensations as if sensations arose from these. Schools commonly call these phenomena [φαινόμενα] objects, as Cicero also seems to speak in the De fato: the object impresses the sight and, as it were, stamps its image on the mind. But Aristotle's word, as I said, is hypokeimenon [ὑποκείμενον], subject; the thing should be understood thus. By this argument the greater part of philosophy, physics and ethics is explained. The subjects of all arts are of this kind, the things occupied by arts already described, consisting of matter and form: so for grammar, rhetoric and logic, and for arithmetic and geometry, the subject is a thing explicable through those arts, which is almost wholly different from the matter and precepts of the arts themselves. The subject of an art is sometimes also called the matter of the art, but ambiguously. Therefore it will be better to call only the matter of the arts, and that which their precepts interpret, matter, and only that about which they are exercised, subject. Campani] The Campanians form part of the kingdom of Naples, and Livy wrote much about their customs: they wished one of the consuls to be a Campanian, they joined Hannibal against the Romans, and then, punished with great severity and stripped of all public honours, they sought right from the Roman magistrate. There is a passage in Propertius, book 2, elegy 1, where the subjects of various persons are given: the sailor speaks of winds, the ploughman of bulls, the soldier of wounds, the shepherd

units.la: de ovibus : ipse autem de amoribus, loquatur. Hoc subjecti argumento Anacharsis arguebat in Scythia no esse tibicines, quia uites non essent. Eodem multo acutius & elegantius Ulysses Achillem habitu muliebri inter puellarum choros occultum deprehendit, cum ipse mercatoris habitu accessisset ad eas, cum variis fœmineis merci bus, inter quas erant arma quaedam virilia, ad quæ Achilles sese protinus convertit. Locus est Metamorph.13.
units.tr: of sheep, while he himself speaks of love. By this argument of subject Anacharsis argued that there were no flute-players in Scythia, because there were no vines. In the same way, much more acutely and elegantly, Ulysses detected Achilles hidden among the choirs of girls in women's dress: he himself came to them dressed as a merchant, with various women's wares, among which were some manly arms, and Achilles at once turned towards them. The passage is in the Metamorphoses, book 13.

units.la: Præscia venturi genitrix Nereia lethi, Dissimulat cultu natum, & deceperat omnes: In quibus Ajacem: sumptæ fallaciæ vestis, Arma ego fœmineis, animum motura virilem, Mercibus inservi: neque adhuc projecerat heros Virgineos habitus, cum parmam haslamque tenenti. Nate dea, dixi, tibi se peritura reservant Pergama: quid dubitas ingentem evertere Trojam? Injecique manum, fortemque ad fortia misi.
units.tr: Foreseeing the coming death, his Nereid mother hid her son in women's dress and deceived them all: among them Ajax, of the garment she had put on as a disguise. I, to stir his manly spirit, offered him arms among the women's wares; nor had the hero yet cast off his maiden dress when he took up shield and spear. "Son of a goddess," I said, "Pergamum keeps for you its ruin; why do you hesitate to overthrow mighty Troy?" I laid my hand on him and sent the brave man to brave deeds.

units.la: Quare locus subjectorum tantæ utilitatis & ubertatis est in rebus divinis, mathematicis, physicis, ethicis, in omni denique ente & no ente.
units.tr: Therefore the locus of subjects is of such great use and fertility in divine things, in mathematics, in physics, in ethics, and in every being and non-being.

units.la: Cap. XI. De A- djuncto.
units.tr: Chapter XI. On the Adjunct.

units.la: ADjunctum, est cui aliquid subjicitur. quod argumentum etsi subjecto est levius, attamen est copiosius & frequentius: Itaque de ejusmodi signis ait Ovidius 2. de Remedio, (vocabit: Forsitan hæc aliquis (nam sunt quoque) parva Sed quae non prosunt singula, multa juvant. Animi corporisq;, & totius hominis bona & mala, quæ dicuntur, adjuncta sunt animi, corporis, hominis: Denique quicquid ulli subjecto extrinsecus accidit, adjûctum ejus est. ut autem Locus, est in subjectis: sic Tempus, est in adjunctis, duratio nempe rerû præterita, præsens, futura: omninoq; qualitates subjectis præter causas, adjunctæ, sive ppriæ sint, q omni foliq; subjecto semper conveniût, ut homini risus, equo hinnitus, cani latratus: sive communes, quæcûq; nō sunt eo modo propriæ. Hoc genere argumenti Fannium Chæream Cicero sp Roscio Comœdo cavillatur: Non ne ipsum caput & supercilia illa penitus ab rasa, olere malitiâ & clamitare calliditate videntur? nonne ab imis unguib.usq; ad verticem summum (si quam conjecturam affert homini tacita corporis figura, ex fraude, fallaciis, mendaciis constare totus videtur? qui idcirco capite & superciliis semper est rasis, ne pilum ullum viri boni habere dicatur. Sic Martialis secundo libro Zoilum ludit:
units.tr: The adjunct is that to which something is subjoined. Although this argument is lighter than the subject, it is nevertheless more copious and frequent. So Ovid, in the second book of the Remedy of Love, speaks of such signs: "Perhaps someone will call these small things (and there are such), but single ones do not help, while many together do." The good and bad things of the soul and body, and of the whole man, which are called adjuncts, are adjuncts of the soul, of the body, of the man. In short, whatever happens to any subject from outside is its adjunct. As Place is in subjects, so Time is in adjuncts, namely the duration of things past, present and future. In general, qualities joined to subjects apart from their causes are adjuncts, whether they are proper, belonging always and only to that subject, as laughter to man, neighing to horse, barking to dog, or common, whatever is not proper in that way. By this kind of argument Cicero mocks Fannius Chaerea against the comic actor Roscius: do not that head itself and those eyebrows, shaved bare, seem to smell of malice and to cry out cunning? Does he not seem wholly made of fraud, deceit and lies, from the bottom of his nails to the top of his head, if a silent shape of the body offers any conjecture? That is why he always keeps his head and eyebrows shaved, so that he may not be said to have a single hair of a good man. So Martial in book 2 mocks Zoilus:

units.la: Crine ruber, niger ore, brevis pede, lumine lusçus:
units.tr: Red-haired, black-faced, short of foot, one-eyed.
