units.la: Sic vestitus & comitatus,res adjunctę sunt.quo circumstatiæ genere, Dido venatum proficiscens, magnificé quarto Aeneidos depingitur:
units.tr: So dress and retinue are adjuncts. In this circumstantial kind, Dido setting out to hunt is magnificently depicted in the fourth book of the Aeneid:

units.la: Oceanum interea surgens aurora reliquit. It portis,iubare exorto,delecta iuventus: Retia rara,plaga,lato venabula ferro: Massylique ruunt equites, & odora canu vis. Regina thalamo cunctante, ad limina primiPoenorum expectant, ostro, insignis & auroStat sonipes, ac frena ferox spumatia mădit. Tandem progeditur magna stipate caterva, Sidonia picto chlamydem circundata limbo: Cui pharetra ex humero,crines nodantur inAurea purpureā subnectit fibula veste.(aurū
units.tr: Meanwhile the rising dawn left Ocean, and with the sun risen the chosen youth went out through the gates: loose nets, snares, and hunting spears with broad iron heads; the Massylian horsemen rush out with the strong-scented pack. The queen, still lingering in her chamber, the chiefs of the Carthaginians wait at the threshold, splendid in purple and gold, and the proud horse stands, champing foaming bits. At last she comes forth, surrounded by a great throng, wearing a Sidonian cloak embroidered with a patterned border; her quiver hangs from her shoulder, her hair is knotted with gold, and a golden clasp fastens her purple dress.

units.la: Est vero adjunctorū ad subjecta,quibus occupātur, usus item magnus. hoc argumēto Plato miseras civitates auguratur,quæ medicorum & judicum multitudine indigeant:quia multam quoq; & intemperantiā & injustitiam in ea civitate versari necesse fit.
units.tr: Indeed the use of adjuncts for the subjects they occupy is also great. By this argument Plato foretells wretched states, those that need a multitude of doctors and judges, because much intemperance and injustice must necessarily dwell in such a state.

units.la: Adjunctum ] Adjūctum dicitur in Organo συμβεβηκος,accidens,πάθος,πάθημα,affectio,ποιότης, σίγασις, circunstātia, ut á Quintiliano appellatur ca.10. lib.5. cūm nempe περίστασιν interpretatur: συμβεβηκὸς accidēs,in Organo complectitur essecta,adjuncta, comparata,ut etiam 4.cap.1.Topi ci di-
units.tr: In the Organon the adjunct is called συμβεβηκὸς, accident; also πάθος, πάθημα, affection; ποιότης, quality; circumstance, as Quintilian calls it in chapter 10 of book 5, when he renders it περίστασιν. The συμβεβηκὸς, accident, in the Organon embraces effects, adjuncts and comparates, as is also said in Topics 4, chapter 1. Properly, however, it is a certain particle of the adjuncts, as will be said shortly. Therefore P. Ramus avoided this name.

units.la: Greek words in the margin of the lower block, set in smaller type, as printed. ti dicitur: & proprie tamen particula quædam est adjunctorum, ut mox dicetur. Quare nomē hoc P.Ramus evitavit. ...
units.tr: ti is said; but properly it is a certain particle of the adjuncts, as will be said presently. Therefore P. Ramus avoided this name. The Greek word [ᾱᾱ] roughly signifies a movement of the mind, and it would not fit here; so it is omitted. The words [πτωσίς] and [πρόσπτωσις] would fit better here, but the Ciceronian term "adjunct" (adjunctum) in the Topics is more apt.

units.la: ti dicitur: & proprié tamen particula quædam est adjunctorum,ut mox dicetur. Quare nomé hoc P.Ramus evitavit.ᾱᾱ, fermé animi motū significat:neq; hic conveniret, ἀpterea est omif sum. πτωσίς & πρόσπτωσις magis hic convenirent: sed (adjunctū) Ciceronis verbum, in Topicis, est aptius ad id exprimendū quo de agitur, quia significat res insuper jūctas, cūm fubjectū nempe aliquod suis caussis integrū constiterit.conjunctum appellatur in Partitionibus,sed minús item est hoc idoneum. Atq; hæc de nomine:hujus autem argumenti res fufiús est exposita, ut antea jam patuit:& locus ipse accidentis, quinquies in Topicis est iteratus,multiq; de accidē te per Philosophiam Aristotelis dispersi loci.
units.tr: The marginal word ᾱᾱ mostly signifies a movement of the mind and would not fit here, so it is omitted. πτωσίς [fall] and πρόσπτωσις [chance occurrence] would fit better here. But adjunctum is Cicero's word in the Topics and expresses the matter in hand more aptly, since it signifies things joined on besides, when some subject has stood whole by its own causes. It is called conjunctum in the Partitions, but this too is less suitable. So much for the name. The matter of this argument has been set out more fully, as was already clear earlier, and the locus of the accident itself is repeated five times in the Topics, and many loci about accident are scattered through Aristotle's philosophy.

units.la: Forsitan] Locus est initio secundi libri: ubi jubet hic medicus amoris, in amica notari vitia singula ad amoris remedium:
units.tr: Forsitan: This is from the beginning of the second book, where the doctor of love bids us note each single fault in the mistress as a remedy for love.

units.la: Tunc animo signa,quæcunq; in corpore menda est, Luminaq; in vitiis illius usq; tene. Tum sequitur: Forsitan hæc aliquis: & mox sequitur.
units.tr: Then mark in your mind whatever blemish is on her body, and keep her faults in view. Then follows: Perhaps someone will say this, and soon after:

units.la: Tu tantúm numero pugna,præceptaq; in unum Contrahe,de multis,grandis acervus erit.
units.tr: Only struggle with the number, and gather your precepts into one; from many, a great heap will result.

units.la: Hoc autem idem notavit Quintil. lib. 4. ca.5: Quid quód interim quę per se levia sunt & infirma,turba valent? Tempus] Tempus Logicé intelligitur ab Aristotele,cúm (Quando)sit categoria una de decem:Tametsi ibidem confunditur,ut locus in genere quantitatis: Tempus autem ejusmodi logicū,duratio dicatur,quia verbum generale aptius nullum est: qualis duratiò significatur à Cicerone primo de Natura deorum, cum ait: Non enim si mundus nullus erat, secula non erant: Secula nunc dico, non ea quae dierum noctiumq; numero, annuis cursibus conficiuntur: fateor ea fine mundi coverfione fieri non potuisse: sed fuit quaedam ab infinito tempore aeternitas, quam nulla temporum circumscriptio metiebatur. Aristoteles autem in Physicis 10.11.12.13.14. cap. 4. lib. de tempore multa diputat, statuitq; esse numerum caelestis motus secundum prius ac posterius: sed tempus hoc physicum est, vel potius physica quaedam logici temporis illius mensura: ut si de horologiis Parisiensis urbis diceretur, Tempus est numerus motus horologiorum Parisiensium secundum prius & posterius: non satis accurate tempus est definitum, sed mensura ipsius quaedam indicata: Sic de coelesti horologio illo, & insigna temporum divinitus in illa sublimi specula collocato sentiendum. Verum P. Ramus hac de re ad illa quinq; capita diligentius consideravit.
units.tr: Quintilian also noted this in book 4, chapter 5: "What of the fact that things which are slight and weak in themselves gain strength from their multitude?" Time: Aristotle understands time logically, since it is one of the ten categories, although even there it is confused, as the place is in the genus of quantity. This logical time is better called duration, because no general word is more suitable. Cicero, in the first book of On the Nature of the Gods, expresses this kind of duration when he says: "For if there was no world, the ages did not exist. I mean by ages not those completed by the number of days and nights in annual courses. I grant that these could not occur without the transformation of the world; but there was a certain eternity from infinite time, which no division of times measured." Aristotle, in the Physics, books 10 to 14, and in the chapter on time, discusses many things and holds that time is the number of celestial motion according to before and after. But this is physical time, or rather a certain physical measure of that logical time. It is as if one said of the clocks of the city of Paris: "Time is the number of the motion of the Parisian clocks according to before and after." Time has not been defined with sufficient precision; only a certain measure of it has been indicated. So too should we understand that celestial clock, and the signs of the times divinely placed in that lofty watchtower. But P. Ramus considered this matter more carefully in those five chapters.

units.la: Propria ἴδιον, proprium Aristoteles 4. cap. 1. Topic. definit, quod non indicat quid est, & soli subjecto vicissim attribuitur. Porphyrius illud ait quod soli, omni, semper convenit: ut homini γελαστικόν, quod suapte natura rideat. Sed addit praeterea proprium triplex: primum, quod soli convenit, nec omni, ut homini geometram esse: secundum, quod omni, non soli, ut esse bipedem: tertium, quod soli, omni, sed non semper, ut canescere in senectute. Sed tria haec commune indicant, non proprium: qualitatesque illae propriae sunt in adjunctis, & solae spectantur in artibus : quales sunt proprietates in variis animalibus à grammaticis notatæ, in leone rugiendi, in tygre runcandi, in urso uncandi, in apro frendendi, in cervo glocitandi, in tauro mugiendi, in equo hinniendi, in ove balandi, in capro mutiendi, in angue sibilandi: in avibus similiter propriæ quædam affectiones insunt, ut in paro tinniendi, in turdo trutilandi, in struno pysitandi, in perdice cacabandi, in cygno drensandi, in accipitre pipandi, in milvo lippiedi, in gallo cucuriendi, in pavone pupillandi, in hirundine trinsandi, in corvo crocitandi, in ciconia glotorandi, in passere pipiendi, in cuculo cucullandi, in cicada fritiniendi, in ape bombiliandi, in vespertilione stridedi. Hujus autem proprii Topicum videtur 28. cap. primi Prior. præcipuè inter argumentorum locus esse propositum. Et 4. cap. 1. Poster. hæc proprietas per se in subjecto inesse dicitur. Itaque horum inter se attributio est quodammodo essentialis.
units.tr: Aristotle, in the fourth chapter of the first book of the Topics, defines the property [ἴδιον, idion] as that which does not show what a thing is, and is reciprocally attributed only to its subject. Porphyry says it is that which belongs to the one alone, to all, and always, as laughter [γελαστικόν, gelastikon] belongs to man, since by nature he is capable of laughing. But he adds that there is also a threefold property: first, that which belongs to the one only but not to all, as being a geometer belongs to man; second, that which belongs to all but not to the one only, as being two-footed; third, that which belongs to the one only and to all, but not always, as growing grey in old age. But these three indicate what is common, not what is proper. Those qualities which are truly proper are found among accidents, and are considered only in the arts. Such are the properties of various animals noted by the grammarians: in the lion, roaring; in the tiger, snarling; in the bear, growling; in the boar, gnashing; in the stag, bellowing; in the bull, lowing; in the horse, neighing; in the sheep, bleating; in the goat, bleating; in the snake, hissing. Among birds, similarly, certain proper affections are present: in the parrot, chattering; in the thrush, warbling; in the starling, whistling; in the partridge, cackling; in the swan, honking; in the hawk, screeching; in the kite, mewing; in the cock, crowing; in the peacock, displaying; in the swallow, twittering; in the crow, cawing; in the stork, clacking; in the sparrow, chirping; in the cuckoo, calling its name; in the cicada, chirring; in the bee, buzzing; in the bat, squeaking. The topic of the property seems to be placed, especially, among the places of arguments in the twenty-eighth chapter of the first book of the Prior Analytics. And in the fourth chapter of the first book of the Posterior Analytics, this property is said to inhere in its subject through itself. Therefore the attribution of these to one another is in some measure essential.

units.la: Caput Physiognomonica quædam hic attinguntur de pilis, de figura tota corporis: qua de re Aristotelis extat philosophia é figuris & affectib. animalium, cujusmodi est etiam Adamantii.
units.tr: Here certain matters of physiognomy are touched upon: concerning hairs, and concerning the figure of the whole body. On this matter there exists Aristotle's philosophy from the figures and affections of animals, and of Adamantius as well.

units.la: Crine ruber Exemplū est Martialis ex eadē physiognomonia, ut intelligatur, totam illam physiognomoniæ doctrinam, ex uno adjunctorum loco deductam esse: hinc prognostica Physicorum de ventis, pluviis: hinc ςημειωτικὴ medicorū, de signis morbi & sanitatis. Tantus loci hujus est usus. Dido Dido regina Carthaginis venatum proficiscēs, variis adjunctis arguitur & explicabat. plicatur: primo temporis, secundo delectæ juventutis, tertio variis venationis instrumentis, plagarum, venabulorum: quarto equitü, quinto canum, sexto nobilium principum, septimo sonipedis mirifico cultu ornati, octavo comitatus & habitus regalis. Adjucti, quod circa subjectu aliqd occupetur: usus perinde est ut talis subjecti. Plato] Locus est Platonis tertio de Republ. ubi multa de necessariis civium generibus differit: neq; judices ac medicos multos requirit, sta tuitq;, vel animo, vel corpore male natos (quibus ob injustitiam & intemperantiam valde fit opus judice & medico) abigedos e civitate. Tale sit argumentū,si cadaver futurū cōjicias, quo advolent vultures. Plinius lib. 10. ca. 7. prodidit triduo ante aut biduo vultures volare eo, ubi cadavera futura sint. Sic secundo Faltorum: Fallimur? an veris prænuntia venit hirundo?
units.tr: With red hair: this is an example from Martial, taken from the same physiognomy, so that it may be understood that the whole doctrine of physiognomy is derived from this one place of adjuncts. Hence come the prognostications of the natural philosophers about winds and rains, and hence the semeiotics of physicians about signs of disease and health. So great is the use of this place. Dido: Dido, queen of Carthage, setting out to hunt, is argued about and explained by various adjuncts: first of time; second, of the chosen youth; third, of the various hunting instruments, nets and spears; fourth, of the horsemen; fifth, of the hounds; sixth, of the noble princes; seventh, of the horses adorned with wonderful trappings; eighth, of the retinue and royal dress. An adjunct, because it is occupied about some subject, is used just as the subject itself is. Plato: This is a place from Plato's third book of the Republic, where he discusses at length the necessary kinds of citizens. He does not require many judges and physicians, and he decides that those born ill in mind or body (who, because of injustice and intemperance, have very great need of a judge and a physician) must be driven out of the city. Such an argument may be used: if you conjecture that a corpse will be there, toward which vultures will flock. Pliny, in book 10, chapter 7, reported that vultures fly two or one days before to the place where corpses are going to be. So also in the second book of the Fasti: Are we deceived, or does the swallow come as herald of spring?

units.la: Mercatores in exteras terras profecturi, studiose adjuncta ista considerant, quæ studia & exercitationes hominum, ad quos lucri faciendi gratia accedunt, ut subjectas eorum moribus & accommodatas merces importent.
units.tr: Merchants setting out for foreign lands carefully consider these adjuncts, and the studies and practices of the men to whom they come for the sake of gain, so that they may bring goods suited and adapted to their customs.

units.la: Cap. XII. De Diversis.
units.tr: Chapter XII. On Diverse Things

units.la: ARgumentū primum consentaneū expositum est, dissentaneū sequitur, quod á re dissentit. Sunt autē dissentanea inter se æquè manifesta, alterumque ab altero æqualiter arguitur: tamen si sua differentione clarius elucescunt. Difsentanea, sunt diversa vel opposita. Diversa, sunt dissentanea, quae sola ratione dissentiunt. Quo de genere sunt illa frequentissima, Non hoc, sed illud: Quanquam tamē, Pro Pomp. Non victoriam, sed insignia victoriae reportarunt. Ovidius 2. de Arte.
units.tr: The first argument of the consequent has been set out; the inconsequent follows, which differs from the thing. Inconsequents are equally evident among themselves, and one is argued from the other in the same way, although they become clearer through their difference. Inconsequents are either diverse or opposed. Diverse things are inconsequents that differ only in reason. To this kind belong the very frequent forms "not this, but that" and "although yet." In the Pro Pompeio: they did not win the victory, but obtained the insignia of victory. Ovid, Ars Amatoria, book 2:

units.la: Non formosus erat, sed erat facudus Ulysses.
units.tr: Ulysses was not handsome, but he was eloquent.

units.la: Virgil.
units.tr: Virgil:

units.la: Hic Priamus, quanquam in media jam morte tenetur:
units.tr: Here Priam, although he is already held in the midst of death,

units.la: Non tamen abstinuit.— Paulo secus in Eunucho:
units.tr: Did not refrain. Somewhat differently in the Eunuch:

units.la: Nam si ego digna hac contumelia Sum maximē: at tu indignus qui faceres tamē.
units.tr: For if I am most worthy of this insult, you are nonetheless unworthy to have done it.

units.la: Item illa aliusmodi. Pro Lig. Scelus tu illud vocas, Tubero? cur? isto.n.nomine illa adhuc causa caruit: Alii enim errorem appellant, alii timorem: qui durius, spem, cupiditatem, odium, pertinaciam: qui gravissime, temeritatem: sceleus praeter te, adhuc nemo.
units.tr: Likewise other distinctions of this sort. In the Pro Ligario: "Do you call that a crime, Tubero? Why? For that case has so far lacked that name: others call it an error, others a fear; some more harshly, a hope, a desire, a hatred, an obstinacy; some most gravely, a rashness. Apart from you, no one has yet called it a crime."

units.la: Diversa] Dissentaneorum categoria sequitur, multis modis a P. Ramo versata, & subinde varie mutata, antequam in hanc politiorem formam perveniret. Dissentaneum autem ut consentaneum, vocabula Ciceronis sunt in hac argumentorum arte: & dissentaneorum nomine comprehenduntur, quæcunq; duo ut difsidentia proponuntur. Diffentaneorum commune eft axioma, inter fe æquè manifefta effe: quod Ariftoteles in Topicis 2.cap.5.lib.item 3.cap.6.lib.fpecialiter de op pofitis ἀμα τῇ φύσει. Oppofitum.n.eft fimul natura. & hoc ipfum, fimul effe natura, eft hic æquè manifeftum effe: cótrá autem fuit in confentaneis. Nam cauffa dicitur natura prior effectis,& fubjectû adjunctis: quia illic fit argumentū clarius & manifeftius. Ergo quod Ariftoteles fpecialiter,id eft,in una diffen taneorum fpecie collocavit, quia generale eft, P. Ramus ex lege Ariftotelis καθόλου πρῶτον, generaliter expofuit. Totū aút hūc diffentaneorū locū Ariftoteles 28. c.1.Prio. repudiavit:fed errori táto refpódetur illic á P.Ramo, & in fingulis generib. Ariftotelis authoritate veriore defendet.
units.tr: Diverse things. The category of inconsequents follows, handled in many ways by P. Ramus and varied from time to time before it reached this more polished form. The terms "inconsequent" and "consequent" are Cicero's in this art of arguments, and under the name of inconsequents are included all pairs that are put forward as disagreeing. The common axiom of inconsequents is that they are equally evident among themselves, which Aristotle states in Topics 2, chapter 5, and in Topics 3, chapter 6, especially concerning opposites, "at once by nature" [ἀμα τῇ φύσει]. For the opposite is at once by nature, and this very thing, being at once by nature, is here equally evident; but it was otherwise with consequents. For a cause is said to be prior by nature to its effects, and a subject to its attributes, because there the argument is clearer and more manifest. Therefore what Aristotle placed specially, that is, in one species of inconsequents, because it is general, P. Ramus, following Aristotle's rule "universally first" [καθόλου πρῶτον], set out in general terms. Aristotle rejected this whole topic of inconsequents in Prior Analytics 2, chapter 8, but such a great error will be answered there by P. Ramus, and he will defend it in each of Aristotle's genera by the truer authority of Aristotle.

units.la: Diffenfione ] Id axioma in fcholis infinitè vulgatum & tritum eft:in toto tamen organo Logico non habetur: fed duobus in Rhetorico Ariftotelis tertio capitib. legitur 2. &17. παραλληλα τὰ ἐναντία μᾶλλον φαίνεσθαι, adverfa é regiõe pofita maximè apparere. Quod ité axioma magis etiā fpecialiter propofitum eft, quàm fuperiús,attamen generale eft,& omniū diffentaneorū commune. Itaq; generaliter proponitur. Categoria aút diffentaneorū tautologias in Ariftotelis bibliotheca multò rariores habet, quàm confentaneorum habuit: habet tamen non paucas. In Organo categoriam unā occupat,eorum nempe quæ funt ad aliquid: deinde permagnum caput de oppofitis:in Analyticis per fpecies varié attingitur: in Topicis infinite iteratur, ut p fingulas fpecies dicetur; in Phyficis vero nomine hujus argumenti, multa etiam cumulantur. Quod principia fint cotraria : item τὰ ἐναντία τῶν ἐναντίων αἴτια ἔναι, adverfas adverforu cauffaseffe,ut 10.cap. 2.de Generatione: item 7. & 8.cap. 4.Meteororum: quod fpecialiter etiam propofitum,generaliter oporteat intelligi:tum de adverfis motibus multa eft in Philofophia illa difputatio. Quare ut materies illa a P. Ramo fecundum Ariftotelis leges & principia fit explicata,ut genera generumq; fpecies generatim & fpeciatim propofitæ, qualis deniq; agricultura fit,attendamus. Confentanea argumenta,ufum magnum habuêre:Diffentaneorū autem quantus fit ufus,declarant Grecorum & Latinorum fcripta innumerabilia,quæ feré tota funt in refutatione errorū & falfarū opinionū : quód é diffentaneis fieri neceffe fit:pars pexigua eft in confirmatione:& quidem ipfa multo fepius etiam é diffentaneis petitur, vel in fchola mathematica, quæ ipfa multo feverioris Logicæ fibi leges impofuit:attamē demonftrationes per impofsibile ex diffentaneorū Topicis deductæ funt. Qua re ut categoria confentaneorum priores dignitatis partes obtinebit,ita categoria diffentaneorum, copiæ & ubertatis opib. longé fuperabit. Diffentaneorum aút doctrina, quamvis fit posterior,quám doctrina cófentaneorū:attamē eft etiam primorum argumentorum, quę re ipfa fe parata effe poffunt à cófentaneis. Diffentanea funt diverfa.]Categoria diffentaneorum prima partitione distribuitur secundā dissensionem ratio‑ nis tantum,tum rationis pariter & rei. diversa il‑ lius primi generis sunt, & usum habet longé fre‑ quentissimum:neq; tamen adhuc satis explica‑ tum & distinctu. P. Pamus in explicadis & poe‑ tis & oratoribus & philosophis,cum fructu tam ordinarium & assiduum cerneret,precepto co‑ prehendit, & primam dissentaneorum speciem hic instituit,quia simplicissima esset dissensio ra‑ tionis tantum.Itaque diversorum alterum affir‑ matur,alterum negatur:vel utrumq; affirmatur negaturve: tantumq; hic distinctio,non autem conclusio quæritur: primum itaq; dissentaneæ categoriæ topicū erit in diversis. Non victoriam] Quinq; sequentia exempla habet dissensionem rationis tantum, quia simul esse reipsa possunt. Non victoriā]Loquitur de Sylla & Murena impe‑ ratorib9, qui de Mithridate ita triuphaverāt, ut postea victus Mithridates victoribus Romanisinsultaret,victoriæq; insignia, triumphi illi fue‑ rint.Formosus]Præceptum Ovidii est, ad concili‑andum amorem: Nec leuis ingenuas pectus coluisse per artes, Cura fit,& linguas edidicisse duas. Tum sequitur: Non formosus erat,sed erat facundus Ulysses: Et tamen æquoreas torsit amore Deas.
units.tr: Dissension. This axiom is endlessly repeated and worn threadbare in the schools, yet it is not found in the whole Logical Organon; it is read in two places in Aristotle's Rhetoric, book 3, chapters 2 and 17: "contraries placed side by side appear more strongly," opposites placed in front of each other appear most clearly. This axiom is also proposed more specifically than the one above, but it is general and common to all inconsequents, and so it is proposed generally. The category of inconsequents has far fewer repetitions in Aristotle's library than the consequents had; yet it has not a few. In the Organon it occupies one category, namely that of things relative to something; then a very large chapter on opposites; in the Analytics it is touched upon variously through its species; in the Topics it is repeated endlessly, as will be told under each species; and in the Physics, under the name of this argument, many things are also heaped together: that principles are contrary; likewise that "contraries are causes of contraries" [τὰ ἐναντία τῶν ἐναντίων αἴτια ἔναι], that adversaries are causes of adversaries, as in On Generation 2, chapter 10, and in Meteorology 4, chapters 7 and 8. Since this was proposed specifically, it must also be understood generally; and there is much discussion in that philosophy about contrary motions. Therefore, let us consider how that matter has been explained by P. Ramus according to Aristotle's laws and principles, so that genera and species of genera are set out generally and specifically, and what kind of art it finally is. Consequent arguments have had great use; but the use of inconsequents is shown by the countless writings of the Greeks and Latins, which are almost entirely devoted to refuting errors and false opinions, which must necessarily be done from inconsequents. Only a small part is devoted to confirmation, and even that is drawn much more often from inconsequents, or in the mathematical school, which imposed on itself the laws of a much stricter logic; yet demonstrations through the impossible have been deduced from the topics of inconsequents. Therefore, just as the category of consequents will hold the first rank in dignity, so the category of inconsequents will far surpass it in the resources of abundance and fertility. The doctrine of inconsequents, although it comes after the doctrine of consequents, is nonetheless also one of the primary arguments, which in fact can be separated from consequents. Inconsequents are diverse. The category of inconsequents is divided by its first partition into dissension of reason only, and of reason and thing alike. The diverse things of the first kind are much the most frequent in use, and yet they have not been explained and distinguished enough. P. Ramus, seeing that they were so common and constant in the explication of poets, orators and philosophers, grasped them in a precept, and established here the first species of inconsequents, because it is the simplest dissension, of reason only. Thus of two diverse things one is affirmed and the other denied, or both are affirmed or both denied; and here only a distinction is sought, not a conclusion. Therefore the first topic of the category of inconsequents will be in diverse things. Not victory: the five following examples have dissension of reason only, because they can in fact exist together. Not victory: this speaks of the generals Sulla and Murena, who had triumphed over Mithridates in such a way that afterwards Mithridates, having been defeated, mocked the Roman victors, and those triumphs were the insignia of victory. Handsome: it is Ovid's precept for winning love: "Let it be your care to cultivate a mind with the arts that are not light, and to have learned two languages." Then it follows: "Ulysses was not handsome, but he was eloquent, and yet he moved the sea goddesses to love."

units.la: Priamus]Priamus Pyrrhū alloqui parat, á quo Polytes Priami filius in cóspectu patris trucida‑ tur. Nam si] Vox est Thaidis ad Chçreá,qui Pāphilam Thaidis puellam vitiarat.& hic ambo di‑ versa sunt affirmata. Scelus] Tubero sceleratum Ligarium vocaverat,propter arma contra Cęsa rem suscepta:cui dissentaneis hisce diversis refpódetur. Qualis illa est aliusmodi distinctio ꝑ Ligario: Nó fuit scelus,sed aut error, aut timor, aut spes,aut odiū,aut pertinacia, aut temeritas. Qualis est etiam diversitas in eadem Ligariana: Fuerint cupidi,fuerint irati, fuerint pertinaces, sceleris veró crimine, furoris, parricidii liceat Cn.Pompejo mortuo,liceat multis aliis carere. Sed hoc argumentum est immensi usus. Verr.ȝ. Non enim furem,sed ereptorem: non adulterū, sed expugnatorem pudicitiæ: non facrilegū,sed hostem sacrorum religionumq; : non sicarium, sed crudelissimū carnificem civium sociorumque,in vestrum judicium adduximus.
units.tr: Priam: Priam is about to address Pyrrhus, by whom Polites, Priam's son, is slain before his father's eyes. For if: these are the words of Thais to Chaerea, who had violated Thais's girl Pamphila; and in this passage both diverse things are affirmed. Crime: Tubero had called Ligarius a criminal because of the arms taken up against Caesar; to this he is answered with these diverse inconsequents. Such is that other distinction in the case of Ligarius: it was not a crime, but either an error, or a fear, or a hope, or a hatred, or an obstinacy, or a rashness. Such also is the diversity in the same Ligarian speech: they may have been eager, they may have been angry, they may have been obstinate, but let Gnaeus Pompey, now dead, be allowed to be free of the charge of crime, of madness, of parricide, and let many others be allowed to be free of it. But this argument is of immense use. In the Verrine orations: "For we have brought before your judgment not a thief but a plunderer, not an adulterer but a violator of chastity, not a sacrilegious man but an enemy of sacred rites and religion, not an assassin but the most cruel butcher of citizens and allies."

units.la: Cap. XIII. De Disparatis.
units.tr: Chap. XIII. On Disparates.

units.la: Opposita,sunt dissentanea, quæ ratione & re dissentiunt, itaq; eidē attribui,fecundum idem, & ad idem, & eodem tempore nõ possunt. Sic Socrates albus & ater non potest eadem parte esse: pater & filius ejusdē: sanus & ægep eodem tēpore: At albus esse potest alia parte,& ater alia:pater hujus,filiꝰ illius:sanus hodie,cras æger:Itaq; ex altero affirmato,alterū negatur,aut contrà. Opposita, sunt disparata, aut contraria. Disparata, sunt opposita, quorū unum multis pariter opponitur, ut viride,cine racēraceum, rubrū, media sunt inter albū & nigrū : q singula extremis, & inter se disparata sunt. Sic liberalitas & avaritia in ter se disparantur: sic homo, arbor, lapis, & ejusmodi res infinitæ disparātur : nec cadē res potest esse homo, arbor, lapis. Virg. i. Aenei. hoc argumento disputat: O quā te memorē virgo: nāq; haud tibi vultū Mortalis: nec vox hominē sonat: O dea certē!
units.tr: Opposites are things that disagree (dissentanea), differing both in reason and in fact. So they cannot be attributed to the same thing, in the same respect, toward the same thing, and at the same time. Thus Socrates cannot be white and black in the same part, nor the father and the son of the same person, nor healthy and sick at the same time. But he can be white in one part and black in another, the father of this man and the son of that man, healthy today and sick tomorrow. Therefore, when one of two opposites is affirmed, the other is denied, or the reverse. Opposites are either disparates or contraries. Disparates are opposites of which one is opposed equally to many things, as green, ash-coloured, grey and red are intermediate between white and black: each of them is disparate from the extremes and from one another. So liberality and avarice are disparate from each other, and so are man, tree, stone and countless other things of this kind; nor can the same thing be man, tree and stone. Virgil, in the first book of the Aeneid, argues with this argument: "O virgin, what shall I call you? For you have no mortal face, nor does your voice sound human: O goddess, surely!"

units.la: Opposita] Hæc definitio fumi potest é Philosophia ad 10. cap. 5. lib. Opposita sunt, quæcunque non accidit simul adesse amborum subjecto. At si dixisset Aristoteles generaliter, quę non accidit in eodem adesse, ut etiam substantiæ & res physicæ oppositæ dicerentur, λογικῶτερον definiviffet. Opposita enim, nō tātum sunt adjuncta, vel accidentia, quæ vocantur, sed etiam substantiæ, sed deniq; τὰ ὄντα καὶ μὴ ὄντα, entia & non entia: quia oppofitio res est logica, & ideo communis rerum omnium : Deniq; opposita sunt, quæ & ratione, & re differentiunt, ideoq; simul esse nō possunt. Nam si Socrates dicatur albus alia parte, alia niger: itē pater hujus, filius illius: fanus hodie, cras æger, sophisticē dicetur: Nec enim tus Socrates ita colorat esset: nec paterna qualitas, qua pater est, refertur ad illum, cujus filius est: nec quādo verè dicitur æger, eodem tempore re dicitur fanus: nec pater & filius opponuntur, sed esse patrem ejusdem, cujus fit filius. Atq; ex oppositorum altero affirmato, alterum negatur: ut, albus est, non igitur niger. Homo non est irrationalis, ergo est rationalis. Quare opposita sunt dissentanea, quæ dissentiunt ratione & re, alteriusque affirmatio, alterius negationem cōstituit: quod in diversis non fuit, propriumq; omnino loci hujus illud est axioma, qd' á P. Ramo i.lib. Scholarum physic. copiose tractatū est, φθαρτικὰ τῶν ἀλλήλων ἐναντία: corruptiva sunt inter se opposita. Sic enim ἐναντία Aristoteles accepit. Itaque circulus, est Arist. in Mechanicis miraculum omnium miraculorum, quia opposita ei videantur inesse, convexum & concavum, motus & quies contrarii motus.
units.tr: Opposites] This definition can be drawn from the philosophy of Aristotle, Categories ch. 10, and Book 5. Opposites are those things which cannot both belong at once to the same subject. But if Aristotle had said generally that they are things which cannot be present together in the same thing, so that substances and physical things would also be called opposites, he would have defined them more logically [λογικῶτερον]. For opposites are not only adjuncts or accidents, as they are called, but also substances; and finally they are things that are and are not [τὰ ὄντα καὶ μὴ ὄντα], beings and non-beings, because opposition is a logical matter and therefore common to all things. Finally, opposites are those which differ both in reason and in fact, and therefore cannot exist together. For if Socrates were said to be white in one part and black in another, or the father of this man and the son of that man, or healthy today and sick tomorrow, this would be a sophistical statement. For Socrates would not be coloured in that way; nor is the paternal quality by which he is a father referred to the one whose son he is; nor, when he is truly said to be sick, is he at the same time said to be healthy; nor are father and son opposed, but to be the father of the one whose son he is. And when one of two opposites is affirmed, the other is denied: as, "he is white, therefore not black"; "man is not irrational, therefore he is rational." Hence opposites are things that disagree in reason and in fact, and the affirmation of one constitutes the denial of the other; this does not hold for things that differ. The axiom peculiar to this place, which P. Ramus has treated at length in his Scholae physicae, book 1, is: opposites are destructive of one another [φθαρτικὰ τῶν ἀλλήλων ἐναντία]. For this is how Aristotle understood enantia [ἐναντία]. Hence Aristotle, in the Mechanics, calls the circle the wonder of all wonders, because opposites seem to be present in it: convex and concave, motion and rest, contrary motions.

units.la: Disparata] Oppositorum divisio deinde bifariam sequitur, in disparata & contraria: quorū differentia sumitur ex eo, quód disparatū, æqué multis disparatum est: contrariū, uni tantū. Hāc differentiam Rodolphus Agricola docuit i. lib. de Inventione, quam P. Ramus sequutus est, sic ut æmulatus in hac arte in primis industriam illius viri, quem in studio logico, post antiquā illam Socraticorum Logicorum scholam (in qua non minús usus artis, quàm sciētia tractabatur) omnibus postea natis Logicis anteponere solitus est, dicereq; palám ab uno Agricola verum germanæ Logicæ studium in Germania primū, tùm per ejus sectatores & æmulos, toto terrarū orbe excitatum esse. Percepit autē Parisiēsis Academia primò fructū illū adventu jacobi Omphalii, Bartholomæi Latomi: sed in primis joannis Sturmii, á quo Logicæ artis utilitas pleniús & uberiús est exposita. Agricola autē, differētia vocavit, quæ P.Ramus disparata dicere maluit, quia differentia totâ dissentaneorum categoriâ cõpleẗi videretur, ut etiâ trito in scholis verbo appellatur differetia comunis, propria, maxime propria:tû qd' differetia ab Aristotele opponeretur similitudini ꝑ dissimilitudine: Disparari, verbū est nō minús Latinū, ꝙ rei accómodatū.
units.tr: Disparates] The division of opposites then follows in two ways, into disparates and contraries. The difference between them is taken from this: a disparate is equally disparate from many things, while a contrary is opposed to one thing only. Rudolf Agricola taught this difference in the first book of De inventione, and P. Ramus followed it, so that in this art he especially emulated the diligence of that man, whom, after the ancient school of the Socratic logicians (in which the practice of the art was no less taught than the science), he was accustomed to place before all the logicians who came after, and he openly said that the true study of genuine logic was first awakened in Germany by Agricola alone, and then, through his followers and rivals, throughout the whole world. The Paris Academy first perceived this fruit through the coming of Jacobus Omphalius and Bartholomaeus Latomus, but above all of Johannes Sturm, by whom the usefulness of the art of logic has been set out more fully and fruitfully. Agricola called it differentia, which P. Ramus preferred to call disparata, because "difference" seemed to comprise the whole category of disagreeing things; and it is also called, in the common school term, "common difference", "proper difference", and most especially "proper", since differentia was opposed by Aristotle to similarity and dissimilarity. Disparari is a verb no less Latin than it is suited to the thing.

units.la: Qui est Imperator diuûm & hominum juppiter, Is nos per gentes,alios in alia disparat.
units.tr: He who is Jupiter, the emperor of gods and men, parts us off, some into one nation, others into another.

units.la: ait Plaut. Cic. 1. de Invent. verbum hoc usurpat pro genere dissentaneorum, contradicentium, ut sapere nō sapere. Et Quint.10.cap.5.lib.difpa rata dicit dura nō duris. At contradicentiū verbum magis ufitatū est in hoc genere. Boetius 1. lib.de syllogismis hypotheticis, disparata dicit, quæ tantûm á se diversa sunt, nulla contrarietate pugnátia: veluti vestis, ignis. Quare verbum pro hac specie P.Ramus usurpavit. ut cõmodissimum & aptissimum: Repugnantia pro eodem aliquando dixerat, sed postea animadvertit repugnantiæ verbum, majoris esse cujusdam oppositionis, quám hic significaretur, ut 2. Philip; Qui tantarum rerum repugnantiâ non videas, nihil profecto sapis. Secundum igitur in dissentaneis topicum erit in disparatis: Disparata autem hic quatuor exemplis declaratur: primum est de coloribus mediis.
units.tr: So says Plautus. Cicero, in the first book of De inventione, uses this word for a kind of disagreeing or contradictory things, such as to be wise and not to be wise. And Quintilian, in book 10, chapter 5, says dura non duris, "hard things not to hard things". But the word contradicentia is more commonly used for this kind. Boethius, in the first book of De syllogismis hypotheticis, calls disparates those things which are merely different from one another, not fighting with any contrariety, as clothing and fire. Hence P. Ramus has used the word for this species as the most convenient and most fitting. He had at one time used repugnantia for the same thing, but afterwards he noticed that the word repugnantia belongs to a stronger kind of opposition than what is meant here, as in Cicero's second Philippic: "Unless you see the repugnance of such great things, you certainly have no sense." The second topic among disagreeing things, therefore, will be that of disparates. Disparates are illustrated here by four examples. The first concerns intermediate colours.

units.la: Cineraceum ] Cinericium vulgò id dicitur. at Plin. ait lib.33. Terra alia est russa, alia cineracea. color etiam cinereus dicitur. Genera autem colorum duo prima sunt, albor & nigror: unde me dia plurima, quæ inter se, & extremis sunt tantûm ditům disparata. Liberalitas] Secundum exemplū sumitur ex 2. Ethico Aristotelis ad Nicomachū filium, cap 8. ubi hæc contraria vocantur ab Aristotele, significatione quadam liberiore & minús distincta: sed tamen interim hoc theorema ethicum proponitur, Extrema videlicet magis inter se opposita esse, quàm ad medium collocata, qua rône, effusio & avaritia magis disparatur, q; effusio & liberalitas, vel avaritia & liberalitas. Sic homo] Tertiū exēplū est de reb.physicis, quarū plures idē esse nó possunt: sed tñ certa diffen sionis lege nó opponūtur, ut homo, lapis, arbor, aqua, terra, ignis, aer, cœlū. Virgilius] Quartū exemplū poeticū est, ubi Aeneas apud Virgiliū di sputat, Venere, quę Spartanę virginis habitū fimulabat, deam tñ esse: argumentum sumitur á disparatis: Virgo non est mortali vultu, nec humana voce: Dea igitur est.
units.tr: Ash-coloured] This is commonly called cinericium, but Pliny says in book 33: "one earth is reddish, another ash-coloured" [cineracea]. The colour is also called cinereus. The two first kinds of colours are white and black, whence there are very many intermediate colours, which are disparate from one another and from the extremes only. Liberality] The second example is taken from Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, book 2, chapter 8, addressed to his son Nicomachus, where Aristotle calls these contraries, in a rather looser and less distinct sense; yet meanwhile this ethical theorem is proposed: namely, that the extremes are more opposed to one another than they are to what is placed in the middle; for which reason prodigality and avarice are more disparate than prodigality and liberality, or avarice and liberality. Thus man] The third example concerns physical things, of which several cannot be the same, yet are not opposed under any fixed law of disagreement: as man, stone, tree, water, earth, fire, air, heaven. Virgil] The fourth example is poetic, where Aeneas in Virgil argues that Venus, who was disguised in the appearance of a Spartan virgin, was nonetheless a goddess. The argument is drawn from disparates: a virgin does not have a mortal face, nor a human voice; therefore she is a goddess.

units.la: Cap. XIIII. De Relatis.
units.tr: Chapter XIV. Of Relatives.

units.la: COntraria sunt opposita, quorum unum uni tátúm opponitur. suntque affirmantia, aut negantia. Affirmantia, quorum utrunq; affirmat, ut relata & adversa, Relata sunt cōtraria affirmātia, quorum alterū constat é mutua alterius affectione: atq;inde nomina sunt relata, ut pater, qui filiū habet: & filius, qui patrem habet: & ob hanc mutuam relationis caussam, relata dicūtur simul esse natura, ut qui alterū perfecte norit, » norit & reliquum. Pro Mar. Ex quo prosecto intelligis, quāta in dato beneficio » fit laus, cūm in accepto tanta sit gloria. Martial.in Sofibianum lib.1.
units.tr: Contraries are opposites, of which one is opposed only to one. They are either affirming or denying. Affirming contraries are those where both terms affirm, as relatives and adversaries. Relatives are affirming contraries, one of which is understood through the mutual affection of the other. Hence they are called relatives, as father, who has a son, and son, who has a father. For this reason of mutual relation, relatives are said to be simultaneous by nature, as one who knows one perfectly also knows the other. Pro Marcello: "From this, you may indeed understand how great is the praise in a given benefit, when there is so much glory in the receiving." Martial, on Sosibianus, book 1.

units.la: Tam servum scis te genitū, blandeq; fateris, Cūm dicis dominum, Sofibiane patrem.
units.tr: You know that you were born a slave, and you admit it flatteringly, when you call Sosibianus your father and lord.

units.la: Sic apud Quintilianum lib. 5. cap. 10.
units.tr: So in Quintilian, book 5, chapter 10.

units.la: Si portorium Rhodiis locare honestū est, & Hermacreonti conducere. Quomodo & in Oratore perfecto Tullius: » Num igitur est periculum (ait) ne quis » putet in magna arte, & gloriosa turpe est se docere alios, id quod ipsi fuerit honestissimum discere? Studium vero quoddam suum Cicero é relatis illis in Orato » re prodidit: jam illa (inquit) matura, uxor generi, noverca filij, filiae pellex. » Quod idem in ferreae aetatis descriptione Ovid. apertius affectavit, 1. Met.
units.tr: "If it is honourable for the Rhodians to let out the harbour dues, it is also honourable for Hermacreon to hire them." Likewise Tully in the Orator perfectus: "Is there then (he says) any danger that someone may think it shameful to teach others in a great and glorious art, when it was most honourable for himself to learn?" But Cicero revealed a certain habit of his own from these relatives in the Orator: "Now (he says) that mature woman, a son-in-law's wife, a stepmother to a son, a daughter's mistress." Ovid, in his description of the iron age, aimed at the same thing more openly, in book 1 of the Metamorphoses.

units.la: —non hospes ab hospite tutus, (est.
units.tr: No guest is safe from his guest,

units.la: Non socer a genero, fratrū quoq; gratia rara Imminet exitio: vir coniugis, illa mariti: Lurida terribiles miscent aconita novercae, Filius ante diem patrios inquirit in annos.
units.tr: No father-in-law from his son-in-law; even the rare kindness of brothers hangs over ruin. Husband against wife, wife against husband. Pale stepmothers mix dreadful aconites, and a son seeks his father's years before their time.

units.la: Itaq; argumentū talis relationis contra riū nihil habet, imo arguit mutuas causas, ut sum tuus pater, tu es igitur meus filius: at cū dico, Sum tuus pater, nō igitur tuus filius, contraria tum veré sunt.
units.tr: Therefore the argument from such a relation has no contrary. Rather, it argues mutual causes: "I am your father, therefore you are my son." But when I say, "I am your father, therefore not your son," then they are truly contraries.

units.la: Contraria] Hæc definitio ab Agricola, ut dixi, facta est: Opposita (ait 1. lib.) sunt quæ repugnant unum uni, sic ut neque alterum de altero, neque ambo de medio dici posint: Opposita vocat, quę Cicero contraria. Contrarii verbum aptius. Porrò differentia eadem unitatis etiam est in Philosophia, sed per species, quód relatio fit ἐνὸς πρὸς ἓν, unius ad unū, ut in Philosophia 6. cap. 4. lib. item ἐναντίον ἐν ἑνί, aduersum unū uni, ut 2. cap. 1. de Cælo, & 6. cap. 4. Meteo. & in Philofophia 4. cap. 10. lib. Manifestum quód non accidit uni plura aduersa esse: & in Interpretatione ne affirmatur similiter, unam negationem duntaxat uni affirmationi opponi, cum de contradictione agitur. In priuatib. res est manifestior: At fi quid unū duobus opponatur, opponetur duplici genere oppofitionis, ut motus motui & quiete ti: ut est 7. cap. 8. Physici. Quare commune est omnium cōtrariorum, unū uni opponi, sed generaliter: quia generale est etiam præponendum: Hæc enim differentia est vera contra disparatorum genus. Hæc aūt unius ab uno dissensio maxima est, quam fexcētis locis Ariftoteles aduerforum oppofitioni attribuit: At communis est omnium contrariorum. Itaq; P. Ramus huc etiam retulit. Plato in Alcibiade fecundo idē pro posuit: Atqui duo aduersa uni rei, quomodo fuerint? Alcib. Nullo modo. Quare cōftet definitio ista, Contraria, sunt opposita, quorū unum uni tantùm tantum opponitur. & contraria intelligamus, quæ Ariftot. vocat ἀντικεἰμενα, ἀντιθέσεις: quomodo in Topicis 3.ca.2.lib. ἀντίθεσις πρᾶξις, oppofi tiones quatuor appellantur. Divisio deinde fequitur in affirmantia & negantia. Affirmantia, quæ vocabulis affirmátibus exponuntur, neq; negationem continétibus, ut Relata & adversa. Hæc definitio est Aristotelis in Categoriis. Ad aliquid autem talia dicuntur, quæcunq; ipsa, quæ sunt, aliorum esse dicuntur. Hic enim mutua relationis affectio exprimitur: sed illic additum est, aut quomodolibet aliter ad aliud. quo additameto, definitio illa vera cofunditur, & pleraq; feré omnia ad aliquid efficiuntur. Cicero in Topicis vocat relata, quę cum aliquo co feruntur. Topicum autem relationis in Logicis valdé celebratum est, sed valdé etiam inconstàter modo fit categoria é decem una integra, modo extra categorias, fit species contrariorum, ut rursus in Topicis, in quibus duodecies citatur. Falce igitur Aristotelei principii καθόλε πρῶτον, ad hanc tautologiam refecádam, opus est, ut generale documentum semel exponatur. Simul esse] Hoc Aristotelis est ἅμα φύσει, quod non tantum ad æquale vim argumeti attinet, sed ad assentiæ reciprocationem & affectionem. Diversa enim & disparata & cætera dissentanea sunt simul natura, neq; quicquam hic prius notitiâ vel posterius: at mutuam essentiæ affectionem non ideo obtinent, ut alterum mutuó per reliquum definiat. Relata veró sunt simul naturâ dupliciter. & quia sunt ęquè nota, & quia mutuę sunt essentiæ, & tiæ, & mutuæ sibi caussæ. Hinc relata πρὸς ἀντιστρέφοντα λέγεται, ad convertentia dicuntur, ut loquitur Aristoteles. Pyrrho ἀλογίαν suę ἀναταλντίας cō firmare nitebatur, quia relata essent æqualiter ignota: Sed æqualitas notitiæ, ignorantię æqualitatem non arguebat.
units.tr: Contraries: this definition was made by Agricola, as I said. "Opposites (he says in book 1) are those that repugnate, one to one, so that neither can be said of the other, nor both of the middle." He calls them opposites, which Cicero calls contraries; the word "contrary" is more apt. Moreover, the same distinction of unity also exists in philosophy, but by species: the relation is [ἑνὸς πρὸς ἕν], of one to one, as in the Philosophy (Metaphysics), book 6, chapter 4; likewise [ἐναντίον ἐν ἑνί], opposed one to one, as in book 2, chapter 1, On the Heavens, and book 6, chapter 4 of the Meteorology, and in the Philosophy, book 4, chapter 10. It is manifest that it does not happen that one thing has several opposites. Likewise in the Interpretation, a single negation is opposed only to a single affirmation when contradiction is treated. In privations the matter is clearer. But if one thing is opposed to two, it is opposed by a double kind of opposition, as motion to motion and to rest, as in book 7, chapter 8 of the Physics. Hence it is common to all contraries that one is opposed to one, but in a general way, because the general must also be put first. For this difference is true against the genus of the disparates. This one-to-one dissent of one thing from another is the greatest, which Aristotle attributes to opposites in six places; but it is common to all contraries. Therefore P. Ramus also referred it here. Plato, in the second Alcibiades, proposed the same: "But how could two opposites be of one thing?" Alcibiades: "In no way." Therefore this definition holds: contraries are opposites, of which one is opposed only to one. Let us understand as contraries those which Aristotle calls [ἀντικείμενα], [ἀντιθέσεις]: as in the Topics, book 3, chapter 2, four kinds are called [ἀντιθέσεις] oppositions. Division follows, into affirming and denying. Affirming terms are those expressed by affirmative words, not containing negation, such as relatives and adversaries. This definition is Aristotle's in the Categories: "Those things are said to be relative to something which are said to be of others." For here the mutual affection of relation is expressed; but there it is added "or in some other way to another," by which addition that true definition is confused, and nearly all things become relatives. Cicero in the Topics calls relatives those which are carried together with something. The topic of relation is much celebrated in the logicians, but very inconsistently: sometimes it is one whole category out of ten, sometimes outside the categories, sometimes a species of contraries, as again in the Topics, where it is cited twelve times. Therefore, to correct this tautology, we need the Aristotelian principle [καθόλου πρῶτον] to be expounded once as a general rule. Simultaneous: this is Aristotle's [ἅμα φύσει], which concerns not only the force of an argument as to equals, but the reciprocation and mutual affection of assent. For different, disparate, and other opposed things are simultaneous by nature, and neither is earlier or later in knowledge; but they do not therefore have a mutual affection of essence, so that one defines the other in turn. Relatives, however, are simultaneous by nature in two ways: both because they are equally known and because they are mutual in essence and mutual causes of each other. Hence relatives are said [πρὸς ἀντιστρέφοντα], to convertible things, as Aristotle puts it. Pyrrho tried to confirm his suspension of judgement [ἀλογίαν] and his equipollence [ἰσοσθένειαν] because relatives are equally unknown. But equality of knowledge does not prove equality of ignorance.

units.la: Servum] Hic relata bis bina sunt, servus dominus, filius pater: Pater est dominus: ergo filius servus, jocus est Martialis in quendam patri tanquam domino & principi adulatem: quomodo hodieq; nobiles appellantur à filiis. Portorium] Usus relationis est magnus ille quidem per sese, sed minus tamen exemplis oratorum & poetarum testatus. Proximum exemplu è Quintiliano sumptū est. Diomedon item publicanorum princeps apud Aristotelę sic argumentatur: Nā si vobis locare turpe non est, nec nobis conducere. Cicero adversus reprehensores, quód vir consularis & tantis rebus gestis ornatus, scriberet de artificio dicendi, arripuit hoc é relatis argumentu in Oratore perfecto, Honestissimum est eloquentiam discere, ergo nō est turpe doce re. Studium]judicium Ciceronis hac de re est in eodem Oratore ad Brutum, manifestum: Nam cum locum Roscianæ defensionis de supplicio parricidarum ita extenuasset: Sūt enim (ait) omnia sicut adolescentis, non tam re & maturitate, quàm specie & expectatione laudati. Tum subdit, Ab hac indole jam illa matura, uxor generi, noverca filii, filiæ pellex. Hoc igitur argumento ab oratore improbitas & libido Sassiæ (quæ mater Cluentii fuerat) exagitatur, quód
units.tr: Slave: here there are two pairs of relatives: servant and master, son and father. The father is master; therefore the son is servant. This is a jest of Martial against someone who flatters a father as master and prince, as nobles are even today addressed by their sons. Harbour dues: the use of relation is great in itself, but it is less attested by examples from orators and poets. The next example is taken from Quintilian. Diomedon, likewise the chief of the publicans, in Aristotle argues thus: "For if it is not shameful for you to let, nor for us to hire." Cicero, against critics who objected that a consular man, adorned with such great deeds, wrote about the art of speaking, seized upon this argument from relatives in the Orator perfectus: "It is most honourable to learn eloquence; therefore it is not shameful to teach." Habit: Cicero's judgement on this matter is plain in the same Orator to Brutus. For when he had weakened the passage of the Roscian defence concerning the punishment of parricides, he said: "For all things (he says) are as with a youth, praised not so much for their substance and maturity as for their appearance and expectation." Then he adds: "From this disposition comes that mature woman, a son-in-law's wife, a stepmother to a son, a daughter's mistress." Therefore by this argument the orator assails the wickedness and lust of Sassia, who had been the mother of Cluentius, because

units.la: g & nomina necefsitudinū, & jura naturę violafset,cúm Melinum generum in amorem pellexif set, filiaque Cluentia expulsa ei nupsisset: Itaq; locrus quæ fuerat, jam est uxor & noverca filii Cluentii, quem odio népe novercali perfequatur:& pellex filiæ Cluentię, cujus nempe virum sibi pellexerit, & quæ tanquam cócubina fit marito filiæ. Ovidius Tullium in hoc videtur imitatus, ut violato toto necessitudinum illarū ju- re,concluderetur id quod ipse conclusit,
units.tr: she violated both the names of the ties of kinship and the laws of nature, since she had enticed her son-in-law Melinus into love, and, after her daughter Cluentia had been driven out, had married him. So she who had been a stranger is now wife and stepmother of Cluentius's son, whom she pursues with stepmotherly hatred; and she is the mistress of Cluentia's daughter, since she had enticed away her husband, and as a concubine she is to the husband of her daughter. Ovid seems to have imitated Tully in this, so that with the whole law of those ties violated, there would follow the very conclusion that he himself drew,

units.la: Victa jacet pietas.
units.tr: Piety lies defeated.

units.la: In hoc autem exemplo,relata alia sunt unius no minis,ut hospes hospitis,frater fratris:alia duobus expressa nominibus, socer generi, conjux mariti,filius patris. Atque hæc exempla proposita fuerūt illius mutuæ relationis, & relationis usus in eo genere magnus est: quod etiam telta ri possunt in locis inventionis tam multæ argumentorum definitiones,per relatione factæ: ut caussæ & effecti,subjecti & adjuncti, dissentanei p diffentaneū,& sic deinceps paria,majora, minora,similia,dissimilia,totum, pars,genus, species,definientur: attamen sic ivœvríwrs nulla est, attum est,sum tuus pater, nó igitur tuus filius: verúm á frequentiore usu nomen est factum.
units.tr: In this example, some relatives are of one name, such as guest of guest, brother of brother; others are expressed by two names, father-in-law and son-in-law, wife and husband, son and father. These examples were set out to illustrate that mutual relation, and the use of relation in that kind is great, since in the places of invention so many definitions of arguments are also made through relation: cause and effect, subject and adjunct, dissent through dissent, and so on; equal, greater, lesser, similar, dissimilar, whole, part, genus, and species are defined in the same way. Yet no such inference is valid: "It is done, I am your father, therefore not your son." But the name has come from more frequent use.

units.la: Cap. XV. De Adversis.
units.tr: Chapter XV. On Opposites

units.la: Adversa, sunt contraria affirmatia, quę inter fe velut è regione perpetuó adversantur. Aeneid. 11.
units.tr: Opposites are affirmative contraries, which stand perpetually over against one another, as it were across a line. Aeneid 11.

units.la: Nulla salus bello,pacem tepofcimus omnes.
units.tr: No safety lies in war; we all ask for peace.

units.la: Sic albor & nigror, calidum & frigi— dum, virtus & vitium opponuntur. Pa— rad. 1. contra Epicureos: Illud tamen ar€te tenent,accurateque defendunt, vo-luptatem, esse summum bonum: quæquidem mihi vox pecudū videtur, nonhominum. Tu cùm tibi five Deus, fivemater(ut ita dicam)rerum omnium natura,dederit animum,quo nihil est præftantius, neque divinius: sic te ipse abjicies ac prosternes, ut nihil inter te atq; inter quadrupedem,interesse putes?Pecudem & hominem, adversa Cicero opposuit. Voluptas, pecudis bonum est: non igitur hominis. Sic libertas & fervitus apud Tibullum 2. lib.
units.tr: So whiteness and blackness, heat and cold, virtue and vice are set against one another. Paradoxes 1, against the Epicureans: "Yet they hold firmly to that and defend stoutly that pleasure is the highest good, which voice seems to me to belong to cattle, not to men. When God, or, if I may so put it, the nature of all things as their mother, has given you a mind, than which nothing is more excellent or more divine, will you so abase and prostrate yourself as to think there is no difference between yourself and a four-footed beast?" Cicero set beast and man as opposites: pleasure is the good of the beast; therefore it is not the good of man. So freedom and slavery in Tibullus, book 2:

units.la: Sic mihi fervitiū video dominamq; paratā: Tu mihi libertas illa paterna vale.
units.tr: So I see slavery and a mistress made ready for me; you, my father's freedom, farewell.

units.la: Pro Mar. Nunquā enim temeritas cum sapientia commiscetur,nec ad cōsilium casus admittitur.
units.tr: Pro Marcello: "For rashness is never mingled with wisdom, nor is chance admitted into counsel."

units.tr: Adversa] According to this topic of affirmative contraries, it is distinguished from relation by this very fact, that it is always set over against its opposite as across a line. Nor are opposites compared with one another as relatives are compared; yet this very thing is to stand over against one another across a line. It is Cicero's, in the Topics: "Contraries", he says, "are of several kinds. One kind is of those which differ most within the same genus, as wisdom and folly.

units.la: » eodé genere plurimûm differunt, ut sapiétia & » stultitia. In eodem aút genere dicuntur, quibus » positis, occurrunt tanquam é regione quædam » cótraria,ut celeritati tarditas non debilitas, qui 5 bus contrariis argumenta talia existunt. Si stultitiam fugiamus, sapientiam sequamur & bonitatem. Definitio autę adversorum generalis est & logica,id est omnis entis & nó entis,quomodo Aristoteles loquitur,cúm dicit,generi subje- 10 ćtas differétias esse ἐναντίας, adversas: quomodo differétias ipsas vocat ἐναντιώσεις, tanquam diceres adversitates. Et sic in categoriis 6. ca.Plurimúm inter se distantia sub eodem genere,adversa dicuntur.quod item repetitur in Philosophia 15 4.cap. 10. lib. Quam adversorum definitionem paulo ante Cicero ab Aristotele mutuatus est, eandem doctrinam infinitis per totam Philosophiam exemplis,Aristoteles approbat.cúm elementa facit ἐναντία, motus ἐναντίσες, & similiter cæ 20 tera.Locus autem est in Categoriis triplex contrarius:primus est 10.cap.in adversis,si subjećtū fuerit,possibile esse inter sese cómutari: nisi naturâ alterum insit, ut cálidum & frigidum mutuó sese expellút é subjećto corpore, nisi alterū 25 infit natura,ut calor inest igni: Hic loc9 videtur sola accidentia facere adversa:quia substátia altera alteri nó accidit,tanquam subjećto. Secundus locus est in cap. de substantia,quód substantiæ nihil sit adversum:quod in Physicis 1. & 5.li. 30 est iteratum.Tertius in cap.de quantitate,quód quátitas nihil habeat adversum. At loci tres illi falsi sunt: Differétiæ enim essentiales magis adversæ sunt, ut rationale & irrationale, quá qualitates adversæ quælibet, ut calor & frigus. Nā, ut Porphyrius ait, qualitates illæ misceri possunt, differentiæ essentiales non possunt, sicuti neq; quantitates, quæ non tantùm sunt in loco, sed complent locum, neq; confusionem patiuntur. Sed judicium controversorum in Aristotelis Philosophia locorum ad leges Aristotelis referatur. Logica tota est entis & non entis: adversorum doctrina, est pars Logicæ: quare entis & nō entis: Peccat igitur categoriarum locus ille triplex, qui adversa tollit é mathematicis & physicis rebus, in quibus in primis usum & præcipuum obtinent. Relatio, facta est communis omnium entium, sic ἰναντίωσις, omnium rerum cómunis fieri debet, neque privari patrimonii sui duabus amplissimis partibus, substantiæ nempe, ut in physicis rebus, & quantitatis, in mathematicis. Adversorum locus, nō sit categoria, ut relatorum: quamvis tamen potius esse debuit, cùm sit amplioris usus: species efficitur contrariorum post categorias, & rectè attingitur in lide Interpretatione, & in Analyticis: in Topicis aut totis, tautologia loci hujus longè omnium maxima: citatur enim novies & quadragies: tũ per Physicam, tum per Ethicam, varie dispersa sunt quædam loci hujus axiomata: Quare redũ dantiam tam alienam, tamq; legibus Aristotelis damnatam tautologiam P. Ramus hoc loco evitavit, & locum adversorum, ut cæteros, semel & generaliter, quia generalis esset, exposuit.
units.tr: "But those are said to be in the same genus which, when one is posited, there occur as it were across a line certain contraries, as slowness to speed (not weakness), and those contraries from which arguments of this kind arise: If we shun folly, let us follow wisdom and goodness." The definition of opposites, however, is general and logical, that is, of every being and non-being, as Aristotle speaks when he says that the differences subject to a genus are opposed [ἐναντίας]; and he calls the differences themselves oppositions [ἐναντιώσεις], as if you were to say adversities. So also in Categories chapter 6: "Those that are most distant from one another under the same genus are called opposites." This is likewise repeated in Philosophy book 4, chapter 10. Cicero borrowed this definition of opposites from Aristotle a little earlier, and Aristotle confirms the same doctrine with countless examples throughout all of philosophy, when he makes the elements opposed [ἐναντία], motions opposed [ἐναντιώσεις], and similarly the rest. In the Categories there is a threefold contrary topic. The first is in chapter 10: "In opposites, if there is a subject, it is possible for them to change into one another, unless one of them is present in it by nature, as hot and cold expel each other from a body that is their subject, unless the other is present by nature, as heat is present in fire." This topic seems to make only accidents opposites, because one substance does not befall another as to a subject. The second is in the chapter on substance, that substance has nothing opposed to it, which is repeated in Physics books 1 and 5. The third is in the chapter on quantity, that quantity has nothing opposed to it. But those three topics are false. For essential differences are more opposed, as rational and irrational, than any opposed qualities, as heat and cold. For, as Porphyry says, those qualities can be mixed, whereas essential differences cannot, and neither can quantities, which are not only in a place but fill it and suffer no confusion. But the judgment of disputed matters in the topics of Aristotle's philosophy is to be referred to Aristotle's own laws. Logic as a whole is of being and non-being; the doctrine of opposites is a part of logic; therefore it is of being and non-being. That threefold topic of the Categories is therefore in error, since it removes opposites from mathematical and physical things, in which they chiefly have their use and principal place. Relation was made common to all beings, so opposition [ἐναντίωσις] ought to be made common to all things as well, and not be deprived of its two most ample parts: substance, namely, as in physical things, and quantity, as in mathematical things. The topic of opposites ought not to be a category, as relatives are; although it ought rather to be one, since it has the wider use. The species of contraries after the categories is produced, and is rightly touched upon in On Interpretation and in the Analytics. But in the Topics as a whole, the tautology of this topic is by far the greatest of all, for it is cited forty-nine times, both through Physics and through Ethics, where various axioms of this topic are scattered in different places. Wherefore P. Ramus, in this place, avoided that tautology, so alien to the reasoning and so condemned by Aristotle's laws, and set out the topic of opposites, like the others, once and in general, because it is general.
