Arĝté]Homo & bestia, adversa quidem sunt:tota tamen enűtiatio (Voluptas est bonum pecudis) non fatis est adversa enuntiationi, Voluptas est bonum hominis ut ex altero affirmato, alterum negandum fit. Sic mihi]Tibulli argumentű sic est, Non ero liber postea, quia servus sum, dominæ amicæ addictus. Tale est ejusdem Tibulli lib.1.
units.tr: Nulla salus] Drances spoke this sentence in the council of King Latinus, when a great defeat had been received from the Trojans; and so peace is demanded of Latinus against Turnus, the author of the war. Arete [ἀρετή]] Man and beast are indeed opposites; yet the whole statement "Pleasure is the good of the beast" is not opposed enough to the statement "Pleasure is the good of man", so that from the one affirmed the other must be denied. Sic mihi] Tibullus's argument is this: I shall not be free afterwards, since I am a slave, bound to my mistress-friend. Such is also this passage from the same Tibullus, book 1:

units.la: At vos exiguo pecori furefq; lupique Parcite, de magno est præda petenda grege.
units.tr: But you, thieves and wolves, spare our small flock; the prey must be sought from the great flock.

units.la: Præda est petenda de magno grege, ergo nö est petenda de exiguo. In hoc exemplo axioma oppositorum pene scholasticé usurpatur, quód opposita simul esse non possint.
units.tr: The prey must be sought from the great flock; therefore it must not be sought from the small one. In this example the axiom of opposites is used almost in the scholastic manner, that opposites cannot be present at the same time.

units.la: Cap. XVI. De Contradicentibus.
units.tr: Chapter 16. On Contradictories.

units.la: COntraria, negantia sunt, quorum alterum ait, alterum negat idem: eaq; sunt contradicentia, aut privantia. Contradicentia sunt cōtraria negantia, quorum alterum negat ubiq; : ut justus non justus, animal non animal, sanguis non sanguis, sunt contradicentia. Sic in defensione Muræna, contradicitur sententiis Catonis & Ciceronis, illius Stoici, huius Academici. Dialogus est his verbis, Nihil ignoveris: Imò aliquid, nō omnia. Nihil gratiæ caussa feceris: Imò ne resistito gratię,cùm officium & fides postulabit.Misericordia commotus ne sis. Etiam in dissolvenda severitate, sed tamè est aliqua laus humanitatis.In sententia permaneto:Enimverò, nisi sentè tia alia vicerit melior. Martialis lib.
units.tr: Contraries are negatives: one of them affirms something and the other denies the same thing. These are either contradictories or privatives. Contradictories are contrary negatives, of which one denies universally, as "just" and "not just," "animal" and "not animal," "blood" and "not blood" are contradictories. So in the defence of Murena, the opinions of Cato and Cicero are opposed, the one a Stoic, the other an Academic. The dialogue goes like this: "Forgive nothing." "Nay, something, not everything." "Do nothing for the sake of favour." "Nay, do not resist favour when duty and good faith require it. Do not let pity move you." "Even in relaxing severity, there is still some praise for humanity." "Keep to your opinion." "Indeed, unless another opinion has conquered it as a better one." Martial, book 1.

units.la: 1. Bella es,novimus:& puella,verum est. Et dives:quis enim potest negare͠? Sed dum te nimium, Fabulla,laudas, Nec dives,neque bella,neque puella es.
units.tr: You are beautiful, we know; and a girl, that is true. And rich: for who could deny it? But while you praise yourself too much, Fabulla, you are neither rich, nor beautiful, nor a girl.

units.la: Cicero 1. Tus. cogit hoc argumento Atticum Epicureum fateri mortuos mi seros nō esse,si omnino nulli sint,ut Epicurei credebant:jam mallem (ait) Cerberum metueres, quàm ista tam incōsiderate diceres. Atticus: Quid tandem? Marc. Quem esse negas, eūdem esse dicis. ubi est acumen tuum?cùm enim mi serum esse dicis,tum qui non sit,esse dicis. Tum post longam disputationem, Atticus ait: Age,jam concedo non esse miseros,qui mortui sunt:quoniā extorsisti, ut faterer, qui omnino non essent, eos ne miseros quidem esse.Sic Terentianus Phædria, Dori Eunuchi dictum elevat,quòd affirmasset priùs quæ pòst inficiaretur.
units.tr: Cicero, in the first book of the Tusculan Disputations, uses this argument to force the Epicurean Atticus to admit that the dead are not miserable, if they are altogether nothing, as the Epicureans believed. "I would rather you feared Cerberus," he says, "than said such inconsiderate things." Atticus: "What then?" Marcus: "Whom you say does not exist, you say is the same as one who exists. Where is your sharpness? For when you say that someone is miserable, you are also saying that one who does not exist exists." Then, after a long discussion, Atticus says: "Very well, I now concede that those who are dead are not miserable, since you have wrung from me that those who altogether do not exist are not even miserable." So in Terence, Phaedria undermines the words of Dorus the eunuch, because Dorus had affirmed earlier what he afterwards denied.

units.la: g 5 Modó Modò ait,modò negat, inquit in Eunucho.
units.tr: "Now he says it, now he denies it," he says in the Eunuch.

units.la: Contradicentia] Contradicentia appellantur sçpé & in Organo, & in Philosophia,affirmatio & negatio:sæpé etiā ex altera parte, ἀποφατικὰ, negantia: Simplicium autem partium, ut caussę,fa⁠ ēta,subjecta, adjuncta,relata,aduersa,privantia, sic negantia per se considerantur.Nomen ἀντιφάσεως,cōtradictionis, hīc proprium est.nam φάναι, ἀποφαῦναι, φάσις ἀπόφασις,negare,affirmare,negatio, affirmatio, communia symbola sunt: & proprie φάσις est,cūm affirmatur: ἀντίφασις, quando negatur contrà. Ἀντίφασις etiam, partem sæpé significat:ac sæpé Aristoteles ἀντιφάσεως nomè commūniter accipit pro omni affirmationis & negatiōnis oppositione.Hoc verò topicum,suam in primis tautologiā, eamq; notabilem habuit in Aristotelis Logica & Philosophia: in Logica, post categorias,fit species contrariorum : totiq; feré duo libri de Interpretatione hīc consumuntur.
units.tr: Contradictories] Contradictories are often called affirmation and negation, both in the Organon and in philosophy. Often, too, from the other side, they are called negatives [ἀποφατικά]. Among simple parts, such as cause, effect, subject, adjunct, relative, contrary, and privative, the negatives are considered by themselves in this way. The name of contradiction [ἀντιφάσεως] is proper here. For to say [φάναι], to declare [ἀποφαῦναι], assertion [φάσις] and denial [ἀπόφασις], to deny and to affirm, negation and affirmation, are common terms. Properly, φάσις is when something is affirmed, and contradiction [ἀντίφασις] is when it is denied in opposition. Yet ἀντίφασις also often means a part, and Aristotle often takes the name of contradiction [ἀντιφάσεως] commonly for any opposition of affirmation and negation. This topic, however, had above all its own tautology, and a notable one, in Aristotle's Logic and Philosophy. In the Logic, after the Categories, the species of contraries is treated, and nearly two whole books, On Interpretation, are spent on it here.

units.la: In Analyticis & prioribus & posterioribus sæpè multiplex est hujus loci doctrina: In secundo priorum,capita decem tota sunt de nugatoria è contradicentib. syllogysmi potestate: de qua libro secundo dicetur ampliūs:In posterioribus, de contradictione frequens est mentio, præsertim de ipsius axiomate.In Topicis citatur locus ipse decies, & ȝ.cap.2.lib.instituitur nomine contradictionis,cosequentia ὑ ἀντάπαλιν inversa, quæ est syllogismi connexi species secunda, ut in eo loco P. Ramus docebit. In Philosophia autem, totus feré quartus liber est de principio contra dictionis. Talem tautologiā habet unica de contrariis species: quæ tamen tam multiplicata doctrina ad Ariftotelis leges á P. Ramo perpurgata, præter unicam in logica invétione definitionem, catholicum nihil habet: cætera paucula, si commodi quid habeant, judicii sunt de enuntiatorum contradictione, de qua 2.lib. Ariftoteles autem in Categoriis & interpretatione 1. & 3. cap.1.lib. negat hic affirmationem & negationem esse, sed velut affirmationem & negationē appellat: sed hoc placitum est hominis: & placitum multo pluribus ejusdem authoris placitis refutatum: ac si nomina sint contradicentium symbola, vocat ὄνομα ὁρισὸν καὶ ἀόριστον, nomen finitum & infinitum: sic ῥῆμα ὁρισὸν καὶ ἀόριστον, verbum finitum & infinitum: Atq; sic utrunq; communiter definit, qd' similiter in quolibet est & ente & non ente: quia de quo justum non dicitur, nō justum dicitur, & de quo sedet nō dicitur, de eo non sedet dicitur. ubiq.] Hæc contradicentiū lex traditur in Categoriis cap.10. In solis enim his necesse est semper alterum verum, alterum falsum esse. Hic igitur proprium factum est κἰνπια φάσεως axioma, multis locis apud Ariftotelem citatum: Quidlibet affirmare aut negare verum, ut est 2.cap.2. Poster. Verum præ cæteris contrariorum generibus cōtradicentium genus á philosophis disputatum est, & cōtradicentium definitio vehementer oppugnata. Anaxagoras inter verum & falsum, aliquid medium posuit: cum tamen nihil inter ens & non ens interjectum sit: Antisthenes dicebat nihil posse dici, nisi propria oratione: unde efficeretur, ut non liceret ἀντιλέγειν. γνῶ contradicere, nec omnino mentiri, quia non propria oratione res tum diceretur: At cúm res falsa pronuntiatur, oratione contrarii dicitur: Anaxagoras dicebat, mistum esse quodlibet in quolibet, & quales res quisq; putaret, ei tales esse: quo uno faciebat omnia falsa: Heraclitus omnia in ppetuo motu & fluxu statuebat, ut bis in eundem fluvium ingredi equus non possit: omniaq; & esse & nō esse: quo uno, faciebat cunêta vera: Cratylus etiam Heraclitum carpebat: Imô veró (dicebat) ne semel quidem eundem fluvium ingredi equus potest: Itaq; eó redierat, ut censeret loquendum non esse, quia rerum natura ante mutaretur, quám oratione pronûtiari posset: sed digitum movebat tantúm: Democritus vacuum & plenum in quolibet ponebat: & hoc ens, illud nō ens appellebat: nihilq; verum esse dicebat, aut certé nobis incertum: Protagoræ sententia, Homo est omnium rerum mensura: Itaq; quod ei videtur & apparet, verum est: contrarium est falsum: Contra quos omnes fanaticos errores, Aristoteles disputavit in libris de Philosophia, eorumq; omnibus argumentis refutatis definitionem & legem cótradictionis vindicavit. Atqui refutationis hujus studio adductus Logicus nescio quis (cujus Logicam in Philos. 4. lib. secutus est Aristoteles) axioma cō tradictionis (Quodlibet affirmare aut negare verum) tantùm extulit, ut principium firmissimum, clarissimum, suppositione non indigens, axiomatum deniq; axioma, & principiorum principium summum constitueret. Atista laus nimis magna videtur cótradicentibus attributa: Cauf farum enim categoria,fontem verę fcientiæ cótinet: Contradictionis topicū, quamvis permagnum & perutile, huc tamen aspirare non pót. tota vis ejus eft in falfo refellendo: inde confeffio quædam veri cogitur,ut id credas deniq;,cujus cauffam nefcias:id eft,verum confiteri cogeris,quod tamen verum effe nefcias:totaq; illa di fputatio Ariftotelis in Philofophia pro contradictione adverfus Anaxagoram, Antifthonem, Heraclitum,Cratylum,Democritum,Protagoram, demonftrat fuiffe Logicos, qui tali principio non affentirentur: at qui negaret principiū cauffarum, omnia videlicet caufsis fuis cóftare, neminem ait Ariftoteles fuiffe:imó (ut antea có ftitit) omnes ad cauffas in primis refpexêre, & in omnibus rebus confecĭati funt: quamvis (ut Ariftoteles putat)non fint affecuti. Stoici] Cicero in ea defenfione, fentiebat Muraenā premi in primis authoritate Catonis: Itaq; ad hanc authoritatem elevādum, Stoica paradoxa, quibus Cato deditus erat,ita cavillatus eft, ut totum judicium rifu compleverit. Itaq; Cato dicitur exclamasse, Dii boni, quám ridiculū Confulem habemus! Ergo huc pertinet exagitatio Stoicę fe ćtæ,quę virum bonum & fapientē, rigidū nimis ac feverum formabat. Bello] jocus eft Fabullæ fićto nomine, in mulierculā gloriosam & vanā, de fuis bonis magnificentiús fentientem. Cerberum]Marcus Tullius difputans cū Attico Epicureo,affirmante mortuos effe miferos,qui omnino nulli effent,unaq; cum corpore, etiam animus mus extinctus esset: interrogat,nū metuat apud inferos Cerberum, Cocytum, &c. tūm Atticus respondet, Adeone me delirare censes,ut ista esse credam? Quare paulò post argumento cōtradictionis convictum, Marcus eludit, quasi multò levius fuerit, inferos admittere, quàm in tá absurdam contradictionis cōfessionem incidere.
units.tr: In the Analytics, both Prior and Posterior, the doctrine of this topic is often manifold. In the second book of the Prior Analytics, ten whole chapters concern the futile power of syllogism from contradictories, which will be discussed more fully in the second book. In the Posterior Analytics, mention of contradiction is frequent, especially of its axiom. In the Topics the place itself is cited ten times, and in the third book, chapter 2, a consequence inverted [ὑπ᾽ ἀνάπαλιν] is established under the name of contradiction. This is the second species of the connected syllogism, as P. Ramus will teach in that place. In Philosophy, nearly the whole fourth book concerns the principle of contradiction. This topic has only one species of tautology, that of contraries; yet this doctrine, so multiplied and purged by P. Ramus according to the laws of Aristotle, has nothing universal apart from the single definition in the invention of Logic. The other few points, if they have anything useful, belong to judgement on the contradiction of statements, which is treated in the second book. But Aristotle, in the Categories and in On Interpretation, chapters 1 and 3, and in book 1, denies that affirmation and negation are here; instead he calls them, as it were, affirmation and negation. But this is the opinion of one man, and an opinion refuted by a great many opinions of the same author. And if names are the creeds of contradictories, he calls them "a defined and undefined noun [ὄνομα ὁρισὸν καὶ ἀόριστον]," that is, a finite and infinite noun; likewise "a defined and undefined verb [ῥῆμα ὁρισὸν καὶ ἀόριστον]," that is, a finite and infinite verb. And so he defines both in common, because in each thing it is alike in being and non-being: for of what is not said to be just, it is said not to be just; and of what does not sit, it is said not to sit. Everywhere] This law of contradictories is handed down in the Categories, chapter 10. For only in these is it necessary that one of them always be true and the other false. Hence this has become the proper axiom [κἰνπια φάσεως], cited in many places by Aristotle: that it is true to affirm or deny anything, as in Posterior Analytics 2, chapter 2. Yet among the other kinds of contraries, the genus of contradictories has been disputed by philosophers more than the rest, and the definition of contradiction has been vehemently attacked. Anaxagoras placed something intermediate between true and false, though nothing is interposed between being and non-being. Antisthenes said that nothing could be said except in its proper speech, whence it would follow that it is not allowed to contradict [ἀντιλέγειν], nor to lie at all, since the thing would then not be stated in its proper speech; but when a false thing is pronounced, it is said in the speech of the contrary. Anaxagoras said that anything is mixed in anything, and whatever sort of things anyone thought them to be, such they are to him; by this one thing he made all things false. Heraclitus established that all things are in perpetual motion and flux, so that a horse cannot enter the same river twice, and that all things both are and are not; by this one thing he made all things true. Cratylus also carped at Heraclitus: "Indeed," he said, "a horse cannot enter the same river even once." And so he had come to think that one should not speak, since the nature of things changes before it can be pronounced in speech; he only moved his finger. Democritus posited the void and the full in anything, and called this being and that non-being; and he said that nothing is true, or at least uncertain to us. The opinion of Protagoras was: man is the measure of all things. Therefore, whatever seems and appears to him is true, and the contrary is false. Against all these fanatical errors Aristotle disputed in the books On Philosophy, and having refuted all their arguments, he vindicated the definition and law of contradiction. But moved by zeal for this refutation, some logician (whose Logic Aristotle followed in Philosophy, book 4) extolled the axiom of contradiction, "that it is true to affirm or deny anything," so highly that he made it the firmest, clearest principle, needing no supposition, the axiom of axioms, and the highest principle of principles. Yet this praise seems too great to be attributed to contradictories. For the Categories contain the source of true science; the topic of contradiction, however great and useful, cannot aspire to this. Its whole force lies in refuting what is false; from this a certain confession of truth is forced, so that at last you believe what you do not know the cause of. That is, you are compelled to confess as true what you nevertheless do not know to be true. And that whole disputation of Aristotle in Philosophy, arguing for contradiction against Anaxagoras, Antisthenes, Heraclitus, Cratylus, Democritus, and Protagoras, shows that there were logicians who would not assent to such a principle. But Aristotle says that no one has ever denied the principle of causes, namely that all things consist of their causes; indeed (as he established before) all have looked chiefly to causes and have been very devoted to all things, although (as Aristotle thinks) they did not attain them. Stoics] Cicero, in that defence, thought that Murena was pressed chiefly by the authority of Cato. Therefore, to lower this authority, he mocked the Stoic paradoxes, to which Cato was devoted, in such a way that he filled the whole judgement with laughter. Hence Cato is said to have exclaimed, "Good gods, what a ridiculous consul we have!" Therefore the attack on the Stoic sect belongs here, which formed the good and wise man as too rigid and severe. To Bellus] This is a joke in a fictitious name, against a boastful and vain little woman who thinks more grandly of her own goods. Cerberus] Marcus Tullius, disputing with Atticus the Epicurean, who affirmed that the dead are wretched who are altogether nothing, and that the soul is extinguished along with the body, asks whether he fears Cerberus, Cocytus, and so on in the underworld. Then Atticus replies, "Do you think I am so deranged as to believe these things?" Therefore, a little later, having been convicted by the argument of contradiction, Marcus mocks him, as if it had been much lighter to admit the underworld than to fall into so absurd a confession of contradiction.

units.la: Locus est act. 4. scen. 4. de virgine stuprata per Chæream: quod factum cūm Phædriæ fratri Dorus affirmat, terretur, & ideo rursum negat. Hinc refutatio testimonii ē tali inconstantia & contradictione.
units.tr: This passage is in Act 4, scene 4, about a virgin ravished by Chaerea. When Dorus tells Phaedria's brother of the deed, he is frightened and so denies it again. Hence the refutation of testimony by such inconsistency and contradiction.

units.la: Cap. XVII. De Privantibus.
units.tr: Chapter XVII. On Privatives.

units.la: PRivantia, sunt contraria negantia, quorum alterum negat in eo tantùm subjecto, in quo affirmatū suapte naturā inest. Atque hic affirmatum, dicitur habitus: negatum autem, privatio.
units.tr: Privatives are negating opposites, of which one denies only in that subject in which the other is by its own nature affirmed. The affirmed term is called a habit, and the denied term a privation.

units.la: Sic motus & quies: sic ebrius & sobrius. Martialis lib. 3.
units.tr: So motion and rest; so drunk and sober. Martial, book 3:

units.la: Ebrius es, nec enim faceres hæc sobrius unquam.
units.tr: You are drunk, for you would never do these things while sober.

units.la: Sic cæcum esse, & videre, pro Cælio:
units.tr: So to be blind and to see, in the words about Caelius:

units.la: Existat igitur ex hac familia aliquis, ac potissimum Cęcus ille: minimum enim dolorem capiet, qui istam non videbit.
units.tr: Let then someone from this family arise, and especially that blind man: for he will feel the least pain, since he will not see that woman.

units.la: Sic pauper & dives opponuntur apud Martialem lib. 5.
units.tr: So poor and rich are opposed in Martial, book 5:

units.la: Semper eris pauper si pauper es, Aemyliane: Dantur opes nullis nunc, nisi divitibus.
units.tr: You will always be poor if you are poor, Aemilianus: now wealth is given only to the rich.

units.la: Talia sunt, mors & vita, in Miloniana: Hujus mortis sedetis ultores, cujus vitā si putetis per vos restitui posse, nolitis? Item tacere & loqui, 1. Catil. Quid expectas authoritatem loquētium, quorum voluntatem tacitorū perspicis? Doleo, cū Respublica immortalis esse debeat, eam in unius mortalis anima cōsistere.
units.tr: Death and life are of this kind, in the Pro Milone: "You sit as avengers of this death; if you thought that his life could be restored through you, would you not wish it?" Likewise to be silent and to speak, in the First Catilinarian: "Why do you wait for the authority of those who speak, when you see the will of those who are silent? I grieve that the commonwealth, which ought to be immortal, should rest in the soul of one mortal man."

units.la: Privantia [Privantia ab Aristotele στερητικὰ appellantur, à στέρησις privatione, parte altera oppositionis, cui opponitur ἕξις, id est habitus, quo bene aut male afficitur affectum, ut scribit Aristoteles cap.20. lib. 5. Philos. Sic 2.cap.4.lib.in Philosophia, negatio & privatio distinguuntur: Absentia enim, negatio illius est: in privatione autem, & subjecta quaedam natura est, secundum quam dicitur privatio. Et 12.ca.5.Phil.Privatio, efficitur alicujus habitus, ne pura ac mera videatur negatio. Locus autem hic modicè proponitur in Aristotelis bibliotheca: post categorias effictur species contrariorū: in Analyticis semel attingitur: in Topicis citatur undecies: Sed in Physicis cōmentum Aristotelis ex hoc loco admirabile exortū est: ut privatio, quae nihil esset, fieret tamē causa, & principiū physicarū rerum omnium. Sed tamen Aristoteles postea in totis operibus physicis cōmentum hoc abundē refutavit: cum efficiente, materiā, formā, finem cōsideret, cōmentitium illud privationis insomniū, in nullo prorsus naturae opere adhibeat. Privatio autē, est negatio cōtrarii habitus in subjecto naturali, ut est in Philosophia 4. cap. 10. lib. Item privatū, dicitur habitus susceptivū, cūm cui naturaliter inesse potest, nō inest, ut est in Categoriis 10. ca. Edentulū enim dicimus, nō quód dentes nō habeat: & cæcū, nō quód visum nō habeat: sed non habere, quādo habere suapte natura debeat, id privari dicitur: aliter q; homo cæcus, aliter talpa dicitur, ut est in Philosophia 22. ca. 5. lib. Itaq; circa idem, habitus & privatio versantur, ejusdemq; rei sunt, δύναμις ἢ ἀδυναμία, potentia & impotentia, ut est in philosophia 4. ca. 10. lib. Atq; horū contrariorum alia sunt, in quibus impossibile est mutuam cōmutationem fieri: ab habitu siquidē in privatione mutatio fit, vt á visu in cæcitate: at á privatione cōtraria & cæcitate in habitū, impossibile putat Aristoteles in categoriis cap. 10. qui tamen alibi author est, effossos hirundinum oculos restitui. Motus & quies] Aristoteles in Physicis sæpé motum & quietem sic opponit. Ebrius] Martialis jocatur in cerdonem, in ludis faciēdis res suas stultē cōsumentē. argumentum est á privantibus. Sobrius, istos ludos nō faceres: ebrius igitur facis. ebrius enim, significat habitum quēdam: & sobrius, habitus ejus privationem: quasi sine ebrio. Existat igitur] jocus Ciceronis est in his privantibus: Appius ille cæcus minimum dolorem capiet, quia non videbit impudicā Clodiam, ad quam objurgandum inducitur. Qui istam] Relativum pro caussali conjunctione positum est, ut alibi Cicero, Actio maluimus iter facere pedibus, qui incommodi-
units.tr: Privantia (privatives) are called by Aristotle στερητικὰ [stericha], from στέρησις [sterēsis], privation, which is the other part of the opposition to which ἕξις [hexis] is opposed, that is, habit, by which a thing is affected well or badly, as Aristotle writes in chapter 20 of book 5 of the Philosophy. Likewise in chapter 4 of book 2 in the Philosophy, negation and privation are distinguished: absence is simply the negation of something, but in privation there is also some subject nature, according to which it is called privation. And in chapter 5 of book 12 of the Philosophy, privation is said to be the production of some habit, so that it does not appear to be a pure and bare negation. This place is only briefly set out in Aristotle's library: after the Categories it is developed as a species of contraries; in the Analytics it is touched on once; in the Topics it is cited eleven times. But in the Physics Aristotle's fiction about privation, which would be nothing yet would become a cause and principle of all physical things, arose from this passage in a remarkable way. Yet Aristotle afterwards thoroughly refuted this fiction throughout his physical works, since when he considers the efficient cause, matter, form and end, he uses that invented dream of privation in no part of natural operation at all. Privation, however, is the negation of a contrary habit in a natural subject, as stated in the Philosophy, book 4, chapter 10. Again, something is said to be deprived when it does not have a habit it could naturally have: we call a toothless man one who has no teeth, not because he lacks teeth altogether, but because he does not have them when by his nature he ought to; a blind man is called so in a different way from a mole, as stated in the Philosophy, book 5, chapter 22. Hence habit and privation are concerned with the same thing and belong to the same thing, as are δύναμις [dynamis] and ἀδυναμία [adynamia], potency and impotency, as stated in the Philosophy, book 4, chapter 10. Of these contraries some are such that a mutual change between them is impossible: from habit there is change into privation, as from sight into blindness; but from privation and blindness back into habit, Aristotle in the Categories, chapter 10, thinks impossible, though he elsewhere affirms that the eyes of swallows, when put out, are restored. Motion and rest. Aristotle in the Physics often opposes motion and rest in this way. Drunk. Martial makes a joke about a cobbler who foolishly squanders his goods in putting on shows; the argument is drawn from privatives: "Were you sober, you would not put on these shows; you are drunk, therefore you do them." For drunk signifies a certain habit, and sober its privation, as if to say "without drunkenness." Let it exist, therefore. Cicero's joke among these privatives is: "That blind Appius will feel the least pain, because he will not see the shameless Clodia, whom he is being brought to rebuke." Who that one. The relative is put for a causal conjunction, as Cicero elsewhere says: "We preferred to make the journey on foot, who had sailed most inconveniently," that is, because.

units.la: Motus & quies, Ebrius, Existat igitur: marginal catchwords in the text as printed. modissimé navigassem: id est quia. Semper eris] Pauper & dives, privantia sunt, quia pauper est, qui nó habet divitias, dives qui habet. unde jocus est Martialis. Mors] Mors, est privatio vitæ, in ea re quæ vitæ capax sit: vita, est habitus quidam viventis. Si possetis vitam Clodio restitue re, nolletis: nó debetis igitur morte ejus ulcisci, Tacere] Tacere, est privatio: Catilinę autem suadet orator, ne à Senatu judiciũ vocis expectet, cũm tacitam damnationem videat. & sic ibidé paulò pòst, Quid vocis expectas contumeliam, cũm sis gravissimo judicio taciturnitatis oppressus? Atq; hæc de generibus contrariorum: quorum maximam ἀντίθεσιν Aristotele's cótradi‐ centibus attribuit: idq; duplici de caussa. Prima est 4. cap. 2. de Interpretatione. quia negatio est ἀντιφατικὴ, magis adversa affirmationi, quám op siti affirmatio: ad eam siquidem oppositi affirmatio revocari dicitur, quia privatio, quædam negatio sit, negatio nempe habitus in suo subjecto, ut est in Philos. 4. cap. 10. lib. & é contrariis, alterum reliqui privatio sit, ut dissimilitudo similitudinis, vitium virtutis, nigror alboris, ut est ejusdem libri cap. 2. De relatis idem fortasse, quamvis non exprimat Aristoteles, vult intelligi, ut seruitus, priuario quædam sit dominatus: &sic cap. 4. 1. Physic. contrariorum quidam termini fiunt ὑπερβολὴ καὶ ἔλλειψις, exuperantia & defectus. Secunda caussa est, quod hæc sola cótraria in re qualibet immediata sint, nec mediũ admittat: Quidlibet est aut nó est. Verúm primæ caussæ responderi potest, adversum adverso multó magis
units.tr: Motus & quies, Ebrius, Existat igitur: marginal catchwords as printed in the text. "Modissimé navigassem": that is, because. Semper eris (You will always be): "pauper" and "dives" (poor and rich) are privatives, because the poor man is one who does not have riches, and the rich one who has them; hence the joke of Martial. Mors (Death): death is the privation of life in a thing capable of life; life is a certain habit of a living thing. If you could restore life to Clodius, you would not want to: therefore you ought not to avenge his death by killing. Tacere (To be silent): to be silent is a privation. But the orator urges Catiline not to wait for the Senate's judgement by voice, since he sees a silent condemnation; and so a little later in the same place: "Why do you wait for an outcry of insult, when you are overwhelmed by the most grave judgement of silence?" So much for the kinds of contraries, of which Aristotle attributes the greatest ἀντίθεσιν (opposition) to contradictories, and does so for two reasons. The first is in chapter 2 of book 4 of On Interpretation: because negation is ἀντιφατικὴ [antiphatikē], more opposed to affirmation than contrary opposites are; for the affirmation of the opposite is said to be reduced to it, since privation is a kind of negation, namely the negation of a habit in its subject, as stated in the Philosophy, book 4, chapter 10. And when one of two contraries is the privation of the other, as dissimilarity is of similarity, vice of virtue, blackness of whiteness, as stated in chapter 2 of the same book. Concerning relatives, perhaps, though Aristotle does not express it, he wishes it to be understood that servitude is a certain privation of lordship; and so in chapter 4 of the first book of the Physics, certain terms of contraries become ὑπερβολὴ καὶ ἔλλειψις [hyperbolē kai elleipsis], excess and defect. The second reason is that these alone are contraries which are immediate in any matter, and admit no middle: anything either is or is not. But to the first reason it can be answered that the opposed is much more opposed to the opposed than the affirmed is to the negated; and that the most excellent divisions of the arts are made into opposites, not into contradictories, since negation produces no science. To the second reason too it can be answered that this immediate division of true and false is common to some opposites as well, as true to false, simple to multiple, and similar pairs; for anything is either true or false. Therefore this reason concludes nothing either way; and even if it concluded most, it would conclude only a scholastic subtlety, and one contrary to the laws of logic too. For it is a logical axiom that the essence of a genus is attributed to this or that species not more or less, but equally to all. Thus by this doctrine, relatives, opposites, contradictories and privatives will be called contraries neither more nor less.

units.la: {h} magis oppositū esse, quám affirmatū negato: & præstátissimas divisiones artiū in adversa fieri, nó in cótradicentia, quia negatio nullá scientiá faciat. Secūdæ item causæ reipóderi potest, istá veri & falsi immediatá divisione, cómunem etiá cum quibusdá adversis esse: ut vero falso, simpli ci, multiplici, & similib. Quidlibet enim verū est aut falsum. Quare causa hæc utraq; nihil cócludit: & si maximè cócluderet, subtilitate tantúm scholasticam concluderet, & Logicæ etiá legib9 contrariā. Est enim Logicum axioma, Generis essentiam non huic vel illi speciei magis aut minús, sed æqualiter omnibus attribui: itaque hac doctrina, relata, adversa, cōtradicentia privantia, neq; magis, neq; minús contraria dicentur.
units.tr: {h} more opposed to the opposed than the affirmed is to the negated; and the most excellent divisions of the arts are made into opposites, not into contradictories, since negation produces no science. To the second reason too it can be answered that this immediate division of true and false is common to some opposites as well, as true to false, simple to multiple, and similar pairs; for anything is either true or false. Therefore this reason concludes nothing either way; and even if it concluded most, it would conclude only a scholastic subtlety, and one contrary to the laws of logic too. For it is a logical axiom that the essence of a genus is attributed to this or that species not more or less, but equally to all. Thus by this doctrine, relatives, opposites, contradictories and privatives will be called contraries neither more nor less.

units.la: Cap. XVIII. De Paribus.
units.tr: Chapter XVIII. Of Equals.

units.la: ARgumenta simplicia ita fuerūt in consentaneis & dissentaneis: cōparata sunt, quæ inter se comparantur: sæpeq; notis brevius indicātur: aliquādo partibus plenius distinguuntur. quæ πρόταεις & ἀπόδοσις, propositio redditioq; nominantur: totaq; propositio argumentum facit, seu verum, seu etiam fictum sit ipsum comparatum. Comparata vero, suapte natura æquè nota sunt, sicut antea oppositā: quamvis alterum alte-ro sit interdum clarius atq; illustrius. Comparatio est in quantitate vel qualitate: Quantitas, qua res cõparatæ, quantę dicuntur: Estq; parium vel imparium. Paria sunt, quorū est una quantitas. Argumentū igitur paris est, cùm par explicatur á pari: ejusq; notæ sunt, par, æquale, æquare, idem quod, tam, quám, tantó, quantó, tot, quot, & non magis, non minús. Virgil. Aeneid. 2.
units.tr: Simple arguments were set out in the same way for agreeing and disagreeing things. Things that are compared are those that are set against one another. This is often indicated briefly by marks, and sometimes more fully distinguished by parts. These are called protasis [πρότασις] and apodosis [ἀπόδοσις], the proposition and its restatement. The whole proposition makes an argument, whether the thing compared is true or fictitious. Compared things are by their nature equally well known, just as the opposites were before, although one of them may sometimes be clearer and more striking than the other. Comparison concerns either quantity or quality. Quantity is that by which the compared things are called quantities, and it is either of equals or of unequals. Equals are those that have one and the same quantity. The argument from equals is therefore when an equal is explained by an equal. Its marks are: equal, equal to, to equal, the same as, as much as, as, as great as, so many as, as many as, not more, not less.

units.la: Par levibus ventis.—
units.tr: Equal to the light winds.

units.la: Aeneid. 3.
units.tr: Aeneid 3.

units.la: Et nunc æquali tecum pubesceret ævo.
units.tr: And now he would have grown up with you in equal age.

units.la: Aeneid. 6.
units.tr: Aeneid 6.

units.la: En hujus nate auspiciis: illa inclyta Roma, Imperium terris, animos æquabit Olympo.
units.tr: Lo, under the auspices of this son, that renowned Rome shall make her empire equal to the lands, and her spirit equal to Olympus.

units.la: Partes deinde distinguuntur. 4. Catil. Cujus res gestæ atq; virtutes, jisdẽ quibus solis cursus, regionibus ac terminis continentur. Aeneid. 4.
units.tr: The parts are then distinguished. 4. Catil. Whose exploits and virtues are confined by the same regions and boundaries as the course of the sun. Aeneid 4.

units.la: Tam ficti pravī tenax, quám nuntia veri.
units.tr: As tenacious of the false and wicked as a messenger of the truth.

units.la: Catul. Tantó pessimus omnium poeta, Quantó tu optimus omnium patronus.
units.tr: Catullus: Worst of all poets by as much as you are the best of all patrons.

units.tr: Cicero, Philippic 9: For he was not more a jurist than a man of justice. So he always referred what proceeded from the laws and from civil law to ease and equity. Nor did he prefer to bring about lawsuits rather than to remove disputes. Ovid, Ars 2:

units.la: Non minor est virtus, quàm quærere parta tueri.
units.tr: It is no less a virtue to keep what has been won than to win it.

units.la: Cic. pro Muræna: Paria cognosco esse ista in L. Murena: atq; ita paria, ut neq; ipse dignitate vinci potuerit, neq; te dignitate superarit. Parium axioma est: Si parium alterum sit reliquum esse: sin alterum non sit, reliquum non esse. Cic. 2. Philip. Quorū facinus commune, cur non eorū præda cōmunis? Hīc é pari affirmato, par affirmatur. Terent. in Adelph.
units.tr: Cicero, Pro Murena: I know these things to be equal in Lucius Murena, and so equal that he could not himself be surpassed in dignity, nor could he surpass you in dignity. The axiom of equals: if one of two equals is, the other is; but if one is not, the other is not. Cicero, Philippic 2: Whose crime is common, why should their plunder not be common? Here, from an equal affirmed, an equal is affirmed. Terence, Adelphi:

units.la: Quando ego nõ curo tuum, nec cura meum.
units.tr: Since I do not care for yours, do not you care for mine.

units.la: Hic é pari negato, par negatur. hujus vero loci sunt consectaria illa, é contrariis quidem orta, sed parium axiomate tractata: ut Martialis illud,
units.tr: Here, from an equal denied, an equal is denied. Of this place, however, are those corollaries which arise from contraries but are handled by the axiom of equals, such as that line of Martial:

units.la: Tum servum scis te genitū blandeq; fateris, Cúm dicis dominum, Sofibiane, patrem.
units.tr: Then you know and sweetly confess you were born a slave, when you call your master, Sosibianus, "father."

units.tr: Arguments from opposites are more frequent. Cicero, Pro Sulla: "Nor indeed can I understand why you should be angry with me. If I defend the man whom you accuse, why do I not also take offence at you, who accuse the man whom I defend? You say, 'I accuse my enemy.' And I defend my friend." So in Tusculan Disputations 5: "Since they admit that there is great power in vices to make life wretched, must it not be admitted that the same power is in virtue to make life happy? For contraries are the consequences of contraries." But the equal passages are those witty ones in Aeschines the Socratic, in which Socrates shows that Aspasia spoke with the wife of Xenophon and with Xenophon himself. "Tell me, I beg you, wife of Xenophon: if your neighbour has better gold than you have, would you prefer his or yours?" "His," she said. "And if she has a finer dress and other women's ornaments of greater value than you have, would you prefer hers?" "Hers indeed," she replied. "Come now, if she has a better husband than you have, would you prefer hers?" Here the woman blushed. Aspasia then began a conversation with Xenophon himself:

Atqui híc Xenophon quoq; ipse tacuit. Hujus etiam tractationis sunt axiomata: Quæ eidem sunt æqualia, inter se sunt æqualia. Quę rationes eidem ratio ni sunt eædē, inter se sunt eædē. Si æqualibus æqualia addantur, tota erūt æqualia. Tum, Si æqualibus æqualia subducātur, reliqua erunt æqualia. Martial. 2.
units.tr: "Tell me, I ask you," she said, "if your neighbour has a better horse than yours, would you prefer yours or his?" "His," he said. "And if he has a better estate than you have, which would you prefer then?" "His, of course, being the better," he said. "And if he has a better wife than you have, would you prefer his?" But here Xenophon himself also fell silent. There are also axioms of this treatment: things equal to the same thing are equal to one another. Reasons that are the same as the same reason are the same as one another. If equals are added to equals, the wholes will be equal. Then, if equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders will be equal. Martial 2.

units.tr: I court your dinners (shame on me!), Maximus, but you court others'; now we are equal. In the morning I come to pay my respects; you are said to have gone before me to pay yours; now we are equal.

units.la: Sū comes ipse tuus, tumidiq, anteābulo regis: Tu comes alterius: jam sumus ergo pares. Esse sat est servum, jam nolo vicarius esse: Qui rex est, regem, Maxime, non habeat.
units.tr: I am your own companion, and you are the puffed-up forerunner of a king; you are another's companion; now we are equal. It is enough to be a slave; now I do not want to be a deputy. Let him who is a king, Maximus, not have a king.

units.tr: Gnatho: Do you know when she mentions Phaedria, or if she praises him, to make you burn with jealousy? Thraso: I understand. Gnatho: To prevent that, this is the only remedy: when she names Phaedria, you name Pamphila. Straightaway, whenever she says "Phaedria," let us bring in a revel; you say "Pamphila," let us call for a song. If she praises his looks, you praise hers in turn. In short, pay back like with like, so that it bites her.

units.la: Paria] Comparatorum locus sequitur, altera species primorum argumentorum. Absoluta enim species fuit in cósentaneis & dissentaneis. Comparata igitur definiuntur, quæ cóparantur inter se: cujusmodi paria imparia, similia dissimilia deinceps erunt. Comparatorū aut inventio, etsi in eadem rerum genera incidit, in quæ absolutorum cogitatio: attamen comparata ex absolutis non oriuntur. Hoc autem problema, de ordine categoriæ hujus diu multúq; P. Ramo deliberatum, neq; dum tamen judicio ipsiu> satis cóco&tum est: sicut nec antea de causa per accidens, deque fine. Interea igitur ordo hic teneatur dum perfectius & accuratius (si quid tamé est) aliquando cernatur. Comparata igitur dicitur in Topicis συμβλητα, 13.cap. 1.lib. & cóparatio ipsa συγκρισις, 3.ca. 1.lib. Fuerit vero operæpretiū recordari, quę antea de causarū & effectorū veluti inundatione dicta sunt: ut doctrina causarū tot libros analyticos, topicos, physicos, phylosophicos implerit: ut ex effectorū loco sex ferè A-
units.tr: "Equals." The place of compared things follows, the second species of the first arguments. For the absolute species was in agreeing and disagreeing things. Compared things are therefore defined as those that are compared with one another, such as equals, unequals, similar, dissimilar, which will follow in turn. The discovery of compared things, although it falls into the same kinds of things into which the thinking about absolutes falls, nevertheless compared things do not arise from absolutes. This problem, concerning the order of this category, has long and much been deliberated by P. Ramus, yet it has not been sufficiently settled by his own judgment, just as earlier with the cause per accidens and with the end. Meanwhile, then, let this order be kept until it is at some time discerned more perfectly and accurately, if there is anything to be discerned. Compared things are therefore called in the Topics [συμβλητα], 13th chapter of book 1, and comparison itself [συγκρισις], 3rd chapter of book 1. It will be worth recalling what was said earlier about the flood, as it were, of causes and effects: how the doctrine of causes filled so many analytic, topical, physical and philosophical books; so that from the place of effects nearly six books of Aristotle A-

Verúm Ariftoteles id valde ac vehementer improbavit,atque in hac quęstione in primis καθόλε πρῶτον ufur pavit.In Philosophia enim, 3. çap.4.lib.affirmat τὰ ἐν τοῖς μαθήμασι ἀξιώματα καλᾶμεν, quę in mathematicis appellantur axiomata, non esse mathematicorum,sed ejus philosophi, cujus fit confiderare περὶ τῶν συλλογιστικῶν ἀρχῶν,de principiis fyl logifticis, deque contradictionis principio. ratioq; Ariftot. prorsus magna hic elt: Hæc (ait) axiomata sunt communia omnium entiū, non autem propria generis unius cujuspiā, ut Arithmetici, & Geometrae crediderūt, Διὰ τὴν τῶν ἀναλυτικῶν ἀπαιδευσίαν, propter analyticorum imperitiā. Hic Aristoteles mathematicos ut logicæ ignaros coarguit, quód logicam doctrinam non exerceât, ut necesse erat, sed quód tanquam mathematicam aliquam in suis præceptis adnumerent. Quin Aristoteles 5. cap. 1. Poster. eandē Logicæ ἀπαιδευσίαν in mathematicis pari severitate reprehēdit, quód proportionum doctrinam in mathematicis elementis permisceant. Itaq; Aristotelis ingeniū hac in re suspiciendū est, quód nobilissimæ disciplinæ confusionem tantā deprehenderit, & quomodo vitanda esset, tam studiosé admonuerit. Videbat nimirum philosophus, si ad difficultatem rerū mathematicarum, etiam doctrinę cōfusio & obscuritas accederet, fore, ut hæc studia jacerent, ut postea tot secula jacuerunt: ut neque quisquam adhuc inventus sit, qui septimus post Hippocraté, Leonté, Theudium, Hermotimum, Euclidem, Theonem, elementa commodiùs & luculentiùs explicare cōtenderet. Itaque & P. Ramus singulari alacritate, Aristotelis illam in Philosophia & Posterioribus vocem, tanquam ad se præcipué pertinentem excepit, totumq; mathematico Aristotelæ agriculturæ studio dies noctesque sese dedidit. Testis vigiliarum & meditationum fui, ut sæpé difficultate rerū & labore pené obrutus, admoneretur à me, ut sibi aliquando parceret, & qdr vix, ac ne vix quidem hominum millia tam multa potuissent, id unum se ne speraret effecturū, quiquibus monitis non deterritus, sed potiús accē su᷑ acrior ad institutū revertebatur: Itaque jam perspicimus, ut Aristotele vindice possessione logicam á mathematicis repetat: neq; dubitet, ut geometricum in logica sit ἄλογον, sic logicum in geometria fore ἀγεωμέτρητον. Neq; veró solúm logica á mathematicis repetivit, sed mathematicas ipsas alienis rebus obscuratas in pristinum splendorem vindicare contendit. Sed hac de re P.Rami mathematicę & artes & Scholę disserét pleniús. Sæpe ] Omnium comparatorum triplex quoddam privilegium est: primum, quód quibusdam notis breviús interdum indicátur: neque enim id convenit cęteris argumentis: tales igitur notæ in singulis generibus comparatorum á P.Ramo studiose proponūtur, quæ tanquam artis magistræ & interpretes, studioso Logicæ dicant, Hoc argumentum est parium, illud majorum, istud minorum, tale similium, aliud quoddam dissimiliū: aliquando partes pleniús distinguuntur: Partes autem comparationis explicatæ & distinctæ, appellantur προτάσεις καὶ ἀπόδοσις, propositio & redditio: est enim quod comparatur, & cui comparatur. Secundum autem privilegium hic est, quód tota προτάσεις vel ἀπόδοσις argumentum facit: non pars altera, seu terminus alter propositionis, aut redditionis: in comparatis autem, terminus proprié dicitur, quanvis sit commune omnis argumenti nomen, ut caussæ vocabulum: quanvis interdum omne argumentū significet: attamé primam speciè proprié significat. Tertium est, quód fiĉta cóparata, verorum verorū etiá argumétorum vim obtinent: Quin Ariftoteles in Rhetoricis lib.2.ca.20. indicat fictarū comparationum inventionem faciliorem esse:verarum tamen utilitatem esse majore. Sed Ariftoteles de apologis & similibus fictis fpecia liter tantum proposuit:hanc gratiam P. Ramus approbavit: Et tamen fi quid fingatur fine comparatione,argumentum veritatis non habebit, sed mēdacii: Itaque merito P. Ramus hoc singulare comparatorum privilegium esse docuit.
units.tr: Thus the place of time and place, and of subject and adjunct, has produced so many chapters in Aristotle's Physics. The place of dissentaneous things, though less so, is nonetheless dispersed variously throughout the whole of Logic, somewhat through Physics, and most widely through Philosophy. The place of comparatives, set out very amply, is first treated in the two very large categories of quantity and quality, but is only lightly touched on in the Analytics. In the Topics, however, it is again poured out most widely, for it is cited by species some one hundred and eighty times. The chief overflow of comparatives, however, has gone into the mathematical arts, so that of the whole faculty of the art of logic, the mathematicians seem to have chosen the place of comparison alone, which they cultivated chiefly not only by examples and practice but also by precepts and teaching. If there is anything great and difficult in the whole of Euclid, or Archimedes, and the other mathematicians, it is chiefly explained by ratios and proportions. Accordingly, in the teaching of ratios and proportions, the eight axioms of the first book, the whole of the fifth book, and the main part of the seventh are spent. Yet Aristotle strongly and vehemently disapproved of this, and in this question he especially used the phrase katholou prōton [καθόλε πρῶτον]. For in the Philosophy, in book 3, chapter 4, he affirms that the things in mathematics which are called axioms [τὰ ἐν τοῖς μαθήμασι ἀξιώματα καλᾶμεν] are not the property of mathematicians but of that philosopher whose business it is to consider concerning the principles of syllogisms [περὶ τῶν συλλογιστικῶν ἀρχῶν], and concerning the principle of contradiction. Aristotle's reason here is entirely great: these axioms, he says, are common to all beings, and not proper to any one kind, as the arithmeticians and geometers believed, because of the lack of training in the analytics [Διὰ τὴν τῶν ἀναλυτικῶν ἀπαιδευσίαν]. Here Aristotle charges the mathematicians with being ignorant of logic, not because they fail to practise logical doctrine as they must, but because they count as mathematical something that is in his precepts. Indeed, in the Posterior Analytics, book 1, chapter 5, Aristotle reproaches the same ignorance of logic among the mathematicians with equal severity, because they mix the doctrine of proportions into the mathematical elements. Accordingly, Aristotle's genius in this matter is to be admired, because he perceived such great confusion in this most noble discipline, and so earnestly warned how it was to be avoided. The philosopher clearly saw that if the confusion and obscurity of doctrine were added to the difficulty of mathematical things, these studies would lie neglected, as they lay neglected for so many centuries afterwards; so that no one has yet been found, the seventh after Hippocrates, Leon, Theudius, Hermotimus, Euclid and Theon, who has striven to explain the elements more conveniently and clearly. And so P. Ramus, with singular eagerness, took up that saying of Aristotle in the Philosophy and in the Posterior Analytics as if it pertained chiefly to himself, and day and night he devoted himself wholly to the mathematical cultivation of Aristotle's field. I am a witness to his watchings and meditations, for often, almost overwhelmed by the difficulty of the matter and by labour, he was reminded by me that he should spare himself at some point, and that he could hardly, or scarcely at all, achieve this one thing, which many thousands of men could not have hoped to achieve; yet, not deterred by these warnings, but rather spurred on, he returned more keenly to his undertaking. Thus we now see that, with Aristotle as his champion, he reclaims logic from the mathematicians as his possession, and he does not doubt that, as the geometrical is irrational in logic, so the logical will be ungeometrical in geometry. Nor has he only reclaimed logic from the mathematicians, but he strives to vindicate the mathematics themselves, obscured by alien matters, to their former splendour. But concerning this matter, P. Ramus's mathematics and arts and school will discuss it more fully. Often... All comparatives have a threefold privilege: first, that they are sometimes indicated more briefly by certain marks, for this does not apply to the other arguments. Accordingly, such marks in the individual kinds of comparatives are carefully set out by P. Ramus, which, like the teachers and interpreters of the art, tell the student of logic: this argument concerns equals, that concerns greater things, this one lesser, another similar, another of dissimilars. Sometimes the parts are distinguished more fully. The parts of a comparison, explained and distinguished, are called protasis and apodosis [προτάσεις καὶ ἀπόδοσις], proposition and rejoinder: there is that which is compared, and that to which it is compared. The second privilege is that the whole protasis or apodosis makes the argument, not the other part, or the other term of the proposition or rejoinder. In comparatives, however, "term" is properly so called, although it is the common name of every argument, as the word "cause" is; although sometimes it signifies every argument, it properly signifies the first species. The third is that fictitious comparisons have the force of true arguments, even of true ones. Indeed, Aristotle in the Rhetoric, book 2, chapter 20, indicates that the invention of fictitious comparisons is easier, but the usefulness of true ones is greater. But Aristotle proposed this only specially for fables and similar fictions. P. Ramus, taking this favour from Aristotle, amplifies it into four parts, and shows that equals, greater, lesser and dissimilar things, even when fictitious, have this force. Therefore, from Aristotle's law, he has made the field of Aristotle four times more fertile and more fruitful. Quintilian, in book 5, chapter 10, calls it kata hypothesin [κατὰ ὑπόθεσιν], and teaches that it can be drawn from all places, because as many species can be fictitious as true. But he adds that the thing about which the question is asked is made like the fiction, and in this he followed Aristotle's elenchus. But the rendering can also be, by fiction, equal, greater, lesser or dissimilar, as P. Ramus has approved by examples. And yet, if anything is feigned without comparison, it will have no argument of truth, but of falsehood. Accordingly, P. Ramus rightly taught that this is the singular privilege of comparatives.

units.la: Natura]Res ante in superioribus locis est definita,quomodo caussa prior effet effectu, & sub jectu adjuncto, & dissentanea simul effent natura: De comparatis nō commemini quicquā definitum esse ab Ariftotele:attamē paria & imparia æquævam notitiā habere videantur: nec for taffe similia & dissimilia repugnabunt, cūm totum id,fit nō e rerum natura,sed e comparatione. Comparatio]Divisio comparatorum fit in cō parationem quātitatis & qualitatis: sed quantitatis verbum ambiguum est in Aristotelis philosophia. Quantitas aliás logicé, aliás mathematicé in philosophia Aristotelis accipitur. Logicé, quod fit una decem categoriarum: generaliter enim & logicé tu accipitur pro quolibet argumento, quo res dicuntur æquales vel inæquales: quomodo & in Phil.2.cap.4.lib.& 2.cap.11.lib. ἰσότης καὶ ἀνισότης, æqualitas & inæqualitas dicitur πρῶται διαφοραί, περὶ αὐδὴ, περὶ τὰ καθ' αὐτὰ πάθη τῶν ὄντων, primæ differentiæ, & species, & per se affectiones entis. hæc logica est significatio quantitatis, quæ etiam totis Topicis ab Aristotele tractatur: sic quantitas loci, temporis, facultatis, & omnino rei cujuslibet appellatur. Atque hæc quantitas est logica:
units.tr: Nature] The thing has been defined earlier, in the preceding places, how a cause is prior to its effect, and how subject, adjunct and dissentaneous things are together by nature. Concerning comparatives, I do not recall that anything has been defined by Aristotle; yet equals and unequals seem to have an equal knowledge, and perhaps like and unlike will not conflict, since all of that comes not from the nature of things but from comparison. Comparison] The division of comparatives is made into comparison of quantity and of quality; but the word "quantity" is ambiguous in Aristotle's philosophy. Quantity is taken in one sense logically, and in another mathematically, in Aristotle's philosophy. Logically, it is one of the ten categories; for generally and logically it is taken for any argument by which things are said to be equal or unequal, as also in Philosophy, book 2, chapter 4, and book 2, chapter 11, equality and inequality [ἰσότης καὶ ἀνισότης] are called first differences, and species, and per se affections of being [πρῶται διαφοραί, περὶ αὐδὴ, περὶ τὰ καθ' αὐτὰ πάθη τῶν ὄντων]. This logical sense of quantity, which Aristotle treats throughout the Topics, is thus called the quantity of place, of time, of faculty, and of any thing whatever. And this quantity is logical.

units.la: at in categoria illa quantitatis, fit divisio quantitatis in numerum & magnitudinē: quæ divisio mathematica est, non logica: neque enim quantitas illa logica, solùm valet in numero & magnitudine, sed in quolibet ente & non ente. Itaque divisio illa quantitatis logicæ in numerū & magnitudiné, vitiosa est in logica arte, partesque toto divisio longé minores & inferiores efficit: & in Mathematicorum sophisma ab Aristotele reprehensum incidit, dum logicam omnisq; entis & non entis doctrinam, speciali numerorum & magnitudinū subjecto attribuit. Parium vel imparium] ἄρτιον, περιττὸν, ἴσον, ἄνισον, Par impar, æquale, inæquale, Mathematici (ut dictum est) sibi usurparunt: paritatemq; & imparitatem numeris, qualitatē & inæqualitatē magnitutinibus attribuerunt. At Logica utrumq; logicé & generaliter suo jure sibi vindicabit: & sic Aristoteles in Philosophia 15.c.5.lib.ait, Aequalia sunt, quorū quantitas una.In Rhetoricis item 23. cap. 2. lib. Æquale, quod neq; magis, neq; minús. Quomodo Cicero in Topicis, Cōparatio pariū (ait) nec elationem habet, neque summisionem: est enim æqualis. Ariftoteles in Topicis paria vocat, quæ similiter insunt: & fere cum similiū argumento confundit, & 4.cap.2.& 4. cap.3.item 4. & 5. ca.5.deniq; 2.ca.7. Attamē ὁμοιότητα, id est similitudinem, á paribus distinxit aliás, ut dicetur suo loco.Deinceps tria comparatorum privilegia in paribus ordine declarātur:ad pariū locum videntur ea referenda esse, quæ tam prolixé per Ariftotelis philosophiam dispersa sunt: Quot modis duo quælibet aut plura, dicātur idem & unum: qui modi sane quatuor omnino sunt é caussis, effectis, subjectis, adjunctis: in quos modos Ariftot. incidit,cúm docet,unū dici, ἐσίας, ποιότης, ὑποκειμένῳ, πάθος. Sed rem totam nomine unius tam cofundit, quám entis nomine: quod modo bifariam, modo trifariá, modo quadrifariá, modo quotlibetfariá dividitur. Proponuntur novem speciales notæ pariū, quæ singulæ suis exemplis illustrātur: tria aut prima exempla, notis tantum indicatur, reliqua latiús. Par levibus]Primę notę exemplum est de simulacro Creusæ, quod Æneæ, conjugem ipsam solicité perquireti apparuit: cúm Æneas memorat, ut respondere, ut complecti conatus sit: Ter frustra comprensa, manus effugit imago, Par levibus ventis, volucri simillima somno.
units.tr: But in that category of quantity, quantity is divided into number and magnitude; this division is mathematical, not logical. For that logical quantity holds not only in number and magnitude but in every being and non-being. So that division of logical quantity into number and magnitude is faulty in the art of logic, and makes the parts far smaller and inferior to the whole. It falls into the sophism of the mathematicians, which Aristotle reproved, when it assigns the whole doctrine of logic and of every being and non-being to the special subject of numbers and magnitudes. Even and odd [ἄρτιον, περιττὸν], equal and unequal [ἴσον, ἄνισον]: as was said, the mathematicians have claimed these for themselves, assigning evenness and oddness to numbers, and equality and inequality to magnitudes. But logic will rightly claim both for itself, logically and generally. So Aristotle in the Physics, book 5, chapter 15, says: "Things are equal whose quantity is one." Likewise in the Rhetoric, book 2, chapter 23: "Equal is that which is neither more nor less." Cicero in the Topics says the same: "The comparison of equals (he says) has neither elevation nor depression, for it is equal." Aristotle in the Topics calls things equal when they belong to a thing in a similar way, and nearly confuses them with the argument from like things, as in book 4, chapters 2 and 3, and also book 4 and book 5, chapter 5, and finally book 2, chapter 7. Nevertheless, he distinguished likeness [ὁμοιότης], that is, similarity, from equality on other occasions, as will be said in its place. Next, the three privileges of comparisons are declared in the order of equals. Those things which are so extensively scattered through Aristotle's philosophy seem to belong to the topic of equals: in how many ways any two or more things are said to be the same and one. These modes are certainly four in all, from causes, effects, subjects and adjuncts; Aristotle falls into them when he teaches that one is said of substance, quality, subject and affection. But he confuses the whole matter under the name of one, just as under the name of being; for it is divided sometimes two-fold, sometimes three-fold, sometimes four-fold, sometimes into however many parts. Nine special marks of equals are set out, each illustrated by its own examples; the first three or four examples are only indicated by the mark, the rest more fully. Equal to light things: The example of the first mark is the image of Creusa, which appeared to Aeneas as he anxiously sought his wife; when Aeneas tells how he tried to answer her and to embrace her: "Three times, grasped in vain, the image slipped from his hands, like the light winds, most like a fleeting dream."

units.la: Et nunc] Secundæ notæ exemplū est: ubi verba ba sunt Andromaches, quæ Hectoris uxor fuërat, & filiū Astyanactë amiserat: quem jam cum Ascanio comparat: O mihi sola mei super Astyanactis imago! Sic oculos, sic ille manus, sic ora ferebat: Et nunc æquali tecum pubesceret ævo.
units.tr: Et nunc] This is an example of the second note. The words are Andromache's, who had been Hector's wife and had lost her son Astyanax, and who now compares him with Ascanius: "O sole image of my Astyanax left to me! Such were his eyes, such his hands, such his face; and now he would be growing up the same age as your boy."

units.la: Cujus] Tertiæ notæ est exemplum, & de Pompejo loquitur, cum Africani, Pauli, Marii, Pompeji laudib. suas orator exaggerat. Anteponatur (ait) omnibus Pópejus, cujus res gestæ atq; virtutes, iisdē quibus Solis cursus, regionib. ac terminis continentur: erit profecto inter horum laudes, aliquid loci nostræ gloriæ. Reliqua exempla cum notis, partes προτάσιν & ἀπόδοσιν explicatas habent. Tam facti] Quartæ notæ exemplum. de fama autem loquitur Virgilius, quæ Didonis & Æneæ amores divulgaverat: fama est tam nutia mendacii, quàm veritatis. Tanto pessimus] Quintæ notæ est exemplum, ex epigrammate Catulli, gratias agentis Ciceroni hoc modo: Disertissime Romuli nepotum, Quot sunt, quotq; fuere (Marce Tulli) Quotque post alii erunt in annis: Gratias tibi maximas Catullus Agit, pessimus omnium poeta: Tanto pessimus omnium poeta, Quanto tu optimus omnium patronus.
units.tr: Cujus] This is an example of the third note. It speaks of Pompey, when the orator heaps his praises alongside those of Africanus, Paulus, Marius and Pompey: "Let Pompey be put before them all," he says, "whose exploits and virtues are contained within the same regions and bounds as the course of the sun. Among their praises there will surely be some place for our glory." The remaining examples have their parts, protasis [προτάσιν] and apodosis [ἀπόδοσιν], explained with the notes. Such a deed] An example of the fourth note. He speaks of rumour, in Virgil, which had spread the loves of Dido and Aeneas: rumour is as much a messenger of falsehood as of truth. The worst by so much] An example of the fifth note, from Catullus's epigram giving thanks to Cicero in this way: "Most eloquent of the descendants of Romulus, as many as there are, and as many as have been, Marcus Tullius, and as many as will come after in the years: Catullus, the worst poet of all, gives you the greatest thanks; by as much as he is the worst poet of all, by so much are you the best patron of all."

units.la: Littora] Sextæ notæ exemplum Ovidii apud Getas exulis, & multitudinem miseriarum suarum comparatione sex parium hyperbolica de monstrantis. Tenerum] Cui sunt innumeræ effigies animatium rerumq; cunctarum impressæ: nec, ut in volucrum notamus ovis, lævitate continua lubricum corpus (quod clarissimi authores dixere tenerum) argumentis indicatur. Plinius lib. 2. cap. 3. & sic Virgil. Eclog. 6. dixit:
units.tr: The shores] This is an example of the sixth note, Ovid's, written in exile among the Getae, who by hyperbolic comparison sets out the multitude of his miseries with six pairs. Tender] Upon it are impressed countless images of living things and of all things; and it is not indicated, as we note in birds' eggs, by a continuous smoothness of a slippery body (which the most distinguished authors called tender). Pliny, book 2, chapter 3, and Virgil, Eclogue 6, said:

units.la: ipse tener mundi concreverit orbis.
units.tr: the tender orb of the world itself had congealed.

units.la: Icariæ] Icarus filius Dædali, fingitur à poetis aliis cera cõpactis maria pervolasse, sed liquefacta Solis ardore cera, decidisse in mare, quod ab ejus nomine Icarium est appellatum. Ovidius,
units.tr: Icarian] Icarus, son of Daedalus, is imagined by the poets to have flown over the seas on wings of compacted wax; but the wax, melted by the heat of the sun, fell into the sea, which from his name is called Icarian. Ovid:

units.la: Icarus Icariis nomina fecit aquis.
units.tr: Icarus gave his name to the Icarian waters.

units.la: Neque] Duæ notæ sequentes, sunt per negationem imparium, septima per negationem majoris, de laude Servii Sulpitii, qui maluit in jurisprudentia Romæ primus esse: quàm Ciceroni in eloquentia secundus. Ergo ita laudatur, ut præstantissimus jureconsultus laudari debeat, qui nō magis juris & scriptarum legum, quàm justitiæ & æquitatis sit consultus & peritus: quique malit controversias tollere, bono & æquo consulendo, quàm alere lites, actionum formulas informando.
units.tr: Neither] The two following notes are by negation of unequals, the seventh by negation of the greater, in praise of Servius Sulpicius, who preferred to be first in jurisprudence at Rome rather than second to Cicero in eloquence. He is praised in such a way that the most excellent jurist ought to be praised: one who is learned not so much in the law and written statutes as in justice and equity, and who would rather remove disputes by advising in accordance with what is good and fair than feed lawsuits by framing forms of action.

units.la: Non minor] Exemplum octavæ notæ, per negationem minoris. Ovidii autem est sententia ad illum locum: Non satis invenisse tibi est, me vate, puellam: Arte mea capta est, arte tenenda mea est.
units.tr: Not less] An example of the eighth note, by negation of the lesser. Ovid's sentiment on that passage is: It is not enough for you to have found a girl through my poetry; she was captured by my art, and by my art she must be held.

units.la: Tum additur, Non minor est virtus, quàm quærere parta tueri: Casus inest illic hic erit artis opus.
units.tr: Then is added: It is no less a virtue to guard what has been won than to seek it. Chance lies in the one; here will be the work of skill.

units.la: Paria] De Sulpitio locus est, qui dejectâ petitione consulatus à Muræna, & ob id indignatus, Muræná accusavit, seq; dignioré fuisse disseruit. At orator, in contentione dignitatis, ut Murænâ servaret, satis habuit æquare utrunq;, & aliis po ftea rebus,ut militaribus artibus, Muræná præponere: In hoc autem exemplo (neque vinci potuerit,neq; superarit) negatio est tum majoris, tum minoris. Est autem rationum, cúm συλλογιστικῶς tractátur, specialis differētia apud Aristotelē,quæ ex rationib. æqualiter vel inæqualiter insunt: quod est Aristoteli ἐνύπαρξις, tanquá dicetur,inexistētia. Tumq; cōparationis argumē. tum est tota protasis,quæ ut pariter vel impariter vera est,ita paris vel imparis argumētum faciet. Axioma] Axioma interdum generaliter appellatur quodlibet propositū,ut Stoici in Logica sunt locuti, ut etiam Aristoteles nonnullis locis:aliquádo specie propositionis per sese clarissimā & evidētissimā significat, quomodo ab Aristotele in Analyticis appellatur: qualia in elementis,duodecim proponūtur ab Euclide: Sed appellantur á Proclo,unico nomine axiomata: à Theone, κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι, p periphrasin. Sed de hac differentia P. Rami Scholę mathematicę loquētur uberius. Parium] Locus est Aristotelis 4. ca.
units.tr: Equals] This concerns Sulpicius, who, when his candidacy for the consulship was rejected by Murena, and indignant on that account, accused Murena and argued that he himself was the more worthy. But the orator, in the contest of dignity, to save Murena, thought it enough to equate the two, and afterwards to put Murena before him in other matters, such as military skills. In this example (he could neither be conquered nor surpassed) there is a negation both of the greater and of the lesser. Moreover, when arguments are treated syllogistically [συλλογιστικῶς], there is a specific difference in Aristotle between arguments that are present equally or unequally, which in Aristotle is inexistence [ἐνύπαρξις], as it may be called. Then there is the argument of comparison, and then the whole protasis, which, as it is equally or unequally true, will make an argument of equal or unequal. Axiom] Axiom is sometimes used generally for any proposition, as the Stoics spoke in logic and Aristotle does in some places as well; sometimes, in the particular sense of a proposition which is by itself most clear and evident, as Aristotle calls it in the Analytics. Of this kind are the twelve which Euclid sets out in the Elements. Proclus calls them, by a single name, axioms; Theon calls them, by periphrasis, common notions [κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι]. But P. Ramus's mathematical school will speak more fully about this distinction. Of equals] This is a passage of Aristotle, chapter 4.

units.la: 2. Topic. Pariū si alterū nō infit, neq; reliquum: & si alterū, & reliquū: Hoc Aristotelis axioma vi detur esse syllogisticum illud quidem, & judicii magis,quám inventionis proprium, videtur enim conclusionis quādam regulam docere, sed quæ vim hujus argumenti etiam explicat. Itaq; cúm varie critica ista & judiciaria axiomata P. Ramus versavisset, tandem reliquit, dum accuratius hic aliqd occurreret. Talia antea ipsi ἀδιά λυσις fuerunt de causa efficiēte per accidens, de fine, de comparatorum genere & ordine. Addit etiam Ariftoteles ad illud axioma parium, valere hoc argumentum in utranque partem, affirmationis nempe & negationis: quod exempla fequètia declarant. Commune facinus] Oratio est, quam M. Antonio Tullius affingit differeti contra Cæsarem: quód Cæsar ab eo sectionem bonorum Pompejanorum repeteret, cúm tamen Antonius bellum cũ Cęsare adversus Pópejum unà fecerit,& unà vicerit. Atq; in hoc exemplo, ex affirmato pari par affirmatur. Quando] Verba sunt Demeæ, actus 5. scena 3. Demea agrestior, é duob. filiis Æschinum dederat adoptandum fratri Mitioni. Ctefiphonem retinuerat fibi, depactufq; erat cum Mitione, ut Æschinum suum curaret, Ctefiphonem sibi curádum relinqueret:postea comperto, Ctefiphonem etiam á Mitione corrúpi,exclamat inter cætera, Quando ego nó curo tuum, nempe Æschinum,ne cura meum,nempe Ctefiphone. Atq; in hoc exemplo negatur par é negato pari: ita par valet in utramq; parte. Consectaria] Hæc Ariftotelis sunt in Topicis 3. cap. 2. lib. ubi instituit é contrariis συμπλοκας complexiones, quas appellat, indeq; duplicem consecutionem,altera τῷ ἐπὶ ταῦτα, ad eadem: quam putat firmam esse in relatis & privantibus. Tum servum] Hoc consectarium é relatis antea fuit: Pater elt dominus : ergo filius est servus. In pretio] Similis est ad eadē confequentia, é privátibus: Dives honoratur: itaq; pauper despicitur. Exemplum Ariftotelis est, Visus est sensus:ergo cæcitas,est ἀναισθησία,sensus impoté tia. At confectariū hoc accuratiús fuerit cōfiderandum, necubi fallat,ut Videns est vivus:ergo cæcus est mortuus : nō sequitur. In relatis autē cósecutio est firma, propter mutuā relationis af sectionem, vel in duobus tantúm,ut Ariftoteles fuit difcipul9 Platonis: ergo Plato fuit magister Ariftotelis. quale feré est illud Quintiliani lib. 5.cap. 11. Si turpis dominæ consuetudo cum fervo, turpis domini cum ancilla. Sylla] Cicero defendebat Syllam amicum suum accusatum á Torquato etiam amico : Itaq; Torquatus ab eo violari amicitiam querebatnr : cui respondet orator ex adversis paribus:quā tamen consequē. tiam Ariftoteles in illo Topico firmam non putat:inftatq; exemplo:Bonus habitus est sanitas: ergo malus habitus est morbus : non sequitur, ait. At medici de instantia illa Ariftotelis viderint. Certé in aliis exemplis perpetuū non erit: ut, Homo est mortalis,ergo bestia est æterna,minimé sequitur. Et quidé Ariftoteles in Ethicis adversus illud axioma citatū á Cicerone (quod contraria contrariorū sint confequētia) disserit, cūm fatetur, in vitio fatis esse cauffe ad miseriā, negat autem in virtute fatis esse roboris ad beatitate: quia corporis & fortunæ bona etiam necessaria sint. quę tamē sentētia valdé mollis est, & indigna philosopho. Fitla] Comparationes generum omnium fingi possunt,ut dixi.Ex pari bus,est Æfchinis illa tota cóparatio,quam Cicero primo de Invētione cóvertit: ubi duplex est ad uxorem Xenophōtis:Tu malles melius aurum, & præcifiorem ornatum vicinæ, quám quâm tuum : malles igitur & virum ipsius meliorem. Item ψέυδος est duplex ad Xenophontem ipsum, Malles & equum, & fundum vicini tui meliorem: malles igitur & uxorem meliorē. Cicero 2.de Inventione,ubi vertit hunc locum, & post Ciceronē Quintilianus, hoc exemplum ad similitudinem retulêre:at paria sunt, Tu malles vicinæ vestem meliorem: ergo malles conjugem. Aspasia Milefia fuit,capta á Pericle: & postea propter ingenii & doctrinę præstā tiam,ducta in matrimonium,docuit autem Socrate Rhetoricas artes,ut est in Epithaphio Pla tonis : ubi & funebris Aspasię oratio recitatur. Tacuit] Post aūt Aspasia( ut habet ibidē Cicero) Quoniā uterqį vestrum (inquit) id mihi solum nō respōdit, quod ego solūm audire volueram: egomet dicam,quid uterque cogitet. Nam & tu mulier,optimū virū mavis habere : & tu Xenophon,uxorem leētissimam habere maximé vis. Quare hoc nisi perfeceritis, ut neqį vir melior, neqį fœmina leētior in terris sit, pfecto id quod semper optimū putabitis esse, multo maximé requiretis: & tu, ut maritus sis cū optima muliere:& hæc,ut quàm optimo viro nupta sit. Quæ eidem] Axioma est primum Euclidis, quod videtur illius Aristotelei ἀντίστροφον quoddam esse: Si parium alterum tertio cōvenit,& reliquum: ergo si duo conveniant eidem,paria erūt. quod etiam tā Logicé & generaliter explicari tractarique potest, quàm illud Aristoteleū, ut apparet in illo Martialis loco:Nā cúm dicit, Capto & captas:perinde est ac si diceret, hoc tibi & mihi pariter cóvenit:quare fumus pares. Cui germanú est illud de rationibus ejdem eisdé propositum 11. p. 5. & infinité totis mathematicis usurpatú: Reliqua duo axiomata Euclidis, Si æqualibus æqualia addantur vel subducantur, tota vel reliqua erunt æqualia: eundem logicum & communem usum habent: nam Martialis idem secúdo & tertio disticho, hoc idem demonstrat, addendo tum Maximo, tum Martiali æqualia facta salutandi, comitandi: unde pares & æquales concludit. Idem porro fiet, si paribus copiis æquo Marte certatú sit, tum reliquas copias pares esse concludatur. Gnatho] Locus est actus 3. scena 1. ubi parasitus consulit Thrasoni, ne purget se Thaidi de amore Päphilæ, sed potiús pari dolore repúgat, ac sicut é paribus fictis cóclufit Martialis pares authores esse, sic ité Gnathonis syllogismus est in doloris & stomachi paris conclusione. Talis est lucta illa duorum pastorum, Damœtæ & Menalcæ, ecloga tertia apud Virgiliú, Dic quib.in terris(& eris mihi magnus Apollo) Tres pateat cœli spatium non amplius ulnas.
units.tr: Topics 2. If one of two equals does not belong to something, neither does the remainder; and if the one does, so does the remainder. This axiom of Aristotle seems to be syllogistic indeed, and more proper to judgement than to invention, for it seems to teach a rule of conclusion, but one which also explains the force of this argument. Therefore, when P. Ramus had turned these critical and judicial axioms over in various ways, he finally left them aside until something more precise should occur. Earlier, for him, there were irresolvable difficulties [ἀδιάλυσις] of this kind concerning the efficient cause by accident, the end, and the genus and order of comparatives. Aristotle also adds to that axiom of equals that this argument holds in either direction, of affirmation and of negation, as the following examples show. Common crime] This is a speech which Tullius (Cicero) ascribes to Marcus Antonius, arguing against Caesar, because Caesar demanded from him a division of the Pompeian goods, although Antony had fought the war against Pompey together with Caesar, and together had won. In this example, from an affirmed equal, an equal is affirmed. Since] These are the words of Demea, Act 5, scene 3. Demea, a rather rustic man, had given Aeschinus, one of his two sons, to his brother Micio to be adopted. He had kept Ctesiphon for himself, and had agreed with Micio that Micio would look after his Aeschinus and leave Ctesiphon for Demea to look after. Afterwards, having learned that Ctesiphon too had been corrupted by Micio, he exclaims, among other things: "Since I do not care for your son, namely Aeschinus, do not care for mine, namely Ctesiphon." In this example an equal is denied from a denied equal; so equal holds in either direction. Consequences] These are Aristotle's, in Topics book 3, chapter 2, where he sets out complexions [συμπλοκάς] from contraries, as he calls them, and from them a twofold consequence: one by the same [τῷ ἐπὶ ταῦτα], to the same things, which he thinks is firm in relatives and privatives. Then the slave] This consequence from relatives was given earlier: "The father is lord; therefore the son is slave." In the price] A similar consequence to the same things, from privatives: "The rich man is honoured; therefore the poor man is despised." Aristotle's example is: "Sight is a sense; therefore blindness is lack of sensation [ἀναισθησία], the powerlessness of sense." But this consequence must be considered more carefully, lest it deceive somewhere, as in "The one who sees is alive; therefore the blind man is dead", which does not follow. In relatives, however, the consequence is firm, on account of the mutual affection of the relation, or in two only, as "Aristotle was a disciple of Plato; therefore Plato was the teacher of Aristotle." Something close to this is in Quintilian, book 5, chapter 11: "If a shameful relationship of a mistress with a slave, then a shameful one of the master with a maidservant." Sulla] Cicero defended Sulla, his friend, when he was accused by Torquatus, also a friend. Torquatus therefore complained that friendship had been violated by him, and the orator replies from opposed equals. Yet Aristotle, in that Topic, does not think this consequence firm, and presses it with an example: "Health is a good habit; therefore disease is a bad habit." It does not follow, he says. But doctors may judge that instance of Aristotle. Certainly in other examples it will not hold always, as "Man is mortal; therefore beast is eternal" by no means follows.
