And indeed Aristotle, in the Ethics, argues against that axiom cited by Cicero (that contraries have contrary consequences), when he admits that in vice there are enough causes for misery, but denies that in virtue there is enough strength for blessedness, because the goods of body and fortune are also necessary. This view is very weak and unworthy of a philosopher. Fitla] Comparisons of all kinds can be framed, as I have said. From equals is that whole comparison of Aeschines which Cicero turns in the first book of On Invention, where there is a double argument: to Xenophon's wife: You would prefer better gold and a finer ornament of your neighbour's than your own; you would therefore prefer her husband to be better as well. Likewise a false argument [ψέυδος] is double against Xenophon himself: "You would prefer a better horse and the farm of your neighbour; you would therefore prefer a better wife." Cicero, in book 2 of On Invention, where he turns this passage, and Quintilian after him, have referred this example to a similarity; but they are parallel: "You would prefer your neighbour's dress to be better; therefore you would prefer a spouse." Aspasia] Aspasia was from Miletus, captured by Pericles; afterwards, on account of her talent and learning, she was taken in marriage, and she taught Socrates the rhetorical arts, as is in Plato's Epitaphios, where the funeral speech of Aspasia is also recited. She fell silent] Afterwards, however, Aspasia (as Cicero has it there) said: "Since neither of you has answered me the one thing I alone wished to hear, I myself will say what each of you thinks. You, woman, prefer to have the best husband; and you, Xenophon, most of all wish to have a most desirable wife. Therefore, unless you bring it about that there is on earth neither a better man nor a more desirable woman, you will certainly always require much more the thing you think is always best: you, that you may be husband to the best of women, and she, that she may be married to the best of men." Which equal to the same] This is Euclid's first axiom, which seems to be a certain converse of that Aristotelian one: "If one of two equals agrees with a third, so does the remainder; therefore if two agree with the same thing, they will be equal." This too can be explained and treated as logically and generally as the Aristotelian axiom, as appears in that passage of Martial: for when he says "captured and captress," it is the same as if he said: this agrees with you and with me equally; wherefore we are equals. A close relative of this is the proposition about ratios equal to the same ratios, book 5, prop. 11, which is used throughout almost all of mathematics. Euclid's other two axioms, "If equals are added to equals or subtracted from equals, the wholes or remainders are equal," have the same logical and common use: for Martial, in the second and third couplets, demonstrates the same thing, adding to Maximus and to Martialis equal acts of greeting and accompanying, whence he concludes that they are equal and alike. The same will happen if, with equal forces and on equal terms, they have fought, and then the remaining forces are concluded to be equal. Gnatho] The passage is Act 3, scene 1, where the parasite advises Thraso not to clear himself to Thais about his love for Phaedria, but rather to answer with equal grief. Just as Martial concluded from equal fictions that the authors were equal, so Gnatho's syllogism is a conclusion of equal grief and equal resentment. Such is that contest of the two shepherds, Damoetas and Menalcas, in Virgil's third eclogue: "Tell me in what lands (and you shall be great Apollo to me) three ells of the sky's space lie open, and no more."

units.la: Cui ænigmati cúm Menalcas respódere non posset, par ænigma reposuit: Dic quibus in terris inscripti nomina regunt Nascantur flores, & Phyllida solus habeto.
units.tr: To this riddle, when Menalcas could not answer, he replied with one of equal difficulty: "Tell me, in what lands do those who are inscribed by name rule over flowers that spring up? And keep Phyllis for yourself alone."

units.la: Hic igitur, ut antea, é paribus silentiis, par utriusque pastoris ignorantia concluditur.
units.tr: Here, then, as before, from equal silences, the equal ignorance of both shepherds is concluded.

units.la: Cap. XIX. De Majoribus.
units.tr: Chapter XIX. On Greater Things

units.la: IMparia sunt, quorum quantitas non est una. Imparis axiomata sunt illa: Si æqualium alterum tertio fuerit inæquale, & reliquum eidem erit inæquale. Si inæqualibus æqualia addātur,tota erūt inæqualia. Si inæqualibus æqualia subducantur, reliqua erunt inæqualia. Impar, est majus aut minus. Majus est,cujus quantitas excedit.Proprię notę sunthujus rationis,non solúm,sed etiā,cúmtúm,malo hoc quám illud, plus, quám. Cicero pro Muræna:
units.tr: Unequal things are those whose quantities are not the same. These are the axioms of the unequal: If one of two equals is unequal to a third, the remaining one will also be unequal to that same third. If equals are added to unequals, the wholes will be unequal. If equals are subtracted from unequals, the remainders will be unequal. The unequal is either greater or less. The greater is that whose quantity exceeds. The proper marks of this relation are not only the words "not only... but also" and "both... and", but also "I prefer this to that" and "more than". Cicero, in the Pro Murena:

units.la: Tollitur é medio— nō solúm ista verbosa simulatio prudētiæ,sed etiam illa domina rerum— Sapientia vi geritur res:
units.tr: It is removed from the midst, not only that wordy show of prudence, but also that mistress of affairs, affairs are conducted by wisdom rather than by force.

units.la: Spernitur orator— non solúm odiosus in dicendo,aut loquax, verumetiam— bonus:horridu' miles amatur.
units.tr: The orator is despised, not only if he is offensive in speaking or talkative, but even if he is good; the rough soldier is loved.

units.la: Hinc sumitur interdum Logica quædam gradatio climaci Rhetorico conjuncta.Pro Mil. Neqj vero se populo solúm,sed etiam senatui tradidit: neqj senatui modó, sed etiā publicis præsidiis & armis : neqj his tantúm, verumetiamejus potestati, cui Senatus totam Rempub. omnem Italiæ pubem, cuncta populi Romani arma commiserat. 2. Agra.
units.tr: From this there is sometimes taken a certain logical gradation joined with a rhetorical climax. Pro Milone: "Nor indeed did he surrender himself to the people only, but also to the Senate; nor to the Senate merely, but also to the public guards and arms; nor to these alone, but even to that power to which the Senate had entrusted the whole Republic, all the youth of Italy, and all the arms of the Roman people." 2. Agrarian (speech).

units.la: » Quæ cúm omnibus est difficilis & magna ratio, túm vero mihi præter cæteros.juvenalis Satyra oćtava:
units.tr: "Although this matter is difficult and great for all, it is especially so for me beyond the rest." Juvenal, Satire 8:

units.la: Malo pater tibi fit Therfites, dummodo tu fis Aeacidæ similis, vulcaniaq; arma capessas, Quám te Thersitæ simile producat Achilles.
units.tr: I would rather your father were Thersites, provided you were like the son of Aeacus and took up the arms of Vulcan, than that Achilles should bring you forth like Thersites.

units.la: Plus admirationis habitura quám gloriæ, pro Marc. Sæpe fine ulla harum notarum; hoc argumentū tractatur, fecundúm illud Aristotelis axioma, Si quod minús videtur inesse, inest, & quod magis. Cic. Pro Arc. Saxa & solitudines voci respondent: bestiæ sępé immanes, cătu fleĉtuntur atq; cõfistunt: nos instituti rebus optimis, non poetarum voce movemur. Aeneid. 1.
units.tr: Destined to bring more admiration than glory. Pro Marcello. Often this argument is treated without any of these marks, according to that axiom of Aristotle: if what seems less to belong, belongs, then so does what seems more. Cicero, Pro Archia: "Rocks and deserts answer the voice; savage beasts are often softened and brought to a standstill by song; yet we, trained in the best things, are not moved by the voice of poets." Aeneid 1.

units.la: O socii (neq;n. ignari sumus anté malorum) O passi graviora, dabit Deus his quoq; finem.
units.tr: "O comrades (for we are not ignorant of evils before now), O you who have suffered worse things, God will give an end to these too."

units.la: » Cicero pro Muræna, Noli tam esse injustus, ut cúm tui fontes vel inimicis tuis pateant, nostros rivulos etiam amicis putes clausos esse oportere. Ovid. 1. de Remedio, ut corpus redimas, ferrum patiêris & ignes, Arida nec sitiens ora levabis aqua: ut valeas animo, quicquâ tolerare negabis? At pretiû pars hæc corpore majus habet.
units.tr: "Cicero, Pro Murena: 'Do not be so unjust that, when your own springs lie open even to your enemies, you think our little streams ought to be closed even to your friends.'" Ovid, Remedia Amoris 1: "That you may save your body, you will endure iron and fire, and will not relieve your parched mouth with thirst-quenching water; that you may be well in mind, will you refuse to endure anything? Yet this part has a value greater than the body."

units.la: Atq; in hac tractatione est illa gradatio septimæ Verrinæ, dissimilis illius superioris: Facinus est vincire civem Romanum: scelus verbarere: propè parricidium necare. quid dicam in crucem tollere? Ficta etiam majora plurimùm valent. 2. Phil. O rem nō modó visu fœdā, sed etiam auditu: si inter cœnam in tuis immanib. illis poculis, hoc tibi accidisset, quís non turpe duceret? in cœtu véró populi, negotium publicum gerens, magister equitum, cui ructare turpe esset, is vomens, fructis esculentis vinum redolentibus, gremium suum & totum tribunal implevit.
units.tr: In this kind of argument is that gradation of the seventh Verrine, unlike the one above: "It is a crime to bind a Roman citizen; an outrage to flog him; close to parricide to put him to death; what shall I say of crucifying him?" Even greater things carry much weight. Second Philippic: "O a thing foul not only to see but even to hear! If this had happened to you at dinner, amid those monstrous cups of yours, who would not think it disgraceful? But in the assembly of the people, when the Master of the Horse, who was conducting public business, and for whom belching would be disgraceful, vomited and filled his lap and the whole tribunal with food and wine-smelling fruits."

units.la: Imparia] Imparia definiuntur definitione oppositâ parium definitioni, quorū quantitas non eadem: hisq; tria axiomata communia majorum & minorum subjiciuntur, ut antea paribus tria subjecta sunt. Si inæquale] Antea fuit, Eidem æqualia, esse inter se inæqualia: cui videtur oppositum, Quę eidē inæqualia, esse inter se inæqualia. at omnium in mathematicis sophisimatū captiosissimum hoc est. est enim falsum. Nam tria, item altera tria sunt inæqualia duobus: & tamē inter se non sunt inæqualia. Itaq; à P. Ramo proponitur imparium primū axioma, uti oportuit: duo sequentia, sunt Euclidis, secundum & tertium, quæ perinde communia sunt: Lumina Solis & lis & Lunæ sunt inæqualia: æqualia addantur utriq; reliquarum stellarum lumina: tota erunt inæqualia. id est, majus, erit majus tantò, & minus, tantò minus: detrahatur utriq; æqualia eadem, reliqua erunt inæqualia: id est, ut antea, majus perinde majus, & minus perinde minus.
units.tr: Unequal: unequals are defined by a definition opposed to the definition of equals, whose quantities are not the same; and to these are subjoined three common axioms of greater and less, just as before three were subjoined to equals. If unequal: before it was, "Things equal to the same are equal to one another," to which the opposite seems to be "Things unequal to the same are unequal to one another." But this is the most captious of all sophisms in mathematics, for it is false. For three and likewise another three are unequal to two, and yet they are not unequal to one another. Therefore by P. Ramus the first axiom of unequals is set forth, as was fitting; the two following are Euclid's, the second and third, which are equally common: The lights of the Sun and the Moon are unequal; if equal lights of the other stars are added to each, the wholes will be unequal; that is, the greater will be greater by as much, and the less less by as much. If equal things are taken away from each, the remainders will be unequal; that is, as before, the greater is greater by the same amount and the less is less by the same amount.

units.la: Impar est majus] Dichotomia servatur perpetuò. Majus in elementis nunquam perspicuè explicatur, sed nomine totius, ut in octavo axiomate primi: & nomine multiplicis, ut tertia definitione quinti, & quinta septimi, obscuriùs comprehenditur: Itaq; majus definitur à P. Ramo è logico & generali quantitatis sensu antea declarato. Propriæ notæ] Propriæ notæ majorum nō tam multæ sunt, quàm parium: sed tamen etiam certè: ut non solùm, sed etiā, cùm tùm, malo hoc quàm illud. Tollitur] Versus sunt Enniani, oratoriis comparationibus majorum illustrati: habent autem versus prosæ interpositi, & gratiam & authoritatè: quod in Ciceroniano P. Ramus plenius adnotavit. Climax] Hic figura rhetorica est, cùm attenditur repetitio sponi continuata multis subinde sententiis: & sonus item figuram verbi efficit: at majora minoribus comparata, præsentis loci argumentum faciunt. Quin potest ista logica esse gradatio sine climace rhetorico: ut apud Terentium, cùm Gnatho Thaidis gratias amplificat pro virgine: Th Magnus vero agere gratias Thais mihi?
units.tr: The unequal is the greater: dichotomy is kept throughout. The greater is never clearly explained in the Elements, but by the name of whole, as in the eighth axiom of Book 1, and by the name of multiple, as in the third definition of Book 5 and the fifth of Book 7, it is comprehended more obscurely. Therefore the greater is defined by P. Ramus from the logical and general sense of quantity declared before. Proper marks: the proper marks of greater things are not as many as those of equals, but they are nonetheless certain: such as not only, but also, not only but even, I would prefer this to that. Tollitur: these are verses of Ennius, illustrated by oratorical comparisons of greater things; verses inserted in prose have both grace and authority, which P. Ramus annotated more fully in his treatment of Cicero. Climax: this is a rhetorical figure, when the repetition of one word is continued through many sentences in succession; the sound likewise makes a figure of the word, but greater things compared with lesser ones produce the argument of the present place. Indeed this logical gradation can exist without a rhetorical climax, as in Terence, when Gnatho magnifies Thais's thanks for the girl: Thais: "Do I really owe him great thanks?"

units.la: Gn. Ingentes. Th Ain tu? læta est? Gn. nō tā ipso qui Dono quàm abs te datum esse, id vero sertio Triumphat. Oratio a majoribus semper crescit: plus enim est, ingentes, quam magnas gratias agere: & plus, triumphare, quam laetā esse: & plus authore muneris, quam munere ipso delectari.
units.tr: Gnatho: "Huge." Thais: "Do you say so? Is she glad?" Gnatho: "Not so much glad at the gift itself as that it was given by you; that indeed she triumphs over." The speech always grows from greater things: for it is more to give huge thanks than great thanks; and more to triumph than to be glad; and more to be delighted with the giver of the gift than with the gift itself.

units.la: Quae cum]Loquitur orator de Consulatus ad ministrandi difficultate, quia nulla generis authoritate, vel commendatione defendatur, si quid offenderit. Therfites] Malo te nobilem patris ignobilis esse filium, quam nobilis ignobilem. Therfites, fuit deformissimus & ignavissimus Graecorum: Achilles autem praestantissimus. De Therfite est 2. Iliad. ut ab Achille, quod illi covitiaretur, ictu pugni sit interemptus. Aeacidae] Aeacus, pater Pelei, avus Achillis: unde jam nepos Aeacides appellatur. Vulcaniaq.] Vulcanus, deus ignis fingitur, & faber armorum jovialium adversus gigantes. Axioma] Habet vero majoris argumentum sua etiam consectaria, sed affirmata tantum: & minus inesse, significat difficilius inesse: Est autem axioma 4. cap. 2. Topici.
units.tr: Quae cum: the orator speaks of the difficulty of administering the consulship, because whatever offence it gives cannot be defended by any authority of birth or by any recommendation. Thersites: I would rather you were the son of a nobody father than a nobody with a noble father. Thersites was the most deformed and cowardly of the Greeks, while Achilles was the most outstanding. Concerning Thersites, in Iliad 2, that he was killed by a blow of Achilles' fist because he reviled him. Aeacidae: Aeacus was the father of Peleus and grandfather of Achilles, whence Achilles is now called the grandson, Aeacides. Vulcaniaq.: Vulcan is imagined as the god of fire and the smith of Jove's armour against the giants. Axiom: it has its own consequences as to the argument of the greater, but only affirmed; and "to belong less" signifies "to belong with greater difficulty." It is the fourth axiom of chapter 2 of the Topics.

units.la: Saxa] Orator multis ante laudibus poetas in defensione prosecutus erat, ut etiam sanctos appellaret & divinos: tum conclusionis loco, comparatio haec inducitur a majoribus: Majus enim & difficilius, saxa & bestias moveri. Quint. li. 8. cap. 3. similitudine hic statuit, sed falso: est enim majorum comparatio, non similium. O socii] Consolatio est Aeneae ad socios tempestate vexatos & dejectos in Africam: Graviora pertulistis, leviora itaq; tolerate. Noli esse] Servium Sulpitium alloquitur, qui (ut antea Torquatus) offendebatur, quod Tullius amicus defenderet » Muraenam, Sulpitii ipsius inimicum Nam si tibi » (ait orator) necesse putas, etiā adversariis amicorum tuorum de jure cōsulentibus respōdere: & si turpe exitiimas, te advocato, illum ipsum, pro quo veneris, caussa cadere. Allegoria autem festiva interponitur, ad placandum : assentatur enim interea, dum jurisprudentiam eloquentia tantō superiore facit, quantō fontes rivulis sint ampliores. Ut corpus] Hoc argumentum cuipiā videatur esse à minoribus: nā corpus, anima minus est: & hoc poeta significat: Attamē pati corporis caussa, difficilius est, & minus videtur inesse:deniq; affirmatio (Tu pateris corporis causa,patere igitur animi) argumētum majoris indicat,quale est illud Horatii,
units.tr: Saxa: the orator had earlier, with much praise, pursued the defence of poets so far as to call them holy and divine; then, by way of conclusion, this comparison is introduced from greater things: for it is greater and more difficult for rocks and beasts to be moved. Quintilian, Book 8, chapter 3: here he sets it up as a similitude, but wrongly, for it is a comparison of greater things, not of like things. O socii: this is Aeneas's consolation to his comrades, harassed and cast down by the storm onto Africa: "You have suffered worse things, so bear the lesser ones." Noli esse: he addresses Servius Sulpicius, who (as Torquatus did before) was offended because Tullius, a friend, defended Murena, the enemy of Sulpicius himself. "For if you think it necessary," says the orator, "to answer even the enemies of your friends when they seek legal advice; and if you think it shameful that, with you as advocate, that very man for whom you came should lose his case." A witty allegory is inserted in order to placate: it flatters him meanwhile, while it makes jurisprudence inferior to eloquence by as much as springs are larger than streams. Ut corpus: this argument might seem to be from lesser things, for the body is less than the soul, and the poet signifies this; yet to suffer for the sake of the body is more difficult and seems to belong less; finally, the affirmation ("You suffer for the body's sake, therefore suffer for the soul's") indicates an argument from greater things, such as that of Horace,

units.la: Ut jugulent homines, furguntde nocte latrones Ut teipsum serves,non expergisceris?
units.tr: Do robbers rise from their beds at night to cut men's throats, and will you not wake up to save yourself?

units.la: Vincire] De Cajo Consano loquitur, quem Verres pro fugitivorū speculatore, quanvis civem Rom. verberibus cæsum, igne candentibusq; laminis excruciatum, tandem in crucem egit.atqui leges Porciæ & Semproniæ, vincula, & virgas à corpore civis Romani, nō solūm crucem sustulerant,ut est pro Rabyrio,& in eadem septima Verrina. atque tres illi gradus, vincire, verberare, necare, quamvis res sint minores, quàm tollere in crucem:tamen ὑπαρξιν difficiliorem habēt, & affirmat deniq;: unde majoris argumentum agnoscimus. Orem] De hoc vomitu sicest 2. Phil. Tuistis faucibus, istis lateribus, ista gladiatoria totius corporis firmitate, tantum vini in Hippiæ nuptiis exhauseras, ut tibi nebi necesse esset in Pop. Rom. conspectu vomere postridie.
units.tr: Vincire] He speaks of Gaius Consanus, whom Verres, though a Roman citizen, had as a spy on runaway slaves. Verres had him beaten with rods, tortured with fire and red-hot plates, and at last had him put to the cross. Yet the laws of Porcius and Sempronius had removed from a Roman citizen's body not only the cross but also the chains and the rods, as Cicero says in the Pro Rabirio and in the seventh Verrine. And these three steps, to bind, to beat, to kill, though they are lesser matters than raising someone on a cross, nonetheless have a harder existence [ὕπαρξιν], and the argument is strengthened at the end. Hence we recognise the argument from the greater. Orem] Of this vomiting he speaks in the second Philippic: "With that throat, those sides, and that gladiatorial firmness of the whole body, you had drunk so much wine at Hippias's wedding that you had to vomit the next day in the sight of the Roman people."

units.la: Cap. XX. De Minoribus.
units.tr: Chapter XX. On Lesser Things

units.la: Minus est, cujus quantitas exceditur. Minus autem, saepe indicatur propriis notis, ut nō solum, sed ne, ante illud quàm hoc: item per grammaticā comparationem, deniq; per negationē parium. Cic. 2. Cati. Nemo non modo Romæ, sed ne ullo in angulo totius Italiæ oppressus ære alieno fuit, quem nō ad hoc incredibile sceleris foedus asciverit. Virg. Eclog. 1.
units.tr: A thing is lesser when its quantity is exceeded. The lesser is often indicated by its own marks: by "not only... but not even," by "before this than that," likewise by a grammatical comparison, and finally by the denial of equals. Cicero, Second Catilinarian: "No one, not only at Rome but not even in any corner of all Italy, was oppressed by debt who was not drawn into this incredible covenant of crime." Virgil, Eclogue 1:

units.la: Ante leves ergo pascentur in æthere cervi, Et freta destituent nudos in littore pisces: Ante pererratis amborū finibus, exul (grim: Aut Ararim Parthʾ bibet, aut Germania Ti Quám nostro illius labatur pectore vultus.
units.tr: Sooner shall the light deer graze in the air, and the seas leave the fish stranded on the bare shore; sooner shall the Parthian drink of the Arar, or the German of the Tigris, than that face of his slip from my heart.

units.la: Ovidius 3. de Trist.
units.tr: Ovid, Tristia 3.

units.la: Sævior es tristi Busiride, sævior illo, Qui falsum lento torruit igne bovem:
units.tr: You are more savage than cruel Busiris, more savage than him who roasted a false ox over a slow fire.

units.la: Atq; hujus ejusdem speciei sunt hæ formulæ, quæ fiunt etiam negatione pariū. Philip. 9. Omnes ex omni ætate, qui in hac civitate intelligentiā juris habuerunt, si unum in locum cōferantur, cum Servio Sulpitio non sunt cōferendi. Cati. 2. til.2. Quanquam illi, qui Catilinam, Maf filiam ire dictitant, non tam hæc quærū tur, quám verentur. Pro Murena: Quod enim fretū, quem Eurypum, tot motus, tantas, tam varias habere putatis agitationes fluctuum, quantas perturbationes & quantos æstus habet ratio comitiorum? Axioma autem est minorū, Si quod magis videtur inesse, nō inest, neque quod minus. quod tantum valet in negando. Pro Marcel. Tantū abes á per sectione maximorum operū, ut fundamenta, quæ cogitas, nondū jeceris. Finguntur etiam minora. Terent. in Heaut.
units.tr: Of this same kind are also those formulas that are made by denying equals. Philippic 9: "All men of every age who have had knowledge of law in this state, if they are gathered into one place, are not to be compared with Servius Sulpicius." Second Catilinarian: "Although those who keep saying that Catiline was going to Mars's daughter [Mamurra's?] are not so much seeking these things as fearing them." Pro Murena: "For what strait, what Euripus, do you think has so many movements, so many and such varied agitations of waves, as the mechanics of the elections has disturbances and tides?" The axiom of the lesser is this: If something seems to be present to a greater degree, and it is not present, neither is the lesser. This holds only in denial. Pro Marcello: "You are so far from the completion of the greatest works that you have not yet laid the foundations you are thinking of." Lesser things are also feigned. Terence, in the Heauton:

units.la: Satrapes si siet Amator, nunq; sufferre ejus sumptus queat, Nedum tu possis. 5. Aeneid. (thor Magnanime Aenea, non si mihi juppiter auspondeat, hoc sperem Italiā contingere cælo.
units.tr: If a satrap were a lover, he could never bear the expense of her, much less you could. Aeneid 5: Magnanimous Aeneas, not even if Jupiter should promise me this, would I hope that Italy should be reached by heaven.

units.la: Atq; hęc de majoribus & minoribus: quorum communis videtur explicatio, ut antea ex paribus paria, sic ex majoribus & minoribus inter se collatis, duorum alterum majus, alterum minus, id est, ex imparibus imparia arguimus. Sic Ovidius amplificat Augusti laudes collatione Romuli, quē (dum ejus facta factis Austis Augusti, minora majorib. cõparat) modis minorem facit, Fast.1. Romule, concedes, facit hic tua magna tuedo Mænia, tu dederas transilienda Remo. Te Tatius, parvi͏ Cures, Ceninaq; sensit: Hoc duce, Romanũ est Solis utrũq; latus. Tu leve nescio quid victa telluris habebas: Quodcunq; est alto sub sove, Cæsar habet. Tu rapis, hic castas duce se iubet esse maritas Tu recipis luco, repulit ille nefas. Vis tibi grata fuit, florent sub Cæsare leges. Tu domini nomen, principis ille tenet. Te Remus incusat, veniã dedit hostibus ille. Cælestem fecit te pater, ille patrem.
units.tr: So much for the greater and the lesser. The common explanation seems to be this: just as from equals we argue equals, so from greater and lesser compared with one another, one of the two is greater and the other lesser, that is, from unequals we argue unequals. Thus Ovid magnifies the praises of Augustus by comparing Romulus, whom (while he compares Augustus's deeds with the greater deeds of Augustus, the lesser with the greater) he makes smaller. Fasti 1: Romulus, you will concede that this great wall of yours, made by the work of Augustus, was a wall that you had made for Remus to leap over. Tatius felt you, and Cures, and Ceninum, the small ones. Under this leader the Roman people is on both sides of the sun. You had some slight thing from the land you conquered; whatever lies under the high sky, Caesar holds. You snatched; here he orders chaste wives to be chaste under his leadership. You took back the grove; he drove out wrongdoing. Your power was pleasing; under Caesar the laws flourish. You held the name of lord; he holds the name of prince. Remus accused you; he gave pardon to enemies. Your father made you a god; he made his father one.

units.la: Sic Cicero pro Murena, imperatorem jureconsulto comparat: Qui potest dubitari, quin ad Consulatum adipiscendũ, multó plus dignitatis afferat res militaris, quám juris civilis gloria? Vigilas tu de noćte, ut tuis cõsultoribus responderas: ille, ut eó quó intendit, mature cũ exercitu perveniat. te gallorum, illũ buccinarum cantus exuscitat. tu actione institutis: ille acie instruit. tu caves, ne tui consultores: ille, ne urbes aut castra capiantur. ille tenet & scit, ut hostium copiæ: tu ut aquæ pluuiæ arceantur. ille exercixercitatus est in propagādis finibus : tu in regendis.
units.tr: So Cicero, in the Pro Murena, compares the general with the lawyer: "Who can doubt that for winning the consulship, military affairs bring far more dignity than the glory of civil law? You keep watch at night so that you may answer your clients; he so that he may reach by dawn, with his army, the place he is heading for. The crowing of cocks rouses you; the sound of trumpets rouses him. You arrange your cases in court; he arranges his battle line. You take care lest your clients..., he takes care lest cities or camps be captured. He holds and knows the forces of the enemy; you know how rainwater is kept off. He has been trained in extending boundaries; you in governing them."

units.la: Minus in Euclideis elementis, pars aut partes appellatur, pars, quando aliquoties sumpta restituit totum: secus partes appellantur, ut prima definitione quinti, & tertia quartaq; definitione septimi. Sed pars ambigué modo refertur ad totum: ut in nono axiomate primi, Totū est majus sua parte: modó ad multiplum. Itaque hanc ambiguitatem P. Ramus evitavit.
units.tr: In Euclid's Elements, a "part" or "parts" is called the part which, when taken a certain number of times, restores the whole; but "parts" are called in a different sense, as in the first definition of the fifth book and the third and fourth definitions of the seventh. But "part" is referred to the whole in an ambiguous way: as in the ninth axiom of the first book, "the whole is greater than its part," and in another way to a multiple. Therefore P. Ramus avoided this ambiguity.

units.la: Notæ hic sunt quatuor, non solúm, sed ne: anté hoc, quám illud: tertió, nota comparationis: quartó, negatio pariū. Præcipua auté est, non solùm, sed ne, opposita illi affirmatæ, nó, solúm, sed etiam. De Catilina loquitur, qui ingenio prorsus admirabili, conflarat tantā improborum manum. Hyperbolica est collatio Tityri: faciliús naturæ leges subvertentur, ut cervi pascātur in æthere, mare are factū destituat pisces, fluminaq; mundi, ut Araris Galliæ, & Tigris Mefopotamiæ, hic in Germaniam, ille in Parthiam influant quám beneficia Cæsaris obliviscar. Tertia nota est minorum per comparationem. Bufiris fingitur á poetis filius Neptuni, crudelitate necatorum hospitum infamis. Itaq; cúm Herculem hospitē mactare vellet ab eo interemptus est. de hoc, 2. Georg. Virgil.
units.tr: There are four marks here: not only, but not even; before this rather than that; thirdly, the mark of comparison; fourthly, the denial of equals. The chief one, however, is "not only, but not even," opposed to the affirmative "not only, but also." He speaks of Catiline, who, with a wholly admirable talent, had gathered so great a band of wicked men. The comparison with Tityrus is hyperbolic: the laws of nature would more easily be subverted, so that deer graze in the air, the sea left dry leaves the fish stranded, and rivers of the world, the Arar flowing into Gaul and the Tigris into Mesopotamia, one into Germany, the other into Parthia, than I should forget the kindnesses of Caesar. The third mark is the lesser by comparison. Busiris is feigned by the poets to be a son of Neptune, infamous for the cruelty with which he killed his guests. Hence, when he wished to slaughter Hercules as his guest, he was killed by him. On this, Virgil, Georgics 2:

units.la: — Quis aut Eurifthea durum, Aut illaudati nescit Burifidis aras?
units.tr: Who does not know the hard Eurystheus, or the altars of the unpraised Busiris?

units.la: Periphrasis est Phalaridis tyranni Agrigentini: cujus exercendæ crudelitati cúm Peril lus Atheniésiş artifex ingeniosus, bovem æneū ita fabricatus esset, ut rei per apertum pectus in clusi, subjectoq; igne tolti, mugitum bovis, non humanam vocem ederent: Phalaris artificii primum periculum in artifice ipso fecit. omnes] Notæ sequentes fiunt negatione parium, Non conferendi, Non tam, quám, Non tot, quot.
units.tr: This is a periphrasis of Phalaris, tyrant of Agrigentum. For the exercise of his cruelty, Perillus of Athens, an ingenious craftsman, made a bronze bull so constructed that men shut inside it through an opening in its side, with fire placed beneath, would give forth the bellowing of a bull, not a human voice. Phalaris made the first trial of his device on the craftsman himself. Omnes] The following marks are made by the denial of equals: "not to be compared," "not so much as," "not so many as."

units.la: Omnes] Laus est Sulpitii magna, quó minores fiunt omnes anté nati Romæ jurisconsulti.
units.tr: Omnes] This is a great praise of Sulpicius, by which all the jurists born earlier at Rome are made lesser.

units.la: Non tam] Catilinarii, ut Ciceroni invidiá crearent, hoc dictitabant. Quod enim ] Hic negatio est parium notarum, tantas, quantas. Freta non habent tantas agitationes, quátas habent comitia. Axioma] Axioma autem Aristotelis, est 4. ca. 2. Topic. Valetq; hic locus tantúm ad negandum, ut superior ad affirmandum. Tantum abes] Cæsar conquestus de suspicione conjurationis, dicebat se satis sibi vixisse: At orator negat Reipublicæ collapsæ, neq; dum restitutæ, satis eum vixisse. Nunc (ait) cúm salutem civium, cunstamq; Rempub. res tuæ gestæ complexæ sint: tátúm abes á perfectione maximorum operū, ut fundamenta, quæ cogitas, nondum jeceris.
units.tr: Non tam] The Catilinarians kept saying this so that they might stir up envy against Cicero. Quod enim] Here is the denial of equal marks: "so many... as," "as great... as." Straits do not have as many agitations as the assemblies have. Axioma] The axiom is Aristotle's, in the fourth book, chapter 2, of the Topics. This place holds only in denial, as the previous one holds in affirmation. Tantum abes] Caesar, complaining about the suspicion of conspiracy, said that he had lived long enough for himself. But the orator denies that he has lived long enough for the collapsed and not yet restored Commonwealth. "Now," he says, "since your deeds have embraced the safety of citizens and the whole state, you are so far from the completion of the greatest works that you have not yet laid the foundations you are thinking of."

units.la: Satrapes] Verba sunt Chremetis, actus 3. scena prima, dissuadentis Menedemo nimiam indulgentiam in amores Cliniæ filii, quia amica nimiúm sumptuosa sit:
units.tr: Satrapes] These are the words of Chremes, in the first scene of the third act, dissuading Menedemus from excessive indulgence in the loves of his son Clinia, because the mistress is too expensive:

units.la: Primum (inquit) jam ancillas secū adduxit plus decē, Oneratas veste atq; auro —
units.tr: First (he says), she has already brought with her more than ten maidservants, weighed down with clothes and gold—

units.la: Satrapes ] Dictio est Persica, quæ latiné persectum significat. Hic igitur fictum est argumentum: Si Satrapes amaret hanc, nō posset perferre hos sumptus: nedum, id est, non solùm nō tu, nedum enim, id proprié significat. Majora vidétur hæc. At ὑπαρξις Aristotelis, & axiomatis negatio, minora demonstrant. juppiter] Fictio est similis : Si juppiter adesset, non posset institutam velificationem sequi: nos igitur non possumus. Vox autem est Palinuri, tempestatem insurgentem prospicientis, cúm ex Africa in Italiam classis Æneæ navigaret.
units.tr: Satrapes] This is a Persian word, which in Latin means "the perfect." Here, then, an argument is feigned: If a satrap loved her, he could not bear these expenses, much less you, that is, not only not you; for "nedum" properly signifies this. These seem to be greater things. But Aristotle's existence [ὕπαρξις] and the denial of the axiom demonstrate the lesser. juppiter] The fiction is similar: If Jupiter were present, he could not follow the course of the sailing begun; therefore we cannot either. The words are those of Palinurus, who saw the storm rising when Aeneas's fleet was sailing from Africa to Italy.

units.la: Colligere arma jubet, validisq; incumbere remis: Obliquatq; sinus in ventum, ac talia fatur.
units.tr: He orders them to gather the arms and bend to the strong oars, and he angles the sail into the wind, and speaks thus.

units.la: Talis est fictio 2. Æneidos, cúm Hecuba Priamŭ deterret ab armis contra victores Græcos: Non tali auxilio, nec defensoribus istis Tempus eget, non si ipse meus nunc afforet Hector.
units.tr: This is a fiction from the second book of the Aeneid, when Hecuba dissuades Priam from arms against the victorious Greeks: Not with such aid, nor with defenders like these, does the situation need them, not even if my own Hector were now present here.

units.la: Talis apud eundem poetam:
units.tr: Another such example from the same poet:

units.la: Non mihi si linguæ centum sint, oraq; centum, Omnia pœnarum percurrere nomina possem.
units.tr: Even if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, I could not run through all the names of the punishments.

units.la: Explicatio] Majorem minorumq; ubertas est permagna: cujus & illud videtur, cúm quæstio est de ipsa majoris & minoris inæqualitatis ratione, eaq; arguitur, illinc é majorib9, hinc é minoribus: quæ modó tamen antecedunt, modó sequuntur: ut in exemplo Ovidii, initium est ab Augusto, reliquæ rationes incipiunt á Romulo: cótrá in exemplo Ciceronis, ratio incipit á Servio, tandem duplex ratio incipit á Muræna. In exemplo autem Romuli, præcipua ejus facta attinguntur. Magna] Romulus fecit Romá quadratam, & quatuor tantúm portarū: Augustus ad sedecim regiones & portas deduxit. Trans-silienda filienda] Romulus ad tutelam novę urbis, validū sufficere putabat, ait Florus. Tatius] Sabinorū rex, in media urbe contra Romanos præliatus, & conditione admissus in partem regni. Cures] Oppidum Sabinorum, cui Tatius præfuit.
units.tr: Explanation: The abundance of the greater and the lesser is very great. This also appears when the question concerns the very reason of greater and lesser inequality, and it is argued from the greater things on one side and the lesser on the other. These arguments sometimes come before and sometimes after. Thus, in the example from Ovid, the beginning is from Augustus, and the remaining arguments begin from Romulus; conversely, in the example from Cicero, the argument begins from Servius, and finally a double argument begins from Murena. In the example of Romulus, his outstanding deeds are touched upon. Great: Romulus made Rome square and had only four gates; Augustus extended it to sixteen regions and gates. Leaping over, leaping over: Romulus thought a strong wall sufficient for the protection of the new city, says Florus. Tatius: king of the Sabines, who fought in the middle of the city against the Romans and was admitted on terms to a share of the kingdom. Cures: a town of the Sabines, over which Tatius ruled.

units.la: Ceninaq] Cenina, oppidum Ceninensium, captum à Romulo & dirutum. Romanum regnū exiguis circa Romam finibus continebatur, sub Augusto tantum fuit imperium, quātum postea fuit unquam. Turapis] Simulatis quippe ludis equestribus, virgines, qę ad spectaculum venerant, prædæ fuêre, ait Florus. Castas] Augustus leges de adulteriis, de pudicitia, de maritandis ordinibus, de divortiis tulit, de quibus Suetonius in ejus vita, cap.34. Vis] Romulus violentus admodum fuit, discerptumq; à Senatu putant, ob asperius ingenium. Leges] Augustus, pace toto imperio cōstituta, geminoq; jano claū so, pronum in omnia mala, & in luxuriam flues sæculū, gravibus severisq; legibus coercuit, ait Florus. Domini] Romulus, Rex vel tyrannus potiús habitus est: Augustus, cúm aliquādo dominus appellaretur, respondit se Cæsarem esse, non dominū. Remus] Remus interfectus á fratre Romulo, quia saltu derisisset foflæ Romanæ angustias. Hostibus] Plerisq; hostibus ignovit, in multis tamen sævus fuit: de quo Suetonius in ejus vita, cap. 13. Cælestem] Romulus, filius Martis creditus est, & ob id consecratus: Augustus autem, julium, á quo erat adoptatus, consecravit. Imperatorē] Exemplum hoc facilius est, nec admodū interprete requirit. Aquæ pluviæ]
units.tr: Ceninaque: Cenina, a town of the Ceninenses, captured and destroyed by Romulus. The Roman kingdom was confined within small borders around Rome; under Augustus there was as much empire as there ever was afterwards. Turapis: for the equestrian games were staged as a pretext, and the virgins who had come to the show became booty, says Florus. Chaste: Augustus passed laws concerning adultery, chastity, the marriage of the orders, and divorces, about which Suetonius writes in his life of him, chapter 34. Force: Romulus was quite violent, and they think he was torn apart by the Senate because of his harsh temper. Laws: Augustus, when peace had been established throughout the whole empire and the gates of Janus were closed, restrained an age inclined to every evil and to luxury with grave and strict laws, says Florus. Masters: Romulus was regarded rather as a king or tyrant; Augustus, when at one time he was called master, replied that he was Caesar, not master. Remus: Remus was killed by his brother Romulus, because in a leap he had mocked the narrowness of the Roman ditch. Enemies: Augustus pardoned most enemies, yet he was cruel in many cases, as Suetonius writes in his life of him, chapter 13. Heavenly: Romulus was believed to be a son of Mars and was on that account deified; Augustus, however, deified Julius, by whom he had been adopted. Commander: This example is easier and does not greatly require an interpreter. Rainwater.

units.la: Aqua pluvia,eadē aqua cælestis dicitur, & pluvialis, Si cui vero aqua pluvia damnum dabit, aqué pluvię actione avertetur aqua, ait Ulpian9.
units.tr: Rainwater: the same water is called heavenly and also pluvial. "If rainwater shall cause damage to anyone, the water shall be diverted by an action concerning rainwater," says Ulpian.

units.la: Cap. XXI. De Similibus.
units.tr: Chapter XXI. Concerning Similars.

units.la: Adhuc coparatio in quatitate fuit, sequitur coparatio in qualitate: qua res coparatę, quales dicutur: nepe similes aut dissimiles. Similia sunt, quorū est eadē qualitas. similitudo, proportio dicitur, ut similia, pportionalia. Notæ similitudinis (quę uno verbo concluditur) sunt, similis, effigies, more, instar, tanquā, sicuti: tum negatio dissimiltudinis, haud secus, non aliter. 1. Aeneid.
units.tr: Thus far there has been comparison in quantity; there follows comparison in quality, in which things compared are said to be of such a kind, namely similar or dissimilar. Similars are those things which have the same quality. Likeness is called proportion, as similar things are proportional things. The marks of similarity (which are summed up in one word) are: similar, image, manner, like, as, just as. Then the negation of dissimilarity: not otherwise, not differently. Aeneid 1:

units.la: Os humerosq; Deo similis.—
units.tr: Like a god in shoulders and face.

units.la: 9. Phil. Quanquā nullū monimentū clarius Servius Sulpitius relinquere potuit, quám effigie morū suorū, virtutis, constantię, pietatis, ingenii, filiū. 1. Trift. Nāq; ea vel nemo, vel qui mihi vulnera fecit Solus Achilleo tollere more potest.
units.tr: Ninth Philippic: Servius Sulpicius could leave no monument more clear than the likeness of his manners, virtue, steadfastness, piety, and talent, his son. Tristia 1: For only he, or he who has inflicted my wounds, can heal them in the manner of Achilles.

units.la: In Pif. Vnus ille dies mihi quidem instar immortalitatis fuit, quo in patriam redii. Verr. 1. Sed repētē é vestigio ex homine tanquam aliquo poculo Cicero, factus est Verres. Pro Pompejo: Itaq; omnes quidē nunc in his locis Cn. Pompejum sicut aliquem, non ex hac urbe missum, sed de cælo delapsum intuentur.3. Aeneid.
units.tr: In Pisonem: That one day was for me indeed like immortality, on which I returned to my country. Verres 1: But suddenly, straight away, Cicero says, Verres was made from a man like some cup. Pro Pompeio: Therefore, indeed, all now in these places look upon Gnaeus Pompey as someone, not sent from this city, but fallen from heaven. Aeneid 3:

units.la: Haud secus ac jussi faciunt. — Terent. in Phorm.
units.tr: They do just as they are ordered. Terence in the Phormio:

units.la: Ego isti nihilo sum aliter, ac fui.
units.tr: To that fellow I am no different than I was.

units.la: Similitudinis explicatę axiomata sunt, Aequalia sunt similia ad idem. &, Idem est simile ad æqualia. cōtraq;, similia ad idem, & atq; idem simile est, sunt æqualia, ut Aiax sic Vlysses ad Achillis arma: & cōtrà, Achillis arma ut ad Ajacem sic ad Vlyssem. Eclog 5. de Daphnide: ut Cereri Bacho, tibi sic vota quotannis Agricolæ facient, damnabis tu quoq; votis.
units.tr: The axioms of the explained similarity are: Things equal are similar to the same thing; and, the same thing is similar to things equal. And conversely: things similar to the same thing, and things similar to the same as the same, are equal. Thus Ajax is to Ulysses as the arms of Achilles are to the arms of Achilles; and conversely, the arms of Achilles are to Ajax as they are to Ulysses. Eclogue 5, concerning Daphnis: As the farmers will make vows yearly to Ceres and Bacchus, so you too will condemn the vows.

units.la: Deinde, Minora sunt similia ad æquè majora: ut duplum est multiplum: sic di midiū est multesimum. Similitudo est disjuncta vel cōtinua. Similitudo disjūcta, est quando termini quatuor re ipsa distinguuntur. Eclog. 5.
units.tr: Next, lesser things are similar to equally greater things: as double is multiple, so half is a multiple-part. Similitude is either disjoined or continuous. Disjoined similitude is when the four terms are really distinct. Eclogue 5:

units.la: Tale tuum carmen nobis, divine poëta, Quale sopor fessis in gramine. —
units.tr: Your song, divine poet, is to us as sleep is to the weary on the grass.

units.la: Carmen ad auditorem, ut sopor ad fessum. termini quatuor distincti sunt. Ad Frat. 1. Quemadmodū gubernatores optimi, vim tempestatis, sic sapientissimi viri, fortunæ impetū persepe supe-
units.tr: The song is to the listener as sleep is to the weary man. There are four distinct terms. To Atticus, Book 1: Just as the best helmsmen cannot always overcome the force of a storm, so the wisest men cannot often overcome the assault of fortune.

units.la: „ rare nō possunt. Hic quatuor suntitem „ termini, ut gubernator ad tempestate, „ sic sapiens ad fortunam.1. Trift. „ Scilicet ut vulvum spectatur in ignib.aurū, Tempore sic duro est inspicienda fides.
units.tr: "Here there are four terms: as the helmsman to the storm, so the wise man to fortune." Tristia 1: Just as gold is tested in the fire, so faith must be examined in hard times.

units.la: „ Cicero 2 Philip. Sed nimirum ut qui- „ dam morbo & sensus stupore, suavitate „ cibi non sentiunt, sic libidinosi, avari, facinorofi, verae laudis gustū non habent. Virgilius fecerat hos versus,
units.tr: Cicero, Second Philippic: "But certainly, just as some people through sickness and numbness of the senses do not feel the sweetness of food, so the lustful, the greedy, and the wicked do not have a taste for true praise."

units.la: (Nocte pluit tota, redeunt spectacula mane: Divisum imperium cū jove Cæsar habet.)
units.tr: Virgil had written these verses: (It rained all night; the shows return in the morning; Caesar holds his power divided with Jove.)

units.la: Batyllus arrogaverat sibi, premiumq; magnum erat adeptus: his igitur similibus Batyllum Virgilius lusit: Hos ego versiculos feci, tulit alter honores. Sic vos non vobis nidificatis aves: Sic vos non vobis mellificatis apes: Sic vos non vobis vellera fertis oves: Sic vos non vobis fertis aratra boves.
units.tr: Batyllus had claimed these verses for himself and had received a great reward; so Virgil mocked Batyllus with similar lines: I made these little verses, another took the honours. So you birds build nests, not for yourselves: so you bees make honey, not for yourselves: so you sheep bear fleeces, not for yourselves: so you oxen bear the ploughs, not for yourselves.

units.la: Aliquādo nulla prsus est nota. Eelog.2. O formose puer, nimiūm ne crede colori: Alba ligustra cadūt, vaccinia nigra legūtur.
units.tr: Sometimes there is no mark at all. Eclogue 2: O handsome boy, do not trust too much in your colour: white privet falls, dark hyacinths are gathered.

units.la: Ficta similitudo, parem vim habet, ut superiora illa. sed præcipuē in hac explicata similitudine Aesopici apologi excellunt. Horat. 1. Epist.
units.tr: A fictional similitude has equal force to those above, but the Aesopic fables especially excel in this explained similitude. Horace, Epistles 1:

units.la: Quód si me populus Romanus forte roget, cur Non ut porticibus, sic judiciis fruar iisdem, Nec sequar, aut fugiã, q diligit ipse, vel odit: Olim quod vulpes ægroto cauta leoni Respondit, referam: quia me vestigia terrent Omnia te adversum spectantia, nulla retror sum.
units.tr: But if the Roman people should perhaps ask me why I do not enjoy the same judgments as the porticoes, nor follow or flee what they themselves love or hate: I will report what the cautious fox once answered to the sick lion: because all the footprints terrify me, all turned towards you, and none going back.

units.la: Atq; hæc disjunctæ similitudinis exempla sunt. Continua similitudo est, quando est ut primus terminus ad secundū, sic secundus ad tertiū. Hic termini sunt tres, lex, magistratus, populus. Afsectio mutua, ut cęterorum antea argumentorum, ita similium est inter se ἀνάπαλιν & ἐναλλάξ, inversé & alterné. ἀνάπαλιν, quando invertitur ordo προηγουμένης & ἀποδόσεως tantúm, aut etiam termino rū. Axioma igitur hic est: Si quędā similia fuerint, ἀνάπαλιν, similia erunt: ut aurum ad ignem, sic fides ad periculum: ergo ut fides ad periculū, sic aurū ad ignē. Item, Ergo ut periculum ad fidem, sic ignis ad aurum. Ἐναλλάξ autem similitu-
units.tr: These are examples of disjunctive similitude. Continuous similitude is when the first term is related to the second as the second is to the third. Here the terms are three: law, magistrate, people. Mutual affection, as with the other earlier arguments, is of similitudes too among themselves, inversely [ἀνάπαλιν] and alternately [ἐναλλάξ]. It is inverse [ἀνάπαλιν] when only the order of the antecedent and the consequent is reversed, or even that of the terms. The axiom here, then, is this: If certain things are similar, inversely they will be similar. As gold is to fire, so faith is to danger; therefore, as faith is to danger, so gold is to fire. Likewise: therefore, as danger is to faith, so fire is to gold. Alternate [ἐναλλάξ] similitude, however, is

units.la: 5 · 10 · 15 · 20 · 25 · 30 — marginal line numbers of the text. do est, quando similitudinis datæ antecedens antecedenti, & consequens confequeti comparatur. Axioma igitur hic est: Si quædam similia fuerint, alterné fimilia erūt. ut aurum ad ignem, sic fides ad periculum: Ergo ut aurum ad fidem, sic ignis ad periculum.
units.tr: 5 · 10 · 15 · 20 · 25 · 30 — marginal line numbers of the text. is when the antecedent of a given similitude is compared with the antecedent, and the consequent with the consequent. The axiom here, then, is this: If certain things are similar, alternately they will be similar. As gold is to fire, so faith is to danger; therefore, as gold is to faith, so fire is to danger.

units.la: Similia] Adhuc primum genus cóparationis fuit in quantitate, secundum est in qualitate: & qualitatem logicé & generaliter intellige, ut Aristoteles intellexit in categoria qualitatis, cum ait, Qualitatem autem dico, secundúm quam quales quidā esse dicuntur. Quomodo & in Philosophia 14. cap. 5. lib. vocat qualitates, differentias ποιὰ ἴσα πάθη, & quaslibet affectiones. item 2. cap. 4. & 3. cap. 11. vocát similitudinem & dissimilitudinem, differentias entis. His igitur locis Aristotelis logicum qualitatis & generalem sensum interpretatur: eumque P. Ramus ex lege πρῶτον ὅρος sequitur: doctrinā verò categoriæ illius de habitu, dispositione, potentia, impotentia naturali, patibili qualitate & passione, figura & forma ethicam, vel physicam, potiùs quàm logicam, ex eadem Aristotelis lege refugit, ne doctrinā generalē specialiter interpretetur. Neque verò qualitas ejusmodi generalis & logica, in illa sola dividitur: cùm in eadē categoria adjicitur rectitudo, curvitas: & dubitetur, utrùm alia possint adjici genera. Hic igitur P. Ramus, ut in cæteris antea locis, eodem instrumento spinas evellit, quo evellendas pater ille Ariftoteles tantopere monuit. Comparationem porrò fimilitu dinis & dissimilitudinis Galenus in opere de placitis Hippocratis, & Platonis mirificé laudavit, eamque fatis esse judicavit, ἀπόδειξις ... ad methodicam cujuslibet artis in ftitutionem Galenus egregio cóparationis fplē dore captus, altiús paulo extulit, quám veritas pateretur.sed hac de re á P. Ramo accuratiús re spondebitur, in quęstione de unica artis methodo. Similia] Definitio est Aristotelis in Philosoph.15.ca.5. ὁμοια, ὧν ποιότης μία: Similia,quorum qualitas una. Locus similitudinis, etsi usus est immēsi, attamē modicé & parcé propositus est ab Aristotele. Primus locus est in categoria qualitatis:secūdus, 14.cap.2.Top. In reliquis Topicis,feré confusus est cum loco parium: aliquando etiam distinguitur,& in confusione illa citatur septies & vicies. Proportio] Græcé ἀναλογία quod nomen est Aristoteli 1. Poster.5. cap. item 5.cap.5.Topic.In Rhetoricis est παραομοίωσις,similitudo.Aristoteles in Philos. multus est in his ver bis,6.cap.9.lib.item 15.cap.5. li.& toto 10.ἑνότης καὶ ταυτότης,unitas & (tanquam diceres)idētitas, valde affines efficiūtur similitudini: tametsi ἑνό- τητ,videt genus esse ταυτότητ ἡ ὁμοιότητος, ut ταυ- τότης sit ἑνότης essentiæ: ὁμοιότης, sit ἑνότης qualitatis adjunctæ. Euclidi est ἀναλογία καὶ ὁμοιότης, proportio & similitudo,ὅμοιον, ὁμόλογον, ἀνάλογον Frequenter autem τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον ἔχειν,eandem ratione habere,pro eodem. Quin ab Euclide pro una similitudinis definitione,quatuor definitiōes accuk 4 mulatæ sunt, quarta, sexta, septima quinti, & viſcesima septimi, quæ à P. Ramo suo loco examinabuntur. Fuit verò de similitudinis argumento, duorum philosophorum valde diversum judicium: qualis antea in contradicentium Topico ἀλογία melancholicorum illorum adversus concertationem, & Logica Aristotelis pro contradictione fuit: species litis hîc est minor, genus sophismatis idem. Euclides Megaricus τὸν διὰ πάρα‑βολῆς λόγον tollebat, quia similibus aut dissimilibus constaret: at si constaret ex similibus, ad res potius, quibus ea essent similia, respiciendum esse: sin è dissimilibus, collationem inutilem esse. Sic enthymemate captiosò, ex argumentis clarissimè Euclides carpebat, ut est apud Laertium, in ejus vita. At pars dilemmatis prima falsa est: Nam etsi ipsa res utcunque appareat, magis tamen illustri similitudine apparebit. At Empedocles, ut est in Philosophia, longè secùs omnia videbatur similitudinis argumento tribuere: ἡ δὲ γνώσις τῶ ὁμοίῳ τῷ ὁμοίῳ. γάιη μὲν γὰρ, φησί, γαῖαν ὁρῶμεν γῆν, ὕδατι δ᾽ ὕδωρ, αἰθέρι δ᾽ αἰθέρα θεῖον, στοργῇ τε στοργήν, νεῖκος τε νείκει λυγρῷ: Cognitio autem similis fit simili: terra enim, inquit, terram inspicimus. aqua verò aquam, æthere autem ætherem divinum, ac amicitia amicitiam, & contentionem contentione perniciosa. Notæ similitudinis] Similitudinis notæ longè plurimæ sunt, primùm ipso similitudinis nomine deinde negatione dissimilitudinis: multa nomina sunt, multaque adverbia, quæ ideo & adverbia similitudinis vulgò à Grammaticis appellantur. lantur. De Ænea loquitur poeta, qui é nube Veneris erumpebat:
units.tr: Similia] The first kind of comparison concerned quantity; the second concerns quality. Take quality in the logical and general sense, as Aristotle understood it in the Categories when he said, "I call quality that by which certain things are said to be of a certain kind." In the Metaphysics, book 5, chapter 14, he likewise calls qualities "affections of a kind" [ποιὰ πάθη] and any affections whatever. In book 2, chapter 4, and book 3, chapter 11, he calls similarity and dissimilarity differences of being. Ramus follows this sense of the passages, taking Aristotle's quality logically and generally, in accordance with the law of the first term [πρῶτον ὅρος]. But the doctrine of that category concerning habit, disposition, natural power and impotence, passible quality and passion, and shape and form, he rejects as ethical or physical rather than logical, by the same law of Aristotle, so that a general doctrine is not interpreted in a special sense. Nor is this general and logical quality divided only in that one place, since in the same category rectitude and curvature are added, and it is doubtful whether other genera may be added too. Here Ramus, as elsewhere, pulls up the thorns with the same tool by which that father Aristotle so strongly urged they be pulled up. Galen, in his work on the opinions of Hippocrates and Plato, greatly praised the comparison of similarity and dissimilarity and judged it sufficient for demonstration [ἀπόδειξις]. But Galen, captivated by the brilliant splendour of the comparison, raised it somewhat higher than the truth allowed when it comes to the methodical establishment of any art. This matter, however, will be answered more accurately by Ramus, in the question on the single method of an art. Similia] This is Aristotle's definition in the Philosophy, book 5, chapter 15: "Similar things are those whose quality is one" [ὁμοια, ὧν ποιότης μία]. The topic of similarity, though used very widely, is proposed by Aristotle only modestly and sparingly. The first place is in the category of quality; the second is in Topics, book 2, chapter 2 (Top. 14, cap. 2). In the other Topics it is nearly confused with the topic of equals, though sometimes it is distinguished, and it is cited, amid that confusion, twenty-seven times. Proportio] In Greek this is analogia [ἀναλογία], a name Aristotle uses in the Posterior Analytics, book 1, chapter 5, and in Topics, book 5, chapter 5. In the Rhetoric it is paraomoiosis [παραομοίωσις], likeness. Aristotle in the Philosophy often uses the words in book 6, chapter 9, and book 15, chapter 5, and throughout book 10: henotes kai tautotes [ἑνότης καὶ ταυτότης], unity and (as one might say) identity, which are very closely akin to similarity, although unity seems to be a genus of identity, so that identity is the unity of essence, and similarity is the unity of an added quality. For Euclid it is analogia kai homoiotes [ἀναλογία καὶ ὁμοιότης], proportion and similarity: homoion, homologon, analogon [ὅμοιον, ὁμόλογον, ἀνάλογον]. Frequently, too, to auton logon echein [τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον ἔχειν], to have the same ratio, is used for the same thing. Indeed, from Euclid, four definitions have been gathered for a single definition of similarity: the fourth, sixth and seventh of Book 5, and the twenty-seventh of Book 7, which Ramus will examine in their place. There was, moreover, a very different judgement of two philosophers about the argument of similarity, just as earlier, in the topic of the contradictor, there was that alogia [ἀλογία] of those melancholic men against disputation, and Aristotle's Logic was on the side of contradiction. The kind of dispute here is smaller, but the genus of the sophism is the same. Euclid the Megarian abolished the argument through comparison [τὸν διὰ παραβολῆς λόγον], because it consists either of similar or of dissimilar things. If it consisted of similar things, one should look rather to the things to which they are similar; but if of dissimilar things, the comparison is useless. Thus, by a captious enthymeme, Euclid attacked the arguments very clearly, as is recorded in Laertius, in his Life. But the first part of this dilemma is false: for although the thing itself may appear in some way, it will nevertheless appear more clearly through a brilliant similitude. Empedocles, however, as stated in the Philosophy, seemed to assign everything to the argument of similarity, quite the reverse: "Knowledge is by like to like. For we see earth by earth, water by water, air by divine air, and love by love, and strife by baleful strife," as he says. That is: knowledge comes from like to like; for we behold earth by earth, water by water, divine air by air, love by love, and contention by pernicious contention. Notae similitudinis] The signs of similarity are very numerous: first the very name of similarity, then the negation of dissimilarity. There are many nouns and many adverbs, which for this reason are commonly called adverbs of similarity by the grammarians.

units.la: Scindit se nubes, & in æthera purgat apertum:
units.tr: Scindit se nubes, et in aethera purgat apertum: The cloud parts and clears itself into the open sky.

units.la: Restitit Æneas, claraq; in nube refulsit,
units.tr: Restitit Aeneas, claraque in nube refulsit, Aeneas stood still, and shone out in the bright cloud,

units.la: Os humerosq; deo similis. Namque ipsa decoram 5
units.tr: Os humerosque deo similis. Namque ipsa decoram with face and shoulders like a god. For his mother herself

units.la: Cæsariem nato genetrix, lumenq; juventæ
units.tr: Caesariem nato genetrix, lumenque iuventae had breathed into her son the graceful locks of hair and the bright light of youth,

units.la: Purpureum, & lætos oculis afflarat honores.
units.tr: Purpureum, et laetos oculis afflarat honores. the purple glow, and the joyful grace to his eyes.

units.la: De luctu Sulpitii filii loquitur, postulantis à Senatu statuam patri. Equidem (ait orator) etiam ad famam Servii Sulpitii filii arbitror attinere, ut videatur honore patri debitum præstitisse. tum hæc loquitur, quæ sunt in litera. sed similitudo est in verbo, effigiem. ut hic metaphora & similitudo sit in unico verbo: vereq; dici posit, omnem metaphoram, similitudinem esse cōtractam ad unū verbū: quod Cicero affirmat 3. Oratorio. Telephus ab Achille vulneratus est in Mysia, dum Ulyssem persequitur: postea oraculo monitus, vulnus sanari non posse, nisi ab eo, qui fecisset: Itaq; ad Achillē rediit, à quo fieri rabigine sanatus esse dicitur. Ut igitur Telephus sanari nō potuit, nisi ab Achille, à quo erat vulneratus: sic Ovidius ab exilio revocari nō potest, nisi ab eo, à quo in exiliū ejectus est. Similitudo igitur hæc in notis illis, Achilleo more, inclusa est. Quale est & illud ejusdē poetę:
units.tr: He speaks of the grief of Sulpicius' son, who asked the Senate for a statue for his father. "Indeed," says the orator, "I think it also pertains to the reputation of Servius Sulpicius's son that he should seem to have rendered to his father the honour owed." Then he says those things which are in the text; but the similitude lies in the word "effigiem" (likeness). So here the metaphor and the similitude are in a single word, and it may truly be said that every metaphor is a similitude contracted into one word, as Cicero affirms in the third book of the Orator. Telephus was wounded by Achilles in Mysia, while pursuing Ulysses; afterwards, warned by an oracle that the wound could not be healed except by the one who had made it, he returned to Achilles, by whose rust [of the spear] he is said to have been healed. Just as Telephus could not be healed except by Achilles, by whom he had been wounded, so Ovid cannot be recalled from exile except by him by whom he was cast into exile. This similitude, therefore, is enclosed in those marks, in the manner of Achilles. Such is also that line of the same poet:

units.la: Tempora labuntur more fluentis aquæ.
units.tr: The times slip away like flowing water.

units.la: Loquitur de reditu ab exilio, quo die urbem est ingressus. Locus est Ciceronis Verr. septima de Verre: qui aliquantisper virum se bonum simularat, sed repente redierat ad sese atque ad suos mores. Verres porcus est non majalis,nequedum castratus. Circeo} Carminibus Circe socios mutavit Ulyßis. ut est 8. Ecclog. Idé initio septimi Æneidos plenius exponitur de leonibus,suibus,lupis: Quos hominum ex facie dea sæva potentibus herbis Induerat Circe in vultus ac terga ferarum.
units.tr: He speaks of his return from exile, on the day he entered the city. The passage is from Cicero's seventh Verrine oration against Verres, who for a while pretended to be a good man but suddenly returned to himself and to his old ways. Verres is a pig, not a suckling pig, and not yet castrated. Circeo Circe, by her spells, changed the companions of Ulysses, as in Eclogue 8. The same comparison is set out more fully at the beginning of the seventh book of the Aeneid, concerning lions, swine and wolves, whom the cruel goddess Circe, with powerful herbs, had changed from human faces into the faces and hides of wild beasts.

units.la: Similitudo igitur in verbis,tanquam Circeo poculo. qualis est illa pro Muræna, de Sulpitio & jurisprudentia: Et quoniam mihi videris istam scientiam,tanquam filiolam osculari tuam, non patiar te in tanto errore diutiùs versari. Cum Pompejum} De continentia Pompeji loquitur, quam auget illa similitudinis collatione. qualis est illa 1.lib. ad Frat. Nã Græci quidem sic te ita viventè intuebuntur,ut quendam ex annalium memoria, aut etiam é cælo divinum hominè efse in provinciam delapsum putent. Hic igitur in verbo tanquam, similitudo includitur: qualia sunt adverbia similitudinis reliqua. Ver. 7.ut ex illo metu mortis,& tenebris, quasi jure libertatis & odore legum recreatus revixisset.
units.tr: The comparison, then, lies in the word, as if it were Circe's cup. Such is the passage in the Pro Murena about Sulpicius and jurisprudence: "And since I see you kissing that science as if it were your little daughter, I shall not allow you to remain any longer in so great an error." Cum Pompejum He speaks of the continence of Pompey, which the comparison enlarges. Such is the passage in the first book of the letters to his brother: "For the Greeks will look upon you, living as you do, as if some divine man, out of the memory of the annals or even from heaven, had come down into the province." Here the word tanquam ("as if") encloses the similitude, as do the other adverbs of comparison. Verrines, book 7: "so that, from that fear of death and of darkness, he had revived, as if restored by the right of liberty and by the fragrance of the laws."

units.la: Haud secus}Sequentes notæ negationem difsi milium continét. Æneas sociis arma imperaverat adversus Harpias: qui protinus obtemperant. Sic pro Muræna Cicero, Non secùs acsi meus frater esset. Ego isti} Actus 3.scena 2.verba sunt Dorionis lenonis conquerentis de Phędria, qui promissum nō persolverit, cúm Dorio iste permaneat in sententia. Sæpe} Superiores notæ similitudinem magis inclusam & involutam habuerunt,sequentes sunt apertiores.
units.tr: Haud secus The following notes contain a denial of dissimilarity. Aeneas had ordered his comrades to take arms against the Harpies, and they at once obeyed. So Cicero, in the Pro Murena: "Not otherwise than if he were my own brother." Ego isti These are the words of Dorio the procurer, in Act 3, scene 2, complaining of Phaedria, who had not kept his promise, while Dorio himself remains of the same mind. Sæpe The earlier notes had the similitude more enclosed and wrapped up; the following ones are more open.

units.la: Axiomata}Axiomata parium & imparium an-tea tea sex fuerût Euclidi, illa quidem ἀξιωματικῶς habita, at similium axiomata, propositiones dubiæ & demonstrabiles, eidem Euclidi fiunt: demonstrantur autem genere demonstrationis, quale Scholæ mathematicæ P. Rami ad eum locum loquétur. Tum vero axiomata illa omnia nomine magnitudinis proponuntur, cum tamen omnia rerum sint communia. Itaq; contra legē καθόλε πρῶ τοῦ, magnum clenchū Euclidi admissum hic Aristoteles diceret, quòd logicum axioma tam generale, infra duos gradus amandatur, à Logica nempe ultra numeros ad magnitudinem.
units.tr: Axiomata The axioms of equals and unequals were formerly six for Euclid, and these were indeed held axiomatically [ἀξιωματικῶς]; but the axioms of similar things, being doubtful propositions which can be demonstrated, are made by Euclid himself. They are demonstrated by the kind of demonstration which P. Ramus will discuss in his mathematical lectures at that place. Yet all those axioms are then proposed under the name of magnitude, although they are in fact common to all things. Therefore, against the rule that what is universal comes first [καθόλου πρῶτον], Aristotle would say that Euclid made a great blunder, since a logical axiom so general is relegated two grades lower, from Logic beyond numbers to magnitude.

units.la: qualiā]Hæc propositio est septima quinti elementorum: Æquales magnitudines ad eādem, eandem habent rationem, & eadem ad æquales: ex qua etiam nona propositio quinti convertitur: Ad eádem, eandem habētes rationē, magnitudines sunt æquales inter se: & ad quas eadē habet eandem rationem, & illæ sunt æquales inter se. Ergo hæc axiomata ex æqualitate terminorū duorū ad inæqualem tertiū, colligunt æqualitatem rationum, id est similitudinē terminorū: & contrā é similitudine & æqualitate rationum, æqualitatem terminorum, ulysses] Nota est contentio de armis Achillis é 13. Metamorp. Ovidii, æquales autem competitores apparebant.
units.tr: qualiā] This proposition is the seventh of the fifth book of the Elements: equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same magnitude, and the same magnitude to equal ones. From this the ninth proposition of the fifth book also follows in reverse: magnitudes that have the same ratio to the same magnitude are equal to one another, and those to which the same magnitude has the same ratio are equal to one another. So these axioms, from the equality of two terms to a third unequal one, infer the equality of ratios, that is, the similarity of the terms; and conversely, from the similarity and equality of ratios they infer the equality of the terms. ulysses] The contest over the arms of Achilles is well known from the thirteenth book of Ovid's Metamorphoses, where the competitors appeared equal.

units.la: Baccho] Locus est de apotheosi Daphnidis: ubi Daphnis & Menalcas, Baccho Cereriq; similes efficiuntur. Itaq; Ceres, Bacchus, Daphnis, velut æquales, fiunt similes in tertio.
units.tr: Baccho] The passage concerns the deification of Daphnis, where Daphnis and Menalcas are made like Bacchus and Ceres. So Ceres, Bacchus and Daphnis, being equals, become similar in the third term.

units.la: Minora] Propositio est decimaquinta quinti: Partes similiter multiplicibus, eandē rationem
units.tr: Minora] This is the fifteenth proposition of the fifth book: parts taken in the same multiples as their wholes have the same ratio to one another.

units.la: habent sumptæ inter se. Quod axioma, sua luce tametsi clarissimū, demonstratum tamen est ab Euclide: sed ea demonstratione, quæ in loco ipso à P. Ramo declarabitur. axioma autē est per totam mathesin utilitatis immensæ: itaq; studiosò hic considerandum, adjungitur huc ab Euclyde undecima quinti. Quæ rationes eidem sunt eædē, inter se sunt eædem. sed hæc propositio comprehenditur primo pariū axiomate, Eidē æqualia, inter se æqualia. & sic aliquando in elementis rationes eædem dicuntur æquales. itaque prætermissum est à P. Ramo, ne generale specialiter contra legem κανόνας πρῶτον repeteretur. Quare quatuor Euclidis propositiones in duo illa axiomata inclusa sunt: ut cōstet, quomodo ex æqualibus & inæqualibus similia nascantur.
units.tr: That axiom, though very clear in itself, has nevertheless been demonstrated by Euclid, by a demonstration which Ramus will explain in its proper place. The axiom is of immense use throughout mathematics, and so it deserves careful attention here. There is added here the eleventh proposition of the fifth book from Euclid: ratios that are the same as one and the same ratio are the same as one another. But this proposition is contained in the first of the common notions, "things equal to the same thing are equal to one another", and so in the Elements ratios that are the same are sometimes called equal. Therefore Ramus has passed it over, lest the general be repeated specially, contrary to the rule of the first [κανόνας πρῶτον]. Hence the four propositions of Euclid are included in those two axioms, so that it may be seen how similar things arise from equal and unequal ones.

units.la: Multesimum] Aristotelis exemplum est de paribus, Si triplū, multiplum, & trīes multesimus: πολλαπλάσιον, P. Ramus vertit multesimum, secutus Lucretium eo loco sexti libri: Quám sit parvula pars, & quám multesima constet.
units.tr: Multesimum] Aristotle's example concerns even numbers: if triple, multiple, and "trice-many" [multesimus]. Ramus renders πολλαπλάσιον as "multesimus", following Lucretius in that passage of the sixth book: "How small a part it is, and how many-fold it is made up."

units.la: Disjuncta vel cōtinua] Genera similitudinis sunt à mathematicis usurpata, sed communia rerum omnium, planeque logica, non propria vel numerorum, vel magnitudinum: ut vel exemplis sequentibus intelligetur. Itaq; P. Ramus, ut antea axiomata parium, impariū, similium, sic denique similitudinis genera, authore Aristotele, vel potius Aristotelea Logicæ sapientiæ lege à mathematicis repetit, quia generalia non specialiter, sed generaliter exponenda sunt. Tale] Verba, sunt Menalcæ collaudatis Mopsum, qui suo carmine ἀπολίωσιν Dapnidis eximiè cantaverat. Quinto fratri tráquillam provinciam prorogatam anno tertio proponit,ut nullæ insidiæ,nulla defectio sociorum,nulla inopia stipendii,nulla seditio exercitus pertimescenda {5} sit,quæ persæpe sapientissimis viris acciderunt: ut quemadmodum,& cætera,quę in litera sunt. Elegia quarta sunt hi versus, ad laudem fidelis amici, Aurum,ait Plinius,quó sæpius arsit,proficit ad bonitatem : aurique ex-{10} perimentum est ignis. Primum autem bonitatis argumentum, est quám difficillimè accendi. De spreta ab Antonio rectè facti gloria loquitur:Recordare igitur(ait)illum diem quo dictaturam sustulisti,pone ante oculos lętitiam{15} Senatus,populique Romani, cúm nundinatione tua tuorumque:túm intelliges quantum inter laudem & lucrum interfit. Talis est Tuscul. 2.similitudo illa, Ut onera contentis corporibus faciliús feruntur, remisis opprimunt: simil{20} limé animus intentione sua pressum depellit omnem ponderum : remisione autem sic urgetur,ut se nequeat extollere. Tales denique partibus expletis similitudines permultæ sunt in Cicerone,& in quovis excellente authore. Hæc historia pleniús in vita Virgilii á P. Ramo narrata est, de spectaculis Cæsaris, cúm tota nocte pluisset,& mané serenitas diei,spectaculis Cæsaris reddita essset.{25}
units.tr: Disjuncta vel cōtinua] The kinds of similarity are used by mathematicians, but they are common to all things and are plainly logical, not peculiar to numbers or magnitudes; this will be understood from the examples that follow. So Ramus, as before with the axioms of equals, unequals and similars, now takes the kinds of similarity from the mathematicians, on the authority of Aristotle, or rather by the law of the Aristotelian logical wisdom, because general things must be set out not specially but generally. Tale] These are the words of Menalcas, after he has praised Mopsus, who had sung most excellently in his song the apotheosis of Daphnis. He proposes to his brother Quintus that a peaceful province be extended for a third year, so that no plots, no desertion of allies, no lack of pay, no mutiny of the army need be feared, which very often befall the wisest men; and so on, as in the text. The fourth elegy contains these lines in praise of a faithful friend. Pliny says that gold, the more often it is fired, the more it gains in quality; and the test of gold is fire. The first proof of quality, however, is that it is very hard to set alight. He speaks of the glory of right action, which Antony had spurned: "Recall, then," he says, "that day on which you abolished the dictatorship; set before your eyes the joy of the Senate and the Roman people, and of yourself and your own; then you will understand how much lies between praise and profit." Such is that comparison in the second Tusculan Disputation: "As burdens are more easily carried by bodies that are tense, but crush those that are relaxed, so the mind by its effort throws off all the weight pressing on it, but by relaxing is so bent down that it cannot raise itself." Indeed, very many such similitudes, fully worked out, occur in Cicero and in every excellent author. This story is told more fully by Ramus in the life of Virgil, about the games of Caesar, when it had rained all night and in the morning the day cleared up for the games of Caesar.

units.la: Querimonia est Coridonis de suo {30} Alexi. Ligustrum, frutex est Francis troefna,cujus flores sunt admodum candidi,& nunc per metonymiam, ligustra dicuntur: grana autem nigra, quę hîc dicuntur vaccinia: quàquam vaccinia Massarius mora agrestia putat ef se: Ruellius vacietum Frácicum putat. Hinc igitur similitudo: ut candidi flores ligustri deciduntgrana nigra colliguntur: sic candor formę deperit, nigror remanet. Fiƈta] Dixi antea de comparatorum tertio isto privilegio, ut etiam fiƈta valeant: fiƈta autem similitudo ejusmodi, in Æsopicis fabulis apologus appellatur, cùm mutis pecudibus Logica quædam attribuitur. Apologi usum permagnum testatur AristotelesRhetorici, ubi apologos istos ἀνεκδότους ἀνὰ πολλὰ, populares ait esse. Et verò prima illa Græcorum philosophia non solúm ethica, sed Logica, ab Æsopo fuit: quanquam Quintilianus lib.5. cap.11. refert ad Hesiodum: Illæ quoque fabulæ (ait) quæ etiam si originem ab Æsopo non acceperint (nam videtur earum primus author Hesiodus) nomine tamē Æsopi maximè celebrantur: ducere animos solent præcipuè rusticorū & imperitorum, qui & simpliciùs quę fiƈta sunt, audiunt, & capti voluptate facilé iis, quibus delectantur, consentiūt. Siquidem & Menenius Agrippa plebem cum patribus in gratiâ traditur reduxisse, nota illa de membris humanis adversus ventrem discordantibus, fabula. Hæc Quintilianus: quibus sumilia sint apud Aristotelem illa Stefichori adversus Phalaridem, & Æsopi pro Demagoro: Nam Stefichorus Phalaridem ab Himereis postulantem custodias corporis, comparavit homini, qui equo adversus cervum persuasit, ut frenos & se sesforem pateretur. & Æsopus Demagorū pecunia publica locupletatū, ob idque apud Samios reum ita defendit, ut compararet populum & ipsum Demagorum, vulpeculæ caninis muscis afflictæ, quas tamē sanguine suo jā exaturatas, ab ericio propelli noluit, ne famelicæ aliæ accederét, quæ reliquum sanguinem exorberent. Quód sit] Horatius prima epistola primi libri apologum vulpis & leonis usurpat, ad irridendum populi judiciū: ut cauta vulpes leonis antrū, sic vir sapiēs populi judiciū refugit. Apologus autē fingit ad leonem ægrotum bestias consolandi causa deficēdisse, nec inde ullā rediisse: propterea cūm id vulpes animadverteret, neq; interea cum cæteris descenderet, interrogata á leone ut accederet, respondit se terreri vestigiis, quæ in antrum adversa essent omnia, nulla retrorsum. Hic igitur termini similitudines sunt quatuor, vulpes, leo, sapiēs, populus: populusq; immanissimę bestiæ comparatur, quod & Horatius adjungit: Bellua multorū es capitū: nā quid sequar, aut quem? Continua] Nona definitio Euclidis videtur esse in 5. lib. hac de re, quód analogia fit minimum in tribus terminis: Hic vero termini quatuor sunt, ut antea, sed ratione tantūm distincti, quin duo tantūm, sed ratione distincti esse possunt.
