Immó verò potest unicus esse, ut in comparatis æ- qualibus: Exemplum autem Ciceronis est initio tertii legum, eique illud additum est: Vereq; dici potest, magistratum, legem esse loquētem: legem autem, mutuum esse magistratum.
units.tr: The lament is that of Corydon about his Alexis. Ligustrum is privet, a shrub which the French call troëne, whose flowers are very white, and by metonymy the word now means the privet itself. The berries, which here are called vaccinia, are black; though Massarius thinks vaccinia are wild mulberries, and Ruellius thinks they are the Frankish vaccinium. So the similitude is this: as the white flowers of the privet fall, and the black berries are gathered, so the whiteness of beauty fades and the blackness remains. Fiƈta] I have said before of this third privilege of comparisons, that they may also be fictitious. A fictitious similitude of this kind, in Aesop's fables, is called an apologue, when a kind of reasoning is attributed to dumb beasts. Aristotle in his Rhetoric attests the great use of apologues, saying that these are popular [ἀνεκδότους ἀνὰ πολλὰ]. Indeed that earliest Greek philosophy was from Aesop not only in ethics but also in logic; although Quintilian, in the fifth book, chapter eleven, refers them to Hesiod: "Those fables too," he says, "which have not received their origin from Aesop (for Hesiod seems to be the first author of them), are nonetheless most celebrated under the name of Aesop. They are wont to win over minds, especially those of rustics and the unlearned, who hear what is made up more simply, and, captivated by pleasure, readily assent to those things they delight in." Indeed, Menenius Agrippa is said to have reconciled the plebs with the patricians by that well-known fable about the human limbs quarrelling with the belly. Thus Quintilian. Similar to these, in Aristotle, are the story of Stesichorus against Phalaris and Aesop's on behalf of Demagorus. For Stesichorus, when Phalaris, from the Himerans, asked for bodyguards, compared him to the man who persuaded a horse against a stag to submit to bit and rider. And Aesop, when Demagorus, enriched by public money and therefore accused among the Samians, defended him by comparing the people, and Demagorus himself, to a little fox afflicted by dog-flies, which, though already sated with her blood, she would not let the hedgehog drive away, lest other hungry ones should come and drain the rest of the blood. Quód sit] Horace, in the first epistle of the first book, uses the apologue of the fox and the lion to mock the judgment of the people: as the cautious fox avoids the lion's den, so the wise man avoids the judgment of the people. The apologue pretends that when the lion was sick, all the beasts set out to comfort him and none came back; so the fox, noticing this, and not going down with the others, when asked by the lion to come in, replied that she was frightened by the footprints, which all led into the den and none out of it. Here then the similitudes have four terms: fox, lion, wise man, people; and the people is compared to a most savage beast, as Horace adds: "You are a monster of many heads; for what shall I follow, or whom?" Continua] The ninth definition of Euclid seems to be in the fifth book on this matter, that an analogy is a minimum of three terms. Here, however, there are four terms, as before, but distinguished only by reason; indeed there can be only two, though distinguished by reason. Nay, there can be a single one, as in comparing equals. The example from Cicero is at the beginning of the third book of the Laws, and to it is added: "And it can truly be said that the magistrate is the law speaking, and the law the magistrate silent."

units.la: Affectio] Adhuc à mathematicis axiomata & differentiæ similium repetitæ sunt: Hic duę alię differentiæ repetuntur. Hæc autem mutua assectio in quibusdam duobus terminis declaratur, ut in causis & effectis, in subjectis & adjunctis, in majoribus & minoribus. In quibusdam comprehenditur uno nomine, ut in dissentaneis, paribus, & nunc in similibus: sed in similibus, assectio dupliciter declaratur, ἀνάπαλιν ἢ ἐναλλὰξ, q sunt Euclidi 12. & 13. definitiones quinti.
units.tr: Affectio] Again the axioms and differences of similars are taken from the mathematicians: here two other differences are taken. This mutual affection is shown in certain pairs of terms, as in causes and effects, in subjects and adjuncts, in greater and lesser things. In others it is comprehended under one name, as in dissentaneous things, in equals, and now in similars; but in similars the affection is declared in two ways, conversely or alternately [ἀνάπαλιν ἢ ἐναλλὰξ], which are the twelfth and thirteenth definitions of the fifth book of Euclid.

units.la: Ἀνάπαλιν] Vt ex causis effecta, & contrá ex efsectis causæ arguuntur sic é propositio similiter redditur, & é reddito vicissim propositum: id duplici modo tractatur á mathematicis, cũ aut invertitur solus ordo protaseos & apodoseos, aut etiam totus ordo terminorum.
units.tr: Ἀνάπαλιν] Conversely [ἀνάπαλιν]: as from causes effects are argued, and conversely from effects causes, so a proposition is similarly rendered, and from the rendered proposition again the proposition is inferred. Mathematicians treat this in two ways: either only the order of the protasis and apodosis is inverted, or the whole order of the terms.

units.la: Ἐναλλὰξ] Euclidis est 12. definitio quinti, unde postea factæ propositiones octo. Nam in quinto libro sunt hujus generis 1. 4. 14. 16. & in septimo, 9. 11. 13. 15. de quib. suo loco dicetur á P. Ramo. De priore autem genere ἀνάπαλιν, nulla propositio facta est, cùm esset tamen par & eadem confingendi occasio. Itaque etiam Campanus illinc propositionem facere tentavit: sed tum P. Ramus respondebit Campano. Atque hæc analogia est, in qua Aristoteles nominatim mathematicos reprehendit 5. cap. 1. Poster. quòd cómunem omnium rerum doctrinam in numeris & magnitudinibus instituerent. Hic verò duo tàtùm termini convertuntur: primus enim antecedēs manet, & ultimus consequens: sed é secūdo antecedente fit cōsequens primus, & é primo consequensequēte, fit antecedēs secūdus: Atqui subtilitas ista & αὐάπαλιν & ἐναλλὰξ, licet in populari & vulgari usu minús trita fit, accidere tn pōt, & utiliter adhiberi: quoniā similitudo nō tantum est ρ tasēos & apodosēos inversæ, sed etiā terminorū inter se. usus tn harū differentiarum αὐάπαλιν & ἐναλλὰξ, in mathematicis præcipuè animadvertitur, quamvis veritas ipsa sit generalis.
units.tr: Ἐναλλὰξ [alternately]: this is the twelfth definition of Euclid's fifth book, from which eight propositions were later derived. In the fifth book the propositions of this kind are 1, 4, 14 and 16, and in the seventh 9, 11, 13 and 15, which P. Ramus will discuss in its proper place. Of the former kind, ἀνάπαλιν [conversely], no proposition has been derived, although there was an equal and similar occasion for framing one. So Campanus also tried to make a proposition from it, but P. Ramus will then answer Campanus. This is the analogy in which Aristotle, in Posterior Analytics 1.5, expressly reproaches the mathematicians for setting out the general doctrine of all things in numbers and magnitudes. Here, however, only two terms are converted: the first term remains the antecedent and the last the consequent, but from the second antecedent the first consequent is made, and from the first consequent the second antecedent is made. Yet this subtlety, both ἀνάπαλιν and ἐναλλὰξ, although it is less familiar in popular and common usage, can occur and be usefully applied, since the likeness extends not only to the inverted protasis and apodosis but also to the terms among themselves. The use of these differences, ἀνάπαλιν and ἐναλλὰξ, is seen chiefly in mathematics, although the truth itself is general.

units.la: Cap. XXII. De Dissimilibus.
units.tr: Chapter XXII. On Dissimilar Things

units.la: Dissimilia sunt comparata, quorum qualitas est diversa. Dissimilitudinis propriæ notæ sunt, dissimile, dispar, differens, aliud, secus. Pro Plan. Quanquam dissimilis est debitio pecuniæ & gratiæ. Ennius:
units.tr: Things are dissimilar when they are compared and their quality is different. The proper marks of dissimilarity are: dissimilis, dispar, differens, aliud, secus. Pro Planc.: although the debt of money is dissimilar to grace. Ennius:

units.la: O domus antiqua, heu quám dispari dominare domino?
units.tr: O ancient house, alas, with how unequal a master do you hold sway?

units.la: Cæsar 1. bell. Gall. Hi omnes, lingua, institutis, legibus inter se differunt. 2. Agrar. Alio vultu, alio vocis sono, alio incessu esse meditabatur. Cic. 2. Nat. Quoniam coepi secus agere, atque initio dixeram. Dissimilitudinis notæ etiam sunt per negationem similium. 3. Orat. Non est philosophia similis artium reliquarum. 2. Aeneid.
units.tr: Caesar, Gallic War 1: "All these differ among themselves in language, institutions and laws." Agrarian Law 2: "He was contriving to appear with one expression, another tone of voice, another gait." Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2: "Since I began to act otherwise than I had said at the outset." Marks of dissimilarity are also given by the negation of similars. Orator 3: "Philosophy is not similar to the other arts." Aeneid 2:

units.la: At non ille, satū quo te mentiris, Achilles Talis in hoste fuit Priamo.—
units.tr: "But not that Achilles, by whose line you falsely claim descent, was such toward Priam, his enemy—"

units.la: Horat.1.Epist. Non eadem est aetas, non mens.—
units.tr: Horace, Epistles 1: "Not the same is age, not mind—"

units.la: 1.ad Frat.Sit annulus tuus, nō tanquam vas aliquod, sed tanquam ipse tu. Dissimilitudinis explicatæ redditio, hîc appellatur ἀντιπόδοσις, dissimilis redditio: Axiomata verò dissimiliū oppositā sunt axiomatis similium: Inæqualium majus ad idem majorem rationē habet, quám minus: & idem ad minus habet majorem rationem, quám ad majus. contraque, Quod majorem rationem habet ad idem, est majus: & ad quod idem majorem habet rationem, est minus. Item, Si æqualium rationum altera fit inæqualis, reliqua eidem erit inæqualis.
units.tr: 1 To Brother (Ad Fratrem): "Let your ring be not as some vessel, but as you yourself." The explanation of dissimilarity by return is here called antipodosis, the dissimilar return. The axioms of dissimilars are opposed to the axioms of similars: of unequals, the greater has a greater ratio to the same than the lesser does, and the same has a greater ratio to the lesser than to the greater. Conversely, what has a greater ratio to the same is greater, and that to which the same has a greater ratio is less. Likewise, if one of two equal ratios becomes unequal, the remaining one will be unequal to the same.

units.la: 3.Philipp. Certus dies non ut sacrificii, sic cōsilii expectari solet. Hoc argumento pastor ille errorem suum confitetur: urbem quā dicunt Romam, Melibœe, putavi Stultus ego, huic nostræ similem.— Et mox: Sic canibus catulos similes, sic matribus hœdos Noram, sic parvis cōponere magna solebam. ut nec canibus catuli, nec matribus hœdi, sic nec Mantua Romæ similis est. Nota plerunq; nulla est, & dissimilitudo etiam etiā pleniús explicatur: Brutus occídit liberos proditionem moliētes : Manlius virtutem filii morte mulćta vit. Catull.
units.tr: Philippics 3: "A fixed day is not usually awaited for a plan, as it is for a sacrifice." By this argument that shepherd confesses his error: "The city they call Rome, Meliboeus, I foolishly thought was like this our city—" And soon after: "Thus I used to know puppies as like dogs, kids as like their mothers, and I used to compare great things with small. As puppies are not like dogs, nor kids like mothers, so Mantua is not like Rome." Often there is no likeness at all, and the dissimilarity is explained more fully: Brutus put to death his sons who were plotting treason; Manlius punished his son's virtue with death. Catullus:

units.la: Soles occidere & redire possunt: Nobis cum semel occidit brevis lux, Nox est perpetua una dormienda.
units.tr: Suns can set and rise again; but for us, when once our brief light has set, there is one perpetual night to be slept through.

units.la: Dissimilia ficta sunt, 6. Aeneid. de immaturo Marcelli funere, deque longioris vitæ (si superfuisset) futura gloria: sed multiplicata fiunt illustriora:
units.tr: Dissimilar things are feigned in Aeneid 6, concerning the untimely funeral of Marcellus, and the future glory of a longer life (had he survived); but when multiplied they become more illustrious:

units.la: Ostendet terris hunc tantum fata nec, ultra Esse sinent. Nimium vobis Romana propago Visa potes, superi, propria hæc si dona fuisset. Quantos ille virum magnum Mavortis ad urbem
units.tr: Fate will show him to the earth only, and will not let him remain any longer. Too much, ye gods, the Roman offspring seemed to you, if these had been your own gifts. What groans will the Field of Mars raise for that great man at the city gate?

units.la: Campus aget gemitus? vel qua Tyberine, vi debis Funera? cum tumulū praeterlabere recentē?
units.tr: Or with what funerals, Tiber, will you honour him, when you glide past his new tomb?

units.la: Nec puer Iulus a quisquam de gente Latinos In tātum spe tollet avos: Nec Romula quondam ullo se tantum tellus jactabit alumno.
units.tr: Nor will any boy of the Julian line raise the Latin ancestors to such hope; nor will the Romulean land ever boast so much of any of her nurslings.

units.la: Heu pietas, heu prisca fides, invictáq; bello Dextra non illi quisquam se impune tulisset Obvius armato: seu cum pedes iret in hostē, Seu spumātis equi foderet calcaribus armos: Heu miserāde puer, si qua fata aspera rūpas, Tu Marcellus eris.
units.tr: Alas for piety, alas for ancient faith, and for the right hand unconquered in war! No one would have met him in arms and come away unharmed, whether he went on foot against the enemy or spurred the foaming flanks of his horse. Alas, pitiable boy, if you break through the harsh fates, you will be Marcellus.

units.la: Sic Cicero Philip. 2. de Varronis Cassi nate fundo, quę Antonius per vim occupaverat, varia dissimilia, sed vera coaggerat. O tecta ipsa misera, quā dispari domino (quanquam quomodo iste do minus s) sed tamen quám á dispari tenebatur! Studiorum enim suorum M. Varro voluit esse illud, non libidinum diversorium. quæ in illa villa anté dicebātur? quæ cogitabantur? quæ literis mandabantur? jura P. Romani, monumēta maiorum, omnis sapientiæ ratio, omnisq; doctrina: At veró te inquilino (non enim domino) personabant omnia vocibus ebriorum, natabant pavimenta vino, madebant parietes, ingenui pueri cum meritoriis, scorta inter matresfamilias versabantur.
units.tr: Thus Cicero, Philippics 2, on the farm of Varro's son Cassius, which Antonius had seized by force, heaps up various dissimilar things, but true ones: "O the poor house itself, held by an unlike master (though how that man is a master I do not know), yet held by one unlike itself! For M. Varro wished that place to be a seat of his studies, not an inn for lusts. What used to be said in that villa? What was thought there? What was committed to writing? The laws of the Roman people, the monuments of our ancestors, the whole reasoning of wisdom and all learning. But with you as tenant (for you are not the master) everything resounded with the voices of drunkards; the floors swam with wine, the walls dripped; free-born boys mingled with prostitutes, and harlots moved among the matrons."

units.la: Dissimilia] Hic locus quandā cum diversis affinitatem habet, & P. Ramum diutiús exercuit: attamen si simplex illic & absoluta duorum dissensio spectetur, hic dissimilis quatuor terminorum comparatio discrimen percipietur. Est veró locus in tota Aristotelis philosophia non admodum propositus. In Categoria qualitatis docetur simile & dissimile uni qualitati esse proprium: Dissimilitudinis sensus talis logicus est. item in Philosophia docetur (ut antea etiā propositum est) similitudinem & dissimilitudinem esse primas differentias entis. hoc etiam logicè & generaliter præcipitur. Decimumquartū caput i. Topici totum consumitur in inventione dissimilitudinum: & differentiarum difsimilitu dinum quidem, in diversis generibus : differentiarum item in iisdem : & ut differentiæ valeant ad definiendum & distinguendum. Ad istud argumentum est formæ, de qua in causis:non est veræ comparationis, dissimilem quatuor termi noꝵum rationem facientis. Isto modo differentia totis Topicis accipitur. At differētia ita sumpta,nullam comparationem ostendit,sed vocabulum comparationis improprie accommodat simplici & absoluto argumento : Symbola autē hujus comparationis idem significantia pleraq; sunt, quinq; autem proponuntur.
units.tr: Dissimilar. This place has some affinity with the diverse, and P. Ramus has spent much time on it; yet if one considers the simple and absolute disagreement of two things, the comparison of four dissimilar terms will be perceived as a distinct thing. This place, however, is not very prominent in the whole of Aristotle's philosophy. In the Categories, in the discussion of quality, it is taught that the similar and the dissimilar are proper to a single quality; this is the logical sense of dissimilarity. Likewise, in Philosophy it is taught (as was also proposed earlier) that similarity and dissimilarity are the first differences of being. This too is taught logically and generally. The fourteenth chapter of Topics 1 is wholly devoted to the discovery of dissimilarities: of dissimilarities in different genera, of differences likewise within the same genus, and of how differences may serve for defining and distinguishing. This argument belongs to form, which is treated under causes; it is not of a true comparison, since it makes a dissimilar relation of four terms. In this way difference is taken throughout the Topics. But difference so taken shows no comparison; it applies the word comparison improperly to a simple and absolute argument. The symbols of this comparison, mostly signifying the same thing, are many, but five are put forward.

units.la: Debitio] Dissimilitudo illa partibus compluribus declaratur eodem loco: Nam qui pecuniam dissoluit (ait orator) statim non habet id quod reddidit, qui autem debet, is retinet alienum : gratiam autem & qui refert, habet, & qui habet,in eo quod habet, refert. Atque hæc proPlanco. Exemplum autem cōtractius positum est tantum propter notā dissimilitudinis. quale in Bruto est illud: Quid est tam dissimile, quàm Demosthenes & Lysias? O Domus] Versus est Ennii i. Offic. de domo, quæ homini honorato & principi decora est: si non domo dominus, sed domino domus honestetur : odiosum est enim, cum á prætereuntibus dicitur, O domus antiqua,&c. Hi omnes] Cæsar loquitur de Gallis, Aquitanis, Celtis, Belgis. Alio vultu] Rulli insolentiam & spiritu his difsimilibus exprimit orator, quod etiam sequetia magis declarant: Vestitu (ait) obfoletiore,corpore inculto & horrido, capillatior quam ante, barbaq; majore,& oculis, & aspectu, ut denuntiare omnibus vim tribunitiam, & minitari Rei publicæ videretur. Philosophia] Hæc etiam dissimilitudo plenius à Cicerone sic exponitur: Nā quid faciet in Geometria, qui nō didicerit? quid in musicis? aut taceat oportet, aut insanus judicetur. Hæc vero quæ sunt in Philosophia, ingeniis eruuntur: & ad id quod in quoq; verisimile fit, eliciendū acutis atq; acribus, eaq; exercitata oratione poliuntur. Et hoc idem exemplū brevioris notæ gratiā, contracte positum est.
units.tr: Debt: This dissimilarity is set out in several parts in the same place. For he who pays back money (says the orator) does not immediately have what he has repaid, whereas he who owes retains what is another's; but he who repays a favour still has it, and he who has it has it in what he repays. And this is said for Plancius. The example is stated more briefly only for the sake of the mark of dissimilarity, as in Brutus: "What is so unlike as Demosthenes and Lysias?" O house: a verse of Ennius, Off. 1, about a house that is fitting for an honoured man and a prince, if the house is honoured not by its master but the master by the house; for it is offensive when passers-by say, "O ancient house," etc. All these: Caesar speaks of the Gauls, Aquitanians, Celts and Belgians. With another expression: the orator expresses the insolence and spirit of Rullus by these dissimilars, which the following words also make clearer: with shabbier clothing, an unkempt and rough body, hairier than before, a greater beard, and eyes and look such that he seemed to threaten everyone with tribunician violence and to menace the Republic. Philosophy: Cicero sets out this dissimilarity more fully thus: "For what will a man do in geometry if he has not learned it? What in music? He must either keep silent or be judged mad. But the things that are in philosophy are drawn out by natural talent, and to elicit what is probable in each case is the work of the sharp and keen, and they are polished by practised speech." This same example is set down in a contracted form for the sake of a briefer mark.

units.la: At non] Vox est Priami, Pyrrho exprobrantis cædem Polytis filii, quòd Achilles non talis in Priamum ipsum fuisset, sed miseratus supplicē, corpus Hectoris reddidisset. Non eadem] Oratio est Horatii postulantis vacationem: Spectatum satis & donatum jam rude, quæris Mecœnas, iterum antiquo me includere ludo,
units.tr: "At non": the words of Priam, reproaching Pyrrhus for the slaughter of Priam's son Polites, because Achilles had not behaved like that toward Priam himself, but, moved with pity for the suppliant, had given back Hector's body. "Non eadem": the speech of Horace asking to be released from service: "You have seen enough of the games and have been given the wooden sword already, Maecenas; do you ask me to shut myself up once more in the old school?"

units.la: Annulus] De officio Prætoris multa sunt in ea epistola ad fratrem, tum fama quadā sinistra laborantem perscripta: ut fit cautior & diligetior, quàm antea: Sint aures tuæ (ait) quæ id quod audiunt existimentur audire: non in quas ficte & simulate, quæstus caussa, insusurretur. Sit annulus tuus, nō ut vas aliquod sed tanquam ipse tu: nō minister alienæ voluntatis, sed testis tuæ.
units.tr: "Annulus": Much is said about the duty of the praetor in that letter to his brother, which was written while he was troubled by some sinister rumour, so that he would become more cautious and diligent than before: "Let your ears (he says) be those which are thought to hear what they hear, not those into which things are whispered falsely and deceitfully for the sake of gain. Let your signet ring be not like some vessel, but as if it were you yourself: not the minister of another's will, but the witness of yours."

units.la: Hic autē annulus fignatorius intelligitur, quomodo & annulo sigilla inprimere Academico 4.dicitur. Atq; hic iterum protasis & anapodosis distinguitur per negationé similitudinis :sed additur simile, tanquá ipse tu. Axiomata] Axiomata disimilitudinis respondent velut é regione, axiomatis similitudinis: ea in logico organo nulla sunt, sed á P. Ramo ex Aristotelis lege é mathematicis, ubi de magnitudine, & specialiter, & tanquá quæstiones dubię ꝓponūtur:quæ tamé communia sunt, & logica, & axiomata per se manifesta. itaq; logicam P. Rami in his excolendis axiomatis agriculturam hic attedamus.
units.tr: Here the signet ring is meant, just as to impress seals with a ring is said in Academica 4. Here again the protasis and apodosis are distinguished by a denial of similarity, but "simile" is added: "as if it were you yourself." The axioms of dissimilarity correspond, as it were directly opposite, to the axioms of similarity. These are not found in the logical organon; they are taken by P. Ramus from Aristotle's rule and from mathematics, where they are put forward concerning magnitude, specifically and as doubtful questions. Yet they are common to both logic and the self-evident axioms. Therefore, in cultivating these axioms, we here apply P. Ramus's logic as a kind of husbandry.

units.la: Inæqualia] Hic tria axiomata disimilitudinis pariter respondent tribus axiomatis similitudinis. Octava propositio quinti, hac de re sic est: Inæqualium magnitudinum major ad eandem majorem rationem habet, quàm minor: & eadé ad minorem, majorem rationé habet, quàm ad majorem. decima deinde sequitur conversa octavæ: Ad eandem rationem habentium, majorem rationem habens,illa major est: ad quam autem eadem majorem habet rationem, illa minor est.
units.tr: "Inaequalia": Here three axioms of dissimilarity correspond equally to three axioms of similarity. The eighth proposition of the fifth book states the matter thus: of unequal magnitudes, the greater has a greater ratio to the same magnitude than the lesser has, and the same magnitude has a greater ratio to the lesser than to the greater. Next follows the tenth, the converse of the eighth: of those having the same ratio to something, that which has the greater ratio is the greater; and that to which the same has a greater ratio is the lesser.

units.la: Certus] Quæritur orator deliberari tardiùs de bello adversus Antonium,frustraq; Calendas januarias expectari: Dies enim afferat(ait) & hora potiùs (nisi provisum est) magnas sæpe clades: Certus autem dies,nō ut sacrificii, &c. Hic partes disimilitudinis plenius explicantur, sed tamen negando similitudinis notam.
units.tr: "Certus": The orator complains that the deliberation about war against Antony is being delayed too long, and that the Kalends of January are being awaited in vain: "For a day (he says), or rather an hour, unless provision is made, often brings great disasters; a fixed day, however, not as of a sacrifice, and so on." Here the parts of dissimilarity are explained more fully, but still by denying the mark of similarity.

units.la: Pastor] Locus est Ecloga prima apud Virgilium, de magnitudine urbis Romæ,cui Mantua disimilis sit,ut canibus catuli, ut matribus hœdi disimiles. Brutus] Exemplum est Quintiliani capite undecimo libri quinti, historia autē de Bruto & Manlio nota est apud Livium, illa secundo libro, hæc octavo. Catullus invitat amicam Lesbiā ad delicias & voluptates in vita perfruendas, quę post mortem nullæ suturæ sunt: ubi sol & vita dissimiliter comparantur, quód ille sæpius abeat & redeat ad nos, hæc nobis semel erepta, nunquam redeat. quod carmē Epicureum & impium est: vita enim sempiterna, sempiternis animis futura est. Protasis est in primo versu, Antapodosis in reliquis duob. In hoc igitur exemplo, termini quatuor distinguuntur, sol, occasus, vita, mors.
units.tr: "Pastor": The passage is the first Eclogue of Virgil, on the greatness of the city of Rome, to which Mantua is unlike, as puppies are unlike dogs and kids unlike their mothers. "Brutus": an example from Quintilian, book 5, chapter 11. The story of Brutus and Manlius is known from Livy, the former in book 2, the latter in book 8. Catullus invites his mistress Lesbia to enjoy the delights and pleasures of life, since after death there will be none. Here the sun and life are compared dissimilarly: the one often sets and returns to us, while this life, once snatched from us, never returns. The poem is Epicurean and impious, for life is everlasting and souls will be everlasting. The protasis is in the first verse, the apodosis in the others. In this example four terms are distinguished: sun, setting, life, death.

units.la: Illustriora Quod antea factum est in reliquis comparatorū generibus, idem & hic agitur, ut dissimilitudinis, præcipuæ opes propalam collocentur: & quidem hic primum exemplo fieto, deinde vero. Marcello Marcellus Octavæ sororis Augusti filius, quem sibi Augustus adoptaverat, in Bajano obiit, decimo octavo ætatis anno. Proponitur autem mors illa immatura duobus primis versibus ufq; ad (Nimium:) ubi dissimile est fictum, Si fuissent hæc propria, id est perpetua. Quantos Iteratur eadem, de interitu immaturo, fusiusq; arguitur & explicatur per gemitus Populi Rom. editos in funere Marcelli. Tumulum Sexcenti funebres lecti tū intrarunt urbem. Campus In Campo Martio sepultus est tum Marcellus. & hic velut epitaphium est Marcelli, ait Servius. quem locū quādo Virgilio recitāte, Augustus & Octavia soror audierunt, obortis lachrymis silentium imperarunt: Octavia autè ipsa animo defecit, proq; sin gulis versibus, denis sestertiis Poetam donavit. Vide P. Ramum in Virgilii vita. Nec puer] Interponitur laus é disimili spe longioris vitæ.
units.tr: "Illustriora": What was done before in the other kinds of comparison, the same is done here too, so that the chief resources of dissimilarity are set out openly; here first by a feigned example, and then in earnest. "Marcello": Marcellus, son of Octavia, Augustus's sister, whom Augustus had adopted, died at Baiae in his eighteenth year. That untimely death is set forth in the first two verses, up to "Nimium", where the dissimilar is feigned: "if these things had been lasting, that is, perpetual." "Quantos": The same theme of untimely death is repeated, argued at greater length and explained through the groans of the Roman people at Marcellus's funeral. "Tumulum": Six hundred funeral couches then entered the city. "Campus": Marcellus was then buried in the Campus Martius, and this is, as Servius says, as it were the epitaph of Marcellus. When Virgil recited this passage, Augustus and his sister Octavia heard it; with tears welling up they called for silence, and Octavia herself fainted. For each verse she gave the poet ten sestertia. See P. Ramus in Virgil's life. "Nec puer": Praise is interposed from the dissimilar hope of a longer life.

units.la: Heu pietas] Αντανάκλασις hic plenius iteratur, de reb. quas gesturus fuerat Marcellus, si diutius vixisset itaq; totum hoc dissimile fictum est. Talis est multiplicatorum dissimilium collocatio
units.tr: "Heu pietas": Antanaclasis [ἀντανάκλασις] is explained more fully here, concerning the deeds Marcellus would have done had he lived longer; so this whole passage is a feigned dissimilarity. Such is the arrangement of several dissimilars placed together.

units.la: 2. Æneidos, de Hectore fœdè contrucidato & quondam triumphante:: In somnis ecce ante oculos mœstissimus Hector Visus adesse mihi, largosq; effundere fletus: Raptatus bigis, ut quondam, aterq; cruento Pulvere, perq; pedes trajectus lora tumentes. Hei mihi qualis erat, quantum mutatus ab illo Hectore, qui redit exuvias indutus Achilli! Vel Danaum Phrygios jaculatus puppibus ignes! Squallentem barbam, & concretos sanguine crines, Vulneraq; illa gerens, quæ circum plurima muros Accepit patrios.
units.tr: Aeneid 2, of Hector foully mangled, once a triumphant man: "Lo, in my sleep Hector, most sorrowful, seemed to stand before my eyes, shedding copious tears: dragged behind a chariot, as once, black with gore and dust, his feet pierced through with swollen thongs. Alas, what a man he was, how changed from that Hector who returned wearing the spoils of Achilles, or who hurled Phrygian fire at the Danaan ships! His beard matted, his hair stiff with blood, bearing those wounds which he received in great number around his country's walls."

units.la: Varronis] Varro fuerat Pompeji legatus in Hispania, tandemq; in Cæsaris potestatem adductus, ut est 1. & 2. Belli civilis: Antonius igitur belli tempore, in fundum Varronis invaserat, & à Cæsare sibi traditum ajebat: quanquam Varro & patriæ, & fortunis restitutus à Cæsare fuerat. Casinate] Casinum in Samnitibus oppidum, unde fundus Casinas. Otella] Versus Ennii jam antea citatus. Studiorum] Doctissimus Romanorum Varro fuit, de quo primo Academicarum Marcus Cicero ita loquitur: Nos in nostra urbe peregrinantes, errantesq; tanquam hospites, tui li
units.tr: "Varronis": Varro had been Pompey's legate in Spain, and at last was brought under Caesar's power, as in the first and second books of the Civil War. Antonius therefore, during the war, had invaded Varro's farm and claimed that it had been handed over to him by Caesar, although Varro had been restored by Caesar to his country and fortunes. "Casinate": Casinum, a town among the Samnites, whence the Casinas farm. "Otella": a verse of Ennius, already cited earlier. "Studiorum": Varro was the most learned of the Romans. Of him Marcus Cicero speaks thus in the first book of the Academica: "We, wandering in our own city like strangers and guests, your books, as it were, have led us home, so that we might at some time recognize who we were and where we were. You have revealed the age of our country, you the descriptions of the times, you the laws of sacred things, you the duties of priests, you domestic and military discipline, you the seats of places and regions, you the names, kinds, duties and causes of all divine and human things. You have brought very much light and words to our poets, and to Latin literature altogether; you yourself have written a varied and elegant poem in almost every metre, and you have begun philosophy in many places, enough to stir the mind, too little to teach it."

Ille mansuetudine & misericordia clarus factus est: » huic severitas dignitatem addiderat.Cæsar dan » do,sublevando,ignoscēdo: Cato nihil largiēdo, » gloriam adeptus est. In altero, miseris profugiū » erat:in altero, malis pernicies.Illius facilitas,hu o jus constantia laudabatur. Postremo Cæsar in » animum induxerat, laborare, vigilare, negotiis » amicorum intentus,sua negligere,nihil denega re, quod dono dignum effet: sibi magnum impe‑ rium, exercitum, bellum exoptabat, ubi virtus ejus enitescere posset: At Catoni studiū modestiæ & decoris, sed maximè severitatis erat: non divitiis cum divite, nec factione cum factiosò: sed cum strenuo, virtute: cum modesto, pudore: cum innocente, abstinetia certabat: Esse, quàm videri bonus malebat: Ita quò minùs gloriâ appetebat, eò magis illam adsequebatur.
units.tr: "…bri": "…they have led us home, as it were, so that we might recognize who and where we were. You have explained the age of the country, the descriptions of the times, the laws of sacred things, the offices of priests, domestic and military discipline, the seats of places and regions, and the names, kinds, duties and causes of all things divine and human. You have brought great light to our poets, and to all Latin letters, and you yourself have written a varied and elegant poem in almost every metre, and you have begun philosophy in many places, enough to stir, too little to teach." This kind of dissimilarity is found in Sallust, splendid and especially magnificent, which P. Ramus greatly praised, concerning the dissimilar characters of Caesar and Cato; therefore I judged it should be added here too. Sallust: "But in my memory there were two men of great ability and different character, M. Cato and C. Caesar. Since circumstances have brought them before us, I did not think it right to pass them over in silence, but to set forth as far as I could the nature and character of each. Their birth, age and eloquence were nearly equal; their greatness of spirit was equal, and likewise their glory, though of different kinds. Caesar was regarded as great for his benefits and generosity; Cato for the integrity of his life. Caesar became famous for gentleness and compassion; to Cato severity had given dignity. Caesar gained glory by giving, relieving and forgiving; Cato by bestowing nothing. For the one, refuge was open to the wretched; for the other, ruin to the wicked. The one's easiness was praised, the other's steadfastness. In short, Caesar had resolved to labour, to keep watch, to be intent on the affairs of his friends, to neglect his own, to refuse nothing that was worthy of a gift; he desired for himself a great command, an army, and a war, where his valour might shine. But Cato's pursuit was moderation and decorum, and above all severity: he did not vie with the rich in wealth, nor with the faction-leader in faction, but with the energetic in valour, with the modest in restraint, with the innocent in abstinence. He preferred to be good rather than to seem so; and so the less he sought glory, the more it followed him."

units.la: Cap. XXIII. De Conjugatis.
units.tr: Chapter XXIII. On Conjugates.

units.la: HActenus prima argumēta sunt ex posita: sequuntur orta de primis: quæ perinde sunt ad id, quod arguunt, sicut prima, unde oriuntur: ut conjugata & notatio, distributio & definitio. Conjugata sunt nomina, ab eodē principio variē deducta, ut justitia, justus, juste. In conjugatis symbolum est consensu taneorum argumentorum. Propertius libro secundo:
units.tr: So far the primary arguments have been set out. There follow those derived from the primaries, which bear on what they prove just as the primaries do, since they arise from them: such as conjugates, notation, distribution and definition. Conjugates are words derived in various ways from the same principle, such as justice, just and justly. In conjugates the sign is the agreement of kindred arguments. Propertius, book two:

units.la: Libertas quoniam nulli jam restat amanti, Nullus liber erit, si quis amare velit.
units.tr: Since freedom now remains for no lover, no one will be free if he wishes to love.

units.la: Hic libertas, causa est cur sis liber. Cicero tertio de Natura deorum, cùm de Dionysio tyranno loquitur: jam mēsas argēteas de omnibus delubris jussit auferri, in quibus (quod more veteris Græciæ) inscriptum esset, Bonorum deorū, uti eorum bonitate velle se dicebat. Dii boni sunt: eorū igitur bonitate est utendum. hic ex effectis ad causas est disputatum. Terent.
units.tr: Here "freedom" is the cause of why you are free. Cicero, in the third book of On the Nature of the Gods, when speaking of the tyrant Dionysius: he had now ordered the silver tables to be removed from all the shrines, on which (as was the custom of old Greece) it was inscribed "of the good gods," and he said that he wished to use them through the goodness of the gods. The gods are good; therefore their goodness is to be used. Here the argument proceeds from effects to causes. Terence:

units.la: Homo sum, humani a me nihil alienū puto.
units.tr: I am a man, and I think nothing human is alien to me.

units.la: Ex subiecto est ad adjunctum. Cōtrá Philip. 2. Non tractabo ut Consulem, ne ille quidem me ut Cōsularem. In Pison. Cúm esset omnis illa causa consularis & Senatoria, auxilio mihi opus fuerat & Consulis, & Senatus.
units.tr: This moves from the subject to the adjunct. Against Philippians 2: "I will not treat him as a consul, nor will he even treat me as a man of consular rank." In Pison: "Since that whole cause was consular and senatorial, I needed the help both of the consul and of the Senate."

units.la: Hactenus] Tráfitus fit á primis argumētis, ad ea quæ sunt de primis orta: quæ symbola quidē primorum sunt, sed tamen viam inventionis diversam indicatia. Origo autem & derivatio primum obscurior est in conjugatis: at in notatione, distributione, definitione, est illustrior & manifestior. Dichotomia vero hic etiam à P. Ramo servata est: sed bis binæ species pro duobus generibus sunt adhibitæ. Ex unitate & multitudine parentum primorum, antecessionis modus agnoscitur. ex unico, oriuntur conjugatio, notatio, ut é singulis apparebit p exempla. At distributio & definitio etiá é coplurib9 sunt. Categoria primi derivati argumēti, tota nominalis est: nec ideo non Logica: Logica. n. est entis & non entis, itaq; etiam nominis: Est tñ Categoria hęc nominalis, omniū parcissima: & parcissimè omnium propositā, minimeq; dispersa. Tautologię absolutorum in cōsentaneis & dissentaneis per totam Aristotelis bibliothecam dić̃ę sunt:dićta etiam comparatorum in mathematicas artes es fusio: hic nihil admodum prodiga philosophia reperiet: ideoq; agricultura P. Ramo leuior & facilior. Conjugata] Aristoteli 3.cap. 2. Topici, συστοιχα dicuntur, quæ proprie cognata dixeris, ut justitia,justus: ubi adverbia é nominibus nata,vocat πτῶσις,casus:sed postea in aliis Topicis & in Rhetoricis,differentiam illam contempsit. Cicero in Topicis,quę videri vult ab Aristotele transtulisse, συζυγια και συζυγίαν,conjugata & cõjugatione dicit: Verbum tamen Ciceronis, quanvis Aristotelis verbo non tam responderet: attamen magis est in hac re tritum & usitatû. Locus conjugatorum parciús appellatur in bibliotheca Aristotelis, particula ejus quædam, paronyma sunt in Categoriis, ut á Grammatica grammaticus, á fortitudine fortis: in Topicis nominatim citatur decies & quinquies. hæc tautologia est quidẽ tam multiplex,quám dixi:sed tautologia feré tantûm nominis,nullius auté prolixioris doćtrinæ: sed tamẽ hæc tautologia ex lege λαβὸντ πρῶτον amputatur á P. Ramo,& generale generaliter ac semel exponitur: Quintilianus autem libro quinto,capite decimo, hunc conjugationis locum ridiculum censuit:At P.Ramus in scholis Rhetoricis ad eum locum respondit Quintiliano:authoritas Aristotelis gravior erit, hunc locum præcipuë celebrantis.Maximè opportuni & communes loci ex oppositis,& conjugatis,& casibus,ait 4.cap.3.Topici.item,Sunt autem opportunissimi locorû, quie casibus & conjugatis:2.cap.7. Topici.Itaq; conjugatorum Topicū Aristotelis authoritate bellé adversus authoritatem Quintiliani defenditur. Sed tamē ut in commendationem contradictionis antea, ita nūc postea in conjugationis laudem Aristoteles profusior videtur. Conjugatorum symbolum est illud quidem egregiam & prædicabile, sed tamen cum nullo priorum, cum nullo item sequetium comparandū: Ergo conjugatis sumus honor esto, sed eo loco & numero, quo par est. Symbolum] Conjugatio est é consentaneis tantúm: In Propertii exemplo quatuor cōjugata sunt, libertas, liber, amans, amare: In quibus caussæ sunt & effecta, sed pauló dissimiliter in (libertas & liber) item in (amans & amare.)
units.tr: So far: the transition is made from the primary arguments to those derived from the primaries. These are indeed symbols of the primaries, but they indicate a different route of invention. The origin and derivation are at first rather obscure in conjugates, but in notation, distribution and definition they are clearer and more manifest. Ramus has kept the dichotomy here too, but two pairs of species have been used in place of two genera. From the unity and plurality of the primary parents the mode of precedence is recognised. Conjugation and notation arise from the single term, as will appear from examples of each. But distribution and definition also arise from several terms. The category of the first derived argument is wholly nominal, yet it is not therefore not logic: for logic is of being and non-being, and therefore also of names. Yet this category is nominal, the most sparing of all, and set out most sparingly of all, and least dispersed. Tautologies of absolutes in agreeing and disagreeing terms are spread throughout the whole library of Aristotle; sayings about comparatives have been poured into the mathematical arts; here philosophy, which is not very lavish in this matter, will find little. Therefore agriculture is lighter and easier for Ramus. Conjugates: In Aristotle, Topics 3, chapter 2, they are called συστοιχα, which you could properly call cognates, such as justice and just. Where he calls adverbs derived from nouns πτῶσις, a case, but later in other Topics and in the Rhetoric he disregarded that distinction. Cicero, in the Topics, which he wishes to seem to have translated from Aristotle, calls συζυγια και συζυγίαν conjugates and conjugation. Yet Cicero's word, though it does not correspond so closely to Aristotle's word, is nevertheless more worn and in common use in this matter. The topic of conjugates is named more sparingly in Aristotle's library; certain parts of it, the paronyms, are in the Categories, such as grammarian from grammar, brave from bravery. In the Topics it is cited by name fifteen times. This tautology is indeed as manifold as I have said, but it is almost only a tautology of names, and of no very extended teaching. Yet this tautology is cut off by Ramus under the law of λαβὸντ πρῶτον, and the general is explained generally and once only. Quintilian, however, in book five, chapter ten, thought this topic of conjugation ridiculous; but Ramus, in his Rhetoric lectures, replied to Quintilian that the authority of Aristotle, who especially celebrates this topic, is weightier. Aristotle says in Topics 4, chapter 3, that the most suitable and common topics are those from opposites, conjugates and cases; likewise, "The most convenient of the topics are those of cases and conjugates," Topics 2, chapter 7. So the Topic of conjugates is well defended by the authority of Aristotle against the authority of Quintilian. But just as Aristotle was more lavish earlier in commending contradiction, so now, afterwards, he seems more profuse in praise of conjugation. The sign of conjugates is indeed excellent and worth proclaiming, but it is not to be compared with any of the preceding or following; so let conjugates be honoured, but in the place and rank that befits them. Symbol: Conjugation is only of agreeing terms. In Propertius' example there are four conjugates: liberty, free, lover, to love. In these there are causes and effects, but somewhat differently in (liberty and free) and likewise in (lover and to love).

units.la: Dionysius ] Historia hæc copiosé exponitur à Cicerone tertio libro de Nat. deorum, ut Fanū Proserpinæ Locris expilarit, deinde jovi Olympio aureum amiculū detraxerit grandi ponderē, atq; in eo etiā cavillatus sit, æstate grave esse aureum amiculum, hyeme frigidū: eiq; laneum pallium injecit, quum id esse aptum ad omne aō nitempus diceret. idemq; Æsculapii Epidauri barbam aueam demi jussit: neq; enim conveniare barbatum esse filium, cūm in omnib. fanis pater imberbis esset. tum sequitur, jām mensas argenteas, &c. Idem victoriolas aureas, & pateras, coronafq; quæ simulacrorum porrectis manibus sustinebantur, sine dubitatione tollebat, eaq; se accipere, non auferre dicebat: Esse enim stultitiam, à quibus bona precaremur, abiis porrigentibus & dantibus nolle sumere. Eūdemq; ferunt, hæc quæ dixi, sublata de fanis in forum protulisse, & per Præconem vēdidisse, exactaq; pecunia edixisse, ut quod quisque á sacris haberet, id ante diem certum in suum quodq; fanum referret. Ita ad impietatem in deos, in homines adjunxit injuriam. In Heaut. cùm Chremes Menedemum de filii absentia tristem videret, cum consolatur: tum Menedemus ait:
units.tr: Dionysius: This history is set out at length by Cicero in the third book of On the Nature of the Gods: that he plundered the shrine of Proserpina at Locri, then took from Jupiter Olympius a golden cloak of great weight, and mocked it, saying that a golden cloak is heavy in summer and cold in winter; and he put a woollen mantle on the god, saying that it was suitable for every season. He also ordered the golden beard of Aesculapius at Epidaurus to be taken off, for it was not fitting that the son should be bearded when the father was beardless in all the shrines. Then follows: "Now the silver tables," etc. Likewise he removed without hesitation the little golden victories, the bowls and the crowns which were held out in the extended hands of statues, and said that he was receiving them, not taking them away; for it would be folly not to accept what we pray for from those who hold them out and give them. They also say that he carried the things I have mentioned out of the shrines into the forum and sold them through a herald, and, when the money was collected, ordered that whatever each person had from the sacred things should be brought back before a fixed day to his own shrine. Thus he added injury to men to impiety against the gods. In the Heautontimorumenos, when Chremes saw Menedemus sad at his son's absence and consoled him, Menedemus then said:

units.la: Chreme, tantúmne est abs re tua otii tibi,
units.tr: Chremes, do you have so much leisure to spare from your own affairs,

units.la: Aliena ut cures? eaq;, nihil quæ ad te attinent.
units.tr: that you care about others' affairs, which have nothing to do with you?

units.la: Chremes respondet, Homo sum, id est, errare possum: attamen humani, id est humanitatis nihil alienum:
units.tr: Chremes replies, "I am a man," that is, I can err; yet nothing human, that is, of humanity, is alien to me:

units.la: Vel me monere hoc, vel percontari puta.
units.tr: Think of it either as advising me of this or as asking about it.

units.la: Hic homo, subjectum est humanitatis.
units.tr: Here "man" is the subject of humanity.

units.la: Cicero in Antonium Consulem liberiús vel petulantiús dicturus, indecori cujusdam reprehensionē á se detestatur: quia Antonius Ciceronem ipsum licet Consularem, id est Consulatu perfunctum, pro dignitate nó tra ctarit. Conjugata hic eadem sunt, Consul, Cófularis, Senatus, Senatorius: ubi Cicero, qui Cófulari potestate, & Senatoria authoritate, Catilinariam conjurationem repressorat, conqueritur Consulem Pisonem, & Pisonis factione Senatum sibi defuisse.
units.tr: Cicero, about to speak more freely or rather more wantonly against Antonius the consul, disclaims any reproach of indecorum on his own part, because Antonius had not treated Cicero himself with proper respect, though he was a man of consular rank, that is, one who had served as consul. The conjugates here are the same: consul, consular, senate, senatorial. Here Cicero, who had suppressed the Catilinarian conspiracy by consular power and senatorial authority, complains that the consul Piso, and through Piso's faction the Senate, had failed him.

units.la: Cap. XXIIII. De Notatione.
units.tr: Chapter 24. On Notation.

units.la: NOtatio, est nominis interpretatio: nomina siquidem, sunt notę rerū: nominumq; vel derivatorum, vel compositorum, si vera notatione fiant, ratio reddi potest ex aliquo argumento primo: ut, homo ab humo. Ovid. 6. Faft.
units.tr: Notation is the interpretation of a name. Names are the marks of things, and the reason for a name, whether derived or compounded, can be given from some primary argument if the notation is true: for example, homo from humus. Ovid, Fasti 6.

units.la: Stat vi terra sua, vi stando terra vocatur. ex caussa est notatio:
units.tr: He stands firm on his own ground, and from standing firm (vi stando) is called earth (terra). This notation is from the cause.

units.la: At focus á flämis, et quód fovet omnia, dict.
units.tr: But the hearth (focus) is named from fire (flammis), and because it warms (fovet) all things.

units.la: Item 4. Verr. O Verrea præclara! Quó enim accessisti, quó nō attuleris tecum istum diem? Etenim quam tu domum, quam urbem adiisti, quod fanum denique, quod non cverfum atq; extersum reliqueris? Quare appellentur sané ista Verrea, quæ non ex nomine, sed ex moribus naturaq; tua cöftituta esse videantur. Ex effectis est notatio. Ovid. 1. Faft.
units.tr: Cicero, Verrines 4: "O famous Verrine! Where did you go, and where did you not bring that day with you? For what house, what city did you enter, what shrine at last, that you did not leave overturned and stripped bare? Therefore those things may rightly be called Verrine, since they seem established not by a name but by your character and nature." This notation is from effects. Ovid, Fasti 1.

units.la: Prima dies tibi Carna datur: dea Cardinis hæc est,
units.tr: The first day is given to you, Carna; she is the goddess of the hinge,

units.la: Nomine clausa aperit, claudit aperta suo. Híc est notatio é subjecto cardine, circa quem numē deæ exercetur. At ex ad junctis notatio est Bambalionis 2. Phil. quia Balbus & stupidus: hinc igit cavillatio in Antonium generum: Tuæ conjugis bonæ fœminę locupletis quidem certè, Bambalio quidā pater, homo nullo numero: nihil illo contemptius, qui propter hęsitantiam linguę stuporemq; cordis cognomen ex contumelia traxerit. rit. Ex adjunctis est notatio. E dissentaneis autem sunt illa apud Quintilianum lib.1. cap. 6. Lucus, quia umbra opacus, parum luceat: & ludus, quia sit longissimé á lusu: & dis, quia minimé dives. Potest etiam é comparatis esse notatio, ut pyropus, quód ignis flammā imitetur. Est verò ut notationi ad suum nomē, sic nomini ad notationem sua affectio: ut, animi plenus, ergo animosus: & contrá, animosus, ergo animi plenus.
units.tr: She opens what is closed by her name, and closes what is open. Here the notation is from the subject: the hinge, around which the goddess's power is exercised. The notation of Bambalio is from adjuncts, in Cicero's second Philippic, because Balbus was stupid: hence his jest against Antony's father-in-law: "Your wife's father, certainly rich, a certain Bambalio, a man of no account; nothing more contemptible than he, who, because of his hesitant speech and dull heart, drew a nickname from an insult." Notation is from adjuncts. From things dissimilar come those examples in Quintilian, book 1, chapter 6: lucus, because it is shadowy and scarcely shines (parum luceat); ludus, because it is far removed from play (longissime a lusu); and dis, because he is by no means rich (minime dives). Notation can also be from things compared, as pyropus, because it imitates the flame of fire. Indeed, just as a notation relates to its name, so a name relates to its affection: as animi plenus, therefore animosus; and conversely, animosus, therefore animi plenus.

units.la: Nominis] Græci (ait Cicero in Topicis) ἐτυ- μολογίαν vocarunt, id est verbum ex verbo, veriloquium: Nos autem novitatem verbi non satis apti fugientes, genus hoc notationem appellamus: quia sunt verba, rerū notæ. Itaq; hoc idem Aristoteles συμβολον appellat, quod Latiné est nota. Hæc ille. Sed tamen P. Ramus non hoc loco instituit notationes rerum, quæ sunt ipsa nomina, sed nominū ipsorum rationes, origines, atq; deductiones, é quibus res argui & explicari possit. Notatio autem á Grammaticis & Dialecticis dissimili ratione tractatur. ab illis, ut accidentia dictionum doceantur: ab iis, ut ex origine & natura res ipsi significationi subjecta arguatur & probetur. Sunt etiam qui originationem potius vocant, ut scribit Fabius, quód origines & argumenta nominum aperiat, unde orta ductaque sint. Topici autè hujus logica Platoni apud Græcos, & Varroni apud Latinos magni pretii fuit. De notatione in Cratylo Platonis longa est disputatio. Nam cum Cratylus nomina rerum naturali quadam veritate, Hermogenes, hominum instituto & lege tantum constare diceret, Socrates, tanquam honorarius arbiter controversiam in hunc modum disceptat: Nominum quaedam esse vera, quę essentias rerum nominatarum significant & quorum recta ratio reddi posit: quaedam esse falsa & quorum notatio diversa sit à re, quae nominatur: quaedam esse primitiva, quorum origo barbara sit, aut certe nobis ignota: Itaq; nomina quidem, arbitrio hominum constare. sed saepe sapienter, & rerum naturis nomina ipsa accommodante, qualia multa & divina & non divina Socrates in Cratylo interpretatur. quo in dialogo notabile est illud, quod Plato affirmat dialectici opus esse, recte nomina rebus imponere, & imposita interpretari: Aristoteles primo capite primi libri de Interpretatione. Hermogenem in hac doctrina sequi videtur, quod vocabula sint κατὰ συνθήκην, ad arbitrium hominis imposita: quod etsi verum est, tamen in Analyticis & Topicis, Cratyli sententiam & Socratis manifeste sequitur, dum notationis argumentum instituit: Notatio enim appellatur ab Aristotele λόγῳ ὀνοματώδης, definitio nominalis, ut 10. cap. 2. Poster. item λόγῳ ἑνόματος, definitio nominis, ut 2. cap. Topici: ité τόπος ἀπὸ τῆς ὀνόματος, locus à nomine, ut cap. 23. 2. Rhetorici. Quare Aristoteles non ita judicavit vocabula rebus imposita, quin eorum si composita praesertim aut derivata essent, ratio reddi posset.
units.tr: Of the name. The Greeks (says Cicero in the Topics) called it etymologia [ἐτυμολογία], that is, word from word, true speech. We, avoiding the novelty of a word not sufficiently apt, call this kind notatio, because words are the marks of things. Accordingly Aristotle calls the same thing symbolon [σύμβολον], which in Latin is nota. So far Cicero. Yet P. Ramus does not here set out the notations of things, which are the names themselves, but the reasons, origins and derivations of the names, from which a thing can be argued and explained. Notation is, however, treated in one way by grammarians and in another by dialecticians: the former teach the accidents of words; the latter teach how a thing subject to the signification is argued and proved from its origin and nature. There are also those who call it rather originatio, as Fabius writes, because it reveals the origins and arguments of names, whence they arose and were derived. The topic of this kind of logic was of great value to Plato among the Greeks and to Varro among the Latins. There is a long disputation on notation in Plato's Cratylus. For when Cratylus said that names of things consist in a certain natural truth, and Hermogenes that they consist only in human institution and convention, Socrates, as an honorary arbiter, settled the controversy thus: some names are true, signifying the essences of the things named, and of which a correct reason can be given; some are false, and their notation differs from the thing named; some are primitive, whose origin is foreign or at least unknown to us. Names therefore consist indeed by human choice, yet often wisely, adapting the names themselves to the natures of things, as Socrates in the Cratylus interprets many names, both divine and not divine. In that dialogue what Plato affirms is notable, that it is the work of the dialectician rightly to impose names on things and to interpret what has been imposed (Aristotle, first chapter of the first book of On Interpretation). Ramus seems to follow Hermogenes in this doctrine, that words are kata synthēkēn [κατὰ συνθήκην], imposed at the will of man. Yet although this is true, in the Analytics and the Topics he plainly follows the opinion of Cratylus and Socrates, while setting up the argument of notation. For notation is called by Aristotle logos onomatōdēs [λόγῳ ὀνοματώδης], a nominal definition (Posterior Analytics 2, chapter 10); also logos onomatos [λόγῳ ὀνόματος], a definition of a name (Topics 2, chapter 2); and also topos apo tou onomatos [τόπος ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀνόματος], a topic from the name (Rhetoric 2, chapter 23). Hence Aristotle did not judge that words were imposed on things in such a way that no reason could be given for them, especially if they were compounded or derived.

units.la: Argumento primo] Id exempla sequentia demȯ ftrant,é singulis primis argumentis deducta.
units.tr: From the first arguments. The following examples, each derived from one of the primary arguments, show this.

units.la: Homo] Quintilianus lib. 1. cap. 6. hanc notationem deridet: Etiamne hominem appellari, quia fit humo natus? quasi vero nō omnibus animalibus eadem origo, aut illi primi mortales ante nomen imposuerint terræ, quam sibi.
units.tr: Homo. Quintilian, book 1, chapter 6, mocks this notation: "Is man also to be called so because he is born from the earth (humo)? As if all animals did not have the same origin, or as if those first mortals had named the earth before themselves."

units.la: Stat vi] Vesta duplex fuit, altera terræ, altera ignis dea. hic Ovidius de terra interpretatur.
units.tr: Stat vi. There were two Vestas: one the goddess of earth, the other of fire. Here Ovid interprets it of earth.

units.la: Verrea] Verres in Sicilia triennium Prætor suit, homo multis scelerū notis, septem libris Verrinarum notatus: hic Marcellea, diem Marcello festum sustulerat: pro iis Verrea reposuerat. ergo sal oratori ex hac notatione quæsitus est, tanquam Verres à verrendo dictus sit, cum tamen verres, porcus sit non castratus, ut antea dictum est. itaq; falsam notationem orator etiam ipse indicat, cum ait, nō ex nomine. Locus aut paulo secus in vulgatis exemplarib. legitur: Hotomannus aut jurecofultus etatis noftrę eximius, ita restitu it. Sic Phip.8. Quid est enim aliud tumultus, nisi perturbatio tanta, ut major timor inde oriatur.
units.tr: Verrea. Verres was praetor in Sicily for three years, a man marked by many notes of crime, branded in the seven books of the Verrines. He had abolished the festival of the Marcellea, held in honour of Marcellus, and in its place had restored the Verrea. So the orator sought his joke from this notation, as if Verres were so called from verrere (to sweep), although verres is a boar not castrated, as was said before. Thus the orator himself indicates that the notation is false, when he says "not from the name." The passage reads somewhat differently in the common editions; Hotomanus, an outstanding jurist of our age, restored it in this way. So also in Philippic 8: "For what else is tumult, unless it is such great disturbance that greater fear arises from it?"

units.la: Carna] Ovid. Carnam à cardine derivat, & cótractio quædam effet, Carna pro Cardinia, argumentum item primum hic manifestum est.
units.tr: Carna. Ovid derives Carna from cardo (hinge), and it was a certain contraction, Carna for Cardinia. The primary argument is also manifest here.

units.la: Bambalioni] Antonius nobilissima familia ortus, uxorem ignobile duxerat, id propter opes: sed pterea hic soceri vilitas, é nominis interpretatione coarguitur. adjuncta hic sunt manifesta.
units.tr: Bambalioni. Antony, sprung from a most noble family, had married a wife of low birth, for the sake of her wealth. But here the baseness of the father-in-law is refuted by the interpretation of the name. The adjuncts here are plain.

units.la: Lucus] A νπίφασιν Grammatici hic appellant, cum res ex contrario nominatur, ut lucus, sylva sacra, & ob arborum densitatem opaca, quia minime nimè luceat. Flammas]Hęc interpretatio fuit antea in Ovidii versu,
units.tr: Lucus. Grammarians call this apophasis [ἀπόφασις] when a thing is named from its contrary, as lucus, a sacred grove, which is dark from the density of its trees, because it scarcely shines at all. Flammas. This interpretation was earlier given of the line of Ovid:

units.la: Clara micante auro flammasque imitante pyropo.
units.tr: Clara micante auro flammasque imitante pyropo. ("Bright with glittering gold, and with the pyrope imitating flames.")

units.la: Quod autè é consentaneis, dissentaneis, comparatis, nomen oriatur, proindeq; notatio troporum, id est modificatio, é Rhetoricis, antea simile quiddam habuit, quæ etiam é distributione tropum deducebat. Affectio] In superioribus argumentorum locis, relatio illa manifestior est: hic etiam est. & quidem Aristoteles nomé ipsum 4.cap.1. Topici ait esse ὅρικόν τι, definitivum quiddam. Itaq; si quæratur, quis inter Græcos verè sapit, respondeas, Socrates: hoc nomine arguere videris & explicare quiddam: ὅριζεν tamen illud metiendum sit quadantenus.
units.tr: That a name arises from things consentaneous, dissentaneous and compared, and so the notation of tropes (that is, modification), which belongs to the rhetoricians, earlier had something similar, since it also derived tropes from distribution. Affectio. In the earlier places of the arguments that relation is clearer; here too it is present. Indeed Aristotle, in Topics 4, chapter 1, says the very word is something horikon [ὁρικόν], definitive. So if one asks who among the Greeks is truly wise, you would answer Socrates: by this name you seem to argue and explain something, though that horizein [ὁρίζειν] must be measured to some extent.

units.la: Cap. XXV. De Distributione.
units.tr: Chapter 25. On Distribution.

units.la: REliquum est ex ortis aliunde argumentis, argumentum distributionis & definitionis: in qua utraq; affectio reciprocationis est omnino propria, illic partium omnium cum toto: hic definitionis cū definito. Distributio, est distinctio totius in partes. Totū, est quod continet partes. Pars, est quę continetur à toto. Atq; ut distinctio totius in partes distributio, sic collectio partium ad constituendum totum, inductio dicitur. Distributio sumitur ex argumentis, toti quidem consentaneis, inter se autem dissentaneis. Itaq; tanto accuratior erit, quanto partium & cum toto consensio, & inter se dissensio major fuerit.
units.tr: It remains to treat, among the arguments derived from other sources, the argument of distribution and the argument of definition. In both, the relation of reciprocity is wholly proper: in distribution, of all the parts with the whole; in definition, of the definition with the thing defined. Distribution is the division of a whole into its parts. The whole is that which contains the parts. A part is that which is contained by the whole. Just as the division of a whole into parts is called distribution, so the gathering of parts to constitute a whole is called induction. Distribution is drawn from arguments that agree with the whole but disagree with one another. So it will be the more precise, the greater the agreement of the parts with the whole and the greater their disagreement among themselves.

units.la: Reliquum] Categoriæ distributionis & definitionis supersunt ex ortis argumetis, & originem suam manifestius ostendunt, quàm conjugatio & notatio: Distributionis enim & definitionis species protinus loquuntur parentes unde ortę & procreatæ sint, sicuti ex earum partibus intelligetur:neq; dubitatio ulla esse potest, quin topica hæc é primis oriátur. Est vero distributionis & definitionis tanta vis & facultas, ut disciplinarum tractatione pené solæ completantur. Nam qui definierit, distribuerit, exemplis illuftrarit, nihil admodum videtur habere reliquum in artibus, præsertim rectè & ex ordine propositis & explicatis. Itaque ars distribuendi definiendiq; valdé à philosophis proposita & tractata est: & Ariftoteles, qui aliquando Logicę inventionem sibi videtur attribuere, attamen 4. cap. 3. Philofoph. hanc distribuendi definiendiq; logicam videtur ad Socratem principem atq; authorem referre. Duo verò sunt (ait) quæ quifpiá attribuerit Socrati merito, id est inductivas rationes, & universalem definitionem. Deniq; laudes definiendi & distribuendi, & ratiocinandi, visæ sunt logicam totam completi. quæ opinio etsi falsa est: nihil enim de logica reliquorum tot argumentorum, de logica enutiati, de logica mothodi loquitur: ostendit tamen maximum & frequentifsimum in his argumentis differendi usum versari. Quapropter distributionis & definitionis vis & facultas est eximia.
units.tr: Reliquum: The categories of distribution and definition remain among the arguments derived from other sources, and they show their origin more plainly than conjugation and notation do. The species of distribution and definition at once name the parents from which they arose and were born, as will be clear from their parts. Nor can there be any doubt that these topics arise from the primary ones. Distribution and definition have such force and power that nearly the whole treatment of the disciplines is completed by them alone. For whoever has defined, distributed and illustrated with examples seems to have almost nothing left to do in the arts, especially when these are set out and explained rightly and in order. So the art of distributing and defining has been expounded and treated at length by the philosophers. Aristotle, who at times seems to claim the invention of logic for himself, nevertheless in 4. cap. 3. Philosoph. seems to refer this logic of distributing and defining to Socrates as its prince and author. He says there are two things which may rightly be attributed to Socrates, namely inductive arguments and universal definition. Finally, the praises of defining, distributing and reasoning seemed to complete all of logic. Though this opinion is false, for it says nothing of the logic of the many remaining arguments, of the logic of enunciation, of the logic of method, it nonetheless shows that the greatest and most frequent use of reasoning lies in these arguments. Hence the force and power of distribution and definition is outstanding.

units.la: Propria] Vitia divisionis duo notantur . cap.
units.tr: Propria: Two faults of division are noted in cap.

units.la: 2. Pofter. si quid in ea redundet, si quid defit: itaque convertitur in legitima divisione totū cum partibus, estque reciprocum & æquale partibus. De definitione idem docetur 2. cap. 2. Pofter. & in Topicis iteratur. Itaq; quod esset partitionis & definitionis commune, P. Ramus communiter & semel ex Aristotelis lege proposuit, tautologias illas evitavit. Hæc autem reciprocatio reperitur in quibusdam & causis & subiectis: ut in forma cum formato, & subiecto cum proprietate: in relatis est etiam simile quiddam. At in toto genere vel causarum, vel subiectorum, ut distributionis & definitionis, id non est perpetuum.
units.tr: 2. Post. if something superfluous creeps into it, or if something is lacking. So in a lawful division the whole is convertible with its parts, and it is reciprocal and equal to the parts. The same is taught about definition in 2. cap. 2. Post., and it is repeated in the Topics. Therefore P. Ramus, following Aristotle's rule, set out once and for all what was common to partition and definition, and thereby avoided those tautologies. This reciprocation is found in some causes and subjects, as form with the thing formed, and subject with property; among relatives there is something similar too. But in the whole genus of causes or subjects, as in distribution and definition, it is not perpetual.

units.la: Distributio] Sed jam separatim de distributione, P. Rami studium diligentiamq; specimus: hic enim præcipue elaboravit. Materies ut antea in causis, effectis, differentiis, comparatis, sic jam denique in distributionis categoria permagna est: collegit igitur P. Ramus omnia quæ tota Aristotelis bibliotheca, quæ in mathematicis ufquam de distributione traderentur: Ea sunt primum in singulis organi logici libris (ne prorsus ullam excipiam) permulta, sed communi distributionis nomine, 32. cap. 1. Prio. item 5. 14. 16. cap.
units.tr: Distributio: But now let us look separately at the study and diligence of P. Ramus concerning distribution, for he laboured especially here. As the material was before in causes, effects, differences and comparatives, so now, finally, in the category of distribution it is very great. P. Ramus therefore gathered everything that the whole of Aristotle's library, and anything in the mathematicians, delivered about distribution. These are first, in the individual books of the Organon (not to exclude any at all), very many, but under the common name of distribution: 3. cap. 2. Prior.; 32. cap. 1. Prior.; likewise 5, 14, 16. cap.

units.la: 2. Pofter atque hæc in Organo. In Physic. 1. lib. de partibus animalium: in Philosophia plurima: in Rhetoricis item nonnulla. Deniq; divisionis logica in artes mathematicas exundavit, & elementa octodecim peperit. Enimvero perjucundum mihi fuit, controversas Logicorum de divisione opiniones é P. Rami prælectione & disceptatione perdiscere: Antea de duobus argumentis cosimilis ludis nobis lusus est: Contradiction ab Heraclito, Anaxagora, cæterisque illis valentibus Logicis explosa de scholis, imo de argumentis erat: Aristoteles patrocinio diligentis & accuratæ defensionis reduxit. Megarensis Euclides, similitudinis argumentum tota sua item dignitate dispoliavit: Empedocles contra exornavit una omnium argumentorum laude & gloria, censuitq; nihil nisi simile simili percipi. Sic Speusippus (ut Aristot. interpretes ajunt in locis Analyticis ante citatis) divisione damnabat, ut exiguam logicæ inventionis particulam. quæ non convenire in omnem quæstionem, quæ infirmus syllogismus esset, & ἀσυλλόγιστον, quod deniq; rem obscuraret, ac, si quid afferre videretur, tamen impossibilis esset: His enim calumniis 23. cap. 1. Prior. & 5. & 14. cap. 2. Poster. divisionis logica appetitur, quibus Aristot. accuratè diligenterq; respondet: neque enim particulam esse specialis cujusdam quæstionis, sed omnis problematis communem doctrinam: id enim 16. ca. 2. Poster. nominatim profitetur, eamq; quamvis sit ἀσυλλόγιστος, ait, ἄλλον τρόπον γνωρίζειν ποιᾶ, alio modo cognoscere facit, modo nempe & more principiorum, quæ sua luce sine ullo syllogismo intelligentiam informant: sic Aristoteles accusatione hanc tuetur. Atqui etiam vel armis Aristotelis licet plenius tueri, dicereque, etiam divisionem cum opus est, syllogisticam esse, æque toto ad partes. ê genere ad species,& contrá, fyllogysmũ concludi posse: Tertium veró probrum illud, quód divisio petat τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ, quod in principio est, id est obscuret, Aristoteles itẽ vehementer inficiatur, aitq; 14.cap 2. Post. Divisio ex contrariis immediatis probat, neq; principium petit. Postrema veró illa Speusippi oppugnatio similiter rejicitur: Divisio(ajebat ille)est impossibilis, quia omnes differentiæ & species essent tenẽdæ: quod homini impossibile est. Imò (respondet Aristote les)satis est animal dividenti, notas esse differentias & species animalis:non autem leonis, equi, necesse est:nisi pariter & illa genera velit dividere:Sic igitur Aristot. condiscipuli Speusippi impetus & conatus adversus divisionis doctrinam refutavit.Sed in Topic.addidit 2. cap. 7. lib.cũm locos é conjugatis & oppositis egregié cõmendasset, tũm é reliquis tenendas esse maximé cõmunes, quia essent efficacissimi, ut singulas partes ac species intueri. quo loco videmus divisionis locum ut efficacissimũ ac præstantissimum commendari. Quapropter his modis defensam & exornatam dividēdi doctrinam perspicimus. Sed Plato in Sophista,Parmenide,Politico,Phædro, multa quidé hujus doctrinæ proposuit, sed illud in Phædro non est hoc loco præterẽundũ, quódimperitos hujus logicæ partitores, similes efficit insulsorum coquorum, qui confringunt carnes, quas scienter secare debeant: inibiq; Socrates ait, si quem offenderit, qui scité & apté unum multaq; possit discernere, τὸν Διώνυ καθόπι- τε μετὰ Ἰχνίαρ, ὥστε θεοῖς: hunc consector á tergo vestigiis,tanquá Deum. Quamobrem P. Ramus hanc de divisione condiscipulorum Speufippi atque Ariftot. litem ita dirimebat. jam videamus quomodo materiam tam multiplicem ad Ariftotelis leges composuerit. Materies magna quidem & ampla,& á nemine (quod quidem constet) post veteres illos philosophos digesta. Citatur á Boetio Adronicus in lib. de Divifiõe, laudatus á Porphyrio, & jamblico. Si Boet. Andronici Logicá de dividendo trâftulit, nihil admodum videtur ea logica fuisse: Itaque jam sequentia confideremus. Distributio, est distinctio totius in partes, hæc definitio est generalis,& communis fequentium distributionum. Totú definitur,quod continet partes: & pars, quæ continetur á toto. At P. Ramus hic & totum & partem cómuniter accipit, ut etiam & integrú,& genus, & subjectum, & adjunctum, totum dicatur, totamque divisionis artem complectitur.
units.tr: 2. Post., and these in the Organon. In the Physics, book 1; in the book on the parts of animals; in very many places in the Philosophy; also some in the Rhetoric. Finally, logical division overflowed into the mathematical arts and gave birth to eighteen elements. Indeed it was most delightful to me to learn from P. Ramus's lecture and debate the controverted opinions of the logicians about division. Before, we had been toyed with by two similar arguments. Contradiction, which Heraclitus, Anaxagoras and the other powerful logicians had driven out of the schools, indeed out of argument altogether, was restored by Aristotle's patronage of a diligent and accurate defence. The Megarian Euclides stripped the argument from similarity of all its dignity; Empedocles, on the other hand, adorned it with the single praise and glory of all arguments, and held that nothing is perceived except like by like. So Speusippus (as Aristotle's interpreters say in the Analytics passages cited above) condemned division as a small particle of logical invention, which did not fit every question, was a weak syllogism and [ἀσυλλόγιστον] unreasoned, and finally obscured the matter; and even if it seemed to offer something, it was nonetheless impossible. Against these calumnies, logical division is defended in 23. cap. 1. Prior. and in 5. and 14. cap. 2. Post., and Aristotle answers them carefully and diligently. For it is not a particle of some special question, but the common doctrine of every problem; he professes this by name in 16. cap. 2. Post., and says that although it is [ἀσυλλόγιστος] unreasoned, it makes things known [ἄλλον τρόπον γνωρίζειν ποιεῖ] in another way, namely by the manner of principles, which inform understanding with their own light without any syllogism. Thus Aristotle defends it against this accusation. Yet one may defend it more fully, even with Aristotle's own weapons, and say that division too, when there is need, is syllogistic, and that from whole to parts, from genus to species, and conversely, a conclusion can equally be drawn by syllogism. As for the third reproach, that division begs the question, [τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ], that is, obscures what is at the beginning, Aristotle denies this vehemently too, and says in 14. cap. 2. Post.: division proves from immediate contraries and does not beg the principle. Speusippus's last attack is rejected in the same way. Division (he used to say) is impossible, because all the differences and species would have to be grasped, and that is impossible for a man. Rather (Aristotle replies) it is enough for the one dividing that the differences and species of animal are known; it is not necessary to know those of the lion or the horse, unless he also wishes to divide those kinds. So Aristotle refuted the assault and attempt of Speusippus, his fellow pupil, against the doctrine of division. But in the Topics, after he had commended the places from conjugates and opposites, he added, in 2. cap. 7., that among the rest the most common ones must be held, because they are most effective for viewing single parts and species. In that passage we see the place of division commended as most effective and most excellent. Therefore we perceive the doctrine of dividing defended and adorned in these ways. But Plato, in the Sophist, Parmenides, Politicus and Phaedrus, proposed much of this doctrine. Yet in the Phaedrus one point must not be passed over here: he makes unskilled partitioners like foolish cooks who break up meat which they ought to carve skilfully. There Socrates says that if he should meet someone who can skilfully and aptly discern the one and the many, he follows that man from behind, tracking his footsteps, as he would a god [διώκω ὥσπερ θεόν]. Wherefore P. Ramus settled this dispute between the fellow pupils of Speusippus and Aristotle in this way. Now let us see how he arranged so manifold a matter under Aristotle's laws. The material is indeed great and ample, and (so far as is known) has been arranged by no one since those ancient philosophers. Boethius cites Andronicus in his book On Division, praised by Porphyry and Iamblichus. If Boethius transmitted Andronicus's logic of dividing, that logic seems to have been nothing much. So let us now consider what follows. Distribution is the distinction of a whole into parts; this definition is general and common to the distributions that follow. The whole is defined as that which contains parts, and the part as that which is contained by the whole. But P. Ramus here takes both whole and part in a common sense, so that even the integral, the genus, the subject and the adjunct are called wholes, and he thereby embraces the entire art of division.

units.la: Atque ut] Distinctio totius in partes distributio appellatur, & argumentum tantúm fit, nunquam autem argumétationis species: Collectio partiú ad conftituendü totum inductio dicitur, nomine quidem recté: at inductio, efficitur species argumentationis, deque ea separatim agitur,ut 33.cap.2. Prio.10.cap.1.Top.
