Verúm inductio argumétationis species non recté efficitur. nec enim forma hic ulla,vel dispositio argumenti traditur, quod argumentatio est: sed tam nudum argumentú est á partibus ad totum, quám est á toto ad partes:utq; eadem via Thebis Athenas,quę Athenis Thebas: sic quod ad rudem inventionis & indigestam materiam attinet, tam nudum est categorema partium, quàm totius ut si inductio à partibus ad totum argumetatio dicatur, etiã distributio totius in partes, argumentatio sit dicenda: quod tamen nemini adhuc in mentem venit, ut auderet in præcepti ponere. Quare P. Ramus à partibus argumentũ facit, & collocat in argumentorũ doctrina: non facit argumentationẽ, neq; judicii dispositionisq; speciem. In eoque commetum logicum nescio cujus ab Aristotele collectũ ex argumentationis definitione rejicit. argumentatio enim dispositionis regula est, nō invētionis, neq; tamē hic de re, sed de rei ordine & loco in logica arte quæstio est.
units.tr: And as distinction of a whole into parts is called distribution, and it is only an argument, never a species of argumentation. The collection of parts to constitute a whole is rightly enough called induction by name, but induction is made a species of argumentation, and it is treated separately, as in Prior Analytics 2.33 and Topics 1.10. But induction is not rightly made a species of argumentation, for no form or arrangement of argument is handed down here, which is what argumentation is. The argument from parts to whole is as bare as the argument from whole to parts, and it is the same road from Thebes to Athens as from Athens to Thebes. So with respect to rude invention and undigested matter, the predicate of the parts is as bare as that of the whole. If induction from parts to whole is called argumentation, then distribution of a whole into parts should also be called argumentation. Yet no one has yet thought of this so far as to dare lay it down as a precept. Therefore Ramus makes the argument from parts and places it in the doctrine of arguments; he does not make it a species of argumentation or of judgement and arrangement. In this he rejects the logical commonplace, gathered by I know not whom from Aristotle, drawn from the definition of argumentation. For argumentation is a rule of arrangement, not of invention; yet here the question is not about the matter but about the order and place of the thing in the art of logic.

units.la: Distributio sumitur] Deinceps paucis verbis magna sententia comprehĕditur, & magnopere animadvertenda, quód distributio fit, in partes illas quidem consentaneas toti, sed inter se dissentaneas: itaq; tantó erit perfectior, quantó partes magis consentient cum toto: ut in causis & essectis magis consentiunt, quám in subjectis & adjunctis: quantoque partes inter se magis dissentient, ut oppositæ magis quám diversę & exoppositis magis cōtrariæ, quám disparatæ, & é contrariis magis affirmatæ, quám negatæ: Itaq; persectio distributionis duobus constat, consensione partium cum toto, & dissensione partium inter se. Illinc sequitur distributiones ex causis effectisq; perfectiores esse: hinc ex contrariis, & præcipuè affirmatis. Sed é partium dissensione, quæstio gravis orta est, in quot partes absoluta distributio fieri debeat, quæ veteres philosophos, phos, Platone in primis atq; Aristotele exercuit. Hospes cùm pleraq; de dividendo in regno Platonis percepisset regemq; à pastorû cæterorumque artificû officiis distinxisset, ac deniq; regiæ facultatis οωσωτιας ηφι αιτιας, concaussas & caussas vellet dividere, tû ait Hospes: Nosti igitur quàm difficile sit dividere ipsas bifariâ: Caussa veró, ut opinor, progredientibus non minûs erit manifesta. Socrat. Itaq; sic agendum. Hosp. Membratim igitur, instar victimæ diviidamus, quoniam bifariam non possumus: Oportet enim in quàm proximum fieri poterit numerum semper dividere. Hæc in Platone hospes Zeno, à quo Socrates Logicam didicit. unde intelligimus, jam primis illis temporibus agitatam esse divisionis διαιρέσεως, præstantissimámque judicatam esse, sed difficilem, Platoniq; ipsi interdum impossibilé. attamen si binarius partium obtineri nō posset, perfecto divisionis binario proximum numerû tenendum esse. Atq; hæc à Platone P. Ramus ita proponebat: tum comparabat in eadé quæstione discipulum Aristotelem, qui 2. & 3. cap. 2. libri de Partibus animalium hoc problema revocavit præcipué adversus Platonis eam doctrinam, ut Michael Ephesius Græcus Aristotelis ad eum locû interpres ait. Sic igitur Aristoteles tum loquitur: Id veró ait, partim est non facile, partim veró impossibile. Aristoteles igitur Platonis magistri difficultate terretur: imó quod Plato se nō posse confitetur, plané discipulus impossibile profitetur. Sed argumenta Aristotelis adversus Platonem audiantur, tria veró ea sunt, cur διχοτο-μίας. μία sit non solùm difficilis, sed plane impossibilis. primum sic est: Nonnullorum (ait) erit differentia sola una, cætera erunt supervacua, ut pedatum, bipes, disipes, multifidum. Deinde additur, secùs tautologiam fore, ut idem dicatur sæpius. At hoc primù Aristotelis argumentum Plato falsum diceret, argumetiq; exemplum magis etiam alienum, rationem deniq; additam argumento & exemplo alienissimam. Neq; enim legitima generis unius unica differentia esse potest, secùs, esset individua species, non genus: & si unica differetia significet hic unicam divisionem, ut alicui videatur: tamen διχοτομία legitimarum differentiarum tautologiâ potiùs sustulerit, quàminduxerit: imò præterminissa generali differentia, necesse sit idem sæpius in specialium differentiarum multitudine repeti. Exemplum vitiosæ divisionis (ut Aristoteles & Aristotelis græcus ille interpres indicavit) captiosi hujus argumentioccasionem præbuit: Nam si Aristoteles legitimam διχοτομίαν sibi proposuisset, tautologiam cô minifci nullam potuisset. Quare hoc primum Aristotelis argumentum Platonicam διχοτομίαν nihil offendit. Secundum Aristotelis argumétumsequitur. Tum verò (ait) non convenit discerpere unûquodq; genus, id est (ut ille interpres interpretatur) species specialissima non est é suo genere in alienum traducenda. Itaq; ut primum argumentum, tautologiam, ita secundum ἐπο-γίναν pro absurdo proposuit. At Plato hoc argumetum multò justiùs abnueret: quia διχοτομία in homogeneis perpetua consistet, itaq; diceret, ut legitima Διχοτομία non genuit illic tautologiam, neq; hic ἐπιφθογγωνυμ gignet, adderetq; exēplo hīc iterum nescio quo discipulū Aristto.abuti, quód aves alix in aquatilium genere, aliæ in alio collo contur: ex subjectis enim divisio avium est ejusmodi, non est totius in propria membra, non generis in suas species: quæ legitima divisio & absoluta esset. Ergo Platonis logica adhuc salva hic est. Tertium Aristotelis argumentū est, quód Διχοτομῆντις, cogerentur per privationem (qua tamen nulla species constitit) dividere. quod item falsum est, & si quādo necesse erit ignotis adversis differentiis per privantes dividere, tum privatione generi subjecta ut animali irrationali & immortale (quas differentias Aristoteles ipse subjicit) aliquid arguetur & explicabitur. Quin Aristoteles ipse privationem tātopere repudiatam, in hac quæstione aliquando pro differentia assumendam monet. Itaq; tertium hoc argumetum, ab authore suo refelli Plato responderet, nequeeo quicquam διχοτομίαν labefactari. Ergo Aristotelis in capitibus illis trium argumentorum disputatio, nihil adversus Platonis διχοτομίαν concludit: imo vero Aristoteles uno disputationis illius loco re ipsa confirmat, quod verbo oppugnavit. Præterea contrariis oportet dividere. Hæc Aristotelis in illa disputatione oratio & sententia est: quæ diligenter animadversa & considerata, totam controversiam dijudicabit. Divisio fieri debet in contrarias partes, ait hic Aristoteles: quod idē repetit & confirmat 14.cap.2. Potter. disputans adversus Speusippum: ait enim illic (ut
units.tr: Distribution is taken in such a way that in a few words a great doctrine is comprehended, and it must be carefully noted: distribution is into parts which are indeed consonant with the whole but dissonant among themselves. Therefore it will be the more perfect the more the parts agree with the whole, as they agree more in causes and effects than in subjects and adjuncts; and the more the parts differ among themselves, as opposites differ more than diverse things, and contraries more than disparates, and affirmatives more than negatives among contraries. Thus the perfection of distribution consists in two things: the agreement of the parts with the whole, and the disagreement of the parts among themselves. From this it follows that distributions by causes and effects are more perfect; from this, that those by contraries, and especially affirmative ones, are more perfect. But from the disagreement of the parts there arose a serious question, into how many parts a complete distribution ought to be made, a question that exercised the ancient philosophers, above all Plato and Aristotle. A stranger, when he had learned much about division in Plato's kingdom, and had distinguished the king from the duties of shepherds and other craftsmen, and finally wished to divide the co-causes and causes [οὐσίας καὶ αἰτίας] of the royal art, says in Plato: "You know, then, how difficult it is to divide these into two; but the cause, I think, will be no less clear as we proceed." Socrates: "So let us proceed thus." Stranger: "Let us then divide limb by limb, like a sacrificial victim, since we cannot do it in two; for one must always divide into the nearest number possible." These words are in Plato, from the stranger Zeno, from whom Socrates learned logic. From this we understand that already in those earliest times division [διαιρέσεως] was debated, and was judged most excellent but difficult, and at times impossible even for Plato himself. Nevertheless, if a binary division of parts could not be obtained, one should keep to the nearest number to a perfect binary division. Ramus set forth these things from Plato; then he compared in the same question Aristotle, Plato's pupil, who in the second and third chapters of the second book of On the Parts of Animals revived this problem, chiefly against Plato's doctrine on this point, as Michael of Ephesus, the Greek interpreter of Aristotle, says on that passage. So Aristotle speaks then: "He says that this is partly not easy, partly indeed impossible." Aristotle, then, is alarmed by the difficulty his teacher Plato admits; indeed, where Plato confesses that he cannot, the pupil plainly professes it is impossible. But let us hear Aristotle's arguments against Plato. There are three of them, showing why dichotomy [διχοτομίας] is not only difficult but plainly impossible. The first is this: "Some differences," he says, "will be the only one, and the rest will be superfluous, such as footed, two-footed, three-footed, many-cleft." Then he adds that it would otherwise be tautology, the same thing being said several times. But Plato would call this first argument of Aristotle false, and the example even more irrelevant, and the reason added to argument and example most irrelevant of all. For a single difference cannot be a legitimate difference of one genus, otherwise it would be an individual species, not a genus; and even if a single difference here means a single division, as it seems to someone, still a legitimate dichotomy would remove tautology rather than induce it; indeed, with the general difference omitted, it is necessary that the same thing be repeated many times in the multitude of special differences. The example of faulty division (as Aristotle and that Greek interpreter of Aristotle point out) gave occasion to this captious argument. For if Aristotle had set before himself a legitimate dichotomy, he could not have invented any tautology. Therefore this first argument of Aristotle does not touch Plato's dichotomy at all. The second argument of Aristotle follows. "Then indeed," he says, "it is not fitting to tear apart each genus," that is (as that interpreter explains) "a most specific species must not be transferred from its own genus into another." So, as with the first argument, tautology, so with the second he put forward the fallacy of denomination [ἐπωνυμίαν] as an absurdity. But Plato would reject this argument much more justly, because a dichotomy among things of the same kind will continue without end; so he would say that just as a legitimate dichotomy did not produce tautology there, so neither does it produce denomination here; and he would add, once again, that Aristotle abuses an example I know not whom, namely that some birds are in the genus of aquatic animals, others in another genus, because they are contained in the same neck. For the division of birds based on subjects is of this kind; it is not a division of a whole into its proper members, nor of a genus into its species, which would be a legitimate and complete division. Therefore Plato's logic is still safe here. The third argument of Aristotle is that those who divide dichotomously would be compelled to divide by privation (which, however, no species consists in). This too is false: and if it ever becomes necessary, with unknown opposed differences, to divide by privatives, then by the privation of a subject genus, such as the irrational and the immortal animal (which differences Aristotle himself subjoins), something will be indicated and explained. Indeed, Aristotle himself advises that privation, so greatly repudiated, is sometimes to be taken as a difference in this question. Therefore Plato would answer that this third argument must be refuted by its own author; nor can I see how dichotomy is at all shaken. Therefore the disputation of Aristotle in those chapters of three arguments concludes nothing against Plato's dichotomy; indeed, Aristotle in one place of that disputation confirms in fact what he attacked in word. Moreover, one must divide by contraries. This is the speech and opinion of Aristotle in that disputation, and whoever considers it carefully and diligently will settle the whole controversy. Division must be made into contrary parts, says Aristotle here; which he repeats and confirms in the fourteenth chapter of the second book of the Posterior Analytics [Potter], disputing against Speusippus. For he says there (as has already been said) that in division there are opposites of which there is no mean [ἀντικείμενα ὧν μὴ ἐστὶ κατὰ ἀντίφασιν], and therefore in division (he says) there is no postulation.

units.la: jam dictum est) in divisione esse ἀντικείμενα ὧν μὴ ἐστὶ κατὰ ἀντίφασιν opposita quorum nō est medium. propereaq; in divisione (ait) non est postulatio. At (inquit P.Ramus) contrariū unum uni tantùm est, ut antea perrelata, adversa, contradicentia, privatia ex Aristotelis ipsius testimoniis patuit. Quare accuratam & absolutam distributionem, necesse est διχοτομίαν esse. Hæc P.Rami de duorū summorum philosophorum sententiis tam accurata disceptatio fuit, unde constat διχοτομίαν magnam quidem & difficilem esse, ut praeclara omnia sunt difficilia: sed tamen & posibilem & necessariā. Rhetores etiam quæstionem hanc de numero partium in dividendo suscepere, sed ad modum dubie & anxie disputarunt. Quintilianus lib. 4. cap. 5. nō probat eos, qui partitionem vetant ultra tres propositiones extendere. Quæ fine dubio, si sit (ait) nimium multiplex, fugiet memoriam judicis, & turbabit intentionem. hoc tamen numero, velut lege, non est alligada, cum posit plures desiderare. Idem eodē capite: Certus est divisionis modus (ait) & evitanda maxime concisa nimium & velut articulosa partitio: in qua multa non membra, sed frusta, nec tam plura, quam minora. Hæc Quintilianus. Verumtamen hic magister nihil docet, dum tam logice rhetoricatur: neq; nimis breve, neq; nimis prolixam divisionem faciendā esse vult. at modi huius fines nullos præscribit: denique de numero partium nihil constituit. Sed de Quintiliani Logica, scholæ Rhetoricæ alibi loquuntur. Quare P.Ramus διχοτομίαν complectitur, quia duo tantum tům contraria esse possunt, non plura. Quinetiá studii sui curá exemplis explicatę adhuc & Grámaticæ & Rhetoricæ & Logicæ demonstrabit: in quibus distributiones bifariam facere contendisset: contrá comparabat exempla artium plurima, quibus artes obscuratę essent & cófusę.
units.tr: But (says Ramus) a contrary is only to one thing, as was shown above; that opposites, contradictories, and privatives are plainly from Aristotle's own testimonies. Therefore an accurate and complete distribution must necessarily be a dichotomy. This was Ramus's account of the views of two very great philosophers, so accurate a dispute that it is clear dichotomy is indeed great and difficult, as all excellent things are difficult, but nevertheless both possible and necessary. The rhetoricians also took up this question of the number of parts in dividing, but they argued about it in a rather doubtful and anxious manner. Quintilian, in the fourth book, fifth chapter, does not approve of those who forbid extending partition beyond three propositions. If it is excessively multiplied, he says, it will escape the judge's memory and disturb his attention; yet this number is not bound by a law, as if it could not require more. In the same chapter Quintilian says: "The mode of division is fixed, and a partition that is too concise and, as it were, jointed must be avoided above all, in which there are many pieces, not members, and not so many as small ones." So says Quintilian. Yet this master teaches nothing here, while he rhetoricizes so logically; he wants neither too brief nor too long a division to be made, but he prescribes no limits to this mode; finally, he establishes nothing about the number of parts. But the schools of rhetoric speak of Quintilian's logic elsewhere. Therefore Ramus embraces dichotomy, because only two contraries can be, not more. Moreover, by careful study he will demonstrate, with examples fully explained, grammar, rhetoric, and logic, in which he contended that distributions should be made in two; on the contrary he compared a great many examples of arts by which the arts were obscured and confused.

units.la: Cap. XXVI. De Distributione ex causis.
units.tr: Chapter XXVI. On Distribution from Causes.

units.la: Distributio prima est ex absolutè côsentaneis, causis nēpe & effectis. Distributio ex causis, est quando partes sunt causæ totius. Hic distributio integri in sua mēbra præcipuē laudatur. Integrum, est totum, cui partes sunt essentiales. Membrū, est pars integri. Sic Grámatica in Etymologiā & Syntaxim: Rhetorica in Elocutionem & Actionē: Dialectica in Inventionem & judicium dividitur. ab his enim partibus artes illę integrantur. Hæc distributio principalis est, cúm rei longioris explicatio suscipitur.
units.tr: The first distribution is from things that are absolutely consentaneous, namely causes and effects. Distribution from causes is when the parts are the causes of the whole. Here the division of a whole into its members is especially commended. A whole is that to which the parts are essential, and a member is a part of a whole. Thus grammar is divided into Etymology and Syntax, rhetoric into Elocution and Action, and dialectic into Invention and Judgement, for these parts make up those arts. This distribution is the principal one, and it is used when an explanation of a longer matter is undertaken.

units.la: 1. Georgic.
units.tr: 1. Georgic.

units.la: Quid faciat latas segetes: quo sydere terram Vertere, Mecænas, ulmisq; adjungere vites Conveniat: quæ cura bou, quis cultus habēdo Sit pecori, atq; apib. quāta experiētia parcis, Hinc canere incipiam.—
units.tr: What makes the fields fruitful, under what star it is right to turn the soil, Maecenas, and to join the vines to the elms; what care oxen need, what tending the flock requires, and how much experience is needed for thrifty bees: from here I shall begin to sing.

units.la: Cic. pro Murœna: intelligo (judices) tres totius accusationis partes fuisse: & earū unam in reprehensione vitæ, alteram in contentione dignitatis, tertiam in criminibus ambitus esse versatam. Hic etiam axioma suum est, Totum est majus sua parte: Quin etiam aliter tractatur hoc argumeti genus per inductionem. Catull.
units.tr: Cicero, Pro Murena: I understand, judges, that the whole accusation had three parts: one of them was concerned with criticism of his life, another with the contest over his dignity, and the third with the charges of electoral corruption. Here too is his axiom, that the whole is greater than its part. Moreover, this kind of argument is also treated in another way, by induction. Catullus.

units.la: Quintia formosa est multis: mihi candida, longa,
units.tr: Quintia is beautiful to many; to me she is fair, tall,

units.la: Recta est: hæc ego sic singula confiteor:
units.tr: And straight: I admit each of these things taken singly,

units.la: Totum illud, formosa, nego: nā nulla venustas,
units.tr: But the whole, beautiful lady, I deny: for there is no charm,

units.la: Nulla in tam magno est corpore mica salis.
units.tr: No grain of salt in so great a body.

units.la: Lesbia formosa est, q̄ cū pulcherrima tota est,
units.tr: Lesbia is beautiful, since she is wholly most beautiful,

units.la: Tū omnibus una omnes surripuit veneres.
units.tr: Then, of all women, she alone has stolen the charms of all.

units.la: Distributio prima] Categoria distributionis bifariam dividitur, ut categoria consentaneorū, unde oritur: in primo genere, præcipué appellatur totum & pars: Itaque communibus præcipué nominibus totius & partis, utrumq; primaria distributionis argumentū appellatur. E caussis vero singulis distributio esse potest. ex efficiente, ut Philosophia scripta est partim à Platone, partim ab Aristotele. ejusmodi distributio fit ex efficientibus caussis. Ex materia similiter distribui potest: Vasorum regiorum alia aurea, alia argentea, si ejusmodi tantum vasa rex habeat, ex materia divisio fit. Vasorum alia sculpta, alia ficta: ex forma videri possit. Ex fine autem est illa Pythagorea distributio, quinta Tusculana, Græcorum ad ludos Olympicos convenientium, gratiâ gloriæ pecuniæ, scientiæ. Nam cum interrogaretur
units.tr: First distribution] The category of distribution is divided in two ways, as the category of the things it arises from. In the first kind, the terms whole and part are especially used, so that by the common names of whole and part, each is called the primary argument of distribution. Distribution can also be made from single causes. From the efficient cause: philosophy was written partly by Plato and partly by Aristotle, and such a distribution comes from efficient causes. Likewise it can be distributed from matter: if a king has only royal vessels, some of gold and some of silver, the division is made from matter. Some vessels are carved and some moulded, which may be seen from their form. From the end, however, comes that Pythagorean distribution, the fifth in the Tusculan Disputations, of the Greeks gathering for the Olympic games, for the sake of glory, money, or knowledge. For when Leon, prince of Phlius, asked Pythagoras who the philosophers were,

units.la: Pythagoras à Leonte Phliasiorū principe, quinam essent philosophi? Pythagoras tum responreturn dit,similem sibi videri vitam hominum, & mercatum eam, qui haberetur maximo ludorū apparatu, totius Græciæ celebritate. Nam ut illic alii corporibus exercitatis, gloriā & nobilitatē coronæ peterent: alii emendi aut vendendi quęstu & lucro ducerentur: esset autem quoddam genus eorum, idq; vel maximè ingenuum, qui nec plausum, nec lucrum quærerent, sed visendi caussâ venirent, studioseq; perspiceret, quid ageretur, & quomodo. Hæc exempla P. Ramus afferebat, ut doceret, ex omnibus caussarum generibus distribui posse, totamq; caussarū facultatem, quantacunq; in topicis quatuor efficientis & materiæ, formæ & finis contineretur, in distributionis categoriam redundare: attamen in hoc primo distributionis genere, integri in membra distributionem longissimè præferebat. Integrum] Huc proprie pertinet definitio Aristotelis in Philosophia 26.cap.5.lib. Totum dicitur, à quo nulla abest pars, ex quibus dicitur totū naturâ. quæ definitio 6.ca.3. Physici repetitur. Itē illa partis definitio 25.cap. 5.lib. Partes sunt, ex quibus componitur totum. Ex his igitur Aristotelis definitionibus, P. Ramus collegit definitiones integri & membri: ē quibus apparet integrum & membra symbola esse caussarum & efsectorum: nam membra singula materiam continent: & sic cap.6. Physici 3. dicitur pars materia totius, membra verò conjuncta, continent materiam & formam integri. Ergo integrum ipsum psum, est effectus talium caussarum : indeq; apparet hic argumentum esse de primis ortum: & primum distribuendi genus & accuratissimum esse integri in membra, quia tum effectus arguitur & explicatur ex caussis. Enim vero una distributio integri in membra, hic præcipua est, appellaturq; Aristoteli in Posteriorib9 ἀνατομὴ, sectio, & partitio Ciceroni in Topicis.
units.tr: Pythagoras replied that human life seemed to him like that great market held at the greatest display of games, the gathering of all Greece. For as some there, with trained bodies, sought glory and the renown of the crown, and others were drawn by the profit of buying and selling, so there was also a kind of people, and the most noble kind, who sought neither applause nor gain but came for the sake of looking on, and eagerly observed what was going on and how. P. Ramus offered these examples to show that distribution can be made from every kind of cause, and that the whole faculty of causes, however many are contained in the four topics of efficient cause and matter, form and end, falls within the category of distribution. Yet in this first kind of distribution, he strongly preferred the division of a whole into its members. Integrum] This properly relates to Aristotle's definition in Philosophy 26, ch. 5, book: a whole is that from which no part is absent, by which the whole is said to be whole by nature. This definition is repeated in Physics, book 6, ch. 3. Likewise that definition of a part in 25, ch. 5, book: parts are those out of which a whole is composed. From these definitions of Aristotle, P. Ramus gathered the definitions of whole and member, from which it appears that whole and members are the counterparts of causes and effects: for each member contains matter, and so in Physics 3, ch. 6, a part is said to be the matter of a whole, while the members taken together contain the matter and form of the whole. Therefore the whole itself is an effect of such causes, and hence it appears that this argument concerns first things, and that the first and most exact kind of distribution is of a whole into its members, because the effect is then argued and explained from its causes. Indeed this distribution of a whole into members is the chief one here, and Aristotle in the Posterior Analytics calls it anatomē (dissection), and Cicero in the Topics calls it partitio (partition).

units.la: · Grammatica] Grámatica vulgo quadrifariā se-catur, in Etymologiā, Syntaxim, Prosodiā, Orthographiā, at duæ postremæ partes sunt fusæ per totā etymologiam & syntaxim. Itaq; P. Ramus in Grámatica tantùm partitionis elenchū sustulit, sicuti pleraq; in descriptione illius artis cósimilia sophismata, quod Grámatica ipsius & Grammaticæ scholæ demonstrant. Rhetorica] Rhetorica distributa est á Græcis & Latinis Rhetoribus in quinq; partes, Inventionem, Dispositionem, Elocutionem, Memoriam, Actionem: At P. Ramus in Rhetoricis in Ciceronē & Quintil. scholis demonstravit, inventionem & dispositionem, partes esse Logicæ: memoriam, tātūm esse umbram dispositionis. Itaque duas tantūm Rhetoricæ partes proprias esse, elocutionem & actionem: quas nos deinde ejus & prælectionibus & observationibus instructi, & consiliis duĉti, ita descripsimus, ut modò Logicam ab eo digestam præceptis, & illustratam exemplis, paulò pleniùs & faciliùs rudiorum gratiâ interpretamur. Dialectica] Hæc partitio una fuit, de qua tantopere á P. Ramo decertatum est: continet enim hæc una partitio commune quoddam lumen universæ Logicæ. Principalis] A principe nempe argumento, id est à caussis perfecta.
units.tr: · Grammar] Grammar is commonly cut into four parts: etymology, syntax, prosody and orthography, though the last two parts are spread through the whole of etymology and syntax. So Ramus, in grammar alone, removed the fallacy of partition, as he did with many similar sophisms in the description of that art, as grammar itself and the grammar schools show. Rhetoric] Rhetoric has been divided by Greek and Latin rhetoricians into five parts: invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. But Ramus, in his Rhetoric and in his commentaries on Cicero and Quintilian, showed that invention and arrangement are parts of logic, and that memory is only a shadow of arrangement. So he held that only two parts are proper to rhetoric, style and delivery. Having been instructed by his lectures and observations, and guided by his counsel, we have described these in such a way that we now expound, somewhat more fully and easily for the sake of beginners, the logic he arranged in precepts and illustrated with examples. Dialectic] This partition was the one over which Ramus contended so vigorously, for this single partition contains a certain common light of all logic. Principal] That is, from the principal argument, namely from the perfect causes.

units.la: Quid faciat] Poeta summam Georgici operis sibi propositi cõpleCtitur hac quadripartita distributione : Prima pars est argumentum primi Georgici de cultu agrorū & de segetibus: secūda de arborib.& vitibus:tertia de pecore: quarta de apibus. Seges] Seges proprié significat nodum demessas truges omnium feminū,unde panis conficitur. Lætas autē dicit poeta, per metaphoram, quę tanquam arrideant & respondeant votis avari agricolę, ut etiam illic poeta ipse loquitur. Sydere] Sydus, proprié est stellarum multarum conjunctio, quæ signum appellatur: qualia sunt numerata ab astrologis 47.in Zodiaco 12.in Septentrione 20.in Meridie 15.
units.tr: Quid faciat] The poet sums up the whole of the Georgics he has undertaken by this fourfold division. The first part is the subject of the first Georgic, on the cultivation of fields and on grain; the second concerns trees and vines; the third concerns cattle; the fourth concerns bees. Seges] Seges properly means a field of standing grain, all of which is harvested to make bread. The poet calls the crops "joyful" (laetas) by metaphor, as if they smile upon and answer the prayers of the greedy farmers, as the poet himself says there. Sydere] A star (sidus) is properly a conjunction of many stars, which is called a sign; of this kind the astrologers number 47 in the Zodiac, 12 in the North, 20 in the South, and 15 ...

units.la: Mecœnas] Nobilis fuit eques Romanus, charus Augusto, studiosus poetarum, & in eos benefic9: unde appellati sunt Mecœnates, omnes fautores studiosorum, artiumq; liberalium studiis deditorum. ulmisq] De vitibus Italiæ loquitur, quæ ulmis & arboribus maritantur.
units.tr: Mecaenas] He was a noble Roman knight, dear to Augustus, a lover of poets and a benefactor to them; hence all patrons of learned men and of those devoted to the liberal arts are called Maecenases. ulmisq] He speaks of the vines of Italy, which are married to elms and other trees.

units.la: Pecoris] Pecoris nomine intelligūtur à grammaticis equi, cameli, caprę, asini, oves, omneq; animal, hominis imperio subjectum, & pabulo terrestri pastum Experientia]Diligentia : id enim proprié est. 5. Verr. Homo navus & industrius, experientisimus ac diligentisimus orator. Hoc igitur exemplū est distributionis quadripartitæ : quæ tamen etiam bipartita esse poterat,in plantas, & animantes mutas cicures: plantas,ut segetes & vites: cicures,ut pecora & apes. Nam si quid hic elenchi fuerit, Αχρηστία nō attulit, sed accepit ē propositō imperfecto physicæ argumento. Murœna] Murœna reus factus erat de ambitu à Sulpitio & Catone, & pleraq; objecta: quę omnia orator in hanc partitionem conclusit. Vitæ) Obiectum est Asia, ad voluptatem, & luxuriā expetita, & Murœna saltator appellatus. Dignitatis] De genere, integritate, indultria. Ambitus] Ambitus est aucupatio gratię, & vitiosa emerendę famę cupiditas: hinc crime largitione affectati magistratus. Hæc autem partitio Ciceronis, etiam bifariam fieri potuit, in contentionem dignitatis, & crimen ambitus: Nam reprehensio vitæ cadit etiam in contētionem dignitatis. Neq; nos Quintilianus hic movebit, lib.14.ca. 5. qui cùm divisionem Ciceronis pro Cluentio reprehensam dixisset, rursus (ait) Nemo tam erit aut injustus, aut stultus, quin eum fateatur optimè pro Murœna esse partitum: Intelligo, &c. Nam sic (ait) & ostendit lucidissimè causam, & nihil fecit altero supervacuum. Hæc Quintiliani est ratio, sed fallax & captiosa: Nam dignitas ex anteacta vita etiam ducitur. Hic etiam] Antea patuit usum distributionis esse multiplicē: primùm illum ἀσυλλόγιστον, è tota nēpe distributionis specie. quo referri posfit Euclidis axioma 9. nam totū hic pro integro intelligitur, & pars pro membro. axioma verò mistum est & comparatione quantitatis & loco distributionis. Itaq; huc relatū. alias verò distributio etiam συλλογιστικῶς ἢ ἀναλυτικῶς tractatur: de quo axiomata affirmata sunt illa 6. cap. 6. Topici:In quo totū est, in illo oportet & partes esse: In quibus partes sunt, & totū necesse est inesse. ibidem negationes oppositæ proponuntur: Si partium vel una desit, totum non esse: at contrà non sequi, Si totum non sit, nullam partem esse: hæc ἀκολουθητικὰ sunt Aristotelis. Quinta] Quidam disputabát é partibus formæ, Quintiam formosam esse, quia esset candida, longa, recta: at inductione illam, ut sophisticá Catullus redarguit, quia pars una formæ desit, venustas nempe: itaque totum inficiatur: Atq; hic poeta artificium genusq; argumenti pené ipse explicat scholastico more, Concedo partes istas singulas: totum illud, formosa, nego. Venustas] Venustas proprié est pulchritudo muliebris, ut dignitas pulchritudo virilis: hic autʼ significat gratiá & leporem vel sermonis vel gestus. Nulla in tam] Allegoria est á cibis insulsis & sine sale ingratis: Nâ sicut sal suavitatē quandā cum mordacitate habet: ita etiam urbanorū joca (ait Quintilianus.) Itaq; sales pro ridiculis & facetiis accipiūtur. Ergo Catulli argumētū est, Deest pars una formę, ergo tota forma nō est. idē Catullꝰ é sex partib. tollit totū in alio epigram. de amica Formiani: Salve, nec minimo puella naso, Nec bello pede, nec nigris ocellis, Nec longis digitis, nec ore sicco, Nec sanè nimis elegante lingua: Decoctoris amica Formiani: Ten' provincia narrat esse bellam? Tecum Lesbia nostra comparatur? O seclum insipiens & infacetum!
units.tr: Pecoris] By the word "cattle" grammarians understand horses, camels, goats, asses, sheep, and every animal subject to human command and fed on land pasture. Experientia] Diligence, for that is its proper sense, as in Against Verres 5: a man vigorous and industrious, the most experienced and diligent orator. This, then, is an example of a fourfold distribution, though it could also have been bipartite: into plants and dumb tame animals; plants, such as grains and vines; tame ones, such as cattle and bees. For if there is any fault in this list, it does not come from achrēstia [ἀχρηστία], uselessness, but was received from the imperfect plan of the physical argument. Murœna] Murena was accused of electoral corruption by Sulpicius and Cato, along with many other charges, all of which the orator brought under this partition. Vitæ] It was objected that he had sought Asia for pleasure and luxury, and that he was called a dancer. Dignitatis] Concerning his birth, integrity, and industry. Ambitus] Ambitus is the hunting after favour, and a vicious desire to win a good reputation; hence the crime of seeking office by bribery. This partition of Cicero could also have been made in two parts: the contest over dignity, and the crime of electoral corruption; for the criticism of his life also falls under the contest over dignity. Nor shall Quintilian trouble us here, in book 14, chapter 5, who, after saying that Cicero's division in the Pro Cluentio had been criticised, said again: "No one will be so unjust or foolish as not to admit that he divided the case excellently in the Pro Murena: I understand, etc. For thus," he says, "he both shows the cause most clearly and made nothing superfluous." This is Quintilian's reasoning, but it is deceptive and specious, for dignity is also derived from a past life. Hic etiam] Earlier it became clear that the use of distribution is manifold: first, the asyllogiston [ἀσυλλόγιστον], that is, from the whole species of distribution, to which Euclid's ninth axiom may be referred; for here the whole is understood as the integral, and the part as the member. That axiom, however, is mixed, both with a comparison of quantity and with the place of distribution; so it is referred here. In other cases distribution is also treated syllogistikōs ē analytikōs [συλλογιστικῶς ἢ ἀναλυτικῶς], syllogistically or analytically; concerning this, those affirmative axioms of Aristotle were stated in chapter 6 of the Topics: in what the whole is, in that the parts must also be; and in what the parts are, the whole must necessarily be in them. In the same place the opposed negations are set out: if one of the parts be absent, the whole is not; but on the contrary it does not follow that if the whole is not, no part is. These are the akolouthētika [ἀκολουθητικὰ], the consequential propositions, of Aristotle. Quinta] Some argued from the parts of form that Quintia was beautiful, because she was fair, tall, and straight; but Catullus refutes this induction as a sophism, because one part of beauty is lacking, namely charm, and therefore he denies the whole. And here the poet himself nearly sets out the artifice and kind of argument in the scholastic manner: I grant those parts singly; the whole, beautiful lady, I deny. Venustas] Venustas properly means womanly beauty, as dignity means manly beauty; here, however, it signifies grace and charm, either of speech or of gesture. Nulla in tam] This is a metaphor from insipid foods, without salt and unpleasant: for just as salt has a certain sweetness together with sharpness, so too are the jests of urbane men (as Quintilian says). Thus salts are taken for witticisms and pleasantries. The argument of Catullus, therefore, is: one part of the form is lacking, therefore the whole form is not. The same Catullus removes the whole from six parts in another epigram, about the mistress of Formianus: "Hail, girl with no small nose, nor pretty foot, nor dark little eyes, nor long fingers, nor dry mouth, nor indeed overly elegant tongue: is the mistress of the bankrupt Formianus said to be pretty? Is our Lesbia compared with you? O foolish and unwitty age!"

units.la: n ʒ Lesbia] Comprehenditur magis quám explicatur inductio fecunda, quód Lesbia habeat omnes partes illas pulchritudinis, sed praeterea fit omnium mulierum venustissima.
units.tr: Lesbia: The fruitful induction is comprehended rather than explained: Lesbia has all those parts of beauty, but moreover becomes the most charming of all women.

units.la: Cap. XXVII. De Distributione ex esse- ctis: ubi de genere & specie.
units.tr: Chapter XXVII. On Distribution from Effects: where concerning genus and species.

units.la: Distributio ex effectis est, quādo partes sunt effecta, ut in navi nautae alii malos scandunt, alii per foros currunt, alii sententiam exhauriunt: gubernator autem clavum tenet in puppi. Distributio generis in species hic excellit. Genus est totum partibus essentiale. Species est pars generis. Sic animal, genus hominis & bestiae dicimus: Animal enim, est totum, cujus essentia (nempe substantia corporea, animata, sentiens) ad bestiam & hominem communiter attinet. Sic dicimus homine & bestiam, species animalis, quia partes sunt animali subjectae, quae animalis essentiam communem habent. Sic dicimus homine, genus hominum singulorum, & leonem, singulorum leonum: contra vero singulos homines, species hominis: singulos leones, leonis. Genus est generalissimum aut subalternum: Species subalterna aut specialissima. Genus generalissimum, cujus nullum est genus: ut in logica inventione. Argumentum est genus generalissimum artificialium & inartificialiū. Species specialissima, quæ est individua in species alias, ut materia & forma singulares. Subalternū genus, ut subalterna item species, quod species hujus, illius autem genus est: ut causa, species est argumenti artificialis, genus materiæ & formæ. Genus verò & species notæ sunt causarum & effectorum: ut in animali, est substantia corporea, quæ materia est ad species communiter attinens: tum facultas vitæ & sensus, quæ forma item communiter ad species spectat. Quare genus continet causas, quæ communiter ad ipsius species attineant: contrà itaq; etiam species, effecta generis sui continent. Hinc universale est insigne ac præstabile, quia causam declarat. Distributio generis in species valdé quidem excellit, sed difficilis est & rara inventu: At tamen illustrationis & exempli gratiâ, asseremus, quod poterimus. Ovid i. Metamor. dividit animal in quinque species, stellas, aves, bestias, pisces, homines: stellis animā tribuit, ut etiā philosophi tribuêre:
units.tr: Distribution from effects is when the parts are effects: as in a ship, some sailors climb the masts, others run along the decks, others bail out the bilge, while the helmsman holds the tiller in the stern. Distribution of a genus into species excels here. A genus is a whole whose parts are essential to it. A species is a part of a genus. Thus we call animal the genus of man and beast, for animal is a whole whose essence (namely corporeal, animate, sentient substance) belongs in common to beast and man. So we call man and beast species of animal, because they are parts subordinate to the animal, which share the common essence of the animal. Likewise we call man the genus of individual men, and lion the genus of individual lions; conversely, individual men are the species of man, and individual lions the species of lion. A genus is either most general or subaltern; a species is either subaltern or most special. The most general genus has no genus above it, as in the invention of logic: argument is the most general genus of artificial and inartificial proofs. The most special species is one that is individual with respect to other species, as matter and form are in particular cases. A subaltern genus, like a subaltern species, is both the species of one thing and the genus of another: thus cause is a species of artificial argument, and the genus of matter and form. Genus and species are known as signs of causes and effects: in the case of animal, corporeal substance, which is matter, belongs in common to the species; and the faculty of life and sense, which is form, likewise belongs in common to the species. Hence the genus contains the causes that belong in common to its species; and conversely, the species contain the effects of their genus. Hence the universal is notable and excellent, because it declares the cause. Distribution of a genus into species is indeed very excellent, but it is difficult and rarely found. Nevertheless, for illustration and example, we will set forth what we can. Ovid, in the first book of the Metamorphoses, divides animal into five species: stars, birds, beasts, fishes and men. He attributes a soul to the stars, as the philosophers also did:

units.la: Neu regio foret ulla suis animalibus orba, Astra tenent cæleste solum, formaque deorū: Cesserunt nitidus habitanda piscibus unda: Terra feras cepit, volucres agitabilis aër. Sanctius his animal, mentisq; capacius alteDeerat adhuc, & quod dominari in cateraNatus homo est. — (posset,
units.tr: Lest any region be bereft of its living creatures, the stars hold the heavenly ground, and the forms of the gods; the bright waters were yielded to fishes to inhabit; the land took the beasts, and the air, a realm of movement, the birds. A more holy animal, and one more capable of lofty mind, was still lacking, and man was born to rule over the rest.

units.la: Sic Cicero i. Offic. Virtutem dividit in species quatuor, prudentiam, justitiam, fortitudinem, temperātiam. Sed omne quod honestū est, id quatuor partiū oritur ex aliqua: aut enim in perspicientia veri folertiaq; versatur: aut in societate hominum tuenda, tribuendoq; suū uni cuiq;, & rerum cōtractarum fide: aut in animi excelsi atq; invicti magnitudine ac robore: aut in omnibus quæ fiunt, queq; dicūtur, ordine & modo, in quo inest modestia & temperantia. Distributio generis in formas specierum cadē est, quia formæ cum genere constituūt suas species: ut animaliū aliud loquens, aliud mutum. Genus & species, non solū tractantur hac simplici divisionis formula, sed etiam separatim alterum ex altero. Pro Archia: Ac ne qs ánobis hoc ita dici forte miretur, quódalia quædā in hoc facultas fit ingenii, atque hæc dicendi ratio, aut disciplina: nec nos quidem huic cuncti studio penitus unquam dediti fuimus: Etenim oes artes, quę ad humanitatem pertinent, habent quoddam commune vinculū, & quasi cognatione quadam inter se continetur. Ars est genus: poetica & eloquetia sunt species. Cōtra genus tractatur per species, ut 4. de Trist. apud Ovid.
units.tr: So Cicero, in the first book of De Officiis, divides virtue into four species: prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance. But everything that is honourable arises from one of these four parts. For it is concerned either with the perception of truth and skill in it; or with maintaining human society, giving each his due and keeping faith in contracts; or with the greatness and strength of a lofty and unconquered spirit; or with order and measure in all that is done and said, in which modesty and temperance lie. Distribution of a genus into the forms of its species is the same, because forms together with the genus constitute their species: as of animals, one speaks and another is mute. Genus and species are treated not only by this simple formula of division, but also separately, one from the other. In the speech for Archias: "And lest anyone should wonder that I say this, that in this there is some faculty of talent, and this manner of speaking or discipline: nor have we ourselves ever been wholly devoted to this study. For all the arts that pertain to humanity have a certain common bond and are held together as by a kind of kinship." Art is the genus; poetry and eloquence are its species. Conversely, a genus is treated through its species, as in Ovid's Tristia, book 4:

units.la: Materiam, tuis tristem virtutibus imple:
units.tr: Fill the sad matter with your virtues:

units.la: Ardua per præceps gloria vadit iter.
units.tr: Glory goes a steep and headlong path.

units.la: Hectora quis nosset, felix si Troia fuisset? Publica virtutis per mala facta via est.
units.tr: Who would know Hector, had Troy been happy? A public way for virtue lies through evils.

units.la: Ars tua Tiphy, jacet. si nō sit in æquore fluctu:
units.tr: Your art, Tiphys, lies idle, if there is no wave on the sea:

units.la: Si valeant homines, ars tua, Phœbe, jacet.
units.tr: If men are well, your art, Phoebus, lies idle.

units.la: Qua latet, ingenii bonis cessat nō cognita rebus, Apparet virtus, arguitur malis.
units.tr: Virtue lies hidden where it is not known, and ceases among the goods of talent; it appears and is proved by evils.

units.la: Exempla igitur specialia, suo generi accōmodata sunt huius loci. 7. ad Atti. Vrbem tu relinquas? ergo idem si Galli venirent? Non est (inquit) in parietibus respub. at in aris & focis. Fecit idē Themistocles. fluctū enim totius barbariæ ferre urbs una non poterat. At idem Pericles non fecit, annum fere post quinquagesimum, cum præter mœnia nil teneret. Nostri olim urbe reliqua capta, arcem tamen retinuerunt.
units.tr: Specific examples, therefore, fitted to their genus, are suited to this place. From Ad Atticum, book 7: "Would you abandon the city? Then what if the Gauls came?" "The commonwealth," he says, "is not in walls, but in altars and hearths." Themistocles did the same, for one city could not bear the onslaught of all barbarism. But Pericles did not do so, nearly fifty years later, when he held nothing beyond the walls. Our people, when the rest of the city had long since been taken, nevertheless kept the citadel.

units.la: Distributio] Secundum hoc Topicum ex essectis quibuslibet (caducis, æternis, nil interest) distributionem instituit. Primum exemplũ est effectorum caducorum, sumptum de similitudine Catonis, qua refellit feneƈtutis reprehensores, qui dicunt, homines senectute avocari ab agendo: Nihil igitur afferunt (inquit) qui in re geréda versari senectutę negant: similesq; sunt, utsi quis gubertoré in navigando nihil agere dicat,cum alii malos scandát, alii per foros cursitent,alii sentinam exhauriant: ille aút clavumtenens, sedeat in puppi quietus, non faciat ea quæ juvenes, at veró multó majora & meliora facit.hæc Cato. Itaq; pars similitudinis hujus p posita est ad exemplum qualecunq; divisionis ex effectis, dum melius & accuratius occurrat: ut interea intelligatur, distributionem ex esseƈtis tam laté patére, quám patet effectorum topicum: sicuti in superiore distributione, tam laté patuit ex caussis distributio, quám caussarũ topicum. Malos]Malus,arbor est navis. Foros] Fori tabulata, quibus perambulatur navis:dicti quód ferant incessus ambulantiũ. Sentina]Sentina, est pars navis infima, quó defluit quicquid instillat aquarũ:ideoq; corrupta, malé olet: unde & nominata sentina, qa gravis ejus odor sentiatur. Gubernator] Proprié rector navis, appellatur gubernator. Clavum]Clavus per metaphorã, hic gubernaculũ navis significat. 5. Æneid. Clavumq; ad littora torquet.
units.tr: Distribution: According to this topic, he sets up a distribution from any effects, whether perishable or eternal; it makes no difference. The first example is of perishable effects, taken from the comparison of Cato, by which he refutes the critics of old age, who say that men are called away from action by old age: "They bring nothing, he says, who deny that those in old age can be engaged in doing things. They are like someone who said that a helmsman does nothing in sailing, when others climb the masts, others run along the decks, others bail out the bilge; he, however, holding the tiller, sits quietly in the stern and does not do what the young do, but does far greater and better things." Thus Cato. Part of this similitude is put forward as an example of any division from effects, so that it may be met more fully and accurately, and so that it is understood in the meantime that distribution from effects extends as widely as the topic of effects does, just as in the earlier distribution the distribution from causes extended as widely as the topic of causes. Malos: the mast is the tree of the ship. Foros: the decks, planks along which the ship is walked over, so named because they bear the footsteps of those who walk on them. Sentina: the lowest part of the ship, into which whatever water drips flows; therefore it is foul and smells bad, and it is named sentina because its heavy smell is perceived. Gubernator: properly the ruler of a ship is called gubernator. Clavum: by metaphor, here clavus means the rudder of the ship. Aeneid, book 5: "and turns the rudder toward the shores."

units.la: Distributio generis] Partitio proprie est integri divisio generis, ut Ciceroni in Topicis placet, nominatim haec interdum confunduntur. Genus] Sequitur de genere & specie ingens materia: De genere enim & specie duo capita sunt Porphyrii magna, & reliqui libri pars maxima in communionibus & differentiis generis & speciei: Regulae sunt in Categoriis de homogeneis & heterogeneis: In Posterioribus Analyticis de genere & specie, 15.ca.2.libri: In Topicis problema unum de genere facti est, quartumq; Topicum tributum: Locus ipse generis & speciei citatus est in Topicis bis & quinquagies: In Philosophia, plurima sunt de genere & specie, deq; ideis, occasione generis & speciei. q tanta materia, quemadmodum ad Aristotelis leges P. Ramus conformarit, ja cosíderemus. Sunt vero Topica generis & speciei, tanto praestatiora, quanto praestantiorum argumentorum symbola sunt. Si quid ex causis atq; effectis artes & disciplinae instituunt, id fere symbolis generis & speciei interpretantur: Si thesis & loci communes a poetis vel oratoribus, ab historicis & philosophis explicatur, explicatio exempla specialia deducitur: Si contra hypothesis fuerit,& specialis aliqua quaestio (quales omnes sunt controversiae forenses, senatoriae, populares) tum ad genus universum recurritur: denique genus & species, omnem fere causarum & effectorum ubertatem complectuntur: industriam itaque P. Rami hic in primis amavi. Definit autem primo genus & speciem e suis & propriis differentiis: deinde speciales differentias generalisimi, subalterni, specialisimi: tum quomodo genus & species, sint caussarum & effectorum symbola: deniq; exemplis usum generis & speciei declarat. Genus est] Hæc definitio generis & speciei, adversas superioris & hujus topici differentias ostendit: illic integrum, sumit essentiā é membris: hic genus, essentiam speciebus tribuit: illic membra constituunt totum, hic species constituuntur á genere: re: Itaq; definitio generis convenit speciei: definitio autem integri, non convenit membro: relatioq; integri & membrorum, cōtraria est relatione generis & specierum. Atqui hęc relatio generis & speciei, Porphyrio satis aperté proposita est, sed nō satis constanter servata. Sed enim Logica P. Rami jam nobis repetenda est, ad exponendum quàm studiosé, quàm accuratè positam generis & speciei definitionem differebat, confirmādo & approbando, é duabus primùm Aristotelis definitionibus in Philosophia 3. cap. 10. libri: quarum prima sic est: Dicitur autem genus, secundùm quod ambo idem dicūtur secundùm essentiam differentia. hæc Aristotelis definitio demōstrat genus esse totum, cujus partes habeát ipsius essentiā cōmunem: & sint eædem in ipsa generis essentia. Altera est generis definitio 7. cap. 10. lib. Tale enim genus voco, secundùm quod ambo unum idem dicuntur, non secundùm accidens, habens differentiam, sive ut materia, sive ut aliter. hæc Aristotelis altera definitio rursus ostēdit, genus esse totum partibus suis essentiale. Ergo definitio generis, quam P. Ramus sequitur, definitio etiam est Aristotelis: sed tamen ne quis Aristotelis definitiones istas captiosas & fallaces arbitretur, multo majus argumentū huc P. Ramus aggregabat, ex usu nepe & observatione rationis, quid homines in vero ratiocinandi usu genus intelligāt: utrūm etiā hominū genus dicatur, ut animalium: Ergo huc exēpla & testimonia proferantur: Plauti, juppiter, q genus colis alifq; hominū: Ciceronis, Dū genus erit hominū: jureconfultorū, qui homine genus dicūt, Stychū & Pamphilū species hominis: itē in mutuo, reddi genus, non specie. Quin Ariftoteles ipse ita sæpe loquitur 1. 3.4. capitib. 3. Philosophiæ. Extrema genera, ut homo. Item, 1.cap.1. Philofophię, Hominum genus arte & ratiocinatione vivit. Ité de lōgitudine vitæ: Hominū genus est diuturnioris vitę, q equorū. Quare P. Rami ftudiū adhuc intelligimus in confirmanda Ariftotelis illa veriore doctrina, & quidē auxiliis ex Ariftotelea facultate copiaq; depromptis duplici definitione, totq; ideonis ad ré locupletibufq; & aliorū, & ipsius testimoniis & exemplis. Ergo hæc generis definitio ita confirmata & approbata est: vocabulū autem genere ris ab Ariftotele in Philosophia 18.cap. 5.libri di citur significare generationē & genitorē, quód fi fit tropus, erit poeticus, potiūs quàm oratorius. Porphyrius addit ad fecundū Ariftotelis fignificatū, etiā vocabulo generis significari patriam: & sic Pindarum dici genere Thebanum, Plato Atheniensem: in quo fallitur apertiūs: nec Thebæ, vel Athenæ, genus: sed Thebanorum &
units.tr: Distribution of genus: Partition is properly the division of a whole into its parts, as Cicero in the Topics prefers; these are sometimes confused by name. Genus: There follows a great matter concerning genus and species. Two great chapters of Porphyry are devoted to genus and species, and the greater part of the remaining books concerns the communities and differences of genus and species. The Categories contain rules on homogeneous and heterogeneous things; the Posterior Analytics, book 2, chapter 15, treats genus and species; the Topics set one problem concerning the genus of a thing and assign a fourth topic; the locus of genus and species itself is cited in the Topics twice and fifty times; and in Philosophy there is very much on genus and species, and on ideas, on the occasion of genus and species. How great a matter this is, and how P. Ramus has arranged it according to the laws of Aristotle, we shall now consider. Indeed the topics of genus and species are the more excellent, the more excellent are the arguments of which they are the symbols. If arts and disciplines set out anything from causes and effects, they mostly interpret it through the symbols of genus and species. If theses and common places are explained by poets or orators, by historians or philosophers, a specific explanation is deduced through examples. If on the contrary there is a hypothesis and some special question (such as all forensic, senatorial and popular controversies), then recourse is had to the universal genus. Finally, genus and species embrace nearly all the richness of causes and effects; so I have especially admired the diligence of P. Ramus here. He first defines genus and species from their own proper differences; then the special differences of the most general, the subaltern and the most special; then how genus and species are symbols of causes and effects; and finally by examples he declares the use of genus and species. Genus is: This definition of genus and species shows the contrary differences between the earlier topic and this one. There the whole takes its essence from the members; here the genus gives its essence to the species. There the members constitute the whole; here the species are constituted by the genus. Hence the definition of genus fits the species, but the definition of the whole does not fit a member; and the relation of whole and members is the opposite of the relation of genus and species. Yet this relation of genus and species was set out quite plainly by Porphyry, though not kept consistently enough. But now the Logic of P. Ramus must be taken up again, to show how diligently and accurately he set out, and confirmed and approved, the definition of genus and species, drawing first on the two definitions of Aristotle in Philosophy, book 3, chapter 10. The first of these runs: "A genus is that of which both are said to be the same according to essence, differing..." This definition of Aristotle shows that a genus is a whole whose parts have its common essence and are the same in the essence of the genus itself. The second definition of genus is in book 7, chapter 10: "For I call such a genus that of which both are said to be one and the same, not according to accident, having a difference, whether as matter or in some other way." This second definition of Aristotle again shows that a genus is a whole essential to its parts. Therefore the definition of genus that P. Ramus follows is also the definition of Aristotle. But lest anyone think these definitions of Aristotle captious and deceptive, P. Ramus adds a much greater argument, namely from the use and observation of reason: what men understand by genus in the true use of reasoning, and whether the human race is also called a genus, as animals are. Accordingly, examples and testimonies are brought forward: from Plautus, "Jupiter, who tends the genus of gods and of other men"; from Cicero, "while there shall be a genus of men"; from the jurists, who call man a genus and Stichus and Pamphilus species of man; likewise in loans, "to be returned as genus, not as species." Indeed Aristotle himself often speaks thus, in book 3, chapter 3 of Philosophy: "The extreme genera, such as man." Likewise, book 1, chapter 1 of Philosophy: "The genus of men lives by art and reasoning." Likewise concerning length of life: "The genus of men has a longer-lived life than that of horses." Hence we understand the zeal of P. Ramus in confirming that truer doctrine of Aristotle, drawing on the resources and abundance of Aristotle's own learning, by a double definition and by so many fitting and rich examples, both from others and from his own testimonies. Therefore this definition of genus is thus confirmed and approved. The word genus, however, is said by Aristotle in Philosophy, book 18, chapter 5, to signify generation and the begetter; if this is a trope, it will be poetic rather than oratorical. Porphyry adds to Aristotle's second meaning that by the word genus the homeland is also signified, and so Pindar is said to be Theban by genus, and Plato Athenian. In this he is more clearly mistaken: neither Thebes nor Athens is the genus, but it is said of the Thebans and the Athenians. Indeed, as animal is the genus of animals, so Athenian is the genus of Athenians, and Theban the genus of Thebans. But the signification of genus for species ought to have been noted much more, since it is by far the most frequent and most usual, as when we say the genera of animals, of causes and of such things. But nevertheless the signification that is necessary for us here

units.la: Atheniefium dicitur: & quidem ut animaliuñ animal,sic Atheniensis Atheniefium,& Thebanus Thebanorũ gen⁹ est. Sed multó magis fuerat notanda significatio generis pro specie,quę longé frequentisima & ufitatisima est:ut cum dicimus,animalium, caussarum & ejusmodi rerum genera. Sed tamen significatio,quæ nobis hic necessaria fit,definitione satis explicatur: cęterę significationes ex usu grámatici sermonis, vel é tropis rhetoricis cognitę,facilé distinguétur.
units.tr: Athenians is said; and just as animal is the genus of animals, so Atheniensis is the genus of Atheniensium, and Thebanus of Thebanorum. But the sense of genus as species, which is far more frequent and common, ought to have been noted much more carefully, as when we say the genera of animals, of causes, and such things. Still, the sense that is necessary for us here is sufficiently explained by the definition. The other senses, known from the usage of grammatical speech or from rhetorical tropes, will easily be distinguished.

units.la: Species] Hæc definitio in Porphyrio pené eadem est: Species, quod sub assignato genere, item : Species,quod ordinatum est sub genere: Ergo definitio speciei sine cóntroversia ejusmodi est. Speciei aút vocabulũ in Topicis Cicero repudiavit,propter casus (specierum & speciebus)asperiores:formarum & formis,maluit. At contrá P.Ramus hic perspicuā logicæ veritatis intelligentiá maluit, quám rhetoricá Ciceronis elegantiam: Cicero enim, formá in caussis nullam intelligebat,quæ tamen in primis intelligę da fit,quamq; P.Ramus Aristotelem secutus antea proposuit:Itaq; si peccádum hic fuerit,multó satius est peccare in voluptatē auriū, quám in rerum notionē & sensum : quod accideret, si duo argumēta uno verbo appellaremus,nec verŏ Cicero tales casus non latinos cėset esse, sed duros. Quare ut species, sic specierum & specie bus, casus á P.Ramo retinentur, meliore & justiore caussa, qá Cicerone rejiciantur. Speciei significationem etiam Porphyrius ꝑponit pro forma,id est pulchritudine, quæ vera quidē est:
units.tr: Species] This definition is almost the same as Porphyry's: species is what falls under an assigned genus; or, species is what is ordered under a genus. So the definition of species is, beyond dispute, of this kind. Cicero in the Topics rejected the word species because of its harsher cases (specierum and speciebus), and preferred forms and formis. But P. Ramus here preferred clear understanding of logical truth to Cicero's rhetorical elegance. For Cicero understood no form in causes, although that must be understood first, and P. Ramus, following Aristotle, had proposed it earlier. So if we must err here, it is far better to err in pleasing the ears than in the notion and meaning of things, which would happen if we called two arguments by one word. Nor indeed were Cicero's cases un-Latin; they were only harsh. Therefore, as species, so specierum and speciebus are retained by P. Ramus, on a better and juster ground, since Cicero rejected them. Porphyry also gives the meaning of species as form, that is, beauty, which is indeed true,

units.la: at species in Aristotele multò saepius significat caussam formalem, ut in Physicis & in Philosophia: aliquādo etiā genus, interdum substantiā, ut P. Ramus ex interpretibus Graecis collegit: Sed tamen totam hanc enumerationem significationum in arte supervacuam judicavit: & eā potissimùm significatione, quae necessaria esset, definitione speciei comprehendit. Atq; haec de generis & speciei definitione, quę valde cōfusa est in bibliotheca Aristotelis ppter alterā utriusq; argumēti definitionem, non contrariam omnino, sed certè valdè controversam. Sed hanc controversiam P. Ramus verioribus illis definitionibus antè confirmatis facilē disceptabat: discoptatio igitur hęc attendatur, audiaturq; generica primū definitio Eubulidis, vel Antisthenis, vel nescio cujus alius Logici, quē etiā Porphyrius & deinde scholastici interpretes universi, veriore illa rejecta ac cōtempta, sunt sequuti. est aūt ejusmodi: Genus aūt est, quod de multis & differentibus speciē in quæstione quid est, dicitur. hæc definitio est 4. cap. 1. Topici, repetita iisdem verbis à Porphyrio: Sed in hac definitione (quòd genus sit categorema multis cōmune) hoc convenit cum veriore illa definitione generis, Genus est totum partibus essentiale: reliquæ duæ partes (differentibus specie in quæstione quid est) diversæ sunt tantùm, non oppositæ, & tamen ita diversæ, ut plane sint ad generis definitionem inutiles & otiosæ, & definitionem primam obscurent, non tollât. Enimverò hoc ipsum (dissere specie) plane nugatorium sophisma est, ex homonymia verbi natũ: etenim cûm de logica specie hic agatur, imò species ipsa definiatur: attamen species pro formali caussa hîc intelligitur, quomodo 7.cap.1.Phys. Unum enim specie dico & ratione idem. hîc enim species & ratio pro forma dicuntur, quod 8.cap.10.Phil.exponitur apertiùs: Quęcunq; in ratione sunt adversa, faciunt differre specie. hi loci, sicuti alii quidam in bibliotheca Arist. docent ea differre specie, quæ differunt essentiali forma: Ergo (inquit P.Ramus) fallacia est valdè insulsa, cûm specie logicâ definias partê generis, in generis definitione verbû speciei, nô pro specie logica, sed p causa formali usurpare. Etenim cûm genus definieris, intelligi vis solas species differre genere, nempe quæ diversis generibus subjiciuntur: ita cûm speciem definieris partê generis, intelligas necesse est, sola genera differre specie, quæ speciem nô eandê habebunt: Sic enim differentiæ relatorum cõparandæ sunt: Differût patre filij, qui patrem habent diversum: Differunt filio patres, qui filium habent diversum. at hîc differre specie dicuntur nô genere, quę specie habeât diversam, sed species quæ formâ diversam habêt.
units.tr: but species in Aristotle far more often means the formal cause, as in the Physics and in the Philosophy; sometimes it also means genus, and sometimes substance, as P. Ramus gathered from the Greek interpreters. Yet P. Ramus judged this whole enumeration of meanings superfluous in the art, and he comprehended under the definition of species chiefly that meaning which would be necessary. So much for the definition of genus and species, which is very confused in Aristotle's library because of the other definition of each argument, not wholly contrary to it, but certainly very controversial. P. Ramus easily settled this controversy by the truer definitions confirmed earlier. Let this dispute therefore be heard, and let the generic definition of Eubulides, or Antisthenes, or some other logician whose name I do not know, be heard first. Porphyry and then all the scholastic interpreters followed it, rejecting and despising that truer definition. It is of this kind: genus is that which is predicated of many differing in species, in the question what it is. This definition is in Topics 4, ch. 1, and Porphyry repeats it in the same words. But this definition (that genus is a predicable common to many) agrees with that truer definition of genus, "genus is the whole essential to its parts." The other two parts (differing in species, in the question what it is) are only different, not opposed, and yet they are so different that they are plainly useless and idle for the definition of genus; they obscure the first definition rather than remove it. Indeed this very phrase (differ in species) is a plainly trifling sophism, arising from the ambiguity of the word. For although the logical species is what is treated here, and the species itself is being defined, yet species is understood here as the formal cause, as in Physics 7, ch. 1: "One I call the same in species and in account." Here species and account are said of form, and Metaphysics 8, ch. 10 explains it more clearly: "Whatever are contrary in account make things differ in species." These passages, like certain others in Aristotle's library, teach that those things differ in species which differ in essential form. Therefore (says P. Ramus) it is a very silly fallacy: when you define a part of genus by logical species, to use the word species in the definition of genus not for logical species but for formal cause. For when you define genus, you want it understood that only species differ by genus, namely those placed under different genera. So when you define species as a part of genus, you must understand that only genera differ by species, namely those that do not have the same species. For thus the differences of relatives are to be compared: sons differ by fathers, who have different fathers; fathers differ by sons, who have different sons. But here things are said to differ in species, not in genus, which has a different species, but species that has a different form.

units.la: Hoc igitur sophisma primû est in illa definitione: quo sublato sententia definitionis erit. Genꝰ est quod dicitur de multis forma differentibus, in quæstione quid est. At (inquit P. Ramus) tû duo quælibet differēt specie, quia formâ differêt, cûm omniû rerum sua & propria forma sit, qua res est id quod est, & differt á cæteris rebus. Neq; audiendû sit, quod dici videtur á Porphyrio,& nonnullis præterea in Aristotelea bibliotheca locis, individua non differre forma essentiali, sed proprietate accidentiū, ut mas & fœmina: quæ accidentia in Hermaphrodito miscentur: Nam tum detractis (quod omnino salte cogitatione fieri potest) accidétibus, omnes homines essent unicus & singularis homo: imó neq; Deus, neq; dæmon, neq; homo, neq; ulla prorsus essentia esset. (quod est ab Aristotele nominatim improbatū, cúm ideale hominę ejusmodi derideat) sed accidentia sola. quod sophisma valde cornutum est, imó barbaræ prorsus & inauditæ impietatis plenum: Quare singuli homines specie, id est forma essentiali differūt, quod etiā Arist.3.cap.10.Philosophiæ cóprobat. Quicquid enim differt, dlffert aut genere, aut specie: genere quidem, quorum nó est communis materia, neq; inter se generatio. Hęc Aristoteles ita philosophatur: unde licet assumere, At singuli homines differunt inter se non genere, quia cómunis eorū materia est, & homo gignitur ex homine: Quare specie seu forma (ut superior illa interpretatio docuit) differūt singuli homines, & sunt species hominis, & homo genus est singulorum hominum. Attamé hanc ipsam formæ differentiā in definitione generis collocare, nugatorium est: quia duæ res quælibet (ut patet é logica formæ definitione) forma differūt. Quapter hic primus elęchus in definitione (quód genus dicatur de pluribus specie differētibus) obscurat tantúm veram definitionem generis, prorsus nihil adjuvat: Secundus elęchus (quód genus dicatur in quæstione quid est) lógioris refutationis non indiget: etenim ré manifeste superuacuâ & falsam proponit. Definitio proprié respondetur ad quæstionem quid est: attamen in definitionis definitione, hæc differentia nô adhibetur: Definito(ait Ariftoteles quarto capite 1.Topici) est ratio quid est, esse significans.hic si necesse fuisset, dixisset Ariftoteles, Definitio, est ratio, quid est, esse significans in quæstione quid est at neque dixit, neq; necesse fuit dici: Nam si nunquam interrogaretur, quid est,constaret tamen usus definitionis: ita si generis proprium esset, responderi ad quæstionem quid est: attamen hæc adventitia esset illi & externa differentia, non essentialis, neque ideo in definitionem adhibeda.at falsum est genus ita respondeTI: quod Ariftotelis doctrina in posteriorib. Analyticis, de quæstione quid est, perspicuë demonstrat: Docet enim,nô genere, sed definitione argui & explicari quæstionem quid est:& quidé vera doctrina docet. Nâ cúm quæritur, quid est Dialectica: si respondeas, est ars:ridiculus habeare. nô enim quæritur, é quo genere rerum fit Dialectica, sed quæ fit ejus sententia & natura. Quare secundus hic elenchus etiam abfurdior est superiore. Generalissimum] Hic privilegium relationis quoddá generis & speciei loco attributum est á Logicis, quod erat tamen aliorum argumetorum commune: idem enim potest esse efficiens hujus, illius effectus: ut homo,effectus Dei:effector ipse infinitorum operum.aliquid est tamen,quod tantum est effi ciens, nempe Deus: aliquid quod tantum essectus, idem in subjectis & adjunctis: Terra est tá‐ tum subjectû aquæ: cælum aeris tantum adjun‐ctû: intermedia sunt subjecta superioris, adjun‐ cta inferioris: sic idem, genus unius esse potest, alterius species: ut oppositû, est genus disparati & contrarii, species dissentanei: aliquid tamen est, quod sit tátum genus, quodq; ideo Aristoteli primum dicitur: ejus autem interpretibus, γε‐νικώτατον, generalissimum, ut in logica inventione argumentum. Sic quædam species est tátum species, ideoq; ἔιδος ἔσχατον, species extrema Aristoteli, interpretibus autem ἀνδικώτατον ἔιδος, specialissima species appellatur, ut in logica inventione exempla singularia & indidua, 28. cap. 1. Pri. genera summa & infima rejiciuntur, tanquâ ex iis concludi non soleat: quem errorem scholæ dialecticæ illic abunde refutarunt: Ergo hæc vicissitudo & relatio est generis & speciei: quæ tamen eadem est in aliis argumentis, etsi minús manifesta, sed vocabula desunt, ut αἴτιον αἰτιώτατον, αἰτιατὸν αἰτιατώτατον: caussa cauffalissima, tanquam diceretur, & caussatum cauffatissimum. Hanc autem relationem generis & speciei cúm Porphyrius multis verbis comparasset, mediorumq; duplicem ratione & cum superioribus, quorum species, & cum inferioribus, quorû genera essent, extremorum duorû summi generis & infimæ speciei, illius ad inferiores species, hu jus ad superius genus, unicam rationem, ut proportio constaret, cócludere debuit: & conclusit quidem recte in summo genere: perversè autê in infima specie, ex illa numeri differetia ratiocinatus, specie fpecialissimâ duplicis esse rationis, & ita definivit: Species est quod dicitur de multis & numero differetib. in quæstione quid est.hęc enim definitio, duobus etiam sophismatis sophistica est: numeri siquidé differetia, quæ dicitur, nil est aliud, quàm speciei differentia ut jam antea ex Aristotele patuit. Quicquid differt (ait Aristoteles) differt genere aut specie. tertiâ hanc numeri differentiâ illic Aristoteles non agnoscit: neq; omnino ufquâ ad legę καὶ παντὸς debuit agnoscere. Quicquid enim præcipitur vel arguitur, generale fit aut speciale, necesse est: ἀιχοτομία ita clarissimæ veritatis cómentitiam numeri differentiâ respuit. Sic Aristot. 2. ca. 2.Phys. opponit ὡς τὸ καθ' ἕκαστον, ἢ ὡς τὸ γένος, singulare & generale, ut sæpe aliàs: Sic Quintilianus 10.ca.12. libri loquitur, cùm ait, oratoris formas differre nō solùm specie, ut signũ signo, & tabulam tabula, sed genere ipso, ut á Græcis Tuscani cæ statuę. Sic omnes deniq; homines ratiocinatur. Itaq; quicunq; vel Eubulides, vel sophistes alius, istam tertiam numeri differentiam attulit, commentum suum, non observatum ex hominum usu documentum prodidit. Quamobrem in logica & vera specialissimę speciei definitione, P. Ramus Porphyrianam illâ numeri disserè tiam sequi né debuit: De secundo elencho (quo species dicitur in qstione quid est) respõsio est eadè quę priús: id esse definitionis, nõ speciei, & id adventitium, non essentiale: imò verò ne adventitium quidem: Etenim ut in Regno verissimé Plato docuit, quicquid species est alicujus, ejus ipsius parté esse necesse est: neq; species logica intelligitur, nisi relatione generis: ut neq; genus nisi relatione speciei. Quapropter ut generis illa, ita hæc specialissimę speciei definitio, duobus sophismatis sophistica est, cúm constet é rebus falsis: aut si veræ sint, alienis. Quamobrem recondemur in hoc uno generis & speciei topico, diligentiam P. Rami, imó curá, sollicitudinem, aliquando etiá stomachú & indignationem, cú sępé in çathedra ipsa, de nostrorú hominum moribus & ingeniis cóquereretur, qui æ tatem in nugis sophisticarum definitionum clamandis consumerent, neq; veritatem ante oculos positam cernerent: tátum inveterata opinio valet, ut anté vita plerúq; quám perversa sentétia relinquatur. attamé agriculturę princeps ille paresq; Aristoteles, lóge alio animo sedulitaté istá susciperet, tantúq; in logicas ipsius leges amoré, vel potiús ardoré mirificé complectere. tur. Genus & species] Declaratur origo generis & speciei, sicut in cójugatione, notatione, integro & mêbro declarata est, & id definitione já cóprehensum est: sed exemplo idem familiariús per caussarum species declaratur, materiam for mamq;, quę species communes in genere comprehenduntur: Itaq; Aristotelis illa ex relatis τῶν τοιούτων ἀποδείξεως, declarat, & id etiá concludit. Genus est αἴτιον speciei: ergo species est αἰτιατὸν generis. hęc cosideranda explicatio, quomodo ge n9 & species, argumeta sint orta de primis, symbolaq; sint caussarum & effectorum. Sic ait Ari ftoteles 24.ca.1. Posteriorū, τὸ ἀλ καθόλ̃υ τίμιον, ὅτι διὰ τὸ αἴτιον: Universale est honorabile, quia declarat causam.atq; inde laudes illæ capite ejusdem libri vicesimo, Generale præstare speciali, quia fit αἰτιώτερον, ἁπλούστερον, ἀρχοειδέστερον, magis & causa, & simplex, & principio simile: ideoq; ἐπιστημονικώτερον εἶναι, scientiæ aptius esse. Simplicius autem esse, indicabit ejus definitio, quæ pauciora cōtinet, quàm speciei definitio. Quare si quis iratorum iltorum adhuc quærat, cur genus & species fiant argumenta orta de primis, & dicantur symbola causarum & effectorum, respondebit cum Aristotele P.Ramus, quia genus significat causam speciei, & species ideo significat efsectum generis: utq; antea conjugatorum, notationis, integri, mēbri, ita nunc generis & speciei topica, originem suā é primis argumentis often dunt: quotiesq; genus explicatur á speciebus, causa arguitur ex effectis: quoties cōtrá species arguitur é genere, effectus arguitur é causis. Quare genus & species sunt symbola causæ & effectus. alia tamē est hic inventionis via quàm illic. causæ enim & effecta subtiliter illic explicantur: hic coprehenduntur. Aristoteles 14. ca.
units.tr: This, then, is the first fallacy in that definition, and once it is removed the sense of the definition will stand. "A genus is what is predicated of many things differing in form, in answer to the question what it is." But (says P. Ramus) any two things differ in species, because they differ in form, since every thing has its own form, by which it is what it is and differs from other things.
