We should not listen to what seems to be said by Porphyry, and by some other passages in the Aristotelian corpus, that individuals do not differ in essential form but in the accidental properties of male and female, which are mixed together in the hermaphrodite. For if the accidents were removed (which can at least be done in thought), all men would be one single and solitary man; indeed there would be neither God, nor demon, nor man, nor any essence at all, only accidents. (Aristotle expressly rejects this, since he mocks such an ideal of man.) This fallacy is very absurd, indeed full of utterly barbarous and unheard-of impiety. Therefore individual men differ in species, that is, in essential form, which Aristotle also proves in the third book, chapter 10, of his Philosophy. For whatever differs, differs either in genus or in species: in genus, of course, those things which have no common matter and no generation from one another. Aristotle reasons thus, and from this one may assume: but individual men differ from one another not in genus, because they have a common matter and man is begotten of man. Therefore individual men differ in species or form (as that earlier explanation taught), and they are species of man, and man is the genus of individual men. Yet to place this very difference of form in the definition of genus is trifling, because any two things differ in form (as is clear from the definition of form in logic). Hence this first refutation, that the genus is predicated of many things differing in species, only obscures the true definition of genus and helps nothing at all. The second refutation (that the genus is said in answer to the question what it is) does not need a lengthy reply: for it puts forward a manifestly superfluous and false point. A definition properly answers the question what a thing is; yet in the definition of definition this difference is not used. Aristotle, in the fourth chapter of the first book of the Topics, says: "A definition is an account signifying what a thing is." If this were necessary, Aristotle would have said, "A definition is an account signifying what a thing is, in answer to the question what it is." But he neither said this nor needed to say it: for even if no one ever asked what a thing is, the use of definition would still stand. So, if it were a property of genus to answer the question what it is, this would still be an accidental and external difference, not an essential one, and therefore not to be admitted into the definition. But it is false that genus answers in this way; Aristotle's teaching in the Posterior Analytics, concerning the question what it is, demonstrates this clearly. For he teaches that the question what it is is settled and explained not by genus but by definition, and indeed this is the true doctrine. For when one asks what dialectic is, if you answer "it is an art," you would look ridiculous: for the question is not from what kind of thing dialectic is made, but what its meaning and nature are. Therefore this second refutation is even more absurd than the first. The most general [genus] — here the privilege of a certain relation of genus and species, which the logicians have attributed to the genus, is set down, though it was common to other arguments as well. For the same thing can be the efficient cause of this effect and the effect of that: as man is an effect of God, and God is the efficient cause of infinitely many works. Yet something is only an efficient cause, namely God; something is only an effect; and the same thing is a subject and an adjunct: earth is only the subject of water, the heavens only the adjunct of air; the intermediates are subjects of the higher and adjuncts of the lower. So the same thing can be the genus of one thing and the species of another: as the opposite is the genus of the disparate and the contrary, and the species of the dissentaneous. Yet there is something which is only a genus, and which for this reason is called by Aristotle the first, but by his interpreters γενικώτατον [the most generic], the most general, as in the logical invention of argument. Likewise some species is only a species, and therefore Aristotle calls it ἔιδος ἔσχατον [the last species], the extreme species, but his interpreters call it the most specific species, as in the logical invention, singular and individual examples (chapter 28 of the first book of the Prior Analytics). The highest and lowest genera are rejected, as one usually does not conclude from them; the schools of dialectic have thoroughly refuted this error there. This interchange and relation of genus and species is therefore the same as in other arguments, though less obvious, and words are lacking for it, such as αἴτιον αἰτιώτατον [the most causal cause], αἰτιατὸν αἰτιατώτατον [the most caused thing]: as if one said "a most causal cause" and "a most caused effect." Since Porphyry had compared this relation of genus and species at length, and had concluded from the twofold relation of the middle terms, both with the higher, of whom they are species, and with the lower, of whom they are genera, and from the two extremes, the highest genus and the lowest species, that the relation to the lower species and to the higher genus constitutes a single proportion: he did indeed conclude this correctly for the highest genus, but wrongly for the lowest species; for he reasoned from that numerical difference and so defined the most specific species as twofold in its relation, saying: "Species is what is predicated of many things differing in number, in answer to the question what it is." For this definition is also sophistical in two ways: the numerical difference which it mentions is nothing other than the difference of species, as already appeared from Aristotle. "Whatever differs," says Aristotle, "differs in genus or in species." He does not recognise a third, numerical difference there, nor at all anywhere ought he to have recognised it under the law of "of every thing and of all" (καὶ παντὸς). For whatever is taught or argued must necessarily be either general or special, and dichotomy thus rejects that fictitious numerical difference as contrary to the clearest truth. So Aristotle, in the second book, second chapter, of the Physics, sets τὸ καθ' ἕκαστον [the particular] against ὡς τὸ γένος [the generic], the singular and the general, as he often does elsewhere. So Quintilian speaks in the tenth book, chapter 12, when he says that the forms of the orator differ not only in species, as a sign from a sign and a picture from a picture, but in genus itself, as the Tuscan statues differ from the Greek ones. So all men finally reason. Therefore whoever, whether Eubulides or some other sophist, brought forward that third numerical difference, has offered his own invention, not a teaching observed from human usage. Wherefore in logic, and in the true definition of the most specific species, P. Ramus ought not to have followed that Porphyrian numerical difference. On the second refutation (by which species is said in answer to the question what it is), the reply is the same as before: that this belongs to definition, not to species, and that it is accidental, not essential; indeed it is not even accidental. For, as Plato truly taught in the Republic, whatever is the species of something must necessarily be a part of that very thing; nor is a logical species understood except in relation to genus, just as genus is not understood except in relation to species. Therefore, just as the definition of genus, so this definition of the most specific species is sophistical in two ways, since it rests on false things, or, if they are true, on irrelevant ones. Accordingly, in this one topic of genus and species, we should commend P. Ramus's diligence, indeed his care, solicitude, and at times even his indignation, since he often complained from the very chair about the habits and abilities of our people, who spend their lives in shouting over trifling sophistical definitions and do not see the truth placed before their eyes: so powerful is long-standing opinion that often a view, however perverse, is kept for life. Yet that prince and equal of agriculture, Aristotle, would have undertaken this diligence with quite a different spirit, and would have embraced with wonderful love, or rather ardour, the laws of logic itself. Genus and species] The origin of genus and species is explained, just as conjugates, notation, whole and part were explained, and this has already been grasped in the definition; but by example the same thing is explained more familiarly through the species of causes, matter and form, which common species are comprehended in a genus. Thus Aristotle declares that illustration from related things of this kind of demonstration, and concludes this too: genus is cause [αἴτιον] of species; therefore species is effect [αἰτιατὸν] of genus. This explanation is to be considered: how genus and species arise as arguments from first principles, and are tokens of causes and effects. So Aristotle says in the twenty-fourth chapter of the first book of the Posterior Analytics: τὸ ἀλ καθόλ̃υ τίμιον, ὅτι διὰ τὸ αἴτιον [the universal is honourable, because it declares the cause]; and from this come those praises in the twentieth chapter of the same book, that the general is better than the special, because it is more causal (αἰτιώτερον), simpler (ἁπλούστερον), more like a principle (ἀρχοειδέστερον), and therefore more fitted to science (ἐπιστημονικώτερον). That it is simpler will be shown by its definition, which contains fewer things than the definition of the species. Therefore if any of those angry men still asks why genus and species become arguments arising from first principles, and are called tokens of causes and effects, P. Ramus will answer with Aristotle that genus signifies the cause of species, and species therefore signifies the effect of genus. And as before with conjugates, notation, whole and part, so now the topics of genus and species take their origin from the first arguments: whenever genus is explained from species, cause is argued from effects; whenever, on the contrary, species is argued from genus, effect is argued from causes. Therefore genus and species are tokens of cause and effect. Yet the way of invention here is different from that there: for causes and effects are explained subtly there, and here they are comprehended.

units.la: 2. Posteriorū. docet é relationis hujus occasione ignotum genus é speciērum definitionibus inveniri: nam quod utrisque speciebus commune ne fuerit, id genus futurum: at inventio hæc non tam valet ad inveniendum genus, quod illic inventum fit, quàm ad cōcludendum. Sed eadem via, si species ignorentur, ajebat P. Ramus divisiones generis inveniri: Quare totū caput illud nil aliud revera dicit, quám divisione generis ostendi species, inductione speciérum colligi genus, quod hic novi nihil elt. Sæpe vero Aristotelés, præcipué in cap. περὶ τὸ ἄμα, docuit species ejusdem generis simul esse naturâ: Quávis enim genus esse prius notiusque specie doceat, & sub eodé genere species oppositas naturâ simul esse profitetur, neq; alteram altera priore aut notiorem: est tamen aliqua differentia ordinis, ut in arte speciem hanc illi præponas. Atque hæc de generis & speciei definitione, cóparatione, origene: unde quæstio de idea (quæ totas Logicorum scholas infinitè vexavit) ex Aristotelis judicio sententiaq; dijudicatur: Ideam nempe, genus esse logicum. sic 8. cap. 2. Posteriorum idea dicitur ἐν ᾗ τὸ αὐτὸ ἐπὶ πολλῶν, unū & idem in multis esse: quæ vera generis est definitio: item 8. cap. 2. Posteriorum, idea dicitur ἐν ᾗ τὸ αὐτὸ παρὰ πολλὰ, unū & idem præter multa: sic enim tum loquitur, & unū idem pręter multa dicit genus ratione separatū à speciebus, in quibus revera cōsistit. Quidam autē Logici veteres perversè philosophati, ideas quasdam reipsa separatas à subjectis speciebus comrnenti sunt, quæ consisterent in mente divina, tāquam imagines quædam rerū, quas Deus intuēs, singularia crearet: eamq; opinionem sem Platonici semique Aristotelei quidā philosophi, ut Porphyrio & Ammonius, Platoni attribuerunt, cūm tamē Plato Socratis ore hoc commentū in Parmenide refellat: & Aristoteles (qui videtur aliquādo hac in re Platonem perstringere) attamē in Philosophia 6. ca. 3. li-
units.tr: 2. Posteriorum. teaches that by the occasion of this relation the unknown genus is found from the definitions of the species. For whatever is common to both species will be the genus. But this discovery is less useful for finding the genus, which is found there, than for drawing a conclusion from it. Yet if the species are unknown, Ramus used to say, the divisions of the genus are found by the same method. So that whole chapter says in truth nothing other than that the species are shown by division of the genus and the genus is gathered by induction of the species, which is nothing new here. Often, however, Aristotle, especially in the chapter on "together" (περὶ τὸ ἄμα), taught that species of the same genus are by nature simultaneous. For although he teaches that the genus is prior and better known than the species, and he professes that opposite species under the same genus are by nature simultaneous, neither prior nor better known than the other, there is still some difference of order, so that in the art you put this species before that one. And so much for the definition, comparison and origin of genus and species. From this, the question about the idea (which has troubled the schools of the logicians endlessly) is decided by Aristotle's judgement and opinion, namely that the idea is the logical genus. So in chapter 2 of Book 8 of the Posteriors the idea is called ἐν ᾗ τὸ αὐτὸ ἐπὶ πολλῶν, one and the same in many, which is the true definition of the genus. Likewise in chapter 2 of Book 8 of the Posteriors the idea is called ἐν ᾗ τὸ αὐτὸ παρὰ πολλὰ, one and the same beside many. For he speaks in this way, and by "one and the same beside many" he means the genus, separated in thought from the species, in which it truly consists. Some of the ancient logicians, however, philosophising perversely, invented certain ideas actually separated from the subject species, which were supposed to subsist in the divine mind, as images of things which God, looking upon them, would create as individuals. This opinion some Platonists and half-Aristotelian philosophers, such as Porphyry and Ammonius, attributed to Plato, although Plato in the Parmenides refutes this invention in the person of Socrates; and Aristotle (who seems sometimes to attack Plato on this point) nevertheless in the Philosophy, chapter 3 of Book 6, openly professes that the ideas of Plato are logical genera.

units.la: 3. libri aperté Platonis ideas logica genera esse profitetur:item 4. cap.13. libri Socrates universalia separata nō faciebat. quod idem 9.cap.ejuf dem libri repetit: Exéplaria autē illa separatim valde & sæpe labefactavit,ut 18.cap.1. Pofteriorum,ubi sic loquitur:ἀλλ᾽ χωρίτω, πρὸ τὸ ἡδὺ γὰρ ὅτι. Species valeāt, prævcétiones enim sunt. In Philosophla autem 7.cap.1.lib.item 4. 5.10.cap.13.libri, longior est disputatio, & in P.Rami metaphysicis Scholis explicatio. Quamobrem imperiti homines Platoni calumniam imponentes, imo Aristotelem tàquam Platonis calumniatorem fingentes derideantur,gratiaq; P.Rami vigiliis habeatur, per quas generis & speciei dostrina tot tenebris circunfusa,tam claré perspicuéque proponatur. Atq; hæc de generis & speciei doctrina:usus & utilitas deinceps,id est demostratio doctrinę & approbatio cōsideretur. Distributio generis Antea dichotomię difficultas pposita est: huc alia difficultas accedit exinvētione specierū, cū etiá genus ipsum inventū fit: Ná tametsi species quædá pateant, attamē proximæ illę duæ,quę differētiis adversis διχοτομίας constituūt,rarissimæ sunt:quin in postremis ge neribꝰ διχοτομία plané impossibilis est,neq; per naturā ulla est:nisi tū forte dicatur fuisse, cū Adam9 & Eva soli homines essent, pariaq; essent specierū talia in singulis generib. Neu regio]Cū Ovidius mundi creationem,elementorū distinctionem docuisset,tum declarat partitione creationem animaliū.Partitio aūt est generis in species,qua nō multó accuratiore Plato in Timæo proposuit: Erant autem (ait) animalium genera quatuor, unum divinum atq; cœleste, alterum pennigerum atque aerium, tertium terrestre, quartum dinin̄ animationis. Primò autem Ἀιχο- τομία fieri potuit animalis, in rationale & irrationale: & deinde rationalis Ἀιχοτομία, ite paganis illis, potuit esse in Deum & homine, sic enim & Plato & Ariftoteles, Deū, animal appellát: poftremò autē, quam Ἀιχοτομίαν species irrationalis habeat, meditandum fuerit: utrūm in pisces & animantes terrestres, ut feras & aues. Mentisque ] Hæc differentia est homini cōmunis cū stellis, judicio philosophorum: itaq; duę species unius generis fuissent. sed á poeta nō fuit Logica accuratior exigēda quám á Platone, qui eléchum eundem in partiēdo fecit. Partitio autem Ovidiana, non solūm est generis in species, sed adjuncti in subjecta: animal enim adjunctum in subjecta etiam dividitur, cælum, aerem, aquam, terram. Sic Cicero] Cūm definitum effet honeftum, tum distributio ista sequitur: Formam qui dem ipsam, Marce filii, & tanquam faciem honesti vides. quæ si oculis cerneretur (ut ait Plato) mirabiles amores excitaret sapiētię. Sed omne, &c. Partitio Ciceronis pro definitis speciebus adhibet definitiones specierum: Poterat orator hic Ἀιχοτομῶν faciliús, quám illic poeta: Virtus enim, est prudētia, aut compositio morum: eaq; temperantia aut fortitudo: justitia autē, est prudentiæ, temperantię, fortitudinis consensio. Separatim syllogistica Aristotelis axiomata de genere & specie, 2.cap. 2. Topici subtiliús dissecta sunt. De genere affirmatum est istud: Necesse enim est, de quibus genus dicitur, de iis fpecierū aliquam dici. sed hæc affirmatio nimis angusta est: Genus enim generaliter vel affirmatum vel negatum, speciem quamlibet includit: ut, Si omne animal vivit, omnis homo vivit: nó tamen cótrá. Affirmati generis exemplū proximū est. Ac ne quis Archias poeta, civis Romanus factus erat: eo jure cúm depelleretur, defensus est á Ci cerone ea defensione, quæ extat. defensionis su fceptæ caussam orator attulit, quód tâquam difcipulus magistro patrocinium præstaret, quia ab Archia effet eruditus, tumque sibi objicit, Tu es orator, ille poeta: quomodo igitur es ab eo eruditus? Tum generis hoc argumetum usurpat, Omnes artes communi vinculo continentur; itaque poetica & eloquentia (quæ sunt artes etiam) continentur. Simile generis argumetum est in Catullo, sed de unica specie; Nulli fe dicit mulier mea nubere malle, Quám mihi non fi fe juppiter ipse petat. Dicit, sed cupido mulier quod dicit amanti. Invento & rapida scribere oportet aqua.
units.tr: 3. Likewise in chapter 13 of Book 4 of the book he says that Socrates did not make universals separate. He repeats the same in chapter 9 of the same book. But he weakened those separate exemplars greatly and often, as in chapter 18 of Book 1 of the Posteriors, where he speaks thus: ἀλλ᾽ χωρίτω, πρὸ τὸ ἡδὺ γὰρ ὅτι [let the species stand, for they are preliminary matters]. In the Philosophy, however, in chapter 1 of Book 7, and likewise in chapter 13 of Book 4 and chapter 10 of Book 5, the discussion is longer, and in the metaphysical schools of P. Ramus the explanation is given. Therefore unskilled men, who impose a slander on Plato, or who imagine Aristotle himself as a calumniator of Plato, should be laughed at, and the labours of P. Ramus should be held in favour, through which the doctrine of genus and species, once wrapped in so many shadows, is set forth so clearly and plainly. And so much for the doctrine of genus and species. Next let the use and utility be considered, that is, the demonstration and approval of the doctrine. ## Distribution of the genus Earlier the difficulty of dichotomy was put forward. Another difficulty is added from the discovery of the species, since the genus itself too is to be discovered. For although some species are evident, nevertheless those two nearest species which constitute the dichotomy by opposite differences are very rare. Indeed in the last genera a dichotomy is plainly impossible, and it does not exist in nature, unless perhaps one should say that it existed when Adam and Eva were the only men, and the species were of such kinds in each genus. Neu regio: when Ovid had taught the creation of the world and the distinction of the elements, he then describes the creation of animals by partition. Partition, however, is the division of a genus into species, which Plato in the Timaeus proposed not much more accurately. There were, he says, four kinds of animals: one divine and heavenly, another winged and aerial, a third terrestrial, and a fourth of the watery kind. Now first a dichotomy of animal could be made into rational and irrational; and then the dichotomy of the rational could be into God and man, for thus both Plato and Aristotle call God an animal. Lastly, one should consider which dichotomy the irrational species has: whether into fishes and land animals, such as beasts and birds. Mentisque: this difference is common to man and the stars, according to the judgement of the philosophers, and so there would have been two species of one genus. But from a poet one should not demand a more exact logic than from Plato, who made the same error in dividing. The Ovidian partition, moreover, is not only of genus into species, but of an adjunct into its subjects: for the animal, an adjunct, is also divided into its subjects, heaven, air, water, earth. Sic Cicero: when honourable had been defined, then that distribution follows: "You see, my son Marcus, the very form of the honourable, and as it were its face; which, if it were perceived by the eyes (as Plato says), would arouse wonderful loves of wisdom." But every..., etc. Cicero's partition, in place of defined species, uses definitions of the species. This orator could divide more easily than that poet: for virtue is prudence or the composition of morals, and this is temperance or fortitude; justice, however, is the agreement of prudence, temperance and fortitude. The syllogistic axioms of Aristotle concerning genus and species, in chapter 2 of Book 2 of the Topics, have been dissected more subtly apart. Concerning the genus this has been affirmed: "For it is necessary that of those things of which the genus is predicated, some one of the species is predicated." But this affirmation is too narrow: for a genus taken generally, whether affirmed or denied, includes any species whatever, as: if every animal lives, every man lives; but not conversely. The nearest example of an affirmed genus is this. Ac ne quis: the poet Archias had been made a Roman citizen, and when on that right he was challenged, he was defended by Cicero with that defence which exists. The orator gave as the reason for the defence undertaken that, as a pupil, he was rendering patronage to his master, because he had been educated by Archias; and then he objects to himself: "You are an orator, he a poet; how then were you educated by him?" Then he makes use of this argument from genus: "All the arts are held together by a common bond; therefore poetry and eloquence (which are arts too) are held together." A similar argument from genus is in Catullus, but about a single species: "My mistress says that she would rather marry no one than me, not even if Jupiter himself should seek her. She says it, but what a woman says to an eager lover ought to be written in the wind and the rapid water."

units.la: Negati generis axioma illud est ibidē: Quod enim generi nō inest, neq; speciei: Hæc negatio proposita est accuratiús, quám superior affirmatio : Itaque negatum omnino genus negat speciem omnem: ut, Si nullum animal sensu caret, nullus homo caret sensu, non contrá. Tale est Lucani argumentum: Nulla fides regni socijs, omnifq; potestas Impaciens consortis erit.—— At Crassus, Pompejus, Cęsar, sunt socii regni & consortes dominatus: propterea infidi.
units.tr: The axiom of the denied genus is in the same place: "For what is not in the genus is not in the species either." This negation is put forward more accurately than the preceding affirmation. Thus a genus denied altogether denies every species: as, if no animal lacks sense, no man lacks sense; but not conversely. Such is the argument of Lucan: "There will be no loyalty among partners in power, and all authority will brook no companion." But Crassus, Pompey and Caesar are partners in power and companions in dominion; therefore they are untrustworthy.

units.la: Contra genus] Axioma de specie affirmatū, sic est. Quæcunque speciei insunt, & generi. & id Quintilianus 5. lib. cap. 10. arripuit: Species firmam probatione habet generis: Nam quod justitia est, utiq; virtus est. Verum speciei affirmatæ axioma, genus tamē specialiter affirmat, non generaliter: ut, Si homo ridet, animal ridet: aliquod nempe, nō utiq; omne.Et quod Aristoteles é consequētia non conversa indicat esse generale, non esset utique verum, si genus generaliter intelligeretur. At præstantius erat axioma de omnibus speciebus, Quæcunq; speciebus omnibus insunt, insunt & universo generi. Homo sentit, bestia sentit: animal igitur sentit. cujusmodi est Ovidianū exemplū. Materia] Hortatur Ovidius vxore, ut in vero cōjugii amore permaneat, pietate rebus adversis illustriore fore. Ardua] Attingitur quæstio generalis, quæ mox clarius cōcludetur. tribus aut specialibus exemplis approbatur: primum est de Hectore, in virtute militari; secundum de Tiphy, in arte gubernandi: tertium de Apolline, in arte medēdi. Tiphy] Tiphys, fuit excellens opifex navium, & gubernator Argonautarum. Ecl. 4.
units.tr: Against the genus: the axiom about the species affirmed is as follows: whatever inheres in the species also inheres in the genus. Quintilian, in Institutes 5, ch. 10, seized on this: "The species has a firm proof from the genus: for what is justice is certainly a virtue." But the axiom of the affirmed species affirms the genus only in particular, not in general, as: "If a man laughs, an animal laughs," that is, some animal, certainly not every one. And what Aristotle indicates from a non-converted consequence to be general would not be true if the genus were understood generally. A more excellent axiom, however, is the one about all species: whatever inheres in all species inheres in the whole genus too. "Man feels, the beast feels; therefore the animal feels." Ovid's example is of this kind. Matter: Ovid exhorts his wife to remain in true love of marriage, which will be more illustrious through piety in adverse circumstances. Arduous: the general question is touched on, which will soon be concluded more clearly. It is confirmed by three special examples: the first is of Hector, in military virtue; the second of Tiphys, in the art of steering; the third of Apollo, in the art of healing. Tiphys: Tiphys was an excellent shipbuilder and steersman of the Argonauts. Eclogue 4.

units.la: Alter erit tum Tiphys, & altera quae vehat Argo, Delectos Heroas.
units.tr: There shall then be another Tiphys, and another Argo to carry the chosen heroes.

units.la: Phœbe] Sic 1. Metamor. Apollo de se loquitur: Inventum medicina meum est, opifexq; per orbem Dicor, & herbarum est subjecta potentia nobis.
units.tr: Phoebe: Thus Apollo speaks of himself in the first book of the Metamorphoses: "My discovery is medicine, and I am called the inventor of healing throughout the world, and the power of herbs is subject to me."

units.la: Quæ latet] Generalis quæstio tandem apertius concluditur: Argumentum igitur est trium specierum in trib. virtutibus, militari, nautica, medica, ad concludendum genus. Axioma negatum hic ab Ariftotele factum est: Quæcunque autem speciei non insunt, non necesse est generi non inesse. & Quintilianus ibidem arripuit, Species infirmam generis refutationem habet: Nam quod non est justitia, potest esse virtus. at multo latius erat ex omnibus speciebus negare genus. Quale est illud Martialis:
units.tr: Which lies hidden: The general question is at last concluded more plainly. The argument, then, is drawn from three kinds within three virtues, military, nautical and medical, to conclude the genus. Aristotle has here set up a rule which is denied: "Whatever does not belong to a species need not for that reason fail to belong to the genus." Quintilian also seized on this, saying that a refutation drawn from a species is weak, for what is not justice may still be a virtue. But it would have been far broader to deny the genus on the basis of all the species together. Such is that epigram of Martial:

units.la: Si quid opus fuerit, scis me non esse rogandum, Bis nobis dicis, Bacchara, terque die. Appellat rigida tristis me voce Secundus: Audis, sed nescis, Bacchara, quid fit opus,
units.tr: If there is anything you need, you know I need not be asked. Twice a day you say to me, Bacchara, and three times too. Secundus addresses me with a stern and gloomy voice: You hear, but you do not know, Bacchara, what is needed.

units.la: Pensio te coram petitur, clareq, palamque: Audis, sed nescis, Bacchara quid fit opus. Esse queror gelidafq; mihi, tritafq; lacernas: Audis, sed nescis, Bacchara, quid fit opus. Hoc opus est, subito fias ut fydere mutus:
units.tr: Your rent is demanded in front of everyone, loudly and openly: You hear, but you do not know, Bacchara, what is needed. I complain that I am cold, and my cloaks are worn thin: You hear, but you do not know, Bacchara, what is needed. This is what is needed: that you suddenly become as mute as a fish—

units.la: Dicere ne possis, Bacchara, quid fit opus.
units.tr: So that you cannot say what is needed, Bacchara.

units.la: Hic tribus speciebus propositis tollitur genera le propositum. Exempla] Exemplorum usus quantus fit, universa omnium artium & invetio & tractatio testis est: Hinc enim sunt ortæ om- nes artes, per observationem & animadversionē: Itaq; Platoni & Ariftoteli principia omnes doctrinę, ἐπαγωγὴ, ἱστορία, inductio & observatio factæ sunt, sicut ad 14.cap.1.Poster.præcipué à P. Ramo declaratū est: Et quidem memini hoc loco, quantum verborū paucorum dogma P. Ramus extulerit, ut artes nō solūm hinc natæ sint, sed etiam cūm mortuæ & extinctæ effent, hinc rursus velut ab inferis excitatę. Grámatica,Rhetorica,Logica multos annos sepultę jacuerunt, quia exempla præstantiū authorū, iis, à quibus artes illę tractatę essent,ignota & occulta erant. poetę & oratores prodiére,exemplorū suorum luminibus tenebras protinus expulerút. Logiçę purioris ac syncerioris exempla insigniora multis seculis nulla in scholis Logicis fuerunt: Itaq; usus artis præstantissimę extinctus est:sophistici tátúm clamores, & quidē de præceptis, remásére. Reducantur exépla nobilia atq; illustria,revivíscet artis honor,Itaque in hac cohor tatióe,P. Ramus Platonis & Aristotelis testimonia illa proferebat: Plato in Theæteto appellat ῳδακλάχμαε, ὁ μύρσε τὰ λόγε, sponsores & prędes rationis:tanquā ab iis fideijussum persolveretur. Sed idem Plato in Regno,maultó mgnificétiús illud celebravit: Difficile est, ô beate, exemplis nó utenté,res magnas explicare : videtur enim unusquisq; nostrúm, tanquam per somniú,nosse omnia,& omnia revera rursus ignorare. Hæc Plato: quem velut studio quodá consimilis laudis æmulatus Aristoteles in Topicis ca. 2.lib.8. idem pari magnificentia prædicavit: Ad perspicuitatem veró, exempla & similia teneda sunt: exépla veró familiaria,& unde res cognoscim9, qualia sunt apud Homerum, non apud Chœrilum:sic enim clarius & manifestius fit quod ,pponitur.hæc Aristoteles.unde sophisma cóvincitur imperitorum,qui ut mendacia quędam in Aristotelis bibliotheca tueantur,negant exemplorú veritatem in logica requiri. Exemplorú vero & in artibus, & omnino omnibus in rebus copiam historia suppeditat: Itaq; cognoscendum rerum gestarum & memoriæ veteris ordinem, maxime scilicet nostræ civitatis, sed imperiosorum populorum & regum illustrium, Marcus Tullius admonet in Oratore. Huc etiam velut axiomaillud 4.Epist.referri potest, Quod exemplo fit,id etiam jure fieri putant. Itaq; & Quintilianus, philosophos & Rhetoras sequutus, doctrinä exemplorum toto capite undecimo libri quinti persequitur: sed exemplorum dissentaneorum comparatorumq;, nō autem horum speciali-um, ad quæ tamen fructus attinet ille, qui à Quintiliano proponitur lib. 3. cap. 8. quod exempla in consiliis plurimum valeant, quia facillimè ad consentiendum homines ducuntur experimentis. item quod 1. cap. 11. lib. Potentiora exempla etiā ipsis artibus, cum eo qui discit, perductus est, ut intelligere sine demonstrante, & sequi jam suis viribus posset. Item lib. 12. cap. 4. præcipit exempla & vetera & nova, ficta etiā & poetica tenenda esse. Nam illa quidem, aut testimoniorum, aut etiam judicatorum obtinent locum: sed hæc quoque, aut vetustatis fide, tuta sunt, aut ab hominibus magnis, præceptorum loco ficta credūtur. Hæc Quintilianus. Ergo P. Ramus exempla tā magnifica philosophorum & Rhetorum fentiā discipulis suis commendabat. Et nos initio interpretationis nostræ, consimili conscientia freti, affirmavimus, quod rursus affirmamus, exemplis, quæ P. Ramus in hac arte collegit, artis ipsius & veritatë, & utilitatë præcipuë demonstrari. Vrbem] Argumēta sunt Ciceronianæ deliberationis adversus Pompejum, qui Cæsaris adventu, Romam reliquit, & in Græciā confugit: ubi postea victus est à Cęsare. primum igitur exemplū est, Romani urbem nō deseruerūt Gallorū adventu: Deinde fingitur Pōpejº causam suā tueri exēplo Themistoclis, qui deseruisset Athenas adventu Xerxis cū infinita multitudine equitū & peditum, tumq; navali prælio vicit, q terrestri victus fuisset: Deinde rursus Tullius opponit exempla duo: primū Periclis, qui Athenas non reliquit, sed in Marathone Persas terrestri prælio superavit. secundum Romanorum, qui capta à Gallis urbe & incensa, arcē capitolinam retinuerunt: tumq; sese & pretio redemerunt, & Camillo duce vindicarunt.
units.tr: Here, with three species set out, the proposed genus is overthrown. Examples: How great is the use of examples is witnessed by the discovery and treatment of all the arts; for all arts have arisen from observation and attention to examples. Hence Plato and Aristotle made induction and observation [ἐπαγωγή, ἱστορία] the principles of all teaching, as was explained above all by P. Ramus at the fourteenth chapter of the first book of the Posterior Analytics. And I recall here how much a few words of P. Ramus's teaching accomplished, so that the arts were not only born from this, but when they had died and been extinguished, were again roused from the dead by it. Grammar, rhetoric and logic lay buried for many years, because the examples of the most excellent authors, from whom those arts had been handled, were unknown and hidden. Poets and orators came forward, and at once drove out the darkness by the light of their examples. For many centuries there were no outstanding examples of purer and sounder logic in the logic schools; and so the practice of that most excellent art was extinguished, and only the clamours of the sophists remained, and indeed only about precepts. Let the noble and illustrious examples be brought back, and the honour of the art will revive. Accordingly, in this exhortation, P. Ramus cited those testimonies of Plato and Aristotle. Plato, in the Theaetetus, calls reason's guarantors and sureties, so that what is owed may be paid as if guaranteed by them. But the same Plato, in the Republic, celebrated the point much more magnificently: "It is difficult, my friend, to explain great matters without using examples, for each of us seems, as in a dream, to know everything, and in truth to be ignorant of everything again." So Plato. Aristotle, imitating him with a kind of zeal for similar praise, in the Topics, book 8, chapter 2, proclaimed the same with equal magnificence: "For clarity, examples and similar cases must be held to; and familiar examples, from which we know things, such as those found in Homer and not in Choerilus, for in this way what is put forward becomes clearer and more manifest." So Aristotle. Hence the sophism of the unlearned is refuted, who, to defend certain falsehoods in Aristotle's library, deny that the truth of examples is required in logic. Indeed history supplies an abundance of examples both in the arts and in all things generally; and so Marcus Tullius, in the Orator, reminds us that we must know the course of events and of ancient memory, chiefly of our own state, but also of the mighty peoples and illustrious kings. To this may also be referred that axiom from the fourth Epistle: "What is done by example is thought to be done rightly as well." And so Quintilian, following the philosophers and rhetoricians, pursues the doctrine of examples through the whole eleventh chapter of the fifth book; but he treats of examples that are dissimilar and compared, not of these particular kinds, to which nevertheless that benefit which Quintilian sets out in the third book, chapter 8, belongs: that examples count for very much in counsels, because men are most easily led to agree by experience. Likewise, in the first chapter of the eleventh book, he says that examples are more powerful even for the arts themselves, when the learner has been led so far that he can understand without a teacher and can now follow by his own strength. Likewise, in the twelfth book, chapter 4, he prescribes that examples, both old and new, and also fictitious and poetic ones, are to be kept. For the former hold the place either of testimonies or of judgments; but the latter also are safe, either through the faith of antiquity, or are believed to be fictions of great men put in place of precepts. So Quintilian. Therefore P. Ramus commended to his pupils examples so magnificent, from the opinion of philosophers and rhetoricians. And we, at the beginning of our interpretation, relying on a similar conviction, affirmed, and affirm again, that by the examples which P. Ramus gathered in this art, both the truth and especially the usefulness of the art itself are demonstrated. The city: These are the arguments of Cicero's deliberation against Pompey, who, at Caesar's coming, left Rome and fled into Greece, where afterwards he was defeated by Caesar. The first example, then, is that the Romans did not desert the city at the coming of the Gauls. Next, Pompey is imagined defending his cause by the example of Themistocles, who abandoned Athens at the coming of Xerxes with an infinite multitude of horse and foot, and who conquered in the naval battle, though he would have been defeated on land. Then again Tullius sets over against this two examples: first that of Pericles, who did not leave Athens but defeated the Persians in a land battle at Marathon; second that of the Romans, who, when the city had been captured and burned by the Gauls, held the Capitoline citadel, and then both ransomed themselves with money and were avenged under the leadership of Camillus.

units.la: Cap. XXVIII. De Distributione é subjectis.
units.tr: Chapter XXVIII. On Distribution from Subjects.

units.la: REliqua distributio est quodammodo cōsentaneorū, ut subjectorum & adjūctorū. Distributio é subjectis est, cū partes sunt subjecta. ut apud Catullū Virginitas nō tota tua est ex parte paretū est: Tertia pars matri data, pars data tertia paTertia sola tua est: noli pugnare duobus, (tri: Qui genero sua jura simul cū dote dederūt: Sic Cicero 5. Tusculan. Sint enim tria genera bonorum, ut jam á laqueis Stoicorum, quib. usum me pluribus quám soleo, intelligo, recedamus. Sint sane {»} illa genera bonorum, dum corporis & externa jaceant humi, & tantummodo, quia fumēda sunt, appellentur bona. Alia autē divina illa, longé lateque se pandant, cælumq; contingant, ut ea qui adeptus fit, cur cum beatū modó & non beatissimum dixerim?
units.tr: The remaining distribution is of things that go together in a way, namely subjects and adjuncts. Distribution from subjects occurs when the parts are subjects, as in Catullus: Your virginity is not wholly yours: a third part is given to the mother, a third part to the father, only a third is yours. Do not fight with two who have given their rights together with the dowry to the son-in-law. So Cicero in the fifth book of the Tusculan Disputations: "For let there be three kinds of goods, so that we may now withdraw from the snares of the Stoics, whom I understand I use more than usual. Let those kinds of goods be granted, provided that the goods of the body and external goods lie on the ground and are called goods only because they must be taken. But those divine goods spread far and wide and touch the heavens, so that for one who has attained them, why should I call him merely happy and not most happy?"

units.la: Reliqua] Secundū distributionis genus est ex quodammodo consentaneis, subjectis nēpe & adjunctis: in quibus proprie neq; totū, neq; partes appellantur: cūm subjectum posit ab adjunctis, saltē cogitatione seperari: Itaq; de iis distributionibus, nulla est in logica Aristotelis mentio: Andronicus (de quo antea diximus) aut certē post Andronicū Boetius, hujus utriusque doctrinā propositui: P. Ramus exemplis, ut cetera, Homericis illustravit. Hoc aūt secundarium distribuēdi genus, ut doctrinę accuratione imperfectius, sic usu multò frequētius: peneq; asiduę distributiones illę sunt, nō solūm in poetis & oratoribus, sed in philosophis, artiūq; & doctrina rū magistris. Distributio ē subjectis, respondet quodammodo distributioni integri in mēbra.
units.tr: Reliqua: The second kind of distribution is of things that go together in a way, namely subjects and adjuncts. In these, properly, neither "whole" nor "parts" are spoken of, since the subject can be separated from its adjuncts at least in thought. Therefore there is no mention of such distributions in Aristotle's logic. Andronicus (of whom we spoke earlier), or at least Boethius after Andronicus, set out the teaching of both. P. Ramus illustrated it, as he does everything else, with Homeric examples. This secondary kind of distributing is as much less exact in doctrine as it is far more frequent in use. These distributions are almost constant, not only in poets and orators but in philosophers and in the masters of the arts and disciplines. Distribution from subjects corresponds in a way to distribution of a whole into its members.

units.la: Catullum] Catullus in epithalamio Manlii & Julię, hortatur juliā, ne fit marito nimium refracta ria: & paulo ante partitionem, versus hi sunt: Et tu ne pugna cum tali conjuge, virgo: Non æquum est pugnare, pater cui tradidit ipse: Cum par connubium maturo tempore adepta es.
units.tr: Catullum: In his wedding song for Manlius and Julia, Catullus urges Julia not to be too stubborn with her husband. A little before the partition, the verses are these: "And you, maiden, do not fight with such a husband. It is not right to fight with one to whom your father himself gave you, since you have obtained a fitting marriage at a ripe age."

units.la: Tum sequitur, Virginitas non tota, &c. Ubi distributionis usus duplex apparet, alter simplicis distributionis, quę tripertita pot in dichotomiam ita redigi, & pene etiam à Catullo redigitur: Virginitas, est partim virginis, partim paretum, patris & matris. & proprie pares in patrem & matrem dividitur. Hic subiecta virginitatis virgo, in qua inest: pater & mater, ad quos attinet, manifesta sunt: alter usus est ἀνοαλλαγτικὸς: Unus maritus habet duas partes tuæ virginitatis, alteram patris, alteram matris: non debes igitur ei resistere. Cicero] Tria bonorum genera ex tribus subiectorum generibus, animo, corpore, fortuna, manifesta sunt. Partitio tamen hic minus aperte facta est: ea autem est apud Platonem plerisque locis, sed quinto Legum ad finem clarius expressa. Cum tria sint omnino, circa quæ universi homines studium suum collocant: ultimum ac tertium est, pecuniarum recte collocatum studium: medium aut, corporis, primum vero, animi. Atqui modo si Respub. quā meditamur, honores ita distribuat, recte erit constituta. Hæc Plato de tribus generibus bonorum, quibus recte & ex ordine distinctis, ut primus honor sit animi bonis, secundus corporis, tertius & extremus, bonis fortunę: bea tam fore civitatem ait. Ita nunc Tullius, Stoicam philosophiam complexus, longissime animi bona cæteris anteponit. Hęc eadem partitio est primo Academico verbis compluribus.
units.tr: Then follows "Virginity is not wholly...". Here a double use of distribution appears. One is simple distribution, which may be reduced from three parts to a dichotomy, and Catullus very nearly does reduce it so: virginity belongs partly to the virgin in whom it inheres, and partly to the parents, father and mother. Properly, the parents are divided into father and mother. Here the subject of virginity is the virgin in whom it inheres, and the father and mother to whom it belongs are plain. The other use is ἀνοαλλαγτικὸς [reciprocal]: one husband has two parts of your virginity, one belonging to the father and one to the mother; you ought therefore not to resist him. Cicero: The three kinds of goods are clear from the three kinds of subjects: mind, body and fortune. The partition is made here less openly, but Plato makes it in many places, and most clearly at the end of the fifth book of the Laws: since there are altogether three things on which all men set their zeal, the last and third is zeal rightly set on money, the middle on the body, and the first on the mind. And yet, if the commonwealth we are contemplating distributes its honours in this way, it will be rightly constituted. Plato says this of three kinds of goods, rightly and in order distinguished, so that the first honour goes to the goods of the mind, the second to the goods of the body, and the third and last to the goods of fortune; and he says the state will then be happy. So now Tully, embracing the Stoic philosophy, puts the goods of the mind far before the others. The same partition occurs in many words in the first Academic book.

units.la: Cap. XXIX. De Distributione ex adjunctis.
units.tr: Chapter XXIX. On Distribution from Adjuncts.

units.la: Distributio ex adjunctis est, quādo partes sunt adjūcta; ut, Hominum alii sani, alii aegri, alii divites, alii pauperes. Sic Virgilius primo Georg. mundū dividit in quinq; partes, mediam torridū, duas extremas frigidas, & reliquas duas temperatas:
units.tr: Distribution from adjuncts occurs when the parts are adjuncts, as: some men are healthy, some sick; some rich, some poor. So Virgil, in the first Georgic, divides the world into five parts: the middle one torrid, two extreme ones frigid, and the remaining two temperate:

units.la: Quinq; tenēt calū zonæ: quarū una, corusco Semper Sole rubēs, et torrida semper ab igni: Quā circū, extrema dextra lævaq; trahūtur Cærulea glacie concreta, atq; imbribus atris: Has inter, mediamq;, dua mortalibus ægris Munere concessæ diuūm.—
units.tr: Five zones hold the sky, of which one, always glowing red with the flashing sun and always scorched by fire, lies in the middle. Around it, on the extreme right and left, are drawn [zones] held fast by blue ice and dark showers. Between these and the middle, two were granted to wretched mortals by the gift of the gods.

units.la: Cesar i. belli Gall. Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres: quarū unā incolunt Belgę, aliā Aquitani, tertiā, qui ipsorum linguā, Celtæ: nostra, Galli appellantur.
units.tr: Caesar, in the first book of the Gallic War: All Gaul is divided into three parts, of which one is inhabited by the Belgae, another by the Aquitani, and the third by those who in their own language are called Celts and in ours Gauls.

units.la: Ex adjunctis]Hæc altera secundariæ distributionis species, refert quodámodo secundá primariæ distributionis speciē. Quinq; tenent]Virgilius cūm per ortus occasufq; syderum, perq; caussas astrorum pleraq; describēda haberet, in hanc mūdi partitionem est deductus. Distributio autem terræ fit nomine cæli, quia partes terræ, cæli partibus respondeant: nec enim cælum torridum, frigidū, temperatum dicitur, sed terra. Ergo ita poeta est intelligendus, tanquam diceret, Terrestris mūdus dividitur in quinq; plagas & regiones, quæ totū undiq; cælum intuentur. Ovidius autem i. Metamorp. paulo facilius exposuit, comparatione cæli & terræ:
units.tr: Ex adjunctis: This second species of secondary distribution somewhat resembles the second species of primary distribution. Quinq; tenent: Virgil, when through the risings and settings of the stars, and through the causes of the stars, he had many things to describe, was led into this division of the world. The distribution, however, is made under the name of the sky, because the parts of the earth correspond to the parts of the sky: for the sky is not called torrid, frigid or temperate, but the earth is. So the poet is to be understood as if he said: the terrestrial world is divided into five zones and regions, which all look up at the whole sky. Ovid, in the first book of the Metamorphoses, explained it a little more easily, by comparing sky and earth:

units.la: Utq; duæ dextra cælum, totidemq; sinistra Parte secant zonæ, quinta est ardentior illis: Sic onus inclusum numero distinxit eodem Cura Dei, totidemq; plagæ tellure premuntur.
units.tr: As two zones on the right, and as many on the left, cut the sky, and the fifth is hotter than those, so the care of God distinguished the burden enclosed by the same number, and as many regions are pressed upon the earth.

units.la: Quarum quæ media est, non est habitabilis æstu: Nix tegit alta duas, totidé inter utramq; locavit: Temperiemq; dedit mista cum frigore flamma.
units.tr: Of these, the middle one is not habitable because of heat. Deep snow covers two, and he placed as many between the two; and he gave temperateness, a flame mixed with cold.

units.la: Media autem hæc regio, inter tropicos patet gradus 47. Torrida] Hæc opinio veterum fuit usq; ad Plinium & Ptolemæum, qui descriptis tamen in eadem regione poculis, docuerút habitabilem, planeq; habitatam regionem: Sed seculo superiore, Hispani multò clarius docuerút, tam multis insulis, novoq; terrarū invento orbe, in quo habitatio temperatissima perhibetur est enim illic caloris diurni cū nocturno frigore summa moderatio & temperatio. Extremæ] Arctică & antarctică plagas dicit, quæ singulæ patent à tropico ad polum 23. gradus, & 30. minuta. Arctica plaga, circa Daniam & Gothiam, glacie quidē riget, locis & temporibus quibusdam. at vel ipsa glacies ab hominibus teritur: quin prælia in ea interdum geruntur. Duæ] Reliquæ duæ plagæ temperatæ significatur, singulæ inter media, & extremas, latæ gradus 43. quarum altera est nostra, quæ primo à geographis trifariam divisa, in Europam, Africam, Asiam altera est nostrorum antipodum, amborum communis est America. Cæsar] Initium est commentariorum Cæsaris, ubi dividitur tantum Gallia, quæ nondū parebat Romanis, quæ proprie comata tū dicebatur, cūm bracchata esset provincia:sed multò major, quá hodie describitur. cõpleƈtebatur.n. Delphinates, Allobroges, Narbonem,Tholofam: Togata autem Gallia,trans Alpes in Iralia fuit.
units.tr: This middle region, between the tropics, extends 47 degrees. Torrida: This was the opinion of the ancients down to Pliny and Ptolemy, who, although they described peoples in that same region, taught that it was habitable and actually inhabited. But in the previous century the Spaniards showed much more clearly, with so many islands and the discovery of a new world, that in it the habitation is most temperate; for there the moderation and temperature between the heat of day and the cold of night are greatest. Extremae: He means the arctic and antarctic zones, each of which extends from the tropic to the pole, 23 degrees and 30 minutes. The arctic zone, around Denmark and Gothland, is indeed stiff with ice in certain places and seasons; yet even that ice is trodden by men, and battles are sometimes fought on it. Duae: The two remaining temperate zones are meant, each lying between the middle and the extremes and 43 degrees wide. Of these one is ours, which the geographers first divided threefold into Europe, Africa and Asia; the other is that of our antipodes. America is common to both. Caesar: This is the beginning of Caesar's commentaries, where only Gaul is divided, the part that did not yet obey the Romans, which was then properly called long-haired, when the province was called Bracchata; but it was much larger than it is described today. For it included the Delphinate, the Allobroges, Narbonne and Toulouse. Togata Gaul, however, lay across the Alps in Italy.

units.la: Cap. XXX. De Definitione.
units.tr: Chapter XXX. On Definition.

units.la: DEfinitio,est ratio quæ explicat qd res fit:eaq; vicissim definito argui potest.Definitio, est perfecta aut impersecta: Illa proprie definitio, hæc defcriptio dicitur.Definitio perfecta, est definitio constans é solis caussis essentiam constituentibus: quales caussæ genere & formâ comprehenduntur. Atq; hocmodo definitur homo,animal rationale:Nempe genere(animal)intelligimus (ut dictum est) essentiam corpoream, plenam vitæ & sensus,quæ materies hominis est, & pars formæ: cum quasi addas(rationale)totam formam hominis comprehendes,vitæ,sensus,rationis facultate : Itaque perfecta definitio, nihilaliud est, quám universale symbolum caussarum,essentiam rei & naturam cõftituentium. Tales definitiones sunt artium, Grammatica est ars benéloquendi: Rhetorica benédicendi: Dialeƈtica benédifferendi: Arithmerica benénumerandi:Geometria benémetiendi.
units.tr: A definition is an account that explains what a thing is, and conversely the thing can be proved from its definition. A definition is either perfect or imperfect: the perfect kind is properly called a definition, the imperfect kind a description. A perfect definition consists solely of the causes that constitute the essence, and these causes are comprehended under genus and form. Thus man is defined as a rational animal. By the genus (animal) we understand, as has been said, a corporeal essence endowed with life and sense, which is the matter of man and a part of his form. Then, by adding (rational), you comprehend the whole form of man, with its faculties of life, sense and reason. A perfect definition, therefore, is nothing other than a universal sign of the causes that constitute the essence and nature of a thing. Such are the definitions of the arts: grammar is the art of speaking well; rhetoric, of speaking well in public; dialectic, of disputing well; arithmetic, of counting well; geometry, of measuring well.

units.la: Definitio] Categoria definitionis, materiâ magnam & nobilem continet: magnitudo proponitur primùm 28. cap. 1. Pr. ubi definitio inter genera mediorum præcipuè tractatur, deinde celebratur, quatuor feré libris: in posteriorib. Analyticis fit principium demonstrationis: & totus liber secundus feré in Logica definitionis occupatur: tres certè Topici libri toti hic consumpti sunt, quintus, sextus, septimus: argumetû ipsum definitionis, totis Topicis duodecies citatum est: In philosophia, loci quidâ sunt de definitione. Materies igitur hujus categoriæ, amplitudinē tantâ continet: nec verò minorē continet nobilitatem. Plato in Theæteto cûm docuisset nomine λόγος significari signû, quo res differat à cæteris tandem ait, Definitionē accipere, & nosse, idem esse hanc definitionis laudem Aristoteles æmulatus, ait 17. cap. 2. Posteriorum: Omnes scientiæ per definitionem parâtur. idemq; repetit in Philosophia 6. ca. 7. libri, quòd fit idem scire, & per definitionē intelligere. Itaq; & Græci Aristotelis interpretes hic veluti rhetoricè exclamant, Definitio omnem principatum obtinet. Quamobrem agite, P. Rami agriculturam attendamus in tam fæcundo nobiliq; agro: imò periculum, quod aliquâdo propterea adierit, recordemur: ut tantò magis amemus, quantò côstantius præclaræ artis instituendæ, ardentiusq; studium cognoscemus. Definitio] Definitio definitionis debuit habere genus innominatum illud distributionis & definitionis commune, ut deinde sua forma distingueretur à distributio-ne: ne: quód illic, quotuplex: hic, quid est, explicatur: ut illic totû distingueretur in partes: hic totum suis partibus componeretur. Definitio autem á P. Ramo adhibita, est Aristotelis 4. cap. 1. Topici. Est autē definitio, ratio quod quid erat, esse significans, hic ab Aristotele genus illud γένος αὐτατον, λόγος, ratio adhibetur: proximum nō exponitur. Nec in eo P. Ramus sibi satisfaciabat: tamen utebatur eo quo poterat, dum melius occurreret. Vocabula hic Græca sunt, ὅρος, ἀφορισμός, ἐφεστικὸς λόγος, ut antea sectionis, divisionis: geomitrica tota sunt utraque vocabula: unde penè intelligimus, quid logica hæc topica pollicean-tur. definitio, tanquam perimetro comprehendit: distributio, veluti diametro dividit. hæc est igitur horum argumentorum vis: quæ facilius animo cócipitur, quám verbis explicari possit. Tria in definitione vulgò præcipiuntur, ut fit dilucida, brevis, propria: & sic Quintilianus libri 7. cap. 3. Finitio, est rei propositæ propria & dilucida & breviter comprehésa verbis enuntiatio. imó verò Aristoteles ipso Topico sexto, plixé perspicuitatem in definitione commédavit: ut si obscura fit definitio, similis (ait) futura sitimaginibus τῶν ἀρχαίων γραφέων, veterum pictorum: quib. nisi adscriptum esset, quorū imagines efsent, animaliū figuræ non agnoscerētur. At perspicuitas, communis est omnis argumenti: Nisi caussæ perspicuæ, nisi facta perspicua, nisi subjecta perspicua, nisi adjuncta perspicua, nisi omni no argumēta perspicua sint, nihil arguent, neq; omnino argumenta erūt: Natura argumenti, est perspicuum planumq; facere: id est enim argue re: Quare definitionis no est hęc virtus ppria. Appelletur itaq; ex Aristotelis lege τον, controversia judicetur: Generalia (dicit Aristoteles) generaliter & semel explicanda sunt, no in specie aliqua specialiter proponeda: Perspicuitas, est virtus & generalis & communis argumenti: generaliter igit & comuniter ac semel exponeda est, no specialiter uni speciei attribuenda. Brevitas vero, derisa est ab Aristotele, ut mox apparebit, & sophi sima brevitati huic oppositu, Aristoteli in Elenchis est πιερίφυαν redundantia, commune vitiu argumentorum. Itaq; brevitas, si virtus sit, virtus erit communis omnium argumentorum, nec ad illam κατόλη πρῶτον lege, specialiter hic docenda: proprietas autem & convertio, est item communis cum distributione, ut jam patuit: Quare si sequi legem illam κατόλη πρῶτον debuit, istorum trium nihil in definiendi doctrina præcipue P.Ramus instituere debuit.
units.tr: Definition] The category of definition contains a large and noble subject matter. Its importance is shown first in chapter 28 of the first book of the Prior Analytics, where definition is treated especially among the kinds of middle terms; then it is celebrated across almost four books. In the Posterior Analytics the principle of demonstration is made from it, and nearly the whole of the second book is occupied with the logic of definition. Certainly the three books of the Topics, the fifth, sixth and seventh, are wholly devoted to it here, and the argument of definition itself is cited twelve times throughout the Topics. In philosophy there are certain commonplaces about definition. The subject matter of this category, therefore, has such breadth, and no less nobility. When Plato, in the Theaetetus, had taught that the word logos signifies the sign by which a thing differs from others, he finally said that to grasp a definition and to know are the same. Aristotle, emulating this praise of definition, says in chapter 17 of the second book of the Posterior Analytics that all knowledge is acquired through definition; and he repeats the same in the sixth chapter of the seventh book of the Metaphysics, that to know and to understand through definition are the same. So the Greek interpreters of Aristotle, as if speaking in rhetorical fashion, exclaim here that definition holds every primacy. Come then, let us attend to the cultivation of P. Ramus in so fertile and noble a field; indeed let us recall the danger that he once faced on account of it, so that we may love it all the more, the more constantly we recognise the study of establishing this distinguished art, and the more ardently we pursue it. Definition] The definition of definition ought to have had that unnamed genus common to distribution and definition, so that it might then be distinguished from distribution by its own form: the one explains how many kinds there are, the other what a thing is; the one divides the whole into parts, the other composes the whole from its parts. The definition employed by P. Ramus, however, is that of Aristotle in the fourth chapter of the first book of the Topics: "Definition is an account of what a thing is, signifying its essence." Here Aristotle uses the account [logos] for that unnamed genus [genos anōnymon, logos]; the proximate genus is not set out. Nor was P. Ramus satisfied with this himself; yet he used it as well as he could until something better presented itself. The Greek terms here are horos, aphorismos, ephestikos logos, as before for section and division; both terms are wholly geometrical. From this we almost understand what the topical logic of these terms promises: definition encloses as with a perimeter, distribution divides as with a diameter. This, then, is the force of these arguments, which is more easily grasped in the mind than explained in words. In definition three things are commonly prescribed, namely that it be clear, brief and proper; and so Quintilian, in the third chapter of the seventh book, says: "A definition is a statement of the proposed thing that is proper, clear and comprehended in brief words." Indeed Aristotle himself, in the sixth Topics, recommended above all clarity in definition: if a definition is obscure, he says, it will be like the images of tōn archaiōn graphéōn [the ancient painters], which, unless it were written beneath them what they were meant to be, would not allow the figures of the animals to be recognised. But clarity is common to every argument: unless the causes are clear, unless the facts are clear, unless the subjects are clear, unless the adjuncts are clear, unless the arguments are altogether clear, they prove nothing, and will not be arguments at all. The nature of argument is to make things plain and manifest; for that is what to argue means. Therefore this is not a peculiar virtue of definition. Let it then be settled, by the law of Aristotle, that the controversy is decided thus: general matters, he says, are to be explained generally and once, not proposed specially in some particular species. Clarity is a virtue both general and common to argument; it must therefore be set out generally and in common, once only, and not assigned specially to one species. As for brevity, Aristotle derided it, as will shortly appear, and the sophistic opposite of brevity, which in the Sophistical Refutations Aristotle calls perittologia [redundancy], is a common fault of arguments. Brevity, then, if it is a virtue, will be a virtue common to all arguments, and it is not to be taught specially here under the law kathólou prōton [the universal first]. Propriety and convertibility, moreover, are likewise common to distribution, as has already been made plain. Therefore, if P. Ramus ought to have followed that law kathólou prōton, he ought to have taught none of these three especially in the doctrine of defining.

units.la: Vicissim] Habet & definitio reciprocationem suam, licet una tantum parte expressam, sicut in notatione antea fuit: ut ex nomine notatio quoque posset argui: duobus autem nominibus expositā est in causis & effectis, in subjectis & adjunctis, majoribus, minoribus, integro, membris, genere, speciebus: fuit autem unicum nomen in dissentaneis, paribus, similibus, dissimilibus argumentis tamen sua etiam reciprocatio fuit, quæ hic deniq; ad extremum artificialium argumentorum genus exponitur. Ut autem definitionis perfectum fuerit argumentum, ita defi niti erit imperfectum: Sed definitionis usus est in illo simplici docendi genere frequentissimus: Aristoteles autē antea nominatim disseruit, efficientem, materiam, divisionem, ἀσυλλόγιστον ef- se: de definitione, lógum problema est in secundo Posteriorum totis septem capitibus, 4.5.6. 7.8.9. quód definitio perfecta, neq; demōstret, neq; demonstretur syllogismo : imperfecta aūt, demonstrari posit: quin tota posteriora Analytica praecipuē docent, nullo praestantiore argumento syllogismum concludi, quám definitione, ut hinc appareat, etiam definitionem syllogisticam esse: quod antea jam docuimus omnis argumenti commune esse: ex omniq; argumenti genere, ut enūtiari, sic & hic concludi modo syllogismi aliquo posse. PERFECTA Partitio est ex Aristotele decimo capite 2. Posteriorum quód definitio fit alia ἀμεσος immediata, alia ἐμμεσος mediata: illa διὰ τι, haec ἐπι appellatur. In Topicis paulò secús idem iteratur definitionis & proprii nomine, & utriq; parti suum topicum integro libro tribuitur. Perfecta] Id est Aristoteli 10. cap. 2. Posteriorum, λόγος ἀπλῶς διὰ τι, περὶ ἀρχῆς: ratio declarans propter quid, & principium. Id obscurius dicitur, facilius á P. Ramo declaratur, cùm causae proferuntur, ipsam rei essentiam constituentes: & particulatim ac minutatim exponitur, quomodo genere & formā causae illę totius essentiae authores continentur: Magna vero est á Platone usque ad Ciceronem & Quintilianum repetita definiendi doctrina. Plato in Theaeteto attigit his verbis: ἴως δ' ἂν λόγος τινὸς ἐφ' ἡμῖν ... {Greek} donec commune aliquid attigeris, illorum nō tibi erit definitio, quorum communitas fuerit. & subdit deinde addendam propriam differentiā, ut definitio fit differētiæ interpretatio. Aristoteles cap. 2. Posteriorum, subtiliūs hāc rem dilatavit, tanquam quidlibet definiendum, esset speciale aut generale: ut omnia necessaria quęrantur, nō communiora tamen genere: deinde tot conjungantur, ut proprium aliquid efficiant. Doctrinā itaq; definiendæ speciei primùm proponit: definiendi contrā generis doctrina eodem capite deinde consimilis traditur: ut é subductarū specierum definitionibus cōmunia eliciantur: Itaque nihil aliud hic Aristoteles præcipit, quām utendū esse divisione generis ad speciem, inductione specierum ad genus definiendum. hæc totius huius doctrinæ summa est, cuius subtilitas Ciceroni in Topicis arrisit, & ab eo ascripta est, hoc modo: Sic igitur veteres præcipiunt, cūm sumpseris ea quæ sunt ei rei, quam definire velis, cum aliis communia, usq; eò persequi, dum proprium efficiatur, quod nullam in aliam rem trāsferri possit. ut hoc, Hæreditas est pecunia, commune adhuc; multa enim genera sunt pecuniæ. Adde quod sequitur: quę morte alicujus ad quempiam pervenit. nondum est definitio: multis enim modis sine hæreditate teneri mortuorum pecuniæ possunt. unum adde verbū, jure: jam à communitate res disjuncta videbitur: ut fit explicata definitio sic, Hæreditas, est pecunia, q morte alicujus ad quempiā pervenit ju» re. Nondum est fatis: adde nec ea aut légata testamento, aut possessione retenta: confectū est. » Hæc Cicero: qui bellæ subtilitatis hujus doctrina, quomodo eam definitionem cōpleverit, jureconsulti viderint. Quintilianus lib. 5. cap. 10. » id breviús repetivit: A genere pervenīedum est » (ait) ad ultimam speciem: ut, Homo est animal: » non est fatis: id enim genus est. mortale, etiamsi » est species, cum aliis tamē communis finitio rationale: nihil supererit ad demonstrādum quod velis. Hæc Quintil. At P. Ramus totum hoc dogma breviús & fuccinctiús & usui aptiús cōpre hendit. hæc enim, quę tam articulosē proponūtur á philosophis, repetūturq; á Rhetoribus, tametsi falsa non sint, attamen obscuriora sunt, & alligant doctrinam definitionis ad leges illas di videndi generis nimiúm difficiles: nulla enim est pars logicæ inventionis, illa una inventione difficilior: Et caussæ rerum per fe interdum faciliús occurrent: quoties tamē proximum genus apparebit, etit assumendum: recteq; & in Analyticis & in Topicis præcipitur, definitionem, genere & differentia, id est, forma perfici & absolvi. Itaq; P. Ramus ad definitionis accuratæ sontem primū recurrit, & symbola illa, tanquam vasa quædā assumit: sed symbola, docet esse fymbola, non archetypa illa exemplaria, quæ fymbolis ostenduntur. Sed tamen de perfecta definitione duplex quæstio magna est, & quòd sit impossibilis, & si possibilis fuerit, eam tamē nō esse logicæ facultatis, sed altioris philosophiæ. Sed primum de prima illa, in tribus antea Topicis certamen simile fuit: primùm Heracliti & Protagoræ adversus contradictionem: Aristotelis contrà pro contradictione: secundum Euclidis adversus similitudinem: Empedoclis contrà pro similitudine: tertium Speusippi adversus distributionem: Aristotelis contrà pro distributione: quartum tandem Antisthenis adversus definitionē; Aristotelis contrà pro definitione. Quæstio hæc tractatur in philosophia 3. cap.8.lib.Itaque dubitatio, quam Antisthenei & similiter immeriti afferebát, jam tēpus est dissolvere, Quód non licet quid est, definire: definitionem enim, esse ratione longam: sed quale quid est, accidit demonstrare: ut argentū quid est, non: quód autem veluti stănum. hęc Aristoteles obscurè: Videtur autem Anthisthenes dixisse, definitionē esse compositam ē multis rebus, quarum singulæ inventione impossibilem haberent, propterea definitionem impossibilem. quo argumento videretur & generis & formæ obscuritate significare: tumq; rem difficilem, nō impossibilē esse concluderet. Alexander Aphrodiseus orationem longam interpretatur, λόγον nempe pro oratione sumi, quasi dixerit Anthistenes, orationem componi non ex uno nomine, sed ē genere & differētia, tanquam ē materia & forma: ut in definitione, Animal rationale. animal, sit materia: rationale, sit forma: tumq; Antisthenis argumento Alexander ita respondet, ut dicat, partes definitionis, esse partes formę, non materiæ: idq; ait ex Aristotelis doctrina patēre. Verum (ajebat hic P. Ramus) ad Aristotelis leges redeamus. Si Antifthenes cenfuit genere folam fpeciei materiam contineri,falfum eft:continetur enim pars formę,ut in litera declaratur : neque κατὰ πᾶντὸς Antifthenes differuerit. Sed Alexander graviús hic etiá peccat,& longiús á κατὰ παντὸς recedit,qui putat, partib. definitionis solam fpeciei formam cōtineri: materia enim etiá cōtinetur:Itaq; definitionis oppugnatio & propugnatio,hic valde varia & anceps: neq; certamen hoc tam aperto marte certatū eft, atq; illa fuperiora certamina: unū hoc eft certū ab Antifthene, definitioné perfectá rarà effe, cúm duabus é reb.cōftet. quarū utraq; per fe fit inventu valde difficilis: ideoq; imperfectā defcriptionis formulam tantúm in plerifq; rebus teneri:attamen veré & conftanter Ariftoteles contrá diffe ruit.nō quia fit difficilis, idcirco effe impofsibilem:juftoq; argumēto motus, imperitiam hanc Antifthenis coarguit. Atq; hęc duarū quæftionū prior eft:pofterior fequitur,utrúm definitionis accuratę doctrina, logicę artis ppria fit, an Philofophię altioris. Ariftotelis hac de re ambiguus locus eft 2.ca. 7. Topici: ... deinde per accurationem quidem,alterius eft confiderationis,precipere, & quid eft definitio,& quomodo oporteat definire. hic locus interpretes commovit,ut putaret argumento πρᾶγματα, primam philofophiam argui & fignificari. Atqui neq; prima philofophia eo loco appellatur:neq; fi appellaretur, vera effet appellatio:Etenim de accurata illa definitio ne plurimus & maximus est in posterioribus Analyticis sermo,ut argumeto ἄλλως πραγματικῶς, analytica illa doctrina significetur. In Philosophia autē prima, nihil præcipitur admodum de definiendo.In tota enim Philosophia, quatuor tantū loci sunt, eorumq; duo falsi, reliqui ex organo inutiliter repetiti. Primus locus & fecundus est 4.& 5.cap.7. quód definitio sit maximē,& primó,& absolutè substantiarum, secundario sit accidentium.quod falsum est. Arithmetica enim & Geometria, quæ sunt accidētium, ut putantur esse, definitiones accuratiores habent,quám Physica. Ergo quicunq; author ille, vel Antisthenes,vel Eubulides, hoc primus attulit,qd' Aristoteles ibi collegit,καθ' αὐτὸ non disseruit. Tertius est 10.& 11.cap. lib. 7. de partibus essentialibus, quæ sunt priores toto. quod verū est:de materialibus, quæ sunt posteriores, est falsum: materia enim,caussa est constituens, ideoq; prior: neq; itē istud καθ' αὑτὸ arguitur, Quartus locus est 4.& 12.cap.7.lib.& itē 6.cap. 8.lib. quód definitio sit una,ratione essentiæ,nō conjunctione partium: ut Ilias, qui locus verus est,sed ex Interpretatione,1.& 10.cap.2.Post Inutiliter iteratur, nec ideo καθόλου πρῶτον arguit. Quare locus ille Topici septimi,ad primam philosophiam ab interpretibus nō potiús quám ad Analyticam doctrinam referri debuit:& si referredus authoris ipsius judicio videretur, falsum tamen id esset judiciū: Etenim Aristoteles ipse, sua lege καθ' αὑτό,judicet logica legicé:theologica(philosophia enim illa,theologica Aristoteli est) theologica, inquam, theologicè docearitur. Cujus igitur doctrinæ (requirebat hic P. Ramus) proprium est de caussis, de genere, de forma, id est de corpore & anima definitionis præcipere? Logicæ propriū id esse, Ariftotelis analytica & topyca refpondebūt: Quamobrem ubi corpus animaq; definitionis fuerit, ecquis dubitabit etiam definitionem collocare? Quare doctrina accuratè definiendi, est Logicæ propria, & quidē tam propria, quàm distribuendi, quàm enunciandi, quàm concludendi, quàm deniq; differendi. Habes igitur adhuc perfectam definitionem constare é caussis naturam rei confti tuentibus: quæ fi genere comprehendantur, & differentia seu forma, symbolis idoneis & aptis, fuccinctior erit definitio: secús etiam definitio perfecta erit, ut fi hominem definieris, quòd cõ stat é corpore atq; anima, vitæ sensus, rationis compote: ex caussis eisdem definieris. Itaque (ut est 2.cap.7.Metaph.) Archytas merito probabat eas definitiones, quæ rei materiam formamq; complectèrentur. Grammatica]Hæc definitio etiam caussas continet: Nam artis nomine, intelligitur compositio dogmatum ad utilē vitæ finem tendentium, quæ materia est & pars aliqua formæ: tum bene loquendi, reliquam & propriam Grammaticę formam, quinetiam formæ conjunctum finem continet. & sic in reliquis artium definitionibus accuratiùs invenietur.
units.tr: Conversely: a definition also has its own reciprocal, though it is expressed in only one part, as was the case with notation earlier, so that a name could also be inferred from the thing named. Notation, however, was set out in two names: in causes and effects, in subjects and adjuncts, in greater and lesser things, in whole and parts, in genus and species. In the case of contraries, like, unlike and paired arguments, there was a single name, yet each still had its own reciprocal, and this is finally set out here, at the end of the kind of artificial arguments. Just as a definition is the perfect argument, so the definition of the definition is imperfect. The use of definition is most frequent in that simple kind of teaching. Aristotle earlier discussed separately that the efficient cause, the matter, the division and the definition are not syllogistic [ἀσυλλόγιστον]. On definition there is a problem in the second book of the Posterior Analytics, in all seven chapters, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9: that a perfect definition neither demonstrates nor is demonstrated by syllogism, while an imperfect one can be demonstrated. Indeed the whole of the Posterior Analytics chiefly teaches that a syllogism is concluded by no argument more excellent than a definition, so that it appears that the definition is itself syllogistic, which we have already shown to be common to every argument: from every kind of argument, just as it can be stated, so it can here be concluded in some mode of syllogism. The division into perfect and imperfect comes from Aristotle, in the tenth chapter of the second book of the Posterior Analytics, that one definition is immediate [ἀμεσος], another mediate [ἐμμεσος]: the former is called by reason of what [διὰ τι], the latter by ... [ἐπι]. In the Topics the same thing is repeated, a little differently, under the name of definition and property, and each part is given its own topic in a whole book. Perfect: this is what Aristotle, in chapter 10 of the second book of the Posterior Analytics, calls a "statement simply by reason of what, concerning the first principle" [λόγος ἀπλῶς διὰ τι, περὶ ἀρχῆς]: an account declaring the reason why, and the principle. This is said rather obscurely, and Peter Ramus explains it more readily, when the causes are set forth which constitute the very essence of the thing, and it is laid out piece by piece and in detail how those causes, by genus and form, contain the authors of the whole essence. The doctrine of definition, moreover, was repeated at length from Plato down to Cicero and Quintilian. Plato in the Theaetetus touched on it in these words: "[ἕως δ' ἂν λόγος τινὸς ἐφ' ἡμῖν ...]", until you reach something common; you will not have the definition of those things whose commonness it is. And then he adds that the proper difference must be added, so that a definition is an explanation of the difference. Aristotle, in chapter 2 of the Posterior Analytics, developed this matter more subtly: as if whatever is to be defined were a species or a genus, all the necessary features are sought, not more common than the genus, and then so many are joined together that they make up something proper. He therefore first sets out the teaching for defining a species; the teaching for defining a genus is then handed down in the same chapter, in similar fashion, so that common features may be drawn out from the definitions of the species that have been collected. Thus Aristotle here prescribes nothing other than that division of the genus should be used to reach the species, and induction of the species to define the genus. This is the sum of the whole doctrine, whose subtlety pleased Cicero in the Topics, and he set it down in these words: "Thus the ancients prescribe that, when you have taken those features of the thing you wish to define which it shares with others, you should pursue them until something proper is made, which cannot be transferred to any other thing. For example, 'An inheritance is money': this is still common, for there are many kinds of money. Add what follows: 'which comes to someone by the death of another.' It is still not a definition, for the money of the dead can be held in many ways without an inheritance. Add one word, 'by law': now the thing will seem separated from what is common. So the definition is explained thus: 'An inheritance is money which by the death of someone comes to another by law.' It is still not enough: add 'nor given by will, nor held by possession': it is complete." These are Cicero's words. How the jurists will have seen how this definition is completed by the teaching of such fine subtlety is their own affair. Quintilian, in the fifth book, chapter 10, repeated it more briefly: "One must proceed from the genus" (he says) "to the last species, as in 'Man is an animal': that is not enough, for that is the genus. Mortal, even though it is a species, is still common with others; the definition is rational: nothing will remain to be demonstrated of what you wish." These are Quintilian's words. But Peter Ramus comprehends this whole doctrine more briefly, more succinctly and more aptly for use.
