For these matters, which the philosophers set out so articulately and the rhetoricians repeat, although they are not false, are nevertheless more obscure, and they tie the doctrine of definition to those rules of dividing the genus which are too difficult: for there is no part of the art of logical invention more difficult than that single invention. And the causes of things, of themselves, will sometimes occur more easily; but whenever the nearest genus appears, it must be taken, and it is rightly prescribed both in the Analytics and in the Topics that a definition is made and completed by genus and difference, that is, by form. Peter Ramus therefore first returns to the source of exact definition and takes up those symbols as it were vessels; but he teaches that the symbols are symbols, not those archetypal models which are shown by the symbols. Yet there are two great questions about perfect definition, both whether it is impossible, and, if it is possible, whether it belongs not to the logical faculty but to a higher philosophy. But first, concerning the first of these, there was a similar contest in the three earlier Topics: first that of Heraclitus and Protagoras against contradiction, with Aristotle contending for contradiction; second that of Euclid against likeness, with Empedocles contending for likeness; third that of Speusippus against division, with Aristotle contending for division; and lastly the fourth, that of Antisthenes against definition, with Aristotle contending for definition. This question is treated in the third book of the Philosophy, chapter 8. "Therefore the doubt which Antisthenes and others similarly unworthy put forward, it is now time to resolve: that one may not define what a thing is, for a definition is long in reason; but it is possible to demonstrate what sort of thing it is, as silver is not what it is, but such as tin." These are Aristotle's words, obscurely expressed. But it seems that Antisthenes said that a definition is composed of many things, each of which would be impossible to find, and so the definition is impossible; by which argument he would seem to signify, by the obscurity of genus and form, that the thing is difficult, not impossible. Alexander of Aphrodisias interprets "long" to mean that [λόγον] is taken for speech, as if Antisthenes had said that speech is composed not of one name but of genus and difference, as of matter and form, as in the definition "rational animal": animal is the matter, rational is the form. Alexander then answers Antisthenes' argument by saying that the parts of the definition are parts of the form, not of the matter, and he says this is clear from the teaching of Aristotle. But (Peter Ramus used to say) let us return to the rules of Aristotle. If Antisthenes thought that only the matter of the species is contained in the genus, that is false, for part of the form is contained too, as is explained in the text; nor did Antisthenes argue in terms of [κατὰ πᾶντὸς] what holds of all. But Alexander errs here even more gravely, and departs further from [κατὰ παντὸς] what holds of all, when he thinks that only the form of the species is contained in the parts of the definition: for the matter is contained as well. Thus the attack on definition and its defence are here very varied and doubtful, and this contest was not fought with such open battle as those earlier contests. This alone is certain from Antisthenes: that a perfect definition is rare, since it consists of two things, each of which is itself very difficult to discover; and therefore only an imperfect formula of description is held in most things. Yet Aristotle argues against him truly and consistently, not because a thing is difficult is it therefore impossible; and by a just argument from motion he refutes this inexperience of Antisthenes. And this is the first of the two questions; the second follows, whether the exact doctrine of definition belongs to the proper art of logic or to a higher philosophy. Aristotle's statement on this matter is ambiguous, in chapter 7 of the second book of the Topics: "... then, that to teach exactly what definition is and how one ought to define belongs to another kind of consideration." This passage has moved the interpreters to think that by the argument [πρᾶγματα] first philosophy is argued and signified. Yet first philosophy is not named in that place, and even if it were named, the naming would not be true. For indeed the most numerous and important discussion of that exact definition is in the Posterior Analytics, so that by the argument [ἄλλως πραγματικῶς] that analytic teaching is signified. In first philosophy, however, very little is taught about defining. For in the whole of philosophy there are only four passages, two of which are false, and the rest are uselessly repeated from the Organon. The first and second passages are in chapters 4 and 5 of the seventh book, that definition is chiefly, and primarily, and absolutely of substances, and secondarily of accidents; which is false. For arithmetic and geometry, which are accidents, as they are thought to be, have more exact definitions than physics. Therefore whoever that author was, whether Antisthenes or Eubulides, who first brought this forward, which Aristotle collected there, did not argue [καθ' αὐτὸ]. The third is in chapters 10 and 11 of the seventh book, concerning essential parts, which are prior to the whole. This is true of the formal parts; of the material parts, which are posterior, it is false: for matter is a constituent cause and therefore prior; nor is this [καθ' αὑτό] argued in that way. The fourth passage is in chapters 4 and 12 of the seventh book, and likewise chapter 8 of the sixth book, that a definition is one by the reason of the essence, not by the conjunction of parts, as the Ilias; which passage is true, but it is from interpretation, chapters 1 and 10 of the second book of the Posterior Analytics. It is uselessly repeated and does not for that reason argue [καθόλου πρῶτον]. Therefore that passage of the seventh book of the Topics ought to be referred by the interpreters to the Analytic doctrine rather than to first philosophy; and even if it seemed, by the author's own judgement, to be referred to first philosophy, that judgement would still be false. For Aristotle himself, by his own rule [καθ' αὑτό], judges logic logically; theology (for that philosophy is theology for Aristotle) is taught theologically. Then (Peter Ramus asked) to which doctrine does it belong to lay down precepts concerning causes, genus, form, that is, concerning the body and soul of definition? Aristotle's Analytics and Topics will answer that it belongs to logic. Wherefore, when the body and soul of definition have been given, who will doubt that definition too is placed there? Therefore the doctrine of exact defining belongs to logic, and indeed belongs as much to it as dividing, as enunciating, as concluding, and finally as disputing. You have, then, a perfect definition consisting of the causes that constitute the nature of the thing; if these are comprehended by genus and difference or form, with suitable and apt symbols, the definition will be more succinct; otherwise the definition will also be perfect, as if you defined man as that which consists of body and soul, sensible of life and possessed of reason, defined by the same causes. Thus (as in chapter 2 of the seventh book of the Metaphysics) Archytas rightly approved those definitions which embraced the matter and form of the thing. Grammar: this definition also contains causes; for by the name of art is understood the composition of doctrines tending to a useful end of life, which is the matter and some part of the form; then the good speaking, the remaining and proper form of Grammar, and moreover it contains the end conjoined with the form. And so in the definitions of the other arts it will be found more exactly.

units.la: Cap. XXXIX. De Descriptione.
units.tr: Chapter 39. On Description.

units.la: DEscriptio est definitio ex aliis etiā argumentis rem definiens: ut, Homo est animal mortale, capax disciplinæ. Hīc cum aliqua caussa miscetur cōmunis itēq; propria circumstātia. Atq; hęc succinĉta brevitas, nō est in hac specie perpetua, sed sæpé illustrioré & magnificentiorem explicationem desideꝛat. Sic gloria describitur in Miloniana: Sed tamē ex omnibus præmiis virtutis, si esset habenda ratio præmiorum, amplissimum esse præmium, gloriam: hanc unam, quę breuitatem vitæ posteritatis memaria consolaretur: quæ efficeret, ut absentes adessemus, mortui viverem⁹: hanc deniq; esse, cujus gradibus etiā homines in cælū videantur ascendere. Sic 4. Aeneid. Fama describitur:
units.tr: Description is a definition that defines a thing by means of other arguments as well, as in: "Man is a mortal animal capable of learning." Here some cause is mixed in, both a common and a proper circumstance. This brief, succinct form is not always suitable, and in some kinds it requires a fuller and more splendid explanation. Thus glory is described in the Pro Milone: "But among all the rewards of virtue, if there were any account to be taken of rewards, the most ample reward is glory, this one thing which consoles the brevity of life by the memory of posterity, which makes the absent seem present and the dead live on, and which at last is that by whose steps even men seem to climb into heaven." Thus Fame is described in the fourth book of the Aeneid:

units.la: Extemplo Libya magnas it fama per urbes: Fama malum, quo non aliud velocius ullū, Mobilitate viget, viresq; acquirit eundo: Parva metu primò, mox sese attollit in auras Ingreditur solo, et caput inter nubila condit. Illam terra parens, ira irritata deorum, Extremam (ut perhibent) Cœo Enceladoq; sorórem Progenuit,pedibus celere, & pernicibus alis: Monstrum horrendum, ingens: cui quot sunt corpore pluma, Tot vigiles oculi subter (mirabile dictu) Tot linguae, totidem ora sonant, tot subrigit aures: Nocte volat caeli medio, terrae per umbrã, Stridens, nec dulci declinat lumina somno: Luce sedet custos aut summi culmine tecti, Turribus aut altis, et magnas territat urbes: Tam ficti pravi, tenax, quàm nutia veri.
units.tr: Straightway Fame goes through the great cities of Libya. Fame is an evil than which none is swifter; she thrives on her motion and gains strength as she goes. At first she is small and timid, but soon she raises herself into the air, walks on the ground and hides her head among the clouds. Her mother Earth, roused in anger against the gods, bore her as the last sister of Coeus and Enceladus, swift of foot and with nimble wings: a horrible, huge monster, for every feather on her body there is a watchful eye beneath it (wonderful to tell), as many tongues, as many mouths that sound, as many raised ears. By night she flies between heaven and earth through the shadows, shrieking, and never lets her eyes sink into sweet sleep. By day she sits as a watchman on the roof of a house or on high towers, and terrifies great cities, as fond of spreading lies and wrong as of carrying the truth.

units.la: Tales sunt descriptiones plantarum, animalium in Physicis: item fluminum, montium, urbium in Geographis & Historicis.
units.tr: Such are the descriptions of plants and animals in the natural philosophers, and of rivers, mountains and cities in the geographers and historians.

units.la: Descriptio [Haec altera species est definitionis, cui Aristot. quintum topicorum attribuit: appellat autem proprium, & ita definit 4. cap. 1. Topici: Proprium autem est, quod nō declarat quid erat esse: foli verò inest, & vicissim attribuitur rei: ut Grammaticæ capax. Hic videtur Aristoteles categorema simplex & unius vocis definire: At exemplum contrà (grammaticæ capax) oratio est. & toto quinto libro declaratur apertius, proprii nomine intelligi descriptionē. & 3. cap. 7. Topici, id etiam nominatim exprimitur: Nam ut plurimum, in cōplexione proprii assignatur. Descriptio Porphyrio dicitur περιγραφή, Rhetorib. periphrasis: Ciceroni in Topicis, ... ϖαϱαγϱαϕὼ: Platoni in Theæteto, σχιαγϱάφημα videtur appellari. Definitio autē differt magis á persecta definitione, licentia quadam & libertate, quám argumentorum primorum genere: tanquam descriptio, fit definitio, quæ non explicat quid fit, ex solis caussis rem cōstituentibus, sed vel ex aliis tantum, vel simul quibusdam & causfis, & non caussis. ut Homo est animal mortale, capax disciplinæ. Exemplū est Aristotelis 1. cap. 5. Topici, ζῷον δυνητὸν, ἐπιστήμης ἀνθρωπικόν. ubi comprehendítur in genere, animal: item circunstantiæ duę, altera communis (mortale) altera propria (capax disciplinę) Descriptiones brevitatis paris sunt illæ: Horatius in epist.
units.tr: Description [This is the second species of definition, which Aristotle assigns in the fifth book of the Topics; he calls it the proper, and defines it in the fourth chapter of the first book of the Topics: "A proper is that which does not declare what it is to be, but belongs only to the thing and is predicated of it in turn, as capable of grammar." Here Aristotle seems to define a simple predicate of a single word; but the example (capable of grammar) is a phrase. The whole of the fifth book makes clearer that by the name of proper is understood description; and in the seventh chapter of the third book of the Topics this is also named expressly, for it is for the most part assigned in the combination of the proper. Porphyry calls description periegraphē [περιγραφή], the rhetoricians periphrasis; Cicero in the Topics calls it paragraphē [παραγραφή]; Plato in the Theaetetus seems to call it skiagraphēma [σχιαγράφημα]. Description differs from a perfect definition more by a certain licence and freedom than by the kind of primary arguments: as a description is made, so a definition is made which does not explain what a thing is from its constituent causes alone, but either from other things only, or from some things together with causes and some non-causes. For example: "Man is a mortal animal capable of learning." Aristotle's example is in the fifth chapter of the first book of the Topics: zōon dynēton, epistēmēs anthrōpikon [ζῷον δυνητὸν, ἐπιστήμης ἀνθρωπικόν], where animal is included in the genus, and there are two circumstances, one common (mortal) and one proper (capable of learning). Descriptions of this kind of brevity are such as these in Horace's Epistles:]

units.la: Ira furor brevis est, — jupiter ita definitur Poetis:
units.tr: Anger is a brief madness; thus Jupiter is defined by the poets:

units.la: — Diuûm pater atq; hominum rex.
units.tr: Father of gods and king of men.

units.la: 2. Philipp. Pax est tranquilla libertas. 2. Amor.
units.tr: Second Philippic: "Peace is tranquil liberty." Second Amores.

units.la: Stulte, quid est somnus, gelidæ nisi mortis imago?
units.tr: Foolish one, what is sleep but the image of cold death?

units.la: Succincta brevitas] Præceptum jam olim á Rhetoribus commendatum, sed ab Aristotele merito derisum 16. cap. 3. Rhetorici: ut si quis pistori interrogāti, durumne an molle pinserer: quid? respondeat aliquis, ἀδύνατον ηχὶ ἐντοῦτα ὁμοίως, an impossibile est & hic convenienter agere? neq; enim vel lōgum, vel breve, hic est τὸ σὺ, ipsum bene: ἀλλὰ τὸ μιτρίως, sed quod apte & congruenter agitur. & id est quod prædixerā, brevitatem ab Aristotele irrisam esse: Sed enim Rhetores imitati philosophū, hoc idem valdē dilatarunt: Sic Tullius. Oratorio secundo ait, in civilibus causis succinctam brevitate perquám puerilem sibi
units.tr: Succinct brevity] A precept long ago commended by the rhetoricians, but rightly mocked by Aristotle, Rhetoric 16, cap. 3. For example, if someone asked a baker whether he kneads hard or soft dough, and someone answered, "Is it impossible, or is it not possible to do this too in the same way?" For here the point is neither long nor short, nor "the good" itself [τὸ εὖ], but "the moderate" [τὸ μετρίως], that is, what is done fitly and appropriately. And this is what I said before: that brevity was mocked by Aristotle. But the rhetoricians, imitating the philosopher, have greatly expanded the same point. Thus Tully, in the second book of the Orator, says that in civil causes a brevity that is cut short seems to him quite childish. For, he says, there is one kind of definition of words when learned men dispute about those very things that belong to the arts, as when it is asked what art is, what law is, what the state is. Another kind is that of matters of civil life among men who are mostly unlearned…

units.la: videri: Alia est enim, ait, cúm inter doctos homines de iis ipsis rebus, quæ versantur in artibus, disputatur, verborū definitio: ut cúm quæritur, quid sit ars, qd sit lex, quid sit civitas. alia est rerum civiliū inter homines plerunq; ineruditos explicatio: etenim definitio primùm reprehenso verbo uno, aut addito, aut dempto, sépé extorquetur é manibus: deinde genere iplo, doctrinā redolet exercitationēq; pené puerilem: tum & in sensum, & in mentem judicis intrare non potest: anté enim prꝑterlabitur, quám percepta est. In quib. est animadvertenda differentia & dissimilis usus duarū definitionum, quód accurata definitione sit utendum in artibus, & cum doctis hominibus. in vulgus autē & imperitorū sensus, descriptiones aptiores esse. Quin eodem in libro Tullius idem iterū apertiūs nomine narrationis: Narrare verò (ait) rem quod breviter jubět (si brevitas appellanda est, cúm verbum nullum redundet) brevis est L. Crassi oratio: si tū est brevitas, cúm tantum verborum est, quantum necesse est: aliquando id opus est, sed sæpé obest vel maximé in narrando: nō solúm quód obscuritatem affert, sed etiam, quód eam virtuté quæ narrationis est maxima, ut jucunda, & ad persuadendum accómodata sit tollit videlicet illa. Hæc Tullius de ridiculo breuitatis præcepto. Quintilianus idem sequutus est 3.cap.7.lib. Agenti verò (ait) quæ tāta est hujus præcisæ comprehensionis necessitas? an si non dixero, Homo est animal rationale, mortale: nō potero expositis tot corporis animiq; proprietatibus,latiús oratione ducta,vel à diis eum,vel á mutis discernere? Quamobrē ex his & philosophorū & rhetorum testimoniis intelligimus, quód non sit omnis definitionis propria brevitas. imó quám ridiculum sit in definitionis doctrina,præceptum brevitatis. Constet igitur Ari stotelis illud,τὸ οὖ ἡ μεγέθος, in accurata definitione suis finibus, causarū nempe rem constituentium genere formaq; definitum. ut jam præcipe re vanū sit, longum an breve: quia quantū esse debeat, sit ita definitū. Cúm præscripsferis lineā bipedalē,frustra sit dicere, vt sit brevis,non longa: nam quantū opus est,tantū est declaratum. Gloria] Locus est in peroratione Milonianæ defensionis, ubi Milo de se magnificé loquitur, & viros fortes contentos esse conscientia recté fa ctorū: se forte esse. tum additur hæc correctio: Sed tamē, &c. quæ ipsa probatur gloriæ descriptione. Hoc enim exemplum etiā syllogisticum est:quomodo per definitionem concludi quidlibet posit. imó (ut antea jam ex Aristotele dictum)optimé & clarisimé posit.
units.tr: For, he says, there is one kind of definition, that of words, which arises when learned men dispute about the very things that belong to the arts, as when it is asked what art is, what law is, what the state is. Another kind is the explanation of civic matters among men who are for the most part unlearned. For a definition, first, is often wrested from one's hands when a single word is challenged, added or removed; then, by its very genus, it smells of learning and a nearly childish exercise; and then it cannot enter into the sense and mind of the judge, for it slips past before it is grasped. In these matters the difference and the unlike use of the two kinds of definition must be noted: a precise definition is to be used in the arts and among learned men, but for the common people and the understanding of the unskilled, descriptions are more suitable. Moreover, in the same book Tullius says the same thing again more openly under the name of narration: "To narrate a matter, which he bids be done briefly (if it is to be called brevity, since no word is superfluous), is the speech of L. Crassus, which is brief. But if that is brevity, when there are only as many words as are necessary, then sometimes this is needed, but often it is a hindrance, especially in narrating: not only because it brings obscurity, but also because it removes that quality which is greatest in narration, namely that it be pleasing and suited to persuasion." These are Tullius' words on the ridiculous precept of brevity. Quintilian followed the same view in 3.cap.7.lib.: "But for one who is speaking, what is the need of such precise comprehension? If I do not say, 'Man is a rational, mortal animal,' shall I not be able, by setting out at greater length the many properties of body and mind, to distinguish him from the gods or from the brute beasts?" From these testimonies of philosophers and rhetoricians, therefore, we understand that brevity is not the proper quality of every definition; indeed, how ridiculous a precept of brevity is in the doctrine of definition. Let that saying of Aristotle stand, [τὸ οὔτε μέγεθος], that in an exact definition things are bounded within their own limits, namely defined by the genus and form of the things that constitute the cause. So it is vain to prescribe whether it should be long or short, since how much it ought to be is already fixed by such a definition. When you have prescribed a line two feet long, it is pointless to say that it should be short and not long, for as much as is needed has been marked out. Glory] This is a passage in the peroration of Milo's defence, where Milo speaks grandly of himself, and says that brave men are content with the consciousness of right deeds, and that he himself is brave. Then this correction is added: "But nevertheless," and so on, which is itself proved by the description of glory. For this example is also syllogistic: it shows how anything can be concluded through a definition, and indeed (as already said above from Aristotle) it can be concluded best and most clearly.

units.la: Extemplo.] Dido regina Carthaginis fingitur á poeta occasione venationis & interea ortę tēpeftatis, in antrū cum Ænea descendisse, & amorib.indulsisse:quod fama ptinus per vniuer fam Africam divulgatū sit. Ergo hinc famæ descriptio oritur. primó ex genere, malum: tū ex minoribus: quód nullum velocius:tū ex adjunctis,effectis,parua,magna,ingredit, cōdit:deinde ex efficiēte causa, matre terra: rursus ex adjunctis,velocitate,pernicitate:iterū ex aliis adjunctis, monstrum horrendum: tum é partibus, oculis, linguis, auribus, sed parium forma expo‐ sitis: rursus ex effectis nocturnis, diurnis: deni‐ que rursus é paribus: tam variis argumentis fa‐ ma describitur à poeta, ut non excellentius co‐ loribus & penicillo Apellis pingi potuerit.
units.tr: Extemplo. The poet feigns that Dido, queen of Carthage, on the occasion of a hunt and of a storm that arose in the meantime, went down with Aeneas into a cave and gave herself up to love; and that the rumour of this at once spread through the whole of Africa. Hence the description of Fame arises. First from the genus, as an evil; then from the lesser things, in that she moves more swiftly than anything; then from the adjuncts and effects, small at first and great afterwards, she enters and hides herself; next from the efficient cause, that Earth is her mother; again from adjuncts, her speed and swiftness; again from other adjuncts, a horrible monster; then from the parts, eyes, tongues, ears, though these are set forth in pairs; again from the effects, by night and by day; and finally again from pairs. By so many varied arguments is Fame described by the poet that she could not have been painted more excellently with the colours and brush of Apelles.

units.la: Plantarum] De quibus libri à Physicis describ‐pti, in omni genere herbarum, arborumque, ita malus medica describitur 2. Georg. Media fert tristes succos, tardumq; saporem Felicis mali: quo non præsentius ullum, (Pocula si quando sæva infecere novercæ, Miscuerunt, herbas, & non innoxia verba) Auxilium venit, ac membris agit atra venena. Ipsa ingens arbos: faciemque similima lauro: Etsi non alium late jactaret odorem, Laurus erat: folia haud ullis labentia ventis: Flos apprima tenax: animas & olentia Medi Ora fovent illo, & senibus medicantur anhelis.
units.tr: This description is from effects, because the fruit of this tree drives out poisons; then from similar adjuncts of leaves and flowers; and again from effects, because it helps breathing. Of animals] Concerning which there are books by Aristotle, Oppian, Pliny, and many natural philosophers; and generally about birds, fishes…

units.la: Hæc descriptio ex effectis, quód fructus hujus arboris abigit venena: tum é similibus adjunctis foliorum & florum: iterumq; ex effectis, quód anhelitum adjuvet. Animalium] De quibus Aristo‐ telis, Oppiani, Plinii, tamq; multorum Physico rú libri: & generatim de avibus, piscibus, feris, quorum omnium etiam imagines pinguntur.
units.tr: This description is drawn from the effects: the fruit of this tree drives out poisons; also from the similar attributes of its leaves and flowers; and again from its effects, that it aids breathing. Of animals: on these there are the books of Aristotle, Oppian, Pliny and many natural philosophers; and generally on birds, fishes and wild beasts, whose images are also painted.

units.la: Fluminum] Sic Rhenus, Rhodan, Padus, Danu‐ bius in Europa: Nilus in Africa: Euphrates, Ti‐ gris, Ganges, Indus in Asia describuntur. Mon‐ tium] Sic Alpes, Olymp in Europa: Atlas in Africa: Taurus & Caucasus in Asia: deniq; geogra‐ phia mundi terreni his definitionibus declara‐ tur. urbium]Talis est Syracufarū descriptio sexta Verrina: urbem Syracusas maximā esse Græcarum urbium,pulcherrimamq; omnium,sæpe audistis. est(judices)ita ut dicitur:nā & situ est cómunito, tū ex omni aditu, vel terra, vel mari pręclaro ad aspectum: & portus habet propé in ædificatione aspectuq; urbis inclusos : qui cūm diversos inter se aditus habeant, in exitu cōjun guntur & confluunt. & deinde tota illa amplifsima descriptio per quatuor partes urbis, Insulam, Acradinā, Tychē, Neapolin. Sed hastenus de definiendi doctrina, quę postremum in ordine artificialium argumentorū locum obtinuit, quia definitio potest ex omnibus illis antecedē tibus argumentis institui: Nec sequitur,si in usu argumentorum & in differendo sit incipiēdum ā definitione, ut ideo doctrina inveniendę definitionis reliquorū argumentorū inveniendorū doctrinā præcedere debeat. hoc argumētum in methodo nullum fit:sed doctrina ea præcedere debet,quæ magis sit communis,& quæ sine cōsequentiū doctrina possit intelligi : At doctrina illa inveniendi caussas & antecedentia cætera, pót intelligi sine ista doctrina definitionis: non contrá,cūm definitio ex illis componatur.
units.tr: Of rivers: so the Rhine, Rhône, Po and Danube are described in Europe; the Nile in Africa; the Euphrates, Tigris, Ganges and Indus in Asia. Of mountains: so the Alps and Olympus in Europe; Atlas in Africa; Taurus and Caucasus in Asia. Finally, the geography of the terrestrial world is set out by these definitions. Of cities: such is the description of Syracuse in the sixth Verrine oration: "You have often heard, judges, that the city of Syracuse is the largest of the Greek cities and the most beautiful of all. It is so, as it is said: for it is both fortified by its site, and conspicuous to the eye from every approach, by land or sea; and it has harbours lying close together in the building and aspect of the city, which, though they have different entrances, join and meet at their exit." Then that whole ample description proceeds through the four parts of the city: Island, Achradina, Tyche, Neapolis. But so far concerning the doctrine of definition, which holds the last place among the artificial arguments, because a definition can be constructed from all the preceding arguments. Nor does it follow that, if in the use of arguments and in disputation one must begin from the definition, therefore the doctrine of finding definitions must precede the doctrine of finding the other arguments. This is no argument in method; rather, the doctrine which is more common, and which can be understood without the doctrine of consequences, ought to come first. But the doctrine of finding causes and the other antecedents can be understood without that doctrine of definition, not the reverse, since a definition is composed from them.

units.la: Cap. XXXII. De Testimonio divino.
units.tr: Chapter XXXII. Of Divine Testimony

units.la: EXposito artificiali argumēto,sequitur inartificiale. Argumētum inartificiale est,quod non sua natura,sed afsumpta artificialis alicujus argumēti vi arguit,testimoniū dicitur. Itaq; cūm exquisita rerũ veritas subtiliús exquiritur, perexiguam vim probationis habet: In civilibus autem & humanis rebus plerunq; hoc argumentũ fidem é moribus testis arguentis efficit, si prudentia, virtus, & benevolētia adfuerint: id uno nomine testimonium dicitur: eftq; divinū vel humanum. In divinis testimoniis numerantur non solúm deorum oracula, sed etiam prodigia, respõsa vatum & fatidicorum: quæ omnia ȝ. Catil. adhibentur: Nam ut illa omittam (ait orator) vi‑ fas nocturno tempore ab occidente facces, ardoremq; cæli, ut fulminũ jactus, ut terræ motus, cæteraq; quæ ita multa nobis Cōsulibus facta sunt, ut hæc quæ nunc fiunt, canere dii immortales videretur. deinde paulò pōst: Quo quidem tempore, cúm Aruspices ex toto Hetruria cōvenissent, cædes atq; incendia, & legum interitum, & bellum civile ac dömesticum, & totius urbis ac imperii occasum appropinquare dixerunt, nisi dii immortales, omni ratione placati, suo numine propè fata ipsa flexissent. Tandem cúm dixisset, ut ex Arusipicũ respõsis ludi facti, & jovis signū majus factū, conversumq; ad oriētem,tum ait:Illud vero nonne ita præsens est, ut nutu jovis optimi maximi factū esse videatur? ut cum hodierno mane per forū meo jussu, & cōjurati & eorū indices in ædē Concordiæ ducerentur, eo iqso tempo re signū statueretur: quo collocato, atque ad vos Senatumq; cōverso, omnia & Senatus,& vos, quæ erant cōtra salutē omniū, cogitata, illustrata & patefacta vidistis.Brevius est illud Tibulli:
units.tr: Having set out the artificial argument, there follows the inartificial. An inartificial argument is one which proves not by its own nature but by the force of some assumed artificial argument, and it is called testimony. Therefore, when the exact truth of things is sought more subtly, it has very little force of proof. In civil and human affairs, however, this argument commonly produces faith in the witness who bears it, if prudence, virtue and goodwill are present. This is called testimony under one name, and it is either divine or human. Among divine testimonies are counted not only the oracles of the gods but also prodigies, the responses of seers and soothsayers; all of these are used. For, to leave those aside, says the orator in the first Catilinarian: "a torch in the night-time flashing from the west, the glow of the sky, the fall of thunderbolts, earthquakes, and the many other things that happened in our consulship, so that these present events seemed to be foretold by the immortal gods." Then shortly after: "At that time, when the haruspices had assembled from all over Etruria, they said that slaughter and fire, the destruction of the laws, civil and domestic war, and the downfall of the whole city and empire were drawing near, unless the immortal gods, fully propitiated, had almost turned aside the fates by their power. At last, when he had said this, games were held according to the responses of the haruspices, and a larger statue of Jupiter was made, and turned to the east; then he says: 'Is not that event so manifest that it seems to have happened by the nod of Jupiter Best and Greatest? That this very morning, by my order, through the forum, both the conspirators and their informers were led into the temple of Concord, at that very time a statue was set up; when it was placed and turned towards you and the Senate, you saw that all the plans which were against the safety of all, both of the Senate and of you, were brought to light, revealed and exposed.'" Shorter is that line of Tibullus:

units.la: Quód si vera canunt sacris oracula templis. Hæc illi nostro nomine dicta refer.
units.tr: If the oracles sing true in the sacred temples, report these things said in our name.

units.la: Hoc tibi conjugium promittit Delius ipse, Felix: ac alium desine velle virum.
units.tr: "Delius himself promises you this marriage, happy one; cease to wish for any other husband."

units.la: Exposito] Categoriæ novem artificialium argumentorum in caussis & effectis, in subjectis & adjūctis,in dissentaneis & comparatis,in nomine, in distributione, in definitioe,sunt adhuc ex veterum authorum,præcipué Aristotelis thesauris depromptæ,expositę,exemplis deniq; excellentium authorum demonstratæ:& illustratę:Decima superest,in testimonio: cujus in tota Aristotelis bibliotheca rariore materiam P.Ramus habuit:quater tantúm in Topicis utcunq; hoc argumentum citatū est: inRhe toricis vero,copiosiús est propositum:unde sequentia feré collecta sunt. Atq; hic nullum fortasse genus argumenti Logicum & cōmune entium & nō entium videatur, quia testimonium tátúm Dei possit esse & hominis: quæ antea P. Ramo conjectura quædá fuit de fine,utrúm logica caussarũ species esset.at hic secús videatur: quanvis enim testimonium Dei tátúm sit & hominis,attamen de quolibet & ente & non ente, testimoniũ esse potest. Inartificiale] Hæc definitio paulo secús instituitur ab Aristotele 2. ca.
units.tr: Exposed] The nine categories of artificial arguments, those drawn from causes and effects, from subjects and adjuncts, from opposites and comparatives, from names, from division, and from definition, have already been set out, drawn from the storehouses of the older authors, chiefly Aristotle, and finally demonstrated and illustrated by examples from excellent authors. The tenth remains, that from testimony. P. Ramus found little material on it in the whole of Aristotle's library: the argument is cited only four times in the Topics, and in the Rhetoric it is treated more fully, so that the following points have been mostly collected from there. Here perhaps no logical kind of argument seems to be common to beings and non-beings, since testimony can be only God's or man's. This was once a conjecture of P. Ramus about the end, whether it is a species of the logical causes. But here the matter seems otherwise, for although testimony is only God's or man's, nevertheless testimony can concern anything, whether a being or a non-being. Inartificial] Aristotle gives this definition in slightly different terms in Rhetoric 1, chapter 2.

units.la: 1. Rhetor.Inartificialia autem dico, quæ non cõ parata sunt á nobis,sed anté extiterunt. Verúm (ut initio jam patuit,cúm de artificialis argumẽ ti definitione dictum est) hæc definitio ex foro nata est,ubi plerunq; testimonia afferuntur á litigatore ad oratorẽ: & topicum præceptum de testimoniis inveniendis, valde ridiculum esset, si artem tradere rei inveniendæ,quæ ab artifice ipso inveniri nõ posset.In rhetorico ad Alexandrum paulo secús eadem definitio instituitur. Atq; hæc argumẽta,dicuntur ωίσεις ἐντίθετοι τοῖς ἀ γομένοις ἢ ἀ ἢ προσλαμβανομένοις,probationes adjunctæ iis quę dicuntur & fiút.Cicero Oratorio secundo, foris assumpta hæc argumenta appellat, quę nõ sua vi,sed extranea sublevantur:ut hæc,Hoc verũ est:dixit enim Qu.Luctatius.Hoc falsum est: habita enim quæstio est. Hoc sequi necesse est: recito enim tabulas. Sic in Partitionibus dicit modó assumpta,modó sine arte,modó remota: in Topicis has probationes ἄτεχνοι, artis expertes, item assumpta nominat. Quintiliani locus jam anté propositus est.ut ab Aristotele traditã partitionem artificialiũ & inartificialiũ, confensu feré omnium comprobatam diceret: Sed & elenchus ille item patuit,generalem doctrinam omnis entis & non cōmunem speciali-ter explicans, testimoniaq; ad usum forensem referens. Sed καθόλε πρῶτον, hujus elenchi remedium suppeditabit, dicetq;, generalem argumenti logici categoriam generaliter explicandam esse. Quare P.Ramus ut Aristoteleam illam sapientię legem sequeretur,inartificiale argumentum definit, quod ex sese artis hujus, id est probationis & fidei nihil habeat,nihilque sua natura arguat: deniq; sit ἄτεχνον,inartificiale & expers artis : ut etymologia nempe nominis,& privatione artificialis argumenti,vis ejus intelligitur,argumétum quidē arguens & declarans aliquid, sed vi artificialium adjunctorum:Etenim ut definitionis hujus veritas clarior & planior fieret,memini quæ tū in categoriæ hujus expositione P.Ramus à Platone & Aristotele repeteret : Plato cōtra testimoniorum inertiam sæpé disseruit, sed præcipuē in Protagora & Gorgia.Socrates Protagoram ridet à re proposita ad quæstionem de poetis digressum,quos citat ut locupletissimos testes:Videtur enim mihi, ait, disputatio de rebus poeticis, persimilis esse cōviviis imperitorum plebejorumq; hominum, qui cūm propter inscitiam, nequeàt invicem propria voce suisq; sermonib.ipsi colloqui, mercede exhibita,tibicines introducunt,& aliena voce, id est tibiarum flatu,convivium transigunt:ubi autē boni præclarique & eruditi viri conveniunt, neq; tibicines,neq; saltatrices, neq; cātatrices ullas videas,sed voce ƥpria,remotis iis nugis jocisq;, có» vivium celebrare, & alternis interrogationibus » refponsionibusq; modeste differere, etiam si vi » num abunde bibant. Eodem modo ad disputa- » tiones huiusmodi si viri conveniût tales, quales 5 esse nostrûm plurimi prędicant: haudquaquam » aliena voce opus est, neq; poetarum, quos per- » contari de his quæ scribunt,nó datur: & qui eo- » rum testimonia in medium afferût, alii hoc, alii » aliud, poetam dicunt sentire: neque tamen con 10 vincere rem possunt, de qua disserunt, aut expe » dire. Tales ergo confabulationes viri sapientes » mittunt, ipsique inter se colloquuntur, vicissim » que ingenii periculum faciût. Disputatores au- » tem hujusmodi,ut arbitror, ego & tu nunc imi15 tari debemus : & poetis posthabitis, nostris rationibus rem ipsam discutere, facereque tam in genii nostri,quám veritatis periculum. Hic primus est Platonis locus, de veritate rerû ex his artificialibus argumentis exquirenda, deque te 20 stimoniorum tenuissima fide. Atque hic in Protagora Platonis locus est. Secūdus locus est in Gorgia: cùm Polus juvenis de beata vita disputans, authoritate testium maximé niteretur, Socrates eum admonet, veritatem in disputando, 25 non ex teste aliquo,sed ex argumento esse pon- » derádam : ut ea disputádi ratio fit optima, cúm » unicus in caussa adversarius ratione convictus » fuerit: At ego unus (ait) tibi nó assentior:non e- » nim me rationibus cogis, sed falsis testibus con 30 tra me productis, ex ipsa veritatis substantia dejicere me moliris: Ego veró nisi te ipsum testem unum adduxero mihi assentientem, nihil existimatione dignum in his, quæ tractamus, persecisse me arbitror: Nihil etiam te profecturũ puto, nisi ego unus folufq; tibi consentiam: tum omissa aliorum testium multitudine, id ipsum efficias. Est igitur unus, ut dixi, iste arguendi modus quemadmodum tu aliiq; multi putatis; Est & alter, quem ego puto: Eos igitur invicë comparantes, utrum & quo pacto inter se discrepët, diligëter cõsideremus. Ergo hæc Plato, qui idë repetit in Charmide & Critone: Quidnã refert (inquit Charmites) ô Socrates, ex quo audiverim? Nihil (inquam) profecto: Neq; enim id cõsiderandum elt, quis dixerit: sed utrum verè dicatur, necne. Probé nũc loqueris, inquit. Rectè, per jovem, inquam. Simile est illud Socratis in Critone, Consideradum est igitur, agendá ne hæc nobis sint, an non: Nam ego is sum, nõ modo nunc, sed & semper, qui meorũ nulli parea, præterquam rationi, quæ ratiocinati mihi optima videatur. In hunc igitur modum Plato contra testimonia, tot locis disseruit. quod Ariftote les 8. capite 1. de Interpretat. breviter & succinctè repetivit: Neq; enim quia affirmatum fit aut negatũ, ideo erit aut non erit. Neq; omnino philosophus unquá ullus tam videtur id propositũ habuisse, quàm Ariftoteles unus, qui contra omnes omniũ hominũ authoritates liberrimè & senserit & scripserit, cuiq; amicus Socrates, amicus Plato, magis tamen amica veritas fuerit. Idëá Cicerone 1. de Nat. feré propositum est: Nõ enim (ait) tam authores in disputando, quàm rationis momenta quærenda sunt. Quare definitio
units.tr: "By inartificial proofs I mean those that are not supplied by us but already existed beforehand." (Rhetoric 1.) But, as was already clear at the start, when the definition of the artificial argument was given, this definition arose from the forum, where witnesses are commonly brought by the litigant to the orator. A topical precept on finding testimonies would be very ridiculous if it were to teach an art of finding something that could not be found by the artist himself. In the Rhetoric to Alexander the same definition is given in slightly different words. These arguments are called [πίστεις ἐντιθέμεναι τοῖς ἀγομένοις ἢ πραττομένοις ἢ προσλαμβανομένοις], proofs added to the things that are said or done. Cicero in the second book of the Orator calls these arguments "taken from outside", those that are supported not by their own force but by something extraneous, as here: "This is true, for Quintus Lutatius said it"; "This is false, for the case was tried"; "This must follow, for I read out the tablets." So in the Partitions he says they are sometimes "assumed", sometimes "without art", sometimes "remote"; in the Topics he names these proofs [ἄτεχνοι], without art, and likewise "assumed". The passage of Quintilian has already been cited above, where he says that the division of artificial and inartificial arguments, as laid down by Aristotle, is approved by almost universal consent. But that elenchus too has been revealed, which explains in general the doctrine of every being and non-being that is not common, and refers testimonies to forensic use. But [καθόλου πρῶτον] will supply the remedy for this elenchus, and will say that the general category of logical argument must be explained generally. Wherefore P. Ramus, to follow that Aristotelian law of wisdom, defines an inartificial argument as one that of itself has nothing of this art, that is, of proof and credibility, and by its nature proves nothing; in short, it is [ἄτεχνον], inartificial and without art. Its force is understood from the etymology of the name and the privation of the artificial argument: the argument indeed proves and declares something, but by the force of artificial adjuncts. And so that the truth of this definition might be clearer and plainer, I recall what P. Ramus, in setting out this category, drew from Plato and Aristotle. Plato often argued against the inertia of testimonies, but chiefly in the Protagoras and the Gorgias. In the Protagoras, Socrates mocks Protagoras for digressing from the matter proposed to a question about the poets, whom he cites as the most authoritative witnesses: "For it seems to me," he says, "that a discussion about poetic matters is very like the banquets of uneducated and common men, who, because of their ignorance, cannot converse with one another in their own voice and with their own words, and so, having hired pipers, they bring them in and spend the banquet with another's voice, that is, with the breath of the flutes. But where good, outstanding and learned men meet, you will see neither pipers nor dancing girls nor singing girls, but they celebrate the banquet with their own voice, with those trifles and jokes set aside, and debate modestly with questions and answers in turn, even though they drink wine freely. In the same way, when men such as most of us claim to be meet for discussions of this kind, there is no need for a strange voice, nor for poets, whom it is impossible to question about what they have written; and those who bring forward their testimonies in the middle, one says that the poet thinks this, another that he thinks that, and yet they cannot convince or clarify the matter they are discussing. So wise men send such conversations away, and converse among themselves, and test their wit in turn. But we, as I think, ought now to imitate such disputants, you and I, and setting the poets aside, to examine the matter itself by our own reasoning, and to test both our wit and the truth." This is Plato's first passage, on seeking the truth of things by these artificial arguments, and on the very slight trustworthiness of testimonies. And this is the passage in the Protagoras. The second passage is in the Gorgias: when the young Polus, disputing about the happy life, relied chiefly on the authority of witnesses, Socrates reminds him that in disputing truth must be weighed not by some witness but by the argument, so that the method of disputing is best when a single opponent in the case has been convinced by reason. "But I alone," he says, "do not agree with you; for you do not compel me by reasons, but you attempt to dislodge me from the very substance of truth by false witnesses produced against me. But I think that unless I bring forward yourself, as one witness agreeing with me, I have achieved nothing worth consideration in the things we are treating; and I think you will achieve nothing unless I alone agree with you; then, leaving aside the multitude of other witnesses, you may accomplish that very thing. So this manner of arguing, as I said, is one, as you and many others think; there is also another, which I think; let us therefore compare these two with each other, and consider carefully whether and in what way they differ." These are Plato's words, who repeats the same in the Charmides and the Crito. "What does it matter," says Charmides, "Socrates, from whom I heard it?" "Nothing indeed," I say; "for it is not to be considered who said it, but whether it is said truly or not." "You speak well now," he says. "Rightly, by Jove," I say. Similar is that saying of Socrates in the Crito: "It must be considered, therefore, whether these things are to be done by us or not; for I am the sort of man who, not only now but always, obeys no one of mine except reason, which seems best to me on reasoning." In this way Plato argued against testimonies in so many places, which Aristotle briefly and succinctly repeated in the eighth chapter of the first book of the De Interpretatione: "For it does not follow that a thing will be or will not be because it has been affirmed or denied." Nor does any philosopher seem ever to have held this purpose so entirely as Aristotle alone, who both thought and wrote most freely against all the authorities of all men; and though Socrates was his friend, and Plato his friend, truth was nevertheless the dearer friend. Cicero also set down this idea almost in the same terms, in the first book of De Natura Deorum: "For in disputing," he says, "one must seek not so much the authors as the weight of the reasons." Wherefore the definition

units.la: tio illa argumenti inartificialis hinc repetita est P. Ramo, quód hoc argumentum ex sese nihil posset,& quod possit,adjuncta artificialium argumentorum fide possit. potestas tamen hæc adventitia, immensa est per omnem hominis vi tam:Nam fi de capite,fama, fortunisque omnibus(quę maxima & sola bona plerifq; existimâtur)contenditur,non aliis feré argumentis controverfia facti transigitur. Quid igitur?inquies. argumentum artificiale nihil probat,& tamen idem probat omnia? Equidem distinctione unam certam animadverto, ut in artium explicatione & accurata demonstratione,his argumentis locus nullus fit: Sic in mathematicis elementis tis(quæ verissimæ disciplinæ putatur)instituêdis, authoritas prorsus nulla est, neq; Pythagorę,neq; Hippocratis,neq; Leontis.neq; Hermotimi,neq; Euclidis,á quibus inventa & constituta narrantur. At in politicis & popularibus rebus,fi de facto quæritur,inartificialiū argumentorū præcipua & ordinaria vis est: sed veritatis caussis adjutorū.quod Quintilianus libro quinto capite primo, breviter complectitur: Sed ut ipsa per fe(ait)carent arte,ita summis eloquentiæ viribus & allevanda plerunq; & refellenda. Itaq; & Ariftoteles & Quintilianus, hic tátúm communes locos instituére confirmandorū & refellendorum testimoniorum: sed totum foro & judiciis accommodarunt. Ariftoteles caussas perfuafionis & fidei adjunctis testimoniis, uno morum nomine ita complectitur fecundo capite primi Rhetorici: Mores, præcipuam fidê habent. bent.fundamentum igitur fidei inartificialis Aristoteles in moribus collocavit:atq; hinc fama & existimatio testatis. Deinde primo capite secundi Rhetorici in tria genera hac morale causam distribuit: Sunt autem hæc,prudetia, & virtus,& benevolentia. Necesse igitur est eum,qui hæc omnia habere videatur, auditoribus fidei plenum videri.Hæc Aristoteles acutè:in his argumentis fide dignum testem haberi,si sapiens, si probus,si amicus. unde contrarium etiam intelligimus ad refellendum testem adhibendum esse:si hæc omnia, vel eorum aliquid defuerit,in dignũ fide testem futurũ:si & stultus, & improbus,& inimicus: vel tantũ si stultus, si improb9: vel etiam cũm sapiens & probus habeatur, si tñ sit inimicus. Sic idem in Phil. docet argumeti fidem præcipuam esse é moribus & cõsuetudine.
units.tr: That distinction of the inartificial argument was taken over here by P. Ramus, because this argument cannot do anything by itself, but can do something when it is joined to trust in the artificial arguments. Yet this borrowed power is immense throughout all of human life. For if a dispute concerns a man's life, reputation and all his fortunes (which most people count as the greatest and only goods), the question of fact is settled by hardly any other arguments. What then, you will say? Does an artificial argument prove nothing, and yet the same argument prove everything? I myself notice one distinction: in the explanation of the arts and in strict demonstration there is no place for these arguments. So in setting out the elements of mathematics, which is thought the most true of disciplines, authority counts for nothing at all, whether of Pythagoras, Hippocrates, Leontius, Hermotimus or Euclid, to whom discoveries and foundations are attributed. But in political and popular affairs, when a question of fact is raised, the chief and ordinary force lies in inartificial arguments, though they are aids to the cause of truth. Quintilian sums this up briefly in book five, chapter one: "But just as they lack art in themselves, so they must often be lifted up and refuted by the greatest powers of eloquence." Accordingly both Aristotle and Quintilian drew up common topics only for confirming and refuting testimonies, but they adapted the whole to the forum and the courts. Aristotle, in the second chapter of the first book of the Rhetoric, embraces the causes of persuasion and of trust, with testimonies added, under the single name of character: "Character holds the chief place in trust." So Aristotle located the foundation of inartificial trust in character, and from this comes the reputation and esteem of the witness. Then, in the first chapter of the second book of the Rhetoric, he divides this moral cause into three kinds: "These are prudence, virtue, and goodwill." It is necessary, therefore, that the man who seems to possess all of these should seem fully worthy of trust to his hearers. Aristotle says this shrewdly: in these arguments a witness is held worthy of trust if he is wise, upright and friendly. From this we also understand the opposite, that a witness must be discredited if all of these, or some of them, are lacking: he will not be worthy of trust if he is foolish, dishonest and hostile; or if only foolish, or only dishonest; or even when he is held wise and upright, if he is nonetheless hostile. In the same way, in the Philippics he teaches that the trust in an argument comes chiefly from character and habit.

Ramo adhibita: primo ex efficientibus causis, solus deus & homo testari possunt:q par titio est in Partitionib9 Ciceronis: Testimoniũ (ait)est diuinũ & humanũ: Diuinum,ut oracula,ut auspicia, & vaticinationes,& resposa sacerdotum,arúspicum, cõjestorum:humanũ,quod spestatur ex authoritate,& ex volũtate,& ex oratione,aut libera, aut expressa: in quo insunt scripta,paćta,promissa, jura,quæsita. Vatum]Vates á fando, quasi fates,divinator, ppheta:faditic9 « autē, qui fata & decreta deorum interpretatur, «
units.tr: Divine: divine testimonies have no logical or true kinds, either of matter or of form. Yet, so that the wide use of this last category may be made clearer by some description, Ramus uses a species of division: first, from efficient causes, only God and man can testify. This is the division in Cicero's Partitions: "Testimony is divine or human. Divine testimony is that of oracles, auspices, prophecies, and the responses of priests, augurs and soothsayers; human testimony is that which is seen in authority, in will, and in speech, whether free or expressed, in which are contained writings, pacts, promises, laws and things sought." Vates: from fando, as it were fates, a diviner or prophet; but a fadicus is one who interprets the fates and decrees of the gods.

units.la: 3.Catil.] Testimonia divina ad gloriā detectæ conjurationis orator mirificè hic adhibuit: sic autem proposuit: Quanquam hæc omnia, Quirites, ita sunt á me administrata, ut deorum immortalium nutu atq; consilio & gesta, & provifa esse videantur: idq; cúm conjectura consequi possumus, quod vix videtur humanis consiliis tantam molem rerum gubernatio consequi potuisse: tum verò ita præsentem his temporibus opem & auxilium nobis tulerunt, ut deos pené oculis videre possemus. hæc Ciceronis generalis est oratio, quód deorum pené præsentium ope, cōjuratio detecta fit: deinde tria divinorum testimoniorum genera exponuntur, primū de meteoris ostentis: secundum de Aruspicum responsis: tertiū de jovis simulacro, eo die collocato, quo conjurati sunt comprehensi. Quódsi] Tibullus infomniū exponit elegia illa, quod præcedenti noćte de Neȩra somniaverat: utq; Apollo optatum conjugium ei promiserit, mandarit que ut amicæ hoc oraculum annuntiaretur.
units.tr: Speech of 3 Catiline: The orator here marvellously brought forward divine testimonies to the glory of the detected conspiracy. He put it thus: "Although all these things, Citizens, have been carried out by me in such a way that they seem to have been done and foreseen by the nod and counsel of the immortal gods, and we can infer this from conjecture, since the management of so great a mass of affairs hardly seems possible through human counsels alone; and in these times they brought such present help and aid to us that we could almost see the gods with our eyes." This is Cicero's general speech, that the conspiracy was detected by the nearly visible help of the gods. Then three kinds of divine testimony are set out: first, that of meteors and portents; second, that of the responses of the haruspices; third, that of the statue of Jupiter, set up on the day on which the conspirators were arrested. Quodsi: Tibullus, in that elegy, interprets the dream he had the night before about Nera, and how Apollo promised him the marriage he wished for and ordered that this oracle be announced to his mistress.

units.la: Cap. XXXIII. De Testimonio humano.
units.tr: Chap. XXXIII. On Human Testimony.

units.la: Testimonium humanum est, generale aut singulare: generale, ut lex & illustris sententia: legis autem & non scriptæ & scriptæ testimonium est pro Milone: Est enim (judices) non scripta, sed nata lex: quam non didicimus, accepimus, legimus, uerúm ex natura ipsa arripuimus, hausimus, expressimus, ad quam non docti, sed facti: non instituti, sed imbuti sumus: ut si vita nostra in aliquas insidias, si in vim, in tela aut latronum, aut inimicorum inciderit, omnis honesta ratio esset expediendae salutis. & ibidem: Quod si duodecim tabulae noctumū furem quoquo modo, diurnum autem si se telo defenderit, interfici impune voluerunt: quis est, qui quoquo modo quis interfectus sit puniendū putet, cum videat aliquando gladium nobis ad occidendum hominem ab ipsis porrigi legibus? Sententiae illustris sunt proverbia: ut, Pares cum paribus facillime congregantur. Spartam nactus es, hanc exorna. Sunt item dicta sapientium: Nosce teipsum, Ne quid nimis, Spode, praesto est detrimentum. Singulare, ut Platonis illud 1. ad Frat. Atque ille quidem princeps ingenii & doctrinae Plato, tum deniq; fore beatas Respublicas putavit, si aut docti & sapientes homines eas regere coepissent, aut qui regerent, omne suum studium in doctrina & sapientia collocassent. Talia sunt in poetis praecipua. 6. Aeneid. Discite justitiam moniti, et ne temnite divos.
units.tr: Human testimony is either general or particular. General testimony is that of law and of a striking saying. The testimony of law, both unwritten and written, is found in the speech for Milo: "For (judges) it is not written but born law, which we have not learned, received or read, but have seized, drawn in and expressed from nature itself; to which we were not taught but made, not instructed but steeped; so that if our life falls into some ambush, into violence, into the weapons of robbers or enemies, every honourable means of securing safety is permitted." And in the same place: "But if the Twelve Tables wished a thief by night to be killed with impunity in whatever way, and a thief by day if he defends himself with a weapon, who thinks that anyone killed in whatever way should be punished, when he sees that the laws themselves sometimes hand us a sword to kill a man?" Striking sayings are proverbs, such as: "Like with like most easily flock together"; "You have got Sparta, adorn it." There are also sayings of the wise: "Know yourself"; "Nothing in excess"; "Give a pledge, ruin is at hand." Particular testimony is like Plato's saying in book 1 ad Frat.: that the most excellent man of intellect and learning, Plato, thought that commonwealths would be happy only if either learned and wise men had begun to rule them, or those who rule had devoted all their zeal to learning and wisdom. Such are the chief examples among the poets, Aeneid 6: "Learn justice, being warned, and do not despise the gods."

units.la: Sic Homerico illo versu Megarenfes, (Αἴας δ᾽ ἐκ σαλαμῖνος ἄγεν δυοκαίδεκα νῆας) cúm de Salamine contenderent, victi sunt ab Athenienfib. Præfentium & vivorum testimonia sunt, non tantū cúm quæritur de fundo aut cæde & ejufmodi negotio aliquo,sed etiam est obligationis,confessionis,jurisjurādi. Obligationis exemplum est 5. Philip. Audebo etiam obligare fidem meam, P.C.vobis populoq; Ro.(quod profecto cúm me nulla vis cogeret, facere non auderem, pertimefceremq; in re maximé periculo-fa, opinione temeritatis) promitto, recipio, spondeo, P.C. Cæsarem talem semper fore ciuē, qualis hodie fit, qualemq; eum maximé velle & optare debemus. Pignus autem, obligatio quædam est. ut apud Virgil.Ecloga 3.
units.tr: So, in Homer's line, the Megarians, when they contested Salamis, were defeated by the Athenians, since the line runs: "Ajax brought twelve ships from Salamis" [Αἴας δ᾽ ἐκ σαλαμῖνος ἄγεν δυοκαίδεκα νῆας]. Testimonies of those present and living are found not only when the question concerns land, murder or some such business, but also in the case of obligation, confession and oath. An example of obligation is in the Fifth Philippic: "I will also dare to pledge my faith to you, Conscript Fathers and Roman people (which indeed, since no force compelled me, I would not dare to do, and I would fear it in a matter most full of danger, and in the reputation for rashness), I promise, I undertake, I guarantee, Conscript Fathers, that Caesar will always be such a citizen as he is today, and such as we ought most to wish and desire him to be." A pledge is also a kind of obligation, as in Virgil, Eclogue 3.

units.la: Confessio,est libera,vel expressa tormentis,quę proprie quæstio dicitur.Tale fuit argumentum contra Milonem, quod á Cicerone deridetur: Age vero, quae erat aut qualis quaestio? heus? ubi Rufcio? ubi Casca? Clodius insidias fecit Miloni? Fecit certa crux. Nullas fecit. sperata libertas. Huc etiā referri potest argumentum quo utimur, cūm affirmarionis nostrae approbationem & expetientiā pponimus. 4. Verr. Ecquis Volcatio (si sua sponte venisset) unam libellam dedisset? Veniat nūc, experiatur: tecto recipiet nemo. Terēt. in Eunucho:
units.tr: Confession is either free or extracted by torments, which is properly called questioning. Such was the argument against Milo, which Cicero mocks: "Come now, what was the question, and of what kind? Hey! Where is Rufio? Where is Casca? Did Clodius lay an ambush for Milo? He did—a certain cross! He did not—hoped-for freedom!" This argument we use can also be referred here, when we put forward the approval and experience of our assertion. In the Fourth Verrine: "Who would have given Volcatius a single small coin, if he had come of his own accord? Let him come now and try it: no one will take him under his roof." units.la: Reciprocatio hic obscurior est: ut quia testatum verum sit, testis sit etiam varax.
units.tr: The reciprocation here is more obscure: since what is attested is true, the witness is also truthful.

units.la: Humanum]Testimonii humani quaedam species hic utcunque colliguntur, primò generale, r quod nulli singulari homini tribuitur,ut lex, ut illustris sententia: hic modó tria numerátur ab Ariftotele 8.cap.ad Alexādrum, testes,jufiuran dum,quæstiones:modó adduntur duo, ut 15.c. 1.Rhetorici,nempe lex & pactum.Quintilianus addidit prejudicia,famam,tabulas,& separatim testes. P. Ramus legem & illustrem sententiam conjunxit, quia sæpe argumenta generalia continent multarum rerum communia: reliqua frequentiús sunt singularium testium.
units.tr: Human: some species of human testimony are gathered here in some fashion. First, the general kind, which is not assigned to any single person, such as law or a striking saying. Here, three kinds are listed by Aristotle in the eighth chapter of the Rhetoric to Alexander: witnesses, oath, and questioning; sometimes two more are added, as in chapter 15 of book 1 of the Rhetoric, namely law and pact. Quintilian added presumptions, reputation, documents, and witnesses separately. P. Ramus joined law and striking saying together, because general arguments often contain what is common to many things; the rest are more frequently those of particular witnesses.

units.la: Scripta] Sic Ariftoteli νόμω& ἰδιῶς ἢ ἔγραφω& καὶ γεγραμμένω, lex communis aut nō scripta & scripta dicitur:Politici autem legumlatores,ut legibus suis authoritatem & fidem majorem tribuerent,deos authores comméti sunt,ut Lycurgus Apollinem, Solon Palladem, Numa Ægeriam nymphā. Est enim] Milo premebatur ab adversariis,tanquam prejudicio Senatus,quasi senatuscófulto judicatū esset, nefas esse eum lucem intueri, quì á se hominem occisum fateretur. Id variis argumētis refellitur á Cicerone, tum hoc in primis testimonio legis naturalis. præcedit veró illud:Insidiatori & latroni quę potest asserri injusta nex?Quid comitatus nostri?quid gladii voluntā quos habere certé non liceret, si uti illis nullo pacto liceret.
units.tr: Scripta] Thus Aristotle calls a common or unwritten law "law" [νόμω], and a written law "written" [ἔγραφω and γεγραμμένω]. Political lawgivers, wanting to give their laws greater authority and credit, attributed them to gods as their authors: Lycurgus to Apollo, Solon to Pallas, Numa to the nymph Egeria. Est enim] Milo was pressed by his opponents, who argued, as if by a decree of the Senate, that it was wrong for a man who confessed he had killed another to look upon the light. Cicero refutes this with various arguments, above all with this testimony of natural law. He had gone before with this: "What unjust killing can be alleged against an ambusher and a robber? What of our escort? What of the swords we would certainly not be allowed to carry, if it were in no way allowed to use them?"

units.la: Est enim] Argumentatur igitur orator á lege naturali: Permissum est defendendi sui caussa, latronem interficere: non igitur cædes omnis est nefaria.
units.tr: Est enim] The orator therefore argues from natural law: it is permitted to kill a robber in defence of oneself; therefore not every killing is wicked.

units.la: Quód si] Hoc item argumentum ex lege scripta, ad eandem quæstionem adhibetur paulò anté, & habet comparationem majorem admistam testimonio.
units.tr: Quód si] This argument from written law is likewise applied to the same question a little earlier, and it contains a larger comparison mixed in with the testimony.

units.la: Proverbia] Proverbiorum quátus usus sit, declarant Def. Erafmi Chiliades ex hoc argumento solo compositæ Aristoteles cóprehendit sub testimoniis, hoc modo: Item paræmiæ, ut dictū est, testimonia sunt: si quis consulit, amicum senem non esse faciendum: proverbium hoc testificatur, Non esse beneficium in senem collocan dū. Quintilianus proverbia subjicit exemplis, nō recté quidé, neq; logicé: sed tamen quo possit præsentem usum adjuvare: Ea quoque (ait) quæ vulgó recepta sunt, hoc ipso quód incertū autorem habent, uelut omnium fiunt: quale est, ubi amici, ibi opes. &c, conscientia, mille testes. & apud Ciceronem, Pares autem (ut est in vetere proverbio) cum paribus facillimé congregátur. Neq; enim durafsent hæc in æternum, nisi vera omnibus viderentur. Cicero Oratorio secundo hunc etiam jocum petit: In hoc genus (ait) cójiciuntur proverbia: ut illud Scipionis: Cúm Asellus omnes provincias stipendia merentem se peragrasse gloriaretur: Agas Asellum, &c.
units.tr: Proverbia] How great the use of proverbs is, the Chiliades of Desiderius Erasmus declare, a work composed from this argument alone. Aristotle includes proverbs among testimonies, in this way: "Likewise proverbs, as has been said, are testimonies: if someone asks whether he should make a friend of an old man, this proverb bears witness that a benefit should not be bestowed on an old man." Quintilian appends proverbs to examples, not rightly indeed, nor logically, but so that they may help the present use: "Those also (he says) which are commonly received, because they have an uncertain author, are, as it were, of everyone: such as, where there are friends, there are riches, etc.; conscience, a thousand witnesses." And in Cicero: "Equals (as the old proverb has it) most easily gather with equals. For these would not have lasted forever unless they seemed true to everyone." Cicero in the second book of the Orator also seeks this jest: "Into this kind (he says) proverbs are thrown, such as that saying of Scipio's: when Asellus boasted that he had travelled through all the provinces serving the state, 'Go on, Asellus,' etc."

units.la: Pares] Cato in Senectute, hoc testimoniū sic usurpavit: Sæpé enim interfui querelis meorū æqualiū: Pares autem cum paribus, veteri proverbio, facillimé congregantur. Spartam] Hoc etiam est á Cicerone 4. ad Attic. cúm de bello ci vili impendente, cū Attico consultaret, & Rem pub. Tullio defendendam suaderet Atticus. Ad monet autem proverbium, ut quam quisq; arté provinciamve naćtus sit, ut in ea exornanda sese exerceat. Sapientium] De quibus ibidé Quintilianus: Nam illa septem præcepta sapientum, nónne quafdá vitæ leges existimamus? Sapientes autem hi, qui & quomodo tripodis argumé to celebrati sint, Laertius primo libro exposuit. Tria apophthegmata sequentia Plato in Charmide ait pro foribus templi Delphici ab Amphi styonibus inscripta esse, tanquá digna deo oracula: sed primum deo tribuit, reliqua duo mortalibus. Plin. li. 7. cap. 32. cuncta tribuit Chiloni. Rursus mortales (ait) oraculorum' societatem dedere Chiloni Lacedæmonio: tria præcepta ejus Delphis confecrādo aureis literis, quę sunt hæc, Nosse se quemq;. &c, Nihil nimium cupere: Comitemq; æris alieni atq; litis, esse miseriam. Quin & funus ejus, cúm victore filio Olympiæ expirasset, gaudio tota Græcia prosecuta est.
units.tr: Pares] Cato in the Old Age used this testimony thus: "For I have often been present at the complaints of my contemporaries: equals, by an old proverb, most easily gather with equals." Spartam] This too is from Cicero, in the fourth book to Atticus, when Atticus was consulting him about the impending civil war and urging him to defend the commonwealth. He admonishes, by the proverb, that each man should exercise himself in adorning whatever art or province he has been given. Sapientium] On these same matters Quintilian says: "For do we not regard those seven precepts of the wise men as certain laws of life?" Those who were wise, and how and why they were celebrated for the tripod story, Laertius explained in his first book. Plato in the Charmides says that the three following sayings were inscribed before the doors of the Delphic temple by the Amphictyons, as oracles worthy of a god; but he assigns the first to the god and the other two to mortals. Pliny, book 7, chapter 32, assigns them all to Chilon: "Again (he says) mortals gave the company of oracles to Chilon the Lacedaemonian, consecrating his three precepts at Delphi in golden letters, which are these: 'Know yourself'; 'Desire nothing too much'; and 'Debt and litigation are a misery.' Indeed, when he died at Olympia with his son the victor, all Greece followed his funeral with joy."

units.la: Nosce] γνῶθι σεαυτόν. De hoc 1. Tusculana sic Tullius. Est illud quidem vel maximum, Animo ipso animum videre. & nimirum hanc habere vim præceptum Apollinis, quo monet, ut se quisque noscat: Non enim, credo, id præcipit, ut membra nostra aut staturam, figuramve noscamus: Neque nos corpora fumus: neq; ego tibi hæc dicens, corpori tuo dico, sed animo. Quum igitur Nosce te, dicit, Nosce animum tuum. nam corpus quidem, quasi vas est, aut aliquod animi receptaculum: Ab animo tuo quicquid agitur, id agitur à te. Hunc igitur nosse, nisi divinum esset, non esset hoc acrioris cujusdá animi præceptum: sic ut tributum deo sit, hoc est, seipsum posse cognoscere. Hęc Tullius: qui-bus bus consimilia ad finem primi de Legibus.
units.tr: Nosce] "Know thyself" [γνῶθι σεαυτόν]. Concerning this, Tully in the first Tusculan says: "That is indeed the greatest thing: to see the mind itself by the mind. And surely the precept of Apollo, by which he advises that each man should know himself, has this force. For I think it does not prescribe that we should know our limbs or stature or figure: we are not our bodies, nor when I say this to you do I speak to your body, but to your mind. Therefore when he says 'Know yourself,' he says 'Know your mind'; for the body is indeed as it were a vessel, or some receptacle of the mind: whatever is done from your mind, is done by you. To know this, then, unless it were divine, would not be the precept of some keener mind; so that it is attributed to a god, namely, that one can know oneself." Thus Tully; and similar things are said at the end of the first book of the Laws.

units.la: Nequid]Μηδὲν ἄγαν. Laertius Pythagoræ tribu it: Aristoteles tertio Rhetorico, Bianti: alii Thaleti, alii Soloni.
units.tr: Nequid] "Nothing in excess" [Μηδὲν ἄγαν]. Laertius attributes it to Pythagoras; Aristotle, in the third book of the Rhetoric, to Bias; others to Thales, others to Solon.

units.la: Sponde]ἐγγύα, παρὰ δ' ἀτη. Hoc Chilonis est, ut 5 patuit é Plinio: quo Tullius allusit ad Lentulū: Dependendum tibi est, quod mihi pro illo spopondisti. á quo tamen paulò secùs exponitur.
units.tr: Sponde] "Make a pledge, and near ruin is at hand" [ἐγγύα, παρὰ δ' ἀτη]. This is Chilon's, as is clear from Pliny; Tully alluded to it with regard to Lentulus: "You must pay what you pledged to me on his behalf," though it is explained somewhat differently there.

units.la: Atq; ille] Locus est Platonis in quinto de Republica: Nisi Philosophi in civitatibus dominetur: vel hi, qui nunc reges potentefq; dicuntur legitimé serioq; philosophentur: in idemq; civilis potentia, & philosophia concurrant: neque (quod nunc fit) á diversis duobus hæc tractentur ingeniis, non erit civitati, vel (ut mea fert opinio) hominum generi requies ulla malorum: neq; priús hæc Respublica, quam verbis exposuimus, orietur pro viribus, & lumen solis aspiciet. Syllogismus hic est ad laudem & cohortationem Quinti Fratris: Respublica quæ regitur á bono & sapiente principe, est beata: Asia regitur á Quint. Fratre, bono & sapiente principe: beata igitur. interseritur de Marco illud, quód universum imperium aliquádo itá beatum fuerit á M. Cicerone: assumptio autem & conclusio syllogismi sic est deinceps in illa epistola: Quod fortasse aliquando universæ reipublicæ nostræ, nuncquidé profecto isti provinciç contigit: ut is in ea summam potestatem haberet, cui in doctrina, cui in virtute atque humanitate percipienda, plurimú á pueritia studii fuisset & temporis. Quare cura ut hic annus, qui ad labo-
units.tr: Atq; ille] There is a passage of Plato in the fifth book of the Republic: "Unless philosophers rule in states, or those who are now called kings and powers philosophize lawfully and seriously, and civil power and philosophy meet in one, and these things are not handled, as now, by two different natures, there will be no rest from evils for the state, nor (as my opinion holds) for the human race; nor will this commonwealth, which we have set out in words, arise as far as its strength allows, or see the light of the sun." This syllogism is made for the praise and encouragement of Quintus the brother: a commonwealth which is governed by a good and wise prince is blessed; Asia is governed by Quintus the brother, a good and wise prince; therefore it is blessed. Into this is inserted what was said of Marcus, that the whole empire was once so blessed by Marcus Cicero. The assumption and conclusion of the syllogism follow in that letter: "What perhaps has sometimes befallen our whole commonwealth, has now indeed befallen that province: that he should have supreme power in it, who from boyhood had devoted most of his study and time to acquiring learning, to acquiring virtue and humanity. Wherefore take care that this year, which has been added to your labour, may seem likewise to have been prolonged for the salvation of Asia; and since Asia was happier in your keeping than we were in your sending away, bring it about that the joy of the province may soothe our longing."

units.la: » rem tuum accessit, idem ad salutem Afię proro » gatus esse videatur: & quoniam in te retinendo » fuit Asia felicior, quàm nos in deducendo:perfi » ce,ut lætitia provinciæ desiderium nostrum leniatur, Poetis]Poetarum verò testimoniis ora- » tores eloquentiam suam in primis exornarunt: » Itaq; Æschines adversus Demosthenē in foro » profitetur à pueris poetas edisci, ut eorum sen- » tentiis in repub. administranda aliquando utantur, Cicero rariùs poetas in civilibus caussis ad » hibuit: At senex in scholis philosophicis multò » frequentiùs: de quo sic 2. Tuscul. cùm poetarū » versibus multum uteretur,tum Atticus:Interea » unde isti versus? non enim agnosco M. Dicam Hercule: etenim recté requiris. Videsne abundare me otio? A. Quid tum? M.Fuisti sæpe credo, quum Athenis esses in scholis philosophorum. A. Vero, ac libenter. M. Animadvertebas igitur (etsi tum nemo erat admodū copiosus) veruntamē versus ab his admisceri orationi: ac multos quidem à Dionysio Stoico. A. Probè dicis. M. Sed is quasi dictata nullo delecto, multa elegātia: Philo & proprium numerum, & elecĉta poemata, & locos adjungebat. Itaq; postquam adamavi hàc quasi senilem declamationem, stu » dise equidem utor nostris poetis: sed sicubi illi » defecerunt: verti enim multa de Græcis,ne quo » ornamento in hoc genere disputationis careret » latina oratio. Hæc Cic. de poeticis testimoniis. unde intelligimus eloquentiam ipsam velut eloquentiorem his argumentis heri. jam verò, ait Quintil.lib, 5.cap.11.sententiis poetarū non orationes modo refertæ sunt, sed libri etiam philosophorum: qui quanquam inferiora omnia præceptis suis ac literis credunt, repetere tamen auctoritatem a plurimis versibus non fastidierunt.
units.tr: Poetis] Orators, moreover, above all adorned their eloquence with the testimonies of poets. Thus Aeschines, against Demosthenes, declares in the forum that from boyhood he learned the poets by heart, so that he might at some time use their sentiments in administering the commonwealth. Cicero rarely brought poets into civil causes; but the old man (Cato) much more often in philosophical schools. Concerning this, in the second Tusculan: "When Atticus used the verses of poets a great deal, Marcus said: 'Where do those verses come from? For I do not recognise them.' Yes, by Hercules, and you ask rightly. Do you see that I have an abundance of leisure? A.: What then? M.: You were often, I believe, when you were at Athens in the schools of the philosophers. A.: Indeed, and gladly. M.: You therefore noticed (though at that time no one was very copious) that verses were mixed into the speech, and many of them by Dionysius the Stoic. A.: You speak well. M.: But he, as if dictating, without any selection, added many elegant things: a proper metre, chosen poems, and passages. Therefore, since I have come to love this, as it were a senile declamation, I eagerly use our own poets; but where they failed, I translated many things from the Greeks, lest the Latin speech should lack any ornament in this kind of discussion." Thus Cicero on poetic testimonies; whence we understand that eloquence itself, as it were more eloquent, is made to shine by these arguments. Moreover, says Quintilian in book 5, chapter 11: not only orations but also the books of philosophers are filled with the sentiments of poets; and although they believe that all lesser things are to be taken from their own precepts and writings, they nonetheless did not disdain to draw authority from very many verses.

units.la: Discite] Phlegyæ vox est cruciati apud inferos, propterea quòd incendisset Apollinis templū.
units.tr: Discite (Learn): this is the cry of Phlegyas in torment among the dead, because he had set fire to the temple of Apollo.

units.la: — Phlegyasq; miserrimus, omnesAdmonet, & magna testatur voce per umbras, Discite, — &c.
units.tr: "And wretched Phlegyas warns them all and calls out with a loud voice through the shades: Learn, be warned, and do not scorn the gods." Virgil, Aeneid 6.

units.la: Homerico] Aristoteles 15. cap. 1. Rhetorici: ἀλλ᾽ 10 ὑμεῖς... μάρτυρι ἐχρήσαντο περὶ Σαλαμῖνος: Athenienses. Homero teste usi sunt de Salamine: quod & Quintilianus repetit apertius lib. 5. c. 11. Neque est ignobile exemplum, Megareos ab Atheniensibus, cùm de Salamine cötenderent, victos Homeri versu: qui tamen ipse non in omni æditione reperitur, significàs Ajacem naves suas Athenienses junxisse. hæc Quintil. Laertius in vita Solonis addit amplius, Solonem tum in illa contentione, nō solùm usum illo Homeri versu, sed etiam effossa in Salamine cadavera demonstrasse ad Orientē conversa, qui mos esset Atheniensium. Vivorum] Hæc testimonia quotidiana fiunt in foro, & sola vulgò testimonia vocantur, & tanti sunt in controversiis forensibus, ut vulgò, testium probatio, anima litis appelletur. 25
units.tr: Homerico (By Homer's testimony): Aristotle, Rhetoric book 1, chapter 15: "but you used a witness [μάρτυρι ἐχρήσαντο] about Salamis," that is, the Athenians used Homer as a witness about Salamis. Quintilian repeats this more clearly in book 5, chapter 11: "Nor is it an unknown example that the Megarians, when they disputed with the Athenians about Salamis, were defeated by a verse of Homer, which, however, is not found in every edition, showing that Ajax joined his ships to the Athenians." So Quintilian.
