Laertius, in the life of Solon, adds more: in that dispute Solon not only used that verse of Homer but also showed the corpses dug up at Salamis lying turned towards the East, which was the custom of the Athenians. Vivorum (Of living witnesses): these testimonies occur every day in the forum, and are commonly called simply testimonies. In forensic disputes they are so important that the proof by witnesses is commonly called the lifeblood of the case.

units.la: Obligationis] συνθήκη, pactum illud dicitur Aristoteli in his testimoniis inartificialibus: in hoc autem exemplo valdé illius apophthegmatis (Sponde, propé est detrimentum) veritas insignis fuit: hinc & Ciceroni, & universæ Reipub. interitus accidit, cùm adolescentulo Octavio 30 cómissus esset exercitus, quo Rempub. subvertit. Pignus Pignus, vulgó noftris hominibus argumentū ftultorum appellatur, qui nempe artificiali argumēto deftituti, huc redeunt: deniq; & poeta hoc imperitis paftoribus congruenter attribuit: Itaq; cúm Damœtas Menalcá fic irritaffet, Menalcas pari argumento refpondet: — Pocula ponam
units.tr: Obligationis (Of obligation): Aristotle calls this kind of thing a contract [συνθήκη], among his inartificial proofs. In this example the truth of that saying was very clear: "Stand surety, ruin is near." Hence came the ruin both of Cicero and of the whole Republic, when the army, which he had entrusted to the young Octavian, was used to overthrow the Republic. Pignus (Pledge): the pledge, which among our people is commonly called the argument of fools, who, lacking an artificial argument, come back to it. Finally the poet fittingly assigns it to unskilled shepherds. So when Damoetas had thus provoked Menalcas, Menalcas answers with an equal argument: "I will set out cups..."

units.la: Fagina cælatum divini opus Alcimedontis, Quæftio Ariftoteles 17. cap. ad Alexandrū ita definit: Quæftio autē, eft confefsio confcii quidem, fed coacti. Rufcio Milonis fervi ad quæftionem á Clodianis poftulati & torti fuerant: Sed quæftiones urgent Milonem (ait orator) quæ funt habitæ in atrio Libertatis. Quibufnā de fervis? rogas? De P. Clodii. Itaq; quæftiones illas elevat orator argumento cōtradictionis & incōftantiæ, tum minis & pollicitationibus adverfariorum, ut fidem nullam mereantur.
units.tr: A beechwood cup, carved, the work of divine Alcimedon. Quaestio (Torture): Aristotle, in chapter 17 of the work to Alexander, defines it thus: torture is the confession of one who is indeed aware, but is compelled. Rufcio (The slaves of Milo): the slaves of Milo had been demanded for torture by the Clodians and had been tortured. But the orator says that the tortures press Milo, which were held in the atrium of Liberty. Concerning which slaves, you ask? Concerning those of P. Clodius. Therefore the orator dismisses those tortures by an argument of contradiction and inconsistency, and by the threats and promises of his opponents, so that they deserve no trust at all.

units.la: Experientiam Etiam βάσανος id appellatur.
units.tr: Experientiam (Experience): this is also called trial [βάσανος].

units.la: Volcatio Initio Verrinæ quartæ, pecuniæ numerantur datę Verri ob corrumpendū judiciū: Verres negabat fe accepiffe: Cicero cōtrá difpu tat, datas effe Volcatio miniftro Verris, & experientiæ hujus teftimonio argumentatur.
units.tr: Volcatio (Volcatius): at the beginning of the fourth Verrine oration, money given to Verres to corrupt the court is counted out. Verres denied that he had received it. Cicero argues the contrary, that it was given to Volcatius, Verres's agent, and he argues from the testimony of this experience.

units.la: Periculum Hæc actus 3. fcena 2. Parmeno laudat Chæream, pro Eunucho deductam ad Thaidem: ubi artes liberales enumerātur, quibus ingenui adolefcentes erudiri folent.
units.tr: Periculum (Trial): this is in Terence's Eunuch, act 3, scene 2. Parmeno praises Chaerea, who was led to Thais in place of the eunuch, where the liberal arts are listed, in which well-born young men are usually educated.

units.la: Quod magis Clausula eft elegię undecimę, fcriptæ ad inhumanum quendam obtrectatorem, qui exulem etiā accufabat, & infectabatur: Itaq; ut credat, quantis miseriis prematur, definatq; ideo maledicere, optat ei experientiam malorum suorum. jusiurandum]jusiurandum, est affirmatio religiosa: jusiurandum, est cum obtestatione divina, indemonstrabilis affirmatio: id est, quae demonstrari non potsit, ait ibidem Aristoteles: Veteres ethnici jurabant per jovem caeterosq; deos, ut apud Virgil. Æneas, per deos superos & inferos testatur se invitum, & divino jussu coactum Carthagine decesisse in Italiam: quae affirmatio Æneae, interpositis diis testibus, jusiurandum est, id est sancta & religiosa affirmatio.
units.tr: Quod magis (The more so): this is the closing line of the eleventh elegy, written to a certain inhuman detractor who was accusing and attacking even an exile. So that he may believe how great the miseries are by which he is oppressed, and therefore cease to speak evil, the poet wishes him the experience of his own misfortunes. jusiurandum (Oath): an oath is a religious affirmation; an oath is an affirmation, not demonstrable, made with divine invocation, as Aristotle says in the same place: that is, an affirmation which cannot be demonstrated. The ancient heathens swore by Jupiter and the other gods, as in Virgil, where Aeneas calls on the gods above and below to witness that he left Carthage unwillingly and under divine command for Italy. This affirmation of Aeneas, with the gods interposed as witnesses, is an oath, that is, a sacred and religious affirmation.

units.la: Reciprocatio] Haec arguendi vicissitudo in tribus tantum argumentis non exprimitur: in definitione enim est obscura, ut é definito definitio arguatur: obscurior in notatione, ut nomine: sed obscurissima in testamento, ut ipsum re testata disputetur.
units.tr: Reciprocatio (Reciprocation): this interchange of arguing is not expressed in only three of the proofs. In definition it is obscure, so that a definition is argued from what is defined; it is more obscure in notation, as in the name; but most obscure in testament, where the thing attested is itself disputed.

units.la: HACTENUS igitur prima pars Dialecticae à P. Ramo nobis ita proposita est, ut meminisse debeamus, argumetorum & rationum Logica esse propositam, ideoq; argumentis & rationib. perpetuo, no autem rebus subjectis semper ita distinctam, quin eadem res esse possit causa & effectus, subjectum & adjunctum, & caetera omnia: Ut Homo efficitur ex suis causis, & alia etiam efficit: subjectu est multorum adjunctorum, & adjunctu etiá cuju sdam subjecti, ut terrae: pluribus opponi & comparari omni modo potest. Hujus item hoc ipsum est nomen & humanitatis atq; humani conjugatum: totum est suarum partium, & pars alicujus totius, ut mundi: genus est Platonis & Ciceronis: species etiam animalis, definitum & testatum esse potest,ut ipsius & definitio & testimonium. Imó idem argumentū in eadem quæstione variis modis accipi potest.
units.tr: So far, then, the first part of Dialectic has been set out by P. Ramus in such a way that we must remember that it is proposed as logic of arguments and reasons, and therefore is always distinguished by arguments and reasons, not by the subjects themselves, so that the same thing can be a cause and an effect, a subject and an attribute, and all the rest. Thus man is produced from his causes, and also produces other things; he is the subject of many attributes, and also an attribute of some subject, as of earth; in every way he can be opposed to and compared with many things. Likewise, this very word is both "humanity" and what is conjugate with "human"; the whole is of its parts, and a part of some whole, as of the world; it is the genus of Plato and Cicero; also the species of an animal; it can be defined and attested, so that both its definition and its testimony are possible. Indeed, the same argument can be taken in various ways in the same question.

units.la: Rullus opprimit populum: non est igitur popularis, effectum est Rulli: est etiam oppositum popularis: ut etiam ex parte conjugatum. Attamē ratio & definitio cujusq; argumenti diversa. Ita que locis his, eaq; ratione distinctis, omnes vias cujusq; argumenti inveniendi propositas habemus. una inventionis doctrina á Rhetoribus præcipué repetita contra legem λαθόντ ωρῶτον,& mille modis per varias quæstiones iterata. primó loci iidem illi caussarum, factorū, & reliquorum,ad forenses controversias de ambiguo, de scripto & sententia, de contrariis legibus, sunt accommodati: deinde ad quæstiones conjecturę, definitionis, qualitatis, translati sunt: cùm genera facta sunt alia demonstrationis in laudando, vituperando : deliberationis in suadendo, dissuadendo : tandem partibus inventionis eadem inventio servire cœpit: deniq; his omnib9 retentis artibus, facta est illa generalis & universalis argumentorum descriptio. At Deum immortalem? quám laboriosé & solicité in Quintilianum & Cic. imó quám evidenter & perspicuè, tautologia ista infinita á P.Ramo disputata est! non esse doctrinam topicam aliam de partibus orationis, aliam de generibus quæstionum, aliam de statibus caussarum,sed unā & eandem sæpiùs iteratam atq; obscuratam. Deniq; quæ doctrina ab Aristotele in Organo contra leges Aristotelis scripta rescriptaque est, eandem millies a Rhetoribus non dissectam generibus, & partibus novis explicatam, sed eadem prorsus mutatis quibusdam verbis & exemplis, odiosissima & importunissima tautologia positam & repositam. Quamobrem fortiter ad extremum P. Ramus pro regia suscepta professionis vigilia custodiaq;, leges illas sanctas & sacras, & a se pro Logicę salute & dignitate juratas tuebatur, concludebatq;, infinitas inventionis artes pro una generali & universali non esse catholicas, ideoq; tollendas.
units.tr: Rullus oppresses the people; therefore he is not popular: this is the effect of Rullus; it is also the opposite of popular; it is also conjugate in part. Yet the reason and definition of each argument are different. Thus, by these places and by this distinct reasoning, we have all the ways of finding each argument set before us. One doctrine of invention, taken mainly from the rhetoricians, against the rule [λαθόντ ωρῶτον], has been repeated in a thousand ways through various questions. First, those same places of causes, of effects and the rest were adapted to forensic disputes about ambiguity, about the written word and its meaning, about conflicting laws; then they were transferred to questions of conjecture, definition and quality; when other kinds of demonstration were made, in praise and blame, and of deliberation, in persuading and dissuading; finally the same invention began to serve as the parts of invention; and at last, with all these arts retained, that general and universal description of arguments was made. But good heavens! How laboriously and anxiously did P. Ramus dispute this endless tautology, and how evidently and clearly, against Quintilian and Cicero! That there is not one topical doctrine about the parts of speech, another about the kinds of questions, another about the states of causes, but one and the same doctrine, often repeated and obscured. Finally, the doctrine that Aristotle wrote and rewrote in the Organon, against the rules of Aristotle, has been placed and replaced a thousand times by the rhetoricians, not divided by new kinds and parts, but in exactly the same form with certain words and examples changed, in a most hateful and troublesome tautology. For this reason, P. Ramus, at the end, bravely maintained, as a watch and guard of the royal profession he had undertaken, those holy and sacred laws which he had sworn for the safety and dignity of Logic, and he concluded that the infinite arts of invention, not being one general and universal art, are not catholic and therefore must be removed.

units.la: P. RAMI DIALECTICAE LIBRI PRIMI FINIS.
units.tr: The End of the First Book of Peter Ramus's Dialectic.

units.la: PETRI
units.tr: OF PETER

units.la: PETRI RAMI DIALECTICAE LIB. II. de judicio.
units.tr: PETRUS RAMUS, DIALECTICAE LIB. II: On Judgement.

units.la: Cap. 1. Quid judicium & enuntiatum, enuntiatio, affirmatio & negatio.
units.tr: Chapter 1. What judgement is; the proposition, its affirmation and its negation.

units.la: DHuc prima dialecticæ artis pars fuit in Inventione: pars altera sequitur in judicio. judicium est pars Logicæ de disponendis argumentis ad bene judicandum: Certa enim dispositionis regula unumquodq; judicatur: unde hæc pars Logicæ & judicium & dispositio pro eodem dicitur. judicium est enuntiati aut syllogismi & methodi. Enuntiatum est dispositio, qua argumentum de argumento enunciatur: pro eodem enuntiatio, pro nuntiatum, pronuntiatio, effatum dicitur. Partes enuntiati duæ sunt: prima antecedens, secunda consequens appellatur, é quibus oriuntur enûtiati affectiones, affirmatio primùm & negatio. Enûtiatum affirmatum, est quando consequens cum antecedente componitur: negatum quando consequens ab antecedente dividitur. hinc nascitur enûtiatorum contradictio, quādo affirmatur & negatur idem consequens de eodem antecedente.
units.tr: Hitherto the first part of the art of dialectic has been invention; the second part follows in judgement. Judgement is the part of logic concerned with arranging arguments so that they may be well judged, for each thing is judged by a certain rule of arrangement. Hence this part of logic is called by the same name both judgement and disposition. Judgement is of the proposition, of the syllogism and of method. The proposition is the arrangement by which one argument is predicated of another argument. It is also called the enunciation, the utterance, the pronouncement or the statement. The parts of a proposition are two: the first is called the antecedent, the second the consequent, and from these arise the affections of the proposition, first affirmation and then negation. A proposition is affirmative when the consequent is joined with the antecedent, and negative when the consequent is separated from the antecedent. Hence arises the contradiction of propositions, when the same consequent is both affirmed and denied of the same antecedent.

units.la: Primæ partis explicatio, P. Rami diligētiam in obseruandis legibus Aristotelis explicauit, cum tam multa ab eo tamq; varia in quatuor & quadraginta Aristoteleis voluminibus præcepta de argumentis subducta, comparata, reformata sint: Materies in hac judicandi parte minor erit. Sex enim tātum libris in Aristotelis bibliotheca judicium logicum comprehenditur, duob9 de Interpretatione, quatuor Analyticis: quorum pars etiam magna abducta est locis argumentorum, de quibus superiore libro actum est. Quare aduersus tautologias, quales in locis inuentionis innumerabiles fuerunt, certamen P. Ramo nullum admodū hic fuit: aduersus tamen obscuritatem, certamen longe grauissimū fuit. Definitur igitur primo judicium, pars Dialecticæ de disponendis argumentis ad bene judicādum. Definita est antea inuentio, pars Dialecticæ de inueniendis argumentis, & nunc analogia seruatur, judicium est pars Dialecticæ de disponendis argumentis. sed additur (ad bene judicandum) qui finis est dispositionis logicæ.
units.tr: In explaining the first part, P. Ramus has set out his diligence in observing the laws of Aristotle, since so many and such various precepts about arguments have been drawn out, compared and reformed from Aristotle's forty-four volumes. The matter of this part of judging will be smaller. For logical judgement is contained in only six books of Aristotle's library, two On Interpretation and four Analytics, and a large part of these has been drawn away into the places of arguments, which were treated in the previous book. Therefore P. Ramus had no great contest here against the tautologies, which were innumerable in the places of invention; but the contest against obscurity was by far the most serious. Judgement is first defined, then, as the part of dialectic concerned with arranging arguments so that they may be well judged. Invention was defined earlier as the part of dialectic concerned with finding arguments, and now the analogy is kept: judgement is the part of dialectic concerned with arranging arguments. But the phrase "for good judging" is added, which is the end of logical arrangement.

units.la: Certa] Tota judicii doctrina enim in sex illis Aristotelis libris, si spectetur ē reipsa, dispositio est: ἐμλωά: est dispositio argumenti cum argumento: analysis prior in componendo syllogismo est dispositio tertii argumenti cum duobus argumentis dubii enuntiati: methodus est dispositio complurium & variorum vel enuntiatorum, vel syllogismorum. Itaque judicii doctrina est disponendi argumenti doctrina, ut inventionis doctrina fuit inveniendi argumenti doctrina. Id P. Ramus hanc judicii definitionem explicans, ē rebus ipsis differebat, non ē testimoniis hominum, quę nulla admodum isto loco ajebat esse quinetiam rursus ē rebus ipsis cōcludebat judicii doctrinam neq; Quintiliano, neq; Ciceroni, neq; etiā ipsi Aristoteli (quamvis ipsis natura & usus minime defuissent) satis explicata fuisse. De Quintiliano res apertior est libri 3. cap. 3. cūm dixisset de Rhetoricæ partibus inventione, dispositione, elocutione, memoria, actione: His adjecerunt (ait) quidam sextam partem, ita ut inventioni judicium subnecterent, quia primū esset invenire, deinde judicare. Ego porrò ne invenisse quidem credo eum, qui non judicavit. Hic rhetor non obscurē loquitur judicandi artem, dispositionis arte minimē sibi videri. sed apertissimē libri 6. cap. 6. idem repetit, cūm de locis inventionis dixisset: His (ait) pro nostra facultatis tractatis non dubitasset transfire pro tinus ad dispositionē, quę ordine ipso sequitur: nisi vererer ne (quoniam fuerint, qui judicium inventioni subjungerent) præteriisse hunc locum quibusdam viderer: qui mea quidem opinione, adeo partibus operis hujus omnibus cōnexus ac miltus est, ut ne à sententiis quidē, aut verbis saltem singulis posset separari: nec magis arte traditur, quàm gustus aut odor. Ideoq; nos quid in quaq; re sequendum cavēdumq; sit, do cebicebimus ut ad ea judicium dirigatur. Hæc Quintiliani verba, manifestam hominis sententiá de nulla judicii doctrina clarissimé demonstrant. Tota verò dispositionis doctrina, quæ ab illo traditur, nullam vel enûtiati, vel syllogismi doctrinam continet: tantùm quiddà de methodo partium orationis continet. Neque verò Ciceronis alia sapientia hîc videtur fuisse, qui in Oratorio secundo, in Oratore perfecto, in Partitionibus, post expositos inventionis locos, quædá de judicio & delectu argumentorum, antequam ad dispositionis doctrinam accedat, interpretatur: neque omnino intelligit, judicii doctrinam dispositione fieri. Quinetiam in Topicis, cùm Stoicá de syllogismis doctrinam cum argumentorum locis complectitur, non arbitratur interea se judicii vel dispositionis ullam doctrinam complecti. Ergo Rhetores hi nullam judicii doctrinam in dispositione versari arbitrantur. Aristotelis sensus videtur idem esse in Organo: siquidem doctrina judicii, prima de enuntiato, secunda de syllogismo, tertia de methodo, variis dispositionis generibus explicatur: judicii nomen aperté núquam à philosopho & manifesté proponitur. atque in Rhetoricis libris prorsus simillis est illorum Rhetorum: neque dispositionis arte, ullam vel enuntiati, vel syllogismi doctrinam instituit. sed tradit tantùm quandam partium orationis methodum. Quamobrem (ajebat hîc P. Ramus) ut Quintiliano, Ciceroni, Aristoteli etiam ipsi judicii naturam & usum quamlibet excellenté attribuas, doctrinam certé exploratam, & dispositionis generibus diftin ctam non possis attribuere: ut nihil mirum sit, scholasticis hominibus, dialectici præsertim usus imperitis, istam judicii doctrinam tam nová,tamq; insolentem videri. Itaq; diligentia hic in primis opus est, & ad leges Aristotelis initio propositas attentione: ut quoniam authoritas hominis deest, nihil nisi perspectæ veritati & ac curatæ considatur.
units.tr: Certa] For the whole doctrine of judgement in those six books of Aristotle, if one looks at the matter itself, is arrangement. The relation of argument to argument is arrangement; the prior analysis, in composing a syllogism, is the arrangement of a third argument with the two arguments of a doubtful proposition; method is the arrangement of several and various propositions or syllogisms. Thus the doctrine of judgement is the doctrine of arranging arguments, just as the doctrine of invention was the doctrine of finding arguments. In explaining this definition of judgement, P. Ramus differed from others, and drew his conclusions from the matters themselves and not from the testimony of men, which he said was of no great weight in this place. Moreover, he concluded again from the matters themselves that the doctrine of judgement had not been sufficiently explained by Quintilian, nor by Cicero, nor even by Aristotle himself, although they had by no means lacked natural ability and practice. With regard to Quintilian the matter is more evident in book 3, chapter 3. When he had spoken of the parts of rhetoric (invention, disposition, elocution, memory, delivery), he says: "Some have added to these a sixth part, so that they join judgement to invention, because it is first to find and then to judge. But I do not think that he has even found who has not judged." This rhetorician speaks plainly enough of the art of judging, and clearly does not think it belongs to the art of disposition. But most openly, in book 6, chapter 6, he repeats the same thing, when he has spoken of the places of invention: "Having treated these according to the measure of my ability, I would not hesitate to pass straight on to disposition, which follows in order; except that I fear (since there have been some who join judgement to invention) that I might seem to have passed over this place, which in my opinion is so connected with all the parts of this work, and so mixed up with them, that it cannot be separated from the thoughts or even from the individual words. Nor is it taught by art any more than taste or smell is. Therefore I shall show what is to be followed and what avoided in each matter, so that judgement may be directed to those things." These words of Quintilian most clearly show that the man's opinion is that there is no doctrine of judgement. The whole doctrine of disposition that he hands down contains neither a doctrine of the proposition nor of the syllogism; it contains only a certain method of the parts of a speech. Nor does Cicero seem to have had any other wisdom here. In the second book of the De oratore, in the Orator, in the Partitiones, after setting out the places of invention, he explains certain things about judgement and the choice of arguments before he comes to the doctrine of disposition; and he does not at all understand that the doctrine of judgement is accomplished by disposition. Moreover, in the Topics, when he embraces the Stoic doctrine of syllogisms together with the places of arguments, he does not think that he is thereby embracing any doctrine of judgement or disposition. Therefore these rhetoricians do not think that any doctrine of judgement lies in disposition. The sense of Aristotle seems to be the same in the Organon: indeed the doctrine of judgement, first of the proposition, second of the syllogism, third of method, is explained in various kinds of disposition; yet the name of judgement is never clearly and openly put forward by the philosopher. And in the books of the Rhetoric he is altogether similar to those rhetoricians, and by the art of disposition he establishes no doctrine either of the proposition or of the syllogism, but hands down only a certain method of the parts of a speech. Therefore (said P. Ramus here), although you may attribute to Quintilian, Cicero and even Aristotle an admirably excellent nature and use of judgement, you cannot attribute to them a tested doctrine distinguished by kinds of disposition. So it is no wonder that this doctrine of judgement seems so new and so strange to scholastic men, especially to those unskilled in the use of dialectic. Therefore diligence is especially needed here, and attention to the laws of Aristotle laid down at the beginning, so that, since the authority of men is lacking, we may rely on nothing but truth clearly seen and carefully examined.

units.la: Pro eodem judicium, pars hæc ex fine appellatur: Græcé illud est λεπτόν, & doctrina ipsa λεπτική: & sic Quintilianus 14. cap. 5. lib. declarat, cùm ait: Dialectici sibi & inveniendi & judicandi vé dicant partes: quarum alteram τεχνική, alteram λεπτική vocát. Aristoteli ἀναλυτικός est ipsa disputationis jam factæ (tanquam diceres) resolutio & exploratio. Quáquam paulò secús de verbo isto Græci interpretes afferunt: quód ἀναλύειν sit ἀποδημούντων περὶ ἀναφερομένων ἐς τὰ εἰκαῖα, peregrinantium & domũ reversorum. At analysis, geometrica metaphora est: sic enim Geometræ nominant quæstionis reditũ ad principia, ut sit inver sio, quę cótrá ex effecto opere revertatur ad prima principia. quales adhuc in Euclide, Archimede Apollonio. P. Rami scholæ mathematicæ adnotabunt: & Aristot. 33. cap. 1. Prior. eum sen sum demonstravit: ubi genesim & analysin op. posuit invētioni, & sic ἀναλυτικά videntur eidem idé esse, quod λεπτικά: & certé 3. cap. 4. libri in Philof. cúm judicandi imperitiam in veteribus phi. losophis reprehendit, ait, διὰ ἀπαιδευσίαν τῶν ἀναλυτικῶν τῶν τόπων ἀρχῶν, propter imperitiam analyticorũ id faciunt. tanquam ἀναλυτικὰ τῆς κειμένα essent eadem. Dispositionis autem verbum ex efficiētia sumitur, quia inde judicium fiat: & variis nominib9 Aristoteli dicitur: in Rhetoricis τάξις in Organo ἀνάλυσις: item θέσις, διάθεσις, γένεσις, positio, dispositio, compositio: θέσις in primo Analytico, capitib. 5. 6. 7. 24. cum de medii ordine & situ praecipitur: διάθεσις duodecimo capite primi Posteriorum, cum agitur de captione syllogismi propter dispositionem: γένεσις autem syllogismo tribuitur 33. cap. 1. Prior. cum genesis etiam enunciato & methodo tribui posit. Ergo haec de definitione & nomine secundae partis. Dispositionis igitur logicae fructus est judicium: sed alius praeterea memoriae confirmandae fructus percipitur: & omnia quaecunque de memoriae arte praecepta sunt, huc redeunt deniq; ut uni ordinis dispositionisq; beneficio debeantur. Itaq; Quintilianus 2. cap. 11. lib. derisis Rhetorum simulacris & imaginibus, Verum (ait) in his quae scripsimus complectendis multum valet, & in his quae cogitamus, continendis, proprie sola (excepta, quae potentissima est, exercitatione) divisio & copositio. Atqui, inquam, ars divisionis & compositionis, in hanc logicae dispositionis artem tota succedit. Itaque Aristoteli 3. cap. 13. libri Philosoph, τάξις, dispositio merito inter τὰ καλὰ μίγιστα ἀλλ, pulchritudinis praestantissimas species numeratur: & in eadem Philos. quarto capite primi libri: Quoniam vero contraria bonis inesse apparent in natura, neq; solum dispositio & pulchritudo, sed cofusio & turpitudo & plura mala bonis & turpia pulchris. Quo loco cotraria oppo- nuntur, τάξις, καλὸν, ἀγαθὸν. ite ἀναξία, αἰσχρὸν, φαῦλον: ut intelligi inde laus secundae partis Logicae no exigua posit. judicium] Partitio judicii bifariā fit, & διχοτομία retinetur à P. Ramo, quae antea studiose servata est, & in hec duo membra subeunt omnia, quae ufquā vel á philosophis, vel á Rhetorib.de logica dispositione vel de logico judicio descripta sunt. Primū genus, enuntiatū dicitur: secundū fine nomine per duas species exprimitur: ut Ariftotelis exēplo locis aliquot antea factum est. Poterat ἐντικὸν, ηθὶ ἀδιαντικὸν judicium fieri, ut ἀδιαντικὸν esset genus fyllogistici & Methodici.
units.tr: Pro eodem judgement: this part is named from its end. In Greek it is [κριτικόν], and the doctrine itself [κριτική]. So Quintilian also declares in book 14, chapter 5, when he says: "Dialecticians call the parts of themselves both invention and judgement; of these they call one [τεχνική], the other [κριτική]." For Aristotle, [ἀναλυτικός] is the resolution and examination of a dispute already completed (as you might say). Yet the Greek interpreters give a slightly different account of this word, namely that [ἀναλύειν] means "to travel abroad and return home", that is, to go back to the things from which one came. But analysis is a geometrical metaphor: for geometers call the return of a question to its principles by this name, so that it is an inversion which turns back from the finished work to the first principles. Such analyses are still found in Euclid, Archimedes and Apollonius; the mathematical schools of P. Ramus will note this. And Aristotle, in book 1, chapter 33 of the Prior Analytics, showed this sense, where he set genesis and analysis against invention; and so [ἀναλυτικά] seem to be the same as [κριτικά]. Certainly, in book 3, chapter 4 of the Philosophy, when he reproaches the older philosophers for their lack of skill in judging, he says: "[διὰ ἀπαιδευσίαν τῶν ἀναλυτικῶν τῶν τόπων ἀρχῶν]", that is, they do this through lack of training in the analytic principles of places, as if [ἀναλυτικά] and the principles were the same. The word for disposition, however, is taken from the effect, because judgement comes from it; and Aristotle names it by various terms: in the Rhetoric [τάξις] (order), in the Organon [ἀνάλυσις] (analysis); likewise [θέσις, διάθεσις, γένεσις]: position, disposition, composition. [θέσις] occurs in the first Analytics, chapters 5, 6, 7 and 24, where the order and situation of the middle term is taught; [διάθεσις] in chapter 12 of the first book of the Posterior Analytics, where the capture of a syllogism through its disposition is treated; and [γένεσις] is attributed to the syllogism in chapter 1 of the Prior Analytics, book 33, where genesis may also be attributed to the proposition and to method. So much for the definition and name of the second part. The fruit of logical disposition is therefore judgement; but there is also another fruit, that of strengthening memory, and all the precepts of the art of memory come back in the end to the benefit of order and arrangement alone. So Quintilian, in book 2, chapter 11, after mocking the images and simulacra of the rhetoricians, says: "But in gathering what we have written, and in holding what we think, division and composition are of great value, and indeed (apart from practice, which is the most powerful of all) these alone." Now, I say, the art of division and composition is wholly succeeded by this art of logical disposition. Therefore in Aristotle, book 3, chapter 13 of the Philosophy, [τάξις] (order), disposition, is rightly numbered among the most excellent species of beauty [τὰ καλὰ μέγιστα]. And in the same philosophy, in the fourth chapter of the first book: "But since contraries appear to be present in nature, not only order and beauty but also confusion and ugliness, and many evils together with goods, and the base together with the fair." In this place the contraries are opposed: [τάξις, καλόν, ἀγαθόν] (order, beauty, goodness), and in the opposite [ἀναξία, αἰσχρόν, φαῦλον] (disorder, ugliness, baseness). From this it may be understood that no small praise of the second part of logic can be given. judgement] The division of judgement is made in two parts, and the dichotomy [διχοτομία], which was earlier carefully observed, is retained by P. Ramus; and under these two members fall all the things that have been described anywhere, either by philosophers or by rhetoricians, concerning logical disposition or logical judgement. The first kind is called the proposition; the second, which has no name of its own, is expressed by two species, as was done a little earlier by the example of Aristotle. It would have been possible for judgement to be [συλλογιστικόν] and [μεθοδικόν], so that the [ἀδιαντικόν] would be the genus of the syllogistic and the methodical.

units.la: Enuntiatum] Primum judicii genus definitur (quomodo prima feré genera definiri possunt) dispositio, qua argumentū de argumēto enūtiatur: hic enim dispositio est argumentorū: quorū autē, & inde cum quibus dicetur postea: & magis per species, res ipsa intelligetur. In Organo feré definitur per speciales affectiones affirmationis & negationis, veritatis & falsitatis: sed tamē aliqd est praeterea generale, quod ipsum potius intelligi fit necesse: itaq; generaliter modo intelligatur enūtiare, ut postea concludere, ut ordine priora praeponere: Enuntiare autē jam Logicis nequaquā verbum grammaticum fit, grammaticis enūntiare, fit extra alteri alicui nūtiare: tibi enim ipsi solus & tacitus hoc enuntiare potes ut concludere, ut ordine disponere: & Aristoteles. 8.c.1. Post. vere admonuit neq; demonstrationem, neq; syllogismum ullum esse sermonis exterioris, sed interioris rationis.λόγῳ & ἐ͏́ξω, λόγος ὁ ἐσω illic dicitur: grecum Ariftotelis verbū προτάσεως hic convenientius erat,& ad sensum logicæ dispositionis aptius:& Ariftoteli προτάσιν προ τάνειν, ita dicitur,ut πρόβλημα προβάλλειν. Sed προτα σις, vel propositionis verbum, ad primam fyllo gifmi parte explicandum proprie usurpabitur. Evitandæ igitur ambiguitatis caufla, P.Ramus πρότασιν hic non aflumpfit. Alia sunt in Organo hujus primi judicii vocabula, sed rariora,λῆμμα, 10 λῆψις, sumptū, fumptio : item ἀξίωμα, θέσις, ὑπόθεσις, poftulatū, positio, suppositio:ἑρμηνεία, interpretatio etiam pro eodem videtur esse in titulo doctrinæ huic operi destinatæ:quanquam Ariftoteles in illo opere id verbum nunquam usurpavit:ἀπόφασις, enuntiatum ex omnibus Ariftotelis verbis latinæ scholæ magis ufurparūt:quanquam de multis illis Ariftotelis nominibus,ἀξίω μα præcipue Cicero interpretatur quinque locis in Philosophia:primum in Faco : Omne enū 20 tiatum,aut verum aut falsum:ibidem enūtiatio: Omnis enuntiatio (quod ἀξίωμα Dialectici appellant) aut vera,aut falsa est. Ite:Explicada vis est ratioque enuntiationum,quę græci ἀξιώματα vocant.at prima Tufculana pronuntiatum:Pro 25 nuntiatum (sic mihi in præfentia occurrit, ut appellarem ἀξίωμα:utar pòst alio,si invenerio meliús)id ergo est pronuntiatum,quod verum est aut falsum,& ibidem pronuntiatio: Omnis pronūtiatio,est vera aut falsa. Effatum autem 4. A-30 cad.dicitur. Fundamentum Dialecticę est,quicquid enuntiatur(id aūt appellatur ἀξίωμα,quod est quasi effatum) aut verum esse, aut falsum. Ergo Ciceronis vocabula, pro Graeco ἀξίωμα vero, quinque sunt, Enuntiatum, Enuntiatio, Pronuntiatū, Pronuntiatio, Effatum: quae ipse, dum rem novam Romanis auribus explicat, in hunc logicum sensum innovavit: & illa veniae praefatione (dum melius invenero) diffidentiam quādam significat verbi nō satis fideliter conversi: haec enim verba omnia, Enuntiatum, Enuntiatio, Pronuntiatum, Pronuntiatio, Effatum, magis sunt externi & grammatici sermonis, quām interioris & logicę rationis: attamē res ipsa per inde intelligatur, ut enuntiatio fit, quanvis sola mente talis dispositio concipiatur. Optabat autem hic P. Ramus, ut Tullius axiomatis verbū usu lanitatis potiús donasset, ut Grammaticæ, Logicæ, & consimilium fecit: ut syllogismi nomen, ut methodi, saltem in scholis facto est: concruentius enim fuisset ad hoc totum axiomaticum judicii genus explicandū, quod per se suaque fide probatur. Atqz haec de primi judicii definitione & nomine. Clinomachus Thurius πρῶτος περὶ ἀξιωμάτων συγγραφὴν, primus de axiomatis conscripsit, ait Laertius libro 2. quod si verū est, principiū doctrinae hujus ei philosopho debeatur, quae deinde translata sit ab Aristotele in librum περὶ ἑρμηνείας.
units.tr: Enuntiatum] The first kind of judgement is defined (as first kinds generally can be) as the arrangement by which one argument is stated of another. Here the arrangement is of arguments, and what kinds of arguments they are, and with what they are stated, will be said later; the thing itself will be understood more clearly through the species. In the Organon it is defined mostly by the special affections of affirmation and negation, truth and falsity, but there is also something more general, which must be understood in itself. So let to state be understood generally, as to conclude and to set prior things before in order. For logicians, however, to enunciate is by no means the grammatical word. For grammarians, to enunciate is to announce something outwardly to another person. You can state this to yourself alone and silently, as you can conclude and arrange in order. Aristotle, in Posterior Analytics 8, c. 1, rightly warned that neither demonstration nor any syllogism belongs to outward speech but to inward reason. There it is called outward speech and inward reason [λόγος ὁ ἐξω, λόγος ὁ ἐσω]. The Greek word proposition [προτάσεως] would have fitted better here and suited the sense of logical arrangement more closely. Aristotle also says to put forward a proposition [προτάσιν προτείνειν], just as one says to throw forward a problem [πρόβλημα προβάλλειν]. But proposition [πρότασις], or the word proposition, will properly be used to explain the first part of a syllogism. So, to avoid ambiguity, P. Ramus has not adopted πρότασις here. The Organon has other words for this first judgement, but rarer ones: lemma [λῆμμα] and lepsis [λῆψις], meaning assumption; likewise axioma [ἀξίωμα], thesis [θέσις] and hypothesis [ὑπόθεσις], meaning postulate, position and supposition. Hermeneia [ἑρμηνεία], interpretation, also seems to mean the same thing in the title of the doctrine destined for this work, although Aristotle never used that word in that work. Apophasis [ἀπόφασις], enunciation, is the word the Latin schools have used more than any other of Aristotle's terms. Cicero, however, explains many of those Aristotelian names, especially axioma [ἀξίωμα], in five places in his Philosophy. First, in the Academics: "Every enuntiatum is either true or false." In the same place: "Every enuntiatio (which dialecticians call axioma) is either true or false." Again: "The force and reason of enuntiationes is to be explained, which the Greeks call axiomata." In the first Tusculan Disputation he has pronuntiatum: "I have, for the present, a pronuntiatum (this is what occurs to me, so that I would call it axioma; I shall use another word later if I find a better one). Therefore that is a pronuntiatum which is true or false," and there, "every pronuntiatio is true or false." Then in the fourth Academic book it is called effatum: "The foundation of dialectic is that whatever is enuntiated (and this is called axioma, which is as it were an effatum) is either true or false." So Cicero has five words for the Greek axioma: Enuntiatum, Enuntiatio, Pronuntiatum, Pronuntiatio, Effatum. While explaining a new thing to Roman ears, he gave these a logical sense, and by that prefatory apology ("until I find a better one") he signals some uncertainty about a word not rendered very faithfully. All these words, enuntiatum, enuntiatio, pronuntiatum, pronuntiatio, effatum, belong more to outward, grammatical speech than to inward, logical reason. Still, the thing itself is understood in the same way, so that it is an enuntiatio even if such an arrangement is conceived by the mind alone. P. Ramus wished, however, that Tully had given the word axioma to common usage rather than to a technical sense, as he did with the words of grammar, logic and similar arts, and as the name syllogism and the name method have been made common, at least in the schools. For that would have been more fitting for explaining this whole axiomatic kind of judgement, which is established by its own nature and its own credibility. So much for the definition and name of the first judgement. Clinomachus of Thurii "first wrote a treatise on axiomata" [πρῶτος περὶ ἀξιωμάτων συγγραφὴν], according to Laertius, book 2. If that is true, the beginning of this doctrine should be credited to that philosopher, and it was afterwards transferred by Aristotle into the book On Interpretation.

units.la: Partes] Partes enuntiati vocantur fere in Organo vocabulis mathematicis, ὅροι, termini. Et sic Aristot. 1. cap. 1. Pri. ὅρον δὲ λέγω, ὡς ὃν διαλύεται ἡ προτάσεις, Terminum aut dico, in quē resolvitur propositio, sed terminus dicitur, ἐγγύμενος, ἐπόμενος anteantecedens, consequens: ut enūtiati (Homo est animal) homo est pars antecedens : est animal, est consequens enunciati. Si dies est, lucet. antecedens est (Si dies est) consequens, (lucet.)
units.tr: Partes] The parts of the enuntiatum are called, in the Organon, mostly by mathematical words: horoi, that is, termini [ὅροι]. So Aristotle, Prior Analytics 1, c. 1: "I call a term that into which a proposition is resolved" [ὅρον δὲ λέγω, εἰς ὃν διαλύεται ἡ προτάσεις]. The terms are called antecedent [ἡγούμενος] and consequent [ἑπόμενος]. In the enuntiatum "Man is animal", man is the antecedent part and is animal the consequent part. In "If it is day, it is light", the antecedent is "If it is day" and the consequent is "it is light".

units.la: Enunciati] In enūtiato duo omnino spectāda sunt quid enuntietur, & quo modo: Quid argumentorum genera côplectitur: quod in ipsa enunciati definitione monuimus generaliter, p species specialiter intelligetur in enūtiato simplici & compositō. modus autem est, quomodo enuntiatū & negetur & judicetur, quæ duo propriam artem requirunt, in hoc primo judicii genere. Prima modi affectio, est affirmationis & negationis: secunda veritatis & falsitatis. Affirmatio & negatio sumitur é partiū cōpositione & divisione: ut cūm dicis, Homo est animal. consequens (animal) componitur cum antecedente (homo) ideoq; affirmatur enuntiatum: Contrá autē (Homo non est animal) consequens idem dividitur ab eodē antecedente, & negatū dicitur enuntiatum. Item Si dies est, lucet consequens (lucet) componitur cum antecedente (dies) contrá, Non si dies est, lucet. consequēs dividitur ab antecedente, & enuntiatum negatur. Deniq; affirmatio & negatio enuntiati, nihil aliud est, quám partium compositio & divisio: Itaque Aristoteli συμβισις περὶ διαιρεσεως appellātur 2. cap. 1. de Interpretatione. Sed per species hæc generalis affectio plenius intelligetur. Contradictio] Ἀντίφασις, quę ad verbum, contradictio, pro quavis enuntiatorum oppositione, sic usurpatur decies octies ab Aristotele in libro de Interpretatione.
units.tr: Enunciati] In the enuntiatum two things altogether must be considered: what is enuntiated, and how. What is enuntiated comprehends the kinds of arguments, which we noted in general in the definition of the enuntiatum itself; the species will be understood specially in the simple and the compound enuntiatum. The mode is how the enuntiatum is both affirmed or denied and judged, and these two things require a proper art in this first kind of judgement. The first affection of the mode is affirmation and negation; the second is truth and falsity. Affirmation and negation arise from the composition and division of parts. For example, when you say, "Man is animal," the consequent (animal) is composed with the antecedent (man), and therefore the enuntiatum is affirmed. On the contrary, "Man is not animal": the same consequent is divided from the same antecedent, and the enuntiatum is said to be negated. Likewise, "If it is day, it is light": the consequent (it is light) is composed with the antecedent (if it is day). On the contrary, "Not if it is day, it is light": the consequent is divided from the antecedent, and the enuntiatum is negated. Finally, the affirmation and negation of an enuntiatum is nothing other than the composition and division of parts. So Aristotle calls it symbasis peri diairesēs [συμβασις περὶ διαιρεσεως], in On Interpretation 2, c. 1. But this general affection will be understood more fully through the species. Contradictio] Antiphasis [Ἀντίφασις], which word for word is contradictio, is used by Aristotle in the book On Interpretation many times, for any opposition of enuntiata.

units.la: s terpretatione, ne quis miretur á P.Ramo ficufurpari: neq; cõtradiction is genus hic aliud eft, quám fuit in fuperiore libro : fed fpecies fubjecta rei eft diverfa : E diffentaneis enim attributis,diffentaneę propofitiones dici poffunt,& diverfæ & difparatæ & relatæ & adverfę & privates:ficetiá cõtradicentes: ut,Homo eft animal: Homo eft fapiens, funt enuntiationes diverfæ. Homo eft animal. Homo eft arbor, funt difpara tæ.Ratio,eft domina voluptatis:Ratio eft serva voluptatis:funt relatæ. Virtus eft laudáda: Virtus eft vituperáda: funt adverfæ. Animal videt: Animal cæcũ eft : funt enuntiationes privátes. qua generali invétionis intelligentia,dici etiam poffent contradicentes. Ignorátia eft fugiêda: Ignorátia eft nõ fugiêda. attamé quia non toto cõfequenti affirmato negatoq;, fed parte confe quétis cõtradicitur,nõ appellatur contradictio enuntiationis: fed tũ demũ appellatur, qñ integrum confequęs affirmatur & negatur de eodê antecedêde.Hæc P.Ramus ita differebat,ut cõcluderęt,enuntiationis cõtradictionem , fpecie contradictionis,vel ejus ipfius, quæ generali argumentorum Topico definiretur:quia, Effe fugiendum,non effe fugiendum,tam contradicetia iunt,quám fugiendum non fugiendum:non tamen omnem contradictionem,enuntiationis contradictionem effe.Separatam verò cõtradictionis doctrinam P. Ramus ideo nõ fecit, quia comunis affectio eft enuntiati: Itaque quodipfius generale eft, commodiús generaliter unā cum genere fubjecto explicatur: quæ fpecialia sunt, per species enuntiati specialiter agetur: ut nunc, dum generaliter definitur enūtiatum, definitur generaliter affirmatio & negatio: postea cúm species enūtiati fiṅplicis & compositi explicabūtur, explicabitur etiam specialiter, quomodo affirmentur, negentur: & quomodo etiam contradictione opponantur. Itaque hic satis est intelligi, contradictionem esse affirmatio nem & negationem ejusdem consequentis de eodem antecedente.
units.tr: interpretatione, lest anyone be surprised that P. Ramus uses it in this way. Nor is this kind of contradiction different from the one in the previous book; only the subject species is different. For from disagreeing attributes, disagreeing propositions may be called diverse, disparate, related, adverse, private, and also contradictory. For example, "Man is animal" and "Man is wise" are diverse enuntiationes. "Man is animal" and "Man is tree" are disparate. "Reason is mistress of pleasure" and "Reason is slave of pleasure" are related. "Virtue is to be praised" and "Virtue is to be blamed" are adverse. "Animal sees" and "Animal is blind" are private enuntiationes. In this general sense of invention, these could also be called contradictory. "Ignorance is to be fled" and "Ignorance is not to be fled" are contradictory. But because it is not contradicted in its whole consequent, affirmed or denied, but in part of the consequent, it is not called a contradiction of the enuntiation. It is called that only when the whole consequent is affirmed and denied of the same antecedent. P. Ramus argued this, so that they conclude that the contradiction of an enuntiation is a species of contradiction, or of that topic which is defined in the general topic of arguments. For "to be fled" and "not to be fled" are contradictory in the same way that "fleeing" and "not fleeing" are, yet not every contradiction is a contradiction of an enuntiation. P. Ramus did not make a separate doctrine of contradiction, because it is a common affection of the enuntiatum. Therefore what is general to it is more conveniently explained generally, together with the subject genus; what is special will be treated specially through the species of the enuntiatum. Thus, now, while the enuntiatum is defined generally, affirmation and negation are defined generally; afterwards, when the species of simple and compound enuntiatum are explained, it will also be explained specially how they are affirmed and negated, and how they are opposed by contradiction. So here it is enough to understand that contradiction is the affirmation and negation of the same consequent of the same antecedent.

units.la: Cap. II. De Differentiis veri & falsi.
units.tr: Chap. II. On the Differences of True and False.

units.la: ENuntiatum deinde est verū aut salsum:verum,quando cōsequens est verum de antecedente : falsum contrá. Enuntiatum verum est contingens aut necessarium. Contingens,quando consequens de antecedēte sic verum est,ut aliquando falsum esse possit,ut,
units.tr: A statement is then either true or false: true when the predicate is true of the subject, false when it is not. A true statement is either contingent or necessary. It is contingent when the predicate is true of the subject in such a way that it could at some time be false, as in:

units.la: Audentes fortuna juvat.—
units.tr: Fortune favours the bold.—

units.la: Fac enim id esse hodie verum,cras salsum esse poterit. Itaq; veritatis hujus contingentis judicium, opinio dicitur, quæ præteritorum & præsentium certa esse potest,futurorum per naturam nō admodum potest.Itaq; Martialis Priscū merito cavillatur:
units.tr: For let this be true today; tomorrow it could be false. Hence the judgement of this contingent truth is called opinion. It can be certain about past and present things, but by nature it cannot be so about future things. So Martial rightly mocks Priscus:

units.la: Sæpe rogare soles, qualis sim Priste futurus, Si fiam locuples:simq, repente potens.
units.tr: You often ask, Priscus, what sort of man I shall be if I become rich and suddenly powerful.

units.la: Quæquā posse putas mores narrare futuros? Dic mihi, si fias tu leo, qualis eris?
units.tr: Do you think you can narrate what manners you will have in the future? Tell me, if you become a lion, what sort of lion will you be?

units.la: Necessarium, quādo consequēs semper verum est de omni antecedente: & illud affirmatū appellat καταπαντὸς, de omni. Impossibile, contra quod de nullo unquam verum esse potest. Necessarium homogeneum, est quando partes sunt essētiales inter se: ut cūm forma de formato, adjunctum de proprio subje< ēto, genus de specie dicitur, id appellatur καθ' αὑτό. Hetoregeneum contrá. Enūtiatum necessarium, homogeneum, reciprocū, est quando cōsequens semper verū est de antecedente, non solum omni & per se, sed etiā reciprocē: ut homo est animal rationale: numerō est par vel impar: lupus est natus ad ululādum. Id appellat καθόλυ πρῶτον, universaliter primum. Tres hæ sunt leges documentorum artis propriorū: prima καπὰ παν-τὸς, lex veritatis. Secūda καθ' αὐτὸ, lex justitiæ: Tertia καθόλυ πρῶτον, lex sapientiæ dicatur. Atq; ejusmodi enuntiatorum ita catholicorum judicium, verissima & prima scientia est.
units.tr: A statement is necessary when the predicate is always true of every subject; this is called affirmed of every [καταπαντὸς], "of every." Impossible is its opposite, that which can never be true of anything. A necessary homogeneous statement is one whose parts are essential to one another, as when form is said of what is formed, a property of its proper subject, or a genus of a species; this is called [καθ' αὑτό], "in itself." Heterogeneous is the opposite. A necessary, homogeneous, reciprocal statement is one in which the predicate is always true of the subject not only of every subject and in itself, but also reciprocally: as "man is a rational animal," "a number is even or odd," "the wolf is born to howl." This is called [καθόλου πρῶτον], "universally primary." These three are the laws of the proper teaching of the art: the first, [καπὰ παντὸς], is the law of truth; the second, [καθ' αὑτό], is the law of justice; the third, [καθόλου πρῶτον], is called the law of wisdom. And the judgement of such universal statements is the truest and first science.

units.la: Enuntiatum] Secūda cōmunis affectio in modo enun-do enundo enuntiati, eft de veritate & falfitate, penes quá Ariftoteli 4.ca. 1.de Interp. definitur enun-tiatum, λόγος ἀποφαντικὸς, ἐν ᾧ τὸ ἀληθεύειν ἢ ψεύδεσθαι ὑπάρχει, Oratio enuntiativa,in qua ineft verū dicere aut mentiri. Sed meliús enuntiatum definietur generaliter,ut jam dictum eft, quám per hanc differentiá veri aut falfi: neq; ipfum verū & falfum,qui termini funt trafcendētes (ut vulgó dicuntur) proprié ad enũtiatum pertinent: nifi compofitio divifioq; vera,aut falfa intelligatur. Quando]Illud eft paulo fecús 8.ca.1. ἐμπνέοντες, ὅτε ὁμοίως οἱ λόγοι ἀληθεῖς, ὥσπερ τὰ πράγματα, Quoniá orationes fimiliter veræ funt,ut res. & fic in Categoriis ad finem de modis Prioris: τὸ γὰρ ἅνευ τὸ πράγμα, ὃ μὴ, ἀληθὲς ὁ λόγος, ὃ ψεῦδος λέγεται, Quod e- nim fit aut nō fit, vera oratio aut falfa dicitur. At quoniam P. Ramus de partium enuntiationis, id eft de argumentorum difpofitione velut á capite primaq; origine omnia deinde deducit,veritatem enuntiati prefsiús definit é partium vera difpofitione,tatúmq; hoc veritatis judicium, enuntiato mirificé vindicavit: ut folum enútiatum verum effet aut falfum: fyllogifino enim cō fequentiam, vel inconfequētiam tribui:methodo,ordinem vel confufionem.Deniq; quicquid per fe verum falfumque judicaretur, enuntiato judicari. Contingēs aut neceffarium]Ariftotelis eft in Organo partitio non femel propofita. Sic 1. c.1.Pri. διαφέρει ἡ ἀποδεικτικὴ πρότασις τῆς διαλεκτικῆς: differt apodictica propofitio á dialectica,quod item iteratur 2.cap.1. Pofter: Sed in utroq; loco fingularis eft explicatio, qd' Apodictica fumat alteram partem contradictionis, Dialectica autem interroget: item quód Apodictica definitè sumat alteram partem cōtradictionis, Dialectica autem utramlibet: De dialectica etiam interrogatione idem dicitur 2. ca. 2. de Interpretatione. Athujus commentitiæ differētiæ commentum jam patuit initio superioris libri, ad Dialecticæ & definitionem & partionem. Nam cúm sit ars una cōmunis bené differendi de entibus & nō entibus, five sumas, ut Aristoteles in tota Philosophia solet, five more Socratis interroges, nihil in re ipsa interest, & totū hoc Eubulidis alicujus ineptissimum commentū est, ut patet ex Aristotelea logici usus observatioe & experientia. ἐνδεχόμενον, id est Aristoteli in tota philosophia, interdum etiam ἀωατόν.
units.tr: Statement] The second common feature in the mode of the statement concerns truth and falsity. By this feature Aristotle, in De Interpretatione 4, ch. 1, defines the statement as [λόγος ἀποφαντικὸς, ἐν ᾧ τὸ ἀληθεύειν ἢ ψεύδεσθαι ὑπάρχει], a declarative speech in which it belongs to speak truly or to lie. But the statement is better defined in general terms, as has already been said, than by this difference of true or false. Nor do true and false, which are transcendental terms (as they are commonly called), belong properly to the statement, unless composition and division are understood to be true or false. When] This is somewhat different in Aristotle, who says in the eighth book, [ἐμπνέοντες, ὅτε ὁμοίως οἱ λόγοι ἀληθεῖς, ὥσπερ τὰ πράγματα], that since speeches are true in the same way as things are; and so in the Categories, at the end of the section on the modes of the Prior Analytics: [τὸ γὰρ ἅνευ τὸ πράγμα, ὃ μὴ, ἀληθὲς ὁ λόγος, ὃ ψεῦδος λέγεται], that is, a speech is said to be true or false according as the thing is or is not. But since P. Ramus derives everything from the arrangement of the parts of the statement, as it were from the head and first origin, he defines the truth of a statement more precisely by the true arrangement of its parts, and he has wonderfully claimed this judgement of truth for the statement alone, so that only the statement is true or false. For consequence or inconsequence belongs to the syllogism, and order or confusion to the method; and in short, whatever is judged true or false in itself is judged in the statement. Contingent or necessary] The division is Aristotle's in the Organon, and he has proposed it more than once. Thus in Prior Analytics 1, ch. 1: [διαφέρει ἡ ἀποδεικτικὴ πρότασις τῆς διαλεκτικῆς], the apodictic proposition differs from the dialectical; this is repeated in Posterior Analytics 2, ch. 1. But in both places there is a peculiar explanation: that the apodictic takes the one part of a contradiction, while the dialectical asks; likewise that the apodictic takes definitely the one part of a contradiction, while the dialectical takes either part at will. The same is said of dialectical interrogation in De Interpretatione 2, ch. 2. The fiction of this invented difference has already become clear at the beginning of the previous book, in the definition and division of dialectic. For since it is one common art of arguing well about beings and non-beings, whether you assert, as Aristotle usually does throughout philosophy, or question in the manner of Socrates, nothing in the matter itself differs; and this whole thing is the most foolish invention of a certain Eubulides, as is clear from the observation and experience of Aristotelian logical use. [ἐνδεχόμενον], that is, contingent, which Aristotle throughout philosophy sometimes also calls [ἀδύνατον], impossible.

units.la: Oratio est Turni 10. Æneid. milites suos exhortatis adversus Trojanos mari advenantes. ut Aristoteles 26. cap. 1. Post. hac de re ita loquitur: ὡς τι λέγεται δόξαν ἄνευ πρὸς τὸ ἀληθὲς μὲν ἢ τὸ ψεῦδος. ἐνδεχόμενον δὲ καὶ ἄλλως ἔχειν τὸ δὲ ἔστιν ὑπόληψις τῆς ἀμέσου προτάσεως, ἢ μὴ ἀναγκαίας: itaq; relinquitur, opinione esse circa verū quidē aut falsum: quod contingit aliter habere: id verò cōjectura immediatæ propositionis ac necessariæ. Quo loco etiam notabis ab Aristotele appellari contingentē propositionem, immediatam, per se claram nempe atque manifestam.
units.tr: It is the speech of Turnus in Aeneid 10, exhorting his soldiers against the Trojans arriving by sea. As Aristotle says on this matter in Post. 26, ch. 1: [ὡς τι λέγεται δόξαν ἄνευ πρὸς τὸ ἀληθὲς μὲν ἢ τὸ ψεῦδος. ἐνδεχόμενον δὲ καὶ ἄλλως ἔχειν τὸ δὲ ἔστιν ὑπόληψις τῆς ἀμέσου προτάσεως, ἢ μὴ ἀναγκαίας], so it remains that opinion concerns what is true or false and what can be otherwise; and it is the assumption of an immediate proposition that is not necessary. In this passage you will also note that Aristotle calls the contingent proposition immediate, that is, clear and manifest in itself.

units.la: Aristotelis sententia est in lib. de Interpret. cap. de futuris contingentibus, enuntiationem præteritorum & præsentium jam manifestè veram aut falsam esse: in futufuturis contingentibus nequaquā similiter: Aristoteles autē ita loquitur, ut affirmet in futuro contingenti parte neutrā ἢ ἀληθὲς ἢ ψευδὲς, jam veram aut falsam esse: & syllogismum hunc concludit: Si futuri contingentis enuntiatio jam vera esset aut falsa, esset etiam necessaria, secundum falsum: falsum igitur primum. Enimvero (ut P. Ramus ad eum locum diligeter subtiliterq;, totū caput illud pene syllabatim examinās, explicavit) cōstat fraudem valdé periculosam isto loco rudibus fieri, si jam verū sit aliquid, protinus esse necessarium: necessarium enim ex conditione philosophus in propositione intelligit & interpretatur: quomodo quidlibet, quod est, quando est, ait necessariō esse, quanvis sit revera & perse contingens. At philosophus idem contra assumptionem disputās, necessarium absolute capit, & eo posito argumentatur, deliberationes hominum cōsiliaq;, leges & politias, vitam deniq; totā peritura esse: ita homonymia verbi illaqueamur & irretimur a philosopho: Propositū erat conditionale necessarium: removetur absolutum. aliud datū est, aliud est repetitum. fallacia igitur est connexæ enuntiationis: Si jam verū, etiam necessariū est. præceps valdé, & lubrica, & magnæ impietati conjuncta: Nam si vero necessarium adjugatur, & veritas necessitatis causa statuatur, quid fiet divina præscientia, cui jā certa & vera sunt omnia, quæ unquam evētura ac futura sunt? Carneades (ut est in Fato Ciceronis) necessitatem, & futuri præscitam veritatem consentaneas res inter se maximeq; cōjunctas {ê}tas judicabat: Ut fi præscitæ res omnes sint, & jam veritas futurorū præsciretur: fatū in actionibus humanis, & in rebus universis necessitas esset: nec animis hominum quicquam liberum seperesset. Itaque cūm aut necessitatem subeundam, aut veram futuri præsensionem tollēdam judicaret, ut damnata necessitate, animi libertatem retineret, divinam præsensionē damnavit, & ut animum sibi liberum faceret, sacrilegū fe- cit, ut verbis utar D. Augustini: Nec enim quia præscivit Deus, iccirco futurum est: sed quia su turum est, præscivit. Non quia video te, iccirco meis oculis objectus es: sed quia objectus es, ic circo te video. Ita, non quia Deus præscivit aliquod scelus futurū iccirco id fiet: sed quia futurū est, ideo præscivit: Nec enim quanvis hominibus (quibus & præsens, & præteritū, jam verū apparet, aut jam falsum) futurū jam verum non appareat, iccirco jam verū non est: nec quanvis ex caussa libera, quę & utrūlibet, & cōtraria possit agere, aliquid evēturum sit: ideo nuntiatio, quæ futurum illud enuntiat, nō est jam neq; vera, neq; falsa: alioqui enūtiatio non esset, si neq; vera, neq; falsa foret: nec veritas, necessitatis est caussa. Atque illud captiose & falso cōnectitur: Si jam verum est, est etiam necessarium: Quicquid enim fore verum est, Deo jam verū est, & verum semper fuit: neciccirco tamen necessarium. Ex caussis necessariis, futurū necessarium est: ex liberis, liberum: ex physicis, physicū: Deniq; quales sunt antecedentes caussæ, talis eventus veritas. Hæc P. Ramus é quinto scholarum dialećti. dialecticarum libro ad verbum repetebat, fructumque Ariftotelæ logicæ primo Interpretationis libro difficillimæ & obfcurisimæ, summatim breviterq; subducebat, valdeque spinosum sophisma perspicué retexebat. Martialis 12.libro deridet Prisci nomine, hominum curiositatem, cupidé futuri temporis evêtus exquirentium: Futurũ sciri nequit: tua quæstio est de futura vita: sciri itaque non potest. atque idem argumentum est ex genere universo. Dic mihi] Reponitur par quæstio : ut sunt apud pastores Virgilianos hæc:
units.tr: Aristotle's view, in the book De Interpretatione, in the chapter on future contingents, is that the statement of past and present things is already manifestly true or false, but not in the same way for future contingents. Aristotle argues that in a future contingent neither part is already either true or false [ἢ ἀληθὲς ἢ ψευδὲς]; and he concludes this syllogism: if the statement of a future contingent were already true or false, it would also be necessary, and the consequence is false; therefore the first is false. Indeed (as P. Ramus explained this passage carefully and subtly, examining that whole chapter almost syllable by syllable) it is clear that a very dangerous error arises here for the unlearned, if it is already true that something is, it at once is necessary. For the philosopher understands and interprets "necessary" in the premise conditionally: as whatever is, when it is, is necessarily so, although it is really and in itself contingent. But the same philosopher, arguing against the assumption, takes "necessary" absolutely, and on that basis argues that human deliberations and counsels, laws and states, and finally the whole of life, will perish. Thus we are ensnared and entangled by the homonymy of the word by the philosopher: the proposition was a conditional necessity; the absolute one is substituted. One thing is given, another is repeated. The fallacy therefore lies in the connected statement, "If it is already true, it is also necessary." It is very rash and slippery, and joined to great impiety. For if necessity is added to truth, and truth is posited as the cause of necessity, what becomes of divine foreknowledge, to which all things that ever will happen or be are already certain and true? Carneades (as is in Cicero's On Fate) judged that necessity and the foreknown truth of the future were things consistent with each other and most closely joined: so that if all things were foreknown, and the truth of future events were already known in advance, there would be fate in human actions and necessity in all things, and nothing free would be left in men's minds. Therefore, since he judged that either necessity must be admitted or the true foreknowledge of the future must be abolished, in order to retain the freedom of the mind by rejecting necessity, he rejected divine foreknowledge; and to make his mind free for himself, he committed sacrilege, to use the words of St Augustine: "For God does not foreknow a thing because it is going to be; rather, because it is going to be, he foreknows it. I do not see you because you are set before my eyes; rather, because you are set before them, I see you." So, God does not foreknow some wickedness to be future and therefore it will happen; rather, because it is going to happen, he has foreknown it. For even though a future thing does not already appear true to men (to whom both the present and the past already appear as true or false), it is not therefore not yet true; nor, though something will happen from a free cause, which can act either way and in contrary ways, is the statement that predicts it therefore neither true nor false yet; otherwise it would not be a statement at all if it were neither true nor false; and truth is not the cause of necessity. And that captious and false inference is drawn: "If it is already true, it is also necessary." For whatever is going to be true is already true to God, and has always been true, and yet is not therefore necessary. From necessary causes the future is necessary, from free causes free, from natural causes natural; in short, the truth of the event is such as the antecedent causes are. P. Ramus used to repeat these things word for word from the fifth book of his school dialectic, and he summarised briefly the fruit of Aristotle's most difficult and obscure logic in the first book of the Interpretation, and clearly unravelled a very thorny sophism. In the twelfth book Martial mocks, under the name of Priscus, the curiosity of men who eagerly seek to know the outcome of future time: the future cannot be known; your question concerns your future life; therefore it cannot be known; and the same argument holds for the whole genus. Dic mihi] A similar question is put, as among Virgil's shepherds here:

units.la: Dic quibus in terris. ——
units.tr: Tell me, in what lands ——

units.la: Ergo ridiculæ quæstionis, solutio etiam ridicula est: Si fias leo, similis eris leonum : ita fi fiam locuples, similis ero locupletum. Siç Pittacus unus é septem fapiétibus, interrogatus quid efset obscurum, respondit futurorum eventus, ut Laertius scribit primo libro. Necessarium] Neceffariũ definitur duabus proprietatibus, quando do cõfequens verum est de antecedente non folum omni, sed semper. De omni] Tres deinceps Ariftotelæ leges de artificiali materia, tot locis á P. Ramo decantatæ explicantur, κατὰ παντὸς, καθ' αὐτὸ, καθόλu πρῶτον. Itaq; quoniá hic proprius est de illis dicendi locus, diligentiús & accuratiús explicandæ sunt, omniaq; huc revocanda, quę à P. Ramo in Posterioribus præsertim proposita sunt, & ad hunc locũ disputata: Definiuntur autem 4.cap. 2. Poster. tres hæ leges primó, tum deinceps explicantur. Lex igitur prima κα- τὰ παντὸς ita definitur : Ac de omni quidé igitur dico, quód fit non in hoc quidem, in illo autem non, neque aliquando quidem, aliquando autem non. Hæc Aristotelis definitio obscura est, quia dissentaneum affirmatum ex consentaneo negato fit intelligendum, nempe quod fit in omni & semper: Itaque prima hæc nota est generalis & necessariæ veritatis. Impossibile] Ἀδύνατον Aristoteli est, quod Cicero in Timæo Platonis convertendo, nefas convertit: at Quintilianus impossibile, verbum usurpat 5. lib. capit. 10. tametsi 8. capit. 3. libri, Ἀδύνατον (ait) nostri possibile nominant: quæ ut dura videatur appellatio, tamen sola est. sed necessarii duabus conditionibus, quod omni, quod semper conveniat, impossibile prorsus opponitur, quod de nullo, quod nunquam dicatur: ut, Lapis est animal. & tamen opponitur ut falsum vero, non autem ut adversum verum, sicut est contingens.
units.tr: So the answer to a ridiculous question is also ridiculous: "If you become a lion, you will be like the lions; so if I become rich, I will be like the rich." So too Pittacus, one of the seven sages, when asked what was obscure, answered that it was the outcome of future events, as Laertius writes in book one. Necessary] The necessary is defined by two properties: when the consequent is true of the antecedent not only in every case but always. Of all] Three further laws of Aristotle about artificial matter, so often praised by P. Ramus, are explained: according to all [κατὰ παντὸς], in itself [καθ' αὐτὸ], and universal first [καθόλου πρῶτον]. Since this is the proper place to speak of them, they must be explained more diligently and accurately, and everything that P. Ramus set out, especially in the Posterior Analytics, and debated at this point, must be brought back here. These three laws are defined in chapter 2 of book 4 of the Posterior Analytics, and then explained in turn. The first law, according to all [κατὰ παντὸς], is defined thus: "And so I say of all things that it is not the case that it belongs to one thing and not to another, nor that it belongs at one time and not at another." This definition of Aristotle is obscure, because an affirmation that is opposed to a negation which agrees with it must be understood as holding in all cases and always. So this first mark is the mark of general and necessary truth. Impossible] Aristotle's ἀδύνατον is what Cicero, in translating Plato's Timaeus, rendered as nefas; Quintilian uses the word impossibile in book 5, chapter 10, though in book 8, chapter 3 he says that our writers call ἀδύνατον possibile. However harsh this name may seem, it is the only one available. But the necessary, with its two conditions, that it belong to all and always, is set absolutely against the impossible, which belongs to none and never, as "a stone is an animal." Yet it is opposed to the necessary as false is opposed to true, not as the contrary of the true, as the contingent is.

units.la: Homogeneum] Συγγενὲς ἡ ὁμογενὲς, id est Aristoteli, quod congener & deneger Latinis esse videatur. Plinius lib. 15. capit. 24. Aliud corpus est terrestribus fragis, aliud congeneri eorum unedo ni. Ergo congener, ejusdem generis, Plinio ita est: cui contrarium est deneger: quæ tamen pro Græcis vix in hunc sensum queas usurpare, & Græca verba Latine declinata, jam frequentia ra sunt in scholis, & ideo à P. Ramo usurpata.
units.tr: Homogeneous] Συγγενὲς or ὁμογενὲς, that is in Aristotle, what seems in Latin to be congener and deneger. Pliny, book 15, chapter 24: "The wild strawberry has one kind of body, and its congener, the unedo, another." So congener, of the same kind, is Pliny's usage, and its opposite is deneger. Yet you could hardly use these as Latin equivalents of the Greek in this sense; and Greek words given Latin endings are now very common in the schools, and so have been adopted by P. Ramus.

units.la: Essentiales] Consentanea, quæ sunt inter se, sunt αὐτὰ καθ' αὑτὸ: absolute, aut modo quodam, ut est 7. cap. 1. Porter. συγγενὲς autem illam absolutam Aristoteles tribus modis interpretatur: Primo, καθ' αὑτὸ, ὅσα ὑπάρχει ἐν τῷ τί ἐστι: Per se autem (ait) quæquæcunq; insunt in ipso quid est. Sic genus de species, sic forma de formato, sic membra de toto, sic definitio de definito, per se dicitur: ut, Homo est animal: Homo est rationalis: Homo constat é corpore & anima rationali: Homo est animal rationale. Secundus est modus per se: Καὶ ὅσα τῶν ἐνυπαρχόντων αὐτοῖς αὐτὰ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ ἐνυπάρχει, τῷ τί ἐστι ἀιλουῶτι: ac quæcunq; ipsa insunt suis attributis, in ipso quid est declaranti. ut nempe species & differetiæ formales generi, ut animal est homo vel bestia: Animal est rationale vel irrationale. Tertio modo, qui Aristoteli quartus est in ipsius litera: ἕτι δὲ ἄλλον τρόπον μὲν δὲ αὐτὸ ὑπάρχον ἑαυτῷ καθ' αὐτὸ: tum vero alio quidem modo, propter se inest unicuiq; per se. Hic obscurè loquitur Aristoteles: sed tamen absoluta illa συγγενεῖα primum secundumq; modum videtur amplecti, quod postea in eodem libro capite vicesimo clariùs comprehendit: ὅταν γὰρ καθ' αὐτὸ ὑπάρχῃ τι, τοῦτο αὐτῷ αἴτιον: cùm enim per se inest aliquid, hoc ipsi est causa. Ergo tres hi modi sunt in Aristotele de absoluta cognatione: reliquum est de quodammodo homogeneis: ἔτι καθ' αὐτὸ, ὃ μὴ καθ' ὑποκειμένου λέγεται ἄλλό τινος: Præterea per se: quod non de subjecto dicitur alio ullo. Hic etiá ex diffentaneo negato affirmatum est intelligendum, ut sit per se hoc modo, quod de subjecto hoc omni & solo dicitur, ut ppria sint adjûcta. Ergo secunda lex Aristotelis, quatuor his modis & obscuré & contra legem καθόλου πρῶτον sophisticé de claratur: Generalia enim generaliter & semel dicenda sunt: at quatuor his specialibus modis quater docetur, quod generaliter & semel dici debuerat: Docueris enim homogeneu enuntia tum esse, cujus partes inter fe essentiales, ut absolute sint caussæ rę constituentes cum effectis, ut quodammodo subjecta cum propriis adjunctis, docueris præcipuè quod hic obscuratur. Atq; hæc de secunda lege. Reciprocum] Sequitur explicatio tertiæ legis καθόλου πρῶτον, quę sic est in eodem illo quarto capite: Καθόλου δὲ λέγω, ὃ ἂν κατὰ παντὸς τινὸς ὑπάρχῃ, καὶ καθ' αὐτὸ, καὶ ἢ αὐτὸ: universaliter autem dico, quod & de omni inest, & per se, & quatenus ipsum. Lex ista minús obscurè quã duę superiores, est proposita: & ea duas superiores etiam amplectitur, sed addit præterea, quatenus ipsum: quod πρῶτον, primũ deinde appellat: idq; interpretatur, quod neq; superius sit, neq; inferius sed par & æquale: ut sunt generalia generalium, specialia specialium: quæ nempe propria sunt inter se atq; reciproca: quod tribus in litera exemplis declaratur: Homo est animal rationale: Quicquid enim est homo, est animal rationale: & quicquid est animal rationale, est item homo. sic in reliquis duobus exemplis. Ergo planũ est, καθόλου πρῶτον Aristoteli idem esse, quod ἀντιστροφον. Et hic Græci Aristotelis interpretes, quamvis docti & diligentes, attamen de usu præsentiū legum nimiúm securi, Themistius & Philoponus, & eos sequuti scholastici terrorem panicũ nescio quem valde ostendunt, dum ajunt, Si necesse fit καθόλου πρῶτον βιοάζειν καὶ ἀντιστρέφειν, æquari & converti, demóstrationem tãtũm definitionis futuram. Ecquid (inquam) nónne none Arist. ipse ita nominatim pfitetur, omnē scientiā definitione parari: attamen nō solā definitioně huc P. Ramus: sed partes de partito, formam de formato, propriam qualitatem de subjecto, huc etiam admittit, aitq; pariter Itaq; quod interpretes illi ajunt in enuntiatis illo modo catholicis, esse demonstrationis τὰ πρῶτα μέτρα, in reliquis (ut cum genus de specie dicitur κατὰ παντὸς, καὶ καθ' αὐτὸ, τὰ ἀδύνα) semisopitos sensus nescio quos ostendunt, cum nominatim Aristoteles tot exemplis & tā illustribus profiteatur nullam esse scientiam catholicam, si generali speciei etiā omni attribuatur. Atq; omnino in arte nulla est definitio, nulla est partitio, nulla est proprietatis explicatio ejusmodi, ubi non convertantur partes enuntiati: secūs, ut verissimē docet Aristoteles, non primo, non quatenus ipsum, id docebitur. Itaq; veluti pumilionis veste gigantem, aut gigantis veste pumilionem, perinde ridiculum corporis habitū induxeris: illa major, hęc minor suo corpore vestis erit. Leges] Equidē cum recordor, qua lætitia P. Ramus toties à se celebratas & decantatas Aristotelis tres istas leges, hoc loco præcipuē celebrarit & decantarit, nō mediocrē ipse animo voluptatē capio, tam breviter & succinctē, tam aperte & perspicuē propositā esse theoremata, tanti per totam philosophiā, adeoque per artes omnino omnes momenti: ut hisce tribus legibus, omnia quæ usquam ab hominib, unquam præcepta sunt in disciplinis & artibus, regi posse & conformari. Has leges Aristoteli P.Ramus attribuit, ut philosopho meritas laudes attribueret. Si quis tamen erit qui de tata re nihil putet Aristotelem cogitasse, ut initio propositum, sed leges istas syllogismo tantum suae be-monstrationis accommodasse, is judicet a P. Ramo nihilominus artibus omnibus instituendis leges accommodari, & misis personarum nominib9 de re ipsa meditetur: sed hac de re plura 9. & 10. Scholarum dialecticarum. Prima lex καθ' αὐτὸ, lex est veritatis necessariae & generalis: Itaque ad eam dece tota Aristotelis capita in posterioribus Analyticis consumpta sunt: Praeceptum artis quodlibet esto καθ' αὐτὸ, ait lex ista prima. Itaq; quomodo generalis necessitatis veritas concipiatur, inductione speciali & sensu observatorum exemplorum, decimumquartum caput 1. Posteriorum interpretatur: quae est ἐπιστήμη, ἀπόδειξις, tam saepe tamq; multis locis adversus Ciceronem & Quintilianum, ad versus Aristotelem ipsum a P. Ramo propositia: quod infinitis nugis Rhetorica & Dialectica ab his doctoribus obscurate sint, quarum tamen nulla e probatis & legitimis exemplis ἐπιστήμης demonstrari posset. Caput decimum octavum secundi Posteriorum hic deinde consumitur, quo modo καθ' αὐτὸ istud ab animo concipiatur, quod animus notitias rerum necessarias & universales, non informatas a natura ipsa capiat, sed colligat facultate intelligentiae sibi naturali & ingenerata: ut oculus colorum species ex utero matris non attulit, sed facultatem naturale omnia colorata cernendi. Itaque generalium & necessaria-rio rió universalium notitiarum non ᵻsɪs habitus, sed δύναμις facultas nostris animis naturalis est. Hæc Logica est capitis illius decimi octavi: De inde ad eandem hanc κατὰ παντὸς legem suadendum, octo capita primi Posteriorum ita referūtur, Omnia artis præcepta sunt κατὰ παντὸς. Itaq; sunt necessariarū rerum & generalium: caput est sextum. non item fortuitarum, neque sensilium: caput est vicesimum quartum. tum verò, universale præstat singulari, quia perpetum, quia αἰτιώτερον, ἁπλούστερον, ἐπιστημονικώτερον, ἀρχοειδέ-στερον, magis caussa, simplicius, scibilius, principio propius: vicesimum caput est. Affirmatum præstat negato, quia cæteris paribus, breviora meliora: quia γνωριμώτερον καὶ πιστότερον, notius & probabilius, quia ἀρχοειδέστερον: vicesimū primū caput. est Δακτυλικόν, ostensivū præstat ducenti ad impossibile & cogēti: vicesimum secundum caput est. Accedit eodem, primam figuram syllogismi præstare cæteris, tanquam ἐπιστημονικωτάτω: undecimum caput hic totum est. deniq; captiones & fallaciæ, quæ negleƈta lege hac accidant, differuntur duodecimo & decimotertio capitibus. Itaq; capitibus decē lex κατὰ παντὸς ab Aristotele tractata est. Studium hoc P. Ramus valdé laudabat, & philosophi diligētiam ferebat in cælum, quód legem tam necessariam reformańdis artibus, tamq; disciplinis omnibus restituēdis opportunam, tam studiosa persuasione pro mulgasset: sed diligentiæ modū in persuasione valdé requirebat, cúm decē verbis disertē dici posset & logicé, quod decem capitib9 illis esset effusum pręfertim cúm in hac orationis effusio ne, falsa essent nonnulla contra legem ipsam κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ. multa autem contra leges reliquas κατ' αὐτὸ, κατὰ ὅσ πρῶτον: de quibus sigillatim dictum ef set ad illa ipsa capita. In grammatica arte anomaliæ multæ sunt cótra generales analogias, at anomaliæ generalib. analogiis additæ κατὰ πάντα τὰ explebūt: Id in artibus reliquis multo est etiam facilius, neq; ullus hic tergiversatori sophistæ locus reliquus est, quód hac lege artes omnes regi nequeát: quód in physicis aut aliis artibus præcepta sint ut plerumq; non semper, erràt, qui id afferút, neq; in physicis ullum Platonis ætate præceptū verū fuit, quod nō hodie verū sit: idem in medicina, & qualibet alia disciplina, cujus vel usus cóje cturalis esse possit, ars tamē tota est κατὰ πάντας, ut veré Galenus admonuit. Teneamus igitur primam in formádis artibus legé esse, ut omnia artis theoremata sint omnino necessarioq; vera & hæc ideo lex veritatis á P. Ramo dicta est. Secunda veró materiæ artificiose lex κατ' αὐτὰ, impensiús á P. Ramo prę dicabatur: parū esse in artib. informandis, quidlibet esse necessariū, nisi esset ité κατ' αὐτὰ. hic Aristotelis capita in primo post.
