Analyt. tria feré versantur, septimum, octavum, nonum: eaq; obscura variis rebus & cósufa, sed tamen unde lex habeatur ad regendos artiū fines, & suum cuiq; tribuendum, valdé necessaria Exemplum Aristotelis hic insigne est, ne quis calumniari posset. Numeri in Arithmetica, magnitudines in Geometria tantùm docéde sunt, secús arithmeticum in geometria ἀγεωμέτρητον, geometricū in arithmetica ἀνάριθμον fuerit, qua una lege, jus, à Lycurgo, vel Solone nullum est unquâ justius institutum. Præcepta artiū distinguantur, usus tamen conjungatur: & sic Aristoteles tribus illis capitibus cūm homogeniâ imperat,ne à genere alio in aliud digressio ulla permittatur: attamen superiorum artium rationes in subalternis & inferioribus concedit. Axiomata logica, Quæ eidem æqualia,& cætera,& numeris & figuris explicandis accommodat:item arithmetica in sonis, in figuris & cæteris numerabilibus rebus, sic geometria in opticis, astronomicis, mechanicis,&sic deinceps:usus enim artiū pro subjectis rebus valet:logicæ, arithmeticæ,geometriæ in omni ente disputabili, numerabili, mensurabili.aliud tamē esse meminerimus præcipere,aliud præceptis uti.Ergo lege ista authore, Philosophia ὑπογίνεσθαι artium segregádo,homogenea ab heterogeneis separavit: quin separabit accuratiús, cúm sese excitaverit.Etiá permulta contra eandem legē in artibus omnibus aliena,quæ ad verbum P. Ramus á se ad 9. ca.1. Post. descripta hoc loco memoriter repetebat: Grammatica(ajebat) Grammaticé, Rhetorica Rhetoricè, Logica Logicé, Arithmetica Arithmeticé, Geometria Geometricé, Musica Musicé tractari debêt,& cæterę deniq; artes suis sibi que cognatis & syngeneis rationib.uti.Plato jubet in Repub. unius artis unū artificē esse. Qui si Platonica lege fuerint (ut feré sunt) artifices distincti,velitq; sutor de texêdo,textor de suen-
units.tr: Essentiales] Things that agree with one another are αὐτὰ καθ' αὑτὸ [in themselves], either absolutely or in some qualified way, as in Porphyry's seventh chapter. Aristotle interprets the absolute kinship (συγγενὲς) in three ways. First, καθ' αὑτὸ [per se], "whatever inheres in the what-it-is" [ὅσα ὑπάρχει ἐν τῷ τί ἐστι]. Things are said to be per se, he says, when they inhere in what a thing is: thus genus is said per se of species, form of the thing formed, parts of the whole, and definition of the thing defined. For example: man is an animal; man is rational; man consists of a body and a rational soul; man is a rational animal. The second way of per se is: "and whatever of the things inhering in them inhere in them of themselves, and declare what they are" [Καὶ ὅσα τῶν ἐνυπαρχόντων αὐτοῖς αὐτὰ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ ἐνυπάρχει, τῷ τί ἐστι ἀιλουῶτι]. That is, the species and formal differences of a genus, as an animal is a man or a beast, and an animal is rational or irrational. The third way, which is fourth in Aristotle's own text, is: "and in another way, that which belongs to a thing per se, inheres in each thing of itself" [ἕτι δὲ ἄλλον τρόπον μὲν δὲ αὐτὸ ὑπάρχον ἑαυτῷ καθ' αὐτὸ]. Here Aristotle speaks obscurely, but his absolute kinship (συγγενεῖα) seems to embrace the first and second ways, which he later sets out more clearly in the twentieth chapter of the same book: "for when something belongs per se, this is its cause" [ὅταν γὰρ καθ' αὐτὸ ὑπάρχῃ τι, τοῦτο αὐτῷ αἴτιον]. So these three modes are in Aristotle on absolute kinship. What remains is the kinship in a certain respect, of things that are alike: "further, per se, that which is not said of a subject to some other thing" [ἔτι καθ' αὐτὸ, ὃ μὴ καθ' ὑποκειμένου λέγεται ἄλλό τινος]. Here too, the affirmative must be understood from the negated opposite, so that per se means in this way: what is said of a subject that is all and only that subject, as proper attributes are. So Aristotle's second law is explained both obscurely and, against the law of καθόλου πρῶτον, sophistically, in these four modes. Generals should be stated generally and once; but through these four special modes it is taught four times what should have been stated generally and once. For he has taught that a homogeneous statement is one whose parts are essential to one another, so that they are absolutely the causes constituting the thing along with its effects, and, in a certain way, subjects along with their proper attributes. He has taught this chiefly, though it is obscured here. So much on the second law. Reciprocum] There follows the explanation of the third law, καθόλου πρῶτον, which in the same fourth chapter reads: "I call universal what belongs to every instance, and per se, and in so far as it is itself" [Καθόλου δὲ λέγω, ὃ ἂν κατὰ παντὸς τινὸς ὑπάρχῃ, καὶ καθ' αὐτὸ, καὶ ἢ αὐτὸ]. This law is stated less obscurely than the two before it. It includes those two, but adds "in so far as it is itself," which he calls πρῶτον, first, and then explains it as meaning that a thing is neither superior nor inferior but equal and matching: as generals are to generals and specials to specials, which are proper to and reciprocal with one another. He illustrates this with three examples in his text: man is a rational animal; for whatever is a man is a rational animal, and whatever is a rational animal is also a man. The same holds for the other two examples. So it is plain that for Aristotle καθόλου πρῶτον means the same as ἀντιστροφον, convertible. Here the Greek interpreters of Aristotle, learned and diligent though they are, are too confident about the use of these laws. Themistius, Philoponus, and the scholastics who followed them show a certain strange terror, saying that if καθόλου πρῶτον must be applied, that is, made equal and converted, then only definition would be demonstrated. Well, I say: does Aristotle himself not openly declare that every science is acquired through definition? Yet Peter Ramus does not admit only definition here, but also parts of the divided, form of the formed, and proper quality of the subject, and he says likewise. So when those interpreters say that in universal propositions of that kind lie the first measures of demonstration, while in the rest (as when genus is said of species κατὰ παντὸς and per se, the τὰ ἀδύνα), they reveal I know not what half-buried senses, since Aristotle himself expressly declares, with so many examples and such illustrious ones, that there is no universal science if a general is not also attributed to every species. Indeed, in any art there is no definition, no partition, no explanation of a property of this kind, where the parts of the statement are not convertible. Otherwise, as Aristotle most truly teaches, that will not be taught first, nor in so far as it is itself. So if you dress a giant in a dwarf's clothing, or a dwarf in a giant's, the body's outfit is equally absurd: the one garment will be too large, the other too small for its body. Laws] Indeed, when I recall with what joy Peter Ramus, having so often praised and sung the three laws of Aristotle, celebrated and sang them especially here, I myself feel no small pleasure in mind. These theorems are set out so briefly and succinctly, so openly and clearly, and are of such weight throughout all philosophy, and indeed throughout all the arts, that by these three laws all the precepts ever given by men in the disciplines and arts can be governed and conformed. Ramus attributed these laws to Aristotle so as to give the philosopher his deserved praise. But if there is anyone who thinks that Aristotle, as was proposed at the start, did not have this whole matter in mind, and that he adapted these laws only to the syllogism of his own demonstration, let him judge that Ramus nonetheless adapts these laws to the founding of all the arts, and that he considers the matter itself, with the names of persons removed. But more on this matter in the 9th and 10th books of the Dialectical Lectures. The first law, καθ' αὐτὸ, is the law of necessary and general truth. Therefore the whole of Aristotle's chapters in the Posterior Analytics are spent on it. The first law says: let any precept of an art be καθ' αὐτὸ. Accordingly, how a truth of general necessity is conceived, Aristotle explains in the fourteenth chapter of the first book of the Posterior Analytics, through special induction and the sense of observed examples. This is ἐπιστήμη, ἀπόδειξις, which Ramus has so often and in so many places put forward against Cicero and Quintilian, and against Aristotle himself. For these teachers have obscured rhetoric and dialectic with endless trifles, none of which could be demonstrated by approved and lawful examples of ἐπιστήμη. Then in the eighteenth chapter of the second book of the Posterior Analytics, Aristotle treats how this καθ' αὐτὸ is conceived by the mind: the mind grasps necessary and universal notions of things, not as they are informed by nature itself, but by gathering them through the faculty of understanding that is natural and innate to it. Just as the eye did not bring the species of colours from its mother's womb, but the natural faculty of seeing all coloured things. Thus the habit (ἕξις) of general and necessarily universal notions is not innate, but a faculty (δύναμις) natural to our minds. This is the logic of that eighteenth chapter. Next, to press this same law κατὰ παντὸς, the eight chapters of the first book of the Posterior Analytics are cited: all precepts of an art are κατὰ παντὸς, and so they concern necessary and general things; this is the sixth chapter. They do not concern chance things or sensible things; this is the twenty-fourth chapter. Then the universal is preferable to the singular, because it is lasting, because it is αἰτιώτερον, ἁπλούστερον, ἐπιστημονικώτερον, ἀρχοειδέστερον: more causal, simpler, more scientific, more akin to a principle; this is the twentieth chapter. The affirmative is preferable to the negative because, other things being equal, shorter is better; because it is γνωριμώτερον καὶ πιστότερον, more known and more credible; because it is ἀρχοειδέστερον; this is the twenty-first chapter. The Δακτυλικόν, the ostensive, is preferable to the reduction to the impossible and the compelling; this is the twenty-second chapter. To this is added that the first figure of the syllogism is better than the others, as being ἐπιστημονικωτάτω, most scientific; the whole of the eleventh chapter is on this. Finally, the captions and fallacies that arise when this law is neglected are discussed in the twelfth and thirteenth chapters. So the law κατὰ παντὸς is treated by Aristotle in ten chapters. Ramus greatly praised this pursuit and extolled the philosopher's diligence, because he had so earnestly promoted a law so necessary for reforming the arts and so opportune for restoring all disciplines. But he greatly required moderation of diligence in such persuasion, since what was poured out over those ten chapters could have been said clearly and logically in ten words. Especially since in this outpouring of words some things were false, against the law itself κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ, and many things were against the other laws, κατ' αὐτὸ, κατὰ ὅσ πρῶτον, which would have been dealt with one by one in those very chapters. In the art of grammar there are many anomalies against the general analogies; but anomalies added to general analogies will fulfil κατὰ πάντα τὰ. In the other arts this is much easier, and there is no remaining place for the evasive sophist, on the ground that the arts cannot all be governed by this law, because in physics or other arts precepts are, as they say, usually but not always true. Those who say this are wrong. Nor was any precept in physics true in Plato's time which is not true today. The same holds for medicine and any other discipline whose use may be conjectural; yet the whole art is κατὰ πάντας, as Galen rightly warned. Let us therefore hold that the first law in forming the arts is that all theorems of an art be wholly and necessarily true, and for this reason Ramus called it the law of truth. The second law, κατ' αὐτὰ, which concerns the artful treatment of matter, Ramus used to proclaim with greater emphasis: it is of little use in shaping the arts for anything to be necessary unless it is also κατ' αὐτὰ. Here three of Aristotle's chapters in the first book of the Posterior Analytics are chiefly concerned, the seventh, eighth and ninth. They are obscure and confused in various matters, but still they give the law by which the boundaries of the arts are governed and each thing is assigned its own. A notable example from Aristotle here, lest anyone might object: numbers are to be taught only in arithmetic, magnitudes only in geometry. Otherwise arithmetic would be ἀγεωμέτρητον, unmeasured by geometry, and geometry ἀνάριθμον, uncounted by arithmetic. By this one law no justice was ever instituted more justly, not even by Lycurgus or Solon. The precepts of the arts are to be distinguished, but their use is to be joined. Thus Aristotle, in those three chapters, commands that homogeneous things be kept together, so that no digression from one genus to another is allowed. Yet he concedes to the subordinate and inferior arts the principles of the superior arts. The axioms of logic, such as "things equal to the same thing are equal to one another," and the rest, he adapts also to explaining numbers and figures. Likewise arithmetic is applied to sounds, to figures and to other countable things; and so geometry to optics, astronomy, mechanics, and so on. For the use of the arts is valid for their subjects: logic, arithmetic and geometry apply to every being that can be disputed, counted or measured. But we should remember that it is one thing to prescribe and another to use precepts. So by this law, Philosophy, by segregating the arts (ὑπογίνεσθαι), separated the homogeneous from the heterogeneous. Indeed, it will separate them more accurately once it has been roused. Also very many things alien to the same law in all the arts, which Ramus himself had described word for word in his ninth chapter of the first book of the Posterior Analytics, he was then repeating from memory in this place: grammar, he would say, should be treated grammatically; rhetoric rhetorically; logic logically; arithmetic arithmetically; geometry geometrically; music musically; and the other arts should in the end use their own and kindred principles. Plato, in the Republic, commands that each art have one craftsman. If, by Plato's law, craftsmen are distinct (as they generally are), and a cobbler wishes to dispute about weaving, a weaver about mending, a fuller about grinding, a painter about stuffing, he will at once be told: "This is not the business of your art and profession." The cobbler criticised the image of Apelles from the sandal; Apelles rebuked him, since he was doing so from his own art. "Let the cobbler not go beyond the sandal," said Apelles.

Hæc Aristotelis exempla tria sunt, in quibus singulis generalis affectio tribuitur speciei: Nam παράλληλισμος etiam obliquis lineis cōvenit: æqualitas triū cum duobus angulorū, reliquis triangulis cōmunis est, & ἀναλογία illa logica plane est omnisq; & entis & nō entis cōmunis. de tribus his in legē καθόλου πρῶτον sophismatis duo prima sunt in Euclide, qui tricesima quinta definitione primi libri parallelismū lineis rectis attribuit, qui idem ἀναλογίαν τῶν ἀναλόγων docuit in magnitudinibus lib.5. & rursus in numeris lib.7.cum tamen 32.P.1. docuerit affectionem angulorum generalem de triangulo. Quid ita? dicat aliquis. nónne idem est de qualibet specie ac de universo genere demóstra re? Reipsa sané (dixerit philosophus) idem est: doƈtrinę commodo non est idem: quia plurib. demonstrationibus doceretur,quod una demó stratione possit doceri. units.tr: As a cobbler, when he criticised a painting of Apelles' image for its sandal, was rebuked by Apelles, who was himself making it according to his art: "Let the cobbler not go beyond the sandal (ne sutor ultra crepidam)," said Apelles. Therefore Aristotle concludes that from this kinship the boundaries and limits of the arts must be distinguished, and he established this law of kinship [συγγενείας] as a kind of prince and mistress of all the arts. By this law, you would say to the grammarian that he divides grammar into the methodical and the historical: you are wrong, because knowledge of the historical matter of poets, histories, astrology and other disciplines is not germane or kin to your art. You would say to the rhetorician, who divides rhetoric into five parts (invention, arrangement, style, delivery, memory): you are wrong, because invention, arrangement and memory belong to method and reason, and so are proper to the logicians, not kin to your art. You would say to the logician, who takes upon himself the doctrine of names, verbs, speech, quantity in number and magnitude, substance in bodies, plants and animals, quality in habit and disposition, passive quality, natural power and impotence, modes, conversions, reductions, powers and syllogistic demonstrations, and many other things not kin to him: you are wrong; these are not yours, since a doctrine is kin only to its own subject genus. You would say to the geometer, who uses logical and arithmetical axioms: you hold what is alien; this doctrine is not yours. You would say to the physicist, who takes up the common causes, motions, place and time explained: you are wrong; these are not kin to you, they belong to the family of the logicians; do not therefore claim what is another's. You would say to that metaphysician, I know not who, who mixes logical disputes through all fourteen books (unless you except the chapters of the fifth book): you are most gravely wrong, master; you have nothing kin; all these things are alien; in them you have nothing of your own. You would say to all the arts: away with the disputes over false opinions and the refutations, the elenchi; here nothing is homogeneous to the use of your learning. With these impediments removed, you will be half shorter and clearer, and one will not hear the sophistical illusions of the inexperienced about the various ends and various uses; for the end and use will be fuller when drawn from distinct arts than from confused ones. Finally, by this one law of kinship [συγγενείας], so grave and so imperious, it will be lawful to govern and arrange the ends of all the arts. Hence P. Ramus greatly praised the great diligence of Aristotle in promulgating this law and persuading all peoples of it, since by the benefit of this law it is lawful above all to reform and restore logic and the other arts too. Yet in three chapters Aristotle said so many things against this very law of kinship and kinship [συγγενείας], not only not per se [καθ' αὐτὸ] but not even in every case [κατὰ πάντα], as has been shown point by point in those three chapters; Ramus strongly disapproved of this and cut back and removed the instrument of the law. Indeed P. Ramus particularly admired the third law, in the setting out and promulgating of which, however, Aristotle used only the one chapter, the fifth of the first book of the Posterior Analytics, confirmed by mathematical examples; and this chapter is known only to the grammarian and the rhetorician, and not unknown to the pupil of that learned dust, but it is firm above all and strong for the protection and guarding of the law itself, so that it cannot in any way be refuted or disproved: whatever precept of an art, let it be universal and first [καθόλου πρῶτον]. And since the affection and nature of the highest, middle and lowest genus is a kind of affection and nature, it must be attributed to what is homogeneous in genus, and homoeides in species [τῷ γένει ὁμογενὲς, τῷ ἰδίᾳ ὁμοειδὲς]. Therefore the teacher of the art will have committed a fault against the law if the general is attributed to the special, or conversely the special to the general. Examples of the former sophism are three of Aristotle: as when someone teaches that straight lines do not meet; that the three angles of an isosceles triangle are equal to two right angles; that the analogy of analogues [ἀναλογίαν τῶν ἀναλόγων] fits number or magnitude. These three examples of Aristotle are such that in each a general affection is attributed to a species: for parallelism [παράλληλισμος] belongs also to oblique lines; the equality of the three angles with two right angles is common to the other triangles; and that analogy [ἀναλογία] is plainly logical and common to every being and non-being. Of these three sophisms against the law of universal and first [καθόλου πρῶτον], the first two are found in Euclid, who in the thirty-fifth definition of the first book attributes parallelism to straight lines, and who likewise taught the analogy of analogues [ἀναλογίαν τῶν ἀναλόγων] in magnitudes in the fifth book, and again in numbers in the seventh, although in I.32 he taught the general affection of the angles of a triangle. He would never have admitted these sophisms if he had set before himself the logical law of universal and first [καθόλου πρῶτον]. It is indeed also remarkable that in the meantime the philosopher handed down, concerning that first sophism, the following on this law: if that general affection of the angles were demonstrated of each species of triangle, the matter would still not be demonstrated except in a sophistical manner. How so? someone may say. Is it not the same to demonstrate it of any species as of the universal genus? Indeed (the philosopher would reply) it is the same in fact, but it is not the same for the convenience of teaching, since what can be taught by one demonstration would be taught by many. Aristotle here brings forward tautology, most pernicious of all the frauds of sophistry in the disciplines; which the philosopher had also put forward in his book On the Parts of Animals, as a law of the legitimate and skilful method proceeding from general things to special ones. So much for the examples of the first sophism. The example of the second sophism in Aristotle is single and brief: if that affection of angles were attributed to the figure; for then the special would be attributed to the general. Wherefore P. Ramus called this one law the law of wisdom, the only law which would make one truly know what is known from its first origin and source, and insofar as it is itself known. For to this properly refer those praises of the first law: according to the whole of everything [καθ' ὅλου τοῦ παντὸς], general and universal, taken generally and universally; and therefore this alone is most simple, most causal, most principial, most scientific [ἁπλούστατον, αἰτιώτατον, ἀρχεαδέστατον, ἐπιστημονικώτατον]; indeed it is the very principle, cause and knowledge [ἀρχὴ αἰτία, ἐπιστήμη]. Nothing more magnificent about the matter of art was ever proposed by Aristotle, yet in no law of logical doctrine was there more frequent transgression. By the instrument of this law, grammar has been made half shorter and clearer, since general matters are explained once and generally. It is commonly divided into four parts: etymology, syntax, prosody, orthography. But the last two, separately from the first, have no art of their own: they are affections of the members of etymology and syntax, which are perpetual. In etymology, species and figure are repeated throughout all the genera of words; but what is said generally and once will be understood equally; there the general is attributed to the special. Comparison is a special affection of certain adjectives, yet on the contrary it is counted among the general accidents of nouns. This is the second sophism, universal and first [καθόλου πρῶτον]. Moreover, in the whole of the rhetorical and logical books, countless tautologies can be corrected and amended by this one law. This was the chief and constant instrument of P. Ramus in the schools, for grammars, rhetorics, dialectics and the other arts of so many kinds: not rarely indeed of all and per se [κατὰ παντὸς καὶ καθ' αὐτό], but far more often and most diligently universal and first [καθόλου πρῶτον], both proposed and treated against so many heaps of repetitions. For Aristotle, the greatest and most serious struggle against the tautologies of the ancients was indeed this, and in the whole field of philosophy he encountered no thorns more harsh or troublesome; yet he could not pluck them all out. Therefore it was a singular plan, full of piety towards posterity, to hand down, promulgate and divulge this law, attested and sealed by so great a seal of examples, so that posterity might have, as from a father of the family, a most effective instrument for removing from the logical field, and indeed from the field of any doctrine, impediments so pernicious to the crops. This husbandry will be far richer and more fruitful, and will truly bring a golden harvest to the liberal disciplines and arts. If anyone maliciously objects that these laws are proper to the artful matter of apodictic science and not common to all arts, this school, and dialectic and mathematics, will reply with the commentary of that Aristotelian apodeixis, by which neither its matter nor its form is found in mathematics at all; and with a monstrous commentary the schools of so many centuries and peoples have been deluded up to now. Let the theorems of any catholic discipline be such, and if anything is special, let it be a theorem [θεώρημα] and a corollary derived from that catholic source, as most things are in geometrical matters. Aristotle bound the axioms of all, per se, universal and first [κατὰ παντὸς, καθ' αὐτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον] to the apodictic syllogism, because he thought that the sciences and arts would be founded on it as on a single instrument; in this he gave the elenchus as much weight as he wished to be held the greatest of philosophers; yet in this he rightly judged that he confirmed the decrees of the disciplines and arts by those laws and conditions. Nor are there any other laws at all in the whole Organon of Aristotle by which the matter of sciences and arts is judged. Concerning the sophistical and the probable, which are to be indicated, the Aristotelians think their laws are set down for themselves in the Elenchi and the Topics; what other laws, then, will they have, if they assign those laws to the syllogism, by which to judge the sayings and decrees of grammar, rhetoric, and even Aristotle's own logic, and of any discipline whatever except the geometrical ones? Finally, Aristotle judged that the particular sciences of each whole discipline are to be governed by these laws; he therefore judged that the whole discipline and art is to be governed by these laws too, because if the parts are such, the whole will be such. Therefore we still have three Aristotelian laws concerning the matter of art and doctrine: the first of universal necessity or truth; the second of essential kinship or justice; the third of property and conversion or wisdom. If these are duly and lawfully observed, a wonderful light will come to all the arts; and therefore they are to be grasped and practised with all zeal and diligence.

units.la: Scientia]ut enuntiati genera, necessarium, cō tingēs:ita judicii in utroq; genere vocabula distincta sunt, alterum scientia,alterum opinio di citur. Scientiæ judiciū Aristoteli ita collocatur in rebus necessariis,26.cap.1.Poster.atq; id judicium dicitur ἀμεταπτωτον,immutabile,2.ca.1.Poster. & ἀμεταπτωτον,indissuasibile, 4. cap.6. Topic.
units.tr: Science: just as propositions are of two kinds, necessary and contingent, so the names for judgement in each kind are distinct. One is called science and the other opinion. Aristotle places the judgement of science among necessary things (Posterior Analytics 1.26), and he calls this judgement immutable [ἀμεταπτωτον] (Posterior Analytics 2.1) and indissuadable [ἀμεταπτωτον] (Topics 4.6).

units.la: Scientia autem principiorū,multo est illustrior scientia aliunde deductorū. atq; talis intelligentia 3.ca.1. Poster.& 18. cap. 2. Poster. dicitur ἐπιστήμη, intelligentia vel intellectus: & idem ad 26. ca. 1. Poster. Philopono dicitur ἀκρότατη νοῦς ψυχῆς ἀνώ- μετ,summa animæ facultas.sed Aristoteli ipsi 14. cap.1. Topic. ὡς ἐν ὀφθαλμῷ, νοῦς ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ: ut visus in oculo,sic intelligētia in anima.Ergo intelligentia appellatur ab Aristotele tale judicium. Est tamen νοῦς,ipsum mentis logicū & universale lumē,his quidē præcipué cōtemplandis idoneum, sed cęteris etiam rebus ęstimandis aptū: Ideoq; P. Ramus hic paulo secus loquitur.Scie tia autem aliquando etiam absoluté veritas appellatur: ideoq; judiciū scientię & veritatis pro eodem est. Enuntiatū autem, tribus his legibus cōsentaneum, appellatur αὐτόπιστον, ἄμεσον, ἀναπόδεικτον, per se probabile, immediatum, indemon strabile: lumen nō solūm sui, sed etiam cōtrarii, ut est 2. cap. 1. Posterior. appellatur ἀρχή, principiū: & principiorum doctrina quædam describitur, quód aliud sit ἀξίωμα, aliud thesis: ἀξίωμα, quod necesse sit habere τὸν μανθάνοντα, eum qui aliquid discere debeat, ut est 2. & 8. ca. 1. Posterior. quodq; ὑπάρχα τέχνης ἢ διδασκαλίας, non ab artifice & magistro (ut Philopon ait) capiatur: ὅρος vero, principium dicitur illud indemonstrabile, nequaquā discenti protinus manifestū, ut definitiones & hypotheses seu αἰτήματα, postulata: de quib. multa verba in Posteriorib. facta sunt. Sed hæc principiorum tam speciosa doctrina, non est in logicis decretis homogenea: tota est inanis & alienā: neq; in cōdendis ad expositas leges artibus, ulla est hic utilitas definiendo, partiendo, proprietatis explicando, quibus artes totæ deducūtur: utrum definitiones, partitiones, proprietatū explicationes, sint axiomata. an theses, hypotheses αἰτήματα, cōsideratio prorsus nulla est: etsi per se clarę sint & manifestę luce sua, id ostē dunt: si quid explicationis præterea requirant, obscuritas ipsa judicio suo lucem sibi necessariā postulabit: nomine thesewς, hypothesewς, αἰτήματα ὁ, hic nihil opus erit: principiorum hæc μαθήματα πίστεις, é mathematicis profecta est, ubi ἀξιώματα & αἰτήματα, hypotheses, ἴσοι definitiones jam ante Ariftotelem nominabantur. Atq; hęc de duo bus judicii generibus, opinione & scientia: quę (ut est 26. cap. 1. Poster.) in idem videntur aliquando concurrere, ut idem sit δοξαστὸν καὶ ἐπιστητόν, opinabile & scibile: ut Hipparcho mathematico insigni, eclipsis lunæ, scientia fuit: Epicuro opinabile, omnia concursione atomorum fortuita conficienti. sed hoc utrumq; opinionis & sciętiæ judicium varië à philosophis acceptum est, plerisq; enim opinio ferè repudiata: Heraclidi enim illud est apud Laertium lib. 9.
units.tr: Principles, however, are much better known than the science of things derived from them, and such understanding is called science [ἐπιστήμη], understanding or intellect (Posterior Analytics 1.3 and 2.18). Philoponus calls it the highest faculty of the soul [ἀκρότατη νοῦς ψυχῆς ἀνώμετ], but Aristotle himself says: as sight is in the eye, so understanding is in the soul (Topics 1.14). Understanding is therefore called by Aristotle this kind of judgement. Yet mind [νοῦς] is also the logical mind itself and the universal light, suited above all to contemplating these things, but also apt for judging other things. For this reason Ramus speaks here a little differently. Science is sometimes also called absolute truth, so the judgement of science and of truth is the same. A proposition that agrees with these three laws is called self-credible [αὐτόπιστον], immediate [ἄμεσον], undemonstrable [ἀναπόδεικτον]: probable through itself, immediate, indemonstrable. It is a light not only of itself but also of its opposite, as stated in Posterior Analytics 2.1, and it is called a principle [ἀρχή]. A certain doctrine of principles is described: one thing is an axiom [ἀξίωμα], another a thesis. An axiom is what the learner must have, the one who ought to learn something (Posterior Analytics 1.2 and 1.8), and what is taken not from the craftsman and teacher (as Philoponus says) but is the basis of the art or teaching [ὑπάρχα τέχνης ἢ διδασκαλίας]. A principle called a term [ὅρος] is that indemonstrable thing which is by no means at once clear to the learner, such as definitions and hypotheses or postulates [αἰτήματα]; many words have been spent on these in the Posterior Analytics. But this so splendid doctrine of principles is not homogeneous with the logical decrees; it is wholly empty and foreign. In establishing the arts according to the laws set out, there is here no use in defining, dividing, or explaining properties, by which whole arts are derived. Whether definitions, partitions, and explanations of properties are axioms, or theses, hypotheses or postulates, is not a consideration at all. Even if they are clear in themselves and manifest by their own light, they show this; if they require any further explanation, their very obscurity will demand the light necessary to them by its own judgement. The names thesis, hypothesis, and postulate are here not needed. This doctrine of principles, the mathematical "conviction" [μαθήματα πίστεις], comes from mathematics, where axioms, postulates, hypotheses and definitions were named even before Aristotle. So much for the two kinds of judgement, opinion and science. As stated in Posterior Analytics 1.26, these sometimes seem to coincide, so that the same thing is both opinable and knowable [δοξαστὸν καὶ ἐπιστητόν]. Thus the eclipse of the moon was a matter of science for the famous mathematician Hipparchus, but an opinion for Epicurus, who made everything arise by the chance concourse of atoms. But each of these judgements of opinion and science has been received variously by philosophers, for most rejected opinion almost entirely. Heraclides' saying in Laertius, book 9, is:

units.la: ὑπὸ νόμως, ἰσρὰ νοσὸς ἐστι, καὶ ὄψεως ψοῦδος.
units.tr: Opinion is a sacred disease, and sight is false. [ὑπόληψις ἱερὰ νόσος ἐστί, καὶ ὄψεως ψεῦδος.]

units.la: Opinio, sacer est morbus, & visus fallitur.
units.tr: Opinion is a sacred disease, and sight is false.

units.la: hic non tantùm opinionem mentis, sed omne sensus judicium tollit. Quæ penè sententia est Parmenidis: — Χρὴ τὸ λέγειν τε νοεῖν τε ἐὸν ἔμμεναι. Ἡ μὲν ἀληθείης εὐπειθὲς ἀτρεκὲς ἦτορ, Ἡ δὲ βροτῶν δόξας, τῶν οὐκ ἔνι πίστις ἀληθής. 20 Oportet verò te omnia nosse: Tum veritatis suasu facilis accuratá sententiá: Tum verò mortalium opiniones, quarũ non amplius fides vera.
units.tr: Here he removes not only the opinion of the mind but every judgement of the senses. This is almost the view of Parmenides: "It must be that what is said and thought is; for it is, but nothing is not." But you must know all things: both the unshaken heart of truth, well persuasive, and the opinions of mortals, in which there is no true trust. [Χρὴ τὸ λέγειν τε νοεῖν τε ἐὸν ἔμμεναι· ἡ μὲν ἀληθείης εὐπειθὲς ἀτρεκὲς ἦτορ, ἡ δὲ βροτῶν δόξας, τῶν οὐκ ἔνι πίστις ἀληθής.]

units.la: Hic duplex judicium videtur attingi, & certæ veritatis, & opinionis. Deinde opinio & sensus, ut ante, rejicitur: Μὴ σε θεὸς πολύσπερον ἀλὸν ἄλλα τὸν δὲ βιάσθω Νωμᾶν ἀσκοπον ὄμμα, καὶ ἠχήεσαν ἀκουήν, Καὶ γλῶσσαν, κρίναι δὲ λόγῳ πολύδηριν ἔλεγχον. 30 Nec te Deus ancipitem viam juxta hanc cogat judicare inconsiderato visu, & resonante auditu, Et linguæ: sed judices ratione ambiguâ sententiâ.
units.tr: Here a twofold judgement seems to be touched on, that of certain truth and that of opinion. Then opinion and sense are rejected, as before: "Let not God force you, by much experience, to judge by the aimless eye, the echoing ear and the tongue, but judge by reason the much-disputed refutation." Let not God compel you to judge, by this path, with the ambiguous way, by careless sight, by resounding hearing and by tongue; but judge by reason, with an ambiguous sentence. [Μὴ σε θεὸς πολύσπερον ἀλὸν ἄλλα τὸν δὲ βιάσθω Νωμᾶν ἀσκοπον ὄμμα, καὶ ἠχήεσαν ἀκουήν, καὶ γλῶσσαν, κρίναι δὲ λόγῳ πολύδηριν ἔλεγχον.]

units.la: Epicurus contrá videtur judiciu veri sensib. attribuisse λέγει ἓν ὁ Ἐπίκουρος, ληπτὴ τὰ ἀληθέα ἕνια αὐδύσεις, ἡ προλήψεις, ἡ τὰ πάθη: ait siquidem Epicurus judicia veritatis esse sensus, & anticipationes, & affectiones. At Aristoteles utrūq; & sensus & intellectus judiciū cōplexus est, intellectumq; sensui longissimé præposuit: Nā tametsi notiones intellectus deducit á sensibus & sensiliū inductione rerū, & animadversione atq; experientia, ut colligit: statuit tn intellectu judiciū ratione visis reb. adjūcta, sensu certius: quantoq; remotiō á sensu notionis genus est, tátó αἰτιωτέρον, ἀρχικώτερον, ἐπιστημονικώτερον, καὶ τῇ φύσει πρότερον, καὶ γνωριμώτερον: causse & principio & scientiæ vicinius, & naturâ prius ac notius: ut jam dictū est, sic sane notionum earum judicium præstantius & excellentius.
units.tr: Epicurus, on the contrary, seems to have attributed the judgement of truth to the senses: Epicurus says that some true things are grasped by senses, or anticipations, or affections [λέγει ἓν ὁ Ἐπίκουρος, ληπτὴ τὰ ἀληθέα ἕνια αὐδύσεις, ἡ προλήψεις, ἡ τὰ πάθη]. For Epicurus says that the judgements of truth are the senses, anticipations and affections. But Aristotle embraces both, the judgement of sense and of intellect, and he places the intellect far above sense. For although he derives the notions of the intellect from the senses, by induction from sensible things, and by observation and experience, as he gathers, he nevertheless holds that the intellect's judgement, with reason added to the things seen, is more certain than sense. And the further a notion is from sense, the more causal, more principial, more scientific, prior by nature, and more knowable [αἰτιωτέρον, ἀρχικώτερον, ἐπιστημονικώτερον, καὶ τῇ φύσει πρότερον, καὶ γνωριμώτερον]: closer to cause, principle and science, and prior and better known by nature. As has already been said, so the judgement of these notions is more excellent and distinguished.

units.la: Cap. III. De Enuntiato simplici.
units.tr: Chap. III. On the Simple Proposition.

units.la: ENuntiatum, est simplex aut cōpositum. Simplex, est quo sententia simplex enuntiatur: itaq; vno verbo continetur, quo affirmato affirmatur, negato negatur: ut, ignis urit, ignis est calidus, ignis non est aqua: hic (ignis) est antecedens: (urit) consequens. Atq; hic prima est inventarū rerum dispositio, caussæ cum effecto, ut in primo exemplo: subjecti cum adjuncto, ut in secundo: dissentanei cū dissentaneo, ut in tertio: quomodo argumentū quodlibet enuntiari potest, exceptis plenis comparationibus & distributionibus: confentanea quidem affirmādo, dissentanea negando. Enuntiatum simplex est generale aut speciale: Generale cùm generaliter enuntiatur. Atque hic contradicētium generalium pars non semper altera vera, altera falsa est, sed contingētium rerum utraque falsa potest esse: ut, Omnis in orbe locus Bajis prælucet amœnis. Nullus in orbe locus Bajis prælucet amœnis. Item non contingentium: ut, Omne animal est rationale: Nullum animal est rationale. Enuntiatū speciale est, quando specialiter enuntiatur: & hic cōtradictionis pars est semper vera, pars salfa. Speciale est infinitum aut proprium: Infinitum, quando species non definitur: ut, Aliquid ignoscendum est: cui generaliter cōtradicitur, Nil ignofcendū est. Proprium, quando de aliquo fingulari enuntiatur: ut, Fabulla est bella: cujus negatio & contradictio est, Fabulla non est bella.
units.tr: A proposition is either simple or compound. A simple proposition is one in which a single judgment is stated. It is therefore contained in one verb: when affirmed it is affirmed, when denied it is denied. For example: "Fire burns," "Fire is hot," "Fire is not water." Here (fire) is the antecedent and (burns) the consequent. This is also the first arrangement of the things invented: cause with effect, as in the first example; subject with attribute, as in the second; disagreeing with disagreeing, as in the third. In this way any argument can be stated, except full comparisons and distributions. Agreeing things are affirmed, and disagreeing things are denied. A simple proposition is either general or special. It is general when it is stated generally. Here, of general contradictories, one is not always true and the other false. With contingent things both may be false: Every place in the world is outshone by the pleasant Baiae. No place in the world is outshone by the pleasant Baiae. Likewise with non-contingent things: "Every animal is rational." "No animal is rational." A proposition is special when it is stated specially, and here one part of the contradiction is always true and the other false. A special proposition is either indefinite or singular. It is indefinite when the species is not defined: "Something must be forgiven," whose general contradictory is "Nothing must be forgiven." It is singular when it is stated of some single thing: "The tale is pretty," whose negation and contradictory is "The tale is not pretty."

units.la: Enuntiatum ] Duplex enantiatiotis affectio communis adhuc exposita est, quid enuntiaretur, & quomodo: modi autem affectio prima, affirmationis & negationis, altera veritatis & salfitatis fpecies enuntiati fequûtur,fimplex & cô pofita:q partitio eft Ariftotelis in Interpr. 4. ca. 1. lib. Ex his vero alia quidem fimplex eft enuntiatio,ut aliquid de aliquo,aut aliqd ab aliquo, aut ex his.conftituta,ut oratio quædam cõposita. Simplicis vero enuntiati doctrina duobus libris περὶ ἑρμηνείας ab Ariftotele tractata eft.fed ager ifte valde neglectus & incultus adhuc jacuit totus feré vepribus obfitus eft. Itaq; P. Rami agriculturam hic operæ pretium fit intueri:fructum enim logicum (quicunque de libris duobus excerpi potuerat) paucis verbis perfpicuè interpretatus eft:Pagina illa fuperior analyfeos pofterioris fruges collegit:pagella hæc, fruges habebit ἐρμωνία: Quare diligêter attendêda nobis eft tam brevis facilifq; P. Rami ἐρμωνία.Simplex enûtiatum,definitur fententia fimplici: ut Philofophus eft ftudiofus fapientię,ideoq; continetur unico verbo. Verbum autem hic appellat,non grammaticũ vocabulum,fed ipfum mẽtis fêfum,quod verbo externo fignificatur: Partes vero enuntiati fimplicis,fpecialibus vocabulis in Organo appellantur,antecedens quidem ὑποκείμενον, fubjectum: cofequens autem κατηγορούμενον καὶ κατηγόρημα,attributum, vulgó in fcholis prædicatum & prædicabile: Sed vocabula hæc Græca longe aliter in Organo & frequenter appellantur:nam κατηγόρημα quodlibet argumentũ & ὑποκείμενον proprié adjuncto accidenti opponitur. Quare cúm doctrina,imó ufus ipfius doctrinæ in fimplicibus enûtiatis intelligi exerceriq; pofsit, abfq; his ambiguis terminorum fubjecti attributiq; vocabulis, P. Ramus has ambiguitis spinas deliberato studio certoq; logicę artis emolumento devitavit: quin etiam majore justioreq; de eauss a prꝛteriit totam illam Ariftote lis Grammaticá de nomine & verbo orationeq; indicante,imperâte, feré quatuor primis capiti bus in primo illo ἐρμηνεία comprehensam: justitia enim illa Aristotelea καθ' αὐτὸ, fines artiumre gi ac definiri jubet: nec quia nominũ verborum que & orationis,totiusq; omnino Grammaticę usus est logicæ arti necessarius, ideo verũ & justum erit,Grámaticam in Logica institui: κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ illud fuerit,non erit protinus καθ' αὐτὸ, nō καθόλου πρῶτον. Quare duabus hisce magnis legib. Grammaticam illam P.Ramus é logica ad Grámaticos remisit: Qua de re si quis curiosiús intelligere plura cupiet, legat P. Rami quintũ libru Scholarũ dialecticarum. Inventarum judicium dispositione cõprehensum & definitũ est: Itaq; in simplici primoq; judicio, simplex & prima debet esse dispositio: quę quatuor primis capitibus primi libri περὶ ἐρμηνείας cõprehensa est: hîc familiariter á P.Ramo explicatur, & quæ generaliter in enuntiato antea proposita sunt, tandem in unaquaq; specie specialiter exponûtur: primó quænam argumeta simplicibus enuntiis enuntientur,ut in exemplis caussa cum essecto, subjectum cum adjuncto, dissentaneũ cum dissentaneo disponitur: Comparata autem pauca simpliciter non enuntiantur: ut, Roma æqualis est Olympo: Roma est major Athenis: Roma est minor Babylone: Roma est similis Carthagini: Roma est dissimilis Mantuę. Comparatio enim plena constat τρφτάσι ἡ ἀπολίσει, quæ simpli ci enũciato cõprehendi nõ possunt. Causa cõsu laris cõsulé requirit: Cõsul à cõsulendo dicitur, conjugatio & notatio est. Partitio nulla sim pliciter enũtiari potest, definitio potest, testimo niũ potest: ut, Dialectica est ars bene disseredi: Cato judicavit Catilinam interimendum esse. Quęcunq; vero simpliciter enũciantur, eadem feré conjunctè possunt enũtiari: Ergo hæc simplex & prima dispositio est argumentorũ in sim plici & prima enũtiatione, & de duobus in logica enuntiatorum doctrina, id primum fuit, quæ argumenta simpliciter enuntiarentur: modus contradictionis & judicii deinde declaratur.
units.tr: Proposition] Two affections of the proposition have so far been explained: what is stated, and how. The first affection, of affirmation and negation, and the second, of truth and falsity, follow the kinds of the proposition, simple and compound. This division is Aristotle's in On Interpretation, chapter 1 (Interp. 4). "Of these, one proposition is simple, stating something of something or something from something, while another is compound, made up of such simple propositions." Aristotle treated the doctrine of the simple proposition in the two books On Interpretation [περὶ ἑρμηνείας]. But this field has been very much neglected and left uncultivated, and it lies almost wholly overgrown with brambles. It is worth our while, then, to look at Ramus's cultivation of it here. He has explained in a few words, and clearly, the logical fruit that could be gathered from those two books. The preceding page gathered the fruits of the later analytics; this little page will yield the fruits of interpretation [ἐρμηνία]. So the brief and easy exposition of Ramus must be attended to carefully. A simple proposition is defined as a sentence with a simple verb, as "The philosopher is zealous for wisdom," and so it is contained in one word. Here he calls "verb" not the grammatical word but the mental sense itself that is signified by an outward verb. The parts of the simple proposition are called by special terms in the Organon: the antecedent is the subject [ὑποκείμενον], and the consequent is the attribute [κατηγορούμενον and κατηγόρημα], commonly called in the schools the predicate and the predicable. But these Greek terms are used quite differently and often in the Organon: for katēgorēma means any argument whatever, and hypokeimenon is properly opposed to an adjunct accident. Since the doctrine, and indeed the practical use of the doctrine, of simple propositions can be understood and exercised without these ambiguous words for subject and attribute, Ramus deliberately avoided these ambiguous thorns, to the lasting benefit of the logical art. Moreover, with greater and more just reason he has passed over that whole grammar of Aristotle's about noun and verb and speech that indicates and commands, which was contained in almost the first four chapters of that first book, On Interpretation. For that Aristotelian justice, "per se," requires that the boundaries of the arts be kept and defined. Nor, because the use of nouns, verbs and speech, and indeed all grammar, is necessary to the logical art, will it therefore be true and right that grammar be taught in logic. What is "the same" (κατὰ τὸ αὐτό) will not at once be "per se" (καθ' αὐτό), nor "first and universal" (καθόλου πρῶτον). So by these two great laws Ramus has sent that grammar out of logic back to the grammarians. If anyone wishes to understand more about this matter in more detail, let him read Ramus's fifth book of the Dialectical Scholae. Judgment is comprehended and defined by the arrangement of things invented. Therefore in the simple and first judgment the arrangement must be simple and first. This is comprehended in the first four chapters of the first book of On Interpretation [περὶ ἑρμηνείας]. Here Ramus explains it in familiar terms, and what was proposed generally above about the proposition is at last set out specially in each species. First, he shows what arguments are stated in simple propositions: as in the examples, cause with effect, subject with adjunct, and disagreeing with disagreeing are arranged. Compared things, however, are not stated simply, as: "Rome is equal to Olympus." "Rome is greater than Athens." "Rome is less than Babylon." "Rome is similar to Carthage." "Rome is dissimilar to Mantua." For a full comparison consists of four or more terms, which cannot be contained in a simple proposition. A common cause asks for a consul: "consul" is derived from "consulendo" (consulting); it is a conjugation and a notation. No division can be stated simply, but a definition can, and a testimony can: "Dialectic is the art of speaking well"; "Cato judged that Catiline should be put to death." Whatever is stated simply can almost always be stated conjointly. So this is the simple and first arrangement of arguments in the simple and first statement. Of the two things in the logical doctrine of propositions, the first was which arguments are stated simply; then the manner of contradiction and judgment is declared.

units.la: Generàle] Partes enuntiati simplicis adhuc ex positę sunt, divisio in quasdam species sequitur generalem & specialem, de quibus duo sunt capita primi de Interpr. quintum & sextum: quod idé iteratur succinctiùs 1. cap. 1 Prior. ταυτολογίαν trium capitũ lex καθόλυ πρῶτον repudiat: at P. Ramus in eam legem in primis juravit: Itaque generalia generaliter & semel explicabit. Comprehenditur autem divisio illa 5. ca. 1. ἐρμ. τὰ μὲν καθόλυ τῶν πραγμάτων, τὰ δὲ καθ' ἕκαστον: rerum aliæ sunt universales, aliæ singulares. Divisionis hoc modo legitimæ διχοτομία est: eodem tamẽ in capite tertium genus proponitur enuntiati, & appellatur τὸ καθόλυ μὲν μὴ καθόλυ, universale nõ universaliter: ut, Homo est albus, Homo non est albus: quod 1. cap. 1. Prior. iteratur, & appellatur ἀόριστον τὸν ἀόριστον τῶν καθόλυ, ἢ κατὰ μέρος: infinitum sine universali aut particulari nota:ut, Cótrariorum est eadem disciplina:ut, Voluptas non est bonum. Ἀδιάϛρον autē videtur Cicero in Fato dicere infinitum, cúm negationes infinitarum cõjunctionum & infinita cónexa dicit: & P.Ramus id ab eo verbū assumpsit. Aristot. autem ἀδιόριστον ali ter intelligit, pro communi quodam ambiguo & incerto, utrū generaliter an specialiter. quod idé iteratur 4. ca.1. Prior. ἀδιόριστον, ὡχὶ τὸ ἐν μέρει, infinitum & particulare enūtiatum in syllogismo idem esse. quod idem videtur iterari initio 7.capit. sed aliud est, infinitum illud valere, ubi particulare valeat:id enim verum sic esset.at 28. ca.1.Prior. ambigua illa inter generalem & specialem sententia iterum proponitur errore consimili. Quod utrumque Eubulidis vel Antisthe nis quoddam est somnium: sententia enim enuntiati mente concepti,est generalis aut specialis: tertium illud vagum,quod neq; generaliter, neque specialiter intelligatur,nihil esse potest:Exi re ex urbe Consul hostem jubet (quod enuntiatur Catilinaria prima) Eubulides ille ἀδιόριστον diceret esse.at σωρίτης,tropus rhetoricus, Eu bulidi resistet, & ex genere speciem docebit intelligi:ut intelligatur, Cicero jubet Catilinā exi re Roma: Cóvincit etiam alterū illud in Analy ticis commentum: infinitum in syllogismo esse pro particulari: Sententia enim enuntiati spectanda est:signa sunt illa quidem & symbola generalis sententiæ & enuntiationis omnis, nullus,quilibet,totus,universus, & similia: attamē ea persæpe nulla requiruntur, imó nulla omni no sunt: & vox generalis generaliter intelligitur, nisi certa restrictio adhibita sit. Quodlibet enim artis enuntiatum, est κατὰ παντὸς, καθ' αὑτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον, generale ideo & universale, & generaliter atq; universaliter intellectû: attamen signis istis universalibus ars nulla utitur. Quinetiam extra artes, homines feré ita differunt:
units.tr: General] The parts of the simple proposition have now been set out, and the division into certain species follows, general and special. Of these two there are chapters 5 and 6 of the first book of On Interpretation, and the same thing is repeated more briefly in chapter 1 of the Prior Analytics. The law of the three chapters, "universal first" (καθόλου πρῶτον), rejects tautology, yet Ramus above all swore by that law. Therefore he will explain general things generally and once only. That division is contained in chapter 5 of On Interpretation: "Of things, some are universal [τὰ μὲν καθόλου], some are singular [τὰ δὲ καθ' ἕκαστον]." That is a legitimate dichotomy of this kind. In the same chapter, however, a third kind of proposition is put forward, called "universal not universally" (τὸ καθόλου μὲν μὴ καθόλου): for example, "Man is white," "Man is not white." This is repeated in chapter 1 of the Prior Analytics, and is called "indefinite without a universal or particular sign" (ἀόριστον), as in: "Contraries have the same discipline," "Pleasure is not good." Cicero, in his On Fate, seems to use "infinite" (infinitum) for the same thing, since he speaks of the negations of infinite conjunctions and infinite connexions, and Ramus took the word from him. Aristotle, however, understands "indefinite" (ἀδιόριστον) differently, as something common, ambiguous and uncertain, whether general or special. This is repeated in chapter 4 of the Prior Analytics: "indefinite, not the part-wise," that an indefinite and a particular proposition are the same in a syllogism. The same thing seems to be repeated at the start of chapter 7, but it is another matter: that an indefinite proposition holds where a particular one holds. For that would be true in that sense. But in chapter 28 of the Prior Analytics that ambiguous sentence between general and special is again put forward, through a similar error. Both of these are a kind of dream of Eubulides or Antisthenes. For the sentence of a proposition conceived in the mind is either general or special; that third vague thing, which is understood neither generally nor specially, cannot exist. "Leave the city, Consul, Catiline is ordered to be an enemy" (as the first Catilinarian is stated): Eubulides would call that "indefinite." But the sorites, a rhetorical trope, will resist Eubulides and will show that the species is understood from the genus: so that it is understood as "Cicero orders Catiline to leave Rome." The commentary in the Analytics also is refuted: that an indefinite proposition in a syllogism stands for a particular one. For the sense of the proposition must be looked to. Those signs, indeed, are the tokens and symbols of general sentences and every general statement, "none," "any," "all," "universal" and similar words; yet very often no such signs are needed, indeed none at all. A general word is understood generally unless a definite restriction is applied. For every proposition of the art is "of all" (κατὰ παντός), "per se" (καθ' αὑτό), "universal first" (καθόλου πρῶτον), and so general and universal, and understood generally and universally; yet the art uses no such universal signs. Indeed, outside the arts too, men mostly speak in this way:

units.la: Virtus est vitium fugere, ait Horar. Tempori cedere sapientis semper est habitum, ait Tullius. Quare tertium genus enū tiati medii inter generale & speciale, P. Ramus ut commentitium sustulit. Bajis]Locus est in prima Horatii epist. Baje, oppidum Campaniæ, in cujus agro aquæ calidæ sunt, & ad voluptatem, & ad sanandos morbos accommodatissimæ: quæ quidem reliquas aquarum calidarum nobilitate antecellunt: fuitq; olim hæc urbs temperie aeris, & Romanorum frequentia, atque ornamētis ædificiorum celeberrima: Martialis lib.epigr.11.ad Flaccum:
units.tr: Virtus est vitium fugere, says Horace: "Virtue is to flee vice." Tully says: "It has always been the habit of the wise to yield to the times." Hence P. Ramus rejected, as a fiction, a third kind of proposition between the general and the special. Baiae: the place is mentioned in the first epistle of Horace. Baiae is a town in Campania, in whose territory there are hot waters most suited both to pleasure and to curing diseases, and which surpass other hot waters in renown. The city was once famous for the mildness of its air, the crowds of Romans, and the splendour of its buildings. Martial, book 11 of the Epigrams, to Flaccus:

units.la: ut mille laudem, Flacce, versibus Bajas, Laudabo digné non satis tamen Bajas.
units.tr: "Though I praised Baiae, Flaccus, in a thousand verses, I would still not praise Baiae worthily enough."

units.la: Infinitum]Enuntiatum infinitum jam perspicué definitur á P. Ramo, pro eo quod particulare vulgus appellat: ejusque ut proprii enuntiati contradictio exponitur: atq; ita cōcluditur simplicis enuntiati doctrina. Veruntamen præter duplicem illam contradictionem simplicis enuntiati, generalem alteram, alteram speciale m, duplex in scholas, jam olim ante Boetii ætate vulgō inducta est: subcontrariæ, Aliquis homo est justus, Aliquis homo non est justus: subalternæ,
units.tr: Infinite: Ramus now clearly defines the infinite proposition as what the common people call the particular, and he explains it as the contradictory of the proper proposition, and so concludes the doctrine of the simple proposition. Yet apart from that twofold contradiction of the simple proposition, the schools have long since, even in Boethius's time, commonly introduced a second, general and special, pair of opposites: the subcontraries, "Some man is just; some man is not just," and the subalterns,

units.la: u
units.tr: u

units.la: Omnis homo est justus, Aliquis homo est justus.vel, Nullus homo est justus, Aliquis homo non est justus. Subcontrariarum autem (quae dicuntur) mentio quaedam est in Organo: sed in eodem etiam Organo magna certaq; est ipsarum refutatio: Etenim (ut est quinto libro dialecticarum Scholarum) definitio contradictionis repetatur, & intelligatur ejusdem affirmatio & negatio, ejusdem (inquam) numero, & de eadem numero, ut Aristoteles in Topicis loquitur: Nam res eadem genere & specie negari & affirmari potest, ut tamen nulla fit contradictio:ut.
units.tr: "Every man is just; some man is just," or "No man is just; some man is not just." There is indeed some mention of the so-called subcontraries in the Organon, but in the same Organon there is also a great and certain refutation of them. For (as is stated in the fifth book of the Dialectical Lectures) the definition of contradiction must be taken up again and understood as the affirmation and negation of the same thing, of the same in number and about the same in number, as Aristotle speaks in the Topics. For one thing can be denied and affirmed in genus and in species, yet there is no contradiction, as in:

units.la: Omnis bos est quadrupes: Nullus equus est bipes.
units.tr: "Every ox is quadruped; no horse is biped."

units.la: Bos & equus, genere sunt idem: quadrupes & bipes genere sunt idem. Item,
units.tr: Ox and horse are the same in genus; quadruped and biped are the same in genus. Likewise:

units.la: Hic homo est Socrates: Ille homo non est Plato.
units.tr: "This man is Socrates; that man is not Plato."

units.la: Specie affirmatur & negatur idem: & tamen contradictio in neutro exemplo est. Quapropter ut contradictio fit, necesse est eandem rem numero, de eadem re numero negari & affirmari. Et genus sibi generaliter oppositum, ideo contradictionem facit, quia res eadem numero, sub eo comprehensae affirmatur & negantur: & idem sumptu specialiter, sibi generaliter sumpto opposito, ideo contradictione facit, quia ex his, quae genere continentur, aliquid idem numero negatur, quod illic affirmatum erat, aut contra. Discernemus igitur oppositā quaestione, hoc modo:
units.tr: The same is affirmed and denied in species, and yet there is no contradiction in either example. Therefore, for a contradiction to arise, the same thing in number must be both affirmed and denied of the same thing in number. A genus opposed to it in general makes a contradiction because the same thing in number, contained under it, is affirmed and denied; and the same taken specially, against its general opposite, makes a contradiction because from those things which are contained under a genus, something the same in number is denied which had been affirmed there, or the reverse. Therefore we shall distinguish the opposed propositions in this way:

units.la: Omnis contradictio idem numero affirmat & negat: Subcontrarietas non affirmat et negat idem numero. Etenim verae simul esse possunt (ut in ipso Interpretationis libro docetur) etiam si infinitae sint: ut,
units.tr: "Every contradiction affirms and denies the same thing in number; subcontrariety does not affirm and deny the same thing in number." For they can be true together (as is taught in the very book On Interpretation), even if they are infinite, as in:

units.la: Homo est albus: Homo non est albus.
units.tr: "Man is white; man is not white."

units.la: Nec enim idem putatur significari hoc enuntiationis genere, atque universalibus significaretur:
units.tr: For this kind of proposition is not thought to signify the same thing as universals would signify:

units.la: Omnis homo est albus: Nullus homo est albus.
units.tr: "Every man is white; no man is white."

units.la: Ut etiam docetur in eodem libro, quanvis inepte. Quare hic nulla est contradictio. & contradictionis verbum κατὰ ἀντίφασιν in his assumptum est, ut dixi. Nec vero fuerit audiedum, quod nescio quis attulerit in his enuntiatis.
units.tr: As is also taught in the same book, though foolishly. Hence there is no contradiction here, and the word contradiction [κατὰ ἀντίφασιν] is used in these cases, as I have said. Nor should we listen to what someone, I know not who, has brought forward about these propositions:

units.la: (Aliquis homo ambulat: Aliquis homo non ambulat.)
units.tr: "(Some man walks; some man does not walk.)"

units.la: eandem rem numero affirmari & negari: nempe de nomine (homo) verbum (ambulat) & affirmari & negari: Etenim valde absurda fit ista captio: Vocabula enim, symbola sunt & signa tantum, nec ex se faciunt contradictionem, sed res symbolis significatae: & orationis qualitas pendet e rerum qualitate. Si autem pars utraque vera fit (ut esse potest) nequaquam res eadem numero in utraque parte affirmat & negatur: Quare nec contradictio erit. Veruntamen (ait Aristoteles in modificatis) impossibile de eodem veras esse oppositas affirmationes & negationes.
units.tr: that the same thing in number is affirmed and denied, namely the verb (walks) is affirmed and denied of the noun (man). For this objection is very absurd: words are only symbols and signs, and they do not make a contradiction by themselves, but the things signified by the symbols do; and the quality of a statement depends on the quality of the things. If, however, both parts are true (as they can be), the same thing in number is by no means affirmed and denied in both parts, and so there will be no contradiction. Yet Aristotle says in the Modals that it is impossible for opposed affirmations and negations to be true of the same thing.

units.la: Et rursus ibidem: Nunquam in eodem simul erunt verae: opponuntur enim. Item ibidem, cum disputat hujus enuntiationis (necesse no esse) negationem non esse (Non necesse est esse) ait, Cótingit enim utrumq; de eodem verum esse. Analy.1.capit. 12. hoc etiam secundo: De omni enim aut affirmatio aut negatio. Sed Analyt.2. capit.15.tota cótroversia hæc dirimitur,ubi docetur hoc genere,
units.tr: And again in the same place, when he discusses the negation of this proposition, "it need not be" (it is not necessary that it be), he says that both happen to be true of the same thing. In the Analytics, I.12, he adds this too: "for of everything either the affirmation or the negation holds." But in Analytics II.15 the whole controversy is settled, where it is taught that this kind of proposition,

units.la: (Aliquis ambulat: Aliquis non ambulat) non revera,sed verbo dūtaxat opponi:ut sic oppositio dicatur. quomodo homo pictus, homo diceretur. Quamobrē Aristoteles oppositas efse non vult subcontrarias, quæ appellantur: & contra ejus opinionem atque sententiá in scholas hæc oppositionis species indućta est:nec authoris sententia ex perverso aliquo & κατ᾽ αχρ κῶς arrepto symbolo comminiscēda est potiús, quám ex tot & tam manifestis: tamque veris lo cis æstimanda: Subalternæ verò sunt ambæ affirmationes vel ambæ negationes,& quidē specialis generali consequens & consentanea: tantum abest,ut sit hic ulla oppositionis forma:cócludereque inde licebit:ut,
units.tr: "(Some man walks; some man does not walk)" is opposed not in reality but only in words, so that it is called an opposition in the way a painted man is called a man. For this reason Aristotle does not want those so-called subcontraries to be opposed, and against his opinion and judgement this species of opposition was introduced into the schools. Nor should the author's opinion be invented from some perverse symbol seized in an extreme way, rather than judged from so many and such manifest and true passages. The subalterns, however, are both affirmations or both negations, and the special one follows from and agrees with the general one. So far is there any form of opposition here that one may infer from it, as:

units.la: Omnis homo albus est: Aliquis igitur homo albus est. Nullus homo albus est: Igitur aliquis homo albus non est. neque id commentum in Aristotelis bibliotheca repertum est. spinæ istæ sunt agri sophistici, unde in agrum logicum tráslatæ sunt:eradicentur igitur, tollanturq;.Ergo contradicétium enuntiatorum genera duo sola sunt, generale & speciale:speciale rursus indefinitū, aut propriū & indefinitum intelligatur,ἀλλοτροπία ista enūtiati generalis & fpecialis, legib. Ariftoteleis & logicis cõsentanea eft, eft καζὰ παντὸς, eft καθ' αὑτὸ, eft καθόλε πρῶτον. Pergamus igitur: Ex occasione vero contradictionis, importuna materies Eubulidi vel Logico nescio cui (quem Ariftoteles secūdo περὶ ἐμμενέας eft imitatus) quæstiones obscuras valdė, nec minús inutiles cõfingendi de confecutionib. enuntiatorũ infinitorũ & modificatorũ infinitorũ é cõsequẽtis parte cõtradicẽ tibus: ut Homo eft juftus, Homo eft nõ juftus. qd' ænigma á grẹcis quibufdá interpretib. ut á Pfello, appellat: At revera fophifma eft infigne, fi ullũ unquá fuit, in quo nulla vel inventionis vel judicii mica eft: imó judicii çaligo fumma. Quare tam alienũ doctrinæ elenchũ contra legė καθ' αὑτὸ, P. Ramus in Logicá fine manifefta fraude inducere non debuit,itaque fuftulit. At veró infigne fophifma illud fuit, fed multó etiá eft infignius de modificatis, id eft(ut vulgus loquitur)de modalibus: quarũ obfcuritas eam in fcholis famá confecuta eft,ut vulgó prædicetur illud, De modalibus nõ guftabit asinus. Modi aũt ipfi fex proponuntur, pofsibile, impofsibile,neceffarium, contingens, verum, falsum. προσδιορίσεις appellat Ariftoteles hos modos, id eft attributiones,ut 2.cap.1. Pr. appellat προσφύσεις,Homine effe album, eft pofsibile: Hominẽ effe divitem, eft cõtingens: Hominem effe animal, eft neceffarium:Hominem effe beftiam, eft impofsibile: Hominẽ effe corporeum,eft verum:Hominem effe marmoreũ, eft falsum. Hi fex mod i funt in hoc capite,pofsibile,cõtingens,neceffarium, rium, impossibile, verū, falsum : Innumerabiles tamē modi sunt: ut, Parentes colere, sanctū est: Suum cuique tribuere, justum est: Socrates disputat sapienter: Zeno respondet subtiliter: Alexander prœliatur fortiter, & similia. Deniq; ex omnibus feré & nominib. & adverbiis, modos ejusmodi liceat enuntiationi addere, ad significandū quomodo catogerema in subjecto insit: ut, Agit bene, incedit obliqué, scribit doctě, & similia: ne quid hic magnæ rei vel novę disputari videatur. De modificatis ejusmodi, doctrina est Aristotelis duplex: altera dicere videtur (quod tamen nominatim non dicit) modificatum negari solo modo negato: ut hæc enuntiatio (Hominem ambulare est non possibile) sit negata: Sed tamen argumento cōtradictionis, error ille per ineptos interpretes in scholas inductus, refelli planeq; convinci potest. Hic enim (Socrates est leo necessario, Socrates est leo non necessario) pars utraq; falsa est. Quare nulla est in propriis illis enuntiatis contradictio, neq; ideo affirmatio & negatio. Quare negationis disserentia in absolutis & modificatis enuntiatis nulla est: Tollatur igitur commentū, lege λαυὰ ωαντὶ convictū. Sophisma aūt de modalium confecutione, ex homonymia verbi (possibilis) contextū est: quod tripliciter capi dicitur, ut modo possibile, res æternas significet, quæ tantum sunt actus: ut, Possibile est Deum esse. modo contingentes, queq; & esse & nō esse possint: ut tū potentia sint. tum actus: ut, Possibile est hominē ambulare. modo significet, quę esse quidem possunt, sunt, neque tamen sunt futura: ut potentia tantum fit: ut, Posibile ignem non calescere. Ergo ex hac ambiguitate nascuntur cōsectaria illa mirifica: quorum tamē judicium non ex enthymematis truncis, qualia sunt in illis consecutionibus, sed é plenis syllogismis sint æstimanda. Accesit ad dumeta illa, spinetum conversionū omnium densissimum asperrimumque: Generalem negationem generaliter cōverti: ut, Nullus lapis est homo, Ergo nullus homo est lapis. affirmationem aut & generalem, & speciale, specialiter tantum cōverti: ut, Omnis homo est animal: Ergo aliquod animal est homo. item, Aliquis homo est animal: Ergo aliquod animal est homo, denique, Socrates est animal: Ergo aliquod animal est Socrates. negationē vero specialem nō necessario convertitur, Aliquod animal nō est homo, vel non est Socrates: Ergo aliquis homo, vel Socrates, non est animal. non sequitur. tum idē in modificatis necessariis contingentibus docetur, omniumq; demonstrationes obscurissimę attexūtur. hic Analytici primi capita duo, secundū & tertiū, integra consumūtur. At exemplis Homericis & humanis hæc minimè omniū sunt inducta: imó ne induci quidé per natură, & rationis humanę sensum possunt: Nam cum quæritur, utrum nullus lapis sit homo: & probare velis controversiam hoc modo, Nullus homo est lapis: ergo nullus lapis est homo. nullum medium extra quæstionem, nullúq; argumentū hic habes: sed quæstionem probas hocipso quæstionis argumento: & si compleas enthymema (Nullus homo est lapis:ergo nullo est homo) sophismatis tă putidi plane te pudeat:hoc nēpe modo, Nullus homo est lapis: Omnis lapis est lapis: Ergo nullus lapis est homo.
units.tr: "Every man is white; therefore some man is white. No man is white; therefore some man is not white." Nor is this invention found in Aristotle's library. These are thorns of the sophistic field, from which they were transplanted into the logical field; let them therefore be uprooted and removed. So there are only two kinds of contradictory propositions, general and special, and the special is either indefinite or understood as proper and indefinite. This alienation [ἀλλοτροπία] of general and special proposition agrees with the laws of Aristotle and of logic: it is [κατὰ παντός], it is [καθ' αὑτό], it is [καθόλου πρῶτον]. Let us go on. From the occasion of contradiction comes an unprofitable matter, the very obscure and no less useless questions devised by Eubulides or some logician I know not who (whom Aristotle imitated in his book On [Persistence] [περὶ ἐμμενέας]), about the consequences of infinite propositions and infinite modal propositions with the contradicting part of the consequent: such as "Man is just; man is not just." Some Greek interpreters, such as Psellus, call this a riddle [αἴνιγμα]. In truth it is a notable sophism, if ever there was one, in which there is no particle of invention or judgement, indeed a supreme darkness of judgement. Therefore P. Ramus should not have introduced into logic such an alien refutation of doctrine, against the law [καθ' αὑτό], without a manifest fraud; and so he removed it. But that sophism was notable, and much more notable is the one about modal propositions, that is (as the common people speak) about modals, whose obscurity has gained such a reputation in the schools that the saying is commonly repeated: "The donkey will not taste of modals." The modes themselves are proposed as six: possible, impossible, necessary, contingent, true, false. Aristotle calls these modes [προσδιορισμοί], that is, attributions, as in chapter 1 of the Prior Analytics he calls them [προσθῆκαι]. "To be white in man is possible; to be rich in man is contingent; to be animal in man is necessary; to be beast in man is impossible; to be corporeal in man is true; to be marble in man is false." These six modes are in this chapter: possible, contingent, necessary, impossible, true, false. Yet there are innumerable modes, as: "To honour parents is holy; to render to each his own is just; Socrates disputes wisely; Zeno replies subtly; Alexander fights bravely," and the like. Finally, it is permitted to add modes of this kind to a proposition, almost from all nouns and adverbs, to signify how the predicate inheres in the subject, as: "He acts well, he walks obliquely, he writes learnedly," and the like; so that nothing of great or new matter seems to be argued here. On modal propositions of this kind, Aristotle's teaching is twofold. One version seems to say (though he does not say it by name) that a modal proposition is negated only by negating the mode; so that the proposition "for a man to walk is not possible" is the negation of the other. Yet by the argument of contradiction that error, introduced into the schools by inept interpreters, can be refuted and clearly convicted. For here (Socrates is a lion necessarily; Socrates is a lion not necessarily) both parts are false. Therefore there is no contradiction in these proper propositions, nor for that reason an affirmation and a negation. Hence there is no difference of negation in absolute and modal propositions. Let the invention therefore be removed, convicted by the law [κατὰ παντός]. The sophism about the consequence of modals is woven from the ambiguity of the word (possible). It is said to be taken in three ways: in one way, the possible signifies eternal things, which are only actual, as "It is possible for God to exist." In another way it signifies contingent things, which can both be and not be, and which are both in potency and in act, as "It is possible for man to walk." In a third way it signifies things which can indeed be, and are, but are not going to be, which are only in potency, as "It is possible for fire not to heat." From this ambiguity arise those wonderful consequences, whose judgement must be weighed not from truncated enthymemes, such as those in those consequences, but from full syllogisms. He came to those thickets, the most dense and rough thorn-brake of all conversions: a general negation is converted generally, as "No stone is a man; therefore no man is a stone." An affirmation, both general and special, is converted only specially: as "Every man is an animal; therefore some animal is a man." Likewise, "Some man is an animal; therefore some animal is a man." Finally, "Socrates is an animal; therefore some animal is Socrates." A special negation is not converted necessarily: "Some animal is not a man, or is not Socrates; therefore some man, or Socrates, is not an animal" does not follow. Then the same is taught in the necessary and contingent modals, and the demonstrations of them all are woven in most obscurely. Here two chapters of the First Analytics, the second and third, are wholly consumed. But these things are least of all illustrated with Homeric and human examples; indeed they cannot even be illustrated by the nature and sense of human reason. For when it is asked whether no stone is a man, and you want to prove the controversy in this way, "No man is a stone; therefore no stone is a man," you have no middle term outside the question and no argument here; you prove the question by the very argument of the question. And if you complete the enthymeme ("No man is a stone; therefore no stone is a man") as "No man is a stone; every stone is a stone; therefore no stone is a man," you should be thoroughly ashamed of such a rotten sophism.

units.la: Hoc judicium conversionis tam ἄλογον erit:unde tamé postea infinitę per tota priora Analytica spinæ in syllogismorū sophisticis & demōstrationib. & potestatibus ortę sunt. Quapropter saxa & asperitates, præsertim tam steriles tăq; logici fructus inanes, imo logico fructui exitiabiles avelluntur à P. Ramo atq; ejiciūtur: Lex λαὰ τὰ παρτες, exēplis Homericis inducta effiagitat: somnia & comenta nunquam probabit: lex λαὰ αὐτὸ, quicquid otiosi & inertęs homines in artibus commenti sunt, pro homogeneo nūquam probabit. Duo capita inserta sunt in eodē secun do libro, alterum de sophismate compositionis & divisionis, alterum quę enuntiationes magis contrariæ sint. At logicæ artis sophistica elĕchtica nulla pars est, ut antea dictum est: & quæstio de magis oppositis, in topico cōtradictionis disceptata satis est. Sed tamen his de rebus major disputatio est P. Rami sexto & septimo dialecticarum Scholarum libro curiosis ingeniis proposita. Quamobrem pagella una de generibus enuntiatorum simplicium & contradictionibus, totum obscurissime duobus in libris ἐμπνεύσεως doctrinæ fructum, semotis sophismatū spinis, P. Ramus ingenuo & liberali discipulo proposuit: non proposuit de enuntiatis & infinitis & modificatis vanum laborem.
units.tr: This rule of conversion will be as irrational (ἄλογον) as it is; and yet from it there afterwards arose endless thorns through all the earlier Analytics, in the sophistries, demonstrations and powers of syllogisms. For this reason Peter Ramus pulls up and throws out these rocks and roughnesses, especially since they are so barren, like empty logical fruit, or rather deadly to the fruit of logic. The law of "according to all" (κατὰ τὰ πάντα), introduced by the Homeric examples, demands it: he will never approve dreams and inventions. The law of "according to itself" (καθ' αὐτό) will never approve as a homogeneous thing whatever idle and inert men have devised in the arts. Two chapters are inserted in the same second book, one on the sophism of composition and division, the other on which statements are more contrary. But there is no sophistical or elenctic part of the art of logic, as was said before, and the question of more opposed things has been argued enough under the topic of contradiction. Nevertheless, a fuller discussion of these matters is set out by Ramus in the sixth and seventh books of his Dialectical Lectures, for curious minds. Therefore Ramus has offered to his free and liberal student one page on the kinds of simple statements and contradictions, which in two very obscure books gives the whole fruit of the teaching of inspiration, with the thorns of sophisms removed; he has not offered a vain labour on statements, infinites and modified propositions.

units.la: Cap. IIII. De Enuntiato copulato.
units.tr: Chapter IV. On the Copulative Proposition.

units.la: ENuntiatū compositū, est quo sententia multiplex conjunctione alia qua compositè enūtiatur.Itaque é conjunctione affirmatur & negata affirmat & negatur: contradictiónisq; pars vera est, pars falsa. Enuntiatum compositū, est cōgregativum aut segregativū:Congregattvum, cujus conjunctio est congregativa.est verò copulatum aut connexum.Copulatū cujus conjunctio est copulativa:ut 1. Aeneid.
units.tr: A compound proposition is one in which several statements are joined by some conjunction, so that it is asserted as a compound. Hence, from the conjunction, what is affirmed affirms and what is denied denies; and in a contradiction one part is true and one part false. A compound proposition is either congregative or segregative. A congregative one is that whose conjunction is congregative, and this is either copulative or connective. A copulative one is that whose conjunction is copulative, as in Aeneid 1:
