units.la: unā Eurusq;, Nothusq; ruūt, crebrq; pcellis Africus.— hic negatio igitur erit & contradictio. Non unā Eurusq;, Nothusque ruunt:creberque procellis Africus.
units.tr: Not only Eurus and Notus rush together, and Africus, thick with storms. Here then is the negation and the contradiction: Eurus and Notus do not rush together, and Africus is not thick with storms.

units.la: Verum enuntiati copulati judiciū pē det ex omnium partiū veritate: falsum saltē ex una parte falsa huic generi assine est enuntiatum relatę qualitatis, cujus conjunctio est ipsa relatio. 5. Eclog.
units.tr: But the judgment of a copulative statement depends on the truth of all its parts; it is false if even one part is false. Closely related to this kind is the proposition of relative quality, whose conjunction is the relation itself, as in Eclogue 5:

units.la: Tale tuum carmen nobis, divine poeta, Quale sopor fessis in gramine.— hic copulatum judicium est: tanquam diceretur, Sopor est gratus fessis: & sic tuum carmë nobis gratum est.cujus negatio est,
units.tr: Your song, divine poet, is to us such as sleep is to the weary on the grass. Here the judgment is copulative, as if it were said: sleep is pleasing to the weary, and so your song is pleasing to us. Its negation is:

units.la: Non tale tuum carmen nobis, divine poetá,
units.tr: Your song, divine poet, is not to us

units.la: Quale sopor fessis in gramine.
units.tr: such as sleep is to the weary on the grass.

units.la: Enũtiatum] Haẞtenus logica enuntiatorũ sim plicių ex Aristotelis Organo fuit,quę quibus argumenta enuntiarentur,& quo tũ contradicendi,tum judicandi genere:quę sequũtur de enũtiatorum compositorum materia, & contradictionis judiciique modo,in Aristotelis philosophia nulla sunt: neq; enim Aristotelis ætate,Logica de compositis & enuntiatis & syllogismis erat inventa: & posteaquám inventa est, damnata à quibusdam,ut á Clinomacho apud Laertiũ 2.lib.qui ex axiomatis, τὰ ἁπλᾶ πρωτἀιχόμενον, τὰ ἐν ἀπλᾷ αὐτῷ, λέγων σωνημμένα καὶ συμπλεγμένα : simpli-cia suscipiens,non simplicia tollebat,nominans connexa & complexa. Sed Clinomachus tam temeré composita enuntiata tollebat,quám antea sustulit negata: Est enim logica compositorũ enuntiatorũ & per se,& in syllogismis maximé necessaria. Discipuli duo, Theophrastus & Eudemus,hanc novalé primi coluére:at Theophrastus tantúm súmmas exequutus est: Eude mus latiorem viam est ingressus: sed ita,ut veluti semina tantúm sparsisse, nullum frugis prové tũm extulisse videatur, ut Boetius nominatim ait libro primo de syllogismo hypothetico.Græci Aristotelis interpretes ad 22.caput 2. Pr.profitentur inventionẽ illam,Theophrasti & Eude mi propriam esse. Quare P.Ramus agricultură illam laboriosam in agro Ariftotelis nullam hic habuit, habuit tamen aliquâ in agro Theophra– fti & Eudemi, vel potiús Boetii: quoniam videri vult initia tantúm ab illis accepiffe, addidiffe de fuo cætera. Superiorem enuntiationis fpeciem, categoricam vocat à parte confequente, quę ληκτηγορικὸν καθ' ὑποθετικὸν: compositá autè, vocat ὑποθετικὸν, conditionalem. At neque rectè, neque Ariftotelis doctrinæ congruenter: Sunt enim compositæ enuntiationes alię præter conditionales: ut copulativa abfoluta, ut difcretiva: Nam connexa & disjuncta, conditionales dici pofsint, & Cicero in disjunctione, códitionem nominat, ut poftea in disjúncto fyllogifmo primo notabitur. Sed ὑπόθεσις Ariftoteli eft quęlibet enuntiatio, quæ pro vera ponitur, feu fimplex, feu compofita, feu cónexa, feu disjuncta, ut poftea in generibus ipfis dicetur. quomodo tota Aftrologia diceretur hypothetica, cúm per hypothefes, non per ἀξιώματα principia progrediatur. & fic 30. cap.1. Prior. ἀναλυτικὸν opponitur τῷ δὲ ὑποθετικῷ: & totis tribus capitib. 2. Prior. 11. 12.13. appellantur ab Ariftotele fyllogifmi hypothetici, fyllogifmi ad impofsibile, qui tamen cóftituúntur é fimplicibus enuntiatis fuppofitis ex conditione. Quare cúm Theophraftus, Eudemus, Boetius appellarûnt omne genus enútiati compofiti ὑποθετικόν, non rectè, neq; magiftri fui doctrinæ convenienter appellarunt. Hypothefeos fignificationem duplicem illi quidem inftituerunt, priorequ; cóplectuntur illam, quam Ari ftotelis effe diximus: pofteriore, confequentiâ conditionalem, quæ connexa P. Ramo cum Cicerone, imó cum Boetio ipso dicitur. Quamobrem hoc sophisma P. Ramus evitavit: generali verbo in genere, specialibus in unaquaq; specie usus est, uti lex καθόλου πρῶτον præcipit. Sed Græcorum Peripateticorum, aut Latini Boetii subtilitas mirabilis huc erupit, ut enuntiationum compositarum, vel (ut ipse loquitur) hypotheticarum modi decies milleni colligeretur, dum tale enuntiatum componitur, modo é duobus simplicibus, modo ex altero simplici, modo ex altero composito, modo ex utriq; compositis, iisque partim affirmatis, partim negatis, partim absolutis; partim modificatis: quod artificium suis artibus egregiù par est visum esse: nec enim tantum laborem in ea re collocassent unquam, si vanitatem ullam subesse cogitasset: Addit etiā Boetius, numerum augeri potuisse si per quantitatem universalem, particularem, si per opposita vel subalternas variare voluissent: Tantum otii hominibus ingeniosis fuit, ad investigandū res nugatorias, & humanæ vitæ inutiles: imó dum leguntur. vel ipsa temporis jactura lectori bus perniciosas. Talis est subtilitas in secundo lib. περὶ ἐμφύτων, de cōsectariis infinitorū & modificatorū, de quibus antea. Itaq; talibus nugis præteritis, P. Ramus necessaria logicæ enuntiationis compositæ genera propositit.
units.tr: Statement. Up to this point the logic of simple statements has come from Aristotle's Organon, with which arguments are stated, and by which kind of both contradicting and judging. What follows, on the matter of compound statements and the mode of contradiction and judgment, is nowhere in Aristotle's philosophy. For in Aristotle's time the logic of compound statements and syllogisms had not been invented; and after it was invented, some condemned it, as Clinomachus did according to Diogenes Laertius in book 2, who, in his axioms, accepting simple things and rejecting non-simple ones, called them connected and complex [τὰ ἁπλᾶ προσλαμβάνων, τὰ μὴ ἁπλᾶ ἀναιρῶν, λέγων συνημμένα καὶ συμπεπλεγμένα]. But Clinomachus rejected compound statements as rashly as he had earlier rejected negated ones. For the logic of compound statements is necessary both in itself and above all in syllogisms. Two disciples, Theophrastus and Eudemus, cultivated this new field after the first master; but Theophrastus pursued only the highest points, while Eudemus entered a wider path, yet in such a way that he seems to have only scattered seeds and to have brought forth no fruit at all, as Boethius expressly says in the first book on the hypothetical syllogism. The Greek interpreters of Aristotle, on chapter 22 of book 2 of the Prior Analytics, declare that this invention belongs to Theophrastus and Eudemus. Therefore Ramus, who had no laborious cultivation in the field of Aristotle here, did have some in the field of Theophrastus and Eudemus, or rather of Boethius, since he wishes it to be seen that he received only the beginnings from them and added the rest himself. He calls the former kind of statement, the categorical, from its consequent part, which is the predicative in place of the hypothetical [ληκτικὸν καθ' ὑποθετικόν]; and the compound he calls the hypothetical, the conditional. But this is neither correct nor consistent with Aristotle's teaching. For there are compound statements other than conditional ones, such as the absolute copulative and the discretive; for the connective and the disjunctive can be called conditional, and Cicero names a condition in the disjunctive, as will be noted later under the first disjunctive syllogism. But for Aristotle a hypothesis is any statement which is put forward as true, whether simple, compound, connective or disjunctive, as will be said later in the kinds themselves. In this way all of astrology would be called hypothetical, since it proceeds through hypotheses, not through axioms [ἀξιώματα] as principles. And so in chapter 30 of book 1 of the Prior Analytics, the analytic [ἀναλυτικόν] is opposed to the hypothetical [τῷ δὲ ὑποθετικῷ]; and in the whole of three chapters, 11, 12 and 13 of book 2 of the Prior Analytics, Aristotle calls them hypothetical syllogisms, syllogisms to the impossible, which nevertheless are constituted from simple statements supposed under a condition. Therefore, when Theophrastus, Eudemus and Boethius called every kind of compound statement hypothetical, they did not speak correctly, nor in agreement with the teaching of their master. They established a twofold meaning of hypothesis: the first embraces that which we have said is Aristotle's; the second, by consequence, is conditional, which with Cicero, and indeed with Boethius himself, is called connective. Therefore Ramus avoided this sophism: he used a general word for the genus and specific words for each species, as the law first in general [καθόλου πρῶτον] prescribes. But the subtlety of the Greek Peripatetics, or of the Latin Boethius, broke out here in a remarkable way, so that the modes of compound, or (as he himself speaks) hypothetical, statements were gathered up to ten thousand, while such a statement is composed sometimes from two simple ones, sometimes from one simple and one compound, sometimes from two compounds, and these partly affirmed, partly denied, partly absolute, partly modified. This device seemed to its makers worthy of their arts; for they would never have spent such labour on the matter if they had supposed any vanity to lie beneath it. Boethius adds that the number could have been increased if they had wished to vary it by universal and particular quantity, or by opposites and subalterns. So much leisure had these clever men, for investigating trifling matters which are useless for human life; indeed, even the mere loss of time in reading them is harmful to readers. Such subtlety is in the second book On Innate Things [περὶ ἐμφύτων], concerning the consequences of infinites and modified statements, of which we spoke before. So, with such trifles set aside, Ramus has set out the kinds of compound statement necessary to logic.

units.la: Affirmata] Affirmatio partiū inter se, negatioq; sumitur é conjunctione ipsa sententiarum variarum, quæ dicitur Aristoteli συλλογισμός, id est, convinctio, ut Quintilianus loquitur.
units.tr: Affirmed. The affirmation and negation of the parts among themselves is taken from the very conjunction of the various statements, which Aristotle calls syllogismos, that is, a binding together, as Quintilian puts it.

units.la: Dividit] Contradictio simplicis enuntiati, nō perpetuo verum falsumq; dividit, propter differentiam generalis affirmationis & negationis: secus est in copositio, in quo nihil generale, nihil speciale, sed συνἀληθεύει tantùm spectaur: itaq; pars altera semper vera est, pars altera est falsa.
units.tr: Divides. The contradiction of a simple statement does not always divide into true and false, on account of the difference between a general affirmation and a general negation. It is otherwise in a compound, in which nothing is general and nothing special, but only joint truth [συναληθεύει] is considered; so one part is always true and the other part is false.

units.la: Congregativum] Congregare & segregare, adversa sunt: unde illius logica partitonis διχοτομία perspicitur. In quo & Peripateticorum illorum error etiā gravior apparet, qui pro quatuor cōpositorum enuntiatorum generibus, cōgregativis duobus, copulato connexoq;, duobus segregatis, discrero disjunctoq;, duo tantum tradiderunt, connexum & disjunctum.
units.tr: Congregative. To congregate and to segregate are opposites, whence the division of this logical partition [διχοτομία] is clear. In this the error of those Peripatetics appears even graver: for of the four kinds of compound statements, two congregative, copulative and connective, and two segregative, discretive and disjunctive, they handed down only two, the connective and the disjunctive.

units.la: und Eurus] Descripturus poeta tempestate, ventos opplitis flatibus maria turbantes inducit. Affirmatum autem est exéplum, quod negatur præpositā negatione: Affirmatio dicebat omnes illos ventos simul flare, negatio ait non simul flare. Homo est natura logicus & arithmeticus affirmatum est. Nō homo est natura logicus & arithmeticus: vel, Homo nō est natura logicus & Arithmeticus. negatū est. At homo est natura logicus, & non arithmeticus: quāuis sit disparatum, non tamen contradicit, neq; negat eundem cōsequentem de eodem antecedente: imò affirmatio est, quia conjunctio (ut) affirmatur. judicium] judicium dispositionis & enuntiationis copulatae verum erit, si partes simul omnes verae sunt: secus falsum: ut, si venti omnes simul flarint, verū erit poetę enūtiatum: si pars una, vel omnes falsæ, falsum. ut, si Eurus non flarit, aut Nothus, aut Africus. Relatio] Hic nulla videtur esse conjunctio: attamen sententiæ duæ sunt: Sopor est dulcis fesis in gramine, & tuū carmen similiter nobis audientib. est dulce. Negatio autem relationis, manifeste postulat præpositionem negationis ante totam enuntiationem, quia notæ ipsæ relationis, faciunt conjunctionem. Tales sunt enūtiationes etiam in relatione quantitatis, ut tantus quantus, tot quot: etiā loci, ut pro Domo: Ibi enim postis, ubi tepli aditus. hæc enim relatio, copulatum quendā sen sum habet. Tullius floruit Romæ, ubi & Hortensius. Homerus Græcis summus est poeta, quantus est Latinis Virgilius. Relatio temporis videt potiūs esse connexa: de qua postea ideo in connexis. Relationis autem copulatæ judicio comparata pleraq; enuntiantur & judicatur: & quidem sæpe judicio necessario, ut analogiæ mathematicæ: Ut est 2. ad 4. sic 1. ad 6. subduplæ ratio ris analogia est necessaria, & sub scientiæ judicium cadit. Potest contingens esse relatio, ut pa storitia illa:
units.tr: And Eurus. The poet, about to describe a storm, introduces winds stirring the seas with opposing blasts. The affirmation is an example, which is negated by a prefixed negation: the affirmation says that all those winds blow together, the negation says that they do not blow together. "Man is by nature logical and arithmetical" is affirmative. "Man is not by nature logical and arithmetical," or "Man is by nature not logical and arithmetical," is negative. But "Man is by nature logical and not arithmetical," although it is disparate, does not contradict, nor deny the same consequent of the same antecedent; rather, it is affirmative, because the conjunction ("as") is affirmed. Judgment. The judgment of a disposition and of a copulative statement will be true if all its parts are true together; otherwise it is false. For example, if all the winds blew together, the poet's statement will be true; if one part, or all, are false, it is false, as if Eurus did not blow, or Notus, or Africus. Relation. Here there seems to be no conjunction; yet there are two statements: sleep is sweet to the weary on the grass, and your song is likewise sweet to us who hear it. But the negation of a relation plainly requires a negative particle before the whole statement, because the marks of the relation itself make the conjunction. Such statements also occur in relations of quantity, as "as great as," "as many as," and of place, as "for home: where the doorpost is, there is the entrance." For this relation has a kind of copulative sense. Cicero flourished at Rome, where Hortensius did too. Homer is the greatest poet for the Greeks, as Virgil is for the Latins. The relation of time seems rather connective, concerning which more will be said later, under connectives. Many statements about relation are made and judged by means of copulative judgment; and indeed often by necessary judgment, as with mathematical proportions: as 2 is to 4, so 1 is to 6. A subduple ratio is a necessary analogy, and falls under the judgment of knowledge. A relation can be contingent, as that pastoral one:

units.la: Tale tuum carmen, &c. potest esse falsa: ut animates, ita stirpes sentiūt.
units.tr: Such is your song, etc. may be false: as animals feel, so plants feel.

units.la: Cap. V. De Enuntiato connexo.
units.tr: Chap. V. On the Connected Proposition.

units.la: ENuntiatum connexum, est congregativum, cujus conjunctio est connexiva: Sicut 2. Aeneid.
units.tr: A connected proposition is a congregative one whose conjunction is connective, as in the second book of the Aeneid:

units.la: —Si miserum fortuna Sinonem Finxit, vanū etiā medacēq; improba finget: Cujus negatio est,
units.tr: —If fortune has fashioned Sinon as wretched, shameless fortune will also fashion him vain and deceitful.

units.la: —Non si miserum fortuna Sinonem Finxit, vanû etiã mĕdacēḡ improba finget.
units.tr: —Not, if fortune has fashioned Sinon as wretched, will shameless fortune also fashion him vain and deceitful.

units.la: Conjunctio etiam hæc interdum negatur apertiùs negando consequentiã: ut pro Amerino: Non cōtinuó si me in sicariorum gregem cōtuli,sicarius sum. De Fato: Nec si omne enuntiatum verũ est aut falsum, sequitur illicó caussas esse immutabiles. Affirmatio enim significat, si sit antecedens, etiã consequens esse. negatio itaq; & cōtradictio statuit, si sit antecedens, non ideo consequens esse. Quare cum judicabis connexũ absoluté verum esse, necessariũ quoq; judicabis: & intelliges hanc necessitatem é necessaria partium connexione oriri: quę ipsa potest esse vel in falsis partib9: ut, si homo est leo, est etiã quadrupes, necessarium connexum est. At si connexio sit contingēs, & pro sua tantúm probabilitate ponatur, judiũ ejus tantúm opinio fuerit: ut Terent. Andr.
units.tr: This conjunction is also sometimes negated more openly, by denying the consequence. Thus in the speech for Amerinus: "It does not follow at once that if I have joined the band of assassins, I am an assassin." In the work On Fate: "Nor, if every proposition is true or false, does it follow at once that causes are unchangeable." For an affirmation signifies that if the antecedent is, the consequent also is. A negation and contradiction therefore states that if the antecedent is, the consequent is not thereby. So when you judge a connected proposition to be absolutely true, you will also judge it necessary, and you will understand this necessity to arise from the necessary connection of its parts. That connection can even hold between false parts: if a man is a lion, he is also a quadruped, is a necessary connected proposition. But if the connection is contingent, and is posited only on its own probability, its judgment will be merely a matter of opinion, as in Terence's Andria:

units.la: Păphile, si id facis, hodie postremũ me vides.
units.tr: Pamphilus, if you do that, today you will see me for the last time.

units.la: Connexo enuntiaro relativum temporis enuntiatum affine est. 9. Eclog.
units.tr: A relative temporal proposition is akin to a connected one, as in the ninth Eclogue:

units.la: Carmina tum meliús, cúm venerit ipse, canemus.
units.tr: Then we shall sing better songs, when he himself has come.

units.la: X
units.tr: X

units.la: Enuntiatum] Hæc secunda species congregativi enuntiati, appellatur à Cicerone cónexa: sic enim loquitur Acad. 4. Ipsa enim ratio cónexi, cum concesserit superius, cogit inferius concedere. Itaq; de Fato: Si quod primum in cónexo est, necessarium est: sit etiam quod sequitur, necessarium. Græci Aristotelis interpretes appellant τὸ συνημμένον: Aristoteles ipse, licet nullam ejus doctrinam instituerit, attamen hanc ipsam enuntiandi speciem, videtur τὸ συνεχὲς appellare, 12. cap. 1. Pr. Scholæ Logicorum vulgò appellát conditionale: verbo, si non Ciceroniano, certè legali & judiciali: Sic enim Martianus jurisconsultus: Solus hæres futurus est omnino, nisi habeat in conditionalem partem substitutum. & Justinianus ait: Sed si conditionaliter enútiata fuerit causa, aliud juris est. Attamen σύνδεσμος seu conditio, iltam conjunctionis speciem neq; Aristoteli, neq; veritati significat, quia tam simplex enuntiatum, quàm compositum copulativum, disjunctumq; tam hypotheticum & dici & esse potest: quàm cónexum. Itaq; cum latinum verbum à Cicerone suppetat certū, ambigua illa, & hypotheticum, & conditionale P. Ramus evitavit: connexum autem, capit omnia argumentorum genera, consentanea affirmando, diffentanea etiam, sed ex iis alterum negando: Enuntiatis autè connexis Mathematici multum sunt usi: & sic magna pars elementorum enuntiatur.
units.tr: Proposition: This second species of congregative proposition is called "connexa" by Cicero, for so he speaks in the fourth book of the Academica: "The very nature of the connection, once the former has been granted, compels us to grant the latter." Likewise in the work On Fate: "If what comes first in a connection is necessary, what follows is also necessary." The Greek interpreters of Aristotle call it to synēmmenon [τὸ συνημμένον]. Aristotle himself, although he set out no doctrine of it, seems to call this very kind of statement to synechès [τὸ συνεχὲς] in chapter 1 of book 12. The schools of the logicians commonly call it "conditional", a word not Ciceronian but legal and judicial: thus the jurist Martianus: "He will be the sole heir altogether, unless he has a substitute in the conditional part." And Justinian says: "But if a case has been stated conditionally, the law is different." Yet syndesmos [σύνδεσμος] or "condition" signifies that species of conjunction neither in Aristotle's sense nor in truth, because a simple proposition, a compound copulative one, and a disjunctive one can all be called and be hypothetical just as a connected one can. Therefore, since Cicero supplies a fixed Latin word, Peter Ramus avoided the ambiguous terms "hypothetical" and "conditional", and called it "connected". This term takes in every kind of argument: those that affirm consistent things, and also those that affirm inconsistent things while denying one of the two. Mathematicians have made much use of connected propositions, and so a large part of the elements is stated in them.

units.la: Si miserum] Sinonis est ad Trojanos hæc infinuatio: quæ affirmatè primùm ponitur, præceptı illustrádi causa, deinde negatū, ut est apud poetam, reponitur. Negatio]Negatio connexi plane cōjunctionem ipsam negat: idq; fit dupli citer: primò simpliciùs pręponendo negationē conjunctioni: secundò apertiùs tollendo consequentiam. primum exemplum est de Sinone.
units.tr: If miserable: This is Sinon's insinuation to the Trojans. It is first put affirmatively, for the sake of illustrating the precept, and then, as in the poet, it is answered by a negation. Negation: The negation of a connection denies the conjunction itself, and this is done in two ways: first, more simply, by placing the negation before the conjunction; second, more openly, by removing the consequence. The first example is that of Sinon.

units.la: Sicariorum]Respodet orator objectioni: quód Roscius Romę tum fuerit, cúm cędes fierent.& connexi cōsecutionem negat. hoc igitur exemplo, consequentia connexi negatur apertiùs, ut sæpé aliàs. Quintil. lib. 2. ca. 21. Nec protinus nō est materia Rhetorices, si in eadem versatur & alius. Nec si omne] Disputat Tullius adversus Chrysippum, qui ex enuntiato disjuncto argumentatur, caussas rerum immutabiles atq; ęternas esse, quæ prohiberét quicquam secús cadere, atq; cāsurum esset. Ergo connexum duobus modis negatur: simpliciter, quando negatio cō junctioni proponitur: apertiùs, quando inconsequentia etiam exponitur: ut, Si dies est, lucet: Non si dies est, lucet. item, Si dies est, nō ideo lucet: vel, Non sequitur lucere. Atq; in hac negatione, hoc solo secundo negádi genere Francus utitur: neq; cōjunctioni negationem prępónit, sed consequentiam negat. Logicum igitur illud axioma Theophrasti, vel Eudemi, vel certé Boe tii, non satis accuratum videtur. Ad cōsequentem propositionem respiciendum esse, ut affirmativa vel negativa propositio cōnexa judicetur: ut, Si est a, est b: affirmativa est, ait Boetius. Si est a, non est b: negativa. At (inquá) tam est affirmativa secunda propositio hęc, quàm illa pri-ma: deceptus est author hujus dogmatis, dissenfionis fpecie:quia illa enuntiata diffentirét, nee fimul effe vera poffent:ideo cótradicentia putavit. At cótradiction, eft affirmatio & negatio ejuf dé de eodé,illic,Si eft a, eft b:affirmatio eft cófe quétis affirmati de antecedéte affirmato: hic, Si eft a, nó eft b:affirmatio ité,fed cófequétis negati de affirmato antecedente: At affirmatio affirmationi nó cótradicit, licet opponatur alio genere. Ergo connexü fic negatur. Quomodo (in quies) verü judicatur? Si neceffaria cójunctio fit,eft neceffarium,ait P.Ramus:fi fit contingés cójunctio,eft item contingens : Connexü auté hîc παράδοξον quiddam efficit,ut totum neceffarium dicatur, cujus partes falfæ, imó impofsibi les fuerint,nedum verae: ut in exéplo, Si homo eft leo,homo rugit:eft neceffarium connexum: pofito enim & cóceffo antecedente, cófequens neceffario fequtur. at antecedens, Homo eft leo: eft impofsibile.Item confequens, Homo rugit. Id fi mirabile tibi videatur,cogitato rerum infirmarum poffe vinculum quoddam effe adamantinum: Vinculo manus divinæ, mundi partes omnes continentur: quæ ipfæ tamen caducæ funt & fluxę.annexæ cónexionis deniq; neceffitas hic æftimatur & judicatur,non rerum connexarum,fed connexionis ipfius necefsitate. Pamphile] Vox eft Charini, Páphilo nuptias Pamphilæ,quas futuras Pamphilº credebat,dif fuadétis,cúm Charinus ipfe Pamphilá cuperet. hęc aút cónexio eft cótingens tantúm:Itaq; nifi códitione, & tanq pacto auditoris admittatur, falfa judicetur,neceffe eft:accepta autem, etiá fi partes veræ sint, opinionis tantū judicių faciet.
units.tr: Of the assassins: The orator answers an objection, namely that Roscius was in Rome at the time when the murders were happening, and he denies that the connection follows. In this example the consequence of the connection is denied more openly, as often elsewhere (Quintilian, book 2, chapter 21): "Nor is it at once not a matter for rhetoric, if another also is involved in the same thing." Nor if every: Tully disputes against Chrysippus, who argues from a disjunctive proposition that causes of things are unchangeable and eternal, and that they prevent anything from falling out otherwise than it will fall out. So a connected proposition is negated in two ways: simply, when the negation is placed before the conjunction; more openly, when the non-consequence is also set out, as: "If it is day, it is light"; "Not if it is day, is it light"; likewise "If it is day, it is not therefore light", or "It does not follow that it is light." And in this kind of negation Francus uses only this second mode of denying, and does not place the negation before the conjunction, but denies the consequence. Therefore that logical axiom of Theophrastus, or Eudemus, or certainly Boethius, seems not accurate enough: that one must look to the consequent proposition to judge whether a connected proposition is affirmative or negative. For example: "If a is, b is", is affirmative, says Boethius; "If a is, b is not", is negative. But I say the second proposition here is affirmative just as the first is. The author of this doctrine was deceived by a kind of disagreement, because those statements disagreed and could not be true together, so he thought them contradictory. But a contradiction is an affirmation and a negation of the same thing about the same thing. In the one case, "If a is, b is", the affirmation is of the consequent affirmed from the affirmed antecedent; in the other, "If a is, b is not", the affirmation is again of the consequent denied from the affirmed antecedent. But an affirmation does not contradict an affirmation, although it is opposed to it in another way. Therefore a connected proposition is negated in this way. How (you will ask) is it judged to be true? If the conjunction is necessary, it is necessary, says Peter Ramus; if the conjunction is contingent, it is likewise contingent. Here, however, a connected proposition produces something paradoxical [παράδοξον]: the whole may be called necessary even when its parts are false, indeed impossible, let alone true. As in the example "If a man is a lion, a man roars": this is a necessary connected proposition, for once the antecedent is posited and granted, the consequent follows necessarily. Yet the antecedent, "A man is a lion", is impossible, and so is the consequent, "A man roars". If this seems marvellous to you, consider that weak things can have some bond of adamant: by the chain of the divine hand all parts of the world are held together, though they themselves are perishable and fleeting. Finally, the necessity of the connection here is estimated and judged not by the necessity of the connected things but by the necessity of the connection itself. Pamphilus: These are the words of Charinus, dissuading Pamphilus from the marriage with Pamphila, which Pamphilus believed would take place, though Charinus himself desired Pamphila. This connection, however, is merely contingent. So unless it is admitted on condition, and as if by agreement with the hearer, it must be judged false; but if it is accepted, even though its parts are true, it will make only a matter of opinion.

units.la: Relativum] Enuntiatum relativum jam antea modis aliquot factum est copulatū: ac cū tempus refertur, videt potiús esse connexū: & Boetius lib. 1. de hypothetico syllogismo, ait hoc enuntiatum (cum homo sit, animal est) hypothetic̄ū, id est connexum esse. & postea syllogismus conexus isto propositionis genere cōcludetur.
units.tr: Relative: A relative proposition has already been made conjunctive in several ways before now; and when time is referred to, it seems rather to be connected. Boethius, in the first book On the Hypothetical Syllogism, says that this proposition ("since man is, animal is") is hypothetical, that is, connected; and afterwards a connected syllogism will be concluded from this kind of proposition.

units.la: Cap. V I. De Enuntiato disjreto.
units.tr: Chapter VI. On the Segregative Proposition.

units.la: ENūtiatum segregativum est, cujus conjunctio est segregativa: ideoq; argumenta dissentanea enuntiat. Enuntiatum segregativum, est discretum aut disjunctum. Discretum, cujus conjunctio est discretiva: Itaque é dissentaneis præcipuè diversa enuntiat. 5. Tusc. Quāquam sensu corporis judicentur, ad animum referri tamen. cujus negatio & contradictio est: Non quanquam sensu corporis judicentur, ad animū tamen referri. vel, Quanquam sensu corporis judicentur, non tamen ad animum referri. Nam (tamen) est hic conjunctio præcipua. Discretum enuntiatū judicatur esse verum & legitimum, si partes non solum verę, sed etiam discretæ sint falsum vel ridiculum, contrá.
units.tr: A segregative proposition is one whose conjunction is segregative, and so it states opposed arguments. The segregative proposition is either discrete or disjunctive. A discrete proposition is one whose conjunction is discretive, and so it states things that are chiefly diverse out of those that are opposed. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5: "Although they are judged by the senses of the body, they are nevertheless referred to the mind." Its negation and contradiction is: "Not although they are judged by the senses of the body, they are nevertheless referred to the mind," or: "Although they are judged by the senses of the body, they are not nevertheless referred to the mind." For here tamen ("nevertheless") is the chief conjunction. A discrete proposition is judged true and lawful if its parts are not only true but also discrete. If they are false or absurd, it is judged the reverse.

units.la: Dissentanea] Segregativū in genere argumen-ta dissentanea enuntiat, ut congregativū in genere enūtiat consentanea. Id Ariftoteles in una specie disjūctionis admonuit, ut mox dicetur, At generale id est, & cómune fegregativi enuntiati: Itaq; generaliter id admonetur á P. Ramo, ne cōtra legem κα offendatur. Congregativi genera duo facta sunt, copulatum & cōnexum: ita nunc fegregativi duo fiunt, difcretū & disjunctum, & conjunctionum differētiis distinguuntur. Diversa] Copulatum & connexū, communia sunt omnium argumentorum relatum, attributum est comparatis: sic modo discretum diversis enuntiandis attribuitur. Quãquam] Disputat Tullius philosophiā Epicuri de voluptate, qui censebat hac usurum cō-penfatione fapiētem, ut voluptatem fugiat, fi ea majorem dolorem effectura fit: & dolorē fuscipiat, majoris efficiētem voluptatis: omniaq; jucunda quanquam sensu corporis judicétur, ad animum referri tamen. Enuntiati autem hujus negatio, ut antea copulati, fuerit præponendo negationem cōjunctioni: Non quanquam cor-poris sensu judicentur, ad animū referri tamen. vel, Quanquam sensu corporis judicentur, non tamen ad animum referri. quia negatio fit in cōpositis enuntiatis negando cōjunctionem: quę hic præcipua est (tamen) quomodo cōnexum dictum est duobus modis negari. Difcretū au- tem, videatur quædam negatio copulati, vel cōnexi: ut fi affirmaretur, Abest á culpa, & caret su spicione: vel, Si ábest á culpa, caret suspicione: tum discretum opponeretur, Quanquam abest á culpa,suspicione tamen nō caret. Ergo hęc có tradiction est discreti. judiciū copulati & discreti, hoc commune habet, quod in utroq; veritas partes omnes veras requirit: at ut in discreto, hoc etiam amplius, quód discretio partium requiratur: Ridiculum enim fit, composita & concsententanea segregare: ut, Quanquam Socrates est homo, tamē est animal rationale, nimirū (quod paulò póst in disjuncto ex Aristotele proponetur) ridiculum fore, si quis interroget disjūcta, quæ naturâ conjuncta sint.
units.tr: Opposed] The segregative proposition in general states opposed arguments, just as the congregative proposition in general states agreeing ones. Aristotle pointed this out for one species of disjunction, as will be said shortly, but the general and common character of the segregative proposition is this, and so Ramus generally warns us, lest we offend against the rule [κανόνα]. There are two kinds of congregative proposition, the copulative and the connective. In the same way there are now two kinds of segregative proposition, the discrete and the disjunctive, and they are distinguished by the differences of their conjunctions. Diverse] The copulative and the connective are common to all arguments, the relative and the attributive being applied to things compared. So too the discrete is assigned to statements of diverse things. Although] Tully discusses the philosophy of Epicurus on pleasure. Epicurus held that the wise man would use this compensation, to avoid pleasure if it were to produce greater pain, and to undergo pain if it would produce greater pleasure. He said that all pleasant things, although they are judged by the senses of the body, are nevertheless referred to the mind. The negation of this proposition, as with the copulative above, is made by placing the negation before the conjunction: "Not although they are judged by the senses of the body, they are nevertheless referred to the mind," or "Although they are judged by the senses of the body, they are not nevertheless referred to the mind." This is because in compound propositions negation is made by negating the conjunction, which here is the chief one, tamen. As was said of the connective, it can be negated in two ways. But a discrete proposition may be given a negation in the manner of a copulative or a connective. If one affirmed, "He is free from blame and is not open to suspicion," or, "If he is free from blame, he is not open to suspicion," the discrete would be opposed by, "Although he is free from blame, he is nevertheless open to suspicion." This then is the contradiction of the discrete. The judgement of the copulative and of the discrete has this in common: in both, truth requires all the parts to be true. But in the discrete there is this further requirement, that the parts be separated. For it is absurd to separate things that are compounded and agree, as in "Although Socrates is a man, he is nevertheless a rational animal." Obviously (as will be set out shortly in the disjunctive, from Aristotle) it would be absurd if someone asked about disjoined things that are joined by nature.

units.la: Cap. VII. De Enuntiato disjunctio.
units.tr: Chapter VII. On the Disjunctive Proposition.

units.la: ENuntiatum disjunctum, est enuntiatum segregativum, cujus cōjunctio est disjunctiva: ut 1. Georg.
units.tr: A disjunctive proposition is a segregative proposition whose conjunction is disjunctive, as in Georgics 1:

units.la: Illic, ut perhibent, aut intempesta silet nox Semper, & obtēta densantur noćte tenebræ, Aut redit á nobis aurora, diemq; reducit.
units.tr: There, as they say, either the unseasonable night is always silent, and the shrouded darkness thickens, or the dawn returns from us and brings back the day.

units.la: De Fat. Omnis enūtiatio est vera aut falsa. Hic significatur, é disjūctis unicū verum esse, Negatio igitur erit & cōtradictio, Non omnis enuntiatio est vera aut falsa. Disjuncti igitur enuntiati contradictione, significatur non necessario alterutrum verum esse: Nam si disjunctio absolutè vera est, est etiam necessaria: partefq; disjunctæ, sunt contrarię sine ullo medio. Veruntamen quamvis absoabsolutè vera disjunctio, necessaria quoque fit: tamen nihil necesse est partes separatim necessarias esse: ut, Homo est bonus, vel non est bonus, disjunctio necessaria est: & tamen, Homo est bonus, non est enuntiatio necessaria. Item, Homo non est bonus: non est enuntiatio necessaria: sed disjunctionis necessitas pendet ex necessaria partium oppositione & disjunctione, non ex earum necessaria veritate. Disjunctio autem plerunq; est ex conditione: ut si quæratur, utrum Cleon venerit, an Socrates, quia ita pactū fit, alterutrum tantum venturū esse. Itaq; si disjunctio sit contingens, non est absolutè vera & tantum opinabilis est: qualis est frequenter in hominum usu. Ovid. in Epistola Leandri, Aut mihi continget felix audacia salvo: Aut mors solliciti finis amoris erit.
units.tr: On Fate: Every statement is either true or false. Here it is meant that of the disjoined parts only one is true. The negation and contradiction will therefore be: "Not every statement is either true or false." The contradiction of a disjunctive proposition therefore signifies that one of the alternatives is not necessarily true. For if a disjunction is absolutely true, it is also necessary, and its parts are contraries with no middle. Yet although an absolutely true disjunction is also necessary, it does not follow that the parts taken separately are necessary. For example, "Man is good, or is not good," is a necessary disjunction, and yet "Man is good" is not a necessary statement. Likewise "Man is not good" is not a necessary statement. The necessity of the disjunction depends on the necessary opposition and separation of its parts, not on their necessary truth. Moreover a disjunction is often conditional, as when one asks whether Cleon has come or Socrates, because it has been agreed that only one of them will come. So if the disjunction is contingent, it is not absolutely true and is merely a matter of opinion, which is common in human usage. Ovid, in Leander's letter: "Either my bold venture will bring me happiness and safety, or death will be the end of my anxious love."

units.la: Disjunctum] Disjunctum enuntiatum respondet connexo, ut discretū respondet copulato. Connexum enuntiavit omnia absolutè consentanea affirmando: Enuntiare non potuit diffentanea medio carentia, nisi alterū negando. Disjunctum contrá, utrumq;, & dissentanea medio carentia enuntiat affirmándo: Aut dies, aut nox est: Aut vales, aut non vales: Aut vidus, aut cæcus es absolutè consentanea enuntiare non potest, nisi alterum negando: Aut nō est ignis, aut urit: Aut non est glacies, aut frigida est: Aut Achilles poterit, aut Hectorn̄ poterit: finge enim pares esse: Aut decem poterunt, aut unus nō poterit: Aut homo non est, aut animal est. Quare segregatis enūtiatis, dissentaneorum locus proprius est: discretis quidem, proprie diversa: disjunctivis, contraria medio carentia. Ergo si de tribus primum illud quæras, quod argumenti genus enuntietur disjuncto enuntiato: dices, contraria medio carentia sola hic affirmari. Theophrastus, Eudem⁹, Boetius decies millenos modos hic obliti sunt, quamvis tamen totidem modos disjuncti fateantur esse, quod sunt cōnexi: quatuor tantūm facit Boetius, ad finem 2. lib. de syllogismis hypotheticis: primum, Aut est a, aut b: qui fit in contrariis medio carentibus. secundū, Aut non est a, aut non est b: qui fit salte in disparatis. tertium, Aut est a, aut nō est b: qui fit ā majoribus ad minora. quartum, Aut non est a, aut est b: qui fit ā minoribus ad majora. Puduit, aut certē piguit (credo) philosophos illos tam singularis philosophiæ: quare & P. Ramus tā beato labore sibi nihil opus esse existimavit.
units.tr: Disjunctive] The disjunctive proposition corresponds to the connective, as the discrete corresponds to the copulative. The connective states all agreeing things absolutely by affirming them, and cannot state disagreeing things without a middle except by negating one of them. The disjunctive, on the contrary, states both alternatives, and states disagreeing things with no middle, by affirming them: "It is either day or night"; "You are either well or not well"; "You are either blind or not blind." It cannot state agreeing things absolutely except by negating one of them: "It is either not fire or it burns"; "It is either not ice or it is cold"; "Either Achilles will be able, or Hector will be able" (suppose they are equal); "Either ten will be able, or one will not be able"; "Either man is not, or he is an animal." So with segregative propositions the proper place of disagreeing things is found, with discrete ones things that are properly diverse, and with disjunctives contraries with no middle. Therefore if one asks first, of the three, what kind of argument is stated by a disjunctive proposition, the answer is that only contraries with no middle are affirmed here. Theophrastus, Eudemus and Boethius have overlooked ten thousand modes here, although they admit as many modes of the disjunctive as there are of the connective. Boethius makes only four, at the end of the second book On Hypothetical Syllogisms: first, "Either it is a or it is b," which occurs in contraries with no middle; second, "Either it is not a or it is not b," which occurs at least in disparates; third, "Either it is a or it is not b," which goes from greater to lesser; fourth, "Either it is not a or it is b," which goes from lesser to greater. I suppose those philosophers were ashamed, or at least grieved, at such a singular philosophy. So too Ramus thought that so blessed a labour was no business of his.

units.la: Illic] Virgilius hoc loco quinq; mūdi Zonas describit, tres inhabitabiles, mediam æstu, duas extremas frigore: Sub Arćto autem esse noćtē perpetuam, ut est, sex continuos mēses: aut diē perpetuum, ut deinde sex reliquos anni mēses: deniq; tot⁹ annus illic uno die, unaq; noćte ter minatur. Vera aut falsa] Disseritur à Tullio sententia Chrysippi:Concludit enim (ait orator) Chrysippus hoc modo, Si est motus sine causa; non omnis enuntiatio (quod ἀξίωμα Dialectici appellant) aut vera aut falsa erit; Caussas enim efficientes quod nō habebit, id nec verum nec falsum erit: Omnis autem enuntiatio, aut vera aut falsa est: Motus ergo sine caussa nullus est unicum.Id Cicero nominatim proposuit in Topicis,in disjunctione, plus uno verum esse non posse:Aristoteles in Philosop.5.cap.10.lib.aliud agēs,idē proposuit cúm ait, per πότερον, utrúm, interrogari oppositionem: Ipsum enim utrúm, in oppositione semper dicimus:ut, Utrúm albū an nigrum? &, Utrùm nigrum an non nigrum? utrúm autem homo,an album, nō dicimus: nisi é suppositione, & scifcitates: ut, Utrúm: venit Cleon, an Socrates? Sed non necesse id in ullo genere: Verúm hoc illic accidit: Opposita enim sola nō accidit simul inesse: quo & hic utitur in eo ipso,utrúm venit:si enim simul accideret,ridicula esset interrogatio. Si autē etiam sit,similiter incidit in oppositionem, in unum,aut multa:ut,Utrúm ambo venerint, an alter. siquidem ipsius(utrúm)interrogatio, semper est in oppositis.Haētenus Aristoteles in Philosophia: quo loco, licet aliud agens, attamen disjunctionis axioma nobis interpretatur, tum de genere argumenti, quod hoc enuntiato pronuntiatur,tū de genere judicii,non solúm necesserio,sed etiá opinabili: & per cōditionem facti. Addit etiam philosophus disjunctionem non tantúm duorum, sed etiam complurium fieri posse, cúm videlicet dichotomia absoluta ignoratur. ]Negatio disjunctionis manifeste, praeponitur ipsi disjunctivae conjunctioni: ut nulla quaestio superfit ejusmodi, qualis in conexo an te fuit. Est vero festivum illud Gelli ca. II. lib. 5. Cum esset (ait Gellius) a quoda rogatus Bias, deberetne uxorem ducere, an vitam vivere celibem: ἢ τοι (inquit) λαλῶ ἴξεις, ἢ ἀσχρᾶν. νῦ δὲ λαλῶ, ἴξεις λοιπῶ, ἢ δὲ ἀσχρᾶν, ἴξεις ποιῶ. Ἑκάτερον δὲ ἓν ἀγαθὸν, ἢ λυπηρὸν ἄρα. Sic autem hoc responsum covertunt, ἢ μὲν λαλῶ ἴξω, ἐπὶ ἴξω ποιῶ, ἢ δὲ ἀσχρᾶν, ἐπὶ ἴξω λοιπῶ, γαμητὸν ἄρα. Sed tum Phavorinus (ut idem Gell.ait) quum facta esset forte mentio syllogismi istius, quo Bias usus est, cujus prima προτάσις (ἢ τοι λαλῶ ἴξεις, ἢ ἀσχρᾶν) non ratu id, neque justu disjunctum esse ait: quoniam non necessarium est alterum ex duobus, quae disjunguntur, verum esse: quod in proloquio disjunctivo necessarium est: Eminentia enim quadam significari formarum turpes & pulchrae videntur. Est autem, inquit, tertiu quoq; inter duo ista, quae disjunguntur: cujus rationem prospectumq; Bias non habuit: Inter enim pulcherrimam foeminam, & de formosissima, media quaedam forma est, quae a nimie pulchritudinis periculo & a summo deformitate odio vacat. Qualis a Qu. Ennio in Menalippa, perquam eleganti vocabulo, Stata dicitur, quae neque λοιπῶ futura fit, neque ποιῶ: q formam modica & modestam Phavorinus, no me hercule insciteappellabat uxoriam: Ennius autem in ista (qua dixi) tragaedia, eas fere foeminas ait incolumi pudicitia esse, quae ista forma forent. Haec Gelius: lius:unde vides axioma de disjunctorum altero tantum vero etiam coprobatu a Phavorino.
units.tr: There] Virgil here describes the five zones of the world: three uninhabitable, the middle one from heat and two extreme ones from cold. Under the Arctic there is perpetual night, for six continuous months, or perpetual day, for the other six months of the year. Finally, the whole year there is bounded by one day and one night. True or false] Tully discusses the opinion of Chrysippus. For the orator says that Chrysippus concludes in this way: "If there is motion without a cause, then not every statement (which the dialecticians call axioma) is either true or false, for a statement that lacks efficient causes will be neither true nor false. But every statement is either true or false. Therefore there is no motion without a cause." Cicero explicitly put this forward in the Topics: in a disjunction, not more than one can be true. Aristotle, in the Physics (though he is dealing with something else), put it forward when he said that questions are asked by poteron, "whether," which is an opposition. For we always use utrum ("whether") in opposition, as in "Is it white or black?" and "Is it black or not black?" But we do not say "Whether it is a man or white," except by supposition and in questioning, as in "Whether Cleon has come or Socrates?" Yet this is not necessary in every kind: it happens here because opposites alone do not occur together. He uses this in the very phrase "whether he has come," for if it occurred together the question would be absurd. If however both occur, the question likewise falls into opposition, between one and many, as in "Whether both have come, or the other." For the question "whether" always concerns opposites. So far Aristotle in the Physics. In that passage, although he is dealing with something else, he expounds the axiom of the disjunctive, both as to the kind of argument stated by this proposition, and as to the kind of judgement, not only necessary but also opinable, and made by the condition of fact. The philosopher adds also that a disjunction can be made not only of two things but of several, when complete division is unknown. The negation of a disjunction is manifestly placed before the disjunctive conjunction itself, so that no question remains of the kind there was in the connective. The witticism of Gellius, Attic Nights 5.11, is well known. When Bias was asked by someone whether he ought to take a wife or live a single life, he replied: "If I marry, I shall get either a good wife or a bad one; if I have a good wife I shall be happy, if a bad one I shall be a philosopher; but either way it is good or bad." [Greek] They rendered this reply thus: "If I marry, I shall have either a good or a bad wife..." but then Favorinus, as Gellius also says, when by chance mention was made of this syllogism Bias used, whose first premise is [Greek], said it was not rightly nor justly a disjunction, since it is not necessary that one of two things that are disjoined be true, which is necessary in a disjunctive premise. For he says that forms that are ugly and beautiful seem to signify some extremes. But, he says, there is also a third thing between these two that are disjoined, which Bias did not take into account or foresee. For between a most beautiful woman and a most ugly one there is a certain middle form, which is free from the danger of excessive beauty and from the hatred of great deformity. Quintus Ennius in Menalippa calls this by a very elegant word, stata, one that will be neither [Greek] nor [Greek]. Favorinus, by heaven, called this moderate and modest form "wife-like," and Ennius in that tragedy (I have mentioned it) says that women of this form are generally those who have their chastity intact. So Gellius. From which you see that the axiom that only one of the disjoined alternatives is true is also confirmed by Favorinus.

units.la: Veruntamen Appendix est ad proximam definitionem ex dissimilib. Necessitas disjunctionis non accipitur ex necessaria partium veritate, sed ex necessaria partium oppositione: ut exemplum docet, Homo est bonus, aut non est bonus: haec disjunctio est necessaria, quia fit ex duabus partib. sic inter se oppositis, ut necesse sit, alteram esse veram: medio liquide carent: neutra tamen harum partium necessaria est, sed ambae versantur in materia contingenti, quae accidere & non accidere potest. Logici autem hujus axiomatis ignoratione, Epicurus, Diodorus, Chrysippus, Tullius etiam, foede ac turpiter lapsi sunt: Epicurus (quem Stoici in Dialecticis tardu & rudem & hebetem dicere solent) cum omne efficientiam fortuitis causis attribueret, disjunctionem ex contrariis veram esse negabat, cum ita efferemur, Hermacus cras aut vivet, aut non vivet: Si enim (ajebat) alterutru concessero ne cessariu esse, necesse erit cras Hermacu vivere, aut non vivere: nulla est aut in rerum natura talis necessitas. Diodor Stoicus, cum omnia vera, necessaria: omnia falsa, impossibilia esse diceret: qualis sit necessitas disjunctionis, & unde fiume da effet, ignoravit. Chrysippus ite deceptus est, cum sic ageret: Necesse est omne enuntiatione vera esse aut falsam: ergo in contradictione rerum enuntiatarum, pars altera necessario vera, pars altera necessario falsa erit. Cicero horum philosophorum sententias disceptans, ad scopulos logicae disjun-
units.tr: However, this is an appendix to the preceding definition, which concerns disjunction from dissimilar parts. The necessity of a disjunction does not come from the necessary truth of its parts but from the necessary opposition of its parts. The example shows this: "Man is good, or man is not good." This disjunction is necessary because it is formed of two parts so opposed to each other that one of them must be true, and there is no middle ground. Yet neither of these parts is itself necessary. Both lie in contingent matter, which can happen or not happen. Logicians, however, through ignorance of this axiom, fell foully and shamefully: Epicurus, Diodorus, Chrysippus, and even Cicero. Epicurus, whom the Stoics in their Dialectics usually call slow, crude and dull, attributed all efficacy to chance causes and therefore denied that a disjunction of contraries is true, when we say: "Hermachus will live tomorrow or will not live." For, he said, if I concede that one of the two is necessary, it will be necessary that Hermachus lives tomorrow or does not live; but there is no such necessity either in the nature of things. Diodorus the Stoic, who said that all true things are necessary and all false things impossible, did not know what the necessity of a disjunction is or where it comes from. Chrysippus too was deceived when he argued: "It is necessary that every statement is either true or false; therefore, in the contradiction of stated things, one part will necessarily be true and the other necessarily false." Cicero, disputing the opinions of these philosophers, ran hard against the rocks of logical disjunction

units.la: disjũctionis vehementer etiá impegit,existimás, si disjũctio necessaria sit, parte ejus altera verá, esse necessariá:partem alterá falsam,esse impossibilem.quod cúm Epcurei inficiantur, Tullius exclamat in eos,O admirabilem licentiá,& miserabilem inscitiam disserendi:cúm tamé in Oratorem sua exclamatio proprié cóveniat. Sed hæc omnia sigillatim P Ramus in illũ Ciceronis locũ pręlectionibus suis plenius exposuit. Cûm igitur ita pronũtiamus,Socrates philosophus est,aut non:disjunctio est necessaria:neutra tamé harum partium est necessaria,sed utraque contingens & mutabilis:unde hoc axioma tenendum est &cócludendum, disjunctionem absolute veram,esse necessariam:non tamen ex partiũ necessitate, sed ex necessaria partiũ oppositione,cúm ita opponuntur,ut verum & salsum distinguát. Aut mihi] Leander Heronis amore captus, Abydo ex Asia interjectum Helle spontum, Sestó ad oppositum in Europa litus, amicæ gratiâ navigans,submersus est: itaq; pro amoris sui conditione,hanc sibi disjunctionem ratiocinatur:quæ tamé disjunctio tantúm opinabilis est.Proculus libro quinquagesimo Digest. (ut P.Ramus differebat hoc loco) Lógicá disjuncti enũtiati á nescio quo Chrysippo desumpsit, nó satis veris Logicæ legibus consentaneam, dum & disjunctivum, & subdisjunc̈tivum interpretatur.Hæc verba,inquit (ille aut ille)non solũm disjunctivę,sed etiam subdisjũctivæ orationis sunt: disjunctivũ est, veluti cũ dicimus,Aut dies est,aut nox est: quorũ posito. altero, necesse est tolli alterū. ité sublato altero, alterum poni. Hoc disjunctivum est Proculo ita definitum, non satis tamen logicè, neq; satis accuratè: Definitur enim enuntiatum, per syllogismum disjunctum, ubi de disjunctis duobus assumitur vel tollitur alterum, ut reliquū in complexione tollatur aut statuatur. Hęc enim pone di tollendiq; lex definitio est syllogistni disjuncti duorum generum, quod non est in omni difjunćto absoluto verum: Nam cum dicitur, Aut decem possunt, aut unus nō potest: vera & legitima disjunctio est: attamen assumpto & posito altero, quale fuit in ipso disjuncto, nempe, At unus non potest: non tolletur reliquum, ut ei contrarium cōcludatur, Ergo decem non possunt. Sequitur de subdisjunctivo Logica etiā spinosior, cum de disjunctivo dictū esset. Ita (ait Proculus) similī figuratione verbū potest esse subdisjunctivum. Subdisjunctivi autē genera duo sunt: unum, cūm ex propositis finibus ita nō potest uterq; esse, ut possit neuter esse: veluti cūm dicimus, Aut sedet, aut ambulat. Nam ut nemo potest utrumque simul facere, ita aliquis potest neutrum: veluti is qui accumbit. Alterius generis est, cūm ex propositis finibus ita non potest neuter esse, ut possit utrūq; esse. veluti cūm dicimus: Omne animal aut facit, aut patitur. nullū est enim, quod nec faciat, nec patiatur. at potest simul & facere, & pati. Hic Proculus duo sub disjunctivi genera nō rectè interpretatur, & tamen in interpretatione ipsa refellit: nam in utroq; exemplo (ut) usurpat pro (quin) & interea salsum docet illud esse (Aut sedet, aut ambulat) cū tertiū doceat esse, nempe quod accumbit. Falsum etiam hoc esse aut certé ridiculum demonstrat, Omne animal aut facit, aut patitur: qa disjungit ea, quæ naturâ conjuncta sunt: Omne enim agens, agendo patitur. Itaq; Proculus juris Romani prudentissimus esse potuit, qui logici juris perinde peritus non esset. Notabilius autē illud est sexto libro Codicis justiniani, ubi disjūctivum ait aliquādo copulativè accipi: ut in interdicto, Quod vi aut clàm, ubi (aut) cōiunctio, ꝑ (&) apertissimè posita est, ait justinianus. Atqui rectior est ista justiniani posterior grāmaticāne an logicaʳ mentis enim & rationis logica tantùm est, verborum latinorum, aut gręcorū, aut cujusquam linguæ symbolorum non est, sed ea grāmaticis subjecta est materia: Itaq; si (aut) copulet, non disjungat, enuntiatū faciet copulatum non disjunctum. Videtur autem interdū (aut) etiam apud Ciceronē copulare: ut in Fato, Nō enim credo nullo præcepto aut cæteros artifices versari in suo munere, aut eos qui divinatione utantur, futura prędicere. Hìc enim adde (neque) pro (aut) eandem sententiā expresseris. Sed adhuc de disjuncto, deq; cæteris enuntiati generib9, id est de toto primi judicii genere, perspecta nobis est P. Rami in agro Aristotelis & Aristoteleorū, Theophrasti, Eudemi, Boetii, diligentia: spinæ hic nō tam multæ, quàm antea, sed tamen graves admodum & molestæ fuerunt, ut gratum opus logicæ artis agricolis propositum hiç esse debeat. Recordemur igitur, é
units.tr: and thought that if a disjunction is necessary, then, with one part true, the other part must be necessary, and that the false part must be impossible. When the Epicureans deny this, Tully cries out against them: "O the admirable licence and the wretched ignorance of disputing!" Yet this exclamation really fits the orator himself. But P. Ramus has set out all these points one by one, more fully, in his lectures on that passage of Cicero. So when we pronounce: "Socrates is a philosopher, or he is not," the disjunction is necessary, yet neither of its parts is necessary; each is contingent and changeable. Hence this axiom must be held and concluded: a disjunction that is absolutely true is necessary, not because of the necessity of its parts, but because of the necessary opposition of its parts, since they are so opposed that they separate true from false. Either to me: Leander, captivated by love of Hero, swam across from Abydos in Asia, over the Hellespont lying between, to the opposite shore of Europe at Sestos, for the sake of his beloved, and was drowned. So, according to the state of his love, he reasons out this disjunction for himself; yet this disjunction is only a matter of opinion. Proculus, in the fiftieth book of the Digest, took the logical disjunctive proposition from I know not what Chrysippus (as P. Ramus explained at this point), and it does not agree well enough with the laws of logic, since he interprets both the disjunctive and the subdisjunctive. "These words," he says, "of this or that are not only of disjunctive but also of subdisjunctive speech. Disjunctive is, for instance, when we say: 'It is day or it is night'; when one of these is posited, the other must be removed, and when one is removed, the other is posited." Proculus defines the disjunctive in this way, but not logically or accurately enough. For a proposition is defined as a disjunctive syllogism, where one of two disjuncts is assumed or removed, so that the remainder in the complex is removed or established. This is the definition of the law of positing and removing, of the disjunctive syllogism of two kinds, and it is not true of every absolute disjunction. For when we say, "Either ten can, or one cannot," it is a true and lawful disjunction; yet when one part is assumed and posited, as it stands in the disjunction itself, namely, "But one cannot," the remainder is not removed so that its contrary is concluded: "Therefore ten cannot." Next, more intricate logic follows concerning the subdisjunctive, now that the disjunctive has been discussed. Thus, says Proculus, the word "can" by a similar figure may be subdisjunctive. There are two kinds of subdisjunctive. One is when, of the proposed ends, both cannot be, yet neither can fail to be: as when we say, "He either sits or walks." For as no one can do both at once, so someone can do neither, as one who reclines. The other kind is when, of the proposed ends, neither cannot be, yet both can be: as when we say, "Every animal either acts or is acted upon." For there is nothing that neither acts nor is acted upon, yet something can both act and be acted upon. Here Proculus wrongly interprets the two kinds of subdisjunctive, and yet refutes himself in the very interpretation: for in both examples he uses "ut" for "quin," and he teaches that the first example, "He sits or walks," is false, although he teaches a third case, namely one who reclines. He also shows that "Every animal acts or is acted upon" is false, or at least ridiculous, because it separates things that are joined by nature: for every agent, in acting, is also acted upon. So Proculus could be the most learned of Roman jurists and yet be no less inexperienced in logical law. More notable is what is said in the sixth book of Justinian's Code, where it says that a disjunctive is sometimes taken copulatively: as in the interdict, "What by force or secretly," where the conjunction "or" is most plainly placed for "and," says Justinian. Yet this later statement of Justinian is more correct as grammar than as logic. Logic belongs only to the mind and reason; it is not a matter of the symbols of Latin, Greek or any other language, but that subject belongs to the grammarians. Therefore, if "or" joins rather than separates, it will make a conjunctive, not a disjunctive, proposition. Sometimes, however, "or" also seems to join in Cicero, as in the work On Fate: "For I do not believe that other craftsmen, or those who use divination, are engaged in their office without any precept, or that they foretell the future." Here you may add "nor" to express the same sense. But so far, concerning the disjunctive and the other kinds of proposition, that is, concerning the whole first kind of judgement, the diligence of P. Ramus in the field of Aristotle and the Aristotelians, Theophrastus, Eudemus and Boethius, has been fully seen by us. Here the thorns are not as many as before, yet they were very serious and troublesome, so that the work of cultivating the art of logic should be thought welcome to the farmers. Let us therefore recall

units.la: quibus vepribus extracta sit nobis primę difpositionis logicæ doctrina. Liber Posteriorum primus fere totus in tribus legibus κατὰ πάντος καθ' αὐτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον, cósumptus est: unde tres triū definitorum versiculi deducti sunt: duo libri Interpretationis, & tria prima capita primi Priorum tantum de enūtiato simplici loquūtur: unde si quintum & sextum capita primi de Interpretatione sustuleris, nihil jā possēs, nisi sentes eruere: Grammatica est de nomine, verbo, oratione. quatuor primis capitib. primi libri: septimum caput est de sophismate ambigui enūtiati: octavum, de doctrina illa impia futuri contingētis: totus liber secundus, de sophismatis infinitorum & modalium, copositionis & divisionis, & quód contradicētia magis opposita videantur, quám adversa. Deniq; tribus capitib. primi Priorū, interátur dicta quinto & sexto capitibus primi de Interpretatione, & novū converforum enuntiatorum sophisma, tanquam superioribus sophismatis corollariū additur. Quamobrem hæc omnia tam multa si quis prætermíssa cōqueratur, cogitet de jure & justitia legis illius καθ' αὐτὸ, alienis & heterogeneis locū in arte nullum esse. Itaq; in Logica, Grammaticis de nomine & verbo verbiq; modis, locum nullum esse: sophisticis verō nugis, nullo prorsus legis cujusquam jure, locum ullum esse reliquū. Tales igitur spinæ, P. Rami agricultura radicitus evulsę sunt: Atq; ut verę fruges liberius uberiusq; succrescant, pręcepta non solum legibus & instrumentis illis Aristoteleis κατὰ πάντος, καθ' αὐτὸ πῇ, τὰ καθόλα πρῶτον congruenter exposita sunt, sed exemplis Homericis illustrata & exornata.
units.tr: from what brambles the doctrine of the first logical arrangement has been drawn out for us. The first book of the Posterior Analytics is almost wholly taken up with three laws, of every, of itself, universal first [κατὰ πάντος, καθ' αὐτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον], and from these three verses of three definitions were derived. The two books On Interpretation, and the first three chapters of the first Prior Analytics, speak only of the simple proposition. So if you removed the fifth and sixth chapters of the first book On Interpretation, you would now have nothing but thorns to dig up. Grammar deals with the noun, the verb and speech: the first four chapters of the first book. The seventh chapter is about the sophism of an ambiguous proposition; the eighth, about that impious doctrine of future contingents; the whole second book, about the sophisms of infinites and modals, of composition and division, and of how contradictories seem more opposed than contraries. Finally, in the three chapters of the first Prior Analytics, the matters said in the fifth and sixth chapters of the first On Interpretation are repeated, and the new sophism of converted propositions is added as a corollary to the earlier sophisms. Therefore, if anyone complains that all these many things have been omitted, let him consider the law and justice of that law of itself [καθ' αὐτὸ], that there is no place in the art for alien and heterogeneous matter. So in Logic there is no place for the grammatical matters of noun, verb and verbal moods, and for sophistic trifles no place at all remains under any law. Such thorns have been rooted out by the cultivation of P. Ramus. So that true fruits may grow up more freely and more abundantly, the precepts have been set out consistently not only in the laws and instruments of Aristotle, of every, of itself in some way, universal first [κατὰ πάντος, καθ' αὐτὸ πῇ, τὰ καθόλα πρῶτον], but also illustrated and adorned with Homeric examples.

units.la: Cap. VIII. De Syllogismo.
units.tr: Chapter 8. On the Syllogism.

units.la: ATque ejusmodi judicium est enū tiati, per fe manifesti: sequitur judiciū syllogismi & methodi. Syllogismo est dispositio, qua questio cum argumento disposita, necessario cōcluditur: Nā si enuntiatio dubia fit, questio efficitur, & ad ejus fidem tertio argumēto opus est, cum quæstione collocato. Syllogismi pars altera antecedit, altera cōsequitur. Antecedēs est, quæ adhibetur ad arguendum quæstionem: duasque partes habet, propositionem & assumptionē: Propositio est prima pars antecedētis, qua quæstionis saltem consequēs cum argumento disponitur: Assumptio est secunda pars antecedentis, quæ assumi tur é propositione. Syllogismi pars cōsequens, est quæ cōplectitur partes quæstionis, eamque concludit: unde cōplexio & cōclufio dicitur. Si qua pars syllogismi defuerit, enthymema dicitur: si quid præter illas tres partes accesserit, prosyllogismus. Partium etiam ordo sæpe cōfunditur: attamē si qua dubitatio
units.tr: Such is the judgment of the self-evident statement. There follows the judgment of the syllogism and of method. A syllogism is an arrangement in which a question, set out together with its argument, is necessarily concluded. For if a statement is doubtful, it becomes a question, and to establish it a third thing is needed, the argument, placed alongside the question. One part of the syllogism comes before, the other after. The antecedent is what is used to argue the question. It has two parts, the proposition and the assumption. The proposition is the first part of the antecedent, in which at least the consequent of the question is set out together with the argument. The assumption is the second part of the antecedent, taken from the proposition. The consequent part of the syllogism embraces the parts of the question and concludes them; hence it is called the complexion and the conclusion. If any part of the syllogism is missing, it is called an enthymeme; if anything is added beyond those three parts, a prosyllogism. The order of the parts is often confused. Yet if any doubt arises on that account, what is missing must be supplied, what is superfluous cut away, and each part brought back to its place in the art.

units.la: y propterea fuerit, explenda quæ desunt, amputanda quę supersunt, & pars quelibet in locum artis redigenda est.
units.tr: Whatever is needed must be added, whatever is superfluous removed, and each part restored to its proper place in the art.

units.la: judicium est enuntiati] judicium enûtiati, est judicium Logicę dispositionis, non solûm primû, sed pené totum: certé totius reliqui judicii fundamentum: hoc enim judicátur omniû artium, omnesque omnino enûtiationes per se clarę & manifestę, qualia feré sunt exépla illa Homerica, prceptis antecedētibus, á P. Ramo adhibita: nec interest, utrûm quæstionis alicujus explicatio fit: Aristoteles (ut antea patuit) efficientem, materiam, partitionem, definitionem, nominatim syllogismi judicio detraxit. at omnis omnino quæstio, cui respondéri nó potest, Ita vel nó: hoc primû enuntiati judicium subit. syllogismi jus aut tribunal nullû agnoscit: ut quid est? quę partes? quale est? ubi est? quádo veniet? Nam si respondeas quod quæritur, acquiescet auditor, quęrereque ultrá ac dubitare desinet, ac postea quicquid judicabitur, ope primi hujus judicii judicabitur. Totæ artes, excepta geometria & geometriæ subalternis, solo enuntiati judicio contentę syllogismû feré nullû requirût, & tamen in geometricis ipsis non pauca sunt, eaque syllogisticorum omnium principia & fundamenta. frequentioris caussam P. Ramus arbitrabatur esse ex obscuritate rerum quę judicio judicari & declarari nó possent: ideo quę syllogisticæ necessitatis judicio convincendæ essent & concludendæ. Itaq; P. Ramus vehementer hoc loco excitabatur ad hominū scholafticorū torporem quendam excitandum, qui nullū putarent usum esse Logicę, nisi diceretur, Sic argumentor, sic argumentaris, nisi denique syllogismus esset aliquis. Enimverò (ajebat, discipulos exhortando) cogitemus de Grammatica simile quippiam: Quando nomina declinātur, verba conjugantur: cujúsnam artis opus illud est? grammaticum nempe. quando nomina cum nominibus, cū verbis passivis, cum adverbiis componuntur, cujúsnam artis est? grammaticum idem respondebis. Quid igitur, si quis assereret ad unam aliquam syntaxeos excellētem regulam, ut verbi activi accusativum regentis, totum grammaticæ artis usum referri, nonne ridicula & temeraria assertio diceretur? At schoLogicorū toto feré terrarū orbe (ne quis Academiæ Parisiensis errorem præcipuum arbitretur) de Logica, grammatistæ illius judicium sequuntur: nullum cēsent usum esse Logicæ, nisi in syllogismo. Itaq; Logica ante divila fuit in Apodicticam, Dialecticam, Sophisticam, id est in syllogismum apodicticum, dialecticū, sophisticum. At (ajebat P. Ramus) quando cōsideras caussam & caussæ genera facta, subjecta, dissentanea, & dissentaneorum genera, & reliqua illa sine syllogismo ullo opera, cujusnam artis opus facis & operaris? Quando tot enūtiatorum modis enuntias simplicis, generalis, specialis, compositi, componendo copulatē, cōnexē, segregādo discreté, disjūctē, quando (inquam) tot modis enuntias, cujus artis facultate uteris? nū Logicæ gicæ & Dialeâ€ticę̂: at syllogismus hic nullus est: Methodus denique, quæ syllogismi doctrinam sequitur. syllogisticum nihil considerat, antecedentis tantúm & consecutionis ordinem intuetur. Ergo totus Logicæ usus in syllogismo non est: magnus quidem & eximius rationis usus in syllogismo versatur, sed non totus: ut Grammaticæ usus est multus in syntaxi verbi actiui, sed non totus, Itaque concludebat P. Ramus, enuntiati judicium non solúm esse magnum per se & amplū, sed reliqui in syllogismo & methodo judicii fundamentum esse.
units.tr: judicium est enuntiati] The judgment of the statement is the judgment of logical arrangement, not only the first but almost the whole of it, and certainly the foundation of all the rest of the judgment. For by this judgment all arts are judged, and all statements that are clear and manifest in themselves, such as are almost those Homeric examples which P. Ramus used in the preceding precepts. It makes no difference whether the explanation concerns some question or other. Aristotle (as was shown earlier) removed the efficient cause, the matter, the partition and the definition from the judgment of the syllogism by name. But any question at all to which one cannot reply "yes" or "no" falls under this first judgment of the statement. The syllogism acknowledges no law or tribunal for such questions: what is it? what are its parts? what kind is it? where is it? when will it come? For if you answer what is asked, the hearer will be satisfied, will cease to inquire further or to doubt, and afterwards whatever is judged will be judged by the help of this first judgment. All the arts, except geometry and its subordinate sciences, rest content with the judgment of the statement alone and scarcely require any syllogism. Yet even in geometry there are not a few such statements, and these are the principles and foundations of all syllogistic reasoning. P. Ramus thought the cause of this frequent failure was the obscurity of things which cannot be judged and made clear by judgment, and so must be proved and concluded by the judgment of syllogistic necessity. Therefore P. Ramus was strongly moved on this point to rouse the kind of torpor found in scholastic men, who thought Logic had no use unless it was said, "I argue thus, you argue thus," or, in short, unless there was some syllogism. Indeed, he would say, exhorting his students, let us think of something similar in Grammar. When nouns are declined and verbs conjugated, whose art is that work? Grammar's, of course. When nouns are compounded with nouns, with passive verbs, with adverbs, whose art is that? You will give the same answer, Grammar's. What then, if someone maintained that the whole use of the grammatical art were referred to a single outstanding rule of syntax, such as the accusative governed by an active verb? Would it not be called a ridiculous and rash assertion? Yet throughout almost the whole world of the schools (lest anyone think this the chief error of the University of Paris), people follow the judgment of that grammarian about Logic: they think Logic has no use except in the syllogism. Hence Logic was formerly divided into Apodictic, Dialectic and Sophistic, that is, into apodictic, dialectical and sophistic syllogism. But (said P. Ramus) when you consider a cause and the kinds of cause, the subject, the contrary, the kinds of contraries, and all those other operations without any syllogism, whose art's work are you doing and performing? When you state a statement in so many modes, simple, general, special, compound, by joining conjunctively, connectedly, by separating discretely, disjunctively, when (I say) you state it in so many ways, whose art's faculty are you using? Surely of Logic and Dialectic; yet no syllogism is involved here. Finally, method, which follows the doctrine of the syllogism, considers nothing syllogistic; it looks only at the order of antecedent and consequent. Therefore the whole use of Logic does not lie in the syllogism. The great and remarkable use of reason does lie in the syllogism, but not the whole of it, just as the use of Grammar is great in the syntax of the active verb but not the whole of it. Thus P. Ramus concluded that the judgment of the statement is not only great and ample in itself, but is the foundation of the rest of judgment, namely of the syllogism and the judgment of method.

units.la: Syllogismi & methodi Duæ species sunt progenere innominato, vel potiús ignoto, sicut antea præmonui hoc igitur sic intelligatur: judicii genus primū est in enuntiato, secundū est in syllogismo & methodo. Syllogismi doctrina quæ sequitur, duobus primis Analyticis ab Aristotele comprehenditur: neque adversus tautologias, legi ἀναλύτικα πρῶτον cōtrarias, agricultura P. Ramo hic magna fuit, fuit tamen omnium maxima gravissimaq; adversus spinas omnium spinarum fo phisticarum longè spinosissimas: ut infinitorū, modalium; conversionum sophismata præ iis nihil esse dicas. Mirabile fit, & vix (nisi oculis intuenti) credibile, quot & quanti veterum Logicorum labores de una syllogismi doctrina ab Aristotele duobus totis Analyticis libris collecti: sint cultura & satio minimé omnium desuerunt Aristotelea colendi, ferendi metendi instrumenta maximé omniú defuerunt. Quapropter P. Rami in his potissimum terris agricultura cótemplemur: Paucæ definitiones & partitiones hic requirebatur, pro quib. sexaginta capita in duob. illis Analyticis omnia omniu fpinarū genera compararút. Ergo hic Ariftoteleorum inftrumentorum opus, hic labor P. Ramo fuerit.
units.tr: Syllogismi & methodi] There are two species under a genus unnamed, or rather unknown, as I warned before. Let this be understood thus: the first kind of judgment lies in the statement, the second in the syllogism and method. The doctrine of the syllogism which follows is comprehended by Aristotle in the first two Analytics [ἀναλυτικά πρῶτα]. Against tautologies and contrary [...] P. Ramus's cultivation here was great, but it was greatest and most serious against the thorns of all the sophistical thorns, by far the most thorny: compared with these you would say the sophisms of the infinite, the modal and the conversions are nothing. It is a marvel, and scarcely credible unless one has looked at it with one's own eyes, how many and how great were the labours of the ancient logicians gathered around the single doctrine of the syllogism by Aristotle in the two whole books of the Analytics. The cultivation and sowing were by no means lacking to those who would cultivate Aristotle; the instruments for ploughing, carrying and reaping were the most lacking of all. Therefore we should contemplate P. Ramus's cultivation especially in these lands: few definitions and partitions were required here, for which the sixty chapters in those two Analytics gather all kinds of thorns. So here was the work of Aristotle's instruments, and here was P. Ramus's labour.

units.la: Syllogismus] Definitio est syllogismi ex genere primum: dispositio enim, genus est fyllogifmi; & fi proximū genus illud syllogismi & methodi nominatum eflet, cōmodiús etiā adhiberetur. at id ignotum est: Arripitur igitur á P. Ramo proximum optimo. ac quamvis genus fyllogifmi & methodi fit ignotum: attamen generalis ejus affectio, ἀφύλη occultatio, non est ignota,ut per species clarius apparebit.
units.tr: Syllogismus] The definition is of the syllogism, from its first genus. For "arrangement" is the genus of syllogism; and if that proximate genus had been named "of the syllogism and method," it would have been more conveniently used. But that is unknown; so P. Ramus takes the nearest genus that is best. And although the genus of syllogism and method is unknown, its general affection, ἀφύλη [occultation], is not unknown, as will appear more clearly through the species.

units.la: Quæstio] Ἐρώτημα, ἐρώτησις, προβλημα, sύτησις, πρᾶγ. μετὰ ἀρχῆς: Interrogatio, propositum, quæstio, res, quod erat ex principio, vocatur in Organo: nó aut omnis quęstio (ut jam dixi) syllogistica, id est syllogismi conclusioni & tanquam jurifdi ctioni subjecta est: sed enuntiatum dubium tantum tūmodo huc attinet, five simplex, five cōpofitū.
