units.tr: Quæstio] Ἐρώτημα, ἐρώτησις, προβλημα, ζήτησις, πρᾶγμα μετὰ ἀρχῆς [question, interrogation, problem, inquiry, matter from a beginning]: in the Organon it is called interrogation, proposition, question, thing, the matter which was from the beginning. Yet not every question (as I have already said) is syllogistic, that is, subject to the conclusion and as it were the jurisdiction of the syllogism. Only a doubtful statement belongs here, whether simple or compound.

units.la: Quæstio cū argumēto] Differētia & forma deinde syllogismi declaratur, é forma dispositionis, qua quæstio cum argumento disposita, necessarió concluditur: Necessitas enim dispositionis hic efficit necessitatem complexionis. atq; fimi le quiddam connexo disjunctoq; cognoscitur. Connexum est necessarium, non ex necessitate partium connexarū, sed necessitate connexionis: Disjunctum est necessarium non ex necesfitate partium disjunctarū, sed ex necessitate disjunctionis: Ita syllogismi complexio necessaria, ex necefsitate confecutionis: ut antecedēs nempe concedi non pofsit,quin cófequens admittatur. neq; hic veritas partiū confideratur: Poteft enim fyllogifmus ex falfis neceffario verum cōcludere:ut, Omnis lapis eft animal: Omnis homo eft lapis: Ergo omnis homo eft animal.fyllogifmus eft cōftans & neceffarius, cúm tamen antecedens totum fit falfum. Sic Ariftoteles 2.3.4.cap.2. Pr.docet ex veris falfum poffe cōcludi:cófecutionis enim difpofitio eft neceffaria. Poteft etiam fyllogifmus ex omnibus paribus falfis & impofsibilibus neceffarius effe: Omnis arbor eft lapis: Omnis leo eft arbor:Ergo omnis leo eft lapis. fyllogifmus eft neceffarius, quanvis partes fint impofsibiles. Quamobrem fyllogifmi judicium nunc refpondet abfoluto neceffarioq; cōnexi & disjunćti judicio, & necesfitas pendet é difpofitionis conftantia & firmitate. Tertio]Argumētum,hic μέσον mediū dicitur,metaphora é topico continuæ fimilitudinis:Illic enim appellatur μέσον ἀνάλογον: & hac metaphora appellatum eft quodlibet argumentum,fed metaphora obfcura,& Grȩcis etiam interpretibus molefta, ut primo libro ad argumē ti definitionem dictum eft.at argumētum in ea fola figura(quæ Ariftoteli prima eft) mediū efse poteft, & iftam antecefsionis & cófecutionis analogiam retinere poteft,in cæteris nō poteft. Quare metaphoras tam obfcuras, imó tam alias tamque difsimiles,P.Ramus evitavit.Syllogifmi autem unicum effe argumentum, ideoq; terminos fyllogifmi tres effe,non plures, 25. ca. primi Priorum disseritur. At doctrina hæc inutilis est, quia é doctrina virtutis, patet refutatio cõtrarii: atq; item quęrere, utrűm tres illi termini,tribus vocabulis exponantur,an longiore o’ rationis ambitu circumscribantur,ad rem logicam nil attinet: Definitiones, distributiones,uno verbo exprimi non possunt,quæ tamē argumenta sunt: & in ipsa inventione monuimus ar gumēti simplicis intelligentiam, interdum verbis plurimis exprimi: & hac de re 36. 37.38.ca.1. Prio. docent tres syllogismi terminos non semper tribus verbis, neq; rectis casibus, sed sæpe longa oratione exprimi. Medii autem illius inventio,jam communiter exposita est: neque in doctrina syllogismi est confundenda,ut Aristoteles vicesimo nono capite primi Prior. confundit,novo quodam inventionis & mirifico gene re, ubi é definitionibus syllogismorum iplorũ, locos inventionis effecit: & quidē tanta obscuritate:ut illic pons asinorũ à scholarum nostrarum doctoribus vulgo appelletur. Figurá quadratam Aristoteles illic instituit, variis triangulis incisam,quibus syllogismi recti & vitiosi notantur: quam qui retexere non possit, asinus vi delicet habeatur. at de hoc asinario ponte diale sticę Scholę accuratiús cõsiderant. quapropter illuc adeat,si quis amplius requirat. Aristoteles 9.& 17. cap.2. Posteriorum ait,argumentũ syllogismi demöstrativi sumi à majore quæstionis extremo,id est consequente: quod non est κατὰ παντὸς: potest enim de utralibet parte assumi. Syllogismi nomen deinceps explicetur:Primó syl-
units.tr: Quæstio cū argumēto] Next the difference and form of the syllogism is explained, from the form of arrangement in which a question set out with its argument is necessarily concluded. For the necessity of the arrangement here produces the necessity of the complexion, and something similar is recognised in the connective and the disjunctive. A connective is necessary not from the necessity of the connected parts but from the necessity of the connection; a disjunctive is necessary not from the necessity of the disjoined parts but from the necessity of the disjunction. So the necessary complexion of the syllogism comes from the necessity of the consequence, so that the antecedent cannot be granted without the consequent being admitted. Nor here is the truth of the parts considered: a syllogism can necessarily conclude a truth from falsehoods, for example: Every stone is an animal; every man is a stone; therefore every man is an animal. The syllogism is constant and necessary, though the antecedent is wholly false. Thus Aristotle, Prior Analytics 2, chapters 3 and 4, teaches that falsehood can be concluded from truths, for the arrangement of the consequence is necessary. A syllogism can also be necessary from all premises that are false and impossible: Every tree is a stone; every lion is a tree; therefore every lion is a stone. The syllogism is necessary, although its parts are impossible. Therefore the judgment of the syllogism now answers to the absolute and necessary judgment of the connective and disjunctive, and its necessity depends on the constancy and firmness of the arrangement. Tertio] The argument is here called the μέσον [middle], a metaphor from the topic of continued likeness: for there it is called the μέσον ἀνάλογον [proportional mean]. By this metaphor any argument at all is called such, but it is an obscure metaphor and troublesome even to the Greek interpreters, as was said in the first book at the definition of argument. Yet the argument can be the middle only in that figure which is first for Aristotle, and it can retain that analogy of antecedent and consequence, but in the others it cannot. Therefore P. Ramus avoided such obscure metaphors, indeed such strange and so dissimilar ones. That a syllogism has only one argument, and therefore that its terms are three and not more, is discussed in chapter 25 of the first Prior Analytics. But this doctrine is useless, for from the doctrine of virtue the refutation of the contrary is evident; and likewise to ask whether those three terms are set out in three words, or are circumscribed by a longer compass of speech, has nothing to do with the logical matter. Definitions and distributions cannot be expressed in one word, yet they are arguments; and in the very discussion of invention we noted that the understanding of a simple argument is sometimes expressed in very many words. On this matter, chapters 36, 37 and 38 of the first Prior Analytics teach that the three terms of a syllogism are not always expressed by three words, nor in the nominative case, but often by a long discourse. The finding of the middle term has already been commonly set out, and it must not be confused with the doctrine of the syllogism, as Aristotle confuses it in chapter 29 of the first Prior Analytics, with a new and marvellous kind of invention, where he makes places of invention out of the definitions of the syllogisms themselves. And he does so with such obscurity that that bridge of asses is commonly called by the teachers of our schools. There Aristotle sets up a square figure, cut through with various triangles, by which correct and faulty syllogisms are marked; whoever cannot unravel it is held to be an ass. But the dialectical schools consider this asinine bridge more carefully; so if anyone requires more, let him go there. Aristotle says in chapters 9 and 17 of the second Posterior Analytics that the argument of a demonstrative syllogism is taken from the major extreme of the question, that is, the consequent; which is not κατὰ παντός [of every], for it can be taken from either part.

units.la: logismus proprie videtur calculū arithmeticū significare, ut collectione, qualis fit ex additione variorum nominum capitumq; summa quaedam: & sic Aristoteles 2. capit. Topic. 6. συλλογισος μὸν usurpat, tanquā συλλογίῳ καὶ ἐπαρίθμησιν. In Philosophia 1. cap. 8. libr. fic loquitur: ἐκ δὲ τῶν ἀριθμῶν συλλογίζεσθαι δεῖ, καὶ συναγαγόντας τὸ κεφάλαιον, τίθεσθαι, ex dictis vero colligere oportet, colligentes summam, finem imponere. & Quintilianus sexto capit. tertii libri syllogismum collectivum interpretatur. Ergo a mathematicis, ut termini, ut medii, ut figurae ac pleraque alia nomina, ita syllogismi nomen ad differendi artem translatū est: λογισμὸς autem, pro eodem in Aristotele sępe legitur, ἐτω γὰρ ὧν ἴσως καὶ λογισμὸς, hic enim fortasse logismus erat. Cap. 18. lib. 2. Post. οἷον δόξα ἡ λογισμός, ut opinio & logismus & 3. ca. 6. Top. ἰσότης ἐναντίων λογισμῶν, equalitas contrariorum logismorum. & 8. c. 2. Physic. ἀρχὴ γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸ ἡ τῆς πράξεως, ἀλλὰ τῆς λογισμός, principium enim ipsum non actionis, sed ratiocinationis. & 1. ca. lib. 1. Philosoph. τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος, καὶ τέχνῃ, καὶ λογισμοῖς ζῇ, genus autem hominum, arte vivit & ratiocinatione, & cap. 7. lib. 11. διὸ ἀδικῶ ἀνθρωπίνῳ λογισμῷ, quare incerta humana ratiocinatione. Ergo λογισμὸς dicitur ut συλλογισμός, quod etiam παραλογισμός, cōpositum verbū pro syllogismo fallaci & captiosō magis indicat: atq; inde dicitur λογιστικὴ p Arithmetica. jam vero, si lubet, agriculturam P. Rami considerēmus & quid ea factus sit melior Logicus Aristotelis ager, attendamus. Quænam igitur, aut qualis est syllogismi organica definitio? Ea vero sic est 1. ca.1. Pr. Syllogismus autem est oratio,in qua positis quibusdam aliud quidpiá á positis ex necessitate accidit, quia hæc sint. Quę definitio idcirco minus aperta est,quia nő satis perspicuas & idoneas syllogismi causas cō tinet.Nam si λόγος,dicatur oratio: syllogismi genus non est:sin autem ratio genus est longé petitum, quod & inventionem & dispositionem universam significat: reliquæ vero partes, formalé caussam obscuriús involvunt, neq; declarant quæstionem cum argumēto disponi,ut necessario concludatur, neq; etiam definitionem propriam efficiunt:Nam quibusdam positis,potest aliquid necessariò consequi, quod hæc ita sunt.neq; tamen erit syllogismus: Omnis enim syllogismus,necessarium: non omne aut necessarium, syllogismus: Quare non si quid accidit quibusdam positis, conádum, ut protinus reducatur in suam formam, sed priús sumendæ sunt duæ propositiones,ut Aristoteles ipse præcipit 3. cap.1. Pr.si quis igitur ita disputat: Venti incubuére mari: Crebris mitat ignib,ether:Défi funduntur ab æthere nimbi: Ergo tempestas est.ex his antecedētibus causis ita positis necessariò tempestas efficitur, neq; tamē syllogismus est. Quamobrem analytica syllogismi definitio, vel Aristotelis ipsius testimonio & judicio,videtur emendari corrigiq;: tāquam ea parum legi κατὰ τωὐτὸς obsecuta sit. Quapropter ad constituendum & definiendum syllogismum,prima illa P. Rami diligentia,Aristotelis non tantum instrumentis,sed manu atque opere adjuta est.Et vero conró consors laboris & cóscius sollicitudinis fui, quoties ista definitio versata, tornata, & ad incudem revocata sit,antequám isto modo confisteret:quo tamen genus illud proximum, quod optaretur,nondum obtinuit. Pars] Partitio syllogismi & enuntiati, cómunibus vocabulis, partes suas appellat:quanquam res est diversa: sed penuria verborū est: atq; etiá syllogismo, antecedétis & cósequentis vocabula magis sunt usitata,quám enuntiato. Adhibetur] Antecedés syllogismi,cótinet argumenti collocationem cum quæstione:ideoq; caussam cócludendi cósequé tis:Pars autē antecedétis utraq; appellatur Ἀνάςτημα intervallū, 4.14.17.26.ca.1.Pr.item. 2.ca.2. Pr.tum 17.18.19.cap.1. Post. Sed metaphora illa est mathematica etiá hïc durior: appellatur etiá pars utraq; πρότασις sppositio, & distinguitur adjectivis,intervallum majus & minus: item propositio major & propositio minor. Sed propositionis nomen, præstabit proprié ad primá parte significandum usurpare,ut Cicero & Quintilia nus usurparunt. Duas autem tantúm partes syllogistici antecedétis esse,disserit Aristoteles 26. cap.1. Pr.secús,si quid præterea sit, e-se προσυλλόγισμον.quod verū quidem est,ut de tribus antea terminis: sed affirmatione virtutis, patet negatio cōtrarii. Propositio] Propositio est pars prima, qua quæstionis saltem consequens cū argumento disponitur quidem, ut in syllogismo simplici: aliás quæstio tota, ut in composito syllogismo:Itaque sive disponatur consequens, sive quæstio,attamen definitio vera erit,& propositio semper complectetur quæstionis cósequēs cum argumento propositionis. Assumptio] Assumtio definitur è posteriore ordinis gradu: & quod assumatur é propositione, nō definitur é dispositione argumenti cum parte quæstionis, quia id non perpetuó verum fit: in simplici enim syllogismo perpetuum est, in composito nō semper:ut, Si dii sunt,divinatio est: dii sunt: divinatio igitur est. Assumptio nil habet quæstionis:qd̄ postea clariùs intelliget. Assumptio Stoicis est πρόσληψις:Peripateticis μετάληψις,ut interpretes Græci adnotarunt 30. cap. 1. Pr. item 21. & 30.ca.1. Poster.ad illud verbum Aristoteli, & hoc Aristoteleis est commune. Unde autem sumatur propositio, quærere jam nō convenit. sumitur enim é locis inventionis argumētum, quod dispositū cum quæstione, propositionem facit. Argumēta autem illa magna jam parte artium decretis comprehensa sunt: Itaque fit, ut propositio syllogismi plerumq; fit é Grammatica,Rhetorica,Dialectica,Mathematica,Philosophia,jurisprudentia:Regulæ enim ac leges,quę primis annis edissuntur, non solúm prima sunt suæ veritatis judicia,sed sunt etiam propositiones & fundamēta judiciorum syllogisticorum, quæ postea cocludimus in specialibus & inde deductis rebus. Quamobrem quod Aristotelēs ἀπορίαν τῶν προτάσεων καὶ τῶν συλλογισμῶν profite tur, tanquā aliquo inventionis titulo, ut nominatim 28.cap.1.Pr.&11.ca.1.Topic.non satis neque accurata, neque logica pefefsio est, neque satis apta inventionis à judicio & dispositione differentia: confusio enim triplicis Logicæ; apo dicticæ, topicę, sophisticæ, huc illa redit, de qua initio primi libri tam diligenter a nobis actum est: ut sophisma tam legibus omnibus Aristotelis infensum & contrarium tolleretur.
units.tr: logismus properly seems to signify an arithmetical calculation, a collection, such as a certain sum arising from adding various numbers together. And so Aristotle in Topics 2, ch. 6, uses the word συλλογισμός as "a reckoning and counting" [συλλογισμὸν καὶ ἐπαρίθμησιν]. In the Philosophy, book 1, ch. 8, he speaks thus: "One must reckon from the numbers, and by adding them together, set down the total; from what has been said, one must draw an inference, and by gathering up the sum, set an end" [ἐκ δὲ τῶν ἀριθμῶν συλλογίζεσθαι δεῖ, καὶ συναγαγόντας τὸ κεφάλαιον τίθεσθαι; ex dictis vero colligere oportet, colligentes summam, finem imponere]. Quintilian, in the sixth chapter of the third book, also explains the syllogism as a collective inference. So, just as terms, middles, figures and many other names were transferred from the mathematicians to the art of disputing, so too the name syllogism was transferred to the art of reasoning. The word λογισμός, meaning the same thing, is often read in Aristotle: "for perhaps here it was logismos" [ἵνα γὰρ ὧν ἴσως καὶ λογισμός], in Posterior Analytics 2, ch. 18: "such as opinion or logismos"; and in Topics 3, ch. 6: "the equality of opposed logismoi" [ἰσότης ἐναντίων λογισμῶν]; and in Physics 8, ch. 2: "for the principle itself is not of action but of reasoning" [ἀρχὴ γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸ ἡ τῆς πράξεως, ἀλλὰ τῆς λογισμός]; and in book 1, ch. 1 of the Philosophy: "the race of men lives by art and by reasoning" [τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος, καὶ τέχνῃ, καὶ λογισμοῖς ζῇ]; and in book 11, ch. 7: "wherefore uncertain by human reasoning" [διὸ ἀδικῶ ἀνθρωπίνῳ λογισμῷ]. Thus λογισμός is used as συλλογισμός; the compound παραλογισμός, which more clearly indicates a fallacious and deceptive syllogism, is also used, and from this comes λογιστικὴ, arithmetic. Now, if it pleases, let us consider P. Ramus's cultivation of the field, and let us observe what he has made of Aristotle's logical field, which is better. What, then, is the organic definition of the syllogism, or what sort is it? It runs thus, in Prior Analytics 1, ch. 1: "A syllogism is a discourse in which, certain things having been laid down, something other than those things follows of necessity because they are so." This definition is for that reason less clear, because it does not contain sufficiently plain and fitting causes of the syllogism. For if logos is taken to mean discourse, it is not the genus of the syllogism; but if ratio is the genus, which is taken from far off and signifies invention and the whole arrangement, then the remaining parts involve the formal cause more obscurely, and do not explain that the question is arranged with the argument so that it is necessarily concluded, nor do they make a proper definition. For, certain things having been laid down, something may follow of necessity from them, that they are so, and yet there will not be a syllogism: for every syllogism is necessary, but not every necessary thing is a syllogism. Therefore, it is not that if something follows from certain things laid down, it is at once to be brought back into its form; rather, two propositions must first be taken, as Aristotle himself prescribes in Prior Analytics 1, ch. 3. If someone reasons thus: "The winds have fallen upon the sea; the ether is sending forth frequent fires; from the ether the rain-clouds pour down; therefore there is a storm": from these antecedent causes so laid down a storm is necessarily produced, and yet it is not a syllogism. Wherefore Aristotle's own analytic definition of the syllogism seems to need emending and correcting, since, as it were, it has been little read and not observed in the same way. Therefore, for constituting and defining the syllogism, Ramus's first diligence was aided not only by Aristotle's instruments but by hand and labour. And indeed I myself was a partner in the labour and a sharer in the anxiety, as often as this definition was turned over, shaped, and brought back to the anvil before it was settled in this form; yet it did not obtain that proximate genus which was desired. Pars: the partition of the syllogism and of the enunciation calls its parts by common names, although the matter is different; but this is due to a shortage of words, and the terms antecedent and consequent are more customary for the syllogism than for the enunciation. Adhibetur: the antecedent of a syllogism contains the placing of the argument together with the question, and therefore the cause of the conclusion of the consequent. Both parts of the antecedent are called ἀνάληψις [anastema], "interval," in Prior Analytics 1, chs. 4, 14, 17, 26, and in Prior Analytics 2, ch. 2, and again in Posterior Analytics 1, chs. 17, 18, 19; but this metaphor is mathematical and here rather harsh. Both parts are also called πρότασις [protasis], proposition, and are distinguished by adjectives: the greater interval and the lesser interval; likewise, major proposition and minor proposition. But the name proposition will be better used properly to signify the first part, as Cicero and Quintilian used it. Aristotle argues, in Prior Analytics 1, ch. 26, that the syllogistic antecedent has only two parts; otherwise, if anything else is added, it is a prosyllogism [προσυλλόγισμον]. This is true, as with the three terms mentioned before; but by the affirmation of the virtue, the negation of the contrary is evident. Propositio: the proposition is the first part, in which at least the consequent of the question is set out together with the argument, as in a simple syllogism; otherwise the whole question is set out, as in a compound syllogism. Thus, whether the consequent or the question is set out, the definition will still be true, and the proposition will always embrace the consequent of the question together with the argument of the proposition. Assumptio: the assumption is defined from the later rank in the order; and what is assumed from the proposition is not defined by the arrangement of the argument with the part of the question, because that is not always true: in a simple syllogism it is constant, in a compound one not always, as: "If there are gods, there is divination; there are gods; therefore there is divination." The assumption has nothing of the question, which will be understood more clearly later. The Stoics call the assumption πρόσληψις [prosēpsis], the Peripatetics μετάληψις [metalēpsis], as the Greek interpreters have noted on Prior Analytics 1, chs. 30, 21 and 30, on that word of Aristotle; and this is common to the Aristotelians. But it is no longer appropriate to inquire whence the proposition is taken. For the argument is taken from the places of invention, and when arranged with the question it makes the proposition. Now those arguments have been comprehended by decrees for the greater part of the arts; and so it comes about that the proposition of a syllogism is for the most part drawn from grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, mathematics, philosophy and jurisprudence. For the rules and laws that are taught in the early years are not only the first judgments of their own truth, but are also the propositions and foundations of syllogistic judgments, which we afterwards conclude in special matters and things deduced from them. Wherefore, what Aristotle professes as "the inquiry into the propositions and syllogisms" [ἀπορίαν τῶν προτάσεων καὶ τῶν συλλογισμῶν], as if under some title of invention, namely in Prior Analytics 1, ch. 28, and Topics 1, ch. 11, is neither an accurate nor a logical exposition, nor a sufficiently apt difference between invention and judgment and arrangement. For the confusion of the threefold logic, apodictic, topical and sophistical, comes back to that, which at the beginning of the first book we treated so diligently, so that the sophism, so hostile to and contrary to all the laws of Aristotle, might be removed.

units.la: Consequens] Aristoteli pars illa dicitur συμπέρασμα ἃ συμπεράνω cocludo: Stoicis est ἐπιφορὰ illatio: Complexio Ciceroni & Quintiliano dicitur: & modo ex quodam conjugatorum argumento explicatur, quod complectitur partes quæstionis.
units.tr: Consequens: Aristotle calls that part συμπέρασμα [symperasma], from συμπεράνω, I conclude. For the Stoics it is ἐπιφορά [epiphora], inference; Cicero and Quintilian call it complexio, the complex; and it is now explained by a certain conjugated argument, which embraces the parts of the question.

units.la: Conclusio] Similiter ex conjugatis definitur, quia concludit: appellatur aut etiam tota ratiocinatio, & argumentatio, conclusio. Cic. in Lucullo: Hæc conclusio quam vim habeat, consider a. Sic Græcum syllogismi verbum videtur proprie complexionem significare: & sic Aristoteles 17. ca. 2. Pr. usurpat, cum ait ex falsis verum concludi posse, ex oppositis non posse: ut in exemplo, Omnis homo est animal, Nullus homo est animal, Ergo nullus homo est homo.
units.tr: Conclusio: likewise it is defined from the conjugates, because it concludes; the conclusion is also called the whole reasoning and argumentation. Cicero, in the Lucullus: "Consider what force this conclusion has." Thus the Greek verb for syllogism seems properly to signify the complex; and so Aristotle uses it in Prior Analytics 2, ch. 17, when he says that from false things the true can be concluded, but not from opposites; as in the example: "Every man is an animal; no man is an animal; therefore no man is a man."

units.la: Ἀ ά, γὰρ ἴναντι ὁ συλλογισμὸς γίνεται τῷ πράγματι: semper enim syllogismus rei adversus efficitur. hic συλλογισμὸς αὐτὶ συμπεράσματος capitur.
units.tr: "For a syllogism is always made against the thing" [ἀεὶ γὰρ ἐναντίον ὁ συλλογισμὸς γίνεται τῷ πράγματι]: here syllogism is taken in place of conclusion.

units.la: Enthymema] Paucis verbis magna historia variorum apud Aristotelem dogmatum comprehenditur: Ista enim ἐνθύμημα est syllogistica, in qua & partium vel defectus, vel redundantia, & ordinis inversio consideratur. Duodecim tota capita sunt ultima in primo libro priorum Analyticorum de analysi syllogismi: quæ si quid habent logici emolumenti, id totum hic no tam succincte quam plane perfecteq; comprehensum est, aut jam antea in syllogismi partibus est declarata. Analysis igitur Aristoteli, est logici operis tanquam telam jam cotextam retexere: Cujus utilitatem certam profert 33. cap.1. Prio. Accidit autem simul & prius dicta confirmari, & clariora fieri, quod sic habeant per antedicta. Necesse enim est omne verum sibi ipsi usquequaque consonum esse. hic fructus est permagnus, quod retexendo syllogismo jam facto, judicium confirmatur & illustratur: sed fructus communis reтe xendo cuilibet argumento, ut definitionis, distributionis: item cuilibet enuntiato & methodo: & analysis interea talis, praecipua in Logica arte doctrinam nullam requirit.
units.tr: Enthymema: in a few words is comprehended a great history of the doctrines of various authors in Aristotle; for an enthymeme is a syllogistic form in which the defect or redundancy of parts and the inversion of order are considered. The twelve last chapters of the first book of the Prior Analytics, on the analysis of the syllogism, are of this kind; and whatever logical benefit they contain has been comprehended here, not so succinctly as plainly and perfectly, or has already been declared earlier in the parts of the syllogism. Analysis, therefore, for Aristotle, is like unweaving a web already woven in the logical work: its certain use he sets out in Prior Analytics 1, ch. 33: "It happens also that what was said before is confirmed and made clearer, since things are thus by the things said before. For it is necessary that every truth be wholly consonant with itself." This fruit is very great: by unweaving a syllogism already made, the judgment is confirmed and illustrated. But this is the common fruit of unweaving any argument, such as a definition or a distribution, and likewise any enunciation and method; and the analysis in this way, being the chief thing in the art of logic, requires no doctrine at all.

units.la: Enthymema] Aristot. 27. ca. 2. Prio. definit hoc modo: ἐνθύμημα μὲν ἐν ἀπὸ συλλογισμὸς ἀτελὴς ἐξ εἰκότων καὶ σημείων: Enthymema igitur est syllogismus imperfectus, e verisimilibus & signis. At postremum hoc additamentum (e verisimilibus & signis) non plus in enthymematis definitione requiritur, quam in syllogismi definitione: ex quot enim argumentis syllogismo pleno concludi potest, ex totidem potest imperfecto concludi. Aristoteles igitur id collegit, non judicavit. Cicero in Topicis, nomine enthymematis omnem sententiam significari ait: ac praecipue eam conclusionem, quae fit e contrariis, qua acutissima videatur. Sed neque Aristotelis illud ex adjunctis, neque Ciceronis e contrariis enthymema modo P. Ramus appellat, sed e quocunque argumenti genere syllogismum parte, de tribus aliqua truncu & impersectum: ad cujus accuratius & perfectius judicium, ciū,fi qua enthymematis dubitatio fit, restituendum est quod defuerit,& sic 33.cap.1.Prio.de propositionibus præcipit Ariftoteles:Et fi ambæ sumptæ non sint, ipse restituas alteram: Interdum enim qui universalem proposuerint, in ea comprehensam non affumunt.neq; fcribentes, neq; interrogantes:per quas autem ipsę cocludunt,præterm̃ittunt:alia vero frustrà interrogant. Cósiderandum vero fi quid superfluūassumptum fit:& fi quid necessariorum prætermissum: & hoc quidem restituendū, illud vero tollēdum, donec ad duas propositiones perveneris. Sine enim his non licet reducere sic inter rogatas rationes.Hæc Aristoteles de enthymemate, aliàs ex ellipsi assumptionis: id enim est quod comprehendi Aristoteles ait in propositione:aliàs ex ellipsi propositionis: id enim est per quod concluditur. & sic Philoponus ait ad hunc locum, propositionē esse,per quam assumptio complexionē colligit. Hic igitur Aristoteles annotavit ellipsin partis utriusq; in antecedente: Ellipsis aliquando etiam est complexionis. Enthymematis vero referta sunt in bonis authoribus omnia,deq; syllogisticis quæstionibus,vix ac ne vix quidem, millesimā pleno syllogismo cōclufam invenies. Hic vero libet é P. Rami exemplis,quibus de enthymemate disserens utebatur, singulas enthymematicas ellipseis illustrare. Cicero in libro de Seneƈt. pro-positionē sic omisit: Senex nec quod speret,habet:At est eó meliore conditione,quàm adolefcens: cúmid quod ille sperat, hic assecutus fit. ille vult diu vivere: hic diu vixit. Adde propositionem generalem, & conclude: (rat: Qui jā est assecutus, beatior est eo, qui se affecuturū sperat Senex assecutus est longa vita, quā adolescens sperat: Itaq; senex beatior est adolescente.
units.tr: Enthymema] Aristotle defines it in the twenty-seventh chapter of the second book of the Prior Analytics: an enthymeme is an imperfect syllogism from probabilities and signs [ἐνθύμημα μὲν ἐν ἀπὸ συλλογισμὸς ἀτελὴς ἐξ εἰκότων καὶ σημείων]. So the enthymeme is an imperfect syllogism from probabilities and signs. But this last addition (from probabilities and signs) is no more required in the definition of the enthymeme than in the definition of the syllogism: for from as many arguments as a full syllogism can conclude, an imperfect one can conclude too. Aristotle therefore gathered this; he did not decide it. Cicero in the Topics says that by the name enthymeme any sentence is meant, and especially that conclusion which is drawn from contraries, by which it seems most sharp. But P. Ramus does not call an enthymeme either Aristotle's (from adjuncts) or Cicero's (from contraries), but any syllogism, from whatever kind of argument, that is cut short and imperfect in one of its three parts. If any doubt about an enthymeme arises, then for a more accurate and perfect judgement what is missing must be restored; so Aristotle prescribes concerning propositions in the first chapter of the second book of the Prior Analytics: "And if both premises are not taken, you yourself must supply the other. For sometimes those who have stated a universal do not assume what is contained in it, neither in writing nor in asking; and they omit those through which they conclude, while others they ask in vain. One must consider whether something superfluous has been assumed, and whether something necessary has been omitted; and what is omitted must indeed be restored, and what is superfluous removed, until you arrive at two premises. For without these it is not permitted to reduce arguments so asked." These are Aristotle's words on the enthymeme: sometimes it arises from an ellipsis of the assumption, for that is what Aristotle says is comprehended in the proposition; sometimes from an ellipsis of the proposition, for that is what the conclusion rests on. So Philoponus says on this passage that the proposition is that through which the assumption gathers the conclusion. Here Aristotle noted the ellipsis of either part in the antecedent. An ellipsis is sometimes also of the conclusion. Good authors are full of enthymemes, and among syllogistic questions you will hardly, if ever, find one in a thousand concluded in a full syllogism. Here it is pleasing to illustrate each enthymematic ellipsis with the examples P. Ramus used when discussing the enthymeme. Cicero in the book On Old Age omits the proposition thus: "The old man has not what he hopes for, yet he is in a better condition than the young man, since he has attained what the other only hopes for. The one wants to live long; the other has lived long." Add the general proposition and conclude: "He who has already attained is happier than he who hopes to attain. The old man has attained the long life that the young man hopes for; therefore the old man is happier than the young man."

units.la: Martialis libro quinto, in sequenti enthymemate assumptionem relinquit: Si quando leporem mittis mihi, Gellia, dicis, Formosus septem, Marce, diebus eris. Si non derides, si verum, lux mea, narras: Edisti nunquam, Gellia, tu leporem.
units.tr: In the fifth book, Martial leaves out the assumption in the following enthymeme: "If ever you send me a hare, Gellia, you say, Marcus, you will be handsome for seven days. If you are not joking, if you tell the truth, my light: you never ate a hare, Gellia."

units.la: Adde assumptionem, syllogismus talis erit: Si quis edat lepore, septem diebus formosus erit: Gellia nunquam formosa fuit: Gellia igitur nunquam edit leporem.
units.tr: Add the assumption, and the syllogism will be this: "If anyone eats hare, he will be handsome for seven days; Gellia was never handsome; therefore Gellia never ate a hare."

units.la: Martialis lib. 1. complexionem omittit: Amissum non flet, cum sola est Gellia patrem: Si quis adest, jussæ prosiliunt lachrymæ. Non luget, quisquis laudari, Gellia quærit: Ille dolet vere, qui sine teste dolet.
units.tr: In book one Martial omits the conclusion: "Gellia does not weep for her lost father when she is alone; if anyone is present, her ordered tears spring forth. Whoever seeks to be praised, Gellia, does not mourn; he grieves truly who grieves without a witness."

units.la: Exple syllogismum, & conclude: Verus luctus est occultus: Fletus Gelliæ non est occultus: Fletus igitur Gelliæ, non est verus luctus:
units.tr: Complete the syllogism and conclude: "True grief is hidden; Gellia's weeping is not hidden; therefore Gellia's weeping is not true grief."

units.la: Prosyllogismus Sic Aristot. dicitur syllogisticę partis exornatio aliqua vel approbatio, ad 26. cap. 2. Prior. ubi προσυλλογισμῶν præcipuė agitur, quod si termini quatuor sint, propositiones tres erunt: si termini quinq;, propositiones quatuor, & sic deinceps: quo capite etiam prosyllogismus appellatur ἀπόδειξις, additio: cujus exemplain singulis generibus frequentia erunt. Pro-
units.tr: Prosyllogism] Aristotle calls it some embellishment or confirmation of a syllogistic part, in the twenty-sixth chapter of the second book of the Prior Analytics, where he treats chiefly of the prosyllogism: if there are four terms there will be three propositions; if five terms, four propositions; and so on. In that chapter the prosyllogism is also called apodeixis, addition [ἀπόδειξις]. Examples of it will be frequent in every kind of argument.

units.la: z syllosyllogismus autem adhibetur nō solúm ad probandum,sed etiam ad occultandū:unde est Ariftotelea <bl>ἀρνῆις</bl> præcipué nominata,de qua præcipitur 20.cap. 2.Prior. & 1. ca. 8.Top. & 14.ca.2.
units.tr: The prosyllogism, however, is used not only for proving but also for concealing; hence Aristotle's denial [ἄρνησις], which is chiefly so named, is treated in the twentieth chapter of the second book of the Prior Analytics, and in the first book, chapter eight, of the Topics, and the fourteenth chapter of the Sophistical Refutations.

units.la: Elench.ne res concludenda præponatur,ne antecedentis partes continuentur,sed rebus alienis misceātur, affectuq; vario turbētur: ut cū quæstio concludetur, quæratur propter quid: quod totum omnibus quidem argumentis,sed præcipué rhetoricis & troporum & figurarum ornamentis efficitur. His autē crypticis Socrates multúm usus est: ideoq; ab iis, contra quos disputat, appellatur incantator,torpedo,Dædalus.ut in Menone: Et nunc ut mihi videris,præftigiis me decipis,veneficiis inficis, & aperté in cantas: ita ut ambiguitatis sim plenus : videris quoq; mihi prorsus (fi quidē licet in te jocari) & forma,& aliis rebus,simillimus torpedini,latifsimo pisci maris:qui hominē sibi propinquātem & tangentem,membris & corpore ftupidū reddit: & tu videris stuporē mihi nūc injecifle: nā & animo & corpore sic obstupui, ut quid tibi refpōdeam,non habeam.Sic Eutyphron Socratem Dædalo comparat:Mihi quidem prope modum videtur ea,quæ dicis, ō Socrates,eadē dicacitate notanda esse : quód enim illa nostra oberrant, neq; sibi constát, non ego sum accufandus:sed tu mihi Dedalus videris:nam quod ad me attinet,illa sic constitissent & mansissent. Thrafÿmachus lib. 1.de Repub.Socratem nominat in sermonibus sycophantā & insidiatorem. Atq; hæc de partium ellypfi & redundátia:ordinis ἀρνὸς brevior est. Propositio & assumptio, licet artis ordine sit illa prior, hæc posterior: usus ordine huc permisset: ut in Grámatica, quâvis suppositû præcedat, appositû sequatur: artis usus tamē, & voluptas auriû id sæpe pervertit: attamen & illic, & hic, cûm exigitur ratio artis, suppositû præponitur, appositû succedit: ita in syllogismo, propositio prima, assumptio secunda erit. Atq; hæc de syllogismi partibus in quibus Aristoteles 26. c. 1. Pr. analogiâ quandâ mathematicâ meditatus est. Omnis erit syllogism⁹ ex propositionib. quidē paribus, terminis imparibus: uno enim plures sunt termini, quám ppositiones. erút aut coplexiones, dimidium ppositionû. Hic Aristoteles Arithmetica ternarii, binarii, unitatis analogiâ reperit, ubi differētia ex cessus, uniras semper essēt. Atqui in hoc exemplo memini P. Ramum excitatum esse adversus scholasticos philosophiæ Aristotelis pfessores nescio quos, qui cûm Euclidis elementû nullû unquam gustassent, attamen auderent philosophiam tam multis partibus mathematicâ prositeri: Etenim cûm mathematica & vocabula λόγον, μέσον, διάστημα, σχῆμα, similiaq;: item exempla de triangulí tribus angulis, de diametro asymmetro, de tetragonismo, ut modo de hac analogia: dicebat ἀναμετρητὴς interpretes (quales toto terrarum orbe pleriq; essent) non plus in Logica Aristotelis videre, quàm Polyphemus ab Ulysse occæcatus, vidisset in illa ovilis sui spelúca. Sed cûm P. Ramus istam Geometriæ ignorantiam deplorassēt: attamē totum hoc & verborum, &
units.tr: So that the thing to be concluded is not put first, that the parts of the antecedent are not continued but mixed with alien matters and confused by varied feelings, as when the question is concluded and one asks for the reason: all this is done in every kind of argument, but chiefly in rhetorical argument with the ornaments of tropes and figures. Socrates made much use of these cryptic devices, and for this reason those against whom he disputes call him an enchanter, a torpedo fish, a Daedalus. So in the Meno: "And now, as it seems to me, you bewitch me with sorcery and poison me, and clearly you enchant me, so that I am full of perplexity. And you seem to me altogether (if it is permitted to joke at your expense) in form and in other things most like the torpedo, the broadest fish of the sea, which makes stupid in limbs and body the man who approaches and touches it. And you seem to me now to have cast such a stupor upon me, for I am so numbed in mind and body that I have nothing to answer you." So Euthyphro compares Socrates to Daedalus: "It seems to me almost that what you say, Socrates, ought to be noted with the same sharpness; for it is not I who am to be blamed that those statements of ours wander and do not agree with themselves, but you seem to me a Daedalus; for as far as I am concerned, those statements would have stood firm and remained." Thrasymachus in the first book of the Republic names Socrates a sycophant and an ambusher. And this is said about the ellipsis and redundancy of the parts. The order [τάξις] is shorter. The proposition and the assumption: although by the order of the art the one is first and the other second, the order of use would permit it here, as in grammar, where what is placed under is first and what is placed after follows; yet the practice of the art and the pleasure of the ears often reverse this. Nevertheless there, as here, when the reason of the art requires it, what is placed under is put before, and what is placed after comes second. So in the syllogism the first proposition will be the proposition, the second the assumption. These are the things about the parts of the syllogism, in which Aristotle, in the first chapter of the second book of the Prior Analytics, pondered a certain mathematical analogy. Every syllogism will have equal numbers of propositions, but unequal terms: for there are more terms than propositions by one. Or they are compounds, the half of the propositions. Here Aristotle discovers, by the analogy of the arithmetic of three, two and one, where the difference of excess would always be one. But in this example I recall that P. Ramus attacked certain scholastic professors of the philosophy of Aristotle, I know not who, who, though they had never tasted the elements of Euclid, nevertheless dared to profess philosophy so largely mathematical. For when they had said that mathematical words such as logos, mesos, diastema, schema and the like, and likewise the examples of the triangle with three angles, of the incommensurable diagonal, of squaring the circle, and just now of this analogy, were the work of mathematics, he said that the anametrētēs interpreters (of whom there would be most throughout the whole world) saw no more in the Logic of Aristotle than Polyphemus, blinded by Ulysses, saw in the cave of his own sheepfold. But although P. Ramus deplored this ignorance of geometry, nevertheless he rejected this whole kind of words and examples taken from the mathematicians from logic,

units.la: exemplorum à Mathematicis genus à Logica rejiciebat, quia καθ' αὐτὸ id in Logica non esset, præsertim cùm posterioris esset disciplinæ, nequedum logicæ artis discipulo perceptæ. Hæc igitur de syllogismi partibus, antecedente propositione & assumptione, item consequente complexione Cicero in veteri Rhetorico, quinque partes ratiocinationi tribuit, ut prima sit propositio, deinde ejus ratio, tum assumptio, quarta ejus approbatio, quinta complexio: à quo differt Quintil. cap.14.lib.5. Mihi (inquit) & pluribus nihilominus authoribus, tres solummodo videntur: Nam ita se habet natura, ut sit de quo quæratur, & per quod probetur: tertium adjicit potest, velut ex consensu duorum antecedentium: Ita prima erit intentio, secunda assumptio, tertia complexio: Nam confirmatio primæ partis, & secundæ exornatio, iisdem cedere possunt, quibus subjiciuntur. Quæ distinctio apud Fabium, numero quidem partium vera est (sunt enim tres tantum syllogismi partes) sed probatione, falsa: intentio enim & complexio una & eadem pars est: nec aliud est intentio, quàm propositta quæstio seu enuntiatio dubia, quæ subducta ratione tandem concluditur: assumptionis autem nomine, propositio & assumptio confunduntur. Sed hæc de syllogismo deq; syllogismi partibus doctrina nobis adhuc arithmetica magnam quidé parte illa fuit: Et verò (ut huc P. Ramus tandé erupit) si quid est in illa arte præclarū, quod in primis logico syllogismi judicio respondeat, regula est quatuor proportionalium, quam aurea
units.tr: because kath' auto [καθ' αὐτὸ] it is not in logic, especially since it belongs to a later discipline, and is not yet understood by a student of the logical art. These things, then, are about the parts of the syllogism, the antecedent proposition and assumption, and likewise the consequent conclusion. Cicero, in his old Rhetoric, assigns five parts to reasoning: the first is the proposition, then its reason, then the assumption, fourth its confirmation, fifth the conclusion. Quintilian differs from him in chapter fourteen of book five: "To me," he says, "and to several authors nonetheless, there seem to be only three: for the nature of the matter is such that there is something about which the question is asked, and something through which it is proved; a third may be added, as from the agreement of the two preceding. So the first will be the intention, the second the assumption, the third the conclusion. For the confirmation of the first part and the embellishment of the second can yield to the same things to which they are subjoined." This distinction in Fabius is true as to the number of parts (for there are only three parts of the syllogism), but false as to the proof: for the intention and the conclusion are one and the same part; nor is the intention anything other than the question proposed, or the doubtful statement, which, once the reasoning is carried out, is finally concluded; while under the name of assumption, proposition and assumption are confused. But this teaching about the syllogism and about the parts of the syllogism has hitherto been, for us, to a large extent arithmetic. And indeed (since P. Ramus has at last burst out here) if there is something excellent in that art which corresponds above all to the logical judgement of the syllogism, it is the rule of four proportionals, which the arithmeticians call the golden rule.

units.la: Arithmetici nominát: ut 2. ad 3. sic 6. ad quem quartus proportionalis quæritur: multiplicatur igitur secundus per tertium, & factus 18 divisus per primum, educit 9. pro quarto: & jam concluditur, ut 2 ad 3 sic 6. ad 9. Quid igitur efficit aurea hæc Arithmeticæ regula? é trib. datis, quartum proportionale reperit: & propter infinitū in rebus humanis usum, aurea dicitur. At syllogismus quid efficit? é duobus manifestis & concessis, tertium judicat & concludit: & quod illic multiplicatio divisioq; hic propositio & assumptio ad colligendum proportionale efficit: sed Arithmetica tribus datis opus habet: ut si duo tantum sint, secundum tamē bis sumitur: Logica duobus contēta est: & syllogismus est judex proportionis Arithmeticæ, & omnium omnino ratiocinationū. Quare syllogismus cūm & paucioribus contentus sit, & omnia complectatur, multò justius aurei cognominis appellationem merèatur, Inauratum est Parisiensis Senatus tribunal illud summum, quo civium, principum, regum deniq; nostrorum controversiæ judicātur: ut syllogismi tribunal non inauratū, sed aureum, sed cælestē potiús & divinum habendū est, quo judicia nostri Senatus, imó omniū, qui usquam terrarum sint, judicantium de enuntiatis dubiis judicia confirmātur & concluduntur. Hæc P. Ramus de syllogismi laude præstantiaq; veré & magnificé prædicabat: & tamen interea vehementer admirabatur vel miserabatur potiús, nullum esse in omnibus disciplinarum studiis hominum genus magis nō ignarum modó, sed fastidiosum logicæ, quàm nostri tëporis juris studiosi pleriq; essent, tanquam ars bené judicandi judicibus futuris esset inutilis. Quâ pestiferam opinionem é scholasticis sophismatis natam conquerebatur: Propterea adolescentes ad juris prudentiam accessuros inprimis exhortabatur ad syllogisticam studiose cognoscendū & exercendum: Hoc enim judicii organum judicibus istis inprimis esse necessariū. Leges justiniani speciales esse judicādi leges, & quidem leges tantum propositionum, ut dixi, quæ sine ipsa generali syllogismi lege & regula exitiales paralogismos essent facturæ: peccaverit enim grammaticus aut Rhetor in judicio verbi aut tropi, judicii barbarismus aut inelegantia ridebitur: at si judex in judicio capitis, famæ, fortunarum peccaverit, peccatum non jam risus, sed luctus & miseria consequetur.
units.tr: As the arithmeticians name it: as 2 is to 3, so is 6 to the quantity sought, the fourth proportional. So the second is multiplied by the third, the product 18 is divided by the first, and this yields 9 for the fourth; and then it is concluded: as 2 is to 3, so 6 is to 9. What then does this golden rule of arithmetic accomplish? From three given quantities it finds a fourth proportional, and because of its endless use in human affairs it is called golden. But what does the syllogism accomplish? From two manifest and granted propositions it judges and concludes a third. Just as there multiplication and division, here the proposition and assumption bring about the collecting of the proportional. But arithmetic needs three given terms; if there are only two, the second is taken twice. Logic is content with two. The syllogism is the judge of arithmetical proportion, and of all reasonings whatever. Therefore, since the syllogism is content with fewer terms and yet embraces everything, it deserves much more justly the name of golden. The supreme tribunal of the Parisian Senate is gilded, the court in which the controversies of citizens, princes, and finally of our kings are decided. But the tribunal of the syllogism should be held not gilded but golden, and rather heavenly and divine, by which the judgments of our Senate, indeed of all judges anywhere on earth, concerning doubtful propositions are confirmed and concluded. Ramus proclaimed these things truly and magnificently in praise of the syllogism. Yet meanwhile he marvelled greatly, or rather pitied, that there was no class of men in all the studies of the disciplines more not merely ignorant of logic but scornful of it than the law students of our time, as if the art of judging well were useless to future judges. He complained that this pestilent opinion arose from scholastic sophisms. Therefore he especially exhorted young men who were about to take up jurisprudence to learn and practise syllogistic diligently, since this instrument of judgment is especially necessary for those judges. The laws of Justinian are special laws of judging, and indeed laws of propositions only, as I have said, which without the general law and rule of the syllogism would produce deadly paralogisms. For if a grammarian or rhetorician errs in judging a word or a trope, a barbarism or an inelegance will be laughed at; but if a judge errs in a judgment concerning life, reputation, or fortunes, the error will bring not laughter but grief and misery.

units.la: Cap. IX. De prima Specie primi generis.
units.tr: Chapter IX. On the first species of the first kind.

units.la: Syllogismus est simplex aut compositus: Simplex, ubi pars quæstionis cum argumento disponitur, cōsequens in propositione, antecedens in assumptione: estq; affirmatus é propositione & assumptione affirmatis: negatus ex altera tantum negata: & uterq; generalis ex utraq; generali: specialis ex altera tantum generali: proprius ex utraq; ppria.
units.tr: A syllogism is either simple or compound. It is simple when a part of the question is arranged with the argument: the consequent in the proposition, the antecedent in the assumption. It is affirmative if both proposition and assumption are affirmative, and negative if only the other is negative; it is general if both are general, special if only the other is general, and proper if both are proper.

units.la: Simplicis syllogismi genera duo sunt, primo argumentum antecedit tantum, vel consequitur tantum. Prima igitur species primi generis est, quando ex argumento antecedente in propositione ut libet in assumptione affirmatè, complexio specialis efficitur, ut in exemplis. Aff. gen. Constantia est virtus: At est confidentia: Quadam igitur confidentia est virtus. Neg. gen. Audacia non est virtus: At est confidentia: Quedā igitur confidentia non est virtus. Aff. spe. Sapiens est laudabilis: At quidam est pauper: Quidam igitur pauper est laudabilis. vel Quidam sapiens est dives: At sapiens est laudabilis: Quidam igitur laudabilis est dives. Neg. spec. Stultus non est beatus: At quidam est fortunatus: Quidā igitur fortunatus non est beatus. vel Quidam stultus est fortunatus:
units.tr: There are two kinds of simple syllogism, in the first of which the argument either only precedes or only follows. The first species of the first kind is when, from an antecedent argument in the proposition, and in the assumption affirmatively as one likes, a special conclusion is produced, as in the examples. Affirmative general: Constancy is a virtue; but it is confidence; therefore some confidence is a virtue. Negative general: Audacity is not a virtue; but it is confidence; therefore some confidence is not a virtue. Affirmative special: The wise man is praiseworthy; but some man is poor; therefore some poor man is praiseworthy. or Some wise man is rich; but the wise man is praiseworthy; therefore some praiseworthy man is rich. Negative special: The fool is not blessed; but some man is fortunate; therefore some fortunate man is not blessed. or Some fool is fortunate:

units.la: Verúm pro judicii claritate usus enthymemate hic ferè cõtentus est. Quçdam cõfidentia est virtus, ut cõstantia: quædam non est, ut audacia.
units.tr: But for clarity of exposition, he here mostly keeps to the enthymeme: Some confidence is a virtue, as constancy is; some is not, as audacity is not.

units.la: Syllogismus] Partitio syllogismi præcessit in partes, antecedente in ppositione & assumptio ne: consequente in complexione: divisio sequitur in species, simplicem, compositum: quç modó verbis iisdem appellantur, quibus appellatę sunt species enuntiati simplicis, compositi: ino​ pia verborum est, tamen definitionibus longé alia demonstratur. Partitio in Aristotelis Organo nulla ejusmodi est: quia é cõpositis syllogismis nullum est in eo verbum: Partitio est Theophrasti, Eudemi, Boetii. Disponitur] Dispositio, genus est primum & summum doctrinæ hujus criticæ: Itaq; á capite speciales omnium syllogismorum, tanquam nervi repetendi sunt, specialesq; omnes differentiæ dirivandę. Simplex igi-turtur syllogismus, est simplex, ubi argumentu disponitur in ppositione cu quæstionis cosequente, in assumptione cum antecedente: ut, si quæstio sit, an omne justum sit honestu, & ita concludatur: Omne laudabile est honestu, Omne justu est laudabile, Ergo omne justu est honestu. Hic (laudabile) argumentum simpliciter & sigillatim disponitur in propositione cum parte quæstionis consequente; item simpliciter & sigillatim in assumptione disponitur cum parte quæstionis antecedente: atq; ita fiet in omnib. syllogismis simplicibus, ut per species intelligetur. Quæ causa ante P. Ramo fuit, propositione & assumptione paulo communius definiendi: & quidem admonuerunt de hac paulo majore diligentia definiendi syllogismi simplicis, hac in re decepti, Theophrast, Eudemus, Boetius, qui syllogismum simplicem e simplicibus, compositum e compositis enuntiatis incautius desiniunt. At simplex syllogismus potest constare ex omnibus enuntiatis compositis: ut, Si laudabile est, honestum est: si justu est, laudabile est: ergo si justum est, honestum est. Hic propositio, assumptio, complexio, compositæ sunt, dispositio tamen argumenti est simplex. quod Theophrastus item animadverterat, docuerat q; hos syllogismos simplicibus ἀναλογίαις, & διὰ τριῶν vocaverat, propter tres partes compositas. At negligentius id ab ipso philosopho est æstimatum ac judicatum: nec enim ἀναλογία, similitudo hic tantum est, sed res ac veritas ipsa. units.tr: Syllogism] The partition of the syllogism came before its division into parts: the antecedent in the proposition and assumption, the consequent in the conclusion. The division into species follows, simple and compound, which are named by the same words by which the species of the simple and compound enunciation are named. There is a shortage of words in this, yet definitions show it quite differently. The partition in Aristotle's Organon is not of this kind, since there is no word in it for compound syllogisms; the partition belongs to Theophrastus, Eudemus, and Boethius. Is arranged] Arrangement is the first and highest genus of this critical doctrine. Therefore all the special kinds of syllogisms are to be traced back to their head, as to sinews, and all their special differences derived from it. So the simple syllogism is simple where the argument is arranged in the proposition with the consequent part of the question, and in the assumption with the antecedent part; for example, if the question is whether everything just is honourable, and it is concluded thus: Everything praiseworthy is honourable; everything just is praiseworthy; therefore everything just is honourable. Here the argument (praiseworthy) is arranged simply and singly in the proposition with the consequent part of the question; likewise it is arranged simply and singly in the assumption with the antecedent part; and so it will be in all simple syllogisms, as will be understood through the species. The reason for this was that before Ramus, proposition and assumption were defined in a somewhat more common way. Theophrastus, Eudemus, and Boethius, deceived in this matter, warned of a slightly greater care in defining the simple syllogism, and they define the simple syllogism from simple enunciations and the compound from compound ones too carelessly. But a simple syllogism can consist of all compound enunciations, for example: If it is praiseworthy, it is honourable; if it is just, it is praiseworthy; therefore if it is just, it is honourable. Here the proposition, assumption, and conclusion are compound, yet the arrangement of the argument is simple. Theophrastus also noticed this, and taught that he called such syllogisms by analogies [ἀναλογίαις] and through three [διὰ τριῶν], on account of their three compound parts. But the philosopher himself esteemed and judged this too carelessly, for here analogy is not mere likeness but the thing and the truth itself. Wherefore, just as those Peripatetic teachers were deceived in defining and naming the compound enunciation, and in dividing and negating the connected one, so they are wrong in defining the simple and compound syllogism from simple and compound enunciations.

units.la: dividendo composito, in negando cónexo, Peripatetici doctores illi decepti sunt:ita sunt falsi in simplici & composito fillogifmo definiendo é simplicibus & compositis enuntiatis. Ex illa definitione simplicis syllogismi bene & accura té posita,sequitur explicatio partium, magnam doctrinæ copiam paucis verbis complexa. Syllogifmus autem licet non definiatur ex enútia to, ex enuntiati tamen differentiis differentias varias capit:ut é partibus antecedentis appelletur affirmatus,negatus é prima nempe affectione enuntiati:generalis auté,specialis,proprius, é differentiis enuntiati simplicis: affirmatus é propositione & assumptione affirmatis: negatus, cúm altera antecedentium partium sola affirmatur. unde intelliges ex omnib. negatis nihil simpliciter concludi. Atq; hæc binaria differentia erit in tribus differentiis reliquis, generali, speciali, proprio. Generalis etiam videtur definiendus ex omnibus generalibus: sed prima species repugnaret, quæ nunquam generaliter concludit. Syllogismus deinde definitur specialis, ex altera tantum generali: potest enim esse altera indefinita, vel propria: & ideo cómuni nomine specialis appellatur á P. Ramo: non autem indefinitus aut proprius,ut cómuni definitione partem utramq; complectatur: Hincetiam percipitur, nihil usquam ex indefinitis sim pliciter concludi. Proprius]Definitur fyllogifmus simplex proprius,qui constat utraq; antecedete propria: Atqui syllogismus hic in Organo doctrinam nulla habet:imo nominatim differitur 24.cap.1. Pr.nullum esse syllogismum sine universali aliquo affirmato. Itaq; quia conclusio haec praetermissa est ab Aristotele, iccirco ab interpretibus Aristotelis etiam damnatur: quia singularia (ajunt) non considerantur in disciplinis: cū theorema quodlibet καθ' αὐτὸ πανταχοῦ. Quae ratio valde ridicula est: Etenim tota Astrologia est de singularibus & propriis ejusmodi rebus, Luna, Sole, & ceteris singularibus stellis: & praecepta tamen catholica sunt & propria? Deinde utrum in Logica praeceptum de syllogismo simplici, proprio, proprium enuntiatum est, non generale? utrum Porphyrii & Aristotelis de specie & individuo doctrina, specialis est, non generalis & universa? Deniq; nisi syllogismus esset entis & non entis, Logicae artis pars non esset. jam vero usus artis spectandus hic fuit: & quidem usus trium Aristotelis in primis figurarum, qui singularibus reb. praecipue continetur, ut in ipsis postea plenius intelligetur, in foro, in curia, in rostris, in totis civitatibus, in agris, in vita hominum: deniq; ubi hypotheses & quaestiones singulares differendae & judicande sunt: Itaq; si laudes Catonem, si vituperes Caesarem, si accusas Clodium, si defendas Milonem, si suadeas Maniliam legem, si Agrariam dissuadeas, Logica nullum syllogistici judicii adjumentum praestabit? & dices agrum Aristotelae Logicae plantis & frugibus istis alendis idoneum non esse? Imo vero natura sua foecundissimus & feracissimus est earum frugum omnium, sed aridus est & ferendus: nec agri, sed agricolae culpa ista est. Quare P. Ramus tam fructuosas stirpes plantavit in syllogismorum agro, fructus eorum demonstravit: Teneantur igitur quinq; illæ communes omnium syllogismorum simpliciû definitiones, affirmati, negati, generalis, specialis, proprii:& quia sunt generales & communes generaliter & semel exponantur, ex lege λαθόντα περὶ τοῦ. At neque in unoquoq; genere, neq; in unaquaque generis cujusque specie, contra illam sapientiæ legem toties & tam sophisticè repetantur atque iterentur, ut in definiendis modis singulorum generum adhuc repetitæ sunt in tribus Organi figuris, atque iteratæ. Res hic exigua videtur: & revera talis est: attamen scio P. Ramo spinam pertinaciorem vix & pervicatiorem nullâ fuisse: tautologia illa ejusdem affectionis tam dênsa, táque in tribus continuis figuris ante oculos erat posita: Ut autem logicũ theorema generale à specialibus definitionibus ad generis originem revocaretur, perdifficilis extricatio, tanquam labyrynthi cujusdam fuit. Ergo postrema agriculturæ huius logicæ aratione, spina hæc evulsa est. Divisio syllogismi simplicis, διχοτομία retinet, quæ in Aristotele τρίχοτομία est, in tres figuras. At unum genus illud est, uno tantum modo disponi, nempe sola vel antecessione, vel consecutione. Quare διχοτομία est λογικωτάτη, sicuti deinde est generis unius in duas species, quæ sunt tertia & secunda figura Aristoteli. Genera enim appellantur ab Aristotele σχήματα, figuræ metaphora geometrica: Nam σχῆμα seu figura, proprie significat lineamentum, ut quadratum, circulum: & sic Aristoteles in Categoriis docet: in totis autem Analyticis, pro specie frequenter usurpat: ut in Philosophia, dicit σχήματα κατηγοριῶν, ut 6. & 7. ca. 5. lib. item 1. cap. 6. lib. item 10. cap. 9. lib. item 3. ca. 10. lib. quę philosophus idem vocat aliàs τὰ γένη κατηγοριῶν, ut 7. cap. 1. Topici, & 3. cap. 2. Elench. quomodo κατα-φατικὸν σχῆμα, 12. cap. 1. Prior. & διαιρετικὰ σχήματα προτάσεως. Et Plato τὰ τῶν πολιτικῶν σχήματα, καὶ ἀλ μυσικὰς σχήματα dicit, 2. & 3. lib. Legum, Deniq; σχῆμα philosophis illis est idem, quod γένος ἢ ἀλλο, genus aut species: Latinis autem sermo iste est insolentior: imò verò etiam Græcis interpretibus ipsis: qui fermè utrique ideo totam hanc judicii syllogistici Logicam ad figuras geometricas retulerunt. At Aristoteles ipse decimoquinto capite secundi Posteriorum, item 3. 6. 7. Topicis, tanquam obscuritatis latebras, metaphoras reprehendit. Quamobrem P. Ramus sciens & prudēs, tropos obscuriores evitavit: propriis & logicis generis & speciei verbis uti maluit, quàm geometricis & alienis. Sed de Logica Aristotelis geometrica P. Ramus persæpe disseruit: atque immodico Geometriæ studio Logicā Aristotelis obscuratam querebatur. Mathematicis nihil erat quondam clarius & illustrius, nec qui eas nesciebat, satis instructus liberali disciplina credebatur. At hodie cùm Grammatica, Rhetorica, Logica antè cognoscantur, quàm quid unitas, vel punctum sit audiatur, magna discipulis mathematicæ disciplinæ ignaris, é geometricis rebus obscuritas in Logica & vocabulis & exemplis, analogiis & reb. ipsis copluribus creatur, κυάλυσις, ὁρᾳ, ἀντιστροφὴ, μίσον, Διάστημα, σχῆς μα, antea fuerunt. nunc accedunt ἀρχαὶ, ἀπαγωγὴ, ἐπιστροφὴ principia, deductio, expositio, adsyllogismorum συναγωγὴ, reductionem. Habent enim geometrę principia definitionum, postulatorum, axiomatum, é quibus problemata suæ artis & theoremata demonstrant: deducunt frequenter ad impossibile, exponunt aliquando singularibus exemplis: figuram ἀμίσρυτον immesurabilem, in aliam, μετρητὸν & mensurabilem reducunt. similem quandam Geometriæ Logicā in syllogismis Logicus quispiam (unde Aristoteles assumpsit) commentus est: principia duo constituit summa, Dici de omni & de nullo de omni, quando nullum liceat subjectum assume re, de quo alterum non dicatur: de nullo similiter: Tum vero syllogismum alium perfectum statuit, alium imperfectum: perfectum, qui præter illa principia, nihil requirat, ut necessarius appareat: imperfectum vero, qui præterea requirat ut reducatur, nō solum ἀντιστροφὴ, sed ἀπαγωγὴ, ἐκθεσις. Enimvero commovebatur isto loco vehementer P. Ramus, & indignabatur, tam aniles nugas, tam sophisticas, tamq; geometricis reb. illis dissimiles atque contrarias, diutius summi philosophi inani potiùs umbra retineri, quàm certissimis ejus legibus expendi & examinari: imò verò ab Alexādro, Porphyrio, Ammonio, tanquā bellissimas maximèque geometricas, summis laudibus efferri ac prædicari. Etenim infinitæ in hac syllogistica Logica obscuritatis fontem lubet é P.Rami scholis & præleẜionib. pauló pleniùs aperire. Demonstratione artium & institutione legitima, nihil est excellentius, cûm definiendo,partiendo,exemplis illustrando, syllogismo etiam,si quid opus sit, concludé do totæ artium liberaliū facultates & opes ex» plicantur. At insana quædam demonstrationis ambitio,Mathematicos in Elementis, & Logicos in syllogismorum figuris, ita transversos egit,ut nulla unquam pernicies major præstātissimis artibus acciderit,perversa ilta demonstrā di cupiditate. De Mathematicis loquétur Scholæ P.Rami mathematicæ,de his logicæ abundé jam loquutæ sunt: summam itaq; colligamus. Hocigitur statuo : quæ totis tribus simplicium syllogismorū figuris in Organo demonstrátur, minimé omnium demonstrabilia fuisse: atq; ubi demonstratio nulla prorsus esse debuerat,septē & sexaginta, incredibili obscuritate cumulatas esse. Etenim totis feré posteriorib. Analy- ticis non aliud cantatur, quám definitionem á demonstratione differre: neq; esse syllogisticā, sed tantum τῷ νῷ,intelleẜu (quod enuntiati judicium est)percipi & judicari, & tanquá principium αὐτόπιτον sumi: totaque tertium,quartum, quintum,sextum,septimū capita secundi Posterior.consumpta in eo sunt,ut doceàt, definitionem demonstrabilem non esse neq; syllogismo, neq; divisione,neq; inductione, neq; sensu,neque digito:Hæc enim totis capitibus illis est Aristotelis doctrina & oratio. Assume: At in trib. figuris syllogismorū simpliciū,definitiones sunt: in prima figura, quatur modorum : in fecunda totidem: in tertia sex, quæ demonstrationibus istis solæ subjiciuntur. Conclude igitur, qui Logicus es: Quare ista definitionum syllogisticarum doctrina non est demonstrabilis, neque ideo ulla principia,ullas ἀντιστροφὰς, ἀπαγωγὰς, ἐκ-θέσεις, ἀναγωγὰς requirit : judicatur prima figura, perspicuitate & luce ipsius figuræ: judicatur secunda, perspicuitate & luce secundæ figuræ: judicat tertia,perspicuitate & luce tertiæ figuræ: neque alia lumen sui judicii ab alia mutuatur, quávis alia sit illustrior & clarior fortasse quám alia. Hæc adversus tam densas tenebras, P. Rami clarissima & evidentissima conclusio fuit: Tum vero κατὰ πίστιν, de singulis obscuritatibus disseruit, ut perversus esset & confusus ordo generum in syllogismis, quia fieret é tribus figuris prima, quæ postrema esse debuerat: & contrà esse tertio loco, quæ debuerat esse prima: nam cùm syllogismus, fit dispositio : necesse est quamque syllogismi speciem tantò priore esse ordine doctrinæ, quató simplicior fuerit. at in tertia, quæ est in Organo figura, dispositio tantum est antecessionis: ut in secunda, est dispositio tantum consecutionis. At in prima quæ facta est, dispositio simul est & antecessionis & consecutionis: & quæ singula sunt in tertia & secunda, eadem universa modo quodam componuntur in prima. Quare quæ facta est tertia, debuit esse prima: & quæ primo loco posita est, debuit esse postremo. Neque hic habenda ratio fuit in methodi & ordinis quæstione, quid affirmatè, negatè, generaliter, specialiter concluderetur: propteraq; quid esset pręstantissimum & nobilissimū. Hę rerū speciales differētiæ, perpetuo plures sunt in specie, quám in genere. & si potestas plures quæstiones concludendi faceret speciem syllogismi priorē, syllogismus cōnexus esset omínū primus, quia quæstionem quamlibet possit cōcludere. Quare ut simplex syllogismus & cōpositus distinguūtur, non simplicium & compositorum enuntiatorum differētiâ, sed simplici & composita dispositione: Ita rursus in ipsa dispositione est intuēdum, si sit aliud alio simplicius, ut est in ordinis antecedsione & consecutione: ut est, universa in unū componi, quæ separata sint in diversis. Quapropter syllogismorum species primò perversæ sunt, magnaq; jam demōstrationis histerologica perversitas hinc apparet, quód demonstratur tertia secundaq; figura per primā, cúm prima ipsa postrema esse debuerit. Tum vero quænam sunt reliqua demonstrationum reductionūq; in singulis figuris argumenta? Cōversio (inquies) deductio, expositio. At (inquam) cōversionis argumentatio, sophismatum omniū sophisma est absurdissimum, ut antea patuit. Deductio autem cogit tantū, non docet, neq; clarissimis definitionum principiis clarius afferre quidquá potest. Expositio autē, est argumentum subjecti exempli ad specialem quæstionem adhibitum, & tertia tantum figura cōclufum: & quidem in tertia tātúm figura demonstranda adhibitū: ut luce tertiæ figuræ clarius nihil afferetur. units.tr: Those learned Peripatetics were deceived in dividing the compound and in denying the connected, just as they are false in defining the simple and compound syllogism from simple and compound propositions. From that definition of the simple syllogism, rightly and accurately laid down, follows an explanation of its parts, which packs a great store of doctrine into few words. Although the syllogism is not defined from the proposition, it still takes various differences from the differences of the proposition. From the parts of the antecedent it is called affirmative or negative, that is, from the first affection of the proposition. It is called general, special, or proper from the differences of the simple proposition. It is affirmative when both the proposition and the assumption are affirmative. It is negative when only one of the antecedent parts is affirmed. From this you will understand that nothing is simply concluded from all negatives. This binary difference will then be found in the three remaining differences: general, special, and proper. The general syllogism also seems to be defined from all the general ones, but the first species would be inconsistent, since it never concludes generally. The syllogism is then defined as special from only one general premise, for the other may be indefinite or proper. For this reason it is called special under the common name given by P. Ramus. It is not called indefinite or proper, so that the common definition may embrace both parts. Hence it is also perceived that nothing is ever simply concluded from indefinites. Proper: the simple proper syllogism is defined as the one that consists of two proper antecedents. Yet this syllogism has no teaching in the Organon. Indeed, in Prior Analytics 1.24 it is expressly denied that there is any syllogism without some affirmed universal. Therefore, because Aristotle passed over this conclusion, the interpreters of Aristotle also condemn it, on the ground that singulars (they say) are not considered in the disciplines, since every theorem is universal in itself (kath' hauto pantachou). This reasoning is very absurd. For the whole of astrology deals with singular and proper things of this kind, the moon, the sun, and the other individual stars, and yet its precepts are universal and proper. Furthermore, is the precept about the simple, proper syllogism in logic not itself a proper statement rather than a general one? Is the doctrine of Porphyry and Aristotle on species and individual not a special doctrine rather than a general and universal one? Finally, if the syllogism were not concerned with what is and what is not, it would not be part of the art of logic. Yet here the use of the art must be considered, and indeed the use of the three figures of Aristotle above all, which are chiefly concerned with singular matters, as will be more fully understood later: in the forum, in the court, on the rostra, in whole cities, in the fields, in human life, and finally wherever singular hypotheses and questions must be debated and judged. So if you praise Cato, censure Caesar, accuse Clodius, defend Milo, support the Manilian law, or dissuade the Agrarian law, will logic provide no aid to syllogistic judgment? Will you say that the field of Aristotle's logic is not fit to nourish those plants and crops? Indeed, by its own nature it is most fruitful and fertile in all those crops, but it is dry and must be cultivated. The fault lies not with the field but with the farmer. Therefore P. Ramus planted such fruitful stock in the field of syllogisms and showed its fruits. Let those five common definitions of all simple syllogisms be held: affirmative, negative, general, special, and proper. Because they are general and common, let them be set out generally and once, by the law of lathonta peri tou [λαθόντα περὶ τοῦ]. But neither in each genus nor in each species of each genus should they be repeated and reiterated so often and so sophistically, as they are still repeated and reiterated in defining the modes of the individual genera in the three figures of the Organon. The matter seems small, and indeed it is so. Yet I know that P. Ramus had hardly any more stubborn and obstinate thorn than this, since that tautology of the same affection was so dense and placed before our eyes in three continuous figures. And to trace the general logical theorem back from the special definitions to the origin of the genus was a very difficult disentangling, like that of some labyrinth. Therefore, by the final ploughing of this logical husbandry, this thorn has been torn out. The division of the simple syllogism retains dichotomy [διχοτομία], which in Aristotle is trichotomy [τρίχοτομία], into three figures. But that one genus can be arranged in only one way, namely by either antecedence or consequence alone. Therefore dichotomy [διχοτομία] is most logical [λογικωτάτη], and so too is the division of one genus into two species, which are the third and second figures of Aristotle. For Aristotle calls the genera schemata [σχήματα], figures, a metaphor from geometry. For schema [σχῆμα], or figure, properly means an outline, such as a square or a circle. Aristotle teaches this in the Categories, and in the whole of the Analytics he often uses it for species. In the Philosophy he says schemata of the categories [σχήματα κατηγοριῶν], as in Topics 1.5–7, 1.6, 1.10 and 3.10. The same philosopher elsewhere calls them the genera of the categories [τὰ γένη κατηγοριῶν], as in Topics 7.1 and Sophistical Refutations 3.2, and calls it the affirmative figure [κατα-φατικὸν σχῆμα] as in Prior Analytics 1.12, and the divisive figures of the proposition [διαιρετικὰ σχήματα προτάσεως]. Plato calls the forms of the state [τὰ τῶν πολιτικῶν σχήματα] and musical forms [καὶ ἀλλὰ μουσικὰς σχήματα] in Laws 2 and 3. In short, for those philosophers schema [σχῆμα] means the same as genus or species [γένος ἢ εἶδος]. But this word is more unusual in Latin, and even for the Greek interpreters themselves, who nearly all for this reason referred this whole logic of syllogistic judgment to geometric figures. Yet Aristotle himself, in Posterior Analytics 2.15 and likewise in Topics 3, 6 and 7, rebukes metaphors as hiding places of obscurity. Wherefore P. Ramus, knowing and prudent, avoided the more obscure tropes. He preferred to use the proper and logical words genus and species rather than geometric and foreign ones. But P. Ramus often discussed the geometric logic of Aristotle, and he complained that Aristotle's logic had been obscured by an excessive devotion to geometry. Once nothing was clearer or more illustrious than mathematics, and one who did not know it was thought not sufficiently educated in the liberal disciplines. But today, when grammar, rhetoric and logic are learned before one hears what unity or a point is, a great obscurity arises in logic, in its terms and examples, its analogies and even its substance, from geometric matters, for students ignorant of mathematics. Formerly there were cyalysis, horos, antistrophe, meson, diastema, schema [κυάλυσις, ὅρος, ἀντιστροφὴ, μέσον, διάστημα, σχῆμα]. Now there are added archai, apagoge, epistrophe [ἀρχαὶ, ἀπαγωγὴ, ἐπιστροφὴ], the principles, deduction, exposition, and the synagoge [συναγωγὴ] or reduction of syllogisms. For geometers have principles of definitions, postulates and axioms, from which they demonstrate the problems and theorems of their art. They often deduce to the impossible, and sometimes they set out things by singular examples. They reduce the amiryton [ἀμίσρυτον], the incommensurable figure, to another that is metrēton [μετρητὸν], measurable. Some logician, from whom Aristotle borrowed, devised a similar geometry of logic in syllogisms. He laid down two supreme principles: dici de omni and de nullo, that is, what is said of all, and what is said of none, when no subject may be assumed of which the other is not said, and likewise of none. Then he set up one syllogism as perfect and another as imperfect. The perfect is the one that, beyond those principles, requires nothing so that its necessity appears. The imperfect is the one that additionally requires reduction, not only by antistrophe, but by apagoge and ekthesis. P. Ramus was greatly stirred at this point, and was indignant that such childish trifles, so sophistical and so unlike and contrary to geometric matters, should be kept for so long by that supreme philosopher as an empty shadow rather than being weighed and examined by his most certain laws. Indeed, Alexander, Porphyry and Ammonius extolled and proclaimed them with the highest praise as most beautiful and most geometric. For it pleases me to reveal somewhat more fully the source of the infinite obscurity in this syllogistic logic from the lectures and schools of P. Ramus. In demonstration of the arts and in lawful teaching nothing is more excellent: when by defining, dividing, illustrating with examples, and concluding by syllogism where needed, the whole faculties and resources of the liberal arts are unfolded. But a certain insane ambition for demonstration has so twisted the mathematicians in their Elements and the logicians in the figures of syllogisms that no ruin has ever been greater for the most excellent arts than that perverse passion for demonstration. The mathematical schools of P. Ramus speak about the mathematicians, and others have already spoken fully about logic. Let us therefore draw up the sum. I therefore lay this down: what is demonstrated in the Organon for all three figures of simple syllogisms was least of all things demonstrable, and where no demonstration at all ought to have been, it has been heaped up with incredible obscurity in seventy-six places. For almost the whole of the Posterior Analytics chants nothing but that definition differs from demonstration, that it is not syllogistic but is perceived and judged only by nous, by the intellect (which is the judgment of a proposition), and is taken as a self-evident principle [αὐτόπιστον]. And the third, fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh chapters of the second book of the Posterior Analytics are wholly devoted to teaching that definition is not demonstrable by syllogism, by division, by induction, by sense, or by the finger. For this is the doctrine and argument of Aristotle in all those chapters. Assumption: but in the three figures of simple syllogisms there are definitions. In the first figure there are four modes, in the second as many, in the third six, and these alone are subjected to those demonstrations.
