Conclude then, you who are a logician: therefore this doctrine of syllogistic definitions is not demonstrable, and so it needs no principles, no antistrophai, apagogai, ekthesis, anagogai [ἀντιστροφὰς, ἀπαγωγὰς, ἐκθέσεις, ἀναγωγὰς]. The first figure is judged by the clarity and light of the first figure itself; the second is judged by the clarity and light of the second figure; the third is judged by the clarity and light of the third figure. Nor does one borrow the light of its judgment from another, even if one is perhaps brighter and clearer than another. This was P. Ramus's clearest and most evident conclusion against such dense darkness. Then indeed, kata pistin [κατὰ πίστιν], he discussed each obscurity, so that the order of genera in syllogisms was perverse and confused. For the third figure, which ought to have been last, was made first, and the one that ought to have been third was placed first. For since a syllogism is an arrangement, each species of syllogism must be earlier in the order of teaching in proportion as it is simpler. But in the third figure of the Organon the arrangement is only of antecedence, and in the second it is only of consequence. In the first figure, as constituted, the arrangement is at once of antecedence and of consequence, and what are separate in the third and second are all combined together in a certain way in the first. Therefore the figure that was made third ought to have been first, and the one placed first ought to have been last. Nor here should account have been taken, in the question of method and order, of what is concluded affirmatively, negatively, generally, or specially, and so of what is most excellent and noble. These special differences are always more numerous in species than in genus. And if the power of concluding several questions made a species of syllogism prior, the connected syllogism would be first of all, since it can conclude any question whatever. Therefore, just as the simple and compound syllogism are distinguished not by the difference of simple and compound propositions but by a simple or compound arrangement, so again in the arrangement itself one must consider whether one is simpler than another, as in the order of antecedence and consequence, and as in bringing together into one what is separate in different things. For this reason the species of syllogisms were first disordered, and a great perversity of demonstration from a later to an earlier position appears here, because the third and second figures are demonstrated through the first, though the first itself ought to have been last. Then what are the remaining arguments of demonstrations and reductions in the individual figures? Conversion, you will say, deduction, exposition. But I say that the argument of conversion is the most absurd of all sophisms, as was shown earlier. Deduction only compels and does not teach, and it can bring nothing clearer than the clearest principles of definitions. Exposition is the argument of a subject by example applied to a special question, and it is concluded only in the third figure, and it is applied in demonstration only in the third figure, so that nothing clearer than the light of the third figure will be brought forward. Therefore that whole apparatus of demonstration and deduction is very rustic and wild for illustrating the judgments and conclusions of simple syllogisms.

units.la: A ftrationis & deductionis instrumenta valde agreftia fylueftriaq; sunt, ad syllogismorum simplicium judicia & conclusiones illustrandum. Atq; in hoc sophismate mathematica imitatio quedam fuit. Eudoxus enim, fiue quis alius est author quinti libri Elementorum, definitiones per cosimilem omnino logicam demonstravit: ut ibi P.Ramus amplius exponet. Reductio aute ista non solum facta est fecundae & tertiae figurae in primam, ut 5.& 6.cap.1.Pr.sed etiam primae in aliam,ut 41.cap.1.Pr.tanquam circulatoriae reductionis judicium institueretur. Sed tamen (quo praecipue P. Ramus angebatur) sophismata tam fatua summis laudibus a tota Peripateticorum familia in caelum tolluntur: φιλογωμίτης Ariftoteles interea praedicatur, reique dissimillimae inanifsima & salsissima affectatio hominibus istis praedicabilis videtur & glorianda. Habent Geometrae (inquiunt) ἀναγωγὴν σχημάτων, reductione figurarum: fateor, est enim in planis figuris parallelogrammum rectangulum menfurabile: in folidis, prifma. Itaq; fi triangulum, fi multangulum, fi circulus metiendus ponatur, ante reducedus est ad rectangulum tumq; reductae figurae mensura capietur. atq; in ista geometrica ἀναγωγή, ut spatium agri, infulae, templi, edificij cujusvis metiare, rem ipsam nihil commutas, sed forma formae aequalem fumis, quam faciliús dimetiare: & utilitas quotidiana in architectura, in re militari, in tota mundi fabrica naturaq; dimetienda, usus mirabiles habet. Verum fyllogifticae istius reductionis usus nullus unquam fuit, neq; erit unquam: neq; logicus hominum sensus tá turpiter unquā delirabit, ut judiciū per se clarū & manifestum, tenebricosis reductionū mæantris conetur é figura alia in aliam reducere: Homeri- ricum, Demostheneum, Virgilianū, Tullianum, Platonicum, Aristoteleum deniq; extra hæc cōmenta, tam inauditæ fatuitatis exemplum nunquam proferetur. Geometra in ipsa dimensione figurarum, atq; in ipso artis suæ usu medio figuram reducit. At quis Logicus cūm in poemate, oratione, in logica, in mathematica, in reliqua philosophia ratiocinaretur, unquā vel solus, vel cum alio quocum dissereret, illam reductione syllogismi, quo uteretur, ad concludedum & judicandum adhibuit? quis vero tam deplorati judicii est futurus, qui adhibere audeat? Quapropter intelligimus jam qualis ista φιλογωμέτρια sit, quámq; syllogisticam Logicam miseré labefacta rit. Neq; jam huc redeundū, ut dicat aliquis, subtilitatem hic artis & perfectionem quæsitū esse: Has enim perversorū ingeniorum fraudes ingenuis artibus nimium diu exitiabiles, P. Ramus in jus sacris legibus appellabat: Totam artiū persectionem in eo consistere, ut theorema nullum habeant, nisi κατὰ πάντις, καθ' αὐτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον. fi quid contrá sit. vanitatem, fraudem, perniciem artis esse. Atqui tota ista reductionum senticeta, legibus illis sunt contraria: é quibus quid nisi Carduus, & duris surgit paliurus acutis. Quare amputentur, & é logico agro tollātur, sicuti jam tum cūm recentiús nata essent, amputata sunt & sublata ab Antipatro & Chrysippo, deinceps á Galeno. Acsi (quod brevi futurum spero) táta logicis scholis felicitas acciderit, ut logicus logicæ artis usus ex idoneis authoribus repetatur, eorūq; amore & exemplo cōformetur & exerceatur, hác tā ἀλογον γυμνιτρίαν, vel potius tam ἀγυμνίστρειον Logicá reformabit, & solidá Logicá ab inani sophistica separabit. Hic igitur cū P. Ramus magnas Aristoteli gratias ageret, qd tam multos labores, vel sui, vel alieni cujus libet ingenii collegisset, multò tñ majores habe das esse prædicabat, quód leges illas nobis tá singulares proposuisset, per quas tā gravia tot difficultatū impedimenta á liberali disciplina tollerentur. Sed tamē inventori taliū in arte syllogistica sophismatum, id nequaquá satis fuit: ad modos legitimæ conclusionis quatuordecim, aggregavit ἀσυλλογίσμους, qui incóstanti nempe & sophistica conclusione fallerent, unū & quadraginta modos, qui ipsi vitiosi conclufionū modi, magis etiam vitiosis demonstrationibus obscurantur. Adhibētur enim huc principia duo, Omni inesse, Nulli inesse: diversa etiá ab illis, Dici de omni, Dici de nullo. per quę vitiosus modus demōstretur, si veré concludat, aliquādo omni, aliquando nullı: id est, concludat aliquando generaliter & veré, aliquando generaliter & falso. Nam si refellere vitiosum concludēdi modum velles, satis erat unum exemplum vitiosum pro ferre: utrúm autem aliquando verum cōcluderet, nihil ad refutationē pertineat: ut si dixero, syllogismum in prima figura propositione sola affirmata constanter concludi: justa unius exēplii inpli instantia me conviceris, si doceas, exemplo non sequi: ut, Omnis equus est animal: Nullus homo est equus: Ergo nullus homo est animal. Syllogismus (inquies) hic tuus est inconstas & captiosus. & verissimo contradictionis argumento me conviceris. Ad hoc igitur refellendum, facere conclusionem aliam, in qua omni inst attributum aliquod: item alia, in qua nulli infit, mera matæotechnia fuerit. Quamobrem videmus in syllogismorum simplicium figuris, omnia nugarum genera accumulari: In quibus tam constanter acriterque refellendis, sæpe demiratus sum P. Rami diligentiam atque constantiam, sepeq; monui, illud fructuosioribus studiis Mathematicæ, jurisprudentiæ, Theologiæ, commodius applicari posse: at subridés, bono me animo jubebat esse, neque ad illos hortos Hesperidum commodé perveniri, nisi superatisanté his rupibus & scopulis. & sibi agriculturæ hujus Aristoteleæ solem, sudorem, pulverem, nunquam adhuc gravem aut molestum fuisse. Sed hæc generalia communiaq; figurarum omnium diligenter attendenda sunt: quinq; nempe definitiones syllogismi simplicis affirmati, negati, generalis, specialis, proprii omnes omnium in tribus Aristotelis figuris syllogismorum definitiones complectatur. Prima] Definitur igitur prima species quadruplici differetia: prima est, quod argumentum ante cedit in utraq; parte antecedentis: secunda est, quod in propositione utlibet, id est generaliter, indefinite, pprie: tertia est, quod assumtio semper affirmetur: quarta quod complexio etiam e genegenerali antecedente, & in syllogismo generali, attamen fit speciális: quæ præcipua est utilitas hujus speciei: tametsi enim cæteris in figuris id etiam fieri possit: id tñ in hac una videtur magis effe familiare, magisq; ordinariū: quod postea etiam magis intelligetur: & quidem specialis complexio, quæ hic concluditur indefinita frequentius est, quàm propria. Prima verò species ista collocat à P. Ramo, quia lex methodi id requirit, ut ante jam disserui, & postea cognoscetur: Ergo prima primi generis species est, quæ ex argumento tantùm antecedente, in propositione quidē utlibet, in assumptione affirmatè, specialiter tātùm concludit. Hæc definitio superioribus quinque definitionibus syllogismi simplicis, affirmati, negati, generalis, specialis, proprii instructa, totos in hac specie modos sine ulla arte nova continet: exempla itaq; nuda à P. Ramo proponuntur. Atqui in syllogistico Aristotelis agro, P. Ramus modos huic figuræ subjectos, ut cunq; propositos, deprehendit: doctrinam modorum ipsam incredibilem in modum obscuratam deprehendit. Ecquid enim obscuritatis figura ista non habuit? Primò definitur definitione valdè spinosa, Quando verò eidem illud quidē omni, hoc verò nulli inest, aut ambo omni, aut nulli. hanc quidem figuram voco tertiam: medium verò in ipsa dico, de quo ambo affirmamus: extrema quidē, attributa: majus autem extremū, quod remotius à medio: minus verò, quod vicinius. Ponitur autem medium extra extrema. Ultimum verò positione, sic in Organo definitur hæc figura, sic medium, sic extrema. At (inquam) definitio figuræ hujus sic informata, nó convenit speciali bus modis in hac figura, cúm hic nihil speciale describatur. Hæc prima est spina, quód definitio hujus figuræ nó cóveniat omni definito, neque sit ideo καθ’ αὐτὸ τὸς: deinde quód cóveniat sophismati, quód ad hanc definitionem fieri possit ex ambabus negantibus: Ergo non convenit soli definito. hæc altera spina est gravior & acrior superiore, qd non fit καθόλε πρῶτον. Scio quibus hic distinctionibus eludi puer in schola soleat, tanquam author definitionis noluerit definire logicam syllogismi virtutem, sed communem syllogismi & paralogismi affectionē: sed captiones politicis logicæ civitatis legibus inimicas & contrarias, logicus civis audiedas nequaquam putabit. Leges κατὰ πάντος καθόλε πρῶτον, istam peccandi tam immoderatam licentiam nunquam ferent. Medium autem & extrema definire, cúm figurâ,id est eorum collocationem definieris: quid aliud est, quám miras tautologiæ nugas cótra legem καθόλε πρῶτον nugari? & quater idem dicere? semel in figura, ter sigillatim in terminis: quod ex lege illa semel dixisse sufficiat? Quare si quis roget, quare P. Ramus hasce definitiones & medii, & extremi majoris, & extremi minoris omiserit, respondebo Aristotelis lege καθόλε πρῶτον esse prohibitū, ne quater idem nugaretur: tum vero extrema definire, quod remotius, quod ppius: in re seria, est nimis aperte auditorem logicę artis ludificari. Nam cúm medium utriq; subjiciatur, hic nihil est propius, nihil remotius. quare delitias istas tã delicatas P. Ramus suis amatoribus concessit. Tum vero μίσον, quod hic appellatur, analogiá illam medii proportionalis (de qua dixi) valdé alienam coarguit: Medium proportionale, est consequens primi, antecedés tertii. at hoc argumentũ semper antecedit, & in his præclaris definitionib9 nominatim dicitur argumetum ἐξω μὴν τῶν ἄκρων. Quare obscuritas illius metaphoræ, de qua dixi, etiam hic ab authore suo damnatur. Modi primæ hujus speciei de finiuntur, iteratis per sophisticam tautologiam illis generalibus affectionibus, quæ sunt quinque definitionibus á P. Ramo comprehensæ: tum vero tantis definitionum sophismatis alia accedũt in quatuor primis modis, é triplici demonstrationis genere, per conversionem, deductionem, expositionem: & ita demonstrationes hic sunt duodecim: quintus per deductionē & expositionem: sextus per coverfionem demonstratur. ita tam sophisticæ demonstrationes sex modorũ hujus figuræ, factæ sunt quindecim: & isti sunt cardui & paliuri, de quibus antea generaliter est propofitū: & in quibus P. Ramus demonstrationem expositionis vehementer admirabatur: in qua demostraretur etiam generalis syllogismus per proprium: ut fi cōclufisses hoc modo: Omnis homo est rationalis: Omnis homo est animal: Ergo aliquod animal est rationale tum per expositionem demonstrares illũ já cōclufum syllogismum, Socrates est rationalis: Socrates est animal: Ergo quoddam animal est
units.tr: These instruments of conversion and deduction are very rustic and wild, fit only for illustrating the judgements and conclusions of simple syllogisms. In this sophism there was a certain mathematical imitation. Eudoxus, or whoever else was the author of the fifth book of the Elements, demonstrated definitions by a logic that is entirely similar, as Ramus will explain more fully there. This reduction was made not only of the second and third figures into the first (chapters 5 and 6, book 1 Pr.), but also of the first into another (chapter 41, book 1 Pr.), so that a judgement of circular reduction might be established. Yet (and this especially troubled Ramus) such foolish sophisms are raised to the heavens with the highest praise by the whole Peripatetic school, while Aristotle is meanwhile proclaimed a lover of geometry [φιλογεωμέτρης]. And this utterly dissimilar and most empty and salty affectation seems praiseworthy and boastful to those men. "The geometers," they say, "have a reduction of figures [ἀναγωγὴν σχημάτων]." I grant it: among plane figures there is the rectangular parallelogram which can be measured, and among solids the prism. So if a triangle, a polygon, or a circle is to be measured, it is first reduced to a rectangle, and the measure of the reduced figure is then taken. And in this geometrical reduction, when you measure the area of a field, an island, a temple, or any building, you change the thing itself in no way, but you make the form equal to a form, which you can measure more easily; and this procedure has wonderful uses in daily life, in architecture, in warfare, and in measuring the whole structure and nature of the world. But the use of this syllogistic reduction has never existed and never will exist, nor will the logical sense of men ever go so shamefully mad as to try to reduce a judgement that is clear and manifest in itself from one figure into another, by the dark windings of these reductions. Never will an example of such unheard-of folly be produced, whether from Homer, Demosthenes, Virgil, Cicero, Plato, or finally Aristotle, apart from these inventions. The geometer reduces a figure in the very measuring of figures and in the very use of his art. But what logician, when he reasoned in poetry, in oratory, in logic, in mathematics, or in the rest of philosophy, whether alone or with another with whom he was disputing, ever used that reduction of the syllogism which he employed for concluding and judging? And who would be of so deplorable a judgement as to dare to use it? Therefore we now understand what this philogeometry [φιλογεωμετρία] is, and how wretchedly it has weakened syllogistic logic. Nor need we return here to say that the subtlety and perfection of the art is being sought. For Ramus used to call these frauds of perverse minds, long deadly to the liberal arts, into court with the sacred laws: that the whole perfection of the arts consists in having no theorem unless it holds per se, universally, and in every case [κατὰ παντὸς, καθ' αὐτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον]; and whatever is contrary to this is vanity, fraud, and ruin to the art. Yet this whole thicket of reductions is contrary to those laws, and from them what arises but "thistles, and the paliurus rises with its sharp thorns"? Therefore let them be cut away and removed from the logical field, just as, when they were newly born, they were cut off and removed by Antipater and Chrysippus, and afterwards by Galen. And if (as I hope will happen soon) such good fortune befalls the schools of logic that the use of the logical art is drawn from suitable authors, and the logician is shaped and exercised by love of them and by their example, then he will reform logic from this illogical gymnastic [ἄλογον γυμνασίαν], or rather from this so unpractised a logic, and will separate solid logic from empty sophistry. So when Ramus gave great thanks to Aristotle, because he had gathered so many labours, whether his own or those of any other talent, he used to declare that we owe much greater thanks, because he had set before us those laws so singular, through which such heavy obstacles of so many difficulties were removed from liberal learning. But for the inventor of such sophisms in the syllogistic art, this was by no means enough: to the fourteen legitimate modes of conclusion he added the non-syllogisms [ἀσυλλογίσμους], which would deceive by an inconstant and sophistical conclusion, forty-one modes, which vicious modes of conclusion are further obscured by even more vicious demonstrations. For two principles are brought in here, Omni inesse and Nulli inesse, and others different from these, Dici de omni and Dici de nullo. By these a vicious mode is demonstrated, if it concludes truly, sometimes universally, sometimes of none: that is, it concludes sometimes universally and truly, sometimes universally and falsely. For if you wished to refute a vicious mode of concluding, it would be enough to produce one vicious example; but whether it sometimes concludes truly has nothing to do with the refutation. For example, if I say that a syllogism in the first figure with only an affirmative premise always concludes correctly, you will convict me by the single instance of a manifestly false example, if you show that it does not follow by example, as: "Every horse is an animal; no man is a horse; therefore no man is an animal." "This syllogism of yours," you will say, "is inconstant and captious, and you have convicted me by a most true argument of contradiction." Therefore, to refute this, to make another conclusion in which something is attributed to every case, and another in which it belongs to none, would be mere trickery. Hence we see that in the figures of simple syllogisms every kind of trifling is piled up. In refuting these so constantly and sharply, I have often admired the diligence and steadfastness of Ramus, and I have often advised him that this could be more profitably applied to the more fruitful studies of mathematics, jurisprudence, and theology. But smiling, he bade me be of good cheer, and said that the gardens of the Hesperides could not be reached conveniently unless one first got past these crags and rocks; and that for him the sun, sweat, and dust of this Aristotelian agriculture had never yet been grievous or troublesome. But these general and common matters must be carefully attended to in all the figures: the five definitions, namely of the simple syllogism affirmative, negative, general, special, and proper, embrace all the definitions of the syllogisms of all three figures of Aristotle. First. The first species is therefore defined by a fourfold difference: the first is that the argument precedes in either part of the antecedent; the second is that in the proposition either, that is, generally, indefinitely, or properly; the third is that the assumption is always affirmative; the fourth is that the complex, even from a general antecedent and in a general syllogism, nevertheless becomes special, which is the chief use of this species; for although this can also happen in the other figures, it seems to be more familiar and more ordinary in this one alone, as will be understood more clearly later; and indeed the special complex which is concluded here is more often indefinite than proper. But Ramus placed this first species here, because the law of method requires it, as I have already discussed before and as will be recognised afterwards. Therefore the first species of the first kind is that which, from an antecedent argument only, in the proposition either way and in the assumption affirmatively, concludes only specially. This definition, equipped with the five earlier definitions of the simple syllogism, affirmative, negative, general, special, and proper, contains all the modes of this species without any new art; so Ramus sets forth bare examples. Yet in the syllogistic field of Aristotle, Ramus found the modes assigned to this figure, however they were proposed, and he found the very doctrine of the modes obscured in an incredible way. For what obscurity did this figure not have? First it is defined by a very thorny definition: "When to the same thing the one belongs to all, the other to none, or both to all or to none." I call this figure the third, and I say that the middle term is that of which we affirm both: the extremes are the attributes, and the major extreme is that which is more remote from the middle, the minor that which is nearer. Moreover the middle is placed outside the extremes. And the last point, in the Organon, this figure is defined thus, the middle thus, the extremes thus. But (I say) a definition of this figure formed in this way does not agree with the special modes in this figure, since nothing special is described here. This is the first thorn: that the definition of this figure does not agree with every definiendum, and so is not per se [καθ' αὐτὸ]; then that it agrees with a sophism, since to this definition one could apply both negative premises: therefore it does not agree only with the thing defined. This second thorn is heavier and sharper than the first, because it is not universal [καθόλου] and first [πρῶτον]. I know by what distinctions a boy at school is usually put off, as if the author of the definition had not wished to define the logical power of the syllogism, but the common affection of syllogism and paralogism. But a logical citizen will by no means think that captions hostile and contrary to the political laws of the logical state should be heard. The laws per se, universally, and first [κατὰ παντὸς, καθ' αὐτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον] will never tolerate such an immoderate licence of error. Moreover, to define the middle and the extremes, when you have defined the figure, that is, their arrangement, what else is this than to talk wondrous tautological trifles against the law universally and first [καθόλου πρῶτον], and to say the same thing four times: once for the figure and three times separately for the terms, when it would be enough to have said it once, according to that law? Therefore if anyone asks why Ramus omitted these definitions of the middle, of the major extreme, and of the minor extreme, I shall answer that the law of Aristotle, universally and first, forbids trifling with the same thing four times. And to define the extremes, what is remote and what is nearer, in a serious matter, is to mock the hearer of the logical art too openly. For since the middle is placed under both, here nothing is nearer and nothing more remote; so Ramus gave these very delicate trifles to his own lovers. Moreover, the term called here meson [μέσον] exposes that analogy of the proportional mean (of which I have spoken) as quite foreign: the proportional mean is the consequent of the first and the antecedent of the third. But this argument always precedes, and in these splendid definitions it is named explicitly as the argument outside the extremes [ἐξω μὲν τῶν ἄκρων]. Therefore the obscurity of that metaphor, of which I have spoken, is here also condemned by its own author. The modes of this first species are defined by repeating, through sophistical tautology, those general affections which are comprised in the five definitions set forth by Ramus; and then to these sophisms of definitions there are added others in the four first modes, from the threefold kind of demonstration, by conversion, deduction, and exposition; and so there are twelve demonstrations here: the fifth is demonstrated by deduction and exposition, the sixth by conversion. Thus the sophistical demonstrations of the six modes of this figure have been made fifteen; and these are the thistles and paliurus of which it was proposed in general before; and in these Ramus greatly admired the demonstration by exposition, in which even a general syllogism is demonstrated through a proper one: as if you had concluded in this way, "Every man is rational; every man is an animal; therefore some animal is rational," and then by exposition you demonstrated that already concluded syllogism: "Socrates is rational; Socrates is an animal; therefore some animal is rational." For thus Aristotle demonstrates the universal mode of the third figure through a proper one. Yet (I say) it is not syllogistic to conclude a general question from a special argument. The question concerns every syllogism of that general kind, and certainly the teacher of logic has been found who would think ... [the passage continues beyond this unit]

units.la: rationale.sic enim Ariftoteles demonstrat univerfalem tertiæ figuræ modum per proprium. Atqui (inquam) fyllogifticum non est, speciali argumento generalem quæstionem concludere. Quæstio est de omni syllogismo illo generali:& scilicet inventus est logicę magister, q speciali syllogismo, imó specialis syllogismi exemplo, putaret eam posse demōstrari: quod eó etiá magis admirandum fit, quód demonstratur syllogismus in Organo institutus, per syllogismū qui in Organo nullus putaretur: Etenim de libra judicii syllogystici, id est constantissimi dubitas:syllogistici judicii inopia est: Demōstrare deinde vis ejus æquitatem, per libram argumentationis, quá tu omnino syllogysticá librá esse ignoras:an nō logici omnino judicii inopia est: Tum veró hisce omnibus obscuritatibus, multó major obscuritas accessit ę vitiosis modis & asyllogisticis decem, totidemq; demonstrationibus ipsorum modorum. Ita demonstrationes quinque & viginti sunt inventæ in hac figura, ubi nulla omnino esse debuerat. Quapropter tá spinosas & hamatas demonstrationes, tam legibus Aristotelis cōtrarias, P. Ramus amputavit, & é logico syllogismorū agro sustulit. Attamen de prima ista syllogismi simplicis specie, quęstio major superest. an omnino nō dico sophismata ipsius tam multa, sed hæc ipsa figura, é logico agro penitus fit ejicienda: etenim Valla, accerrimi vir ingenii, sustulit, quód ejus figurę nullus usus ufquá appareret: ac si quis isto modo concludere vellet, ridiculū futurū: quin si quis omnino usus esseт,ex aliis figuris haberi. Argumentum Vallæ permagnum videatur: est enim lex κατὰ πάντος, ἱστορία, ἐμπειρία, ἀξίωσις, ἐπαγωγὴ. Equi-dem P. Ramum hic valdé dubium anxiumque animadverti, planeque confitentem, nullum fibi etiam curiosius inquirenti, figurę hujus exeplum usquam plena disposition cŏclusum occurrisse, quo Vallæ tam validum argumentū in firmaret: attamē cùm Vallæ ingeniū suspiceret, nō penitus illud ei concedebat, si nulla generis hujus conclusio plena pfectaq; in scriptis libris occurreret, ideo nullum protinus ejus usum efse: neque sequi, ut rejiciendum sit conclusionis genus, si posset alio genere cocludi: Etenim syllogismus hic, omnium syllogismorum & simplicissimus & clarissimus est, quanvis comprehensus magis, quàm plena forma dispositus. Quoties enim specialis ejusmodi quæstio aliqua fuerit, Animal quoddā est rationale, ut homo. Homo quidam est philosophus: ut Socrates: quæstio est hic syllogistica enuntiati nempe dubii, & explicatio licet enthymematica & imperfecta, attamē etiā syllogistica: Quāvis enim verba auribus vel oculis enthymema & imperfectum syllogismum repræsentent, mens tamen absolutum protinus perfectumq; concipit: tum enim argumentū illud sub utramq; parte quæstionis subjectū simul intelligitur, quod homo sit & rationalis, & animal: quòdque Socrates sit & philosophus, & homo: indeque propter tam naturalé, tamque logico hominum sensui popularé enthymematis syllogismū, fieri P. Ramus arbitrabatur,ut nulla plenior ppositionis & assumptionis explicatio dispositioq; requireretur: & illa est Aristoteli nimirū ἐνδιαιτος, quā instar principii nó syllogismo, sed τῷ νῷ judicavit. Itaq; judice atq; authore Aristotele,P.Ramus concludebat,figurā hanc syllogismi (quam philosophus ipse postremā fecisset) esse non solum primā & simplicissimā, sed clarissimā omnium atq; facillimam: Atqui tamē in tali expositionis exēplo, si qua dubitatio esset partes antecedentis syllogistici,& propositio,& assumptio, distinctius esse sent ordinandæ & explicandæ, ut syllogismi cō stātia evidētior appareret: eumq; artis pprium fructū esse, si quid forte naturalis judicii cōclusio laboraret. Quamobrem P.Ramus argumento Vallæ, usum artis requirenti, ita respōdebat, ut confiteretur, nullum sibi partibus explicatæ ratiocinationis exemplū in memoria & in próptu esse:usum tamē occurrere in illis exemplorum expositionibus assiduū perpetuūq;, neq; verum esse,nedum cōsequens,si quid idem alia figura concluderetur,id illico esse repudiandū: Nā prima figura, expositio ejusmodi nequeat, nisi tortuose,cōcludi: ut si dicas, Omnis homo est rationalis: Aliquod animal est homo : Ergo aliquod animal est rationale.Item, Socrates est Philosophus:Quidā homo est Socrates: Quidā igitur homo est philosophus. nec enim tā logicū est, in his assumptionibus speciē de genere, quām in illis, genʼ de specie affirmare. Quāobrem cùm P.Ramus tanta solicitudine,tam laboriosæ furculationis & runcationis figurā horū syllogismorum tot sentibus ac rubis expurgasset, fructum e purgato loco aliquem capere voluit: locum ipsum penitus amittere noluit.
units.tr: So Aristotle demonstrates the universal mode of the third figure by a proper (instance) example. But (I say) it is not syllogistic to conclude a general question by a special argument. The question concerns that whole general syllogism. A master of logic was indeed found who thought it could be demonstrated by a special syllogism, even by the example of one particular syllogism, and this is all the more remarkable because a syllogism set out in the Organon is demonstrated by a syllogism that no one would think belonged in the Organon. For you doubt the scales of syllogistic judgment, which is the most certain of judgments; this is a lack of syllogistic judgment. Then you undertake to demonstrate its fairness by the scales of argument, which you do not even recognise as syllogistic scales at all. Is this not a complete lack of logical judgment? Moreover, to all these obscurities there was added a far greater obscurity: the faulty and non-syllogistic ten modes, and ten demonstrations of those very modes. Thus twenty-five demonstrations have been invented for this figure, where there ought to have been none at all. Therefore Ramus cut away these thorny and hooked demonstrations, so contrary to the laws of Aristotle, and removed them from the field of logical syllogisms. Nevertheless, concerning this first species of simple syllogism, a greater question remains: whether this figure itself, not to mention its many sophisms, should be wholly cast out of the logical field. For Valla, a man of most keen intellect, removed it, because no use of this figure appeared anywhere; and if anyone wished to conclude in this way, it would be ridiculous; indeed, if there were any use at all, it would be had from the other figures. Valla's argument seems very weighty, for it is the rule [κατὰ πάντος] (by all), history, experience, judgment, and induction. For my part, I noticed that Ramus here was quite doubtful and anxious, and he plainly confessed that, though he inquired most carefully, no complete and perfect conclusion of this figure had ever occurred to him in any example, by which Valla's so strong argument might be weakened. Yet, since he admired Valla's intellect, he did not wholly concede to him that, if no complete and perfect conclusion of this kind occurred in written books, there was therefore no use of it at all. Nor does it follow that a kind of conclusion should be rejected because it could be concluded by another kind. For this syllogism is the simplest and clearest of all syllogisms, although it is more often comprehended than set out in full form. For whenever there is some question of this special sort, "some animal is rational, as a man is; some man is a philosopher, as Socrates is," the question here is the syllogistic statement of what is doubtful, and the explanation, though enthymematic and imperfect, is nonetheless syllogistic. For although the words represent to the ear or eye an enthymeme and an imperfect syllogism, the mind immediately conceives it as complete and perfect: for then that argument is understood at once under either part of the question, that man is both rational and an animal, and that Socrates is both a philosopher and a man. From this natural enthymematic syllogism, so natural and so popular to the logical sense of men, Ramus thought that no fuller explanation or arrangement of the proposition and assumption was required; and this, by Aristotle's own judgment, is the [ἔνδοξος] (generally accepted), which he judged to serve as a principle, not as a syllogism, but [τῷ νῷ] (by the intellect). Therefore, on the judgment and authority of Aristotle, Ramus concluded that this figure of syllogism (which the philosopher himself had placed last) is not only the first and simplest, but the clearest and easiest of all. Yet in such an example of exposition, if there were any doubt about the parts of the antecedent syllogism, both the proposition and the assumption ought to be ordered and explained more distinctly, so that the consistency of the syllogism might appear more evident; and this is the proper fruit of the art, if the conclusion of natural judgment should happen to labour in any way. Wherefore Ramus, answering Valla's argument that demands the use of the art, replied as follows: he confessed that he had no example at hand in memory of a reasoning set out in its parts, yet that the use of this figure occurs constantly and perpetually in those expositions of examples; and it is not true, let alone that it follows, that if the same thing were concluded in another figure it should immediately be rejected. For in the first figure such an exposition cannot be concluded except in a roundabout way, as when you say: "Every man is rational; some animal is a man; therefore some animal is rational." Likewise: "Socrates is a philosopher; some man is Socrates; therefore some man is a philosopher." For it is not so logical to affirm a species of a genus in these assumptions as it is to affirm a genus of a species in those. Wherefore, since Ramus with such care had cleared away, from so many briars and brambles, this figure of syllogisms, which was laboriously hoed and weeded, he wished to gather some fruit from the cleared ground, and he was unwilling to abandon the ground itself altogether.

units.la: Cap. X. De secunda specie primi generis.
units.tr: Chapter 10. On the second species of the first kind.

units.la: SEcunda species est, ubi ex argumento consequente affirmate in sola propositione vel assumptione: in propositione definite complexio antecedenti similis efficitur.
units.tr: The second species is the one in which, when the consequent argument is affirmed only in the proposition or the assumption, the complexion of the proposition is made similar to the antecedent.

units.la: GEN. I.
units.tr: GEN. I.

units.la: Turbatus non bene utitur ratione: Sapiens bene utitur ratione: Sapiens igitur non est turbatus.
units.tr: The troubled man does not use reason well: the wise man uses reason well: therefore the wise man is not troubled.

units.la: Hoc judicium ita fit a Cicerone tertia Tusculana: Et quemadmodum (ait) oculus conturbatus non est probe affectus ad suum munus fungendum: & reliquae partes, totumq; corpus a statu cum est motum, deest officio suo ac muneri: sic conturbatus animus non est probe assectus ad exequendum munus suum: Munus autem animi, est ratione uti: & sapientis animus ita semper affectus est, ut ratione optime utatur: Nunquam igitur est perturbatus.
units.tr: Cicero proves this judgement in the third Tusculan Disputation in this way: "Just as (he says) an eye that is disturbed is not in good condition for performing its function, and the other parts, and the whole body, when they are moved from their state, fail in their duty and office, so a disturbed mind is not in good condition for carrying out its task. The task of the mind, however, is to use reason; and the mind of the wise man is always so disposed that it uses reason in the best way. Therefore it is never disturbed."

units.la: GEN. 2
units.tr: GEN. 2

units.la: Res mortalis est composita: Animus non est compositus: Animus igitur non est mortalis.
units.tr: What is mortal is composite: the soul is not composite: therefore the soul is not mortal.

units.la: Cicero prima Tusculana, hoc syllogismo judicat animum immortalem esse. In animi autem cognitione (inquit) dubitare non possumus (nisi forte in physicis plumbei sumus) quin nihil sit animis admixtum, nihil concretū, nihil copulatum, nihil coagmentatum, nihil duplex. Quod cū ita sit, certe nec secerni, nec dividi, nec discerpi, nec distrahi potest: nec interire igitur. Est enim interitus, quasi discessus & secretio ac dirempatus earum partium, quae ante interitum, junctione aliqua tenebantur.
units.tr: In the first Tusculan Disputation Cicero judges by this syllogism that the soul is immortal. "In knowing the soul," he says, "we cannot doubt (unless perhaps we are leaden in our physics) that nothing is mixed into the soul, nothing is compounded, nothing joined, nothing fitted together, nothing double. Since this is so, it certainly cannot be separated, divided, torn apart or pulled asunder; therefore it cannot perish either. For perishing is, as it were, a departure and separation and dissolution of those parts which were held together by some joining before their perishing."

units.la: SPE. I.
units.tr: SPE. I.

units.la: Lividus non est magnanimus:
units.tr: The envious man is not magnanimous:

units.la: Maximus est magnanimus:
units.tr: The greatest man is magnanimous:

units.la: Maximus igitur non est lividus.
units.tr: Therefore the greatest man is not envious.

units.la: Hoc judicio Ovidius tertio de Ponto elegia 3. concludit:
units.tr: By this judgement Ovid concludes in elegy 3 of the third book of the Pontic Epistles:

units.la: Livor, iners vitium, mores nō exit in altos: utque latens ima vipera serpit humo. Mes tua sublimis, supra genus eminet ipsū: Grandius ingenio nec tibi nomen inest. Ergo alii noceant miseris, optentque timeri: Tinctaque mordaci spicula felle gerant. At tua supplicib. domus est assueta juvādis: In quorum numero me precor esse velis:
units.tr: Envy, a sluggish vice, does not rise to lofty minds, but creeps low on the ground like a viper hiding in the depths. Your mind is lofty, rising above its very kind; no greater name than yours is found in genius. So let others harm the wretched and wish to be feared, and let them carry darts dipped in biting gall. But your house is accustomed to help suppliants; I pray that I may be among their number.

units.la: SPE. 2.
units.tr: SPE. 2.

units.la: Saltator est luxuriosus: Muræna non est luxuriosus: Muræna igitur non est saltator.
units.tr: The dancer is dissolute: the lamprey is not dissolute: therefore the lamprey is not a dancer.

units.la: Cic. pro Murœna: Nemo enim feré saltat sobrius(nisi forte insanit) neq; in solitudine,neq; in convivio moderato atq; honesto intēpestivi convivii, amoœ ni loci,multarum deliciarum comes extrema saltatio. Tu mihi arripis id, quod necesse est omnium vitiorū esse postremum: relinquis illa, quibus remotis, hoc vitium omnino esse nō potest. nullum turpe convivium,non amor nō comessatio, non libido,nō sumptus oftendi-tur:& cum ea nō reperiantur, quæ voluptatis nomen habent, quæq; vitiosa sunt,in quo ipsam luxuriā reperire non potest, in eo te umbrā luxuriæ repertum putas:Hoc judicii modo Ovidius tripliciter concludit, dum carminū suorum excusationem exponit:
units.tr: Cicero, in the speech for Murena: "For hardly anyone dances while sober (unless perhaps he is mad), neither in solitude nor at a moderate and respectable dinner; the dance comes last, as the companion of an untimely drinking party, of an amorous place, of many pleasures. You seize on what must be the last of all vices and leave aside those things which, when removed, this vice cannot exist at all. No shameful dinner, no love affair, no drinking bout, no lavish expense is shown, and since those things are not found which bear the name of pleasure and are vicious, you think that in the man in whom luxury itself cannot be found, a shadow of luxury has been found in you." Ovid concludes in this manner of judgement three times, while setting out the excuse for his poems:

units.la: Carmina proveniūt animo deducta sereno: Nubila sunt subitis tempora nostra malis Carmina secessum scribētus, & otia quærūt: Me Me mare, me venti, me fera jactat hyemsi Carminib. metó omnis abest : ego pditus ense Hasurum jugulo jam puto, jamq; meo. Hac quoq; quæ facio, judex mirabitur æquus: Scriptaq; cum venia, qualiacunq; leget.
units.tr: Poems come forth drawn from a serene mind: my times are clouded by sudden misfortunes. Poems seek retreat and leisure for writing: the sea, the winds, the savage winter toss me about; with poems all is absent from me; I, undone, think that the sword will soon be at my throat, and soon at my own. Even these things that I do a fair judge will wonder at, and he will read what I have written, whatever it is, with forgiveness.

units.la: PRO. I.
units.tr: PRO. I.

units.la: Agesilaus non est pictus ab Apelle: Alexander est pictus ab Apelle: Alexander igitur non est Agesilaus.
units.tr: Agesilaus was not painted by Apelles: Alexander was painted by Apelles: therefore Alexander is not Agesilaus.

units.la: PRO. 2.
units.tr: PRO. 2.

units.la: Cæsar oppressit patriam: Tullius non oppressit patriam: Tullius igitur non est Cæsar.
units.tr: Caesar oppressed the fatherland: Tullius did not oppress the fatherland: therefore Tullius is not Caesar.

units.la: Secunda species primi generis definitur totidem differentiis, quot prima. Primò argumentum hic tantùm sequitur: illic tantùm antecedebat. Secundò alterutra pars antecedentium est negata: Ex omnibus enim affirmatis in hac specie nihil concluditur: ut, Omnis homo est animal: Omnis equus est animal: Ergo omnis equus est homo: veris antecedétibus cóplexio falsa. Ergo hic altera pars ancedentium necessario est negata: Atq; ut primæ speciei peculiare fuit, tantùm specialiter concludere: ita nunc secundæ speciei proprium erit, tantùm negaté judicare. In prima autem specie, pars secunda necessariò affirmatur, & prima interdum etiâ potest affirmari. Tertiò prima pars definita est, generaliter nempe aut proprie. sic enim definitū enuntiatum P. Ramus ab indefinito distinxit. propositone siquidem indefinita, nihil concluditur: ut, Aliquod animal nó est rationale: omnis homo est rationalis: ergo aliquis homo non est rationalis. Illic prima pars libera fuit, ut esset generalis, vel indefinita, vel propria. Quartó cõplexio est similis antecedenti: nempe ut sit similis utriq; antecedentis parti: vel si diversæ sint, debiliori: Itaque cum propositio vel assumptio negetur negabitur: Si pars utraq; sit generalis, erit generalis: Si altera tátúm generalis, erit specialis indefinitè aut proprié: Si utraque propria sit, erit specialis indefinitè aut proprié: quomodo feré antea syllogismus est definitus. Aristote les hanc cõplexionis analogiā & similitudinem cum antecedente adnotavit 24. cap.1. Prior. Manifestum quod etiam in omni syllogismo, aut utrasq; aut alteram propositionem similem necesse est esse complexioni: Item 28. cap.1. Prior. Similis enim est quaelibet complexio principiis. quod deinde Theophrastus apertiùs exposuit: cum docuit, cõplexionem debiliori antecedentium parti similem esse, ut Græci interpretes 9. cap.1. Prior. adnotarunt. At id verum est tantum in secunda specie, & in secundo genere: Quare non est κατὰ πάντος: nec ideo quod speciale erat generaliter P. Ramo exponendum fuit: sed ut κατὰ πάντος, & καθόλου πρῶτον servaret, speciale specialiter fuit explicandum. Similitudo igitur & analogia consequentis cum antecedente sic intelligenda est, & in utraq; specie primi generis, quadruplex differentia sic erit. Atq; hæc de secúdę speciei definitione, quæ in Organo tam accurata est, quá fuit definitio primæ speciei: Sic enim est 5. cap. 1 Prior. Quando autem idem huic qui dem omni, illi verò nulli inest, Aut utriq; omni, aut nulli, figuram quidem talem voco secundâ. medium autem in ipsa dico, quod attribuitur utrisq;: extrema verò, quibus id attribuitur: majus aut extremû, quod propiús adjacet medio: minus autem, quod remotiús à medio: Ponitur autem medium extra extrema, primúm quidê positione. Hæc figuræ definitio non convenit omni definito, quia speciali bus modis nō convenit: deinde non convenit soli definito, quia cōvenit sophismati é duabus negātibus. Quare nihil est κατὰ παντὸς, nihil καθόλς πρῶτον: ideoq; tollitur à P. Ramo tantũ sophisma, logicæ politiæ legibus tam vehementer obnoxium. Nugæ illę é definitionibus medii extremorum, simillimæ atq; in prima specie huc redeunt: & eadem de caussa á P. Ramo rejiciūtur, ne sæpius adversus eadem sophismata lex καθόλς πρῶτον iteretur: Et hic videlicet excusabitur author definitiōis, ut antea, quód noluerit instituere definitionem logicam, sed communem logicę & sophisticę figuram: quōd voluerit sigillatim & medium, & extrema sic definire. At excusatio voluntatis legibus contrarię & licentię bonis artibus nimiúm periculosæ ferenda diutiùs non est: Leges logicæ civitatis, ut jam dixi, nō patientur, nō sinét, non ferent: neq; hic argumentum, μέσον appella ri poterit, sicuti neque potuit in prima specie: & nominatim etiá hic ut antea, ab authore doctrinæ analyticæ, dicitur ἐξω τῶν ἀναφωνῶν. Ergo in secúda specie eædem spinæ sunt, quæ fuerant antea in prima specie, & à P. Ramo iisdem illis legum politicarum instrumentis avulsæ, & ex agro ejectæ. Duo autem modi antea quilibet in prima specie differebant affirmatione & negatione, quód primus esset affirmatus, secundus negatus: at hic cum uterq; sit negatus, alia differentia quæ renda fuit, quód prior haberet propositionem negatam, posterior affirmatam. Poteßt ista figura indefinita quæstio concludi: ut,
units.tr: The second species of the first kind is defined by as many differences as the first. First, here the argument only follows, whereas there it only preceded. Second, one of the antecedents is negated; for from affirmative premises nothing is concluded in this species, as in: "Every man is an animal; every horse is an animal; therefore every horse is a man," where the antecedents are true but the complexion is false. Hence here one of the antecedents must necessarily be negated. And just as it was peculiar to the first species to conclude only particularly, so now it will be peculiar to the second species to judge only negatively. In the first species, however, the second part is necessarily affirmed, and the first can sometimes also be affirmed. Third, the first part is definite, that is, either general or proper; for Ramus distinguished the definite proposition from the indefinite, since nothing is concluded from an indefinite proposition, as in: "Some animal is not rational; every man is rational; therefore some man is not rational." There the first part was free, so that it could be general, indefinite or proper. Fourth, the complexion is similar to the antecedent, namely so that it is similar to each part of the antecedent; or, if they are different, to the weaker one. Therefore, since the proposition or assumption is negated, it will be negated: if both parts are general, it will be general; if only one is general, it will be particular, indefinite or proper; if both are proper, it will be particular, indefinite or proper, as the syllogism was defined in the same way before. Aristotle noted this analogy and likeness of the complexion with the antecedent in chapter 24 of book 1 of the Prior Analytics: "It is clear that in every syllogism either both propositions or one of them must be similar to the complexion." Likewise in chapter 28 of book 1 of the Prior Analytics: "For every complexion is similar to its principles." Theophrastus then set this out more clearly when he taught that the complexion is similar to the weaker part of the antecedents, as the Greek interpreters noted in chapter 9 of book 1 of the Prior Analytics. But this is true only in the second species and in the second kind. Therefore it is not [κατὰ παντός] (of every); nor for that reason was what was particular to be explained generally by Ramus; but, so that the [κατὰ παντός] and [καθόλου πρῶτον] (first universal) might be preserved, what was particular had to be explained particularly. The similarity and analogy of the consequent with the antecedent must therefore be understood in this way, and in both species of the first kind the fourfold difference will be as follows. So much for the definition of the second species, which in the Organon is as accurate as the definition of the first species was. For thus it is in chapter 5 of book 1 of the Prior Analytics: "When the same thing belongs to all of one and to none of the other, or to all of both or none of both, I call such a figure the second. I call the middle term that which is attributed to both; the extremes are those to which it is attributed; the major or extreme is that which lies nearer the middle, the minor that which lies further from the middle. The middle is placed outside the extremes, first of all by position." This definition of the figure does not fit every definition, because it does not fit the specific modes; further, it does not fit only the definition, because it fits the sophism from two negatives. Therefore there is nothing [κατὰ παντός], nothing [καθόλου πρῶτον]; and so Ramus removed only the sophism, which is most strongly subject to the laws of the logical commonwealth. The trifles about the definitions of the middle and the extremes, very like those in the first species, come back here; and for the same reason they are rejected by Ramus, lest the law of [καθόλου πρῶτον] be repeatedly violated against the same sophisms. And here too the author of the definition will be excused, as before, on the ground that he did not wish to set out a logical definition, but the common figure of logic and sophistry, because he wished to define the middle and the extremes separately in this way. But an excuse based on will, which is contrary to the laws and too dangerous a licence for the good arts, must not be tolerated any longer. The laws of the logical state, as I have already said, will not allow it, will not permit it, will not bear it. Nor can this argument be called the middle, as it could not be in the first species; and by name too, here as before, it is said by the author of the analytic doctrine to be [ἐξω τῶν ἀναφωνῶν] (outside the utterances). Therefore in the second species there are the same thorns that were before in the first species, and they are torn away by Ramus with those same instruments of the political laws and cast out of the field. Moreover, in the first species the two modes differed in affirmation and negation, since the first was affirmative and the second negative; but here, since both are negative, another difference had to be given, namely that the former has a negative proposition and the latter an affirmative one. This figure can conclude an indefinite question, as:

units.la: Nullus turbatus utitur ratione: Aliquis sapiens utitur ratione: Aliquis igitur sapiens non est turbatus.
units.tr: No troubled person uses reason: some wise person uses reason: therefore some wise person is not troubled.

units.la: Sed tamen cum quæritur indefinitum illud (utrum aliquis sapiens utatur ratione) ut in prima specie: multò magis propria est: & rara quæstio generis hujus infiniti: In artibus omnia generaliter & universaliter agitur: in negotiis & rebus quotidianis, hypothesis & rerum propriarum singulares quæstiones differuntur: Itaque & P. Ramus exemplis singularibus hic usus est: ars tamen assumptionis & complexionis utcunq; specialis, est una & communis. Demonstrationes modorum jam antea quales essent, explicatæ sunt sed huc unam primi in hac secunda specie modi singularem P. Ramus é Dialecticis scholis repetebat. Syllogismorum hujus figuræ definitiones (ajebat) si legitime constituantur, per se claræ sunt & illustres: At per eas definitis modis, si requiras quamobrem talibus conclusionibus insit syllogisticæ conclusionis necessitas, id est, quamobrē unicuiq; speciei suum genus adsit: adferam generis ipsius definitione, quia sit dispositio, qua quæstio cum argumeto disposita, necessario cōcluditur. Si longius pergas, dicam te Aristotelis Logicam nescire, & proposi{ 5}tionis immediatæ medium quærere. Deinde si petas à demōstrationibus & deductionibus ad impossibile rationē aliquam, mōnebo te, in cōversionibus & deductionibus ad impossibile, nullum medium, nullamq; caussam quæstionis{10} tuæ contineri: teq; in rem prorsus ridiculā conversione tua cōverti. Ecto nobis primi modi secundæ figuræ demōstratio per cōversionē: ut,
units.tr: But when this indefinite question is asked (whether some wise person uses reason), as in the first species, it is much more proper, and this kind of indefinite question is rare. In the arts, things are treated generally and universally; in business and everyday affairs, hypotheses and singular questions of particular matters are put off. So Ramus too has used singular examples here, yet the art of assumption and complexion, however special it is, is one and the same. The demonstrations of the modes, what they are like, have already been explained, but Ramus used to repeat here one singular point about the first mode of this second species, taken from the schools of the dialecticians. He would say that if the definitions of the syllogisms of this figure are properly laid down, they are clear and evident in themselves. But if, by means of those defined modes, you ask why such conclusions have the necessity of a syllogistic conclusion, that is, why each species has its genus, I will bring forward the definition of the genus itself, since it is an arrangement by which a question, set out with its argument, is necessarily concluded. If you go on further, I will say that you do not know Aristotle's logic and are seeking a middle term for an immediate proposition. Then, if you ask for some reason from the demonstrations and the deductions to the impossible, I will warn you that in conversions and in deductions to the impossible no middle term and no cause of your question is contained, and that by your conversion you are turned into something utterly ridiculous. Let us take the demonstration of the first mode of the second figure by conversion, as follows:

units.la: Nullus improbus est sapiens:
units.tr: No wicked person is wise:

units.la: Omnis philosophus est sapiens:{15} Nullus philosophus igitur est improbus.
units.tr: Every philosopher is wise: therefore no philosopher is wicked.

units.la: Reducatur nobis hic syllogismus per cōversionem ad primam figuram: Cōvertatur igitur propositio:
units.tr: Let this syllogism be reduced for us to the first figure by conversion. Let the proposition therefore be converted:

units.la: Nullus improbus est sapiens:{20} Ergo nullus sapiens est improbus.
units.tr: No wicked person is wise: therefore no wise person is wicked.

units.la: Hoc siquidē lumine, atq; hoc judicio illuminatur & judicatur nostra reductio. At ista conversio, est enthymema secundæ figuræ:& si absolvatur, eodem plane modo, sed sine argumen{25}to ita concludetur:
units.tr: For by this light and by this judgement our reduction is illuminated and judged. But this conversion is an enthymeme of the second figure, and if it is completed, it will be concluded in exactly the same way, but without an argument, thus:

units.la: Nullus improbus est sapiens:
units.tr: No wicked person is wise:

units.la: Omnis sapiens est sapiens:
units.tr: Every wise person is wise:

units.la: Nullus igitur sapiens est improbus.
units.tr: Therefore no wise person is wicked.

units.la: Atq; ita judicii modus idem, per eundem ju{30}dicii modū, imò syllogismus ex argumento suo costans, & partibus absolutus, per syllogismum nullo argumento compositum parte una truncum, ridiculé atque inepté judicatur. Hæc P. Ramus fine stomacho recitare nó poterat: tam indignabatur, quosdá professores artium, in agro logico nimiúm securos agricolas esse, nimiúm illi & falsitatis & impietatis fundaméto cósidere: quód quæcunq; in libris Aristotelis haberétur, ea oía legitima & catholica esse crederét. Inertia ista nimiúm supina delicataq; est, laborifq; nimiúm insolés ac fastidiosa: Instrumenta tibi comparavit Aristot. quibus agrum tibi legatú coleres: tu fructus expectas, & arandi difficultatem respuis? & his iratus maledicis, qui aratrú cylindrúmve inducent, qui occabunt, qui deni que lætas segetes sudore suo tibi comparabút? Verúm perge: demonstratio primi modi talis suit. Demonstrationes reliquorum modorum nihilo sunt præstantiores: tres primi modi per cō versionem & deductionem, quartus per impossibile demonstratur: atq; ad hos sophisticarum demonstrationú carduos & paliuros, accedunt vitiosi modi duodecim, & totidem demonstrationes: ut nemo jam mirari debeat, tam obscurá esse talem syllogismorum doctrinam, ad quam obscurandam tot noctes sint continuatæ.
units.tr: And so the mode of judgement is the same, and by the same mode of judgement, indeed a syllogism consisting of its own argument and complete in its parts, is judged ridiculous and absurd when it is maimed in one part by a syllogism composed without any argument. Ramus could not recite these things without bitterness: he was so indignant that certain professors of the arts were too careless as farmers in the logical field, and placed too much trust in them as the foundation of falsehood and impiety, because they believed that everything found in the books of Aristotle was entirely lawful and Catholic. This sluggishness is too lazy and dainty, too unaccustomed to labour and disdainful. Aristotle has provided you with the tools to cultivate the field committed to you; do you expect fruits and reject the difficulty of ploughing? And will you rage at and curse those who bring in the plough or the roller, who harrow, and who at last prepare for you fertile crops with their own sweat? But go on: the demonstration of the first mode was of this kind. The demonstrations of the remaining modes are no better: the three first modes are demonstrated by conversion and deduction, the fourth by the impossible; and to these thistles and brambles of sophistical demonstrations are added twelve faulty modes, and as many demonstrations. So no one should now wonder that such a doctrine of syllogisms is so obscure, when so many nights have been spent in making it obscure.

units.la: Tertia Tusculana] Tullius de lenieda ægritudine in ea Tusculana disputat, ex Stoicorú philosophia, quód philosophus sit ἀπαθὴς, sine animi affectione & pturbatione. Syllogismi igitur huius quæstio est, utrúm sapiés sit turbatus, animi nempe perturbationibus & affectibus, voluptate dolore, spe, metu. argumentum est ex effectis sapientis, quód ratione bene utatur: ordoq; partium servatur. Sed propositioni & assumptioni sua probatio est, quæ hic προσυλλογισμὸς dicitur, prosyllogismus propositionis habet similitudinem perturbatarum corporis partium, quę ossicio propterea suo desint: assumptio item prosyl logismum suum habet, ex animi proprio fine & munere. Prima Tusculana] Prima Tusculana, longa est disputatio de animorum immortalitate: Illud modo videre (ait orator) ut Deum noris: & si ejus ignores & locum, & faciem, sic animū tibi tuum notum esse oportere, etiási ejus ignores & locum, & formá. In animi autem, &c. Ordo autem artis totus hic pervertitur, & partes ipsæ suis prosyllogismis magis sunt implicatæ: Assumptio præcedit, Animus non est compositus: sed prosyllogismus additur ex adjunctis, quódideo dividi non possit. Nec interire] Complexio magis nudé ac simpliciter est exposita.
units.tr: Tusculan Disputations, Book 3: Cicero, in that Tusculan work, disputes on the alleviation of sickness, from the philosophy of the Stoics, that the philosopher is apathes [ἀπαθὴς], free from affection and disturbance of the mind. The question of this syllogism is therefore whether the wise man is troubled, namely by the disturbances and affections of the mind: pleasure, pain, hope, fear. The argument is drawn from the effects of the wise man, that he uses reason well and the order of the parts is preserved. But the proposition and the assumption have their own proof, which here is called prosyllogismos [προσυλλογισμὸς], a prosyllogism. The prosyllogism of the proposition has a likeness to the disordered parts of the body, which for that reason lack their proper office. The assumption likewise has its own prosyllogism, drawn from the proper end and function of the mind. Prima Tusculana (Tusculan Disputations, Book 1): The First Tusculan is a long discussion of the immortality of souls. The orator says only this: that you should see to it that you know yourself, just as, if you do not know God's place and face, you should know your own mind, even though you do not know its place or form. But the order of the art is wholly reversed here, and the parts themselves are more entangled with their prosyllogisms: the assumption comes first, The mind is not compound; but a prosyllogism is added from its attributes, that it therefore cannot be divided. Nec interire (nor perish): the complexion is set out more plainly and simply.

units.la: Est enim] Sententia propositionis cū suo pro syllogismo hic est involuta: Mortale est compositum: quia mori, est partibus antè cõpositis secerni ac separari. Atque hi duo modi generales, nó genere affirmationis & negationis, sed ordine tantúm differunt: quomodo etiam differunt speciales duo qui sequuntur. In quibus tamē as-sumptio & complexio propria est, non indefinita: & illud est, quod antea monui, usum specialis syllogismi frequentiús esse quæstionis propriæ, quám indefinitæ.
units.tr: For it is: the sense of the proposition is here involved with its prosyllogism: What is mortal is compound, because to die is for things previously compounded to be separated and parted. These two general modes differ not in the kind of affirmation and negation but only in order; just as the two specific modes that follow also differ. In these, however, the assumption and the complexion are proper, not indefinite; and this is what I said before, that the use of the specific syllogism is more frequent for a proper question than for an indefinite one.

units.la: Livor] Ovidius scribit ad Fabium Maximum 3. de Ponto elegia tertia:
units.tr: Envy: Ovid writes to Fabius Maximus, in the third book of the Letters from Pontus, the third elegy:

units.la: Si vacat exiguum profugo dare tempus amico? O fidus Fabiæ, Maxime, gentis ades.
units.tr: If there is a little time free to give to an exiled friend? O Maximus, faithful one of the Fabian race, be present.

units.la: Et mox.
units.tr: And soon after:

units.la: Conveniens animo genus est tibi: nobile nam Pectus & Herculeæ simplicitatis habes.
units.tr: The race is fitting to your spirit: for you have a noble breast and the simplicity of Hercules.

units.la: Tandem sequitur hic syllogismus, cujus singulæ partes ordine positæ sunt, & suis profyllogismis ornatæ. Livor] Propositio exornata è diverso & simili: Lividus non est magnanimus, sed abjectus humo, ut vipera.
units.tr: Finally this syllogism follows, whose separate parts are placed in order and adorned with their prosyllogisms. Envy: the proposition is adorned by contrast and likeness: The envious man is not great-spirited, but cast down to the ground, like a viper.

units.la: Mens] Assumptio est, duplici collatione minorum illustrata: Tu es magno animo, majoreq; quam tuum est & genus & nomen. Ergo] Complexionis sententia dissimilitudine comprehenditur, per speciem concessionis. Alii noceant & timeantur: tu fis liberalis & benignus. Finita] Allegoria militaris est, quod aliquando in bello milites inficiant sagittas veneno, ut plaga quæ libet sit exitialis. Saltator] Exemplum est secundi modi specialis è defensione Murænæ, qui cum designatus esset Consul, repulso Ser. Sulpitio, accusatus est ambitus à Servio ipso, & Catone. Cato autem inter cætera accusationis capita, quod fuerat, quod Murena saltator esset: Ergo id à Cicerone defenditur: Saltatorem (ait) appellat Lu. Murænam Cato. Maledictum est (si vere objicitur) vehementius accusatoris: sin falso, maledici convitiatoris. Quare cum ista fis authorate, Cato: non debes arripere maledictum ex trivio aut ex scurrarum aliquo cōvitio: neq; temere Consulem Pop. Rom. saltatorem vocare: sed aspicere, quibus præterea vitiis affectū esse necesse sit eum, cui vere istud objici posit: Nemo enim, &c. Nemo] Propositio prima est ejusq; prosyllogismus est e dissentaneis: Saltator est convivator sumptuosus, quia nemo saltat sobrius. Tu mihi] Assumptionis prosyllogismus explicat sophisma quoddam vitiose differetis: tanquam consequentem complexionem postulantis, non propposito neq; probato antecedente.
units.tr: Mind: the assumption is illustrated by a double comparison of lesser things: You are of a great mind, and of greater worth than your birth and name. Therefore: the sense of the complexion is comprehended by dissimilarity, through the figure of concession: Others may harm and be feared; you are generous and kind. Finished: this is a military allegory, because sometimes in war soldiers poison their arrows so that any wound may be deadly. Dancer: this is an example of the second specific mode, from the defence of Murena, who, when he had been designated consul, with Servius Sulpicius repulsed, was accused of electoral corruption by Servius himself and by Cato. Cato, however, among the other heads of accusation, alleged that Murena was a dancer. Therefore this is defended by Cicero: Cato, he says, calls Lucius Murena a dancer. It is a reproach, and if it is truly brought against him, it is the more serious accusation of the prosecutor; but if falsely, it is the reproach of an abusive railer. Wherefore, since you, Cato, have such authority, you ought not to snatch up an insult from the crossroads or from some railing of the buffoons, nor rashly call a consul of the Roman people a dancer; but you should consider what other vices must necessarily belong to the man to whom this could truly be objected: For no one, etc. No one: the first proposition, and its prosyllogism, is drawn from things inconsistent: A dancer is a lavish feaster, because no one dances while sober. You to me: the prosyllogism of the assumption explains a certain sophism, faultily differentiated, as if it demanded a consequent complexion without the antecedent being proposed or proved.

units.la: Nullum turpe] Assumptio est per partes explicata. Et cum] Complexionis sententia illustrata est minoribus, Non reperis causam saltationis, quomodo reperies saltationem ipsam velut umbram? Tripliciter] Ovid. i. Tristium excusat minorem versuum suorum elegantiam:
units.tr: No base thing: the assumption is explained part by part. And since: the sense of the complexion is illustrated by lesser things: If you do not find the cause of dancing, how will you find dancing itself, as though it were its shadow? Thrice: Ovid, Tristia, Book 1, excuses the lesser elegance of his verses:

units.la: Ut peragas mandata, liber, culpabere forsan: Ingenii minor laude ferere mei. judicis officium est, ut res, ita tempora rerum Quaerere: quaesito tempore, tutus eris.
units.tr: That you may carry out your commands, little book, you will perhaps be blamed: you will be borne with less praise for my talent. It is the duty of the judge to seek the time of things as well as the things themselves; with the time sought out, you will be safe.

units.la: Deinde sequitur triplex syllogismus, unius tamen complexionis: Carmina proveniunt, &c.
units.tr: Next follows a threefold syllogism, all with one complexio: "Poems come forth, etc."

units.la: Primus est syllogismus: Bonus poeta est laetus: Ovidius non est laetus: Ovidius igitur non est bonus poeta.
units.tr: The first syllogism: A good poet is cheerful; Ovid is not cheerful; therefore Ovid is not a good poet.

units.la: Secundus est: Bonus poeta est otiosus: Ovidius non est otiosus: Ovidius igitur non est bonus poeta.
units.tr: The second: A good poet is at leisure; Ovid is not at leisure; therefore Ovid is not a good poet.

units.la: Tertius syllogismus est: Bonus poeta est securus: Ovidius non est securus Ovidius igitur non est bonus poeta.
units.tr: The third syllogism: A good poet is free from care; Ovid is not free from care; therefore Ovid is not a good poet.

units.la: Hic Híc argumenta tria sunt ex adjunctis, lętitia, otio, securitate: complexio una est omnibus cōmunis: & profyllogismi assumptionum é differen taneis ponuntur pro ipsis assumptionibus.
units.tr: Here there are three arguments from adjuncts: cheerfulness, leisure, and freedom from care. The conclusion is common to all of them, and the prosyllogisms, which differ, are put in place of the minor premises themselves.

units.la: Hæc utraq; historia est in epistola Ciceronis ad Luceū, de duobus Regibus, Agesilao Laconum, Alexandro Macedonum: Neq; enim (ait orator) Alexander ille gratiæ caussa ab Apelle potisimúm pingi, & á Lysippo fingi volebat: sed quód illorum artem cúm ipsis, tum etiam sibi gloriæ fore putabat. Atq; illi artifices, corporis simulachra ignotis faciebát nota: quæ vel si nulla sint, nihilo sunt tamen obscuriores clari viri. Nec minús enim est Spartiates Agesilaus ille perhibēdus, qui neq; dictam, neq; fictá imaginem suá passus est esse, quám qui in eo genere laborarunt. Unus enim Xenophontis libellus in eo rege laudando, facilé omnes imagines hominum statuasq; superavit.
units.tr: Both of these stories are in Cicero's letter to Lucceius, about two kings, Agesilaus of the Spartans and Alexander of the Macedonians. For the orator says that Alexander did not want to be painted mainly by Apelles or sculpted by Lysippus merely for the sake of favour, but because he thought it would bring glory both to those artists' art and to himself. Those artists made likenesses of bodies familiar to people who did not know the men. And even if such likenesses did not exist, famous men would be no less obscure for that. Agesilaus the Spartan deserves to be named no less than the others who laboured in this field, for he would not allow either a spoken or a painted image of himself to exist. Indeed, a single little book by Xenophon in praise of that king easily surpassed all the images and statues of men.

units.la: Cæsar] Hęc altera historia est notissima, de Cę fare, qui patriæ libertatem armis oppressit: pro qua Cicero gravissimos labores, mortem denique tádem subiit. Ergo hæc exempla P. Ramus attulit propriorum in hac specie syllogismorū, quorum usus frequens esse posit, cúm de duobus quæritur, utrúm sit unus & idem. Atq; hæc de secunda specie primi generis: quę una re quidem copiosior est superiore, quód concludere posit etiá generaliter: sed una re est infirmior, quód affirmaté concludere non posit: & quód in prima specie, simplici illo expositionis sensu judicatur, in hac specie judicari non posit: vel potiús potius ut expositio, precipua laus est prime speciei: sic negata conclusio secundæ: in quam ne pe dissensio rerum negatioq; frequentius incurrit. Itaque sua cuique speciei & propria laus atque perfectio est.
units.tr: Caesar. This second story is very well known: it concerns Caesar, who crushed the liberty of his country by arms, and on account of whom Cicero endured very grave labours and at last death. So Ramus has brought forward these examples of syllogisms of this kind, which are of their own sort. Their use can be frequent when the question is whether two things are one and the same. So much for the second kind of the first genus. It is indeed richer in one respect than the previous kind, because it can conclude even in general terms; but it is weaker in one respect, because it cannot conclude affirmatively. And whereas in the first kind a judgment is reached by that simple sense of exposition, in this kind it cannot be judged in that way. Or rather, as exposition goes, the chief praise belongs to the first kind, while the negated conclusion belongs to the second, into which disagreement of things and negation most often fall. Thus each kind has its own praise and perfection.

units.la: Cap. XI. De secundo Genere syllo gismi simplicis.
units.tr: Chapter XI. On the second genus of the simple syllogism.

units.la: ADhuc fuit species utraq; primi generis, unde secundum genus coponitur. Syllogismus simplex secundi generis est, ubi ex argumento antecedênte in propositione definitè, consequente in assumptione affirmatè complexio antecedenti similis efficitur.
units.tr: Both kinds of the first genus have so far been treated, and from them the second genus is formed. The simple syllogism of the second genus is one in which, from an antecedent argument in a definite proposition and a consequent in an affirmative assumption, a complexio similar to the antecedent is produced.

units.la: Aff. gen. justum est utile: Honestum est justum: Honestum igitur est utile,
units.tr: Affirmative, general: What is just is useful; what is honourable is just; therefore what is honourable is useful.

units.la: Quod Cic. 2. Off. ita concludit: Summa quidem authoritate philosophi, severè sanè atq; honestè, hæc tria genera confusa, cogitatione distinguūt. Quicquid enim justum sit, id etiam utile esse censent: itemq; quod honestum, idem justū. Ex quo efficitur, ut quidquid honestum sit, idem sit utile.
units.tr: Cicero concludes this in the second book of On Duties: "Indeed, philosophers, with the highest authority, and quite severely and honourably, distinguish in thought these three kinds, which were confused. For they hold that whatever is just is also useful, and likewise that whatever is honourable is also just. From this it follows that whatever is honourable is also useful."

units.la: Neg. gen. Timidus non est liber:
units.tr: Negative, general: The timid man is not free.

units.la: B Avarus est timidus: Avarus itaq; non est liber.
units.tr: B. The miser is timid; therefore the miser is not free.

units.la: Hoc ita concluditur & judicatur ab Horatio 1. Epist. Quo melior servo, quo liberior sit avarus, In triviis fixum cum se demittit ob assem, Nō video: nā qui cupiet, metuet quoq; porro Qui metuēs vivit, liber mihi nō erit unquā.
units.tr: Horace concludes and judges this in the first book of his Epistles: "What is a slave better off for, how much freer is the miser, when he stoops at the crossroads for a penny? I do not see it. For he who desires will also fear from then on, and he who lives in fear will never be free, in my view."

units.la: Sic Terent. in Eunucho concludit & iudicat: Consilii expers consilio regi non potest: Amor est consilii expers: Consilio itaq; regi non potest.
units.tr: So Terence in the Eunuch concludes and judges: Without counsel, one cannot be governed by counsel; love is without counsel; therefore one cannot be governed by counsel.

units.la: Syllogismus his verbis sequitur: Here, quia res in se neq; consilii, neq; modum Habet ullum, eam consilio regere non potes: In amore omnia hac insunt vitia injuria, Suspiciones, inimicitia, inducia, Bellū, pax rursum. incerta hac si tu postules Ratione certa facere, nihilo plus agas, Quām si des operā, ut cum ratione insanias.
units.tr: The syllogism follows in these words: "Here, since the thing in itself has no counsel and no measure, you cannot govern it by counsel. In love all these vices are present: injury, suspicions, enmity, truce, war, and peace again. If you demand to make these uncertain things certain by reason, you will achieve no more than if you took pains to be mad with reason."

units.la: Aff. spe. Cōsules virtute facti, studiose Rep. tueri deCicero est virtute factus Consul: (bent: Cicero igitur Remp. studiose tueri debet.
units.tr: Affirmative, specific: Consuls made by virtue ought to guard the Republic zealously. Cicero was made consul by virtue; therefore Cicero ought to guard the Republic zealously.

units.la: Sic orator diligētiam suam Agraria secunda cōcludit & judicat: Nam cúm omnium Cōsulum,ait,gravis in Republica custodienda, cura ac diligētia debet esse: tum eorum maximé,qui nō in incunabulis, sed in campo sunt Consules facti:Nulli populo Romano pro me majores nostri spoponderunt:mihi creditum est:á me petere,quod debeo,me ipsum appellare debetis. Quemadmodum cúm petebā,nulli me authores generis mei vobis commendarunt: sic si quid deliquero, nullæ sunt imagines, q me á vobis deprecentur. Quare modó ut vita suppetat ( quāquā ego sum is, q eā possim ab istorū scelere infidiisq; defendere/polliceor hoc vobis,Quirites, bona fide,Rēp.vigilāti homini,nō timido: intelligenti, non ignavo cōmisistis
units.tr: So the orator concludes and judges in his second speech on the agrarian law: "For while the care and diligence in guarding the Republic ought to be great in all consuls, it ought to be greatest in those who were made consuls not in their cradles but on the Campus. Our ancestors pledged nothing to the Roman people on my behalf; the trust was given to me. What I owe, you must seek from me, and you must summon me yourselves. Just as, when I was seeking office, no sponsors of my family commended me to you, so if I do wrong, there are no images that will plead for me with you. Therefore, as long as life suffices for me (although I am the man who can defend it from the crimes and plots of those men), I promise you this, Quirites, in good faith: you have entrusted the Republic to a vigilant man, not a timid one, to an intelligent man, not an idle one."

units.la: Si quid optatum redierit,gratum est: Lesbia Catullo optata rediit; Grata igitur est.
units.tr: If something desired has returned, it is pleasing. Lesbia, desired, has returned to Catullus; therefore she is pleasing.

units.la: Catullus sic concludit:
units.tr: Catullus concludes thus:
