units.la: Si quicq; cupidoq; optantiq; obtigit unquā,et Insperanti,hoc est gratum animo proprie. Quare hoc est gratū, nobis quoq; charius auQuód te restituis Lesbia,mi cupido. (ro, Restituis cupido, atq; insperāti ipsa refers te: Nobis ô lucem candidiore nota? Quis me uno vivit felicior? aut magis hac Optandū vita, dicere quis poterit? (quid
units.tr: If anything that a man desires and wishes for has ever come to him unhoped for, that is properly pleasing to the mind. Therefore this is pleasing, and dearer to us than gold, that you restore yourself to me, Lesbia, my desire. You restore yourself, my desire, and you bring yourself back unhoped for. O light to me, marked with a brighter sign! Who lives happier than I with this one thing? Or who could say that anything is more to be wished for in life than this?

units.la: Neg. spec.
units.tr: Negative, specific.

units.la: Deceptor amantis puella non est laudandus, Demophoon est deceptor amantis puella, ut Phyllidis: Demophoon igitur non est laudandus.
units.tr: A deceiver of a loving girl is not to be praised. Demophoön is a deceiver of a loving girl, as he was of Phyllis. Therefore Demophoön is not to be praised.

units.la: Phyllis apud Ovidiū ita judicat Demophoontem laudandum non esse:
units.tr: Phyllis in Ovid judges that Demophoön is not to be praised:

units.la: Fallere credentem, non est operosa puellam Gloria: simplicitas digna favore fuit. Sum decepta tuis et amās, et fœmina verbis:Dii faciant laudis summa sit ista tua.
units.tr: To deceive a trusting girl is no glorious achievement; simplicity was worthy of favour. I have been deceived by your words, lover and woman that I am. May the gods grant that this be the highest of your praises.

units.la: Aff. pro.
units.tr: Affirmative, for.

units.la: Octavius est heres Caesaris: Ego sum Octavius: Sum igitur heres Caesaris.
units.tr: Octavius is the heir of Caesar. I am Octavius. Therefore I am the heir of Caesar.

units.la: Neg. pro.
units.tr: Negative, for.

units.la: Antonius non est filius Caesaris: Tu es Antonius: Non es igitur filius Caesaris.
units.tr: Antonius is not the son of Caesar. You are Antonius. Therefore you are not the son of Caesar.

units.la: Adhuc] Compositio secundi generis ex utraque specie primi generis modo per partes plenius intelligetur. Syllogismus] Haec definitio manifeste demonstrat figuram, quam Aristotelesprima fecit, esse tertiam, magisq; esse specialem, quam duae superiores fuerunt. Nam in definienda specie, adhibentur generalia & antecedentia, tia,nó contrá: At in hac definienda figura, adhibentur quę in utraq; specie primi generis fuerunt:neq; quicquam hic adhibetur,nó colleētū ex illis : ut plané constet, hác figurá ex illis esse cópositam.Nam primó quód argumentū antecedat in prima parte,est é prima specie:quód sequatur in secúda parte , est é secúda specie : qᵭ ppositio sit definita,est é secúda specie:quód af sumptio sit affirmata , est é prima specie : quód cóplexio sit antecedéti similis, est é secúda: qᵭ bini modi distinguantur affirmatione & negatione, est é prima specie : quód speciales modi sint assumptionis cóplexionisq; frequétiús propriæ,quám indefinitæ, est é secúda specie. Itaq; si syllogismi prima differentia nominata non est set vocabulis simplicis & cópositi, syllogismus tribus Aristotelis figuris conclusus, commodé ita diuideretur in simplicem & compositum:& simplices essent adhuc expositi in utraq; specie primi generis:compositus ex utraq; illa,in modis sequentibus.Sed quanvis verba nó succurrant satis idonea,res tamen ipsa nihilominùs á P.Ramo perspicuè proposita est. Quamobrem justa methodi lege , postposita est figura, & de tribus facta est tertia, quá Aristoteles primá fecerat. Enimveró P. Rami agriculturá in hac agri parte,cum Organi deserta illa atque inculta Arabia comparemus:definitionem figuræ cẹte raq; illa anté jam in superioribus figuris considerata subducam⁹.Quomodo igitur figura ista definitur:Quádo igitur termini tres sic habuerint inter se, ut extremus in toto sit medio, medius in primo fit, aut non fit: necesse est extremorum esse syllogismum perfectum: voco autem medium quidem, quod & ipsum in alio, & aliud in ipso est quod & positione fit medium: extrema autem, cum idem in alio fit, & in quo alius est, Haec definitio est Organi, duarum in duabus ante figuris definitionum una re dissimilis. in ea quidem καθ' αὑτὸ nihil est: nec enim definitio ista speciali bus & propriis modis convenit: At sophisma alterum hic non est admissum, quod antea, ut definitio soli definito non conveniret: Hoc uno elencho minus est vitiosa definitio: at media & extrema consimiliter definiuntur, & tautologiam consimilem ostendunt.
units.tr: "Up to now": the composition of the second kind, out of each species of the first kind, will be understood more fully part by part. "Syllogism": this definition clearly shows that the figure which Aristotle made first is the third, and is more specific than the two before it. For in defining a species, general and prior terms are used, not the reverse; but in defining this figure, the things that belonged to each species of the first kind are used, and nothing is used here that is not gathered from those. So it plainly appears that this figure is composed of them. For: that the argument precedes in the first part is of the first species; that it follows in the second part is of the second species; that the proposition is defined is of the second species; that the assumption is affirmed is of the first species; that the conclusion is similar to the antecedent is of the second; that both kinds are distinguished by affirmation and negation is of the first species; that the special modes are more often proper to the assumption and conclusion than indefinite ones are, is of the second species. Therefore, if the first difference of syllogism is not named by the terms simple and compound, a syllogism concluded by Aristotle's three figures would fittingly be divided into simple and compound, and the simple ones would still be set out in each species of the first kind, and the compound one from both of those, in the following modes. But although the words do not come readily enough, the thing itself has nonetheless been set out clearly by P. Ramus. Hence, by the just law of method, this figure has been placed after, and of three figures one has been made a third, which Aristotle had made first. Indeed, if we compare P. Ramus's cultivation of this part of the field with that desert and uncultivated Arabia of the Organon, we shall deduce the definition of the figure, and of the others considered earlier in the previous figures. How, then, is this figure defined? When three terms stand to one another so that the extreme is in the whole and the middle is, or is not, in the first, it is necessary that the syllogism of the extremes be perfect. I call the middle that which both is in another and has another in itself, and which is also made middle by its position; the extremes are those when the same is in another, and that in which another is. This definition is from the Organon, and in one respect it differs from the two definitions of the earlier figures. In the one there is nothing [καθ' αὑτὸ, "in itself"]; for this definition does not fit the special and proper modes. But the other sophism, which was present before, that the definition should not apply to the thing defined alone, is not admitted here. By this one elenchus the definition is less faulty, but the middle and extremes are defined in the same way, and they show a similar tautology.

units.la: Definitio enim figurę legitima, id communiter explicaret, quod per partes hic inutiliter iteratur. Attamen medium in hac figura, solummodo est justa antecessionis & consecutionis metaphora nominatum, ut antea dixi. tam secus fuit de lege καθ' αὑτὸ, de lege καθόλου πρῶτον qui primus argumentum hic medium nominavit. Obscuritas sophismatis tā multiplicis prima est in hac Organi figura, quod figura prima, quod me diu, & extrema tam sophistice definiantur: sed multis obscuritatibus praeterea cumulata. Modi quatuor demonstrātur praeclaris demonstrationib. principiorum, dici de omni, & dici de nullo: quarum unicum pro omnibus hoc loco P. Ramus è Scholis dialecticis examinabat et retexebat: Enimvero (ajebat) organica demonstrationem primi modi videamus: quaestionem esse de modi primi definitione meminerimus: an si primum mum fit in medio toto, & medium in toto postremo, necesse propterea sit esse universalem syllogismum extremorum, & primum esse in toto postremo? Hæc enim verba sunt in Organo, & ea est ad demonstrádum proposita quæstio. Quęnam igitur ratio ad primum sophisticę Aristotelis figuræ modum demonstrandum affertur? Si enim, ait Aristoteles, α de omni β, & β de omni γ: necesse est α de omni γ dici: prius enim dictum, quomodo de omni dicimus. Hæc tota demonstratio est: Argumentum igitur & medium demostrationis hujus videamus, quâ complexionis caussam contineat, æstimemus. Principium est (inquies) dici de omni. At hoc principium, est sententia definitionis, quæ demonstranda proponitur, mutatis tátùm verbis cõprehensa, definitionem etiá tertii in eadem figura modi cõsuse cõplexa: Quod de toto dicitur, si quid vel generaliter, vel specialiter assumas, de eo quoq; dicitur. Hoc axioma cõpleētit primi & tertii modi definitioné: itaq; ad definitiones ipsas demóstrandũ, si afferatur, idem per idem demóstrabitur: aut si quid diversum putes, posterius & obscurius erit. Cõstet enim definitio primi modi, de quo nunc agitur, ex suo genere suaque differentia: dicaturque syllogismus simplex secundi generis affirmatus & generalis: clarius & evidētius nihil esse potest. Nulla igitur hujus definitionis esse demonstratio potest: & quicquid afferetur ad eam demonstrádum, posterius & obscurius erit. Definitio est principium, nec omni no demonstrari potest, ut quinq; capitû senten-tiâ tiá nos antea Aristoteles docuit: Ergo frustra & contra Aristotelis doctrinam ista demonstratio tentatur. Iam vero nonne in Organo docetur, duos modos primę figurę, omniū syllogisimorum clarissmos esse ad eosq; cęteros omnes re vocari? Imó vero docetur in Posterioribus, hūc modum generaliter affirmatum, demonstrationis excellentissimæ & omnium præstantissimę modum esse: Si vis igitur probare primi hujus modi definitionem per alium quempiam syllogismi modum, nónne vehementer erras? & solem tanquâ stella aliqua illuminare vis? Quamobrem intelligimus, quó sese ingeniorum præstátium luxuries effuderit. Apollonius summus Mathematicꝰ, quod erat in totis mathematicis clarissimum & evidentissimum (Quæ eidem ęqualia) demóstrare voluit: & nunc Aristoteles, in logicis videlicet Apolloniꝰ, demóstrare vult clarissimum & evidentissimum syllogismi judicii. Hic elenchus inertibus ingeniis accidere nó solet: impetus est luxuriantis ingenii, genio que suo indulgentis, neque satis accuratė ad logicas illas bene docendi leges attēdentis. Quāobrem obsecrabat hic etiam P. Ramus philosophos omnes, ut aliquádo sese excitarent ad studium percipiendæ cognoscendæque veritatis & intelligerent tandem aliquando, quę præstantissima Logicæ mysteria judicassent inani vanitatis inauditæ fuco sophismata inducta esse, eaque vulgó probari & laudari, quia excellétis philosophi nomen prætexeretur. At philosophus ipse tali argumento, taliq; syllogismo nunquá
units.tr: For a legitimate definition of the figure would explain in common what is here uselessly repeated part by part. Yet the middle in this figure is named only by a fitting metaphor of precedence and sequence, as I said before. It was otherwise with the law [καθ' αὑτὸ], and with the law [καθόλου πρῶτον], which first named the argument here as the middle. The obscurity of so many-sided a sophism is first in this figure of the Organon, because the first figure, the middle, and the extremes are defined so sophistically, and are further heaped with many obscurities. Four modes are demonstrated by the famous demonstrations of the principles "to be said of all" and "to be said of none". P. Ramus, from the dialectical schools, examined and unravelled a single one of these on behalf of all. Indeed, he said, let us look at the Organon's demonstration of the first mode. Let us remember that the question concerns the definition of the first mode: whether, if the first is in the whole middle and the middle in the whole last, it is therefore necessary that there be a universal syllogism of the extremes, and that the first is in the whole last. For these are the words of the Organon, and this is the question proposed for demonstration. What reason, then, is offered to demonstrate the first sophistical mode of Aristotle's figure? For, Aristotle says, if α is said of every β, and β of every γ, then α must be said of every γ, since the prior is said of all, as we say of all. This whole demonstration is as follows. Let us look at the argument and middle of this demonstration, and weigh the cause it contains of the connection. The principle, you will say, is "to be said of all". But this principle is the meaning of the definition which is proposed for demonstration, only expressed in different words, and it also confusedly combines the definition of the third mode of the same figure. "What is said of the whole is said also of whatever is taken, either generally or specially." This axiom comprehends the definition of the first and third modes; so if it is brought forward to demonstrate the definitions themselves, the same will be demonstrated through the same. Or if you think it something different, it will be later and more obscure. For the definition of the first mode, which is now under discussion, consists of its genus and its difference: it is said to be a simple syllogism of the second kind, affirmative and general. Nothing can be clearer or more evident. Therefore there can be no demonstration of this definition, and whatever is brought forward to demonstrate it will be later and more obscure. A definition is a principle, and cannot be demonstrated at all, as Aristotle taught us in the sentence of the five chapters. Therefore this demonstration is attempted in vain and against the teaching of Aristotle. Now indeed, is it not taught in the Organon that the two modes of the first figure are the clearest of all syllogisms, and that all the others are reduced to them? Indeed, it is taught in the Posterior Analytics that this general affirmative mode is the most excellent of demonstrations and the best of all modes. If you wish, then, to prove the definition of this first mode by some other mode of syllogism, are you not greatly mistaken, and do you not wish to light up the sun as if it were some star? Hence we understand into what excess the luxuriance of the more outstanding minds has poured. Apollonius, the chief mathematician, wished to demonstrate what was the clearest and most evident of all the mathematical things, namely that things equal to the same thing are equal to one another; and now Aristotle, in logic, that is, Apollonius in logic, wishes to demonstrate the clearest and most evident principle of the syllogism of judgement. This error does not usually befall sluggish minds; it is the impulse of an exuberant mind, indulging its own genius and not attending closely enough to the laws of teaching logic well. Wherefore P. Ramus also here begged all philosophers to rouse themselves at last to the study of perceiving and knowing the truth, and finally to understand that the sophisms which had been introduced as the most excellent mysteries of Logic were, by the vain paint of an unheard-of vanity, commended and generally approved only because the name of an outstanding philosopher was put forward as a pretext. But the philosopher himself never taught that philosophy must be handled by such an argument and such a syllogism; he set forth the laws of judging more accurately and of philosophising more steadily, and this was the foundation of P. Ramus for founding and building the art of logic. Such is again the demonstration of the second mode, from the principle "to be said of none", which I will not pursue piece by piece, since I am summarising...

units.la: philosophiam tractandam esse docuit: leges accuratius judicandi, constantiusque philosophandi propósuit. & hoc P. Rami fundamentum adhuc fuit logicæ artis fundandæ & ædificandæ. Talis est iterum demonstratio secundi modi, ex principio dici de nullo: de qua ne minutatim persequar, quod summatim completi possum, idem est dicendum, quæstionem non esse demonstrabilem: Deinde principium illud esse ex definitione secundi & quarti modi collatum: aut si diversum sit, posterius definitionib. illis & obscurius esse. Definitiones tertii & quarti modi simul coĕ funduntur, & ex iisdem principiis, consimili caligine demonstrantur: demonstrationes sunt quatuor in modis quatuor rectis: Atque ita pro definitionib. & claris exemplis, demonstrationes nil demonstrantes & exempla nullius rei exempla adhibita sunt, quæ totam hac doctrinam valde conturbant. An nodum obscuritatum finis est? Imo vero vix est initium. Quatuor modis recte concluditur in primo simplici genere: novemdecim modis vitiose concluditur in eodem genere, ut nominatim hic docetur: pluribus vero, ut interpretes enumerant. Demonstrationes igitur hic etiam novendecim prioribus additæ, tres & viginti demonstrationes in hac figura constituunt. At (ajebat hic P. Ramus) sophistica elenchorum non est homogenea Logicæ syllogismorum: & de tanto tamque in Organi libris frequenti sophismate, jam infinite coactus, repeto, cum doceo: in Organi libris, pro Logica sophistica esse traditam: repeto, inquam, quod antea proposui, fui, syllogismos omnes esse perfectos sua definitione, lumine externo non indigere. Ac si jam obstinatus aliquis & pervicax roget, Quae sunt syllogismorum principia? An (inquam) id nondum satis expolui? an nojam toties Aristotelicam philosophiā proposui? Definitus est syllogismus, divisus est in species, species definitae: quaeris an genus speciei conveniat? & primus modus, definitus sit syllogismus, id est constas & perpetua conclusio? hic si ratio aliqua sit quā obrē, sanē sola fuerat syllogismi definitio. Si requiras praeterea definitionis rationē, nihilo plus agas (ut inquit ille) quām si des operā, ut cum ratione insanias. Sic Aristoteles affirmat genus differentiam atque ex iis conflatā definitionē, demonstrari non posse, sed principia demonstrationis esse: Ergo syllogismorum definitiones, sunt syllogismorum principia.
units.tr: philosophy ought to be treated in that way. He set out more exact laws of judging and a more consistent way of philosophising, and this became the foundation on which P. Ramus founded and built the art of logic. Again, such is the demonstration of the second mode, from the principle that something is said of nothing. I will not pursue it in detail, but what I can state briefly applies equally: the question is not demonstrable. Next, that principle is derived from the definitions of the second and fourth modes, or if it differs from them, it is later and more obscure than those definitions. The definitions of the third and fourth modes are confused together and demonstrated from the same principles in equal darkness. There are four demonstrations for the four modes, and so, in place of definitions and clear examples, demonstrations that demonstrate nothing and examples that are examples of nothing are offered, which greatly disturb the whole doctrine. Is this the end of the knot of obscurities? Indeed it is hardly the beginning. Four modes are validly concluded in the first simple figure; nineteen modes are wrongly concluded in the same figure, as is taught here by name, but more according to what the commentators enumerate. Therefore the demonstrations added here to the nineteen earlier ones make twenty-three demonstrations in this figure. But (said P. Ramus here) the sophistical refutations are not of the same kind as the logic of syllogisms; and, having been compelled again and again about so great and so frequent a sophism in the books of the Organon, I repeat, when I teach that in the books of the Organon sophistical logic has been handed down in place of logic. I repeat, I say, what I proposed before: all syllogisms are perfect by their definition and need no external light. And if some stubborn and obstinate person asks, "What are the principles of syllogisms?", should I say (I ask) that I have not yet explained this sufficiently? Have I not already so often set out Aristotelian philosophy? The syllogism is defined, it is divided into species, the species are defined. Do you ask whether the genus belongs to the species? And the first mode: is the syllogism defined, that is, a constant and perpetual conclusion? If there is some reason for this, then surely the definition of the syllogism alone would have been enough. If you further demand a reason for the definition, you will achieve no more (as that man says) than if you took pains to go mad with reason. So Aristotle asserts that genus and difference, and the definition made from them, cannot be demonstrated but are the principles of demonstration. Therefore the definitions of syllogisms are the principles of syllogisms.

units.la: Summa quidē] De utilitate Tullius eo loco differt Stoicum paradoxum, utile nihil esse, nisi honestū. Sed in hoc verbo (ait eo loco Tullius) lapsa consuetudo deflexit de via, sensimque eo deducta est, ut honestate ab utilitate secernens, constitueret, honestum esse aliquid, quod utile non esset: & utile, quod nō honestum. Qua nulla pernicies major hominū vitae potuit afferri. Summa quidem, &c. Tum sequitur: Quod qui parum perspiciūt, ii saepe versutos homines & callidos admirantes malitiam, sapientiam judicant. Quorum error eripiendus est, opinioque omnis ad eam speciem traducenda, ut honestis consiliis, justisque factis, non fraude & malitia se intelligant ea quę velint, consequi posse.
units.tr: Summa quidem] Cicero, in that place, discusses utility, and the Stoic paradox that nothing is useful unless it is honourable. But he says there that custom has slipped into this word and turned from the right path, and by gradually leading it there has come to separate the honourable from the useful, so that it holds something to be honourable that is not useful, and something useful that is not honourable. No greater ruin could be brought upon the life of men. "Summa quidem," etc. Then it follows: "Those who see this too dimly, often admiring cunning and shrewd men for their wickedness, judge them to be wise. This error must be removed, and every opinion must be turned to this view: that by honest counsels and just deeds, not by fraud and malice, they may understand that they can attain what they wish."

units.la: Summa quidem] Propositionis est prosyllogismus, ex authoritate Stoicorū, qui reipsa cōjunctum honestū cum utili cēsebant esse, cogitatione autem separabant. Itemᵋ] Assumptio.
units.tr: Summa quidem] The proposition is a prosyllogism, on the authority of the Stoics, who held that the honourable is in fact joined with the useful but separated in thought. Item] The assumption.

units.la: Ex quo] Complexio.omnes autem syllogismi hujus partes, sunt relata, enuntiata: & tamen ex iis simpliciter concluditur: quia dispositio argumenti est simplex cū singulis partibus quæstionis. Sic autem concludit Ovidius 1.Fast.
units.tr: Ex quo] The complexion. All the parts of this syllogism are relatives and enunciations, and yet a conclusion is drawn from them simply, because the arrangement of the argument is simple, with each part of the question.

units.la: Dic age, frigoribus quare novus incipit annus: Quæstio est. tum syllogismus sequitur:
units.tr: Thus Ovid concludes in Fasti 1: Dic age, frigoribus quare novus incipit annus: Tell me, come, why does the new year begin with the cold? This is the question. Then the syllogism follows:

units.la: Bruma novi prima est, veterisq; novissima solis:
units.tr: Bruma novi prima est, veterisq; novissima solis: The winter solstice is the first of the new year and the last of the old sun's course:

units.la: Principium capiunt Phœbus & annus idem.
units.tr: Principium capiunt Phœbus & annus idem. Phoebus and the year take the same beginning.

units.la: Principium solis est anni principium:
units.tr: Principium solis est anni principium: The beginning of the sun is the beginning of the year:

units.la: Bruma est principium solis:
units.tr: Bruma est principium solis: The winter solstice is the beginning of the sun:

units.la: Bruma igitur est anni principium.
units.tr: Bruma igitur est anni principium. Therefore the winter solstice is the beginning of the year.

units.la: Talis syllogismus Catonis, quod mors senibus sit bona, quia secundum naturā. Omnia verō (ait) quæ secundum naturā fiunt, sunt habenda in bonis. Quid est autem tam secundum naturam, quam senibus emori? quod idem cōtingit adolescentibus, adversante & repugnate na tura: Itaq; adolescētes mori sic mihi videtur, ut cum aquę multitudine, vis flammę opprimitur: senes autem sic, ut sua sponte, nulla adhibita vi, consumptus ignis extinguitur.
units.tr: Such is the syllogism of Cato, that death is good for old men because it is according to nature. Yet (he says) all things that happen according to nature are to be counted among good things. What is so according to nature as for the old to die? The same happens to the young, though nature resists and opposes it. So the young die as a flame is extinguished by a multitude of water and its force is overpowered, but the old die as a fire goes out of its own accord, with no force applied.

units.la: Horatio] Horatius primo libro Epistolarū ad Quintium, paradoxum Stoicum concludit, Omnes avaros esse servos. Complexio præcedit cum propsyllogismo é paribus & effectis. Cupiet] Id est, avarus erit: & assumptio est syllogismi.
units.tr: Horatio] Horace, in the first book of his Epistles to Quinctius, concludes the Stoic paradox that all the avaricious are slaves. The complexion comes first, with a prosyllogism from like things and effects. Cupiet] That is, the avaricious man will be; and this is the assumption of the syllogism.

units.la: Qui metuens] Propositio est syllogismi. Notabis autem etiam hic partes relati compositas, attamen in syllogismo simplici. Here] Act.1.Scen.1. Parmeno leno Phædriæ adolescêti hero suo amati suadet, ut sese redimat captū quáti queat: neq; præterquám quas ipse amor molestias habet,addat & illas quas habet,rectè ferat. Here] Propositio relata sine syllogismo: illud videlicet ponitur.In amore] Assumptiōis tertia comprehenditur profyllogismo variorum adjunctorum.Incerta] Sententia complexionis profyllogismo pariū comprehensa. Speciales modi antea, uti diximus,habet speciale sæpius proprium,quàindefinitū: & hic rursus est idem. E propositis generalib.exeplis,indefinita facies hoc modo: Omne justum est utile. Aliquod honestum est justū: ergo aliquod honestū est utile. Itè: Nulla res cōsilii expers,cōsilio regi pōt: Aliquis amor est expers cōsilii: Aliq̄s igitur amor cōsilio regi nō potest. At quæstio hęc indefinitæ rei,melius expositione breviūsq; comprehenditur (ut antea jam dixi) & propriarū rerū quæstio frequetior.
units.tr: Qui metuens] This is the proposition of the syllogism. Here you will also notice the composite relative parts, yet in a simple syllogism. Here] Act 1, Scene 1: Parmeno the pander advises Phaedria, a young man in love with his master, to ransom the girl as well as he can, and to bear patiently, besides the troubles that love itself brings, those that it also brings. Here] A proposition of relatives without a syllogism: this is what is laid down. In amore] The third part of the assumption is contained in a prosyllogism of various adjuncts. Incerta] The sense of the complexion, contained in a prosyllogism of equal things. As we said, the special modes have, before, a special and more often proper form rather than an indefinite one, and here again it is the same. From the general examples proposed, make the indefinite form in this way: Every just thing is useful. Some honourable thing is just; therefore some honourable thing is useful. Likewise: No matter lacking counsel can be ruled by counsel; some love lacks counsel; therefore some love cannot be ruled by counsel. But this question of an indefinite thing is more fittingly and briefly comprehended by exposition (as I said before), and the question about proper things is more frequent.

units.la: Nam cum] Locus est in peroratione fecundæ Agrariæ: ubi conversus orator ad latores legis Agrariæ,qui turbare omnia conabatur, Hęc(inquit) vos concupisse pro vestra stultitia atq; intemperantia non miror: sperasse me Cōsule assequi posse,demiror. Nam cum,& cætera.
units.tr: Nam cum] The passage is in the peroration of the second Agrarian speech, where the orator, turning to the proposers of the agrarian law, who tried to throw everything into confusion, says: "I am not surprised that you have desired these things, given your folly and intemperance; I am surprised that you hoped to attain them while I am consul. For since..." and the rest.

units.la: Nam cum] Propositio prima est,cum profyllogismo majorum & diversorum: In incunabulis fuere Consules (ait) qui majorū gratia & favore honorem illum assequerentur. Campo]In cāpo po Martio antea comitia habebātur creādis magistratibus: & in Campo magistratus fieri dicit, qui pro sua virtute deliguntur.
units.tr: Nam cum] The first proposition, with a prosyllogism of greater and different things: "In early times (he says) there were consuls who obtained that honour through the favour and goodwill of the greater men. Campo] In the Campus Martius elections for creating magistrates were held formerly, and he says that magistrates are made in the Campus: those who are chosen for their virtue."

units.la: ] Sententia assumptionis cū profyllogis mo diversorum illorū. Eadē illa diversa tractantur per collatione similitudinis.
units.tr: The sentence of the assumption, with a prosyllogism of those different things. Those same different things are treated by a comparison of likeness.

units.la: ] Cōplexio, cum profyllogismo variorum diversorum. Si quid] Catulli exemplū est item propriæ cōplexionis: & cōcludit simpliciter, é propositione tamē connexa, ut modis omnibus intelligatur error Theophrasti, Eudemi, Boetii. Catullus autem poeta, amicā nomine Lesbiæ, multis poematis celebravit: significat autē hoc loco antecedentis cujusdam offensionis reconciliationem, & reditum in gratiam.
units.tr: The complexion, with a prosyllogism of various different things. Si quid] Catullus's example is likewise of a proper complexion, and it concludes simply, from a connected proposition, so that the error of Theophrastus, Eudemus and Boethius is understood in every way. Catullus the poet celebrated his mistress under the name Lesbia in many poems. Here he means the reconciliation after some earlier offence, and a return to favour.

units.la: Si quid] Propositio est sine profyllogismo, quia ἀμιϛον quippiam & αὐτόπιϛον complectitur.
units.tr: Si quid] A proposition without a prosyllogism, because it embraces something self-evident and self-manifest.

units.la: Quare] Cōplexio est cū profyllogismo minorum. Quód te] Assumptio est totidem verbis repetita. O lucem] Iteratur sententia complexionis ex adjuncto. Legitur in Aldino codice: O mihi chara magis candidiore nota.
units.tr: Quare] The complexion, with a prosyllogism of minors. Quod te] The assumption, repeated in the same words. O lucem] The sentence of the complexion is repeated with its adjunct. It is read in the Aldine codex: "O dearer to me than a whiter mark."

units.la: Quis] Iteratur eadem complexio é minoribus. Phyllis] Phyllis Lycurgi filia, regina Thraciæ, Demophoonte Thesei filiū é bello Trojano illuc eiectū, hospitio & cōjugali lecto exceperat: Itaq; cum Demophoo Athenas ad occupandū patris regnū profectus, nō rediret, Phyllis inter cætera apud Ovidium hoc conqueritur.
units.tr: The same complexion is repeated from the minors. Phyllis] Phyllis, daughter of Lycurgus, queen of Thrace, had received into her hospitality and marriage bed Demophoon, son of Theseus, who had been cast there from the Trojan war. So when Demophoon set out for Athens to seize his father's kingdom and did not return, Phyllis complains, among other things, in Ovid as follows.

units.la: Fallere] Propositio cum profyllogismo adjun stæ simplicitatis.
units.tr: Fallere] A proposition with a prosyllogism of an adjunct of simplicity.

units.la: Sum decepta] Assumptio, ubi nominatim repetuntur propositionis partes. Sed amàs, pro credens: & fœmina, pro puella dicitur.
units.tr: Sum decepta] The assumption, where the parts of the proposition are repeated by name. But "amas" is used for "believing", and "femina" for "girl".

units.la: Dii faciant Complexionis loco, imprecatio est: quę paulò post enumeratis majorū titulis, ita concluditur:
units.tr: Dii faciant] In place of the complexion there is an imprecation, which, after the illustrious titles of the ancestors have been enumerated, is concluded thus:

units.la: Hæc tua post illos titulo signetur imago:
units.tr: Let this, your image, be marked with a title after those:

units.la: Hic est, cujus amans hospita capta dolo est.
units.tr: This is the one whose lover, a hostess, was taken by trickery.

units.la: Octavius Exempla de historia ficta, sunt duo sequētia: de qua Suetonius in Octavio 8. & 10. capitibus: ut Octavius hæres à Cæsare sit relictus, & Antonius tamē Cōsul ab adeunda hæreditate deterrere conaretur. Adhuc de prima Aristotelis figura nobis actū est, quā Aristoteles II.cap.1.Post. præstare cæteris judicat, quia per eā investigetur & cōcludatur scientia ἀιόπι, quæ est λυσιωλοκα. At hāc utramq; caussam P. Ramus in Posteriorib. ipsis plenissimē confutavit, cùm docuit, quæstionem ipsam ἀιόπι, syllogisticā non esse, scientiasque omnes & disciplinas, solis definitionibus, partitionib9, exemplis, sine syllogismo ullo institui posse. Tertia Aristotelis est ratio de præstantia hujus figurae, quia cæteris non egeat, cùm tamē ad eam cæterē reducātur. quæ ratio quàm ridicula sit, patuit è sophismatis reductionum antea disputatis: hoc enim argumento, duæ superiores præstarent, quia sunt simpliciores, & ad eas potius redigenda figura hęc esset, si reductione ulla esset opus. Quare primi generis prima species suam laudē habet ex illa expositionis familiaritate: secūda é negationis conclusione. Secundum hoc genus ex illa utraq́ue compositum, etiam laudes compositas copletīplectitur: sed generalis affirmationis laudé propriam sibi vendicavit. Veruntamé totú hoc excellentię problema, otiosæ elegātiæ multó plus habet, quám solidæ doctrinæ. Philosophus 7.c. 1.Poster. deridet ridiculas in Geometria qstiones, utrúm recta sit pulcherrima linearū: Derideтo igitur, ac multó justiore caussa, quęstiones in Logica plané ludicras, utrū figura prima sit pulcherrima figurarum: Cognitio enim præstantiæ hujus, nihil ad cōclusionis judicium, nihil ad syllogismi usum attinet. Tale fuit in contradictionis Topico problema, quód contradicentia, maxima essent omnium oppositorum: & tales quæstiones de comparatione duorum vel trium argumentorum ludicrorum disceptari possunt, quæ sit pulcherrima causarum, quæ sit præstantissima comparationum, quæ frequentissima enuntiationum. At hæc omnia ad bené differendum nihil attinent: nihil habet in Logica λογικὰ: propterea tá bellus artis fucus á P.Ramo sublatus est: Sed tamen infinitum sit, si quis omnia, quę in trium figurarum argumento Logicorum scholæ commentæ sunt, expendere conetur. Dictum est de tribus figuris, earumq; propriis modis: capita supersunt duo & triginta, de syllogismo simplici, mirabilis sophisticæ plena: Primó septimum caput 1. Pr. duos communes omnium figurarum modis instituit: quos é Scholis dialecticis P.Ramus huc repetebat: sic autem in Organo proponuntur: Cùm autem affirmativus & privativus, & universaliter sumptus privativus, semper fit syllogismus minoris
units.tr: Octavius. The two examples from fictitious history are these: the first is in Suetonius, Octavius, chapters 8 and 10, where Octavius is left as heir by Caesar, while Antony, the consul, tries to deter him from accepting the inheritance. We have now dealt with the first figure of Aristotle, which in Posterior Analytics 2, chapter 1, he judges superior to the others, because through it scientific knowledge, which is demonstrative [ἀποδεικτική], is investigated and concluded. But P. Ramus, in the Posterior Analytics, has thoroughly refuted both of these grounds, when he taught that the question itself, whether knowledge is demonstrative, is not a matter for syllogism, and that all sciences and disciplines can be established by definitions, partitions and examples alone, without any syllogism. Aristotle's third reason for the excellence of this figure is that it needs no others, although the others are reduced to it. How ridiculous this reason is became clear from the sophisms about reductions discussed earlier: for by this argument the two former figures would be superior, because they are simpler, and this figure would have to be reduced to them, if any reduction were needed. Therefore the first species of the first kind has its praise from that familiarity of exposition, and the second from the conclusion of negation. The second kind, compounded of both, also takes up compound praises, but it claimed for itself the praise of general affirmation. Yet this whole problem of excellence has far more of idle elegance than of solid doctrine. The Philosopher, in Posterior Analytics 1, chapter 7, mocks the ridiculous questions in geometry, such as whether the straight line is the most beautiful of lines. So I too mock, with a much more just cause, the questions in logic that are plainly frivolous, such as whether the first figure is the most beautiful of figures: for knowledge of this excellence contributes nothing to the judgment of a conclusion, nothing to the use of a syllogism. Such was the problem in the Topic of contradiction, that contradictories are the greatest of all opposites; and such questions can be disputed about the comparison of two or three arguments, as to which is the most beautiful of causes, which the most excellent of comparisons, which the most frequent of propositions. But none of these matters for arguing well: there is nothing logical [λογικά] in them; therefore P. Ramus removed this pretty ornament of the art. Yet it would be endless if someone tried to weigh everything that the schools of the logicians have devised in the argument about the three figures. Enough has been said about the three figures and their proper moods; there remain thirty-two chapters on the simple syllogism, full of wonderful sophistry. First, chapter 7 of Prior Analytics 1 lays down two modes common to all the figures, which P. Ramus here recalls from the dialectical schools; they are set out in the Organon thus: when the affirmative and the privative, and the privative taken universally, are present, a syllogism of the minor extreme to the major is always made, as if A belongs to all B, or to some, but B to no A: for when the propositions are converted, it is necessary that A not belong to some A.

units.la: C noris extremitatis, ad majorem: ut si α quidem omni β, vel alicui: β autem nulli α: coverfis enim propofitionibus, neceffe α alicui α nō inefie: Similiter aute in aliis figuris: femper enim fit per converfionem fyllogifmus. hos duos modos Græci quidem κατὰ ἀντικατάστιν ἀντικαταστρέφει (id est ἀντιστροφὴν καὶ ἀντιστρέφοντας), fecundum converfionem & converfos nominant: vulgus in noftris fcholis appellat Fapefmo & Frizefomorū.
units.tr: ...of the extremes, to the major: as when α belongs to every β, or to some β, and β belongs to no α. For once the propositions are converted, it necessarily follows that α does not belong to some β. The same holds in the other figures, since a syllogism is always made through conversion. The Greeks name these two modes by conversion and converted [ἀντιστροφή, ἀντιστρέφοντα], that is, "according to conversion" and "converted"; the common people in our schools call them Fapesmo and Frizesomorum.

units.la: Exemplis autem exponamus, quo faciliùs ineptiæ deprehendentur. Exemplum Fapefmo in prima figura Ariftotelis:
units.tr: Let us illustrate these with examples, so that the faults can be detected more easily. An example of Fapesmo in the first figure of Aristotle:

units.la: Omnis philofophus eft laudandus:
units.tr: Every philosopher is to be praised:

units.la: Nullus fophifta eft philofophus:
units.tr: No sophist is a philosopher:

units.la: Aliquis igitur laudandus non eft fophifta:
units.tr: Therefore some who are to be praised are not sophists.

units.la: Coplexio directa erat, Nullus igitur fophifta laudadus: ea vero non procedebat: quare per converfionem, cotorta coplexio eft hoc modo, Aliquis igitur laudandus non eft fophifta. Vides quàm volubili rota figulus hujus operis coplexionem convertat. Simile eft fecundæ figuræ exemplum:
units.tr: The direct conclusion was "Therefore no sophist is to be praised," but that did not follow; so by conversion the conclusion is twisted into this form: "Therefore some who are to be praised are not sophists." You see with what a rolling wheel the potter of this work turns the conclusion. A similar example is of the second figure:

units.la: Aliquis philifophus eft laudandus:
units.tr: Some philosopher is to be praised:

units.la: Frizefomorū: Nullus fophifta eft philofophus:
units.tr: Frizesomorum: No sophist is a philosopher:

units.la: Aliquis igitur laudadus nō eft fophifta:
units.tr: Therefore some who are to be praised are not sophists.

units.la: In fecunda tertiaq; figura hæ coclufiones non habent ab ufitatis modis collocationem diversam, nifi quòd fecundo loco propofitionem ftatuunt, aflumptione primo: & quòd coplexione habent in fecunda figura fpecialem: Secudæ enim figuræ primo & tertio, tertiæ fecudo & fex to modis concluduntur in fecunda figura, fic: Omnes improbi sunt miseri? Fapesmo: Nulli sapientes sunt miseri: Ergo aliquis improbus no est sapiens. Aliquis sapiens est beatus:
units.tr: In the second and third figures these conclusions do not have a different arrangement from the usual modes, except that they place the proposition second and the assumption first; and in the second figure they have a special conclusion. For the first and third moods of the second figure, and the second and sixth of the third, are concluded thus in the second figure: "All the wicked are wretched?" Fapesmo: "No wise men are wretched: therefore some wicked man is not wise. Some wise man is blessed."

units.la: Frizesomorum: Nullus improbus est beatus: Aliquis igitur sapiens no est improb.
units.tr: Frizesomorum: "No wicked man is blessed: therefore some wise man is not wicked."

units.la: In tertia figura idem prorsus erit: pone igitur priore loco, quod secundo est, omnia congruent ad artis legem, quae est secundae figurae modis quatuor illis: ut, Nulli sapientes sunt miseri: Fapesmo: Omnes improbi sunt miseri: Aliquis igitur improb. no est sapiens. Nulli improbi sunt beati: Frizesomorum: Aliquis sapiens est beatus: Aliquis igitur sapiens no est improb.
units.tr: In the third figure it will be exactly the same: put first what is second, and everything agrees with the rule of the art, which is the four moods of the second figure, as: "No wise men are wretched:" Fapesmo: "All the wicked are wretched: therefore some wicked man is not wise. No wicked men are blessed:" Frizesomorum: "Some wise man is blessed: therefore some wise man is not wicked."

units.la: Mutatio autem loci, nec legem, nec specie syllogismi variat: & syllogismi parte metimur non loco, sed sententia & collocationis ratione. & liber Interpretationis vere docet, transmutata nomina & verba idem significare. Ergo haec nova est de duobus communibus concludendi modis syllogistica. At quis isto modo ratiocinatur, aut argumentatur? Proferant hujus doctrinae doctores, Homericum aliquod, Platonicum, Aristotelem etiam, extra haec commenta, ullum naturale exemplum: Recordentur Aristotelicae doctrinae, in Analyticis etiam tantopere celebratae, principia artium, singularium exemplorum inductione non solum colligi, sed collecta, cum traduntur aliis, illustrari: artium omnium mater experientia & observatio (ait Aristoteles) inducatur.
units.tr: But a change of place alters neither the rule nor the kind of syllogism, and we judge a part of a syllogism not by its place but by its meaning and the order of arrangement. And the book On Interpretation truly teaches that transposed nouns and verbs signify the same thing. Therefore this new way of concluding by the two common modes is syllogistic. But who reasons or argues in this way? Let the teachers of this doctrine produce some example from Homer, from Plato, or even from Aristotle, outside these inventions, that is natural. Let them recall the principles of the arts in Aristotle's doctrine, so celebrated also in the Analytics, which are gathered not only by induction of single examples, but when they are handed down to others are also illustrated by what has been gathered: experience and observation, the mother of all arts (says Aristotle), are to be brought forward.

units.la: Ergo nobis hujus artis hujus regulæ vera & natu-ralia exempla é præstantibus authoribus deducta & observata, proponātur. Atqui non solùm ejusmodi nulla reperiëtur, sed si fingantur, portinus sophisticam suâ indicabūt: hæc enim commētitia & captiosa sophismata, é tenebrico fis cōversionum sophismatis educta sunt. Atq; hæc in 7.cap. logica syllogistica est, de duobus modis cōmunibus: ad cæteros autem duobus Analyticis priorib. syllogisticæ artis tribulos re spiciens exhorefco tantâ otiosorum ingeniorū in sterilibus avenis fertilitatem exitisse, hic enim P.Ramus logicas Musas & Charites implorans, attonitus hærebat, cūm tam incredibiles tenebras à doctissimis quidé & & ingeniosismis hominibus invétas intueretur. Quis enim putet ab inertibus & stolidis ea unquam meditata & commentata esse, quæ vel diligētissimis & acerrimis ingeniis intelligere tantùm & cognoscere sit difficillimū? Superiorem verò syllogisticam é mathematica schola profectā, tam multa & vocabula, & exempla, & similia plane demonstrarunt: Et conjectura nō aliena sit indidem reliqua hæc orta esse. Itaq; homines eruditi, & ingenio otioq; abundantes, cùm sesē in reconditis illis obscurisq; artibus vehementer exercuissent experiri placuit, quicquid de syllogismo dici potest, vtrūm κατὰ πάντος, καθ' αὐτὸ, καθ' ἓλης πρῶτον, cura (ut apparet é rebus ipsis) nulla omnino fuit: Ergo P. Ramus labyrinthum hic quendā reputans, errores & mæandros anfractuum tam varios admirabatur: sed minimè gētium, minimé temporum, minimé hominū, minimé deniq; logicarū & Aristotelearū legū, obscuritates istas in lucis & perspicuitatis doctrina convenire arbitrabatur. Primo Analytico capita sunt deinceps quatuordecim post septimū ad vicesimum secundum, de syllogismo e modificatis enuntiatis tum puris, tū permistis, & inter se, & cū absolutis. Octavum caput est, quód syllogismus ex omnibus necessariis necessariū cōcludat in tribus figuris, eadem arte, quæ jam tradita elt: Quod non est καθ' αὑτὸ: nam etsi error accidere non potest, ut antea de negatis modificatis intellectum est: attamen negatio non est, Necesse est nullum hominem esse bestiam: sed affirmatio est, quia consequēs (est necesse) affirmatur de antecedente, Nullum hominem esse bestiam: nec ideo tales affirmationes ad regulam artis pro vera negatione possunt admitti. hæc P. Rami ratio est adversus syllogismū e modificatis necessariis. Tria capita proxima, 9. 10. 11. habent μίξιν ἀναγκαίᾳ καὶ ὑπαρχόντως, mistione necessarii & absoluti: ut ex propositione necessaria, & assumptione absoluta, necessariū concludatur. At Theophraftus jam olim id refutaverat, docueratque, complexionem debiliori partium antecedentium similem esse, ideoque ex necessario & absoluto nō posse, nisi absolutum concludi. hoc igitur non est κατὰ παντὸς, sed plane falsum est. Duodecimo capite significatio cōtingēris necessarii & nō necessarii proponitur, non necessarii frequentis & utlibet, cujus affirmatio in negationem covertatur: ut, Contingit homihominem esse divitem, & contingit hominem non esse divitem: quae negatio tamen enuntiati non est: quia attributum cotingit, non negatur: deinde enuntiati cotingentis sententia duplex efficitur, ut, cum dicitur (Omne currens cotingit cadere) intelligatur, quod currit, cotingit cadere: Item quod contingit currere, contingit cadere. At secunda haec sententia commentitia est, exemplisque vel organici authoris abunde in Scholis dialecticis cofutata. Itaque doctrinam reliquarum miftionum in totis decem reliquis capitibus deinde deductam (cum a tali comento profecta fit) fallace & captiosam judicari necesse est. Causa vero tati sophismatis in eo cofistit, quod cotinges, significationis vage fit & in certe, & in propositione aliud, in assumtioe aliud tempus comprehendat, unde complexio nulla coftans posit effici: ut si ita concludas, Omne currens contingit hominem esse, Omne equum contingit currere, Omne igitur equum cotingit hominem esse: propositionis contingentia (ut ita dicam) aliud tepus, aliud assumptionis contingentia respicit: Itaq; complexionis inco statia inde nascitur: neq; quicquam καθ' αὐτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον, doctrina haec efficit. Haec Logica igitur est quindecim capitum: Septede cim capita deinde sunt prima in secundo libro priorum Analyticorum, de syllogistica potestate plura concludendi ex uno dato syllogismo. & hic videtur geometricum simile quiddam quaesitum esse, Potestas lineae est quadratum. Itaque geometricorum Logicorum acumen hic elaboravit, ut dati syllogismi potestas eliceretur: & hic septem sunt inventæ: sed (bone Deus) quàm dissimiles, quàm toto genere diversæ. Potestas syllogismi legitima & logica est e duobus cōfes fis & cōcesis tertium judicare & concludere, modo simpliciter, modo compositè, & singulis utriusq; generis differentiis aptè & accommodatè: quæ potestas tanta est, ut non modo tribunalium civitatumq; & regnorum atq; imperiorum judices, rectores, reges, imperatores, in terris omnibus de dubio propositio, sed ne in cælo quidem ipso Jupiter cum Pallade absq; syllogismo recte judicare possit. At potestates septem hic institutæ sunt illius legitimæ potestatis infolentissimæ & impotentissimæ. Sed de singulis consideremus: Prima potestas est per conversionem complexionis. At iste conversionis paliurus nimium fruticatur: Genuit e suis spinis omnes syllogisticarum demonstrationum sentes, & latiùs tamen hucusq; extenditur. Amputetur igitur, vel stirpitus evellatur: quoniam talis potestas nullam syllogismi potentiam, sed solam absurdi sophismatis impotentiam arguit: quæ nullum usum habuit unquam, quæ nunquam habere ullum posset: ut antea jam nos e sua origine docuit. Itaq; potestas ista non est καθ' αὐτό. Dialectica est ars bene differendi: conversio factę cōclusionis, nil ad bene differendum pertinet. Secunda potestas fit assumēdo à generali propositione, vel assumptione vel etiam complexione: ut, Omne animal est substantia: Omnis homo est animal: Omnis igitur homo est substantia. Potestes tes enim aliud assumere ex eadē propositionē: sic, Omne animal est substantia: Omnis equus est animal: Ergo omnis equus est substantia. Itē ex eadē assumptione, Omnis homo est animal: Socrates est homo: Socrates igitur est animal. Item ex eadem complexione, Omnis homo est substantia: Plato est homo: Plato igitur est substantia. Atq; hæc secunda potestas est argumenti generalis, non est argumentationis, nō est syllogisticæ dispositionis. neq; quicquam hic κατὰ παντός habetur. Hæc vero utraq; potestas & conversionis & assumptionis, primo capite brevius comprehenditur: reliquæ potestates quinq;, ternis capitibus continētur. Tertia, quod ex falsis syllogismus fiat in omni figura. At illa potestas non potius est syllogismi, quàm connexi enuntiati, quàm disjuncti: quod ex falsis etiam necessarium esse possit: imo syllogismi potestas nulla est, sed partium syllogisticarum, quæ in syllogismo constant & absoluto aliàs veræ, aliàs falsæ possunt esse. Quarta potestas est, cū ex facti syllogismi complexione & conversione terminorum, in altera antecedētium parte, reliqua pars terminis itē conversa circulatur: ut cūm ita cōcluseris. Omnis homo est rationalis: Omne ridens est homo: Ergo omne ridēs est rationale, circulabis ita propositionem, Omne ridens est rationale: Omnis homo est ridens: Ergo omnis homo est rationalis. Hic vides circulatam propositionem: jam circuletur assumptio conversa propositione: sic, Omne rationale est homo; Omne ridens est rationale: Ergo omne ridens est est.
units.tr: Therefore let there be set before us true and natural examples of this rule of this art, drawn from and observed in outstanding authors. But not only will no such examples be found, if they were invented they would betray the sophistry itself, since these made-up and deceptive fallacies have been drawn out of the murky sludge of the sophism of conversions. This is the seventh chapter of the logic of syllogisms, on the two common modes. As for the other chapters, I look back on the thorns of the syllogistic art in the two Prior Analytics and shudder that such fertility of idle wits could have sprung up in such barren oats. Here P. Ramus, invoking the Muses and Graces of logic, stood dumbfounded, seeing such incredible darkness invented by men who were indeed very learned and very clever. For who would think that things were ever thought out and devised by sluggish and dull men, things which it is most difficult even for the most diligent and sharpest minds merely to understand and recognise? The earlier syllogistic, which came from the mathematical school, displayed plainly so many terms, examples and similar things; and it is not an unreasonable guess that these others arose from the same source. So learned men, abounding in wit and leisure, when they had exercised themselves vehemently in those hidden and obscure arts, chose to test whatever can be said about the syllogism, whether it holds of every case, of itself, and first of the whole [κατὰ πάντος, καθ' αὐτὸ, καθ' ὅλης πρῶτον]; yet (as appears from the matters themselves) there was no care at all for this. Therefore P. Ramus, considering this labyrinth, admired its errors and winding turns, so various; but he judged that those obscurities agreed least of all with the doctrine of light and clarity, least of all with the times, least of all with the peoples, least of all with the men, and least of all with the laws of logic and of Aristotle. The first Analytic has fourteen chapters after the seventh, from the twentieth to the twenty-second, on the syllogism from modalised propositions, both pure and mixed, both among themselves and with assertoric ones. The eighth chapter says that a syllogism concludes what is necessary from all necessary premises in the three figures, by the same art already handed down; this is not per se: for although error cannot arise, as was said before about negated modals, nevertheless it is not a negation when one says "It is necessary that no man is a beast", but an affirmation, because the consequent ("it is necessary") is affirmed of the antecedent, "No man is a beast"; and so such affirmations cannot be admitted under the rule of the art as a true negation. This is P. Ramus's argument against the syllogism from necessary modals. The three next chapters, the 9th, 10th and 11th, have a mixture of the necessary and the assertoric, so that from a necessary proposition and an assertoric assumption a necessary conclusion is drawn. But Theophrastus had long ago refuted this, and taught that the combination is like a weaker part of the antecedents, and therefore that from the necessary and the assertoric nothing can be concluded except the assertoric. This therefore is not of every case, but is plainly false. In the twelfth chapter the meaning of the contingent and the non-necessary is set out: the frequent and the non-necessary, whatever, whose affirmation is converted into a negation, as "It is contingent that a man is rich" and "It is contingent that a man is not rich"; yet this is not the negation of the statement, because the attribute "is contingent" is not negated. Then the sense of a contingent statement becomes double, so that when one says "Every runner is contingently falling", it is understood that what runs is contingently falling, and also that what is contingently running is contingently falling. But this second sense is invented, and has been abundantly refuted in the dialectical schools by examples, even from the Organon's own author. Therefore the doctrine of the remaining mixtures, deduced then in the whole of the ten remaining chapters (since it proceeds from such an invention), must necessarily be judged fallacious and deceptive. The cause of so great a sophism lies in this: that "contingent" is vaguely and uncertainly significant, and in one premise it comprehends one time and in the assumption another, whence no stable combination can be made. For example, if you conclude thus: "Every runner is contingently a man; every horse is contingently running; therefore every horse is contingently a man": the contingency of the proposition (so to speak) regards one time, and the contingency of the assumption another; and so an inconstancy of the combination arises from this, and this doctrine produces nothing per se, universal and first [καθ' αὐτό, καθόλου πρῶτον]. This logic therefore has fifteen chapters. Then seventeen chapters follow, the first in the second book of the Prior Analytics, on the syllogistic power of concluding more from one given syllogism. Here something geometrical seems to be sought, like "the power of a line is a square". So the acumen of the logical geometers has laboured here, so that the power of a given syllogism might be drawn out; and here seven have been discovered: but (good God!) how dissimilar, how entirely different in kind. The lawful and logical power of a syllogism is to judge and conclude a third from two granted and conceded premises, either simply or compoundly, and aptly and suitably to each difference of either kind. This power is so great that not only the judges, governors, kings and emperors of tribunals, cities, kingdoms and empires throughout all the lands may rightly judge a doubtful proposition, but even Jupiter with Pallas in heaven itself cannot judge rightly without a syllogism. But the seven powers instituted here are of that lawful power the most insolent and most impotent. Let us consider each. The first power is by conversion of the combination. But this buckthorn of conversion grows too wildly: it has begotten from its thorns all the thorns of syllogistic demonstrations, and yet it extends itself more widely up to now. Let it therefore be pruned away, or torn up by the roots; since such a power proves no power of the syllogism, but only the impotence of an absurd sophism, which has never had any use, and never could have any; as we have already shown above from its origin. Therefore this power is not per se. Dialectic is the art of disputing well; the conversion of a drawn conclusion has nothing to do with disputing well. The second power arises by assuming from a general proposition either an assumption or even a combination, as: "Every animal is a substance; every man is an animal; therefore every man is a substance." For one may assume something else from the same proposition: thus, "Every animal is a substance; every horse is an animal; therefore every horse is a substance." Again from the same assumption: "Every man is an animal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is an animal." Likewise from the same combination: "Every man is a substance; Plato is a man; therefore Plato is a substance." And this second power belongs to general argument, not to argumentation, not to syllogistic arrangement; nor is anything of every case held here. Both these powers, of conversion and of assumption, are comprehended more briefly in the first chapter; the remaining five powers are contained in threes of chapters. The third: that a syllogism arises from false premises in every figure. But that power belongs not so much to the syllogism as to a connected proposition or a disjunctive one, since even from false premises a conclusion may be necessary; indeed there is no power of the syllogism at all, but of the syllogistic parts, which make up the syllogism and which, taken absolutely, may at one time be true and at another false. The fourth power is when, from the combination of a drawn syllogism and the conversion of its terms, in one part of the antecedents the remaining part is circulated with its terms likewise converted; as when you have concluded thus: "Every man is rational; every laughing thing is a man; therefore every laughing thing is rational." You circulate the proposition thus: "Every laughing thing is rational; every man is laughing; therefore every man is rational." Here you see the circulated proposition. Now let the assumption be circulated by converting the proposition, thus: "Every rational thing is a man; every laughing thing is rational; therefore every laughing thing is is"

units.la: 292 est homo. Enimvero potestas ista in speciem peracuta perque arguta videatur, cum sic é complexione propositio assumptioque, & é propositione atque assumptione, complexio tam subtiliter & eleganter efficitur: At res penitus animadversa plané circulatoria est. Primum non potest ista conversio nisi reciprocis & propriis cóvenire: aliorum terminorum syllogismus circulari non potest, neque igitur ista est potestas dispositionis syllogisticæ, sed terminorum syllogistica dispositione conclusorum. Deinde si fuerit syllogismus partibus antea cófessus, quid erit opus ilto circulatorio syllogismi ludicro, ad probandum & concludendum, tanquam rem dubiam & incertam quæ confessa concefsaq; antea fuerit? Nullus hic est syllogistici judicii fructus, sed puerilis otii lusus valdé ridiculus: & sanè potiús histrionicus, quám philosophicus: si quidem philosophos in arte gravi & seria delicias istas agere, minimé omnium deceat. Quare potestas ista non est καθ' αὐτὸ in arte syllogistica, neq; ad rectè judicandum quicquá attinet. Tres reliquæ potestates totis decem capitibus explicatæ, ex uno contradicentiū loco & topico derivantur: de quo quám multa sint á veteribus Logicis coscripta, in ipso loco & Topico á nobis declaratū est. Hinc igitur potestas syllogismi triplex est inveta, sophistimatis, omniū quę adhuc fuerunt, stolidissimi & absurdissimi. Ergo de septem potestatib9 quinta est, cum ex generali contradictione complexionis cum altera antecedentium reliquæ, contradictio quęlibet
units.tr: 292 is a man. Indeed, this power may look very sharp and clever, since the conclusion is put together from the proposition and the assumption, and the proposition and assumption are drawn out of the conclusion, and the whole thing is made so subtly and elegantly. But when the matter is examined closely, it is plainly circular. First, this conversion can work only with reciprocal and proper terms; a syllogism with other terms cannot be circled. So this is not a power of syllogistic arrangement but a way of arranging conclusions by the arrangement of terms. Second, if the syllogism has already been granted in its parts, what need is there for that circular syllogistic game, to prove and conclude something that was previously conceded and admitted as doubtful and uncertain? There is no fruit of syllogistic judgement here, only a childish idle play, very ridiculous, and indeed more theatrical than philosophical, since it would least of all befit philosophers to perform such trifles in a grave and serious art. Therefore this power does not belong per se to the syllogistic art, and contributes nothing to judging correctly. The other three powers, explained in ten chapters, are derived from one topic of contradictories, and how many things the ancient logicians have written about that topic we have already declared in the topic itself. Hence the threefold power of the syllogism has been devised, the most stupid and absurd of all sophisms that have ever existed. So the fifth of the seven powers is this one: from the general contradiction of the combined proposition with the other of the antecedents, any contradiction whatever is concluded:

units.la: Lines marked 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 are line numbers, not notes. libet concluditur: Omnis homo est rationalis: Omne ridens est homo: Ergo omne ridens est rationale. Concludetur ita contradictio assump-tionis in secunda figura, Omnis homo est rationalis: Nullum ridens est rationale: Ergo nullum ridens est homo. Hic contradictio assumptionis est cóclusa in secunda figura: oppositio propositionis in tertia figura similiter cócludetur, Nullum ridens est rationale: Omne ridens est homo: Aliquis igitur homo non est ratio-nalis. Ergo potestas quinta est ejusmodi. Enim veró quis hæc attente considerans existimet talia sophismatum monstra hominum potiús, quám pecudi proposita esse? Nec enim primus syllogismus homini, sed hominis trunco & stipiti incóstans videri potest: Et tamen si incóstans videatur, quomodo secundus in obscuriore & obscurioris figuræ modo constans apparebit? Ergo qui magister hanc syllogisticam primus docuit, videtur sibi pro discipulis, nō animantes rationis compotes, sed pecudes nescio quas sibi pro posuisse: Ita omnia hæc ab humano & logico sensu lógissime abhorrent. Sexta potestas est p impossibile concludendi, cúm nempe specialis contradictio conclusionis sumitur cum altera antecedentium, unde cótradictio specialis reliquæ partis concluditur: Hæc enim sola potestatis hujus differentia est á superiore: ut si conclusum ita fuisset, Omne animal est substantia: Omnis homo est animal: Ergo omnis homo est substantia. tum si trúcus ille stipesq; hominis negarit admisso antecedente, complexioné: petereturtür specialis contradiction coplexionis cum altera antecedentium: & reliquæ contradictio ita cocluderetur in tertia figura, Aliquis homo nō est substãtia: Omnis homo est animal: Ergo aliquod animal non est substantia. hic specialis có tradictio propositionis concluderetur. Verum deductio ad impossibile syllogismū anté factū: cujus constantia probetur, nullum requirit, ut constat é mathematicis deductionibus in toto Euclide: in quibus extremum nominatim illud est,ὅπερ ἀδύνατον. Et adversus stolidum illum tam cōmunis sensus expertem, qui syllogismi judicium non videat, disputare, non video quid sit aliud, quám velle cum ratione ipsa insanire: flagris enim illic sit opus, nō argumentis. Deinde (quod antea aduersus cōsimilem stuporem disferui) qui tam plumbeus est, ut syllogismi antè conclusi judicium improbet: quomodo postea conclusi judiciū probabit? Prius illud in figura prima,id est Aristoteli clarissima fuit: hoc posterius in tertia & postrema: Quomodo lumen laternæ clarum ei fuerit, cui lumen Solis fuerit obscurum? Atq; hic interea decimum quartum caput consumptum est in differentia ostensivi syllogismi & ad impossibile: quę ipsa tam aliena est in logicæ artis præceptis, quâ tota hæc sophisticarum potestatum ἀκατάληπτον. Potestas ultima superest é contradicentibus, longé omniū nobilissima, longeq; clarissima. Quæ nulla esse dicitur in prima figura, sed tátúm in secúda aut tertia: ut, Nulla scientia est bona: Omnis scientia est bona: Nulla igitur scientia est scientia. O
units.tr: is concluded: Every man is rational; every laughing thing is a man; therefore every laughing thing is rational. The contradiction of the assumption is concluded in the second figure thus: Every man is rational; no laughing thing is rational; therefore no laughing thing is a man. Here the contradiction of the assumption has been concluded in the second figure. The opposite of the proposition is concluded similarly in the third figure: No laughing thing is rational; every laughing thing is a man; therefore some man is not rational. So the fifth power is of this kind. Indeed, who, considering these things carefully, would not think that such monsters of sophisms are set before men rather than cattle? For the first syllogism cannot appear inconsistent to a man, but only to a man's trunk and stump. And yet if it appears inconsistent, how will the second, which stands in the more obscure mode of the more obscure figure, appear consistent? Therefore the man who first taught this syllogistic seems to have set before his pupils not creatures endowed with reason, but I know not what beasts. All these things shrink far from human and logical sense. The sixth power is the concluding by the impossible, when the particular contradiction of the conclusion is taken with the other of the antecedents, whence the particular contradiction of the remaining part is concluded. For this is the only difference of this power from the one above: as if the conclusion had been: Every animal is a substance; every man is an animal; therefore every man is a substance. Then if that trunk and stump of a man, granting the antecedent, should deny the combination, the particular contradiction of the combined proposition would be sought with the other of the antecedents, and the contradiction of the remaining part would be concluded in the third figure: Some man is not a substance; every man is an animal; therefore some animal is not a substance. Here the particular contradiction of the proposition would be concluded. But a reduction to the impossible requires no previously made syllogism whose consistency is to be proved, as is clear from the mathematical demonstrations throughout Euclid, in which the final step is named precisely ὅπερ ἀδύνατον [which was to be shown impossible]. And to dispute with that stupid fellow, who lacks all common sense and cannot see the judgement of a syllogism, I do not see what else it is than to wish to go mad with reason itself: for there he needs whips, not arguments. Next (as I argued earlier against a similar stupidity), he who is so leaden that he rejects the judgement of a syllogism already concluded, how will he afterwards approve the judgement of the concluded syllogism? The former was clear to Aristotle in the first figure; the latter, in the third and last. How can the light of a lantern be clear to one for whom the light of the sun is dark? And here meanwhile the fourteenth chapter has been spent on the difference between the ostensive syllogism and the reduction to the impossible, which difference is as alien to the precepts of the logical art as the whole of these sophistical powers is incomprehensible. The last power remains from the contradictories, by far the noblest of all and by far the clearest. It is said to be found in no first figure, but only in the second or third: for example, No science is good; every science is good; therefore no science is a science. O

units.la: mores logicos (exclamabat hic P.Ramus) ô têpora philosophica? huccine rationis doctrina rediit, ut tales syllogismos nobis argumétetur? Equidem reliquum nihil esse suspicor, quó tanta nugarum licétia longiús posit erumpere: & certé interpretes quosdam tâ putidi sophismatis sic puduit, ut syllogismû hic ullum negarent esse: Appellatur tamen in Organo syllogismus, & revera est syllogismus: sed tamen cui, homini nè an pecudi propositus? utrúm hominem fore sperámus, cui contradictio antecedétis vera videatur, ut inde contradictio consequentis vera possit videri? Superior potestas utraq;, quinta generalem, sexta speciale cótradictionem potulavit: sed ejus partis, quam bubulcus ille negaffet: at hic protinus proponitur & assumitur cótradictio. Ecquis (inquam) opilio, bubulcus, aut in aliquo educatus stabulo, syllogismi hujus antecedés sic admittet, ut inde cótradictio alia concludatur? Aristoteles respódet hoc loco, in duobus sophisticis & contentiosis syllogismis, duas ejusmodi cõclusiones posse cótingere: itê si propositio cõplectatur contradictione aliquâ generalem, unde speciales cótradictio cõcludatur: ut, Omnis scientia est opinio & nõ opinio: Medicina est scientia: Ergo est opinio & nõ opinio. Hæc Aristoteles in hoc capite ita respódet: Verùm duo illi syllogismi, non sunt unus syllogismus, neq; propterea est potestas syllogismi, sed syllogismorum: & duæ illæ in duobus syllogismis complexiones, non facient unius syllogismi altera propositionem, altera assumtionê, ut hic requiritur. Deinde in hoc secundo modo, truncum illum hominis (qui in generali propositionis contradictione nihil motus fuerit) quo rationis sensu in speciali complexionis contradictione putamus moveri posse? Contradictio est Aristoteli (ut antea jam dictum est) principium omnium maximum & clarissimum: & tamen logica syllogismi potestas hic est inventa, qua contradictio alicui homini vera videatur. id est, qua suu logicæ artis fundamentu evertatur. Itaq; potestas syllogisticæ artis hic nulla est, sed extrema sophistice impotentia. Eadem enim sapientia, potestates syllogismorum quæreretur e causis, factis, subjectis, adjunctis, singulisq; topicis. Quamobrem ut tota illa superior intervalorum, mediorum, figurarum reductionum, ita nunc ista potestatum geometria valde est ἀλογος, vel logica potius valde ἀγωνιστική. Commentationes excellentium ingeniorum vigiliasq; hic elaborasse satis cōstat, sed frustra, sed inutiliter, contra legem logicarum decreta: tot capitū primo secundoq; de syllogismis Analytico commentata, hominis unius commenta esse non arbitror: Spinas tam aculeatas unus homo tam multas non reperit: multorum ingeniorum labor & sudor ille fuit: quem deinde Aristoteles e multis voluminibus & libris in hæc capita coegit: quæ si relegere & retractare, & ad suas leges expendere per ætate potuisset, P. Rāmo contentio tam gravis, tamq; laboriosa subeunda nunquam fuisset: totam hanc speciosam geometriæ umbrā à corpore logico, lumine legum
units.tr: logical manners! (cried P. Ramus here), O philosophical times! Has the teaching of reason come to this, that they argue such syllogisms to us? Indeed I suspect there is nothing left by which such license for trifles might break out further, and certainly some interpreters were so ashamed of such a foul sophism that they denied it was a syllogism at all. Yet it is called a syllogism in the Organon, and in truth it is a syllogism; but to whom is it proposed, to a man or to a beast? Do we hope it will make a man, for whom the contradiction of the antecedent appears true, so that the contradiction of the consequent can appear true from it? The two previous powers, the fifth with its general contradiction and the sixth with its particular contradiction, laid claim to a part which that cowherd would have denied; but here the contradiction is immediately proposed and assumed. Which shepherd, cowherd, or one brought up in some stable (I ask) would admit the antecedent of this syllogism in such a way that another contradiction is concluded from it? Aristotle answers at this point that in two sophistical and contentious syllogisms two such conclusions can occur, namely if the proposition embraces a general contradiction from which a particular contradiction is concluded: for example, Every science is opinion and not opinion; medicine is a science; therefore it is opinion and not opinion. Aristotle answers thus in this chapter: But those two syllogisms are not one syllogism, nor is there therefore a power of one syllogism but of syllogisms; and those two combinations in two syllogisms will not make one proposition of one syllogism and the other assumption, as is required here. Next, in this second mode, that trunk of a man (who was not moved at all by the general contradiction of the proposition), by what sense of reason do we suppose he can be moved by the particular contradiction of the combination? Contradiction is, as already said, for Aristotle the greatest and clearest of all principles; and yet a power of the syllogistic art is devised here by which a contradiction seems true to some man, that is, by which the foundation of the logical art is overturned. Therefore there is no power of the syllogistic art here at all, but the extreme impotence of sophistry. For by the same wisdom the powers of syllogisms would be sought from causes, effects, subjects, adjuncts, and each topic. Wherefore, as that whole superior geometry of intervals, middles, figures and reductions was, so now this geometry of powers is very irrational, or rather, as a logic, very contentious. It is clear enough that the commentaries of excellent minds and their vigils were laboured over here, but in vain, uselessly, against the decrees of the logical law; the many chapters of the first and second books on syllogisms in the Analytics I do not think were the inventions of one man. One man does not find so many thorns so sharp: that was the labour and sweat of many minds, which Aristotle afterwards gathered from many volumes and books into these chapters. If he had been able to reread and revise them, and weigh them by his own laws, over time, such a grave and laborious contest would never have had to be undertaken by P. Ramus, and he would have removed this splendid shadow of geometry from the logical body, by the light of the laws.

units.la: gum catholicarum longisimé disputiffet. Sed tamé hic P.Ramus Ariftoteli beneficiū immor* tale debitum prædicabat, á quo instrumēta suppeditata nobis essent logicæ artis tam importunis tamq; perniciosis impedimentis sublevandæ. Quamobrem si revivīsceret Aristoteles, & tot postea seculis natum sibi successorem intueretur, á quo logicum agrum tot sentibus ac spinis,tam multis carduis & paliuris expurgatumcerneret,legitimum Peripateticæ familiæ discipulum agnosceret: Id enim magister studiosé studuerat,idemque sui studiosis studium præcipué mandaverat.
units.tr: ...had discussed at great length the catholic matters. Yet Ramus here professed that he owed Aristotle an immortal debt of gratitude, since from him we had been supplied with the tools for relieving the logical art of such troublesome and pernicious hindrances. Wherefore, if Aristotle were to come back to life and see a successor born so many centuries after him, by whom the logical field had been cleared of so many thorns and brambles, so many thistles and buckthorns, he would recognise a legitimate disciple of the Peripatetic family. For this was what the master had eagerly studied, and he had especially enjoined the same zeal upon his students.
