units.la: Elufmodi syllogismus simplex fuit: Syllogismus compositus est syllogismus, ubi tota quæstio est pars altera propositionis affirmatæ & compositæ,argumētum est in reliqua parte. Sed ar* gumentum aliás est consequēs antecedenti quæstionis,aliás est tota proposi* tionis pars reliqua:tumq; in assumptione solúm assumitur. Tollere aūt in composito syllogismo,est specialem contra dictionem ponere. Syllogismus cōpositus est connexus aut disjunctus. Syllogismus connexus est syllogismus compositus,cujus ppositio est cōnexa:estq; duorum modorū: Primus modus assu* mit antecedens & consequens concludit. Quomodo Cicero judicat & cõclu dit fecundo de Divinatione:
units.tr: Such was the simple syllogism. A compound syllogism is one in which the whole question is the one part of an affirmed and compound proposition, and the argument lies in the remaining part. But the argument is sometimes the consequent of the antecedent of the question, and sometimes it is the whole remaining part of the proposition; and then it is assumed only in the assumption. To remove something in a compound syllogism is to posit its specific contradiction. A compound syllogism is either connected or disjunctive. A connected syllogism is a compound syllogism whose proposition is connected, and it is of two kinds. The first kind assumes the antecedent and concludes the consequent. This is how Cicero judges and concludes in the second book of On Divination:

units.la: Si dii sunt, divinatio est: Sunt autem dii: Divinatio est igitur.
units.tr: If there are gods, there is divination. But there are gods. Therefore there is divination.

units.la: 3. Off. Atq; si etiam hoc natura præscribit, ut homo homini, quicūq; sit, ob eā ipsam caussam, quód is homo sit, cōsul tum velit homini: necesse est secūdum eandē naturā, omnium utilitatē esse cōmunem. Quod si ita est, una cōtinentur omnes & eadē lege naturæ. idq; ipsum si ita est, certe violare alterū lege naturæ prohibemur: verum autem primum, verum igitur & extremum.
units.tr: From the third book of On Duties: "And if nature also prescribes that a man, whoever he is, should wish to look after another man for the very reason that he is a man, then it necessarily follows, according to the same nature, that the advantage of all is common. If this is so, then all are bound together by one and the same law of nature. And if this too is so, then we are certainly forbidden by the law of nature to harm another. But the first is true; therefore the last is true too."

units.la: Frequenter hic non assumitur idem, sed majus: ut prima Catilinaria: Si te parentes timeret atq; odissent tui, neq; illos ulla ratione placare posses, ut opinor, ab eorum oculis aliquò concedëres. Nunc te patria (quæ communis est omniū nostrūm parens) odit ac metuit: & jamdiu de te nihil judicat, nisi de parricidio suo cogitare: hujus tu neq; auctoritatem verebere, neq; judicium sequêre, neq; vim pertimescēs? Concludendi modus hic idem est, quando pro positio est relata temporis: quo genere nympha Oenone, apud Ovidium concludit errorem stultitiæ suæ:
units.tr: Here the same thing is often assumed, but in a greater form, as in the first Catilinarian: "If your parents feared and hated you, and you could not in any way win them over, as I think, you would withdraw from their sight somewhere. Now your country, which is the common parent of us all, hates and fears you, and has for a long time judged nothing about you except that you are plotting her parricide. Will you neither revere her authority, nor follow her judgement, nor fear her force?" The mode of concluding here is the same when the proposition is a relation of time. In this kind the nymph Oenone, in Ovid, concludes the error of her folly:

units.la: Cùm Paris Oenone poterit spirare relicta, Ad fontem Xanthi versa recurret aqua: Xanthe retro propera, versæq, recurrite lymSustinet Oenonē deferuisse Paris. (pha:
units.tr: When Paris can breathe with Oenone left behind, the water of Xanthus will flow back to its spring. Xanthus, hasten backward, and you waters, turn and run back: Paris is bearing that he has deserted Oenone.

units.la: Compositus] Syllogismus simplex ejufq; genera, differētiæ, ac proprietates declaratę sunt: spinæ de logico syllogismorum agro, si nō omnes at plurimæ tamen sunt avulsæ: Cōpositus syllogismus sequitur: quē nullū Aristoteles agnovit, imó verò disseruit 22. c.1. Pr. nullā prēter tres ex positas syllogismi speciem esse, hoc nempe argumento: méto: Si igitur necesse est aliquid sumere utriq; cómune, idq; tripliciter accidat: aut enim «de γ,&γ de β dicentes,aut γ de utrisq;,aut utraq; de γ:eæ verò dictæ sunt figuræ : constat omne syllogismum necessario fieri per aliquam harú figurarū. Hęc Aristotelis disputatio involuta est: in suas partes retexta, facilius sic intelligetur: Si mediū triplici figura disponitur, omnis etiá syllogismus eadem cócluditur: Sed primum verum. nam argumentū vel antecedit & sequitur, & prima figura est: vel sequitur tantúm,& secúda est:vel antecedit tantúm,& est tertia. Quare & secúdum verum est, omnisq; syllogismus triplici figura cócluditur.Hoc Aristotelis est judicium. At judicium assumptionis fallit ipsum có clufionis judicem:neq; enim quęlibet argumēti dispositio aliquam sequitur é tribus expositis figuris speciem: in connexis enim & disjunctis syllogismis factio propositionis & assumtionis longe alia est,quám fuit antea. Quare quod Ari stoteles ait, argumentū in omni syllogismo bis antecedere,aut bis sequi, aut partim antecedere,partim sequi:verum tantúm est in tribus expositis figuris : falsum autem est in connexis & disjunctis:nec iccirco recté ab eo judicatū,nul; lam præter simplices speciem syllogismi esse.Et quidem mirabile hoc ipsum quod dico, cōsideranti videatur: cúm Aristoteles disputat nullos præter expositas figuras syllogismos esse, interim utitur syllogismo cónexo, nulla trium figurarum comprehenso : syllogismus enim illé, Si medium triplici figura disponitur, syllogismus
units.tr: Compound] The simple syllogism and its kinds, differences and properties have been set out, and the thorns have been pulled out of the logical field of syllogisms, if not all, then at least most of them. There follows the compound syllogism, which Aristotle did not recognise; indeed, in chapter 22 of the first Prior Analytics he argues that there is no species of syllogism apart from the three set out, and he gives this argument: "If, then, it is necessary to take some term common to both, and this can happen in three ways (for either α is predicated of γ and γ of β, or γ of both, or both of γ), and these are called the figures, it is established that every syllogism is necessarily made through one of these figures." This argument of Aristotle is involved; unfolded into its parts it will be understood more easily as follows. If the middle term is placed in a threefold figure, then every syllogism is concluded in the same way. But the first is true, for the argument either precedes and follows, and this is the first figure; or it only follows, and this is the second; or it only precedes, and this is the third. Therefore the second is true too, and every syllogism is concluded in a threefold figure. This is Aristotle's judgement. But the judgement of the assumption deceives the very judge of the conclusion. For not every arrangement of the argument follows one of the three set-out figures in form. In connected and disjunctive syllogisms the making of the proposition and the assumption is quite different from what it was before. Therefore what Aristotle says, that in every syllogism the argument either precedes twice, or follows twice, or partly precedes and partly follows, is true only of the three set-out figures, and false of connected and disjunctive syllogisms. Nor is he right to judge on that ground that there is no species of syllogism apart from the simple ones. And indeed this very thing that I am saying will seem remarkable to anyone who considers it: when Aristotle argues that there are no syllogisms apart from the set-out figures, he meanwhile uses a connected syllogism, which is comprised under none of the three figures. For that syllogism, "If the middle is placed in a threefold figure, the syllogism is concluded in the same way; but the first is true; therefore the second", is a connected syllogism of the first kind, as will soon be understood.

units.la: D eadem concluditur. Sed primum verum : fecŭdum igitur. est syllogismus cōnexus primi modi,ut mox intelligetur. Quapropter Aristotelis disputatio, Aristotelis exemplo testimonioque refellitur. Neq; jam adversus Aristotelis Logicā ulla contentio P.Ramo fuit: Quicquid est reliquum de syllogismorum doctrina, erit à Theophrasto, Eudemo, Boetio. Compositus] Admonuimus in definiendo enūtiato composito, Peripateticos Aristotelis successores abusos esse verbo συνθετικός pro composito, quia hypothesis potest esse simplicis enuntiati: & sic Aristoteles 30.cap.1. Prior.syllogismum διαιρετικὸν ... ostensivum & conditionale opponit: quòd ἐν διαιρετικῷ λαβ' ἀληθὲς ἀμφοτέρα τίθεται ... προτάσεις, secundùm veritatem propositiones ambæ ponuntur. syllogismi vero hypothetici, διὰ συνθήκην ὁμολογούμενοι τούτως, ex pacto & cōditione cōsessi omnes. Atq; syllogismi Aristotelis hypothetici modó sunt simplices, ut 11. 13. cap.1.Prior.syllogismi ad impossibile in tribus figuris simplicib. appellantur hypothetici: & nominatim dicitur vicefimofecŭdo capite primi Prior. syllogismŭ ad impossibile, partem esse hypothetici. Aliquâ do etiam syllogismi apud Aristotelem, hypothetici sunt syllogismi compositi (quamvis syllogismos ipse præter simplices nullos putet esse) ut 40.cap. primi Prior. Si non est una quædam facultas contrariorum, nec una est scientia: Sed non est una quædam facultas contrariorum, ut salubris & insalubris: simul enim idē esset salubre & insalubre: Quare non est una cōtrariorŭ scientia. Antecedens probatum est, consequês non est probatum. Confiteri tamen necesse est, non autem ex syllogismo, sed ex hypothesi. Hic Aristoteles nomine syllogismi, argumentū & argumentationem complexus, syllogismū absolute negat esse, sed ex hypothesi syllogismum: nec tamen syllogismi compositi sunt hypothetici, si propositio assumptioque verae sunt & certę: ut, Si homo est animal, sentit: Sed homo est animal: Sentit igitur: hic vera & certa sunt omnia, nil est hypotheticum. Eadem porrò differentia ἁπλοῦς καὶ ὑποθετικός repetitur vicesimo tertio capite primi Priorum. Sed tamen tota haec ἁπλοῦς καὶ ὑποθετικός differentia, nihil ad artem logicam: una enim est communis utriusque inventionis & judicii doctrina: Quapropter si quis jam requirat, quamobrem bella haec differentia ἁπλοῦς ὑποθετικός, à P. Ramo praeterita fit: respondebo, capitibus octo hic consumptis, 22. 23. 30. 40. in primo Prior. item quatuor, de quibus jam dictum est, 11. 12. 13. 14. in secundo, sophisticam inanem contineri: Logicam logicis legibus consentaneam prorsus nullam instituit: ideoque à P. Ramo haec omnia veprium genera, tam multa extra logici agri fines ejecta esse.
units.tr: Therefore Aristotle's argument is refuted by Aristotle's own example and testimony. Nor was there any longer any dispute between Ramus and Aristotle's logic. Whatever remains of the doctrine of syllogisms will come from Theophrastus, Eudemus and Boethius. Compound] In defining the compound proposition, we have pointed out that the Peripatetic successors of Aristotle misused the word συνθετικός [synthetikos, compound] for compound, since a hypothesis can be of a simple proposition. Thus Aristotle, in chapter 30 of the first Prior Analytics, sets against the disjunctive syllogism [διαιρετικὸν] the demonstrative and conditional one, because in the disjunctive "both propositions are posited as true in fact" [ἐν διαιρετικῷ λαβ' ἀληθὲς ἀμφοτέρα τίθεται ... προτάσεις], that is, both propositions are posited according to truth. But the hypothetical syllogisms are all agreed "by compact and condition" [διὰ συνθήκην ὁμολογούμενοι τούτως], that is, arranged by agreement and condition. Moreover, Aristotle's hypothetical syllogisms are only simple, as in chapters 11 and 13 of the first Prior Analytics, where the syllogisms to the impossible in the three simple figures are called hypothetical; and it is said by name in chapter 22 of the first Prior Analytics that the syllogism to the impossible is a part of the hypothetical. Sometimes also among Aristotle's syllogisms the hypothetical ones are compound syllogisms (although he himself thinks there are no syllogisms apart from simple ones), as in chapter 40 of the first Prior Analytics: "If there is not one faculty of contraries, neither is there one science; but there is not one faculty of contraries, as of healthful and unhealthful; for at the same time the same thing would be healthful and unhealthful; therefore there is not one science of contraries." The antecedent is proved, the consequent is not proved. Nevertheless it must be conceded, though not from the syllogism but from the hypothesis. Here Aristotle, taking the name of syllogism to comprise argument and argumentation, denies that it is a syllogism absolutely, but a syllogism by hypothesis. Nor are compound syllogisms hypothetical if the proposition and the assumption are true and certain, as in: "If man is an animal, he feels; but man is an animal; therefore he feels." Here everything is true and certain, and nothing is hypothetical. The same difference, ἁπλοῦς [haplous, simple] and ὑποθετικός [hypothetikos, hypothetical], is repeated in chapter 23 of the first Prior Analytics. But this whole difference between ἁπλοῦς and ὑποθετικός has nothing to do with the logical art, for there is one doctrine of invention and judgement common to both. Therefore, if anyone now asks why this fine difference between simple and hypothetical was passed over by Ramus, I shall answer: with eight chapters consumed here (22, 23, 30 and 40 of the first Prior Analytics, and likewise four others already mentioned, 11, 12, 13 and 14 of the second), empty sophistry is contained; he set up no logic at all in harmony with logical laws. Therefore by Ramus all these kinds of thorns, so many, were cast out beyond the bounds of the logical field.

units.la: Syllogismus compositus] Definitur copositus syllogismus e genere & forma: Genus est syllogismus: forma colligitur e differentiis propositionis ab ea propositione, quę fuit in simplici syllogismo: primo propositio est affirmata: illic etiā negata esse potuit: secundo propositio est compositā: illic etiā simplex esse potuit: tertio tota quaequæstio est pars altera propositionis: argumen tū est in reliqua parte. Ex his igitur tribus differentiis, forma syllogismi compositi colligitur.
units.tr: Compound syllogism: A compound syllogism is defined by its genus and its form. The genus is syllogism. The form is gathered from the differences between its proposition and the proposition in a simple syllogism. First, the proposition is affirmed; there it could also have been denied. Second, the proposition is compound; there it could also have been simple. Third, the whole question is one part of the proposition, and the argument lies in the remaining part. From these three differences the form of the compound syllogism is gathered.

units.la: Alias consequens] Argumentum est aliquando nudum: ut, Si Socrates est homo, Socrates est animal: Socrates est homo : Socrates igitur est animal. hic argumetum (homo) est in propositione consequens antecedenti quæstionis (Socrates) At in syllogismo, Si virtus est laudanda, vitium est vituperandum: virtus est laudanda: Vitium igitur est vituperandum: argumentum (Virtus est laudāda) est tota pars propositiōis reliqua: Et assumptio, præter argumentū, nil assumit quæstionis: quod tamē fit sēper in simplici syllogismo. Specialem]id est,ut é generali speciale, vel cōtrá: aut é pprio ppriū αντιφατικὴν ponatur, quod est cōmune in cōnexo & disjuncto.
units.tr: Otherwise, consequent: An argument is sometimes bare, as in: If Socrates is a man, Socrates is an animal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is an animal. Here the argument (man) is, in the proposition, the consequent of the antecedent of the question (Socrates). But in the syllogism: If virtue is to be praised, vice is to be blamed; virtue is to be praised; therefore vice is to be blamed. The argument (virtue is to be praised) is the whole of the remaining part of the proposition, and the assumption, apart from the argument, takes nothing from the question, though this always happens in a simple syllogism. Specific: that is, the specific is posited from the general, or conversely, or the contradictory is posited from the proper to the proper, which is common in the conditional and the disjunctive.

units.la: Connexus aut disjunctus] Διχοτομία hic servatur eadē, quæ adhuc perpetua fuit: Quamvis enim species enuntiati quatuor factæ sint, congregativum copulaté & cōnexé, segregativum discreté & disjunctē: copulatū in simplici syllogismo duntaxat propositio esse potest: discretum syllogismi, propositio esse nō potest, iudiciumq; habet ἀσυλλόγιστον: Itaq; duę tantum pronūtiati species reliquūtur, quæ possint cōpositi syllogismi ppositioné cōponere cōnexam & disjūctā.
units.tr: Connected or disjunctive: The same division holds here as has been constant until now. For although the kinds of statement are four, the congregative (copulative and connective) and the segregative (discrete and disjunctive), a copulative can be the proposition of a simple syllogism only; a discrete statement cannot be the proposition of a syllogism, and it has an unsyllogistic judgement. So only two kinds of statement remain that can make up the proposition of a compound syllogism: the connected and the disjunctive.

units.la: Syllogismus connexus] Definitio hæc é genere,ité & forma constituitur: Genus est syllogismus cōpositus: in quo omnes illas antè expositas differentias intelligimus: forma autē é propositione cōnexa perficitur. Syllogismus autem cōnexus, appellat à Grecis interpretib.ad 22.c. 1.Pr-φυλλογισμὸς ὁ ἀξ ἀνολυθίας, ἢ τὼ ἀνολυθίαν λαβ̈ασονδά-ψε: ex confequetia, & consequentiâ comparans partefq; ipsæ ab interpretibus iisdē, imò ab Aristotele ipso aliud agente, dicitur ὑσούμενον ἢ ἀνὸ λόγον. Duorum modorum] Διχοτομία item hic est, licet sine nominibus. Hic duplex modus ab Aristotele comprehenditur 2. cap.2. Top.pro argumento ab antecedentibus & consequentibus. Considerandum verò, ait, id in proposito, quod cùm fit, propositum est: aut quid est ex necessitate, si propositum fuerit. Hic Aristoteles de mediis & argumetis inveniendis præcipiens, jubet antecedentia rei & consequentia speẞtari: deinde syllogisticas leges, licet aliud agens, attamen coprehendit, ut mox dicam. Assumit] Assumere, hic est non affirmare, sed repetere omnino, quale propositum erat: si affirmatū, affirmatè: si negatum, negatè. Aristoteles verò hunc connexi modum ita complectitur: Confiderandū itaq; confirmare volenti, quod cùm fit propositum, erit ex necessitate: Nam si demonstratum fit illud esse, propositum quoq; demöstrabitur. & Theophrasti Eudemique rivulos, é fontibus Aristotelis irrigatos esse constat: Non appellat syllogismū Aristoteles, nec in arte syllogismorum docuit: imò verò artem nullā hic esse disseruit: attamen reipsa ac veritate arte ipsam proposuit. Divinatione] Divinatio Latinis omnis præsensio rei futuræ, sive á deo, sive ab homine fieret: & futura præsentire aut prædicere, deorū propriū videbatur: indeq; á divis divinatio, est nominata,ut ait Cic.de Divin. Duos in eo argumento libros Cicero conscripsit: in primo, Q. Frater divinationem é Stoicorum sententia cōfirmat:Marcus refellit secundo. Itaq; Stoicū syllogismū hic adhibitū, Marcus ut propositione connexa inconstantem cavillatur: Vester deus (ait de Stoicis)potest non impertire, ut nihilominùs mundum regat, & hominibus consulat. Cur igitur vos inducitis in eas captiones, quas nunquâ explicetis?Ita enim cúm magis properant,cócludere solent: Si dii sunt, est divinatio: Sunt autē dii:Est ergo divinatio. Multó est probabilius, Non est autem divinatio:non sunt ergo dii. Vide quám temeré committant,ut si nulla sit divinatio,nulli sint dii.Divinatio enim per spicué tollitur. deos esse retinendum est.
units.tr: Connected syllogism: This definition is made up of genus and form. The genus is the compound syllogism, in which we understand all the differences set out above. The form is completed by the connected proposition. The connected syllogism, however, is called by the Greek interpreters, on Aristotle's Prior Analytics 2.c.1: [συλλογισμὸς ὁ ἐξ ἀκολουθίας ἢ τὴν ἀκολουθίαν λαμβάνων], a syllogism from consequence, or taking the consequence; and the parts are compared by the same interpreters, or even by Aristotle himself while he is treating of something else, and it is called [ὑπούμενον ἢ ἀνάλογον], supposed or by analogy. Of two modes: The division here is likewise of two modes, though without names. Aristotle includes this double mode in Topics 2.c.2, under the argument from antecedents and consequents. "We must consider," he says, "in the matter proposed, what is when it is, or what is of necessity if it is proposed." Here Aristotle, in giving precepts on finding middles and arguments, bids us look at the antecedents and consequents of a thing; then, though treating of something else, he nonetheless includes the syllogistic laws, as I shall say shortly. Assumes: To assume here means not to affirm but to repeat entirely what the proposition was: if affirmed, affirmatively; if denied, negatively. Aristotle indeed embraces this mode of the connected thus: "Therefore one who wishes to confirm must consider that what is proposed will be of necessity; for if it is shown that this is so, the proposition too will be shown." And it is agreed that the streams of Theophrastus and Eudemus were watered from the springs of Aristotle. Aristotle does not call it a syllogism, nor did he teach it in the art of syllogisms; indeed he argues here that there is no art at all, yet in fact and truth he has set forth the art itself. Divination: For the Latins, divination was any foreknowledge of a future thing, whether it came from God or from man; and to foresee or foretell future things seemed to be a property of the gods, whence divination is named from the gods, as Cicero says in On Divination. Cicero wrote two books on this subject: in the first, Quintus, the brother, confirms divination from the opinion of the Stoics; Marcus refutes it in the second. So Marcus, mocking the Stoic syllogism used here as a connected proposition as unsteady, says (of the Stoics): "Your god, he says, may not impart it, and still govern the world and care for men. Why then do you lead us into those tricks which you never explain? For when they hurry most, they are accustomed to conclude thus: If there are gods, there is divination; but there are gods; therefore there is divination. Much more probable is: But there is no divination; therefore there are no gods. See how rashly they commit themselves, so that if there is no divination, there are no gods. For divination is clearly abolished; the gods must be retained."

units.la: Si dii]Partes syllogismi nudæ sunt sine profyllogismo:argumentum autē est ex caussis,Deus est autor divinationis. Atq; ȝ. Offic.Tullius quę stionem de cóparatione utilitatis & honestatis disputans,eó descendit,ut judicet, homini non licere alterum violare: quod conficit sorite qua tuor graduū: Cóciliatio hominū inter se est naturalis: ideoq; cómunis & utilitas & lex: unde sequitur injurię prohibitio.Duo sunt igitur pro syllogismi,ad propositionem: Si hominū naturalis est conciliatio,injuria prohibetur:quia utilitas sit communis,etiam lex communis erit.
units.tr: If there are gods: The parts of the syllogism are bare without the prosyllogism, but the argument rests on causes: God is the author of divination. And in On Duties 3, Tullius, disputing the question of comparing usefulness and honesty, descends to judge that it is not lawful for a man to harm another. He makes this out by a sorites of four degrees: the union of men with one another is natural; therefore both utility and law are common; whence it follows that injury is forbidden. So there are two for the syllogism, to the proposition: If the union of men is natural, injury is forbidden; because utility is common, the law too will be common.

units.la: Dido] Æneas & hospitio & lectulo conjugali exceptę à Didone regina Carthaginis, ut á Virgilio fingitur: ac cū jovis mādato in Italiá vocaretur,insciaq; regina discessū pararet, hac ratio ne admonetur, ut maneat. Mene] Complexio est, cum prosyllogismo obsecrationis variarum partium.
units.tr: Dido: Aeneas, received with hospitality and with the marriage couch by Dido, queen of Carthage, as Virgil feigns, is warned by this reasoning, when he is called into Italy by Jove's command and the queen, unaware, is preparing his departure, that he should stay. Me: This is a complexion, with a prosyllogism of an entreaty of various parts.

units.la: Hymenaos] ὑμὴν, pellicula est puellis, quae primo coitu rumpitur: hinc Hymenaeus deus nuptiarum. Te propter] Assumptio cum prosyllogismo variorum effectorum. Libycæ] Libya, Africa est, mundi pars tertia: ubi fuit Carthago à Didone condita: & gentes illæ Didonem oderant, quod suorum principum connubia contempsisset. Nomadum] Nomades, à νέμω pasco, dicti in Scythia, qui sunt hodie Tartari: dicti itē eodē nomine in Africa, quales hodie sunt Arabes, qui Africam pervagantur, & stipendiariam feré totam tenent. Tyrii] Tyrus, inclyta civitas Asiæ, quondam insula, victoria Alexandri facta peninsula: illinc Dido in Africá profugerat, unde Carthaginienses dicti Tyrii.
units.tr: Hymenaeus: ὑμήν is the membrane in girls that is broken at the first intercourse; hence Hymenaeus is the god of marriages. On your account: The assumption with a prosyllogism of various effects. Libyan: Libya is Africa, the third part of the world, where Carthage was founded by Dido; and those peoples hated Dido because she had scorned the marriages of their chieftains. Of the nomads: Nomads, named from νέμω, to pasture, were in Scythia, and are today the Tartars; they were named by the same name in Africa, and such today are the Arabs, who roam through Africa and hold almost all of it tributary. Tyrians: Tyre, a famous city of Asia, once an island, made a peninsula by Alexander's victory; from there Dido had fled into Africa, whence the Carthaginians are called Tyrians.

units.la: Cui me] Complexio est.
units.tr: To whom me: This is a complexion.

units.la: Restat] Addit hic etiam poeta.
units.tr: Remains: The poet adds here too.

units.la: Hoc solum nomen, quoniam de conjuge restat.
units.tr: This name alone, since of the spouse there remains.

units.la: Majus] Assumptio sequentis syllogismi, videtur ἀσυλλόγιστον quippiam facere, quia quartum terminum adhibere videatur: ut, Si te parentes timerent, concederes ab eorum oculis. assumptio recta erat: At te parentes timent, pro qua assumitur, At te patria timet. Verum in hoc majore assumpto, etiam minus illud comprehenditur: itaque re ipsa assumitur idipsum, quod erat propositum, sed aliquid praeterea amplius. Si te parentes] Propositio est syllogismi sive prosyllogismi, ut antea, quia connexum feré est ἀντάκτιον νε αμιστον: secus absolute verum non esset. Ideoque rarus hic est prosyllogismus.
units.tr: Greater: The assumption of the following syllogism seems to make something not syllogistic, because it seems to admit a fourth term, as in: If your parents feared you, you would withdraw from their eyes. The assumption was correct; but for it we assume: "But your parents fear you," in place of which is assumed: "But your country fears you." Yet in this greater assumption the lesser is also included; so in fact the same thing is assumed that was proposed, but with something more besides. If your parents: The proposition is of a syllogism or prosyllogism, as before, because the connected is almost always ἀντάκτιον, and otherwise would not be absolutely true. Hence this prosyllogism is rare.

units.la: Oenone] Oenone, Pyritie fluvii & Creusę filia, adamata a Paride expositο, posteaqu ab eo (spręta, cum Helena rapuisset: unde ad eum revocandum, Ovidii fingitur epistola. Narrat autem nympha paulo ante mores arboribus inscriptos, aitque:
units.tr: Oenone: Oenone, daughter of the Phrygian river Cebren and of Creusa, loved by Paris while he was a shepherd, and afterwards, having been spurned by him when he had carried off Helen, is feigned by Ovid in a letter to call him back. She tells how, a little before, she had inscribed her feelings on the trees, and says:

units.la: Populus est memini, fluviali consita ripa, Est in qua nostri littera scripta memor.
units.tr: I remember a poplar planted on the river bank, in which a letter of mine is written, mindful of me.

units.la: Populę vive precor, quae consita margine ripae, Hoc in rugoso cortice carmen habes.
units.tr: Poplar, I pray you, that grow along the edge of the bank, you hold this song in your rough bark.

units.la: Tum sequitur, Cum Paris, &c. Propositio est testimonio Paridis. Xanthe] Xanthus fluvius Troadis in Lycia, oriens inter Telmesum & Pataram oppida, tandem cum Simoente miscetur.
units.tr: Then follows, When Paris, etc. The proposition is by the testimony of Paris. Xanthus: The Xanthus is a river of the Troad in Lycia, rising between the towns of Telmessus and Patara, and at last mingling with the Simois.

units.la: Xanthe] Complexio est secunda, cum brevi prosyllogismo partium. Sustinet] Assumptio est. Atque haec de primo connexo, ubi antecedens assumitur. Est autem apud jureconsultos conexum antecedentis disjuncti pro copulato: unde controversia captiosa oritur. Sic autem est: Si filius meus sine liberis, vel sine testamento, decesserit, Sempronius meus haeres esto: nam si assumatur, At decesit sine liberis, vel sine testamento: cum nepe intestat obierit, & ad disjuncti veritate veritas partis sufficiat: & concludatur, Sempronius igitur haeres meus esto. Hic jureconsulti admonet copulate assumendum esse: Sed decesit sine liberis & sine testamento: ut concludatur Quare Sepronius haeres meus esto. Tale antea fuit in enuntiato disjuncto, aut, pro &, accipi. Utrum vero testatoris negligentia vel imperitia quædam hic fuérit? Veruntamen quicquid hic statuatur, ratum illud & logicum esto: in primo connexi modo, semper assumēdum antecedēs, ut consequēns concludatur: nec si cujusquam soloecismus aut elenchus excusetur: ideo Grāmaticam soloecismis, aut Logicam elenchis subjeĉtam esse.
units.tr: Xanthus: This is the second complexion, with a brief prosyllogism of parts. Sustains: This is the assumption. And this is said of the first connected mode, where the antecedent is assumed. Now among the jurists the connected of an antecedent disjunctive is taken for the copulative, whence a captious controversy arises. It is as follows: If my son dies without children, or without a will, let my Sempronius be my heir. For if it is assumed: "But he died without children, or without a will," since he died intestate, and the truth of one part suffices for the truth of the disjunctive, the conclusion is: "Therefore let Sempronius be my heir." Here the jurist warns that the assumption must be made copulatively: "But he died without children and without a will," so that the conclusion follows: "Wherefore let Sempronius be my heir." Something like this was formerly taken in the disjunctive statement, or in place of "and." But whether this was some negligence or inexperience of the testator, I leave aside. Yet whatever is decided here, let that be fixed and logical: in the first mode of the connected, the antecedent must always be assumed, so that the consequent may be concluded; nor, if anyone's solecism or fallacy is excused, is it therefore the case that grammar is subject to solecisms, or logic to fallacies.

units.la: Cap. XIII. De Con.2.
units.tr: Chapter XIII. On the Connected [Syllogism], 2.

units.la: SEcundus modus connexi tollit cōsequeus, ut tollat antecedens. Si ulli rei sapiens assentietur usquā, aliquando etiam opinabitur: Nusquam autem opinabitur: Nulli igitur rei assentietur. Eodē syllogismo, Ovidius 2. de Tristib, stultitiam suam indicat: Si saperem, doĉtas odissem jure sorores, Numina cultori perniciosa suo: At nunc (tāta meo comes est insania morbo) Saxa memor refero rursus ad iĉta pedem.
units.tr: The second mode of the connected [argument] removes the consequent in order to remove the antecedent: If the wise man will ever assent to any thing, he will sometimes also opine: but he will never opine: therefore he will assent to no thing. By the same syllogism Ovid, in the second book of the Tristia, indicates his own folly: If I were wise, I would rightly have hated my learned sisters, divinities ruinous to their worshipper: but now (so great a madness accompanies my disease) I, mindful, bring my foot back again to the stones that struck it.

units.la: Secundus] Specialis autē contradiĉtio hic præcipuē requiritur, secūs ἀσυλλόγιστον fuerit: ut, Si omne animal est irrationale, omnis homo est irrationalis: sed nullꝰ homo est irrationalis, Ergo nullum animal est irrationale: antecedēte vero falsum est cōsequens. Hiç veró modus primus 2.cap.2.Top.sic ab Aristotele proponitur: Considerandum veró refellere volenti, quidnā est, si propositum est: Nam si demonstremus illud proposito consequens nõ esse, propositum tollemus. Atqį hic modus rursus ab Ariftotele ȝ.capit.2. Top. minimé tamē de syllogismis cogitate, comprehēditur: primó rursus nomine τὼν ἀ- ποληθων. ὥστ ἐπoιωνῶν ἰνὸς τῶν ἀνοληθων ἀναιρεθέντος, ἀναιρεῖται καὶ τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ,itaqį quolibet uno confequentium sublato,tollitur & quod erat in principio. Secundó nomine τῆς κατὰ τὸν ἀντίφασιν ἀνολυθύοντος ἀναιρεῖ, secundúm contradictionem confecutionis inversæ: tollitur enim confequēs, cúm sumitur ejus ἀντίφασις.Si ulli] Disseritur Academica ἐπιχή ex Arcefilæ syllogismo in Lucullo, q de duobus Academicis libris á Cicerone primúm conscriptis, & postea tamē damnatis, fuperefl:
units.tr: Secundus] A special contradiction is chiefly required here; otherwise it would be an unreasoned (ἀσυλλόγιστον) argument, as in: If every animal is irrational, every man is irrational; but no man is irrational; therefore no animal is irrational. Here the antecedent is false, and so the consequent is false. Aristotle sets out this first mode in Topics 2.2 as follows: one who wishes to refute should consider what the proposition is, for if we show that it does not follow from the proposition, we shall remove the proposition. Yet Aristotle treats this mode again in Topics 3.2, though by no means as concerning syllogisms. First he states it under the name of those things that follow one from another [τῶν ἀκολουθῶν]: "so that, when one of the consequents is removed, the thing in the beginning is also removed [ὥστε ἑπομένων ἑνὸς τῶν ἀκολουθῶν ἀναιρεθέντος, ἀναιρεῖται καὶ τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ]." Second, under the name of the consequence [τῆς κατὰ τὸν ἀντίφασιν ἀκολουθοῦντος], according to the contradiction of an inverted consequence: for the consequent is removed when its contradictory is taken. If any] The Academic suspension of judgement is discussed from the syllogism of Arcesilaus in the Lucullus, which Cicero first wrote in two Academic books and afterwards condemned; it survives.

units.la: Sic igitur illic ait Tullius: Quid igitur loquar de firmitate sapiētis ? quem quidē nihil opinari tu quoq; Luculle concedis ? Quod quoniá à te probatur,ut præposterè tecum agam, mox referam me ad ordinē,hæc primúm cóclufio, quam habeat vim, cōsidera:Si ulli rei sapiens assentietur unquam,aliquando etiam opinabitur: Nun quam autem opinabitur: Nulli igitur rei assentietur.hanc conclusioné Arcefilas probat: Confirmabat enim primum & fecundū: Carneades nonnunquam fecūdum illud dabat, assentiri aliquando id assequebatur etiam,opinari. Quod tu nō vis:& rectè,ut mihi videris. Sed illud primum (Sapientem, fi assensurus esset, etiam opinaturum) falsum esse & Stoici dicunt,& eorum astipulator Antiochus. Posse enim eum falsa á veris,& quæ nō possint percipi,ab his quæ possint,distinguere.hęc Tullius.unde intelligimus propositionis connexione reprehendi, ubi generi species inconstanter adnectitur: Nec enim si animal est, homo est: assensio enim, est genus scientiae & opinionis. Quare si sapiens assentiatur, non protinus opinabitur: poterit enim scie tia judicare, non opinione. Atque in hoc Arcesi lae exemplo notabis diserte expressam contradictionem speciale: qualem P. Ramus in definitione posuit: ulli rei assentiri, nulli rei assentiri: Aliquando opinari, nunquam opinari. Si faperem] Ovidius eo loco deplorat exilii causam, tanquam Musae & poesis in carminibus amatoriis ei causam calamitatis attulerint:
units.tr: Thus Tully says there: "What then shall I say of the firmness of the wise man, whom, Lucullus, you too concede to opine nothing? Since this has been proved by you, I shall, to argue with you out of order, soon return to the proper sequence. First consider what force this conclusion has: If the wise man will ever assent to anything, he will sometimes also opine; but he will never opine; therefore he will assent to nothing." Arcesilaus proves this conclusion. For he confirmed the first and the second premise; Carneades sometimes granted the second, that assent sometimes also follows opinion. This you do not want, and rightly, as it seems to me. But the first premise (that the wise man, if he were going to assent, would also opine) is false, say the Stoics and their supporter Antiochus. For he can distinguish false things from true, and things that cannot be perceived from those that can." Thus Tully. From this we understand that the proposition is faulted by its connection, where a species is inconsistently joined to a genus: for it does not follow, if it is an animal, that it is a man; assent is a genus of both science and opinion. Hence if the wise man assents, he will not straightway opine, for he can judge by science, not by opinion. And in this example of Arcesilaus you will note a special contradiction clearly expressed, such as P. Ramus put in his definition: to assent to some thing, to assent to no thing; sometimes to opine, never to opine. If I were wise] Ovid in that passage laments the cause of his exile, as though the Muses and poetry, in his amatory poems, had brought him the cause of his calamity:

units.la: Deme mihi studium, vitae quoq; crimina demes:
units.tr: Take away from me my study, and you will take away also the crimes of my life;

units.la: Acceptum refero versibus, esse nocens.
units.tr: I credit my verses with the fact that I am guilty.

units.la: Hoc pretium vitae, vigilatorumq; laborum,
units.tr: This is the reward of my life and of my wakeful labours

units.la: Cepimus: ingenio poena reperta meo.
units.tr: that I have received: a punishment devised by my own talent.

units.la: Tum sequitur:
units.tr: Then follows:

units.la: Si saperem, &c. unde insipientia suam judicat: Si saperem, odissem Musas: At non odi: Non sapio igitur hic contradictio est specialis propria.
units.tr: If I were wise, etc. whence he judges his own unwisdom: If I were wise, I would hate the Muses; but I do not hate them; therefore I am not wise. Here the contradiction is special and proper.

units.la: Numina] Profyllogismus est propositionis, ex adjuncto detrimento.
units.tr: Numina] This is a prosyllogism of the proposition, drawn from the added loss.

units.la: At nunc] Assumptio, cum profyllogismo allegoriae, ab offensione pedum. Tanta] Complexio hic inclusa est, per parenthesin.
units.tr: At nunc] An assumption, with a prosyllogism of allegory, from the stumbling of the feet. Tanta] The complexion here is enclosed by a parenthesis.

units.la: Usitatissimae] Duo modi connexi, frequentissimi sunt omnium syllogismorum, quia duo sint organa maxime omnium argumentorum communia: quocunque enim argumento in ceteris syllogismis concludi potest, potest etiam his connexis: tum vero ex plerisque argumentis multo
units.tr: Usitatissimae] The two modes of the connected [syllogism] are the most frequent of all syllogisms, because they are two instruments most common to all arguments: whatever can be concluded by means of other syllogisms can also be concluded by these connected ones; and moreover, many arguments are concluded here much

units.la: E faci-
units.tr: more easily

units.la: faciliús hic concluditur,quá in aliis syllogismis: Paria enim,majora,minora, similia, hanc præcipué dispositionem subeunt.Et quidem Aristoteles, qui connexorum syllogismorū artem nullam cognovit, tamen istorum syllogismorum usum tam familiaré expressit, ut etiam syllogismi definitionem iis modis concluderet & judicaret:Ná 2.cap. 2. pri.cúm disputat Aristoteles in syllogismo ex veris falsum cócludi nó posse, id est,syllogismi definitioné demonstrat, sic ait: Primúm igitur,quód ex veris non liceat falsum syllogismo cócludere,hinc manifestum.sic cúm a sit,necesse est ß esse:cúm ß nó fuerit,necesse est a non esse: hic secundus est modus,quo tolliturß consequens,ut tollatur antecedens a.Si igitur verū est a,necesse est & ß verū esse,hic primus est modus,quo ponitur antecedés a,ut ponatur cō sequens ß.Quin ejus ratio additur: Aut accidet idé simul & esse,& nō esse:id veró est impossibile. Quarto autem capite,ex secundi cōnexi lege affertur caussa,quamobrem ex falsis verum aliquando concludatur in sillogismo. causa veró est,quoniam cúm duo ficse habeát inter se, ut si sit alterū,necesse sit alterū esse: cúm hoc quidénon sit,nec erit alterum: si veró sit, nonnecésest esse alterum: At cúm idem sit, & non sit,impossibile est ex necessitate esse idem. Si veri cónexi(ait Aristoteles)consequens falsum sit, salsum erit antecedens:non autem,si consequensverū sit,antecedés etiam necessario est verum. At in syllogismo,res est ut in cónexo: Quare syllogismi consequente vero, non necesse est ante cedens cedes esse verum, sed falsum esse potest. Sic igitur Aristoteles connexis syllogismis concludit & judicat, tametsi nullam horum syllogismorum doctrinâ teneat: ut animantes tam multi videt, neque tamen ἐπ᾽ ἀλλήλων, & artem videndi tenent. Usum vero etiam horum syllogismorum valde celebrem esse demonstrat illud conclusionis compendium, Ciceroni imprimis usitatum, cum in primo modo assumitur & concluditur hoc modo: Sed illud, hoc igitur: Sed primum verum, potius igitur: vel secundum igitur: item, ante cedens verum, igitur & consequens. In secundo modo, Non aut hoc, nec illud igitur: vel, secundum falsum, primum igitur: item, consequens salsum, antecedens igitur: de quibus compendiis sic à Laertio in Xenone scribitur: Modus, est verbi figura rationis, velut talis est: Si est primum, est secundum: atqui primum, secundum igitur.
units.tr: more easily than in other syllogisms, for equal, greater, lesser and similar things undergo this arrangement especially. And indeed Aristotle, who knew no art of connected syllogisms, nevertheless expressed the use of these syllogisms so familiarly that he also concluded and judged the definition of syllogism by these modes. For in the second book, chapter 2, of the Prior Analytics, when Aristotle argues that a falsehood cannot be concluded in a syllogism from true premises, he demonstrates the definition of syllogism, saying thus: "First, then, that it is not permitted to conclude falsehood from true things in a syllogism is clear from this: since a is, it is necessary that β is; since β is not, it is necessary that a is not. This is the second mode, by which the consequent β is removed so that the antecedent a is removed. If therefore a is true, it is necessary that β is also true; this is the first mode, by which the antecedent a is posited so that the consequent β is posited. The reason is added: otherwise it would happen that the same thing both is and is not, and that is impossible." In the fourth chapter, from the law of the second connected [mode], the cause is given why a truth is sometimes concluded from false premises in a syllogism. The cause is that since two things are related to each other, so that if one is, the other must be, then since this is not, the other will not be; but if it is, it is not necessary that the other is. Yet since the same thing both is and is not, it is impossible by necessity that the same thing is. "If the consequent of a true connected [proposition] is false, the antecedent will be false; but if the consequent is true, the antecedent is not necessarily true also." But in a syllogism it is as in a connected [proposition]; so when the consequent of a syllogism is true, the antecedent need not be true, but can be false. Thus Aristotle concludes and judges connected syllogisms, although he holds no doctrine of these syllogisms, just as many animals see without holding the art of sight, nor does one see [ἐπ᾽ ἀλλήλων] by means of another. Moreover, that the use of these syllogisms is very common is shown by that compendium of conclusion, especially used by Cicero, which in the first mode is assumed and concluded thus: "But this; therefore that. But the first is true; therefore rather the second; or the second, therefore." Likewise: "The antecedent is true; therefore also the consequent." In the second mode: "Neither this nor that; therefore," or "the second is false; therefore the first"; likewise "the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent." Of these compendia Laertius writes thus in the life of Xenon: "A mode is a figure of reasoning, such as: If it is the first, it is the second; but the first; therefore the second."

units.la: Logotropus autem est, quod ex utrisque est compositum: ut, Si Plato vivit, Plato respirat: atqui primum, secundum igitur. Inductus est autem logotropus, ne in longiorum argumentationum structura, longa assumptio complexioque dicē da esset, sed breviter concluderetur. Primum autem est, secundum igitur. Suidas idem repetivit: sed vitiose apud eundem λογότροπος pro λογότροπος legitur. quo etiam ratiocinationis compendio Aristoteles alicubi usus est: ut 4. ca. 9. Metaph. Si igitur ipsum β impossibile est esse, necesse est & α impossibile esse: At primum est, ergo secundum. Sic igitur in exemplari Latino vetere ad verbum translato: at in Graeco secus est. Atque hæc de duobus cónexi syllogismi modis: quib, duo præterea à Theophrasto, Eudemo, Boetio sunt additi, é propositione antecedētis negati, & consequentis affirmati: primoq; tolli antecedens, ut cōsequens tollatur: secundo assumi consequens, ut concludatur antecedens: ut, Si dies nō est, nox est: Atqui dies est: Nox igitur nō est. Item, Si dies nō est, nox est: Atqui nox est: Dies igitur non est. atque consequētiam hic necessariam statuerunt, necessitate tamē rei, non syllogismi: id enim Boetius, ne quis addubitaret de modo propositionis illius, octies in diversis locis primi libri de syllogismis hypotheticis affirmavit: Primó, cúm ait, Quantū ad rei naturam, ita est: quantúm verò ad cōplexionis ipsius attinet conditionem, minimè sequitur. Secundó, Quantúm ad syllogismorum complexionem attinet, nullum efficit syllogismum: quátúm ad rem naturá, consequētia est necessaria. Tertió, Necessitas est in rebus, nō in cōplexione. Quartó, Valet ex necessitate rerum, non complexionis. Quintó, Secundúm cóplexionis naturam, nullus syllogismus efficitur. Sextó, Nó propter complexionis naturam, sed propter terminorum contrarietatem. Septimó, Non facit necessitatem complexio, sed terminorum natura. Octavó, Syllogismum, non complexionis, sed terminorum proprietas metitur. his igitur octo locis in uno libro Boetius, Theophrasti & Eudemi sententiā eandē pronuntiavit, quód in his duobus modis, necessaria cōsequentia oriatur é ter minorū natura, contrarietate, proprietate, nō é com-
units.tr: A logotropus is what is composed of both, as: If Plato lives, Plato breathes; but the first; therefore the second. The logotropus was introduced so that in the structure of longer arguments a long assumption and complexion would not have to be stated, but the conclusion could be drawn briefly: "the first; therefore the second." Suidas repeated the same, but in him λογότροπος is faultily read for λογότροπος. Aristotle also used this compendium of reasoning somewhere, as in Metaphysics 4.9: "If therefore β is impossible to be, it is necessary that α is also impossible; but the first is; therefore the second." So the old Latin version, translated word for word, has it; but in the Greek it is otherwise. These are the things on the two modes of the connected syllogism, to which Theophrastus, Eudemus and Boethius added two more, from a proposition with the antecedent denied and the consequent affirmed: first, the antecedent is removed so that the consequent is removed; second, the consequent is assumed so that the antecedent is concluded, as: "If it is not day, it is night; but it is day; therefore it is not night." Likewise: "If it is not day, it is night; but it is night; therefore it is not day." They held that the consequence here is necessary, yet by necessity of the thing, not of the syllogism. For Boethius, lest anyone doubt about the mode of that proposition, affirmed the point eight times in different places in the first book of his work on hypothetical syllogisms. First, when he says: "As far as the nature of the thing is concerned, it is so; but as far as the condition of the complexion itself is concerned, it by no means follows." Second: "As far as the complexion of syllogisms is concerned, it makes no syllogism; as far as the nature of the thing is concerned, the consequence is necessary." Third: "The necessity is in the things, not in the complexion." Fourth: "It holds by the necessity of things, not of the complexion." Fifth: "According to the nature of the complexion, no syllogism is produced." Sixth: "Not on account of the nature of the complexion, but on account of the contrariety of the terms." Seventh: "The complexion does not make the necessity; the nature of the terms does." Eighth: "The property of the terms, not of the complexion, measures the syllogism." In these eight places in one book Boethius pronounced the same opinion as Theophrastus and Eudemus: that in these two modes the necessary consequence arises from the nature of the terms, their contrariety and property, and not from the necessary condition of the complexion.

units.tr: of the necessary condition of the connexion. So they decided that there is no syllogism here, just as P. Ramus had earlier contradicted...

units.la: hac eadem de re differente, falsis etiá exemplis, in tertio connexionis modo inductū deprehen diffet: suspicari cœpit, nullá é rebus ipsis, nedū é syllogismis, necesitate hic esse. Boeti9 enim, dum explicat Ciceronis locū illū in Topicis, à repugnantibus, simplicitate suam valdè prodidit: Cū m enim Tullius primum & secundū connexi syllogismi modū coprehendiffet, sic de tertio loquitur: Cū m autem (ait) aliqua cōjuncta negaris, & his alia negatio rursus adjungitur: & ex his primum sumpseris, ut quod relinquitur, tollendū sit: is terti9 appellatur cōclusionis modus. hæc Ciceronis verba sunt: quibus interpretādis, utitur Boetius syllogismo cōnexo, & ait: Nam quia consequens esse intelligitur, ac verū est, Si dies est, esse lucē, repugnat & falsū est, Si dies est, nō esse lucem. quæ denegata, rursus vera est ita, Nō si dies est, lux nō est. & sit cōsimilis affirmationis, Si dies est, lux est. quia facit affirmationem geminata negatio. Atqui (ajebat hic P. Ramus) cūm Cicero, & post Ciceronē Boetius affirmant assumpto antecedente tolli consequens hoc modo, Non si dies est, lux non est: Atqui dies est: Lux igitur est. totū id fallax & captiosum deprehenditur: iisdem enim vestigiis falsum ex antecedente vero consequens efficietur. Esto enim inconstans connexio, Si dies est, non pluit. cōtradictio firma erit, Non si dies est, nō pluit. Assume igitur, At dies est: Pluit igitur. Dato antecedente vero, poterit consequēs esse falsum. Itaq; cūm P. Ramus Boetium tā simplicem in credendis, aut certè tegendis erroribus aliealienis animadvertit, quærere cœpit, nunquid aliquando exempla quoq; horum modorū sallerent, quę philosophi illi perpetua cōstantiaq; judicassent, quæq; P. Ramus ipse ejusmodi per annos quinq; & viginti expertus esset: tandem cum nihil hic procederet, & quæreret exemplum vitiosum, nisi specialis contradictio serva retur: incidit in exemplum modi tertii, etiá ad Theophrasti, Eudemi, Boetii Logicam falsi: ut, Si nullū animal est irrationale, omnis homo est rationalis: Sed aliquod animal est irrationale: Ergo aliquis homo non est rationalis. quod cū sæpius versasset, nō protinus sibi ipsi persuadere potuit, tenere se, quod tādiu quæsitū, nunq̃ inveniisset, quódq; desperatū abjeciisset: imo cujus oppositū sibi & authoritate philosophorū, & longa variorū exemplorum inductione plane persuasisset: Itaq; cum amicis conferre, & comunicare, & omnia se cōtra dicere: Etenim objiciebatur, licet falso, contradictionem non specialem, sed qualemcunque assumendam esse: ac si generalis contradictio antecedētis assumeretur, syllogismum constanté fore. Ergo ad hunc etiam aggerem subruedum, aries idem convertitur, exemploq; prompte refellitur: ut, Si nullū animal sentit, omnis homo est cæcus: Sed omne animal sentit: Ergo nullus homo cæcus est. hic contradictio est generalis: & tamen antecedentę vero, consequens falsum esse potest. Noli veró (quisquis hæc legis) jam quærere, qua tū lætitia P. Ramus affectus est, eo se tā diuturno judicii morbo esse liberatum, cujus medicinā an-
units.tr: Differing on this same point, and with false examples too, he found that the third mode of connexion was induced here. He began to suspect that there is no necessity here in the things themselves, much less in the syllogisms. Boethius, while explaining that passage of Cicero's in the Topics about opposites, greatly betrayed his own simplicity. For when Tully had covered the first and second modes of the connected syllogism, he speaks thus of the third: "But when some conjoined things are denied, and another denial is added to these again, and you have taken the first of these, so that what is left must be removed, this is called the third mode of conclusion." These are Cicero's words, and in explaining them Boethius uses a connected syllogism and says: "For because the consequent is understood to follow, and is true, If it is day, there is light, the contradictory is false and opposed to it, If it is day, there is not light. This denied, is again true in this form: Not if it is day, is there not light. And there is a like affirmation: If it is day, there is light, because a doubled negation makes an affirmation." Yet (said P. Ramus here) when Cicero, and after Cicero Boethius, affirm that, once the antecedent is assumed, the consequent is removed in this way: "Not if it is day, is there not light: but it is day: therefore there is light," the whole of this is found to be fallacious and captious. For by the same steps a false consequent will follow from a true antecedent. Let the connexion be inconstant, If it is day, it does not rain. The contradiction will be firm: Not if it is day, it does not rain. Assume then: But it is day: therefore it rains. Given a true antecedent, the consequent can be false. Therefore, when P. Ramus perceived that Boethius was so simple in believing, or at least in covering up, the errors of others, he began to ask whether perhaps examples also might deceive in these modes, which those philosophers had judged to be of constant and perpetual validity, and which P. Ramus himself had found to be such for twenty-five years. At last, since nothing progressed here and he was seeking a faulty example unless a particular contradiction were preserved, he hit upon an example of the third mode, which is also false for Theophrastus, Eudemus and Boethius' Logic: "If no animal is irrational, every man is rational: but some animal is irrational: therefore some man is not rational." When he had turned this over many times, he could not at once persuade himself that he held what he had sought so long, had never found, and had given up in despair. Indeed, he was thoroughly persuaded of its opposite both by the authority of the philosophers and by a long induction of various examples. So he conferred with his friends, communicated the matter, and contradicted everything. For it was objected, though falsely, that a contradiction must be assumed not as particular but of whatever kind, and that if a general contradiction of the antecedent were assumed, the syllogism would be constant. Therefore, to overthrow this mass too, the same ram is turned against it and readily refuted by example: "If no animal feels, every man is blind: but every animal feels: therefore no man is blind." Here the contradiction is general, and yet with a true antecedent the consequent can be false. Now, whoever you are who read this, do not ask with what joy P. Ramus was moved that he was freed from so long-lasting a disease of judgment, the remedy for which he had never been able to find before.

units.la: tea nullam invenire unquá potuisset. Ergo hue pené Archimedis ⟨Greek⟩ erupit. Tantū Philosophis animis veri studiū, tantusq; amor inest: ut ejus invētione, nullius thesauri, quamlibet pretiofi, inventio apud cupidos atq; avaros homines coparanda videatur. Enimvero (si quis forté caussam tantæ lætitiæ requirat) peccatur cæteris in artib. sed peccato multo leviore, quám in Logica, ut jam prædictum est. Galenus disseruit barbarismos & soloæcismos nullá eruditionis culpam esse, Demosthenes in tropo reprehensus ab Æschine, negavit in uno verbo res Græcorū periclitari: Quintilianus docet ignoratione Geometriæ multa á Geographis pecca ri.sed peccata hæc præ sophismatis logicorū judiciorum, levissima sunt: Potest enim, ut prædixi, de fortuna, fama, capite deniq; judicium, his falsis judicandi legibus constitui, peccato longé gravisimo ac periculosissimo. Itaq; tam exitialem, tamque capitalem sophismatis fraudem pestemque protulisse, illustrasse, sustulisse, verifsima philosopho animo lætitia fuit. Quapropter paliurus iste, spinis tam acutis tamque multis perniciosus, radicitus evellitur á P. Ramo. De- cies millenos modos connexorum pronuntiarorum philosophi tres illi antea jam nobis invenerant: nūc septuaginta modos syllogismorum connexorum, occasione aculeatissimi & cornutissimi hujus sophismatis, invenerunt: ut nugarum istarum studiosi in Boetio dinumerare poterunt. Atqui decies illi milleni modi, uno tantùm modo á P. Ramo antea comprehensi sunt: & hi jam septuaginta modi,nunc duobus comprehenduntur. Quamobrem & hanc P.Rami agriculturam tam logicam,imo agriculturæ logicæ fructum potiùs tam suavem ac jucundum, exanimo complectamur.
units.tr: Hence he almost burst out with Archimedes' "Eureka" [εὕρηκα]. So great is the love of truth and so great the affection in philosophical minds that the discovery of it seems to be worth more to eager and greedy men than the finding of any treasure, however precious. Indeed (if anyone perhaps asks the cause of such great joy) errors are committed in the other arts too, but with a far lighter fault than in Logic, as has already been said. Galen argued that barbarisms and solecisms are no fault of learning; Demosthenes, reproved by Aeschines for a trope, denied that the affairs of the Greeks were endangered by a single word; Quintilian teaches that many errors are made by geographers through ignorance of geometry. But these faults, compared with the sophisms of logical judgments, are the lightest. For, as I said before, a judgment on fortune, reputation, and even life itself can be settled by these false laws of judging, a fault far more grave and dangerous. Therefore it was a truly philosophical joy to have brought forth, illuminated and removed so deadly and capital a fraud and plague of sophism. Wherefore that buckthorn, so harmful with such sharp and numerous thorns, is torn up by the roots by P. Ramus. Those three philosophers had earlier found for us ten thousand modes of connected propositions; now, on the occasion of this most prickly and horned sophism, they have found seventy modes of connected syllogisms, as the students of those trifles may count in Boethius. Yet those ten thousand modes were comprehended by P. Ramus in a single mode before, and these seventy modes are now comprehended in two. Wherefore let us embrace with a sound mind this agriculture of P. Ramus, so logical, or rather so pleasant and agreeable a fruit of logical agriculture.

units.la: SYllogismus disjunctus, est syllogismus compositus, cujus propositio est disjũcta:modi duo sunt:primus tollit unum, & reliquum cõcludit:ut, Aut dies est,aut nox est: At dies nõ est:Nox igitur est. Ciceronis p Cluëtio judiciũ tale est:Sed cúm esset hęc illi proposita cõditio,ut aut justè picq; accusaret,aut acerbè indigneq; moreretur: accusare quoquo modo posset, quã illo modo mori maluit.Disjunctio clarior sic erit:
units.tr: Syllogism disjunctive is a compound syllogism whose proposition is disjunctive. There are two modes. The first denies one alternative and concludes the other, as: Either it is day or it is night; but it is not day; therefore it is night. Cicero's argument in defence of Cluentius goes like this: "Since the alternative offered to him was either to accuse, justly and fiercely, or to die shamefully and disgracefully, he could accuse by whatever means, which he preferred to dying in that way." The disjunction will be clearer if set out thus:

units.la: Aut accusandum,aut moriendum;
units.tr: Either he must accuse, or he must die;

units.la: Non moriendum:
units.tr: But he must not die;

units.la: Accusandum igitur.
units.tr: Therefore he must accuse.

units.la: Sic idem 2.Philipp.ratiocinatur:Nũquámne intelliges tibi statuēdum esse, utrum illi, qui istam rem gesserunt, homicidæ sint, an vindices libertatis? Attende enim paulisper, cogitationemq; sobrii hominis ad punctum temporis suscipe. Et ego,qui sum illorum(ut ipse fateor)familiaris:ut á te arguor,socius:
units.tr: In the same way, in the second Philippic, he reasons: "Will you never understand that you must decide whether those who carried out that deed were murderers or defenders of liberty? Pay attention for a moment, and give your sober mind to the question. I, who am (as I myself confess) familiar with them, am, as you charge, their associate:"

units.la: » nego quicquam esse medium. confite-» or illos,nisi liberatores populi Romani conservatoresque Reip.sint,plús quám sicarios, plús quám homicidas, plús quám parricidas esse: si quidem est atrocius patriæ parentem, quám suum occidere. Tu homo sapiens & considerate, quid dicis? Si parricidæ, cur honoris causá á te sunt & in hoc ordine, & apud populum Rom. semper appellati? cur M.Brutus,te referente,legibus est solutus, si ab urbe plús quám decem dies abfuisset? cur ludi Apollinares incredibili M.Bruti honore celebrati? cur provinciæ Cassio & Bruto datæ? cur Quæstores additi? cur Legatorum numerus auctus? Atque hæc acta per te. Non igitur homicidæ: Sequitur ut liberatores, tuo judicio, sint: quandoquidem tertium nihil potest esse. Si partes disjunctæ propositionis sint duabus plures, judicandi concludendique ars erit eadem. Sic Cicero judicat Rabyriü cum Consulibus esse oportere: Atqui videmus (ait) hæc in rerum natura tria suisfe,ut aut cum Saturnino esset, aut cum bonis,aut lateret.Latere autem mortis erat instar turpissimæ: cum Saturnino esse furoris & sceleris: virtus, & honestas, & pudor, cum Cosis. esse cogebat.
units.tr: "I deny that there is any middle ground. I confess that those men, unless they are the liberators of the Roman people and the preservers of the Republic, are more than assassins, more than murderers, more than parricides; for it is more monstrous to kill one's country's father than one's own. You, a wise and thoughtful man, what do you say? If they are parricides, why have they been called by you, in this order and before the Roman people, by honourable names? Why was Marcus Brutus, on your proposal, released from the laws, if he had been absent from the city for more than ten days? Why were the Apollinarian games celebrated with incredible honour to Marcus Brutus? Why were the provinces given to Cassius and Brutus? Why were quaestors added? Why was the number of legates increased? And all these acts were done through you. Therefore they were not murderers; it follows that, by your judgment, they are liberators, since there can be no third option." If the parts of the disjunctive proposition are more than two, the art of judging and concluding will be the same. Thus Cicero judges that Rabirius ought to be with the consuls. "But we see," he says, "that there were three courses open to him in the nature of things: that he be with Saturninus, or with the good men, or that he lie hidden. Now to lie hidden was like a most shameful death; to be with Saturninus was a matter of madness and crime; virtue, honour and modesty compelled him to be with the consuls."

units.la: P.Rami diligentia in perpurgando syllogismorum connexorum agro, magna nobis apparuit: de disjunctis syllogismis agricultura ipsius attendatur. Primo syllogismus definitur è genere, quod sit syllogismus compositus: tum è forma, quod propositione habeat disjunctam: ut enim antea, connexa, ita nunc disjuncta enuntiatio addita generi, facit differentiam compositi syllogismi. Logicam vero disjunctorum syllogismorum hic etiam P. Ramus è fontibus Aristotelis derivabat, ut jam antea derivavit Logicam syllogismorum connexorum: neque tam à Theophrasto & Eudemo invetam horum syllogismorum doctrinam, quàm digestam & excultam profitebatur. Aristoteles enim, licet de argumentis tantum cogitans, nihil de argumentationum & syllogismorum Logica consideràns, has etiam argumentationum formas aperuit: Sic enim 2. ca. 2. Topic. præcipit: Quibuscunque vero necesse est solum alterum inesse, aut non inesse: ut homini morbum, aut sanitatem: si ad alterum facile diferere valeamus, quod infit aut non infit: ad reliquum quum quoq; facile valebimus: Id vero convertitur ad utrumque. Hæc (inquam) Aristoteles ita præcipit: & reipsa syllogismi disjuncti formam describit, quamvis de argumento tantum cogitans, nil suspicans de nova syllogismi specie aut figura. Quamobrem partis etiam hujus gratiâ AristoAriftoteli acceptam P.Ramus referebat.
units.tr: The diligence of P. Ramus in clearing the field of connected syllogisms has appeared great to us; let us now consider his cultivation of the field of disjunctive syllogisms. First, the syllogism is defined by its genus, namely that it is a compound syllogism; then by its form, namely that it has a disjunctive proposition. For just as before the connected proposition, so now the disjunctive proposition, added to the genus, makes the difference of the compound syllogism. Moreover, Ramus here too derived the logic of disjunctive syllogisms from the sources of Aristotle, just as he had earlier derived the logic of connected syllogisms; and he professed that the doctrine of these syllogisms was not so much discovered by Theophrastus and Eudemus as arranged and refined. For Aristotle, though thinking only about arguments and taking no account of the logic of argumentations and syllogisms, nonetheless laid open these forms of argumentation as well. Thus in the second book, chapter two, of the Topics he prescribes: "But where it is necessary that only one of two things belongs or does not belong, as health or disease belongs to a man, if we can easily show that one does or does not belong, we shall also easily be able to do so for the remainder; and this conversion holds for both." Aristotle, I say, prescribes this, and in fact describes the form of the disjunctive syllogism, although thinking only of the argument and suspecting nothing of a new species or figure of syllogism. For this reason Ramus acknowledged that the credit for this part too was owed to Aristotle.

units.la: Duo]Διχοτομία hic etiam fervatur, & disjûctorum binarius cum binario connexorum analogiam retinet. Primus modus generalis omnino est quocunq; modo partes disjunctionis afficiantur,five affirmatæ sint omnes, five omnes ne gatæ,five mixtum fit hic aliquid. Tollit]Contradictio hic quelibet videtur poni posse,seu generalis,seu specialis: nam fi propositio ipsa fit é generaliter disjûctis, etiam natura rerum feret, ut generalis cotradictio aflumi possit: ut, Omnis homo est rationalis,aut nulla bestia est irrationalis:Sed omnis bestia est irrationalis: Ergo omnis homo est rationalis. At fi disjûctio vera esse non possit,nisi é specialiter disjunctis, non poterit,nisi specialis cotradictio aflumi. ut, Aut omnis homo est rationalis, aut nullum animal est rationale. hic nó potest veré aflumi,Sed omne animal est rationale : sed tantúm aflumi poteft,Aliquod animal est rationale. unde concludetur,Ergo omnis homo est rationalis. Et cauf fa est, quod alterû tolli fatis est, quoquo modo tolli possit, cúm reliquû maneat idem prorsus, sicuti propofitû fuerat.Hic veró modus fpeciatim sic ab Ariftotele 2. ca. 2. Topic.proponitur. Si veró quod non est,docuerimus:reliquum in esse docuerimus. Ergo hunc etiam modum Ari ftoteli merito P.Ramus attribuit. Sed cúm]Primus modus trib. exemplis declaratur,quę singula sunt propria : Aut dies est,aut nox est.sententia est, Aut hoc tempus est diurnum,aut nocturnum. Cluentio] Secundum est exemplum: Cluentius veneficii reum fecerat Oppianicum vitricum suum. Itaq; hæc accusatio, quia turpis videbatur, excusatur ab oratore. Hūc igitur hominem (ait orator de Oppianico) tam audacé, tam nefarium, tam nocentem, nūquam accusas set Habitus, judices, si id pretermittere, salvo capite suo, potuisset. Erat huic inimicus Oppiani cus. erat, sed tamē erat vitricus: crudelis: & huic infesta mater: attamē mater postremō nihil tam remotū ab accusatione, quām Cluentius, & natura, & voluntate, & instituta ratione vitæ. tum sequitur, Sed cūm esset, &c. Conditio] Etiam videmus hic ab oratore disjunċti conditione ap-. pellari: ut disjunctum tam coditionale dici possit, id est ὑποθετικὸν, quām connexum.
units.tr: Two [Dichotomy: Διχοτομία] is preserved here too, and the binary of disjunctives keeps an analogy with the binary of connected propositions. The first mode is wholly general, whatever way the parts of the disjunction are affected, whether they are all affirmed, or all denied, or some mixture. Denies: any contradiction seems able to be posited here, whether general or particular. For if the proposition itself is made of generally disjoined terms, the nature of things will also allow a general contradiction to be assumed, as: Every man is rational, or no beast is irrational; but every beast is irrational; therefore every man is rational. But if the disjunction cannot be true except from specially disjoined terms, only a particular contradiction can be assumed, as: Either every man is rational, or no animal is rational; here the second cannot truly be assumed, but only this can be assumed: Some animal is rational; from which it will be concluded: Therefore every man is rational. And the reason is that it is enough to deny one alternative, however it may be denied, since the remainder stays exactly the same as was proposed. This mode is set out specifically by Aristotle in the second book, chapter two, of the Topics: "But if we have shown what is not, we have shown what remains." Ramus therefore rightly attributes this mode to Aristotle too. But since: the first mode is illustrated by three examples, each of which is proper: "Either it is day or it is night," meaning, "Either this time is diurnal or nocturnal." Cluentius: this is the second example. Cluentius had charged his stepfather Oppianicus with poisoning. And so this accusation, because it seemed shameful, is excused by the orator. "This man," says the orator of Oppianicus, "so bold, so wicked, so guilty, you never accuse; judges, he could have passed over it, saving his own head." Oppianicus was an enemy of Cluentius; he was, but nevertheless he was his stepfather; cruel; and to him his mother was hostile; yet, in the end, nothing was so remote from accusation as Cluentius, both by nature, by will and by the principle of his life. Then follows: "But since it was, etc." Condition: here too we see the orator call the disjunctive a condition, so that a disjunctive may be called conditional, that is hypothetical [ὑποθετικὸν], just as a connected proposition may be.

units.la: Aut jusse] Propositio est velut ἀμφὶ αὐτέπιϛ. Accusare] Complexio hic coprehenditur.
units.tr: Either he must accuse: the proposition is, as it were, an ambiguous proposition [ἀμφὶ αὐτέπιϛ]. To accuse: the complex is comprehended here.

units.la: Quam illo] Assumptio, per remotionem partis alterius hic comprehenditur. Nunquámne] Tertium exemplum paulo copiosioribus profyllogismis exornatum: & λογικώτερον, velut in schola, certamen disceptatur. Constituitur igitur primum propositio cū profyllogismo, é disjunctionis axiomate. Attende] Locus est attentionis: ubi tanquam Logicus aliquis judex atq; stima tor conclusionis exposcitur. Confiteor] Profyllogismus propositionis alter é collatione majorum. Tu homo] Attentio altera, ad assumptionis profyllogismum, ex effectis Antonii.
units.tr: Than to die in that way: the assumption is comprehended here by the removal of the other part. Never: a third example, adorned with somewhat fuller prosyllogisms, and argued more logically, as in a school disputation. First, then, the proposition is set up with its prosyllogism, from the axiom of the disjunction. Attend: this is a place of attention, where a kind of logical judge and assessor of the conclusion is called for. I confess: the second prosyllogism of the proposition, from the comparison of the greater. You, a man: a second attention, to the prosyllogism of the assumption, drawn from the deeds of Antony.

units.la: Provincia] M. Bruto Gallia togata, alteri Bruto Creta, Cassio Libya, Trebonio Asia, Cimbro Bithynia. Nonigitur] Concluditur profyllogismus gisimus assumptionis. Sequitur]Complexio disjuncti cum prosyllogismo authoritatis Antoniane, & axiomate ipsius disjuncti. Si partes]Dichotomia perfectę divisionis, ideoq; disjunctionis, vix perpetuó retineri potest: & tamen syllogismi ratio in tollendo ac retinendo par est.
units.tr: Provinces: to Marcus Brutus Cisalpine Gaul, to the other Brutus Crete, to Cassius Libya, to Trebonius Asia, to Cimber Bithynia. Therefore not: the third prosyllogism of the assumption is concluded. It follows: the complex of the disjunctive with the prosyllogism of Antony's authority, and the axiom of the disjunctive itself. If the parts: a dichotomy of perfect division, and therefore of disjunction, can scarcely be kept throughout; and yet the reasoning of the syllogism is equally valid in denying and in retaining.

units.la: Atqui]Tullius Rabyrium perduellionis reum, imò damnatum & cruci pené jam suffixum, de sensione illa quæ extat, & in quam P. Rami praelectiones ēditæ sunt, liberavit: accusatus autem fuerat à suborñato per Cæsarē Labieno, quód Saturninum Trib. plebis quadraginta ante annis necasset. Saturnino] Tribuno plebis seditioso: ad quem coercendum, Marius Consul Senatusconsulto armatus fuerat. Bonis]Bonos, appellat optimates, qui tum ad Saturninū opprimendum convenerant. Coss.]Mario & Valerio, qui tum fuêre,
units.tr: But: Cicero freed Rabirius, charged with treason, indeed already condemned and almost hanged on the cross, by that speech which survives, and in which the lectures of P. Ramus were published; he had been accused by Labienus, who was suborned by Caesar, because he had killed Saturninus, tribune of the plebs, forty years before. Saturninus: the seditious tribune of the plebs, against whom Marius, the consul, had been armed by a senatus consultum to restrain him. The good men: he calls the optimates "good men," who had then gathered to crush Saturninus. The consuls: Marius and Valerius, who were then in office.

units.la: Cap. XV. De Disjunctio 2.
units.tr: Cap. XV. De Disjunctio 2.

units.la: DIsjunctus secundus ē propositione partibus omnibus affirmata assumit unum, & reliquum tollit: ut, Dies est, aut nox est: At dies est: Nox igitur non est.
units.tr: The second disjunctive syllogism, from a proposition with all its parts affirmed, assumes one part and removes the rest: for example, "It is day or it is night; but it is day; therefore it is not night."

units.la: Sic juno cum jove de Turno concludit, decimo Aeneidos: — Quid si quod voce gravaris, (ret? Mete dares? atq; hac Turno rata vita maneNunc manet insonte gravis exit: autego veri
units.tr: So Juno, in the tenth book of the Aeneid, concludes with Jupiter about Turnus: "What if you are troubled by a word? Will you give life? And will this life remain fixed for Turnus? Now he remains, and a grievous end awaits him, though innocent; or else I am carried along in vain..."

units.la: Vana feror, quod ut ô potius formidine falsa Ludar, et in meli⁹ tua, q potes, orsa reflectas.
units.tr: "...that I am deceived by a vain fear, and that you may turn to a better course the undertakings you are able to turn."

units.la: Ejusmodi syllogismus efficitur ê pro positione copulata negata, quę negata complexio dicitur:
units.tr: A syllogism of this kind is formed from a negated conjunctive proposition, which is called a negated complexion:

units.la: Non & dies est, & nox est:
units.tr: It is not the case that both it is day and it is night.

units.la: At dies est:
units.tr: But it is day.

units.la: Non igitur nox est.
units.tr: Therefore it is not night.

units.la: Secundus] Secundus modus non tam generalis est, quàm primus, quia certis & specialib. legibus astringitur: ideoq; postponitur primo, ut lex methodi requirit. Affirmata] Secus fit ἀσυλλόγιστον: ut, Aut decem poterunt, aut unus nō poterit: Sed unus non poterit: Ergo decem nō poterunt. Vero antecedente, falsa complexio hinc posset effici. Tollit] Specialis contradictio hic exigitur: secus si generalis contradictio concludatur, captiosum fit & ἀσυλλόγιστον: ut, Aliquod animal est irrationale, aut omne animal est rationale: Sed aliquod animal est irrationale: Ergo nullum animal est rationale: ex vero antecedente, falsa cöplexio efficietur. Quare necessaria est hic specialis contradictio. Aristoteles etiam 2. cap. 2. Top. hunc modum complexus est. Nam si docuerimus, ait, quòd inest alterum, docuerimus reliquū non inesse. Sed hęc Aristotelis definitio, etiam hoc uno peccat, quód neq; partes affirmatas, neq; specialem complexionis cōtra dictionem definit. Turno] Æneas motus Pallantis cæde à Turno interempti, exarsit cupiditate vindicandi amici: Itaq; magna hostium ftra ge ædita, Turno exitium afferebat: Quare juno periclitantis salutem á jove deprecatur, Quid] Præponitur quæstio, quæ deinde concludenda fit. Si] Optatio, qualis interdum hac conjunctione exprimitur 6. Æneid.
units.tr: Second: The second mode is not as general as the first, because it is bound by certain and special rules; therefore it is placed after the first, as the law of method requires. Affirmed: Otherwise it becomes a fallacious inference [ἀσυλλόγιστον], as in: "Either ten will be able, or one will not be able; but one will not be able; therefore ten will not be able." From a true antecedent, a false complexion could be produced in this way. Removes: Here a specific contradiction is required; otherwise, if a general contradiction is concluded, it becomes captious and fallacious [ἀσυλλόγιστον], as in: "Some animal is irrational, or every animal is rational; but some animal is irrational; therefore no animal is rational." From a true antecedent a false complexion would follow. Hence a specific contradiction is necessary here. Aristotle also described this mode in the second chapter of the second book of the Topics.
