For, he says, if we have shown that one of the two inheres, we have shown that the other does not inhere. But this definition of Aristotle errs in this one respect as well: it defines neither the affirmed parts nor the specific contradiction of the complexion. Turnus: Aeneas, moved by the slaughter of Pallas, who had been killed by Turnus, burned with desire to avenge his friend; and so, after a great slaughter of the enemy had been made, Turnus brought destruction. Therefore Juno, pleading for the safety of one in danger, entreats Jupiter. What: The question is put first, and is then to be concluded. If: An optative, of the kind sometimes expressed by this conjunction in the sixth book of the Aeneid:

units.la: Si nunc se nobis ille aureus arbore ramus Ostendat, nemore in tanto.
units.tr: If now that golden bough on its tree should show itself to us in that great grove.

units.la: Nunc] Propositio disjuncti, aut Turnus peribit, aut juno fallitur. Vana] Proprie vana veri, ut contrarium, plena veri. Sic 1. Georg.
units.tr: Now: The disjunctive proposition: either Turnus will perish, or Juno is deceived. Vain: Properly "vain" of truth, as the opposite is "full of truth." So in the first Georgic:

units.la: Expectata seges, vanis elapsa avenis. id est vacuis. Quod] Assumptio, cum profyllogismo optationis, At utinam juno potius fallatur. In melius] Sententia complexionis in hanc á textoribus allegoriam includitur. Ejusmodi] Negatu copulatum ex sese nullum syllogismu facit: sed hic vim disjunctionis obtinet, & præterea communius quiddam complectitur neq; partes hic affirmatas esse necesse est: ut, Non & homo est, & animal nō est. utrumlibet hic licet assumere, ut reliquum tollas: Sed homo est. Ergo animal est. vel, Sed animal non est: Ergo homo non est. Complexio] A Græcis interpretibus ad 22. cap. 1. Prior. dicitur ἀποφατικὴ συμπλοκή. Est autem genus hoc enuntiandi rarum, & quo nullum ex omnibus enūtiandi generibus sit distor tius, ut ait in Fato Cicero. Itaq; propter eas cortiones, hoc etiá syllogismi genus rarius erit.
units.tr: The expected crop, slipped away into empty oats, that is, empty ones. That: The assumption, with an optative prosyllogism: "But would that Juno were rather deceived." Into better: The sense of the complexion is enclosed by the commentators in this allegory. Of this kind: A negated conjunction does not by itself make any syllogism; but here it has the force of a disjunction, and moreover embraces something more general, and the parts here need not be affirmed, as in: "It is not the case both that a man is and that an animal is not." Either part may here be assumed in order to remove the other: "But a man is; therefore an animal is." Or: "But an animal is not; therefore a man is not." Complexion: Among the Greek interpreters, on the twenty-second chapter of the first Prior Analytics, this is called a negative conjunction [ἀποφατικὴ συμπλοκή]. This kind of statement is rare, and of all kinds of statement none is more distorted, as Cicero says in the De Fato. Therefore, because of these things, this kind of syllogism will also be rarer.

units.la: Atq; hæc de syllogismorum disjunctorum modis duobus, in quib. Theophrastus, Eudemus, Boetius, paulo partiores & frugaliores fuerūt, quám
units.tr: And so these are the two modes of disjunctive syllogisms, in which Theophrastus, Eudemus and Boethius were somewhat more sparing and economical than

units.la: quàm fuerant antea in connexis: Tametsi Boetius totidem modos & propositionum disjunctivarum, & syllogismorum disjunctivorum fieri posse putat, quot antea modi facti connexarum propositionum, & syllogismorum conexorum. Attamen neq; hîc decies millenos modos disjunctivarum propositionum, neq; septuaginta modos disjunctivorum syllogismorum collegit: contentus fuit quatuor modis propositionis disjunctivæ: & decem modis syllogismi disjunctivi: Nam cûm modis quatuor propositio disjunctiva varietur: ut, Aut est a, aut est b: Aut nô est a, aut nô est b: Aut est a, aut non est b: Aut nô est a, aut est b. è prima propositione utrinque affirmata, quatuor modos efficit, duos retinêdo alterutrum, duos tollêdo: é reliquis propositionibus binos efficit tollêdo alterutrum. At hos decem bellos modos duobus modis & breviùs & elegantiùs P. Ramus comprehendit, ut antea septuaginta modos illos pari binario comprehenderat. Sed hactenus de syllogismi & argumentationis generibus & differentiis, quibus adjecta sunt pro novis argumentationum generibus, inductio, exemplum, dilemma, sorites: quæ omnia in arte præterita sunt à P. Ramo, quia nullum catholicum præceptum adferant: Etenim (ut de tribus primis illis primùm dicam) tam sophisticum est & vitiosum, argumentorum genera pro argumentationum generibus in Logica proponere, quàm antea fuit, argumentationum formas pro simplicibus argumentis instituere. Aristotelis antea in figuris connexorum & disjunctorum syllogismorum
units.tr: they had been before in connected ones. Although Boethius thinks that as many modes of disjunctive propositions and disjunctive syllogisms can be made as there were earlier modes of connected propositions and connected syllogisms. Yet he has collected neither the ten thousand modes of disjunctive propositions nor the seventy modes of disjunctive syllogisms: he was content with four modes of disjunctive proposition and ten modes of disjunctive syllogism. For while the disjunctive proposition varies in four modes, as: "Either it is a, or it is b"; "Either it is not a, or it is not b"; "Either it is a, or it is not b"; "Either it is not a, or it is b." From the first proposition, with both parts affirmed, he makes four modes, retaining one or the other in two of them and removing one or the other in two; from the remaining propositions he makes two each by removing one or the other. But P. Ramus comprehends these ten fine modes more briefly and elegantly in two modes, just as he had earlier comprehended those seventy modes in an equal binary. But so far concerning the kinds and differences of syllogism and argumentation, to which have been added, as new kinds of argument, induction, example, dilemma and sorites. All of these have been passed over in the art by P. Ramus, because they bring no sound precept. For (to speak first of those first three) it is as sophistical and faulty to set out kinds of arguments as kinds of argumentation in Logic, as it was earlier to lay down forms of argumentation as simple arguments. Earlier, in Aristotle's treatment of the figures of connected and disjunctive syllogisms,

units.la: F rum elenchus hic fuit, dum pro topicis antecedentium, consequentium, oppositorū argumētorum categoriis, syllogisticas arguinétandi figuras interpretatur: nūc alter elēchus est, cūm pro syllogisticis argumentandi figuris, topicæ partium, speciei, oppositorū categoriæ demonstrantur: Inductio enim, & exemplum & dilemma, argumentorū illorū nomina sunt. De inductione, præcipitur 2⅓. cap. 2. Prior, quód é partibus totū colligat: ut, Omnis & homo & bestia est essentia: Omne igitur animal est efsétia. Hic si dispositionis & argumentationis species formaq; spectetur, nulla prorsus est nova. Enthymema est figurę apud Aristotelem primę: quod addita assumptione expletus syllogismus demonstrabit, hoc modo: Omnis & homo & bestia est essentia: Omne animal est homo bestiáve: Omne igitur animal est essentia. Tum verō quód author ille nescio quis argumentationis inductivæ ait in illo capite syllogismum differre ab inductione, quód inductio concludat majus extremum de medio per minus, ut in propositā inductione: syllogismus autem concludat majus de minore per medium: ut, Omne animal est essentia: Omnis & homo & bestia est animal: Omnis igitur homo bestiáve est essentia. Verū hæc differentia est valde ridicula & valdé falsa: Primó non omnis syllogismus concludit majus de minore per medium. Nullus enim syllogismus figuræ apud Aristotelem tertiæ sic concludit. Dein de cūm ex propriis agitur, ut definitione, subjecto, proprio, nil majus medium aut minus est: omnia sunt æqualia & reciproca. Postremo hęc differentia est argumenti, unde concluditur, nō est syllogisticę dispositionis: nullam enim novā concludendi figuram inductio requirit. & per hāc bellam Dialecticam, liceret ex omnibus argumentis fingere argumentandi species: Nā si à partibus ad totū species est argumentationis, & à toto ad partes, à genere ad speciem, à specie ad genus, à causa ad effectū, ab effectu ad causam, & à cæteris deniq; argumentis nova argumentandi species effet. Quare quisquis primus in logicas artes inductionem partium ad totū, pro nova argumentationis specie induxit, ignavum sophisma, nō catholicum dogma induxit. Itaq; P. Ramus inductionem ex agro logico nō tollit, sed in suo solo & naturali loco constituit. Exemplū simili sophismate venit in species argumentationis. Caput hic vicesimum quartum secundi Prior.consumptum est, quando medio extremū inest per simile tertio: ut, Bellum cum finitimis est perniciosum, ut Thebanorum contra Phocenses: At bellum Atheniensium contra Thebanos est bellum cum finitimis: Bellum igitur Atheniensium contra Thebanos est perniciosum. Hic propositionis profyllogismus est Aristoteli, per exemplū simile medio: at hoc exemplum nō est simile medio: sed est speciale: Similitudo enim hic nulla est: Exempla autem rebus generaliter propositis ita singularia solent adhibere: quomodo in specie topico ante declaratū est: Deniq; exemplum, argumenti nomen est, neque argumentationis aut syllogismi figuram,
units.tr: the refutation was this: while he explains the syllogistic figures of arguing by the topics of antecedent, consequent and opposite arguments; now there is another refutation, since the topical categories of parts, species and opposites are shown in place of the syllogistic figures of arguing. For induction, example and dilemma are names of those arguments. Concerning induction, it is laid down in the second chapter of the second Prior Analytics that it gathers the whole from the parts, as: "Every man and every beast is a substance; therefore every animal is a substance." If the form and kind of the arrangement and argumentation is examined here, it is not new at all. The enthymeme is the first figure in Aristotle, which, with an added assumption, will show a complete syllogism, in this way: "Every man and every beast is a substance; every animal is man or beast; therefore every animal is a substance." Then again, that author, whoever he is, says in that chapter that a syllogism differs from induction in that induction concludes the major extreme from the middle through the minor, as in the induction proposed; but a syllogism concludes the major from the minor through the middle, as: "Every animal is a substance; every man and every beast is an animal; therefore every man or beast is a substance." But this difference is very ridiculous and very false. First, not every syllogism concludes the major from the minor through the middle; for no syllogism of the third figure in Aristotle concludes in this way. Next, when we argue from proper things, as from definition, subject, property, there is no major or minor middle: all things are equal and reciprocal. Lastly, this difference belongs to the argument from which the conclusion is drawn, and is not a matter of syllogistic arrangement: for induction requires no new figure of concluding. And by this fine dialectic it would be permissible to invent kinds of argumentation from all arguments: for if a kind of argumentation is from parts to whole, and from whole to parts, from genus to species, from species to genus, from cause to effect, from effect to cause, and finally from the other arguments, there would be a new kind of arguing from each. Therefore whoever first introduced into the logical arts induction from parts to whole as a new kind of argumentation introduced a lazy sophism, not a sound doctrine. So P. Ramus does not remove induction from the logical field, but places it in its own soil and natural place. Example has come into the kinds of argumentation by a similar sophism. The twenty-fourth chapter of the second Prior Analytics is concluded here, where the extreme is in the middle through something similar to the third: "War with neighbours is destructive, as the war of the Thebans against the Phocians; but the war of the Athenians against the Thebans is a war with neighbours; therefore the war of the Athenians against the Thebans is destructive." Here Aristotle's prosyllogism of the proposition is by a similar example for the middle; but this example is not similar to the middle, but is particular: for there is no likeness here. Examples are usually adduced in this way, singular for generally proposed things, as was explained earlier in the topical kind. Finally, example is the name of an argument, and signifies neither a figure of argumentation nor of syllogism, nor an arrangement or order; and it is as foolish to set up a kind of argumentation in an example as in an induction. Therefore, concerning example, P. Ramus has said what is to be said in Logic in its proper place; it is not sophistically repeated at a foreign time among the rules of judgement.

units.la: F 2 dispositionem, ordinem significat: tamq; fatua res est, argumentationis speciem in exemplo, quàm in inductione statuere. Quare de exéplo dictum est à P. Ramo suo loco, quod in Logica dicendum fit: in judicii regulis alieno tempore sophisticè non iteratur: deniq; in familiarem & naturalem locum restituitur. Dilemma cõsimili sophismatis elencho, pro nova argumentationis specie acceptum est:ut enim inductio à partibus,exemplum à specie: sic dilemma à contràriis medio caretibus argumentũ est: & ut inductio & exemplũ,assumptione ὑπυμνηματικῶς cõclu di solet:ut Martialis est illud ad Domitianũ li.2.
units.tr: F 2 It signifies arrangement or order, and it is a foolish thing to set up a species of argument in the example rather than in induction. Hence P. Ramus rightly discussed the example in its own place, where it belongs in Logic; in the rules of judgement it is not repeated out of place as a sophism, and it is finally restored to its familiar and natural place. The dilemma, which resembles the sophistical elenchus, has been accepted as a new species of argument. For just as induction is an argument from parts and the example an argument from a species, so the dilemma is an argument from contraries that have no middle, and, like induction and the example, it is usually concluded by a restatement [ὑπομνηματικῶς], as in Martial's lines to Domitian, book 2:

units.la: Hæc,si displicui, fuerint solatia nobis:
units.tr: "If I have displeased you, let these be our consolations;"

units.la: Hæc fuerint nobis præmia,si placui.
units.tr: "let these be our rewards, if I have pleased."

units.la: Adde huic propositioni assumptionem:
units.tr: Add to this proposition an assumption:

units.la: Sed placui aut displicui.
units.tr: "But I have either pleased or displeased."

units.la: Tum conclude:
units.tr: Then conclude:

units.la: Quare solatia erunt,vel præmia,quæ dabis,
units.tr: "Therefore the things you will give will be consolations or rewards."

units.la: Atq; in cornutũ argumentandi genus quidã arbitrantur esse,quia duobus utrinq; veluti cornibus feriat. Dilemma igitur, ut inductio, ut exemplũ, nullam novam argumentationis figurã docet,sed argumenti speciem indicat. Itaq; concludebat hoc loco P.Ramus,Topicã & Criticã, duas Logicæ partes diversas esse : Argumetum in Topica, argumentationem in Critica docendam esse & declarandam. Qui judicii & dispositionis regulas in locis invētionis proponit, peccat in legë methodi, quia posterius naturâ priore loco constituit:contrá qui locos inventionis in judicii regulis proponit, in pari vitio est, qa natura prius, posteriore loco praecipit: At qui tradit pro argumentis argumentationes (ut in connexis & disjunctis factum est) quiq; pro argumentationibus argumenta (ut nunc fit in inductione, exemplo, dilemmate) no tantum methodum pervertit, sed in κατὰ πάντως turpiter offendit. Sorites vero progressio est enthymematica: ac qua minutatim ac gradatim addit, & paulatim, veluti congestis granis, acervum efficit, σωρείτης, acervalis appellatur: ut, Socrates est homo: Homo est animal: Animal est substantia: Ergo Socrates est substantia. Hic duo sunt enthymemata: priori complexio deest: ut, Animal est substantia: Homo est animal. Complexio .n. (Homo igitur est substantia) non exprimitur. Posteriori deest assumptio: Animal est substantia: Ergo Socrates est substantia. Assumptio enim (Socrates est animal) praeterita est. Saepe autem sorites una multis gradibus connexa propositione continetur: Itaq; sorites in rebus inter se necessario connexis utiliter inventus est: quod in longioribus mathematicis demonstrationibus, magnum plerunq; compendium attulerit: sed in ceteris etiam rerum generibus valet: ut 3. Off. Atq; si etiam hoc natura praescribit, ut homo homini, quicunq; fit, ob eam ipsam causam, quod is homo fit, cofultum velit: necesse est secundum eandem naturam, omnium utilitatem esse communem. quod si ita est, una continentur omnes & eadem lege naturae: idq; ipsum si ita est, certe violare alterum lege naturę prohibemur. Verum autem primum: verum igitur & extremum. Hic syl-
units.tr: Some think it is a kind of horned manner of arguing, because it strikes on both sides as with two horns. The dilemma, then, like induction and the example, teaches no new figure of argument but indicates a kind of argument. So P. Ramus here concluded that Topic and Critic are two different parts of Logic: argument is to be taught and explained in Topic, argumentation in Critic. Whoever sets out the rules of judgement and arrangement among the places of invention sins against the law of method, because he puts what is naturally prior in a later position. Conversely, whoever puts the places of invention among the rules of judgement is at fault in the same way, because he teaches what is naturally prior in a later place. But whoever hands down arguments as if they were argumentations (as was done with connexives and disjunctives), or argumentations as if they were arguments (as is now done with induction, example and dilemma), not only pervertes the method but offends shamefully in every respect [κατὰ πάντως]. The sorites, however, is an enthymematic progression, which adds little by little and step by step, and gradually, like grains piled together, makes a heap; it is called the acervalis [σωρείτης]. For example: Socrates is a man; a man is an animal; an animal is a substance; therefore Socrates is a substance. Here there are two enthymemes. In the first, the complexion is missing: Animal is a substance; man is an animal. The complexion (therefore man is a substance) is not expressed. In the second, the assumption is missing: Animal is a substance; therefore Socrates is a substance. For the assumption (Socrates is an animal) is left out. Often, however, a sorites is contained in a single proposition connected through many steps. Hence the sorites has been usefully devised for things that are necessarily connected with one another, since in longer mathematical demonstrations it has usually brought great economy. But it holds also for other kinds of things, as in Cicero's De Officiis 3: "And if nature also prescribes this, that one man should wish well to another, whoever he is, for the very reason that he is a man, then it is necessary, according to the same nature, that the advantage of all is common. If this is so, all are bound together by one and the same law of nature; and if this is so, we are certainly forbidden by the law of nature to harm one another. But the first is true; therefore the last is true too." Here the syllogism is a connexive of the first mode, whose proposition has a sorites of four steps; but it could have more steps and be assumed and concluded in another way. Indeed, a sorites within a single syllogistic proposition sometimes takes in many arguments, as in the discussion of Fate: "If the cause of appetite is not placed in us, then appetite itself is not in our power. If that is so, then not even those things that are brought about by appetite are placed in us. Therefore neither assents nor actions are in our power. From this it follows that neither just praises nor blames, nor honours, nor punishments are just. Since this is faulty, they think it is probably concluded that not everything that happens happens by fate." Here the syllogism is a connexive of the second mode, whose proposition has a sorites of five steps, of which the fourth and fifth are connected enthymematically. So no art here is new, and the sorites does not produce a new species of argument; yet the use of a sorites of gradation is dangerous unless the things cohere firmly with one another. P. Ramus discussed the sorites in this way, which is why he passed it over together with induction, example and dilemma.

units.la: logisf. logisimus est conexus primi modi, cujus propositio soritem habet quatuor graduum: possit autem & graduum compluriū haberi, & alio modo assumi concludiq;. Quin sorites in una syllogismi propositione, capit interdum argumentationes multas. ut de Fato, At si caussa appetitus nō est sita in nobis neipse quidem appetitus est in nostra potestate. quod si ita est:ne illa quidē, quæ appetitu efficiuntur,sita in nobis sunt. Nō igitur neq; assensiones, neq; actiones,in nostra potestate. Ex quo efficitur, ut neq; laudationes justæ sint,nec vituperationes,nec honores,nec supplicia. Quod quū vitiosum sit, probabiliter cocludi putant,non omnia fieri fato,quæcunq; fiant. Hic syllogismus est connexus modi secundi,cujus ppositio sorité habet quinq; graduū: quorū quartus & quintus,enthymematicé connectītur. Quare ars nulla hic nova est:neq; novam speciem argumentationis sorites efficit,& tamé gradationis sorticæ captio periculosa sit, nisi res firmé cohæreant inter se. Hęc P.Ramus de sorite differebat, cur ab eo cum inductione, exemplo, dilemmate pręteriretur:Quapropter habemus adhuc in P. Rami agricultura logicá syllogistici judicii doctrinam maximis & gravi simis impedimentis liberatam, & quidé quæ ad huc calumnia caruerit: in primo illo enuntiati indicio-leges κατὰ παντὸς, καθ' αὐτὸ, καθόλε πρῶτον ἀ quibusdam si nō aperté improbantur, certę malitiose eluduntur:at syllogismi constantiam,qui inficiari aut elevare auderet, nemo(quod sciá) extitit,sed logicá syllogismi á P. Ramo strenuē vindicatâ habemus: imò verò singula i judicio descriptâ & explicatam: ut si Logici veteres illi, unde Aristoteles tâ multa in duos libros prioris Analyseos coduxit, Logicû agrum sic aratû satumq;, sicundiq; lætissimis frugibus nitentê & luxuriâtem videant, agnoscât sui generis atque ordinis aratorem, plerisq; inertibus agricolis & diligentiorem, & melioribus certé instrumétis instructioré: Aristoteles verò, legû suarû logicum diligentissimum, retinentissimû, amâtissimum cõfiteatur, qui tot annos tanto tamq; pertinaci & indefatigato studio nunquâ desuerit, non modò in cæteros omnes, sed in seipsum acerrimé ac vehementissimé inquirere: neq; antè unquâ conquieverit, quâm opus inchoatû, aut perfectum, aut certé affectum reliquerit.
units.tr: For this reason we still have, in P. Ramus's logical husbandry, the doctrine of syllogistic judgement freed from the greatest and most serious impediments, and one that has so far escaped calumny. The laws of "of every" [κατὰ παντὸς], "per se" [καθ' αὐτὸ], and "universal first" [καθόλου πρῶτον], which some openly reject and others maliciously mock in that first indication of judgement, have not been dismissed, but the constancy of the syllogism, which no one (as far as I know) has dared to deny or diminish, has been vigorously vindicated by P. Ramus. Indeed, each thing has been described and explained in the judgement. If those old logicians, from whom Aristotle drew so much into the two books of the Prior Analytics, could see the field of Logic so ploughed and sown, and flourishing and luxuriant with the most joyful crops, they would acknowledge a ploughman of their own kind and order, more diligent than most idle farmers and certainly better equipped with better tools. And Aristotle, the most diligent, most retentive and most devoted logician of his own laws, would confess that for so many years, with such persistent and tireless study, he never ceased to inquire most keenly and vehemently not only of all others but of himself, and never rested before leaving the work either begun, or completed, or at least carried forward.

units.la: Cap. XVI. De Methodo secundum Aristotelem unica.
units.tr: Chapter 16. On the single method according to Aristotle.

units.la: METHODUS est dispositio, qua de multis enûtiatis homogeneis, suoq; vel syllogismi judicio notis, disponitur primo loco absoluta notione primû, secundo secundû, tertio tertiû, & ita deinceps: ideoq; ab universalib. ad singularia perpetuó progreditur. Hac enim sola & unica via proceditur ab antecedentib. omnino & absolutè notioribus, ad consequentia ignota declarandû. eamq; solam Methodum Aristoteles docuit.
units.tr: Method is an arrangement by which, among many homogeneous statements that are known by their own judgement or by that of the syllogism, the first is placed first, the notion that is absolutely first; the second is placed second, and the third third, and so on. Therefore it always proceeds from universals to singulars. For this is the one and only way in which one proceeds from antecedents that are wholly and absolutely better known to consequents that are unknown, so that they may be made clear. And this is the only method that Aristotle taught.

units.la: F 4 Methos
units.tr: F 4 Methos

units.la: Methodus] E secúdo judicii genere, species altera in syllogismo declarata est, superest altera, in methodo. Cujus definitionem tanquam legē logicarum artis informandæ legum longissimé principē, dies aliquot P. Ramus in regia cathedra, tâquam publica logicorum undiq; excitorum cócione suasit. Meminimus quanto studio Ariftotelea trium superiorū de artis materia legum suafio celebrata fit, & quot locis ab Arifto tele repetita: Meminimus quanto studio aurea syllogismi regula ab infinitis elechis vindicata fit: attamen materies illa methodi tantum fuit. Quantum verò studium methodo, id est formę artium omnium, & tanquam animæ debitū ar- bitramur. Ergo hac extrema perorationè in primis ingenii atq; industriæ vires P. Ramus excitavit, ad legem legum omnium maximé legitimam, maximeq; omnibus artibus salutarem de monstrandum, promulgandum, suadendum, fe rendum: & quidem ad Ariftotelis summam gloriam, ut quicquid in antecedētibus logicæ partibus ab Ariftotele fit offensum, abundé tamen fit cum methodi præstātia atq; excellentia com pensatum. Itaq; hac in extrema parte certamen est P. Ramo adversus Aristoteleorū sophisticas ineptias & nugas ,p Ariftotelis singulari laude & gloria: Sigillatim igitur parte unamquamq; persequamur. Dispositio] Definitio methodi colligitur é genere primū: Dispositio enim, genus est universi logici judicii, cujus duo genera sacta, primum enuntiatum, & secundum sine nomine, fuit genus syllogismi & methodi. Itaq; si genus hoc notum & nominatū esset, adhiberetur in hac definitione:sed inopia proximi,adhibetur proximo vicinum. Meminerimus igitur methodū esse dispositionem,nō esse rem dispositionis propositā, ut est semper argumetum,ali quando etiam enūtiatum & syllogismus: Argumentum enim res simplex & nuda cōsideratur: Enuntiatum est dispositio argumentorum : sed ipsum rursus disponi pót,ut in syllogismo : Syllogismus dispositio est enūtiatorū , sed ipsemet etiā disponi pót, ut in methodo. Nec veró nos moveat,quód fieri possit, ut methodȝ etiā quedam teneri possit in syllogismo ut ꝓpositio generalis prima sit,assumptio inde orta subsequatur,complexio ex utraq; fit extrema. Nam neq; id in syllogismo est perpetuum:ut in tertia Aristotelis figura,ut etiam in prima. ubi tam potest ex speciebus de genere,quám ex genere de speciebus concludi.nec in syllogismo atteditur dispositio absolutè prioris & notioris, sed arguméti sic vel sic antecedētis vel cósequentis. Atque ut de argumentis antea dictū est, in unā & eádem rem subjectam posse cadere:sic de syllogismo & methodo respódebis,in uno & eodem exemplo utrumque posse deprehendi,rationes tamen & definitiones distinctas esse : aliudque esse syllogismi,aliud methodi ordinem & dispositionem sequi. Quare syllogismus etiam materia erit methodi: at methodus dispositio est omnium dispositionum ultima, ultra quam dispositio alia in logicis nulla est. Itaq; Aristoteles,Cicero, Quintilianus in Rhetoricis, cúm disposi-tiotionem faciunt secundam Rhetoricæ partem, συνδοχικὴς nomine dispositionis intelligunt nō enuntiatum, non syllogismum, sed methodum. Quapropter methodi genus nobis erit dispositio. De enuntiatis] Argumenta nuda absque enuntiatis in usu nulla sunt, ut patuit, nec eorum simplicium ulla methodus esse potest: Nam tametsi in nudis partitionum tabulis (quales vulgo ab artium magistris fieri solet) videatur methodus adhiberi: illic tamen enuntiata é verbo aliquo intelligi necesse est: secus nulla sententia conciperetur. Meminerimus igitur materiâ methodo propositam in enuntiatis esse, eorumq; multorum unam perpetuamq; formam esse methodum. Homogeneis] Ars omnis constat ex homogeneis, ut antea já dictū est in lege καθ' αὑτὸ: ut essent præcepta uno & eodem genere cōpre hensa, ut etiam é generalibus & antecedentib9 rationes ad subalternas artes deduci possent ut à logica in mathematicas omnes, ab arithmetica in musicā, & reliquas: & geometria in omnes artes geometricis figuris innexas: quæstionem autem quamlibet unam continentia enuntiata, sunt item quodammodo homogenea: Itaq; quæ in tota vel Iliade, vel Æneide, quæ in qualibet Demosthenis aut Ciceronis Philippica, sunt enuntiata, ea sunt homogenea: si non absoluta illa, & ante definita ratione, certè hactenus, dum finem eūdem respiciunt. ὑπόθεσις siquidem, etiam á poetis in poemate reprehensa est: quamvis poetis multo justior licētia sit: Notum enim est Horatii præceptum:
units.tr: Methodus: The second kind of judgement has been explained in the syllogism; the other species remains, in method. Its definition, as the law that most of all governs the forming of the art of logic, P. Ramus recommended for several days from the royal chair, as a public sermon of logicians gathered from every side. We remember with what zeal the persuasion concerning the matter of the art, the three earlier laws of Aristotle, was celebrated, and how often it was repeated from Aristotle; we remember with what zeal the golden rule of the syllogism was defended against countless refutations. Yet that matter was only the matter of method. But how much zeal is owed to method, that is, to the form of all the arts and, as it were, their soul? Therefore, in this final peroration P. Ramus has roused the powers of his wit and industry, to demonstrate, promulgate, recommend and bring forward the law of all laws, the most lawful and the most useful to all the arts. And indeed this is for the highest glory of Aristotle, so that whatever has been found offensive in Aristotle in the preceding parts of logic may be more than made up for by the excellence and pre-eminence of method. Accordingly, in this final part P. Ramus contends against the sophistical absurdities and trifles of the Aristotelians, with Aristotle's singular praise and glory. Let us therefore pursue each part separately. Dispositio: The definition of method is gathered from its genus, first. For arrangement is the genus of all logical judgement; of its two kinds, the first, the statement, and the second, which has no name, were made, the genus of the syllogism and of method. So if this genus were known and named, it would be used in this definition; but for lack of the nearest term, a neighbouring one is used. Let us remember, then, that method is an arrangement, not a thing proposed for arrangement, as an argument always is, and sometimes also a statement or a syllogism. For an argument is considered as a simple and bare thing; a statement is an arrangement of arguments; but it in turn can be arranged, as in the syllogism. The syllogism is an arrangement of statements, but it too can be arranged, as in method. Nor should it trouble us that method can also be found in some way in the syllogism, when the general premise comes first, the assumption follows from it, and the conclusion is formed from both. For this is not constant in the syllogism, either in the third figure of Aristotle or in the first, where a conclusion may be drawn from species to genus as well as from genus to species. Nor in the syllogism is an arrangement regarded as absolutely prior and better known, but as this or that antecedent or consequent of the argument. And just as was said earlier about arguments, that the same thing can fall under one and the same subject, so you will answer about the syllogism and method: in one and the same example both can be detected, yet their rationes and definitions are distinct; and it is one thing for the syllogism to follow an order, and another for method to follow an order and arrangement. Wherefore the syllogism will also be the matter of method; but method is the last of all arrangements, beyond which there is no other arrangement in logic. Accordingly Aristotle, Cicero and Quintilian in their rhetorics, when they make arrangement the second part of rhetoric, by the name of [συνδοχικὴς] of arrangement understand not the statement, not the syllogism, but method. Therefore for us the genus of method will be arrangement. De enuntiatis: Bare arguments without statements are of no use, as has been shown, nor can there be any method of such simple things; for although method seems to be applied in bare tables of divisions (such as are commonly made by teachers of the arts), yet in them the statements must be understood from some word, or else no sense would be conceived. Let us remember, then, that the matter proposed to method lies in statements, and that method is the one and constant form of many of them. Homogeneis: Every art consists of homogeneous things, as was said above under the law per se [καθ' αὑτὸ]: so that the precepts are comprehended in one and the same genus, and so that reasons can be deduced from general and antecedent things to subordinate arts, as from logic to all the mathematical arts, from arithmetic to music and the rest, and from geometry to all the arts bound to geometrical figures. Statements that contain any one question are also in some way homogeneous. Accordingly, what are statements in the whole of the Iliad or the Aeneid, or in any Philippic of Demosthenes or Cicero, are homogeneous, if not by that absolute and previously defined reasoning, at least so far as they look to the same end. For hypothesis [ὑπόθεσις] has also been blamed in poems by the poets, although the poets have a far more just licence. For the precept of Horace is well known:

units.la: Humano capiti cervicem pictor equinam jungere si velit, & varias inducere plumas, Undiq; collatis membris, ut turpiter atrum Desinat in piscem mulier formosa superne: Spectatum admissi risum teneatis amici?
units.tr: If a painter should wish to join a horse's neck to a human head, and to spread varied feathers over limbs gathered from everywhere, so that a fair woman above ends shamefully in a black fish, could you, my friends, hold back your laughter at the sight?

units.la: Credite Pisones, isti tabulae fore librum Persimilem, cujus velut aegri somnia, vanae Fingentur species, ut nec pes, nec caput uni Reddatur formae.
units.tr: Believe me, Pisos, that a book like that will be like a picture, whose dreams, as of a sick man, are feigned as empty images, so that neither foot nor head is given to one form.

units.la: Pauloq; post ita concluditur:
units.tr: A little after, he concludes thus:

units.la: Deniq; sit quodvis, simplex duntaxat, & unum.
units.tr: In short, let whatever it is be simple at least, and one.

units.la: Notis] Enuntiata, quae methodo collocanda proponuntur, necesse est ante esse nota, id est, explorata & judicata suo vel syllogismi judicio: Quid enim ordinem ignotorum quaereres? aut cur praeteritis antecedentibus judiciis, extremum hoc arriperes? Quare pars haec ultima Logicae artis, proponit sibi universalem formam & exae dificationem summa rerum, de quibus in antecedentibus logicae partibus agitur, statuitq; sibi res inventas homogeneas, judicatas etiam separatim enuntiato, vel syllogismo, ad collocandum & disponendum. Neque porro exististimandum, ut quibusdam videtur, P. Rami placitum hic agi: tanquam haec aliqua nova sit hypothesis, Potulare in methodo, ut res inventae & judicatae sint, antequam methodice disponantur. Haec enim est naturae hypothesis, haec Platonis, Aristotelis, Ciceronis, Quintiliani, omnium denique, qui unquam de hoc ordine praeceperunt, hypothesis est: ut inventio antecedat, judicium & dispositio sequatur: Tum vero e judicii partibus, prima fit enuntiati doctrina, necesse est: secunda syllogismi: tertia methodi: nec ad extremum, nisi a primis per media, perveniri potest. Materies igitur (ut perspicue concludam) per methodum formanda & collocanda est in enuntiatis homogeneis & notis.
units.tr: Notis: The statements that are proposed to be placed in method must necessarily be known beforehand, that is, tested and judged by their own judgement or that of the syllogism. For why would you seek the order of unknowns, or why, passing over the earlier judgements, would you seize upon this last point? Therefore this final part of the art of logic proposes for itself the universal form and the building up of the sum of the things that the preceding parts of logic treat of, and it takes for itself the discovered things, which are homogeneous and judged separately by statement or syllogism, to be placed and arranged. Nor should we suppose, as some think, that P. Ramus's opinion is being debated here, as if this were some new hypothesis: namely, that in method things should be discovered and judged before they are methodically arranged. For this is the hypothesis of nature; it is the hypothesis of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, Quintilian, and of all who have ever given precepts about this order: that invention goes before, and judgement and arrangement follow. Then indeed, of the parts of judgement, the doctrine of the statement must come first, the syllogism second, and method third; nor can one arrive at the last except from the first through the middle ones. Matter, therefore (to conclude clearly), is to be formed and placed by method in homogeneous and known statements.

units.la: Absoluta] Magna philosophia est de comparatione cognitarum rerum, utra de duabus notior, quae de pluribus notissima, ut in methodico ordine notior praecedat ignotiorem: Quae quaestio ex antecedentibus categoriis & topicis argumentorum repetenda nobis est, & e judicio Aristotelis inprimis explicanda: illinc enim optime verissimeque judicabitur. De causis igitur, materia materiato, efficiens effecto, itemque forma formato, notior & clarior est, denique etiam finis finito, sicut antea ex Aristotele dictum est. Quare causa omnino & absolute causato (ut ita dicam) notior est & clarior: subjecto item quodammodo notius est proprio adjuncto: ut etiam ex Aristotele patuit: Sic causa & effectum consentanea ἀπλῶς antea facta sunt: subjectum & adjunctum, ϖῆ. Dissentanea autem & comparata sunt aeque nota: reliqua de illis, parentum (a quibus procreantur) natura referunt. Quare si vere ratiocinari judicareque ex illa Aristotelis philosophia volumus, duobus modis aliud alio notius & illustrius erit, causa & subjecto: sed quod per causam notius & illustrius est, proprie absolute notius est & illustrius. Itaque Aristoteles ex eodem illo causarum loco, tanquam prima claritatis luce, definit 2. ca. 1. Post. Scire esse per caussam nolle propter quam res est.indeq; methodi ordine deducit,quód omnis scientia progrediatur à caussis primis & immediatis, tanquam à rebus clarissimis & notissimis. Sed eodem loco,notius duobus modis dividitur, nobis & naturà:Priora veró & notiora dupliciter, ait Aristoteles:Non enim idem prius naturá,& ad nos prius:neque notius, & nobis notius.Dico quidem ad nos priora & notiora,quæ sensui viciniora sunt, absolutè autè priora & notiora,quæ remotiora. Sunt autè remotissima universalia maximé:proxima autem singularia.& hæc opponuntur inter se.Hic locus Aristotelis ostè dit generalia & universalia absolutè notiora esse. Sed addit specialia esse notiora nobis, quiapropiús accedunt ad sensum. Quod idem repetitur ȝ.ca. 6,Top. quód aliud fit notius nobis, aliud absolutè:quod nobis aliás alia magis nota: Rudioribus enim sensilia notiora,peritioribus autem,contrá. Sed Aristoteles idem eodem capite seipsum interpretatur:& hoc discrimen,no bis,& absolutè: & absolutè dicit notū, quod est nobis mente bene affectis notum. Fortasse autem etiam absolutè notum est,ait philosophus, non quod omnibus est notum,sed quod mentebene cöpositis:veluti absolutè salubre bene habentibus corpore. Hac igitur sententia Aristotelis,non solúm absolutè , sed etiam nobis animo atque ingenio bene affectis,id est bene noscentibus generalia atque universalia sunt notiora. Eadem notionis differentia,imó eadē differentiæ caussa in Philosophia 1. ca.2.lib. pauló secùs dedemóstratur. Fortasse etiam cum difficultas sit duplex, non in rebus, sed in nobis caussa ipsius est: ut enim vespertilionū oculi ad diurnum lumen habent, sic & mēs animæ nostrę,ad ea quę clarissima omnium sunt natură.Itaq; uniuersalia per se clariora,singularia autem,nostrę imbe cilitati, idem 11.cap.ʒ.lib.in philosophia proponitur: Priora notione esse alia secundúm rationem, & alia secundùm sensum: secundúm ratio nem universalia:secundúm sensum, singularia. Verúm totum hoc intelligentiæ & cognitionis discrimē iteratur 4.ca.ʒ. Eth.ad Nicomachum, Voluntati subjeᴄtum bonū dicitur, non quod cuique appareat,sed quod absoluté & secūdúm veritatem bonum sit, quód q; viro bono tale ap pareat,qui rectė iudicat de singulis: cúm sit velut regula ipsorum ac mēsura.ut corporibus be ne affectis (ait) salubria, q revera salubria sunt, talia apparent.Deniq; ut absolutė bona bonis, absosuté sana sanis, sic absoluté notiora nobis mente bene affectis notiora sunt.Hæ similes Aristotelis collationes,sensum habét apertū. Idē notius esse nobis & naturâ, & Aristoteleos ne- scio quos de sua ptinatia monere debeát. Quare si me interroges de duobus in arte enútiatis utrū præcedere debeat : respondebo,ex Aristo telis sententia,quód notius absoluté evidétiusque sit,id est quod caussam,vel subjeᴄtum cótineat sequentis.Sic igitur methodicæ legis definitio á P. Ramo ad Aristotelis gloriam explicabatur:addebatur etiá notatio nominis : ex quo præcipue á cupidis hominibus, neq; satis rerū peritis, controversiæ infinitæ excitátur: ὁδὸς viâ significat: hinc μέθοδος, breve compendiū Quintiliano dicitur: Ciceroni ratio & via: quomodo jam vulgó in Scholis methodi nomen percrebuit apud interpretes Græcos Latinosq; : quia methodus nos deducat via compédiaria ad cognitionem artium rerumq; hoc ordine dispositarum, cúm perpetua serie appareat velut ante oculos suo loco quidque collocatum. Sic Philoponus ad 1.ca.1.Physici: μέθοδός ἐστιν ἕξις ὁδοποιητικὴ τινὰ μετὰ λόγου: methodus est habitus viam faciès cum ratione: Alexáder feré idem, sed paulò obscurius: Philoponi ὁδοποιητικὸν illud, præsentis ςp grefsionis viam magis ostendit. Itaque licet methodi vocabulum, quodlibet & argumēti, & docendi, & disputationis genus significet: attamē significatio certa hic definita & explicata est á P.Ramo, quá in hac parte Logicę sequitur. Itaq; etiam atq; etiam hic admonemur, in tantę lucis perspicuitate, tenebras malitiosé affectádas nō esse: nec enim dubitatio já ulla potest esse, quid methodi nomine, & quam Dialecticæ partę P. Ramus comprehendat: rem definit definitione illustri & præclara: nominis etiam rationem reddit, idoneis & locupletibus authoribus affirma tam. Methodus invētionis hic nulla agitur: tradita enim est primo libro amplissimè, quomodo & artes & res omnino oēs sint inveniendæ, tradita etiá in distributionis loco via, quá sine arte artes primó observatione & inductione essent inventæ: methodus inquá inventionis vel artium vel cuiuscunq; argumenti hic nulla agitur, ne quis hallucinetur in hac quæstione, quæ præcipua à scholasticis hominibus P. Ramo, ut postea patebit, molestia est: neque item methodus ulla vel enuntiati vel syllogismi hic agitur: tota enim hęc doctrina præcessit. Methodus disponendæ materiæ & inventæ suis partibus omnibus & perfectionibus etiam quaque declarantur explicatæ, æstimatæ, judicatæ: methodus (inquam) dispositionis universalis, generalis, totá variorum enuntiatorum & etiam syllogismorum formam complectentis agitur.
units.tr: Absolute Philosophy has long debated how known things compare: which of two is better known, and which of many is best known, so that in methodical order the better known comes before the less known. This question must be drawn from the earlier categories and the topics of arguments, and explained chiefly from Aristotle's judgement, for it is from there that it will be judged best and most truly. Thus causes are better known and clearer than what they cause: matter than what is formed from it, efficient cause than effect, and likewise form than what is formed, and finally end than what is ended, as was said earlier from Aristotle. Hence a cause is better known and clearer than its effect absolutely and, as I may say, without qualification. Likewise the subject is in some respect better known than its proper attribute, as was also shown from Aristotle. So cause and effect were earlier treated as simply [ἀπλῶς], and subject and attribute as in some respect [πῇ]. Things that are opposed or compared are equally known, and the rest of this concerns the nature of the parents from whom they are born. Therefore, if we wish to reason and judge truly by that philosophy of Aristotle, one thing will be better known and clearer than another in two ways, by cause and by subject; but what is better known and clearer through its cause is properly and absolutely better known and clearer. So Aristotle, from that same place on causes, as from the first light of clarity, defines in the second book of the Posterior Analytics, chapter 1, that to know is to know through the cause on account of which a thing is. From this he deduces, in the order of method, that all science proceeds from first and immediate causes, as from things most clear and best known. But in the same place he divides "better known" in two ways, for us and by nature. Aristotle says that things are prior and better known in two ways: for what is prior by nature is not the same as what is prior for us, nor what is better known absolutely the same as what is better known to us. I say indeed that those things are prior and better known to us which are nearer to the senses, but those are prior and better known absolutely which are more remote. The most remote things are universals, and the nearest are singulars, and these are opposed to each other. This passage of Aristotle shows that the general and universal are better known absolutely. But he adds that the particular is better known to us, because it comes nearer to sense. The same is repeated in the sixth chapter of the Topics: one thing is better known to us, another absolutely, since sensible things are better known to the less skilled, but the reverse to the more skilled. Yet Aristotle interprets himself in the same chapter, and says that this distinction, to us and absolutely, is that what is absolutely known is what is known to those whose minds are well disposed. Perhaps, the philosopher says, something is also known absolutely not because it is known to all, but because it is known to those whose minds are well constituted, just as what is absolutely healthy is healthy to those whose bodies are in good condition. By this opinion of Aristotle, then, the general and universal are better known not only absolutely but also to us whose judgement and wit are well disposed, that is, to those who know them well. The same difference of notion, indeed the same cause of the difference, is shown a little differently in the first chapter of the second book of the Physics. Perhaps also, since the difficulty is twofold, its cause lies not in things but in us: for as the eyes of bats are adapted to daylight, so the minds of our souls are adapted to those things which are by nature the clearest of all. Hence the same chapter of the eleventh book of Physics (?) proposes that universals are clearer in themselves, and singulars are clearer to our weakness: that some things are prior in notion according to reason and others according to sense; universals according to reason, singulars according to sense. But this whole distinction of understanding and knowledge is repeated in the third chapter of the fourth book of the Nicomachean Ethics: the good that is the object of the will is said to be not what appears to each person, but what is good absolutely and according to truth; and what appears such to the good man, who judges each thing rightly, since he is as it were the rule and measure of them. Just as (he says) wholesome things appear to bodies in good condition, and really are wholesome, so the absolutely good appear good to good men, and the absolutely healthy to the healthy; thus things absolutely better known are better known to us whose minds are well disposed. These similar comparisons of Aristotle have an obvious sense. That what is better known is so both by nature and to us, I do not know what Aristotelian obstinacy should warn anyone about. Therefore, if you ask me which of two statements in an art ought to come first, I will answer, according to Aristotle's opinion, that what is absolutely better known and more evident is the one that contains the cause or subject of what follows. Thus the definition of the methodical law was explained by P. Ramus to the glory of Aristotle. To this was added an etymology of the name, from which infinite controversies are stirred up, especially by eager men who lack sufficient knowledge of things. Hodos [ὁδὸς] signifies way; hence method [μέθοδος] is called by Quintilian a short cut, and by Cicero a plan and way; and so the name of method has now become common in the schools among Greek and Latin interpreters, because method leads us by a short way to the knowledge of arts and things arranged in this order, since in a continuous series each thing appears placed in its own place, as if before our eyes. So Philoponus, on the first chapter of the first book of the Physics: method is a habit making a way with reason [μέθοδός ἐστιν ἕξις ὁδοποιητικὴ τινὰ μετὰ λόγου]; Alexander says nearly the same, but more obscurely. That word of Philoponus, the road-making [ὁδοποιητικὸν], more clearly shows the way of present progress. Therefore, although the word method may signify any kind of argument, teaching or disputation, yet the certain meaning defined and explained here is that of P. Ramus, which he follows in this part of logic. So again and again we are reminded here that in such clarity of light we should not seek to create darkness by malice: for no doubt can now exist about what P. Ramus comprehends under the name of method and under which part of dialectic. He defines the thing with an illustrious and excellent definition, and he also gives the reason for the name, affirming it by fitting and abundant authorities. No method of invention is treated here: for that was set out at length in the first book, how arts and all things must be discovered, and the way was also set out in the place on distribution by which arts without art were first discovered by observation and induction. I say, no method of invention of arts or of any subject is treated here; so that no one may be deceived about this question, which scholastic men have especially made a trouble for P. Ramus, as will later be clear. Nor is any method of the statement or of the syllogism treated here, for all that doctrine has gone before. The method of disposing matter once discovered, with all its parts and also its perfections, is here explained, estimated and judged. I mean the method of arrangement that is universal and general, embracing the whole form of various statements and also of syllogisms.

units.la: Ideoq; ab universalibus Consectarium hoc certamen ingens cōtinet á multis & magnę authoritatis doctoribus incredibili contentione certatum. Invētionis & syllogismi logica reprehensionis calumnia caret, á nemine improbatur: logica de enuntiatis artificiosis, sed præcipuæ de methodo disponendę artis mirabiles turbas excitavit. Hæc enim singularia sunt instrumenta re formandę & constituendæ cujusvis disciplinæ, quod si sine cujusquam offensione fieri posset, nihil esset P. Ramo, doctis & eruditis hominibus charis, nihil amabilius, nihil præstantius: At iis telis petitur Aristoteles, petitur Euclides, petitur Galenus, omnes omnium artium summi doctores petuntur. hinc lachrimę rerum, attamen consolutio certissima est: nulla remedia tam faciunt dolorem, quam quę maximè sunt salutaria. His instrumentis grammatica, rhetorica, mathematica, omnesq; liberales & ingenuę artes emendantur, illustrantur, decorätur: & dolor iste est fatuę & rusticæ opinionis, non est philosophicę menmentis: & tamen ut prædixi, P. Ramus in hac disceptatione pro Aristotele philosophorum omnium (ut adversarii opinantur) principe præliatur. Itaque alacri animo rem aggrediamur. P. Ramus ex Aristotelis sententia unicam artis ordinandæ methodū Aristoteleam & singularem esse cōtendit, ut sit γνωριμώταλον primo loco, μέσαν ἀπὸ μέσου medio, ἀδιαίρετα infimo: cōtrà nationes quędam ac familiæ scholasticorum interpretū sunt positæ, asserentiū artis ordinādæ varias ac multiplices methodos esse. Ergo illa P. Rami suasio legis omnium legum maximæ ac præstantissimæ diligenter attendatur. Hic igitur tanquam in foro res ageretur, Prætorque quæstione decrevisset, ita P. Ramus primo antecedētia argumenta, deinde artiū ipsarum rerumq; omnium, quæ quidem perspicuè doceri vellent, testimonia producebat: id est totos logicæ inventionis & artificialis & inartificialis fontes huc aperiebat ac derivabat: id est, Aristotelis palmariá laudem manibus pedibus totisque viribus adversus importunè & fatuè Aristoteleos tuebatur ac vindicabat. Quæ omnia summa fide referenda mihi proposui. Ac ne qua de verbo cōtroversia oriretur, quid generale sit & universale, Aristotelem 4. ca. 1. de Partibus animaliū primo pro-ferebat: universalia autem, cōmunia: nam quæ pluribus insunt, universalia dicimus. Hæc Aristotelis definitio perspicua est: & sic locis aliis philosopho litera magis universalis & generalis, quàm syllaba, syllaba quā dictio, & dictio q̄ oratio: sic unitas quàm binarius, binarius quàm ternāternarius: sic punctum quám linea, linea quám superficies, superficies quám corpus, quia ante cedentia illa insunt in pluribus. Nam fi posteriora hæc sunt, illa priora etiam erunt: non contrá. Hoc modo loquitur Ariftoteles in cap. de modis Prioris, & 4.cap.1. Posterior. & 3. cap.6. Topic.ac locis præterea fexcentis. Sic in Logica argumentum magis est universale, quám enuntiatum, & enuntiatum quám syllogismus,& fyllogifmus quám methodus. neque hic generale & speciale,pro generis & speciei simplicibus & unius tantùm vocis categorematis intelliguntur á P. Ramo, cúm dicit, ex enûtiatis homogeneis alia aliis esse magis generalia aut specialia. Deniq; in methodica quæstione,ex homogeneis enûtiatis magis commune, universale, generale dicitur quod possit intelligi fine proprii,fingularis,specialis intelligétia. Sic enim doctrina generaliū potest intelligi fine doctrina fpecialiū, non contrá. Quam definitionem P. Ramus hoc loco præcipué inculcabat, quód vereretur, ne qui scholasticis categorematū tricis apinisque impediti, istum methodicę quæstionis sermonē non fatis attenté considerarét. Hanc,inquá,definitioné folicité repetebat & inculcabat, & affirmabat antecedentib.dialecticę partib.perceptis nihil in toto methodicæ dispositionis huj9 opere præter hác definitioné cõsiderandū esse: ut de partibus materiæ ad methodicé collocan dũ propositæ, singulæ ordine alphabeti notatæ effent a,b,c,&c.tantũ notas illas in disponendo spectares, ut quæ notá primæ literæ haberet,ea primo loco effet, quę fecūdę.ea fecūdo, & deinceps cōsimiliter: atıla universalis & generalis definitio tibi tanquā digito mōstrabit & dicet: hic elta, hic b, hic c, quia hoc per fe fine reliqs, reliqua fine ipso nequeat intelligi. Quapropter definitione ista diligenter explorata & animad versa,probata & concessa, P. Ramus ait methodū á generalibus ad specialia perpetuó progredi, quia sola hac via absolutè & nobis notiora præcedūt:Hæc caussa summa est, & qua major, vel antiquior reddi nulla possit: sed quæ multó clarior & illustrior efficietur,fi cōtraria rationū mometa,quæ in hanc quęstionē cadunt,conseratur.Firmameta ergo caussæ primó confirmentur, tum cōtrariis respondeatur. Differebat igitur P. Ramus ad suasionem methodicę legis,ab Aristotele methodū á generalibus ad specialia unicá & singulare esse propositam,deq; Aristotelis laudibus nullam esse præstabiliorē. Agitedū,suasionis locos ex Aristotele deinceps recē seamus,in Logica,in Ethica,in Physica,in Philosophia. Primū singularis methodi eulogiū est in Logica,loco antea jā citato,2.c.1.Post. Scire(ait philosophus)est rem per causam nosse propter quā res est. Ideoq; omnis scietia proficiscitur á caussis primis,immediatis. deincepsq; per tota posteriora Analytica latissimé diffusus est hic locus,nomine principiorū generaliū & univer-saliū. Secundū methodi singularis Aristoteleū eulogiū est in Ethica philosophia dissimile primo pauloq; obscurius:Disserit enim 3. cap.1. Ethic.ad Nicomachum,in morali philosophia nō G exigendas ab Ethico,tanquam á Geometra aliquo,immutabilium & necessariorum argumétorū demonstrationes: quia morū natura subtilitaté & accurationé ejusinodi nó ferat. idemq; 2.cap.2.Eth.repetit.Illud auté(ait)antea confitendum est,quód omnis de rebus agédis ratio, τύπῳ ἢ ἐν ἀκριβῶς figura quadā, non auté accurate explicanda est: ut initio,diximus,quód secū, dúm materiá rationes expetédę sint. Tum veró in eodem tertio cap.primi libri,addit ea sequenda esse,quæ nó levibus & intéperatis,sed liberalibus beneq; moratis ingeniis probabiliora fideq; digniora videátur. Deinde quæstioné ean dem quarto capite repetit: Ne veró nos lateat (ait) quód differūt rationes á principiis, & ad principia:rectę namq; de eo dubitabat Plato,& quærebat,utrúm á principiis, an ad principia es set via:velut in stadio, ab athletis ad metam, an contrá. Incipiendum enim est á notis:hæc auté dupliciter:alia enim nobis,alia absoluté. Fortasse igitur incipiendum ab iis, quæ sunt nota nobis.Huc igitur locus ille de duobus notionis generibus,ex Analyticis & Topicis revolvitur,& declaratur,ingenué & liberaliter institutis ingeniis notius esse in moribꝰ, quod absoluté sit notius.similia enim illa fuerűt, absoluté bona bonis,absoluté sana sanis. Res nullæ hic admodū sunt necessariæ: nec item caussæ aut demonstrationes necessariæ semper erunt, sed tales, quales sunt res ipsæ. Itaq; á talibus Ethicam philosophiam esse ordiendam & contexendam philosophus concludit.Tertium methodi singularis
units.tr: Therefore from the universals This consequence contains a great dispute, which many teachers of great authority have contested with incredible vehemence. The invention and the syllogism of logic are free from the charge of faulty reasoning, and no one disapproves of them. Logic in its artful treatment of propositions has not aroused any great storm, but the teaching on the method of arranging the art has. For these are unique instruments for shaping and organising any discipline whatever. If they could be used without offence to anyone, nothing would be more beloved by learned and educated people than Peter Ramus, nothing more pleasing, nothing more outstanding. But it is at these weapons that Aristotle is attacked, that Euclid is attacked, that Galen is attacked, and all the greatest teachers of all the arts are attacked. Hence come the tears of things, yet the consolation is most certain: no remedies cause pain as much as those that are most wholesome. By these instruments grammar, rhetoric, mathematics and all the liberal and noble arts are corrected, illuminated and adorned. That pain belongs to a foolish and rustic opinion, not to a philosophical mind. And yet, as I said before, Ramus in this dispute fights on behalf of Aristotle, the prince of all philosophers (as his opponents suppose). So let us approach the matter with a willing mind. Ramus contends, following the opinion of Aristotle, that there is one Aristotelian and singular method of arranging the art, so that the most known [γνωριμώτατον] comes first, the middle from the middle [μέσον ἀπὸ μέσου] comes in the middle, and the indivisibles [ἀδιαίρετα] come last. On the other side, certain factions and families of scholastic interpreters have taken up the position that the art of arrangement has various and manifold methods. Therefore let that persuasion of Ramus, the law of all laws and the most excellent, be carefully considered. Here, then, the matter would be handled as if in a court of law, and the praetor had given his decision on the question. Ramus would first produce the arguments that come before, and then the testimonies of the arts themselves and of all things, which would wish to be taught clearly. That is to say, he was opening up and deriving here the whole sources of logical invention, both artificial and inartificial. That is to say, he was defending and vindicating Aristotle's chief praise with hands, feet and all his strength against those who attack him unreasonably and foolishly as an Aristotelian. I have resolved to report all these things with the utmost good faith. And lest any dispute over a word should arise, what is general and universal, Aristotle in Book 4, chapter 1, of On the Parts of Animals first sets forth: "universals are common, for we call universal those which are present in many." This definition of Aristotle is clear. And so in other places the philosopher uses general and universal of a letter more than of a syllable, of a syllable more than of a word, and of a word more than of a sentence; of unity more than of the binary, of the binary more than of the ternary; of a point more than of a line, of a line more than of a surface, of a surface more than of a body, because those prior things are present in more instances. For if the latter things exist, the former will also exist, but not the reverse. Aristotle speaks in this way in the chapter on the modes of the Prior Analytics, and in Posterior Analytics 4.1 and Topics 3.6, and in six hundred other places. Thus in logic the argument is more universal than the proposition, the proposition more than the syllogism, and the syllogism more than the method. Nor are the terms "general" and "special" understood by Ramus here in the sense of the simple categorematic words of a genus and a species of one single term, when he says that among homogeneous propositions some are more general or special than others. Finally, in the question of method, that is called more common, universal or general among homogeneous propositions which can be understood without the understanding of what is proper, singular or special to others. For thus the doctrine of general matters can be understood without the doctrine of special matters, but not the reverse. Ramus especially impressed this definition at this point, because he feared that some, hindered by the scholastic tricks and snares of categorematic terms, would not attend closely enough to this language of the question of method. This definition, I say, he repeated and impressed with care, and he affirmed that, once the earlier parts of dialectic have been grasped, nothing in the whole work of this methodical arrangement needs to be considered beyond this definition. Suppose that the parts of the matter proposed for methodical arrangement were each marked with letters of the alphabet, a, b, c, and so on; you would look only at those marks in arranging, so that whatever had the mark of the first letter would be in the first place, whatever had the second would be second, and so on in the same way. Then the universal and general definition will show you, as with a finger, and say: "here is a, here is b, here is c," because this one cannot be understood through itself without the others, and the others cannot be understood without it. Therefore, once this definition has been carefully examined and considered, approved and conceded, Ramus says that method always proceeds from the general to the special, because only by this way do things which are absolutely and to us more known come first. This is the chief cause, and no greater or older one can be produced; but it will be made much clearer and more illustrious if the opposing arguments that fall into this question are set beside it. Therefore the supports of the cause should first be confirmed, and then the objections answered. Ramus therefore, in persuading the method's law, proceeded to show that, according to Aristotle, the method from general to special is the only and singular one proposed, and that no praise of Aristotle is more notable. Let us now gather in order the passages of persuasion from Aristotle, in Logic, in Ethics, in Physics, in Philosophy. The first praise of a singular method is in Logic, in the passage already cited, Posterior Analytics 2.1: "To know is to know a thing through its cause, on account of which the thing is." Therefore every science proceeds from first and immediate causes. And this passage is extended very widely through the whole of the Posterior Analytics under the name of general and universal principles. The second praise of Aristotle's singular method is in Ethics, somewhat different at first and rather obscure. For he argues in Nicomachean Ethics 1.3 that in moral philosophy one should not demand from the ethical writer, as from some geometer, demonstrations of unchangeable and necessary arguments, because the nature of morals does not bear such subtlety and exactness. And he repeats the same in Ethics 2.2: "Moreover, it must be admitted at the outset," he says, "that every account of things to be done is to be given in outline and not with exactness," as we said at the beginning, since the reasons must be sought according to the matter. Then, in the same third chapter of the first book, he adds that those things are to be followed which seem more probable and more worthy of trust, not to light and undisciplined but to liberal and well-mannered minds. Then in the fourth chapter he repeats the question: "Lest it escape us," he says, "that the reasons differ from the principles and toward the principles; for Plato rightly doubted this and asked whether the way was from the principles or to the principles, as in a race-course, from the athletes to the goal, or the reverse. For one must begin from what is known. But things are known in two ways: some to us, others absolutely. Perhaps, therefore, one should begin from those things which are known to us." Here then that passage about the two kinds of knowing, from the Analytics and the Topics, is turned over and explained: that for those with minds liberally and nobly trained, what is known in morals is more known than what is absolutely known. For those were similar, good things being absolutely good for good people, sound things absolutely sound for the sound. No matters here are very necessary, and likewise causes and demonstrations will not always be necessary, but such as the things themselves are. Therefore the philosopher concludes that Ethics must be begun and woven from such things. The third praise of the singular method...

units.la: ris Aristoteleŭ eulogium est in Physica, sed varis subinde locis consignatum: Primus locus 1. cap. 1. Phys. cúm methodum tractandæ ejus philosophiæ Aristoteles proponit: Manifestū quód etiam conádum sit primo loco principia 5 Physicæ scientiæ declarare. Ratio profertur ea dem illa superior: Videmur enim (ait) unumquodq; nosse, quádo caussas cognoverimus primas, & principia prima ufq; ad elementa. Hic Aristoteles in physica philosophia methodum á 10 caussis manifesté sibi proponit. Secúdus locus est ejusdem libri ca. septimo. Est enim secundū naturam, cómunia primó dicere: sic de unoquoque proprié considerare. Hic methodum vides á communibus ad propria proponi. Tertius locus est 1. cap. 3. Phys. cúm Physicus ait philosophiá de loco, vacuo, tépore, infinito, præponendá, quæ illa sunt cómunia & universalia. & addit: Posterior enim est de propriis consideratio, de cómunibus consideratione. hic, ut antea, communia præponuntur, propria succedunt. Quarto loco iteratur eadem methodus 3, ca. 3. de Cælo. Quoniá in omnibus cognitio fit per prima: prima aút eorū q insunt, elementa sunt. Hic sermo est, qui fuerat 1. ca. 1. Phys. Quinto iteratur eadé 25 methodus 9. c. 2. de Gener. Facilius enim sic singula constéplabimur, quádo primum sumpserimus de universalibus. hic universalia præponuntur, singularia sunt postposita. Verumenimveró in Physica ad hác methodici ordinis questio 30 nē, physicorū locorū præclarisimus locus est 1. ca. 1. lib. de Partibus animaliū. Quæstio enim de methodo artis instituendæ nominatim ita proponitur, utrûm oporteat assumédo unamquamque essentiâ, de ipsa per se constituere, an communiter omnibus convenientia, cōmuniter instituere: mox verò rejicit priore viam à speciali bus, & tautologiá necessario ei conjunctâ interpretatur. Manifestû autem ait, quód etiam particulatim quidem dicentes de multis, dicemus ipse eadē. Eodem capite quæstio mox eadem itera tur: Itaq; non est ignorandû, quomodo fit consideranda. Dico autem utrûm communiter primûm de genere, deinde posteà de propriis agēdû, & de unoquoq; protinus. Quarto capite libri ejusdem oppositio tautologiæ sophismate, tertiûm iteratur eadē quæstio, & solvitur ut antea: Necesse est aut universalia priús dicere, aut sæpius idem repetere, uti dictum est. Hoc eulogium P. Ramus mirificè celebrabat, à generalibus & universalibus esse progrediendum. Cur ita? secus, respondet Aristoteles, In fœdum tautologiæ sophisma incurres, & idem in specialibus sæpius dices, quod in generali & universali semel dictū satis superq; in omnibus specialibus fuisset. Deniq; sophistam ignavū hic Aristoteles appellat, qui in artibus aliam quàm à generalibus viam sequitur. Ergo singularis methodi eulogia Aristotelea nobis adhuc fuerút é Logica, Ethica, Physica: postremū est é Philosophia nobilissimū 2. cap. 1. lib. cùm docuisset philosoph9 primo capite, scientiam ab admiratione & experientia rerum singularū ad primas rerum causas & universales ascendisse: Atqui, ait, necesse nobis est constituere ordinem ipsius contrariũ inquisitionibus, quę ab initio præcesserunt: Omnes ab admiratione philosophari cœperunt, tanquā spectarent in theatro θαυμάτων τωτόμαϊα, mirabilium rerum machinas per se mobiles: sic in mundo conversiones solis, in Geometria dia metri ἀσυμμετρίαν admiratos, & ad causarum inquisitionem adductos esse: Oportet autē in cōtrarium, & in melius (iuxta prouerbiū) definere: quemadmodum in iis cum didicerunt: nihil enim geometra mirabitur, utrum diameter sit mēsurabilis. Hęc philosophus accuratē, nec obscurē. Duo igitur prima capita compara: quód philosophia inventa sit observatione specialiū ad generalia ascendēdo: sed cum parta fuerit, á generalibus caussis ad specialia descendendo, contraria via deducendam esse. hic Alexander ait ab Aristotele tradi viā & rationem cōparandæ sapientiæ: idq; rectē: cæterũ cotrarias primó observādę atq; inveniēdę, deinde coformādæ & collocandę artis vias negligentiùs hic animadvertit. Sententia Aristotelis est, aliter artes observari, aliter informari & doceri. Quapropter Aristotelis problema, Utrum á generalib. ad specialia progrediendū sit, an cōtrā regredie dū á specialibus ad generalia, satis perspicue atque aperte propositū est: repetitū subinde ab interpretibus Græcis. At Galenus, ἰδοιτορία διττή, ἰᾷ ἀναλυτικὴ καὶ διριστικὴ. αὐτοῦ συνθετικὴ ἢ γνῶσις: Progressio (ait) duplex, itio resolutiva & divisi va: reditio cōpositiva vel compositionis. Itaq; si methodus varia esset & multiplex, attamen duplex tátum effet, altera á generalibus ad fpecialia, altera á fpecialib. ad generalia: Acfi quæras, unde ifta fit Ariftotelis disjunctio bipartita, resfpódebo ex antecedentiu definitione in methodo, enuntiata effe homogenea: ideoq; alia aliis, generalia aut fpecialia: tertiu hic & mediu nihil effe. Quæritigitur Ariftoteles, de duobus contrariis medio carentibus, quorū alterū effe neceffe fit, utrū: & quæftioni fuæ refpódet idé népe, quod antea docuit, priore viá á generalibus ad fpecialia tenendá effe. hæc philofophi eft fententia: fed tñ fententia philofophi nihil nos moveat, fententiæ ratio cauffaq; fit potior: Cauffa fa né (fi quis forté nondū fatis animadvertit) illa ipfa eft, qua major in artiu quæftione, & excellétior effe nulla pofsit: quia illa via eft fcientiæ & intelligentiæ. Quamobre dices: quia(refpodebit Ariftoteles) generalia funt αʼrɩwrόρα ἀρχεαδις γόρα, ἀπλήσρόρα, ideoque ἐπισημεινωτόρα: quia etiá (addebat huc P. Ramus) difpofitio illa ordinis tá perfpicui, táq; fuccincti, eft memoriæ & cófti tuēdę & cófirmandę fola & fingularis magiftra: ordo enim memoriæ pater eft: At hic ordo perfectisimus eft & abfolutisim9. Ergo duæ ma- ximæ humani ingenii dotes, methodico Arifto teleç difpofitionis genere cötinentur, intelligē tia & memoria. Difponito artes hoc ordine, facilé intelligentur, facilé edifcétur. hęc mágna & fingularia funt: Neq; tamé philofopho fatis fuit, demóstrasse legitimæ methodi á generalib9 ad fpecialia progredientis emolumentu illud tam eximium effe, fed viæ á fpecialibus ad generalia contrariæ, contrarium etiā detrimētum duob. in eodē libro capitibus cōparavit: Si voles (ait Aristoteles) á specialibus ad generalia progre‐ di,in duo ignavisima contrariorū elenchorum sophismata incurres: Primó obscurabis ea quæ vis illustrare: quia procedes ab obscurioribus absolutė & ignotioribus ad absolutė illustriora & notiora,totamq; intelligentiā mentis conturbabis: Seçúdó memoriā obrues multitudine & confusione repetitarū rerum: quia necesse erit in singulis specialibus generalia quælibet nondum definita & demonstrata repetere. Ergo ut illa ex bonorū caussis ἀπόδειξις in priorem viam cohortatur: ita hæc ē malorum adjunctis ἀναγωγὴ revocat à posteriore ac dehortatur.Hic literā Pythagorę ad herculis Xenophontei tanquam ancipitē illam non vitę,sed doctrinę viam P.Ramus comparabat. Quid multa?hunc utrunque Aristoteleę & ἀποδείξεως & ἀναγωγῆς syllogismū, in hac quæstione tātum affirmabat esse,quantū in totis mathematicis artibus nullū unquā deprehendere potuisset:Illa via,& intelligentię & memoriæ mater est:hæc & intelligentiæ & memoriæ noverca est. Quare teneatur illa,hæc sugiatur.Ergo hæc in physicis artibus sententia est Aristotelis de methodo á generalibus ad specialia:sententia in logicis & ethicis antea etiā constans & una & perpetua. Iustumque P.Rami ρ Aristotele patrocinium sanctūmq; Aristoteleis omnibus,si resipiscant,videri necesse est. Quid deinde? quid authoritate testimonii ullius præterea nobis opus est? Certė ad rei firmitatem veritatem, nihil ad fcholafticorum & imperitorum interpretum & ufum difciplinarum ignorantium pervicaciam convincendum: ad fplen dorem fufceptæ fuafionis & dignitatem, fortaffe plurimum. Aggregabat igitur huc P. Ramus Hippocratem, Platonemq; ad Ariftotelis fentétiam roborandũ. Etenim Hippocratis locus ille eft infignis citatus á Galeno 9. libro de placitis Hippocratis & Platonis: Medicus ille fummus, comparandam ægrotantis faciem cum facie valentis admonebat, corporumq; valetudiné fimilitudine & diffimilitudine judicabat: fed ad fimilitudiné & difsimilitudiné deprehendé, dũ, viá á generalibus fequebatur. Similiáne fint (inquiebat) an diffimilia, primúm á maximis & facilimis, á notis omnino ufquequaq; quæ & vi dere & audire liceat, queque liceat percipere & vifu, & naribus, & lingua, & mente (quibus cognofcimus) omnib. liceat cognofcere. hæc Hip pocratis oratio de fimilitudinis & difsimilitudi nis cognofcendæ via, vera eft, & eam methodũ docet, quam Ariftoteles docet, & quam ex Ariftot. P. Ramus fequitur: ab iis nempe incipiendũ, quę maxima funt ... ufu & facultate, ut veré Galenus interpretatur: & prorfus notifsima funt, tum fenfui, tum menti: hæc enim Hippocratis maxima facillimaq;, fut Ariftotelis illa notiora tum abfoluté naturaq;, tum etiam nobis: res enim eft in Hippocrate & Ariftot. una, diuerfa tantúmverba, hæc (inquá) Hipp. methodicæ progrefsionis ratio vera eft, qua principia primo loco difponantur, quia facillima
units.tr: Aristotle's praise of this single method occurs in the Physics, but at various points. The first passage is in Book 1, chapter 1 of the Physics, where Aristotle sets out the method for treating that philosophy: "It is clear that we must first explain the principles of natural science." The reason given is the same as the earlier one: "For we think we know each thing when we have known its first causes and principles, down to the elements." Here Aristotle plainly proposes a method that proceeds from causes. The second passage is in the seventh chapter of the same book: "It is according to nature to state common things first; so one should consider each thing properly." Here you see the method proposed as proceeding from the common to the proper. The third passage is in Book 1, chapter 3 of the Physics, where the natural philosopher says that the philosophy of place, void, time and the infinite should be put first, since these are common and universal things. He adds: "For the consideration of proper things comes later, and that of common things earlier." Here, as before, the common things are placed first and the proper things follow. The fourth repetition of the same method is in Book 3, chapter 3, of On the Heavens: "Since in all things knowledge comes through first things, and the first of the things that belong to bodies are the elements." This is the argument of Physics 1.1 again. The fifth repetition of the same method is in Book 9, chapter 2, of On Generation: "For we shall more easily grasp each thing if we first take up the universals." Here universals are placed before, and singulars are placed after. But in the physical works the most distinguished passage on this question of methodical order is in Book 1, chapter 1, of the book On the Parts of Animals. There the question about the method of constructing an art is put explicitly: whether one ought, by taking each essence in turn, to establish something about it in itself, or to set out in general what belongs to all things in common. Aristotle then rejects the first way, because of the particulars, and interprets the tautology necessarily joined to it. He says it is clear that even if one speaks of many things particularly, one will say the same things. In the same chapter the question is repeated at once: "So we must not be ignorant of how things are to be considered. I mean, whether one should first treat the common, that is the genus, and afterwards the proper, and deal with each thing directly." In the fourth chapter of the same book, with the sophism of tautology opposed to it, the same question is raised a third time and resolved as before: "It is necessary either to say the universals first, or to repeat the same things often, as has been said." Peter Ramus greatly celebrated this praise, that one must proceed from the general and universal. Why so?
