Otherwise, Aristotle replies, you will fall into the shameful sophism of tautology, and you will say often in the particulars what, once said in the general and universal, would have been more than enough for all the particulars. Finally, Aristotle here calls lazy the sophist who in the arts follows any other way than from the general. So the Aristotelian praises of this single method have so far come from Logic, Ethics and Physics. The last and most noble is from First Philosophy, Book 1, chapter 2. There the philosopher, having taught in the first chapter that science rose from wonder and from experience of single things to the first causes and universals, says: "But we must establish the order of the reverse of the inquiries that began at the start. All men began to philosophize from wonder, as if they were looking in a theatre at wonders [θαυμάτων αὐτόματα], machines that move by themselves; so, in the world, at the turnings of the sun, and in geometry at the incommensurability [ἀσυμμετρίαν] of the diagonal, they were amazed and led to the inquiry into causes. But one must end, as the proverb says, on the contrary and for the better: as geometers do when they have learned; for no geometer will wonder whether the diagonal is measurable." The philosopher says these things accurately and not obscurely. Compare therefore the two first chapters: philosophy was discovered by observing particulars and ascending to generals; but once it has been acquired, one must descend from general causes to particulars, and the way must be taken in the opposite direction. Here Alexander says that Aristotle taught the way and method of acquiring wisdom, and rightly so. But he has less carefully noted that the ways of discovering and observing the arts are one thing, and the ways of forming, arranging and teaching them are another. Aristotle's opinion is that arts are observed in one way and informed and taught in another. Therefore Aristotle's question, whether one should proceed from generals to particulars, or on the contrary go back from particulars to generals, has been set out quite clearly and openly, and it was repeated afterwards by the Greek interpreters. But Galen says: "The progress is twofold: the way [ὁδὸς διττή] is the resolutive and divisive [ἀναλυτικὴ καὶ διαιρετική], and the return is the compositive or composition [συνθετικὴ ἢ σύνθεσις]." So, even if method is varied and manifold, it is nonetheless only twofold: one way from generals to particulars, the other from particulars to generals. If you ask whence this bipartite division of Aristotle's comes, I answer from the definition of the preceding statements in method: they are said to be of the same kind, so that one is generals and another particulars; there is no third or middle thing here. Aristotle therefore asks, concerning two contraries without a middle, of which one must be the case, which of them it is; and he answers his own question with the same thing he taught before, that by the former way one must proceed from generals to particulars. This is the philosopher's opinion. But the philosopher's opinion should not move us; the reason of the opinion is the stronger. The cause (if anyone has not yet noticed it well enough) is that very cause which is greater in the question of the arts and cannot be more excellent: because that way is the way of science and understanding. Therefore, you will say: because (Aristotle will reply) generals are prior and more known, and more simple, and therefore more known in the sense of knowledge. Peter Ramus also added here that this arrangement of an order so clear and so succinct is the sole and singular teacher of memory, of retaining and of confirming: for order is the father of memory. And this order is most perfect and most complete. So the two greatest gifts of the human mind are contained in this methodical arrangement of Aristotle's, understanding and memory. If you arrange the arts in this order, they will be easily understood and easily learned. These are great and singular things. Yet it was not enough for the philosopher to have shown that the advantage of a legitimate method proceeding from generals to particulars is so excellent; he also compared the opposite way, from particulars to generals, with its opposite disadvantage, in two chapters of the same book. "If you want," says Aristotle, "to proceed from particulars to generals, you will fall into two most lazy sophisms of the opposite refutations. First, you will obscure the things you wish to illustrate: for you will proceed from things that are absolutely more obscure and unknown to things absolutely clearer and better known, and you will throw the whole understanding of the mind into confusion. Second, you will overwhelm the memory with a multitude and confusion of repeated things: for in each particular it will be necessary to repeat generals that are not yet defined and demonstrated." So just as demonstration [ἀπόδειξις] urges us, by the good causes, towards the former way, so leading back [ἀναγωγὴ], by the attendant evils, calls us back from the latter and dissuades us from it. Here Peter Ramus compared the letter of Pythagoras to the two-faced path of Xenophon's Hercules, which is a way not of life but of teaching. What more? He asserted that in this question this double Aristotelian syllogism of demonstration [ἀπόδειξις] and leading back [ἀναγωγὴ] was worth as much as any he could find in all the mathematical arts. The one way is the mother of understanding and memory; the other is the stepmother of understanding and memory. Therefore the one is to be held and the other shunned. So this is Aristotle's opinion in the physical arts about the method from generals to particulars: an opinion that in logic and ethics also was constant, one and perpetual. And it must seem just and sacred to all Aristotelians, if they come to their senses, that Ramus should stand for Aristotle. What then? What further need have we of the authority of any testimony? Certainly, for confirming the firmness and truth of the matter, none is needed; for convincing the obstinacy of the schoolmen and unskilled interpreters, who are ignorant of the practice of the disciplines, perhaps a great deal is needed. To add splendour and dignity to the persuasion undertaken, Ramus therefore also brought in Hippocrates and Plato to strengthen Aristotle's opinion. Indeed that passage of Hippocrates, cited by Galen in the ninth book of On the Opinions of Hippocrates and Plato, is notable. That supreme physician advised that the face of the sick be compared with the face of the healthy, and judged the states of bodies by likeness and unlikeness; but in finding out likeness and unlikeness he followed the way from generals. "Whether things are alike or unlike," he said, "first from the greatest and easiest things, from things entirely known in every respect, which it is possible to see and hear, and which it is possible to perceive by sight, by nostrils, by tongue and by mind (by which we know), it is possible for all to know." This speech of Hippocrates about the way of knowing likeness and unlikeness is true, and it teaches the method that Aristotle teaches, and that Ramus follows from Aristotle: one must begin, that is, with those things which are greatest ... in use and capacity, as Galen rightly interprets, and which are wholly most known, both to sense and to mind. For these things are, in Hippocrates, the greatest and easiest, just as in Aristotle they are the more known both absolutely and by nature and also to us; the thing is one in Hippocrates and in Aristotle, and only the words differ. This rule, I say, of Hippocrates' methodical progression is true: that the principles should be arranged first, because they are the easiest, because they are the greatest, that is the best known and most general, because they are most causal and most scientific; then, concerning the principles, the consequences in second place, the second in third, the third in fourth, and so on for the rest, as they are greater and easier.

units.la: [Greek phrase in the line 'maxima funt' rendered as printed: κατὰ χρῆσιν περὶ δυνάμεως] cillima, quia maxima,id est notissima & genera lissima: quia αὐτιώτατα, ἐπιστημονικώτατα:tū de principiis consequentia,loco fecundo fecunda,tertio tertia, quarto quarta,ac deinceps reliqua,ut sunt majora facilioraq;. Atq; hæc ordinis collocationisq; præceptio generalis & cōmunis est omnium disputationum, omnium artium: nec solum ad judicandum,quæ similia & dissimilia, sed omnino ad omnem vel unius argumenti,ut simplex rei unius & unica explicatio demonstratioue fuerit, vel lögioris disputationis quęstioné perpendendū & æstimandū. Quamobrẽ Hippocrates methodo Aristoteleus est, aut potiús Aristoteles Hippocrateus: & summi me dici Logicā imitatur: sed sine nomine, ut ferétotam ab eo Physicam,licet Hipprocratem nun quā nominarit. Quid verò philosophorũ Homerus,& tanquam deus Plato, quid de methodo philosophatur? Prorsus idē, sed Socraticė, id est graviter & ornatė. Hic igitur P.Ramgna animi alacritate,nobilissimi philosophi sententiam é tribus locis proferebat, é Charmide, Phædro,Philebo.Etenim Socrates in Charmide, medicæ curationis exemplo, Aristoteleam methodum succinctė complectitur, dum remedium ad curãdos oculos ei pollicetur,sed priús sanandum caput,imó totum corpus, quàm animum censet esse,ad eamq; rem, ἐπῳδὴν incantationem quandam adhibendam.Est autem ejusmodi,ait,ut non possit caput solùm sanum sacere,sed quemadmodum etiam forte de præstantibus medicis inaudisti, cúm quis oculis æger ad eos accesserit, respondent utiq; solos oculos curari non posse, sed necessario simul caput curandum esse, si bene habituri sint oculi: ac rursus putare caput ipsum per se fanari posse, sine totius corporis curatione, magna esse dementia.
units.tr: [Greek phrase in the line 'maxima funt' as printed: kata chrēsin peri dynameōs] ...most easy, because most general, that is, most known and most general, because they are most primary and most scientific [αὐτιώτατα, ἐπιστημονικώτατα]. Then, from the principles, the consequences follow: second in the second place, third in the third, fourth in the fourth, and so on through the rest, as they are greater and easier. This precept of order and arrangement is general and common to all disputations and all arts, not only for judging what is alike and unlike, but for any single subject whatever, whether a simple and unique explanation of one thing is being demonstrated, or the question of a longer disputation is being weighed and assessed. For this reason Hippocrates is Aristotelian in method, or rather Aristotle is Hippocratic, and the greatest of the Logicians imitates him, though without naming him, just as he takes almost all his Physics from him, although he never names Hippocrates. But what do Homer, the prince of philosophers, and Plato, as if he were a god, teach about method? Exactly the same, but in the Socratic manner, that is, weightily and elegantly. Here, then, P. Ramus, with a cheerful spirit, set forth the opinion of that most noble philosopher from three passages: from the Charmides, the Phaedrus and the Philebus. For Socrates in the Charmides, using the example of medical treatment, sums up the Aristotelian method briefly, when he promises a remedy for curing the eyes, but holds that the head must first be healed, indeed the whole body rather than the soul, and that for this purpose a certain epōdē [ἐπῳδὴν], an incantation, must be applied. It is of such a kind, he says, that it cannot make only the head sound, but, as you have perhaps heard from the excellent physicians, when a patient with bad eyes comes to them, they answer that the eyes cannot be cured alone, but the head must of necessity be cured at the same time, if the eyes are to be well; and again, to think that the head itself can be healed by itself, without curing the whole body, is great madness.

units.la: Ex qua sane ratione dietæ ad universum corpus conversi, cum toto partem curare & sanare instituunt. Hæc Socratica logicæ curationis incatatio, non solum medicis, sed chirurgis ac tonsori bus notissima est, & in ore perpetua, In curandis morbis, à generalibus & universalibus progrediendum esse: Et quidem ne quis sua sponte perire volens, hic periclitetur, vere tali curatione proceditur à generalibus: Nam si curetur oculus necesse est curari caput, non contrà: item si curetur caput, necesse est curari corpus, nō contrà. itaq; curatio corporis magis est generalis & plurib. communis, quàm capitis, & capitis quàm oculi: & idem nempe est Aristoteli generale & universale, quod pluribus commune fit: & Aristotelea methodus est revera medicina infinitorum in artibus modorum. Deniq; de tribus curationibus, prima est γνωστική, secunda ἀπαλλαγῆς, tertia διαιρετική. hoc primum de unica artis methodo à generalib. ad specialia, Platonis testimonium est illustre: hęc nobilis in primis & animadvertenda est incantatio. Cantando rumpitur anguis, ait poeta: carmine igitur isto Platonico perversæ opiniones publicis studiis perniciosæ rumpantur. Secundum Platonis testimonium paulò clarius est & illustrius in Phædro. Circùferebatur Athenis oratio Lysiæ de amore: re: quâ tamé ut ἀμίλοδον, & præstantissima logicæ disposi-tionis laude carêtem, Socrates merito derisit: quia rerum talium ὁ τὴν σύρεσιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν διάθεσιν ἐπαινετὸν, non inventio, sed dispositio laudanda: deinde docet dispositionis nullam ratio nem à Lysia habitam esse, quia neque primò definitus in ea oratione esset amor, neque deinde distributus in genera, sed temerè quodque primum postremo, postremum primo loco projectum: Tumque Socrates cum Phædro. So. Atqui arbitror te dicturum esse oportere omnem disputationem, instar animalis, suo quodam corpore compositam esse, neque sine capite, neque sine pedibus, sed mediis & extremis non solùm inter se, sed toti congruentibus conformatum. Ph. Quidnì? So. Cōsidera igitur amici tui orationem: utrùm sic, an aliter habeat: & invenies, nihil ab epigrammate differre, quod nonnulli Midæ Phrygii inscriptum ajunt esse. Ph. Quódnā hoc, & quale? Soc. Est nempe ejusmodi: Χαλκῆ παρθένος ἀμί, Μίδα δ᾽ ἐπὶ σύματι κεῖμαι. Ὄφρ᾽ ἂν ὕδωρ τι ναίῃ, ἡ δὲ δένδρεα μακρὰ τεθάλῃ. Αὐτὴ τῇδε μίνυσα ἀωλυπλαύτως ἐπὶ τύμβῳ, Ἀγγελίαν παρίσαι, Μίδας ὅτι τῇδε τέθαπται. id est, Aenea virgo sum, Midæ sepulchro imponor: Quādiu & aqua fluet, et longæ arbores virescet: Ipsius hic manens lamentabili in tumulo, (est. Nuntio prætereūntibus: Midas quód hìc sepultus
units.tr: From this very reasoning, those who turn to the whole body in diet undertake to cure and heal the part together with the whole. This Socratic incantation of logical cure is not only most familiar to physicians but also to surgeons and barbers, and is constantly on their lips: in curing diseases one must proceed from the general and universal. And indeed, lest anyone, wishing to perish of his own accord, be put at risk here, cure truly proceeds in this way from the general: for if the eye is cured, the head must necessarily be cured, not the reverse; likewise if the head is cured, the body must necessarily be cured, not the reverse. Thus the cure of the body is more general and common to more things than that of the head, and that of the head than that of the eye. And the general and the universal, for Aristotle, is indeed the same as what is common to many; and the Aristotelian method is really the medicine of the infinite modes in the arts. Finally, of the three cures, the first is gnōstikē [γνωστική], the second apallagēs [ἀπαλλαγῆς], the third diairetikē [διαιρετική]. This first point, concerning the single method of an art from the general to the special, is a famous testimony of Plato; this incantation is especially noble and worthy of attention. "The snake is burst by singing," says the poet; so by that Platonic charm let perverse opinions, harmful to public studies, be burst asunder. The second testimony of Plato is a little clearer and more illustrious, in the Phaedrus. A speech of Lysias on love was being circulated at Athens, which Socrates rightly mocked, since it was without amilodon [ἀμίλοδον] and lacked the highest praise of logical arrangement, for in such matters the praiseworthy thing is not the invention but the disposition [ἡ διάθεσις]; not invention, but arrangement, is to be praised. Then he teaches that Lysias had no principle of arrangement in that speech, because love was not first defined in it, nor then divided into kinds, but each thing was rashly put first in place and the last thing first. And Socrates then speaks with Phaedrus: "Socrates: Yet I think you will say that every discourse ought to be composed, like an animal, with a body of its own, neither without a head nor without feet, but with middle and extremes fitted together so as to agree with one another and with the whole." "Phaedrus: Why not?" "Socrates: Consider then the speech of your friend: whether it is so arranged or otherwise; and you will find that it differs in no way from an epigram which some say is inscribed on the tomb of Midas the Phrygian." "Phaedrus: What is that, and of what kind?" "Socrates: It is of this kind: Chalkē parthenos eimi, Midas d' epi sēmati keimai, hōphr' an hydōr ti nai ē de dendrea makra tethalē, autē tēde minysa aōlaupluōs epi tymbō, angelian parisai, Midas hoti tēde tethaptai [Χαλκῆ παρθένος εἰμί, Μίδα δ᾽ ἐπὶ σήματι κεῖμαι. Ὄφρ᾽ ἂν ὕδωρ τι ναίῃ, ἡ δὲ δένδρεα μακρὰ τεθάλῃ. Αὐτὴ τῇδε μίνυσα ἀωλυπλαύτως ἐπὶ τύμβῳ, Ἀγγελίαν παρίσαι, Μίδας ὅτι τῇδε τέθαπται]." That is: I am a maiden of bronze, I lie on the tomb of Midas. As long as water flows and tall trees grow green, here I shall remain on this tomb, weeping without end, and announce to passers-by that Midas is buried here.

units.la: Quod verò nihil interest, quamlibet ejus partem primam vel postremâ dici, intelligis: ut opinor. Atqui hæc Socratis Logica, unicam & fingularem methodum à capite per intermedia membra ad ultimos ufq; pedes nobis adubravit: ut oratio,tanquam animal unum, in quo primum fit caput aliquod, deinde membra intermedia, tum pedes ultimi, membrorum omnium fymme‐ tria proportioque, & inter fe, & toti consentiat. A'πόδειξις est egregiæ similitudinis: tum additur ἀπαγωγὴ, é ridicula epigrammatis similitudine: cujus nihil interfit, quid primū postremúmve statuatur. Atq; hæc elt adumbratio Ariltotelæ methodi, á capite per intermedia mēbra ad pedes progredientis: Sequitur luculenta pictura, é duarum idearū coloribus expressa, quam præcipuis tantúm præceptis attingam. Mihi quidē videntur cætera alia per jocū transacta esse: harum vero duarum fpecierū, quę forte nobis excideruntt, fi quis ipsam facultatem arte possit as sequi,res non ingrata fuerit. Ph. Quarúmnam? Soc. In unam ideam intuens, cogat varié difper fa: ut unumquodq; definies, manifestum faciat quod dicere instituet. Ph. Alteram specie ó Socrates, quámnam dicis? Socr. Rursus fecúdum species posse articulatim dividere, ut rerum natura tulerit: neq; imperiti coqui more, partem ullam frangere. Ph. Verissimé dicis. Soc. Harū quidem,ó Phędre,& divisionum & collectionū amator ipse sum,ut dicere sapereque possim: Si vero quempiam aliū arbitrabor pro natura posse unum & multa prospicere, hunc vestigiis poné tăquam Deum confector. atq; hac facultate præditos,utrúm tamen recte an non, Deus novit: voco igitur hactenus Dialecticos. Adhuc Socrates animalis illius methodici figuram formamq;
units.tr: That it makes no difference which part of it is called first or last, you understand, I think. Yet this Socratic logic has pointed out to us a single and unique method, from the head through the intermediate members to the very last feet, so that the speech, like one animal, in which there is first some head, then intermediate members, and finally feet, agrees with all its members in their proportion and symmetry, both among themselves and with the whole. Apodeixis [ἀπόδειξις] is of an excellent likeness; then apagōgē [ἀπαγωγὴ] is added, from the ridiculous likeness of the epigram, of which it makes no difference what is placed first or last. This is the outline of the Aristotelian method, proceeding from the head through the intermediate members to the feet. There follows a brilliant picture, expressed in the colours of two ideas, which I shall touch upon only in its main precepts. Indeed, the other matters seem to have been passed over in jest. But if anyone could attain the faculty itself by art, of those two kinds which perhaps have slipped from us, the matter would not be unwelcome. "Phaedrus: Which two?" "Socrates: Looking at one idea, to gather together things scattered, so that by defining each one you make clear what you are going to say." "Phaedrus: What is the other kind, Socrates, which you mean?" "Socrates: Again, to be able to divide by parts, according to species, as nature has given them, and not, like an unskilled cook, to break any part." "Phaedrus: Most true." "Socrates: Of these divisions and collections, O Phaedrus, I myself am a lover, so that I may be able to speak and think; and if I think that someone else can by nature see one and many, I follow him as after a god. But whether they are rightly so endowed, God knows; so far I call them Dialecticians."

units.la: Ioan. 3. mamq; duarum idearum coloribus expressit: primo loco res summa ita definiatur, ut genera quaecunq; ei subjecta sunt, apte proprieq; comprehendantur. haec definitionis prima idea est, quae varie dispersa cogit, quaeq; ideo συναγωγὴ dicitur: Secunda est, ut genera ita comprehensa, deinde separatim dividantur. haec est idea altera: Earumq; idearum duarum amatorem fe Socrates profitetur: amorisq; caussam idoneá reddit, ut dicere sapereq; possit, tanquá & eloquentiam & sapientiam Aristotelea in definitionib. & partitionibus methodus complexa sit. Antea fuit incantatio logica, nunc eloquetiq & sapientiq ludus est: sed multò majus & excellétius laudis elogium additum est, quód methodicæ hujus facultatis participem compotemq;, Διώκειν λατρικῶς μὲν ἰχνίου, ὥστε θεοῖς, tanquam deum verecundeq; & religiose colat ac veneretur: eūq; Logicū appellat: Ergo laus Aristoteleae methodi, non est laus acuminis & subtilitatis cujufdam, ut in inventione: non ex sese perspicuq veritatis, ut in enuntiatione: non deductae ex aliis, & conclusae, ut in syllogismo: haec enim omnia sunt humana. sed (quod penè captum humani ingenii superat) laus methodi, laus est cujusdá divinitatis. Aristoteleus igitur, qui Aristoteli tot & tantas laudes detrahit, videat quàm sit in Aristotelem non ingratus modó, sed agrestis & barbarus. Neq; vero philosophus ὑπερβολὴν in his laudibus loquitur: vera res est: Si homo, Dei imago & species est, nusquam alia species est divinae mentis & imago clarior apparebit. Homines mutis bestiis præstát syllogismo:sed homines hominibus excellùt methodo. Ergo Logicus hanc logicam methodicæ dispositionis facultatem adeptus, tanquam deus aliquis á Platone colitur:& Aristoteles methodi hujus doctor, patron9, author post magistrũ Platonem patrimoniũ tantæ celebritatis æmulatur. Sed tertium Platonis testimonium super est, omnium clarissimũ & illustrissimũ, ideoq; diligentissimé considerandum. Charmides incantatione sua unicam doctrinæ methodum á generalibus ad specialia, medicorum exemplo docuit:Phædrus unicam doctrinæ methodum á generalib. ad specialia, é proportione animalis, & definitionis partitionisq; ordine docuit: Eandem Philebus postremó docebit. Locũ Platonis hunc tertium trifariam dividemus,in proœmium,expositionem methodi, & exempla,ut cómodiús intelligatur. Cúm igitur in Philebo dictum esset,Logicæ cujusdam naturalis impetum nostris animis ingeneratũ, pené furiosum esse, nisi velut habenis cohiberetur: ratioq; regendi hujus impetus & conformandi quæreretur: tum Socrates cum Protarcho ita loquitur.
units.tr: John 3. Socrates has, up to now, expressed the figure and form of that methodical animal in the colours of two ideas: first, a sum is to be defined in such a way that all the genera subordinated to it are aptly and properly comprehended. This is the first idea of definition, which gathers things scattered in various ways, and which is therefore called synagōgē [συναγωγὴ]. The second is that the genera, so comprehended, are then divided separately. This is the second idea. Socrates professes himself a lover of these two ideas, and gives a fitting reason for his love, so that he may be able to speak and think; as if the Aristotelian method in definitions and partitions were a combination of both eloquence and wisdom. Before, it was a logical incantation; now it is a game of eloquence and wisdom. But a far greater and more excellent eulogy of praise is added: that he who shares in and is master of this methodical faculty, diōkein iatrikōs men ichnyou, hōste theois [Διώκειν λατρικῶς μὲν ἰχνίου, ὥστε θεοῖς], he cherishes and venerates with reverence and piety as if a god, and calls him a Logician. Therefore the praise of the Aristotelian method is not the praise of some sharpness and subtlety, as in invention; nor of clarity drawn from itself, as in enunciation; nor of what is derived from other things and concluded, as in the syllogism. For all these are human. But the praise of method, which almost exceeds the grasp of the human mind, is the praise of a certain divinity. Therefore the Aristotelian, who takes away from Aristotle so many and such great praises, let him see how not only ungrateful but rustic and barbarous he is towards Aristotle. Nor indeed does the philosopher speak with hyperbolē [ὑπερβολὴν] in these praises; the thing is true: if man is the image and likeness of God, nowhere will the image and likeness of the divine mind appear more clearly. Men surpass the mute beasts by syllogism, but men surpass men by method. Therefore the Logician who has attained this faculty of logical methodical arrangement is worshipped by Plato as some god; and Aristotle, the teacher, patron and author of this method, after his master Plato, emulates the inheritance of such celebrity. But there remains the third testimony of Plato, the most famous and most illustrious of all, and therefore to be considered most diligently. In his incantation, Charmides taught the single method of doctrine from the general to the special, by the example of physicians; Phaedrus taught the single method of doctrine from the general to the special, by the proportion of an animal and the order of definition and partition; Philebus will finally teach the same. We shall divide this third passage of Plato into three parts: a proem, an exposition of the method, and examples, so that it may be understood more conveniently. Therefore, since in the Philebus it had been said that the impulse of a certain natural logic, implanted in our minds, is almost furious unless it is held back as if by reins, and the manner of governing and shaping this impulse was sought, then Socrates speaks thus with Protarchus.

units.la: Soc. Nulla veró est via pulchrior ea,neq; possit esse,cujus amator perpetuó sum : persæpe autè effugiens,solum me ac solicitum destituit. Pro. Quę nam porró hęc,dicatur modò. Soc. Quam declarare quidem non valde difficile ,usu autè expromere perdifficile. Omnia enim artib. cóprehensa, quæcunq; unquam inventa sunt, per hanc viam plana facta sunt : cócipis veró quam dico? Pro. Dic tátúm. Soc. Deorum quidem ad homines donum, ut mihi quidé videtur, alicunde à diis per quendam Promethcum unâ cum igne clarissimo delapsum. Atq; majores nostri nobis prĕstantiores ad deosq; propiús accedentes,hoc oraculum prodiderunt. Adhuc Platoni cum methodicę legis proœmium est: cujus verba pené singula, magnorû mysteriorum plena sunt: Methodici ordinis perpetuus amator Socrates fuit: hæc philosophia videlicet est, hic amor sapientiæ. Amatores tales philosophi post homines natos perpetuò fuêre, & erűt quádiu genus erit hominum: sed amica hęc velut superba & fastidiosa, amatores suos effugiens, sepe solos & anxios deserit: O Socraticos amores sæpe inanes & fallaces! Nemo unquâ ad philosophandum, nemo ad docendum quicquam unquam, vel voce, vel scripto accessit, qui methodum non impense amaverit, nō omni studio sequi contenderit. At quotusquisq; ex infinita docentium multitudine, potiri? quotusquisq; assequi potuit? Quâ declarare nō difficile: Etenim unico verbo tâta res cōtinetur; Absoluté notiꝰ pcedat: at exercere, at in usu actūq; deducere,
units.tr: Socrates: There is no path more beautiful than that one, and none could be, and I have always been its lover. Yet very often it escapes me and leaves me alone and anxious. Protarchus: What then is this path? Tell me. Socrates: It is not very hard to state, but it is extremely hard to put into practice. For all the arts, whatever has ever been discovered, have been made plain by this path. Do you grasp what I mean? Protarchus: Just tell me. Socrates: It is a gift of the gods to men, I think, sent down from the gods somehow through a certain Prometheus, together with the very bright fire. And our ancestors, who were better than we are and came closer to the gods, handed down this oracle. Still, the proem of Plato's methodical law is this, and nearly every word of it is full of great mysteries: Socrates was the perpetual lover of the methodical order. This is philosophy, clearly, this is the love of wisdom. Such lovers of philosophy have existed continually since men were born, and will exist as long as the human race does. But this mistress, proud and disdainful as she is, escapes her lovers and often leaves them alone and troubled. O Socratic loves, so often empty and deceptive! No one has ever approached philosophy, or ever attempted to teach anything by word or in writing, who has not loved method intensely and strained with all his zeal to follow it. But of the endless crowd of teachers, how few have been able to master it? How few have been able to attain it? To state it is not difficult: the whole matter is contained in a single word. It can be grasped perfectly well, but to practise it, to bring it into use and action,

units.la: Hoc opus, hic labor est: pauci quos æquus amavit juppiter, aut ardens evexit ad æthera virtus.
units.tr: This is the work, this is the labour: few whom fair Jove has loved, or burning virtue has raised to heaven.

units.la: Quid igitur (inquies) unde est difficultas tâta? Omnia, inquit Socrates, artiû decreta & documenta, quæ unquam ab hominibus inventa sunt, per hanc viâ plana facta sunt. Via inveniendi multiplex est, via enuntiádi multiplex est, via concludendi multiplex est: at via doctrinę, & di H spositio seu methodus, unica & singularis est: p hanc unicam & singularem viam artes progrediuntur: & ea Socrati difficultas est tanta: Etenim ut Socraticę difficultatis huj9 magnitudo percipiatur, meminerimus quę ceteris in partibus difficultates singulae sint, has simul universas in hanc partem extremam concurrere: Neq; enim methodi intelligetia potes uti, nisi omnia argumentorum, enuntiatorum, syllogismorum genera notissima & exploratissima habeas: neque exercere, nisi omnia illa multiplicib. & variis omnium meditationum comentationumq; generibus exercueris. Labor invetionis magnus est, labor judicii in enutiato major est, labor judicii in syllogismo maximus est: sed labor methodi, ex omnibus illis antecedentibus laboribus cumulatus est: praeterea longe summum longeq; gravissimum adjungit in provisione & cotemplatio ne dispositionis universae. Qui posit in Repub. partem aliquam politici muneris obire, pleriq; reperiuntur: qui statum civitatis universum partibus omnib. pspicere & tueri possint, rari erunt. Ergo methodu doctrinae declarare, facillimum quidem est: at exercere usuq; expromere, difficilimum: Veruntamen ne magnitudine difficultatis quisquam logicae artis studiosus deterreatur: haec difficultas est doctoris & magistri, non est audi toris, no est discipuli: est artem aedificatis & construentis, no est aedificata arte cognoscentis: est agricolae arantis, iteratis, tertiantis: est ferentis, no est metetis: radices deniq; praeceptori & compositori amarissimae sunt, fructus aut discipulo suavissimi: & tamen etiam quavis difficultate magnitudo dignitatis & amplitudo major & amplior ante oculos conditori ipsi subjicitur. Itaque non hominum inventum, sed donum deorum, methodica lex efficitur, Prometheusque in schola deorum Logicam hac edoctus, ad homines detulisse dicitur: poeticis fabulis argumentum, quod Prometheus auxilio Minervae ignem de caelo clepsit,
units.tr: What, then, you will ask, is the reason for so great a difficulty? Socrates says: all the rules and teachings of the arts that have ever been discovered by men have been made plain by this path. There are many ways of discovering, many ways of stating, many ways of concluding; but the way of teaching, and the arrangement or method of exposition, is one and unique. It is by this one and unique way that the arts advance. And this is the great difficulty for Socrates. For to grasp the magnitude of this Socratic difficulty, let us recall what difficulties each of the other parts has, and see that all of them together converge on this last part. For you cannot use the understanding of method unless you have a thorough and well-tested knowledge of all the kinds of arguments, propositions and syllogisms; nor can you exercise it unless you have practised all of those in the manifold and varied kinds of all meditation and study. The labour of invention is great, the labour of judgement in the proposition is greater, the labour of judgement in the syllogism is greatest; but the labour of method is heaped up from all those preceding labours, and besides this it adds by far the highest and by far the heaviest task, namely the foresight and contemplation of the whole arrangement. Many people will be found who can carry out some part of the political office in the commonwealth; few will be able to survey and keep in view the whole state of the community in all its parts. So to state the method of a discipline is very easy, but to practise it and bring it into use is most difficult. Nevertheless, so that no student of the logical art may be discouraged by the magnitude of the difficulty, this difficulty belongs to the teacher and master, not to the listener or the pupil. It belongs to the one who builds and constructs the art, not to the one who knows an art already built. It belongs to the farmer who ploughs, harrows and tills; it belongs to the one who bears, not to the one who reaps. Finally, the roots are very bitter for the instructor and the compiler, but the fruit is sweetest for the pupil. And yet, despite whatever difficulty, the greatness and the breadth of the dignity is set before the eyes of the founder himself, larger and wider. Thus the methodical law is made not a human invention but a gift of the gods, and Prometheus, having been taught logic in the school of the gods, is said to have brought it to men. The poetic fables have as their subject that Prometheus, with the help of Minerva, stole fire from heaven:

units.la: Posti ignem aetherea domo subductum, ait Horat. Deinde, ut Ovidi, hoc igne homine Finxit in effigiem moderantium cuncta deorum.
units.tr: After fire had been drawn from its ethereal home, says Horace. Then, as Ovid says, with this fire he shaped into the image of the gods who rule all things man.

units.la: Etenim hoc igne caelesti Prometheus, seu Logicus (quisquis primus ille fuit) in artium constructione, idem quod Deus in elementorum compositione effecit. Quid in prima nascentis mundi origine, nonne
units.tr: Indeed, with this heavenly fire Prometheus, or the logician (whoever he first was), accomplished in the construction of the arts what God accomplished in the composition of the elements.

units.la: Frigida pugnabant calidis, humentia siccis? Mollia cum duris, sine pondere habentia pondus?
units.tr: Cold things were fighting with hot, moist with dry, soft with hard, things without weight with things that have weight.

units.la: Quid deinde ait poeta?
units.tr: What does the poet say next?

units.la: Hanc Deus, & melior litem natura diremit: Nam caelo terras & terris abscidit undas: Et liquidum spissso secrevit ab aethere caelum.
units.tr: A god, and a better nature, parted this strife: for he cut the lands from the sky, and the waters from the lands, and separated the clear heaven from the dense air.

units.la: Sic porro in prima humani generis aetate, omnia quae postea comprehensa sunt artibus, vaga disperseque ferebantur: in grammaticis literae, in rhetoricis tropi & figurae, in logicis argumentum, enuntiatum, syllogismus, methodus: in arithmeticis & geometricis, numeri & magnitudines: caeteraque in caeteris artibus genera: Tum Prometheus, tanquam provisor caelestis & divinus instituit, & suis quoque terminis ac finibus concludit: primum & generalissimum summo in solio,
units.tr: So too, in the first age of the human race, all the things that were later comprehended by the arts were wandering and scattered: in grammar, letters; in rhetoric, tropes and figures; in logic, argument, proposition, syllogism, method; in arithmetic and geometry, numbers and magnitudes; and kinds of the same sort in the other arts. Then Prometheus, as a heavenly and divine provider, arranged them and also bounded and limited them within their own terms and borders: the first and most general he placed on the highest throne,

units.la: H intermedias fubalternarũ differétias & ideas in medio spatio,infimas in ultimo collocavit.Et fi vera est de tempore, Platonis interpretatio, de patriarchis Hebræorum Noeus aliquis Prometheus hic fuit,tot annorum millibus antequam in Græcia Logicæ vel Dialecticę nomẽ esset au ditum Logicæ itaq; methodi prudentia, & difficultatem,& dignitatem tantam obtinet,ut divi num potiús donum, quám humanum invétum Platoni videatur. Atq; Socraticum methodicæ legis proœmium adhuc esto: Lex ipsa deinde á generalibus ad specialia describitur. Cúm ex uno quidé & multis constent entia, quæ perpetuó dicuntur esse,finemq; & infinitate in seipsis insitá habeant:necesse est his ita cöstitutis. semper unam ideam de unoquoq; statuentes,quærere:inveniemus enim,cúm infit: ac ubi sumpserimus, post unam duas considerare : sin minústres aut alium quempiá numerü: deinde unum quodq; istorü rursus similiter, donec noveris, quod ab initio,cúm propositum est, non solúmquod unum & multa,aut infinita,sed etiá quot: Infiniti veró ideam non priús ad multitudinemadhibere, quám omnem ipsius numerum pervideris, qui est intermedius inter infinitü & unü: tum verò unumquodq; in infinitum abeuntiüpræterea​s,ac valere sinas. Dii igitur (uti dicebam) hanc nobis viam cömonstrarunt, mutuæinter nos & disciplinæ & doctrinæ. Adhuc Socratica methodicę legis informatio descriptioque fuit eadé, q in Phædro antea fuerat: Illic ideæ duæ in ppetua bene cöpositi animalis forma nominabátur, definitionis generalis altera, altera specialis subinde partitionis, Híc λογικώτερον ἢ πλατωνικώτερον, tota perpetuaq; artis forma duob.finib.terminifq; finitur ac terminatur, ᾧτι ἢ ἀπείρια, fine & infinitate: In Phædro illud πρῶτον ἢ ὕστατον, primum & extremū dicebatur: Cŏprehensa aūt duob.his finib. intermedia genera proprio nomine hîc nō appellátur, q ἀντάλλαξ Aristoteli antea fuerunt. Ergo cùm hæc omnia homogeneorū genera constiterint,ideæ, 10 quę fuerát in Phædro appellantur paulò secús: Primo loco una exigitur,generalis nēpe & universalis definitio, quá Socrates ideo nos inventuros affirmat,quia ea fine dubio inest: Secundo loco διχοτομία generū postulatur, si sit: illa enim est difficultas,de qua in categoria distributionis tractatum est. Quapropter si perfectus ille distributionis numerus defuerit: quemvis alium proximum Socrates permittit: & hîc non secunda idea, sed duæ,tres, aut quotlibet á Socrate dicuntur: Tertió ut distributa genera rursus pariter & definiantur & distribuátur ad extremam ufq; infinitorum multitudinem, pręcipitur, donec propositum initio totum subjectū genus modis omnibus exploratum & perspectum fit: non solùm quæ unitas, & quæ multitudo, sed etiá quám multiplex in eo quidq; fit: infinitatis autem idea (qui terminus infimus est) non priús ad cōcludendum adhibeatur, quám totus intermediorum & subalternorū generū numerus tractatus & explicatus fit: Postremó infinitorū & individuorū multitudo rejiciēda.
units.tr: the intermediate differences and ideas of the subordinate kinds in the middle space, and the lowest in the last place. And if the interpretation of Plato about time is true, that among the patriarchs of the Hebrews some Noah was this Prometheus, then he was many thousands of years before the name of logic or dialectic was heard of in Greece. So the wisdom of logical method holds such difficulty and such dignity that it seems to Plato a divine gift rather than a human invention. Let the Socratic proem of the methodical law stand as it is. The law itself is then described from the general to the special. Since the beings which are said to be always consist of one and many, and have limit and infinity inherent in themselves, it is necessary, once these things are so established, always to seek one idea of each thing as it is laid down. For you will find it when it begins; and when you have taken it up, to consider two after the one, or three or some other number; and then each of these again in the same way, until you know the whole that was proposed at the beginning, not only that it is one and many or infinite, but also how many. But the idea of the infinite is not to be applied to the multitude before you have surveyed its whole number, which lies between the infinite and the one; then, indeed, you may let each of those going off into infinity go, and be well. Thus, as I was saying, the gods have shown us this way, a mutual way between us for learning and teaching. Again, the Socratic account and description of the methodical law was the same as it had been earlier in the Phaedrus. There two ideas were named in the perpetual form of a well-composed living thing, one of general definition and the other of special partition in turn. Here, more logically or more Platonically, the whole and perpetual form of the art is bounded and terminated by two ends and limits, the limit and the unlimited, end and infinity. In the Phaedrus the same was called first and last, the first and the extreme. The intermediate kinds, comprehended between these two ends, are not here given a proper name, which before were called middle by Aristotle. Therefore, since all these are the kinds of homogeneous things, the ideas which in the Phaedrus were named somewhat differently are these: in the first place one is required, namely the general and universal definition, which Socrates affirms we shall find because it is undoubtedly present; in the second place, the division of the kinds is demanded, if there is one. For that is the difficulty about which a treatise was written under the category of distribution. Wherefore, if that perfect number of distribution is lacking, Socrates allows any other nearby number, and here he speaks not of a second idea but of two, three, or however many. Third, it is prescribed that the distributed kinds be defined and distributed again in the same way, down to the extreme multitude of the infinite, until the whole genus proposed at the beginning has been examined and viewed in every way: not only what is the unity and what the multitude, but also how manifold each thing is in it. The idea of infinity, which is the lowest limit, is not to be applied to the conclusion until the whole number of intermediate and subordinate kinds has been treated and explained. Finally, the multitude of infinite and individual things is to be rejected.

units.la: hîc Socrates cælestem Promethei ludum cócludit:Hæc schola(inquit) deorũ,cúm hominũ magistri & doctores essēt:hic ludus olim fuit, quonos inter nos artes & discere & docere valeamus. Atq; Socraticę definitionis propositę ἀπό διαῥέσεως ejusmodi est,ἀναγωγὴ etiá quędam additur. Eorum vero hominũ qui sapientes perhibētur, unum quidem utlibet assecuti sunt,& multa,celeriús tardiúsve expediunt, quám deceat: postunum vero, infinita repente; media aût ipsos effugiút, quibus discretum separatumq; est illudgenus quoq; Dialecticæ rursus, & quo litigioserationes inter nos cóferimus.Hic Socrates Dialecticum appellat,qui methodicam istá differendi facultate adeptus sit, ut possit institutá quæstionem á summo fine per intermedias ideas ad infinitatem ultimam deducere: Sophistam contrá, qui nullam intermediorũ generũ methodũ sequutus, repete á summo decidat ad infimum. In Charmide, Dialecticus factus est medicus animi:In Phędro, Dialectic9 ille inter homines, táquam deus aliquis habitus est:In Philebo autem dono deorum beatus efficitur. Aristotelis ἀναγωγὴ deducebat ignorantię & oblivionis viâ, si vera & legitima intelligentiæ & memoriæ via relinqueretur:Platonis ἀναγωγὴ deducit philosophicæ & artificiosæ methodi ignarum aut contemptorem, nō dialecticum illum deo cuidam similem,sed captiosum, fallacemq; nebulonem ac sophistam futurũ.Deniq; cúm duos summos tot feculorũ, tot populorũ magistros iu unitate methodi tam mirabiliter cósentientes & confpi rantes animadvertimus, qui Platonicu: qui Aristoteleum philosophum putemus, qui contraria tantę veritati sophisinata tueatur. Pars tertia testimonii Platonici tertii e Philebo superest, de exemplis, quibus expositam methodi definitio nem philosophus illustravit: Exempla autem tria sunt, primum de Grammatica, alterum de Musica, tertium de motibus corporis, quorum propter longitudinē, satis erit summa proposuisse. Grammatica Platonis tempore, erat in literis scribendis & legendis. Vox quidē (ait) nobis utiq; est. & rursus, infinita est multitudine, & omnium, & cujusq;. Neutro horū, ait Socrates, Grammatici efficimur: sed comprehensione generum intermediorum in vocalibus & consonis, & speciebus utriusq; generis. Sic in musica, vox est una: deinde species duæ, grave & acutū: & tertium genus ἁρμονία, quibus item musicus esse nō possis, sed perceptis intervallorum quibusq; modis atque harmoniis. Tertium exemplū de motibus ipsius corporis: in quibus ejusmodi quædam afsectiones insunt, p numeros in rhythmis & metris dimensę. his vero propositis exemplis, rursus Socrates contraria via ab infinitate specialissima per intermedia genera ad generalissimū fi nem ascendendo, docet, artes omnes inventas esse: idq; Grammaticæ rursus exemplo: quod Grammaticæ primus inventor, primo in singulas literas inciderit, numero & multitudine infinitas: tum collegerit certum numerū: unde species vocaliū consonarumq; diviserit: deinde vocalium & cōsonarum genera magis universalia
units.tr: Here Socrates concludes the heavenly game of Prometheus: "This school of the gods," he says, "was once the game by which we, among ourselves, might be able both to learn and to teach the arts, when the teachers and doctors were men." The Socratic definition proposed by division [ἀπό διαῥέσεως] is of this kind, and an ascent [ἀναγωγὴ] is also added to it. Of those men who are called wise, some have indeed attained it in some way, and they carry out many things more quickly or more slowly than is fitting; but others suddenly reach the infinite, while the intermediate steps escape them, by which that genus is separated and distinguished. This is the genus of Dialectic too, by which we conduct our contentious debates with one another. Here Socrates calls the Dialectician the one who, having gained this methodical faculty of disputing, is able to lead the question under inquiry from the highest end, through the intermediate ideas, down to the final infinity. The Sophist, on the other hand, who follows no method of intermediate genera, falls from the highest to the lowest at once. In the Charmides, the Dialectician is made a physician of the soul. In the Phaedrus, that Dialectician is regarded among men as a kind of god. In the Philebus, he is made happy by a gift of the gods. Aristotle's ascent [ἀναγωγὴ] led by the way of ignorance and forgetfulness, if the true and lawful way of understanding and memory were left aside. Plato's ascent [ἀναγωγὴ] leads the man ignorant of, or contemptuous of, the philosophical and artful method to become not a Dialectician like a god, but a crafty, deceitful rogue and sophist. Finally, when we see the two greatest masters of so many ages and so many peoples agreeing and conspiring so wonderfully in the unity of method, who would think that one of them is the Platonic philosopher and the other the Aristotelian, and that one defends sophisms contrary to so great a truth? The third part of Plato's testimony, from the third book of the Philebus, remains, concerning the examples by which the philosopher illustrated the proposed definition of method. There are three examples: the first about grammar, the second about music, the third about the motions of the body. Because of their length, it will be enough to set out their substance. In Plato's time, grammar was concerned with writing and reading letters. "Voice," he says, "is indeed for us a single thing; and again it is infinite in multitude, both as a whole and in each part." By neither of these, Socrates says, do we become grammarians; but by the grasp of the intermediate genera among the vowels and consonants, and the species of each kind. So in music, sound is one; then there are two species, low and high; and a third genus, harmonia [ἁρμονία], by which again one cannot be a musician, but by perceiving the intervals and the various modes and harmonies. The third example concerns the motions of the body itself, in which there are certain affections of this kind, measured by numbers in rhythms and metres. Having set forth these examples, Socrates, again by the opposite way, ascending from the most specific infinity through the intermediate genera to the most general end, teaches that all arts have been invented. He uses the example of grammar again: the first inventor of grammar, having first fallen upon the single letters, which are infinite in number and multitude, then gathered a certain number from them, whence he divided the species of vowels and consonants; then the more universal genera of vowels and consonants.

units.la: H diviserit: deniq; ait de Teutho Ægyptio inventore Grammaticæ: Cúm autem videret á nemine nostrúm, neq; unum ipsum per sese sine universis ipsis percipi posse: vinculū ratiocinatus, quod esset velut unum, atq; hæc universa unū quodámodo efficeret: artem, quæ una in seipsa esset, cognominádo Grammaticam appellavit. Hunc extremum tertii testimonii versiculum, P. Ramus valde commédabat, quod methodus á Platone valdé idoneo nomine vinculum artis nominaretur, quo tota artis universę materia & coagmentatio vinciretur. Homerus 8. Iliados σάφλω χρυσέιλω, catenam auream fingit, qua Iupiter mundum universum colligatū regit: Quam Platonem in Theæteto de solo interpretatur. At P. Ramus ad Platonis laudem, vinculum hoc methodicum, catenæ illi aureæ mirificé cóparabat, cum jus annulis persimiles essent in methodo generum, specierum, differentiarum, proprietatum, connexi inter se colligatiq; modi. Platonem igitur intelligimus tam multis, tamque mobilibus testimoniis in affirmatione singularis methodi Aristoteleū esse, aut potius Aristotelem esse Platinicum, magnamque utrique philosopho contumeliæ notam ab iis inuri, qui commenta sophismatum contrariorum tam obstinatè defendunt. Quapropter suasionis confirmatio adhuc argumentis suis declarata est, & rationibus illis intelligentiæ memoriæque summis, & testimoniis Aristotelis, Hippocratis, Platonis: Sed tamen quoniam ita recepimus, contraria quoq; nobis agenda atq; audienda sunt. Quid igitur cótra tantam & veritatem & authoritatê dici potest:Certê verbo plurima á plurimis scriptoribus effusa sunt, re nihil.Principium omnis in tota philosophia erroris illud unum fuit,credere omnia quæ usquam ab Arist.in Aristotelea bibliothecam collecta essent,velut oracula esse: nullas leges judicandi propositas habere: denique nequaquâ tales Aristot. discipulos esse,qua lis Aristot.Platonis fuisset, nó philosophico,sed servili ingenio. hic error interpretū Arist.Græcorum Latinorumq; perpetuus fuit, & eorum deinde hominum, qui tales interpretes sunt secuti. Offenderút igitur Alexander,Ammonius, Porphyrius, cæteriq; ejusdem familiæ philosophi,doćti quidem homines (utsæpe dićtum)& multis bonis artibus eruditi: sed tamen neq; judicio satis liberi,neque satis usum artis assecuti, de cujus præceptis disputarent. Enimveró excitabatur hic P.Ramus, & philosophos omnium gentium in tanta quæstione attentos esse cupiebat:Etenim quæstio ista fundamentum est philosophiæ universæ stabiliendæ, & cujusvis doćtrinæ confirmandæ: quæstio est de prima sum maq; logicæ civitatis lege, qua cóservata, salus artium,táquam civiū, retineatur. Si methodus legitima sit accepta, oēs artes facilé(ut dixi)intelligentur,facilé ediscentur:Eadem autē repudiata,omniū artium jura violari perfringiq; necesse est:artes oēs infinita caligine & difficultate obruétur ac sepeliêntur.Quare diligenter attenteq; hoc unū consideretur.Si interpres quis quâ, multiplices & varias methodos inducere cupiebat primũ Ariftotelei philosophi persona erat deponenda: deinde Ariftot.illa & sententia, & sententiæ demostratio de unica doctrinę methodo, expugnanda. Quomodo enim Aristoteleus videatur, qui Ariftot.etiam virtutem infectatur? quomodo vera fuerit cotradictionis tã manifestę pars utraq;?Unica est artis method9, ait Aristoteles: Nó est unica artis methodus, ait interpres.unica est artis methodus (ait Aristoteles) à generalibus ad specialia: quia sola hæc via est intelligentiæ & memoriæ: cótraria à specialibus ad generalia, & intelligétiam & memoriam cófundit. Quid hic interpretes, qui omnia Aristotelis dicta velut oracula tuentur, quid ad ista respondent? obstupescunt & obmutescunt: qua enim fronte dicere auderet, viam in artib. instituendis eam tenendam esse, qua intelligentia rerum impediatur, qua memoria consundatur? Etenim quamlibet fabrorum incudem cerebro suo antè disperserint, quam vel tantillam methodi hujus veritatem queant imminuere. Sed tamẽ ut error iste penitus & radicitus ex animis hominũ evelleretur, omnia sibi discutienda P.Ramus proposuit, quæ simplices & credulos homines in errorem impellere potuerũt,& alia, quæ ipsi nunquá fortasse cogitarunt, tamẽ pro eorũ defensione in mediũ proferre statuit: omnes Aristotelis hac de re locos expendere é Logica, Physica, Ethica, Philosophia prima: denique quicquid contrà omnino disputatum fit ab interpretibus, aut disputari possit, studiose accurateque discutere. Questio igitur ante oculos habeatur, An unica fit mothodus doctrinæ collocânde:omnifq; disputationis ad bené & per spicuè docendum ordinandę, à generalibus ad specialia. Hanc esse unicam P.Ramus ,p Aristotele cofirmat:interpretes inficiantur:inficiationis igitur causlam,quæcunq; reddi posit,attendamus.Multi sunt in Aristotelis bibliotheca contrarii loci de multis methodis : interpretes etiá græci contrarii sunt: Hæc enim erat P.Ramo bipertita refutatio. Quid tum,inquâ? An leges in Aristotelis civitate nescimus esse, quib. qui pareant,boni & justi cives habentur ? rebelles autem, seditiosi, scelerati, exterminantur? sic antea contradicétium rerum pars altera, quæ sine dubio vera esset, est cófervata à P.Ramo: opposita, rejecta & explosa est. Sed audiamus Aristotelis locos qui cótra unitate methodi ab interpretib. afferantur. Primus est Aristotelis locus in Categoriis de priore, quod aliud alio prius quinque modis dicatur: hinc methodi quinq; scilicet interpretibus videbûtur,quia methodus disponit propria priore loco. At his modis omnibus generalia specialibus priora sunt,& unica methodus Aristotelea hos omnes modos recipit: & ta mè quinquepartita ista distributio, quibusdam suis partib9 ad methodum nihil attinet. Primò quidè & præcipuè secúdúm tempus,quo senex juvene prior dicitur. Esto,inquam: sic enim generalia specialib9 in natura rerû priora sunt: sic in procreatione hominis priùs tempore est animatû,quàm animal: & animal, quàm homo: & generis tota natura pfectè explicari intelligiq; popotest absque specie. & tamen hic modus nihil attinet ad questionem methodi: in methodo enim qritur notitię, claritatis, intelligentię ordo, non temporis: Omnia comprenhésa disciplinis & artibus perpetua ponuntur, nihil statuitur tē porarium, ut ex lege λατὰ ϖᾶντὸς priús est intellectum. Deniq; in ordine methodico, & in collocandis præceptis, ista temporis cõsideratio nulla est: neq; prius illud primó & pcipué rećté dicitur. Secundúm, quod non cõvertitur ad essentiæ consequentiam. Sic unum est prius duob9, quia si duo sunt, est unú, non contrá. Atqui hoc etiá modo, generalia sunt priora specialib. Nec hic consequentia convertitur á generali ad speciale: & illo cósequentiæ ordine generalia & universalia ab Aristotele antè definita declarantur: ut unum magis fit universale & generale, quám duo: Sic punćtū magis universale, quám lineá, quarto ca. 1. Poster. fecit Aristoteles. Hic modus propiùs ad questionē attinet: cófecutio enim á speciali ad generale, nó contrá, methodicam ordinis antecessionem comprehendit: Atque id multó magis præcipuum in methodica prioris quæstione fuerat. Et tamé in isto consequentiæ nó conversæ judicio, diligenter attendendū est, quid dicatur. Si homo est, animal est, nó cótrá: Ergo animal (ais) est quiddam magis generale, quám homo: & doćtrina de animalis natura generalior erit, quā de natura hominis. Atsi ita disseras, Omne animal vivit: Ergo omnis homo vivit, non contrá. non protinus idcirco judicabis secundá propositionem magis esse generalem prima. Illa enim consecutio, Si homo est, animal est, non contrá. animal genus nō assumit generaliter, sed specialiter: nec aliud dicis, quàm si diceres, Si homo est, aliquod animal est, non contrá. At in secundo exemplo genus assumis generaliter, ideoque consequentię conversio contraria est, Si omne animal est, omnis homo est, non contrá: Ideoque antea monuimus in Topico generis & speciei, genere generaliter affirmato, affirmari speciem, non contrá: ut specie quolibet modo affirmata, affirmaretur genus specialiter, nō cōtrá: & hic repeto, ne quid ea res quenquam posset coturbare, putetque specialia quæ sunt, illo cōsequentiæ converse judicio, generalia fieri. Revertor igitur ad tertium prioris modū: Tertium secundū quendam ordinem: ut in demonstrativis scientiis principia sunt priora lineamētis: in Grammatica, literæ priores syllabis. Atqui hic tertius modus, totus est methodicæ quæstionis: Sic enim generalia in Artibus Aristoteles priora ait esse: quin & principia & elementa, ad illum Aristotelei universalis & generalis ante positā definitionem, Generalia & universalia sunt, cùm infinit in pluribus. sed tamē hic modus quæstionem methodicam tantùm continet, quæstionis explicationem nō continet, neq; docet, quid antecedere, quidve sequi debeat: ut secundus modus docuit universalia & generalia singularibus & speciali bus priora esse. Præterea præstabilius ac honorabilius, πρότερον τῇ φύσει, prius naturā videtur, ut in civitate, principes reliquis civibus. Quarto igitur modo, quod honore antecellit, prius dicitur. Sed hic modus (ut etiam nominatim ait Aristeles) feré est alienissimus: ut revera quæstionis methodicæ est alienissimus: in qua queritur præstátia notitiæ & claritatis, non auté dignitatis & potentiæ. Et tamen hic alienissimus modus, etiam generalibus convenit, quæ Aristoteles hocipso honoris verbo antea jam in topico generis honorabiliora dixit esse, quia caussam contineant: Ergo ut temporis, sic dignitatis ordo, nihil ad methodū. Interea causus (τῆ φύσει) notetur nobis ad quęstionē aliam postea differendum: quod latiné reddendū (naturā) ablativo casu, non (naturæ) dativo. Additur præterea & quintus Prioris modus: Ex his quæ convertuntur (ait) secundum essetiæ consequentiā, quod caussa est, quodámodo alteri ut sit, dicatur meri τὸ τῆ φύσει πρότερον, naturā prius: ut vera definitio. Quisquis tamen hunc quintum Prioris modū sic ad convertentia allegavit, peccavit in legem λαθόντ προτοτ: quia generale specialiter exposuit. Quicqd enim caussa est alteri, sive reciprocū, sive nō reciprocū, prius est caussā & naturā: Quin etiam hinc téporis & ordinis prioritas, tanquā diceretur, existit: Itaque generaliter ita præcipi debuit, Quicquid est caussa, prius est: & tum generalia diceretur hoc etiam quinto modo priora specialibus, cùm generalia sint specialiū caussæ, ut toties ex Aristotele repetitum est. Quare de quinque modis Prioris ultimus hic & quæstionem, & quæstionis explicationem (licet parum logicé) attamé coplectitur. Deniq; quinqui sti isti modi Prioris, non quinque modos methodi faciunt, sed omnes unicæ Aristotelis methodo à generalibus ad speciali a conveniunt: primusq; temporis, & quartus dignitatis, præcipuè nihil huc spectant: é reliquis, tertius habet quæstionem nem, quam secundus non reciprocæ consequentiæ, & quintus reciprocę caussæ interpretantur: ut tanquâ notius præcedat, omnino quicquid caussa sive reciproca, sive non reciproca fuerit: At in hoc quinto modo memoria teneatur etiā manifestior dativus, τῇ φύσει cùm quod caussâ sit notius & prius, id notius & prius dicatur τῇ φύσει hoc enim ad quæstionem aliam, ut prædixi, attinebit. Quapropter concludebat hic P. Ramus, totum hunc locum de quinque modis prioris, cŭ illa Aristotelea methodi singularis & unicæ philosophia consentire: & tamen hæc quinquepartita distributio Prioris refellitur ab Aristote le ipso in proximo capite, cùm docet, ἅμα simul duo quælibet esse, primò κατὰ τὸν χρόνον, ut quorum ortus est simul: deinde τῇ φύσει, ut quæ convertuntur, neque alterum alteri caussa est: ut relata, duplū, dimidium: ut species sub eodem genere oppositę: De quinq; modis illis, duos hic tátúm philosophus retinet, tempus & naturam seu caussam: cùm tamen tempus in quæstione methodi & ordinis, nullum momentum habeat, ut jam dixi. Quare ad methodicam quæstionem de antecedentiū & consequentium ordine, sola caussa spectanda est, ut absolutè prius & notius dictū est, quod esset caussa. Atq; interea notabimus in hoc capite, dativū (τῇ φύσει) quater in hoc sermone adhiberi, ut bis antea adhibitus est: ne que τῇ φύσει, aliud esse, quàm τῇ αἰτίᾳ. Quamobrē ut hęc plusio cōcludatur, primus hic ex Arist. bibliotheca locus neminem turbare debuit, ut artis methodū multiplicē opinaretur, quia tam multos Prioris modos videret, cūm hi modi in unā methodum singularem conveniant: vel potiús, quód ex omnib. quinq; modis, unus causfæ modus ad hanc methodicā quæstionē solus referendus fit. Secunda Prioris divisio est 2. ca.
units.tr: Finally, he says of Theuth the Egyptian, the inventor of grammar: "When he saw that none of us could perceive any one thing by itself without all the rest, he reasoned that there must be a bond which would make the many, as it were, one, and he named the art that is one in itself Grammar." P. Ramus greatly commended this last little verse of the third testimony, because Plato had called method by the very fitting name of the bond of the art, by which the whole matter and structure of the art is bound together. In the eighth book of the Iliad, Homer imagines a golden chain [σειρὴν χρυσείην] by which Jupiter holds the whole world bound together, and Plato, in the Theaetetus, interprets this only as a figure. But P. Ramus, to the praise of Plato, compared this methodical bond wonderfully to that golden chain, since the rings of method, namely of genera, species, differences, properties and the connected and linked modes, are joined to one another. We understand, then, from so many and such varied testimonies, that Plato was in agreement with Aristotle's single method, or rather that Aristotle was a Platonist; and that a great mark of disgrace is branded upon each philosopher by those who so stubbornly defend the inventions of contrary sophisms. Therefore the confirmation of this persuasion has been set forth in its own arguments, and in those supreme reasons of understanding and memory, and in the testimonies of Aristotle, Hippocrates and Plato. Yet since we have accepted it in this way, we must also set out and hear the opposing case. What, then, can be said against so great an authority and truth? Certainly, in words, very many things have been poured out by very many writers, but in substance nothing. The one source of all error in the whole of philosophy has been to believe that everything which Aristotle's collected library contains is like oracles, to hold that no rules of judgement have been laid down, and finally that his disciples were by no means such as Aristotle was to Plato, not with a philosophical but with a servile mind. This error has been perpetual among the Greek and Latin interpreters of Aristotle, and then among those men who have followed such interpreters. Thus Alexander, Ammonius, Porphyry and the other philosophers of the same family stumbled, learned men indeed (as has often been said), and trained in many good arts, but not sufficiently free in judgement, nor having attained sufficient use of the art whose precepts they were discussing. Indeed P. Ramus stirred himself and wished the philosophers of all nations to give their attention to so great a question. For this question is the foundation for establishing the whole of philosophy and for confirming any teaching whatever: it is a question about the first and chief law of the commonwealth of logic, which, if preserved, keeps safe the arts as the citizens of a state. If the lawful method is accepted, all the arts will be easily understood and easily learned (as I have said); but if it is rejected, the rights of all the arts must necessarily be violated and broken, and all the arts will be overwhelmed and buried in infinite darkness and difficulty. Wherefore let this one point be considered carefully and attentively. If any interpreter wished to introduce many and various methods, he would first have to lay aside the character of the Aristotelian philosopher, and then to overthrow Aristotle's view and the demonstration of that view concerning the single method of teaching. For how could he be an Aristotelian who also attacks Aristotle's own virtue? How could either part of so manifest a contradiction be true? "There is only one method of the art," says Aristotle; "there is not one method of the art," says the interpreter. "There is only one method of the art" (says Aristotle), "from the general to the specific, because this way alone is the way of understanding and memory; the contrary way, from the specific to the general, confounds both understanding and memory." What do the interpreters, who guard all the sayings of Aristotle as oracles, answer to these things? They are astonished and fall silent; for with what face would anyone dare to say that the path to be followed in establishing the arts is one which hinders the understanding of things and confounds the memory? Indeed, however many smiths' anvils they may have scattered from their brains beforehand, they could not diminish even the smallest part of the truth of this method. But so that this error might be utterly and radically torn out of men's minds, P. Ramus proposed to examine all the points which could have led simple and credulous men into error, and he resolved to bring forward in their defence other points which perhaps they themselves never considered: to weigh all the passages of Aristotle on this matter in the Logic, Physics, Ethics and First Philosophy; and finally to examine diligently and accurately whatever has been argued, or can be argued, by the interpreters against all this. Let the question therefore be kept before our eyes: whether there is one method for arranging teaching, and for ordering every discourse for teaching well and clearly, from the general to the specific. P. Ramus affirms from Aristotle that this is the only one; the interpreters deny it. Let us therefore consider the cause of the denial, whatever reason can be given for it. There are many passages in Aristotle's library which speak against many methods; the Greek interpreters too are opposed to them. For this, P. Ramus said, was the twofold refutation. "What then?" I say. "Do we not know that there are laws in Aristotle's commonwealth, by obeying which men are held good and just citizens, while rebels, seditious and wicked men are cast out?" Thus the one part of the contradictory pair, which would undoubtedly be true, was preserved by P. Ramus; the opposed part was rejected and driven out. But let us hear the passages of Aristotle which the interpreters bring forward against the unity of method. The first is the passage in the Categories on "prior," where it is said that one thing is prior to another in five ways; from this the interpreters think there are five methods, because method arranges things in their proper prior place. But in all these ways the general is prior to the specific, and the single Aristotelian method admits all these ways; and yet that fivefold division, in some of its parts, has nothing to do with method. First and chiefly, prior according to time, in which an old man is called prior to a young man. Granted, I say: for in this way too the general is prior to the specific in the nature of things; thus in the generation of a man the animate is prior in time to the animal, and the animal to the man; and the whole nature of a genus can be perfectly explained and understood without the species. Yet this mode has nothing to do with the question of method: for in method we seek the order of knowledge, clarity and understanding, not of time. All things comprehended in disciplines and arts are set down as continuous; nothing temporal is laid down, so that by the rule "according to all" [κατὰ παντός] one thing is understood before another. Finally, in methodical order and in the arrangement of precepts, this consideration of time is of no account, nor is that which is first and chief rightly said to be prior in this sense. Second, prior is that which is not convertible with regard to the consequence of essence: thus one is prior to two, because if there are two there is one, but not the reverse. Yet in this way too the general is prior to the specific; nor here is the consequence converted from the general to the specific; and in that order of consequence the general and universal, which Aristotle defined earlier, are explained: so that one is more universal and more general than two. Thus Aristotle, in the fourth chapter of the first book of the Posterior Analytics, made the point more universal than the line. This mode bears more closely on the question: for the following from the specific to the general, and not the reverse, contains the methodical priority of order; and this would have been far more important in the methodical question about what is prior. And yet in this judgement of a consequence which is not converted, careful attention must be paid to what is being said. If a man is, an animal is; not the reverse. Therefore (you say) the animal is something more general than man, and the doctrine concerning the nature of the animal will be more general than the doctrine concerning the nature of man. But if you argue thus: every animal lives, therefore every man lives, not the reverse: you will not at once judge the second proposition to be more general than the first. For that consequence, "if a man is, an animal is," not the reverse, does not take the genus generally but specifically; nor do you say anything other than if you were to say, "if a man is, some animal is," not the reverse. But in the second example you take the genus generally, and therefore the conversion of the consequence is the opposite: "if every animal is, every man is," not the reverse. Hence we warned earlier, in the Topic of genus and species, that when the genus is affirmed generally, the species is affirmed, not the reverse; so that when the species is affirmed in any way, the genus is affirmed only specifically, not the reverse. And here I repeat this, lest anything in that matter should disturb anyone, and lest anyone think that specifics, which are what they are, become generals by that converted judgement of consequence. I return therefore to the third mode of prior: third, a certain order: as in demonstrative sciences the principles are prior to the lines, and in grammar the letters are prior to the syllables. Yet this third mode is wholly the matter of the methodical question. For in the arts Aristotle says that the general things are prior in this way; indeed the principles and elements too, according to that definition of the universal and general which Aristotle laid down earlier: "general and universal are those which are found in many." But this mode contains only the methodical question; it does not contain the explanation of the question, nor does it teach what ought to precede and what to follow, as the second mode taught that universals and generals are prior to singulars and specifics. Moreover, the more excellent and honourable, "prior by nature" [πρότερον τῇ φύσει], seems to be prior as in a commonwealth the rulers are prior to the other citizens. Fourth, therefore, that which excels in honour is said to be prior. But this mode (as Aristotle also says by name) is well-nigh most alien, just as it is truly most alien to the methodical question, in which we inquire into the excellence of knowledge and clarity, not into dignity and power. And yet this most alien mode also belongs to the generals, which Aristotle had already called more honourable, by this very word of honour, in the Topic of genus, because they contain the cause. Therefore, as the order of time, so the order of dignity has nothing to do with method. Meanwhile let the case ("by nature," τῇ φύσει) be noted by us, to be discussed later in another question: it should be rendered in Latin by the ablative case, naturā, not the dative, naturae. Besides, the fifth mode of prior is added: "of things which are converted (he says) according to the consequence of essence, that which is the cause of the other, in some way, that it may be, is said to be prior by nature," as a true definition. Yet whoever cited this fifth mode of prior in this way, in relation to convertible things, has offended against the rule of the prior [κατὰ τὸ πρότερον], because he explained the general in a specific way. For whatever is a cause to another, whether reciprocal or not reciprocal, is prior as cause and by nature. Indeed, from this too the priority of time and order seems to follow, as if it were said. So it ought to have been laid down generally: whatever is a cause is prior; and then this too would be called a general which, by the fifth mode, is prior to the specifics, since generals are the causes of specifics, as has so often been repeated from Aristotle. Therefore, of the five modes of prior, this last one, though rather unlogically, embraces both the question and the explanation of the question. Finally, these five modes of prior do not make five methods, but all of them agree with the single method of Aristotle, from the general to the specific: and the first, of time, and the fourth, of dignity, chiefly have nothing to do with this; of the rest, the third contains the question, which the second interprets as the consequence that is not reciprocal, and the fifth as the reciprocal cause; so that whatever is a cause, whether reciprocal or not, precedes as the more known, entirely. But in this fifth mode the dative τῇ φύσει, which is more evident, should be kept in mind as well, since what is the cause is more known and prior, and it is said to be more known and prior by nature [τῇ φύσει]; for this will belong to another question, as I said before. Wherefore P. Ramus concluded that this whole passage on the five modes of prior agrees with that Aristotelian philosophy of a single and unique method; and yet this fivefold division of prior is refuted by Aristotle himself in the next chapter, when he teaches that two things are at the same time [ἅμα], first according to time, as those whose origin is simultaneous; then by nature [τῇ φύσει], as those which are convertible, and neither is the cause of the other, as relatives, double and half, or as species opposed under the same genus. Of those five modes the philosopher here retains only two, time and nature or cause; yet time has no weight in the question of method and order, as I have already said. Therefore, for the methodical question about the order of antecedents and consequents, cause alone is to be considered: that which is cause is prior and more known in an absolute sense, as has been said. Meanwhile we shall note in this chapter that the dative (τῇ φύσει) is used four times in this discourse, as it was used twice before, and that τῇ φύσει is no other than τῇ αἰτίᾳ. Wherefore, to conclude this point: this first passage from Aristotle's library ought not to have disturbed anyone into thinking that there is a manifold method of art, because they saw so many modes of prior; since these modes agree in one single method; or rather, because of the five modes only the mode of cause is to be referred to this methodical question. The second division of prior is in chapter 2 [of the Posterior Analytics]…

units.la: 1. Poster. quæ jā nobis explicata est, quód prius & notius dupliciter dicatur, nobis & naturā: unde valētes hi Logici, duo methodi genera invenerunt, alterū à notioribus naturā, alterū ab iis quę sunt notiora nobis. At partitio ista à quocū que Aristoteles collegerit, inepta & ridicula est: & si legitima maximē esset, maximēq; logica, at tamē duas methodi artificiosæ species nō cōstituerēt: De partitionis elegantia primū dicatur: etenim totus hic de duob. prioris & notioris generib. locus, Eubulidē potiús authore quám Aristotelē judicē ostendit: Consideretur igitur qd ista prioris & notioris bipartita distributio præcipiat. Notiora nobis esse, ait hic locus, quæ sen sui viciniora sint: remotiora autē, ἁπλῶς καὶ τῇ φύσει, absolutē & naturā esse notiora. Ecquid illud (Nobis) inquam, significat? nónne hominibus? Quid illud (τῇ φύσει) nónne idē quod ἁπλῶς? Quę nam igitur erit ista comparatio rerum cognitarum? Singularia sunt homini notiora, Singularia sunt absolutē & naturā ignotiora. Rogabat hic P. Ramus, quódnā & quàm logicum genus comparationis id effet: Nam cum dicis, Generale eft notius abfolute & natura: hic modum notitiæ declaras: cui non exponis. cum autem dicis, Speciale eft notius nobis. hic cognitore causæ definis, hominem quippe: modum autem cognitionis non exprimis. Ergo illic judex & cognitor, non judicii, non cognitionis modus declaratur: hic vero, modus judicii & cognitionis declaratur, reticetur iudex & cognitor. Quare Logica comparationis huius valde eft λόγος: & interpretes hic ualde fudarunt: alii interpretantur(nobis) ideft noftris fenfibus: τῇ φύσει, id eft menti: quomodo & Ariftoteles loquutusvidetur antea κατὰ τὸν λόγον, κατὰ τὸν ἀδηλοιν, fecudum rationem, fecundum fenfum. At (inquam) fpe ciale hic no nifi propriu fit & individuu, fub fen fum cadere non poteft: cuiufmodi tame fpecia lia in artib9 (excepta aftrologia) nulla Ariftote les admittit, fefilia omnia rejicit, univerfalia tántum retinet. Quid igitur? quid hac mifera prioris & notioris diftributioe fiet? Alii interpretes nefcio quam nova huc interpretationem attulerunt. Deus bone, commemini abhinc annos quindecim, cum philofophus quidain hac urbe nefcio unde peregrinus, ad P.
