Ramum fuper hac queftione folicite ac fepius ventitaret, tandem meditatam & diu comentatam folutione Gordii hujus nodi attuliffe, quod diceret cafu (τῇ φύσει) no ide effe quod ἁπλῶς, fed τῇ φύσει, naturæ per dativu cafum interpretabatur: ficuti docti homines in quibufdam Ariftotelis locis latine effent interpretati: & per naturam, dicebat à I philophilosopho Deŭ intelligi: ut (Nobis & Naturę) significaret homini Deoq;: & Aristoteli placuisse, specialia esse homini notiora generalibus, generalia Deo absolutè esse notiora specialib. quē 5 philosophū recordor tum comiter & festivè à P.Ramo acceptū esse: Beasti me (ait) ò philosophe: Memoria tenes quid Aristoteles de modis Prioris & Simul in Categoriis precipiat: προτέρον τῇ φύσει, interpretaris naturę, id est Deo: Ergo πρό 10 τόρου τῷ χρόνῳ, τῇ τάξει, τῇ ἀκολουθήσει, τῇ τιμῇ, τῇ αἰτίᾳ, in eodem sermone Aristotelis & eadem re quid significabunt? An notius tempori, ordini, consecutioni, honori, causę? Tempus erit deus Saturnus credo aliquis. honor etiā numē divinitatis 15 inveniet. at logica causę, consequentię, ordinis numina quænam erunt? Tum nostra quęstione methodica quid fiet? de disciplinis humanis loquimur, qua via, non Deo, qui scholis nostris nihil egeat, sed homini tradendæ sint: & Aristoteles nominatim profitetur deducendas esse ab absoluté prioribus, id est (ut tu vis) naturæ seu deo notioribus. deorū scholam hic Aristoteles, non hominum instituerret: deniq; casus ille divinus (τῇ φύσει) sexies in capitib. de modis Prioris 25 & Simul, accipitur, non divinitus, sed ad nostrū hunc sensum humanitus: & illic τῇ φύσει, idem est quod τῇ αἰτίᾳ: & recte, cùm natura rei nihil aliud sit, quàm essentia ex causis suis constituta. Itaque 7. cap. 8. Phys. προτέρον τῇ ὁσίᾳ dicitur pro eodem, quod in Logica Organo πρότερον τῇ φύσει καὶ 30 τῇ αἰτίᾳ imò quod in eodem illo 7. capit. 8. Phys. τῇ φύσει. Quin apertissimum illud 11. cap. 5. lib. in philosophia, rem totam planissimam facit: ubi κατὰ τὸν λόγον, κατὰ τὴν φύσιν, pro τῇ φύσει à philoso-pho usurpatur. Quib auditis, philosophus ille erubuit, nec apparuit postea. Ergo videmus anxietatem hominum mirabilem, dum tam sophisticam notioris partitionem, ab Aristotele ipso praesertim reprehesam retinere cupiunt. Da mihi (inquam) ut sensus coparationis requirit, notam speciem, notum genus: & quære, utrum sit notius: nec adde jam, vel hominini vel naturae: Satis enim constat, neq; ad deos, neq; ad animates mutos & rationis expertes hanc quæstionē attinere, & hominū caussa id quæri: tū enim captio comparationis intelligetur. Comparato solem cū stella fixa aliqua, & quære de duab. stellis utra clarior: comparatio logica & legitima erit. quæstio erit claritatis, non tēporis: tumque tibi respōdebit Astrologus, solem esse clariorē: quia luce solis stella fixa accenditur, non contrà: Ita respōdebit hic Logicus, genus esse clarius & illustrius specie, quia species illustretur & definiatur genere, non cōtrà, ut antea in inventione patuit. Falsum igitur est, specialia esse nobis notiora generalibus: Nec verò sequitur, si species ante cognoscatur, quā genus, specie nobis esse notiore genere: nec ex eo concludi potest, genera minus esse nobis ac nostris sensibus, quàm species nota: nō enim efficitur, si ex tenui candela magnā aliquā facem accendero, non esse nobis & nostris sensibus facē cādela clariorem. Ita minime efficeretur, genera quàm species, quanvis ab illis orirentur, non esse notiora clarioraque.
units.tr: Aristotle's Posterior Analytics 1, which has now been explained to us, says that the prior and the better known are spoken of in two ways: for us and by nature. From this, these clever logicians found two kinds of method: one from things better known by nature, the other from things better known to us. But this division, whoever it was that Aristotle collected it from, is inept and ridiculous. Even if it were entirely legitimate and most logical, it still would not establish two species of artificial method. Let us first speak of the elegance of the division. This whole passage on the two kinds of prior and better known shows Eubulides rather than Aristotle to be its author. Let us consider, then, what this bipartite distinction of prior and better known prescribes. The passage says that things nearer to the senses are better known to us, while things further away are better known absolutely and by nature ([haplōs kai tē physei]). What, I ask, does that word "to us" mean? Does it not mean "to men"? And does tē physei not mean the same as haplōs? What, then, will this comparison of known things be? Singulars are better known to man; singulars are less known absolutely and by nature. P. Ramus asked what kind of logical comparison this was, and how logical it was. For when you say "the general is better known absolutely and by nature," you declare a mode of knowing but do not say to whom. When you say "the special is better known to us," you name the knower as man, but do not express the mode of knowing. So in the one case the judge and knower is declared, but not the mode of judging and knowing; in the other, the mode of judging and knowing is declared, while the judge and knower is left out. Hence the logic of this comparison is very much a mere play on words [logos], and the commentators have sweated hard over it here. Some interpret "to us" as "to our senses," and tē physei as "to the mind," just as Aristotle seems earlier to have spoken of [kata ton logon, kata ton adēlon], that is, according to reason and according to sense. But (I say) a special, if it is only proper and individual, cannot fall under the senses; yet Aristotle admits no such special things in the arts (except astrology). He rejects all singulars and retains only universals. What then? What will become of this wretched distinction of prior and better known? Other interpreters have brought in some new interpretation here, I know not what. Good God, I remember that about fifteen years ago a certain philosopher, a stranger to this city, I know not from where, used to visit P. Ramus often and anxiously on this question. At last he brought a solution to this Gordian knot, one he had pondered and long meditated. He said that the case (tē physei) is not the same as haplōs, but tē physei should be interpreted as "of nature" through the dative case, just as learned men have translated certain passages of Aristotle into Latin. He said that by "nature" the philosopher meant God, so that "to us and to Nature" would mean "to man and to God"; and that Aristotle had been pleased that specials are better known to man than generals, and generals better known absolutely to God than specials. I recall that Ramus received this philosopher courteously and wittily: "You have made me happy, philosopher," he said. "Do you remember what Aristotle prescribes in the Categories about the modes of prior and simultaneous? You interpret prior by nature as 'of nature,' that is, of God. Then what will prior in time, in order, in sequence, in honour, in cause [proteron tō chronō, tē taxei, tē akolouthēsei, tē timē, tē aitia] signify, in the same discourse of Aristotle and about the same thing? Are they better known to time, to order, to sequence, to honour, to cause? Time will be, I suppose, the god Saturn; honour will find its own deity too. But what will be the gods of logical cause, consequence and order? And then what becomes of our present methodical question? We are speaking of human disciplines, which must be taught in a way that suits man, not God, who needs nothing from our schools. Aristotle expressly declares that they must be derived from things prior absolutely, that is (as you would have it) from things better known to nature or God. Would Aristotle here be founding a school of gods rather than of men? Finally, that divine case (tē physei) occurs six times in the chapters on prior and simultaneous, and there it is not divine but human, in our sense. There tē physei is the same as tē aitia, and rightly so, since the nature of a thing is nothing other than its essence constituted from its causes. So in Physics 7.8, prior in substance [proteron tē ousia] is said in the same sense as prior by nature and by cause in the Organon, indeed in the same chapter 7.8 of the Physics as tē physei. Moreover, that most evident passage in Metaphysics 11.5 makes the whole matter perfectly plain, where the philosopher uses [kata ton logon, kata tēn physin], according to reason, according to nature, in place of tē physei." When they had heard these things, that philosopher blushed, and was not seen again afterwards. So we see the remarkable anxiety of men, who want to keep this so sophistical distinction of the better known, especially since Aristotle himself reproves it. Give me (I say), as the sense of the comparison requires, a known species and a known genus, and ask which is better known. Do not now add either "to man" or "to nature." For it is clear enough that this question concerns neither gods nor animals that are dumb and lack reason, and that it is asked for the sake of men; only then will the trap of the comparison be understood. Compare the sun with some fixed star, and ask of the two which is brighter. The comparison will be logical and legitimate, and the question will concern brightness, not time. Then the astronomer will answer that the sun is brighter, because the fixed star is lit up by the light of the sun, not the reverse. So this logician will answer that the genus is clearer and more illustrious than the species, because the species is illuminated and defined by the genus, not the reverse, as was made clear earlier in invention. It is therefore false that specials are better known to us than generals. Nor does it follow, if the species is known before the genus, that the species is better known to us than the genus; nor can it be concluded from this that genera are less known to us and to our senses than species are. For it does not follow that if I light a great torch from a thin candle, the candle is not clearer to us and to our senses than the torch. So it would by no means follow that genera, though they arise from species, are not better known and clearer than species.

units.la: Imó
units.tr: Nay.

units.la: Imo vero totum contrá est: Quantó enim comz munior cognitio fuerit, tantò nobis notior: ut lumina tantó sunt illustriora clarioraque, quantó majora atque ampliora. Quinetiam singulis rebus percipiendis,generales illę notitiæ in primis vel in sensus occurrunt: Priùs animal, quod eminús movetur, quàm homine esse dicimus. & hominem,quàm Socratem,quod Aristoteles in Physicis docet:imó inde Theorema opticum factum est Halaceno 72. numero lib. 2. & Vitellioni 72. Theoremate 3. Quod generales visibilium species prius occurrunt oculis quám speciales.Quamobrem quisquis vel Eubulides,vel Antisthenes,vel quivis alius, genera notioris ita partitus est,ut diceret,é notis alia esse notiora nobis , alia naturâ, cruciatum discendi cupidis proposuit: Vix enim credibile est, quot ex hoc uno velut abyssi puteo, tenebræ & caligines per omnes artes dispersæ sint. Sed tamen si qua logici salis mica hinc assumi possit, illa est, quæ ab Aristotele in Topicis in prima Philosophia anté nobis est exposita: Alia nobis rudibus & rerum imperitis notiora sunt,alia ingenio maturiore clariora: quo tempore & nobis, & naturâ sunt eadem notiora prioraq; : Neque Eubulidis partitio jam tum vera fuerit.& quidé si de duob9 coloribus quęratur, uter sit clarior: aut de sonis,uter acutior:non quęretur, uter cę cis aut lippis sit clarior, uter surdis aut surdastris sit acutior : sed uter visu, uter auditu bene affeĉtis:& illa sunt Aristotelis nimirũ similia absoluté bona bonis,absoluté sana sanis, absoluté nota doctis & eruditis. Ergo fecunda ista partitio Prioris est ridicula & inepta: Sed (quod erat secundum) si maxime esset legitima maximeque logica: attamen duplex methodus ordinandae artis & informandae minime omnium hinc aliter ab interpretibus potuit: Quid enim dicerent hic interpretes, priore illa a notioribus nobis & specialibus via artes inveniri? id enim etiam dicunt. At in hac quaestione, de artis ordine, cum inventa separatim; judicata materia sit, valde inepte atque imperite respondent: haec enim pars Logicae, de inveniendis generalibus per inductionem specialium, praemonstrata est in Categoria distributioris, in topico generis & speciei: neq; hic omnino quaestio est de rebus inveniendis. Itaq; sic respondere, sic interpretari, est aperte ludificari, aperte nugari. Tum vero quid Aristoteli interpretes hoc ipso in capite respondere debuit? Quanvis duo modi sint (ait Aristoteles) Prioris, attamen omnis ars & scientia a causis primis & immediatis procedit. Quare partitio Prioris non solum inepta & fatua est, sed ad multiplicem ordinandae artis methodum prorsus nihil efficit. Ac si jam nobis ex eodem erroris sonte locus idem ex Ethicis & Physicis & Philosophia prima proferatur, de duobus illis prioris & notioris modis, nobis & natura, propterea que duas esse artis methodos, Aristoteles interpretibus suis respondebit, quod jam respondit: Non propterea formandae & figurandae artis duas formas, duas figuras esse. In Ethicis res apertior & manifestior est, & antea jam satis explicata: At in Physicis (inquiét) res longé urgétior & vehemé tior est. Quid igitur hic Ariftoteles premit vel urget? id (inquá) qd' P.Ramus: Nam cúm philosophus præcepisset, in explicáda physica, á caus fis & principiis ordiendū esse: tū ait: Naturalis est nobis via é notioribus nobis & clarioribus, ad clariora naturâ & notiora. Quod interpretes Græci sic interpretantur, ut dicát, ab Aristotele tradi modum declarandi principia, si quid difficultatis habeant: A principiis est ordiedū, ait Aristoteles. tū si quis dicat, principia non omnib, semper esse notiora, ut rudioribus & imperitis: nihilominus respondeat Aristoteles, Est abiis incipiendū. sed si subobscurum principium aliquádo fuerit, declarádū erit inductione aliqua sensilium & familiarium exemplorū, explicatio ne communium & popularium argumentorū, hæc Græcorum interpretū vera & Aristotelæ philosophiæ in primis consentanea interpretatio est. Quapropter Physicus hic locus, duarum methodorum non potest, nisi sponte errátibus, errorem adferre. Eadem partitio iteratur 5. ca.
units.tr: Indeed the very opposite is true. For the fuller a knowledge is, the better known it is to us, just as lights are the brighter and clearer the greater and larger they are. Moreover, in perceiving particular things, those general notions come to the senses first. We say that the animal, which is moved from a distance, is known before man, and man before Socrates, as Aristotle teaches in the Physics. Indeed, an optical theorem has been drawn from this by Alhazen, book 2, number 72, and by Witelo, theorem 72 (3): that the general species of visible things meet the eyes before the special ones. Therefore whoever it was, whether Eubulides or Antisthenes or anyone else, who divided the better known into what is better known to us and what is better known by nature, set a torment before those eager to learn. For it is hardly credible how many shadows and darkness have been spread through all the arts from this one pit, as if from an abyss. But if any little crumb of logical salt can be taken from it, it is that which Aristotle set out earlier in the Topics and in First Philosophy: some things are better known to us, who are untrained and inexperienced, and others are clearer to a more mature mind. At that stage, they are the same as the better known and prior both to us and by nature. Nor would Eubulides' division have been true even then. And indeed, if one asks which of two colours is clearer, or which of two sounds is sharper, one does not ask which is clearer to the blind or the half-blind, nor which is sharper to the deaf or the hard of hearing. One asks which is clearer to those well-disposed in sight, and which is sharper to those well-disposed in hearing. Those are, of course, Aristotle's similar cases: good things absolutely to good things, healthy things absolutely to healthy things, things known absolutely to the learned and erudite. Therefore this second division of the prior is ridiculous and inept. But (which was the second point) even if it were most legitimate and most logical, a twofold method of ordering and forming an art could in no way be derived from it, as the commentators have supposed. For what would these commentators say, that arts are discovered by that first way, from things better known to us and from specials? For they do say this. But in this question, about the order of the art, the matter having already been treated separately under invention, they answer very foolishly and ignorantly. For that part of logic, on finding generals by induction from specials, was already set out in the Categories, in the topic of genus and species; nor is the question here at all about discovering things. So to answer thus, to interpret thus, is openly to mock and openly to trifle. Then what ought the commentators to have answered to Aristotle in this very chapter? Although there are two modes of the prior (says Aristotle), yet every art and science proceeds from first and immediate causes. Hence the division of the prior is not only inept and foolish, but accomplishes nothing at all toward a manifold method of ordering an art. And if the same passage is now brought forward from the same source of error, from the Ethics and the Physics and First Philosophy, concerning those two modes of prior and better known, to us and by nature, and therefore that there are two methods of the art, Aristotle will answer his interpreters as he has already answered: there are not for that reason two forms and two figures for forming and shaping an art. In the Ethics the matter is more open and manifest, and was already sufficiently explained earlier. But in the Physics (they will say) the matter is far more pressing and forceful. What then does Aristotle press or urge here? That (I say) which P. Ramus says. For when the philosopher had prescribed that in explaining physics one must begin from causes and principles, he then says: the natural way for us is from things better known and clearer to us, to things clearer and better known by nature. The Greek interpreters so interpret this as to say that Aristotle hands down a way of explaining principles, if they have some difficulty: "one must begin from principles," says Aristotle. And if someone says that principles are not always better known to everyone, as to the rougher and the inexperienced, Aristotle would nonetheless reply: one must begin from them. But if some principle is at any time rather obscure, it must be made clear by some induction of familiar and sensible examples, by explanation through common and popular arguments. This is the true interpretation of the Greek interpreters, and the one most consonant with the philosophy of Aristotle. Wherefore this passage of the Physics cannot bring in a twofold method, except to those who err of their own accord. The same division is repeated in chapter 5.

units.la: 1. Physic. clarius & manifestiús, quod notiora alia sint secundúm rationem, alia secundúm sensum: secundúm rationem, universalia, secúdúm sensum singularia. Iteratur Prioris partitio, sed trifariá. 7. capit. 8. Physic. nempe τὴ ἀκολουθίαν, τῷ χρόνῳ, κατὰ τὸν λόγον. ubi λόγια jā pro αἰτία ponitur. Sed satis superque respósum, tempus nihil esse methodicæ quæstionis: consequentiam autem & essentiam seu caussam, in unicam Aristotelis & singularem methodum cógruere. Quarto loeo eadem revocantur in philosophia 1. ca. 5. lib. quód principium fit aliquādo, unde optimè res inchoatur: ut in disciplinis, nō à primo semper inchoatur sed unde discipulus facillimè condiscat. Sed locus idé jam fuit ad 1. caput 1. Physic. 5 & de partis alicujus inductione sic intelligi locum necesse est. Licet igitur Alexander etiā errorem suum indidē revocet, quód Aristoteles illic inceperit à sensilib9: at incepit à principiis maximè generalibus & universalibus. Genera 10 verò notioris & prioris in eadē philosophia repetuntur 11. capit. 5. lib. quód prius fit loco, tempore, motu, potentia, ordine, notione: eaq; duplici, ut antea citatum est: item natură, quæcunque accidit esse sine aliis, alia verò sine illis mini 15 mé: qua divisione usum Platonē Aristoteles illic āit: & id antea fuit prius consequentia, item prius subjecto. Hic igitur genera Prioris octo ē sophista aliquo per Aristotelem colliguntur. At locus cadit in ordinis prioratum, ut natura & 20 subjectum in rationem: neq; resposition mājorem hæc confusio requirit. Neq; verò in Philosophia id tātūm fuit: Ibidē notioris duo genera 4. capit. 7. lib. repetuntur. Aristoteles disputat urus adversus ideas universales, ait à sensilib9 25 & in materia positis incipiendum. Operæpretiū enim (ait) trāsfire ad notius. Omnis enim disciplina sic fit omnibus per minus nota naturā ad nota magis. & hoc opus est, ut in actionibus fe- * cisse ex cuiq; bonis omnino bona, unicuiq; bo- 30 natsic ex iisdem notioribus, naturā nota, ipsi nota. Hic locus extremus etiam videatur interpretibus é duobus notioris generibus duo quoq; artificiosæ methodi genera facere: & incipiendum á speciali b.potiús esse : quia ut Legislator é bonis singulorum universale & absolutè civibus bonum colligit: sic doctor artis, ex iis quæ ipsi,id est(ut Alexáder interpretatur)ignoranti nota sunt,deducit naturâ nota. hic primó notabis dici cuique notum,quod antea nobis notū dicebatur:& ὅλως ἢ τῇ φύσει,jam pro eodè acci- pi,ut antea ἁπλῶς, τῇ τῇ φύσει, κατὰ τὸν λόγον, κατὰ τὴν φύσιν. Neq; hic locus de universę artis ordinatio ne,sed de inductione singulorum ad universale declarandū loquitur,ut locus ille ad 1.ca.1.Physic. quod & ejuídem loci consequens litera clariús ostendit: Singulis nota & prima quadantenus nota sunt,& parum aut nihil habet entis,id est(ut Alexander ait) veritatis.hic philosophus prima dicit,quæ dixerat antea priora: & taliū rerum cognitione ait esse infirmę,aut potiús nullius veritatis. tum sequitur, Attamen ex malé quidem notis , ipsi aut notis, omnino nota nos se conandum est,transfeudo (uti dictum est) per hęc ipsa. His verbis Ariftoteles plpicué docet, specialia homini nota esse ἰδίμα τῇ χωλῶς, quadantenus & malé id est imperfectè generalia, ὅλως τῇ τῇ φύσει, omnino & naturâ. Ut jam partitio tota hæc Eubulidea, nihil aliud significet, quâ quod antea dictum est: é notis, alia esse quodammodo & ex conditione captuque ingenii notiora, alia esse ἁπλῶς, ὅλως, κατὰ τὸν λόγον, τῇ φύσει: absolute, omnino, secundum rationem, naturâ notiora: & nostrum philosophum, τῇ φύσει, id est naturæ, tanquam Deo interpretantem, valde ridiculum efficit. Veruntamen postremus hic Aristoteles locus ab Aristotele ipso temere inductus est: Erat enim illi de essentia tum physica & sensili, tum divina & separata differendum: cumq; sibi prius agedum de physicis & sensilibus statuetet, unde lucis aliquid ad divinas intelligedum accederet, (ut ex scholis P. Rami Metaphysicis ad eum locum percipies) tum, inquam, theorema hoc induxit temere, quia q progreditur a Physica ad Theologiā, progreditur a naturā clarioriAC magis communi ad naturā obscurius & magis speciale: quod Aristoteles etiā facere voluit, qui τὰ μετὰ τὰ φυσικὰ physicis substituit. Quamobrem valeat Eubulides, cum prioris & notioris sui partitione, qua totas omnium disciplinarū scholas tam vehementer obscuravit: prioris & notioris genera modo quinq;, modo duo, modo tria, modo octo: neq; quinq;, neq; duas, neq; tres, neq; octo artis ordinandae collocandaeque methodos Aristoteli Aristoteleam illam intelligentiae viam recordati persuadebunt. Atq; hoc primum de multitudine methodorum argumentum, videmus quomodo sumptum sit ex Aristoteleae bibliothecae locis perverse detortis, neq; ad rem quicquam attinentibus. Secundū est ab interpretibus Aristotelis, qui duas methodos in Organo, analysin & genesin, id est resolutionē & compositionem commeti sunt: ut per Analysin, cogitemus primo summū finem: deinde fini proxima: postremo reliqua, ut erūt propinqua vel remota, ita prius posteriūsve cogitemus. Per I.5 genesin cótrà, opus ordinemus ex eo loco, ubi analysis desierat: tandemq; concludamus, ubi analysis inceperat. Simplicius in Categoriis appellat Διωρίζω τὴν πρᾶξιν, contemplatione & actione, & explicat exemplo domus, cujus primùm finis cogitetur, tum tegumentu, deinde parietes, fundamenta, fossio terræ deniq; : & hæc illi est analysis seu Διωρία, à cuj9 extremo deinde πράξις incipiat, à fossione nempe, tum ad fundamenta, deinde parietes, tandem ad tectum perveniat. At hoc exemplū de unius singularis ædificii architecto mente architectonicam complexo hîc & falsum & ineptum est. Nam cúm architectus de ædificio certo cogitat, totam simul ideâ ma-teria formaq; comprehensam complectitur, deinde ad opus accessurus materiam primùm é lapide, ligno, cæmento comparat, deinde coagmétat & architectatur: Sic cum grámatico vel logico loquendum aut differendum est, primó copiam verborum vel argumentorum, deinde syntaxim vel dispositione meditatur. At interpretes isti beati non animadvertût hic quæstionem non esse de usu artis inventæ & conformatæ, sed de artis (cum totæ ejus partes inventæ & separatim judicatæ fuerint) forma & collocatione. Tum verò quód ajunt artes inveniri primùm à summo fine per subalternas partes descen dêdo ad infima: imperitissimè ac turpissimè labuntur, nec recordantur quę sunt ab Aristotele 14.1.Post.& 18.cap.2.Post.tam magnificé tamq; copiosé propositá, inductione singularium rerū generalia & universalia artium documéta inveniri, tandem qz cū particulatim inventa fuerunt, incipiendo á natura prioribus & notioribus generatim collocari, ut tot Aristotelis locis já patuit. Quare interpretes Aristot.se sprsus ignaros vel immemores Aristoteleę philosophiæ in his tā anilib. deliramētis profitētur. Et tñ hæc methodꝰ interpretū duplex videtur é tertio capite tertii Ethici ad Nicomachū deducta esse: ubi Aristoteles ait, deliberationē, esse inquisitionē & invētionē quandā, nō finis, sed ad finē deinceps mediorū, donec perventū fit ad primā caussam, q ultima fit in invētione: mediaq; ista invenire, perinde esse, ac figurā geometricā retexere: tan demq; ultimū in analysi seu resolutione, esse primum in genesi seu generatione. Hęc Aristotelis verba de consultatione & consultationis executione, verba sunt interpretū de duabus methodis. Logica deniq; Aristotelis de genere deliberativo, videatur interpretibus Logicam de duabus methodis attulisse: Sed tamen neq; hic Aristotelis locus verus est, neq; interpretes sententiam Aristotelis ad duas methodos rectè trāstu lerunt. Aristoteles ait finem nō quæri in deliberatione, sed assumi: quod verum est. Videtur autem hic certum invētionis ordinem præcipere: quod tamen perpetuum nō est. Ac ne quis scholasticus & imperitus rerum in deliberatione civili res ualdę reconditas & abstrusas agi putet, testimonia adhibebūt Demosthenis & Ciceronis deliberationes in amplissimis civitatib. habitæ, in quibus non certo illo ordine cōnexa in ter se argumenta, sed consentanea, dissentanea, comparata, omnia deniq; argumentorum genera, ut res tulit, adhibentur. Somnium igitur est philosophi de logica inventione, & deliberationis & omnisquæstionis cómuni, non satis accurate recordátis: Deinde comparatio ἀναλύσεως γραφικῆς deliberativæ cum geometrica, valdé est hic absurda: Genesis enim, q dicitur á Geometris, est á principiis generalib. deducta cóclusio. Analysis est item explicatio inversa é suppositá cóclusione ad ipsa principia, ut patet in Euclidis elementis, I.2.3.4.5. ppositi.13. & in Archimede 2. de sphæra, & Pappo l. 7. Imo qualis vera & utilis analysis est in quadrati & circuli laterib. & radici b9 retexédis: nā in cæteris illis locis est sophisma plane deridendum: ut P. Rami scholę illic oftendunt: quale hic in deliberatione nihil est: Analysis enim, quæ modo Aristoteli dicitur, est ipsamet deliberatio disputatioq; deliberantis: quæ á generalibus esse posit, ut quælibet alia discreptatio: nō est illa retexta Penelopes tela: Genesis autem deliberationis omnino nullum est logicum opus, sed ipsa μηχανή πράξις, id est administratio & effectio rei, quæ non argumētis, sed manibus & pedibus, cæterisq; corporū instrumentis peragitur. Sic deliberationis Manilianę analysis, Ciceroniana fuit oratio: γένεσις aut Popeiana, tot millibus hominū terra mariq; armatorum expeditio. Quamobrem tota hæc deliberativæ ἀναλύσεως περὶ γενέσεως & descriptio, & cum geometrica analysi genesiq; comparatio, fallax admodum & captiosa est. neq; etiam si vera sit, ab interpretibus rectè translata est ad duas methodos: Primó finem interpretes cogitandum præceperunt, quem Ariftoteles ponédum effe dicit: deinde genefin fumpferunt pro compofitione argumétorum, non pro executione & effectione fumpti confilii, ut Ariftoteli placuit. Quare interpretes toto cælo híc aberrarunt, & turpi fœdoq; fophifmate philofophiam deinde contaminarunt: Hinc enim pleriq; alii interpretes feductí(in quibus Galenus numeratur) cómenta ifta methodorū per omnes artes difperferunt. Enimvero ex interpretibus Ariftotelis, Galenus omnium nobilifsimus, cujufq; in Ariftotelis Logicam varia monumenta extiterunt, de multitudine methodorū fcholas omnes præcipué complevit, præcipueq; P. Ramo objecto eft,ideoq; precipué animadvertendus. Vir hic, ingenio fingulari fuit, eruditione varia & multi plici, eloquentia licet ἀσιαπινωτάτη, attamé legentibus nó ingrata: judicio ab omni opinionis fervitute liberrimo, ut Hippocrati, Platoni, Ariftoteli, addictos, fervos appellet. Verùm quamvis tantus tamq; egregius philofophus, attamé huc neq; ingenii, neq; doctrinæ, neq; eloquetiæ, neque judicii dignum quicquá attulit: nec Ariftoteli fanctior Galenus in Logicæ erroribus effe debuerit: quáin Ariftoteles Galeno fuit in erroribus anatomiæ: Appellat igitur Galenus methodum, modó fuo ipfo methodi nomine, modó Θεωρίαν, ut fimplicius, modó διδασκαλίαν τάξεως, initioque noni libri de placitis Hippocratis & Platonis ita definit: Ego veró (ait) affirmo, quæfitarum rerum veritatem te adepturũ effe, fi primum » primúm viæ ad eam ducentis initium cognove » ris, á qua aberrans in multos rationum errores » incides.Iisdem autem indiciis, quibus principi- » um adeptus fis, obtinebis, quid é principio se5 cundum, deinde similiter tertium, ac deinceps unumquodq; consequatur. Hæc methodi definitio Galenica,est obscura: videtur enim Simplicii analyfin & Διωρίαν dicere, sed mox ibidé de Hippocrate apertiús loquitur: quód Hippocra 10 tes initium faciat ab iis,quæ sunt maxima, & omnibus cognitu facillima:Hæc (ait tum Galenus) qui assecutus erit, poterit facilé ad proxima inter fe & conjuncta defcendêdo paulatim pervenire.Hic Galenus clarior est, & Hippocra 15 tis methodum anté propositam,rectè & perspicué declarat: ut videatur definire methodum, quam P.Ramus definivit. Sed Galenus methodum ita definitam,modó unicam, modó duplicem, modó triplicem, imperitis quibusdam & 20 P.Ramo in hac quæstione obstrepentibus videtur efficere. Primus igitur est locus, dū illo ipso Hippocraticç methodi argumêto probare vult, similitudinis & dissimilitudinis accuratam notionem ad methodicam cujuslibet artis consti25 tutionem satis esse. At qui Galeni authoritate hic abutitur, hanc artificio sæ dispositionis formam in hoc Hippocratis loco non animadvertit,sed quæstionem, ad quam disceptandâ & deducendam, methodus hæc ab Hippocrate adhi 30 bebatur,pro methodo ipsa accepit:& similitudinis dissimilitudinifq; quæstionem, pro quæstionis ipsius explicatione & tractatione sumpsit:si militudinemq; ac dissimilitudinem nobis tradidit pro methodo,quæ principia, quę maxima & facillima, & notisima, deq; iis derivata fecunda,tertia,quarta,suis quæq; locis institueret. Similitudo quidem & dissimilitudo, argumenta (fi apté fumantur) illustria quidem illa & fplendida sunt, & Empiricorum analogifmum illum continent,de quo in optima secta Galenus tam multa disserit,& in Empiricæ sectæ compēdio. At ordinis nullam nobis viam ostendunt: Nec Hippocrates, similitudinis & dissimilitudinis argumentū illud; pro dispositione & ordine artis tradidit,sed viam & hoc, & cæteris argumētis utendi docuit.Materia domus, est in lapidibus,lignis,cæmentis : forma domus est in lapidum,lignorum, cæmentorum apta compositio ne & collocatione:lapis,forma domus non est. Ita est in methodico ordine,materia est in caufis,effectis, genere,specie,toto, parte, fimilitudine, dissimilitudine : forma methodicæ difpofitionis est in ordine primorum,fecundorum,tertiorum.Et quidem Galenus quamvis interpretum commenta illa verbis loqui videatur,attamen reipfa & exemplis docet,similium & difsimilium nominibus nequaquam perpetui in arte tota ordinis formam sibi propositā esse, cuíh idem & diversum,commune & proprium,fimile & dissimile pro eodem capiat.Itaq; veré judicabat P. Ramus temerè Galenū hic sibi objici. Atq; id scholasticum magistri alicujus fomniū fuisse suspicabatur: Galeni inventum & judiciū nullum esse arbitrabatur, errorem hunc totum
units.tr: Let us take the first point: Physics 1 says that things are better known in two ways, some by reason and some by sense. By reason, the universals are better known; by sense, the singulars. The division of the Prior is repeated, but in three ways (Physics 7, ch. 8): namely in order (τὴν ἀκολουθίαν), in time (τῷ χρόνῳ), and according to the account (κατὰ τὸν λόγον), where the word λόγια is already put for cause (αἰτία). But it has been answered more than enough that time has nothing to do with method, and that sequence and essence, or cause, agree in one single and distinctive method of Aristotle. In the fourth place, the same things are recalled in Philosophy, Book 1, ch. 5: that a beginning is sometimes where a thing is best started, as in the disciplines, which do not always begin from the first point but from where the pupil can learn most easily. But this same place was already discussed at Physics 1, ch. 1, and it is necessary that the division of some part be understood in this way. Therefore, although Alexander here also repeats his error, that Aristotle began there from sensibles, Aristotle in fact began from the most general and universal principles. The kinds of what is better known and prior are repeated in the same philosophy at Book 5, ch. 11: that what is prior is prior by place, time, motion, power, order, and notion (and this twofold, as was mentioned before); likewise by nature, whatever can exist without others while others cannot exist without it; and Aristotle there says that Plato used this division. And previously it was prior by sequence, likewise prior by subject. Here, then, eight kinds of the prior are gathered by Aristotle from some sophist. But the place falls under the priority of order, as nature and subject fall under reason, and this confusion does not require a longer reply. Nor was this all in Philosophy: in the same place, at Book 7, ch. 4, the two kinds of what is better known are repeated. Aristotle, disputing against universal Ideas, says that one must begin from sensibles and from what is placed in matter. For (he says) it is worth the effort to pass over to what is better known. For every discipline thus proceeds by way of what is less known by nature to what is more known; and this is necessary, as in actions, to make all good things out of good things for each person, so also out of the same things better known by nature to what is known to us. This extreme passage also seems to interpreters to make from the two kinds of better known two kinds of artificial method, and that one should begin rather from the particular: because just as the lawgiver gathers the universal and absolute good for citizens from the goods of individuals, so the teacher of an art deduces from what is known to himself, that is (as Alexander interprets it), what is known to the ignorant, things better known by nature. Here first you will note that what is known to each is said to be what was previously said to be known to us, and that ὅλως or τῇ φύσει [wholly, or by nature] is now taken for the same thing as previously ἁπλῶς, τῇ φύσει, κατὰ τὸν λόγον, κατὰ τὴν φύσιν [simply, by nature, according to the account, according to nature]. Nor does this place speak of the ordering of a whole art, but of the induction of singulars to declare the universal, as that place at Physics 1, ch. 1, does; and the following sentence of the same passage shows this more clearly: "To individuals what is known and first is known in some measure, and has little or nothing of being, that is (as Alexander says) of truth." Here the philosopher calls prime what he had previously called prior; and he says that knowledge of such things is weak, or rather of no truth. Then follows: "Yet from things known badly, yet known to us, we must strive to know things altogether, passing through these very things (as has been said)." By these words Aristotle plainly teaches that the particulars are known to man in some measure and badly, that is imperfectly, while the generals are known wholly and by nature (ὅλως τῇ τῇ φύσει). So that this whole Eubulidean division means nothing other than what was said before: that of things known, some are in a way better known, according to condition and capacity of mind, and others are better known simply, wholly, according to the account, by nature: absolutely, wholly, according to reason, by nature. And it makes our philosopher, who (as it were) interprets nature as God, appear very ridiculous. Yet this last place of Aristotle was rashly introduced by Aristotle himself: for he had to discuss the essence of both the physical and sensible, and also the divine and separate; and since he had first resolved to deal with physical and sensible things, from which something of light might come to the understanding of divine things (as you will perceive from the Metaphysical school lectures of P. Ramus on that place), then, I say, he rashly introduced this theorem, because whoever proceeds from Physics to Theology proceeds from what is clearer and more common by nature to what is more obscure and more special; which Aristotle also wished to do, he who placed τὰ μετὰ τὰ φυσικὰ [the things after the physical] in place of physics. Therefore let Eubulides go, with his division of prior and better known, by which he has so vehemently obscured the whole schools of all disciplines: the kinds of prior and better known, now five, now two, now three, now eight. Nor will those who recall the path of understanding to Aristotle, that path of his, persuade us that the methods of ordering and placing an art are neither five, nor two, nor three, nor eight. And this is the first argument concerning the multitude of methods: we see how it has been taken from places of Aristotle's library perversely twisted and having nothing to do with the matter. The second comes from the interpreters of Aristotle, who have committed the error of finding in the Organon two methods, analysis and genesis, that is resolution and composition: so that by analysis we think first of the highest end, then of what is nearest to the end, last of the rest, and as they are near or remote, so we think of them earlier or later. By genesis, on the contrary, we order the work from the point where analysis left off, and finally we conclude where analysis began. Simplicius in the Categories calls it Διωρίζω τὴν πρᾶξιν [I define the action], contemplation and action, and explains it by the example of a house: first the end is thought of, then the roof, then the walls, foundations, and at last the digging of the ground; and this for him is analysis, or Διωρία, from whose end then the πρᾶξις [action] begins, namely from the digging, then goes on to the foundations, then the walls, and at last reaches the roof. But this example, of a single particular building, with the architect conceiving it in mind as a whole, is both false and inept here. For when the architect thinks of a definite building, he grasps at once the whole idea comprehended by matter and form; then, about to set to work, he first procures material of stone, wood, and mortar, and then fits and builds. So when one must speak or discourse with a grammarian or a logician, one first considers the store of words or arguments, and then their syntax or arrangement. But those blessed interpreters do not notice that the question here is not about the use of an art already invented and formed, but about the form and placing of the art (once all its parts have been invented and separately judged). Moreover, when they say that arts are first invented from the highest end by descending through subordinate parts to the lowest, they fall most unskilfully and shamefully, and do not recall what Aristotle says at Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 14, and Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 18, so magnificently and copiously set forth: that the general and universal precepts of arts are found by induction of singular things, and finally, when they have been found piece by piece, are arranged generally, beginning from nature, from what is prior and better known; as has already been made clear by so many places of Aristotle. Wherefore the interpreters of Aristotle profess themselves, once more, ignorant or forgetful of Aristotle's philosophy in these so childish follies. And yet this twofold method of the interpreters seems to be drawn from the third chapter of the third book of the Ethics to Nicomachus, where Aristotle says that deliberation is a certain inquiry and invention, not of the end but of the means that follow on to the end, until one arrives at the first cause, which is the last in invention; and that to find these intermediate things is just like unravelling a geometrical figure; and finally that the last thing in analysis or resolution is the first in genesis or generation. These words of Aristotle about consultation and the execution of consultation are, for the interpreters, words about two methods. Finally, Aristotle's Logic on the deliberative kind is thought by the interpreters to have brought in the Logic of two methods. But neither is this place of Aristotle true, nor do the interpreters rightly render Aristotle's meaning into two methods. Aristotle says that the end is not sought in deliberation but assumed; which is true. But he seems here to prescribe a certain order of invention, which nevertheless is not constant. And lest any scholastic and inexperienced person think that very recondite and abstruse matters are treated in civic deliberation, the speeches of Demosthenes and Cicero, delivered in the most important states, will serve as witnesses: in them the arguments are not linked together in that fixed order, but are agreeing, disagreeing, compared, and in short all kinds of arguments are used as the matter required. So it is a dream of the philosopher, not sufficiently carefully remembered, about logical invention, and about the common character of deliberation and every question. Then the comparison of the deliberative ἀναλύσεως [analysis] with the geometrical is utterly absurd here: for the genesis, which is so called by geometers, is a conclusion deduced from general principles. Analysis is likewise an explanation running back from a supposed conclusion to the principles themselves, as is plain in Euclid's Elements, Books 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, Proposition 13, and in Archimedes, On the Sphere and Cylinder 2, and in Pappus, Book 7. Indeed, what true and useful analysis there is in unravelling the sides of a square or circle and the roots of numbers: for in those other places it is a sophism to be plainly laughed at, as the schools of P. Ramus show there. Such a thing has no place here in deliberation: for analysis, which is now said by Aristotle to be deliberation itself and the disputation of the one deliberating, can proceed from general things like any other debate; it is not that unravelled web of Penelope. But the genesis of deliberation is no logical work at all, but the μηχανή πράξις [mechanical action], that is the management and effecting of the thing, which is carried out not by arguments but by hands and feet and other bodily instruments. Thus the analysis of the Manilian deliberation was Cicero's speech; its genesis, or that of Pompey, was the expedition of so many thousands of armed men by land and sea. Wherefore this whole description of the deliberative ἀναλύσεως περὶ γενέσεως [analysis concerning genesis], and its comparison with geometrical analysis and genesis, is very fallacious and deceptive. Nor, even if it were true, has it been rightly transferred by the interpreters to two methods. First, the interpreters taught that one must think of the end, which Aristotle says must be assumed; then they took genesis for the composition of arguments, not for the execution and effecting of the chosen plan, as Aristotle intended. So the interpreters have wandered here wholly off course, and then contaminated philosophy with a shameful and foul sophism. For from this many other interpreters, led astray (among whom Galen is counted), spread these fictions of many methods through all the arts. Indeed, of the interpreters of Aristotle, Galen, the most noble of all, whose various monuments on Aristotle's Logic have survived, filled all the schools with the multitude of methods, and it is chiefly against him that P. Ramus has made his objection, and therefore he must be considered especially. This man had a singular genius, varied and manifold learning, eloquence indeed ἀσιαπινωτάτη [most unpolished], yet not unpleasant to readers; a judgment most free from all servitude to opinion, so that he calls those devoted to Hippocrates, Plato, and Aristotle slaves. But although so great and so excellent a philosopher, yet here he has brought nothing worthy of his genius, his learning, his eloquence, or his judgment; nor ought Galen to have been more sound than Aristotle in the errors of Logic, just as Aristotle was not sounder than Galen in the errors of anatomy. Galen therefore calls it method, sometimes by the very name of method, sometimes Θεωρίαν [theory], as a simpler term, sometimes διδασκαλίαν τάξεως [teaching of order], and at the beginning of the ninth book of On the Opinions of Hippocrates and Plato he defines it thus: "I affirm (he says) that you will attain the truth of the things sought, if you first come to know the first beginning of the way leading to it, from which, wandering, you will fall into many errors of reasoning. And by the same signs by which you have grasped the beginning, you will obtain what follows from the beginning in second place, then in similar manner third, and so each thing in its order." This Galenic definition of method is obscure: for it seems to speak of the analysis and Διωρία of Simplicius, but soon after, in the same place, he speaks more openly about Hippocrates: that Hippocrates makes the beginning from those things which are greatest and most easily known to all. "Whoever has attained these (says Galen then) will be able to come easily, by descending gradually, to what is nearest to them and connected." Here Galen is clearer, and rightly and perspicuously declares the method of Hippocrates set forth before, so that he seems to define the method which P. Ramus defined. But Galen, by making method defined in this way sometimes single, sometimes double, sometimes triple, seems to some unskilled persons, and to P. Ramus who is clamouring against him in this question, to bring about confusion. The first point, then, is where he wishes to prove by this very argument of the Hippocratic method that an accurate notion of similarity and dissimilarity is enough for the methodical constitution of any art. But he who abuses the authority of Galen here does not notice the form of artful arrangement in this place of Hippocrates; instead he takes for the method itself the question for which this method was used by Hippocrates to be argued and deduced; and he took the question of similarity and dissimilarity for the explanation and treatment of the question itself. He handed down similarity and dissimilarity to us as the method, which should establish the principles, the greatest, easiest and best known, and the second, third and fourth derived from them, each in its place. Similarity and dissimilarity, indeed, are arguments (if rightly taken) that are bright and splendid, and they contain that analogism of the Empiricists, of which Galen discourses so much in the best sect and in his Compendium of the Empiric sect. But they show us no way of order: nor did Hippocrates hand down that argument of similarity and dissimilarity as the arrangement and order of the art, but taught the way of using this and his other arguments. The matter of a house is in stones, wood, and mortar; the form of a house is in the fitting composition and placing of stones, wood, and mortar: a stone is not the form of the house. So it is in method: the matter is in causes, effects, genus, species, whole, part, similarity, dissimilarity; the form of methodical arrangement is in the order of firsts, seconds, and thirds. And indeed Galen, although he seems to speak in the words of the interpreters' fictions, yet teaches in fact and by examples that the form of order in the whole art is by no means set before him in the names of similar and dissimilar, since he takes the same and different, common and proper, similar and dissimilar for the same thing. So P. Ramus judged rightly that Galen was rashly objected to here; and he suspected that this was a dream of some schoolmaster; he judged that Galen had no invention or judgment in this, and that the whole error

units.la: non aliunde profectum, sæpe jam in Ariftotelicorum interpretum erroribus monuit, quàm quia Logica definita his nulla fit, partium nulla distributio facta fit, ut intelligeretur methodus ipsa deniq; in certa Logicæ & sua parte cōstituta. Hęc igitur Galeni logica est, de prima methodo similitudinis & dissimilitudinis: cujus etiam Platoné pari atq; eadē fide faceret authoré, atq; Hippocraté fecerat. Plato enim similitudinem & dissimilitudinem sæpe adhibuit & laudavit. methodum tamē artis ordinandæ in similitudine & dissimilitudine nullam usquam collocavit. Secunda Galeni doctrina est de duabus methodis, ad artiū cōstitutionem maximè (ut ait) necessariis. altera Διαιρετικὴ vocat, à primo & generalissimo per medias differentias ad individua. Illa est interpretū ἀναλυτικὴ seu διωρητικὴ: alteram vocat συνθετικὴν, quę contrà ab individuis per medias differentias ascendit ad generalissimum & primum: & ista videatur πρᾶξις, σύνθεσις, γνῶσις interpretum. Atqui P. Ramus tot locis antea productis, secundam istam methodum quā universæ artis ordinandæ Galenus videtur efficere, propositis duobus illis fœdissimis ex una tautologia sophismatis, tam acriter refutavit, ut nō pigeat modò, sed pudeat repetere. Sed tamē magis est admirabile hoc etiam loco adversarii ingenium, quàm in prima methodo fuerat. Methodum similitudinis & dissimilitudinis antea probare contenderat authoritate Hippocratis & Platonis: qui uterq; nihil unquam de tali methodo cogitasset: Hic vero duas istas ἐλὰς τῇ ἀνάλυσι memethodos, clarisimis illis & illustrisimis ePhe dro Phileboque testimoniis affirmare nititur, duasq; Platonis illas ideas definitionis partitio nisq;. putat esse methodos duas, σωϑετικὼ ἡ διαιρετικῶ. At mirifice methodice, ajebat hic P. Ramus, quid hic agis: utrum nobis duobus Phaedri Philebiq; locis persuadere vis, duas contrarias esse contrariis inter se viis methodos, cum unica & singularis a generalib. ad specialia tam splendide tamq; magnifice praedicetur quaeq; sola perfecti animalis formam in Phedro celebratam refert, cum primo definiat, deinde partiatur? Haec? sola(ut Philebus testatur) omnes artes ignis sui luce clarissima hominibus perspicuas effecit: solaq; catenae suae vinculo, artes in unum corpus copofuit ἐπιστήμης quidem in Phi lebo Socrates proposuit: αὐτόλω σωϑετικῆ artes qui dem primo repertas esse docuit, sed contraria ἀλλ' ἀναιρετικῆ tradendos esse descendendo a summo illo fine per media ad infinitatem. Quamobrem P. Ramus hoc loco philosophos omnes ob testabatur & orabat, ne quid simpliciter crederent, Platonis locos cum his Galeni dogmatis conferrent, cernerētq; oculis, quod animis vix persuaderi posset. Galenus Platonem, Aristolelem, Pollucem praeceptore, aliosq; permultos, ut simpliciter credulos irrisit, qui nullo adhibito judicio, nullo de rebus experimento sumpto, temere scriptis atq; auditis rebus & opinionibus stultis (ut ipse loquitur) credidissent. Virtutem igitur Galeni imitemur: nec hominis gratia eorum similes efficiamur, quos merito a Galeno leno pro fatuis idiotis reprehensos arbitramur. Optima ille voluit, nos idem velimus: non omnia potuit, nos aliquid pro nostra parte conemur: in Galeno, Galeni virtutes imitemur, nec inerte inexperientiâ, omnis erroris ac temeritatis magistram (ut Plato, ut Ariftoteles cêsent) á Galeno interprete tantopere damnatá, in Gale no sequamur: attamen si quis æquior esse volet, intelliget é Galeni exemplis Galenum nihil hic de perpetua artis collocatione cogitasse, sed juedicasse duas ideas divisionis & definitionis ad omnê tractatione singulares esse. Sed interpretû verbis ambiguè utitur, & incautos fallit: neque logicâ distinctá habuit. Verûm his tam multis cômentis adhuc infolentiora sunt eą quæ de tertia methodi doctrina objiciûtur. Sunt enim tria capita, ait Galenus: Primû circa cöpositionê & divisionê: secundû circa cöfequentiû & repugnantiû cognitionê: tertium præterea, quod circa mutuâ rerum cöparationem, tum majorû, tum pariû, tum similiû: quibus respondet ejusdê & diversi cognitio. Hæc adhuc Galeni verba sunt, quib. tres novæ methodi ad totas artes disponendû dicûtur proponi. at inquâ potius texerentur superiores etiâ jam cötextæ. Methodus similitudinis & dissimilitudinis unica primum facta est: hac trium methodorû partitione á Galeno damnaretur: nec certé ulla præcipué de tribus efficitur. Διαίρεσις ἡ σύνθεσις, duæ diverse methodi factæ priûs erant: hic é duabus una cô ficitur. At impossibile est, unam & eandê artem utroq; ordinis genere simul instituì. Secûdo capite,consequentiū & repugnantiū cōsideratio, methodus efficitur. At μαχόμενα, repugnātia quę Galeno dicūtur,si sint Aristotelis αὐτοπαθῆ, opposita,argumenti quidē logici magnū & amplū locum copleƈtuntur: ordinis tamen & methodicæ difpofitionis fymbolū nobis nullum often dūt:ἀκόλουθα, cōsequentia, exceptis diffentaneis, & difsimilibus, omnia feré argumentorū genera cōtinent:cauffæ enim ex effectis plerunq;, & vicifsim ex caufsis effecta cōsequuntur:& in cęteris argumentis eodē feré modo. At argumenta materiam artium & difputationum ( ut antē jam dixi)præbet formam, fpeciem, collocationem,id eft methodū,non præbent. Tandem verō cōparatorum genera, majorum,minorū, parium, fimiliū, quam artificiosæ collocationis & methodi vel obscurifsimam notam habent? Ingentem librum parabolis & cōparationibus impleveris: quid obstabit,quō minus liber ifte cō fufifsimē ,ac fine ulla methodo progrediatur? Nec enim cōparatio, ut ejusdē ac diverfi cōfide ratio,ullam cōtinet in fe admonitionē, quid pri mū,quid fecundū, quid tertiū effe debeat:id eft, methodi nullum fymbolum, nullū fignum,nullum documētum habet: materies eft informis. Nihil igitur ifto loco Galenus Aristotelis unicā ordinandę artis methodum offendit, nihil refel lit, temerēq; ab imperitis hominibus P. Ramo objicitur : neq; enim judicio his verbis Galenū quicquā de perpetua ordinatione totius artis cogitasse, & obtrectationis adversus unicā Aristotelis methodū calumnia manifestior eft.Tot igi-
units.tr: This error arose from no other source than what Ramus has often pointed out in the mistakes of the Aristotelian commentators: no definition of logic was given, no division of its parts was made, so that method itself was never understood to be established in a fixed place within logic and in its own part. This, then, is Galen's logic of the first method, of similarity and dissimilarity. Galen would have made Plato its author with the same weight and the same credibility with which he made Hippocrates its author. For Plato often used and praised similarity and dissimilarity, but nowhere did he set out a method of arranging an art based on similarity and dissimilarity. Galen's second doctrine concerns two methods, which he says are especially necessary for the constitution of the arts. The first he calls diairetikē [Διαιρετικὴ], which goes from the first and most general thing through intermediate differences to the individuals; this is the analytic or diōrētikē [ἀναλυτικὴ ἢ διωρητικὴ] of the interpreters. The other he calls synthetikē [συνθετικὴν], which on the contrary rises from individuals through intermediate differences to the most general and first thing; this seems to be the praxis, synthesis, and gnōsis [πρᾶξις, σύνθεσις, γνῶσις] of the interpreters. Yet Ramus, after so many passages cited earlier, refuted this second method, which Galen seems to think constitutes the whole ordering of an art, so sharply, by exposing the two most disgraceful sophisms built on a single tautology, that I am not only unwilling but ashamed to repeat them. Yet this adversary's cleverness is still more remarkable here than it was in the first method. Ramus had earlier tried to prove the method of similarity and dissimilarity by the authority of Hippocrates and Plato, though neither of them had ever thought of such a method. Here, however, Galen strives to affirm these two methods, the synthetic and the diairetic, by the very clear and famous testimonies of Plato in the Phaedrus and the Philebus, and he thinks those two Platonic ideas of definition and division are two methods. But how marvellously methodical you are, Ramus would say, what are you doing here? Do you wish to persuade us, from two passages in the Phaedrus and Philebus, that there are two methods opposed to each other by contrary paths, when the single and unique method, from general things to particulars, is praised so splendidly and magnificently, and it is the only one that, in the Phaedrus, presents the form of a perfect animal, since it first defines and then divides? This method alone, as Philebus testifies, has made all the arts clear and visible to men by the most brilliant light of its fire; and it alone has joined the arts into one body by the bond of its chain. Socrates in the Philebus did indeed propose the knowledge [ἐπιστήμης] of these things, and he taught that the arts were first discovered by the synthetic method [αὐτόλω συνθετικῆ], but that they must be handed down by the opposite, the analytic method [ἀναιρετικῆ], descending from that highest end through the intermediate steps to the infinite. Therefore Ramus in this place called all philosophers to witness and begged them not to believe anything simply, but to compare Plato's passages with these doctrines of Galen and to see with their own eyes what could scarcely be persuaded to their minds. Galen mocked Plato, Aristotle, Pollux his teacher, and very many others as simple-minded believers, who, without applying any judgment or taking any experience of things, had rashly believed writings and heard opinions and foolish views (as he himself puts it). Let us therefore imitate Galen's virtue, and for the sake of no man let us become like those whom we rightly judge to have been rebuked by Galen as foolish idiots. He wished the best things; let us wish the same. He could not do everything; let us strive for something on our own part. In Galen, let us imitate Galen's virtues, and let us not follow in Galen the sloth and inexperience, the teacher of every error and rashness (as Plato and Aristotle said), so greatly condemned by Galen the interpreter. Yet if anyone wishes to be fairer, he will understand from Galen's examples that Galen had not thought here of a perpetual arrangement of the art, but had judged that the two ideas of division and definition are each singular for every treatment. But he uses the words of the interpreters ambiguously, and deceives the unwary, and he had no distinct logic. Yet even more outrageous than all these many fabrications are those things that are objected concerning the third doctrine of method. For there are three heads, says Galen: first, concerning composition and division; second, concerning the recognition of consequents and conflicting things; third, besides these, that which concerns the mutual comparison of things, of greater, of equal, and of similar things, to which the knowledge of the same and the different corresponds. These are still Galen's words, by which three new methods are said to be proposed for arranging whole arts; but I would say rather that the earlier ones, already woven together, are being woven again. The method of similarity and dissimilarity was made first, alone; by this division into three methods it would be condemned by Galen, and certainly no single method is produced from the three. Division and composition were two different methods made earlier; here one is made from the two. But it is impossible to set up one and the same art by both kinds of order at once. In the second head, the consideration of consequents and conflicting things, a method is produced. But the conflicting things [μαχόμενα], which Galen calls conflicting things, if they are Aristotle's opposites [αὐτοπαθῆ], fill a large and wide place in the logical argument, yet they offer us no sign of order or methodical arrangement. Consequents [ἀκόλουθα], excepting things that are contrary and dissimilar, contain almost all kinds of argument: causes generally follow from effects, and conversely effects follow from causes, and in other arguments in almost the same way. But arguments provide the matter of the arts and of disputations (as I said before), not the form, the species, the arrangement, that is, the method. Finally, what do the kinds of comparison, of greater, of less, of equal, of similar things, have that is even the most obscure mark of an artful arrangement and method? You could fill a huge book with parables and comparisons: what would prevent such a book from proceeding in the utmost confusion and without any method? For the consideration of the same and the different, as a comparison, contains no admonition in itself as to what should be first, what second, what third: it has no symbol, no sign, no instruction of method; its material is formless. Therefore Galen in this place found no single method of arranging an art belonging to Aristotle, refuted nothing, and what is rashly objected to Ramus by unskilled men is not so; for it is more manifest than anything that by these words Galen had not thought, in any judgment, of a perpetual ordering of the whole art, and that the charge of detraction against Aristotle's single method is clearer still. So many, therefore,

units.la: igitur tamq; varias methodos tibi Galenus effi cit: modo unam, modo duas: modo unam illam relinquit, & é duabus his unicam facit, duasque alias instituit: omniaq; hæc tà varia, tamq; sine methodo effusa in uno & eodé libro tradit. Postrem? supurest Galeni de methodis loc?. Tres sunt (ait in Arte medica) omnes doctrinæ, quæ ordinem & dispositionem sequuntur. Prima qui dem ex finis notione & intelligetia secundum solutionem instituta: Secunda vero ex eorum compositione, quæ per resolutionē fuerint inventa: Tertia autem ex definitionis dissolutione, in qua nūc insistimus: vocare vero licet ejus modi doctrinam, nō solùm definitionis dissolutionem, sed etiam explicationē, ut quidam nominarūt: aut resolutionem, aut divisionem, aut (ut nonnulli alii) explanationem, aut expositionem, ut alii. Hę trium methodorum Galeni definitiones sunt: in duabus primis Galenus côtra morem suum, vehementer obscurus est, iisq; illud interpretū ἀναλύσεως καὶ γνώσεως commētum cōplectitur. Prima methodus, ait, est ex notione finis per ἀνάλυσιν: ut interpretum ἀναλύσεις τῆς χώρας, plane fit Galeni ἀνάλυσις τῆς σωστεως, resolutio & compositio: tantumq; pro interpretum verbo γνώσεως, Galenus verbum σύνθεσις usurpavit. Galenus ipse id affirmat, quia docet prima methodo res inveniri, secunda res invetas componi: nominatim quidem de prima in ipsa prima id nō dicit, sed nominatim dicit in secunda, cūm dicit secunda componi quæ per resolutionē primæ sint inventa: sed ne qua dubitatio fit, utrūm Galenus dicat artes prima methodo resolutiva seu divisiva inveniri, Galenus ipse in libello de Constructione artis medicæ, testis locupletissim9 est: ubi sibi nominatim proponit á notione finis methodû eamq; philosophis omnibus p. batam ait esse: neq; satis esse desiderium veri ad inventionem eorum quæ invenieda proponantur, nisi viam ea ipsa inquirendi expeditam teneas: deniq; toto libro nihil nisi invetionem & investigationem loquitur: & in ore semper habet architecturæ exemplû ab interpretibus Aristotelis sibi traditum: bonaq; pars libri in exemplii illius odiosa iteratione cõsumitur. Quæ Galeni sententia cum ejusmodi sit, certé Galenus secutus est commentum illud Aristoteleorû interpretum: & in utrisq; Analysis est una, Galeni que synthesis, interpretumq; genesis vna: analysis; sic á fine generalissimo primoq; deorsum per subalterna ad specialissima descendens, αυτός erit, quâ Galenus appellavit antea: synthesis cõtrà, á specialissimis per subalterna sursum ascendens ad finem primum & generalissimum, synthesis erit eadem, quæ dicta & definita priús est. Tertia methodus satis aperté explicata est, quæ nempe ex definitione, & definitionis explicatione cõstat. Verumeninvero, per Deum immortale (exclamabat hic P. Ramus) ô Philosophi, ô Galeni sectatores & æmuli (quorum in Academia Parisiensi, & in reliquis orbis Christiani academiis doctissimû, & in omni literarû doctrinarumq; genere florentissimû numerum & prædicabat libenter, & ex animo coplectebatur &. colebat) mecum studiose & attente quæstionem infinitis hominum scriptis agitatam perpendite. Alicui vestrum forasse (cui adversus Aristotelem dicere, audacia tantum videretur) furor hic esse videbitur, Quód in Galeni (quem gentes ac nationes omnes pro maximis ejus in hominum genus meritis, jure meritissimo in cęlum pene tollunt: quem ipse omnibus post illa aurea vetustatis liberaq; secula, philosophis antepono) quód in Galeni methodos (inquam) liberiús inquiram: sed furor hic, Platonis furor fuit, Aristotelis furor fuit, Galeni deniq; furor fuit: quo incensi, vigiliis, laboribus, studiis sapientiæ totos se penitus dediderunt: ejusq; gratiá, homini nemini pepercerunt, & veras atque humanæ vitæ necessarias artes quærere & parare modis omnibus contenderunt: falsas & inutiles refellere & damnare nō formidarunt. Philosophia Platonis, Aristotelis, Galeni, magnam quidem partem, præstantium artium confirmatio est: sed multò maximam, vanarū opinionū refutatio est: imó, si decem in partes horum hominum philosophiam doctrinamque totam diviseris, vix ac ne vix quidem decima pars in solidę utilisque scientiæ confirmatione fuerit, reliquæ omnes partes in refutationibus occupatæ reperientur. Quare si quod Plato, quod Aristoteles, quod Galenus in primis cum sua summa gloria fecerunt, id enitor & contendo, cur á Platonis, ab Aristotelis, á Galeni sectatoribus & ęmulis de studio simili judicium tam dissimile nunc audio: Platonis, Aristotelis, Galeni consilium, voluntas: principium meum, meum consilium, mea voluntas, meum principium est: experientiam, usum, utilitatem, finem rerum in tradendis artibus sibi proposuerunt: opinione magistrorum & authoritate nullam sibi propofuerunt. Sic P. Rami pro philosophica methodo exprômebatur amor: Et memini, cum Italorum & Germanorum quorundam philosophorum & medicorum diligentiam doctrinamque admiraretur, ut immoderatum tamen quoddam in his erroribus defendendis studiu deploraret, Nam si colligatur quae à medicis de sophisticatis historium ordinum scripta sunt, oceanus videatur. Ergo missa Galeni authoritate, Galeni methodos specitemus. videamus, utrum artificiosae materiae jam inventae ac judicatae dispositio, forma, collocatio, triplex, an unica fit: utrum tres sint τάξεις διδασκαλίαι, ἀνάλυτική, συνθετική, ὁρισμοί vel ὁρισμοί. Docet Galenus, analyticam methodum dignitate principem esse: id verum est. docet hac methodo finem primo, deinde finem sequentia, secunda secundo, tertia tertio, quarta quarto loco paulatim constituit: & illud est, quod de unica & singulari methodo tantopere, & tam saepe ex Aristotelis & sententia & philosophia dicitur, quod generalissimum primo, deinde subalterna, tum specialissima, vera methodus constituat. At Galenus docet ista via artes inveniri: id falsum est: artes enim (ut jam dixi) omnes inductione singularium & specialium per subalterna, ad generalissimum ascendendo, sunt inventae, ut Plato docuit, ut Aristoteles tantopere confirmavit: imó, ut Galenus ipse plurimis locis de Empiricis disputans, exponit, cum docet, singularium exéplorū experientia, observatione, historia, generalia artiū documenta inveniri, & ratione cō firmari: Et Galenus optimé mortalium omniū didicerat, medicine observationes primó fingulares in Æsculapii templo cōsecratas esse, unde Hippocrates generalia medicinæ decreta cōstituisset: ut inde satis constet, Galenum cum hæc scriberet, scholasticis nugis captum, cætera illa minimé recordatum esse. Quare Galenus hic lapsu interpretum labitur, & ab his fallacibus magistris falsa doctrina decipitur. Neq; hic excusandi Galeni gratia dicere jam possum imperitā vel obtrectatione vel calumnia eorū, qui P. Ramo adversantur: Galeni sententia talem & talibus verbis conceptā Aristoteles aversabitur: salsam, falsam (inquam) affirmabit esse. Est enim interpretum falsa illa analysis, quam antea refutavimus: & tamen Galenum de tali inventionis methodo in hac dispositionis constituta & definita methodo opponere, impudens sophisma fuerit: neq; enim hic de logica inveniendarū artiū agitur. Ars enim inveniendi (ut prædictum est) & artes & reliquas omnino res omnes, prima pars fuit logicæ artis, talisq; methodus primo artis libro fuit. Hic (inquam) nulla quæstio est de inventione artium, sed de tota ipsarum conformatione, cum singulæ ipsarum partes inventæ, imó separatim judicatæ fuerint. Quapropter te merè opponis à Galeno cōtra quæstionē dispositionis methodicæ, Methodi inventionis alia effe:tanquá confusé de qualibet methodo,nõ aute de artificiosæ & scientificæ collocationis methodo ageretur.Itaq; & res falsa objiciatur,quia ista via nullæ artes primó inventæ sunt, & si maxime vera esset, nihil tamē ad rem attineret. Aristoteles unicam artis collocandæ viā aitesse, & tu contrá ais aliam esse inveniendæ,& in una objectione duplicē elechum facis & falsi & aliei ni. Sed de prima Galeni methodo & falsa & ad præsentem quæstionē inepta & aliena , hoc habemus,ab eo dici nunc ἀναλυτικὴ methodū,quę διαιρετικὴ dicta prius est ab eodem. Secundam methodū συνθετικὴ facit,eandē videlicet, quam antea à specialissimis per subalternaad primū finem & generalissimum. Affirmat artes superiore methodo inventas per hanc methodum tandem disponi & collocari : quod item falsum esse reclamabunt Hippacrates, Plato, Aristoteles, & interpretum somnium de compositione damnabunt: imó Galenus ipse, si affirmatione hanc diligentiùs attenderit,sine dubio reclamabit, & tales duas methodos improbabit: docebitque totum contrá esse, & artes inductione singularium & individuorum per subalternas differentias ad generalissimum finem ascéden-do inveniri:ficinventam inprimis esse medicinam,sic denique artes omnes:& sic inventas disponi & doceri ordine planè contrario á generalissimo fine per subalternas differentias & specialissima & individua descendendo.Improbabit(inquam) Galenus totam hanc sophisticam, & ea se deceptū á scholasticis magistris esse confitebitur:ut tandē etiam in exemplis aperte cōfitebitur. Cætera de methodis á Galeno quæ P. Ramo objiciuntur, ad imperitiam referri possunt eorum, qui tanti viri authoritate abutūtur:
units.tr: So Galen makes for you such varied methods: now one, now two. Now he drops that one and turns two of these into a single method, and sets up two others. He delivers all these various methods, poured out so carelessly, in one and the same book. Last of all, what remains is Galen's passage on methods. In the Art of Medicine he says: "All teachings that follow order and arrangement are of three kinds. The first is founded on the understanding and knowledge of the end, by resolution. The second is from the composition of what has been discovered by resolution. The third is from the dissolution of definition, which is what we are now engaged in. Such teaching may be called not only the dissolution of definition but also explanation, as some have named it; or resolution, or division; or, as others have it, unfolding or exposition." These are Galen's definitions of the three methods. In the first two, Galen, contrary to his usual manner, is very obscure, and in them he includes that invention of the interpreters of Aristotle, analysis and synthesis [ἀναλύσεως καὶ γνώσεως]. The first method, he says, is from the notion of the end by analysis [ἀνάλυσιν]. Just as the interpreters' analyses of the region [ἀναλύσεις τῆς χώρας] plainly become Galen's analysis of the ... [ἀνάλυσις τῆς σωστεως], so Galen used the word synthesis [σύνθεσις] only in place of the interpreters' word for knowledge [γνώσεως]. Galen himself affirms this, since he teaches that by the first method things are discovered and by the second the things discovered are put together. He does not say so by name of the first method in the first method itself, but he does say it by name of the second, when he says that the second composes what has been discovered by the resolution of the first. But lest there be any doubt whether Galen says that the arts are discovered by the first method, which is resolutive or divisive, Galen himself is a most abundant witness in his little book On the Construction of the Art of Medicine. There he expressly proposes to himself a method from the notion of the end, and says it has been approved by all philosophers; and he says that a desire for truth is not enough to discover what is to be found unless you hold the way of inquiring into those things made ready. Finally, throughout the whole book he speaks of nothing but invention and investigation, and he always has on his lips the example of architecture handed down to him by the interpreters of Aristotle; and a good part of the book is spent in the tedious repetition of that example. Since Galen's opinion is of this kind, Galen certainly followed that fiction of the interpreters of Aristotle. In both of them there is one analysis, which is Galen's synthesis, and one genesis of the interpreters. The analysis, descending from the most general and first end downwards through subalterns to the most special things, will be that which Galen called earlier. The synthesis, on the contrary, ascending from the most special things through subalterns upwards to the first and most general end, will be the same synthesis that was described and defined earlier. The third method has been explained clearly enough, namely the one that consists of definition and the explanation of definition. But truly, by the immortal God (cried P. Ramus here), O philosophers, O followers and rivals of Galen (whose most learned number in the Academy of Paris and in the other academies of the Christian world, and most flourishing in every kind of letters and learning, he was wont to proclaim gladly, and to embrace and cherish with his whole heart), consider with me diligently and attentively a question debated in countless writings of men. To some of you, perhaps, who would think it mere audacity to speak against Aristotle, this madness will seem to be that I inquire rather freely into the methods of Galen, whom all peoples and nations, on account of his great merits toward the human race, lift almost to heaven with the fullest right, and whom I myself place before all philosophers after those golden and free ages of antiquity. But this madness, I say, was the madness of Plato, was the madness of Aristotle, was the madness of Galen as well: inflamed by it, they wholly devoted themselves to vigils, labours and studies of wisdom; for its sake they spared no man, and they strove by every means to seek and acquire the true arts necessary to human life, and did not hesitate to refute and condemn the false and useless ones. The philosophy of Plato, Aristotle and Galen is, for the most part, a confirmation of the excellent arts; but by far the greater part of it is a refutation of vain opinions. Indeed, if you divide the whole philosophy and teaching of these men into ten parts, scarcely, or hardly even, a tenth part will be found to contribute to the confirmation of a solid and useful science; all the other parts will be found occupied with refutations. Therefore, if I strive and contend to do what Plato, Aristotle and Galen especially did with their great glory, why do I now hear from the followers and rivals of Plato, Aristotle and Galen, in the same study, a judgement so unlike? The plan and will of Plato, Aristotle and Galen was their principle; my principle is my plan and my will. They proposed to themselves experience, use, utility, the end of things in delivering the arts; they proposed to themselves nothing from the opinion of masters or authority. Thus P. Ramus expressed his love for the philosophical method. And I remember that when he admired the diligence and learning of certain Italian and German philosophers and physicians, he nevertheless lamented a certain immoderate zeal in defending their errors: for if one were to gather together what physicians have written about the sophistical orders of diseases, it would look like an ocean. So, setting aside Galen's authority, let us examine Galen's methods. Let us see whether the arrangement, form and placing of material already discovered and judged for art is threefold or single; whether there are three orders of teaching, analytic, synthetic, and definitional or definitions [τάξεις διδασκαλίαι, ἀνάλυτική, συνθετική, ὁρισμοί]. Galen teaches that the analytic method is pre-eminent in dignity: that is true. He teaches that by this method one first sets down the end, then the things that follow the end, the second things in the second place, the third in the third, and the fourth gradually in the fourth place. And this is what is said so greatly, and so often, on the authority of Aristotle and in his philosophy, about the single and unique method: that it establishes first the most general, then the subalterns, then the most special, which is the true method. But Galen teaches that arts are discovered by this way: that is false. For arts (as I have already said) have all been discovered by induction from singulars and specials, ascending through subalterns to the most general, as Plato taught and Aristotle so strongly confirmed; indeed, as Galen himself, discussing the Empirics in many places, sets forth when he teaches that the general precepts of the arts are found, and confirmed by reason, from the experience, observation and history of single examples. And Galen, best of all mortals, had learned that the observations of medicine were first consecrated singly in the temple of Aesculapius, whence Hippocrates established the general decrees of medicine; so that it is sufficiently clear that Galen, when he wrote these things, was caught by scholastic trifles and did not at all remember those other things. Therefore Galen here slips in the mistake of the interpreters, and is deceived by these fallacious masters into false doctrine. Nor can I here, to excuse Galen, say that the ignorance or the cavilling and calumny of those who oppose P. Ramus is to blame: Aristotle will reject Galen's opinion, conceived in such a way and in such words, and will affirm that it is salse, false, I say.
