For that false analysis of the interpreters is what we refuted before; and yet to oppose Galen's view of such a method of invention to the method of this constituted and defined arrangement would be a shameless sophism: for here we are not dealing with the logic of discovering the arts. For the art of inventing (as has been said) and the arts and all other things whatever were the first part of the logical art, and such a method was in the first book of the art. Here, I say, there is no question about the invention of the arts, but about their whole ordering, since their individual parts have been discovered, and indeed judged separately. Wherefore you rashly oppose Galen against the question of methodical arrangement, saying that there are other methods of invention, as if it were a confused discussion about any method at all and not about the method of artful and scientific placing. So also a false thing is objected, because by that way no arts were first discovered; and even if it were wholly true, it would still have nothing to do with the matter. Aristotle says there is only one way of arranging an art, and you on the contrary say that there is another way of inventing, and in one objection you make a double refutation, of falsehood and of irrelevance. But concerning Galen's first method, which is both false and inept and foreign to the present question, we have this: he now calls it analytic [ἀναλυτικὴ], which he had earlier called divisive [διαιρετικὴ] himself. The second method he makes synthetic [συνθετικὴ], namely the same one which was before from the most special, through subalterns, to the first and most general end. He affirms that arts discovered by the former method are at last arranged and placed by this method; and Hippocrates, Plato and Aristotle will likewise cry out that this is false, and they will condemn the dream of the interpreters about composition. Indeed Galen himself, if he attended more carefully to this affirmation, will without doubt cry out and reject those two methods of that kind; and he will teach that the whole thing is the reverse, and that arts are discovered by induction from singulars and individuals, ascending through subaltern differences to the general end; thus medicine was first discovered, and so all the arts; and thus discovered they are arranged and taught by the plainly contrary order, descending from the general end through subaltern differences to the most special and individual things. Galen, I say, will reject this whole sophistry, and he will confess that he was deceived by the scholastic masters in it, as he will at last openly confess even in examples. The other matters from Galen which are objected to P. Ramus can be referred to the inexperience of those who abuse the authority of so great a man.

units.la: At vel judice Galeno attentiús & accuratiús in formato, tam perversa tamq; præpostera, quód artes inveniantur descendedo á generalissimo per subalterna ad individua, quod sic inventæ contrá disponantur ascendendo ab individuis per subalterna ad generalissimū, tam perversa interpretum (inquam) tanque præposlera sophisma-ta fine dubio rejicientur á Galeno, & é Galeni placitis tollentur. Sed hoc judicium Galeni in proximo capite de exemplis cōmodiús audietur. Atque hęc de secunda methodo satis, falsa quidem illa, ut superior fuit, non tamen aliena. Aristoteles ait, artium partes omnes invē tas disponendas esse á generalissima parte per intermedias ad individuas: Galenus cum interpretibus aperte contrá loquitur disponēdas esse ab individuis per intermedias ad generalissimam. Cōtradictio manifesta est: vera autem est Aristotelis affirmatio, falsa igitur inficiatio Galeni. Quid? definitiva methodus (quam tertiam Galenus hic efficit, quámque se secuturum in constructione τέχνης ἰατρικῆς præedicit) quá viam proponit? quid habet in hac quæstione potius, quám similium, dissimilium, pariu m, majorum: minorum collatio, quám consequentium & repugnantium cognitio, quám ejusdem & diversi consideratio? cur, inquam, in hoc potiús argumento, quám in cæteris methodus exīstimatur?
units.tr: But even if we judge more attentively and accurately with Galen as our judge, the claim that arts are discovered by descending from the most general to subordinate and then to individual things, and that the arts so discovered are arranged by ascending from individuals through subordinates to the most general, is so perverse and preposterous that these sophisms of the interpreters, I say, will undoubtedly be rejected by Galen and removed from his opinions. But Galen's judgment on this will be heard more conveniently in the next chapter, on examples. So much for the second method, which is false, as the previous one was, yet not foreign to the ancients. Aristotle says that all the parts of the arts, once discovered, must be arranged from the most general part through the intermediate parts to the individual ones. Galen, with the interpreters, speaks openly against this, saying they must be arranged from individuals through intermediates to the most general. The contradiction is plain. Aristotle's affirmation is true, so Galen's denial is false. What of the definitive method, which Galen makes the third and which he predicts he will follow in constructing the art of medicine [τέχνης ἰατρικῆς]? What does it propose? What does this question have to do with anything except the comparison of like and unlike, equal, greater and lesser, and the knowledge of consequents and contraries, and the consideration of the same and the different? Why, I ask, is method judged to belong to this subject rather than to the others?

units.la: Definitio argumentum est, materiaque est, quæ disponenda, & ordine collocanda proponitur: non èlt dispositionis, non ordinis, nò methodi formula quę moneat, quid in arte primū, quid fecundū, quid tertium ac deinceps esse debeat: materia est, inquam, quæ locis illis gradatim disponitur. Si definitio generalissima fit, erit primo loco statuêda: si subalterna, medio: si specias lissima, infimo. At definitio per se nulla methodicæ collocationis est significatio, non magis quàm genus, quod summū, medium, infimum similiter esse diceretur. Nò magis quàm caussa, quæ summa, media, infima diceretur, nec tamē cuiquam adhuc in mentem venit, methodum genericam aut caussalē fingere. Utrúm veró possit in tertia methodo Galenus excusari, quód non intellexerit definitivam methodum reipsa differentem ab aliis duabus, ejusque rei á Galeno argumentum esse, quód hic dicat definitivâ ipsam definitionis διάλυσιν, ἀνάλυσιν, διάιρεσιν, διάςτασιν, διάλυσιν, διάλυσιν, dissolutionem, resolutionem, divisionem, explicationē, explanationem, expositionem. Certé sic Galenus hic loquitur: at idem loquitur tres methodos, nò duas & trisariam dividit, & differentiam etiam ostendit, quód definitiva vincatur á refolutiva ἀξιώματι τε πρὸς μεθόδω, dignitate & ordine: at vincat σωφίᾳ τῇ μνήμῃ compendio & memoria: imò quód definitiva fit essentialis, aliæ duæ sint accidentales: & dicit in hoc ipso libro se definitivam secuturum esse: unde si liberè judicare voles, nihil aliud judicare possis, quàm Galeno licet in logicis (ut eft prima Dialecticarum fcholarum τὴν λογικὴν (?) logicam tamen nullam diftinctam fuiffe,ut intelligeret logicá aliam, συνθετικὴν, aliam ταξικὴν, αρτητικὴν : ut cogitaret methodum difponedæ artis unam præcipuam logicæ partem effe. Itaque imprudenter,uel impudéter potiús P. Ramo in hac diftincta logicæ parte tres iftæ methodi objiciuntur. Sed fatis de Galeni methodis. una in fimilitudine & difsimilitudine,duabus in defcē fu á generalibus,vel afcenfu ad generalia: In tribus, prima in genefi & analyfi, fecunda in confequentium & repugnantium cognitione tertia in comparatione:itemque tribus aliis, prima in analyfi, fecunda in genefi, tertia in definitione: In quibus fi quis dixerit per repugnátium,comparationis, fimilitudinis, difsimilitudinis, definitionis methodos, intelligi nō perpetuá iftam artis collocationem, fed fingularia argumenta, libéter P. Ramus affentietur: fed tota illa ἀδιάτακτα ρἰα ἀδὶς ἡ ἀνώδις, excufationem hanc capere non poterit : reliquiæ iftæ hærebunt in falebra. quin Galenus (ut proximo capite dicetur) exemplo teftimonioq; fuo fcholaftica hæc de tot methodis commenta refutabit, & judicio fuo condemnabit. Verum enimvero interpretū natio magna eft: é quibus nonnulli doĉti & modefti reperientur fortaffe,qui nondum fuafione tam accurata moveantur,dicantque,methodum á generalibus præftante quidem illam effe,fed perdifficilem, planeq; interdum impofsibilem : ut ideo fola non fit. At P. Ramus perdifficilem quidem effe confitetur: fed doctori : & cauffam nō folúm solùm á Platone, sed à seipso tantæ difficultatis magnam attulit. Sed difficultatem hanc,auditoris & discipuli nullam esse confitetur:imó facilitatem summam,quia fit illi intelligentiæ ac memoriæ via facillima: sed tamé in facilitatis argu
units.tr: A definition is an argument and a matter, and it is set forth as something to be disposed and placed in order. There is no formula of arrangement, no formula of order, no formula of method, that tells us what should come first in the art, what second, what third, and so on. The matter, I say, is what is gradually disposed in those places. If the definition is most general, it will be placed in the first place; if subordinate, in the middle; if most specific, in the last. But a definition in itself signifies no methodical placement, any more than a genus would, which could likewise be called highest, middle, or lowest. Nor does a cause signify it, which could be called highest, middle, or lowest either, yet no one has ever thought to devise a generic or causal method. Could Galen be excused in the third method on the ground that he did not understand that the definitive method is really different from the other two, and that the proof of this is that he calls the definitive method the dissolution, analysis, division, distinction, explication, explanation and exposition of the definition, namely dissolutionem, resolutionem, divisionem, explicationem, explanationem, expositionem? Certainly Galen speaks in this way here. Yet he also speaks of three methods, not two, and divides them threefold, and he shows a difference too: that the definitive method is surpassed by the resolutive in dignity and order [ἀξιώματι τε πρὸς μεθόδω], but surpasses it in brevity and memory [σωφίᾳ τῇ μνήμῃ]. Indeed, the definitive is essential, and the other two are accidental. And he says in this very book that he will follow the definitive method. So if you wish to judge freely, you can judge nothing else than that Galen, in logic (as is the first of the Dialectical schools, the logic [τὴν λογικὴν]), did not have a distinct logic, so that he might understand one logic as synthetic, another as taxic, another as apodeictic; and so that he might think the method of disposing an art is one principal part of logic. Thus imprudently, or rather impudently, these three methods are attributed to Ramus in this distinct part of logic. But enough about Galen's methods. In one (on similarity and dissimilarity), two (on descent from generals, or ascent to generals), in three (first on genesis and analysis, second on the knowledge of consequents and contraries, third on comparison), and likewise in three others (first on analysis, second on genesis, third on definition): if someone says that by the methods of contraries, comparison, similarity, dissimilarity and definition we are to understand not a perpetual arrangement of the art but singular arguments, Ramus will gladly agree. But that whole disordered utterances, a labour pain without pain [ἀδιάτακτα ῥήματα, ἀδὶς ἡ ἀνώδυνος] will not be able to accept this excuse; those remnants will stick in the mire. Indeed Galen, as will be said in the next chapter, by his own example and testimony will refute these scholastic inventions about so many methods and condemn them by his own judgment. But truly the race of interpreters is large, and among them perhaps some learned and modest men will be found who are not yet moved by so careful a persuasion. They will say that the method from generals is indeed better, but very difficult and sometimes altogether impossible, and so it is not the only one. But Ramus admits it is indeed very difficult, but for the teacher; and he has brought the cause of this great difficulty not only from Plato but from himself. Yet he declares that this difficulty is nothing for the hearer and the pupil; indeed it is the greatest ease, since for them the way of understanding and memory is most easy. But the interpreters persist in their argument about ease,

units.la: mento instent interpretes:citét Platonem in Ti mæo, de duplici genere differendi, cum duob9 rerum generibus congruente,ut res necessariæ & immutabiles,necessariis & immutabilibus argumentis exponátur:instabiles & infirmæ, probabilibus & verisimilibus. Appellent Ciceronē duo genera hominum similiter partiētem, alterum indoctum & agreste, alterum expolitū & liberale: proptereaque duas methodos duob. hominum generibus accommodandas esse disputét. At hic P.Ramus respondere solitus est, Eubulidem illum (de cujus partitione jam soties dictū est) idem ipsum dicere, aliis alia esse notiora.Itaque quod adversus illa duo notioris generarefponfum est, adversus Platonis Ciceronifq; partitiones responsum esto : tametsi uterque author de argumentis loquitur, non de perpetua enútiatorum collocatione.Quare locus Timæi,locus Ciceronis, Ariftoteleam ordinandæ artis unicam methodum nihil offendit, nihil refellit. Sed tñ da mihi (ajebat P. Ramus) exempli gratiâ, Grammaticam docendam esse: dabis Grammaticum profefforem omnibus artis suis partibus perfecté eridıtū, qui,ut methodica quæstio requirit,habebit materiam methodi totam in promptu inventam, figillatimq; judicatam:ordinis sola quæstio supererit,quo difcipu cipulum ducat. Si discipulus ingenio alacri paratoque fuerit: confiteris á generalibus ad specialia Grammaticam ordiendá esse: & hanc effentialem atque universalem methodum lógiffimè præstare. Hoc igitur tanquam confessum confectumq; teneatur. Sin erit discipulus idem rudis & hebes, à specialibus ais incipiendum ef fe. Ergo ,p Ariftotele P.Ramus, vel potiùs ipsemet Ariftoteles pro Ariftotele tibi respondebit: nō bajulis ac remigibus, bubulcis & porcariis, id est natură fervis, sed ingenuis & liberalibus ingeniis, artium liberaliū ludos aperiri. Sed tamen fit truncus hominis quivis, modo utcunq; difcipline capax: nihilo minus á generalibus ru dem hunc & hebetem informandū esse Ariitoteles respondebit: quia via facilima clarissimaque: Si principiū generale aliquod ei fuerit obfcurum, ut definitio, ut partitio Grammaticæ, aut aliud deinceps quidpiam: obscuritas hæc erit exemplis familiaribus inducenda, & é medio sumptis argumentis & popularibus declaranda: Sic Ariftoteles, sic (inquam) Ariftoteles huic objectioni, eheu, quot capitibus & locis re fpondit: Principia sunt ἀρχαί, sunt αὐτόπιστα, sunt καταδέξαντα: attamen fi cui forte sint aut ignota, aut obscura: inductio (ait philosophus) prefenti remedio erit. neque tamen in artis quibusque præceptis inductiones hæ sunt adhibendæ: extremis tantum & fpecialifsimis in locis exempla adhibenda sunt. Adhibendæ sunt ejusmodi inductiones á doctore, ubi discipulum hærere deprehenderit. Remedium illud catholicum in docto-
units.tr: citing Plato in the Timaeus on the twofold kind of discourse, corresponding to the two kinds of things: necessary and immutable things are to be explained by necessary and immutable arguments, unstable and weak things by probable and plausible ones. They cite Cicero, who similarly divides men into two kinds, one untaught and rustic, the other polished and liberal, and who therefore say that two methods must be fitted to the two kinds of men. But Ramus has been accustomed to reply that Eubulides (whose partition has been mentioned so often already) says the same thing, that different things are better known to different people. So what has been answered to those two better-known kinds may be answered to the partitions of Plato and Cicero, although both authors speak of arguments, not of the perpetual arrangement of propositions. Therefore the passage in the Timaeus and the passage in Cicero do not offend or refute Aristotle's single method of ordering an art. But grant me, Ramus used to say, for example, that grammar is to be taught. You will grant a grammar professor who is thoroughly learned in all the parts of his art, who, as the methodical question requires, will have the whole matter of the method discovered and judged in detail and at hand. Only the question of order will remain: by what route he is to lead the pupil. If the pupil is lively and prepared in mind, you concede that grammar is to be begun from the general and that this is the essential and universal method, which serves best. Let this therefore be held as agreed and settled. But if the pupil is rude and dull, you say one must begin with the specific. Then, Ramus, on the side of Aristotle, or rather Aristotle himself will answer you on behalf of Aristotle: the arts liberal are not to be opened to porters and rowers, cowherds and swineherds, that is, to natural slaves, but to free and liberal minds. But even if the person is a mere trunk of a man, provided he is in any way capable of discipline, still Aristotle will answer that this rude and dull person must be instructed from the general, because that is the easiest and clearest way. If some general principle is obscure to him, such as a definition or a partition in grammar, or anything else after that, the obscurity is to be met by familiar examples, and explained by arguments taken from the middle and from common things. So Aristotle, I say, replied to this objection, alas, in how many chapters and places! The principles are archai, they are self-evident, they are katadexanta; yet if any of them happen to be unknown or obscure to someone, induction, says the philosopher, will be the present remedy. Nevertheless, such inductions are not to be used in the precepts of each art; examples are to be used only in the extreme and most specific places. Such inductions are to be used by the teacher when he sees the pupil stuck. That universal remedy must lie in the mind of the teacher, not in the appearance and form of the art.

units.la: doctoris mēte, non artis specie & forma esse ne cesse est. Si pergas dicere, viam à specialibus fa‐ ciliorem: imó (dicit philosophus) partibus infi‐ nitis difficilior erit: turbabit enim intelligentiā, memoriamque obruet: denique totam illam é primo de partibus animalium ἀπόδειξιν τῆ ἀπαγω‐γῷ reponet. Itaque quantò rudior & hebetior discipulus erit, tantò diligentiús & accuratiús hac via ducendus erit. Ecquid (ajunt hîc homi‐ nes isti eruditi) si absoluté notiora defuerint, quid futurum est? nónne impossibilis á genera‐ libus methodus fuerit? Sanè (respondebat hîc P. Ramus) si res artis unius homogeneæ sint in ventæ judicatæque, ut definitio methodi requi‐ rit, utque tria tota Aristotelis capita, septimum, octavum, nonum in primo libro Posteriorum, ἀποδείξεως istà amplissimo certissimæ sponsionis vadimonio confirmant: nunquam futurum est, ut desint generalia specialiaq;, aliis alia absolu‐ té notiora: fieri tamen fortasse poterit, ut definitio aliqua partitioque ex adjunctis quibusdam aut dissentaneis cōparatisve sumatur: necideo argumentū arguta re sit absoluté notius. Quod si sit, commune erit etiam viæ á specialibus ad generalia: quia materies utriusque formæ com‐ munis erit: attamen totum enuntiatū rei utcun‐ que definitæ aç partitæ, generale speciali com‐ paratum, semper erit absoluté notius: ut si essentiam, aut corpus, aut animatum, aut animal, nō absoluté nōtioribus argumentis definieris aut diviseris, argumenta illa nuda, nō erunt absolu‐ té notiora: at arguta res ipsa generalis, semp e‐ rit absoluté notior speciali clariusque & notius erit á generalibus illis descendere, quia res illæ genera sunt inferiorú: ideoque & caussá notio res:taliaque enuntiatorum posteriora categoremata erunt in arte universa, tanquam in perpetua magni cujufdam corporis forma nævi quidam: Quód fi totam aliquam artis partê ignoratã esse dixerint, ut in metrica, pars magna Stereometriæ: ut in Grámatica Francica, de brevibus & longis sillabis prosodia: sané ubi materia defit,ibi formam requirere non debes: sed tamen neque tuam á specialibus methodum adhibebis: quia ubi materia nulla est, ibi forma nulla potest esse.via nostra á generalibus,in hoc exemplo clausa erit: sed via quoque erit á fpecialibus obstructa: neq; tamen methodus iccirco singularis & unica esse desinet. Ná fi quodam orbis loco muti homines aut fatui essét:ibi Grámaticæ,rhetoricæ,Dialecticæ usus nullus effet: veræ tamé nihilominus effent artes, & apud loquentes & sapientes, usum fructumq; suum retinerent.Quapropter hæc adhuc interpretú fere sunt argumenta:quibus P. Ramus refponden dum judicaret: unum tamen erat omnium grauiffimum, & ipsi periculosissimum, cui dicebat fe nunquam respondisse,neque refpófurum effe.Ecquódnam,inquies? Contumeliæ,inquam, probra,injuriæ,maledicta, similiaque fopifmata ægrotorum hominum,qui fi lapidibus appetere medicú,ut verbis,potuissent, lapidatio valde formidabilis P.Ramo fuisset jugulaffent medius fidius homine. At P.Ramus vanos istos velut anserum sibilos perpetuò contempsit,sufce‑ ptamq; methodicę legis suafione eò alacriús cõ stantiusq; sustinuit, non solùm confirmatus il‑ lis & argumentorum, & authorũ tantis momé‑ tis,sed bonæ atq; integræ mentis cõscientia fre‑ tus:quod patrocinium in hac caussa tam studio sum tamq; accuratum, consideret esse & homi‑ nibus utile,& Deo non ingratum.
units.tr: If you go on to say that the way from the specific is easier, the philosopher says that on the contrary it will be more difficult by infinite parts: it will confuse the understanding and overwhelm the memory. Finally he puts that whole demonstration by leading [ἀπόδειξιν τῆ ἀπαγωγῷ] from the first book of On the Parts of Animals in its place. So the ruder and duller the pupil, the more diligently and accurately must he be led by this way. What, these learned men say, if absolutely better-known things are lacking? What then? Will the method from the generals not be impossible? Certainly, Ramus replied, if the matters of one homogeneous art are discovered and judged, as the definition of method requires, and as the three whole chapters of Aristotle, the seventh, eighth and ninth in the first book of the Posterior Analytics, confirm with the broadest guarantee of certain surety, then there will never be a lack of generals and specifics, some better known in one way, some in another. Yet it may perhaps happen that a definition or partition is taken from certain adjuncts, or from things dissimilar or compared, and then the argument itself is not absolutely better known. If so, it will also be common to the way from specifics to generals, since the matter of each form will be common. Yet the whole proposition of a thing, however defined and divided, when the general is compared with the specific, will always be absolutely better known. For instance, if you define or divide essence, or body, or animate, or animal, not by absolutely better-known arguments, those bare arguments will not be absolutely better known. But the thing itself, being general, will always be absolutely better known than the specific, and it will be clearer and better known to descend from those generals, because those things are the genera of the inferior ones, and so they are better known as causes. Propositions of this kind, namely the posterior predicaments, will be in the whole art like certain marks on the form of some great body. But if they say that some whole part of an art is unknown, as in metrics, or a large part of stereometry, or as in French grammar, the prosody of short and long syllables, then surely where there is no matter, you must not look for form there. But you will not use your method from the specifics either, because where there is no matter, there can be no form. Our way from the generals will be closed in this example, but the way from the specifics will also be blocked. Yet the method will not on that account cease to be single and unique. For if in some part of the world men were mute or foolish, there would be no use of grammar, rhetoric, or dialectic there; yet the arts would nonetheless be true arts, and among speakers and wise men they would keep their use and fruit. Therefore these are still almost all the arguments of the interpreters, to which Ramus judged he must reply. Yet one argument was the weightiest of all and most dangerous to him, and he said he had never replied to it and would never reply. What is it, you will ask? Insults, I say, reproaches, injuries, abuse, and similar sophisms of sick men, who, if they could have assailed the physician with stones as with words, would have stoned him, and, by my faith, would have killed the man in a very frightening way. But Ramus has always despised those empty hisses, as of geese, and undertook the persuasion of the method of the law all the more cheerfully and steadfastly, not only strengthened by such great arguments and authorities, but relying on the consciousness of a good and sound mind, since he considered that this defence, in a cause so zealously and carefully pursued, is both useful to men and not unwelcome to God.

units.la: Cap. XVII. De Prima methodi illu‑ stratione per exempla artium.
units.tr: Ch. XVII. On the first illustration of method through examples from the arts.

units.la: MEthodi exempla præcipua sunt in artibus:in quibus quãvis omnes regulæ generales sint & universales,ta‑ men earum gradus distinguũtur, quan‑ tóque unaquæque generalior erit, tan‑ tó magis præcedet. Generalissima lo‑ co & ordine prima erit, quia lumíne & notitia prima est:subalterne consequẽtur,quia claritate sunt proximæ: atque ex his naturâ notiores præponẽtur,mi‑ nús notæ substituentur: tandemq; spe‑ cialissimę constituentur.Definitio itaq; generalissima,prima erit:distributio se‑ quetur: quæ si multiplex fuerit,p̃cedet in partes integras partitio, sequetur di‑ visio in species , partefq; ipsæ & species eodẽ ordine sunt rursus tractãdę ac de‑ finiędæ,quo distributæ fuerint: & trãsi‑
units.tr: Method's principal examples are found in the arts. In these, although all the rules are general and universal, they still have degrees of generality, and the more general a rule is, the earlier it comes. The most general rule will come first in place and order, because it is first in light and knowledge. Subaltern rules follow, since they are closest in clarity. Of these, the ones better known by nature are placed before, and the less known are put after. Finally, the most specific rules are set down. Therefore the most general definition will come first, and the distribution will follow. If the distribution is manifold, a partition into integral parts will come first, and a division into species will follow. The parts and species are then to be treated and defined again, in the same order in which they were distributed, and they are to be bound together by transitions.

units.la: tionum tionū vinculis, fi longior inter eas inter fit explicatio, colligādę sunt: Id enim auditore reficit & recreat. Atq; ut res fami liariūs accipiatur, exemplo quoq; familiari nobis utendum est. Omnes definitiones, distributiones, regulæ Grammaticæ repertæ sint, atq; unaquæq; sigilla tim judicata: omniaq; hæc documēta, variis tabellis inscripta, unā confundantur & cōturbentur in urna aliqua, ut in Ollę ludo fieri solet: Hïc si quæras, quæ pars Dialectice te doceat has regulas ita cōfusas disponere, & in ordinē redi gere: Primo locis invētionis nihil opus est, cūm sint omnia reperta: neq; primo enūtiationis judicio, cūm unaquæq; e- nūtiatio probata & æstimata fit: neq; se cūdo syllogismi judicio opus erit, cum sint oēs singularum rerū controversiæ his de rebus disceptatæ & cōclufæ. sola methodus superest. Dialecticus igitur, lumine methodi artificiosæ seliget in hac urna definitionem Grāmaticæ (id ēnim est generalissimum) & primo loco statuet, Grammatica est doctrina be ne loquēdi: tum requiret in eadem urna partitionem Grammaticæ, & collocabit secundo loco: Partes Grammaticæ sunt duæ, Etymologia & Syntaxis: de inceps in eodem vase, definitione Etymologiæ de vocib. separabit, & tertio gradu antecedentib. adjunget: tum vocis partes in literis & syllabis, speciesque in vocibus numeri & sine numero collocabit, exitusque trasitionibus aptis colligabit. Atq; ita omnium etymologiæ partium definitiones, distributiones, colligationes ordinando, ad exempla specialissima in singulis descendet: Idemq; in syntaxi faciet. Hanc viam omnes artes sibi proposuerunt.
units.tr: by transitions. If the explanation between them is rather long, they must be tied together, for this refreshes and restores the listener. So that the matter may be grasped more easily, we must also use a familiar example. Suppose all the definitions, distributions and rules of grammar have been found, and each has been judged separately; and suppose all these teachings, written on various tablets, are mixed up and jumbled together in some urn, as is usually done in the game of Ollæ. If you ask here which part of dialectic will teach you to arrange these mixed-up rules and put them back in order, the answer is this. First, there is no need for the topics of invention, since everything has already been discovered. Nor is there need for the judgment of the proposition, since each proposition has been tested and assessed. Nor will the judgment of the syllogism be needed second, since the controversies of each single matter have been disputed and concluded. Only method remains. So the dialectician, by the light of artful method, will choose from this urn the definition of grammar (for that is the most general), and will place it first: "Grammar is the teaching of speaking well." Then he will seek in the same urn the partition of grammar and place it second: "The parts of grammar are two, etymology and syntax." Next, in the same vessel, he will separate the definition of etymology from the definitions of words, and join it to the preceding ones in the third degree. Then he will arrange the parts of a word into letters and syllables, and the species of words into those with number and those without, and he will bind the endings together with suitable transitions. And so, by ordering the definitions, distributions and connections of all the parts of etymology, he will descend to the most specific examples in each. He will do the same in syntax. This is the path all the arts have set for themselves.

units.la: Quanuis] Methodica lex adhuc multis & magnis præsidiis & rationum & authoritatum confirmata est: refutata etiā, quæ contra dici posse videbatur: Superest ut inquirantur testimonia ipsarum artium, omniumq; omnino rerū, quæ perspicue doceri velint: ad eamq; rem reliqua methodicæ artis doctrina referatur, contraria que (ut antea factum est) etiam comparentur. Prima porrò monitio constituitur, quanvis generalia in artibus sint omnia, attamen gradus esse summos, medios, infimos: & specialia, quæ dicuntur, non esse illa ἄτακτα, quæ Platoni: neq; illa ἄτομα, quæ Aristoteli dicuntur: sed minus communia, magis communibus comparata. Itaque Hippocratis μίγιστον καὶ ἐλάχιστον. Platonis τὸ ἀρχὴ μονάς.
units.tr: Although] The law of method has already been confirmed by many great supports, both of reasons and of authorities, and the objections that seemed to be raised against it have been refuted. It remains to look for the testimony of the arts themselves, and of all things that are meant to be taught clearly. The rest of the doctrine of the method of art is to be referred to this matter, and the contrary views are also to be compared, as was done before. First, this warning is set down: although everything in the arts is general, there are still highest, middle and lowest degrees; and the so-called specific things are not those "unordered" things of Plato, nor those "indivisible" things said to belong to Aristotle, but are less common and are compared with the more common. So Hippocrates' "greatest and least" (megiston kai elachiston), and Plato's "the beginning is a unit" (to archē monas).

units.la: Dicendi Ariftotelis γνωριμώτατον, primo loco erit: Platonis et μεταξύ ἰδέαι, ὑπάλληλοι Ariftotelis διαφοραί subsequentur: Platonis ultimæ ideæ, Ariftotelis species specialissimæ, ultimo loco erunt. Multiplex autem in distributionibus ejusdem rei variis præcedere debet partitio, quia ex caussis est, ut antea patuit.
units.tr: Of saying: Aristotle's "most knowable" (gnōrimōtaton) will come first. Plato's "intermediate ideas" (metaxy ideai) will follow, and Aristotle's "subordinate differences" (hypallēloi diaphorai). Plato's ultimate ideas and Aristotle's most specific species will come last. In distributions of the same thing, a manifold partition ought to come before the various others, because it comes from causes, as was shown before.

units.la: Eodem ordine] Id in præceptis collocare, ridiculum fortasse videatur: at vitia cōtrarii sophismatis P.Ramus vicesimo libro dialecticarum Scholarum in magnis authoribus adnotavit.
units.tr: In the same order] To place this among the precepts may perhaps seem ridiculous. But P. Ramus, in the twentieth book of his Dialectical Scholars, noted the faults of the opposite sophism in great authors.

units.la: Transitionum] Transitio inter figuras rhetoricas à Cicerone numeratur: Propositio (ait Orator tertio) quid dicturus sis, & ab eo quod est dictum, sejunctio. Quintilianus, ejus laudem minime partitionis libro quarto capite quinto cō plexus est: Reficit quoq; auditorem (ait) certo singularum partium fine: non aliter quàm faciētibus iter, multum detrahunt fatigationis, notata inscriptis lapidib9 spatia. Nam & exhau &ti laboris nosse mensuram, voluptati est: & hortatur ad reliqua fortius exequenda, scire quantū supersit: Nihil enim longū videri necesse est, in quo quid ultimum sit, certū est. Grammaticæ]
units.tr: Of transitions] Transition is counted among the rhetorical figures by Cicero. The orator says in the third book: "A statement of what you are about to say, and a separation from what has been said." Quintilian, in the fourth book, chapter five, which he praises very little for partition, embraces it: "A certain end of each part also refreshes the listener," he says, "just as for those making a journey, spaces marked with stones on the road greatly lessen the weariness. For it is a pleasure both to know the measure of the labour already spent, and it encourages us to carry out the rest more bravely to know how much remains. Indeed, nothing needs to seem long when it is certain what its end is." Of grammar.

units.la: Inductio P. Rami, ad confirmādam methodi unitatē, magna prorsus incipit, quód omnes artifices, poetæ, oratores, historici, omnes deniq; homines, qui perspicuè docere lōgam aliquam materiam statuerunt, illam methodum unicam á generalibus ad speciália consectantur, licet omnibus partibus nō assequantur: Primū exemplum est de Grammatica, ad quod declarandū, ludus Ollę (quam vulgus Blancham vocat) cō paratur: ut intelligatur, in quæstione de methodo, nihil opus esse præceptis Logicæ antecedētis: neq; hic requiri inventione rerum, aut enūtiati, vel syllogismi judicium: in quo feré totus est error interpretū, qui methodi nomine, modo totam Dialecticam, modó partē quamlibet intelligūt. At in Ollæ ludo, cæcus est, qui tabellas educit ex urna: qualis Logicus noster minimé omniū esse debet, sed oculis acutissimis, divinoq; potiús, quám humano lumine præditus.
units.tr: P. Ramus's induction, to confirm the unity of method, begins in a very grand way. All artisans, poets, orators, historians, and finally all men who have set out to teach some long matter clearly, follow this single method from the general to the specific, although they do not reach it in all its parts. The first example is grammar. To explain it, the game of Ollæ (which the common people call Blancha) is brought in, so that it may be understood that, in the question of method, the precepts of the preceding logic are not needed, nor is the judgment of the invention of things, of the proposition, or of the syllogism required here. In this the interpreters have mostly erred, since they understand by "method" sometimes the whole of dialectic, sometimes any part of it. But in the game of Ollæ the one who draws the tablets out of the urn is blind. Our logician should by no means be like that, but should be endowed with the sharpest eyes, and with a divine rather than a human light.

units.la: Grammatica] Grammaticam totam Platonicis & definitionum & partitionum ideis ita P.Ramus persecutus est: & licet in materia aspera & refractaria, quæque feré nullam analogiam catholicā, sine anomalia aliqua, reciperet: attamē methodicam logici ordinis figuram elegantem admodum impressit: ut beneficio talis ordinis, Grammatica partibus artis numerisq; omnib. absoluta, multis partibus tamen & breviorr & facilior habeatur: & homines huic singulari methodo tantopere adversarii, excitari commoverique debeant hoc exemplo, cúm videant artē quæ minimé videbatur, attamen legibus κατὰ πάντος, καθ' αὐτὸ, καθόλης πρῶτον á generalib. ad specialia sic esse dispositam & conformatam.
units.tr: Grammar] P. Ramus pursued the whole of grammar with the Platonic ideas of both definitions and partitions in this way. Although it is a rough and stubborn matter, which would hardly admit any catholic analogy without some anomaly, he nonetheless gave it an elegant figure of logical order, a method. Through the benefit of such order, grammar, complete in all its parts and numbers of art, is held to be both shorter and easier in many parts. And men who are so hostile to this singular method should be stirred and moved by this example, when they see that an art which seemed least suited to it has nonetheless been arranged and shaped by the laws of "according to all, according to itself, first in the universal" (kata pantos, kath' auto, kathologou prōton), from the general to the specific.

units.la: Partes Grammaticæ] Partes Grammaticæ vulgó quatuor factæ sunt, Etymologia, Syntaxis, Prosodia, Orthographia: at duæ ultimæ, sunt velut sanguis spiritusque per totum corpus susæ, etymologiaq; literarum nihil aliud est, quám prosodia de sonis, & orthographia de charactēribus literarum: Sic in syllabis, de colligatione ipsarum, & quantitate: sic in dictionibus, de accentu & notatione literarum in principio & fine: sic in tota oratione, de incisis, membris, periodis pronuntiandis & scribendis. Itaq; dichotomia primæ partitionis legitima est. Quantū verò é methodo lucrum arti Grámaticæ accesserit, P. Rami Grammatica & Latina & Græca & Francica abundé explicabit: Grammatica tamen quorumlibet Grammaticorum, seu Græcorum, seu Latinorum, id etiam iter ingredi atque insistere voluit: Itaque de literis primò, tū de syllabis, tertiò de dictionibus, postremò de tota oratione præcipit: Interroga quamobremresponderent Grammatici ita aliis alia præposuisse, quia putarent antecedentia consequentibus esse magis communia & generalia, antecedentiaque sine consequentibus intelligi posse.
units.tr: Parts of grammar] The parts of grammar are commonly made four: etymology, syntax, prosody, and orthography. But the last two are, as it were, blood and breath spread through the whole body. The etymology of letters is nothing other than prosody concerning sounds, and orthography concerning the written forms of letters. So too in syllables, it concerns their combination and quantity. So too in words, it concerns accent and the marking of letters at the beginning and end. So too in the whole speech, it concerns the cola, members and periods to be pronounced and written. Therefore the dichotomy of the first partition is lawful. How much gain the art of grammar has gained from method, P. Ramus's Grammar, in Latin, Greek and French, will explain abundantly. Yet he wished that the grammar of any grammarians, whether Greek or Latin, should also enter and keep to this path. Thus he teaches first about letters, then about syllables, third about words, and last about the whole speech. Ask why the grammarians have placed one before another in that way; they would answer that they thought the earlier things were more common and more general than the later ones, and that the earlier could be understood without the later.

units.la: Artes] Rhetorica nostra, P. Rami non solū prælectionibus rhetoricis adjuta est, sed logicis legibus præcipuè digesta compositaq;: Neq; verò Rhetorica nostra solúm, sed Rhetorica Aristotelis, Ciceronis, Quintiliani, hunc etiā ordinè sequi voluit: licet aliena plurima hi authores afsūpserint, ut Dialecticam inveniendi & disponendi. Et quanquam multis in locis plurimā cōtra leges artificiosæ materiæ & formę peccaverint, attamen si roges, cur inventionem primā, disposi-tionem secundam, elocutionem tertiā, memoriā quartam, actionem quintam fecerint: logicęmethodi lege à generalibus ad specialia factum fuū defendent. Dialectica adhuc à P. Ramo descripta, cúm artium reliquarum magistra esse velit,legi suæ in primis obsequi & obtéperare debuit. Neq; porró P. Rami Dialeêtica id solü præ stitit, sed Aristotelis etiá logica præstare voluit: Aristotelis enim Logica(ut antiquissimi & nobilissimi Peripateticorū, Adrastus ejusq; adstipulatores censuerunt) habebat invētionē primo loco in Categoriis & Topicis, dispositionē deinceps enuntiati in ἑρμηνέα, syllogismi in priore analysi, methodi in posteriore : vitia tum inventionis, tum dispositionis, in Elenchis. atq; hic á generalibus ad specialia paulò justiús pro cedebatur: interpretes verò, qui eo ordine Logicam Aristotelis disposuerunt, quo nunc est, chaos omnibus Logicis legibus contrariū commenti sunt: attamen interrogati de ordine, cur illa præposuerint, respondebűt præcedētia magis communia, magisq; generalia sibi visa esse, & sine consequentibus intelligi posse. Arithmetica & Geometria, eam testimonii fidem atque religioné é P.Rami vigiliis, proximis annis manifestiús explicabunt. Sed tamen Elementa Euclidis ex his duabus artibus, licet locis plerisq; magis confusa, quám composita, attamen speciem legis nostrae in una saltem Geometria prę textum:pun&tum, lineam, superficiem, corpus deinceps ordinando: & sic ʒ.ca.6.Topic. Aristo teles nominatim ait, pun&tū esse prius notiusq; linea, & lineá superficie, & superficiē corpore. Astrologia una artium omniū confusissima est: attamen etiam Ptoleměus in constitueda & cōponenda astrorum doctrina, interdū logicę methodi legem nominatim prætexit. Phifica porró Ariftotelis tota, mirabili porfus & laudabili ftudio methodum á generalibus ad fpecialia cŏ fectatur,definiédo communiter naturam, tum in genera fimplicis & compofitæ naturæ partiē do:fimplicis,in cælo & quatuor elementis:com pofitæ,in brutis & animatis reb9. In Ethicis autem,definitur primó fummum bonũ ĕ virtutis actione,tum virtutis genera fpeciefque & differentiæ ad extremum deinceps explicantur.|Ne que veró philofophus methodũ á generalibus ad fpecialia in Ethicis tátúm fequutus eft,fed fe fequutũ effe nominatim libri tertii capite quinto prædicavit. Quid multa?Si qua virtute præftitit Ariftoteles(qui certé plurimis & maximis præftitit)hac una nom modó reliquos philofophos,fed feipfum longifsimé fuperavit: fedita tamé fuperavit, ut Socraticos amores illos multis partibus effugientes, nō obfcuré oftenderit.
units.tr: The arts] Our rhetoric, P. Ramus's, was not only aided by rhetorical lectures, but was arranged and composed chiefly by the laws of logic. Nor did he wish only our rhetoric, but also the rhetoric of Aristotle, Cicero and Quintilian, to follow this same order, although these authors have taken over much that belongs to others, such as the dialectic of invention and arrangement. And although in many places they have sinned much against the laws of artful matter and form, yet if you ask why they put invention first, arrangement second, style third, memory fourth, and delivery fifth, they will defend their deed by the law of logical method, from the general to the specific. Dialectic, as described by P. Ramus so far, since it wishes to be the teacher of the other arts, ought above all to obey and submit to its own law. Nor did P. Ramus's dialectic achieve only this; he wished it to achieve also the logic of Aristotle. For Aristotle's logic (as the most ancient and noble of the Peripatetics, Adrastus and his supporters, judged) had invention first, in the Categories and Topics; then the arrangement of the proposition in the Hermeneia, of the syllogism in the Prior Analytics, and of method in the Posterior Analytics; and the faults of both invention and arrangement in the Elenchi. Here too the procedure was somewhat more just, from the general to the specific. But the interpreters, who arranged Aristotle's logic in the order it now has, have devised a chaos contrary to all the laws of logic. Yet when they are asked about the order, why they put the earlier things first, they will reply that the earlier things seemed to them more common and more general, and could be understood without the later. Arithmetic and geometry will, in the coming years, explain more clearly the trust and reverence that this testimony has gained from the watchings of P. Ramus. Yet the Elements of Euclid, from these two arts, though in many places more confused than composed, nonetheless show the appearance of our law at least in geometry alone, by ordering in turn the point, the line, the surface, and the body. And thus Aristotle, in the third chapter of the sixth book of the Topics, expressly says that the point is prior and better known than the line, the line than the surface, and the surface than the body. Astrology is the most confused of all the arts, yet even Ptolemy, in establishing and composing the doctrine of the stars, sometimes expressly puts forward the law of logical method. Moreover, the whole physics of Aristotle, with a wonderfully admirable zeal, pursues method from the general to the specific: it defines nature in general, then divides it into the genera of simple and composite nature. Simple nature is divided into the heavens and the four elements; composite nature into brute and animate things. In ethics, the highest good is first defined as the activity of virtue; then the kinds, species and differences of virtue are finally explained in turn. Nor did the philosopher follow method from the general to the specific in ethics alone; he expressly declared in the fifth chapter of the third book that he had followed it. What more? If Aristotle excelled in any virtue (and certainly he excelled in very many and very great things), he surpassed not only the other philosophers in this one thing, but also himself by far. Yet he surpassed himself in such a way that, while in many respects escaping those Socratic loves, he did not obscurely show them.

units.la: Quamobrem omnes liberales difciplinæ, locupletisimo & luculētissimo testimonio,unicam & fingularem artis methodũ á generalibus ad fpecialia teftificantur.hæc P.Rami præmittebatur inductio & inquifitio. Grámatica, Rhetorica, Dialectica, Arithmetica, Geometria, Aftrolo gia, Phyfica,Ethica,á P.Ramo inquam producũ tur,quæ una voce omnes verifsimum jufiurandum jurarent, fibi aliá quám á generalibus viá nullam unquam placuisse. Agite igitur,interpretes Ariftotelis (ubicunq; terrarum eftis) inductionis hujus & anquisitionis fidem explorate & perpędite. Ad Philofophorum omniũ principia, ad usum artium & doctrinarum (de quarũ methodo & ordine potissimúm differim9) ad experientiá redeamus, legem καθ' αὐτὸν hic in primis usurpemus: ac pro omnibus, unus aliquis exoriare, qui interpretum, qui Galeni tot, tamq; varias methodos legitimas arbitrere. P. Ramus tam studiose disseruit, methodum disponendæ artis, semper á generalibus procedere: hæc alii caussas, alii elementa, alii initia, alii principia, alii simplicia: imó Aristoteles ipse iis omnibus nominibus appellat, qui ἀρχὰ, qui στοιχεῖα, qui ἀρχαί, qui ἀπλᾶ nominat. At de verbis ne curiose soliciti simus, ut verissimé jubet Plato, ut sæpissimé Galenus admonet: rē potiús teneamus. Omnibus artium scriptoribus unicam methodū á generalibus placere P. Ramus pro Aristotele contendit, ut á primis & immediatis prę notionib. per subalternas ad specialissimas descēdatur: quodq; in artib. primo loco statuūt, id illis generalissimū videri, quia possit ej9 doctrina facilé sine consequentibus accipi: consequentium nō item, sine præcedentis doctrina. Non dicit (inquam) omnes artifices id penitus assequi, neq; nusquam labi, neq; nufquá Socraticis amorib. affici: sed ista via sola & unica vele progredi: & artis eam partem, quam cæteris primo loco præponant, illis generalissimam, na turaq; primam & notissimam videri: quam medio loco subjungát, subalternam: quam infimo, specialissimam. Quamobrē (iterabat hic P. Ramus, ut pertinacia ingenia diligētiús commonefaceret) facito in omnibus artibus periculū:
units.tr: Wherefore all the liberal disciplines, by the fullest and clearest testimony, attest that art has one and only method, proceeding from general things to special ones. This was the induction and inquiry that P. Ramus set before his work. Grammar, Rhetoric, Dialectic, Arithmetic, Geometry, Astrology, Physics and Ethics are brought forward by P. Ramus, I say, and all of them would swear with one voice the truest oath that no way but from the general has ever pleased them. Come then, interpreters of Aristotle, wherever on earth you are, test and weigh the trustworthiness of this induction and inquiry. Let us return to the principles of all the philosophers and to the practice of the arts and doctrines, whose method and order we are chiefly discussing, and to experience. Here above all let us use the rule by itself. And for all of them, let someone arise who judges so many and such varied methods of the interpreters and of Galen to be legitimate. P. Ramus has argued so earnestly that the method of arranging an art always proceeds from the general. Some call these things causes, others elements, others beginnings, others principles, others simples. Indeed Aristotle himself uses all these names, calling them beginnings [ἀρχά], elements [στοιχεῖα], first things [ἀρχαί], and simples [ἁπλᾶ]. But let us not anxiously fuss over words, as Plato very truly bids and Galen very often warns; let us hold to the thing itself. P. Ramus contends, on Aristotle's behalf, that all writers on the arts agree on one method, from the general: one descends from the first and immediate notions, through the subaltern ones, to the most special. What they place first in an art, they regard as most general, because its doctrine can be grasped easily without its consequences, whereas the consequences cannot be grasped without the doctrine that precedes them. I do not say (I insist) that all craftsmen fully achieve this, nor that they never slip, nor that they are never touched by Socratic loves; but that they proceed by this one way alone. The part of the art that they put first before the rest seems to them most general, first by nature and most known; what they put in the middle is subaltern, and what they put last is most special. Wherefore (P. Ramus repeated this to admonish stubborn minds more carefully) make the trial in all the arts:

units.la: experiéris hác methodum solùm adhiberi, quæ á maximis & notissimis tum menti, tum sensui procedat, ut Hippocrates censuit: quæ á capite per media ad pedes descendat, ut Phædro placuit: quæ ab unitate per medium numerum ad infinitatem descendat, ut in Philebo monstratum est: quę etiam á notione finis incipiēs, proxima quæq; partiens ac collocás, secundo loco secunda, tertio tertia, quarto quarta, quinto quinta, ac deinceps similiter in ultimis particulis acquiscat, ut Galenus docere debuit. jam verò in reliqs cōmentitiis methodis facito (si lubet, quó magis res confirmetur) idem de iisdem artibus periculum, remq; præsentē, ac velut oculis subjectam, experientia præsenti disceptato: hęc experientia controversiæ finem adferet. Cerā ean dem variis formis informari, si quis affirmáti tibi negaverit, præsentis operis exemplo affirmationis tuæ fidem facies: in calefacta & emollita cera Achillem, leonem, Cęsarem effinges. Similimum certamē nobis est: Galenus rectē docet (ut affirmas) eandem artis partibus omnibus inventæ & judicatæ materiam pluribus methodis variisq; ordinibus totā disponi posse: id verò inficiatur P. Ramus ac pernegat: Unicam, eamq; Aristoteleam á generalibus prænotionibus esse dicit. Esto igitur nobis artis unius tota materia, sed rudis & indigesta, informis & profusus confusa: mistæ sint definitiones & partitiones, regulæ omnes ac institutiones perturbatę: ludus Ollæ deniq; nobis huc redeat. Agé, duas Galeni methodos, compositivam & definitivá hic experire,σωφρονίζω priús adhibe: Sit hæc materies artis tam cófusa Grammaticę: quid secundum hanc Galeni methodū facies? si primo statuas specialissima, medió subalterna, postremó generalissimum (ut Galenus tibi præcipere videtur) quid ages? Si duos annos in grammaticis puer tibi fit instituendus ad tuam istam methodum, primū annū consumes in regulis Syntaxeos, ultimis primū, deinde mediis, tū primis, partiumq; orationis nondū cognitarū mirificā structurā instituēs. Anno fecūdo, cùm docueris syntaxin, ad etymologiā venies, & partes orationis explicabis, conjunctiones primùm & adverbia, verba deinde & nomina, item syllabas, & literas declarabis: sic enim retrogradus á naturā posterioribus ad naturā priora cóscendes: atq; in tenebris viatori lumen tutioris vię non præferes, sed poné vagante, & errante in umbra corporis videlicet occultabis: Qua stultitia, quæso te, quæ nam major in artibus instituendis fingi cogitariq; potest? jámne sentis, ô philosophe (si quis in hac pertinacia philosophus esse posit) jámne sentis verá Aristot. ἀπαγωγὴν illam fuisse: regressionēq; illam á specialibus ad generalia, ignorantiæ & oblivionis viá esse? Quid in Geometria quid facies? quomodo γραμμίνγει ἀποδείξις illæ tantam doctrinæ perturbationē ferent? Elementorum libri sunt quindecim: decimus quintus tibi primus erit, decimus quartus tibi secundus & deinceps sic invertetur reliqui, aut si qua fit illustrior σοιχεῖωσις (qualem P. Rami spero suturam) attamē solida primùm, tum superficies, tertio loco linea fuerit, tandem desines in punſtū,& magnitudinis affectiōes primas. At quas demonstrationes hic ordo compositivus habebit’ex antecedētibus theorematis & problema tis consequentia,analytica via demonstrantur: an etiam contrá, per hanc viam poterunt Eucli dis posteriores ppofitiones ē prioribus nondū cognitis demonstrari’an consequentes,principia erunt antecedentium’an Geometras putaſmus istam methodū sine risu audituros esse’nō potiús radio & pulvere talē sophistā é cathedra abaćturos’Quare secūda methodus Galeni, secunda ordinis doćtrina nó modó facilis nō est (ut antea temeré objiciebatur) sed pdifficilis, sed plané impossibilis:nec adhuc á mortali(qd’ fando auditū fit)quoquam tentata: Ac fi qui ex iis, qui hos errores tá crassos, tamq; palpabiles obstinate defendunt, ad rem,ad opus,ad exemplum,ad effigiem & veritate adducantur,& his interrogationibus urgeantur,utrūm grammatica possit aliter disponi, quám ut primo loco sit litera,secundo syllaba,tertio diƈtio,quarto oratio: ité utrúm geometria aliter disponi possit,q̄ ut precedat puĉtum lineam , linea superficiem, superficies corpus, negant aliter disponi posse, sed logicæ confusiús perceptæ mirificas ambages,de caussarum præsertim generibus permiscent: neq; cōsiderant tamé, ista quæstione caussas omnes jam invētas, imó judicatas proponi, nec aliam considerationem relinqui, quám quę prima naturā sit & claritate,quæ secunda, quæ tertia: Deniq; rei consensio hic summa est, ver-boborum & authoritatū mirabilis dissensio: ut in isto Galeni errore verbis defendendo, cûm docet Galenus artes antea inventas disponi, á spe cialissimis per subalterna ad generalissimū finē. Cæteri errores illi de similitudine & aliis argumentis pro methodicæ dispositionis doctrina assumptis, errorem simplicem habuerūt: At hæc inventarum artium dispositio á specialis-simis per subalterna ad generalissimū finē, apertissimé in sophisticas sordes ignorantiæ & oblivionis ab Aristotele propositas incurrit. Si diceret Galenus, artes unico modo collocari ab uni versalib. ad specialia, ut de litera, syllaba, dictione, oratione, ut de pun&to, linea, superficie, corpore dictum est: Attamē collocationis hujus triplicem ratione reddi posse: aliquid licet falsum, attamē minus absurdū diceret. At dicere, quód exemplo, usu, experimento neq; audierit neq; legerit unquam, imó quod vel opere qualicunque sine rubore fingere nō audeat, materiam artium prius inventam & judicatam, tandē disponi á specialissimis per subalterna ad generalissimum finem: Id verò, ut prędixi, neq; Hippocrates neq; Plato, neq; Aristoteles, neq; attētior ipse Galenus feret, dormientis vel stertentis potius insomniū esse profitebitur. Perge ad definitivam methodum, signumq; ejus in eadem illa rudi, cujus voles artis, materia imprime: quid ex ejus forma primum, quid secūdum, quid tertium, quod deniq; ordinis indicium ac vestigiū cernes ante Varronem, Donatum, Diomedē, Priscianum, veterefq; Grammaticos, Gramma-
units.tr: you will find that only this method is applied, the one that proceeds from the greatest and most known things, both to the mind and to the senses, as Hippocrates thought; the one that descends from the head through the middle to the feet, as Phaedrus liked; the one that descends from unity through the middle number to infinity, as was shown in the Philebus; and the one that, beginning from the notion of the end, divides and arranges the nearest things, so that second things come in second place, third in third, fourth in fourth, fifth in fifth, and so on in the same way down to the last particulars, as Galen ought to have taught. Now, in the remaining fictitious methods, make the trial as well (if you like, so the matter is more firmly established) on the same arts, and let the present matter, set before you as if before your eyes, be debated by present experience; this experience will bring the controversy to an end. If someone denies to you that wax can be shaped into various forms, you will prove your affirmation by the example of the present work: in warmed and softened wax you will fashion Achilles, a lion, Caesar. Our contest is very similar. Galen rightly teaches (as you affirm) that the same material of an art, once discovered and judged, can be arranged entire by several methods and in various orders. But P. Ramus denies this and utterly rejects it; he says there is only one, and it is Aristotle's, proceeding from general preconceptions. So let us take the whole material of one art, but rough and undigested, shapeless and poured out in confusion; let definitions and divisions be mixed together, and all rules and precepts be in disorder. Let the game of the pot, at last, return to us here. Come, first take heed [σωφρονίζω], and then try on this same material the two methods of Galen, the compositive and the definitive. Let this material of grammar be as confused as you like. What will you do according to this Galenic method? If you first set down the most special things, in the middle the subaltern, and last the most general (as Galen seems to direct you), what will you do? If a boy must be instructed in grammar for two years for the sake of your method, you will spend the first year on the rules of syntax, beginning with the last, then the middle, and then the first, setting out the wonderful structure of the parts of speech before they are known. In the second year, when you have taught syntax, you will come to etymology and explain the parts of speech, first conjunctions and adverbs, then verbs and nouns; likewise you will explain syllables and letters. For so, retracing your steps from nature, you will climb from later things to things earlier by nature. You will not hold up to the traveller in darkness the light of a safer way, but will hide it from him, putting him behind, wandering and erring in the shadow of his own body. What folly, I ask you, what greater folly can be imagined or conceived in teaching the arts? Do you now perceive, philosopher (if anyone who is so obstinate can be called a philosopher), that the apagoge [ἀπαγωγήν] of true Aristotle, that regression from the special to the general, is the road of ignorance and forgetting? What will you do in geometry? How will those geometrical demonstrations [γραμμικαὶ ἀποδείξεις] bear such great confusion of doctrine? The books of the Elements are fifteen. The fifteenth will be your first, the fourteenth your second, and the rest will be inverted in turn. Or if there is some clearer elementary exposition [στοιχείωσις] (such as I hope P. Ramus will produce), nevertheless solids will come first, then surfaces, third lines, and finally you will end at the point and the first affections of magnitude. But what demonstrations will this compositive order have? Will the theorems and problems that follow be demonstrated by the analytic way from the preceding ones? Or, on the contrary, by this way, could the later propositions of Euclid be demonstrated from the earlier ones, which are not yet known? Will the consequents become the principles of the antecedents? Do we think that geometers will hear this method without laughing? Will they not rather drive such a sophist from the lecture hall with rods and dust? Therefore the second method of Galen, the second order of doctrine, is not only not easy (as was rashly objected before), but very difficult, and plainly impossible. Nor has any mortal yet attempted it, so far as one has ever heard. And if some of those who obstinately defend these errors, so gross and so palpable, were brought to the matter itself, to the work, to the example, to the image and the truth, and were pressed with these questions: whether grammar can be arranged otherwise than with the letter first, the syllable second, the word third, and the sentence fourth; and whether geometry can be arranged otherwise than with the point preceding the line, the line the surface, and the surface the body, they would deny that it can be arranged otherwise. Yet they would muddle, with wonderful circumlocutions, the logic that they perceive too confusedly, especially concerning the kinds of causes. Nor do they consider that in this question all causes are already discovered, indeed already judged, and that no other consideration is left than which is first in nature and clarity, which second, which third. In the end, there is the greatest agreement in the matter itself and a marvellous disagreement over words and authorities. Such is the case with Galen's error, which he defends in words when he teaches that arts already discovered are arranged from the most special, through the subaltern, to the most general end. Those other errors, about similarity and other arguments assumed for the doctrine of methodical arrangement, had only a simple error. But this arrangement of discovered arts from the most special, through the subaltern, to the most general end, runs most openly into the sophistical filth of ignorance and forgetting, which Aristotle set forth. If Galen said that the arts can be placed in only one way, from the universals to the special, as has been said of the letter, syllable, word and sentence, or of the point, line, surface and body, then even if it were false, his claim could be given a threefold justification and would be less absurd. But to say that the material of the arts, already discovered and judged, is finally arranged from the most special, through the subaltern, to the most general end, when he has never heard or read of this in example, practice or experiment, and when he would not dare to invent it even in some rough work without blushing, that, as I said before, neither Hippocrates, nor Plato, nor Aristotle, nor Galen himself, however attentive, would bear. He will confess it to be the dream of a man asleep, or rather snoring. Proceed to the definitive method, and impress its mark on that same rough material of whatever art you wish. What first, what second, what third in its form, and what finally, do you see as an indication and trace of order before Varro, Donatus, Diomedes, Priscian and the old grammarians? The rules of grammar were once scattered, and these were at last comprised briefly and easily by the short road of the logical method. What if, before grammar had been so adorned, you had consulted Galen about ordering grammar, and he had answered that the definitive method must be followed, the thing must first be defined: what would you have done?

units.la: ticæ artis regulæ dispersę quondam fuerūt, quę tandem compendiaria logicæ methodi via facilé breviterq; sunt coprehésę. Quid si antequàm Grammatica sic ornata esset, Galenum de ordinanda Grammatica cósuluisses, tibiq; responderet, definitivam methodum sequendam esse, rem primùm definiendam, quid fecisses ? Hoc enim respóso, nescires quid primū, quid secundum, quid tertium debuisses definire, quá definitionem de tam multis præponere, quá postponere, & quidquid hic sursum deorsū miscueris ac turbaris, quia per definitiones procedes, & definitivam methodum adhibebis : nihil ad istam Galeni logicam peccabis, qua ἀλογία quid ἀλογώτερον fingi potest ? Experire idé in reliquis artibus:idem reperies. Quare tertia hæc methodus, nulla est methodus. Verumenimvero quæstionem hanc primùm cum philosophiæ salute, cumq; Aristotelis laude, deinde quoad fieri poterit, cum Galeni excusatione concludamus, sicut antea dubiam hac de re locis aliquot Aristotelis sententiam conclusimus. Galenus de artiū constitutione & cōpositione tam multa præceperit, in iisq; præceptis, contra veram Aristot. methodum P.Ramo objicitur. Galenus experientiam, usum, utilitatem, præceptorum omniū & dogmatum magistram unicá esse docuit: experientia verò, usus, utilitas Grammaticæ, Rhetoricæ, Logicę, Mathematicę, & liberalis cuiusvis doctrinę, unicá methodum illá á generalib9 ad specialia, ab universalibus ad Particularia requirit, ut facilius discatur ut facilius exerceatur :
units.tr: ...ticæ artis regulæ dispersæ quondam fuerunt, quæ tandem compendiaria logicæ methodi via facile breviterque sunt comprehensæ. What if, before grammar had been so adorned, you had consulted Galen on how to arrange grammar, and he had replied that the definitive method must be followed, with the thing to be defined first: what would you have done? For on that answer you would not know what ought to be defined first, second and third, which definition to put before so many others and which to put after them. Whatever you mix up and throw into disorder here, above and below, because you proceed by definitions and will use the definitive method, you will commit no fault against that logic of Galen. What more unreasonable thing [ἀλογία] than this [ἀλογώτερον] can be imagined? Try the same in the other arts: you will find the same. Therefore this third method is no method. But let us conclude this question first with the safety of philosophy and the praise of Aristotle, and then, as far as possible, with an excuse for Galen, just as we earlier settled Aristotle's doubtful opinion on this matter in several passages. Galen gave so many precepts on the constitution and composition of the arts, and in these precepts Ramus is objected to as contrary to the true method of Aristotle. Galen taught that experience, use and utility are the sole teacher of all precepts and doctrines. But the experience, use and utility of grammar, rhetoric, logic, mathematics and every liberal discipline require that single method from general to special, from universals to particulars, so that it may be learned more easily and practised more easily.

units.la: Hoc igitur satis superq; mihi fuerit, ad concludendu pro Ariftotele, quod institui, unicá artis ordinádę viá esse á generalib. ad specialia: neq; cúm superet Aristoteles Galenū veritate, par erit Aristotelē á Galeno authoritate superari. Re prehensus est Aristoteles in qbusdá veré cóstáterq; á Galeno, patietur vicissim & Galenȝ se ve ré & cóstáter ab Atistotele de tanto methodorū sophismate reprehēdi: Quod ut minimé nostris hominibus mirum videatur, efficient duo summi in Italia Germaniaque philosophi, Hieronymus Cardanus & Iacob. Schekius, aperté professi, quám valentem logicum Galenum existimarent. Ridicula sunt (ait Cardanus in sua dialectica) quæ Galenus jactat de demostratione. Schekius vero in apodicticis suis cúm plerosq; Galeni in logicis errores adnotasset, affirmat Galenū nō semper demonstrationū intelligentissimū fuisse. Itaq; Galeni libros de demostratione nō magna posteritatis jactura periisse. Verum tamen Galeni judiciū de Galeno ipso antea á P. Ramo recepimus: & hic postrem̄ locus id potissimum exigit.
units.tr: This, then, will be more than enough for me to conclude on behalf of Aristotle what I set out to show: that the one way of ordering an art is from general to special. And since Aristotle surpasses Galen in truth, it is not fitting that Aristotle should be surpassed by Galen in authority. Aristotle has been truly and consistently criticised by Galen on some points; in turn, Galen must allow himself to be truly and consistently censured by Aristotle for so great a sophistry about methods. That this may not seem strange to our people, two of the greatest philosophers in Italy and Germany, Girolamo Cardano and Jacob Schegk, will make it plain: they openly declared how able a logician they judged Galen to be. "The things Galen boasts about demonstration are ridiculous," says Cardano in his Dialectic. Schegk, having noted in his Apodictics many of Galen's errors in logic, affirms that Galen was not always the most understanding of demonstrations. And so the books of Galen on demonstration perished without great loss to posterity. But we have already received from P. Ramus Galen's own judgment of Galen, and this last point especially requires it.

units.la: — Video meliora, proboque, Deteriora sequor. — ait poeta ille. At ego contrá, ajebat hic P. Ramus, cósirmo Galenum á scholasticis doctoribus, & Aristotelis præsertim interpretib. deteriora didicisse, scriptoq; prodidisse, usu autē atq; opere, id est mentis ac judicii veritate, secutū esse meliora. Quid ita? aut quomodo tándem id probari potest? Attende (inquam) homo es, deus non es, nec tui sermones tuis actionibus semper respondet: Si igitur ubi liber es, ubi quod velis potes: ubi etiā vitę tuę profesio singularis famaq; versatur, ibi uno modo semper agas, ubi judicium tuum vis existimem? Certè (opinor) in perpetua actionum, præsertim laudabiliū constantia. Hoc usus argumēto atq; judicio P. Ramus grammaticos Donatū, Diomedem, rhetoras Quintilianum. Ciceronē, philosophos & mathematicos Aristolem, Euclidem de maximis rebus appellavit, & admonuit, magistroq; artium usu fallaces artium institutiones plerafq; refutavit. Ponatur igitur hæc hypothesis atq; caussa: ibi Galeni judicium esse, ubi perpetuus Galeni usus, tanquā nempe perpetua approbatio fuerit. Si quis igitur de Galeni libris tam multis ullus sequatur aliam methodum, aliamq; dispositionem quàm Aristoteleam ab universalib. ad singularia: aut si quis ejus liber totus & integer, artem aliquā integram & totam, sola similitudine & dissimilitudine artificiose componat (quę prima methodus ejus est) aut à specialissimis p media ad generalissimum artificiose progrediatur (quę copositio ejus est) aut sola consequentiū & repugnantium consideratione artificiose constituat (quæ methodus alicubi de tribus ei secūda est) aut sola comparatione majorum, minorum, parium, aut eiusdem & diversi consideratione artificiose cōficiat (quæ tertia) aut solo definitiōis ordine deducat (quæ de tribus postremis ultima est) ego me(ajebat P.Ramus) in Galeni sententiā authoritatemq; servum sponte devoveā. & quod non videam, attamen quia Galenus dicit, videre me dicam: & quod non teneam: quia Galenus nō dicit, coprehendere me fatear. Sin unicam à generalisfimo per subalterna ad specialissima viam Galenus in libris omnibus sibi propofuit, hoc nó fcholafticum á magiftris, fed proprium & verum Galeni judiciū effe pro unica Ariftotelis methodo cócludatur & teneatur. At Galenus ex omnibus philosophis quamvis diverfis locis, diverfis temporibus, diverfis oc cafionibus, nunc difcipulorum & amicorum rogatu, nunc obtrectatorum impulfu, incredibile quedam librorum numerum confcripferit: via tamé illam, quam primó divifivam, quam etiam poftremó refolutivam vocat á prioribus naturā & notioribus, ab univerfalibus & generalib. ad fingularia & fpecialia fequi vehementer voluit: fic in omnibus difputationib. fuis fummá quæftione proponit, eamq; toto opere dividendo & refolvendo partes exequitur: quę ab univerfalibus & generalibus via eft: nufquam à fpe cialiffimis per fubalterna ad generalifsimū artem ullam totam & integram inftituit, quod reditus compofitivi effet exemplum: nufquam cęterarum methodorum una aliqua fola unam artem tradit. Falfaq; & fallacia funt exempla, particularibus & accidentalibus methodis Galeni errores excufantium: umbrę tantum funt magnarum authoritatū fimplicibus imponētium, artem nullam totam illis fuis commentitiis for mis efformarunt, neq; efformabunt unquā. Quamobrē Galenus judicio suo unicam Ariftotelis á generalibus methodū approbat, in eoq; egregiam quandam præstátis ingenii naturá ostendit,quę tam fallacibus fcho lafticorum magiftrorū documentis nihil impedita aut retardata|fit, quo minus in usu ipso ferioq; opere unitatē methodi, veritatēq; fequeretur. Statuamus igitur, Galeni studiosos philosophos in ista caussa temerē tumultuari,& abiis tam fœdas notas turpiter tanto viro tanquam probatas & æstimatas inuri. unum fi ad hoc Galeni confirmandum judicium addidero, peroratum arbitrabor.Multa cótra Galeni methodos,vel potius cótra nescio quos Galeni doctrina abutētes fatuos P. Galenus in libro de Arte medica dicit fe definitivā methodum secuturum, quæ ab Ariftotelica illa sin-
units.tr: "I see the better things and approve them; I follow the worse." So says that poet. But I, on the contrary, said Ramus here, maintain that Galen learned the worse things from the scholastic teachers, and especially from the interpreters of Aristotle, and handed them down in writing; but in practice and in his work, that is, in the truth of his mind and judgment, he followed the better things. How so? Or how can this finally be proved? Consider, I say: you are a man, not a god, and your words do not always match your actions. If, then, where you are free, where you can do what you wish, and where your distinctive way of life and your reputation are at stake, you always act in one way, is that where you would want your judgment to be assessed? Surely (I think) in the constant consistency of one's actions, especially the praiseworthy ones. By this argument and judgment P. Ramus called to account the grammarians Donatus and Diomedes, the rhetoricians Quintilian and Cicero, the philosophers and mathematicians Aristotle and Euclid on the greatest matters, and admonished them; and, with practice as his teacher, he refuted most of the deceptive instructions of the arts. Let this hypothesis and case therefore be laid down: that Galen's judgment is wherever his constant practice is, as it were a constant approval. If anyone, then, among so many books of Galen, follows any method or arrangement other than the Aristotelian one from universals to singulars; or if anyone, in a whole and complete book, skilfully composes some whole art by similarity and dissimilarity alone (this is his first method); or skilfully progresses from the most special things through intermediates to the most general (this is his composition); or skilfully constitutes an art by considering consequences and contradictions alone (which is his second method, somewhere among the three); or skilfully makes it by comparing greater, smaller and equal things, or the same and the different (the third); or deduces it by the order of definition alone (the last of the three final ones), then I, said P. Ramus, will willingly devote myself as a slave to Galen's opinion and authority. And what I do not see, I shall say I see, because Galen says it; and what I do not hold, since Galen does not say so, I shall confess I hold. But if Galen in all his books set before himself the single way from the most general through intermediates to the most special, let it be concluded and held that this is not a scholastic view derived from the teachers but Galen's own true judgment, in favour of Aristotle's single method. But Galen, among all philosophers, though in different places, at different times and on different occasions, now at the request of pupils and friends, now at the instigation of detractors, wrote an incredible number of books; yet the way which he calls first divisive and finally resolutive, proceeding from what is prior and better known by nature, from universals and generals to singulars and specials, he strongly wished to follow. So in all his disputations he sets forth the chief question, and in the whole work he carries out its parts by dividing and resolving; this is the way from universals and generals. Nowhere does he establish any whole and complete art from the most special things through intermediates up to the most general, which would be an example of the compositive return; nowhere does he teach any art by any one of the other methods alone. False and fallacious are the examples of those who excuse Galen's errors by appeal to particular and accidental methods. They are mere shadows of great authorities, imposing on simple people; they have formed no whole art by those invented forms of theirs, and never will. Let them drop their confused examples drawn from physics, metaphysics and medicine, by which they deceive themselves and their followers. Let them try, in some Platonic example about mere letters, free of trickery: let them try with letter, syllable, word, sentence, point, line, surface and body, whether they can be skilfully arranged in several ways. They will at once understand that they are shamefully deceived and disgracefully mistaken. Therefore Galen, by his judgment, approves the single Aristotelian method from generals, and in this shows an outstanding natural talent, which was in no way hindered or delayed by the deceptive teaching of the scholastic masters, so that in actual practice and serious work it followed the unity of method and truth. Since this is so, who will now doubt Galen's judgment? What student of Galen will begrudge him so philosophical a nature, so unconquered by scholastic fables? By example, by work and by the whole truth of accurate judgment, Galen agrees with Aristotle about the single method of arranging an art. Let us grant, then, that the philosophers who study Galen rush about rashly in this cause, and that such foul marks are shamefully branded on so great a man, as if he had approved and valued them. If I add one more thing to confirm Galen's judgment, I shall consider the speech finished. P. Ramus has argued much against Galen's methods, or rather against certain foolish men who abuse Galen's teaching; for if there were one method among them, the others would not be methods, nor would they be ways of arranging arts and forming them in continuous order. Galen says in his book on the art of medicine that he will follow the definitive method, which seems to some to differ greatly from that single, unique and most general Aristotelian method proceeding through intermediates to the most special.
