Quid igitur? si Galenus hanc nostram divisivam & resolutivam (ut appellat) á generalibus ad specialia methodū in hoc etiam ipso libro sequatur,& á generalissimo p sub alterna ad specialissima pgrediatur? quid si alibi dicat secundum hanc ad divisivam methodū in hujus operis exeplo se progredi, quid pluribus Galeni judicium confirmandū sit,cum ipse suo facto, suo exemplo, suo testimonio, suo ore cōfirmet? & re vera ac veritate doceat, quod antea dubitavimus, definitivam illam methodum nullam ordinandæ artis & conformandæ viam ab hac divisiva & resolutiva diversam esse? At progreditur, medicamq; artem costituit partiedo á summo capite per medias differētias ad infima & individua, nēpe per salubria, insalubria, neutra in corporibus, caussis signis: & partitionibus & divisionibus in hoc toto libro ppetuis utitur, & revera ac veritate docet definitivam, quam tantopere per somnium nescio quod amp plexatur, accidentalem esse in perpetui ordinis deductione, resolutivam autē & divisivam, quā accidentalem dicebat esse, substātialem potius in ordine & principalem, quia sine definitione methodus, vel ea ipsa quam sequitur, constituatur. Quare quod antea proposui, Galenus aperti ssimē demonstrat, logicam nullam sibi distinstā fuisse, ut methodum vel ordinem, vel viam conformandæ & collocandæ artis, intelligeret unam peculiarem logicæ disciplinæ parte esse:
units.tr: What then? If Galen in this very book follows our divisive and resolutive method (as he calls it), from general to special, and progresses from the most general through intermediates to the most special? What if elsewhere he says that he proceeds in this divisive method in the example of this work? Why should Galen's judgment need further confirmation, when he confirms it himself by his deed, his example, his testimony and his own words? And in truth and fact he teaches what we doubted earlier: that the definitive method is no way of ordering and forming an art different from this divisive and resolutive one. But he does proceed, and he constitutes the art of medicine by dividing from the highest head through middle differences down to the lowest and individual things, namely through healthful, unhealthful and neutral things in bodies, causes and signs; and he uses partitions and divisions continually throughout this whole book. And in truth he shows that the definitive method, which he so greatly embraces as if in some dream, is accidental in the deduction of a continuous order, whereas the resolutive and divisive method, which he said was accidental, is rather substantial and principal in order, since no method, not even the very one he follows, can be constituted without definition. Therefore what I proposed earlier, Galen most openly demonstrates: he had no logic distinct from his own, so that he would understand method or order, or the way of forming and arranging an art, to be one peculiar part of the discipline of logic.

Quamobrem ad extremum P.Ramus exclama bat, & philofophos omnes invocabat, ut meminiffent, quantum certamen pro Ariitotelis gloria, quâm fortiter & conftanter certaviffet: fe logicum in notandis aliarum partiū Ariftoteleis elēchis, in topicis invētionis, in criticis & enuntiati & syllogismi severum fuisse, se etiam in nobilissima logicae parte, quam Plato donum deorum, cujusq; participem deum appellarit, acre Aristotelei laudis patronum ac defensorem futurum. Caetera Aristotelis encomia magna quidem illa esse in physicis, ethicis, & logicis reliqs, sed hoc esse divinum, primaq; causam reliquorum. Aristotelis interpretes (quos Galenus verbo sequitur) via artis, cum omnes partes inventę judicatę q; fuerint, collocadae ab individuis per subalternas differentias ad generalissimum, fabulose, immo disciplinis omnib. perniciose comenti sunt.
units.tr: And those who maintain that Galen was an Asiatic should also admit that on this same argument he was a poor logician. Yet in this example Galen follows the method from the general to the particular; indeed he professes that he is following it. For in his compendium of the empirical sect, while citing Herophilus, who set out medicine in this way and divided it threefold, he says that the method in this example is divisive. Galen therefore followed Aristotle's judgment on the single order for arranging an art, not moved by any scholastic persuasion, but led by the steadiness of a more mature judgment and by the truth of constant use. So let us set aside the calumnies of the troublesome abusers of Galen's writings, and praise Galen's freedom, his philosophical and sincere zeal for truth, and above all his experience, which rests on these foundations. Indeed let us thank Galen, who by the example of his own virtue and freedom roused us to seek better and more useful things; who gave us a rule for judging his writings, not a foolish opinion of him, but a sure knowledge of things through experience. Let us banish the scholastic dreams and untested inventions of so many empty methods, which Galen drew from scholastic commentaries and lectures and did not observe in true and excellent examples. Therefore at last P. Ramus cried out and called on all philosophers to remember how great a contest he had fought for the glory of Aristotle, and how bravely and steadily; that he had been a severe logician in marking the elenchi of Aristotle's other parts, in the topics of invention, and in the criticism of the proposition and the syllogism; and that he would also be a keen patron and defender of Aristotle's praise in the most noble part of logic, which Plato called a gift of the gods, and of which a god is the partaker. Aristotle's other encomia are indeed great in physics, ethics and the remaining parts of logic, but this one is divine and the first cause of the rest. The interpreters of Aristotle, whom Galen follows in words, have fabulously, and indeed ruinously for all the disciplines, invented that the way of the art, once all its parts have been discovered and judged, is to be arranged from individuals through subordinate differences up to the most general.

units.la: Etenim quavis in commentis impudentibus tā audaces, attamen salvo pudore audeat in coponenda grammatica orationem dictioni, dictionem syllabę, syllabā literae, vel in disponenda geometria corpus superficiei, superficiē lineę, lineā puncto praeponere: audeat, inquā, sua compositiva methodo tentare vel aggredi. Hic clypeus Achillis, haftaq; P. Ramo est in ppugnado Aristotele. Extorqueant, si possint. At licet in summa impudentia, attamen pudor erit contrā vel hiscere vel cogitare.
units.tr: For in shameless commentaries, however bold they are, someone may still dare, without loss of decency, in composing grammar, to put speech before word, word before syllable, and syllable before letter; or in arranging geometry, to put solid before surface, surface before line, and line before point. Someone may dare, I say, to attempt or undertake this with a compositive method. This is the shield and spear of Achilles for P. Ramus in attacking Aristotle. Let them wrest it away if they can. But although it would be the height of impudence, it would also be a shame even to gape at it or think against it.

units.la: Quare palmā istā Aristotelis tā gloriosam teneamus, & statuamus, collocādae artis, cum partes ejus omnes invētae & judicatae fuerint, a generalibus ad specialia unicam methodum esse, & fallaciū mendaciumq; interpretum ignorantia calumniaq; vindicemus. Aristotelis interpretes (quos Galenus est secutus) varias & diversas methodos nugatoriis somniis cofinxerunt. Arist. igitur veram doctrinā a scholastica fallaciū & medaciū interpretū inertia tia vindicemus: unicá deniq; Ariftotelea ab uni verfalibus & generalibus ad fingularia fpeciali-aq; methodu Hippocratis, etiá Platonis, quin& etiam Galeni methodum teneamus.
units.tr: Therefore let us hold fast to this so glorious palm of Aristotle, and establish that for arranging an art, once all its parts have been discovered and judged, there is one method, from the general to the special, and let us vindicate it from the ignorance and calumny of the fallacious and lying interpreters. The interpreters of Aristotle, whom Galen followed, have contrived various and diverse methods out of trifling dreams. Let us therefore vindicate Aristotle's true doctrine from the scholastic inertia of fallacious and lying interpreters, and finally hold to the single Aristotelian method, proceeding from universals and generals to singulars and specials, which is also the method of Hippocrates, even of Plato, and indeed of Galen.

units.tr: Chapter XVIII. On the second illustration of method through the examples of poets, orators and historians.

units.tr: But method is employed not only in the matter of arts and disciplines, but in all things which we wish to teach easily and clearly. Therefore poets, orators, and writers of every kind, whenever they set an audience before themselves to teach, want to follow this way, although they do not enter upon it and keep to it in every respect. Virgil in the Georgics distributes his proposed matter into four parts, as I said before. In the first book he pursues common matters, such as astrology and meteorology, and discourses on crops and their cultivation, which was the first part of the work. Then he uses a transition at the beginning of the second book: "Thus far the cultivation of fields and the stars of heaven; now I will sing of you, Bacchus."

units.la: Sic igitur poeta generalissimum primo,subalterna medio, specialissima extremo loco ponere studuit. Sic Ovid. in Fastis, dispositionis hujus gratiā sequitur: proposuit initio summam operis:
units.tr: Thus the poet has sought to place the most general matter first, the subordinate in the middle, and the most specific last. So Ovid in the Fasti follows this order for the sake of arrangement. He set out at the beginning the sum of the work:

units.la: Tempora cũ caussis Latiũ digesta per annũ, Lapsaq; sub terras ortaq; signa canam.
units.tr: "The seasons of Latium arranged through the year with their causes, and the signs that rise and set, I will sing."

units.tr: Soon after, having made an invocation, he sets out the division of the year, first made by Romulus into ten months, which he criticises: "When the founder of the city arranged the seasons in the year, he set the months at five pairs in his year."
