Tum vero expositis Legationis criminibus transitio ad Præturam sequitur: Verum ad illa jam veniamus præclaram Præturam, criminaqueea,quę notiora sunt his,qui adsunt,quānobis,qui meditati ad dicendum paratique venimus. Transitio hæc imperfectior est sine epilogo: tādem principio quartæ orationis,transitio est confimilis ad quartam partem de Prætura Siciliensi: Multa mihi necessario, judices, prætermittenda sunt, ut possim aliquo modo de iis rebus,quæ meę fidei commissa sunt, dicere: recepi enim caussamSiciliæ, ea me ad hoc negotium provincia attraxit.Sic Livius summam septingentorum annorum initio compleƈtitur, tum per decades dividit.
units.tr: Orators, in the exordium, narration, confirmation and peroration, aim at this order, and they call it the order of the art, of nature and of the matter, and sometimes they aim at it with great care. In an accusation, Cicero first proposes and then divides: "You were quaestor, he says, under the consul Gnaeus Papirius fourteen years ago; and from that day to this I call you to judgment for what you have done. No hour will be found free of theft, crime, cruelty and disgrace." This is the proposition and definition of the whole matter; from it, as in a general division of the case, there follows: "These are the years, he says, spent in the quaestorship, the Asiatic legation, the urban praetorship and the Sicilian praetorship. Therefore this will be the fourfold distribution of my whole accusation." He handled these four parts, and the smaller parts of those parts, each in its own order and place, and joined them by transitions; the first three he joined in the third book: "Therefore, he says, now that your quaestorship has been shown, and the theft and crime of your first magistracy have been seen clearly, attend to the rest." Then, when the charges of the legation have been set out, the transition to the praetorship follows: "But now let us come to that famous praetorship, and to those crimes which are better known to those who are present than to us, who have come prepared and ready to speak." This transition is more imperfect, with no epilogue. Finally, at the beginning of the fourth speech, the transition to the fourth part, on the Sicilian praetorship, is much like it: "Many things, judges, must necessarily be passed over by me, so that I can in some way speak of those matters which have been entrusted to my good faith. For I have undertaken the cause of Sicily; that province drew me to this business." So Livy, at the beginning, embraces the sum of seven hundred years, and then divides it by decades.

units.la: Materia autem] Methodus est artiū & doƈtrinarum præcipua illa quidem, sed tamen etiam adhibetur in omnibus omnino variis enuntiatis, homogeneis, suoq; vel syllogismi judicio notis: Deniq; ut enuntiatum enuntiandi, syllogismus cōcludendi quid, quoq; modo enūtiari cō cludive possit: sic methodus, omnis materiæ, quæ quidem methodi ordinis capax fuerit, ordinandæ & concludendæ cōmune instrumentum est: Itaque ad superiorem artium inductionem, & poetæ, & oratores, omnisq; omnino generis scriptores, quanvis in jus non vocati, atta mē sua sponte accurrūt, profitenturq; , quoties docere volūt, nō aliā viā, quām à generalib. sibi propositā fuisse. Exéplis igitur res declaratur.
units.tr: Materia autem] Method is the chief instrument of arts and disciplines, but it is also employed in absolutely all varied and homogeneous statements, which are known by their own judgment and by that of the syllogism. Finally, as the statement states what is to be stated, and the syllogism what can be concluded and in what way, so method is the common instrument for ordering and concluding every matter that is capable of the order of method. Therefore, to the induction of the arts described above, poets, orators and writers of every kind, though not summoned to the law, nevertheless hasten of their own accord, and profess that whenever they wish to teach they follow no other way than the one set before them from the general. The matter is therefore made clear by examples.

units.la: Quanvis non] Amores Socratici hīc valde apparēt: & in poetis atq; oratoribus multi sunt & frequentes lapsus, errorefq; multi: sed tamen cōsensus est unus & idem, á generalibus ad specialia progredi cupientium. Exemplū Virgilii gra d9 methodici hujus ordinis valdé notabiles habet: Astrologiam primo, Meteorologiam secundo, segetum culturam tertio, arborum communem considerationem propriamque de vitibus quarto: deniq; de animalibus quinto: nam primum illud sine cæteris inteligi potest, non contrā: secundum sine primo non potest, potest autem tem sine reliquis & sic deinceps. Methodus igitur genere ipso servata est: tametsi accuratiō in partibus aliquid esse potuit: Astrologia & Meteorologia, proximæ quidem sunt: in plantis, præter arbores vitesq;, aliquid esse potuit: in animalibus ité plenior distributio esse potuit. Has tenus] Trásitio plena, epilogus est primę partis expeditæ de cultura segetem & Astrologia: & propositio est secundæ, de cultu vitium.
units.tr: Quanvis non] Socratic loves appear here very clearly. Among poets and orators there are many frequent slips and many errors, yet there is one and the same agreement among those who wish to proceed from general things to specific ones. Virgil's example has a very notable arrangement of this methodical order: astrology first, meteorology second, the cultivation of crops third, the general consideration of trees and the particular one about vines fourth, and finally animals fifth. The first can be understood without the others, but not the reverse; the second cannot be understood without the first, though the first can be understood without the rest, and so on. Method, then, was observed in its general kind, although the parts could have been arranged more accurately. Astrology and meteorology are indeed close neighbours. Among plants, something more could have been done beyond trees and vines, and among animals a fuller distribution could also have been made. Has tenus] This is a full transition: it is the epilogue of the first part, on the cultivation of crops and astrology, and the proposition of the second, on the cultivation of vines.

units.la: Imperfectior] Transitio imperfecta, est conveniențior, quádo longa partis disputatio nó fuerit, ut memoriæ renovatione minimé sit opus. Te quoq;] Hic propositio tátúm est tertiæ partis, — Quæ cura boum, quis cultus habendo Sit pecori. — epilogus secúdę partis omissus est. Talis est trásitio quarto Georgico: Portinus aerii mellis silvestria dona Fexequar. —
units.tr: Imperfectior] An imperfect transition is more fitting when the discussion of the earlier part has been short, so that there is no need to renew the memory. Te quoq;] Here there is only the proposition of the third part: — What care of oxen, what cultivation there is for keeping the flock — The epilogue of the second part has been omitted. Such is the transition at the start of the fourth Georgic: — I shall now go on to the wild gifts of the airy honey —

units.la: Sic] Ovidius in Fastis, id est in descriptiõe an ni per menses singulos, & singulorum mensiū dies festos, profestos, fastos, nefastos, huius methodi studiū perspicuū demonstravit. Propositio est igitur illa primū, Tempora cū caussis, etc. ac paulo póst etiá pleniús fasti definiút hoc modo: Sacra recognosces annalibus eruta priscis, Et quo sit merito quæq; notanda dies. Invenies illic & festa domestica vobis: Sæpe tibi pater est, sæpe legendus avus. Quæque ferant illi, pictos signantia fastos: Tu quoq; cum Drufo præmia fratre feres.
units.tr: Sic] Ovid in the Fasti, that is, in his description of the year month by month and of the festival days, working days, fasti and nefasti, clearly demonstrated the practice of this method. The proposition, then, is first The seasons with their causes, etc., and a little later the Fasti define it more fully in this way: You will recall the sacred rites drawn from the ancient annals, and why each day is to be marked. You will find there festivals of your own household: often your father, often your grandfather is to be read. And those which the painted calendars mark for those who bear them: you too will receive rewards with your brother Drusus.

units.la: Imploratione] Imploratio gemina Ovidii est: prima præcedit,
units.tr: Imploratione] Ovid's invocation is double: the first comes before,

units.la: Excipe pacato Cæsar Germanice vultu,
units.tr: Receive me, Caesar Germanicus, with a calm countenance,

units.la: Et mox iterum:
units.tr: and soon again:

units.la: Annue conanti per laudes ire tuorum.
units.tr: Grant assent to me as I try to go on through the praises of your family.

units.la: Romulus, primus rex Romanorum, annum distribuerat in menses decem, Marcii, Aprilem, Majum, junii, Quintilem, Sextilem, Septembrem, Octobre, Novembrem, Decembrem: Erroris autem illius excusationem Ovidius affert duplicem, quod mulier decem menses & gerat uterum, & maritum mortuum lugeat: denique (ut ait poeta)
units.tr: Romulus, the first king of the Romans, had divided the year into ten months: March, April, May, June, Quintilis, Sextilis, September, October, November, December. Ovid gives a twofold excuse for that error: that a woman carries a child for ten months, and that a husband, once dead, is mourned; and finally (as the poet says):

units.la: Scilicet arma magis, quam sydera, Romule, noras: Curas finitimos vincere major erat.
units.tr: Clearly, Romulus, you knew arms better than the stars; it was a greater concern to overcome the neighbouring enemies.

units.la: Periphrasis est Romuli, a quo Roma condita fuerat. Bis quinq; phrasis est poetica. Cicero bis quinos dixisset: ut bis bina, septies octonos. Quomodo etiam Virgilius:
units.tr: A periphrasis for Romulus, by whom Rome had been founded. "Twice five" is a poetic phrase. Cicero would have said bis quinos as he said bis bina and septies octonos. So Virgil also:

units.la: Bis quinos silet ille dies.
units.tr: That one is silent on the twice five days.

units.la: Numa, secundus rex Romanorum, justitia & pietate insignis, religionem & ceremonias, sacerdotes, ac pleraque alia instituit: inter quae, Astrologia fuit anni ad Solis cursum accomodati, unde creditus est Pythagorę discipulus: falso tamen, cum Tarquinio regnante, Pythagoras e Samo in Italiā venerit. Numa igitur duos menses addidit anno Romuli, januarium in honore jani: geminiq; jani templum condidit, quod apertum, belli: clausum, pacis insigne esset.
units.tr: Numa, the second king of the Romans, distinguished for justice and piety, established religion and ceremonies, priests, and many other things. Among these was an astronomy of the year adjusted to the course of the sun, whence he was believed to have been a disciple of Pythagoras, though falsely, since Pythagoras came from Samos to Italy in the reign of Tarquin. Numa therefore added two months to the year of Romulus, January in honour of Janus, and built the double temple of Janus, which, open, was the sign of war and, closed, of peace.

units.la: Periphrasis est Februarii: Februum, purgamentum Sabina lingua dicitur: hinc (ut auctor est Festus) februarius mensis dictus est, quod populus februaretur, id est, lustraretur ac purgaretur. Per duodecim enim dies cōtinuos Februarii celebrabatur Februa: hisque diebus, pro impetranda mortuorum animabus quiete, omnis populus piaculis, sacrificiis, circa sepulcra accesis facibus cereisq; intentus erat, hactenus Festus. Ergo nunc poeta per avitas umbras, intelligit Februarium mensem. Differentias] Has differentias Ovidius ita proponit: Nec tamen ignores variorum jura dierum, Non habet officium juppiter omnis idem.
units.tr: A periphrasis for February: Februum is called "purgation" in the Sabine language. Hence (as Festus says) the month was named February because the people were februati, that is, purified and cleansed. For the Februa was celebrated for twelve continuous days in February, and on these days, to obtain rest for the souls of the dead, all the people were busy with expiations and sacrifices around the tombs, with torches and waxen candles lit. So far Festus. Now the poet, through "ancestral shades", means the month of February. Differentias] Ovid sets out these differences thus: Nor should you be ignorant of the laws of the various days: Jupiter does not hold the same office on every day.

units.la: Deinde fastum diem & nefastum ita definit: Ille nefastus erit, per quem tria verba silentur: Fastus erit, per quem lege licebit agi,
units.tr: Then he defines the fasti and nefasti thus: That day will be nefastus on which three words are kept silent; it will be fastus on which it is lawful to transact business by law.

units.la: Verba autem Praetoris erant jus populo reddentis, Do, Dico, Addico: Do, cum dabat potestatem vocandi in jus: Dico, cum sententiam dicebat: Addico, cum rem controversam attribuebat victori. Deinde poeta dies intercisos definit, qui mane essent nefasti, a meridie fasti: Nec toto perstare die sua jura putaris: Qui jam fastus erit, mane nefastus erat.
units.tr: The words of the praetor, by which he rendered justice to the people, were Do, Dico, Addico: Do when he gave the power of summoning to court; Dico when he pronounced judgment; Addico when he assigned the disputed thing to the victor. Then the poet defines divided days, which were nefasti in the morning and fasti from midday: Do not think your rights hold for the whole day: what is now fastus was nefastus in the morning.

units.la: Comitialis] Dies comitialis, quo die populi conventus & comitia habebantur. nundinalis, cum tribus rusticis, dies octo rusticu opus fecissent, nono die cessarent, Romamq; ad mercatum & audiendas leges convenirent. Calendarum] Calendae, primus est dies cujusq; mensis: numeratur autem in mense antecedente. Nonarum] Nonae sunt in Martio, Majo, junio, Octobri, dies a Calendis sex proximi: in reliquis, sunt tantum quatuor. Nonae dictae, tanqua novae praeter initium observatae lunae.
units.tr: Comitialis] A comitial day is one on which assemblies of the people and the comitia were held. A market day (nundinalis) was when the country tribesmen, having done eight days' work, rested on the ninth and came to Rome for the market and to hear the laws. Calendarum] The Calends are the first day of each month; it is counted in the preceding month. Nonarum] The Nones fall in March, May, June and October on the sixth day before the Calends; in the other months they are only four days before. The Nones were so named as if they were new, observed after the beginning of the moon.

units.la: Iduum] Idus, dicuntur illi dies, qui in singulis mensibus nonas sequùtur. Iduare, est dividere, Hetrusca lingua: hinc Idus, tàquam d visiones, quia dividunt nonas à calèdis. Atri] Dies ater, religiosus, infaustus, quo Respub. malè & infeliciter gesta esset. Atri verò dies omnes Romanis erant postridie Calèdas, Nonas, Idus: Ideoque Ovidio dies ille proximus appellatur, ab aliis postriduanus. has autem quatuor differètias ultimas Ovidius ita complexus est: vendicat Æusonius junonis cara calèdas: Idibus alba jovi grandior agna cadit. Nonarum tutela deo caret omnibus istis: Ne fallare, cave: proximus ater erit.
units.tr: Iduum] The Ides are those days which follow the Nones in each month. To "idue" means to divide, in the Etruscan language; hence the Ides are so called as if they were divisions, because they divide the Nones from the Calends. Atri] A black day is a religious and unlucky day, on which the Republic had been conducted badly and unhappily. For the Romans, all black days were the day after the Calends, the Nones and the Ides; so for Ovid the nearest day is called "black", and by others "postridian". Ovid embraced these last four differences thus: Aeson's Juno claims the Calends as dear to her; the white lamb falls to Jove on the Ides. The Nones lack the protection of any god among all these: beware of being deceived; the day nearest them will be black.

units.la: A generalibus] Hæc (inquit) hęrètia tòtis fastis, id est communia generaliaq;, semel dicta erunt. Lex enim est toties cantata, Generalia generali ter & semel dicenda esse: & illud est ordinis methodici beneficiū singulare, quòd suo quidq; loco positum semel dicitur. Seriem] Hìc poeta videtur Aristotelis ἀπόδειξιν, vel ἀπαγωγὴν significare, nisi à generalib. ad specialia procedatur, ordi-nis confusionem & tautologiam futuram: Itaq; ut recèus esset ordo, generalia communiaq; præposuit. Ergo videmus in hoc etiá poeta, methodici ordinis amores: sed amores Socraticos per multis enim locis effugiunt. Sed tamè ad P. Rami inductionem, testimonium poetarum hoc erit, methodum à generalib. affectàtium. Oratores] Indu&ti sunt primo inquisitionis loco artifices & doctores artiū, secundo poetæ, tertio tàdem & oratores ad eandem fidem testes adducùtur: Oratores enim Græci pariter & Latini, methodicũ quendam ordiné in partib.ordinis sequuntur, cũm jubeant primo loco esse proœmium, secundo narratione, tertio confirmatione, quarto perorationé: hæc enim primi, secundi, tertii, quarti loci collocatio, methodica forma est: de quibus tamen partib. Aristoteles primam & ultimam non necessarias ait esse. Quicquid tamen fit, sive partes illæ quatuor adhibeátur, siue duę tátùm: quoties orator perspicuè docere velit, súma quędá caufę pręponitur: partes, si multiplex ea fit, deinde diuidúdur, ac dein ceps explicantur. De ordine verò partiũ orationis, quæ præcipiuntur ab oratoribus, varia sunt & incerta: Tullius Oratorio secũdo collocationem duplicem facit: Altera est (ait) quam affert natura causarum: altera, quæ oratorum judicio & prudentia cõparatur. Nam ut aliquid ante rē dicamus, deinde ut rē exponamus, pòst ut eam probemus, nostris præsidiis confirmandis, contrariis refutandis: deinde ut concludamus, atq; ita peroremus: hoc dicendi genus, natura ipsa præscribit. Ut verò statuamus ea, quæ probádi, docendi, persuadendi caussa dicenda sunt. quèadmodum cõponamus, id est vel maximè proprium oratoris prudentiæ. Hæc Tullius de duplici methodo, altera naturæ & artis altera judicii & prudentiæ. At methodus hæc altera prudentiæ, κρύψις quædam est methodi, nó methodus, ut postea dicetur. In Partitionibus, varias ordinis species ad varias quęstiones Tullius ac commodavit: In demonstrativo genere, aut réporũ servantur gradus (ait) aut generum distributiones, aut á minorib. ad majora afcēdimus, aut á majorib. ad minora dilabimur, aut hęcinę quabili varietate distinguim⁹, cūm parva quędam magnis, simplicia cōjunctis, obscura dilucidis, læta tristibus, incredibilia ṗbabilibus inteximus: quæ in exornationem cadunt omnia. Hæc methodorū varietas feré est Galeni: at tēporum gradus, & generum distributiones, in unam veram methodum cadunt: quia generalia etiam speciatim distributa, tempore quoq; priora sunt: & quæcunq; tēpore priora sunt, modo sint homogenea, sunt etiam magis generalia & communia: ut raptus Helenæ ad interitum Hectoris: quia illud, hujus est caussa communis, & aliorum malorum, quę tota Iliade continentur. Ascensus autem á minoribus ad majora, & descēsus á majoribus ad minora, videtur viam Galeni & reditionē anté disputatas significare, aut certē comparationem, quam Galenus complexus est: de quo satis antea dictum est. Inæqualis autē varietas, potest delectationis ordine quendam docere, de quo mox in ἀφύψα methodi dicetur. Addit eodem loco Tullius, ordinem in consiliis necessarium feré partium esse: in accusando, rerum ordinem, contrarium in defendendo. Hæc varietas methodorum est in Cicerone, nō ad docendū tantūm: illic enim unicum naturæ & artis, rerūque ipsarum ordinem profitetur: sed ad delectandū & movendum, id est ad sallendūauditorem. Quintilianus autem dispositionis doctrinam nullā in omnes materias certam tradi posse docuit: eandem multitudinem methodorum, quam á Cicerone didicerat, toto septimo libro ppofuit: de quib. rhetoricæ Scholæ P. Rami. Accusatione unum Ciceronis exemplum materiæ apud oratorem maximé proponitur. Actio autem Verrina illa duplex fuit: quá utramq; antecesserant divinatio & oratio secunda. Actio prima tota in testium interrogatione fuit: itaque scripta non est: Secundæ actionis superfunt libri quinque: Initio autem tertii libri, qui primus est actionis secundæ, hæc propositio partitioque adhibetur.
units.tr: A generalibus] He says: these things, which are common and general to all the fasti, will be said once. For the rule is so often repeated: general things are to be said once, and not three times or more; and this is the singular benefit of methodical order, that each thing, placed in its proper place, is said once. Seriem] Here the poet seems to mean Aristotle's demonstration [ἀπόδειξιν] or induction [ἀπαγωγὴν]: unless one proceeds from general to special things, there would be confusion of order and tautology. So, that the order might be more correct, he placed general and common things first. Thus we see in this poet too the loves of method, but Socratic loves, since in many places they escape. Yet for P. Ramus' induction the testimony of the poets will serve as evidence of method that proceeds from general things. Oratores] Witnesses are brought forward for the same point, in the order of inquiry: first the artists and teachers of the arts, second the poets, and third the orators. For Greek and Latin orators alike follow a certain methodical order in the parts of an oration, since they require that there be first a proem, second a narration, third a confirmation, fourth a peroration. This placement in first, second, third and fourth position is a methodical form, although Aristotle says that of these parts the first and last are not necessary. Whatever happens, whether those four parts or only two are used, whenever the orator wishes to teach clearly, a summary of the cause is set out first; the parts, if the cause is complex, are then divided and afterwards explained in turn. Concerning the order of the parts of a speech, which orators prescribe, opinions vary and are uncertain. Tully, in the second book of the Orator, makes a double arrangement: one which the nature of the case supplies, and another which is acquired by the judgment and prudence of the orator. For that we say something before the matter, then set out the matter, then prove it, strengthening our own arguments and refuting the opposing ones, then conclude and so sum up: nature itself prescribes this kind of speaking. But how we arrange what is to be said for the sake of proving, teaching and persuading, that is especially the proper prudence of the orator. So Tully on the double method, one of nature and art, the other of judgment and prudence. But this second method of prudence is a certain concealment of method, not a method, as will be said later. In the Partitions, Tully adapted various kinds of order to various questions: in the demonstrative genus, he says, either the degrees of things are observed, or the distributions of kinds, or we ascend from smaller to greater, or descend from greater to smaller, or we distinguish these by a certain variety, when we weave small things among great, simple among joined, obscure among clear, cheerful among sad, incredible among probable, all of which serve ornament. This variety of methods is almost Galen's. But the degrees of time and the distributions of kinds fall under one true method, because general things, when distributed into their species, are also prior in time; and whatever is prior in time is, provided it is of the same kind, also more general and common: as the rape of Helen is prior to the death of Hector, because the former is the common cause of this and of the other evils contained in the whole Iliad. The ascent from smaller to greater and the descent from greater to smaller seem to signify Galen's way and return, discussed earlier, or at least the comparison which Galen embraced, about which enough was said before. An unequal variety can teach a certain order of delight, of which more will be said soon in the discussion of the [ἀφύψα] of method. Tully adds in the same place that the order in deliberative speeches is almost wholly determined by the parts: in accusing, the order of things; in defending, the contrary. This variety of methods is found in Cicero, not for teaching alone: there he professes one order of nature and art and of the things themselves, but for delighting and moving, that is, for beguiling the hearer. Quintilian, however, taught that no fixed doctrine of arrangement can be handed down for all subjects, and in the whole seventh book he set out the same multitude of methods which he had learned from Cicero. Concerning these, the rhetorical schools (of P. Ramus) ... Accusatione] One example from Cicero's matter is set before the orator above all in the accusation. The Verrine action was double, preceded by both the Divinatio and the second speech. The first action consisted entirely in the questioning of witnesses, and so it was not written down. Five books of the second action survive; at the beginning of the third book, which is the first of the second action, this proposition and partition is used.

units.la: Quas partes] Partitio, genera magistratuum spectauit, non criminum: Tertia itaq; Verrina, crimina Quæsturæ, Legationis Asiaticæ, Præturæ urbanæ comprehenduntur: totaq; triu partiutransitio duplex est: quatuor reliquis Verrinis, explicata est Siciliensis Prætura: quarta Verrina est de jurisdictione, quinta de frumento, sexta de signis, septima de suppliciis. Quáobre Ciceronis actio, quinque libris perpetuis perorata, methodu á generalibus ad speciala sibi propofuit. Ergo oratorium etiam testimonium est.
units.tr: Which parts: the partition looked to the kinds of magistracies, not to the crimes. Accordingly the third Verrine oration embraces the crimes of his quaestorship, of his legation to Asia, and of his urban praetorship. The whole transition between the two parts is double. In the remaining Verrine orations the praetorship of Sicily is set out: the fourth is on jurisdiction, the fifth on grain, the sixth on statues, and the seventh on punishments. So Cicero's speech, concluded in five continuous books, proposed to itself a method moving from general to special matters. Therefore this too is oratorical testimony.

units.la: Livius] Postremi testes inquisitionis sunt historici: historia enim, etsi res disipatas & plerumque valde disimiles sequatur, attamen gradus tempora feré sequitur, & proponit aliquando summam propositumq; partitur: Sic Livius supra septingentorum annorum historiam proponit: deinceps, etsi non nominatim, attamen reipsa per decades, per singulos annos opus universum distribuit. Florus historiá eandem breviter proposuit, & in quatuor ætates distribuit,
units.tr: Livy: The last witnesses of the inquiry are the historians. For history, although it follows scattered events, which are often very dissimilar, nevertheless generally follows the order of time, and sometimes sets out a summary and divides up its subject. Thus Livy sets out a history of more than seven hundred years; then, although not by name, yet in fact, he distributes the whole work by decades and by individual years. Florus set out the same history briefly and divided it into four ages,

units.la: N aper-
units.tr: ... more clearly,

units.la: apertiore logici ordinis studio. Quamobrè etiam hic P. Ramus anquisitionis inductionem concludebat, poetas & oratores historicos in poematis & orationibus methodum a generalibus ad specialia studiose consectari.
units.tr: with a more evident concern for logical order. Hence P. Ramus also concluded the induction of the inquiry here, that poets and orators, in their poems and speeches, and historians, eagerly pursue a method from general to special matters.

units.la: Cap. XIX. De Crypticis Methodi.
units.tr: Chap. XIX. On the Cryptic Methods.

units.la: HAec igitur in variis enuntiatis homogeneis,suoque vel syllogismi judicio notis methodus erit, quoties perspicuè res docēda erit. At cùm dele statione motúve aliquo majore in parte aliqua fallendus erit auditor,homogenea quædam rejicientur, ut definitionum, partitionum, transitionumque lumina: quædam pro his assumētur heterogenea, velut digressiones à re, & in re commorationes: sed præcipuè rerū ordo initió invertetur, antecedentiaque nonnulla consequentibus postponentur. Itaq; ad illā perfectę methodi regulā, hæc alicubi imperfectior forma, nō solúm detractis rebus mutila est, vel superadditis redūdat, sed ordinis sui quibusdā gradibus inversis præpostera est. Quod poeta facit majore quadam artificii specie, dum populum ducendū sibi proponit, id est, belluam multorū captum: ideoq; variis modis decipit: incipit á medio, ibique primum sæpe comprehendit, postremû deniq; incerto aliquo & inopinato casu cõcludit. Sic (ut Horatius ait) Homerʾ Iliada disposuit: Nec gemino bellû Trojanû orditur ab ovo: Semper ad eventû festinat, & in medias res, Non secús ac notas, auditorem rapit: & quæ Desperat tractata nitescere posse, relinquit: Atque ita mentitur, sic veris falsa remiscet, Primo ne medium, medio ne discrepet imum.
units.tr: These, then, will be the method in the various homogeneous statements, marked by their own judgement or that of the syllogism, whenever a matter must be taught clearly. But when the hearer must be deceived by some greater shift of position or movement in some part, certain homogeneous elements are rejected, such as the lights of definitions, partitions and transitions; in their place certain heterogeneous elements are taken, such as digressions from the subject and lingering within it. But above all the order of things is first inverted, and some preceding matters are placed after the following ones. So this less perfect form, departing from the rule of the perfect method, is not only mutilated by things removed or redundant by things added, but is also reversed by the inversion of some of the steps of its order. A poet does this with a certain greater appearance of art, when he sets out to lead the people, that is, the beast of many heads, and so deceives them in various ways: he begins in the middle, there often seizes first on what comes there, and at last concludes with some uncertain and unexpected turn. Thus (as Horace says) Homer arranged his Iliad: "Nor does he begin the Trojan war from its twin egg; he always hastens to the outcome and seizes the hearer in the middle of things, as if they were known; and what he despairs of making shine when handled, he leaves out. And so he lies, and mixes false things with true, so that the middle does not clash with the beginning, nor the end with the middle."

units.la: Sic Virgilius Aeneam á Sicilia excepit, & in cõvivio Carthaginis, præterita narrante fecit: postrema variis perturbata casib. induxit. Sic comici poetę, tametsi magno cõsilio judicioque, comœdias per actus, scenas, officia personarum distinguunt: efficiunt tamẽ, ut omnia fortuita & inopinata videantur. Oratores veró in civilibus caussis ad victoriâ omnia referunt. Itaque non tam docẽdi, quám permovendi gratiá, firmissimum quodq; primum ab iis collocatur: dum tamen ea quæ æquè excellent, servent-tur etiâ ad extremum, & Homerica dispositione, mediocria in mediâ turbam atque in gregem conferantur.
units.tr: So Virgil took up Aeneas from Sicily, and made him narrate past events at the banquet in Carthage; he brought in the final events disturbed by various misfortunes. So the comic poets, although they distinguish their comedies by acts, scenes and the roles of the characters with great deliberation and judgement, nevertheless make everything seem accidental and unexpected. But orators, in civil cases, refer everything to victory. Therefore the strongest point is placed first, not so much for teaching as for moving the hearer; yet what is equally excellent is kept even to the end, and, in the Homeric arrangement, middling points are gathered into the middle, into the crowd and the herd.

units.la: Hæc igitur] Epilogus est methodicę regulę ha stenus ētenus expositæ: cui additur admonitio κρύψεως, occultationis methodicę cujusdam in poetis & oratoribus, id est imperfectæ methodi, quę non tam ad docendum, quam delectandum, vel movendum pertineat. Itaq; hic proprie methodus & ordo non est, sed methodi atque ordinis quędam perversio: quæ tamen vix tanta esse potsit ut vel poema, vel oratio tota á speciálibus ad generalia fursū versus progrediatur: sed initio hysterologiam aliquam habet, ut intelligetur. Est autem κρύψις methodica in ellipsi & redūdantia partium, vel in earum ordine perversō: tametsi enim methodica κρύψις proprie opponitur ordini: attamen cūm hic universi corporis forma spectetur, tunc trunca fit necesse est: ut redundantes supervacuæ: quale utrunq; est in syllogismo. ut enim enthymema syllogismo detraxit, profyllogismus addidit, ordoq; trium partium sæpe per versus est: ita nūc ista κρύψις ἀμέθοδον, legitimę imperfectæq; methodo detrahit quædam necessaria, instar enthymematis: quædam non necessaria adjungit, instar profyllogismi: hysterologiá quarundam partiū principio præsertim efficit. P. Ramus, quę generaliter præcipi poterant, breviter hic admonuit. Primū ad enthymema methodi, detrahantur (ubi periculum fuerit) lumina propositionis, partitionis, transitionis: Nam » est nonnunquam (ait Quintilianus libri quarti » capite quinto) dura propositio: quam judex fi ³⁰ præ videt, non aliter reformidat, quám qui ferrum medici, priusquám curetur, aspexit, at si re » non ante propositā, securum ac nulla denuntiatione tione in se coverfum intrarit oratio, efficiet qdf promittenti non crederetur: interim refugienda non modo distinctio quaestionum est, sed omnino tractatio. Affectibus perturbadus, & ab intentione auferendus auditor: Non enim solum est oratoris docere: sed plus eloquentia circa movendum valet: Cui contraria est maxime tenuis illa & scrupulosa in partes sectae divisionis diligentia, eo tempore, quo cognoscenti judicium conamur auferre. Haec Quintilianus de enthymematica ellipsi methodicarum partium: unde intelligimus, cur illa detrahenda intelligentiae lumina, ad eum perturbandum, qui docendus alioqui fuerat. Ac quod Quintilianus ait, non modo partitionem, sed etiam partium tra ͥtationem interdum praetereundam esse, Ciceronis est documentum Oratorio secundo, de partibus quidem rebus; dispositis, sed unde dispositionis species immutatur. Mea aute ratio (ait Antonius) in dicendo haec esse solet, ubi boni quod habeat, id ampleͤtar, exorne, exaggerem, ibi commorer, ibi habitem, ibi haeream: a malo autem vitio; caussae ita recedam, non ut id me de fugere appareat, sed ut toto bono illo exornando & augendo dissimulatum obruatur. Ac pauͤ lo post: Duo (inquit) mihi fumo: unum, ut moſto aut difficili argumento aut loco nonnunquam omnino nihil respondeam: confiteor; me, si quae premat res vehementius, ita concedere solere, ut non modo non abjecto, sed ne rejecto quidem scuto fugere videar: sed adhibere quandam in dicendo speciem atq; pompam, & pugne
units.tr: Hæc igitur] This is the epilogue to the method's rules explained so far. To it is added a warning about κρύψις, a certain methodical concealment found in poets and orators, that is, an imperfect method, which serves less to teach than to delight or move. So strictly speaking there is no method or order here, but a certain perversion of method and order. Yet this could hardly be so great that a whole poem or speech proceeds upward from particulars to generals; rather it has some hysterology at the beginning, as will be understood. The methodical κρύψις consists in ellipsis and redundancy of parts, or in their inverted order. For although methodical κρύψις is properly opposed to order, nevertheless, since here the form of the whole body is in view, it must be truncated, and the redundant parts superfluous. Each of these occurs in the syllogism. For as the enthymeme removes a part from the syllogism and the prosyllogism adds one, and the order of the three parts is often reversed, so this κρύψις, being ἀμέθοδον, removes from the legitimate and complete method certain necessary parts, in the manner of an enthymeme, and adds certain unnecessary parts, in the manner of a prosyllogism, and above all brings about a hysterology in the beginning of some parts. Ramus briefly warned about what could be laid down in general terms. First, where there is danger, the lights of the proposition, partition and transition should be removed from the methodical enthymeme. For, as Quintilian says in the fifth chapter of Book Four, "a proposition is sometimes harsh; when the judge sees it beforehand, he shrinks from it no differently than one who has looked at the surgeon's knife before he is treated. But if the speech enters without the matter having been announced beforehand, and turns the hearer on himself, unwarned and unsuspecting, it will achieve what would not have been believed had it been promised." Meanwhile, not only the division of questions but the whole treatment of them must be avoided, and the hearer must be stirred by the emotions and drawn away from his attention. For it is not the orator's only task to teach; eloquence has more power in moving. The opposite of this is that thin and scrupulous diligence in dividing things into parts, which is most harmful at the very moment when we try to take the judgment away from one who knows. These are Quintilian's words on the enthymematic ellipsis of methodical parts. From them we understand why those lights of understanding should be removed, so as to disturb the one who otherwise ought to be taught. And as for what Quintilian says, that not only the partition but sometimes the very treatment of the parts is to be passed over, this is the teaching of Cicero in the second book of the Orator, on the disposition of things. There the species of disposition is changed: "My method in speaking," says Antonius, "is usually this: where there is something good, I amplify it, adorn it, exaggerate it, there I linger, there I dwell, there I cling; but from a bad point I withdraw from the case in such a way that it does not appear that I am fleeing, but that the bad is overwhelmed and hidden by the whole adorning and enlarging of the good." And a little later: "There are two things," he says, "I observe. One is that with a dangerous or difficult argument, or at some point, I sometimes answer nothing at all; I confess that when a matter presses on me too hard I am accustomed to yield in such a way that I seem not to flee with my shield cast away or even rejected, but to bring in a certain show and pomp in speaking, a flight like that of a fighter who is not escaping the enemy but yielding as if to seize a position. The other is what I think the orator must most guard against and foresee, and what usually troubles me most: I do not labour so much to help my cause as to avoid harming it; not that effort should not be made in both, but it is far more shameful for an orator to seem to have harmed his cause than not to have helped it." These are Tully's words, before Quintilian. Therefore Ramus rightly taught that the lights of things are to be removed, when the things themselves are to be passed over altogether. This, however, must be understood of some part of the proposed case, or of some principal argument, not of the whole and entire case. For if the whole case is passed over, there will be no form of the omitted matter. The whole case can indeed be omitted, as in that kind of defence by Scipio in Livy, Book 48: when ordered to plead his case before the Senate and the Rostra, without any mention of the charges, he began with a speech so magnificent about his own deeds that it was clear no one had ever been praised more fully or more truly. For they were spoken with the same spirit and talent by which they had been done, and there was no weariness of the ears, because they were not referred to the danger but to glory. A similar defence was made before the people; nothing was answered to the charges, but they went up to the Capitol and to all the shrines of the city. Therefore what Ramus says is passed over is not of such a kind as to contain the whole case: for in Scipio's speech the method could have been complete; but it concerns some part, as will soon appear. Finally, the elliptical κρύψις of method is related to method as the enthymeme is to the syllogism: just as in the syllogism either the proposition, the assumption or the conclusion is omitted, so here either the definition, the partition or the transition is passed over. And just as the syllogistic enthymeme omits some syllogistic part, not all, so this methodical enthymeme omits some methodical part, not all of them. And the ellipsis of this kind is like an enthymeme. Redundancy, on the other hand, is twofold, ἐνσροχίνεια and περισσολογία. And this whole difference is from true and absolute method. In ellipsis and redundancy, proposition, partition and transition are of especial praise in the one case, and in the other would be faults if continued; digression and delay would there be sophistical and blameworthy, here they occupy the chief place of virtue. Thus, with the hearer's disposition changed, as with his stomach, the same things are at one time wholesome and at another poisonous. Yet an inversion of the whole order can never occur in method, so that one proceeds upward from particulars to generals; it is rather an inversion of some part. This inversion is more frequent in the parts of the syllogism, but because the parts are few, it is less noticed. In method, however, with very many parts, among which the light depends on their order, confusion is far more conspicuous and produces a much greater confusion of judgment. In poets and orators the matter is different, and so it will be set out in its own place.

units.la: Marginal numbers 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 mark every fifth line of the column. » pugnæ similé fugá: cósistere vero in meo præsidio, sicut non fugiendi hostis, sed capiédi loci causâ cessisse videar. Alterum est illud, quod ego oratori maximé cavendum & providendū puto, quódqꝫ me solicitare summé solet: Nō tam ut prosim caussis, elaborare soleo, quàm ut ne quid obsim, non quin enitendum fit in utroque, sed tamē multo est turpius oratori nocuisse videri caussæ, quàm non profuisse. Hæc Tullius ante Quintilianū. Quapropter recté P. Ramus docuit, lumina rerum tollenda, cúm etiam res ipsæ præterēundæ sint omnino: quod tamē de parte aliqua caussæ propositæ, aut de præcipuo aliquo argumento, non de tota & universa caussa est intelligendū. Nam si tota caussa prætereatur, forma pteritę materiæ nulla erit: Tota quidem caussa potest omitti. quale Scipionis illud apud Liviū lib. 48. defensionis genus est: In curia & rostris jussus dicere caussā, sine ulla criminum mētione, oratione adeó magnificam de rebus ab se gestis est exorsus, ut satis constaret neminem unquam neqꝫ meliùs, neqꝫ veriùs laudatum esse: Dicebantur enim ab eodē animo ingenioqꝫ, á quo gesta erant: & aurium fastidium aberat, quia pro periculo non ad gloriam referebantur. Consimilis defensio in concione fuit, neqꝫ criminibus quicquam est responsum, sed inde itum est in Capitolium, & ad omnia urbis pulvinaria. Quare quę prætériri dicuntur á P. Ramo, non sunt ejusmodi, ut totā caussā cōtineant: Potuit enim in Scipionis disputatione methodus integra esse: sed de parte aliqua, ut inox mox apparebit. κρύψs deniq; elliptica methodi erit, velut enthymema est syllogismi: utque illic propositio, vel assumptio, vel coplexio: ita hic definitio, vel partitio, vel transitio prætermittitur: deniq; ut enthymema syllogisticū, est omissio partis cujusdam syllogisticæ, non omnium: sic hoc velut enthymema methodicū, est omissio partis cujusdam methodicæ, non universarū. Atq; ellipsis velut enthymematica ea est. Redundantia autē opposita est duplex, ἐνσροχίνεια, & περισσολογία. Atque hæc tota differentia est à vera & absoluta methodo. In ellipsi & redundantia, propositio, partitio, transitio, illic præcipuæ laudis sunt, hic continuatæ essent vitiosæ: digressio commoratioq; sophisticæ illic essent & vituperandæ: hic precipuum virtutis locum oc cupaverút. sic mutato auditoris ingenio, tanq; stomacho, eadē modó salubria sunt, modó sunt venenata. Ordinis tamen totius inversio in methodo nunquam omnino esse potest, ut sursum versus à specialibus ad generalia procedatur, sed partis alicujus quædam est inversio. Hæc in syllogismi partibus inversio frequentior: sed quia partes sunt paucæ, id minús attenditur: at in methodo partium plurimarum, quarum inter se lumē pendet ex ordine, cófusio longé notabilior est judiciiq; confusione multó majorem efficit. Res in poetis & oratoribus diversa est: itaq; spe ciatim illic exponetur.
units.tr: Marginal numbers 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 mark every fifth line of the column. ...to appear to have fled like a beaten enemy; but to stand firm in my own defence, as if I had given ground not to escape the enemy but to seize the position. The other point is the one I think an orator must guard against and provide for above all, and which most often troubles me: I usually labour not so much to help my causes as to avoid harming them. Not that one should not strive in both respects, but it is far more disgraceful for an orator to seem to have harmed his cause than to have failed to help it. These are Tully's words, before Quintilian. Therefore Peter Ramus rightly taught that the lights of things are to be removed, since the things themselves are sometimes to be passed over altogether. This, however, must be understood of some part of the proposed case, or of some principal argument, not of the whole and entire case. For if the whole case is passed over, there will be no form of the matter left. The whole case can indeed be omitted, as in that kind of defence of Scipio's in Livy, book 48: ordered to speak his case in the senate-house and on the Rostra, without any mention of the charges, he began with a speech so magnificent about his deeds that it was plain no one had ever been praised either better or more truly. For they were spoken with the same spirit and genius by which they had been done, and there was no weariness of the ears, because they were not referred to the danger but to glory. A similar defence was made before the assembly: nothing was answered to the charges, but the people went up to the Capitol and to all the altars of the city. So the things that Ramus says are passed over are not of such a kind as to comprise the whole case: the method in Scipio's speech could have been complete, but the omission concerns some part, as will soon appear. krypsis [κρύψις], finally, will be the elliptical form of method, just as the enthymeme is of the syllogism: as there the premise, or the assumption, or the conclusion is left out, so here the definition, or the partition, or the transition is omitted. Finally, just as an enthymematic syllogism is the omission of a certain part of the syllogism, not of all of it, so this is like a methodical enthymeme, the omission of a certain part of the method, not of all of it. And ellipsis of this kind is, as it were, enthymematic. Redundancy, however, is opposed to it in two forms: ensorochineia [ἐνσροχίνεια] and perissologia [περισσολογία]. And this is the whole difference from true and complete method. In ellipsis and redundancy, the proposition, partition and transition are of especial praise in the former case, while in the latter they would be faulty if continued; digression and amplification would be sophistical and blameworthy in the former, but in the latter they occupy the chief place of virtue. Thus, with the hearer's mind changed, as it were his stomach, the same things are at one time wholesome and at another poisonous. Yet an inversion of the whole order can never occur in method, so that one proceeds upwards from the particulars to the generals; it is rather a certain inversion of some part. Such inversion is more frequent in the parts of a syllogism, but because the parts are few, it is less noticed; but in method, where there are very many parts, whose light depends on their order, confusion is far more conspicuous and produces much greater confusion of judgement. In poets and orators the matter is different, and so it will be set out there, case by case.

units.la: Belluam multorum capitum]Horatianum est illud primo Epistol. de populo: (quem Bellua multorum es capitum: nam quid sequar, aut
units.tr: The beast of many heads: This is the Horatian line in the first Epistle, on the people, where he says: "You are a beast of many heads, for what shall I follow, or..."

units.la: Incipit ]Κρύπτινα sunt Aristotelis trib. locis,2o. cap.2.Prior.1.cap.8. Top.14.cap.2.Elenc.de quibus antea jam in syllogismo.Methodicæ autem ἀρχῆς duo genera P. Ramus pposuit, poeticū & oratoriū. Proprium autem poeticę ἀρχῆς illud videatur,á medio incipere,tum per occasionem aliquam præterita narrare,deniq; notabili aliquo casu cõcludere: qd in arte poetica multo etiā clariùs & accuratiùs ab Aristotele est ex positum. Sed hæc ordinis perversio non admo‐ dum magna est: Homerica enim hysterologia, itemq; Virgiliana secundo libro terminatur:cætera directam methodum habent: nec omnino poeta á medio unquam sic incipit, quin propo‐ nat antea generale quippiá: Sic enim Homerus:
units.tr: Incipit: The cryptic [κρύπτινα] things are in three places of Aristotle: Prior Analytics 2.2, Prior Analytics 1.8, Topics 1.14, and Sophistical Refutations 2, which were discussed earlier under the syllogism. P. Ramus proposed two kinds of methodical beginning, the poetic and the oratorical. The distinctive mark of the poetic beginning seems to be starting from the middle, then relating past events as occasion arises, and finally concluding with some striking event. Aristotle explains this in the Poetics much more clearly and accurately. But this reversal of order is not very great. Homer's Iliad is a case of hysterology, and Virgil's second book ends this way too, while the rest keep the direct method. Nor does a poet ever begin from the middle without first proposing something general. Thus Homer:

units.la: Μῆνιν ἄειδε θεὰ Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος.
units.tr: Μῆνιν ἄειδε θεὰ Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος. [Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles, son of Peleus.]

units.la: Iram pande dea Pelidæ Achillis.
units.tr: Unfold the wrath, goddess, of Achilles son of Peleus.

units.la: Item Virgilius:
units.tr: Likewise Virgil:

units.la: Arma virumq; cano, Troiæ qui primus ab oris, Italiam fato profugus Lavinaq; venit Littora.
units.tr: I sing of arms and the man, who first came from the shores of Troy, a fugitive by fate, to Italy and the Lavinian shores.

units.la: Generalis quædā est propositio: Itaq; poeta caput summo loco statuit,mébra media medio, pedes infimo loco retinet, & á generalib.ad specialia progreditur:sed in proximis quædá confusio, quód consequentia quędam præponātur. Homerus igitur propter ordinis hujus inversio nem talé,dicitur ab Aristotele θεῖος divinus, præ cęteris poetis,quia bellum Trojanū aggressus,cóstans & principio,& medio & fine,nó totum complexus fit,sed amputarit prima,quędá & extrema: tantumq; illustria, assumptis etiam externis,retinuerit.Iliadis artificium hoc ὑφυντὶ κὸι Horatius in arte poetica interpretatur.
units.tr: There is a general proposition here. So the poet sets the head in the highest place, the middle parts in the middle, and the feet in the lowest place, and he advances from general to specific. But in the opening lines there is some confusion, since certain consequences are placed before the principles. For this reversal of order, Aristotle calls Homer divine above all other poets. Homer undertook the Trojan war, but he did not embrace all of it, with its beginning, middle and end. He cut off some of the first and last parts and kept only the most striking things, adding outside material where needed. Horace, in the Art of Poetry, explains this craft of the Iliad as "weaving the middle."

units.la: Ovo] Fingunt poetæ cõcubitu jovis & Ledæ natum esse geminū ovum Pollucis & Helenæ: quæ rapta,materies belli Trojani fuit. Ergo Homerus interprete Horatio, Iliadem non repetivit ab ultima belli origine,id est ortu Helenæ.
units.tr: Ab ovo: The poets feign that from the union of Jupiter and Leda twin eggs were born, of Pollux and Helen. Helen, when she was seized, became the matter of the Trojan war. So Homer, by Horace's interpretation, did not begin the Iliad from the very origin of the war, that is, from the birth of Helen.

units.la: In medias] Aristotelicū est illud, á medio incipere: & medię res intelligendę sunt, quę tempore sunt mediæ inter primâ originė & fine ultimū. Ac notas] Et hoc item logicū est, á medio incipere, tanquam á notissimo, ut antecedētium luce nil opus sit. Incipitur autē Ilias á precibus Chrysę sacerdotis: & secundo libro in catalogo naviū,præterita cöprehendūtur: duo deinceps & viginti libri,gradib.tēporum ordinē rectū sequūtur. Nitescere] Sic Aristoteles in poetica: Si Homerus totū cõplectéretur,id esset nimis magnum, ἡ ἐπ συνωυπηθεν, neq; satis illustre: Nunc autem cūm una parte assumpta, episodiis ipsorū multis est usus,ut navium catalogo, & aliis episodiis,quibus poesin distinguit. Episodiū Aristoteli, est adventitium acroama jucundumq; á verbo ἐπάσωμι,ingredior.
units.tr: In medias: It is Aristotelian to begin from the middle, and "middle things" must be understood as those that lie in time between the first origin and the final end. Ac notas: This too is logical, to begin from the middle, as from what is most known, so that nothing is needed from the light of what comes before. The Iliad begins with the prayers of Chryses the priest, and in the second book the past is gathered up in the catalogue of ships. The twenty-two books that follow keep the true order of time by steps. Nitescere: So Aristotle says in the Poetics: if Homer had embraced everything, it would have been too large, and not clear enough. But as it is, he took one part and made use of many episodes, such as the catalogue of ships and other episodes, by which he gives variety to the poem. For Aristotle, an episode is an incidental and pleasing addition, from the verb meaning "to come in" [ἐπάσωμι].

units.la: Mentitur] De laudibus Homeri una est illa apud Aristotelé in illo opere: docuit verò maximè Homerus & alios falsa dicere,uti convenit. Quinetiam ipsum mentiendi artificium é connexi syllogismi secundi paralogismo (ut ibidem est) docuit. Materia verò poematis, est res verisimiliter cõfiēta: alioqui si poeta describit historiā,ut Lucanus: aut doctrinam aliquā, ut Empedocles,poeta non videbitur. tur.Itaq; ait Ariftoteles ibidem, nihil Empedocli & Homero commune, præter metrũ : meritoq; Homerus poeta, Empedocles philosophus appellatur. Ε᾽πααόδια nimirum sunt illa ad gratiam poematis extrinsecús assumpta.
units.tr: Mentitur: One of the praises of Homer in that work of Aristotle's is this: Homer taught others, above all, to tell falsehoods as is fitting. Indeed, he taught the very art of lying through the false inference of the second connected syllogism, as Aristotle says in the same place. But the matter of a poem is something plausibly feigned. Otherwise, if a poet describes history, as Lucan does, or some doctrine, as Empedocles does, he will not seem a poet. So Aristotle says in the same place that Empedocles and Homer have nothing in common except meter, and that rightly Homer is called a poet and Empedocles a philosopher. The episodes are, of course, those added from outside for the charm of the poem.

units.la: In hac tamen veri falsiq; mistura, portio symmetriaq; corporis servatur: & quam vis à medio tempore incipiat, est tamé corporis universi primũ, medium, infimũ: estq; sua suoq; modo perfecta, perfectiq; tanquã animalis forma. finis autē Iliados, est cædes Hestoris: cæteraq; consequentia, ut prima antecedentia, sunt amputata, quia nō satis illustria fuissent: Deniq; etiam Homerus à generalibus ad specialia, licet imperfecte attamé progressus est. Secundum est exemplũ secundi & post Homerũ principis poetæ, qui Homericum artificiũ imitatus est, & methodum à generalibus ad specialia pari modo tenuit: neque incipit ab excidio Trojano. Locus est statim libro primo: Vix é conspectu Siculæ telluris in altum Vela dabant læti, &c.— Tempestas nempe exorta describitur.
units.tr: Yet in this mixture of truth and falsehood, the proportion and symmetry of the body are kept. Although it begins at a middle time, it still has the first, middle and last parts of the whole body, and it is perfect in its own way, like the form of a living creature. The end of the Iliad is the slaughter of Hector, and the consequences that came before and after have been cut off, because they would not have been striking enough. Finally, Homer too advanced from general to specific, though imperfectly. The second example is the second poet after Homer, the prince of poets, who imitated Homer's craft and in the same way kept the method of moving from general to specific. He does not begin from the destruction of Troy. The place is at the very start of the first book: "Scarcely out of sight of the Sicilian land, the happy crews were setting sail on the deep..." A storm that has arisen is described.

units.la: Secundus liber est Æneidos:
units.tr: The second book is of the Aeneid:

units.la: Conticuére omnes, intentiq; ora tenebant, &c. Multis & variis præliis, & utrinq; magna cæde factis, tandem Turnus ab Ænea interficitur, in ultionem Pallantis: ut Hector illic ab Achille in ultionem Patrocli. & hic Æneis item cócluditur. Quapropter uterq; poeta logicam methodum á generalibus ad specialia cõsimiliter secutus est.de materia & prima & extrema nonnihil nonihil amputavit,addiditq; alia: Et hæc formę prima imperfectio eft é materia: tum etiam temporum ordinem invertit, complexus in medio quædá præcedentia.ideoq; & hæc altera eft inverfio:attamen uterq; & fummam operis initio propofuit: & licet in medio quędam turbarit, at tamen multò maximam partem ordine collocavit: Duoq; humines diligentiam ridiculam hic navarunt, Qu. Calaber, ut quatuordecim libris Iliada: Maphęus,ut unico Æneida abfolverent: Erat enim utrūq; opus accurato opificis fui judicio abfolutum & perfectū. Comici Tertium exemplū de comicis. Difpofitio enim comœdię per actus, & actuū fcenas, & fcenarū perfonas, in progreffu προτάσεως, ἐπιτάσεως, καταστροφῆς, propo fitionis, intentionis, coverfionis, artificiū comici poetæ magnum demonftrant: cura tamen ordinis initio inverfi in comico poemate eft, ne ordine cofequentia prævideátur: tametfi prologus generale quiddam proponit initio: & actus fcenæq;,rem totam, fi nō logica partitione, certe partium comica diftinctione dividunt. Atq; hic etiam methodus á generalibus ad fpecialia, ficut in Homero Virgilioq;, fervatur: nec toto genere poetica difpofitio alia eft,quám philofo phica: fed quia delectandi potiús,quám docendi caufa adhibetur: iccirco quod voluptati cóceditur, detrahitur intelligentiæ. Oratores Oratores quoties docere rem juftam aperté ftatuerunt,methodum plená fequuntur: At infidiantur animis audientium quandoq;,& voluptaté, aut grauiorem aliquem motū, præcipué é Rhetoricis præstigiis, ad pervincédos audientium animos quǫrunt:sed occultiús, ne injustitia suo ipsa indicio pereat. Itaq; solam docédi speciem præ se ferút,ep∉sodiaq; illa digressionum, commorationum,cum poetis habent communia.
units.tr: "All fell silent, and held their faces intent..." After many and varied battles, with great slaughter on both sides, Turnus is at last killed by Aeneas, in vengeance for Pallas, just as Hector was killed by Achilles in vengeance for Patroclus. So the Aeneid too ends here. Therefore both poets followed the logical method from general to specific in the same way. Both cut and added something to the first and last parts of their material. This is the first imperfection of form arising from the matter. They also reversed the order of time, weaving in some earlier events in the middle, and this is the second reversal. Yet both set out the sum of the work at the beginning, and although they disturbed some things in the middle, they arranged the greater part in order. Two men took ridiculous pains here: Quintus Calaber, who wrote the Iliad in fourteen books, and Maphaeus, who finished the Aeneid with a thirteenth book. Each work was complete and perfect by the careful judgment of its own maker. Comedies: The third example is from comedy. The arrangement of a comedy by acts, by the scenes of the acts, and by the persons of the scenes, shows the great skill of the comic poet in its progress of proposition, intention, conversion [προτάσεως, ἐπιτάσεως, καταστροφῆς]. Yet in a comic poem the order is reversed at the beginning, so that the consequences are not seen in advance, although the prologue proposes something general at the start. The acts and scenes divide the whole matter, if not by logical partition, at least by a comic distinction of parts. Here too the method from general to specific is kept, as in Homer and Virgil. Indeed, the arrangement of poetry is in its whole kind no different from that of philosophy, but since it is used for delight rather than for teaching, what is granted to pleasure is taken away from understanding. Orators: Whenever orators have openly undertaken to teach a just matter, they follow a full method. But at times they lay snares for the minds of their hearers, and they seek pleasure or some heavier emotion, chiefly by the tricks of rhetoric, to win over the hearers' minds. They do this more covertly, so that injustice does not perish by its own evidence. So they display only the appearance of teaching, and those episodes of digressions and delays they share with the poets.

units.la: Firmissimū]Ex omnib. quæ á Cicerone, quęq; á Quintiliano de hoc ordine præcipiuntur, id præcipuè est notabile,quod ordinem non intelligentiæ,sed victoriæ sibi præponút : ut poetæ, ordinem voluptatis & gratiæ,de quo Tullius secundo Oratorio sic ait: Atq; etiam in illo repre hédo eos, qui quæ minimé firma sunt,ea prima collocát:In quo illos quoq; errare arbitror, qui si quando(id quod mihi nunquam placuit)plu res adhibent patronos,uti quemq; eorum minimum putant esse,ita eum primum volunt dicere.Res enim hoc postulat,ut eorum expectatio ni,qui audiút, quám celerrimé succurratur: cui si initio satisfactū nō fit, multó pl9 fit in reliqua caussa laborádum. Male enim se res habet, quæ nó statim ut dici cœpta est,melior fieri videtur. Ergo ut in oratore, optimus quisq;, sic & in oratione,firmissimū quodq; sit primum:dum illud tamen in utroq; teneatur,ut ea quę æquė excellant, servétur etiá ad perorandū:si quæ erūt mediocria(nam vitiosis nusquá esse oportet locū) in media turbá atq; in gregem cōjiciantur.Hæc Tullius: quæ Quintilianus deinde repetit lib.5. cap.12. Quæsitū etiá, potétissima argumēta primône ponēda sint loco, ut occupét animos: an summo, ut inde dimittát: an partita primo summoq;, ut Homerica dispositione, in medio sint infirinfirma: an à minimis crescant. Quę prout ratio causæ cujusq; postulabit, ordinabūtur: Imò (ut ego censeo) excepto, ne à potentissimis ad levissima decrescat oratio. Homerica autē dispositio illa est Nestoris 4. Iliad. Equitibus acie prima præmisis, levior armatura in secunda acie, fortioribus, & valetiorib. tanq; triariis, in extrema collocatis. Atq; hic ordo oratorius, quanq; turbatior est, q; poeticus, qa nō evidentia docendi, sed movendi potētiā tantūm spectat: attamē hoc ipso potentiæ argumēto, satis significat, nō nisi à generali & propositione & ratioe aliqua ad hypothesin (quę specialis quæstio est) sese descendere: nec unq; à specialib. ascendere ad generalia. Quamobrē P. Ramus hoc extremo perorationis loco, Musas oēs dialecticas & Charites logicas appellabat, atq; implorabat, ut tantę quæstionis conclusioni præsiderent, judicioq; tot annos de legitima omniū artiū, omniū (quę docendi caussa suscepte sunt) disputationum forma, adeoq; anima disceptato, authoritate suā interponeret, hominū in tenebris errantiū mētibus lumina præferret. P. Rami quæstio est, quód methodus artis instituendę, atq; informādę unica sit à generalib. ad specialia. Causa nō in foro, ad judices: non in curia, ad Patres: nō in rostris, ad Quirites: sed ad omniū locorū, omniū temporū omniū ingeniorū præsides illas deas agitur: & argumētis & testimoniis omniū argumētorū & testimoniorū longé gravissimis, longéq; firmissimis: qa methodus hęc sola fit intelligentię me moriēq;, & qdem ab Aristotele, Hippocrate, Platone tone singulariter & unicé ꝑbata & laudata: vanaq; & comentitia sunt omnia, quæcunq; contrá fingi vel excogitari unquam potuerút. Hæc argumenta sunt: quia artes omnes ingenuæ, Grammatica, Rhetorica, Dialectica, Arithmetica, Philosophiaq; tota in jus appellatæ viva voce testificantur, hanc unicam methodum sibi cognatam & familiarem esse: Poetæ, Oratores, Historici eandem testimonii fidem teftimo nii quoq; fui fide confirmant: qui etiam, licet aliqua parte aliquando voluptati aut utilitati potius, quam doctrinæ inserviant: attamen cæteris partibus majoribus ꝑgrediuntur á generalibus ad specialia. Quid plura? humani ingenii natura adhuc non tulit, ut ars ulla, aut disputatio longior ulla tota â specialibus ad generalia progrederetur. Quapropter methodus á generalibus ad specialia, in omnibus rebus perfpicuê docendis, unica erit: in quibus autê rebus aliquid erit occultandum, aliquid etiam ipsius occultabitur: sed ita ut ê capite ac partibus reliquis forma corporis & species appareat.
units.tr: Most firm: Of all that Cicero and Quintilian teach about this order, the most notable point is that they place before the order of understanding the order of victory, just as poets place the order of pleasure and charm. Cicero says of this in the second book of his Orator: "And in reproving those who put first what is least firm, I think they are wrong too, who, when they use several advocates (as I have never liked), think the weakest of them should speak first. For the matter requires that the expectation of the hearers be met as quickly as possible. If this is not satisfied at the start, much more labour must be spent on the rest of the case. For a case is in a bad state if it does not seem to improve as soon as it is begun. So, as in the orator the best man is first, so in the speech the firmest point should be first, provided that in both cases the things that are equally excellent are kept back for the peroration. If there are some middling points (for weak points should nowhere have a place), they should be thrown into the middle of the crowd and flock." Quintilian repeats this in the fifth book, chapter twelve. He also asks whether the strongest arguments should be placed first, to take hold of the minds, or last, so as to send the hearers away with them; or divided between first and last, with the weaker ones in the middle as in Homer's arrangement; or whether the argument should grow from the least to the greatest. These will be arranged as the reasoning of each case demands. Indeed (as I judge), the one thing to avoid is letting the speech sink from the most powerful points to the lightest. Homer's arrangement is that of Nestor in the fourth book of the Iliad: horsemen sent out in the first line, lighter armour in the second line, and the stronger and more vigorous men, like the triarii, placed in the last line. This oratorical order, though more disturbed than the poetic one, looks only to the power of moving, not to the clarity of teaching. Yet this very proof of power shows well enough that one descends only from a general proposition and some reasoning to the hypothesis (which is a specific question), and never ascends from the specific to the general. Therefore P. Ramus, at this final point of the peroration, used to call all the dialectical Muses and logical Graces, and implored them to preside over the conclusion of so great a question, and to interpose their authority in the judgment of the disputed form of all arts and all disputations undertaken for teaching, which had for so many years been the soul of the matter, and to set lights before the minds of men wandering in darkness. Ramus's question is that the method of forming and instructing any art is one only: from general to specific. The cause is not argued in the forum before judges, nor in the senate before the Fathers, nor on the rostra before the citizens, but before those goddesses who preside over all places, all times and all minds, with arguments and testimonies of all arguments and testimonies, far the weightiest and firmest. For this method alone belongs to understanding and memory, and it has been approved and praised uniquely and exclusively by Aristotle, Hippocrates and Plato. Everything else, whatever could ever be feigned or devised against it, is vain and made up. These are the arguments: all the liberal arts, grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic and all of philosophy, when summoned to court, bear witness with one voice that this one method is their own kin and familiar. Poets, orators and historians confirm the same faith of testimony by their own witness. Although at some points they serve pleasure or usefulness rather than teaching, in their greater parts they proceed from general to specific. What more? The nature of the human mind has not yet been able to bear that any art or any longer disputation should proceed wholly from specifics to generals. Therefore the method from general to specific will be the only one for all things that are to be taught with clarity. In those matters where something must be kept hidden, something of the thing itself will also be concealed; but so that the form and appearance of the body still show through from the head and the remaining parts.

units.la: HABES (LECTOR) AUDOMA- RI TALAEI PRAELECTIONES IN DIALECTICAM, EXTREMA IPSIVS VELUT OLORIS VOCE ITA MODULATAS, UT E MU- LTIPLICIBUS SUAVIS ET ACUTI INGENII MONUMENTIS, FACI- LE HOC UNUM SUAVITATE ET ACUMINE PRINCEPS HABEA- TUR. SIC NEMPE
units.tr: Here you have, reader, the lectures of Audomarus Talaeus on dialectic, which at their close are modulated, as it were, from the very voice of the swan, so that among the many monuments of his subtle and sharp wit this one may easily be counted the prince for sweetness and keenness. Thus indeed:

units.la: DULCIA DEFECTA MODULATUR CARMINA LINGUA, CANTATOR CYGNUS FUNERIS IPSE SUI.
units.tr: Sweet songs the dying tongue modulates, the swan who sings his own funeral.
